text:
“Hee mae mg!” (fool), my grandpa yells, his teeth clenched in frustration.

“Grandpa, what is it? Do you need your urinal bottle? Or do you want water?”

“Hee mae mg!!!”

Four years ago, I became my grandpa’s caretaker. Interpreting his needs was not easy. His face held no expression except a furrowed brow and tight lips that mouthed “Hee mae mg”.

“Mom, how do you never get tired of his shouting?” I asked.

She showed me a photo of my grandpa and said, “From morning till night, your grandpa used to sell tofu, tirelessly riding his bicycle in the heat. I never complained because I always reminded myself of the life he used to have.”

Looking at his pictures, I began to see the person he used to be. One struck me: he was spinning and swinging his arms in the air. Now, he was confined to his bed, watching the world pass him by. I quickly realized then that he must have been scared of losing touch with life itself. Perhaps his screams were a mask for that fear. Feeling guilty for misunderstanding him, I decided to change the way I communicate with him.

Sensing the impact photos had on me, I wondered if they might have the same effect on him. I crafted my own album to share with him.

Recognizing how isolated he must have felt, I began collecting the moments we missed together. I stood beside him and showed him pictures of my family’s Osaka trip, where we rode a Harry Potter-themed rollercoaster—my mom and I with our eyes shut, and my brother and dad’s eyes sparkling with excitement, their mouths wide open. I wanted to share these exciting and memorable feelings with him, to make him feel included in our family. When my grandpa calmed down, I felt relieved. We created our own silent language—it may not have been like others, but it was enough for my grandpa and me to understand.

Reflecting on our way of communicating, I realized that I could use the language I created to address the communication barriers that Laotians face due to the lack of access to literacy resources that limits their expression of ideas. Since Lao is a language built on compound words, I had the idea of putting a photo on top of each word. That way, Laotians could associate the composition of each word with an image, developing their literacy skills. Furthermore, inspired by the lessons learned through my grandpa’s stories, I created a visual storybook where Laotians can read with their family and share meaningful moments together. With these combined visions, I created LittleStories, an early-education reading tool.

While I was at my cousin’s house, I met five-year-old Somphone and decided to test the efficiency of my books. From reading Emma’s Passion to The Hardworking Turtle, I taught her how to read, write, and pronounce words in Lao. Every time she differentiates the word pattern between mae (bus) and maae (mom), I am reminded of creating language to communicate with my grandpa, using pictures to express what words could not. Watching Somphone learn new words and seeing my grandpa’s warm look, I’m amazed by how communication stretches beyond words.

The room next door no longer echoes “Hee mae mg.” It's empty now, filled only with memories. Yet, I still visit to talk to my grandpa, whose presence is captured both in the frames that decorate our shelves and the photo albums resting on our tables. From the start to the end, our communication was never “normal,” but we still managed to understand one another across generations and cultural differences. In college, I hope to keep discovering new forms of communication—verbal or otherwise.

At three a.m., I found myself once again surrounded by the wreckage of my broken promises. The dim glow of my phone revealed a familiar scene of defeat: a sea of crumpled chip bags, grease-stained pizza boxes, and donut crumbs. I swore I wouldn’t binge again, yet each time, the urge would drown my determination like a wave swallowing a storm. My life unfolded like The Truman Show; I watched myself follow a path of scripted choices I couldn’t escape. Why did I keep repeating the same cycle? Was it comfort, or was I avoiding something worse? If I was serious about change, I knew I had to look inward, questioning the comfort I found in self-sabotage and confronting the truths I had avoided for so long.

The summer after my sophomore year, I immersed myself in studying human biology. YouTube videos on eating behaviors became nightly rituals, starting with Professor Andrew Huberman’s series on how dopamine pathways control reward-seeking behaviors. I kept rewinding the episode, taking notes as he explained intricate concepts foreign to me. Day after day, “just one more video” turned into late-night research dives, my cravings for junk food replaced with a hunger for knowledge. Eventually, the videos weren’t enough—I began poring over the precision of scientific literature.

Gaining new vocabulary like 'endorphins' and 'serotonin' helped me see my cravings differently—suddenly they became patterns I could understand, not impulses I had to obey. Each binge brought a numbing endorphin high, but as serotonin levels dipped, relief soon turned to anxiety. As my understanding of human health grew, I started to approach each urge with curiosity rather than judgement. When I felt the familiar pull toward the fridge late at night, I practiced deep breathing to calm my racing thoughts. I began journaling each time I overcame an urge to record these small victories. Slowly, these actions built a foundation of resilience, transforming my relationship with food and allowing me to regain control. Overcoming my own battle awakened a new hunger to use my experience to support others with their own limitations. This time, the urge pushing me forward was constructive and aligned with my values. My internship at the Houston Rheumatology Center took on new meaning as I realized my struggles had equipped me to offer genuine understanding and support to patients like never before.

One evening, an elderly patient approached me, gripping her walker tightly as she watched younger patients enjoying physical therapy together. “I just can’t keep up like I used to,” she sighed. I could see how the stiffness in her joints left her feeling trapped in her own body. My struggle with binging taught me that discomfort—physical or mental—could make small tasks feel impossible. I wanted to help her regain a sense of control by creating exercises that respected her limits yet rekindled the joy of movement. That night, I researched physical therapy, looking for evidence-based strategies tailored for patients with limited mobility. Inspired, I used Canva to design simple brochures with simple instructions and colorful graphics, then printed them in bulk. I offered them to patients who expressed interest or mentioned pain when trying standard exercises, hoping the knowledge within those pages could help them reclaim their independence. The overwhelming support from patients inspired me to organize community events, where I led elderly patients through these accessible exercises. Through their feedback, I saw how scientific knowledge, when paired with empathy, could uplift an entire community by giving them the tools to regain control over their lives.

Three a.m. used to be a time of broken promises and uncontrollable cravings. Now, I’m kept up by a different desire - one to bring comfort, resources, and empowerment to those who are in need. As I walk this path, I hope to offer others the empathy and support I once needed, bringing my hard-earned understanding to those facing their own battles.

The year is 1983. My father’s family flees Sri Lanka at the peak of Black July. Their home was vandalized by Sinhalese mobs. In the north, his uncle rides home with mangoes tied to the spokes of his bicycle. He is stopped in the street by two men, who ask if he is Sinhalese or Tamil. He answers Tamil. They shoot him. A few miles away, my mother crouches under a bus seat as shells rain down outside the vehicle. She survives. Her parents put her on a train back to Colombo, praying she will escape the hotspot of political violence.

2001. My father and mother, newly married, move into their first apartment in America. The shoebox-sized studio has barely enough space to move, but it is home. They eat cold bagels and cereal and toaster strudel. True American delicacies.

2014. My first trip to Sri Lanka. I am seven years old. Moisture weighs down the air wherever we go. The floors look dirty to me, not like American floors. Bumps the size of small moons pepper my arms and legs, gifts from the mosquitoes. Selfishly, I rage at my parents for bringing me to this place. We go to the temple in the morning, drink tea, and hide from the afternoon heat in my grandmother’s foyer. We wait and wait and wait. Neighbors come and go through the open door. Palm trees share hushed whispers in the ocean’s breeze. The light flickers, on, off, on, off. I wonder what we are waiting for.

2020. I attend my first protest for Black Lives Matter. My sister and I proudly hoist our sign; a big, dark fist emblazoned on Amazon cardboard. Five minutes into the march it begins to rain. Behind my hood and mask, my unsmiling face is barely visible. I clear my throat and join in the chants. No justice! No peace! The only response is the rain beginning to fall harder, and cars honking as they go by. In support or in jest, I don’t know. Something inside tells me to yell louder, stand up taller. It says yes, here. This is what I’m meant to do.

2022. My last trip to Sri Lanka. I am fifteen years old. My grandparents’ driver waits in line for three nights to get petrol and cooking gas for the house. On the streets, others do the same. They wait and wait and wait, falling asleep in their rickshaws. Fuel is quickly running out. Protestors camp outside Parliament in masses. They call it aragalaya, struggle, and wave flags. Like the lion on them, they roar—Go home, Gota! The government passes a national curfew, then they begin using tear gas and water cannons. The protestors become more inflamed. They are sick of waiting. They unleash fire on the prime minister’s house and storm the presidential palace. They jump in Gota’s pool, sleep in his bed, and dance exuberantly to trumpets in the hallways. The president flees to the Maldives. Smoke spirals in the sky. I forget about the mosquitoes.

Sri Lanka has shown me waiting in many forms. Irritated by the stupor of my childhood visits, I looked down on the country from the comfort of my American standards. After my first protest, I didn’t know it’d mark the start, not the end, of my journey to speak out. What I did understand was that fighting for justice isn’t always loud or immediate. It’s built over time, and waiting is simply preparation for action. My family’s sacrifices in escaping persecution and the protests manifesting in Sri Lanka forty years later show true advocacy is perseverance. It’s a never-ending cycle, from injustice, to progress, and back again. These acts of defiance, however loud or quiet, are important.

Sri Lankans are patient. They can wait for a long time, but not forever. I, too, am ready to fight for the change I want to see.

I was practicing “Waltz in A Minor” at the piano in the school's music room, trying to get the timing of my cascading scales right for the recital scheduled for the following week. “Attention Students!” My fingers froze at our school director's sonorous voice on the PA system. Seconds became eternity before he announced, “I declare with pleasure the results of the student council election. The president-elect for 2023-2024 is [Name] Abraham…”. Everything around me blurred, and waves of emotion—pride, self-doubt, excitement, and disbelief—washed over me. A quiet voice whispered, “Girl! You did it! But how?”

I was transported two years back when I transferred to a school renowned for its IB curriculum. Readying for my first day, I was assailed with thoughts of starting again, making friends, finding mentors, and proving myself anew. In the cafeteria, whispers and glances, both warm and cold, followed me. Cliques occupied tables, and I wondered where I would fit in. Over the next few days, the path of least resistance made me gravitate towards a student group that shared similar opinions, from pop culture to politics. We reinforced each other’s beliefs without challenging them, and I settled in, delighted at having found my comfort zone.

During a class debate on the government’s renewable energy programs one morning, I supported a complete shift to green energy. A classmate countered me, raising concerns about infrastructure costs and the threat of unemployment. Instead of listening and responding, I felt challenged and reacted. We both argued for the last word, refusing common ground.

Reflecting on this, I realized I’d built my own echo chamber with my small coterie, a space where my opinions were validated without room for growth. I decided to expand my horizons by seeking people with divergent experiences and perspectives.

Going to the movies with my different-abled friend, Rohan, made me realize how uncomfortable and inconvenient the place I enjoyed was for him due to its lack of inclusive infrastructure. Participating in a food distribution drive for underprivileged people outside a neighborhood temple had me wonder how malnutrition might impact worldviews. I tried to draw out Abeer, a reticent orchestra member, who shared that she felt stifled growing up in a conservative family, discovering poetry as her expressive outlet. The exchanges of personal stories and unhurried listening freed me from binary thinking and honed a more compassionate mindset.

Going beyond local experiences, I explored “Why are We Yelling” by Buster Benson on the art of productive disagreement, “When Inclusion Becomes Intrusion” by Indian author Devdutt Pattanaik, and the “Good Influence” Podcast series to challenge preconceived notions, which made me see value in viewing the world through multiple lenses and confronting cognitive dissonance.

I became aware of a dogmatic "Us vs. Them” mindset on social media and at family and friend meet-ups. Similarly, polarized attitudes among students seemed to divide my school community and threaten school spirit. Our physical and digital identities were still developing, and I saw value in encouraging open dialogue to nurture compassion and tolerance. Could I be that changemaker who fosters a broader shift toward openness and understanding? School is a microcosm of the world, and to become a future changemaker, I had to start right here.

I decided to run for school president. It was a risky proposition, as I was pitted against school veterans. My campaign focused on implementing a “school spirit week” to celebrate diversity, a buddy system between junior and senior students to mitigate bullying, and programs that promoted open dialogue in safe places within the school community. It lacked flashy appeal and the promise of more parties or sports events, but I believed in my cause.

Even if I made one person feel seen, heard, or included, I would've made a difference. Becoming the change I wanted to see taught me that being authentic is better than being “always right.”

I thought mastering yoga would make me a superhero; it turns out I was right. As I take a step onto the mat, a sense of calm prevails as all the worries in the world slowly dissipate. The familiar feel of the spongy cushion and the stimulating aroma of the rubber scent ground me. As I begin my routine with the Urdhva Hastasana—the upward salute pose—I feel every part of my body come alive and work together in harmony. My arms stretch with agility, complementing the flexibility of my spine. Having moved between three countries during high school, my identity often felt lost and I was unsure of my roots. Yoga has provided the grounding I needed, being a constant in my life that never made me forget who I was.

From the very first time I caught sight of my mom doing yoga as a five-year-old, I was obsessed with mimicking her every movement with my chubby hands and little stout feet. Despite falling over and over as I attempted the child pose, I was resilient in my approach. I just wanted to do it as eloquently as my mom did. Just as I learned to hold the pose, eventually, I learned to hold my ground during challenges. My diagnosis of Scoliosis my freshman year didn’t prevent me from undertaking 4 varsity sports, nor did my family’s immigration issues deter me from building an inspiring science community, AspireSTEM, in every place I called home.

The beauty of every pose, complexity of every stretch, and dynamics of the breathing technique always filled my head with endless thoughts. “Ma, what is the science behind the breathing technique?” “Ma, how does the pose get its name?” Each question led me to a new path. That childhood fascination stayed through all of my adolescence, slowly blossoming my curiosity into an insatiable desire to learn, not just about yoga but the world around me. From Aristotle's philosophies to Mendelian genetics, I spared nothing that I got my hands on.

Yoga fueled my unparalleled desire to try new poses as I mastered the basics. Eagle pose, frog pose, cow pose—you name it. I still remember vividly the day I finally mastered the child pose, or I felt like I did, swelling with pride as if I had conquered the world. That feeling mirrored the pride I felt growing my first micro-green at age ten or when I rooted for Mohawk, Africa’s oldest lion, to survive another day in the documentaries I obsessively watched.

Ending my yoga session with Savasana, joy and sadness bubble within me. I am devastated that the ritual has to come to a closing but grateful that I will be able to do it all over again tomorrow. Importantly, I gain mental clarity on my journey in yoga, and life. Yoga has given rise to an unbreakable bond with my mom who inspires me every day, and I am confident I will find fellow yoga enthusiasts to connect and forge bonds with, sharing stories, laughter, sweat, and even tears.

The balance I find on the mat reflects my pursuit of balance in other aspects of my life, from dance rehearsals and basketball practices to computational biology research. As I take a step closer to adulthood, I carry with me lessons yoga has taught me. I will always be the googly-eyed toddler who can’t wait to do yoga, and the mat will always remain my superhero training ground to connect with myself when life gets challenging. As I step off the mat, my session doesn’t end here; rather I see a cape ready to be put on for my next adventure, finding passions both on and off the mat. I will pursue each experience with purpose and enthusiasm, honoring the beauty of the journey itself. With each deep breath, I remind myself life, like yoga, is not perfect but infused with lifelong memories.

“The Perfect Sourdough Recipe” yielded mountains of discarded sourdough starter, failed loaves, and a battlezone-like kitchen. Quite imperfect. My mouth puckered as I took a bite of the flat lump-shaped loaf. Where did I go wrong? Did I not follow the recipe correctly?

The stirring confusion and spiraling lack of control transformed me back into the 7-year-old [Name] who tried to connect the dots of the English language. If “G” has the “ga-” sound and “J” has the “ja-” sound, why wouldn’t “change” be pronounced “chan-ga” or spelled “chanje.” Did I do something wrong?

Academics accelerated past the constant velocity at which I read when I transferred to a new school with new faces and a new curriculum in the first grade. Daily readings, spelling quizzes, and worksheets on foreign math concepts scattered around my kitchen table—like a battlezone. Following "the perfect academic recipe" of my previously underfunded school, where I had not even learned first-grade-level vocabulary, I expected the comfort of an underbaked curriculum that even a kindergartener understood.

I sought out comfort in following “objective” standards in everything—especially in the perfection of mixed flour, salt, and water according to “The Perfect Sourdough Recipe,” from which I also expected a delicious loaf. However, following the recipe exactly—flour measured by the gram, 11 minute dough kneading time, and five hour dough rising time—I witnessed seven failed attempts, still empty of the perfect loaf. Ms. Tosio’s description of why we deviate from typical English pronunciation for words like “change” came to mind: tailored rules. I started to question: Why does the recipe instruct me to use 400 grams of water? Why not 415 grams? Could the recipe be wrong?

Adding 15 more grams of water, my loaf transformed from dense and gummy to soft and luscious. Experimenting with shortened dough rise times, my loaf finally achieved the perfect harmony of mild tanginess and sweetness as opposed to overpowering sourness. Every two weeks, I scrutinized these variables and realized the tailored rules of sourdough.

Chewing on the perfect slice, I smiled after eight months of deviating from the “perfect recipe.” From the crispy, golden crust to honeycombed pockets, I knew that I had finally perfected my Zhou-erdough recipe—the most comforting snack that was birthed out of change.

I started discovering tailored rules in how I followed “the perfect recipes” to winning lacrosse games, helping students understand mathematical and literary concepts that I once struggled with, and especially working at i-Tea.

My role as a barista transformed after repeatedly hearing “how do you make this drink?,” seeing rows of incorrect drinks with an hour-long queue, and working in a battlezone-like store. I began to reimagine the training program—a supposedly “perfect recipe”—as I sought to uncover and adapt its tailored rules.

Asking questions like “What drinks are hardest to make?” and “What resources would help?” to new trainees pinned a starting point—like identifying what variables of the sourdough recipe to be changed. The “300mL water (1-1.5), T1 (5g), T234 (15g), BT/GT sugar (check color)” directions to make a cup of tea were difficult to comprehend, which I transformed into a mnemonic device: “We Bring Power So Customers Ingest Sweets,” representing the process of “Water, Brew, Pour, Sugar, Creamer, Ice, Shake.” Like adjusting the water proportions for my sourdough recipe, I constructed a study guide for our barista-training process, bringing increased drink-making accuracy, faster service speed, as well as smiles to my colleagues’ faces.

I would not have found the comfort of indulging in my perfect Zhou-erdough bread or productively working against rush hour as part of a well-trained team if I had stayed indifferent to the mouth-puckering taste of bad bread and disorganized combat as a barista. Thus, my answer to why imperfect results come from “perfect recipes” will forever be tailored rules—so long as “change” is pronounced as “chanje” yet spelled the way it is.

“I’m more of a son than my brothers are anyway,” chimed the voice in my head. I fumbled with a red strip of fabric pilfered from Ayah’s closet dangling around my neck like a self-bestowed medallion. The phone on the desk played a video: How to Tie a Tie (EASY).

I pinched the wide end of the tie and crossed it over the narrow one, forming an X. This––the voice declared––was justice!

A batik-patterned shawl sulked at the desk’s edge, protesting at being forsaken. I ignored it, of course. Why must I, a grown 13 year old, listen to a deceptively beautiful leash?

“Wear this to the wedding,” Ibu said earlier, shoving the shawl into my hands alongside an overly-embellished dress that made an impossible feat of walking without tripping. I stopped myself from asking her “why?”––a word she surely is sick of hearing by now since I abused it at every opportunity: why are speed bumps called “sleeping officers”? Were police killed as ritual sacrifice and buried there? Why are many bowls decorated with roosters? To affirm the superiority of the Rooster zodiac? Why can’t I wear what my brothers wore––loose, minimal, while free of scrutiny? Some questions she answered briskly, others vaguely, oftentimes with the dreaded “that’s just how it is.”

Being the only daughter meant noticing double standards early, how I wasn’t allowed to do certain things my brothers could, and neither could Ibu, who compliantly stopped leading prayers to let my brothers, much younger and less experienced, lead, who dismissed feminism as a “western-import,” who often answered my questions with “that’s just how it is,” who did not question at all.

I looped the wide end under the narrow one. Despite being a daughter, I knew I could become the ideal son. When Ibu complained that none of her sons were doing their jobs by watching soccer with Ayah, I stepped in, sitting with other men on benches to shout “GOAAAL!” to all the wrong times.

I pulled the tie through the loop and tugged down. Engaging and competing in martial arts became proof of my value. In Taekwondo practice, when a boy hits hard, I’d try hitting harder.

I slipped the wide end underneath, through the opening. At school, I insisted on wearing trousers over skirts, negotiating with teachers to tweak the uniform policy to accord all students greater freedom to choose.

Knot cinched, the tie was a rather meaningless defiance. But it was something others would not allow and that made it worthwhile.

In the car, I sat next to Ibu. She glanced at me. “Why are you wearing that?! It looks ridiculous. I gave you the shawl.”

I couldn’t hold in the W-word anymore. “Why do I have to wear that?”

“Dress code.”

“So, I have to wear it while they–,” I pointed to my brothers, ”–don’t?”

“What? No! Everyone’s using it. Look, Armand’s already wearing his.”

I twisted from my seat to look at my brother. To my horror, there he was. Sitting. Shawl over his shoulders.

Guilt settled as realisation dawned: I had fancied myself superior for being a skeptic and based my self-worth on my ability to be the “better son,” to surpass others’ expectations, real or perceived. In my insecurity, I became quick to make assumptions and shut my ears, creating a falsified image of others, of my own mother. As a successful woman and engineer, she had battled expectations herself and won––victories I foolishly dismissed. I questioned everything, yet I failed to question myself and my facile judgments.

Beyond learning how to ask for clarifications, I began to appreciate the nuance in others’ beliefs and experiences: I’ve come to value debates with family and friends, seeked their life stories, and go opinion-hunting––even if we’ve disagreed.

Nearing the venue, I pulled out the shawl and confessed to Ibu: “I’m not sure how to wear this.”

“Here. I’ll help.”

Singed hair is never a good smell, but that is all I smelt after the propane from my turbojet reignited while I was behind it. For my junior year of high school, I decided I would try my hand at building a jet engine. I did some research and decided to make a turbojet engine which utilizes a turbocharger like what can be found on a truck or car, I bought the turbocharger and took some measurements of the intake and exhaust which allowed me to start working on the combustion chamber formulas which would supply the engine with its fuel. Once the formulas for the combustion chamber were solved it gave me the information I needed to start building the chamber.

For the combustion liner, I used a 2.5" 304 stainless pipe (a high chromium and nickel iron alloy) with 64 quarter-inch holes drilled in it. That piece was then welded onto a three-eighths piece of stainless steel with a four-inch diameter. For the housing, I had a 4" piece of 304 stainless pipe with a 20-degree taper into the turbocharger; this taper allowed proper airflow between the edge of the liner and the four-inch housing. After these two pieces were welded together, I drilled and tapped the top plate for the spark plug and hose barb fitting. The spark plug was then wired to an ignition coil like what is on a car, this allows it to spark and ignite the propane that is being fed through the hose barb fitting. Through testing the combustion chamber, I saw there was some uneven burn but not enough to affect anything in a major way. The final step was just to bolt it to the turbocharger and hook the propane to it and start it up, but nothing is ever that easy.

Once everything was bolted up and together, I decided to start it, first turning on the oil pump, then spooling the turbine up with an air compressor blower, and finally turning the propane on and sparking the ignition. Sure enough, it ran but not under its own power which was odd I thought. I checked all of my math and even had a teacher at school look it over too, but it just wouldn't run on its own. That had me stumped for over a week tinkering and trying to change stuff and in trying to change what I should have left alone I walked behind the exhaust that was still cherry red from running less than thirty seconds before, some residual propane ignited and singed all the hair from off my calf.

What turned out to be wrong with the engine was the propane was not under enough pressure. It had been at 30 psi when it should have been at 67 psi, it was an extremely simple formula I had forgotten to do that would have saved me time and my hair. However, through this, I realized that slowing down to look work over instead of rushing in and trying to change things is extremely important and could have saved me from the headaches rushing into it caused.

The main goal of this project was to build a turbojet engine that could run on many different fuels and generate electricity. Similar to biodiesel, this turbojet was able to run on used cooking oil, used motor oil, and many other byproducts of daily life. Doing this and being able to convert this energy into electricity allowed me to run tools and lights with liquids that would usually have been thrown out.

His sharp words and erratic behavior frustrated me. My fury boiled over when my brother smashed my computer in yet another argument. I snapped words meant to stab.

“You always complain about Dad being the problem, but the role he plays in your life – you play that exact role in mine.” My brother, who was never at a loss for words, stood silent.

I won! I finally silenced him.

But the triumph was hollow, dissipating almost as quickly as it came. In the aftermath, I was left with unsettling questions that refused to be ignored. Where was the issue?

One evening, after yet another argument with our mother, he stormed into my room. “I hate myself for how I act. All I want is to get along with everyone.” His vulnerability caught me off guard. He expressed insecurities and pain he had never expressed before. For the first time, I saw beyond his anger and saw someone struggling with his loneliness. That moment cracked the shades of resentment. I began to see how my resentment had blinded me –- not only to his humanity but also to the capacity of my own.

“Want to watch a movie?” he’d ask, and I’d always reply, “Not now, I’m busy.” I couldn’t understand why he couldn’t just watch the movie on his own. I was only protecting my time, but now I realized how often I had dismissed his attempts to connect. Our conflicts weren’t about winning or losing; they were cries for understanding, both his and mine. Compassion began to seep into spaces once filled with anger. I discovered the power of empathy — not as an obligation but as a choice that could set me free.

“Want to watch a movie?” I asked. He just smiled and said a big, “Sure!” I began to see that connection was such a simple human need but meeting that need was transformative. The simple act of reaching out first began to change our relationship. I couldn’t meet him where he was at all times, but fury was replaced with understanding and bonding.

I sat down and came to reflect on that change, wondering how often others might feel the same loneliness my brother did but had no place to belong to. I thought about what I could implement in my community in the roles I was in. When I founded the Korean American Student Association at my high school, my goal was to connect people of shared heritage. But as I grew, so did my vision. People from different backgrounds often wanted to join but hesitated, unsure if they could truly belong. I saw this as a chance to create a space they would also feel welcome in.

What is the best way to bond different people? A good challenge. That’s how the Spicy Buldak Challenge was born. I thought about how laughter and the shared struggle to eat something impossibly spicy could bring people together. Coordinating the event wasn’t easy, but I believed it was worth it. Thirteen participants braved the spicy Buldak challenge, cheered on by an audience of over thirty students from diverse backgrounds. Students came up to me to express how much fun they’d had and signed up to join the club. The event was a success! The club grew to become a safe space where students could feel connected where they might feel lost in the mass.

My brother’s display of vulnerability broke my mindset free and shined insight: despite the complexity of human relationships, everyone inherently sought connection. I felt like I succeeded in seeking out connection first to bring people together.

**Ramps.** To most people, they’re just inclines or flat stairs. I know ramps as launchpads for creativity.

It started eight years ago when I became a scooter fanatic. Skateparks became my second home, a place where I learned tricks and made lifelong friends. Then the pandemic hit, locking down my community.

So, I built my own park.

Armed with a few sheets of plywood and an excess of optimism, I hacked together my first ramp. Hours later, mid-360 attempt, it collapsed beneath me. Lesson learned: recklessly improvising a curved take-off with a rusty saw doesn’t cut it—literally.

Swallowing my pride (and some sawdust), I decided to try again, NASA-engineer style. This time, I sketched a blueprint full of detailed measurements and set course to Home Depot in the hunt for 2x4s. Hours later, a robust kicker ramp lay before me, proudly spray-painted with “N-A-S-A.” As I flew through the air (new knee scrapes and all), I realized that while my off-the-cuff excitement helped me quickly hammer together ramps, it was detailed planning that helped them last. Ramp [Name] was ready for liftoff.

“Who wants to match some poop?!” I announced. I wheeled my rubber poop cart into the museum for a new round of Scat-Match: an animal-feces matching game. Thinking these children would be well behaved, like the volleyball kids I coach, I was unpleasantly surprised to see them just flinging the scat around, ignoring my explanations.

I had to ramp up their curiosity.

I turned toward Eddie, a 4th grader stumped at the lumps. I tried ramping him up to the answer: "Do you have cats? Have you seen their poop?" Eddie picked up the mountain lion scat, placed it with the cougar photo, and said, “It kinda looks like this one!” Nearby, Nari was confused between the deer and the snake scat. “The lion’s scat is big and chunky,” I prompted, “what might a snake’s look like?” With a bit of spontaneous improvisation, just as I had carefully carved that curved take-off years prior, I now guided each student to solve the puzzle themselves. When Eddie asked, “Why is some poop round and some long and squiggly,” quickly followed by “Why do people study poop and can I go poop?”—I knew I started a learning movement. (More than just a bowel one, at least.)

This time, my ramp let their questions take flight.

It was horror-movie night with friends. After “Bird Box,” I suddenly proposed a themed hide-and-seek: the seeker would be blindfolded like the movie’s protagonist, while the rest of us hid as “invisible monsters.” You could see their excitement visibly ramp up. Chaos soon erupted as Kris squeezed his chubby frame behind the TV, nearly toppling it, and Jason wriggled under the sofa. I quickly hatched a plan: I lifted my hand… 1, 2, 3. Tony, our poor protagonist, was bombarded with couch cushions and Nerf darts, crumpling in defeat.

Exhausted, we all sprawled on the carpet as we watched the next film, the Taiwanese horror film “Incantation.” As Ronan performed the ritual to remove the curse from her daughter Dodo on screen, I noted parallels to the Korean horror film “The Wailing.” 
“It’s like when the shaman and priest try to save Hyo-jin in The Wailing, but rooted in different cultural beliefs.” Tony added: “Yeah, seems to be Buddhist versus Korean shaman and Christian beliefs. But the common theme—unrelenting parental love.” As we discussed, I felt our curiosity gaining traction. “And both toy with trust—like is the Jap evil?” commented Andrew. As we chatted for hours, that movie night became our most memorable because we left room for spontaneity.

From crafting a Superman-worthy kicker ramp to keeping a kid’s learning momentum rolling to movie nights that bring Nerf fights and philosophy, I’ve learned planning gives you a strong foundation, but spontaneity makes you airborne.

My mom has always been the breadwinner in our family. While she worked long hours, my dad ran our home. For twenty years, he'd cooked our meals, paid the bills, and made sure the laundry never piled up. I never thought much about it. It was just what he did. Then one morning, my mom called me into the kitchen. Her voice was soft, careful.

“Your dad’s tests came back. It’s cancer.”

The words settled over me, heavy and quiet. A week later, I was sitting next to him on a flight to Turkey. I watched him stare out the window, his reflection faint in the glass. I could feel his fear in the way he squeezed my hand as the plane landed. The hospital room was cold, the kind that makes you realize how far from home you are. While he rested after surgery, I tried to take care of the bills. I accidentally paid the wrong ones—twice—and spent an hour on hold with the Airbnb host, trying to explain the mistake in broken Turkish. We had to stay longer than planned, and the old landlady kept trying to kick us out. I sat in the dark, frustrated but laughing at how badly I was handling things.

Eventually, I came back to Mongolia. Our house felt emptier without him moving from room to room, humming as he cleaned. The fridge was empty, the laundry unfolded, and bills sat unopened. I stood there, waiting for him to walk in and fix it all like he always had.

At first, I tried to copy him—the way he folded clothes or scribbled grocery lists on receipts. I burned rice, my brother was late from school once again, and I paid another bill late. It felt like patching things together, but none of it was quite right.

Over time, the house felt less fragile. Folding laundry became less about finishing a chore and more about preserving the calm he brought to our home. Grocery lists weren’t just about food but became a way to make sure things felt familiar when he returned.

That experience didn’t just change how I saw my dad. It made me notice the quiet efforts shaping the world around me. At school, I saw the janitor wiping desks long after the hallways emptied and the classmate leading group projects without stepping into the spotlight. I began to realize how often people carry responsibilities that go unnoticed—how care isn’t loud but holds everything in place.

Growth didn’t arrive all at once. There was no single moment that made me feel like I had it figured out. But in those months, whether I was halfway across the world in a hospital or home in our kitchen, I learned how to be still with uncertainty. I grew more patient, more intentional with the little things, and more aware of how people quietly take care of one another.

When my dad finally came home, thinner but smiling, I realized the most important thing I learned wasn’t how to cook or pay bills—but how to carry the invisible work that keeps a family together.

As I helped him inside, he glanced around and smiled.

“You did good,” he said.

I smiled back, swallowing the lump in my throat. Now, when people ask what my dad does, I tell them the truth.

“He takes care of us,” I say. And now I do too.

In small ways, I’ve tried to pass that forward. I began volunteering at food drives and organizing donation bins at school, inspired by how small actions ripple outward. I used to think community was built through big gestures, but I’ve learned it’s often shaped by the unnoticed details—the quiet care, the small favors, the invisible acts that keep everything moving. I’m still learning to navigate that space, but I know now that care isn’t just something you give at home. It’s something you carry with you wherever you go.

I was diligently jotting down each definition from my AP Psychology textbook when one word struck a chord: temperament. It was described as having a set of immutable characteristics, like middle C on a piano. Yet as the polysemous word lingered, I questioned—did this definition encompass the complexity of temperament?

This notion of temperament didn’t resonate with my past twelve years as a concert pianist. I understood temperament as a method of tuning pianos to alter how notes sounded in relation to each other. This definition suggested dynamic flexibility, not monotonous rigidity.

As I tried to reconcile these clashing definitions, I was suddenly transported back to the volleyball court, sitting in the forming circle as the fuzzy voices became clearer. “Last night was crazy! Remember when…” outside-hitter Jill said. “It was so funny when…” middle-blocker Audrey chimed in. What happened last night? I thought as I listened to my teammates’ crescendos of laughter. I could only stifle an awkward snicker, like an off-key middle C note; I had not been invited to the previous night’s birthday party.

I mean, I couldn’t blame them. I wasn’t the most talkative person on the team. Trouble often came when I tried to harmonize with others—even dialing in a pizza order could make my heart race. But I was tired of feeling like an off-key C note hidden in a larger symphony. It was time to bend my introversion into confidence and tune myself to society.

To calibrate my temperament, I got a job at Kaldi’s Coffee, working as the first point of service for customers. Every Saturday and Sunday at 6 AM, I clocked into a world where I needed to harmonize with each customer’s personality. My conversations—from the controversies in up-charging milk alternatives to talking about my dreams of advancing healthcare using AI and precision medicine—pushed me to hold up my end of any discussion. In a place where diverse perspectives flowed as freely as coffee, I learned the importance of finding common ground.

To further challenge my introversion, I swapped out the familiar environment of my high school for the rigorous, collaborative one of Washington University in St. Louis, where I’ve spent the past two years pursuing my interest in bioinformatics and cellular research. My social experiences at Kaldi’s carried into the lab, where I used my newfound confidence to highlight research problems in staff meetings, like when there was no effect on cancer invasion in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells with varying cholesterol concentrations, or when my code caused errors in graphing peaks while developing Pycallingcards, a Python module. My evolving temperament made me question the connection between my computational research and my cellular findings, sparking my curiosity in the potential bridges between AI and medicine.

I’ve come a long way from the limited C note I once hid behind, finding my voice and passion through fine-tuning my temperament. I now embrace all 88 piano keys, rejecting the fixed definition of temperament from my AP Psychology textbook. Instead, I’ve formed my own meaning.

tem·per·a·ment: An individual’s characteristic response patterns that evolve through harmonizing academic, social, and personal experiences and can be tuned over time and across situations.

I’m eager to continue discovering who I am through my complex definition of temperament, especially as I transition from my comforting childhood room to the dynamic dorm I will soon call home. I’ll be omnipresent in research labs, tuning into my intellectual curiosity as I explore the connections between AI and medicine. Or I’ll be with my community in a nearby cafe, embracing freshly minted friends (and a hot cup of coffee) and sparking conversations about the latest NCAA volleyball tournament. As I leave my introverted middle C note behind me, I enter into a new chapter with a full 88-key range of my capabilities.

“You smell nice” is the compliment I receive most often.

Concocted with precision, my own perfume consists of 40mL of alcoholic base blended with 2mL of bergamot, 1.5mL of narcissus, 2mL of patchouli, and 2.5mL each of vanilla and tonka. See, a perfume isn’t a single scent; it’s a composition of layers that unfold over time. In perfumery, "notes" refer to these layers—top, heart, and base. Each note emerges at its own pace according to the volatility of its molecules, with the top notes providing the initial burst of scent, the heart notes forming the fragrance’s core, and the base notes lingering the longest, leaving the final impression. The carefully chosen components of my perfume reflect different facets of me—the layers that reveal themselves as you get to know me better.

If you’re my classmate in the chemistry lab, leaning over a flask while I measure drops of sulfuric acid with a pipette, you’ll likely catch the bright, citrusy burst of bergamot. It’s sharp, fresh, and slightly tart, like a freshly zested lemon twist. Curious and energetic, focused on the thrill of discovery, it’s the part of me that thrives in moments of intellectual exploration in the classroom, whether through dissecting a sheep liver during biology or engaging excitedly in a debate on the US’s recent EV tariff in economics.

Spend a little more time with me, though, and the heart notes make their presence known. During the academic council meeting at lunch, as I coordinate student feedback on the school’s peer tutoring program, patchouli’s grounding depth mirrors my focus and strategic planning. Later, if you’re on the tennis team following my lead through warm-ups, or in my Science Society club listening to me present our latest initiative on a STEM day with village school students, you’ll notice the floral and green, the bold and slightly animalic edge of narcissus taking the center stage.

But if you’re my younger brother running into my arms, outstretched and waiting for me at the school gate, or my grandmother in her hospital bed as I gently blow on a spoonful of soup before offering it back, you’ll catch the warm, powdery scent of tonka and vanilla, carrying the quiet patience and unwavering love I extend to those who mean the most to me.

Much like with a fragrance, the deeper someone engages with me, the more dimensions of my personality they uncover. Recognizing these layers in others has taught me to approach people with patience and curiosity. First impressions, like the bright top notes of a perfume, are easy to notice but often incomplete. Once, a classmate famous as the 'fashionista' for her flawless makeup and waist-length hair styled intricately once surprised everyone by cutting it into a short bob. When I asked her why, she shared that she donated it for cancer patients’ wigs. Inspired, I asked if she would like to lead a cancer support initiative in my medical club—today, she’s our most dedicated member and vice president. Similarly, a teammate on our badminton team known for a stone face and an aggressive playing style surprised me when I saw him chatting tenderly with his grandmother as he pushed her wheelchair. I invited him to join me in volunteering at a nursing home—now, he’s my Sunday afternoon volunteer buddy.

By approaching others with openness and attentiveness, I’ve learned the value of making space for their complexities, strengths, and struggles. It’s in these hidden layers—unexpected depth and nuance—where true meaning and strength reside. And if you’re patient enough to appreciate someone’s ‘base note,’ they’ll resonate long after the moment has passed.

The market was alive with colours, sounds and smells that made my senses overload. At just four years old, I stepped into the chaos of São Paulo’s Mercado Municipal, where my eyes locked onto an old map of Brazil. Its edges were frayed, its words foreign, but I couldn't look away. Despite not knowing the meaning at the time, I pleaded to take it home, and when we returned, I bluetacked it above my bed, where it remained until I needed it most.

As the years passed, the map followed me. It was there when my mother was diagnosed with cancer – a word that I didn’t fully understand at that time, but its presence brought anarchy to our home. As she battled for her life, time itself seemed to dissolve, standing still in moments - like waiting in hospital, watching her chest slowly rise and fall as I watched the hours crawl past. I continued to deteriorate, sobbing quietly as I questioned why cancer had chosen my mother.

In the midst of this, the map showed the same deterioration that I felt. Its edges had weathered, its colours had dulled, and its once precise lines had become faint, as though time was gradually eroding the place it once depicted. Seeing it deteriorate sparked the start of the quiet rebellion against my lack of control I felt, and so I decided to cycle it to the frame shop, carefully folding it into the large pocket of my school backpack. Reframing it wasn’t just practical; it marked a shift. Encased in its frame, its frayed edges were shielded from time’s wear, and seeing that reminded me of my mum's strength, inspiring me to embody her ‘Latina fire’ as I searched for ways to help her.

Initially, I tried to comfort her by creating playlists of her favourite artists, hoping the soothing voices of Maria Bethania and Joao Gilberto would ease her pain, but my gesture felt futile, as though I were using a teaspoon to bail out a sinking ship.

Desperate for something more, I turned to research. Late nights at my laptop became a ritual as I scoured the internet, learning about foods that could combat inflammation and boost immunity. Dr Greger’s How Not to Die became my bible, teaching me about how curcumin had anti-inflammatory properties that might help her chronic inflammation, or how the polyphenols in green tea could support her cellular health. More interestingly, I found studies showing that reconnecting with cultural identity can reduce cortisol levels, reducing anxiety and increasing emotional well-being (turns out my playlists weren’t totally useless!).

Armed with this knowledge, I found my battleground – the kitchen. My first weapon was bone broth, simmering for hours with turmeric and ginger, both known for their anti-inflammatory properties, enriching the soup further with coriander and garlic, both staples of Brazilian cuisine, to help nourish both her body and mind. Each warm cup was a step closer to healing and soon came along feijoadas, then moqueca. I was finding so much joy in these small acts, especially seeing my mother’s mood start to change, saying my food made her feel ‘home’. I even started sharing my recipes with family friends, hoping they too, might benefit from dishes that remind them of home.

As she started to recover, I found myself again, being drawn to the map, like I had been back in the Mercado Municipal. But now, when I look at the map, I see it for what it truly is: not just a map of Brazil, but a mirror of my family. It had become a symbol of my family’s culture, with the outline of the nation fading as we lost traditions but fighting the forces of time when we practiced our heritage most.

Though I can’t stop time, I will use the little I have to carry with me the spirit of the map, ensuring that cultural legacies, like my mum's ‘Latina fire’, continue to shine whether through food, supporting economic empowerment, or fostering greater access to opportunities.

As I looked ahead, my body felt weak. The uneven rocks, fallen tree branches, and the edge of the overlook were all too much for me. This must be a mistake, I thought to myself. Surely, we had made a wrong turn; perhaps we had veered off course. But as I looked up to my parents, expecting their steps to falter alongside mine, I instead found myself lagging behind, watching as they continued forward.

Panicked, I begged to turn back. “It’s too dangerous,” I argued; “I’m tired,” I complained. I mustered up every excuse I could find. Unfortunately, it didn’t work. My parents, aware of my bluffs, assured me that I had nothing to worry about. So, reluctantly, I proceeded forward.

As we found our footing on the first rock, the vast forest beneath us, with trees appearing to be the size of thumbtacks, caught my eye. Immediately, my stomach sank; tears began to weigh down in my eyes. I became paranoid. I envisioned tripping on tree branches, slipping on pebbles, and my shoes giving out on me. A wave of heat came over me as I stood there, unable to move.

Seeing this, my dad encouraged me to focus on my steps, not on each small detail. After taking time to compose myself, I followed his instructions, looking ahead for a spot to place my next step. Pushing aside each worst-case scenario and what-if in my head, I gradually made my way through.

Looking back from the trail’s end, this section no longer seemed as dangerous as I first perceived it to be. Blinded by my worries on smaller issues, I lost sight of my goal: reaching the other side. I realized that when put into perspective, the challenges weren’t as substantial as I thought.

Now, I’ve learned to remember that my perception can shape my challenges. When I first started performing piano recitals, I would be terrified to take the stage. In the days leading up to performances, my eyes would be glued to my scores, copying down note names and reciting them over and over again. I’d barrage my teacher with questions like “Am I playing the second sixteenth note of this measure slightly too late?” and “Should I move my elbows to the side or to the side and up?”

Though my intentions were to improve my performance, my fixation on every detail did the opposite. I realized that by attempting to account for each aspect at each moment in my performances, I lost track of my goal: making music. Instead of thinking about phrases, I was thinking about individual notes. Instead of learning to express myself, I was rehearsing pre-planned movements. With this shift in attitude, performances no longer felt like a challenge to regurgitate notes on a score. Instead, they became opportunities to share a part of me and grow as a musician. In this way, taking that first step towards the piano no longer felt so difficult and I came to enjoy performing.

Beyond this, whether it’s those last-second doubts that linger in my head before I publish a new article on my blog, the anticipation of arriving at one of my recitals, wondering how many people showed up, or the awkward silence at the start of a cohort meeting, I remember that these are all only as significant as I make them out to be.

As I enter college, I remind myself that the way I see my challenges shapes how they affect me. So, as I prepare to enter a new building, start a conversation with someone new, and sign up for an event, I’m focused on the trail ahead, not the pebbles in front of me.

I tried to jump to the moon.

No, I’m not a lunatic. I’m just an ex-umchina. “Umchina” is a Korean slang for a perfect child, often used by mothers (alongside a slipper) for scolding their children to do better. Ever since I could remember, I had a craving for perfection. When I was cutting out an apple, my 8-year-old friends were curious why it was taking me so long. Well, I was trying to cut out an actual apple instead of irregular polygons that barely resembled the intended form. As I cut along the outline, I intensely focused on ensuring that the blade of the scissors did not touch a single bit of the white space. I tried to be perfect in every task, as if I was tightrope walking between two skyscrapers, where a single mistake would cost my life. Still, the hurdles I had to jump over were very low, and I had no problem achieving perfection in my childhood. At first, my strive for perfection came purely from myself. I savored the sense of accomplishment from producing a perfect outcome not to mention the bonus of praises and compliments. However, my image as an “umchina” slowly started to strangle me. As my family moved to different countries (from Korea to France, then Chad, and then Cameroon), I had to repeatedly break into preexisting “bubbles” of local communities. Something I was good at often acted as the catalyst for my friends to reach out to me, and I developed a misconception that others liked me because of my perfection. I began to fear doing something that I’m not already good at in front of others. Unless I appeared perfect, they would no longer like me as much. The hurdles I had to jump over grew taller and taller as my tasks became increasingly complex and time-consuming, and eventually, the inverse proportion between my energy and demand for perfection led me to face the impossible: I had to jump to the moon instead of a mere hurdle. I jumped. Of course, I failed. Although I had already known that true perfection is unattainable, a failure to uphold my own standards of perfection broke me down. Immediately, I became a procrastinator. The overwhelming pressure to be perfect made me push things back as I felt like I couldn’t achieve it. The rush of a deadline was the only thing that could defeat the fear of imperfection. The destructive cycle wore down my mental and physical health until I lay down sick with malaria.

My English teacher, noticing the change, continuously reached out to me, asking me about what I’m going through. After a few days, I honestly told him everything I was going through and received comfort and advice. While the “umchina” image is a part of me, it was my first time fully revealing my inner, vulnerable self to another. I have empathized with and counseled many friends, but, ironically, I have never poured out my struggles or emotions to someone else. After this point, I no longer had trouble opening up my imperfect self to others. Through the process, I learned that they found value in me purely as myself rather than my perfectionist image. I broke down major tasks into steps and installed a camera in my room to track myself.

Failure no longer meant rejection; it only left me with laughter, improvements, and upcoming success. Still, approaching something as a “rough draft” that could freely be modified helped me overcome the perfection-induced procrastination. Now I strive for excellence rather than perfection.

I can’t jump to the moon. But, I can build a spaceship to get there.

“What is your dream?”

In the sweltering heat of an afternoon, I stood before a classroom of eager yet uncertain faces. The middle school students, many of whom had never left their small town in Henan Province, sat in simple wooden desks. Their village was hours away from the nearest train station, a world apart from the bustling cities I was accustomed to. Before starting to teach them sing, I started with that simple question.

“I don’t know… I just want to escape this place, even just in my mind.”

Shocked and uncertain, I remained silent for a moment. Not knowing what to respond, I started teaching them singing.

That child’s response lingered in my mind. It reminded me of a conversation I had with a friend—a home renovator I met during a hip-hop music collaboration. He told me that he was living in Hangzhou, a city next to Shanghai, and had to spend months of savings just to purchase a train ticket to Shanghai. At first, I couldn’t believe what he said, until he showed me a picture of his home: a roughcast apartment with a single bed, taking over all the space. The walls, once intact, now yellowed and cracked. A small window, bare and unadorned, inviting all the harsh light of the world. Thus, he had to travel to another city to a rental apartment we called “Dreamhub,” where a community of Hip-hop artists gathered to produce music for free.

The more friends I met at Dreamhub, the more I discovered their shared struggles. At night, they poured all their thoughts into their flows and lyrics. As another day starts they, they were waiters, nurses, sneaker sellers, and home renovators, earning enough to live more comfortably.

I couldn’t shake the guilt that I never thought of their predicaments, nor tried to help. I set out to Henan just to help people, but people who needed the help were right around me: They had dreams too, but many of them didn’t have the tools or resources to chase them.

To help them, I first offered to cover the cost of a two-hour recording session in a professional studio. They thankfully refused my gesture. Consequently, I could only ask them to collaborate with me, promoting their music on my channel with my streams. With the profits we earned through our streams, we upgraded the microphone for our shared studio in the rental apartment and invited more artists so that they can have access to the equipment they need to pursue their dreams in music. I was struck by their gratitude and the realization that, for many of them, hip-hop was more than just a form of expression—it was their lifeline.

“At least we have a dream,” one of them told me.

“Hip-hop showed us a way out.”

And it wasn’t just them. All over China there were remote provinces like Henan where children were trapped in the cycles of poverty and limited education. For them, education was the only escape, but it shouldn’t have to be the only lifeline. They should be given more options to break free from the shackles imposed by their economic status.

To directly support the underprivileged teenagers, I hosted a charity concert in China last summer, called “emotional dumpster.” It was recorded and played to a group of kids in Guizhou. The money, over three thousand dollars, helped fund the renovation of homes and cover the transportation and ticket fees for twenty children to watch a Music Festival in Shanghai.

The concert was held in a small, intimate venue in Shanghai. My friends performed as guest artists, the nurse, the sneaker seller, and of course, the room renovator, pouring their hearts into every verse, every beat, every rhyme. It wasn’t just music; it was a message—a message of hope, of possibility, and of resilience. As the night unfolded, I could see the audience caught in the rhythm, the pulse of the music, but more importantly, in the cause we were championing. We weren’t just raising money for a charity. We were creating a space where people could see beyond the conventional idea of success as they didn’t have to be the only measures of a future.

As the last beat of the concert faded, I felt a shift in my heart. At that moment, I realized that I have a more important mission. I once wanted to be a famous artist, but now I know that the real art is in empowering the underprivileged with equal opportunity because the greatest reward isn’t recognition—it’s knowing I’ve made someone’s world a little bit bigger.

I was only 4 years old when I stepped into São Paulo. The market was alive, vibrant with colours, sounds and smells that made my senses overload. Though, amidst the chaos, my eyes locked onto something – an old map. Its edges were frayed, its words foreign, but I couldn’t look away. I didn’t know what it meant at the time, but I felt it pull at me, as though it held a secret I needed to uncover. My small chubby hands clutched it like a lifeline, an instinctive grasp for something bigger than myself. I insisted on taking it home, and when we returned, I pinned it to my wall.

As the years passed the map followed me. It came with me when I moved houses. It came with me when I changed rooms. Everywhere I went, I took pride in keeping it safely hung above my bed. But when I turned eleven, everything changed. My mother was diagnosed with cancer – a word that I didn’t fully understand at that time, but its presence brought chaos in our home. My mum was forced to battle for her life and as she did, time itself seemed to dissolve. There were moments where it stood still – waiting in hospital, watching her chest slowly rise and fall as I watched the hour go past. Other times, it seemed to blur the days and weeks together into a long, indistinguishable fog.

In the midst of this, the map showed the same deterioration that I felt. Neglected for months, it had become subject to time’s scarring. Its edges had weathered, its colours had dulled, and its once precise lines had become faint, as though time was gradually eroding the place it once depicted. I decided to take my map to the frame shop, carefully folding it in the large pocket of my school backpack. Reframing the map wasn’t just a practical choice but marked the start of my quiet rebellion against my lack of control.

Then, in the kitchen, I found my next battleground. Bone broth became my next act of defiance, but I didn’t just want to make it, however, I wanted it to be perfect. To me it wasn’t just a meal, but something that carried healing and made me feel as though I was contributing to my mother’s fight. I experimented with different ratios of vegetables and adjusted the stove to ensure that I could supply my mum with an infinite supply of cups of support.

Slowly, my mother started to recover, and with each small improvement in her health, I felt my own mental state shift. The weight of uncertainty that had clouded my world began to shift, and the chaos that had once filled out home began to fade. And it was in these moments of healing where I found myself again, being drawn to the map, like I was back in São Paulo.

But now when I look at the map, I see it for what it truly is: not just a map of Brazil, but a mirror. The faded lines, the cracks, the edges that had once been crisp and bold, now soft and blurred, were things I lived through all this time. Each tear or imperfection held a piece of me, a moment I thought I had forgotten. When I traced an unfamiliar tear in the corner something in me shifted. Time hadn’t broken the map; it had moulded it. I understood that time wasn’t something to fight against as it was the force that carried me forward, and the map was proof of it.

On the surface, my house was rich with noise—siblings playing, voices overlapping, and moments of innocent chaos. It appeared to outsiders as the boisterous energy of a large family of nine. People often mentioned that my childhood seemed to be filled with excitement and joy, but behind closed doors a more difficult reality existed. My home was often a battleground of cutting words, unresolved grievances, and bitter tension. Love was something I was expected to give unconditionally despite being surrounded by clashing personalities.

For years, I had believed that this dynamic was normal—the tension meant we were simply that close. I had naively clung to the happy moments convinced that they outweighed the difficult times. But as I grew older, I began to see how warped this perception was. The affection in the family was tangled with conflicts and misunderstandings that felt like an ugly paradox.

I started to resent certain family members, especially my older brother, Pattrick, who is ten years older than me. He was once my favorite playmate, but as I got older, his behavior frustrated me. I couldn’t reconcile how someone whom I had admired could act in ways that hurt me. Slowly, he became the embodiment of everything I feared and didn’t want to become.

Suppressed resentment boiled over into a ruthless war. He broke my computer with his fists. I broke his heart. I snapped loudly, “You always complain about Dad being the problem, but the role he plays in your life—you play that exact role in mine.” Pattrick, who was never at a loss for words, stood silent.

I won! I finally silenced him.

However, my satisfaction was fleeting. The questions that had laid dormant in my subconscious trickled to the surface. Why were we always fighting? Why was I so quick to anger? I contemplated it for many months. My anger was rooted in fear—the fear of being trapped in the same dysfunctional patterns as my brother and sister who have been draining our family emotionally and financially. Yet, every argument chained me closer to the same fate.

I heard the harsh noises of my brother arguing in yet another battle with our mother. The words got louder and closer until they burst through my door and I found Pattrick’s sorrow gushing out to me. He was ashamed of himself. His goal wasn’t to always be in conflict. My chest tightened. His fragility and insecurities resonated throughout my room.

The strong reverberations of his woes placed a small fracture in my tough exterior and empathy for him slowly seeped out. Neither of us had ever extended the compassion that we both needed. Looking through the shades of resentment, I couldn’t see beyond my pain or his missteps, and that narrow focus isolated us both. But his display of vulnerability broke my mindset free and shined insight on how our struggles and mistakes were deeply human. This encounter reframed my perspective, helping me to understand the complexity of human emotions and relationships.

These shifts helped me to see others as intricate individuals. My challenges evolved from sources of frustration into chances to build patience, emotional awareness, and compassion. Instead of chaos, I now heard the conversations—voices full of complexity and understanding—transforming the noise that once trapped me into energy of connection and growth.

In embracing the truth of human complexity, I reframed my interactions and reinterpreted my approach to conflict and hardship. I began to forge a path forward built on emotional strength, openness, and connection. This insight continues to inspire me to lean into vulnerability, as it fosters resilience and a deeper sense of humanity in both myself and my relationships.

“You smell nice” is the compliment I receive most often.

But when I ask, “Thanks. What do I smell like?”, I’m met with puzzled faces cycling through fleeting eureka moments—bright with sudden certainty, only to fall back into contemplation. Eventually, everyone arrives at the same conclusion: “I can’t describe it. It just smells like you.”

It’s a fair answer. A perfume isn’t a single scent; it’s a composition of layers that unfold over time. In perfumery, "notes" refer to these layers—top, heart, and base. Each note emerges at its own pace according to the volatility of its molecules, with the top notes providing the initial burst of scent, the heart notes forming the fragrance’s core, and the base notes lingering the longest, leaving the final impression.

Concocted with precision, my own perfume consists of 40mL of alcoholic base blended with 2mL of bergamot, 1.5mL of narcissus, 2mL of patchouli, and 2.5mL each of vanilla and tonka. These carefully chosen components reflect different facets of me—the layers that reveal themselves as you get to know me better.

If you’re my classmate in the chemistry lab, leaning over a flask while I measure drops of sulfuric acid with a pipette, you’ll likely catch the bright, citrusy burst of bergamot. It’s sharp, fresh, and slightly tart, like a freshly zested lemon twist. Curious and energetic, focused on the thrill of discovery, it’s the part of me that thrives in moments of intellectual exploration in the classroom, eagerly diving into the unknown much like the zesty effervescence of bergamot.

Spend a little more time with me, though, and the heart notes make their presence known. During the bustle of a lunch break, as I lay out plans for our next playdate, presenting my grand vision for how we’ll maximize every minute of our precious time together, patchouli’s grounding depth mirrors my focus and strategic planning. Later, if you’re on the tennis team following my lead through warm-ups, or in my club listening to me present our latest initiative, you’ll notice the floral and green, but bold and slightly animalic edge of narcissus taking the center stage.

But if you’re my younger brother running into my arms, outstretched and waiting for you at the school gate, or my grandmother in her hospital bed as I gently blow on a spoonful of soup before offering it to you, you’ll catch the warm, powdery scent of tonka and vanilla, carrying the quiet patience and unwavering love I extend to those who mean the most to me.

Just as one experiences all the layers of a perfume only by staying attentive to how it evolves throughout the day, the more deeply someone engages with me, the more dimensions of my personality they come to uncover. Recognizing these layers in others has taught me to approach people with patience and curiosity. First impressions, like the bright top notes of a perfume, are easy to notice but often incomplete. The most energetic kid in class might secretly grapple with unspoken challenges, like a perfume’s sparkling opening masking a more somber base. Similarly, a quiet, distant classmate might reveal profound thoughtfulness and empathy over time, akin to a soft floral note that blooms only after darker, woodier scents have dissipated.

It is through noticing these subtleties that builds genuine connections. Like a perfume’s evolving scent, every person carries a unique blend of traits that may initially seem contradictory but ultimately form something cohesive and extraordinary. By approaching others with openness and attentiveness, I’ve learned the value of making space for their complexities, strengths, and struggles. It’s in these hidden layers—unexpected depth and nuance—where true meaning and strength reside. When you’re patient enough to appreciate someone’s ‘base note,’ they’ll resonate long after the moment has passed—like the lasting impression of a perfume’s final scent.

I’ve always been fascinated by ramps.

It started eight years ago, when I became a scooter-fanatic. Skateparks became my second-home as I learned tricks and made life-long friends. Then the COVID-19 pandemic hit, locking-down my community.

My solution? Build my own park.

With a few sheets of plywood and a bit of wood glue, I hacked together my first ramp—which collapsed hours later as I tried a 360. I found recklessly improvising a curved take-off with a rusty saw doesn’t cut it — literally.

Swallowing my pride (and some sawdust), I decided to try again, NASA engineer-style. This time, I sketched a blueprint full of detailed measurements before heading to Home-Depot. I hunted down 2x4s for the ramp’s inner-supports and plywood for the ramp faces. Hours later in my garage, a robust kicker ramp spray painted with “N-A-S-A” lay before me.

Grinning ear-to-ear as I flew through the air (despite a few new scrapes on my knees), I realized that while my off-the-cuff excitement helped me quickly hammer together ramps, it was detailed planning that helped them last.

“Who wants to match some poop?!”

I wheel my rubber poop cart into the museum, preparing a new group of kids for Scat-Match: a matching-game with animals and their feces.

Thinking that the children would be well-behaved, like the kids I coached in volleyball, I was unpleasantly surprised to see them flinging the scat around, ignoring me as I carefully explained the activity and takeaways.

I had to ramp-up their curiosity somehow.

I turned toward Eddie, a 4th grader stumped at the lumps. I tried guiding—ramping—him to the answer: "Do you have cats? Have you seen their poop?" Eddie finally picked up the mountain lion scat, placing it with the cougar photo, “My cat’s poo kinda looks like this one!” Nari, confused between the deer and snake scat, realized the snake’s would be misshapen once I hinted, “The lion’s scat is big and chunky, so what might the snake’s look like?”

Just as I carefully carved that wooden, curved take-off many years prior, I guided each student through the activity with a bit of spontaneous improvisation. And when Eddie asked, “Why do people study poop?”, followed quickly by “why is some poop round and some long and squiggly?” with a newfound flicker of curiosity, I know I've started a learning movement — more than just a bowel one. And this time, it would continue rolling onwards.

After watching the horror movie Bird Box, I proposed a themed game of Hide-and-Seek to my friends: Tony, the brave protagonist, would be blindfolded while the rest of us hid around the room, playing the invisible monster. As the soundtrack Undercurrents blasted in the background, the living room turned into a comedy of errors: Kris squeezed his chubby frame behind the TV, nearly knocking it over, while I wriggled desperately under the sofa. Tony stumbled around, arms out, all of us bursting out laughing when he caught someone. The next round, I orchestrated a plan: I lifted my hand… 1, 2, 3. Jason, the poor seeker, was bombarded with couch cushions and Nerf darts, as he crumpled to the ground in defeat.

After watching the scene in the Taiwanese horror film Incantation where the mother performs the ritual in the tunnel to remove the curse from her daughter, I compared it with the Korean horror film The Wailing's climax, where the father rushes to save her daughter from the mysterious curse. We discussed that while the villainous forces in the movies are inspired by different cultural beliefs, there was a common thread: the unrelenting ferocity of parental love.

By balancing planning with the movie night, spontaneity with the game, and a mix of both in planning our discussion, I learned there’s a time and place where planning can help promote improvisation.

Whether I'm crafting a Superman-worthy kicker ramp or designing a lesson that not only teaches kids, but also gives them enough momentum to keep their curiosity rolling, I’ve learned that by balancing careful planning and improvisation, I’m able to succeed in my ambitions. I’ll continue to ramp my way step-by-step to my dreams.

Buk buk buk buk ba-GAWK! 
The clucking of thirty-one chickens greets me each morning as they ruffle their feathers, briskly rubbing their backs in the grey, dampened soil. Loudy starts his morning crescendo crows, Blackbeard flaunts her…black beard, Princess Leah observes me with her opaque left eye (pecked out by a rival clique), albino Gary strikes my midnight blue crocs, which are two sizes too big for my feet. Life as a backyard chicken farmer is as unglamorous as you’d expect, filled with frantic scrambles to retrieve escaped hens and the occasional indignity of chasing one around the yard in socks. Chickens aren’t known for their brilliance–they’d often peck at their reflections in windows, convinced another bird was challenging their supremacy, or perform an iconic “left-left-right” scratch on the same 2-by-2-inch section of dirt, expecting something new. And yet, I still found myself fascinated by how a brain so small could orchestrate survival instincts, pecking orders, and surprisingly endearing personalities. 
As I tossed sweet potato scraps into the feeding grounds, I noticed that the chickens' pecking frenzy followed an almost rhythmic pattern. The same alpha hen always struck first, while the others waited their turn. The pecking order was just that–an order–and every chicken knew just where they fit, indicative of a social hierarchy.
