Years later, while researching zebra finches’ song patterns as part of a behavioral neuroscience project, I found myself recalling those early mornings. To me, mapping neural pathways felt like a natural extension of watching the hens; both were puzzles waiting to be pieced together, and I felt butterflies after uncovering a deeper order beneath the surface chaos, as if I’d cracked the shell into something greater. 
While some people might look at a flock of chickens and just see chickens, I think that everything presents a puzzle waiting to be solved. 
The first time I held a 5x5 Rubik’s cube, I immediately needed to take it apart to see how it worked. At first, I just wanted to solve the cube faster, but later, I found myself drawn to the physical science underlying how it fits together. This growing fascination with problem-solving and understanding complex systems reaffirmed my desire to pursue the “holy trinity” described by my peers (“triple sciencing” in biology, chemistry, and physics) my junior year, dropping a study hall while filling its position with HL Biology. 
Through this scientific journey, creating systems to overcome obstacles became second nature, and I found my flock by sharing those resources with others. In history class, I struggled to present my Cuban Revolution Socratic seminar points, so I taught myself LaTeX, making a simple user-guide to organize evidence, allowing me to fully communicate my ideas and rebut or concur with others. Egged on by my classmates’ positive feedback, my initial project snowballed into a full-stack History Bowl website where I created practice problems, a queryable database to search related questions, and single-player and multiplayer functionality to simulate real competition scenarios. My classroom and club resources remind me that the “chicken or the egg” problem of creativity often resolves itself through action: once I begin creating something, new ideas emerge naturally for what to do next. 
Small, everyday moments can seem so unremarkable at the time. But chasing chickens in the backyard, for instance, is what shapes who you are. Observing chickens made me inquisitive. The mechanisms underlying Rubik’s cube sharpened my focus on science. Struggling with history notes inspired me to build resources that help others. Small curiosities have an uncanny way of coming home to roost. And life is a living, breathing science experiment if you have a curious mind that is eager to understand how everything works. I’ll continue ruffling my feathers, carrying on my love for chasing questions, solving problems, and building connections into every new experience. After all, I’m no spring chicken, but I'll sure crack open an opportunity to see what hatches.

I like to call myself a curator. Not of art, nor of rare zoological specimens, but of inanimate objects that sit atop my nightstand. This 17-year-old piece of furniture is a microcosm of my mind—hosting the ideas, experiences, and objects that shape who I am.

First, a stack of books, high enough to mimic a game of Jenga but just short of toppling over. It’s a contradictory yet amalgamated tower, blending dystopian sagas, postcolonial critiques, and works of my favorite poet, Rupi Kaur. This delicate mix defines my curiosity: the tension between the world as it is and the world as it could be.

Hidden behind my literary Tower of Pisa is a miniature race car emblazoned, “MONACO”. My fascination with Formula 1 taught me the principle of constant evolution. In motorsport, addressing even minor “pit”falls can shave off milliseconds during races. Marginal gains—small, consistent improvements that generate exponential progress—are everything. This philosophy underpins my approach to leadership, driving me to ensure that each new version of myself is stronger than the last.

Though you’ll smell before you see them, my nightstand is populated by a mini-city of candles. From Endless Weekend to Coconut Grove, my collection represents my personal mission: being a guiding light for others. I aim to illuminate the world around me using candles of knowledge, advocacy, and justice. By mentoring underclassmen for debate competitions or voicing youth perspectives to my city’s Mayor, I’m passionate about helping others feel supported and heard. I’m also drawn to the theoretical aspects of change-making; captivated by the Jemez Principles for Democratic Organizing and pursuing research on global human rights. This interplay between theory and practice is perfectly encompassed by Aristotle’s praxis—putting ideas into action—which I’ve adopted as a reminder that meaningful change emerges when we align our values with our actions.

These values come to life in one community in particular: DECA. Atop my books is a hot-pink bracelet with the letters “NM DECA”, representing my initials and the New Mexico state officers who gifted it to me. Wearing this bracelet daily represents my commitment to mentorship and meaningful connections. What started as “just” a business club became the most transformative experience of my high school career, allowing me to collaborate for equity by lowering barriers to access, and make friends in every state.

Australia to Ceylon non-stop. A vintage airline commercial with my native country’s colonial name depicts a saree-clad woman before Sigiriya Rock- it’s a print I purchased in the coastal town, Galle. Glancing at the image brings me back to my heritage, stirring my nostalgia for the rolling landscapes of Sri Lanka. Simultaneously, it’s proof of why justice is so central to my identity. The civil war and genocide my parents endured affected Tamil people across continents and generations, but their struggles didn’t happen in vain. This print is a daily reminder of my family’s resilience and why I strive to make sure no voice, including my own, is silenced.

The final stop on my nightstand tour: a turquoise tub of Play-Doh. While I no longer consume it in disturbing quantities, Play-Doh teaches me that innovation can coexist with intellectual rigor and confers the malleability of ideas. Whether harmonizing with my a cappella group or telling stories through Bharatanatyam dance, I embrace creative expression as a way to temper the intensity of my other pursuits. Play-Doh allows me to reshape my thoughts, approaching obstacles from new angles and constantly seeking inventive solutions.

These objects, each a small artifact of my life, are more than just random trinkets. Whenever I’m feeling scattered, I take comfort in knowing that I can simply close my eyes while focusing on the objects I hold dear. When I wake up, I’ll gaze upon a complex landscape of my life’s biggest inspirations; a mosaic of the person that I am and the person that I hope to be.

“Want some tea?”

You’d think the last thing a high school student would want to do after working nine hours straight in a research lab is spend an entire hour making tea. However, walking to the only supermarket on the university campus despite the scorching summer sun, picking out the freshest patch of mint leaves, washing individual mint sticks, and then serving my friends mint tea wasn’t something I did to just bury myself in more work; it was a way for me to help those who have helped me.

It didn’t come naturally to me to ask others for help. I used to believe I was able to accomplish everything on my own. I would study for exams without thinking to ask the teacher for help and would end up on top every time. Thus, walking into the Saudi Research Science Institute (SRSI), a research program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), I was sure the same approach would net the same result.

But after scoring 29/100 in my mini research paper report, I felt crushed. What could I have done better? I was sure my paper was flawless. I even included expected results! However, when the top mini-paper winners were given the stage to debrief their success in front of us all, I realized what I had been doing wrong: I was working all on my own, without even thinking of asking for feedback.

Determined to remedy my loss, I decided to approach the upcoming poster competition with a new mindset. This time, I would actively seek out help from others. Their feedback would surely help me win an award. After forming overnight study sessions with a couple of peers, I released my endless barrage of questions.

As we worked on our posters over the dim lighting of the study rooms at KAUST’s student center, we shared stories from home. Slowly, my focus shifted from utilizing my friends as “feedback machines” to learning more about my friends’ interests, which made me notice their homesickness. Rather than push them more with my research questions, I felt inclined to help in a meaningful way. In Saudi, we would shower guests with tea, so I decided to give my friends a semblance of home by brewing tea for everyone.

Although brewing tea at KAUST was no easy task, the smiles everybody greeted me with as I walked from study room to study room serving tea were the driving factor in the process. Every “thank you” or “you don’t know how much I needed this” I was met with made me feel intense joy, and it was this joy that drove me to not only succeed but also help those around me succeed, too. Eventually, this process was integrated into my daily routine.

After the competition, as I walked on stage for achieving top-five posters alongside my friends, I felt happy—not just because I had accomplished my goal, but because of the claps and cheers surrounding me. Walking into SRSI, I was certain I would win something, and I did: I won membership in a new family.

On the program’s last day, as people lined up to have one last cup of tea before going on the bus ride to the airport, I realized overcoming challenges isn’t about facing them alone, but rather approaching them from many different perspectives, and by asking others for help, I got to view my work from a different set of eyes, which allowed me to see flaws I never could have seen alone.

Just as there is a positive correlation between x and y values in linear graphs, the more people I ask for help, the larger my improvements. Looking forward, I hope to continually improve as part of a much larger family in college, and form new friends along the way over cups of tea.

From suburban San [Name], California, to the sprawling metropolis of Johannesburg, South Africa, my family moved continents when I was young and I experienced an exciting shock. Five minutes from us lay the biggest informal settlement in Africa, Soweto, where street vendors hustled to make ends meet and music blared from streetside hair salons and food stalls. Having only lived there only a year, I kept to myself, realising my American interests of baseball and Pokemon did not harmonize with the rugby and Ben10 of my peers. I remember on the first day of school stating that I was fond of soccer (a lie, I wasn’t), a habit I carried throughout my time there.

When we moved back to California I remember speaking to my friends about some of the hobbies I had acquired abroad like my new excitement for Football Panini (a collectible soccer sticker book), which left them with blank stares and shrugs of disinterest. To my surprise however, I didn’t mind. Then my parents informed me that we would be relocating to Kenya that following summer. Again, I was gripped by the fear of not fitting in. Would I have to live another lie? Tailoring myself to blend in with everyone else? No. Instead I tried to see moving to Kenya as an opportunity to be confident from the start and not to compromise this time. On the first day at my new international school, the class icebreaker seemed like a blank canvas for me. I expressed my passion for baseball, finding an unusual feeling of satisfaction in the puzzled expressions that played across my peers who reigned from 13 different countries. I thought that my answer would be seen as unengaging as no one could relate to it, but to my shock it raised questions (“how do you score a goal in baseball?”) and prompted further discussion. This ignited a newfound confidence in myself to embrace my individuality, as it reinforced that I didn’t need to compromise to fit in.

I carried this confidence in me to own who I am, what they now coin a third culture child. I attended a summer hockey camp in Minnesota and again felt that familiar apprehension of admitting I was from Kenya, fearing it could leave me an outsider. But I embraced it and instead had many campers asking questions, curious about what life was like in Africa. When I moved continents once again to attend high school, I had years of experience under my belt. I was an American from Kenya attending a British boarding school - talk about different! But I had gained much confidence over the years that I once again, owned my unique upbringing this time with pride. This reinforced my desire to approach everything with a bold step, embracing who I am, as opposed to being left with an endless void of what ifs and imposter syndrome.

My interactions with diverse cultures have also shaped me into a more adaptable person. From sharing supper with my Ethiopian friend and her family, finding myself immersed in her tradition of sitting on the floor, eating with no cutlery, and even feeding one another! To attending the baptism of our nanny’s daughter, crammed in a room smaller than my bedroom with over 25 Kenyans, none of whom spoke English but with whom I managed to communicate with using sign language and shared laughter, this range of experiences instilled an ease in myself adapting to new situations.

Moving to new places wasn't exciting to my younger self, yet all of the experiences I’ve had have taught me that different geographical locations do not need to be isolating. I do not fear things that are new and different. I am open minded and adaptable, a social chameleon. I’m grateful to have had such a rich upbringing where unfamiliarity was the norm and just another opportunity to grow and learn.

A couple months into quarantine, my dad and I looked through dusty boxes in the garage to find something interesting to do. We found a box with my childhood toys, another with my dad’s collection of creepy face jugs, and one with beads, wire, and other tools. As I picked up a maroon statement necklace, my dad heartwarmingly recalled how he used to make matching sets of bracelets and necklaces for my mom. A week after restarting this hobby, I picked up one of his books inside the box named “Wirework Techniques,” to which he said he bought the book but never had the chance to learn it. Intrigued, we started with the book’s basics. With time, our designs completely diverged and transformed. My wire wrapping designs became extremely detailed with wire wrapping around a bead to create designs of flowers or trees, while my dad’s designs remained abstract with swirls and lines over a bead.

I was also taking a photography class at school, where our assignments were to take photos of anything around the house. Every time I took a photo of an object, there was a lack of sentimental meaning because the pandemic prevented me from photographing people, leaving my pictures feeling empty. When I asked my friends to model, they posed awkwardly, unsure of what to do. Dejected, I sought my dad’s advice. “Try connecting with them,” he suggested, “make it feel natural and relaxing.” Taking his words to heart, I approached a girl in my neighborhood for a shoot. Recognizing her bubbly personality, I chatted and cracked horrible dad jokes to put her at ease. As I clicked the shutter, her laughter illuminated the frame which transformed my photos and taught me the power of connecting with people.

When I became the Virginia Junior Classical League (VJCL) historian, I put my improved, conversational photography skills to use. During VJCL convention, I wanted to capture as many events as possible within the two days. When students were waiting to turn in Classics-related art projects, such as a crocheted Cerberus or a rendition of ancient pottery, I asked them what their inspiration for the project was before taking a picture of them standing with their artwork. Just by walking down a line of students, I created so many new friends who asked to hang out when I was free. At other events, I captured moments of students celebrating their tournament wins, competing in spirit contests, and singing karaoke in their togas. When I came home to develop my photos, I sat jaw-dropped to see that I captured around 3,000 photos in two days. Several schools even reached out to ask me to edit certain photos. While it was tough to narrow down the photos, I took the ones that captured VJCL the brightest to put into a scrapbook.

Applying the creativity I developed from my dad, I designed the scrapbook cover by airbrushing a wooden plate with a swirling purple galaxy splashed with gold stars. I then carefully drilled holes into the wood to form the constellation Auriga to represent ingenuity, the theme of my scrapbook. I cautiously threaded star-shaped beads through the holes, illuminating them with fairy lights. Over the past few months, I’ve poured countless hours into perfecting my scrapbook, practicing what my dad taught me and often staying up until midnight to refine each spread. All my hard work paid off when I received first place for my scrapbook against 35 other states at the national Latin convention.

Every project I’ve worked on with my dad—whether it was crafting jewelry, capturing candid moments, or designing this scrapbook—has nurtured a mindset of ingenuity in me. Now, I’m learning how to do woodworking and 3D printing with him. As I prepare to begin college without him, I’m proud to carry forward his excitement to create what comes to mind, not just in regards to crafts.

When I first met Mr. Chen, we were standing outside his motel in Zhuchang, my hometown. He was middle-aged, stout and short, listening to my chatter about this place and the youngsters I hopefully could befriend in the upcoming summer. Rumor has it that he was a retired mafia boss, but I felt from his eyes something much tender than his toughened facial lines, when his low voice permeated the humid air: "Here hold many stories of families with troubled kids. I hope you could listen to them, please."

Our conversations struck me as unexpected. The word "troubled kid" was familiar to me. Ever since the age of 12, I was often branded as rebellious, in defiance of discipline. These "accusations" certainly had some credit for my indiscretions at school, but I was also unnerved by my angst which was rooted in a hyper-sensitivity to how others perceived me. The growing mustache, the deepening voice, and the change in my physique all mirrored my inner questioning. My personality, as told, had become unreasonable, but no one seemed to care to explain why.

I was inspired by Mr. Chen: what do people know about "troubled" kids? What do I know about myself? In seeking those answers, I traversed the town's muddy roads in the following days. I visited family-owned barbershops and noodle stores, knocked on humble brick-built ranch homes, and waited outside teen calligraphy teaching centers in search of families I could interview.

It was undoubtedly difficult to swallow all these rejections, countless times, as the parents were defensive toward a stranger poking into daily matters or their children just hiding themselves from accusations. After sharing some corn on the stools of a sidewalk, Miss Zhang, the owner of a small metal and tool store, told me her son once locked himself in his room and almost ran away from home during a massive fight about phone usage. Her cheek blushed into a rosy red when she asked me whether I, as a teen, could offer an explanation for her "wild" son for whom her love failed to smooth those hurtful moments.

Those unfinished conversations in Zhuchang urged me to speak with more parents and teenagers on different occasions. Back in the parks of Shenzhen, I interviewed and learned more stories of anxiety, miscommunication, and discoveries of self-identity, those often dismissed by strained relationships with people close to life. With each person I met, I slowly realized that the awkwardness of adolescence was not rooted in neglect or prejudice, but in a mutual lack of understanding.

Looking back on my past six years, it was, at times, chaotic and often at odds with my own mind. Yet it was also my immature adolescent sensitivity that pushed me to walk through the rain-soaked streets for conversations from different generations. I envisioned a space where compassion can clear the misunderstanding of the tumult of adolescence. In 2022, therefore, I opened up a new channel, "A Stranger's Ear," an online platform where "troubled" kids could open up with an anonymous peer listener.

As a humble listener, I realized the insecurity of adolescent times intertwined with personal predicaments that often reveal our deep vulnerabilities. The anonymous platform helped the teenage voice challenge those moments of self-doubt. I spoke with the sister struggling to afford treatment for her brother's autism and the high-schooler facing punishment for his homosexuality. I shared my own haunting memories of bullying with the girl who endured years of sexual assault by classmates. These ongoing weekly sharing sessions connected our lives with peer support across gender, class, and social factors; sharing encouraged us to regain the confidence, confronting the lurking anxieties with which we, as teenagers, truly empathize.

Separated by a socially distant world, we can still be bonded to navigate the time of "awkward growth." Adolescence, after all, can bridge childhood to adult life, from the fear of change to an embrace of growth, to a community with endless potential ahead.

An earthly waft of the coarse-grained wood drifted beneath my nose, as I sipped a fresh green apple juice. The mellifluous sound ringing from the strings of the Tonkori blended with the whirring of skateboards. In the rural field in front of me children happily tossed frisbees around in front of the screen showcasing the community’s films. After two long weeks of work, I wanted to cherish this feeling… and Japan.

I have admired Japan for as long as I can remember. Unlike my life in Hong Kong or the UK, which feels quite isolating, time spent in Japan felt communal and comfortable. This notion of collectivism stems from the fact that Japan was an isolated society for a long time. This required people to work in perfect harmony with each other, avoiding confrontation, and putting others' needs over individual desires. In addition to daily actions, these sentiments are present in the Japanese language. Phrases like sumimasen are used to mitigate conflict and honorifics like -san are a way to convey respect and deference.

Having attended high-performing schools my whole life, it was inevitable that an element of competitiveness would linger. Naturally, people would also be biased towards their own opinions due to their unique experiences, and be protective of their own suggestions. I often believed that I needed to do more and constantly compare myself to my peers, leading to endless amounts of self-induced stress.

Being cooped up in my dorm or my room at home, I fantasised about trying something new and spending time in an environment less about competition and more about collaboration for the common good. So, I signed up for a summer internship at the Niseko Hirafu Green Park, built from the ground up with reclaimed wood, highlighting the creative endeavors of the locals. I arrived in Japan hoping for an immersive cultural and linguistic experience but quickly realised this experience would mean so much more. On my first day, I worked on building the park’s café. Not wanting to embarrass myself with my amateur carpentry skills, I took extra caution with every swing of the hammer. Realising how timid I was acting, my fellow volunteers, with a smile and empathetic gaze, went out of their way to make me feel at ease. Despite my best efforts, I ended the day feeling like I had contributed little to the group's effort.

This feeling brought me back to group projects at school, everyone pushed their own agendas and ignored the fact that it was supposed to be a collaborative effort. These weren’t traits within the Japanese community as everyone carried a respectful and open-minded attitude. As I grew accustomed to the kindness Japan has treated me, I realised that my time there was not about my own individual contributions to building the park, but rather about coming together as a community to create something meaningful. I was determined to ignore my embarrassment: if my Japanese wasn’t perfect, that’s okay; if a piece of wood was too heavy, that’s fine too, as long as I was trying my best. During the day, I would be helping design the billboard for sponsorships or assist building the cafe hands-on. At night, I would stay up until 1AM, trying to create the sleekest social media posts. My enthusiasm inspired other volunteers, and together we fostered a spirit of hard work and collaboration. The park became a canvas for our collective creativity, and I felt the sense of belonging I had long sought.

The sky grew dimmer as the two weeks swiftly passed. As I wiped the sweat off my forehead, sharing gyoza with my friend Bodai, we ran through the collection of vinyls that the DJs used after a long day of hard work. I realised how important it is to have a support network. Whilst I will always value healthy competition, I now understand the power of collaboration.

Harsh dissonances burst out of my phone speaker, filling my practice room with chaotic echoes. Clutching onto my viola, I craned my neck towards the Pierrot Lunaire sheet music, trying to understand Schoenburg’s abstract harmonic language. Pausing the YouTube video, I sighed. I felt uncertain whether I could master the viola part of these monstrous songs for the upcoming Wigmore Hall audition.

With a packed schedule of concerts, exams, and outreach trips, I only managed to look at the music six days before the audition. My academic side urged me to give up and run back to my dorm to study for my next A-level Maths exams. After all, I didn’t even like the piece. However, my musical side reminded me of my Wigmore Hall debut—when my quartet became one in the unforgettable ambiance. Dying to relive that sensation, I pushed through both as always.

This wasn’t the first time such a thing happened. As I sought academic opportunities at a music school, events clashed almost biweekly. Math olympiads and concerts were often on the same day, and success in one meant falling short in another. On top of that, there were no clubs or advanced classes—I had to pave my own path. Like how the slightest deviation from consonant notes creates a clash, my anomalous passion was inharmonious at my school. I was like the dissonances in Pierrot Lunaire.

Despite discouraging ‘failures’, I planned and practiced more strategically each time, learning from countless previous attempts. This time, I finally made it. Getting to the point of solving Mechanics questions and playing Pierrot Lunaire in my dreams, I not only got the grades and another opportunity to perform on my dream stage—I proved to myself the power of persistence. Even when the daily Wigmore rehearsals clashed with math competitions, I handled everything with more enthusiasm than ever.

As we had 5-hour-long weekend rehearsals, the same topic came up every break: ‘Do you enjoy Pierrot Lunaire?’. Interestingly, the debate always looked different. One by one, my ensemble started discovering the piece’s inexplicable charm. Even the enduring Schoenburg-haters eventually admitted that it’s not that horrible.

Being one of the first to move to the ‘pro-Pierrot’ group, I ended up liking the piece so much that I couldn’t stop singing the dissonant 7-note motif. I didn’t know why. I knew dissonances naturally sound unpleasant due to the interference phenomenon of overtones, but my odd fascination contradicted this mathematical explanation.

After days of reading research articles, I realized that our perception of dissonance evolves. The tritone, called the devil’s interval in the Medieval times, is now prominent in the Blues scale and dominant seventh chords. Indeed, dissonant frequencies clash, but it adds exciting tension. Knowing how Beethoven and Wagner revolutionized harmony with this added spice, I realized that dissonance should be embraced, not avoided.

Having considered my math enthusiasm to be a dissonance, I was inspired by this notion of embracement. Rather than exploring my ‘unusual’ interests alone, why not try spreading this joy? With nervous excitement, I sent out a survey about my plans for creating academic clubs. Surprisingly, many students responded with enthusiastic suggestions and messages of appreciation. Realizing that those with academic interests hesitated to explore it due to inaccessibility, I was even more motivated to develop a supportive academic scene.

After months of running around to negotiate with teachers, make posters, and give speeches in assemblies, I finally established the first academic clubs at Purcell. As expected, not many people came due to clashing music commitments. Walking back to my room with barely touched biscuits often felt disheartening. Nevertheless, the enthusiasm of the few people who appreciated my clubs was enough to keep me going.

I am still a dissonance. It is still difficult to juggle multiple concerts and competitions or to teach myself unoffered courses. But as I find beauty in my dissonance, others do too. From introducing interesting math puzzles to teaching the unoffered courses to my peers, I aspire to embrace my dissonance to create a unique harmony.

The mask felt heavier than it should have. The sun scorched above the Thailand field, glaring down at us like a spotlight on the stage of some unforgiving drama. It was forty degrees Celsius, and I was wearing a mask. Why was I wearing a mask? Even I didn’t fully know.

I tugged at the elastic bands around my ears as I jogged onto the field, but the fabric clung to my face as if stitched into my skin. Every breath felt like a wager against the heat, each inhale thinner than the last. I didn’t stop running. I couldn’t. Maybe it was stubbornness, or maybe I just wanted to prove something—to myself, to my teammates, to no one in particular.

My teammates' shouts were muffled as if we were playing underwater. Sprint. Stop. Pivot. The game didn’t pause for the heat, and neither did I. But the mask tightened around me like a noose, its presence more noticeable than the game itself. I ignored it. Until the world tilted.

One second I was mid-stride, the next my knees were pressed into the turf. The sky twisted above me like a kaleidoscope, the roughness of the turf grounding me. I couldn’t hear the whistle or the stampede of footsteps rushing toward me. All I could hear was my own breath, shallow and frantic. The sun flickered in and out of focus, blurring my vision. And for the first time, I thought: Maybe I’m going to die right here, on this field, in this ridiculous mask.

I woke up under the harsh glare of fluorescent hospital lights. The mask sat quietly on the bedside table, almost mocking me. That mask is armor. A shield I had worn long before pandemics were part of our vocabulary. A defense I built to hide the pieces of myself I wasn’t ready to show the world.

Lying in that bed, I felt stripped bare, as if the mask had been more than just cloth. But staring at it, I realized safety was an illusion. The mask, the persona I wore around others, protected nothing real. I had been living too cautiously, mistaking comfort for happiness.

Returning to school felt different after that hospital stay. Friends tore their masks off the moment they could. I kept mine on. Partly out of habit, partly because I wasn’t sure who I was without it. But I started to wonder if I’d hidden behind it for too long. Growth, I realized, wasn’t just about surviving the heat. It was about stepping out of the shade.

That day on the field stuck with me. The fear of embarrassment and the need to fit in—they all disappeared at that moment. What stayed was the desire to live fully. I had spent so much energy avoiding judgment that I forgot to trust myself. There was nothing to lose by showing the world who I really was.

A week after returning to school, I removed my mask during lunch for the first time. I felt exposed, but lighter. A friend noticed. "I almost didn’t recognize you," he said with a grin. I felt the cool breeze for the first time in months, unfiltered by cloth. It felt real. We laughed, and I realized how long I’d been holding back. That small moment—just a shared joke—felt like a step toward something bigger.

As I stood in front of the mirror one morning, I felt foolish taking the mask off, as if exposing something fragile. But I realized the bravest thing I could do was embrace that vulnerability. Being foolish, I realized, wasn’t a weakness but my growth. Living without fear of judgment wasn’t just the point; it was freedom. The next time I step onto that field, the heaviest thing I carry won’t be the mask. It will be the strength I’ve earned.

“A deaf concert?"

The skepticism in the volunteers’ voices was unmistakable as I shared my idea of organizing a music concert for the Deaf. Despite the doubts, I continued to explain our vision, often sharing stories of my encounters with Feng.

I met Feng at a pop-up market two years ago, a place I had only agreed to volunteer at simply because my friends were participating. Watching them shout enthusiastically to attract customers, I stood in the crowd, unsure how to make myself heard in the chaos. But among the frenzy, I noticed a figure that mirrored my stillness. Standing alone by her food stand, her lips remained closed, eyes carefully scanning the faces of passersby. Before I knew it, I felt my body slowly moving towards her.

"How much is this?"

Silence hung in the air. It wasn’t until she pointed to her ears that I realized: she wasn’t just quiet; she was deaf. The quiet I thought we shared suddenly became a wall separating us: the world of sound on my side and the world of silence on hers. But that wall, instead of separating us, drew me closer to her.

Over the next few weeks, I visited Feng at the bakery where she worked. I would watch as the bakers glide from station to station, instructing each other with silent commands, all while attending to the customers at the counter—no words needed. I began to see how their silence wasn't passive; it was filled with drive and initiative—something mine was lacking until that point. As I spent my weekends there, learning Chinese Sign Language, packaging baked goods, and immersing myself in their world, I began to hear things in their silence.

There was so much they wanted to say; many just didn’t know how to listen. A wall divided our worlds, but I was determined to break it down. And so, we decided on the idea of a Deaf concert, where the bakers’ voices could reverberate through music.

Organizing the concert, however, was anything but simple. I recruited student volunteers, negotiated venue locations, and organized logistics. But rehearsals were tough, especially without the typical auditory cues most musicians rely on. When I got frustrated at the lack of synchronization between the Deaf performers, Feng cupped her palms over her ears.

Close my ears? I was confused at first, but then it hit me. She was urging me to listen to a music that transcended sound—a music only felt, not heard; one that was entirely theirs. So, I closed my ears, opened my heart, and followed their lead in creating a concert not meant for the ears, but for the heart. From there, we designed a system of visual and tactile cues to guide the performers: lights that pulsed with rhythms, flags to mark transitions, and vibrations through the stage to signal movements.

The final performance was unforgettable. As the audience signed applause, I discovered a new meaning of voice. Before meeting Feng, I equated voice with volume, with loudness. But now I understand that voice is the initiative I show. Though mine may be quiet, it carries a weight and clarity that speaks louder than any words. I’ve carried this lesson forward by founding a service club to continue championing the Deaf community and creating Utopix Magazine to amplify the voices of underrepresented groups that often go unheard.

I now understand that being quiet doesn't mean staying silent. Instead, it's a chance to listen, to listen with our hearts, and in doing so, I've discovered how to speak and act in ways that truly resonate. That's how we reach people through walls—not by shouting louder, but by taking action to chip away at the barrier bit by bit. As I move forward, I aspire to create more inclusive spaces through active listening and compose a symphony of voices that can penetrate any wall.

En garde. Pret. Allez!

I squatted to parry Andy’s hit as he charged toward me. I flicked my sword at his rusted lame, turning my light green. Point after point, I became recognized by the most prestigious sabre coach in Vancouver, himself a national champion, as a fencing prodigy. I eventually ranked second in sabre and was on track to make the Canadian Junior Olympics team.

I trained under my coach, my lungs burning with each breath. Every morsel of my being worked to keep up with the older, more muscular boys my coach challenged me against in training. My sabre, like me, was pushed to its limits, repeatedly hit but never breaking.

Coach was my idol. Although he routinely struck my legs and arms with his sabre, leaving stinging, deep purple bruises, I never once doubted his methods. I didn’t want to, as a path of greatness lay ahead. As days passed, he became more aggressive, and his anger translated into the roughness with which he handled my limbs, correcting my weaknesses. His strength, overpowering, controlled my body and mind like a puppet.

Though I held my sabre, a symbol of courage and strength, behind it, I felt powerless. Blinded by childlike trust, I followed his every shout of guidance: “You can rest when you win,” his motto, which became mine. This damaging mindset consumed me. If this were what it took to get to the Olympic piste, I would persist.

Soon after, anxiety attacks took over, followed by asthmatic symptoms. They were triggered by the constant fear of punishment or humiliation if I failed Coach. The layers of my fencing whites and lame felt suffocating, reflecting the mental stranglehold of authority he had over me. Despite my worsening mental health, I didn't want to give up, too scared to face his wrath or my own disappointment.

As a young girl, I didn’t recognize his harm until I lost my period for years. This led to my amenorrhea diagnosis. The physical and mental abuse I endured from him, combined with being admonished for resting, resulted in a choice between my Olympic dreams and my well-being.

Closing the chapter on fencing wasn’t a decision made lightly, nor was it an instant epiphany. Instead, it was months of painful debate, building distrust, and climbing clarity. I spent months in therapy unravelling my years of rationalizing the neglect of health, knots of dread, and burying my identity. I often internalized that I left due to my weakness; however, finding others silenced due to a belief in discipline allowed me the strength to forgive myself.

Reflection helped me piece together what I endured, which was not only wrong but an injustice faced by many others. A fire burned in me, different from the one before that burned for success but is now alive for change. Struck with a sense of purpose, I joined Marlinaires, a humanitarian organization, where I helped fundraise over $2500 for Covenant House, a shelter supporting young women facing abuse. As Vice-President of Marlinaires, I spearheaded initiatives to collect menstrual hygiene products for low-income youth, educating and raising awareness about abuse among 50+ members.

To further my advocacy, I founded a nonprofit organization called TrailBlaze Youth Foundation, which recasts marginalized women and youth as the next generation of leaders. Through facilitating workshops on public speaking and leadership training, I empower young women to find their voices and lead on topics they are passionate about. Since launching Trailblaze, over 20 young women have joined together on a collective journey to advocate for women’s rights.

Fencing taught me how to endure pain, push limits, and fight; however, it also taught me that these factors do not define strength. Strength is knowing when to step away, reclaim your voice, and channel your pain into action. I aim to become a litigator, empowering young women to become the next generation of leaders and change-makers.

**It’s too late.**

As death approached, I closed my eyes and accepted my fate.

But in that split second, as if fireflies in the dark, memories blazed across my mind: falling belly-deep into a puddle with buwa (grandpa), painting over our accidental living room ink splash with Siddha (cousin), and savoring Goldee’s BBQ brisket with mama (uncle). A split second later the darkness vanished as mom swerved a heartbeat away from death.

I was alive.

Alive with one question pressing against my brain for days after: If that was the end, would I have been happy with the life I’d lived? I wasn’t so sure. Nonetheless, I promised myself to start welcoming life to prepare for death’s sudden arrival.

Not knowing where to start, I started small with appreciation. I made it a daily habit to jot down 5 “reasons to smile” in my worn-out bonded leather notebook. From “the taste of soggy parle-g biscuits drenched in milk” to “successful your mom jokes,” I left nothing out. Though it was a slow start, it gradually made me realize there was a lot to be grateful for that went unnoticed. For example, I never noticed being told that it was cold outside was a blessing as I hadn’t already felt the breeze from the inside. Growing increasingly appreciative of simplicity was rewarding, but I knew this wasn’t enough.

Given the uncertainty of the end, I couldn’t be content with being just a memory; I want(ed) to be remembered, leading me to start something worthy of lasting appreciation. Reflecting on my early days in the US and my communicative struggles, I started envisioning a project that would help students find their voice–just as debate had done for me. Starting with hundreds of cold emails to school principals, I prayed that just one would be interested in an untested idea. Weeks went into planning lectures breaking down topics like logical fallacies while not missing out on integrating the occasional Suits clips to keep my lessons engaging. Hours of Zoom meetings and dozens of denied requests taught me to find a balance between bold ideas and practicality. Each setback reminded me of my reason for starting this journey–to guide students to build the confidence I once struggled to discover.

The first session was rough. My Messi vs Ronaldo icebreaker couldn’t quite crack through these students’ hard surfaces of awkwardness, especially the youngest’s–Suravi. However, it wasn’t until the topic of vegetarianism on Day 3 that Suravi finally showed her true colors, shaking the room with her masterful analogies. After 18 lectures, the big day was finally here. The final round of the tournament; in front of the entire school. After a little pep talk to channel their inner Harvey Specter and [Name] Sitaula, I couldn’t help but tear up with pride during the grand cross and secretly throughout the award ceremony. I couldn’t keep my tears a secret for long, though, as all 8 of my students delivered a hilarious thank-you speech. Seeing the students fearlessly imitate my American accent in front of everyone made me feel ready to die happily anytime.

On the flight back, staring at the Saraswati figurine that my students gifted me, I looked back at the near-miss. I smirked at the realization that it took the power of death for me to live life carefree. I now know that the next time I close my eyes to accept my fate, it won’t be in fear but with pure gratitude. Gratitude towards the legacy I’ve worked to build and the people who I built it with. I am now fearless of death but petrified by the idea of missing opportunities. I’ve now come to appreciate that near-miss, as it was a call to embrace each day as if it’s the last one I have, seek significance over convenience, and leave behind something timeless in the little time I have.

It’s 3 A.M. For most, the day has long ended, but for me, it has just begun. I walk to my closet, grey MacBook Pro in one hand and Samsung LevelOn headphones in the other. I make a makeshift studio, surrounded by hanging t-shirts, ready to produce music.

The foundation of any good piece of music is having a mesmerizing melody. I go for a raging synth layered with chords and plucks to add more oomph, something non-typical for a Hip-Hop beat. I’ve always wanted to push boundaries, forcing me out of my comfort zone. This same drive led my younger self to start a YouTube channel detailing the personal side of my life. It provided a platform of self-expression, from my highest highs to my lowest lows. I finish laying a myriad of high and low notes, and the synth starts to build momentum. Blaring instruments flow through my ears, and I start to bring in the drums.

I lay down the hi-hats, repeating four times per second, weaving flow and rhythm into the track. But there’s a fine line: too much, and it becomes overwhelming, sometimes irritating. For me, I tipped towards irritation. When pushing boundaries, my back was up against a wall. I felt the pressure to constantly elevate the quality of my videos, a pursuit that cost hundreds of dollars and countless hours—time I could’ve devoted to friends or schoolwork. My idea of perfection that I had desperately fought for could never come to fruition due to doubts and negativity lurking in my mind. Despite slipping grades, I forced myself to keep going, and now it’s time for the snare.

The snare repeats once every four bars, a unique approach that adds groove. Though not constantly present, its impact is undeniable, giving the track a sense of structure. It serves as a reminder that less is more, and how I should navigate life: stop to reflect. My friend Cristian, my biggest critic, urged me to focus on shorter videos that resonate deeper with people, saying a well-crafted narrative leaves a lasting impression. This shifted my perspective, and I was able to enhance storytelling, refine editing, and take my time to express myself. I found motivation to push myself further, and with this mindset, I turned to the final part of the beat, the 808, determined to make it resonate with purpose.

The Spinz 808 is the most important part, as it’s the loudest. It causes the tamest songs to break bass in cars and flip moods from somber to upbeat. Its key role is to express the energy in the beat. This energy drove me to improve and elevate my videos. My Season 6 Fortnite video, created in one month, captured my emotions, every high and low I experienced, and reminded me why I loved creating. It wasn’t perfect, but I embraced the process, expressing myself unapologetically through every frame. With my rekindled love for creating, the beat is now complete.

Amid self-doubt and negativity, I found strength through creation. Each beat was a testament to perseverance, and pushing forward with passion was key to growth and self-expression. In the end, I was able to provide an outlet for my frustrations. Music, like life, is about creation without the need for universal approval. Confident in what I’ve created, it’s now 4 A.M, and I’m ready to move on to the next beat.

With the conclusion of Advanced Baking and Pastry, Chef Kogi gave each of her students an award just for them. She deemed me “Tidy Composting Titan.”

My mom was tired of seeing me sneak strawberry stems into my mouth. “Why waste when I can eat,” was my rationale. Eventually, we bought a bokashi composting bin to replace me. Each night throughout my freshman year, I added vegetable and fruit scraps we had accumulated throughout the day; the sweet, tangy, and fermented aroma never failed to clear my nostrils (or my mom’s) while burying the finished compost.

Seeing the garlic and lettuce in my garden growing healthier than ever before in my nutrient-rich soil made me realize the potential of organic materials: the ability to transform from a liability into an asset. Whether it’s creating a renewable energy source in the form of biogas via anaerobic digestion or a rich fertilizer by accelerating decomposition, these methods of turning what was once seen as a burden into a valuable commodity fascinates me. They give me hope that the monetary value of these goods in conjunction with their environmental benefit will serve as a bridge to close the growing division between humans and the natural world.

Currently, I collect and compost food waste from my school’s kitchens as my way of bringing the two spheres together. There are icky sides to it that still surprise me sometimes—pill bugs rolling, flies buzzing, and roaches scurrying out of unexpected places—but I wouldn’t trade it for anything else. With each week, I notice the compost pile shrink as the food waste decomposes until it transforms into “black gold” and wealth is spread to the rest of the city. This is my type of wealth—one that contributes to both the human and natural spheres.

In addition to its environmental and horticultural benefits, compost drew me to people who became equally important. Despite delivering waste every week, I still remember the first day I brought my buckets to the composting site—a community center. Children rushed inside, curious about what they contained, and wanting to contribute, they emptied the buckets onto the compost piles and even went through the trouble of cleaning them for me. I was touched by their thoughtful gesture in the moment, but I came to realize that systems are not just tools to solve problems but conduits for others to engage and find meaning in the work themselves—systems are only as impactful as the people they invite to participate.

Beyond composting, I see immense potential in addressing the root of the problem: substituting synthetic materials with biodegradable alternatives. Plastic alternatives particularly call my attention as we interact with it daily—most of us are wearing it right now. And since Earth’s anthropogenic mass recently surpassed all biomass, we are now at a crossroads of whether to continue as we have or start converting from synthetic to biodegradable materials. The latter transition is one I wish to bridge.

Bridging this transition is not only about reducing pollution but also about protecting our memories. The pollinators buzzing outside my window remind me of the culinary treasures they produce: coffee, chocolate, and vanilla. These have been the ingredients of my most cherished memories: the excitement I felt as I went door-to-door, seeking my favorite chocolate bar, the heavenly scent of vanilla extract in my Cakes and Tortes class that provides the underlying flavor in my pastries, and the bitter notes of Nespresso I smell emanating from my parents every morning. These are the moments I hope to preserve.

The “black gold” I have returned to the earth reminds me of the tremendous promise organic waste holds, but it also reminds me of the people it has introduced and the memories I hope they can remember. To ensure these memories can be created in the future, I, Tidy Composting Titan, will strive to make “biodegradable” the new norm.

Center-backs are usually labeled ‘the restricted ones’ on the field. While strikers can soar across the field, my role as a center-back is supposedly glued to a limited patch of turf right in front of the goal. However, I felt center-backs can influence the game quietly and crucially. By zooming out to the entire field, I can see the entire pitch—the players, the ball, the strategies at play—transforming the field into an elaborate chessboard where every movement counts.

This wide range of perspectives often overwhelms me, especially under the pressure of a match. Each subtle shift has implications that extend far beyond my individual performance. Observing the dynamic nature of football—strategies in the games, unpredictable weather, the crowd's reactions—initially filled me with anxiety. On the other hand, I was fueled to better myself to bring the team a better chance of winning. Instead of zooming out, I began to zoom in—on my own tangible efforts, on how I could contribute to my team, and on the impact one player can have. Worried I wasn’t fit enough, I hit the treadmill and lifted weights at the gym. And when I felt my techniques weren’t sharp enough, I attended one-on-one sessions to work on my touch. Every worry turned into a motive to push me harder. Each effort was a step toward gaining control over the chaos of the game. My passion for self-improvement took me from barely making the team to steadily improving until I was playing at a professional academy and captaining my school’s first XI.

In honing this focus on personal improvement, I could be better aware of other players' movements, which required a different lens—one that allowed me to zoom in on the nuances of their actions. Each teammate’s strengths and weaknesses became essential. For instance, a senior teammate once criticized a junior player for missing a game-winning goal in a critical regional competition, but I noticed from their motions that the senior's previous passing fault had produced the predicament. He was just covering up his mistake with anger. As I zoomed in to examine the reason behind it, I discovered that our senior player was dealing with his own burdens—academic pressures, the weight of meeting expectations of others, and fear of taking the loss… all led to his distorted performance.

I could see how the nuanced factors, both from the senior player’s perspective and a broader picture, caused a ripple effect in the game. It was clear that unexpected mistakes are part of our lives, but if we allow frustration to take over or make excuses to hide the truth, we will fail as a team. It’s not about being perfect; it’s about staying honest, learning from what happened, and sticking together through the tough moments. Determined to confront the situation, I approached him, offering empathy rather than judgment, acknowledging that we were facing each game as well as a broader future together. “We’ll make it next time,” I reassured him with an honest smile. He felt embarrassed when I gently implied his faults, but the mixture of self-blame and shame vanished when he saw all the team members, including the junior who had previously taken the blame for him, hugging together.

I took the initiative to reflect on how I constantly learned from the loss and became a professional soccer player. What I confessed revealed courage and honesty, which resonated deeply within the team. A team spirit was further fostered by embracing our imperfections and reflecting on how we could better ourselves as a team. Returning to the pitch, I positioned myself to the familiar role of center-back, zooming out for openings and every detail that could be crucial to winning. I felt grounded, steady, and united with my teammates as I zoomed in, seeing the honesty, confidence, and unspoken connection in everyone’s eyes.

I gather oak wood, plan each slab, then begin building. When the bridge stands, I polish it with resilient paint, though some cracks and undersides remain unfinished. 
When I began high school, I naively came out as queer. The expression wasn’t naive—I had known since I was five—but the repercussions were. At school, I was out, while at home, I remained closeted. This divide led to secrecy: I ensured friends never visited my house, avoided homecoming pictures with my parents, and carefully compartmentalized my personal and public lives. 
So, what did I do? I built a bridge. On a Friday night during my sophomore year, I confidently came out to my family. Overcoming this challenge helped me recognize the clear struggle that exists from being divided. As a result, I began constructing bridges for two interconnected issues: social and economic marginalization. My initiatives in creating a cultural mural in my school library, raising money for amputees’ prosthetic hands, and distributing freshly cooked meals to the homeless in Minneapolis reflect this passion. 
The bridges I’ve built aren’t flawless; undersides and cracks still require paint, preferably violet. Sure, I’ve advocated within my community, but I have yet to make a national mark. The campus without walls is where I will achieve this. For the next four years, I plan to perfect my bridges by contributing to the McSilver Institute for Poverty, Policy, and Research, using my major in economics to alleviate systemic inequities in America and create change for others.

An inflated head with a Dora the Explorer haircut. Oversized frames. “NERD & Proud of It” emblazoned below.

“Did you lose this? It’s at security waiting for you!”, the announcement screeched as I realized the email was sent to the entire pre-college program. It was like someone had hung my blazing pink underwear on a balcony for all to gawk at — not just embarrassing, but exposing. Except I didn’t lose my underwear; it was my pin instead—both a badge of pride and a burden of expectation.

The pin was from a small business specializing in artwork that celebrated oft-disparaged elements of the Bay Area stereotype: a STEM-minded startup founder ready to conquer in a Steve Jobs uniform. My school prized such characteristics: surrounded by peers chasing STEM careers, I felt an unspoken pressure to follow suit—even if it meant sidelining my passions. That pin wasn’t just a quirky accessory; it was my ticket into being “normal”, my daily reminder that I should belong. I wanted to be like my best friends—a non-profit pioneer to inspire girls in STEM and a cardiovascular researcher hoping to cure my mother’s cardiomyopathy. After a long lineage of regretful housewives in my family, they advised that STEM was the safest key to being an independent woman. But as I chased the STEM ideal, I felt an eerie unease. The harder I attempted to mirror their ambitions, the more I felt like a shadow of myself.

I began filling the 1.5 x 1.5-inch void: volunteering to teach neighborhood children the beauty of Akbar the Great’s empire or William Jennings Bryan’s fiery Cross of Gold speech, concert hall-hopping, and convincing dozens of friends around me to read Human Acts, despite their initial hesitance towards historical fiction.

My oboe case, bare and pinless, became colorful with a handmade Gerda Lerner sticker to a Walt Disney Concert Hall sticker. I’m starting over on my own interests. By choosing pieces like Coping, which addresses anxiety and depression, I found a way to express emotions I had kept bottled up—the unease of pretending to fit in, the pressure of chasing someone else’s dream, and the quiet struggles that come with self-discovery. A single mom told me after the performance that my oboe’s voice encouraged her to continue fighting the occasional bouts of anxiety, connecting both of our experiences despite contrasting backgrounds. Supporters like her inspired me to be an artist-activist: amplifying voices—mine and theirs—deserving to be heard.

Exploring my heritage through books like Wild Swans: Three Daughters of China and Daughters of the Flower Fragrant Garden, I realized history has shaped me as a woman. My own great-grandmother sold all of her heirlooms and mahogany furniture to feed seven children during the Great Famine. My grandmother hid the existence of my uncle during the One Child Policy, preventing her from raising a family without apprehension. The superficial validation of my pin contrasted with the meaningful “badges” of resilience they wore. I realized struggling to cram myself into constructed expectations mirrored their battles to preserve what mattered most: authenticity. Although their genuine push into STEM never aligned with me, their bold strength inspires me to pursue music and history with the same unwavering determination.

You might be wondering if I ever got the pin back. The answer: no.

When I asked if I could retrieve my pin, the security guard, eyebrows raised in surprise, told me that somebody had already claimed it. Losing the pin wasn’t a loss I realized; it was liberation—a chance to shed the universal experience of wearing badges that pierce instead of embrace. College offers a pen instead of “pin”-ning me down, where I can continue to draw my own path filled with individuality and authenticity. While someone else has given my pin a new home, I’ve replaced something deeper—a sense of purpose rooted in my love for history, music, and storytelling.

I was in a rush, afraid of being late for my Asian Physics Olympiad preparation, an opportunity I had earned after many rounds of selection. I hurriedly grabbed items from my desk, putting them into my backpack, and it felt as if nothing could disrupt me. Then, the sound of footsteps behind my door broke my focus. I recognized the rhythm instantly and knew the owner would call my name.

“Arvin,” the soft voice called. I froze, caught between the urgency of my Olympiad schedule and the weight of that voice. It was my sister, Tsolmon, who has lived with an intellectual disability for 36 years. Every call from her carried significance I couldn’t ignore.

This time, she needed help turning on the TV. “What do you want to watch?” I asked, masking my hastiness. She struggled to name anything specific, murmuring softly, “Something fun.” I quickly selected a Mongolian comedy series she hadn’t seen yet and set it up. As I reached the door, holding the handle tightly, I called back, “When this episode ends, try to watch the next one by pressing the button I taught you.” Without waiting for her response, I stepped out and shut the door behind me.

Every time I closed that door, guilt settled over me. It felt like I wasn’t just shutting the door, I was shutting her life, leaving her alone with a TV she barely knew how to use. I hated myself for prioritizing my own goals over being a good sister. But that guilt didn’t break me. It fueled me. With the mantra, “You left your sister there to come here,” I pushed myself to the fullest. I convinced myself I had no choice but to succeed, to make every moment of leaving her worthwhile. But no matter what I achieved, even mastering Schrödinger's wave function, I would come home to find her still struggling with the same TV. The contrast between my learning world of quantum physics and her constant struggles with the simples crushed me once again.

Over time, this cycle of guilt and pursuit taught me to see life through her eyes. The apartment’s entrance keypad wasn’t just a device, it was a barrier that left her stranded outside in the -38C cold when she forgot the digits. The TV remote wasn’t just buttons, it was an obstacle that left her staring at a blank screen for hours. YouTube’s infinite shorts weren’t entertainment, they were a trap that overheated her phone.

These experiences opened my eyes to silent failures beyond the obvious. I began noticing gaps elsewhere: how silent bus route apps left visually impaired individuals stranded and how, in an era of folding phones, people still crossed streets with basic canes. These observations drove me to act. Using my growing knowledge of physics and technology, I began designing solutions. They were small, but impactful: a smart backpack for navigation, a smart cane for mobility. These projects marked a turning point. I was no longer the helpless younger sister waiting for someone else to solve these problems, and I was becoming that “someone.”

For the first time, I saw my guilt differently. It wasn’t there to hold me back; it was there to transform me. Every moment I hated myself for leaving her to attend physics class had shaped me into the person who could change her world. Every time I closed that door, I was also opening another: one that led to this moment.

I am no longer just a younger sister filled with guilt. I am a creator, an observer, and a builder of solutions. My journey has shown me that the guilt I once feared could guide me to create a world where everyone, like my sister, can experience the joy, value, and presence that technology offers. I am ready to open her door and many others to let the light of possibility flood through.

In 2015, opening my dad’s MacBook to watch “Gangnam Style” for the 492nd time, I noticed a peculiar yet inviting button at the top right of YouTube’s homepage—a sharp, gray arrow pointing up, towards something yet to be discovered. Clicking on it unveiled a corner of YouTube I had never seen before—the upload page. It interested me more than watching videos ever could.

Soon, I learned how to program Arduino boards using C++ to make a pair of LEDs blink. Turning my thoughts into reality through seemingly meaningless syntax felt groundbreaking. I felt the need to teach the world what I had just learned, and what each word of the code meant. I picked up my Lumia 640, filmed an eight-minute video, and turned to the upload button.

Watching the blue progress bar trickle to the end—my first video made its way to the world. As I learned about microcontroller programming—I kept sharing these experiences with the world. The iTech Everything channel became a platform for me to make the most out of the technology I had access to, and share with the world how they can do the same—from video editing and graphic design tutorials to product reviews and analysis. I spent hours optimizing the keywords in my video description—not least because I could get more views, but instead so that I could get more people closer to the answers they wanted. That simple change in perspective has not only helped me impact a larger audience, but it has also influenced the way I make my videos: keeping the viewer—not just myself—in mind.

Sooner rather than later, my world of twenty family members would evolve into an audience of over half a million viewers.

During the lockdown, I discovered the Shortcuts app on my iPad. It opened up a world of possibilities for personal automation. I started automating repetitive and cumbersome tasks in my day-to-day life. I created AttendCut—a way to track attendance for teachers during online classes—to spice up online school while I was still locked in my room. I would scour the r/Shortcuts subreddit to help users facing challenges with Shortcuts, and I spent hours preparing detailed guides to solve their problems. Seeing my enthusiasm, followers on Twitter and friends at school would often ask me to help them automate their workflows in different ways. Over time, my collection grew to over 700 automations—and for hundreds of thousands of people, my work became their first introduction to the world of automation. I couldn’t be happier to have played a part in their journey.

When I realized that Shortcuts were no longer sufficient to accommodate my ideas—I knew I had to start developing software. Through Stanford Online’s CS193p and the 100DaysOfSwiftUI course, I started learning SwiftUI. When I finally released my apps through Starlight Apps—I open-sourced them for people to see—hoping they serve as valuable resources for others to learn from, just as I benefited from exploring open-source projects during my learning journey. Whenever I spotted clever design techniques inside existing apps, I looked up how to replicate them, only to realize that some programming questions were left unanswered to gate-keep what made the best apps possible. I spent countless days to come up with solutions to these problems myself—and made these answers more accessible through my blog—so that others could save time.

My story has been about recognizing that as humans, we all encounter the same problems, yet solutions are often kept under wraps. I strive to provide value that others fail to provide—to fill the gaps in our problem-filled world—and make answers more accessible and democratize complex technology.

What would most people do the weekend before final exams? I, for one, ended up running around my living room at 4 AM, celebrating wildly. That day, my dad had declared that we had to watch our favorite team, Suwon Bluewings, play in the relegation playoffs. Looking at the never-ending pile of notes on my desk, I wasn’t too keen on spending two hours watching soccer.

But my dad was insistent that I take a break. And when Suwon scored a last-minute winner, my dad and I went crazy, singing and jumping all around our living room at 4 in the morning, even blowing hard on vuvuzelas, a type of trumpet played at soccer games.

Yes, my dad is not like most doctors of nuclear engineering, at least on the weekends. Most Saturdays, you can expect him to be wearing a full-body skinsuit, zooming around on a carbon-fiber bike at 20 miles per hour. Even in his stressful routine filled with meetings and business trips, he still makes sure to incorporate fun into his life.

My father’s love of fun rubbed off on me over the years. But where my dad separated his times of fun and work, I learned to combine the two. During a physics project in which we had to construct a full-sized boat out of cardboard, my group often found ourselves stressing over our grade on the line. Still, even through the long hours of designing, cutting, and taping, I made sure that we took a break. Every once in a while, I would play a game of pool with someone, or we would go to get ice cream from a nearby convenience store.

It was during those breaks that we came up with a theme: a banana boat. We went the whole nine yards; we taped actual bananas to the side of our boat; we showed up wearing monkey costumes, ties, and sunglasses to the competition. Even as we waited our turn in the pool, laughter never ended from our group as we posed for pictures in our ridiculous outfits. As I looked at the photos after the event, I noticed that beyond the silliness of the photo, a kind of beauty existed. There we were, with the biggest grade of the quarter on the line, yet still with the biggest smiles on our faces. I realized that day that that was how beauty was found: by having fun in mundane, even stressful moments.

How would one describe staying up until 5 AM studying fossils? Early morning summer workouts for soccer? Some would say tiring. Others might say tedious. But I would describe it as beautiful. During a Science Olympiad competition, the WiFi unexpectedly cut out as my partner and I scrambled to finish our research. However, I remember being unable to keep the smile off my face as I ran around the entire school, holding my computer up, searching for a connection. Some of my best memories are of cold, rainy mornings, running 10x400s with my teammates, when jokes and energy never ceased to exist even through the sound of panting and gasping for air. To me, there’s nothing more beautiful than these moments.

Throughout my life, my father’s emphasis on having fun, whether it be through his peculiar obsession with cycling or his passionate support for Suwon, helped remind me of the importance of “fun” in life. Most importantly, I came to see the beauty that can be found by simply enjoying myself for a moment, even in the most stressful, high-pressure moments. I hope to bring these values with me wherever I go, helping to make my community a more vibrant and energetic place by helping others find enjoyment and beauty in their everyday lives.

Thursday nights were my pasta nights. I always made my go-to: an authentic Fettuccine Alfredo, not the Americanized version slathered with cream and parsley, but the original, born in a small trattoria in Rome. It was here that the mastermind behind the dish, Alfredo Di Lelio, combined just three simple ingredients—pasta, butter, and Parmesan—resulting in the rich and creamy dish that I enjoyed every Thursday. Every time I made the dish, I worked carefully, imagining an Italian nonna watching over my shoulder. "No!" she might interject. "That's too much cheese and sauce!"

Growing up, my parents taught me to value the authenticity of cuisines. 'Taco Bell? That's not real Mexican food,' my father would declare. 'Just like Olive Garden isn't real Italian, and Panda Express isn't real Chinese.' In hearing this, I've grown accustomed to following recipes; they weren’t just instructions but artifacts enshrined through generations. I'd pour over online forums, search for the authentic masala blend, and curate the appropriate wet-dry ratio for lavash dough. Rarely deviating from what was written out of fears of making the dish "inauthentic," I was not to let creative freedom tarnish any dish's humble beginnings.

Soon, adhering to these recipes became a challenge. I developed [] in 8th grade, limiting me to a menu, barring starch, dairy, and many spices. I could no longer enjoy my favorite dishes, let alone cook them. Biryani was fundamentally changed without the spice blend, and pasta’s silky texture was compromised without fresh wheat noodles. These were omissions no self-respecting culture enthusiast would allow. Food became distant from me, no longer an enjoyment but rather an unpalatable commodity. Routine joys like kneading dough for naan became futile when I could no longer touch wheat flour. I would sometimes skip meals entirely, finding it easier to starve than to grapple with the negative connotation food had taken on.

But still, I always found ways to emulate the cooking experience brainstorming new recipes as I always had. Some foods were still possible with modifications. Initially, I made simple swaps: lentils instead of rice, lettuce instead of sandwich bread. These swaps allowed me to keep cooking, even if cooking had become more tolerable than enjoyable. But as I continued to make these dishes, cooking pulled me into a tug of war between tradition and innovation. Bending culinary rules mattered. There was hope even if that meant abandoning "traditional" recipes.

I started to experiment more boldly. Instinctively, I went back to my favorite Fettuccine Alfredo, a dish I didn’t think I’d be able to enjoy again. I blended almonds and nutritional yeast into a creamy sauce that mimicked the richness of cheese and played around with spiralized zucchini for noodles. As I tasted the fresh and nutty accents, I realized that my changes weren't stepping on the toes of those generations of Italian cooks, but instead honoring their work for new audiences.

As I dabbled, adapting recipes has not just been acceptable but essential. Bending the rules has its place and time, even when we’ve been instructed to play it safe. And when we’re confined by limitations, who’s to say “we can’t”? I’ve realized I’ve bent rules unknowingly all the time. When playing piano, I've started to blend my techniques—the traditional with the modern—realizing that using both doesn’t lessen the integrity of either. In conducting physics research, I've realized that building on other people's findings forms the foundation of scientific understanding, even when additions may be unconventional. It's often the unorthodox discoveries that push knowledge forward. Cooking with [] has shown me limited ingredients can often be deceptive; boundless possibilities appear once I start truly exploring. In a world of set recipes, I want to be challenged to mix and match. In doing so, making Paella with cucumbers or halo-halo with chicken livers won't have to sound so ‘unusual’ after all.

Fairouz’s mesmerizing voice rouses me from a deep sleep. Her melodies flow through the air like steam from my Arabic coffee with some Syrian musk. The oud joins in, its soulful timbre echoes my mother’s joyful heart. Determined to keep her smiling forever, at seven, I taught myself the oud to play her favorite songs. While traditional Arabic music has been the soundtrack to my life, I wondered, “What distant melodies exist beyond the familiar notes I’ve listened to since childhood?”

One afternoon, I met Diego, chef of La Tarantula, who introduced me to the vibrant, Spanish flavors of his world-class paella. A culture with such flair for creativity would likely have similarly evocative music. Searching online, I connect with discovered Sako, a Rumba Flamenco artist who plays with an infectious energy I'd never heard before. I reached out, and despite our language barrier, music became our way of communication and understanding. Feeling SAKO’s optimism through every chord, I wanted to bring that same feeling into my music. Foregoing the traditional oud feather, I replicated the flamenco guitar approach and used only my fingers. With this new more tactile technique, I suddenly experienced a more lively, pure musical spirit.

After hearing Lead Belly's “Goodnight, Irene” one evening, my musical antennae perked up. The wistful passion of blues would apply beautifully to my oud. While falling love with a genre is easy; making it your own is wholly different. After hours wrestling with blues’ unique phrasing, my music still didn’t sound right. “Where’s your character?” my oud whispered gently into my ears. I believe that an oud’s advice should never be ignored. So, recognizing that both genres share similar rhythmic structures and emotional expressions, I decided to layer my own Syrian harmonies into traditional American Blues phrasing. After playing my blues interpretation of my mother’s favorite Fairouz masterpiece, ‘AL Bent Al Shalabia,’ I saw her smile widen with pride. My creative success inspired me to continue finding new, unlikely musical combinations. I even expanded my curiosity to other areas, like food (apparently ketchup pairs well with chocolate cake).

As I creatively explored new musical frontiers, my love for traditional genres also deepened, as the soulful melodies of John Coltrane became a refuge and way of navigating challenges and stress. Jazz also trained me in deep listening and, through albums like Meditation by Joe Pass, I learned to appreciate the silences between notes. I didn’t know how valuable this lesson would be until I traveled to Panama for the World Robot Olympiad. The pressure to represent Syria felt immense, but from the outset our robot struggled to identify and handle key objects. Rather than panic, I listened—carefully—to the problems, to my teammates, to the tiny notes that could shift everything. Every suggestion, like to adjust the light sensitivity of the sensors, became a part of a larger composition. Jazz is often not about playing notes perfectly, as robotics isn’t always about flawless coding. They’re both about adjusting, improvising, and finding harmony among the chaos. Through careful listening, I realized that unexpected factors, like unanticipated lighting variations and surface textures were confusing our robot. Recalibrating to embrace these new environmental changes, our robot was back on track and we were awarded the silver medal.

Next to Fairouz's posters, my oud rests proudly, carrying the weight of countless lessons in each of its strings.
