As I embark on my college journey, I can’t wait to meet people from all corners of the globe and explore every facet of their culture and music. Whether it’s a hidden jazz club or a soft melody on the koto, I’m eager to cross the threshold and create a symphony of shared stories and new friendships. And with every challenge, I’ll bring the curiosity that led me to flamenco, the perseverance that created Syrian Blues, and the improvisational spirit of jazz to make college uniquely magical!

While physicists credit the start of the universe to the Big Bang, I say that mine started with the Big Fizzle. Two of them.

My mother was divorced twice. And each time, my world was left empty and chaotic. Divorce turned nights of laughter, jumbled Mahjong tiles, and sharing peeled grapefruit into ones of bitter feud and heartbreak. When my sister refused to accept a stepfather, arguments escalated into broken doors and police visits, shattering our family.

As a kid, I didn’t understand our family situation. All I knew was that I longed to return to the life of nightly board games and home-cooked feasts. Desperate to regain the social connection that had gone with my father and stepfather, I turned to playing online games with friends—oftentimes in lieu of my homework—to the dismay of my study-oriented mother.

One night, my sister and mother got into a huge quarrel—angry and refusing to do her homework, my sister had locked herself in the bathroom. It escalated, and eventually, the police came. As they talked to my sister in the frame of the front door, my mother sat dejected at the kitchen table.

“Er Zi”, lamented my mother with tears in her eyes. “I don’t know what to do. I feel like I have failed you as a mother.” She told me I deserved a complete family, apologizing for her frustrations as a single mother after being laid off. Tears flowed from my eyes as I realized my mistake. Although I no longer enjoyed board game nights with my family, my mother had lost so much more. Amidst her deepening eye bags and fracturing heart, she was also contending with two naive rebels. She didn’t fail me. I had failed her. I wasn’t sure how to proceed, but I knew avoiding my studies was not the answer.

Nonetheless, I knew I had always been fascinated by the mysteries of the universe. Outside of evening board games and video games, Ted Ed riddles and science fiction were the joy of my childhood, so I turned to physics.

Downloading a textbook from online, I voraciously began filling sheets of paper, problem by problem. Pages of scribbled equations turned into stacks of manuscripts, and late nights scouring the depths of Physics Stack Exchange while my mother toiled away on the floor below me, writing the code that fueled our existence, transformed physics into not just an intellectual pursuit but one of atonement as well. Each question was another coin refilling our family’s vanquished fountain, and as I weaved together information from the textbook and Stack Exchange to understand vague solution manuals and puzzling atwood machines, I gained an appreciation for my mother tirelessly programming away errors late into evenings whilst shielding off family discord and heartbreak. Eventually, I finished the textbook, cover to cover, and I had a large stack of papers to show for it.

Gradually, I also began applying the laws of physics in the real world. In the practice room, I harnessed gravity and angular momentum to drive my drumsticks into my drums. In the gym, I saw myself using pivots and torques to shorten moment arms and optimize my weightlifting technique. Eventually, physics even entered our family dinner conversations, and even though they still carried a hint of strain, I knew, with my studies in line, my mother had one less thing to stress over.

When, six months later, my mom congratulated me for earning a Bronze Medal in the U.S. Physics Olympiad, I knew I had done right. For what I had gained in accomplishment, I had thrice gained in curiosity, gratitude, and repentance. It is only by moving past family trauma that I have been able to navigate past divorce and truly discover what the world has to offer. Although my life started with a fizzle, it will certainly end in a bang.

“I like the smell of books,” said the girl sitting next to me, as she flipped open her freshly purchased paperback. Her name was Ayaka. She was the kind of person you meet once in a lifetime—someone who leaves an unforgettable mark and then inevitably pulls you apart.

“Well, I don’t,” I replied, with a tone a little sharper than intended. “And don’t get me wrong, I read. A lot.”

“Then you probably don’t really understand what reading means,” she said, her words carrying a quiet certainty that stung more than it should.

I would proudly say I am a book nerd. I had the credentials to prove it, too—a medallion from the National Library for outstanding readership, not to mention the novel I’d written myself. Still, her words unsettled me.

“I read for content,” I said, slightly defensive, as though I’d just been accused of some literary heresy.

“Books are more than just reading,” she said to me and turned to her book, as if it was just a simple phrase.

It was the beginning of a friendship, one defined by late-night conversations and the quiet sharing of ideas. Books became our common language, though we approached them in completely different ways.

One afternoon, months after Ayaka and I had drifted apart, I found a package waiting in my locker. It was wrapped neatly in brown paper, sealed with strips of tape in red, green, and black, and topped with a small note. The handwriting, looping and elegant, was unmistakably feminine. “Happy birthday,” it read.

There was no name, no “from,” no “to.” Just those two words. My birthday was a month ago, so it couldn’t possibly be for me. Then again, the cursive handwriting looked familiar. I stood there for a moment. Who could have left it?

I peeled back the layers of tape, carefully so, trying not to tear the envelope. Questions raced through my mind: What if it wasn’t meant for me? What if I ruined someone else’s gift? When I finally opened the package, my breath caught.

Inside was a book. Not just any book.

Norwegian Wood.

Raising the book to my nose, for a moment as memories flooded in. Ayaka. The conversations. The stories she has told. I remembered the night she told me how Norwegian Wood had changed her life. It was her favourite book, she’d said, but also the one that had left her most shaken. To her, it was a symbol of life’s bittersweet extremes. We never discussed the plot; it wasn’t about that. It was about the connection the book had sparked between us. Holding the book now, I knew exactly who had left it for me. We were not bound by faith, but we are connected by memoir, by books that hold memories.

“I get it now,” I whispered, lifting the book to my nose and inhaling its faint, woody scent. The act felt almost ceremonial, a quiet acknowledgment of the memories it carried.

That evening, as I slid Norwegian Wood onto my bookshelf, I took a moment to read the spines of the other books there: The Count of Monte Cristo, Bobby Fischer Teaches Chess, Stephen Hawking: Unfettered Mind, The Spessart Inn, Theoretical Physics, and The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F***.

Not one of them was a book I’d purchased. Each one had been a gift—a teacher’s encouragement, a parent’s love, a friend’s thoughtfulness. Each holding a story; not just the ones within the pages but stories of people who gave it to me.

I sat there looking at my bookshelf for a while. I was no longer seeing them as papers with printed inks. I was looking at a tapestry of moments and people, a story uniquely mine. She was right. Books are more than just for reading. They are pieces of life. Vessels of connection. Embodiment of memories that shaped your life.

Dr. Hughes, my Pre-Calculus teacher, walked from the SMART board to the whiteboard, continuing his explanation of limits, and I was troubled. We were growing from algebra to calculus, and with the pinnacle of algebra accelerating toward us, there appeared to be a finite range to mathematics. I knew calculus followed, but when we eventually passed that mark, it seemed as though we’d just examined algebra in greater depth. While it was possibly the single most fascinating event of my education, no new factors came into play beyond an aspect I hadn’t previously considered: the way the function changed. With defined working materials, that of algebra, an end to the rabbit hole of math approached. What could be left to do?

This isn’t physics, where laws of the universe are revealed through discoveries in the physical world, from velocity/acceleration, to gravity, to the melting point of balloons. These laws are, in effect, a lineup of equations that command every natural process. To me, this is absolutely incredible–that math isn’t limited to deciphering the world, but can explain it and provide a reason for it. Math isn’t constrained to demonstrating what is, but can explain why it is; a set of perfect explanations, the greatest poetry of all. The beauty of these perfect explanations, I worried, mathematics were exempt from.

Yet math has laws of its own, rules that compound and grow through discoveries about math and its design. ‘Laws of the universe’ is too narrow a term here. Math governs the universe, but these laws govern math and its very fabric. This is number theory, which explains the most essential property of math: standalone numbers. It infuses reason into integers by constructing principles and equations to categorize and understand them. It is, in effect, the physics of mathematics and brings deeper logic for the most basic logic there is. For as man realizes categories, number theory explores, framing equations and laws to determine math’s fundamental rules, from prime to perfect numbers. And as with physics, each category’s laws are formed through other factors. For instance, the equation for even perfect numbers (when a number’s divisors added equal that number) is based on Mersenne primes (prime numbers less than 2^n-1).

To me, number theory is perhaps the most breathtaking aspect of math. That numbers, the most fundamental element of math, can be interpreted through systems of processes and mathematical laws is even more amazing than the fact that the universe can be. Every door of mathematics is open, for math is only as finite as the thought and ingenuity of humankind. Thus, the rabbit hole does, and forever will, keep going. That math possesses infinite complexity is a trove of endless incredible value.

The consequence of this, however, is that there’s always an answer unsolved, a solution to reap. We still don’t definitively know whether all the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall on the critical line. But it means there’s more to solve. When there’s more to solve, there are deeper buried truths (fellow nerds, rejoice). Take the laws of the universe, for instance. Can these laws be overlayed and explored through the lens of number theory, and unveil the hidden secrets and explanations of the cosmos? Through number theory, can real world values be organized and grouped as a piece to a greater puzzle? As our understanding of math waxes to higher levels of illumination, for it always will, these are questions that must be answered and understood. These questions among others, I believe, need to be pursued wherever they may lead.

It always begins with a simple question: “XXX XXX?” This question pops up at every critical moment; I treat it as both a challenge and a motivation. In fact, it’s even the reason I’m sitting here, typing this essay.

In Year 9, frequent traffic accidents on Tai Chung Kiu Road brought this notorious traffic black spot into the headlines. These accidents not only caused economic losses but also put countless lives to a tragic halt. Watching such tragedies unfold, whether on TV or in front, I questioned myself: “Should I try to develop a solution to address this problem, saving those innocent lives from the hands of death?” “XXX XXX?” And I dive into action the next second.

Developing the solution was no easy task. Traffic simulation – the topic never mentioned in school or easily accessible online, forced me to dive into uncharted territory. Through self-learning, I gained essential knowledge to test my ideas: coding, conducting traffic simulations, data analysis, etc.

Along the way, with their unconditional guidance from online forums, research papers, and even strangers who generously shared their expertise online, AmbuFlow was born – a smart traffic system that utilizes machine learning and novel self-proposed algorithms to optimize traffic light phases while providing automatic green-light clearance for emergency vehicles.

Encouraged by my teacher, I entered multiple competitions to present my project. But the journey didn’t stop with the initial version; through each competition I entered and each conference that I attended, I constantly asked myself: ‘XXX XXX take it a step further? There is always space for technical improvements. Pushing the project to be theoretically significant, and practically achievable.

This persistent self-questioning brought me to the publication of my first research paper, with the second one completed and undergoing the publication process. Along the way, achievements were gained, but these statistics weren’t even salient in front of the potential of my work: the lives that could and should be saved. This project has been far more than a technical challenge. It’s a personal mission.

In Year 11, this project brought me to ISEF, where another ‘XXX XXX’ moment came into my life in Los Angeles which could potentially change my life. As I stood at my booth, zoning out, an admissions officer approached me, and after some chit-chat, he asked, ‘Did you plan to study abroad in the US?'. I answered honestly that I wasn’t sure, and his question echoed in my mind even after I returned to Hong Kong. One night, as I lay awake, turning and tossing in my bed, with the question echoing, I asked myself, ‘Why not?’

The conversation at ISEF wasn’t the start of my journey but rather a turning point, the straw that broke the camel’s back. I realized that deep down in my heart, I love such an environment where diverse ideas collide, and where dedication and collaboration can make a difference.

Why not just step out of my comfort zone and embrace something new? Why not challenge myself to collaborate with some of the most talented and passionate students in the world to do something great? Why not take my mission and myself a step further?

‘Why not?’ This simple, two-word question has always been my loyal companion, driving me forward at every vital junction, and pushing me to seize every opportunity I could. And now, it brings me here, ready to take the next step — to arm myself with advanced tools and knowledge, collaborate with like-minded peers, and open up the road ahead taking the mission to the next level, because…… WHY NOT?

I strain my ears to hear the priest’s chants over the crackle of the fire pit, the dry wood sputtering in staccato jabs. The dancing flames enrapture me, warming me as I sit in traditional vajrasana pose. In Hindu culture, flames do more than warm, though—they’re considered divine, serving as a link between humans and the gods. The Rig Veda, one of our holy books, states that flames symbolize purity and cosmic order, bringing light and life in periods of darkness. Yet, as I gaze into the fire, its unpredictability unsettles me. I recall my grandma’s story of the 1944 Bombay Dock fire, devastating the city. These “divine” flames seem more like creatures with untamable minds of their own.

The priest’s conclusion of the annual havan ritual breaks my reverie. He’s been leading us through prayers and offerings to the gods, using havan samagri—a mix of herbs, roots, and leaves. Every year, we perform a havan at home, requesting blessings from the deities to fulfill our wishes and desires.

After the ritual ends, I tentatively approach the priest: “Panditji, why do we worship the flames if they have such destructive capabilities?”

He smiled and chuckled: “Some things are not always as you see. Life needs both light and dark, blessings and hardships. As you get older, you’ll see.”

This moment, from when I was thirteen, may seem inconsequential, but the more I considered the priest’s words, the more I began noticing that fire symbolized both order (as a divine mechanism) and chaos. Inspired, I knew that I wanted to navigate chaos to find order and understand the need to destroy order to create new life—the duality of being.

Reasons like these helped me develop a passion for both religious studies and physics. I became fascinated with how religious scriptures provided the structure to understand the world. Physics also enthralled me, as it sought to understand, predict, and control chaos itself. I began recognizing trends of how human civilizations were carved out of torrents of disarray, like the fall of the Roman Empire. When Europe entered the Dark Ages—a time of upheaval—it encouraged the development of new customs, providing the foundation for the Renaissance. Scientists in this era, like Thomas Bradwardine, also worked on the study of motion, which became the basis for Newtonian and classical physics. Humanity’s cyclical relationship between periods of chaos and order underlines the outlying principle of civilization’s progress and resilience.

Even more so, religious studies and physics are not just parallel interests; rather, they both use multiple perspectives to explain how chaos gives rise to order. Religion takes the symbolic approach; physics uses mathematical and empirical approaches. In Norse mythology, for instance, there exists a void called Ginnungagap, which is the birthplace of creation. In particle physics, a similar relation between matter and antimatter exists. When they collide, the force that occurs is essential for understanding the universe’s structure. My exploration of each field proves that they are not opposites, but interdependent ways of understanding our world’s fundamental truths.

This journey led me to found HarmonyNexus, an organization exploring the intersections between religion and STEM. Our work is based on regular online collaborations, where ideas are discussed and converted into papers accessible worldwide through repositories and journals. With a diverse team of researchers, scholars, and scientists from around the globe, we aim to integrate religious wisdom and scientific knowledge to create new paths of knowledge. Through this process, I strive to lead by pushing the conventional boundaries of our work.

I’m like the havan flames—spontaneous yet full of creative potential and energy. Flames symbolize opportunity, bringing growth through destruction. This duality between the unpredictability and potential of innovation inspires me, and I aim to share this mindset in college. Now, when I pray to a sacred flame, I feel satisfied that I am a witness and part of the building blocks of the future to come.

Nine. Out of 25.

“You know, even if you doubled your score, it’d still be less than his.”

Adding salt to my wound. Thanks Dad. I’d failed my first competitive math test, the AMC-8, while my friend Skyler nearly aced it. I braced for my dad’s pointed criticism, but instead, my dad clapped me on the back, saying, “Practice makes perfect. Just keep working at it.” Nothing motivates an Asian child more than expectations rolled in surprise praise. By the eighth grade, I made the Distinguished Honor Roll, scoring 23 out of 25 on the AMC-8 —the top 1%.

Unrelenting hard work did indeed seem to pay off, except when it came to my legs, apparently.

During my first freshman cross-country race, my legs pounded the sandy earth, my labored breathing sounded like a donkey in its death throes, and the oxygen-deprived organs of my body were screaming. The only thing louder was the silence behind me—because I was dead last. Everyone else crossed the finish line as I was still forcing my shattered muscles along.

After this disaster, clinging to my dad’s advice, I thought to myself, “I’ll just work harder.”

During the entire winter off-season, I threw myself into training, running four-mile loops around my house every day. Rain or shine, cold or hot, I pushed through the exhaustion and my lungs begging for mercy.

Winter turned to spring, and as the track season began, I toed the starting line, brimming with confidence.

“BANG!”

The starting pistol fired, and I exploded forward, my muscles moving in sync. For a moment, it felt like all that work had paid off. Then the pack surged ahead, leaving me behind once again.

This wasn’t the last sting: months of relentless running had taken a toll, and I developed tendonitis in my right foot, landing me in a brace for the rest of the season. As I watched my teammates progress, my motivation crumbled. By sophomore year, I was still running but without the same intensity–I couldn’t bear the thought of putting in so much torturous effort, only to fail again. By junior year, I ran without purpose, caught in a hamster wheel of effort that never moved me forward. My coach commented on my dedication, “I always see you putting in so much effort. And that makes you one of the most valuable team members. But is this something you really want to do?”

That spring, I quit. The guilt was intense– I was violating every childhood lesson I'd been taught about determination and hard work leading to success. But I also felt relief.

In the end, stepping away from competitive running didn’t make me a failure–it taught me the value of letting go of something that wasn’t right for me. In my intellectual pursuits, my improvement depended largely on factors I could control: strategy, creativity, and effort. Improvement in running depended on factors I couldn’t: recovery times, genetic limits, and the blunt fact that I wasn’t built for it. I chose to stop pouring energy into something that didn’t serve me and redirected it toward something that did.

I immersed myself into the world of computer science, turning my focus to competitive coding. For years, I had been stagnating in USACO Gold, stuck on problems like _______. With dedicated effort, putting in _______ and working on _________, I finally achieved USACO Platinum, the highest division of the USACO competition. It was the kind of tangible improvement I’d never found in cross-country—a stark contrast to those years of Sisyphean toil.

Sometimes, I’ve realized, it’s okay to move on. Struggles aren’t always about “overcoming” through perseverance and dedication: they can also be about knowing when to let go and find something that truly aligns with my strengths and passions. Sometimes, you need to know what’s the right game to “double your score.”

“On a piece of paper, write down a word, any word, and I will guess it.”
“Any word?”
“Any word.”
“Ok, I’ve got it.”
“Watch. You wrote down Watch.”
“Uh, no.”
“Book?”
“No.”
“Dog?” 
No.
“Did you even write down a word [Name]?”
“Yes.”
I wobbled back to my room in protest and shut the door. Why can’t I get it right! Dennis did it to me at the magic parlour show a few nights ago: he told me to write down a word, I did, and he guessed it! There must be a tell that shows people’s thoughts so I can read their minds. My 10 year old hands took to my parent’s keyboard:

How to read people’s minds. Enter.
Quora: Become a mentalist; someone who is so well-researched on the way humans think and act that they can basically read minds.

Fascinated at the possibility of becoming a mentalist-mind-reader, I immediately began reading: The Definitive Book on Body Language; How to Analyze People; What Every BODY is Saying; Emotions Revealed; many, many more…

Seven years later (10th grade): A pile of mind-body-language-reading books clutter the dusty confines of an attic closet. I have, unfortunately, realized that mind-reading is impossible, so gone are my dreams of becoming a true mentalist. But still, my study of body language remains in the recess of my subconscious. I had a new first period teacher that year. Let’s call him Dr. O. He was energetic, happy, and exceptionally inspiring. Yet, intriguingly, and uncharacteristically of his cheerful personality, Dr. O would, at random instances of speech, break out into a long, pensive stare at the pipes that ran along the classroom ceiling line. I thought on a Thursday:

It’s almost as if he’s thinking about something deeply troubling. Maybe I should ask him about it. I snapped out of it: Stop daydreaming! Class ended.

Friday morning was different. Dr. O placed his messenger bag to the right of his desk with grace, and slowly unbuttoned his suit while simultaneously taking a seat. He scratched his forehead and pushed his glasses up his nose’s upper ridge. He looked at us, and, in French, said:

I will tell you a story now. A few months ago, my wife had a miscarriage. Since then, my life has never been the same…

As Dr. O continued, sniffles began to congest his speech, and, revealed by the faint reflection of classroom lights onto his face, tears began to crowd his eyes. Overwhelmed with emotion, I listened to Dr. O as he revealed to our class a side of him no one had ever seen, one I could have never read. Dr. O no longer seemed like a forever-happy, coffee-energized teacher, but a deeply reflective and courageously vulnerable person.

The following Monday, I hoped to have a conversation with Dr. O after class. I walked into first period, and sitting at Dr. O’s desk was an interim teacher. Dr. O had taken an indefinite leave of absence, and I have never been able to reach him since.

I cannot help but think that, if I had acted on my ridiculous–yet, as I now realize, somewhat reasonable–observations, if I had taken action, then maybe I could have had a conversation with Dr. O before he left. From then on, I developed the courage to ask. I now choose action instead of letting fleeting thoughts pass by. I choose not to comfortably stay within the confines of my imagination, but rather to strive to be unabashedly outgoing, because, as I’ve learned, the only way to find a real answer–the truth–is to take action. To be brave. To be bold. To ask:

“Hey [Name]! Remember when I told you to write down a word seven years ago?”
“Oh… Actually yes!”
“What did you write down?”
“Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious.”
I sighed with a smile. “Alright. Whatever [Name].”

Where is Home for you?

From meeting new friends to connecting with classmates, I’ve been asked this question, or a variation of it, hundreds of times. But growing up at the intersection of cultures, I've often felt like I was walking between worlds.

When I was barely seven, my grandmother’s early-onset Alzheimer’s brought my family to China for an extended Sabbatical. There, Laolao's fourth-floor apartment was filled with the rich smells of Jiao zi (dumplings) mixed with fresh chives and Yóutiáo (fried dough-sticks) peppered with home-grown scallions. Her balcony was an oasis, a garden flourishing with a panoply of plants used for cooking and medicine. But after nearly two years, our trip came to an end. My world shifted from Laolao’s bustling kitchen to Nana's homegrown garden in rural Indiana.

Half Native American, half Hungarian-Jewish, Nana would meticulously section out wooden beds for her garden. I spent hours hunched over, always placing exactly four seeds in each hole as per her instruction. Truthfully, I resented the work. With every seedling, I felt the lactic acid and soreness build in my arms and legs as I continued planting. But, as I glanced left at Nana’s relentless dedication and right at the prairie coneflowers starting to blossom, I began to enjoy the feeling of dirt clinging to my fingernails; the sound of bees trumpeting from ear to ear; the beading of dew during 7AM planting sessions. The Earth would speak, beckoning me to continue, each shovel and sprinkle of seeds bringing me closer and closer to my roots.

Inspired by Nana’s garden, I started my own. I’d spend hours at my dad’s side planting family traditions -- sage, banana trees, Jamaican cherries, sweet lychees, and mulberries. My tools? A spade for digging roots, a switchblade to prune. Spending hours at Clearwater Library researching grafting techniques, I’d fixate on each new line, imagining the look on my family’s faces when I’d show them my enormous garden.

As Nana’s vitality slowly waned, my parents hosted a small family get-together for her. During the weeks leading up, I worked tirelessly in our garden, azaleas slowly blooming in delicate shades of pink as the towering sunflowers beamed at the sky. Scents of the garden deepened day by day, the crisp aroma of chives mingling together with hints of citrus and jasmine. My cultures, once abstract, became tangible artifacts situated at the heart of my Home.

The day of the get-together, I prepared a feast. Starting with Jiao zi, I carefully stuffed them with chives and pork, meditatively rolling, pinching, and sealing the dough. Nana’s Matzah ball soup came next, pot brimming with hand-picked carrots and parsley from my garden. The Cheyenne finish? A corn and squash pie, seasoned with wild sage and sumac, earthy flavors coming to life. Sitting down to eat, I study the faces of my family. Serving the Jiao zi, Matzah ball soup, and squash pie, I felt both the presence and absence of my respective grandmothers. Laolao's memories continued to wilt with time. Nana’s calloused hands, once steady in the soil, trembled, weakened by osteoporosis.

I sit down, and wait. I wait for each one of my relatives to pick up their utensil, and take their first bite. Only then do I pick up my own, and enjoy the fruits (and vegetables) of my labor.

Where is Home for you? Home isn’t a place. It’s a legacy. Even so, the definition of Home is vague, as legacy isn't fixed; it's a living story woven into the fabric of heritage, shaping and reshaping as life moves on. It's Lunar New Year. I bring wild rice stir-fry, Jiao zi with my own twist on corn masa, and Sichuan-style salmon chili. Soaking in the warmth of burning Jin zhi (incense paper) in memory of Nana, smoke from the burned paper curls upward, marking the beginning of the new year.

**Color or Colour? Meter or Metre?**

These were the usual debates in my classroom, where one half of my classmates pronounced "Lieutenant" as “Left-enant” while the other said “Leeyoo-ten-ant.” Growing up in an Indian school in the UAE, we were given the freedom to gamble with English in its American and British counterparts, all while learning “Indian” English from our teachers. We would end the debates with a quick fix: choosing “one accent a day” at random.

Yet, one evening as I completed my English homework on “Food Cultures around the World,” I faced the familiar roadblock between choosing “flavour” and “flavor” to describe my appreciation for a French croissant. “Let me take a different approach,” I mused, closing my eyes and playing with each word in its respective accent. As I pronounced “flavour,” I was transported to the tiny pastry shop my family visited in Bristol, lined with mouthwatering pies and scones. “Flavor,” however, took me to the chicken gyro we ate from a local deli as we watched the Niagara Falls at sunset. I realized that giving the word a different light each time I spoke it allowed me to see the world through two different lenses.

Excited by this newfound perspective, I began to think about other facets of my life where I could apply it. What about dance? In two months, I was set to perform a solo Bharatanatyam piece as a milkmaid—an archetype often portrayed as clumsy and naive. Yet, this perspective made me reconsider the character on my own terms. How could I make her more relatable? I slowly wove a story, showing the other side of the face. Every step, every gesture, I embodied a different side of the character, speaking through my eyes. “Look at me. I am not daydreaming. I am not clumsy. I am a wife concerned about my family at home. I am a sister struggling to make ends meet, a mother unable to cure her son due to a lack of money. I have been through the ups and downs, just like you.” At the end of the performance, the audience erupted into thunderous applause, many in tears, reflecting on their struggles in a foreign land far from home. By breathing new life into this traditional role, I allowed my audience to see beyond societal expectations and relate to the character on a deeper level. Through this, I discovered my own inner diversity.

I continued to explore this duality in academic pursuits. Over the summer, I conducted research on the role of the Apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) gene in increasing Alzheimer’s risk in women. Halfway through, I hit a roadblock: my findings on APOE4 couldn’t be generalized to women from different racial, geographic, or age backgrounds due to limited data on inheritance rates. Instead of halting, I shifted focus to explore how estrogen decline might amplify APOE4’s effects, leveraging emerging data on diverse groups. This led me to hypothesize that APOE4 might elevate Alzheimer’s risk during menopause, especially in women with declining estrogen levels. What began as a study on a neurological disorder evolved into a convergence of genetics, endocrinology, and cell biology, as I embraced the complexity of human biology from multiple perspectives.

This duality—of viewing problems from different angles—is how I aspire to shape the world. I will bring this critical yet empathetic lens to every venture I undertake, seeking to explore uncharted territories and find answers to unanswered questions. Whether it’s creating technology for cancer detection rather than cure or using VR to bridge the gap in sign language communication, I am committed to forging solutions that respect diverse perspectives and empower communities. Just as my classmates and I once debated spellings as a way to navigate shared yet distinct identities, I will continue to bridge differences, bringing empathy and critical thought to the forefront of every endeavor.

In West Houston, beside a little mall where roads I-10 and 99 cross, there stands a small restaurant named Freddy’s that has the best burgers in the world. Consisting of a juicy smash patty, onions, special sauce, and three-inch pickles that always find a way to fall off, Freddy’s burgers were made simple. My joy was to go there on weekends or after a long day of football practice.

On the grill, teenagers cranked out as many orders as they could. I watched, captivated by their swift movements and eager to taste the food I loved. I thought Freddy’s would be with me forever.

Then, when I was ten years old, I had to move back to Japan. Anxious about starting a new life, I felt devastated to leave behind my home and my precious burgers.

After returning to Japan, my cravings for Freddy's hit almost immediately, so I vowed to do whatever I could to replicate Freddy’s in my new home. My first attempt was trying a teriyaki chicken burger; I found it difficult to enjoy the awkward mix of sweet and savory. Then came my clumsy homemade burgers. After hours in the kitchen, I took my first bite, expecting joy but instead biting into dry meat and limp buns. The pickles lacked their distinct flavor, and each failed attempt at recreating Freddy's in Japan made me feel farther away from my life in America.

It wasn’t until six years later, at a conveyor-belt sushi restaurant in Tokyo, that I started to question my desires. At dinner, my friend Xavier from Australia mentioned how jealous he was that I had access to good, cheap sushi.

This struck me. My mind rushed back to something I'd long forgotten: how much I craved Japanese food when I lived in Houston. My family and I traveled several hours just to visit a “real” ramen restaurant run by a Japanese chef. Once we moved back to Japan, I eagerly anticipated the weekends when we could enjoy the delicate crunch of tonkatsu or the sharp tang of umeboshi.

My mother often quoted a Japanese phrase: nai mono nedari, "to beg for things you don’t have”. It took a casual comment at a sub-par sushi chain for me to understand how trapped I was in my own feelings of nai mono nedari. When I finally answered Xavier, I told him how grateful I was for the cheap sushi and for every day I was in Japan.

Although I can no longer take in the vast Texas skies or rejoice in their genuine Southern hospitality, I now find joy in other experiences. Seeing the majesty of Mt. Fuji on my bike to school and having my monthly chat with my barber feel much more meaningful than they once did. Each experience becomes a treasure, reminding me to appreciate every moment. I've learned to embrace, savor, and live in the present because there might not be another day to taste the pickles that slip out of my burger.

As I look ahead to university, my perspective about what it means to achieve my goals has changed. I strive to be a straight-A flag football Olympian, yet I view this dream not as a distant target to rush toward, but as a culmination of each moment on the field, every catch and celebration. Though I'm still an ambitious and driven individual - begging for things I don’t have - I've come to recognize gratitude even in the moments of challenge, because I know these will be the memories I value most in the future. Continually, this sense of nostalgia will empower me to embrace both my dreams and the present.

So I’ll cherish every bite of Japanese food I have now, knowing that America and my next Freddy’s await me.

As I lay in the quiet of my room, memories drifted in like long-lost songs—familiar yet distant. They grew heavy, settling over me like layers of blankets, pressing down on my chest. Each shallow breath, each flicker of my eyelids, seemed to echo dreams I had let slip away. The faces of my grandparents, former teachers, and old classmates from China surfaced, washing over me with a wave of bittersweet nostalgia. Before moving to the States in fourth grade, I thought I had made peace with my goodbyes. With my childhood innocence, I couldn’t fully grasp the true significance of those farewells. Only now do I feel the weight of those partings, the fleeting nature of moments I hadn't known I needed to hold cherish and close.

Those goodbyes, once layered with expectations, now feel like heartfelt wishes from those who truly cared. My classmates hoped that I would thrive in my new school, their eyes misting up yet sparkling with hopeful smiles. My Erhu teacher didn't mind that it would be my last time touching the instrument; she wanted me to have a happy life. Even my grandparent’s parting advice to be a good and healthy student, words that irritated me at the airport, now feels like a priceless gift.

In the end, I just don't want to feel that bitter taste each time I look at old pictures. Seven years have passed, and though time has blurred their faces, it has left behind only the faint echo of their unfulfilled wishes—wishes I now carry with a sense of purpose and determination.

A single tear, like a lone raindrop tracing its path down a window, slid down my cheek quietly and unhurriedly. Another memory surfaced, one that reminded me of my first childhood dream. Walking the bustling streets of Shanghai, I would often see them—people old enough to be my grandparents, still pushing enormous carts of recyclables or standing at intersections each day, holding up signs to collect discarded items. Their struggles pierced my heart, but their tenacity sparked my first ambition: to earn enough to uplift my community and make a real difference in people’s lives.

As more raindrops accumulated on the windowpane, I tried to push my memories away. Yet, when my mind turned to the present, only frustration and regret streamed in. Somewhere along the way, I had grown stagnant; I had let time slip by and lived my days without a purpose, just like a phoenix buried in its ashes.

The ashes had been drifting down for years, but by freshman year, they had completely consumed me. Everyday, as I strolled through the hallways, I was trapped in a never-ending cycle, with no purpose to propel me forward. Most days, I avoided human interactions and was lost in the monotony of homework and video games. It felt as if I had forgotten to rise from my own debris. That night, those poignant memories reignited something within me—a spark that began to lift me up, breathing life into embers I thought had long burned out.

By my sophomore year, I had spread my wings and attended my first club meeting. I didn't speak to anyone, but just sitting in that room felt like a step toward flight. With each new challenge, I shed those layers of ash, a process that was uncomfortable but essential to uncover my hidden potential. Every step—joining a club, attending an event, or assuming responsibility—marked the end of an old chapter. I began to turn a new leaf and embrace the light of a new beginning.

There have certainly been moments of doubt and lingering shadows. But a phoenix doesn't rise just once; its journey is a cycle of constant rebirth. I know that I will rise again with each challenge, stronger and more determined than before. In the future, I intend to carry the weight of my dreams and people’s heartfelt wishes with purpose and resolve, to continue to soar with the resilience of a phoenix, embracing every rise and fall as part of my unwavering ascent.

Cotton — called "white gold" in Uzbekistan — was harvested through state coercion. Each laborer toiled to fulfill an arduous 30-kilogram quota. When my cousins Diyorbek and Umarbek countered my offer to assist our family with an invitation to play, how could a ten-year-old boy convince them to help?

Learning from my mother, who made multiplication fun by drawing times tables in chalk squares on the pavement, I blended work with play by turning cotton picking into leapfrog games. Instead of picking parallel to rows, I invented a perpendicular approach — vaulting over cotton plants and racing to clear the most ground. Soon Umarbek, Diyorbek and I were leaping through the field, each determined to gather the most.

It all ended quickly: We abandoned actual picking after one incomplete row. Instead, we hopped between plants like frogs on a lily pad hunt. The grand finale? Me, face-planting spectacularly into a cotton bush (those fluffy plants aren't as soft as they look). When my father discovered our antics, I simply replied that I wanted to help. Smiling, he said “You did your best, thank you, son!”

***

Junior year, while my schoolmates flooded into the medical office with burning throats, chest pain, and persistent coughs, our school mandated masks. As founder of Eco-Union, watching my schoolmates struggle to breathe ignited my search for solutions.

Our school, nestled between a major highway and construction sites in already-polluted Tashkent, was at risk. I secured a beta attenuation monitor from State Eco-Party Chairman Oybek Raximov and conducted PM2.5 measurements using cyclonic separation and beta radiation absorption analysis. The results — 76.5 µg/m3 — exceeded WHO standards threefold. Through recycling and Eco-Party fundraising events, the raised $1,200 enabled my ambitious planting: 12 conifers, 10 poplars, 2 greenhouses, and various bushes. With new volunteers I recruited, we expanded our total green area to 6,200m² — a 38% increase from where we started.

My next focus was on our dorm residents — 20 students from regions with clean air whose lungs weren't accustomed to Tashkent's atmosphere. Using 3D-printed fans, MERV-13 filters, and Arduino-controlled monitoring, the smart purifiers activated based on city pollution levels. Reading parents' letters about their children breathing easier made every moment of work meaningful.

***

In Moynaq, ten-year-old Yulya carries both an inhaler and her family's intricate history with the Aral Sea. Three generations of her family are intertwined with this place: her great-grandfather was forcibly relocated here to work on the Aralsk-7, her grandparents thrived as fishermen when the sea was full, and today her parents work in the textile industry — a reflection of how the region's economy flowed away with water to white gold.

I met Yulya when I chose to spend my summer volunteering with The International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea, while my peers prepared for college entrance exams. Teaching English and mathematics to fifty local children, I watched her struggle with asthma attacks precipitated by toxic dust from the sea's exposed bed.

The dust that triggers Yulya's asthma doesn't stay in Moynaq: laden with salt and agricultural chemicals, it travels thousands of miles, carrying the Aral Sea's legacy to Japan's shores, Greenland's glaciers, and even Antarctica's penguins. I joined phytomelioration efforts to fight this global threat, planting hardy species like black saxaul, halostachys, and halocnemum to stabilize the exposed sandy bottom. While I couldn't reverse decades of damage, each saxaul sapling I planted joined thousands of others in a growing green barrier — a small contribution to cleaner air not just for Yulya, but for everyone under the same sky affected by the Aral's legacy.

***

Whether preparing breakfast in bed for my sick roommate or spotting them during bench presses; whether setting up the prayer zone for Jumuah prayer in the student Muslim community or cleaning the shared shower in the dormitory hallway; whether making the Sahara green again or bringing all dried seas back to life — I give my maximum effort to help.

**In second grade, I told my friends that my dad was a billionaire. Every night, he’d scan his handprint on a hidden wall panel, revealing a secret high-tech expanse where my three bionic siblings lived. I ripped it straight from a Disney XD show I loved. I said it so many times that one day, I came home, ran my fingers along the walls, thinking—just maybe—I’d willed it into existence.**

**By the time I was a little older, I cringed at my young brain’s absurdity. But years later, I wished I could actually harness such a world-morphing power.**

**The summer before my sophomore year, my dad walked into my room, eyes grim and silent, and handed me his phone. “Visa Denial” —Two simple words endorsed by a mockingly proud eagle, screeching away at the life I’d known for fifteen years.**

**Landing in Chennai, my Thaatha (grandpa) embraced me at the airport. “It’s okay, it’ll be fine,” he said with a cautious smile. His joy was real, but it carried the same angst I felt. Every moment of happiness in the following weeks—playing Kabaddi with cousins, eating Arun Ice Creams, exploring monkey-filled temples—felt muted because I knew this wasn’t a vacation.**

**This was my new life.**

**As I sat down in the peach-colored corridor to start my online classes—from 7 P.M. to 2 A.M.—I’d fume at the sight of my online school’s laggy portal. I hated my classes, the time zone difference, and the fact that I wasn’t home.**

**One night, I was lying on my grandma’s lap, reminiscing as she petted my hair, her red sari draped over me like a blanket. “Dei, you could’ve built a skyscraper with just your mouth as a kid,” she joked. I laughed, covering my face—not wanting her to know that I knew it was true too. I was instantly swept back to second grade, to those days of pressing my palms against the walls, searching for the seams of some imaginary hand scanner. My words had been so powerful, so convincing, that even I’d started to believe them. What if I used that power again?**

**So, I decided to start small, changing the little words.**

**I didn’t have to attend K12 INDLS; I got to attend. I didn’t have to pump water every morning with my Thaatha; I got to share those moments with him. I didn’t have to endure the relentless heat on daily walks to Arun Ice Cream; I got to savor the sweetness of Kesar Pistachio at the end. Bit by bit, the days became lighter, the colors more vivid.**

**The painful weight of the visa rejection lifted as I slowly clung to a new belief: I will eventually always find a way to win. I began repeating it daily, trying to get it ingrained into my being. I said it to my grandparents, to the pesky lizards crawling around the walls, and most importantly to myself.**

**When I wanted to enroll in non-existent AP courses, I emailed over two hundred independent AP course providers, facing rejection after rejection—“No,” “Budget constraints,” “District rules.” But I kept emailing, with my religious conviction that I would eventually succeed. Finally, an executive from Indiana Online replied: “Yes!” That one word, earned after countless no’s, felt like the validation for my efforts that I was searching for.**

**Eight months later, when my visa was finally approved, I hugged my grandparents with joy and sadness, but also clarity.**

**I hadn’t willed this outcome into existence, not even an iota.**

**Life is random, chaotic, and often too cruelly indifferent for my efforts to always bear fruit. I have a lot to do and big, messy problems to solve—ones that require unabashed honesty about the world around me. But if reshaping my reality with words gives me the best chance of succeeding in this pursuit while also being happier, maybe that’s the kind of power even my bionic siblings would envy.**

I used to go by my mom’s name, Hao.

“Hi, this is Hao. I wanted to confirm the pediatrician appointment I made for Allison Wang?”
“Hi, this is Hao. I wanted to follow up on the pest situation in our crawlspace?”
Hi, this is Hao—but it wasn’t, and I hated it.

For four years, it was just me, my mom, and my baby sister. It was hard on us, and I had to take charge of responsibilities from managing schedules to keeping up with my sister’s school’s PTA. I naively felt robbed of my time and failed to see how tight of a grip exhaustion had on my mom. When I was folding laundry one day, I overheard my mom on the phone telling my grandpa that she was “done.” I stayed silent, not daring to breathe as I imagined what life without my mom would be like. I envisioned the things I’d taken for granted—the breakfasts that magically appeared when I woke up, the blanket draped over me after afternoon naps. I realized just how much she poured into us, even as she was running on empty.

I didn’t want to stay oblivious to how she felt, but how could I gain her trust? I reached out to my grandparents and aunt for advice. At first, 7,400 miles and a partial language barrier led to awkwardness. However, I kept trying, learning the language and learning who they were. My choppy “How are you?” turned into smoother “How would you define fulfillment? How would mom?” To cheer me on, they sent me supportive proverbs and cute Chinese character emoticons ♡〜٩( ˃▿˂ )۶〜♡. Our exchanges grew warmer, and through their stories, I saw new dimensions of my mom’s strength. I practiced ways for mom and I became more transparent, and began carving out time to sit with her after dinner and ask about her day, her worries, and her aspirations. Sometimes she’d laugh, sometimes she’d cry, sometimes she’d do both, but I always listened. I began to understand humility. I realized that my perspective—however valid it felt—wasn’t the only one that mattered. My mom’s sacrifices, my grandparents’ wisdom, and my baby sister’s sweet “thank you”s painted a fuller picture. The family felt bigger and closer than ever, and my “heart grew three sizes [in those few months.]”

Throughout these hardships, I realized my love for stories. Specifically, the raw and untold. After a call with my grandpa, I carefully arranged my workspace, setting out brushes, ink, and a photograph of the street vendor from Shanghai. I reached for a thin stick of white charcoal, illustrating the man wiping his sweat and fanning the smoke rising into his tent. I dipped a thin brush into black ink, practicing methods from traditional Chinese shui-mo-hua to mirror the crisp rustle of plastic as the vendor arranged his goods, the melodic chatter of customers haggling over prices, and the muted roar of the city beyond. My grandpa knows this man. Despite living in one of the economically strongest areas in the country, rapid urbanization and an influx of wealth drove up the cost of living and created a divide between the affluent and those who struggled to keep pace. However, the vendor remained rich with spirit, working long hours to hold out hope to provide his children with a comfortable life. As I stepped back to assess my work, the piece radiated the world I hoped to share.

As a team, my grandpa and I began capturing these stories with our cameras and brushes. He takes pictures, and I diffuse his candids after recreating them in my own style. Dozens of stories in, I’m proud of the lives we’ve been able to capture. Still, in college, I want to create an initiative that combines art and interviews to highlight diverse voices on campus. I envision organizing exhibitions and workshops that invite others to share their narratives and spark dialogue about global experiences. I hope to encourage others to see the world not just through their own perspectives but through stories they’ve yet to see.

Even when my dad returned and I was able to retire my pseudonym, I felt blessed for having needed to use it in the first place. Being "Hao" taught me to see life through different eyes, to appreciate what I have, and to display a more open heart. This borrowed identity ultimately helped me build my own—one of a storyteller.

A Category 4 typhoon. 24 paramedics. 112 firefighters. A labyrinth spanning 10 square kilometers—and one drone equipped with SparAI.

My co-founder Josua Chan’s voice crackled through the phone: "Sabrina Lee, a 17-year-old student, is missing in MOS Country Park."

After noticing HK’s search and rescue (SAR) operations had quadrupled since 2022, I'd partnered up with the Fire Department (HKFSD) to build SparAI for them—a program that dives into drone footage to help spot missing people during emergencies.

Normally, SparAI was used to locate lost hikers, but I hadn’t anticipated a typhoon flattening the terrain into an impenetrable maze. Not only had the storm separated Sabrina from her family, it also made our existing SparAI features unusable.

Scrambling to my laptop to help HKFSD and rescue teams "see" through the densified foliage, I powered through 11 hours of manually splitting drone footage into frames and labeling 12,164 images of hikers, rescue workers, and a few curious stray animals. With the data ready, I booted up my Azure Virtual Machine, adjusted batch sizes, and began retraining the model.

Despite our hard work Sabrina was still lost after 28 hours. Unable to sleep, at 3 a.m., I finally implemented SparAI’s multispectral imaging system. Once we deployed the updates, it could now filter out irrelevant detections and hone in on heat signatures to pierce the dense foliage for HKFSD.

Except now, a new problem emerged: the processing times were through the roof! At the rate we were going, it would take three weeks to find Sabrina.

Josua argued that we needed more GPU power, worried that code optimization alone might fail. But I remained firm on my stance– upgrading the GPU would push Sabrina’s rescue even farther back, by five days at least.

If I learned anything from this emergency, it’s that even back-up plans need back-up plans. To ease Josua’s concerns, I proposed a compromise: he’d handle a fallback GPU upgrade, while I removed redundant layers from the neural net. After an 8 hour hackathon, the optimized model had managed to remove three seconds per frame! Finally, after a 7-day pursuit and processing 10,325 images, we found Sabrina. She was huddled beneath a Mimosa Pudica plant, hidden from sight--but not from SparAI.

Watching the rescue team escort her to safety, my hands trembled with exhaustion and exhilaration. For me, this moment wasn’t just about finding Sabrina or seeing through the typhoon; it was about leveraging tech to see and help humanity.

After countless rescue operations, and turning our office in a co-founder sleepover club, I’m proud to say that SparAI has become Hong Kong’s #1 search and rescue software. Over the last 9 months, I’ve also had the fun of partnering with government and private entities including the Hong Kong International Airport, Baguio Group, and NWD Group to deploy SparAI for airport baggage injury prevention, dense crowd safety analysis, and—believe it or not—rodent detection!

Yes, you read that correctly: this past summer, I spent my weekends clicking on 7,000 rats scurrying through alleyways on my Dell monitor. The evenings before that, we were on Zoom calls with Baguio Green Group’s Chief Strategy Officer, fine-tuning model parameters before deploying what I nicknamed the “Project Rattrap” across 200+ cameras in HK.

The typhoon may have ended, but my work has only begun. I want to take SparAI further—to global crises where its empathetic lens can continue to create tangible change, protect the vulnerable and empower communities. By bridging technology and humanity, I aim to show how algorithms aren’t just made of 0s and 1s, but made to serve and save real people in real time.

**Essay:**

It was an open-and-shut case, or so I thought. He was a convicted felon charged with negligent use of an illegally obtained firearm. Was there any reasonable doubt?

This summer, I interned for my county’s District Supervisor in an area where being Black means being almost three times more likely to be incarcerated than a White person. I chose to research the problem of Black incarceration as part of a capstone project to study ways to improve the county.

As research for my project, I attended an active trial to see for myself how felony court worked. The defendant was a Black man in his 20s, whom the prosecutor referred to as a “repeat offender.” The jury saw the security camera footage of the defendant committing the offense, and on the stand, he admitted to firing the gun. But then, during his testimony, something changed.

I listened intently while he was on the stand, recounting his fear of the group of men threatening his life, of that same group of men later finding him and beating him unconscious. I nodded along when he explained that his prior felony conviction made it nearly impossible to find steady work. I understood how living in poverty sometimes means not having the full protection of the law, and how living as a Black man is to live in distrust of law enforcement.

To the defendant, carrying a gun was a means of self-sufficiency—a means of protection that became necessary when he was threatened—especially in East Oakland, where violence had been the backdrop to his life. In instances like this, the law becomes hazy. The facts show one story, and the human experience shows another. He could’ve been lying, sure. But I saw him on the stand. I heard him speak—you can’t fake that kind of truth.

His words, and the trial, stuck with me. They reinforced a belief I’ve always held—that everyone, especially those overlooked and cast aside by the system, deserve a second chance. This same belief, this unwavering commitment to justice and fairness, have fundamentally shaped the course of my academic and extracurricular pursuits.

As President of the Diversity Matters club, I’ve tried to spread this vision of justice and understanding within my school community. Both in and out of the classroom, I’ve helped make Diversity Matters an integral part of Valley Christian’s cultural fabric, spreading awareness and education, spearheading social justice for the marginalized in San Jose through community service, and promoting diversity and inclusion on campus.

My commitment to a better world is unwavering, which is why every summer, I, along with fellow members of the Diversity Matters community, volunteer with the Kids Time program at the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. At the Pine Ridge Reservation, one of the poorest regions in the country and home to the Oglala Lakota tribe, we empower the next generation through educational workshops, teaching children essential life and career skills to improve their lives. Ultimately, I believe that a desire to involve yourself in problems such as poverty and discrimination is vitally important, and that concrete action should be taken by all educated people to do this.

Although the world is deeply unjust, my summertime experiences have driven me to always seek ways to rectify inequality, even if by just a little bit or in the face of enormous adversity. You may call me naïve or even foolish. But throughout my life, I’ve chosen to believe in people—in my understanding that all people contain a deep intrinsic morality, a buried integrity. This past summer, I saw it in a courtroom with my own eyes. Like much of life itself, there are no open-and-shut cases. Only more questions.

In Mandarin, the words “hen kuai” mean “soon.” But whenever my dad used it, it was void of meaning: a pointless suffix at the end of his sentences that didn’t provide any solace.

For seven years, my dad had a gambling addiction. He often neglected us for long hours or even several days to be at the casino. During the rare moments he actually answered my mom’s phone calls and was asked when he’d return, he’d always reply with “hen kuai.” Though I initially felt despair when he lied to us, I grew numb to his phrase over the years.

I was eleven when I was first responsible for my dad’s negligence. During a midnight argument in the kitchen, my mom urged him to quit gambling. But, consumed by total addiction, he generated almost enough strength to rip the door off the mahogany cabinet. My eyes instantly darted to the cracked handle and fallen hinge. I feared him. Yet, even worse, when I saw his bloodshot gaze, I was in utter shock at seeing who my dad had become. Helpless, adrift, and torn apart, I sank into my bed afterwards. However, when I heard my mom well up in tears in the morning after my dad left to gamble again, I wanted to shoulder some of her burden by cleaning up his mess. So, I heaped wood debris and splinters into plastic bags. I walked thirty minutes to Home Depot to purchase a pack of nails and hinges and finally drilled the door back in place. From that incident onwards, my dad wouldn’t be home “hen kuai,” which meant I had to inherit all the household duties he had given up. Each time I toiled away, I felt internally proud of how my father’s addiction indirectly made me a more responsible and dependable son, who was a pillar of support for his mother.

When I was fifteen, my dad claimed we would “hen kuai” be bankrupt. His plan was simple: to scare me into guilt-tripping my mom to give him more funds to gamble. I knew he wanted to recoup his heavy losses, but I hardly expected he would go as far as exploiting my innocence to do so. I asked him to show me any financial documents that could verify our alleged circumstances. But he firmly refused. His excuses coupled with attempts at making me doubt myself were what gave away his plan and further shattered the trust I had in him. Afterwards, I strengthened my logical thinking to prevent my emotions from taking full rein in my decision-making process. Being both logical and perceptive meant I could better understand my father.

A year later, however, my dad’s “hen kuai” finally began to hold its intended meaning. Perhaps it was his excessive losses or the bitter realization that his absence isolated him from any meaningful connection. Perhaps it was both. Regardless, though I couldn’t forgive my father, I was glad to be able to see him at the dinner table more often, conversing with us and being there for our family after all these years. I understood the importance of not dwelling on the painful moments in life but rather the more pleasant ones.

In Mandarin, the words “hen kuai” also make up “hen kuai le,” to be happy. Just as the characters are borrowed, my experience of my father’s gambling addiction is now just a chapter of our larger family story. Through navigating these emotional tempests, I’ve learned I can overcome anything to find greater happiness. Now, as I watch my dad recently make efforts to quit gambling to support my dreams, I know I won’t just work hard to persuade him that his efforts are meaningful but to mold the best version of myself.

With this sacred treasure, I summon, Eight-Handled Sword Divergent Sila Divine General: Mahoraga.

Summoned using a special incantation, Mahoraga, known for his ability to adapt to any type of attack, is a popular character in the hit anime Jujutsu Kaisen. His resilience and versatility has allowed him to defeat foes that, at first, seemed more powerful, making him a fan-favorite. Through analyzing his opponent's attacks by exposing himself to them, Mahoraga slowly turns a wheel on top of his head. Once that wheel has made a complete turn, he has found the winning formula, and is now able to overcome any obstacle thrown his way.

Last year, I was hit with the punch of having to suddenly leave home with my siblings and mother. Due to a parental split, we had no choice but to end up at our closest relatives house. With much of my belongings still at my father's home and having limited living space to work with, my life was turned upside down. School was only a week away, and since we had no car and neither me nor my mother could drive, I had to act quick.

*TURN*

Next, the weight of academic pressure crushed me. With my external exams around the corner and incredible opportunities and competitions ahead, my quality of work and study had to be top-notch. Unfortunately, the environment wasn't too conducive in my new house; there was no office space and the family always got together in the afternoons and evenings, so I couldn't get much work done.

*TURN*

Finally, as the eldest of my siblings, the obligation of being an authority figure to them held a choking grip on me. Having my cousins in the same house meant that my siblings' typical squabbles were much more severe, and with the absence of their father and that they were just entering their rebellious state, I had to put them back on track.

*TURN*

My wheel has made a full revolution. I have found my winning formula, able to block the punches, lift the pressure, and free the grip that suffocated me.

*BLOCKED*

Luckily, my grandfather had an extra old beater car, and with the help of numerous YouTube tutorials, I learned how to repair and maintain it. I convinced my uncle to give me driving lessons, and in the nick of time, me and my siblings could make it to school and back, and my mother could make it to work.

*LIFTED*

I made a small makeshift office in the storage room using an old desk propped on a broken printer and a stool to use for work. I realized that if I shifted my sleep schedule to sleeping after school, I could mitigate the afternoon and evening buzz when all my relatives got together. This way, I spent most of my nights in that storage room, and was able to get through one of the toughest times academically in my life with great success.

*FREED*

Noticing that most of my siblings' and cousins' arguments were on who had the gaming console at what time, I got them Overwatch, a multiplayer game, so they could play together instead. With time, my siblings realized that it was my job now to be there for them, so their respect for me grew naturally.

Now, having moved out to my mother's own house, I look back and compare myself to who I was only a year ago, seeing how much I've changed. Through adapting to less than favorable circumstances and making the most out of the cards I am dealt, I have taught myself so much about who I am and what I'm capable of, and have allowed myself to carve a new version out of myself I can be proud of, one with a new name: The Divine General.

A cutting board rests on the aisle, my mom sifting flour while the aroma of boiling broth fills the air. She’s making my favorite soup, bantan. It’s a Mongolian traditional soup with ground meat, flour, and onion. It was the only soup that didn’t trigger my severe allergy.

Growing up, my mom would make two dinners with different ingredients because of my dad’s diabetes and my atopic dermatitis. By the time I became the chef of my home, my mom got glomerulonephritis, a chronic kidney disease that left her the possibility of only 5-10 years of lifespan. In order to keep her kidney from failing, she had to follow a strict diet that focused on limited protein intake.

I scoured the internet for recipes, determined to create meals that met each family member's specific needs. But nothing I found was perfect. The “healthy” recipes I read online had ingredients too sugary for my dad, too allergenic for me, or too proteinaceous for my mom. So, I started experimenting.

My search bar has transformed. Instead of “healthy dinner recipes,” it was now “spinach’s benefits” or “vitamins in peppers.” The more I researched, the more I understood the digestive system and the human body's needs.

How potato preparation can make its glycemic index lower which can benefit my dad’s blood sugar level or how too much protein can damage the nephron of my mom’s kidney. Armed with this knowledge, I began crafting my own recipes: low-carb chicken soup, vegan salad, and countless others.

At dinnertime, when I presented the dishes along with each ingredient’s health benefits, both my parents would compliment my food, saying it was tasty, and praise how my cooking was improving day by day. Seeing them savoring every meal I made, leaving no scraps behind, made me realize these meals were more than a plate of food. They were my way of bringing comfort and a sense of hope to my family’s dinner table. Visiting the hospital with my mom and hearing the doctor say her body was improving because she’d been following her diet so well filled us all with joy and relief that my mom jumped like a little kid. Doctor’s words were more than a diagnosis, they were motivation which sparked my desire to help others in similar conditions.

I started sharing my recipes online with people who have glomerulonephritis. After posting 5 recipes, people started showing their support under my posts. One mom whose daughter has kidney disease, said “my low-protein pasta with roasted vegetables has turned into her daughter’s favorite food.” Another man who has the same diagnosis as my mom said “my cabbage rolls reminded him of her late wife.” Although creating one recipe took at least four hours, knowing my meals brought comfort and joy to others made every minute worthwhile. It felt like a small way to spread hope and healing beyond my own family’s table.

At first, cooking healthy meals felt like the only way I could support my struggling mom. But as I spent hours in the kitchen, cooking became both a science and an act of love. Sharing my recipes and reaching others through cooking has shown me the joy of giving. At college, I hope to expand my ability to help others using science to promote healthier lives while still sharing recipes online and bringing healthy tarts to classes. I’m eager to be a source of hope for families like mine, families who fight illness with love and resilience, one meal at a time.

I have been using a fake last name for 5784 days.

This thought wandered to my mind as I looked for the car keys on the table, glimpsing at my father’s ID and sensing reading different letters in our last names than usual. Instead of Smith, I saw Johnson or Jonson. Until today, I still sometimes leave any paper with my name scuffed with traces of pencils and erasers.

Instantly, my heart raced with confusion and thought of countless scenarios. Am I [Name] Johnson or [Name] Smith.

I soon learned that my grandfather had requested to change our last name—secretly—from the largest tribe in the country to one that was more niche and reflected the town we were from [X]. The change occurred the day after his death. I felt furious. Not only did I now belong to a new tribe, but I also felt a disconnection from myself. My thoughts wandered on how strange it would feel looking at my old name soon, replaced by one I hadn't asked for.

To cope and seek stability, I got involved in new absurd activities. I started with gardening, learning Mandarin, playing chess in the English classroom during breaks, and spending extra hours in the lab. Every day felt like piling more sand onto my personality to discover who I was beyond my last name. Little by little, things started to fall into place. Eventually, my tomato seeds grew into cherry tomatoes. My Mandarin strokes became legible. My chess techniques improved enough to beat my cousin. I earned the highest number of awards on my research out of all finalists. And I realized I enjoyed writing the letter “J” in cursive more than “S.”

I began a habit of giving away one valuable item annually to someone in need, a habit I picked up from my grandfather. He was the most generous person I knew, always assisting orphans across the street and giving them some of his sheep during Eid, which he treated like his own children. This act of giving has helped me detach from possessions upon realizing nothing lasts forever.

In this ugly adversity, I found beauty in change. From my favorite chess piece becoming the rook as it always moves forward instead of the knight that steps two steps backward in the opposite direction, from selecting avocados randomly to picking them with precision, from using my middle name on tests to proudly saying “I am [Name] Johnson Smith” during my graduation speech, from my Subway sandwich containing ranch sauce only to trying to mix and match different combinations, from reading a book's description to reassure myself that it has a happy & perfect ending to reading any book that interests me, even with two-star ratings on Goodreads, from always keeping my Draw Two card in UNO to use them when someone places theirs first to using them whenever it feels right - even it means being the first card to draw in, from foxes being my favorite animal to goats, and from preferring the pool since its safer to explore to the ocean as there's always something to think about when visiting.

Each of these small changes felt like a grain of sand building my core. Like quartz, I discovered I could adapt and thrive under different conditions while keeping my essence. I now see my 4 last names as unique grains of sand, each with its composition, origin, and shape, coming together to form my distinct quartz. My grandfather’s choice, which used to feel like a crab invading my castle, now turned into a popping shell that reminded me he was a man who felt homesick to his town that he left and longed to see in his name, even if it felt like a crab invading mine. The sea tides became stronger to keep the crab away from sight and keep me building my quartz and castle.

"Questions can set you free, even when answers remain elusive."

This is 15-years old me: a strict Muslim kid surrounded by faith, who doesn’t even listen to Music, believing it is prohibited by Islam. I am watching Islamic scholars preaching Islam on social media. Their speeches are powerful, proving why is Islam the best and other religions not and should be avoided.
