What is faith? Is it the inner conviction that drives you to score a game-winning basket? Or is it the chants you hear from rallying fans, compelling you to make that contested shot?

Growing up, I was anathema to relying on others. I often witnessed my parents struggle to understand my sisters and their mental health battles. My problems of gossip circles or finding a prom date were nothing in comparison, making it seem heartless to ever open up. Instead, I adopted a mentality of self-care. I refused to be a burden.

When I tore my meniscus cutting towards a basketball in my sophomore year, it was instinctive to blame myself. Surgery was on the table, but a year-long recovery was a reality I couldn’t accept. The thought of depending on my family to even walk was unutterable. For two months, I fought to defy my piercing knee aches and diminish my injury. But my bravest efforts fell short as surgery became my only chance at relief.

Rehabilitation led me to an unexpected beacon of hope: my physical therapist Carly. When I fell the first time I tried to run, she assured me that one day, I’d be elegantly ice skating beneath the dazzling stars of Rockefeller Center. When I thought I’d miss watching the solar eclipse because of an appointment, we shared vintage protective glasses to marvel at the sky. Even after 54 sessions, I never once felt like just another patient. But when Carly rushed me to the ER because of a suspected blood clot in my leg, I shut her out. It was all because of three words.

“Faith is coming,” she consoled me as I lay restless on a hospital gurney. How cliché, I thought. Was this platitude solely a part of her job description? Maybe I was just another patient. Vulnerable and abandoned, I began to question the sincerity of our friendship.

Limping into the clinic the next week, a girl drew my attention as she wrestled uncomfortably with her arm sling. Six months ago, I would have kept to myself. But something propelled me toward her. As I gently guided her arm, she let out a sigh of relief. I met her face with a smile, and we began to connect over the mutual strains of our injuries. We vowed that one day, we’d both heal and attend each other’s games. As she reached for the door to leave, I shouted across the clinic for her name. “Faith,” she mouthed.

I now realize that Carly’s words were not intended as motivation. She was merely reading an alert off her pager that a patient named Faith had arrived. But in retrospect, I don’t see it as just a coincidence. Shortly after that interaction, Carly took a two-week medical leave that became an indefinite hiatus. In her absence, I found spirit in her voice inside me. She reminded me that my return was within arm's reach—it was coming.

Since my surgery, I’ve developed plica syndrome that elicits chronic knee pain. It’s this certainty of never being the same that haunts me the most. It’s the knowledge that tingly numbness will always greet me in the morning or the ghastly realization that I may never play sports again. However, as I begin to bear these facts, I choose to look for faith. Carly’s goodbye was a sign for me to embrace others and hold belief in their encouragement. Faith is about accepting support and trusting that it’s pure. I believe in my heart that I have my parents’ undivided advocacy, no matter how long my journey to healing takes.

Today, I listen for my family’s cheers in the stands every time I step up to take a decisive free throw. With any adversity I face, I know people are rooting for me. Even when I can’t seem to hear them, I remind myself: Faith is coming.

Tick, tick, tick, tick. The rhythmic sound of the metronome fills the room as my father guides me through the four-count measures of La Campanella. My fingers dance across the polished ivory keys gleaming under the soft glow of the toy lightsaber resting nearby. Squeezed together on the piano bench, the scent of my father’s freshly laundered clothes grounds me. His presence, warm and unwavering, feels as constant as the Force itself.

It was my father who first introduced me to Star Wars, sharing stories from a galaxy far, far away of hope, struggle, and resilience. The Force connects all living beings through the past, present, and future, much like time does. Time felt like an ally, its steady rhythm used to measure progress and growth. I could not have imagined how swiftly its steady beat could falter.

A decade later, I found myself in the cold sterility of the ICU, my father’s once-steady presence fading as my metronome’s reliable tempo gave way to waning beats of a weakening heart. Unbeknownst to us, my dad had severe coronary artery disease and required a triple bypass. My father, who had guided and raised me, now lay in a medically induced coma. I saw him not as the invincible figure of my childhood but as a man fighting his mortality. I barely noticed the discomfort of my legs going numb from sitting so long; all I could hear was the beeping, a constant, cruel reminder that he's here but not really here, alive but lost in the silence.

Memories I’d taken for granted overwhelmed me: his late-night math help, his support as a single parent, comforting me through my panic attacks, standing up against my mother’s harassment, even missing his father’s funeral to care for me when I was ill.

Like Anakin Skywalker, who sought control in the world shaped by his own struggles, I realized no power could halt time or erase regret. As my father lay between life and death, the jarring sound of the flatline echoed like the hiss of an extinguished lightsaber, cutting through the fragile thread of hope. Yet, unlike Anakin, I was granted a second chance. “Clear!” The hum of life returned, tentative but steady. My father had survived. Time, mercifully, granted me a second chance to say everything I had left unsaid. The words written in smudged ink now felt tangible and alive. In my father’s recovery, I found clarity and resolve, a gift Anakin never received. Unlike Anakin, who was consumed by grief and anger, I chose to embrace the fleeting nature of time. By embracing time as opportunities rather than an enemy, I found the strength to move forward with intention.

As I stood backstage preparing to play Anakin in our senior homecoming performance, gripping my lightsaber, I closed my eyes and took a trembling breath. In this fragile moment, the weight of everything I’d endured emerged, and I thought of Anakin—not the notorious Darth Vader, but the broken boy searching for purpose. I wasn’t just stepping onto a stage; I was stepping into a role that mirrored my own tale of struggle, resilience, and resolve.

Tick, tick, tick. The metronome’s steady rhythm returns, a reminder that time is both fleeting and precious, a Force that perpetuates growth and transformation. My lightsaber, once a childhood toy, now represents my ability to illuminate paths for others to forge, driven by a deep desire to make meaningful contributions to society through social reform, political advocacy, and academic research.

My house was aglow with lights, illuminating my family and friends as they filled the room with laughter and singing. Kids ran around the house, laughing and screaming while I ensured they didn’t break anything. When it was time for pooja, my father led the prayers, perfectly singing each one, while my cousins and I stumbled through the Sanskrit verses. Later, the karaoke machine was turned on and the room was booming with an off-key version of “Jai-Ho.”

I moved through the chaos, making sure every guest had what they needed. The faces I saw when someone bit into the food I helped prepare or played the games I helped set up made the hours of preparation worth it. The noise of the celebration wrapped around me, but there was a small part of me that felt a little out of place. That part of me craved a quieter corner to just calm down and breathe.

A few months later I found myself in India, surrounded by my relatives. One of them was my great-uncle who was born with Down Syndrome, Birender Mama. He lives with my grandparents, who assist him with daily tasks: eating, bathing, and even walking. Watching them, I felt unsure of how to connect with him. He didn’t speak, and his movements were slow, so I hesitated.

One afternoon, I asked my grandmother to make me my favorite noodle dish: Maggi. She made two plates, one for me and one for Birender Mama. We sat across from each other and ate in silence. As I was about to ask for more, my grandmother walked over to our table and refilled my great-uncle’s plate. His eyes lit up. I paused, realizing he was as excited about the meal as I was. We proceeded to devour our newly refilled plates, eating silently, yet it felt like the most meaningful conversation I’d had in a while.

Over the next few days, I found myself noticing the things he enjoyed doing. I started helping him from his room to the living room, letting him lean on my arm so he didn’t fall. We watched TV together, and whenever he started to laugh I’d also laugh. I didn’t have the right words, but gestures and small actions began to feel enough. I’d bring him snacks, sit beside him during meals, and wait for him to finish, even if it meant sitting in silence.

One day, as I was helping him walk from his room to the kitchen, I felt him squeeze my hand. Even if it was the smallest of actions, I could feel him trying to communicate something with me. I started to feel an understanding between us. We had started to communicate in our own ways, using universal body language and a mutual desire to connect.

When it was time to leave, my grandmother told me he really liked having me here. I nodded, a sense of warmth filling my body as I felt I had built a strong connection with my great-uncle through a language I didn’t even know before I met him.

Back in the U.S., I volunteered at Bristol Hospital, where the rooms were a cacophony of machines beeping, conversations between doctors, and footsteps echoing through corridors. I checked on patients; some were speaking languages I didn’t know, and others were struggling to speak in general. I remembered Birender Mama’s small gestures, the way he communicated with just a squeeze of his hand, and I code-switched. Sitting at a patient’s bedside, I offered a simple smile or a nod, watching as they responded with small gestures, just as he had. With another patient, I cracked a joke, lifting the mood just like when he laughed beside me. These moments reminded me connections could be formed without words, and a handheld or a smile shared could convey understanding as deeply as any spoken language.

I am a butterfly child. When I entered the world, a red, bulging blister unfurled—a cruel brand on my back under the glow of fluorescent lights. Doctors shuffled perplexedly through their distant medical journals, informing my mother days later, faces ashen: “Your son has Epidermolysis Bullosa (EB). He is a butterfly child.”

Only later did I understand what that meant: EB is a rare genetic disorder affecting 0.002% of children, making my skin as fragile as the wings of a butterfly. Before I could speak or see, I carried a burden of fragility.

As a baby, even crawling became an obstacle course. An inch forward on marble floors would leave an inch-long fissure on my knees. Polished wood was like splintered lumber; frayed edges, even loosely woven sweaters from my grandmother could mean weeks of recovery. They called me a butterfly child, but I felt more like a helpless caterpillar—clinging to the ground, constrained by my physical form.

School was an entirely new battle. Side-eyes from classmates felt painfully obvious. My classmates’ innocent questions—“Can we be near you? You aren’t contagious, right?”—reminded me constantly of the feeling of a repellent aura surrounding me. During recess, I would stay in the classroom as all the other children went to the playground, trying to avoid an environmental reaction. The deafening silence of the classroom, the feeling of emptiness—it matched how I felt constantly. Isolated, overwhelmed by how different I was.

Yet, there was a place that offered me refuge: the stage. Participating in debate and oratory, the crowd below me was a captive audience, replacing silence and isolation with hundreds of watchful eyes. Under the spotlight, I dictated others’ perception of me. I could go from debating AI regulatory policy to reciting Hamlet in a single breath; I could choose whether “to be or not to be” more than just a boy restrained by his condition. I felt unbounded from my physical limitations. Here, I felt powerful. Though my skin refused to harden, it was unbeknown to me, thickening.

As my confidence grew, I embraced this gift to rebel against my chrysalis. The cold metallic dilator sliding down my esophagus biyearly, and its sterile smell, became wind shaping my wings, teaching me patience and strength. I realized the manifestations of my condition, while bringing discomfort, acted as tests of resilience. EB became a mentor, teaching me how to pick myself up after every missed exam, and every missed day. My struggles subliminally strengthened me, providing me with the required power to emerge from my pupa.

I slowly realized my struggles weren’t unique. The fight with EB was not only against flawed collagen genes, but a lack of awareness and resources. It wasn’t enough for me to overcome my own challenges; I didn’t want anyone else to feel as isolated as I did, suffering the pain alone.

Inspired by the influence my stage presence had, my answer was to found the DIYC—the DEBRA International Youth Council. In the DIYC, I gathered youth with EB from across the globe. My evenings were filled with discussing techniques used to mitigate symptoms, grief support, and creating a network for every young caterpillar stuck in their chrysalis.

Gradually, DIYC became more than a support group; here, we cherished small victories—celebrating degrees completed in Santiago, Chile or applauding marathon completions in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

Having hosted conferences around the world, the DIYC has brought a youth perspective to the global discussion of EB. Speaking to a global audience of scientists and other youth now, I can’t help but smile. I felt unstoppable, truly realizing my potential for the first time. When I finally saw my wings, the butterfly child was already flying.

Today, I carry the EB flag as a banner of resilience. I am both the butterfly and the caterpillar within, proof that strength can come from fragility. As butterflies pollinate gardens, I will continue to share and spread the lessons I learned through my own metamorphosis. That’s what being a butterfly child means to me.

The warmth of summer nights engulfing me, my father’s salt lamp maintaining a soft navigational glow and the sound of my younger sister's rhythmic breathing: I escaped.

In these stolen moments, Starry Messenger by Neil deGrasse Tyson became my companion, and immersed in its interstellar view of humanity. Its blend of cosmic vastness with empirical science revealed how universal truths—derived from observation and experimentation—shape our understanding of the universe. These truths often contrast to the biases that mold human perceptions of others. Tyson’s commentary illuminated a “cosmic perspective”—one of an astronaut above earth, seeing only the interconnectedness of existence and importance of science—and I began to see its relevance to my world.

“She’s a pleasure to have in class, but too shy. She should speak more.” These words, reverberations of which were repeated from teachers to relatives, became a label I carried. In classrooms and birthday parties alike—nails digging into my palms, forming crescent-shaped scars—my thoughts brimming but my words caught between hesitation and fear. Yet, this “shyness,” wasn’t an unchanging truth; it was simply situational.

“Come. You’ll be fine.”

My friend grasps my hand, offering a comforting smile as she leads me into the debate society’s weekly meeting. The room buzzed with energy—energetic voices exchanging arguments, laughter filling the gaps. I feel like an outsider, standing at the edge, my heart pounding, words tangled in a knot. “You’re new?” a senior smiled as he approached. I nod, my stomach flipping. “Just listen and watch today to learn—no pressure. If you need help, I’m here.” His kindness cut through my apprehension. In the coming meetings, my hesitant rebuttals gave way to confident exchanges, passionately taking on the ethics of AI, to the relevance of UN policies in a polarized world. Each risk I took—each word I spoke—chipped away at my fear. Shyness wasn’t who I was; it was one of many layers, evolving as I embraced challenges.

By junior year’s parent-teacher meetings, the label had shifted. Fulfilling my duties as Student Council Representative, I could not attend my own. I spot my father leaving my English teacher’s office, red-faced from laughter. “She talks too much in class now,” he relays, ruffling my hair with a chuckle. “Good—but a little distracting.” The new label reflected change, much like scientific hypotheses evolving with new evidence. Viewed through the lens of a cosmic perspective, these labels were not fixed scientific truths, but situational reflections of growth.

“One. Two. Three. Stomp!” as soda bottles crunch under excited feet, rockets shoot upward, propelled by air pressure. The kids’ wide-eyed enthusiasm mirrors my own, as I guide them through the principles behind rocket thrust during a workshop I co-led at the British Council Library. With glue-covered hands and a shared curiosity, we build rockets together, balancing theory with experimentation. Volunteering with Exploration: Cosmos to Classroom, I saw the transformative power of education—not just in teaching science but in fostering a sense of connection and shared responsibility for Earth, reminiscent of an interstellar view. Weaving curiosity and collaboration, I realized that science isn’t a collection of formulas; it’s a language free of labels, bringing people together to solve problems and imagine possibilities.

Now, as Head Girl of my school, the cosmic perspective continues to shape my approach. Working with the student council, I’ve helped create lunchtime groups to support younger students struggling with isolation and launched a tutoring program, pairing juniors with seniors for tailored academic help. These initiatives apply the interconnectedness Tyson writes about—by looking out for one another, we can create meaningful change.

As I look to the future, I carry the lessons of these moments—from the glow of summer nights to rockets soaring under a child’s foot—and hope to combine them, alongside the cosmic perspective, with the insights and voices of future peers and mentors, working together to build a better reality on, as Carl Sagan said, “this pale blue dot.”

“[Name], pass the ball!” My teammate shouted, but fueled with individuality and overconfidence, I dismissed him. I kicked the soccer ball hard–but my aim faltered, the shot weak and unpracticed. WHAM! The opponent’s goalie deflected the ball easily, tackling me down to the ground; blood pooled the grass within seconds.

When finally conscious, I had received four stitches to my head, but it’s the four wake-up calls and miracle recovery that I’ll always remember.

The first thread to flesh stitched more than skin - it wove patience. Just like I was eager to get the soccer ball into the goal, I wanted a speedy recovery, but struggled with chronic migraines and nausea, which continued to affect many of my daily activities. Doctors in Indonesia couldn’t conclusively explain my lingering symptoms. The uncertainty of my condition caused much stress, and eventually forced my parents and me to travel to Singapore to seek help from other doctors. After a few MRIs and CT scans, we learned that if the ball had struck an inch differently, my memory nerves would have been damaged. Hearing that news made me realize I needed to be patient and not rush my recovery.

The second stitch didn’t just knit my gash closed, it unraveled deeper layers of vulnerability. Prior to this accident, I cloaked myself in pride and thought I was better off doing everything independently. I refused any help during the earlier parts of my recovery, thinking I’d look weak with someone babysitting me, but that arrogance deterred my recovery as the doctor told me I had overworked myself and slowed the process. This forced my mom to take time off work to care for me full time as I struggled to perform daily tasks and battled with my self-esteem. As I watched my mom tirelessly care for me, I realized it’s okay to rely on others for support.

The third stitch healed more than physical wounds as it taught me resilience. Constant medical check-ups, migraines and absences from school became challenges when I was met with a mountain of missing assignments and quizzes. I kept trying to find ways to successfully learn, but I was clueless as I watched countless YouTube videos on concepts such as geometry, the human nervous system and English grammar. With the deadline nearing and me barely scratching the surface, I made an attempt to ask my best friends to teach me the necessary material the best they could. With their help, I eventually submitted over 10 assignments by the deadline and passed my final exams.

The last needle-to-skin was a sharp awakening, a stinging realization that I can’t let fear or hesitance control me. When the doctors finally cleared me to carry out my daily activities, I found myself reluctant to play sports, fearing another injury that would put me through the same misery. It made me distant with friends, because I refused all invitations to play casual soccer games after school. My friends all progressively got better while I watched sadly from the sidelines, wishing I had the courage to play again. I wasn’t happy or living my life. It occurred to me I was given a second chance, and I needed to use it to not miss out on life opportunities. Slowly, I pushed myself out of my comfort zone, playing only with my closest friends who wouldn’t be too aggressive, and later mustered enough courage to try out for the school soccer team where I was selected from 30 boys. I gained confidence in myself again and was happy with my choices.

The injury that I once viewed as a misfortune became a catalyst for profound personal growth. I now embrace that uncertainty is part of life, and as I move forward, I’m confident these lessons I learned will help me positively contribute to any new community I find myself in.

My fascination with chemistry began in seventh grade when I learned about the periodic table. The idea that controlling the atoms could possibly transform waste into valuable applications captivated me, driving countless nights of online courses and self-studying chemical theories. Eager to test them with hands-on experiments, I competed for a spot on the National Chemistry Olympiad training team and the Chemistry Talent Development Program. I reveled in the scent of organic compounds and the warmth from neutralization reactions, but these experiments somehow felt too confined to the walls of the laboratory.

A weekly hike awakened my dream of tackling real-world problems. Spotting a pile of pea pods outside a farm, I asked the owner if I could help process them. He smiled and led me to a storage room––inside was a towering heap of plum seeds. "These are the hardest to deal with," he said, "they don't degrade naturally." My eyes lit up as I asked to take a few for experiments. Moments later, I found myself crammed into the backseat with a massive bag of plum seeds on the way home.

With approval from Professor Ping-Shan Lai at National Chung-Hsing University's Chemistry department, I began transforming plum seeds into antibacterial materials to combat oral diseases in aging populations. Carbon quantum dots intrigued me with their potential to generate reactive oxygen species under light exposure, effectively killing bacteria through oxidative damage. Since previous studies mainly synthesized them from organic solutions, I explored methods for hard biowaste precursors. Without direct guidance from graduate students, I collaborated with college and graduate labmates from physics, chemistry, and biology majors, learning how to operate box furnaces, analyze spectrometer data, and culture bacterial plates.

Shuttling between high school and the lab was not the hardest part—I always caught the bus, fueled by anticipation for experiment results or the pressure to make it to exams. What challenged me was the unpredictability of research: thrilling yet daunting results revealed whether my methods were correct.

My first attempt to pyrolyze plum seeds was a disaster. I stared in disbelief at the white remnants, which emitted a strange odor that made my labmate frantically search the furnace for roasted lab mice. Another sniffed the air and said, “It doesn’t smell like mice—more like pigeons.” Only then did they realize the smell came from my burnt plum seeds.

Determined to move past this embarrassment, I unpacked a box of Costco’s roast chicken and joked, “My plum seeds still smell, but here is a real roasted chicken.” Laughter broke the tension, and we sketched ideas: Was the carbon escaping? Shortening duration only left the seeds intact. Increase the temperature? They were burned on the outside and raw inside. Finally, we tried a mild condition filled with nitrogen gas. The seeds emerged perfectly charred, and the air stayed clean—a triumph of precision and brainstorming.

After modifying the quantum dots with edible acids to enhance their antibacterial effect, I took a bold yet tempting step: dispersed them in water, assumed they were non-toxic, and rinsed my mouth—there was a plum aroma! When I spat them out, brown residues appeared. Two labmates speculated they might carry food particles or bacteria—and decided to try it themselves.

Watching them with a smile, I recalled the early days of my research when I worried I could not offer value in return for the guidance, resources, and kindness I received. Over time, I realized that by connecting people across fields, I could spark curiosity, inspire new ideas, and deepen the shared passion for scientific discovery. With humor and thoughtful gestures, I have learned to turn failures into opportunities for connection.

This journey has introduced me to the transformative power of quantum chemistry, which I believe will unlock new principles through interdisciplinary collaboration.

As the clock strikes 2:30 AM, the faint rustling of crumpled, ink-drenched notes echoes through the apartment corridors. The curtains refuse to close completely, leaving a sliver of moonlight to snake in. Under this luminescence, the IDANÄS IKEA coffee table perches at the center of the room, listening.

“Think of parameters as a recipe,” I rehearsed, my vocal cords beginning to rupture. “Like a recipe, parameters define the data you need and how to use it,” I croaked, hoping the table would finally nod in agreement, just as I wished my coding class would do tomorrow.

This serene space was supposed to be my battlefield for tackling the complexities. Circling the table counterclockwise, teaching imaginary students—this was how I grasped the most challenging concepts. Memorizing the citric acid cycle reactions? Programming Hermite spline interpolations? With my IKEA table beside me, these topics become mere stepping stones.

And yesterday was supposed to be my moment, my first faceoff with non-imaginary students. After years of circling in solidarity, I could finally test my skills outside the apartment. Yet, with a sigh of failure, I found myself back at home, navigating the familiar wooden corners of IDANÄS. The haunting whispers of students saying “I don’t get it” lingered, weighing on me in a way I hadn’t expected.

I couldn’t let things end there though; the next day, I arrived 40 minutes early to class.

I quadruple-checked each laptop, ran through all 26 slides, and scanned the classroom for contingencies—every worksheet perfectly in place, each cable secured, and every explanation rehearsed. I was ready.

That is, until the 13 munchkins shuffled in, yawning in perfect unison. One started doodling stars across my worksheets; another tilted her chair, crossing her mini-legs on the table. These mischievous creatures were more cunning than I had anticipated.

“Let’s start with a video review,” I suggested, trying to sound discerning by deepening my voice—only to have two students mimicking my hand gestures and another glued to his screen, watching cat videos he’d somehow downloaded on the computer.

Plan B. I threw up the Kahoot I’d spent weeks fine-tuning, smirking inwardly. Who doesn’t love competition? But within seconds, they’d teamed up, whispering like little generals plotting their strategy, ending the game with nearly identical scores.

Fine, I thought. You want games? I’ll give you games. The next day, I dashed into the classroom with cones, poles, and a blindfold.

“We’re coding today—kind of,” I announced, as my assistant, now blindfolded, stumbled around the room. It was a game I created where students ‘programmed’ my assistant, navigating him around the poles and other classroom obstacles to gather and score cones. One by one, they took turns shouting commands.

“Left!”
“More left! Wait NO, your other left!”
They cackled as he narrowly avoided the wall.

For every new tactic the stubby hobbits threw my way, I’d have a recalibrated lesson ready to go. And soon enough, back at home, instead of rehearsing speeches around the IKEA table, I was jotting down notes on engagement and behaviors like experiments. The two weeks flew by before I knew it.

Three years have passed since that first volunteering opportunity. I’ve taught, assisted, and observed across seven institutions since then; yet, I still find myself asking the same question I began with: what makes a good teacher? Is it someone who makes the class laugh? Someone strict? Someone meticulously prepared? No matter how long I circled that IKEA table, the answer always seemed out of reach.

Only in these chaotic moments, when I broke away from the table, did I finally realize that, much like in engineering, good teaching isn’t about following a single formula: it’s about embracing the unexpected through tenacious adaptation. Though mindlessly revolving around students as if they were IKEA furniture no longer works, ironically, it’s that very predictable unpredictability that brings me ever closer to the heart of teaching.

There’s one question I dread having to answer: “How will you spend your break?”

The bottoms of my feet ache after a fourteen-hour shift. My mom gently shakes me awake from my thirty-minute nap on top of the rice bags, pulling me from my dream where middle-aged moms were prohibited from ordering Diet Coke. Outside, Christmas lights flicker and families are busy with holiday movie marathons and eggnog. My family’s version of this festive night was preparing cream cheese wontons for tomorrow’s rush.

Reluctantly, I swing my feet to the ground, wincing at the stiffness that comes from sleeping with the posture of a banana, I take a final look at my hands before they become crusted with flour. In contrast, my mom’s hands are calloused, accompanied by burns from the fryer. My exhaustion is replaced with a mixture of guilt and gratitude.

Instead of the usual silence, while assembling these cheesy creatures, she asks me to teach her a few words in English. In exchange, she teaches me Taishanese, the language she grew up speaking.

Ga: Family.

Her calloused hands fold each one with precision, a muscle memory honed through years of relentless work. Mine, by comparison, were a mess: crooked folds, weak seals. Outside of the kitchen, I’m well acquainted with forgetting orders and spilling drinks. My mistakes never bothered her, she only cared that I was there, hunched over the counter folding one after another. Not once has she scolded or raised her voice, telling me that mistakes are a part of the process. It’s in the moments of shared laughter when I pinch too tightly and the filling bursts everywhere. These small acts of togetherness remind me that ga isn’t just about sharing the same last name, but about sharing the weight of life’s burdens and the warmth of its fleeting joys.

Nou lek: Hard work.

Like many parents, my mom rambles on about the importance of being nou lek. It was what she grew up with and wanted me to understand, even if it wasn’t always easy or clear. Deep down, I know she’s right. The restaurant must go on. Customers will be lined up waiting to feast at 11 AM sharp. The smell of grease will linger on my clothes despite my best efforts with Tide’s Ultra Stain Release, but being nou lek means contributing to something far greater than yourself.

Hei mong: Hope.

As I continue to teach her, the differences between our trays become glaringly obvious. Yet this is her hei mong, that I’ll escape the confines of the grueling restaurant life and chase after my dreams. The truth is, I can achieve them here. To me, hei mong means using what I’ve learned and taking advantage of the privileges I’ve been given to uplift those around me. Whether it’s helping Martin (who got fired for the 4th time) find a new job or organizing a food drive for those in need, hei mong is about creating opportunities, and believing that small actions can lead to a future where everyone can thrive.

Our holiday tradition doesn’t come wrapped in ribbons or framed in sparkling lights. It doesn’t smell like hot cocoa, nor does it resemble the picture-perfect celebrations I once imagined as a child. But it’s a tradition full of lessons I’ll take with me wherever I go. It’s no less meaningful than those of any other family. In fact, it’s one I can say is uniquely ours. The next time someone asks: “How will you spend your break?” I’ll answer with: “Folding wontons and getting a headstart on my New Year’s resolution” because while each wonton is shaped with my hands, each one shapes me too.

A loud clang broke through my thoughts. A tool had slipped from the hands of the mechanic’s young assistant. The boy froze, and before he could recover, the mechanic’s voice thundered with anger. I opened my mouth to intervene but stopped, unsure of what to say. For a moment, I saw myself in him—stuck, powerless, unsure of how to change the situation.

The classroom was heavy with silence. I stared at my exam paper, its blank spaces a reflection of my own emptiness. A year ago, I would have approached it with confidence, eager to showcase my hard-earned knowledge. Now, I felt like a shadow of that person—drained, defeated, and unrecognizable. But it wasn’t always this way.

I stepped into my new high school with ambitious goals of academic success and personal growth. The building felt like the gateway to a bright future, but the reality was far less forgiving. Struggling to keep up, I found the lectures moving at lightning speed. My teachers didn’t know me as well as at my old school, where guidance was personal. Here, I was just another face in a crowd. I missed my old friends who felt like family, unlike my new peers who were kind but distant.

Isolation eroded my confidence, and my grades fell. Every day felt heavier, and I withdrew further into myself, convinced I wasn’t good enough. One such gloomy evening, I mindlessly flipped through a newspaper. An ad for '150% financial aid' caught my eye, sparking hope.

The next weekend, my father and I attended the educational expo. Representatives from universities spoke of possibilities. For the first time in months, I allowed myself to dream again—of walking across a stage in a graduation gown, my family’s proud faces in the audience.

But dreams have a way of meeting roadblocks. When I shared my aspirations with a school counselor, his dismissive response extinguished my spark. He said, “Scholarships are traps,” leaving me adrift once more.

Then, on a sweltering July afternoon, life once again jolted me. I was at a mechanic's shop when a loud bang startled me. Unable to watch the boy endure such abuse, I stepped in. "Stop treating him like this," I said, my voice more assertive than I felt. But the boy's response left me speechless: “It’s okay, sir. I do this so my siblings can go to school. At least they’ll have a better life.”

It was as if the sun and the boy's quiet courage burned away the doubt clouding my path. The impact of his words lingered long after I left the shop. Here was a child, facing unimaginable challenges, yet carrying himself with quiet strength and purpose. In that moment, my own struggles felt insignificant. The boy’s resilience lit a fire in me, reminding me that adversity doesn’t have to break us—it can drive us to rise.

Determined to act, I reported the abuse, leading to authorities and an NGO helping the boy. This small victory gave me the courage to confront my own struggles head-on.

I restructured my life, enrolling in a remote coaching centre and persevering through the commute to improve my academic standing. I found a small sports club, reigniting my love for teamwork and discipline. At school, I organised students and parents to push for policy reforms, creating solutions for challenges that once felt insurmountable. My most rewarding effort was creating a community for young people to share struggles, which grew into a district-wide network fostering resilience.

Today, as I pass by that mechanic’s shop, I am reminded of the boy's quiet strength and the lesson of resilience he unknowingly taught me. I no longer see myself as the defeated boy in the classroom but as someone capable of building a hopeful future. With every challenge I face, I aim to be a towering tree, offering shade to those who seek refuge, just as I once did.

The nursing home air is as stagnant as time itself. We came bearing boxes of homemade cooking—crispy pan-fried dumplings, fragrant sweet rice. My grandparents disliked the Western taste of the cafeteria food. There was a time when the two of them would meet us at the door, brimming with questions about our lives. My grandma in particular loved to ask, “[Name], when will I see you dance?” But I demurred, always saying it wasn’t the right time: I wasn’t in costume, their room was too small, I didn’t have permission. During the pandemic she passed, and my unfulfilled promise to share my dance sat heavy, deep within me. We still visit my grandfather, but now he remains rooted in his chair by the TV, as if he doesn’t have energy for much else. Only a sterile chill lingers in the empty doorway.

Family and culture are irrevocably tied to my dance practice. I specialize in traditional Chinese folk dance. My instructor says the most important aspect of Chinese dance is expressing deep emotions through your quality of movement and facial expressions. But in the competitive circuit, the scratch of pens on rubrics reduces me to a number, inevitably stripping away my personal connection to the dance. There is rarely a separate category for cultural styles, so I compete in the “Open” category. In competition, doing tricks earns you more points, and if I want to win, I have to twist my art to fit their requirements. So, I alter my routines to include techniques foreign to Chinese tradition. My reward? Waiting alone in my traditional costume during awards, feeling as though I’ve made an imbalanced compromise long before my name is even called out.

This past Chinese New Year, I found myself on a new “stage”—at the nursing home, surrounded by folded plastic tables and mismatched chairs. I lined up with the other volunteer performers by the cafeteria wall, but there was no competitive pressure. Just dingy tiles and creased, attentive eyes.

When my turn came, I didn’t just walk out—I ran. My dance flowed freely, unshackled by checkboxes. I adjusted my movements to avoid colliding with furniture and the crowd, but these changes didn’t feel like sacrifices. Before a mostly non-Chinese audience, each of my motions narrated an unfamiliar time and place: the peacock wakes up, the “Bird of Sun,” flaunts her beauty and grace. Through flexible arm movements, I invisions the peacock’s wings, tail and head, becoming one with the bird, full of life and spirit. At that moment, I fulfilled my promise to my grandma. Her presence felt palpable as I shared this piece of us.

As the music faded, applause erupted throughout the cafeteria, echoing off the walls in the suddenly expansive room. I caught sight of my grandpa, his face alight with happiness and pride. Before I could reach him, the audience surged forward to meet me, aged countenances animated with wonder, voices competing to know the meaning of my dance. On that makeshift stage, the nursing home grew warmer, alive with the echoes of music and applause.

My grandpa is at the age when words have long since escaped him. But he used to tell me, “Remember who you are.” That day at the nursing home, dance served as a language that transcended barriers, speaking directly to the heart and achieving what words couldn’t. That performance meant more to me than any trophy ever could; it was about bridging differences of age, race, and culture, bringing joy to those who matter most, and creating a space for my story when none existed. This is the legacy I want to build—not one of accolades, but of connections I forge through my art. At college and beyond, I hope to expand this space, using dance to unite and inspire, just as it has always done for me.

I look at my grandpa and respond “Dāngrán”—of course. If not now, then when?

A sharp voice shattered the stillness of the night. My mother clutched my hand, her trembling fingers betraying her calm facade. “We’re going to visit Nani,” she whispered, a lie wrapped in urgency. The frantic packing told the truth: we were fleeing after my father’s business collapsed, leaving behind threats and danger.

Eight years ago, “asylum seeker” was a foreign phrase. Overnight, it became my reality—a heavy cloak that obscured the life I knew and forced me to redefine myself.

We landed in Boston with nothing but hope, squeezing eight people into my uncle’s apartment. Privacy vanished, and nights became a rotation of couch corners. When my uncle lost his job, homelessness followed. Shelters and borrowed couches blurred into a relentless survival marathon. At ten, while my parents waded through asylum paperwork, I found purpose in small acts: cooking, cleaning, ensuring what little we had stretched further.

But survival wasn’t living. I missed school—not just math problems, but the sense of routine and belonging. In a life filled with uncertainty and displacement, I yearned for something, anything, that I could control. One afternoon, while rummaging through my cousin’s things, I found an old computer. Its flickering screen didn’t matter; it worked. I stumbled onto Codecademy and started coding to pass time. Soon, it became an obsession. Amid the instability of our lives, coding gave me something rare: control. The power to build, debug, and fix.

But even coding couldn’t shield me from life’s next challenge. When my mother fell ill with Lyme disease, I watched her push through pain with outdated YouTube tutorials, and I felt helpless—until I realized I could apply my learning.

Coding, once my refuge, became my solution. While playing Just Dance with my sister, I noticed how the game awarded points based on how well our movements matched the on-screen dancers. Curious, I researched and discovered pose estimation, a technology that uses cameras and algorithms to track and analyze body movements. What if this technology could ensure physical therapy exercises were done safely?

That question consumed me. My bedroom transformed into a makeshift lab, cluttered with sticky notes, tangled cables, and endless lines of code. Building Therapose was no simple task. The early prototypes misread stretches as jumping jacks and crashed mid-session. Debugging became a marathon: I retrained the model for accurate joint detection, adjusted algorithms, and even rigged desk lamps to resolve lighting inconsistencies. When the app correctly identified movement patterns for the first time, I ran to show my mother. When she completed her first exercise without pain, her smile erased months of frustration.

But Therapose was never just about the code. It was about people. Testing with over 2500 users across 18 rehabilitation centers revealed more than technical bugs; it revealed emotional barriers. Interfaces were overwhelming, encouragement was missing, and progress felt abstract. So, I redesigned layouts, added visual progress trackers, and built encouragement messages—reminders to celebrate tiny victories.

Local news outlets shared my story, and suddenly, for the first time, I was no longer the outsider but the innovator. Presenting Therapose before Congress, I realized it wasn’t just code. It was a bridge to equitable care. Zainab Farah, a Therapose user, put it simply: “After my surgery, I could garden again.” Her words reminded me that resilience, paired with action, transforms hardship into service. Now, in my senior Capstone project, I’m developing AI-powered wearables to complement Therapose, focusing on affordable diagnostics to break down barriers to care, especially for communities like mine.

“Asylum seeker” is no longer just a phrase. It’s a badge of pride. Coding became my refuge, my voice, and my path forward, transforming chaos into opportunity and resilience into innovation. More importantly, it became a tool for service.

Eight years ago, I was clinging to survival. Today, I’m building—a seeker of knowledge, a coder with a cause, and a future computer scientist driven to shape a more equitable world.

Lucky kick in my butt and the best words from my mom: “You are ready”—those were the last things I remember when leaving my home. Before that, I woke up five minutes before my alarm, even though I slept only four hours. However, I didn’t feel tired (which was weird as the caffeine from Redbull hadn’t yet entered my bloodstream), probably because of the adrenaline-cortisol cocktail emerging from my kidneys. But why would I be so stressed? I have been preparing for that day for two years, with countless nights sacrificed for learning and revising material. Today, I will show everyone how much I have learned over the past four years and will know the future of my academic career as this exam will be the last one in high school and will determine which university I will be able to go to. Today, I’m writing a maturity exam—matura.

On my way to the school, I remembered when last week I, Ignacy, and Jan did a study session at Jan’s house. Before, we were supposed to go to the gym, but Ignacy (as always) overslept, and while we tried to reach him, we discovered that he had to move coal to his new house. Knowing that it would take a while (and he had fifty minutes to get to us), we decided to watch the Premier League. We made predictions for the final score of Fulham vs Manchester City, and at the last minute, Julián Álvarez scored a penalty for my predicted score of 4:0 for Citizens. Luckily, Ignacy arrived, and we started our studying; our heads emerged into a pile of tests from recent years, as we were discovering weirder exercises with each next one. But after a while of sweaty work, we started to make dinner together. After a short trip to the nearby shop, we figured out that the best meal for today would be Italian Tomato Pasta. In the kitchen, everyone did their task with coordination as one organism. Around 6 pm, heads swimming with formulas and Newtonian Laws, we stumbled outside for some fresh air. In the crisp air on Jan’s balcony, we looked up at the moon. I couldn’t believe how powerful the power of gravity is. We didn’t end up staying up all night to study, and a previous version of myself would have seen this as a failure, but seeing the stars made it all worth it. I will never forget this day.

After a month, it was time to receive my score. My friends gather around me to congratulate me on my 57%. Ignacy remarks how it must have been a long way to achieve this score. As he gives me a pat on the back, I consider that I am happier I have his friendship and our experiences doing meetings and going out together to prepare than I am about the score itself.

I spent all of January locked away in my room, feeling like a Gollum watching his “precious treasure” in his cave (I didn’t even go to the New Year's Eve Party). When I emerged in February, I missed my friends, and I realized, too, that I had missed restaurant visits, going to the cinema, and shared gym training, too. I introduced a calendar to my life in which I can plan hours where I learn and hours where I spend time with the most precious people in my life. The next exam, I not only felt better with how I was spending my time, making more memories in my last year of high school, and helping my friends, but I had scored better on my exams, as well. I felt there was a value in appreciating our road rather than focusing on success itself.

I plan to be very ambitious in college—I am eager to complete research, my app with intention to help unhoused people, and get a major in physics. However, I know now that I should not let everything I do in my free time with my friends be forgotten as valuable parts of my college journey beyond any graduation.

After a long day of school, I find comfort at the table.

As I step through the front door, the scent of freshly toasted arepas and warm spices wafts from the kitchen. I trace it to the wooden structure that has seen my math homework sprawled across its surface, countless cups of spoiled milk, and more conversations than I can remember. My father, already sitting down, begins discussing a Halloween event at his office with my ten-year-old sister and me, while my mother carefully places dishes of warm food between us. Tonight, it's “pabellón criollo”—a mix of shredded beef, black beans, and sweet fried plantains, with arepas nestled alongside. With one hand on my stuffed arepa, I listen to my family's voices melt into a comforting melody. Amidst their warmth and laughter, the day’s worries seem to gradually fade away.

After a grueling soccer match, I find relief at the table.

“Uno. Dos. Tres. Greengates!” Having shouted the team chant, we all rushed to our school’s main entrance, our hearts still racing from the thrill of the game. Dining at Marqueé, a small local restaurant two blocks away from campus, is my soccer team’s tradition after every match. Being so many, we pull the tables together to fit us all, transforming what would otherwise be a regular dining place into our own lively gathering spot, with one, large, unified table at its center. Once I finally sit down, laughter and stories flow as easily as the food, and the tackles, sprints, and bruises endured during the game all become worthwhile, reminding me that true value doesn't come from the score, but from the bonds strengthened and memories created together.

After an afternoon of storytelling, I find purpose at the table.

Shy whispers, excited smiles, and curious faces are a rough picture of what I see when I come into the children’s home. As we gather around the table, they lean forward, hands inching towards the colorful covers of the books stacked in front of us. I open the first page, and a hush settles as their eyes widen, following each line, each turn of the page. Laughter bubbles up when a character stumbles, and gasps ripple across the table when a twist unfolds. Here, at the table, with the children I had organized a book collection for, a deep sense of purpose fills me as I turn through the pages: a purpose rooted in each story I share, each smile I spark.

After hours of innovation, I find achievement at the table.

This one is covered in a mix of laptops, notebooks, half-scribbled sketches, and surrounded by students deep in thought. This afternoon is just one of many spent at the AI club I co-founded. After dedicating numerous weekly sessions to developing a code that implements a decision tree algorithm for sorting books in our school’s library, we finally achieved a working model, successfully classifying each book by genre, publication date, and age rating. Each project, problem, and algorithm solved brings purpose to our efforts, and by the end of each session, I’m reminded of the impact we create when in collaboration.

I am grateful for the table.

Though I might not always return every night to the same kitchen, every evening to Marqueé, and every Wednesday afternoon to my school’s workshop, I am and will remain grateful for the lessons the table has taught me. I’ve learned to become a more attentive son and brother, find purpose in service to others, and lead communities with empathy, lessons I will carry forward wholeheartedly—no matter which table I’m sitting at.

“Oops! What I did that’s blunder move” was my realization that losing in chess felt similar to failing to convince evaluators that PVC was a better choice than PTT for our prototype's building material. Back in the first semester of Grade 10, I faced challenges with material detection arguments.

My capstone teacher advised me, “Your discussion isn’t effective this way; you should respect your teammates’ points. Improve your persuasive skills.” Initially, my teamwork abilities were lacking, and it reflected when my team received a low evaluation in our exhibition test. This setback urged me to turn lemons into lemonade by joining the debate club.

In the second semester, my capstone teacher encouraged me to join the debate club. The topic “Should the voting age be lowered to 16?” was my first debate. Reading “Thank You For Arguing” taught me essential debate skills like using enthusiastic expressions such as “Let’s examine this from another angle together,” and understanding Aristotle's rhetorical appeals: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos. These skills allowed me to win my first debate!

When discussing with teammates about “Is social media more harmful than beneficial to our society?” I presented our argument effectively, using research to support our stance, and highlighting that social media contributes to a 39% reduction in Egyptian students’ academic levels according to ResearchGate.

In the first semester of Grade 11, as I improved my teamwork skills, I mediated a disagreement in my capstone project on whether to use ESP32 or Arduino. This breakthrough felt like winning chess games again!

By the semester's end, my team achieved the highest evaluation score in the exhibition test among 32 teams. We were able to respond to challenging questions and present a united front. Leadership often requires teamwork skills, which also helped me in discussions with the math club management to develop new plans.

The child’s heart had a hole between its chambers.

A pungent metallic odor filled the cool air of the operating room. The vital signs monitor steadily beeped in the background. The cardiac surgeon and his team were preparing to repair a ventricular septal defect.

I perched beside the operating bed, hovering nervously as the surgeon made his first incision. A suture here, an incision there, heart tissue in hand, he expertly manipulated the delicate anatomy, giving the boy a new life.

As he closed the incision, I stood awestruck. It was magic, a medical mechanic changing another’s life with his very own hands.

After the surgery, we hurried to inform the patient’s parents that everything went perfectly. Watching the anxiousness melt off their faces, I felt deeply inspired and compelled by the power of this seemingly magical act for this family. I remember thinking, “What can I do now?”

The next day, I had an opportunity. I watched Dr. Srimanarayana perform EKG tests when he asked me if I wanted to conduct some under his supervision. I was flabbergasted: “I’m doing this on a real patient!!”

I firmly placed the color-coded electrodes on different locations of the patient’s body. I glanced at the monitor. A crisp line danced across the screen. Any doubts I had evaporated; I felt oddly confident. A joyous smile spread across my face.

“Nice to meet you Akhi, I’m Leo!”

Leo was the first kid I met at Buddy Up Tennis. He would look at me with a sparkle in his chocolate brown eyes and give me a fist bump every time I taught him a basic technique. Leo loved tennis.

As we worked together, I never saw Leo let his Down syndrome define him. He gave his best, laughed, and loved every moment.

Leo strived for excellence, so he grew distraught whenever he missed shots. I desired to help him. I told him, “Tennis is an expression of creativity and inner beauty. Let your imagination empower your game and forget about results.” I reminded him this every session. Leo implemented this, and combined with his relentless love for the sport, he played tennis with immortal happiness and confidence.

Leo also taught me a special lesson: believe in your own, magnificent self.

I experienced the power of confidence countless times, whether it was conducting EKG tests in the hospital, trusting myself in piano, or Leo’s ironclad self-belief. 6:40 a.m. on a rickety yellow school bus, my friend’s eyes are glued to her screen, filled with wonder. “Aren’t they amazing?” she says. She stares at me with admiration, as if I held the key to the enchanting world in front of her. Puzzled, I blankly stared at her. “You can understand them!” she exclaims. “You can watch their shows, sing their songs—you’re so lucky.” I nodded to the beat and laughed it off. Of course, I can—I’m Korean. Yet, even as I smiled, something didn’t sit right. I understood them, sure, but not in the way she did. At eleven, I had just realized that despite being Korean, I wasn’t connected to what my friends associated with my culture. I didn’t fully understand what truly being Korean entailed.

In fourth grade, K-pop suddenly became the new rave, and as the designated Korean in my class, I became the go-to K-pop help desk. “Are stores full of albums real? Have you ever seen an idol? What’s it like living in Korea?” they asked. My answers were vague; I didn’t even know if they were correct, but I figured they wouldn’t know either. Until then, I had never doubted how Korean I was. I understood the language, the culture, and the traditions. Growing up in an international environment, that had always seemed enough. But as K-pop grew, it hit me: I wasn’t “socially” Korean. To my friends, being Korean wasn’t about reciting customs or traditions. It was about K-pop, and I didn’t get it. It was ironic: the globalization of something so distinctly connected to my country, my culture, made me feel less Korean. For the first time, my culture was accepted, appreciated, and even admired, but I simply did not understand it.

When this strange sense of disconnection formed within me and no one offered a solution to reconnecting, I figured I had to find my own way to (pop) culturally integrate. Thus began my ultimate guide to being a Korean tween. Surprisingly, Korea’s pop culture taught me more than I had anticipated. I picked up new words, phrases, and nuances—terms kids my age used and their intriguing Chinese origins. This knowledge unexpectedly proved invaluable when I moved to China. My understanding of Korea’s linguistic history allowed me to grasp Chinese idioms and puns easily, allowing me to build cross-cultural friendships with some of my closest friends today.

Music and storytelling became windows into Korean society—they did not just guide me on where to go or what to eat, but also illuminated my academic pursuits. They sparked my curiosity about Korea’s distinct history – not one told by Western historiography or international textbooks – and about my family’s narrative. This enabled me to connect with my loved ones through my academic passions, leading me to write research linking my family’s experiences during Korea’s independence movements to the broader phenomenon of national sovereignty, drawing from the most valuable primary sources: my family members.

Ironically, K-pop, something globalized and seemingly far from tradition, redirected my journey toward self-discovery. Cookie-cutter definitions of culture had created an unattainable ideal of what it meant to be Korean. For someone navigating a third-culture identity, intercultural understanding through unconventional means became crucial in defining my sense of home. My discoveries inspired me to create an intercultural understanding playlist, helping my community reconnect with their own cultures through unexpected platforms. The goal wasn’t simply to spread appreciation for different cultures but to prompt reflection about your own. Today, when my friends ask, “I thought this was really popular in Korea; don’t all Koreans know it?” I no longer feel the pressure to have all the answers. I can confidently say, “I don’t know,” without feeling embarrassed to represent where I come from. I am proud of my heritage but even prouder of what makes me unique.

An inflated head with a Dora the Explorer haircut. Oversized frames. “NERD & Proud of It” emblazoned below.

“Did you lose this? It’s at security waiting for you!”, the sentence amplified as I realized the inquiry was sent to the entire pre-college program. It was like someone had hung my blazing pink underwear on a balcony for all to gawk at—not just embarrassing, but exposing. Except I hadn’t lost my underwear. I’d lost a pin— both a badge and burden.

The pin was from a local small business specializing in artwork that celebrated the oft-disparaged elements of the Bay Area stereotype. Instead, my school prized such stereotypes. Surrounded by peers chasing careers in STEM, I felt an unspoken pressure to follow suit, to prove I belonged—even if it meant sidelining the passions that truly made me feel alive. I wanted to be like my best friends—trailblazers for girls in STEM and a cardiovascular researcher hoping to cure my mother’s cardiomyopathy. But even as I chased these ideals, I felt an eerie unease. The harder I tried to mirror their ambitions, the more I felt like a shadow of myself.

"Would you jump off a cliff if your friends did too?” It’s a cliché question, but in my case, following the crowd forced me to confront a hard truth. I was chasing someone else’s dream, not my own. A 1.5 x 1.5-inch void stared back at me, hollow and unfulfilled—just like how I felt. While my peers thrived in coding and lab experiments, I found myself daydreaming about Akbar the Great’s empire or William Jennings Bryan’s fiery Cross of Gold speech. I ignored what my heart wanted and clung to STEM as the ‘“safe cliff.” I was ready to fill the void with true self-discovery.

My oboe case, bare and pinless, became a fresh canvas—a symbol of starting over on my own terms. By choosing pieces like Coping, which addresses anxiety and depression, music became more than a hobby—it was a way to connect and advocate. A single-mom told me after the performance that my oboe’s voice had encouraged her to continue fighting the occasional bouts of anxiety. Supporters like her gave me the determination to stop muffling my voice; instead, uplift others musically. Now I see music as a form of activism.

Discarding my pin allowed me to venture outside its rigid constrictions. By exploring my heritage through books like Wild Swans: Three Daughters of China to Daughters of the Flower Fragrant Garden, I realized history has shaped me as a woman. My own great-grandmother sold all of her heirlooms and mahogany furniture to feed seven children during the Great Famine. My grandmother hid the existence of my uncle during the One Child Policy, preventing her from raising a family without apprehension. Powerful women in my family have taught me that strength isn’t just about survival—it’s about the courage to act. While their actions were born from necessity, they’ve inspired me to pursue my own passions with the same determination, even when societal pressure suggests otherwise. Their legacy reminds me that I owe it to myself to live authentically, embracing the things that bring me purpose and joy.

You might be wondering if I ever got the pin back? The answer: yes and no. When I asked if I could retrieve my pin, the security guard, with his raised eyebrows in surprise, told me that somebody had already claimed it. At first, I felt a pang of loss, but I soon realized I didn’t need it anymore. College offers a pen instead of pinning me down, where I can continue to draw my own path filled with individuality and authentic passions. I don’t need a pin, sticker, or label to define my identity or give validation to what I pursue. While someone else may have given my pin a new home, I’ve found mine within myself.

It’s too late.

As death approached, I closed my eyes and accepted my fate. At that moment, the approaching darkness was momentarily shadowed by bright recollections: falling belly-deep into a puddle with buwa (grandpa) after trying to jump across it, painting over our living room ink splash with Siddha (cousin), and tasting Goldee’s BBQ brisket with mama (uncle).

Suddenly, I was ripped out of my memories and sent flying into my seat as my mom accelerated just in time. After some particularly profane exchange of words, we shared a much-needed hug.

I couldn’t believe it. I couldn’t believe I was seconds away from being a memory instead of making one. For the next few days, everything I did, I questioned its purpose.

“Is this really what I want to do?” 
“Would I be doing this if I knew the end was near?”
“Could the end be today?”
“Would I be happy with myself if it was?”

With these questions pacing in my mind, I was struggling to be my old self. Just sitting in my room wasn’t enough anymore, knowing there was a chance I couldn’t tomorrow. Having been near death, I decided I had to get closer to life. After all, I had a whole Christmas break to spend.

I soon understood I had a difficult task to tackle. Somehow, I had to cherish life to a point where I wouldn’t hesitate to let go. Not knowing where to start, I started small with appreciation. I made it a habit to jot down 5 “reasons to smile” in my worn-out bonded leather notebook. From “the taste of soggy parle-g biscuits drenched in milk” to “successful your mom jokes,” I left nothing out. Though it wasn’t much, it slowly made me realize there was a lot to be grateful for that went unnoticed. For example, I never noticed being told that it was cold outside was a blessing as I hadn’t already felt the breeze from the inside. Growing increasingly appreciative of simplicity was rewarding, but I had just begun.

Next, I started showing my appreciation. I placed little thank you notes underneath buwa’s plates, did the dishes behind aama’s (grandma’s) back, surprised papu (dad) at work with my daily culinary “masterpieces,” and seasoned mamu’s (mom’s) aachar. Excluding mamu, the reactions from this simple gesture made me elated beyond words. It was unbelievable how such little actions made such lasting impacts. These little actions made me realize that there is no present as precious to me as the presence of my loved ones and their love for me. However, I was still one step short.

Finally, I started working towards being appreciated. Given the uncertainty of the end, I couldn’t be content with being just a memory; I want(ed) to be remembered. With this in mind, I took it upon myself to make an impact and started planning for something meaningful. After hundreds of emails to school principals, weeks of lesson planning, and hours of Zoom meetings, I was finally ready. That summer, I taught a month-long debate course to 8 bright students, hosted a debate tournament, and volunteered as an assistant science teacher in Nepal.

Seeing the students’ fear of public speaking disappear, tears of joy during the award ceremony, and imitation of my American accent made me feel ready to die happily anytime.

On the flight back, staring at the Saraswati figurine I was gifted, I looked back at the day of the near accident. I smirked at the realization that it took the power of death for me to live life carefree. I now know that the next time I close my eyes to accept my fate, I won’t do it in fear but in appreciation. I am now thankful for the end because if it weren’t for death, I would’ve kept living life without making it life-worthy.

Creativity comes from a shower thought. As I close my eyes, a vision appears in my mind; I grasp it and seize it. My hair is still damp as I barely dry off, sit, open my laptop, and write it.

The internet was the outlet of my childhood creativity—namely Google. I mastered the transcendental realm of Google Slides, pasting vibrant borders, planting animated GIFS, and enhancing each slide with seamless transitions. A young Google guru, I also dived headfirst into the world of Google Docs, where I wrote 30-page-long children's books, Minecraft guides, and suspenseful, attention-grabbing, epic renditions of games of hide-and-seek. Creativity then didn't come from the shower; it was who I was, a carefree, wild kid with dreams of becoming a famous author.

"You have to shower, Ben!" yells my mom as time approaches for me to sleep. Yet my middle-school mind is stuck to the screen, immersed in the world of Roblox. My eyes light up as one sale comes in after another from other Robloxians like me. Life is all about Roblox, the game that consumed most of my screen time during the Covid-19 lockdown. Yet, I wasn't just any typical player. I was a developer, conjuring up new designs every day for colorful streetwear to sell on the busy marketplace.

Vivid memories linger in my head of creating advertisements in Photoshop, tweaking angles and editing out blanks, and finding the perfect combination of light and dark. Being a Roblox developer, I escaped the chaos of the pandemic through creativity. Every shower before bed, I let new ideas spawn in my mind like a whirlpool. I'd think of new logos, advertisements, or designs and store them in my memory, ensuring they stayed until the next morning. Creating on Roblox, I combined my limitless creativity with my inherent desire to succeed, turning my art into a form of business.

Standing alone in the shower, water patters on my skin, and I feel a random eagerness to create. I'm now in the busiest era of my life: high school. As I hop out of the shower, I open Canva and begin working on a design. The design adds more and more layers as I incorporate aspects of Blade Runner, Off-White design, and Japanese symbols. Fueled by my Roblox development venture several years earlier, my creation unfolds—a T-shirt. I expand my sights further—one shirt leads the next, and into hoodie designs, and accessories. I splatter a bit of Greek art onto one and some Roman onto another.

Curious, I search for marketing videos and clothing-creation courses. After a few weeks, ALLOR is born. My creativity doesn't just stop at clothing; it moves into the fabric of social media, where I begin to post videos and pictures of my clothing using Photoshop, and an audience starts growing. I incorporate organic audio, follow different trends, and add unique twists to each. I create business cards, film videos, and take modeling photoshoots with my friends.

As I close my computer after a long day of creation and step into the shower, I make a crucial revelation. As the water splashes on my skin, I realize the shower is a gift. The shower water allows me to splash my own authentic creativity into the world. Whether it be through the form of a new shirt design, an essay, a social media post, a senior day speech, or a new improvised solo, I let the water take control and unlock doors filled with the essence of my childhood creativity. As the water rains, I find I'm soaked with the creativity within me, the creativity of a kid who didn't need to look for his creativity in the shower—and as I grab my pen and pencil, minutes later, my paper is wet with imagination.

At eight years old, my world was dictated by my father’s seemingly arbitrary rules. “Turn off your light,” my dad would say as we were about to leave the house. I’d sigh, knowing I was already running late. As I started up the stairs to turn off my bedroom light—“No,” he’d interrupt, “take your shoes off first.” His words were sharp, his tone unyielding. Annoyed, I’d kick off my sneakers, bolt up the stairs, flick the switch, and hurry back down. Only then would we finally get in the car and head off.

As a child, this felt arbitrary, even stifling. Surely one small lightbulb couldn’t wreak havoc on our energy bill. But my dad’s lesson wasn’t about electricity—it was about discipline. He believed that paying attention to the small things today made room for bigger things tomorrow. Back then, I didn’t fully understand the purpose behind these small habits. I simply turned off the light.

Unlike my father, my grandmother—Achi, as I call her—never scolded me for being undisciplined. She showed me. She had always been a model of resilience, fighting as a widowed mother to raise my mom and uncle. When I was three years old, she was diagnosed with breast cancer. Her survival after chemotherapy and surgery was a victory I only came to appreciate as I got older. But regardless of how much pain she was going through, she never gave up. I remember peeping over the counter as Achi baked for the holidays, even through her anxiety attacks, all so we could freely enjoy the sweet taste of love cake on Christmas morning.

This duality of freedom and discipline began to shape my own approach to life. By high school, I was managing more than most adults I knew. As I dove into the world of competitive swimming, my world became grueling 5 am practices. Homework and projects that stretched into the early hours. Research inspired by Achi’s story. Kung fu and Piano fitting in between. But I was rarely overwhelmed. I enjoyed everything I did, so I rarely needed to summon discipline to get through it. Swimming laps wasn’t a chore—it was a challenge. Writing code wasn’t work—it was an adventure.

Of course, there were moments when love and enjoyment alone weren’t enough. There have been hundreds of days when I felt like I couldn’t do it. I’ve failed innumerable times: missing intervals in workouts, breathing off the walls, exceeding goal times in VO2 max sets, and falling short of time standards, despite the work I put in. But with every setback, my dad’s stern voice in my head tells me to show up, every day, ready to do the unglamorous work, just like Achi standing at the stove even when she felt too weak to stand. Winning races hasn't made me a better swimmer—it’s the discipline, applying my father’s attention to details as I analyzed Michael Phelps’ races for tiny stroke corrections or trained at the YMCA during the off season.

Over time, I began to see discipline not as an enemy of freedom but as its greatest ally. The act of turning off the light—a habit so small it felt inconsequential—had taught me that consistency in the little things gives you the freedom to pursue the big ones. Doing things correctly now clears the path for doing meaningful things later. Looking back, I realize that everything I do stems from intent. Whether it’s swimming down the pool or writing lines of code, I approach every act with the same intent and purpose I saw in my grandmother’s kitchen. I see it every time I persevere through a long day or find joy in solving a complex problem. And when I reach for the light switch, I’m reminded of how much these small moments have shaped who I am.

During my fragile transition from childhood to adolescence, my world seemed to value stature over substance. When tiptoeing around at school only received ridicule, I tried wearing height boosters, thinking no one would notice. But as I lost balance and fell walking to class—my extra-cushioned insoles slipping out—my insecurity was revealed to the world. I realized I needed real growth, not temporary solutions.

It wasn't hard to find that nutrition, exercise, and sleep were key to boosting growth. However, my insatiable curiosity—my greatest asset by day—became my biggest obstacle by night. Mentally drowning in a vat of questions every night, I'd pace my room and stare blankly at walls.
