I spent four hours in the operating room, donning a surgical mask, safety goggles perched awkwardly over my -5.5 prescription glasses, and an apron tied slightly off-center. My hands, steady as a surgeon’s, were covered in stained red gloves. The procedure was delicate: drilling a hole right through the center of the paw.

The operation was successful—I made a red paw-shaped keycap for the control key of my keyboard from epoxy resin. I am a self-proclaimed epoxy resin specialist, and the abandoned community room on our rooftop is my operation theater, where I spend hours performing artistic surgeries and dissecting art scraps to make new art. Over the years of mixing resin and hardener in a 2:1 ratio, I found a way to blend my creativity with a purpose.

My neighbor adopted Toby, a stray cat from an animal shelter, after he had a severe road accident that left one of Toby's forelimbs paralyzed. As soon as Mr. Rahman brought Toby home, my wheels started turning. How can I help this defenseless cat regain some of its mobility and independence? Maybe a crutch? No, he will tip over. How about a sling? It does not sound practical.

After countless days of sketching, prototyping, scrapping, and failing—a lot—along with a few scratches from Toby, I made a customized resin tray with screwed-in wheels and a cushion on top. Toby could sit on it and push himself slowly with one of his hindlimbs. This month-long project proved successful as my neighbor sent me videos of Toby going to bed alone, sitting on that tray. That was the birth of Toby’s cat Uber. This experience strengthened my commitment to helping rescued animals. Inspired by Toby's success, I began selling my creations—resin pendants, cup holders, and pet collars—to raise funds for local animal shelters, ensuring that more rescued animals like Toby can find safe homes.

However, my resin works were not just limited to art; they soon became a medium for connecting with people.

I packed the remaining products as the busy day ended, raising about $97 (11,599 BDT). ‘Is the event over?’ I looked at a little girl in school uniform, standing before my stall, breathing heavily as she handed me an envelope with a used pet collar and a dried blue orchid petal. ‘I got the collar from your first fundraising event for my dog. He passed away a week ago. Could you make something of it so I can hold onto his memories?’ It took me a second—what if I cannot do justice to her grief? —but I agreed. I had two days to cut the collar, arrange the charm and petals in a mold, dry, sand the pendant, and deliver it to her address. Her teary-eyed ‘Thank you’ reminded me why I loved what I did.

I could not realize how my crafts expanded beyond quirky projects to being significant parts of people’s lives. The honor of framing wedding bouquets for newlyweds or making handmade coasters of wilted flowers for a client’s parents’ anniversary became more than work commitments, I was a small part of the story people carry with them.

Toby’s Uber project taught me that there is a certain freedom in failing—and in failing often—because it keeps me persistent in attaining perfection. It also sparked my fascination with prosthetics, mobility aids, and biomaterials. The later experiences enabled me to understand how a simple craft can be a form of care: bridging the gap between loss and healing, a new beginning or celebrating milestones, combining innovation, and empathy. As I step outside my operating room to face a new world of biomedical engineering, I am prepared. I aim to work with resins, not just the ones I use for crafting, but also researching cationic exchange resins, which work against antibiotics to prepare lifesaving vaccines in labs and engineer mobility aids to transform lives positively.

For every Indian raised in the Gulf, life is a familiar dichotomy. My school life was a blend of shawarma nights and Arabic poem recitations, while the customary journey of over 2857 kilometers from Abu Dhabi, UAE to Allapuzha, Kerala involved swapping sneakers with sandals and dining from a vaazhayila (banana leaf) instead of a plate.

This experience was culturally fulfilling, yet paradoxically, draining. At school, I faced mockery from other kids for “not speaking English properly” and was assumed to not be able to assimilate. Ironically, returning to India intensified my sense of isolation - my cousins scrutinized my “posh” choice of track pants and hoodies and branded me as the “foreigner girl”.

I somehow didn’t quite exist, too Arab to be Indian, and too Indian to be Arab. This “in limbo” identity perplexed me in my selection of subjects in school, and my decision about my future: am I a psychology student, or a future biologist? An obedient daughter or a staunch non-conformist? When I wore my “I’m In Shape, Round Is A Shape” T-Shirt to Diwali I didn’t simply stand out, it was like a fabled roc had sauntered past my grandmother. For much of my life, I felt guessed at, unknown, unseen, unverifiable, both a particle and a wave – mythical, per my namesake: for my name is [Name].

“Hello [Name]. This is [Name], your English tutor. How are you?”

The pandemic marked a profound moment in history, bringing the world to a standstill. For some, it ignited new beginnings and hobbies; for others, it brought death, disease, and conflict. Cooped up at home with my anime-loving brother, I was determined to spread my knowledge to those in need and signed up as an English tutor to [Name] Slukina, a 17 year old from Kyiv, Ukraine. It was nerve racking, transitioning from occasionally helping my classmates with classwork to becoming a full-time teacher. Yet, I was excited and spent the days up to my meeting scouring YouTube and Cambridge English “Resources for English Language teacher”.

“Hi, I am doing ok. How are you?…s-sank you for this session.”

I noticed her hesitation while expressing her gratitude. In Ukrainian, the “th” sound is uncommon, often replaced with an "s”. I quickly switched gears, forgoing my planned notes and spending the next few weeks demonstrating the elusive sound: placing the tip of the tongue between my teeth and releasing it to make the “th” sound. This was partly selfish, for without being able to pronounce this phoneme, she wouldn't be able to pronounce my name; I reasoned I would be out of reach, even further away than the 5,305.5 kilometers and cultural gap that separated us. We were both nomads; though we hailed from different families, we shared the challenge of fitting in. It was a sobering realization - while I grappled with two identities, Arab and Indian, [Name] was on the verge of losing hers. In the process of this close friendship, I realized the power of individuality - molding your personality based not on who you were asked to become but on who you chose to be. [Name] and I were together on her birthday, when we watched “Spiderman: No Way Home”, and, happily, when she had the chance to emigrate to Poland with her family.

I am still [Name], still a nomad, a girl with many imperfections and diverse origins. But I have done something for myself that I would not have done before I met [Name], and began reflecting on my goals, for myself, mythical as I may be: I have taken a gap year. Breaking the empirical chain of cause and effect, spending time reading “The Brain Changes Itself” while slowly understanding my goals of improving global healthcare and finding answers to incurable diseases. Gaps, discontinuities, flukes, coincidences. I accept myself as someone who doesn't fit in; I seek my niche, and if I cannot find it, I will make it for myself.

My cutter zipped up and in, flinching the batter just enough to earn a called inside corner strike. "Let's go, Kenny!" cheers erupted from behind me and from my bench. On the next pitch, I threw a slider aiming at his chest before it broke away at the last moment as strike three. This mental chess match - pitcher vs. hitter (and vice versa) - with so many strategies to employ and moving parts to consider is what makes baseball thrilling. While some moan about the sport as a slow game and a fading pastime, I find that the game within the game and its complexities are intellectually stimulating and mirror life.

I admit, I’m no Shohei Ohtani (sigh). Since my T-ball days - when I swung at pitches like a piñata three feet above my head - I’ve always been smaller than most players. At every tryout, I just hoped to make the cut and stay “afloat” until I hit my growth spurt, clinging to the naive belief that I’d inherited my Dad’s six-foot height. Lacking physical prowess and feeling like David facing Goliath, I relied on my baseball IQ and soft skills to excel. In high school, I spent countless hours (unlikely 10,000) personally refining my arm mechanics and analyzing pitch sequencing, studying YouTube videos, and deciphering research papers on arm injuries. Though my four-seam fastball topped out at 81 mph, it was still far from college recruitable speed. Starting last season as the unofficial fifth-string pitcher on my varsity team, I unassumingly climbed up the depth chart to become the team’s ace, culminating in an unexpected league Honorable Mention and an invitation to pitch in the league’s Underclass All-Star Game.

Baseball is also truly a game of constant failure - Hall of Famers "fail" at the plate nearly 70% of the time. On a traditional grading scale, that would translate to a grade of “G”. Yet, success in baseball often comes through small, strategic moves that may seem like failures in the moment. Sacrifice flies, bunts, or groundouts to advance runners or bring in runs are tradeoffs that can lead to a team’s success, and they matter more than individual statistics and achievements. These quiet victories, however modest, deserve recognition, whether it’s a pat on the back or a high five. Baseball, and life, isn’t just about glory in the big moments, but also the countless small failures and successes at every turn. You can strike out one inning and hit a home run the next, humbly teaching you to stay optimistic and persistent. The repetitive nature of these so-called failures has also made me more empathetic toward teammates and everyone outside the chalked-white lines. These positivity and compassion are qualities that I want to continue to cultivate and share with others as a way to forge stronger team camaraderie.

From T-ball to varsity baseball, and kindergarten to high school, I've come to appreciate that opportunities are not guaranteed. That constant self-improvement is essential before seizing them (“Fortuna Eruditis Favet" [“chance favors the prepared mind"]), a philosophy drilled into me by my baseball coaches. Inspired by my parents' immigrant mindset of appreciating every opportunity, I co-founded a nonprofit, collecting used sports gear to provide students at underprivileged schools with the chance to play. Our success led to expansion to multiple local high schools. Hearing the appreciation from the students using our donated equipment was incredibly rewarding. It felt almost as if I created opportunities for others the way my parents did for me.

When I hang up my cleats from competitive baseball, the game will continue to guide me through new journeys to anything and anywhere. The subtleties and nuances of baseball make it more than just a game; they offer a way to understand and appreciate life’s constants.

6:58. I wait on the platform. 7:05. I’m not on the train? 7:09. I step on. Cigarette smoke corrupts my nose, an all-too-familiar reminder of my father’s cigarettes between cutting chicken. Murky puddles. Discolored stains. Jagged graffiti scratching windows. I worry the train will stop, stopping me from exploring beyond the sidewalk by my family’s restaurant. Can’t escape the smoke.

Food’s on the table when I get home. Mom washes my dishes after her umpteenth order of fried rice. She’ll restock soda how I once helped out. Mom and Dad sometimes say, “All that matters is each generation lives better lives than the last.” So I slink away, two floors above their long hours. Above my mother selling cigarettes, my father smoking.

Pages flipping. Mental gymnastics, that better life. Footsteps pound up the stairs. Dad leans against my bed, catching his breath. “Huh? I can’t feel my mouth. . .” Book forgotten, what do I even do? My brother would’ve already helped, but I scramble for instructions.

“Get a towel.” I wipe sweat off his forehead.
“Call Mom.” Mom forgets the restaurant.
“Call 911.”

Half an hour later, misshapen Mandarin stumbles out as everyone awaits my translation. My brother would’ve found the words, but I could barely speak Mandarin or understand the Chinese proverbs we hang up for New Year’s. For all my studying two floors above, I can’t communicate with my parents. Can I save them?

Mom worries, “Something’s in the fryer.” I snap. “We’re in the hospital, and you’re still thinking of the restaurant?” How could they value that restaurant over their lives? They value my life over theirs. Immigrating to a cramped Chinese restaurant, sacrificing traditions for survival. As long as I get a better life. That’s the essence of selflessness and love. It’s about working hard for people I care about above all.

Dad breathes, “What if I were gone? Dad’s growing old.”

“Please, don’t smoke another cigarette.” I’d tried so often to warn him, but I couldn’t utter the thought he could die. It curses us in his frail eyes. There’s only so long to learn who we were. Only so long to relearn Mandarin from them. My alienating English races through my head. How can I appreciate life disconnected from my family? I should cherish the time I spend with people.

An hour later, he pushes through hospital doors, finds his lighter, and lights a cigarette.

What happens to a dream deferred? Cigarettes slowly extinguish my parents’ lives, but their hope lights my resilience and persistence in following my curiosity, making the most of the world they’ve given me. Seeing how little they had and how much they’ve sacrificed to give me more, this is love, the cruelty of “each generation lives better lives than the last.” Their suffering doesn’t weigh me down, it grounds me. With all the lows in this world I’ve grown up in, I know I must make it a better place.

I choose what to make of my life. I’ve faced struggles, but I know they pale against my parents’ and I still feel privileged to have more choices than they did. I choose to speak Mandarin to Mom and Dad. Their hours at the woks won’t be lost to the American melting pot. It costs nothing to give back to those who’ll always root for me. I choose to seize opportunities, collaborate on the world’s problems, improve lives, and hopefully inspire the next generation. In everyone I help by volunteering or teaching, I see my family and everything they’ve lived without. The opportunity to explore. The opportunity to see this world’s beauty. The freedom to truly live. Every morning, I take that train knowing I’ll make it. Cigarette smoke awaits inside, but the train always comes.

This is that better life.

To the room I’ve left undecorated for 17 years,

A bed in the middle of the desert is the best way I could’ve described you. If I hadn’t learned a lesson from making candy with my Tantee, I would’ve never been able to shape you into the oasis you are today. Initially, I didn’t see the point in investing my time in you, sorry. Unknowingly, you represented my confidence and what I loved; however, an empty room couldn’t reflect my best self, and it showed. Like your walls, my mind was blank, and expressing myself to people was a challenge. I didn’t have the space to develop my interests. I went about my day, accepting my shyness and lack of expression until my family arrived.

Besides you, the next best thing that brings out my personality is family. During the summer, my family from Grenada visits. Each time, my authentic self radiates just like the tropical sun. I abandoned you again as a guest room, distracting me from personalizing you. My Tantee was the one who took care of you during then, draping our flag over your walls. A yellow-green-red pattern with floral decorations brightens the room with pinks and lavender. I became jealous as I never felt I had the opportunity to transform you into something I’d be proud of.

Later, I’d spot Tantee in the kitchen making one of my favorite candies, tamarind balls. This was my first time seeing it homemade, so I leaped to join her. At the table, we collected the peeled fruit and poured the sugar into the batch, now it was time to knead it in. Before mixing I felt uneasy, I was so eager to jump in, but now intimidated by the task of making the sugary spheres. Tantee noticed and guided me saying, “Don’t let the tamarind knead you.” Even though the message was confusing, I had the affirmative to dive in. By the end, I had made the best tamarind balls of my life.

While eating my delicious creation, I reflected on the moment with Tantee. Before kneading I was stuck, once again I drew a blank, but Tantee reminded me that I was in control. My rebound in that moment taught me an important lesson: life is like tamarind. Everything within my life is in my hands, waiting for me to dig in, whether it’s the opportunities I take or how I set up my room. From that point on my Tantee’s words echoed, and I began to approach life as I had approached tamarind—taking control.

With Tantee back in Grenada, I went back to you. I noticed Tantee had left something behind, her flag. It was still draped over you, and I felt the warmth of family. Like a domino effect, I began to decorate you with posters and souvenirs. Gradually, no longer did I shy away from expressing my interests; I proudly wore my bracelets from Grenada and admitted my love for Power Rangers, even if I got strange looks. The memories we shared ignited my passion to take control. I knew that if I could take space at home, I could dominate no matter where I was. For example, I used to freeze during Model UN debates, but Tantee’s lesson helped to ground me. As a delegate, I participated in nerve-wracking debates; the competitive environment challenged me, and I had to adjust. Each time I walked out of the conference room, I knew I tried my hardest.

Now, I see an elaborate collage of posters and objects that reflect my identity and interests. You’re no longer just a space but a testament to my journey. The lessons I learned from kneading tamarind with Tantee—about taking control and embracing my uniqueness—continue to guide me. I owe it to you and Tantee for allowing me to shape my life in ways that truly reflect who I am.

“Turn off your light,” my dad would say just as we were about to leave the house. At eight years old, I sighed, knowing I was already running late. I began up the stairs to turn off my bedroom light. “No,” he’d interrupt, “take your shoes off first.” His words sounded sharp, his tone unyielding. Annoyed, I’d kick off my sneakers, bolt up the stairs, flick the switch, and hurry back down. Only then would we finally get in the car and head off.

Back then, I didn’t understand why he cared so much. The light would only be on for an hour or two—why did it matter? I thought he was being strict just for the sake of it. I’d misread him entirely. In hindsight, my dad wasn’t angry. His firmness wasn’t rooted in frustration but in care. I’ve come to understand why love and anger are painted in the same color. I had been conflating the two; the moments I mistook for irritation were lessons in disguise—discipline, attention to detail, and patience. I was foolish. I still am.

These lessons were apparent when I dove into the world of competitive swimming. The early 5am practices, the countless meters spent refining my strokes, and the mental endurance required to push through a gruelling VO2-max set taught me that success isn’t about talent—it’s about showing up, every day, ready to do the unglamorous work. And yet, there have still been hundreds of days when I felt like I couldn’t do it all. I failed, and continue to fail, countless times: missing intervals in workouts, breathing off the walls, and hence falling short of time standards, despite the work I put in. But with every setback, I hear my dad’s stern voice in my head. It isn’t about perfection; it’s about persistence. It isn’t the big, dramatic moments when I win a race that make me a better swimmer—it’s the quiet ones, the repetitions that no one sees.

This mindset became even more important when I encountered AI several years later during an internship at Chirp. What began as a project to build a human activity recognition model quickly became something much more personal. For years, my grandmother—Achi, as I call her—has been a symbol of resilience for me. When I was young, she was diagnosed with breast cancer, and though I don’t remember those years in detail, I grew up with an awareness of her quiet strength. Her survival was a victory I only came to appreciate as I got older. The topic of breast cancer also resurfaced years later when my mom was asked to undergo her first mammogram screening. I was reminded of how vital early detection is, yet I couldn’t stop thinking about the years of waiting, the uncertainty, and the cost that make screenings inaccessible for so many. I wanted to do something meaningful to resolve these barriers.

That’s when I started my research on using AI for breast cancer detection. Debugging code for hours, reworking flawed models for weeks—the process was grueling. But I kept going, driven by my grandmother’s quiet strength and my dad’s enduring lessons. It was the first time I felt a responsibility beyond myself. My goal wasn’t just to build something functional, but to create something impactful. The thought that my work might help someone detect cancer earlier made every late night worthwhile.

Sometimes, I’ll catch myself flicking off a light switch, and I’ll think of my dad. I’ll think of the way he’d stand at the door, waiting for me to put my sneakers back on. His patience, his consistency, his commitment to doing the little things right—these are the values that have guided me through every race, every project, every single action. They’re the same values I’ll carry with me wherever I go next. Whether it’s pursuing AI research, training for Olympic trials, or simply turning off a light, I’ll keep showing up. Not because someone’s watching, but because I’ve learned that’s how you leave behind something that lasts.

"Manya, come down for lunch!" my mom called.

"Coming, Amma!" I lied, rushing through the last few questions of Buzzfeed's "What Pizza Topping Are You?" quiz. As I pressed submit, a big red box appeared at the bottom of my screen.

"You're an olive!" it proclaimed.

I groaned. I hated olives.

Despite my disappointment, it made me think. I've always found personality tests silly yet fun: from MBTI (I'm an ENFJ, by the way) to Love Languages (I’m "Quality Time"). Over time, however, I realized they drew me in because of something deeper: a desire to understand a complicated world by building models, frameworks, and systems.

Take Taekwondo, for instance. At my studio, True Martial Arts, we start every class with the same instructions: "chit-ee-yet kin-yet" - a call to attention, and a bow to show respect. We end with "chom-bo-ney-o" - the Instructor's goodbye. In the time between, we'd master stances that built up kicks, that made up forms, that let us achieve the next rank.

Taekwondo was my first case study in the power of systems. It showed me how directed effort could transform hard work into tangible results. I carried that mindset into other areas of my life - whether mastering "up down" brushstrokes making up hand lettered words or coloring in each box on a summer reading challenge.

When I became Washington DECA State President, I approached leadership the same way: systematically. I led monthly self-evaluations, set SMART goals for our officers, and prioritized efficiency. By every metric, it seemed like Team Infinity was doing great.

Still, something felt off. My team didn’t seem to trust me, and our conversations were awkward. Meetings were quiet, filled with polite nods but little engagement. One officer rarely spoke; another struggled to meet deadlines. It felt like they didn’t trust me enough to ask for help.

The turning point came at our spring retreat. After dinner, I asked everyone to share a personal challenge they were facing. At first, the responses were hesitant: "I’ve been falling behind in school," one officer admitted. Another said, "I’m struggling to balance my part-time job with this role."

Their honesty opened my eyes to how much I had overlooked by treating them as "DECA Robots."

Determined to change, I began holding monthly one-on-one check-ins. I learned about their struggles and worked to lighten financial burdens and tailor roles to their strengths. Slowly, trust grew, and I realized leadership means building systems that empower people - not the other way around.

However, not all systems work for everyone. One afternoon, I asked my mom why she was usually the one to change my baby sister’s diaper.

“Because women’s bathrooms are more likely to have changing stations,” she explained.

Her answer made me pause. I’d never noticed this before, but it struck me as deeply unfair. This everyday inequality reflected how many systems - whether in bathrooms, workplaces, or schools - are built with biases that exclude or disadvantage certain groups.

It was a realization that fueled my passion for advocacy. From organizing healthier school lunch initiatives to addressing menstrual inequity in my district, I’ve worked to challenge systems that don’t serve everyone, and I’ve seen how small changes can make a big difference.

Looking ahead, I see how systems will shape the future. As technology advances, innovations in AI and machine learning - some of the most complex systems - offer the potential to improve billions of lives or deepen systemic inequities. As someone who understands both the power and pitfalls of systems, I’m excited to ensure tomorrow’s innovations work for everyone.

Even personality quizzes, with all their quirks, remind me of this. They don’t define who I am, but they’ve helped me ask better questions - about myself, others, and the world around me. And that, I’ve learned, is the best place to start.

What would you expect a doctor of nuclear engineering to do on his weekends? Probably not wearing a full-body skinsuit, zooming around local roads at 20 miles per hour. But my dad is not like most people. Even in his stressful routine filled with meetings and business trips, he still makes sure to incorporate his hobbies into his life.

One spring during sophomore year, my dad insisted we watch our favorite soccer team, Suwon Bluewings, play in the relegation playoffs. Initially, I was skeptical.

“I can’t, dad, I have so many finals to study for.”

But my dad was insistent that I took a break. And when Suwon scored a last-minute winner, my dad and I went crazy, singing and jumping all around our living room at 4 in the morning, even blowing as hard as we could on vuvuzelas, a type of trumpet played at soccer games.

During a physics project in which we had to construct a full-sized boat out of cardboard, my group often found ourselves stressing over our grade on the line. Even still, we came up with a theme, a banana boat, and taped on actual bananas to the side of our boat. On the day of the competition, my group showed up wearing monkey costumes, ties, and sunglasses. Even as we waited our turn in the pool, laughter never ended from our group as we posed for pictures in our ridiculous outfits.

My dad attended university during a time where Korea was dominated by protests pushing for democratic reforms. Watching the news about rallies ongoing in Korea, he would tell me stories of marching in the streets, of facing beatings by riot police, of friends who were arrested for protesting. Social awareness was a value he tried to instill in me at an early age; I remember he took me to a Presidential rally in Korea, where he put me on his shoulders so I could see the stage properly. I even got to shake the hand of the future president of Korea, Moon Jae-in.

Having been exposed to some of my dad’s activism, I wanted to learn more about the issues that needed change in my time. At international Model UN conferences, I spoke about some of the biggest issues in today’s world, such as abortion rights and censorship. Like my dad advocated for democracy in the 90s, I pushed for the values of freedom of speech. As I passionately delivered speeches pushing for increased education of law enforcement and media literacy campaigns, and eventually incorporated these plans into the final resolution, I became better connected to the world around me.

After a trip to Mexico, my family’s flight back from North Carolina to Albany had been canceled due to snow, leaving us with only summer clothes, no chargers, and a 14 hour drive to get back home. My dad, though, joked, “Now we get a vacation AND a road trip.” To me, trying to keep warm in a T-shirt and shorts in the backseat, his view of the world seemed alien to me, at least initially.

How would one describe staying up until 5 AM studying fossils? Early morning summer workouts for soccer? Some would say tiring. Others might say tedious. But I would describe it as beautiful. During a Science Olympiad competition, the WiFi unexpectedly cut out as my partner and I scrambled to finish our research. However, I remember being unable to keep the smile off my face as I ran around the entire school, holding my computer up, searching for a connection. Some of my best memories are of cold, rainy mornings, running 10x400s with my teammates, where jokes and energy never ceased to exist even through the sound of panting and gasping for air. This awareness of beauty is what keeps me going.

Throughout my life, my father has affected some of the most crucial parts of myself, whether it be through his peculiar obsession with cycling, his democratic demonstrations, or his ability to find beauty. I came to understand the importance of “fun” in life, developed a better connection to the world around me, and became more aware of the beauty that exists in unexpected places. I hope to bring these values with me wherever I go, helping to make my community a more vibrant and energetic place by helping others find enjoyment and beauty in their everyday lives.

My mother wasn’t allowed to hold me when I was born. The moment I entered the world, a corrections officer whisked me away and like a stork, dropped me into the hands of my anxious father waiting down the hall. I was immediately embraced by the tribe of artists and academics that is my family. They showered me with love, and imparted to me only the best of themselves. In this environment, I quickly found my own creative outlet: a Lego Batman set I was given when I was five.

I was obsessed. While other children were stuffing them in their mouths, the idea that a pile of plastic blocks could be assembled into any configuration imaginable enthralled me. I began with box directions but quickly discovered that muti-set, Frankensteinian amalgamations were much more stimulating to create.

Attaching a tattooed, muscular arm from a Ninjago set to my newest creation, it reminded me of sitting with my father while he wrote lyrics on his lined, yellow notepad, preparing for his next face-off. He was a battle rapper, artist, amateur stand-up comedian, and my idol. I once peeked at his scribbles, expecting vulgarity, and was surprised to find complex rhyme schemes, literary references, and even humor. I never told my dad about my discovery before his death, but from then on, my eyes sparkled whenever someone mentioned his name. Clicking a plastic microphone into the arm’s circular hand, I appreciated all that my father had taught me: never be afraid of putting myself out into the world and never take myself too seriously.

There was a knock on my door. My grandfather stood in the frame and surveyed my Lego-covered carpet. “It looks like every piece you’re using is from a different set. Don’t you want to follow the directions?” Pausing impatiently, like an interrupted architect, I explained that what made Legos so fun was taking the coolest parts from each set, and making one that has everything.

I stuck my hand into the Lego bin again, in search of another perfectly eclectic limb or odd accessory. Like a deep sea fisherman, I pulled out a black cape from a G.I. Joe set that I found in my closet, left there by my uncles when they were kids. They grew up in the same house as I did, and I often felt that being raised by the same parental figures in the same environment was like having “ghost siblings.” Once, I asked my grandparents to paint in the garage, and was met with panic. Only after they calmed down did I discover that 30 years prior, one uncle spray-painted the garage walls until they looked like a New York subway. Even though I was told no, I didn’t mind, as facing the same backlash that my uncle had felt like having an older brother, and connected me to the family lore.

“CLICK,” the Lego figure was complete.

In some way, these creatures represented me and the pieces in myself left by the metaphorical “village” that raised me. Drawing on the best parts of each of them helped me become the determined and adaptable person I am today. From my Grammy award-winning grandfather, I learned creativity in my pursuit of music, picking up 3 instruments over the last 10 years. From my two published author grandparents, I learned open-mindedness in my reading and writing, and from my artistic father, I learned resourcefulness and gained inspiration in my painting and poetry.

These traits and values I carry with me, and the greatest thing about being a Lego is that I can always swap out or add parts to become the best version of myself. As I encounter new people, I can learn from them and borrow what makes them unique, even if it means stacking a red pirate hat onto a neon green NASCAR helmet.

Growing up in the Dominican Republic, I would watch through the backseat window of my dad’s truck on our trips to the beach as tall buildings gradually gave way to dirt roads and stacked houses in impoverished communities. Kids my age in these neighborhoods often worked long hours just to put food on the table for their families. By contrast, I was born into privilege, free to pursue my interests without looking back.

These contrasts made me reflect on Jean-Paul Sartre’s philosophy, particularly in his book *Being and Nothingness*. He describes how every human is born into conditions outside of our control—our facticity—but also highlights our ability to surpass these barriers—our transcendence.

It was during badminton tournaments that I first witnessed the reality of Dominican society and its remarkable ability to transcend hardship.

Many of the athletes competing were kids with torn shoes and broken rackets, which contrasted greatly to our school team. Unfortunately, these young athletes played the sport out of necessity rather than passion, sparking a curiosity that has set me on a journey to understand their daily struggles and lifestyle—a quest to bridge the gap between privilege and its absence.

Outside of tournaments, I began donating badminton equipment to underprivileged teams, such as the Neyba regional team, creating new friendships by bonding over common interests like sports, music, and video games. I was invited to their practice spaces on the outskirts of the city and returned the favor by bringing them to my school’s state-of-the-art facilities. Even though this was a new experience for me, it felt entirely natural, as I believed I was giving everyone an equal opportunity to transcend their facticity—something that was otherwise impossible given their circumstances.

Around the same time I started playing badminton, I also joined the debate team at my school. When it came time for international tournaments, the script was suddenly flipped—I was now the one coming from an under-resourced background, representing the Dominican Republic in the largest speech and debate tournaments across the United States. Instead of sticking to the style of debate I had known and studied for years in my country, I embraced the challenge. I adapted my traditional Dominican case format to the traditional cut-card format used in American debate, and I also learned new techniques that complemented my skills, such as incorporating theoretical arguments from policy debate and the use of critiques, or "K's," to strengthen my evidence-based arguments.

Being on both ends of the stick has led me to a position where I don’t belong in any specific group, I’m just sort-of in the middle, bridging both sides of the worlds that I now have been exposed to. I again find myself reflecting on Jean-Paul Sartre, but now under a different concept—his interpretation of bad faith as a form of self-deception, where individuals deny their own freedom and responsibility by conforming to societal expectations or roles. In my case, I set myself free, confronting the societal differences in my country in order to develop bonds that transcend barriers.

I have found immense satisfaction in the impact I have had on other people's lives, and it has defined one of my goals in life: to bridge the gaps between different levels of society and provide opportunities to those who are not as fortunate as I am. Whether through sports or debate, my experiences have taught me that meaningful connections can surpass the barrier of privilege.

This journey is not just about my personal growth; it’s about creating a legacy of support and understanding, ensuring that the next generation has the tools and opportunities to transcend their circumstances, and it all starts with me.

My mom never really mastered driving on the frozen icy roads of Edmonton. She frequently got lost and found parking challenging. Even as a four-year-old, I was her navigator. I used to sit with an old paper map of the city, guessing our location based on the shape of the roads because I couldn’t yet read English. I was right more often than not, and this became a routine. I was keen on taking over her role, to assist her with the horror she calls driving.

I attempted my first long-distance drive a month after I got my license. My eyes were acutely focused on the road, hands at the three and nine o’clock positions, passing through turquoise lakes and snow-capped mountains. It was tough, but the driving gave me a boost of confidence. I felt free; the flow state of the highway was addictive. I passed many semi-trucks along the way, chugging across the twisty mountain roads. Occasionally my dad chided my aggressive passing technique, but I brushed him off in my driving daze.

My parents dozed off after hours of driving without issue. I began approaching a semi-trailer hauling logs. Instinctively, I signaled left and began to pass, despite a yellow sign indicating the lanes would merge. I gained on the semi, eventually reaching the cab area. However, the semi was uncomfortably close. I was being squeezed, with my left tires driving onto the shoulder. The rumble strips on the shoulder shook the car, and in a split-second decision, I floored the gas pedal and surged ahead.

Needless to say, I was satisfied and exhilarated by my driving. It was as if I was winning a race. I felt euphoria akin to a risky gamble that ultimately hit the jackpot.

Later that night, surrounded by silent darkness, an unexpected thought surfaced. What if I had not made it out in time? The truck would have run us off the road and the picturesque scenery I passed would have become tainted with smoke and burning metal.

It truly hit me when I realized my parents and I could have become a statistic, our lives cut short due to the teenage desire to feel better than others. I had allowed my emotions to dictate my actions. I completely underestimated the gravity of that situation, and that humbling realization brought a newly profound sense of responsibility.

In the two years since, it feels as though that incident has aged me. Now, whenever I sit behind the wheel, I’ve come to embrace a sense of calm. It is remarkable how the act of overtaking, something I’ve done dozens of times, turned into such a crucial experience for me. I feel a constant sense of responsibility, to myself and to others around me. I realized that overconfidence, which feels empowering, can quickly lead to recklessness if left unchecked. I realized I need to learn how to control my emotions and set aside my ego to make the right choices. I’ve been plagued countless times by thoughts such as “I cannot study today” or “missing one swim practice won’t hurt.” Truthfully, I knew I wasn’t good enough to miss studying or practice. Before I would have given in to the temptation of short-term dopamine, but with my newfound resolve, I looked past the short-term benefits to think long term. My self-control has given me the ability to do what needs to be done, and to forgo my emotional impulses. I have a schedule, the week planned out. No matter what I feel, whether I want to do it or not, I have developed a sense of duty, a personal responsibility to do it and do it well.

Although I am still not perfect, I have learned invaluable lessons on self-control and responsibility. Now I finally feel ready to take over my mom’s role, to drive and navigate the frozen icy roads myself.

Early Sunday morning, as I anxiously waited for my phone to ring, my heart pounded in my chest and my hands shook. My thoughts raced and I could picture the neurons in my brain firing at lightning speed. I had been anticipating this call for months, yet I was still questioning whether I was ready to answer the call.

Ring! I was momentarily paralyzed, debating whether I should let the next responder answer. 
“(Name) Crisis Hotline, this is (name) speaking, how may I help you?” I held my breath as I waited for the response of my first caller. I had enthusiastically pursued the opportunity to become a crisis center responder, envisioning myself skillfully using the power of words and conversation to heal people during their desperate times. 
I could hear breathing on the other line, but no words. I rushed to fill the silence with the befriending techniques I had learned, extending a warm greeting and an invitation to talk about any topic. 
“James” eventually opened up with a stream of family problems. His somber demeanor devolved into scorn when I did not give him a solution. It was against the hotline's policy to provide direct advice, and I resisted the urge to problem solve with every fiber of my being, feeling muzzled at times. 
"I am so sorry, ‘James.’ I wish I could tell you what to do. But I am here to listen and offer additional resources if you need them," I feebly consoled. 
Silence followed. The line disconnected. James had hung up. 
Disappointedly, I typed a call report, filing the document into a shared database filled with thousands of previous caller files. I was a drop in the ocean, a pebble on a mountain, a single isolated neuron with no impact. What use was I to callers? 
Then “Steve,” a cancer patient, called. I was startled by the volume of his voice. He spoke loudly, quickly, and angrily. He launched into a frenzy talking about the problems in his life, his voice trembling with agitation as he jumped from topic to topic.
I struggled to find the right words to comfort him, weighed down by the gravity of the situation. As I internally questioned my effectiveness to callers at their time of crisis, “Steve” continued his seemingly unrelated tangents. I responded sincerely with affirmation and validation, but mostly, silent reflection and risk assessment. As our call continued, I noticed the volume of his voice shift lower, and he became melancholy. At the end of what was my longest call, “Steve” thanked me for listening and said, “I will be okay.” 
His call impacted me more than he would ever realize. I then understood the wisdom of Samaritan’s focus on active listening and connectedness. Just as neurons have more dendritic receptors for sensing input than axons for creating output, I listened more than I spoke to "Steve. I had made an asymmetric connection.

I thought about “Steve” as I sat on my research laboratory bench. I stared mesmerized at the neurons dancing on the computer monitor. Every fiery bright light represented electrical impulses transmitted from neuron to neuron, forming a circuit of interconnected neural communities. Each neuron would be rendered useless in isolation, but were powerful through interactions with others. The neurons and patterns of activation were not uniform and repetitive: they were different and dynamic, a result of asymmetric connections. 
It is easy to quantify the effects of words as I continue to use my voice to advocate for mental wellbeing, but what is not so apparent are the effects of listening that promote connectedness and understanding. “Steve” and other callers showed me that the greatest impact is generated through the delicate balance of listening and speaking.

Most don’t remember their first shared meal with their mother. But I do—vividly. I was eight. It was a steamed pork bun from the Seven-Eleven at Narita Airport. After years in an orphanage in Korea, my Korean mother finally came back to me. She had left me to work alone in Japan, she said, to earn enough to give me a better life. As I chewed the bun, warm and soft, I noticed her uneaten one sitting in her lap. I didn’t know it then, but her fear of food had shaped her for years.

By ten, I was cooking for both of us–morning, lunch box, dinner–out of necessity and love. Meals became experiments: twenty kinds of salads where spinach hid rice, carrots became flowers, and daikon-wrapped ground pork. Yet, every effort came with a sense of helplessness, a recognition that her struggle wasn't something I could solve in the kitchen. Anorexia, I learned through quiet observation, was a battle fought deep within the mind, rooted in trauma and fear.

My mother’s battle with anorexia taught me early on that psychological disorders are not just personal struggles; they are societal challenges shrouded in silence. I wanted to help her and others like her. But as I searched for available therapies, I realized that they fell short, treating symptoms without addressing the underlying fear-conditioning in the brain. I began to wonder: What if we could disrupt this fear at its core? At sixteen, I set a personal mission to create an EEG-based neurofeedback to treat anorexia. Without mentors, funding, programming skill, or fluent English, I armed myself with determination, an Oxford Dictionary, a 975-page Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain, and a second-hand Fujitsu laptop.

Late nights became my classroom. I taught myself to code using Harvard’s CS50 course and scraped together equipment from openEEG and Arduino. I soldered EEG, HR, and GSR amplifiers and assembled electrodes, feeling like an explorer. The first time I recorded brain signals and decoded emotion with my custom AI, I was overwhelmed—proof that even the most invisible battles could one day be healed.

My first prototype trained the brain to rewire fear responses. It wasn’t perfect, but with support from Dr. Yoshida at Tokyo University and national recognition for my work, this project grew into a published study.

Through this project, I have come to deeply believe in the power of neuroengineering. This drives my continued work on EEG-related scientific research, as I strive to create tools that address a spectrum of psychological disorders.

But even as I gained accolades, I realized that science alone can’t create change.

In my rural Japanese town, conversations about mental health were clouded by stigma and avoidance. I decided to change that. I began holding talks at schools and adult daycare centers. Initially, I was met with rejection. But gradually, schools and daycare centers started to invite me. They were moments of connection, where parents opened up about their fears for the first time, and children learned to empathize with friends silently carrying invisible burdens. Watching a community awaken was as transformative as building my neurofeedback, and I hope to create the same at University.

Today, my mother eats with me again. Through love and the neurofeedback system I built, she overcame her fear of food.

Reflecting back, I now see my mother not only as my greatest guide but as my first challenge. Her battle with anorexia forced me, as a child, to grapple with fear—ultimately igniting the resilience and ingenuity that define me today. Society glorifies parenthood as endless sacrifice and perfect model, yet it is through the adversity parents inadvertently create that children uncover their strength. To the child I was, wondering in the orphanage if I was worthy: you are. Your mother returned, and from those struggles, you rose—not just worthy but extraordinary, shaping tools to heal others and mastering a killer daikon-wrapped pork recipe along the way.

“You’re not ready.”

Those three words struck me harder than any punch I had ever taken. After months of relentless training–countless hours fine-tuning basic four-punch combinations and unraveling intricate jiu-jitsu grappling techniques–I thought I was finally prepared for my black belt test. Yet my Sensei’s three simple words stopped me cold, spoken as casually as describing the color of my uniform. For years, I believed that sheer perseverance through every challenge was enough to overcome any obstacle. But, when it mattered most, my perseverance did not suffice. For the first time, I felt stuck. How could all those years of training and pushing through lead to nothing?

As I lay awake in the comfort of my room laying on my bed, my gaze wandered to the Formula 1 car silhouette hanging above my headboard. I thought of the races I had spent countless hours watching: each team operates by analyzing laps to the millisecond, weighing the trade-offs between three to four pit stop strategies and five distinct tire compounds, and adjusting plans accordingly. They don't blindly persevere through their roadblocks; they adapt and pivot to different strategies—informed by performance history and specific future objectives—to improve race pace.

F1 had revealed that brute force without a strategy wouldn’t succeed. Could I adopt the same methods? I realized I needed to shift my approach; I needed to combine perseverance with detailed strategies to train effectively.

With this new perspective, I approached training like an F1 team fine-tuning their car for optimal performance. Every hour I spent training was now focused on strategy; it wasn't just about maximizing my hours; I had intent and a plan.

I began with my roundhouse kick, dissecting the motion to identify the improvements. A slight adjustment rotating my hips a fraction of second earlier with the pivot of my foot generated a newfound speed and power. Encouraged, I turned to improving my grappling technique. Consulting my sensei like a driver relies on his race engineer, I asked for his feedback. He said that I hesitate when transitioning to a takedown, so I experimented by adjusting my foot placement–but it only worsened the maneuver. I found myself fumbling and getting pinned. Stepping back, I paused to strategize, perhaps shifting my weight to the balls of my feet to be more explosive and changing the takedown angle could improve my takedowns. After implementing these changes, I noticed smoother, well-controlled grappling entries.

When the 2024 black belt test arrived, I experienced a readiness that was as mental as it was physical. This time, my mind and body worked in harmony, and I was confident that my approach had significantly improved my skills. My Sensei’s nod of approval carried a weight that no words could match. It was an unspoken affirmation: You are ready. I went on to earn my black belt, not just through determination, but by tailoring each move to every challenge I faced.

The more I developed and honed my jiu-jitsu skills, the more I noticed how the benefits of strategy and precision began shaping other aspects of my life. Initially, in my financial real estate internship, I approached property owners in mortgage foreclosure with a standard pitch, offering a broad explanation of why working with our company was a good opportunity. But much like in jiu-jitsu where a calculated adjustment can shift the outcome of a match, I needed to shift my approach to be tailored to customer needs. Instead of relying on one-size-fits-all outreach, I studied each property mortgage foreclosure situation and created customized strategies that emphasized financial investment solutions assigned with their specific circumstances. This mindset, honed through the discipline of MMA, became the cornerstone of how I tackle challenges.

Now, the F1 car silhouette and black belt plaque on my walls hold a deeper significance. They serve as reminders that true growth demands a balance of endurance, strategy, and adaptability—not just one in isolation.

150 marks, 16 long forms, and 23 calls home: My stat line across 13 years of education. I am a talker—the most criminal quality a student could have. My early elementary school days often involved the shameful trudge of placing my behavioral folder in the teacher’s bin to be marked with the details of my latest disruptions. Whether I was blurting answers or asking questions without raising my hand, each teacher viewed what I thought was curiosity as an annoyance. The harder I tried to restrain myself, the more my chatty impulses kicked in. For years, I felt ashamed that I did not fit the mold. I saw silence as the standard for success and my talkativeness as a flaw.

Entering high school, my voice changed—not just in pitch but in purpose. The enthusiasm that had once defined me as "the talker" started to fade as I became more aware that the world seemed to reward quiet, disciplined learners. I tried to mute myself, hoping to erase my reputation as a disruptor.

Yet I constantly found myself struggling to hold it in on the tennis court. During a particularly brutal practice match, after my third double fault, Andy—our senior captain—approached my court. He didn't offer the usual empty encouragement. Instead, he shared the story of his sophomore year, how he would often lose control during matches, throwing rackets and snapping at teammates when his emotions got the best of him. As we practiced serves in the fading afternoon light, his words carved a path through my self-doubt. Andy’s guidance taught me that sometimes all it takes is a voice willing to reach out—and I wanted my voice to have that same positive impact on others.

So, I stopped trying to silence myself and instead tried to direct my voice towards my classmates. Any person I found myself with, I attempted to befriend. In biology, conversations with my lab partner often turned to his passion for soccer. Our English reading group dove into debates on current political issues, while in math, my tablemate and I would brainstorm different career paths. Beyond school, I took this approach with me everywhere—whether sparking a conversation with an opponent on the tennis court or sharing insights with family friends at our occasional get-togethers.

In theory, these conversations with my peers should have been a place to channel my classroom insights. However, instead of blurting out the first thought that came to mind, I found myself leaning into thoughtful inquiry. If we were discussing their vacation, I would ask about the cultural aspects they experienced, or if they were detailing their career goals, we would explore the passion behind these goals. Each question prompted our discussion beyond typical small talk, drawing us closer.

For most of my life, talking has been instinctive, a need as basic as breathing. I filled every silence with words, every pause with thoughts spilling over, my voice constantly seeking to be heard. It is through these insightful conversations that I have learned to create a space where the people I talk to feel valued and share a part of themselves they might not otherwise reveal. As a child, I was not just looking for an audience; I was searching for shared understanding and a sense of belonging.

150 marks, 16 long forms, and 23 calls home later; I am still labeled as “the talker.” But now, I see those marks not as failures but as milestones of growth. My voice has found its purpose—not just in expressing myself but in creating a space where others feel comfortable to share and connect.

While I may still be a talker, I have come to realize that the most powerful part of my voice lies in the silence it allows for others.

“Unmonitored fish populations can destroy our ecosystems.”

Shocked, I leaned back in my chair. The news article described how goldfish and koi dumped in local ponds could lay hundreds of thousands of eggs, reproducing at a rate that could eradicate native species.

Earlier that overcast Saturday, I’d walked by a retention pond and noticed small red dots moving below the surface. My shoes sank into the damp soil as I curiously stepped closer to investigate. Surprisingly, the dots were goldfish. “Where did they come from? No way they are native,” I told my friend.

Seeing those “red dots,” my thoughts went back to my childhood when grandpa took me to catch minnows with leftover bread and bring them home as pets. Memories like those drive me to find a solution—quickly, I returned to the pond with a fish net, caught a few goldfish, felt their slimy bodies in my grasp, and smiled. Shortly after the excitement, I realized the pond was too big—these catches wouldn’t make a difference.

I started contemplating why fish were dumped in the first place. After scrolling through numerous articles, forums, and videos, the picture became clear. Many shared my alarm, emphasizing how the problem was rooted in pet owners who opted to release fish as a humane way to dispose of them.

Naturally, as a fish enthusiast, I brainstormed a solution: I could adopt these unwanted fish. Eager to get started, I ordered the necessary aquarium supplies: tanks, heaters, aerators, substrates, and sponge filters, followed by pictures of my setup on Craigslist to promote the free adoption service: Aquadop.

Within the first week, I got four responses. With the first adoption at 30 miles away, doubts crept in: Will he show up? Is the fish healthy? But as Bill, a middle-aged man in a white hoodie, introduced me to the fish family—50 colorful plecos and guppies in a 20-gallon tank—excitement quickly vanquished my apprehension. After moving the tank to my trunk, with a mixture of gratitude and anxiety in his voice, Bill shared how he’d been worrying about what to do with the fish amid his upcoming move, and that I solved his problem.

After several successful adoptions, my tanks began to get crowded. To make matters worse, guppies started breeding. After witnessing two male plecos fight for territory, I realized that offloading some fish would be necessary to make the adoption sustainable.

With a mindset shaped by early ventures—like trading paintings for mechanical pencils and earning income on YouTube by streaming Pokémon gameplay through a self-coded Arduino—it felt natural to offload the fish through a business channel. I started by researching local fish stocks and prices, aiming my prices at 50% of the market, where the margin is still healthy as my fish sources are free adoption and in-house breeding. Craigslist brought me several transactions, but the inventory needed to move faster. Conversations with fellow fish enthusiasts led me to a fish-selling group on Facebook. There, I actively answered questions from other members, attaining the “top contributor” badge. This community allowed me to make constant sales while replenishing stocks through ongoing adoption and breeding efforts.

Through countless ads, promotions, texts, calls, pickups, and deliveries, I practiced marketing, negotiation, and sales skills in real-world situations. In time, these skills seemingly translated into my service with International Buddy, a non-profit dedicated to helping neurodivergent children. I developed marketing posters and promotions to recruit new volunteers, negotiated a free ski field and 25% equipment discount for ski camps, and applied sales skills to raise $5,000 in collaboration with my team at Microsoft fundraisers.

Since that gloomy Saturday at the pond, I’ve adopted hundreds of fish while sustaining the business through constant revenue, all to help stop more “red dots” from being released. In college, I’ll explore new ways to use my entrepreneurial drive to make positive impacts, beyond my local ecosystem.

Winter had just begun, and New York City’s Union Square Subway Station pulsed with life. Home for Christmas, I decided to sing for an audience of strangers for the first time. For years, I’d kept my voice to myself previously, but today, I wanted to push beyond that comfort zone and share what I had long cultivated.

My hands shook as I readied my equipment. Commuters surged around me, and I still hadn’t chosen my song. Charlie Puth or Jay Chou? Instinctively, I leaned toward Charlie Puth, the familiar American artist, but fearing imperfection, I chose Jay Chou. The Chinese lyrics would mask any flaws for my American audience.

I began to sing, the notes spilling out as the lyrics brought a feeling of home. I turned up the volume, letting my voice swell as it did in the privacy of my dorm room. A woman in an elegant white jacket leaned against the wall, eyes closed, swaying to the rhythm. After the third song, she approached me. My heart clenched, unsure.

“These songs are so beautiful,” she said softly, with a genuine warmth. “I don’t understand the lyrics, but the melodies—they’re moving.” She reached into her bag, pulling out a twenty-dollar bill, a bag of chips, and a soda. “This is all I have, but your voice deserves more.”

In that moment, the world felt smaller, more intimate, and I smiled, thinking of my songs—the ones I’d never shared, too raw, too uncertain. Peers had labeled my compositions “not hip-hop enough” or “not mandopop enough,” leaving me unsure. But her kindness emboldened me, affirming that music can transcend language. I started singing No One to Confide In, a song born of loneliness, far from my family. A Dominican couple approached me, their expressions soft as they enjoyed the melody. Their quiet appreciation reminded me that my music didn’t need to fit a genre—it simply needed to connect.

“Could we share a song with you?” they asked, smiling as they joined me. I nodded, searching for their request. Pulsating beats filled the station, and their energy was contagious. Despite not knowing the lyrics, I couldn’t help but ad-lib and join them. Huddled around a single microphone, December’s chilly wind whisked away forgotten lyrics and imperfect pitches, leaving only the joy of a shared moment.

In embracing my homeland’s music, I found the strength to share my voice; in sharing my voice, I connected with others beyond language and background. Music was no longer just mine—it was a bridge, a way to reach strangers. I carried that thought with me, feeling renewed purpose.

That summer, I returned to China and organized a small concert to raise money for teenagers’ mental health in rural areas. I closed the show with No One to Confide In, the melody filling the hall as it had filled Union Square. I saw recognition on audience faces, like I’d seen months before. Smiling, I invited them up. Fifteen people joined, swaying together as I sang:

“There are too many worries, but I have no one to confide in.”

The lyrics spoke of isolation, but in that moment, the weight of loneliness dissolved. We weren’t alone; the music had made us one, united in rhythm, no longer solitary but bound together by sound.

As I left Union Square that day, I knew I wasn’t just singing. I was inviting strangers to pause, to listen, and perhaps recognize something of themselves in my music. I found strength not in perfection, but in openness. From New York’s underground to a concert hall in China, I realized my voice wasn’t simply about music—it was about sharing pieces of myself, risking vulnerability, and narrowing the distances between us through something as simple as a song. My goal isn’t perfection or applause. Instead, it’s the simple hope that offering my voice, even briefly, brings us all a little closer to each other.

There are two types of smiles in this world. Happy Smile is the fan favorite—and rightfully so. But Happy Smile has a lesser-known, frightening brother: Guarded Smile.

Tug up the corners of your mouth. Unless you're beaming from my brilliant introduction, that subtle lift is Guarded Smile—a smile one hides their emotions behind.

So why is Guarded Smile so scary? As an escapee of his grasp, I’ll explain.

Coming home in elementary school to my swollen-eyed mom after arguments with my dad, Guarded Smile was all too familiar to me growing up. Knowing anything but a smile would add to my mom’s worries, I smiled. I smiled when my awkward English-Busan dialect sparked snickers in my Seoul classroom. I smiled alone at lunch, unsure how to fit in. But most importantly, I smiled in front of (and for) my mom.

So every day, I hid my emotions behind my crooked teeth, letting Guarded Smile shield me from genuine connection as long as it kept up the illusion of happiness. But my tennis coach, of all people, had other plans.

"Aditya, [Name], court three." Doubles—not singles—and with my polar opposite at that. Aditya’s loud, expressive personality clashed with my focused intensity. During our first match, I stayed laser-focused while he cracked jokes and laughed off his mistakes, unbothered by whether we won or lost.

But observing Aditya from the safety of Guarded Smile showed me that while my silence held us back, his energy lifted us both. His cheers permeated when we upset heavy favorites West Valley, and again with Ridgeline. Slowly, I started to crack. A cautious high-five after a well-placed shot. A “nice one” during a crucial rally. Aditya’s grin in response felt like a reward, nudging me to keep opening up. I learned that winning a match paled in comparison to laughing with Aditya after he hit me on the head with his serve or strategizing game plans on the bus. Happy Smile was winning me over.

As I grew more confident, poetry became my outlet. Words I’d held inside for years finally found paper. One day, I visited my local coffee shop, Roost, during a live poetry reading event. Inspired by others’ stories about divorce and the death of their daughter, I shared a piece I’d written about the layers of smiles. My hands shook, but I didn’t hide. I spoke with raw honesty, and the small crowd clapped, not because I smiled through it, but because I didn’t.

I was free. But there was still another victim I had to save.

I knew the smile my mom gave me hid untold stories behind her wrinkles. After mustering up courage for months, I finally spilled it all out while making bibimbap together for dinner. I softly asked, “Mom, what makes you sad?” She curled the corners of her mouth at first, but then gingerly began opening up. Slowly, that reflexive smile faded as she explained the loneliness of moving across the Pacific, the struggle to make ends meet, and the guilt of not being able to give me everything she wanted.

We cried that night—deep, wrenching sobs. For the first time, my mom saw my unguarded self. But instead of fear, I felt relief. I hugged her, grateful for a new kind of connection—one rooted in the courage to be vulnerable (together). In that embrace, I knew Guarded Smile no longer stood between us.

If you see me smiling on campus, you’ll know that it's genuine, one I no longer feel the need to hide behind. Whether flying custom-made kites with friends or teaching cadets about aviation, each Happy Smile symbolizes the courage it took to stand on that coffee shop stage. Wrangling Guarded Smile taught me to embrace openness, fueling my current efforts to share Happy Smile with others.

There are still two types of smiles in this world. But for me, now there’s only one.

An inflated head with a Dora the Explorer haircut. Oversized frames. “NERD & Proud of It” emblazoned below. “Did you lose this? It’s at security waiting for you!”, the sentence amplified as I realized the inquiry was sent to the entire pre-college program. It was like having your blazing pink underwear being aired out on a balcony for all to see. But I didn’t lose my underwear, I lost a pin.

Why was I so embarrassed, to the point that I refused to bring myself to the security desk? I dreaded approaching security to say “Hi! I am the one who lost the neon nerd pin and would like to have it back.” I thought this pin completed me. The pin was from a local Asian-owned small business, creating artworks that celebrated the often disparaged parts of being a Bay Area stereotype. Instead, my school prized such stereotypes, as a majority of those around me pursued STEM and devoted themselves to become the next generation of software engineers, neurosurgeons, and developers of world-altering AI.

Inspired by the dedication and pure talent around me, I followed my peers. I wanted to be like my best friends who were a light for girls in STEM, a cardiovascular researcher hoping to cure my mother’s hypertrophic nonobstructive cardiomyopathy, an owner of a glitzy loft by the ripe age of 21, a glowing symbol that proved I won in life. I needed to be that.

Would you jump off a cliff if your friends did too? Although a ridiculous bandwagon fallacy, the leap of faith led to a needed awakening. A 1.5 x 1.5 inch void was erected. I was hollow because the pin was never tailored to me in the first place. From taking classes that did not spark the same glow as learning about Akbar the Great and the eloquence of William Jennings Bryan’s “Cross of Gold” speech or being embarrassed every single time somebody asked me what an oboe was, I ignored what my heart wanted as my head embraced the “safe cliff” of STEM.

My oboe case, bare and pinless, now offered me a fresh canvas, an opportunity to create my own stage. Now, I post videos of me performing pieces that resonate with me, hoping to motivate beginners and showcase that performing is a form of activism. It all started at SFCM’s mini-concerts. Although casual, my chamber group performed a piece I discovered, “Coping”, dedicated to sufferers of anxiety and depression, a topic far from casual. Parents and classmates alike would come up and tell me how intriguing the oboe’s soprano-like voice could convey human thought.

Discarding my pin allowed me to venture outside its rigid archetype. By exploring my heritage through books like Wild Swans: Three Daughters of China to Daughters of the Flower Fragrant Garden, I realized history has shaped me as a woman. My own great-grandmother sold all of her heirlooms and mahogany furniture to feed seven children during the Great Famine. My grandmother hid the existence of my uncle during the One Child Policy, preventing her from raising a family without apprehension.

Powerful women in my family have made me realize that I have no excuse not to do what I truly want even under societal pressure.

I can’t time travel back to my history, but I can mend the disconnect with what I realized from the past. I don’t need a pin, sticker, or label to find meaning in what I devote myself to in life. Now, I am pin-less and free.

You might be wondering if I ever got the pin back? The answer: yes and no. When I asked if I could retrieve my pin, the security guard, with his raised eyebrows in surprise, told me that somebody had already claimed it. Although I never got it back, I like to think that somebody found a better home for my beloved.

The whirring lathe and piercing shrill of a vertical bandsaw couldn’t mask the overlapping chatter of students and mentors speaking unfamiliar jargon. Amidst the mechanical storm filling the tiny portable, I awkwardly held the unfamiliar weight of a drill and squinted through foggy safety glasses to learn the basics of fabrication from a student lead.

I’d heard of the team since a young age, idolizing local newspaper photos of engrossed kids hunched over robots and wielding unfamiliar tools with confidence. And, now, I watched in awe as experienced members flew around the shop in a cloud of sawdust, unpacking CAD models, assembling prototypes, and soldering electrical components.

Whisked into this tornado, long hours of my early training were spent following directions from my mentors and leads. I’d “drill here” and “staple there,” unsure of how everything I was doing truly fit together. I was expected to learn by observing, scrambling to help where I could while hastily picking up bits and pieces of knowledge.

And, at one of these typical meetings, a mentor began by doling out a foreign-sounding list of instructions, something I was certain at least the leads would understand. I looked around for someone to follow - someone who would show me exactly what I needed to do, just as I was accustomed to. Instead, taking me aback, one of these student “experts” raised his hand and asked the question I’d been avoiding: “How do we do that?”

I’d been convinced that asking would make my peers think less of me, but I’d only been masking my weak foundation. Attempting to reach these high standards simply by imitating others, my own fear of judgment blinded an understanding of the larger picture. Through my frazzled attempts at acquiring a displayable list of skills, I was failing to learn the overall process, the knowledge of how things worked and why we needed to do them – all underlying knowledge that would allow me to truly contribute to our team.

Moved by observing an expert confident enough to admit doubt, I began my sophomore year with a new attitude. Though I was a (somewhat) experienced student, I hesitantly and repeatedly glanced toward the new members' training, where they asked questions I remained curious about. Although I wanted to be with the returning students, I felt drawn to listen in and relearn, and so I slowly joined their training. As I quietly asked my own questions, my foggy safety glasses began to clear and the storm quieted.

I soon dedicated myself to get a new feel for the shop, signing up for organization projects and continuing to ask for help as I gained a new understanding of the world around me. I trained (and re-trained) in advanced machinery, finally being the one filling the shop with the lathe’s whirring sounds.

Becoming a lead my junior year, I knew the new members would see me as a confident, talented upperclassmen. Yet, as I set up to demonstrate power tools, I saw my reflection on their cloudy safety glasses and recognized: no matter how much I wanted to be inspirational, I am inevitably still—and always will be—a learner. I am proud of the knowledge I’ve acquired and the skills I’ve demonstrated, but I’ve discovered growth is anything but linear; I’ve gone back and forth, surging ahead and then relearning as needed.

Ready to pass on the weight of the drill, I realized that what any learner needs most is not a perfect role model with a toolkit full of expertise but rather one who remains as eager to learn as they are to lead. Now, as I forge my way closer to the eye of the storm, I don’t let the clouds fill the path behind me. When I stumble, fall, and ask for help, I hope everyone else starting their journey sees too.

When my family visits, the nursing home air feels as stagnant as time itself. We came bearing boxes of homemade cooking since my grandparents disliked the Western taste of the cafeteria food. There was once a time when the two of them would meet us at the door, brimming with questions about our lives. My grandma, in particular, loved to ask, “[Name], when will you dance for me?” But during the pandemic, she passed, and my promise to dance for her remained unfulfilled. We still visit my grandfather, but now he stays by the TV as if he doesn’t have energy for much else. Only a sterile chill lingers in the empty doorway.

Family is irrevocably tied to my dance because I specialize in the traditional Chinese style. But in the competitive circuit, each scratch of pens on rubrics reduces me to a number, inevitably stripping away my connection to the dance. There is rarely a separate category at competitions for cultural styles, so I usually compete in the “Open” category. And if I want to win, I have to twist my art to fit their requirements. For example, my teacher would say the most important thing about Chinese dance is to express deep emotions through your quality of movement and facial expressions. But in competition, doing tricks earns you more points. So, I alter my routines to include techniques that aren’t native to Chinese tradition, and my reward is feeling like I’m already singled out when I wait alone in my traditional costume during awards, long before my name is even called out.

This past Chinese New Year, I found myself on a new “stage” at the nursing home, surrounded by folded tables and misplaced chairs. I lined up with the other volunteer performers by the cafeteria wall, but there was no competitive pressure. Just dingy tiles and quiet, attentive eyes.

When my turn came, I found myself finally able to let go when performing. This dance was only about me, the music, and the story I was telling. My dance ran free from the walls of checked boxes. I adjusted movements to avoid colliding with furniture and the crowd, but these changes didn’t feel like sacrifices. Before a primarily non-Chinese audience, each of my motions told of an unfamiliar time and place. I reached for their hearts while sharing a glimpse of my Chinese heritage. This performance was the only way I could try to fulfill my promise to my grandma now. I wasn’t performing alone. I was sharing a piece of us.

Applause erupted through the cafeteria as the music came to a close, echoing off the walls that warmed the seemingly expanding room. I caught sight of my grandpa, his face alight with joy and pride. Before I could go to him, the audience surged forward to meet me, aged faces exclaiming with wonder and asking me more questions about the meaning of my dance. On that makeshift stage, I felt like the nursing home was a little warmer, a little more lively with the echoes of music and applause.

Dance had served as a language that transcended barriers and spoke directly to the heart, achieving what words couldn’t. This performance meant more than any trophy ever could; it was about connecting with people, bringing joy to those who matter most, and creating a space for my story when none existed. If I could truly move people, this was the legacy I want to build—not of accolades, but of connection.

My grandpa is at the age when words have long since escaped him. But I remember he would often tell me, “Remember who you are.” These are the words behind my answer that day: “Dāngrán”—of course.

Cancer is a term known by many, yet fully understood by few. I am one of the unfortunate. My father, diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer, granted me this fate.
