I spent many sleepless nights in a chilling hospital room, with the dim lights that flickered being my sole company. On a couch-turned bed, I spent my early youth trying to learn.

Amidst my boredom in the hospital, I stumbled upon a language that enamored me. The language of mathematics spoke to me in ways I never thought possible. Its beauty hid behind a wall of complexity, compelling me to uncover its secrets. While uncovering its beauty its complex surface masked the complexities of my own life.

Fond of both my father and math, I found a way to combine the two through the path of an engineer. An engineer who would integrate his love for mathematics and a passion for the betterment of society as well as the world. But, I couldn't focus on the world just yet. Trying to be a better caretaker for my father, I sought knowledge in health science. I learned the basics of CPR and other life-saving techniques. However, knowledge is nothing without the experience to put it into action. So when the faithful night came to make use of it, I could only sit and watch my efforts be of no avail, as the life of my father slowly slipped away from my hands. With my father's passing, I didn’t know where to continue. He was my vision, my mural, and I was left blind without a canvas to paint on. I had aimed for success so that he would be proud. Yet, despite having missed me growing up and not fully grasping what I sought, he had already been proud of the person I was striving to be.

Conversations about colleges came and went. His response always being “If it helps you in life, go for it, I’ll be proud of you regardless.” However, he always hid his fear of being abandoned so as to not burden my conscience. Yet, he left me before I ever could. As I carried him to his grave, I wore the necklace he had prided himself on. A heirloom that was meant to be passed down after every son’s graduation. Despite having yet to graduate, I wear it to symbolize my past. The hours I worked to earn money so we wouldn’t struggle as much, the days I would spend in hospitals taking care of him. Like engineers, who get their rings to remember the power they hold, I wear it as my symbol, not of power, but of those I carry with me as I pursue my goals.

His death only pushed me further in the pursuit of my goal. The goal of using the language that I love so dearly for the creation of something innovative, and unique. He, despite not having been there fully for me due to his condition, has made me the person I am today. Because, while he wasn't there fully, he was still always present in the back of my mind, as he was the reason I was willing to wake up and fight every day. Even now, he stands by me watching me pursue my goal of using my love for math for the betterment of society. Whether that be to lay a foundation for someone else to build upon, or to solve a complex problem it doesn’t matter. So long as the betterment of society and people is there, my father and I will stand together proud. Because where I am, he is, for his blood flows through my veins, and like him, I won't give up until I achieve my goal.

Every afternoon in Ethiopia, the rich, earthy aroma of freshly roasted coffee beans fills the air. Outside the open windows, my family gathers around the scent’s source, not just for a drink but for a shared moment of connection, wisdom, and community. Yet, in this familiar setting, surrounded by my people in my homeland, I felt out of place.

During our summer visit, I watched in awe as my younger cousins effortlessly conversed in our family's native tongue, wishing I could do the same. Even my own mother conversed with her relatives with ease while I remained on the sidelines. What was initially a cherished gathering now reminded me of my linguistic shortcomings. Each word I found perplexing, each joke I didn’t grasp, revealed the connections I was missing out on. Beneath nods and polite smiles, I grappled with my inability to connect. My fear of admitting confusion silenced my questions. I thought about how embarrassing it was to identify as an Ethiopian without understanding Amharic.

On the plane ride home, my thoughts kept returning to the disconnect I felt in Ethiopia. I had been excited to meet my relatives face-to-face, confident that it would bridge the gap between us. But physical proximity didn’t give me that satisfaction. I compared the surface-level phone conversations we'd had prior to the complex dialogues I'd heard in Ethiopia. Ironically, sitting in a circle shoulder-to-shoulder with my loved ones only highlighted my estrangement. From this experience, I recognized that language was a bridge to the stories, wisdom, and warmth that people offer. With renewed purpose, I approached my mom once we returned: "Mama, I want to learn Amharic."

Seeing my interest, she enrolled me, where learning Amharic proved extremely challenging. The sentence structure, the unfamiliar script, the pronunciation, and the complex conjugations all felt like hurdles. I would stand in front of the bathroom mirror, recording myself as I repeated phrases, twisting my mouth to match the sounds, yet they never seemed to come out right. My frustrations mirrored my mother’s struggles with English, and I gained a deeper appreciation for her efforts.

Aware of our culture's deep religious roots, I then turned to the Amharic Bibles we kept at home. Comparing the 1962 and 1986 versions, I discovered a discrepancy: “Mama, did you see this?” I pointed to a verse that had changed from "guest on the earth" to "refugee." Intrigued, she joined me, and as we talked, we uncovered that this change represented Ethiopia’s turmoil following the monarchy's fall. This experience brought me closer to my mom, who sought new beginnings in America after the upheaval. It was through inquiry and understanding that the duty to preserve our heritage transformed for me. No longer did it feel imposed upon me; I embraced it.

Transitioning from student to teaching assistant at Nuni’s School of Amharic gives me the platform to explain proverbs like “dir biyabiri anibesa yasiri.” I hold up a ball of cotton, explaining that "dir" refers to thread in the process of being spun. I describe how in Ethiopia, women would sit together, spinning cotton, their conversations weaving through the air, how it’s a communal experience, a way of strengthening social bonds.

“A single thread might seem weak,” I continue, “but when many threads are spun together, they become strong enough to trap a lion.”

Through teaching, I’ve discovered the subtleties of language. It’s more than vocabulary; it’s tradition and experience passed down through generations. I’m lucky to contribute to a movement that encourages others to embrace their cultural roots. This experience helped me realize that my identity is my societal contribution, where I carry with me the rich aroma of Buna and the wisdom of my ancestors. Through their empowerment, I seek to create a future where every voice is heard, every story is told, and every bond is cherished.

I’m a lawyer. Except, my cases reside on 2.25” wide morsels of sticker paper and my opening statements are composed of a white bun, two pickles, and a golden-brown medallion of chicken. The clanging of metal pans on worn countertops calls the courtroom to order as I wage war on the opposing council: growling stomachs.

As an expeditor at Chick-fil-A, my case objective is to ensure speed and accuracy. The routine is rehearsed, exploitatively optimized, and resistant to change. But…what if we could reduce food waste through decreasing speed and increasing intentionality? Could bagging fries separately facilitate more desirable temperatures? My probing nature not only advocates for operational change, but societal as well.

After observing the disconnect between Hollywood’s portrayal of mental illness and unscripted reality, I was eager to fuse my primary form of protest—film—and my devotion to practical social impact. I began the process of discovery, engaging in post-psych-class consultations about schizophrenia with Professor Eik and spending weeks analyzing publications by Bleuler and Skinner. After the scenes were captured, recaptured (pro tip: remember to turn your mic on), and stitched together, my cinematic protest boasted an accurate depiction of mental illness—one that could hopefully begin to reshape public opinion.

***

Amidst the smell of unleaded gasoline and someone’s cacophonous “It’s not a phase, mom” playlist, a silver, 2016 Ford escape identifies two of my Chick-fil-a cinematic universe characters. Every other day, 3PM, Jordan and her daughter are lined up ready to obtain their post-ballet practice meal: three large fries—no salt. Whether it’s rating a new Mexican restaurant’s authenticity or simply remembering their order, each seemingly insignificant interaction has created a patron loyal to more than our waffle-shaped fries.

To claim I’ve never felt embarrassed by holding a job in fast-food would be perjury. Yet, Each time I help a customer to their car through torrential downpour—soggy socks and all—or geek out with a stranger on their Fire Red Jordan 4s, I learn to appreciate my position more. Every customer is an opportunity to redefine public opinion of service workers and, through genuine interactions, slowly shift fast-food culture to something more desirable.

***

Everything, everywhere, all at once: indie filmmaking’s gift to humanity, but also a reliable descriptor of the restaurant at close. As the doors are secured and dubious stains of ketchup (I hope) scrubbed, I double-knot my oversized apron, attiring myself for the great dish crusade. The unassuming dish sink becomes my makeshift think-tank. Between each eviction of unwanted lemon pulp I’m left wondering how fast-service culture has shaped America. How would a federal minimum wage affect the fast food industry? Does tipping culture benefit the working class or disservice it?

These questions often persist, prompting many 2AM searches through literature, YouTube’s uncharted peripheral, and my communities. Whether it’s debating my mom while eating homemade popcorn or sparking conversation by writing a “question of the day” on our setup board at Chick-fil-a, I ensure my pursuit is never deprived of community rebuttals.

***

Most consider service work an obstacle to be overcome—a temporary source of income; however, its contribution to my life has been much more than a paycheck.

With each smile exchanged and sandwich assembled, I’m left wondering why my restaurant, society, and country function the way they do. Sometimes that means being left, wholly unsatisfied, after finding that not all questions come with answers. Yet, the restaurant has also taught me that meaningful change takes time: speed is not the primary objective when bagging chicken nuggets, or when advocating for change in border policy.

I can’t pretend that change will ever be a linear progression, but whether my opposing council presents itself as hunger or inequity, I resolve to push for a better outcome through slow, methodical processes. That is the lens through which I effectuate change, and the methodology I hope to bring to a university campus and the justice system.

Growing up, I loved to draw. But not on paper.

My grandpa is a retired mechanical engineer, and his toolbox was my treasure trove. Waving around metal compasses and vernier calipers, I left my “artist’s signature” wherever I went.

Perhaps out of desperation to rescue the remaining furniture from my vandalism, my grandpa taught me how to draw, and this time, actually on paper. Taking a scrap of newspaper, he drew two overlapping squares and swiftly connected the four pairs of corners. I blinked. Those scattered, unassuming lines were suddenly pulled taut, transforming into something entirely new.

A Cube.

“See? This is ‘Perspective’.” He looked at me gleefully. Like Mr. Square in Abbot’s Flatland suddenly awakening to the dizzying reality of the third dimension, my flat world shattered, and I tumbled “down” the rabbit hole.

With this newfound power of capturing reality on paper, I immersed myself in a perpetual state of observation. Through sketching, I discovered mathematical beauty. Points stretch into lines; lines converge to form planes; and planes fold into a massive, geometrical construct that is the world. I found comfort in the structure that “perspective” offered, and it became the gospel truth I religiously followed.

However, my aesthetic world was shaken to its core when I began learning modern art in school. Impressionism’s daring brushstrokes. Fauvism’s breathtaking colors. But what startled me the most was Picasso’s Cubism.

Despite its name, it was nothing like the cubes my grandpa taught me. One of his most iconic works, Guernica, haphazardly pieced together fractured forms of humans, animals, and abstract shapes simultaneously captured from multiple angles. Why? What about perspective? Confusion sparked curiosity. I brought my pen and A5-sized sketchbook beyond still-life studies into the streets, and I fell in love with urban sketching.

Sitting along Telok Ayer Street in Singapore’s heartland, I often found myself joined by curious children, eager to offer their hilariously blunt opinions of my art. More amused by their innocence than annoyed at their interruption, I’d invite them to add new lines to my drawing as a friendly gesture. These squiggles disrupted the flow of my detailed sketch – floral majolica tiles, phoenix motifs, and intricate woodwork. But it added something else – unfiltered personality. Till now, these bold, expressive strokes remain my most cherished memory from those trips, reminding me that there’s no rule in art, and to always view the world with an open mind.

During my trip to Romania for a physics tournament, our student guide Mihai generously treated us to Mititei – a traditional Romanian barbecue. While my teammates were busy salivating at the savory aroma of sizzling sausages, I hastily sketched the scene. To my surprise, the messy spontaneity of hurried strokes, smudged with flecks of barbecue grease, captured the moment better than a photograph ever could. Mihai and I didn't speak the same language, but a quiet understanding passed between us when he smiled at my drawing. It was then that I realized that art is beyond depicting observations, but conveying emotions that words cannot express.

With time, I’m no longer after the technical precision I once dreamt of attaining. While my scientific instincts urge me to reside within the tower of objectivity built upon firm foundations of theorems and postulates, urban sketching pushed me to look beyond the cyclopean view and appreciate the world with greater sentimentality and sensitivity. Like Cubism, the human experience defies any singular perspective.

Today, lines flow freely, and colors bleed organically across my sketches. Rather than imitating reality with Chiaroscuro or Sfumato, I now craft entirely new worlds within the pages of my sketchbook, where observation, emotion, and imagination coalesce into something far greater than the sum of its parts.

In many ways, Cubism is also me. Grounded yet unorthodox. Logical and imaginative. Composed but chaotic. I hope to carry these lessons I gained from art forward into my scientific endeavor – looking past mere empirical truths and exploring deeper questions about humanity with romance and awe.

A cube will always have six faces, eight vertices, and twelve edges; but there are infinite ways to look at it.

**The child’s heart had a hole between its chambers.**

A pungent metallic odor filled the cool air of the operating room. The vital signs monitor steadily beeped in the background. The cardiac surgeon and his team were preparing to repair a ventricular septal defect – a hole in the tissue that separates the heart’s chambers.

There I was, standing beside the operating bed. I watched nervously as the surgeon made his first incision. I witnessed medical masterclass unfold. A suture here, an incision there, heart tissue in his hand, he expertly manipulated the delicate anatomy, giving the boy a new life.

As he closed the incision, I stood there in awe. It was magic to me, a medical mechanic changing one’s life with his very own hands.

After the surgery, we went to the waiting room to inform the patient’s parents that everything went perfectly. Watching the anxiousness melt off their faces, I felt deeply inspired and compelled by the power of this seemingly magical act for this family. I remember thinking, “What can I do now?”

The next day, I had an opportunity. I watched Dr. Srimanarayana perform EKG tests when he asked me if I wanted to conduct a few under his supervision. Sure! I felt confident with my observations. I firmly placed the color-coded electrodes on different locations of the patient’s body. I looked at the monitor. A crisp line danced across the screen. A joyous smile spread across my face: my debut intro.

**It’s going beautifully. Keep it moving. Wait, what if I mess up under this pressure?**

My piano performance came crashing down. I was playing Invention #8 at my local recital. After that thought, I missed a couple notes. Dissonant sounds pierced the air. I froze, forgetting my place in the piece. I left the bench in shame.

After the performance, I asked my piano teacher how to overcome the pressure of performing. She told me to perform more. I had to face my fear.

Over the following weeks, I played my songs in school, in front of public audiences, and in more recitals. There were occasional mistakes, but my confidence grew from my experience, helping me befriend pressure.

The Dorothy Sutton state recital was approaching fast. I played excellently in the qualifying audition, but the recital had an audience. “I’m gonna cook,” I thought.

Invention #8, performed by [Name] Velaga! My turn. I walked onto the stage, sat on the bench, and started. I trusted myself unconditionally, even when I felt the temptations of pressure. I performed the piece majestically: conflict overcome.

**Nice to meet you Akhi, I’m Leo!**

Leo was the first kid I met as a volunteer coach at Buddy Up Tennis. I remember that every time I taught him basic techniques, he would give me a fist bump and look at me with a sparkle in his eyes. I could see his deep love for tennis.

Leo never let his Down syndrome define him. He gave his best, laughed, and loved every moment. We were like brothers. Our relationship was my favorite part of the program. Buddy Up helped me share my love for tennis and inspired me to continue service. Leo taught me to cherish every gift and every moment: the moral.

My stories are different – from various genres. Each story has helped me develop a key goal, skill, or takeaway.

Meeting those parents in the ICU solidified my desire to pursue a pre-med path at university because I want to dedicate my life to bringing families that same joy. Piano helped me develop the confidence to overcome pressure. Buddy Up Tennis taught me the value of service: both the relationships and the lessons.

As I write this next chapter of my life in college, I’ll bring these lessons with me to make a difference, one story at a time.

I spent most of my childhood summer afternoons in the suburbs of Zaporizhzhya, Ukraine, playing pretend Toy Story with my father in my grandma’s perfectly manicured backyard. I was always Woody, my dad, Buzz Lightyear, and my Grandma, Andy, the person who brought us both into the world, and who gave us such joy. But in the spring of my freshman year in high school, she passed. In just three months, overgrown grass and my father’s countless cigarette butts replaced the laughter that once filled grandma’s backyard. Losing her left an invisible wound on both my father’s and my hearts. However, seeing my dad slip into the cold stages of grief felt like someone was rubbing salt in mine.

My grandmother was conservative, in the typical Ukrainian manner. When I had come home one day in 7th grade, brimming with excitement after learning about psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, she dismissed me, seeing this work as something akin to phrenology. Despite her dislike for psychology, she always encouraged me to help others. So, when my father struggled with grief after her passing, I thought about psychology's healing power more deeply.

I combined hours of independent research on grief with what I’d learned from Kübler-Ross. After-school sessions with my school psychologist also introduced me to narrative therapy—reframing stories to foster healing. Using these insights, I created what I called a “grief support loop” where the act of sharing stories helps the patient break out of the haze of grief. When I initially suggested this to my father, he resisted my support. But, by modeling vulnerability, and shakily opening up about my own experiences first, I got through to him. Loop by loop, my father began to rediscover his happiness, and I found my own. Witnessing his growth empowered me to do the same for others.

Through the online mental health advocacy group I had started sophomore year, I got to know Thomas, a high school student in Nigeria. He confided in me about his stress over disappointing his parents, compounded by the stigma surrounding mental health in his culture. After several hours-long, late-night conversations, we set a goal to host a series of mental health workshops at his school. A month later, with the generous financial support of some people in my school community, and driven by the conviction that mental health support should know no borders, I found myself speaking to 20 eager students in Port Harcourt, Nigeria.

Working with kids tested my patience. Despite weeks of preparation, my workshop was met with incessant fidgeting and watery yawns. A call from the headmaster revealed the real issue: my voice. My accent made the stories feel too Oyinbo—too foreign.

So next time, I encouraged the students to take the lead. As I saw them sharing stories in pairs, I noticed a shift in their attitudes: their voices were kinder, more curious. I felt overwhelmed with pride as they completed their final assignment: a backpack drawing filled with reframed perspectives and experiences. Something that had been so difficult for my father came so naturally to them.

As my time with the students came to an end, I wanted to continue supporting them beyond the workshops. With the help of my school psychologist, I developed an AI chatbot that creates personalized support loops to reframe users’ stories. After months of training the chatbot on different types of data, I shared the web app with the schools. Hearing stories of transformation from school officials, I felt ecstatic with my efforts—but I knew that a web app like this was not enough on its own.

As I move forward, I'm excited to continue blending my love for storytelling and working with diverse voices by becoming a practicing psychologist. With each step, I hope to help others process their stories, guiding them through the plot twists of their lives until they, too, can move to infinity and beyond.

After the usual hour-long piano lesson to satisfy my mom, we’d pull into my favorite place on Earth: Michaels. Drawn by the strange charm of its scent of cloying pine and cinnamon, I’d walk in, eyes lighting up as I scanned through never-ending rows of creative freedom—a maze that I would allow myself to get lost in.

In my youth, I refused to leave Michaels without a gallon of Elmer’s glue from the glue section. Carefully combined with the right ratio of borax to water, the entire gallon would be turned into a delightfully sticky mess: slime. Inspired by the slime stores with 1M+ followers, I made my own account. Starting with @bluefishslimes__123, I began experimenting with types of glues, from clear to wood glue, learning to handle the viscosity and unique features of each glue.

Michaels also had aisles of tiny treasures waiting to be discovered: pom-poms, beads, and even foam balls from the floral section. I was drawn to unexpected combinations. Would it mimic a jar of maraschino cherries if I added red pom-poms to a clear base? Could I embed tiny seashells and sand into a clear slime to recreate a beach? I tested and tweaked, sometimes ending up with spectacular fails—but they were never discouraging, instead invitations to try again, to innovate.

The limitations of the tools at my disposal only made me more resourceful. Without any understanding of how to purchase a domain or start an online store, I turned to Wix, crafting a professional-looking website to “sell” my creations for church donations. I created a logo using the “Insert-Drawing” feature on Google Docs, since I didn’t have apps like Procreate or Adobe Illustrator for graphic design. I organized the slimes I’d “sell” on a Doc, priding myself on my ability to come up with innovative designs I’d never seen on the Instagram of famous slime stores. Each creation was a mini science experiment crossed with art, a tangible manifestation of my curiosity and drive to create.

This creative experimentation extended beyond the medium of glue. More recently, I revisited Michaels, but with a focus on the styrofoam section.

On my walks to the subway station by my house, I would pass a group of stray cats lounging in a nearby parking lot. In the summer months, they basked contentedly on the sun-warmed asphalt, their bellies exposed to the gentle heat. But as winter approached, the group dwindled, and the cats I did see would be huddled in the corners of buildings, hiding from the biting wind and snow.

Coming home to my cat, purring contentedly and spread across my bed in blissful warmth, I couldn’t stop thinking about the strays enduring below-freezing temperatures. So, armed with determination and a little creativity, I set out to build shelters for them.

I began with materials I had at home: cardboard boxes for structure, duct tape and garbage bags to waterproof the exterior, and fabric salvaged from old clothing to provide bedding and insulation. I carefully assembled these makeshift shelters, testing different ways to layer the materials so they could keep out rain and trap warmth. Still, they felt too flimsy to withstand the brutal New York winter. I researched insulation materials and discovered that styrofoam was both lightweight and excellent at retaining heat. After a quick trip to Michaels, I lined the interiors of the boxes with styrofoam to create an insulating layer. I then experimented with the materials to make the shelters both sturdy and unobtrusive—something that would blend in with the urban environment to avoid attracting attention from passersby but still provide a safe haven for the cats and keep warmth in.

After setting up the shelters in the corner of the parking lot with the permission of the building’s security, I monitored them over the following weeks, making adjustments based on what I saw. I moved them to areas with better wind protection and left food nearby to attract the cats. The first time I saw a stray slip into one of the shelters, I felt an overwhelming sense of accomplishment.

What began as a childhood fascination with fake flowers, glue, and glitter has grown into a commitment to making, problem-solving, and giving back. Whether I’m building shelters for stray cats or creating art for a non-profit organization’s event, each trip ignites a new spark of inspiration, pushing me to transform ordinary materials into something meaningful. Michaels has always been more than a store to me—it’s where my creativity finds purpose, where curiosity takes shape, and where, amid aisles of possibility, I find myself.

**Essay:**

“Good night Aaron,” I said to my five-year-old brother as we went to bed.

“Good night Aaron,” he echoed back instead of “Good night, Timmy.”

I’d watched movies of siblings adventuring together—building treehouses, playing catch, roughhousing—so I was eager to do the same with my brother, just two years younger. However, it was frustrating when Aaron would seemingly ignore me and turn around to enter his own world. When my parents revealed Aaron’s diagnosis of autism spectrum and ADHD, I wasn’t old enough to understand what those terms meant, but I sensed that something was different about Aaron, and as his older brother, I felt obligated to help him come into his own.

Aaron’s learning disabilities led to struggles with his schoolwork. Since I had already learned the material, I offered to help with his fractions homework. To me, it was clear: You take the bottom right and top left and add it to bottom left and top right all over the bottoms multiplied. It was simple in my head; I didn’t get how Aaron couldn't understand it. My early study sessions with Aaron often ended with me impatient and exasperated, storming to my room and leaving my mom to finish the job.

My mom’s patience and malleability in her way of working with Aaron contrasted with my one-dimensional teaching method. Despite her difficulty with English and caring for three kids, her patience shone through. She slowly worked through each step with Aaron, backtracking when needed and molding his path to the answer in a way he would understand. Over time, I attempted to learn and emulate these elements that provided such success with Aaron: her patience and versatile teaching methods and understanding of others’ perspectives.

Given how different each subject can be, I knew Aaron required different methods for studying each. Through much trial-and-error and observations over time, I’ve developed approaches unique to him. With math, I can work through a parallel problem with him, and he’ll be set. In science, mere definitions don’t work. We have to work out the different relationships and interactions between systems—like cell organelles. And in ELA, we have to slow it down and work through each scene in a book individually. Sometimes, my new methods don’t work, but I know with different approaches, I can slowly reach an answer with Aaron.

Swimming is a sport that especially demands a personalized approach for each swimmer. Everyone’s bodies are so different, and working through a foreign medium—water—only heightens those differences. I’ve experienced this firsthand. As a swimmer for over ten years, I’ve journeyed through different stroke techniques and training approaches, taking what works for me and ultimately refining my training program to what it is today. I’ve taken the perspectives I learned through my own journey to others. As a swim coach, I enjoy taking a struggling swimmer aside and teaching them something meaningful—something they wouldn't be able to figure out on their own. During swim lessons, I love the challenge of translating a concept so simple to me yet foreign to them into something comprehensible by a five-year-old: “shoot your arm out like Superman,” or “lay your head back like you’re cloud watching.”

Today, Aaron continues to struggle, but he is learning to grapple with challenges independently. I’m grateful to him and my mother for the patience and perseverance I’ve come to accrue from watching and helping him develop. I’ve learned the most meaningful way of assisting others is by guiding them to an answer they’d otherwise be unable to reach on their own. In college, I hope to be elevated by others and learn to solve more complex problems, whether it be helping a classmate out or coaching the next Olympic swimmer.

With a Barbie Car clutched in one hand and a tower fan in the other, I pedaled the six-mile journey home on my bike, my grip slipping with every bump on the road. To any bystander, I looked pretty ridiculous. Here I was, a scrawny twelve-year-old lugging broken-down appliances nearly as tall as himself, just one wrong move away from crashing into a car. Despite the humiliating stares, I inched forward one revolution at a time, reminding myself that beneath the rust-speckled surface of the junk were hidden treasures waiting to be rediscovered.

Once I finally arrived home, I would dive into the mechanical carcasses, carefully popping out each security screw and prying open the plastic gussets to reach the scrumptious mechanisms inside—in this case, the high-torque motors I needed for a robot arm’s rotating base. This weekend routine of scouring for free listings was far from easy, but in the first two years of tinkering, it was what fueled my passion through a period where I lacked financial resources. Deep down, I loathed these restraints. I yearned to construct something beyond salvaged materials, freed from the shackles of money and resources.

In high school, local makerspaces, the robotics garage, and even my friend’s financial support suddenly granted me these resources. My wish had come true, yet a void lingered: something felt … off. My projects had evolved in complexity, but they felt hollow and devoid of substance inside, almost less personal.

I couldn’t quite pinpoint why this was until I launched STEM Without Borders, an initiative where I spent countless weekends prototyping, manufacturing, and packaging STEM kits for underprivileged communities across the globe. I had initially created it after witnessing the deep disparity in opportunities when mentoring FIRST teams in Lesotho, Africa, and it became a way for me to share something I loved with those who may not be lucky enough to experience it. Since launching, I’ve expanded STEM Without Borders to four countries and nearly ten local nonprofits, reaching hundreds of students worldwide. Having delivered dozens of interactive lessons, I was delighted to see that I could help kids develop an interest in STEM, but unexpectedly, they imparted something equally valuable to me.

Each week, I witnessed my kits morph into innovations beyond my original intent, shaped by the experiences and creativity of the children who used them. Kids from under-resourced SF neighborhoods adapted the circuit components from depth-sensing cars to make practical sensor-activated floor lights. Children with autism reconfigured planetary gear kits, finding calm in their predictable rotations. These kids had been able to innovate in situations far more restrictive than mine, whether it was monetarily, psychologically, or even physically. Despite all their hurdles, they came out of it stronger, tougher, and more vibrant than they were before.

I began to understand what had been missing in my creations. It turns out my scrappy, idiosyncratic beginnings were never liabilities. Scarcity had forced me to think on my feet, envisioning how each odd piece fit into the puzzle of my project. Each appliance I’d torn apart, from the circuitry of a microwave to the layers of a monitor, left behind a blueprint for my own designs. While I finally gained access to resources I’d only dreamed of, the creative thrill of fabricating a piece from eclectic parts seemed to diminish. With this realization, I dusted off the hot glue gun in the corner of my closet and pieced together something unrefined yet full of a unique essence—something that can’t be found anywhere else. Something that finally felt like home.

Moving into college, I’ll carry this lesson forward, recognizing that challenges along the way are only molds that shape my identity and craft. As I pedal across campus, seeking out these new experiences, I’ll remember that some of the best journeys start with a wobbly bike and a dream of what could be.

Twist. Peer. Discover. A burst of colors flooded my vision, and for a moment, the world felt like magic. I was eight, sitting cross-legged on my bedroom floor, my heart pounding as I peered into my most treasured possession. An enigma of endless possibilities contained in one tiny tube. A kaleidoscope.

Just hours earlier, my workspace had been a delightful chaos of materials. Empty toilet paper rolls leaned haphazardly against a small mound of colorful plastic beads, while shards of a broken vanity mirror glinted under the warm glow of the overhead light. Shadows flitted across the table as I eagerly began to assemble the pieces. Little did I know, this homemade creation would become a lens into my world, each twist revealing layers I was only beginning to understand.

As I meticulously arranged the tiny glass shards into an imperfect triangular prism, I began constructing the core of my kaleidoscope. Bhubaneswar, India—the city where my journey began, where my parents' roots run deep under the foundation of my early years. Here, I cultivated my identity amidst vibrant cultural diversity and the realities of societal adversity. Yet, I found beauty within every corner; within the resilience and spirit of those around me. From the young children, to whom I taught math and science, to my father working until the depths of the night to support his family. From my passionate Bollywood dance teacher to my daily optometry patients. Each interaction became a fragment, a mirror reflecting the lives I encountered, coming together to form the core of my character.

With each chemical reaction explained in Odia, I grew to cherish the endless questions, each one a spark of curiosity ignited by dedication and persistence. With every night, the soft rhythm of my father’s fingers clacking on the keyboard filled the room, echoing the power of love in the tireless efforts of an overworked parent. With every dance step that flowed through me; each pair of gleaming eyes followed by a radiant smile post-eye exam, I found how passion could bring joy and breathe life into every moment. I crafted my identity piece by piece, using my experiences from India.

As I dropped the mismatched beads into the kaleidoscope, I marveled at how they shifted and intertwined, revealing dazzling mosaics of light and color. My childhood unfolded as a series of choices that felt both significant and inconsequential at the time. Would I spend the afternoon in the kitchen, attempting to caramelize balsamic vinegar over roasted strawberries? Or lost in the charcoal smudges on my canvas, chasing the fleeting sensation of bringing something intangible to life? I once thought I had to choose—science or art, experiments or expression—constantly worrying I would have to abandon one passion for the other. But over time, I realized that each fascination, whether it lasted a moment or stretched over years, left a mark, adding a gem to my growing collection. What seemed like unrelated pursuits—beads of various shapes and colors—have gradually intertwined to form something unmistakably my own.

My days of trial and error in the kitchen eventually led to countless hours in my neurobiology lab—another world of curiosity, free to ask endless “what ifs.” As I delicately navigate the layers of the mouse brain, the precision I once honed with a paintbrush transforms into a new form of artistry. The thoughts I once sketched to capture emotion now find a voice in articles advocating for women’s empowerment in the sciences. Each bead I have collected, each distinct lesson learned, continues to shape new patterns and perspectives.

Peering through the kaleidoscope, I realize the true magic lies not in a single, fixed view but in the endless spectrum of shifting patterns that emerge with every turn. As I gather the fragments of my life, I’m eager to uncover the boundless potential and possibilities that come with each moment of discovery, with every twist.

My first kidnapping victim is my best friend. I grab him up in my chubby fingers, imprisoning him in a makeshift jail. With his ironclad body and athletic agility, I want to be just like him. And what better way than to have him all to myself? Sure, Clawde is also encrusted with barnacles and reeks of rotting fish – minor drawbacks. I stole him from his home for six long years, keeping him in a spacious terrarium where he lived a comfortable life. Until the morning he died.

I dress in all black to cremate him in his tinfoil tomb, my grandmother serving as the sole witness (and, honestly, fire warden) to what might have been the world’s first funeral for a crab.

I love crabs. I like the clever, algorithmic way they skitter sideways between ocean and shore in search of food. I’m enraptured, observing their bubbles as they flexed and aerated their gills, allowing them to absorb more oxygen. The underappreciated Turings of the ocean, their carefully engineered burrows give life to entire ecosystems. And yet they’re regarded merely as dinner.

It's Clawde I think of, years later, as I boredly scroll Google News awaiting my morning bus. A headline catches my attention: Tyre dust: the ‘stealth pollutant’ that’s becoming a huge threat to ocean life. The article warns that toxic chemicals shed by tires are washing into waterways, causing mass marine die-offs and threatening keystone species. Tires crunching against gravel snaps me back to reality. The extended-length bus pulls up on no fewer than six tires. Was my route to school secretly destroying the environment?

I open a jStor account and dive into the literature.

I learn that tires annually contribute to over 200,000 tons of microplastics entering the ocean. And that’s just the beginning. The chemical 6PPD, a common rubber stabilizer used since the 1970s, wears off as the tire is used, reacting with ozone to form 6PPD-quinone. It’s like the black plague to sea life, killing indiscriminately - and we’re all unwittingly responsible for spreading it.

Unlike the auto industry, which is governed by strict regulations to limit and reduce emissions, the tire industry is a lawless game. Worse yet, even as vehicle emissions decrease with the uptake of electric vehicles, tire pollution has soared because these ‘green’ cars have greater weight and torque, shredding tires exponentially faster.

And nobody is talking about it.

I establish The Traction Initiative to raise awareness about tire pollution and work towards solutions. I take an internship with a sustainability start-up that uses AI to monitor corporate fleets, ensuring tires are replaced before they become worn out, since weakened tires emit more pollutants. I email Dr. Scholes, a professor of Civil Engineering at UBC who studies contaminants in urban water systems. What can we do?

Look at rain gardens, she advises.

Her research found that these interventive ecosystems can prevent harmful pollutants from entering our marine environment. And – serendipitously – the city has just opened applications to become stewards of local gardens.

We apply, becoming the caretakers to a rain garden a few blocks east of the Knight Street bridge, one of the city’s busiest thoroughfares. We launch a slate of educational programs, helping people understand the threat of tire pollution—and the ways our communities can meet those challenges.

Over this journey I’ve learned about the chemistry of rubber production, the physics of tire wear and torque, the history of environmental regulations, and the future of urban planning. The more I learn, the more I want to learn.

As a kid, I wanted to be just like Clawde. Having an armor-like exoskeleton and claw-hands seemed cool. But standing in the rain garden, hands dirty, wet from the Vancouver rain, I realize I’m more like him than I thought. I’m a builder, a problem solver, a scientist, and a shepherd for my environment, stewarding an ecosystem towards environmental change.

In Korean, chummul means to quietly endure hardships without complaint. My mom raised me to chummul: if something was hard, you pushed through. If something hurt, you didn’t show it. I believed strength meant solving problems on my own and keeping my struggles inside.

That belief changed three days before my budget calculator app was due. My code was broken. I stared at my screen, heart pounding, as error messages flashed like warning lights. I scrolled through line after line, every one of them seeming correct, yet something didn’t work. Hours passed, and my frustration turned into doubt. Maybe I wasn’t good enough to do this. At lunch, the words slipped out before I could stop them: “I’m stuck.” Tom, sitting across from me with Dorito dust still on his fingers, paused mid-bite. “With what?” he asked. My pride screamed at me to stay silent, but desperation was louder. I hesitated, then pushed my laptop toward him. That afternoon, he sat beside me in Informatics class, studying my code. “Ah,” he said, pointing at the screen. “Your input logic doesn’t handle edge cases like 0 or 100.” Relief hit me like a wave, but so did shame. I thought about chummul and how it had stopped me from asking earlier.

Letting someone see my weakness wasn’t easy. It felt uncomfortable, even scary. But it taught me something I hadn’t realized before: strength isn’t about enduring alone. It’s about trusting others to help you when you need it.

A week later, I thought about that moment while mentoring first-generation Hispanic students at Breakthrough. After proposing coding lessons to the director, I led our first workshop. I noticed Jeremy sitting at a corner table, his shoulders slumped, his pencil frozen over his notebook. “Hey,” I said, sitting beside him. “What’s going on?”

He hesitated, then whispered, “I don’t think I belong here. Everyone else is better at coding than me.” His words hit me like a memory of my own voice, staring at my broken code and wondering if I was good enough. I leaned closer. “I know how you feel,” I told him. “Last week, I couldn’t figure out my own code and had to ask for help. That doesn’t mean you don’t belong. It just means you’re learning.”

As we talked, Angel and Mia joined us, sharing their struggles with coding. One by one, other students came over. Soon, our quiet corner became a circle of voices, laughter, and shared stories. I realized that creating a space for others to feel supported was as important as teaching coding itself. It reminded me of how letting go of chummul had helped me move forward.

Studying Informatics: Artificial Intelligence has changed how I solve problems, pushing me to embrace collaboration. Experimenting with AI tools to build predictive models sparked my interest in how machine learning can solve problems. One idea I’m passionate about is creating a financial app that uses AI to analyze spending patterns and help families avoid debt. It would generate personalized savings plans, giving people the tools to build financial stability. Becoming an AI systems engineer will allow me to build algorithms that solve big societal issues while prioritizing fairness.

Whether it’s helping families break out of debt, expanding educational resources globally, or diagnosing diseases more accurately, I want my systems to create opportunities for people who might otherwise be left behind. At university, I imagine debugging code with peers in late-night hackathons, brainstorming ideas with students from diverse backgrounds, and bringing our shared visions to life. I want to develop tools that not only work but truly serve the people who need them most.

When I think back to chummul, I realize my mom’s lesson taught me to endure. But my experiences taught me a new kind of strength: the courage to let others in and build something together. Strength is not about facing challenges alone. It’s about creating systems that empower others to thrive.

Fifty delicate thin mints, neatly packed in parchment, stared back at me as I tied my red and green scouts neckerchief around my collar. Fidgeting, I compulsively straightened my Outdoor Adventure Skills badges.

“You can do it,” my mom encouraged, a warm smile on her face.

Trudging down the sidewalk, beads of sweat condensed on my forehead. The bright summer sun beamed down on my mints, subtly melting the layer of milk chocolate. But that wasn’t the only thing on the verge of melting.

A tornado of doubt tore holes in my confidence. What if I was disturbing them? How long would my cookies last? What if I didn’t have enough change?

“Let’s do this house,” my mom encouraged, her eagerness contrasting with the greenhouse of butterflies fluttering in my stomach.

For the next few hours, I’d go from door to door, attempting to solicit a few dollars for my now sticky mints. Every house would be different. At some, my hesitation was met with impatience, a stutter losing the attention of busy neighbors frantically packing for a flight. At others, gentle grandmothers welcomed a weary salesman with cookies of their own.

On the way up every driveway, I’d count the cookies left. With a face of unease from the anxiety that followed every ring of the doorbell, I’d lose a bit of patience: 45. 32. 27…

By the end of the day, I was left with a puddle of liquid peppermint, sugar, and chocolate in a congealed mess representing 22 thin mints unsold.

Sitting on our front steps in the orange of the sunset, my mom still had an unshakeable sense of optimism. “What’s the matter?” She seemed insensitive to my frustration. “You’ll get it. One day, you’ll be the best cookie seller in town.”

“Right,” I thought. “Sure thing, mom.”

Despite the metaphorical eye-rolling my answer conveyed, I’d be forced to sell many more as I earned my Cub Scout Community Service pins. And as I worked my way down the dizzying variety that was the scouts’ cookie catalog, I’d notice different symptoms of my anxiety disappear. After a day selling oatmeal-raisin, each step down the street would drown out a voice of doubt. Through strawberry sugar, every smile I cracked seemed to smooth out a stutter in my sales pitch. And through chocolate chip, every successful sale would quiet a fluttering butterfly.

With the echo of my mom’s words in my ear, I’d slowly become somewhat of a cookie brokering master. And although my ability to efficiently liquidate a fundraiser’s leftover cookies did impress, the lessons I learned would find their true value beyond the scouts community.

Instead, the cookies I sold would project my voice when I stood at my school door in sixth grade, calling for donations of toques for the homeless shelter in the winter. It would give me the confidence to explain my brutally abstract piece of eighth grade art at a local art show. In the ninth grade, it would give me the bravery to run for student council by setting the aggressive goal of meeting every single person in my grade. And in the eleventh grade, it would give me the drive to call for non-gendered pronouns in my school board’s policy documents.

The biggest gift from my time as a cookie salesman would prove to be the voice that it gave me—the confidence to share what I believed in and inspire others of the causes I valued.

As a natural introvert, that isn’t to say I still don’t want to shrink into a corner at times. As a student trustee, I still feel the same heat of anxiety when I represent 78,000 students to my school board’s board of trustees, my words broadcast to the entire city.

But whenever that happens, I look back on those fifty thin mints, and every cookie I’ve sold since.

“It’s just how it is! You question too much.”

Mr. Park sighed, rubbing his temples. 
“But there must be a reason . . .” 
Furrowing his brows, he asked. 
“What do I always say?”

Reluctantly, I replied—don’t ask, just memorize.

In Korean schools, where exam scores of academic subjects define students, my questions were often seen as pointless. Students sneered when I raised my hand; teachers rolled their eyes at my questions after class. All that mattered was how accurately we filled the blanks with memorized information.

But, why?

Returning home, I opened my laptop. 
G,o,o,g,l,e, Enter. 
As my fingers sprinted across the keyboard, information surged onto the screen, quenching my thirst for answers beyond the A4-sized test sheets.

From a young age, I always enjoyed asking why—I’d question everything, from a math formula to the color of the sky. Everything had a reason, and discovering each one delighted me. Hours flew by as I dived into research; even when 404 Not Found blocked my search and complicated theories gave me headaches, my questions continued in the local library and through documentaries.

When grandma’s diagnosis of diabetes and stroke took over our daily lives, a question arose again. Why us? Grocery shopping together became impossible as her trembling legs kept her at home. Our dining table was now split between flavorful dishes and the bland, minimally seasoned dishes. But this time, no research or documentaries could answer the question.

However, I wasn’t the only one confused. Facing life’s biggest challenges, my grandma’s smile faded, leaving her depressed and lethargic. So instead of discovering answers, I changed my questions—why to how. How can I help her adapt to this new reality? Soon, dance classes to trot music and painting her favorite flowers replaced our grocery trips. To share our meals again, I began creating diabetes-friendly dishes.

Recreating diabetes-friendly recipes wasn’t easy. To tackle the bitter, rubber dough and bland sauce in cream gnocchi, I gathered from food science journals to my 8th-grade Health textbook. If glutinous powder doesn’t work, what about water or yogurt? Maybe kneading less, or boiling longer? Exhausted by mountains of dishes and failed attempts, I still questioned why I failed and how to improve—her illness became less a tragedy but more an opportunity to solve.

Combining why and how, I could create positive changes not only at home but also in others.

While teaching English to disadvantaged students, I met a student who refused to speak; several meetings passed with awkward one-way conversations.

Any questions? Silence. 
I’d love to hear your ideas! Silence. 
Would you try reading the passage? Silence.

Why is she so demotivated? Despite teaching passionately until my throat hurt, her small nods drained my energy. This time, I closed the book and asked her.

What comes to mind when you think of English?

Her answers astonished me: poor grades and incompetence. Constantly falling behind in school but unable to receive additional support, she was discouraged. As her story echoed the rejection I got from Mr. Park, why transformed into how—How can I engage her?

With advice from teachers and friends, I began changing materials and methods monthly, trying to connect her interests to English. Vocabulary cards, learning games, translating movie clips. . . planning and preparing each one took me days.

Finally, one method lit up her eyes—translating songs. Working through the lyrics, I slipped in key grammar and synonyms. Her grades soared; watching her speak every word in confidence compensated for every hour I devoted.

Often, questions don’t have clear answers for why. 
However, I now know that I can make meaningful differences as I focus on how.

I aspire to empower others to overcome their obstacles in health, education, or finances; I hope to create a world where everyone can fully enjoy their daily lives and basic rights.

As I solve problems asking why and how, the world becomes even more intriguing.

On one of the coldest nights of February, I listened as my dad tried to save his company.

I recall the clatter of keyboards, the howl of the wind against the window, and the constant buzz of phone calls that echoed through my father’s office. He was speaking on the phone, although his voice lacked its usual strength and confidence. His glasses were fogged up, and I lost count of how many times he adjusted his posture as he shifted restlessly in his chair.

I couldn’t stand the heavy atmosphere and asked, “Dad, let’s go home and play Madden together.” He hesitated, sighed, and turned to me with weariness and sadness in his eyes. He explained that an IT firm that his company relied on had been locked down by a COVID-19 outbreak. It kept the technicians at home, unable to install the smart locking software for the cloud cabinets on site. His business was operating at a loss, he explained, as pain showed on his face. I suddenly realized that his desperate calls were to seek help to save the company.

For a moment, I was lost in thought. To me, my father had always been a pioneering figure, taking a leap of faith to move from rural Donghai to build his business in the city. But now, faced with challenges he had never encountered, he appeared more vulnerable than ever.

I couldn’t shake the feeling there had to be a solution. Scrolling through TikTok absentmindedly, I paused on a CSGO video that suddenly reminded me of my computer’s frame rate issue three days ago. A technician on Xiaohongshu had used GameViewer to control my screen remotely. The thought suddenly burst into my head – could my dad use this to overcome his issues?

Excited by my realization, I was eager to share my idea. I ran to my father’s study, where he sat surrounded by stacks of papers, his head resting heavily in his hands. When I saw the look on his face, I hesitated. “What if it’s just a game solution, too simple for business?” I thought to myself. But then I remembered the exhaustion in his eyes and how desperately he needed a solution. Mustering my courage, I asked my father, “Dad, could we install the program remotely?”

His face softened, and a glimmer of hope appeared in his tired eyes. He said, ‘Whether it works or not, I’m willing to try.’

Eager to prove my idea, I set up an experiment to test the process. Using two computers at home, I logged into GameViewer on one device to generate a remote code, and then used it to control another computer. I tested the setup by playing games and watching videos remotely, monitoring the ping values. To my surprise, the connection was smooth – proof that this approach could be applied to remote software installation. I summarized the tutorial into a PDF and sent it to my father’s staff.

Two days later, my father told me the client’s server lacked storage space for my solution, and that they needed a NAS hard drive. However, the drive was only available in Shanghai, and the pandemic delay made prompt delivery impossible. Determined to overcome this latest setback, I scoured a second-hand marketplace, filtering for local sellers. After a full afternoon of 4 hours of searching, I found one that fit the client’s needs and got the drive just in time for installation.

As we finished installing, I saw the weight lift from my dad’s shoulders. He looked at me with a relieved smile and said, ‘I couldn’t have done this without you.’ The man who had always lifted me up now leaned on me. Helping him showed me that challenges can bring us closer, creating moments of connection where we truly grow. Through that, I discovered a strength I never knew I had—a strength born from love.

At T-10 minutes, my dad had just one question: “What’s the chance of success?”

Twenty percent, I told him, but his question still nags at me as I struggle to insert an igniter into the engine. Born in 1958, Dad grew up with his eyes glued to the TV, captivated by the Apollo 11 era. Although he’d pursued finance, his rocketry fascination stayed — and it rubbed off on me, too. We’d grown up launching small rocket kits or watching launches from the Florida beach. Now, to teach myself engineering, I’d been trying to land a rocket like the SpaceX boosters we’d watched at Cape Canaveral. I’d meticulously simulated today's flight, confident I’d addressed prior issues.

With a final look to my dad, I initiated the launch: 3… 2… 1! My rocket lifted off slowly, vectoring the engine to hold course. Finally! Then, as if it had cruelly read my mind, it flipped and slammed nose-first into the ground with a sickening crunch.

For my dad, who always approached problems analytically, the clichéd mantra he later repeated — “Failure is crucial to success; keep trying”— sounded like empty words. Usually, I just accepted another loss. Today, I explained that I couldn’t interpret his advice. How could failing lead to progress?

Dad smiled wisely and handed me one of his favorite books, Thinking in Bets. As I read, I learned that results don’t necessarily reflect the quality of the decisions that led to them — unknown factors affect all outcomes! Even though I’d been improving my rocket, my pride kept me from realizing there were factors I hadn’t noticed that could cause failures. I’d been so focused on perfecting the design I overlooked the need for nuanced analysis.

To address this, I added an SD card to record over 18,000 data points per flight. As I reviewed the data, I began to notice patterns. For example, I saw that my altitude measurements drifted, which led me to replace a faulty sensor. After analyzing the relationship between engine angle and rocket orientation, I did research and found my simulation lacked actuator delay. Comparing landing burn initiation times revealed igniter inconsistencies, prompting me to implement a thrust-bleed divert maneuver. After each failure, I ran to plug in my SD card, excited to search the data for clues to guide my next iteration. After another year, I became the first person to land any rocket without throttling, landing me an internship at SpaceX!

While an SD card was a clear-cut approach to uncovering neglected issues in my rocket, I’d need a new approach to help identify other problems. Including others, I’ve learned, is my best bet. At SpaceX, I brought the voices of production line technicians into engineering design reviews, using their input to raise problems about factory integration that even senior engineers couldn’t have noticed from their desks. When my Chinese grades dropped unexpectedly, I didn't panic. Instead, I sought my teacher’s help and discovered my tones needed work. After scheduling weekly meetings to refine my pronunciation, I eventually won the sophomore Chinese award!

Now, I know how to act on my Dad’s saying. “Failing leads to success” isn’t as simple as it seems. After all, I had been failing a lot without much improvement. Now, though, I see what I’d done wrong. My desire to improve was too passive: only once I gave up my ego and included outside perspectives — whether it was my dad, Chinese teacher, or SpaceX technician friends — could I improve. This is what I hope to bring to college: the willingness to bring in others while solving exciting problems. So, when my dad asks me, “What’s the chance of success?” about my next ambitious challenge, I’ll have the support I need to say 100%.

“BOOM!” The cannonball streaks across the sky, finding its target in a soldier across the field. I nervously survey the situation. One wrong move could mean the end.

That is, the end of an intense chess match between my mother and me. My mother first taught me the rules of Xiang Qi in third grade. Since then, we have shared Sunday afternoons on our couch with a beige-colored Chinese chess board between us. Other than a fun way to bond with my family, Xiang Qi has taught me values that extend far beyond the game.

Clack. My mother moves her rook to the edge of the board. I considered the effect of her move holistically. Like a mutation in a single nucleotide, a change in one pawn’s position affects others across the board. The ability to examine cause-and-effect situations has not only come in handy during chess matches, but also while working in my research lab. I found my passion for cell biology while observing the microscopic structure of leaves in freshman-year Biology. I furthered my interest by interning at the Oliver Lab at Stanford, where I tested virion entry on melanoma cells. By the end of my internship, I had strengthened my analytical abilities while solving problems and troubleshooting failed experiments.

I move my cannon to the center of the board. My mother’s eyebrows shoot up in surprise. Trading my cannon for her horse pawn is a risky move, but I enjoy stepping outside my comfort zone to deviate from traditional chess patterns. Coincidentally, being able to create new high-risk, high-reward strategies has been an integral part of serving my community.

Creating Stepping into STEM was full of new experiences. In sophomore year, I noticed that the students I tutored often despised STEM due to the way their schools taught abstract science concepts with long lectures. Growing up in a low-income family, I also had limited access to out-of-the-classroom education experiences and sought to increase access to hands-on science for underserved students. I started with nothing but a bold plan, teaching myself to write grants, cold emailing local school district officials, and pitching my plan to principals along the way. Using my creativity to create engaging curriculums and taking initiative to found my program, I created a project larger than myself and brought together a community of diverse students united by their shared love for science.

It’s time for the endgame. With our remaining pawns scattered across the board, my mother and I resort to moving measly soldiers one square at a time. A successful offense only comes from a strong defense. And a strong defense comes from patience. However, patience doesn’t always end in victory.

Sometimes, a two-hour game concludes from a simple misstep or from overlooking a powerful opposing pawn. While frustrating, I quickly began to see losses as prologues to more triumphant wins. I used every failed RNA extraction to improve my research techniques. Each Stepping into STEM workshop gave me valuable feedback on how to better structure our next one to be more engaging. Every game was a lesson to learn from; every match another chance to try a new strategy. The possibilities are endless.

I am ready to begin this new chapter of my life with the skills I have gained from playing Xiang Qi. With my analytical ability, creative risk-taking, and patience, I hope to continue my work in serving underserved populations as a pediatric physician. By splitting my time between treating domestic and global patients, I will broaden my worldview while providing quality care to the children that need it the most. PHEW! My king survives and I win this match. But I know that even if my strategy fails, I can learn from my mistakes and adapt in the next game. More importantly, I am ready to learn and adapt on the playing field of life.

Have you ever wondered how a mere electron rearrangement at the molecular level can significantly alter a molecule’s properties? I have — sometimes obsessively. As a child, I was even (unknowingly) haunted by the thought of a molecular misstep in the form of a spontaneous combustion! But at UChicago, where questions spark deeper exploration in and out of the classroom, my curiosity will not lead to fear — it will lead to thrill and discovery.

And, even though I’m no longer daunted by pushing boundaries, at UChicago, I will be encouraged to — it is something to be celebrated. I have been in classrooms, been in learning environments where questions seemed to be confined to the textbook, but I know that won’t be the case at UChicago. At UChicago a community where curiosity thrives, where theory is the very essence of teaching. From striking comparisons between MLK and the Ancient Greeks in Philosophical Perspective I to Quantum Mechanics, where complex mathematical equations point to what has not yet been translated into practice, at UChicago, comparisons between intangible permeate the classroom. At UChicago, knowledge isn’t confined to what’s practical but by one’s curiosity.

Most importantly, at UChicago, childhood fears will be replaced by the excitement of learning, of chemistry. At UChicago, striking a balance between theory and practice as early as freshman year will convert my doubts into awe. Specifically, engaging in hands-on research under Professor Henning Lin’s mentorship, whose interests in the regulation and targeting of enzymes that control post-translational modification align with my past experiences in biochemistry, will glimpse and develop my interests in the elaborate interplay of biological systems at their most fundamental level. Under Professor Lin, I will learn synthetic pathways of enzyme modification and protein identification, which, given my interests, will prepare me for my post-graduation outlook. UChicago’s theoretical aspects translated into practice through an honors thesis will expand my chemical knowledge from more to more. The complexity of the human body will not daunt me, as at UChicago, hands-on experience and deep thinking will instill confidence.

And, definitely, it is not confined by a major — because, as much as I love chemistry, I know it isn’t all there is to learn. Through the core, I’ll not only have the intellectual freedom to develop my critical thinking linguistically, culturally, societally, and scientifically — something that is so pivotal to science — but also find no place for boredom. Boredom haunts me — in classmates, in myself, everywhere. But at UChicago, I’ll find plenty to keep me engaged, both off and on campus. On campus, whether it’s through relaxing walks by the Botany Pond as I sip my $1 milkshake or those study nights at the McCormick Lounge, I won’t be exhausted or bored mentally — one-half of what’s needed. And it is precisely off campus where I’ll find the other half (physical), through those long cycling rides with fellow Maroons in the Veló Club wherein my body regains control of itself, cycling for me without even thinking of it. At UChicago and through its community, I’ll find comfort — one wherein fear and boredom are nonexistent.

Ultimately, UChicago’s focus on theory and intellectual freedom will prepare me to tackle challenges analytically in an ever-changing field. And there’s no better place to develop as a chemist than at UChicago, where humanity first unleashed the power of the atom. At UChicago, I won’t fear chemistry; rather, I’ll fear how much I’ll love it.

I thought I did everything right, but the delicate, skeletal bodies of my lifeless ornamental shrimp laying belly-up on the moss soil proved otherwise. Despite my extensive efforts to carefully acclimate them in pH-adjusted water, only a few of the Galaxy Pinto, Blue Bolt, and Orange-Eye Blue Tiger shrimp remained. Stunned, I was confronted with my failure, listless shrimp lying motionless at the bottom of their tank.

Like other projects I've undertaken, this endeavor required some convincing and strategic ignoring of objections. My mom's concerned gaze while I hauled five gallons of reverse osmosis water into the playroom is a look I've seen before. But I have always been stubbornly optimistic, rarely dissuaded by others' doubts. When faced with a less-than-desirable outcome, I see a puzzle to be solved or a person to be understood.

It is this stubborn optimism that prompted 8th-grade me to call Bob Lewis, the Radon Division Manager at the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (PA DEP), after our home was selected for a year-long radon monitoring study. A nearby house had recently been found to have the highest ever recorded level of radon – a carcinogenic gas – and I wanted to learn more. Watching my grandfather suffer from an aggressive cancer, the result of occupational radiation exposure, I know a hazard you can't see or smell can still kill. When I learned that Pennsylvania doesn't require radon testing in schools despite having the 3rd highest average radon levels, I wanted to do something.

I've since addressed the threat of radon exposure in our schools from multiple angles – research that demonstrates students are potentially exposed to hazardous levels of radon in school, tutorials on radon testing/mitigation for HVAC students, and presentations to local and state legislators. Sometimes, I am congratulated on my work; other times, I am listened to politely and told that it is unlikely that the proposed legislation will pass.

But with each discussion and each new data point, my perspective grows. From stuttering conversations as a skinny 8th grader to speaking on a TEDx stage, my confidence has also grown. And I've learned that analogies are my friend when explaining that our community is at risk for radon exposure. Describing how the EPA action level of radon, 4 pCi/L, is equivalent to smoking 8 cigarettes/day paints a picture that is hard to ignore.

As the only high school speaker at TEDx Northampton Community College, I didn’t want to waste this opportunity, practicing my presentation until I could give it in my sleep. However, with the initial jolt of stepping onto the stage, the lights blinding, I became frozen momentarily. Taking a deep breath and reminding myself of what was at stake, I faced an audience I could not see. I explained why our area had high levels of radon and what we could do about it. When friends, neighbors, and teachers share that they have tested/mitigated their homes due to my efforts, I’m gratified, knowing that they are safer.

What started out as a quick call to the PA DEP in 8th grade has turned into an unexpected journey. I’ve worked with public health advocates from multiple states and learned that introducing a bill and shoring up bipartisan support amidst the constraints of a state budget is as challenging as research and science. My future goals now include work that combines policymaking and research in order to advocate for those who cannot.

For my remaining delicate shrimp, I set about making changes, adding mineral sticks to help molt their exoskeletons and enhancing their diet with microorganisms. Slowly, these shrimp adapt to their new home; the dark blue color that indicates stress fading as they slowly turn light blue, a sign of good health. My efforts are rewarded several weeks later. Little blue and white lines in the tank—undeniable proof that my shrimp had adjusted to the tank. Baby shrimp.

"Names may carry weight, but legacies carry the world." A ten-year-old me couldn't fully understand the meaning of these words till the first Eid after my grandfather's passing. As my cousins and I lined up for our customary Eid gifts, my uncle paused as I approached and handed me 200 riyals, rather than the usual 50, and said, "This is because of your name." The whispers from my cousins were immediate. In their eyes, I was no longer just [Name]—I was [Name] Abdulaziz Alangari, my grandfather's namesake. The playful rivalry between us suddenly felt different, burdened with both unearned privileges and expectations that I could only now begin to grasp.

More than just a successful businessman to me, my grandfather embodied quiet generosity. He founded Hafiz, a non-profit that provides educational tools to those in need and transforms lives without seeking recognition. I never saw myself as confined by his name, but I always carried it with a subtle pressure; I saw it as a challenge to build something of my own—something that would leave a meaningful, lasting impact on the world, just as he had.

This sense of purpose fueled my curiosity. I would be staring at houses made of bricks, wondering what composed each one. This curiosity led a younger me to explore further, eventually drawing him upon Dalton's Atomic Theory—a eureka that felt akin to unlocking the universe's hidden code. Suddenly, atoms were all around me—water splitting into hydrogen and oxygen, metals transferring electrons to form strong bonds, and gasses colliding in constant motion. I was mentally dissecting the world, atom by atom, envisioning their electrons, orbitals, and energy levels, all obeying the invisible laws of quantum mechanics. The more I learned, the more I felt drawn to this hidden world of possibilities.

My early fascination never left me; in fact, it soon became the foundation for everything I pursued, and I refused to let the looming pressure of becoming "[Name] the Second" define my purpose. My focus was on the joyous serendipity of discovery, on scientific challenges that made me think harder, and on the thrill of dealing with complex interactions. I was driven by more than just a legacy—I was driven by a relentless curiosity to understand how even the smallest particle could drive large-scale impact.

Fully immersed in my research on chemical catalysis, I often think back to Hafiz. In Arabic, Hafiz refers to something that facilitates and accelerates a process, much like an effective catalyst in a well-balanced reaction. I've come to realize that my journey wasn't just a series of random steps—it was a process of facilitating change. My work has been more than academic; it has embodied the same values my grandfather instilled. Except now, I could not only shape lives—I could shape molecules, too.

Explaining my work to my family, I used Hafiz to describe the catalytic process, and they smiled knowingly. Looking back, that was the moment that I could comprehend that I hadn't been running from legacy, I had actually been living it all along. My name was no longer a burden, heck it never even was; it is a foundation upon which I could build. I feel at peace with the weight of being [Name] Abdulaziz Alangari.

The previous burden of a name has now become the bedrock of my identity; it has transformed many of my doubts into purpose. My grandfather's legacy isn't something I need to live up to—it's a source of inspiration, and the realm of molecular exploration equips me to forge my own path, one that honors the past while innovating for the future. I'm ready now to build upon the foundation he laid and add my own contributions to the legacy he began.

Names may carry weight, but it's the legacies we build through action that shape the world.

“Is anybody...home?”

I pressed my ears against the damp wooden door, catching only indistinct murmurs. Amid the Cao Bang mountains, a journey to provide assistance had become a search for sound. I knocked again, burning to try the handle. Each knock wasn’t just a request to enter, but a quiet rebellion against a world overshadowed by illness.

Growing up, I inherited my mom’s dedication to study Thalassemia—a genetic blood disorder. I wanted freedom for future generations, whose choices were bound by medical constraints from birth due to a lack of access to preventative tools. I embraced my struggles with chemistry and started developing a Thalassemia-carrying gene diagnostic test. Achieving 70% accuracy was more than a scientific milestone; it was a hope of liberating lives.

When my mom planned to visit marginalized communities battling Thalassemia in Cao Bang, I eagerly set off. I carried a full backpack and an even fuller heart, convinced that science could unlock the doors of liberty for those trapped by this disease. I even wondered how I would respond to their warm welcomes. Except, only silence awaited me.

My voice grew weaker with each call, my knuckles swollen. As I kept knocking, the doors started to crack half-opened. Behind some were tears. Behind others, wary gazes. They opened my eyes to a stark reality, where freedom means just leaving pain and discomfort to fate.

As the ridges faded from the windows on our way back, the distance between my ideals and the reality I faced felt insurmountable. But I wasn’t accepting defeat. The silence behind those doors was a truth I needed to confront: if I wanted to empower others, I had to redefine freedom—not as something I could simply give, but as something to learn from others.

I poured my thoughts into conversations with Mom and her colleagues, diving into their insights while challenging my past understanding. The more I learned, the more questions I uncovered, fueling my relentless search for true answers long after the trip ended.

“Tell you what,” a small boy held me back one day as I left the treatment room. “Sometimes I think God was putting us under some sort of magical transformation into super beings, but He just forgot a few steps.”
