His words struck me—what if freedom wasn’t about fixing lives, but empowering people to reclaim their stories?

I decided to do something different: visiting treatment rooms, not to run tests, but to ask patients about their lives, their hopes, and their definitions of freedom.

There, I saw the world anew. For a trio of 7-to-8-year-olds, freedom was playing soccer. For a single mother, freedom was reuniting with her children. For a teenage girl, freedom was neither book nor clothes, but the ease in completing everyday tasks.

Each unique lens reshaped my worldview, and the test I once saw as a key to liberation now seemed incomplete. What good is a positive result if people choose to ignore it—or worse, if their beliefs were opposed to it?

I learned that freedom isn’t something you just give through science, for science alone cannot unlock doors if the people it’s meant to help feel disconnected from its purpose. True progress isn’t just about technical breakthroughs, but about understanding the fears, beliefs, and values of the individuals it serves. Without addressing these human factors, even the most precise tools risk becoming meaningless.

So as I step forward, I’ll keep knocking—on doors, on barriers, on assumptions—guided by the boy’s dream of transformation and the lives science can connect. After all, what is science if not a bridge between people and the freedom they seek?

I always felt normal. Just like the letters in normal: 
N stood for necessary. 
O stood for ordinary. 
R stood for regular 
M stood for manage. 
A stood for average. 
L stood for logic. 
I tried to be like everyone around me, being the puzzle piece in everyone's picture, afraid of showing what I cared about. Like everything else, being a doctor was the only thing acceptable in my parent's eyes. Because of this, I chose it despite not knowing what I actually wanted to do. My pathway was solidified on Christmas of 2022 when my grandpa passed away; after my grandpa's passing, my mom was in shambles; her health deteriorated to the point where she would not leave bed for hours on end. Besides that, she locked herself in the bedroom, crying day and night. This situation worried me as it was not normal for my mom to be like this; she was always the one who was happy and cheerful, but looking at her state scared me.

Mission: help mom – in action. From cooking to cleaning, I did all of it. Due to my mom's condition, she would require assistance, so no matter the task, I would always make sure that I did it for her. Every day, I would bring her a new cup of water every two hours for her to use to drink her medicine. I also got her breakfast, lunch, and dinner and returned it downstairs when she finished. I remember constantly running back and forth around the house to ensure everything was fine for my mom.

Mission: completed. Slowly but surely, my mom's condition improved; she got out of bed more often and became more of herself. Because of this experience, it sparked anger at myself as I wished I helped my mom more and stopped her from all the hurt she felt. The experience made me realize I never want anyone to endure such pain, igniting my passion for becoming a doctor. Without any resources, what can I do? Although TV shows do not accurately represent what happens in real life, Grey's Anatomy taught me the basics, such as the uses of different medical instruments and how a hospital works. In Grey's Anatomy, I love the scenes where I see the hospital in action, such as the episode "Time Has Come Today." Through this episode, I learned more about hospitals' procedures to ensure that disease does not spread throughout the hospital. It intrigued me as I never understood how much precaution is needed to ensure contamination does not run rampant throughout the hospital. Was this how doctors felt during the Covid-19 pandemic?

Future mission – learn more about the field of medicine. Something I love about the medical field is that there are a lot of areas you can study within. I know I can find something I love, from public health to pediatrics. Over the summer of sophomore year, I started to explore my interests. I attended sessions at my local police station to learn more about their operations. I learned about CPR and stopping the bleeding in one of these sessions. Even in school, I attended our medical club (Medfinify), where I learned more from the guest speakers and events such as suturing. Besides this, I continued to explore my interests outside of school during the summer of my Junior year; I volunteered at my local hospital and attended medical events such as PCOM and Johns Hopkins' Global Health Leadership Conference. From these opportunities, I was able to explore more about the medical field by watching procedures and talking with professionals, showing me that medicine is something that I want to go into. In college and beyond, I hope that I will be able to enhance my skills and be someone who can make a change in the medical space.

Footsteps rushed the silent halls that I walked to get to my next class. Sitting in the corner of the class, I began taking out my materials until I heard someone faintly mutter: "When was he in this class?" As I came home, I replied to my mom's question of how my day went: "School was great, I got an A on my-" before being interrupted. This was a common interaction as the needs of my siblings overshadowed my own. Ever since my brother was diagnosed with Autism, I was labeled as the high-functioning child who provided help to my siblings at any given moment. However, this limited the voice of my needs and issues to be something that had to be independently taken care of. This repression became more apparent during my father’s recovery from his emergency surgery, as I not only had to juggle my siblings' needs, but it was also up to me to assist him.

I grew up wanting to be heard. There was not a single day that passed where I did not feel the desire to speak uninterrupted or without being told to speak up. I realized the voice of my own was microscopic in my everyday life, as it was overshadowed by the voices of others. Yet, it was the voice of others that helped me find mine. I acknowledged that while I lacked a voice, I did not lack the passion to find it. I did so through surrounding myself with like-minded club members who aspired to become medical professionals. It was a way to help me observe and create a formula for how to convert thoughts into words. Through participating in meetings, I was able to fortify this formula through repetition and began finding my voice. However, I wanted more.

I took it upon myself to transform this formula from an extracurricular into a dual-enrollment class at my local community college, Communications 121. There, I began to understand how I could communicate with others effectively by utilizing vocal projection. This formula was now a formalized and structured set of operations that culminated in a final where we were tasked to either write an essay or give an oral presentation. Before, I would have chosen the essay. I now knew that would not have been of any benefit to me. I thought if I wanted to see change, I needed to prove to myself that I could utilize my voice. I repeated the same lines I revised thousands of times like a mantra. However, I knew that if I heard the snickers and giggles of the crowd that all my previous memories of going unheard, being interrupted, and my silenced voice would come back with full strength.The day came where I presented in front of dozens of people: “Today I’ll be presenting about the amygdala”. With an applause, I realized that nobody judged me, nobody snickered at me, nobody could detect my nervousness. Instead, they listened attentively about my passion for becoming a medical professional that I had never seen before in anyone I spoke to. That was my real voice. As they applauded me, I saw the culmination of finding my unique voice.

My voice was once a cauldron of untapped potential, silenced by my own fears and difficult experiences. Through grit, I realized that the only way to truly be heard was to confront fear and adversity head on. By embracing this challenge, I finally was able to discover the strength of my voice. However, this experience is shared by thousands of others who may feel their voices are lost amongst the individuals who interrupt or overshadow them. As I step onto campus, I hope to empower the voices of students who face similar challenges, inspiring anyone I meet to embrace their fears and find their unique voice.

“Doheny Beach?” The text seemed ordinary, just two words, but to me, it was everything. I sent it out of desperation, hoping to break the silence that had become suffocating. When their reply came, “Sure, see you there,” it felt like someone had thrown me a life ring, pulling me from deep water I didn't even know I was drowning in.

At Doheny Beach, we played volleyball, laughed over soggy sandwiches, and watched the sun dip below the horizon. Building the courage to share, I hesitated then I quietly sighed, “I’m stuck on my comp sci project.” For days, I had been wrestling with a block of code that refused to run, the frustration building up with every failed attempt. Admitting my struggle was freeing but hard as being vulnerable with my friends was new territory for me. My hands fidgeted, what was seconds seemed like hours. Tom smiled. “Me too.” Gary leaned forward, his face puzzled. “Wait, I thought you were finished. Do you want help?”

Their words surprised me. They did not need me to have it all together. They just needed me to be real. For the first time, my self-reliant pride cracked open and I felt the connection as I unloaded my frustration with my friends. I no longer had to pretend I did not need help.

The next day, we sat together in our Informatics: Artificial Intelligence class, laptops open, ready to tackle our frustrations. My error, dividing by zero in the monthly spending calculations, had stalled progress for days. When Tom spotted it, the code finally worked, and I had an idea. “What if we combined our projects?” I asked. With our instructor’s approval, I split the tasks. Tom refined the graphs, Gary polished the interface, and I integrated the components.

For the first time, coding did not feel lonely. Leading the team, I realized how much faster solutions came through collaboration. We caught each other’s mistakes, built on one another’s ideas, and created a better budgeting app than if we did it alone plus it was more fun. That project did not just teach me to debug code. It showed me the power of leadership is asking for help and collaboration is important to building apps.

But my aspirations did not stop there. My goal is to become an AI systems engineer, connecting systems because AI is often so complex that even its creators do not fully understand it. Designing ethical and accessible tools requires ensuring algorithms work fairly for everyone, especially underserved communities. After volunteering at a food pantry, where I saw parents juggling rent and groceries, I thought programs could be designed that provide financial education helping users track spending and save effectively. Additionally, I learned that algorithms can carry biases, such as credit-scoring models penalizing people in low-income neighborhoods based on zip codes rather than their actual financial history. Securing personal financial data from hackers is equally critical to building trust in these systems. AI can not just analyze data but empower people by offering accessible solutions.

At university, I want to collaborate and find my own “PayPal Mafia,” a group of peers who push me and inspire me to build something as breakthrough as PayPal to solve financial insecurity or cure diseases or programs for wearable devices reducing anxiety. I picture myself joining teams at hackathons, brainstorming and creating apps that solve a problem that assist marginalized populations or address global challenges like climate change.

Standing on Doheny Beach that night, watching the waves smooth the sand, I realized I was like the shoreline, constantly shaped by the people and experiences around me. Just as my friends helped me break through my silence, I want to create systems that help others break through barriers. Whether it’s financial tools or curing diseases, my goal is to solve problems one coding project and one connection at a time.

Every eye in the history classroom was on me, and my heart hammered so loudly I could barely think. I stood frozen, searching for words I’d rehearsed but suddenly couldn’t remember. I wonder why I had ever thought memorizing a script would save me.

Weeks before, I never imagined I’d be so tongue-tied. I had grown up in a home alive with overlapping accents; Najdi, Eastern, and English from traveling relatives; and I’d always assumed I “knew” all the languages.

Then I transferred to an international school, and suddenly, the comfort of my old life vanished. The first day, when I introduced myself – “Me name is [Name]” – a few students snickered. During math class, I wrote equations right to left, triggering confusion and whispers. During lunch, I wandered through the crowded cafeteria as I watched groups huddled together, their easy camaraderie a stark reminder of the warmth I once knew.

At home, I tried to fix myself by perfecting my English. I turned off the Arabic subtitles on my favorite show, The Amazing World of Gumball. I replaced my beloved Arabic copy of Diary of a Wimpy Kid with the English edition. But as Gumball and Darwin chatted, I struggled to catch their jokes. Greg’s simple language felt strangely distant without translations. I forced myself to memorize vocabulary and recorded my speech. I managed to say new words correctly by the fifth week, but something still felt off. I could parrot sounds, but they refused to stick in my mind or settle comfortably in my throat.

That’s when I realized that the problem wasn’t about English; it was about what I was willing to give up to sound “right.” I chased ideal perfection in English, yet I lost myself during the process. So I changed tactics. I let the episodes play instead of pausing. I read Diary of a Wimpy Kid without jumping to translations. I started speaking aloud; messing up but going on; mistaken long vowels, and double constants; I’m still struggling. Yet in each small group project, I realized that my classmates looked beyond my mispronunciation; they focused on genuine communication. This made me embrace my accent, my heritage, and my quirks.

Before I knew it, I was standing in front of my history class, assigned to summarize a chapter of World Civilizations. During the night before, I rehearsed beneath the soft glow of my desk lamp, the words echoing in my mind until I could deliver them flawlessly. But when I stood in front of the class, I froze. My mind went blank. After ten seconds of silence that felt like an eternity, I realized there was only one option: improvise. Taking a deep breath, I began to speak from my heart. I explained ancient trade concepts by relating them to how my family exchanged dates and coffee with our neighbors during Ramadan. I expected laughter, but as I moved from slide to slide, no one laughed. When I finished, the class erupted in applause.

Standing there, I understood that I didn’t need to hide behind perfect English. My accent, my cultural references, and my personal touch were strengths, not weaknesses. This realization didn’t stop at the classroom door; I started expanding my message to everyone around me. Through mentoring and guiding students from underrepresented areas, leading environmental awareness campaigns from all across our school, speaking openly about my English journey, and discovering myself, I now stand against self-doubt and use my voice to make an impact.

Today, when I speak English, I don’t try to hide my roots. I lean into my authenticity. Instead of chasing perfection, I use my voice. While my R’s sound heavy, and my T’s sound British, I learned to embrace my language’s sincerity instead of purity. Moving forward, I’m excited to use my Najdi accent, along with an Eastern one, to break down social barriers and make it my own trademark.

“Is anybody…home?”

My voice grew weaker with each repetition, my knuckles swollen. Amid the mountains of Cao Bang, what began as a trip to provide medical aids for ethnic communities battling Thalassemia had turned into a strenuous search for sound. Fifteen minutes passed, still no response. I pressed my ear against the damp wooden surface, only to catch some indistinct murmurs. Hesitantly glancing at Mom, I was burning to just try the handle.

Not every door greeted us with silence. Some half-opened to skeptical frowns or timid stares. Others flooded with tears, revealing struggles too immense for words. Many closed quietly, as if we’d never come. But these doors did have one thing in common: they opened my eyes to a stark reality where people wished to just leave every pain and discomfort to fate.

This experience challenged me to the core.

Growing up, Mom was my inspiration. I inherited more than her love of science, from owning a collection of medical conference merchandise to binge-watching videos on the Krebs cycle without understanding a single word.

But fighting Thalassemia meant more than honoring Mom’s scientific work. For me–an advocate of freedom–it was also a question of choice. In most “Freedom for All” efforts, help is often directed toward people without financial means or those with physical and mental impairments. But what about these Thalassemia patients, whose choices were replaced with syringes and blood transfusions even before birth?

That very question pushed me through a love-hate relationship with chemistry to study this disease. I’ll never forget the day Mom and I celebrated when the rapid diagnostic test I developed reached 70% accuracy. My heart raced at the thought of liberating lives with science.

As the ridges faded from the windows on our way back, the distance between my ideals and the reality I confronted felt insurmountable. I came here thinking I understood freedom, but now, I doubted I knew anything. The silence I faced was indeed a loud statement: If I wanted to set someone free, I couldn’t simply offer some assistance and say, “Take it. This is what I call liberty.” It doesn’t work that way.

I poured my longing for answers into conversations with Mom and her colleagues, hoping for insights. As my mind was further puzzled by numerous biological mechanisms, I remained yearning for an anchor months following the trip.

I decided to do something of my own: visiting patients, not to run tests, but to ask about their lives, their hopes, and their definitions of freedom.

The smell of disinfectant stung as I stepped into the treatment room. I blushed at the fleeting gazes of patients and their family members, their eyes holding stories I was only beginning to understand.

Papers and pens in hand, I began a simple yet incredible exploration. I saw the world anew: a trio of 7-to-8-year-olds whose love for soccer was confined to the hospital, a single mother counting the days to reunite with her children, and a teenage girl struggling with everyday tasks, indifferent to neither books nor clothes. Each unique story deepened my sense of purpose.

That was also when I realized: one day, I may resolve my questions about freedom, but throughout my search, I will continue to nurture my own version of science–one that doesn’t just address cold, hard facts, but listens deeply to the people it serves. After all, what is science if not a bridge between lives and the freedom they seek?

“Tell you what,” a small boy held me back one day as I left the treatment room. His eyes sparkled as he whispered with absolute certainty.

“Sometimes I think God was putting us under some sort of magical transformation into super beings, but He just forgot the final step.”

“Hmm? Shall we remind Him so that next time He will remember?”

The boy nodded. And that was the happiest smile I had ever seen.

I was once missing something.

The responsibility of keeping a younger sister in check with everything is deeply rooted in my mind as an older brother. From setting screen time limits on Roblox to giving social life advice to her, I did it all. But they don’t tell you one thing about playing the older sibling.

I vividly recall walking the hallways on the first day of freshman year with an outfit I took so much pride in. Judgmental glares didn’t meet my eyes, so I was left oblivious to the actual train wreck I was.

My wardrobe consisted of skinny blue jeans and Aeropostale t-shirts that you would only find teens in 2012 wearing. In my mind, these pieces of clothing were timeless as they were personally handpicked by my Gen X mother, whom I trust with everything. I couldn’t fathom the difference between the outfits of my peers and mine until my sister decided to let me in on a little secret: my outfits were unflattering. I protested. As a fashion expert, she was eager to offer a few words of advice, but frankly, fashion wasn’t something profound in my eyes.

“Just listen to Em [an endearing Vietnamese term to refer to a younger sibling],” my mother reassuringly urged me. Even she trusted my sister. I’m one who easily caves in because of encouragement, so I let my sister completely run the show.

I found myself fully immersed as a client to the personal stylist that was my sister. Sitting in the corner of our gray mini couch that hosted styling advising sessions, she scoured triumphantly through Pinterest, in search of inspiration images for outfits that are still wonderfully preserved in my camera roll. Our occasional trips to Lenox Square always include her intentional selection of shirts and pants that was so well harmonious with my outer appearance; I must thank her every time. Gradually, up-to-trend tops, baggy jeans, and accessories adorned my new wardrobe. And here I am now, stuck in the fashion rabbit hole which would've never crossed the mind of my freshman year self.

While it may be unorthodox for an older brother to actively seek words of advice from a younger sister, I recognize that a two-way street is an inherent aspect of any great sibling dynamic. Beyond fashion, I resorted to her for other advice, which included smoothie recipes and skincare regimens. Some say I’m too reliant on her. Even so, I realized I needed to be all ears to the insights that I would’ve otherwise overlooked, and that is not limited to only the words she shared.

Joined by a close friend, we hosted a lesson about Vietnamese dialects to a group of curious 12-year-olds at my temple. I opened the floor, and a boy who spoke the Central dialect added insights that were uncommon to hear of to our vocabulary explanations. His comments sparked endless discussions that strayed from our initial lesson plan. I was hooked, longing to hear more. To me, this experience of the mentor switching roles with the student was very familiar, as I faced it with my very own sister. Ever since, my Vietnamese lessons have become more of open discussions–where civil debates about pronunciations and meanings of slang arose–rather than typical lectures. After each lesson, I leave with so many takeaways such as the new Vietnamese jokes that I’m always excited to crack with my mainland relatives on FaceTime.

Being all ears and eyes to seemingly trivial comments put me in shoes that were never on my bingo card. In my continuous search for insights from unexpected sources, I unknowingly discovered what I was missing as an older sibling: to take notes from my Em.

After all, I didn’t inherit my mother’s large ears for nothing. I’ve got to put them to use by listening out for more thoughts, unconventional or not.

After coming back from school I dropped my backpack from what felt like a ton of bricks. Sighing in relief, I silently sat on my bed, with the breeze sedately hitting the hair behind my ear. As my room fell silent I heard a mix of heavy and faint footsteps approaching my bedroom door. “Akua Fa wo nwoma kan.” (Pick up a book and read). Unfazed by the millionth time at my parents comment, I began to unpack the contents of my bag and placed my unsolved chemistry notes on my bedroom floor.

My parents always made reading a standard practice in our household. It never occurred to me why they were so adamant at putting reading into practice but now I finally understand; reading is the product of awareness, awareness is the product of insight and insight is the product of light.

20 years ago, in Accra, Ghana the youngest daughter of five fended for her family in order to provide means for them. Her mother suffered from the numbing of her limbs resulting in the amputation of her leg. She sold at the open marketplaces day and night while trying to keep everything from falling apart; only for her home to catch on fire in return. All of her hard work and dedication, gone. Unable to keep up with the situations life threw at her, she dropped out of school. Day by day, I am motivated by the clapped hands of my father, who works tirelessly every night to help put food on the table. I am driven by the sore back of my tenacious mother, who never stops working even though she can't read or write.

Their hard work has impacted the trajectory of my life. I take advantage of opportunities that I'm willing to indulge in for personal growth. And kThis ultimately led me to start book drives to underfunded areas and schools in the Bronx and Ghana. Knowledge is something that can’t be taken away nor is something that is ever completed since there will always be exploration for more. A few months later, I came to Ghana and saw how children utilized their education with the books that were given to them. The teachers expressed how the students' performances improved compared to the beginning of the school year. Seeing kids utilize what they were given, gave me insight that these kids would be able to develop a better future and produce something valuable in a world where things aren’t fully comprehensible. I’ve lived long enough to realize that the books I’ve had access to have helped me grow in my actions, reactions, experience and mistakes in which I am forever grateful for —I live every day as if my knowledge is something that is not fully comprehensible; and it isn’t but I can always look forward to the future expecting myself to gain more every single day.

I like to think that part of me resonates with books: I find myself lost in thought and find myself falling asleep. I feel comfortable and at peace as if I’m meant to stay awake a little longer and hear the sound of ruffling pages just a bit more evoking a sense of belonging before I finally go to sleep.

I watched, horrified, as my army lay pulverized and misshapen in a pool of red. My once pristine, sharp-edged deck of Bicycle cards now sat paint-splattered and warped after a stray slap in a fierce game of Egyptian War.

The summer after my junior year, I spent a month at UCLA for the California State Summer School for Mathematics and Science (COSMOS). My excitement for the projects to come was quickly contrasted by the slow first day. Pacing around the halls, after a tour of campus, I suddenly remembered I had brought my deck of cards. Tucking them into my pocket, I headed to the dorm room lounge, ready to quell my solitude and unfamiliarity.

In the lounge, I found two students I had met earlier that day in the cafeteria. I pulled out my deck of cards and we deliberated what game to play. Poker? Blackjack?

“Egyptian War?” Sumedh suggested.

“What’s that?” Lawrence and I asked in unison.

As Sumedh explained the rules, I realized I knew the game by a different name: Egyptian Ratslap. Despite its simplicity—just slap the cards—Sumedh embarrassed us with his expertise, winning game after game. The walls of unfamiliarity began to fall as we chatted over the deafening slaps. Sumedh and I discovered our shared love for the Golden State Warriors, even as he labeled me a traitor to the Lakers. Lawrence shared his interest in botanical journaling; later that week, on a walk in the garden, he showed me how to sketch Dracaena aletriformis and write notes about all the plants he saw.

Though I had found my footing, many of my peers were still grappling with homesickness and anxiety, often isolating themselves during group activities. Aiming to foster a sense of community, I organized card games in the lounge, encouraging anyone who wanted to find friends to play. From poker to rummy, the lounge soon buzzed with dozens of students duking it out through their favorite card games. Still reeling from my humiliation at Sumedh’s hands, I set up my cards every night and challenged anyone willing to play Egyptian War. I triumphed over a roller coaster enthusiast from Pasadena who taught me about “dive loops” and “ride ops.” My experimental strategies failed against an avid fisherman from San Francisco who built robots. As the program ramped up, we shifted our focus to research projects, where the camaraderie we built through card games paid off. Everyone’s strengths took center stage as we were comfortable enough to rely on each other.

Helping draw in others for equitable inclusion goes beyond cards. Where I cannot take my deck of cards, I carry the expression and communication skills I have developed through years of speech and debate. When I learned that the local middle school attended by half of my friends did not have a debate program, I partnered with a fellow student to create one. We prepared students for tournaments, taught them essential research skills, and most importantly, instilled confidence and fundamental speaking skills. The most rewarding moments came when I witnessed shy middle schoolers transform into confident speakers who could hold their own against even high schoolers. Even without my cards, I found success in empowering others.

In COSMOS’s final days, I faced Sumedh again, and all my practice paid off: I finally managed to defeat him. Through our countless matches, we both formed a valuable friendship. As I turn towards college, I will continue using the power of communication to foster inclusivity—whether it’s hosting card game nights in the dorms or organizing study sessions. I want to help create an environment where everyone feels comfortable sharing and discussing their ideas through open dialogue. I hope to carry my deck of cards with me, continuing my conquests: making new friends, building new connections, and cultivating community—one brutal card game at a time.

“You’re not ready.”

Those three words struck me harder than any punch I had ever taken. After months of relentless training and countless hours spent perfecting basic four-punch combinations to intricate jiu-jitsu grappling techniques, I thought I was finally prepared for my black belt test. But my Sensei’s three simple words stopped me cold.

My heart sank. For years, I believed that pushing through every challenge and persevering through any obstacle was enough. I pushed my body further and further every day, allowing my muscles to grow exhausted and sore. I convinced myself that simply remaining determined would prepare me sufficiently. Yet, when it mattered most, my perseverance fell short. For the first time, I felt stuck. How could all those years of training and pushing through feel like they had amounted to nothing?

As I lay awake in the comfort of my room, my gaze wandered across the familiar walls, washed in a soft blue hue, then to the calm white ceiling, before finally resting on the Formula 1 car silhouette hanging above my headboard. I thought of the races I had spent hours watching, my eyes glued to the screen unbudging in my captivation, where strategy constantly trumped brute force. The roaring engines, sleek cars, and complex strategies that teams like Mercedes and Ferrari implemented were inspiring.

Each team operates under a strict cost cap, balancing multimillion-dollar investments with long-term strategies while navigating within limited resources. They don't blindly persevere through their roadblocks; they adapt and pivot to different strategies—informed by performance history and specific future objectives—to improve race pace. By analyzing the finances of F1 teams, it's clear that they don't succeed by just pouring money into upgrades blindly; instead, they plan and spend strategically.

In my free time, I found myself revisiting old F1 races, noticing tactics I might have missed in my MMA training: a new strategy, an unusual move, or an adaptation to tricky situations. For example, race engineers guide drivers step-by-step through changing conditions, helping them adapt instead of leaving them to speed as fast as they can.

F1 had shown me that simply forcing something without a strategy wouldn’t work. Could I use the same methods? Could I, like the teams, create a plan, adapt, and train with intention rather than use blind force? I realized I needed to shift my approach; I needed to combine perseverance with detailed strategies to train effectively.

With this new perspective, I returned to training with an adapted mindset. I analyzed every move, refining my techniques down to the finest details. I deconstructed my training into parts: adjusting my footwork, fine-tuning the chambers and extensions in each kick and punch, increasing the fluidity of my jujitsu moves as needed, and analyzing minor mistakes in every combo, strategizing methods to target and eliminate them. Every hour I spent training was now focused on strategy. I wasn't just maximizing my hours; I had intent and a plan.

When the 2024 black belt test arrived, I experienced a readiness that was as mental as it was physical. This time, my body and mind worked in harmony, and I was confident that my strategic approach had significantly improved my skills. My Sensei’s nod of approval carried a weight that no words could match. I went on to earn my black belt, not just through determination, but by tailoring each move to every challenge I faced.

Now, the F1 car silhouette and black belt plaque hung up on my walls take on a new meaning. They testify to the fact that real growth requires endurance paired with strategy and adaptability, not just one or the other.

The principles I have learned throughout my journey with MMA extend far beyond earning my black belt. This new perspective has instilled a different definition of resilience in me, equipping me with the mindset I need to overcome any challenge I face in my future.

Match point. Sweat poured down my face as I reached the end of the 3rd set in the team district tennis championships. This match decides whether the whole team progresses to the next round. I was down two match points; one missed shot could crush our dream of winning districts. Thinking the match was over, people in the stands started packing up to leave. My teammates watched eagerly, sick with apprehension, but I was undeterred by the pressure, determined to fight for the sake of my teammates.

Cardiac surgery, the artistic manipulation of the human heart, can change the course of a patient’s life. As a child, I never imagined myself exploring this field. I had no idea what I wanted to pursue in the future. One day, I came across a documentary about Dr. Vivian Thomas, which introduced me to cardiac surgery. Although it initially seemed scary, there was something genuinely mystical and unreal about it. It was incredible that surgeons held the fate of the patient in their own hands, carefully suturing and restoring the heart back to health. While visiting my grandparents in India, I decided to explore this further by shadowing Dr. Srimanarayana at Andhra Hospital, where something unexpected and truly special occurred.

In the tennis match, a miracle happened. I saved the two match points. Point by point, I fought as my teammates cheered me on, motivating me to give it my all despite my failing body. The sun was slowly setting, and the cool afternoon breeze gently blew against my face as I went up 6-5, 40-15: my very own match points. I hit a blistering first serve and emerged victorious. As I staggered out of the court with thoroughly exhausted, cramping legs, I was re-energized by the smiles on the faces of my teammates. We spent months of grueling effort as a team to prepare for the tournament, so their happiness was the biggest reward of the match. I could not have won without their invaluable support.

At Andhra Hospital, I had the opportunity to watch an open-heart surgery on a 6-year-old pediatric patient. He had a ventricular septal defect: the child’s heart had a hole between its chambers. I stood beside the surgeon as he worked his magic, expertly utilizing his hands as a violin maestro wields his bow. It was fascinating to watch how the surgeon manipulated the delicate heart tissues to fix the problem and give the patient a new life. Although surgery is stressful and a single mistake could cost a life, the surgeon worked with extreme composure. The surgeon was not the only one contributing. He worked closely with anesthesiologists, perfusionists, nurses, and primary care doctors; he needed the support of a team, just as I needed the support of my team. After the surgery, we went to the waiting room to inform the patient’s parents that everything went well. Their relief and happiness were priceless, and their smiles were worth more than gold.

Although seemingly disparate, I noticed that tennis and surgery share many similar principles. Both require composure, especially during the most challenging moments. In both, a single mistake can have lasting consequences. Both require collaboration with a team.

These experiences have taught me invaluable lessons that I will bring to campus. I have learned to embrace pressure and treat it as an opportunity through tennis. I have learned to remain composed during high-pressure situations and perform the task at hand. I also learned about the vital role of collaboration. Meeting those parents in the ICU solidified my desire to pursue a pre-med path at university because I want to dedicate my life to bringing families that same joy. During my undergraduate studies, I plan to continue using the lessons I learned from tennis and the operating room to continuously improve and make the most of my college experience.

Parallel to the Control Panel operated by emotions, I have a Code Switch operated by Mandarin, English, German, French, and Taiwanese. Each language brings its core values, shaping my belief system and guiding me through life’s experiences.

Mandarin, my primary language, embodies diligence and patience. 
“That’s still not right,” Dad said. “The last stroke needs to be diagonal.”
I held in the tears to not ruin the page as I rewrote my name for the tenth time. 
As I spent nights writing character after character, Dad’s insistence on making each stroke perfect frustrated me. However, it was only later that I realized the cumbersome but consistent process taught me more than just writing characters. At school, as I poured over literature, calculated mathematical functions, and studied historical events, Mandarin took over and reminded me that progress comes with time and practice, just like writing a perfect stroke.

English unlocked a different part of me—one that craved expression and creativity. This alter ego binge-read The Hunger Games, filled up my diary, to eventually found its full potential in Model UN. Trembling as I stood on the podium to deliver my first speech as the delegate of Israel, English transformed into a diplomat, voicing our nation’s stances. As English honed its skills conference after conference—persuading countries to lift economic sanctions as Russia, building Arctic consensus as Canada, and fostering dialogues as a Chair—I realized how English sparked my creativity and empowered me to share my voice confidently.

German, on the other hand, is observant. I started learning the language just months before moving to Germany, and its complex grammar (the notorious noun declension and verb conjugation) has trained my eye for detail. This attentiveness carried over to when I did cheerleading in Germany. While learning stunts like Extensions and Liberties, I stayed quiet at first, absorbing every detail from hand placement to counts. But as we progressed to the Basket Toss, I noticed that the slight difference in the timing of our throw affected our success. As I voiced my observations and improved our success rate, I realized that German has empowered me with observation of details.

French, a recent addition, brings the joy of discovery. What began as a surprise greeting of "Bonjour" in my German high school soon blossomed into an unexpected passion for the language. Learning French feels like solving a delightful puzzle; with its similarities to English and German, I relish connecting the linguistic dots between new vocabularies and grammar structures to familiar ones. The same joy extended to my time in the Humanities and Social Science Scholars Program. That summer, I read Benedict Anderson’s theories on nationalism while watching Taiwanese athletes compete in the Paris Olympics. After observing the nationwide unity, I realized the Olympics beautifully exemplified modern nationalism. As I crafted connections in my thesis, drawing from the joy I found in learning French, it unlocked a new way of exploring the world around me.

Finally, there’s Taiwanese, the language of comfort and home. Spoken primarily with my relatives, my go-to phrase is “Have you eaten?” Yet, Taiwanese is more than just a language; it’s the bridge to my heritage. Whether cooking for family during Lunar New Year or hosting Taiwanese-themed dinners for friends from abroad, these traditional recipes are my way of preserving our culture. As the golden-brown edges of the sweet rice cakes sizzle in hot oil, the familiar aroma reminds me that I’ll stay connected to the island that nurtured me.

Growing from monolingual to multilingual, I’ve watched these lessons shape me into who I am today. My languages are not just tools of communication; they are the core of my identity, instilling the values that guide me in every step of my journey. As I navigate between languages with my Code Switch, I strive to use the core memories to embrace new challenges and contribute to my community.

At seven, life felt ordinary—until I dared to seek the extraordinary.

In My Little Pony, I saw infinite possibilities. My imagination was ignited as I watched Princess Twilight Sparkle unleash nebula-like bursts of energy to protect Equestria. I began searching for a spark in my own life—wouldn’t it be amazing, I thought, if I had a superpower, too? Inspired by Twilight’s powers, I set out to find magic in the world around me.

Of course, even at seven, I knew magic wouldn’t manifest with a determined stare. Instead, I turned to the wonders of my everyday life—how did our cucumber plant climb poles? How did sparrows soar? The more I questioned, the more fascinated I became. Each discovery, from genetics’ secrets to the universe’s origins, enriched my world with new possibilities.

But the more I learned, the more I believed that by mastering knowledge, I would unlock the universe’s secrets, becoming magical too. Driven by hunger, I studied and studied, chasing the boundless power that knowledge promised. I devoured textbooks until, like a firebird consumed by its flame, I burned out, unable to summon the passion that once drove me.

But from ashes, firebirds rise again—gaining strength after every pain.

As I rebuilt my life, I experienced a magic beyond knowledge. At the Georgia Governor’s Honors Program, I formed a group of female mathletes to tackle challenging weekly PSETs together. In the face of an all-male group that excluded us, we empowered each other to succeed. We shared strategies, explained permutation algorithms, and helped struggling friends, ensuring everyone had the chance to thrive. Through this, I realized that magic doesn’t lie in what we know, but in how we use it to uplift others.

So, it’s fine if I can’t master every concept. Magic isn’t about hoarding knowledge for ourselves—it’s about sharing it to empower others.

Determined to pass on this gift, I’ve found purpose in my Computer Science Club. As I teach Python to my students, I shape my lessons to spark curiosity and build confidence. There’s August, who once struggled to grasp loops but never stopped asking questions. One day, after careful explanations, he exclaims “I get it now!” His electric joy as he watches the Mandelbrot set bloom on his screen fills me with pride. I’m reminded of knowledge’s true magic—creating moments of wonder for others.

Holding my grandmother’s hand as I play the sweet melodies of “Bésame Mucho,” I’m sure the same magic lives in music. Channeling music’s power through every note, I watch as her smile brightens, cherished memories returning. Inspired by her reaction, I began performing for Memory Care residents at a nursing home. As I play Debussy’s Arabesque No. 1, I shape every phrase with intention, understanding how dynamics and tempo can speak to the heart in ways that words can’t. After one performance, an elderly woman approaches me, tears in her eyes—“Your music moved me. I haven’t felt this way in years—thank you!” The smiles of the residents reflect more than joy—they reveal loneliness lifted. In these moments, I feel the true power of knowledge—not in my musicality’s mastery, but in how I can use it to create lasting moments of connection.

I’m no Princess Twilight Sparkle, but my journey parallels hers in remarkable ways. We’ve both learned that magic isn’t about mastering every spell—it’s about using what we learn to light up others’ lives. Though I’ve let go of perfection, I'll never lose my love for learning. In fact, I'm continually discovering new ways to nurture it—each challenge I face is an opportunity to bring understanding to life. Whether I'm inspiring young minds through coding or playing music that heals, my passion only grows as I share it—because my true power lies not in knowledge alone, but in using it to empower others. And that is a magic I’m determined to keep sharing.

My childhood summers unfolded over a sea of jigsaw pieces strewn across the bedroom floor, my father and I cross-legged amid the chaos, eager to construct the promised fairytale landscape. I’d always found comfort in the logic of assembly, mirroring my obsession with science. While poet John Keats lamented that science would "clip an Angel's wings/Conquer all mysteries by rule and line," I found beauty in transforming disorder into order, conquering the mystery before us piece by piece.

But alongside my fascination with the scientific, I harbored another, quieter, irreconcilable love: poetry. Ever since stumbling upon my dad’s weathered copy of Leaves of Grass in third grade, I was smitten with rhythm and verse. At first, poetry bewildered me. Unlike the Pushkin and Chukovsky stanzas that lulled me to sleep as a child, most poems didn’t adhere to set lengths or predictable structures; from Basho's haikus to Byron's sprawling epics, each was unique. And yet, I was drawn to poetry's unpredictability, how works so stylistically diverse could still spark similarly ineffable emotions. I found myself embroiled in a love triangle, caught between two seemingly antithetical worlds: the rigid structure of science and the boundless freedom of poetry.

Enter Computer Science 09, where I met Ada Lovelace, creator of the first computer algorithm. Probing her biography, I learned Lovelace's brilliance lay in her ability to harmonize the empirical with the enigmatic. She called herself a "poet of science," and for the first time, I realized embracing one side of myself didn’t have to mean sidelining the other. Recognizing myself in Lovelace, I discovered how these two identities could not only coexist but thrive in symbiosis. Writing for my school's century-old literary magazine, I began to see words as instruments not unlike microscopes and spectrophotometers—tools that allow us to chip away at perennial existential questions. That same year, I won my first statewide poetry award for a poem I wrote to grapple with my grandmother's Alzheimer's diagnosis. Yet, even as I found catharsis through poetry, I itched for a clear-cut explanation and solution to her affliction, returning to science in search of a way to help women like my grandmother. I joined the Icahn School of Medicine, working with a team formulating a novel follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)-blocking antibody to treat neurodegenerative disease in female mice.

Entering the lab, I expected research to be methodical and orderly, like the puzzles I'd solved with my father years ago. What I found was something more akin to poetry. Human biology, with its intricate networks of atoms, proteins, and cells, wasn't merely systematic—it was lyrical. Just as Lovelace saw poetry in algorithms, I saw poetry in my work, from the biochemical marriage of antibody and ligand, to the ruby-red glow of FSH receptor transcripts on hypothalamic neurons. Poetry taught me to read between the lines, question the obvious, uncover unexpected connections the same way one crafts a metaphor. I noticed links between seemingly disparate phenomena: rising FSH levels post-menopause, increased ovarian cancer rates in older women, and our antibody's potential to modulate FSH activity. The pieces slowly assembled in my mind: Could a therapeutic we’d used against Alzheimer’s bridge a gap in women’s health? With that, I engineered an independent study to combat ovarian cancer. I found the beauty of the scientific process in soaring through a hazy sky of unknowns, discovering the serendipitous connection, the fresh simile, and watching the clouds part—only to ascend anew.

Keats feared science would clip angels' wings, strip life of its poetry. Becoming a scientist in my own right, I can't help but disagree: With every answer unearthed, a thousand novel questions emerge in its place, and the puzzle expands. As a poet-scientist, I’m committed to forging wings that fly to uncharted spaces where the analytical and artistic meet.

My cracked screwdriver would expose me as a fake handyman.

As I wrestled with curtain rods and faux blinds, I honed in on the mechanics' long-nose pliers, stud finders, and power drills. With loose nails scattered on the floor, I transformed my laundry room into a workshop station, delving into the world of craftsmanship.

When our TV stand became wobbly, I crafted a wooden L-bracket of the perfect dimension to stabilize its legs. I salvaged colorful rubber bands from styling my low buns, fixing them into U-shaped anchors (a fake wrench) to tighten bolts on broken office desks. Surely, I could repair any problem seamlessly with the right instruments, making the flaw obscure.

***

Three years ago, I strolled into my grandmother’s living room and noticed her struggling to lift herself off the couch, her hand trembling. Involuntarily. Months later, the devastating diagnosis came: Parkinson's Disease. I couldn't believe the words. What was Parkinson’s disease? What did dopamine deficiency even mean?

I applied my handyman skills- finding precise angles to strengthen my grandmother. While cold-emailing neurologists, I learned about the essential role of folate, vitamin B12, and B6 in tremor development. Although my grandmother is one of the sweetest people I know, she is an unbelievably picky eater who stays true to her African dishes such as ______ and _____. Scavenging online forums for diet plans, I pinned up a weekly schedule of high-fiber and antioxidant-rich meals, crafting ways to fuse these nutritious foods with our traditional Ghanaian cuisine. I’m no chef. Yet, my grandmother seemed to enjoy the odd mixes of oats and fruit bowls with yams and tomato stews.

The next step was to add daily walks after school to help maintain her mobility. With nimble fingers, I created cardboard NBA rims, sizable enough to host living room basketball tournaments. Despite my spectacular track record of defeat, our makeshift competitions kept her walking regularly, although her fingers trembled slightly. Surprisingly, her hands launched the ball into the basket while trying to dunk for the first time!

Yet, my efforts weren't enough. My grandmother’s hands quivered with a new intensity. Her cane became an extension of her arm as she shuffled across the sidewalks. I felt frustrated. What was it that made my efforts fall short, I wondered.

I re-doubled my efforts. After school, I folded sketch papers into identical pieces to hold my origami lessons. Every Tuesday and Thursday at 5 PM, I taught my grandmother inside reverse, squash, and swivel folds to transform these one-dimensional flat pieces of printer paper into soaring jets, springing frogs, and flappable cranes. As she maneuvered the paper, I could see the quiet pride in her eyes as she admired each piece she created.

***

A month later, after a stroll home, my grandmother, shaking slightly, stops. She holds my shoulder and says, “At first, when I got diagnosed, I didn't know what would happen. But then, you showed up almost every day to me through my pain. Thank you for everything you have done. You have made me a stronger person now”.

I stared across the distance of the street, struggling to keep my tears from falling onto my face. As she held onto my shoulder, I sniffled and continued our path home.

It was easy to think that being a handyman was just about fixing things, but when Grandma got sick, I realized that the real value rests not in flawless restoration but in the heartfelt adventures of empathy and care. As caregiving is often seen as an irreparable hardship, I aspire to change this perception. Even if I couldn't reverse my grandmother’s illness, I could create new origami designs and experiment with nutritional mixes, bringing a smile to her face. Moving forward, I aim not only to solve practical problems but to fix the objective questions I can answer and look for ways to create bonds and nuance in life's less pliable corners.

Jolting up from my bed, I peered into the hallway to investigate a startling sound. My gaze swept past shattered plates and bowls to my father, sprawled on his right, clutching a torn tablecloth that couldn’t prevent his fall. I rushed towards him and shook his shoulders frantically. After an eternal minute, his eyes opened.

What followed was a blur: my mother helped him sit up as I brought him water. After taking a sip, my father instructed me to leave so he could speak privately with my mother. I stepped out of sight—but secretly listened.

“...stress...suddenly fainted…”
“...H-1B visa…11 days to get a job…deported to India…”
“...no time…talk later.”

At age 13, I’d heard of H-1B visas—but I’d never thought that a ticket into America would have an expiration date. Terrified, I began scavenging through immigration articles, desperate for any path to avoid deportation. After grappling with legalese like “Form I-129” and “Form I-140,” I discovered the solution: permanent residency.

“With a green card, Appa can't get deported for being unemployed," I told my parents later that day. I knew they’d realize I'd eavesdropped—but their relief was my priority.

Yet, their eyes weren’t relieved—just defeated.

“Adhi…we filed for a green card six years ago.”

Countless questions flooded my mind, but the exhaustion in their faces convinced me to hold them back. Instead, I spent the night poring through policy papers until I pieced together our predicament: immigrants of each nationality were limited to just 7% of employment-based green cards granted annually. This country-cap disproportionately constricted Indian immigrants, creating a 195-year wait for permanent residency.

Why did society ignore this inequity?

In the week approaching potential deportation, tension escalated with every day that passed; finally, my father revealed our fate.

“Adhi…”

My gut tightened.

“I got hired. We can stay.”

With tearful eyes, we embraced, grateful that we’d escaped deportation. Yet, I couldn’t escape indignation. When millions of Indian immigrants silently teetered on the tightrope above deportation, I needed to bring our plight to light.

I began by describing the green card backlog to my friends—ultimately, their curiosity and empathy fueled my courage. I sent several letters to Congress, pushing for immigration reform. Though each letter was met with silence, I expanded my efforts undeterred, entering an essay contest with a piece condemning immigrant discrimination. Placing among the top entries earned me an invitation to speak at the Stop the Hate Ceremony in Cleveland.

I accepted, ready to make my written words spoken.

***

Gripping the lectern, I scanned the dim auditorium. Five hundred faces stared back. Doubt gripped me—until I found my father's reassuring smile in the crowd. Soon, words began to flow.

“Society condemns illegal racism but ignores legal racism,” I denounced, thinking of 400,000 Indian immigrants expected to die before being naturalized.

“Each voice added to the chorus amplifies the call for immigrant justice,” I declared, rallying the audience to advocate for reform.

I wasn’t speaking for applause, but to ensure no child would witness a parent collapse from stress caused by systemic injustice.

After my five-minute speech, dozens approached the stage—not just with praise, but with their own stories of injustice. “Go into politics,” urged an African-American gentleman, as he recounted the discrimination he endured for his skin color. “Run for Congress,” encouraged a Czech lady, sharing her father’s struggles immigrating to Canada.

My father’s fall ignited a fire within me, but that night, my words sparked the same in others. As once-strangers shared heartfelt stories, I realized the power of words to forge unity. Injustice looms large—but does the yearning for change. True reform arises when voices converge into movements. I’m determined to ignite that convergence with my voice—uniting others and forging a legacy of impact—both in college and beyond.

***

As I stepped off stage, my father awaited, beaming. With tearful eyes, we embraced—not for escaping deportation but for parlaying our pain into purpose.

Sitting and watching the waves at Doheny Beach, endlessly reshaping the shore, I remembered how a month ago, they reshaped me too. That was the day I learned strength isn’t about staying silent; it’s about connection.

Growing up, silence was my armor. My Chinese dad and Korean mom believed in carrying burdens quietly, in Korean, my mom says, “chummul.” So I swallowed my worries and fears, sealed them up tight believing it made me strong. At school, I laughed when my friends laughed, nodded at their stories, but I never let them in. I was too afraid of looking weak. Lonely, the silence felt like a weight pressing on my chest, heavier every day.

That changed at Doheny Beach. Feeling desperate, I sent a text I almost didn’t: “Beach trip?” To my shock, they said yes. We played volleyball until our arms stung, ate chips that crunched with sand, and watched the sunset. Mustering up courage, I quietly said, “I totally bombed the math quiz.” My throat tightened. Tom smiled. “I’m failing chemistry.” Someone else laughed. “Same.” We kept going, trading struggles and funny stories. For the first time, I felt free. Vulnerability wasn’t weakness; it was strength.

That moment stayed with me. Life isn’t something to face alone; it’s meant to be shared and built together. I carried this lesson into my Informatics: Artificial Intelligence (AI) class, where collaboration turned confusion into clarity.

One afternoon, my partner and I were debugging a budget calculator that kept crashing. Error messages piled up on the screen like a losing game of Tetris. Frustration set in until I suggested, “What if we add graphs to show spending patterns?” The suggestion worked. While they redesigned the interface, I focused on fixing the equations. We tested, failed, adjusted, and tried again. After hours of work, the program finally ran. Seeing it come to life wasn’t just about the code—it was about the teamwork that made it possible.

That same excitement drives me to learn. In Informatics: Artificial Intelligence (AI), I tested a language model’s ability to answer real-world questions. I asked, “How do I save money if I don’t make enough?” Watching it adapt fascinated me. It inspired an idea for a financial literacy app that analyzes spending, warns users about overspending, and suggests savings tips. While volunteering at a food pantry and with Breakthrough, I’ve met people who feel like saving is impossible. Tools like this could break cycles of poverty.

My goal is to become an AI systems engineer, designing ethical and accessible tools. AI systems are often so complex that even their creators don’t fully understand them. I want to develop tools to audit algorithms for fairness, ensuring they work for everyone, especially underserved communities. Whether it’s helping students manage loans, improving healthcare access, or predicting disasters, I want to build systems that leave no one behind. To me, AI isn’t just about solving problems—it’s about creating progress everyone can share.

At university, I want to collaborate with peers and professors to solve bigger social challenges like poverty, mental health, or healthcare. I can already see myself at a hackathon, sketching app ideas on a whiteboard at midnight, writing and debugging code alongside a team, and watching our vision take shape. I want to work on projects that explore how AI can serve marginalized populations, address global challenges, and drive real change. I hope to find my own “PayPal Mafia”—a group of peers who inspire me, challenge me, and build something extraordinary with me.

Standing on Doheny Beach that day, watching the waves reshape the shore, I realized I was like the sand, shaped by the people and experiences around me. I want to carry those lessons into my future as an AI systems engineer, ensuring the tools I create empower people, solve meaningful problems, and leave the world better than I found it.

Beyond the Blank Page

As my uncle's restaurant neared closing time, I slowly unboxed a new pack of fortune cookies at the front counter. But, when I was almost finished placing them into the table box, a cookie slipped and hit the ground. Unable to resist my curiosity to read the fortune paper, I stopped midway through restocking and broke the cookie open. I found myself not being impatient for the satisfying crunch of the cookie, but rather intrigued by the fortune paper that held wise words of luck and advice. I anticipated a wise saying or a lucky omen, but the paper inside held an unexpected surprise: a blank fortune.

I blinked in disbelief, questioning whether I was hallucinating behind my newly prescribed pair of glasses. Yet the two-inch sheet of rectangular paper stared back at me revealing nothing but emptiness. Discombobulated, I shoved the paper in my pocket and returned to the cashier register, drumming my fingers and waiting for customers to arrive. A blank fortune?

Father calls out behind the kitchen, asking me to take the soup container and start his car. As I listen to his directions, I realize I always followed others’ advice and instructions without questions. I have always been a ‘listener’, rather than the one adding my own voice. Whether it was a friend's conversation about a favorite song, my mother’s demands to come home earlier instead of going to after-school clubs, or a teacher’s philosophical question, I never had my own solid opinions before hearing what others had to say. With decisions, I waited for my parents’ guidance. With conversations, I listened to my peers. With advice, I followed it meticulously.

The pocketed empty fortune reminded me of my own blank voice, and it inspired me to make a difference. As a student who never earned a full score in participation, I gradually challenged myself to make a conscious effort to communicate. Instead of waiting for class to begin and passively completing the “Do Nows”, I used the first few minutes of class to ask my teachers for clarifications on any unclear concepts from the previous lesson. I became more proactive during group work rather than waiting for another classmate to take the initiative.

Furthermore, I chose to pursue extracurriculars that excited me and were connected to my homelife. Inspired by my parents’ medical challenges, I found “Inspiration Through Ink”, a card-making organization to uplift the mental spirits of nurses and patients through written messages. When helping my mother schedule her doctors’ appointments, I no longer wait for a translator to support her. Instead, I take the initiative to communicate with the medical staff directly.

Ironically, it was the blank fortune that helped me realize that I am in charge of my life. Each time I speak up or take action that demonstrates my informed decisions, I feel the empty fortune cookie being replaced with my story of building the confidence to express myself. I have come to realize that my voice matters because my opinions and choices shape my experiences, and that I can and should take ownership of my life. This epiphany will continue to inform my choices as I challenge myself, follow my passions, and pursue my curiosities. I still leave the blank fortune on my desk as a reminder of my journey to self-discovery for my voice.

For most families, when night falls, the atmosphere is peaceful, as spouses and children settle in to recharge for the next day. However, when the sun went down when I was a child, my father would be out gambling. One night when he came home, he beat my mother. But he also burned my drawing books because of his addictive behaviors. I looked at my mother, tears running down her face, and I knew everything was about to change. My mother packed our clothes to move to my grandma’s house. I knew my family was broken, but I could not do anything. I understood it was best for my mother and father to go their separate ways.

The effects of my parents’ divorce upended my life, but perseverance against adversity paved the way to a new and stronger reality. My biological father seemed to have forgotten about me, with not even so much as a “happy birthday.” My mother rode an outdated bike to take me to school and get to her workplace. She worked twelve hours a day, seven days a week to earn enough money to raise me. Her hands were calloused and often bloody because of the physical work that she did to support us. Her eyes were dry and red from long hours laboring. I witnessed the toll of hard work and this made me determined to educate myself to better provide for myself and my future family. Our first move took us from northern Vietnam to the south, leaving behind my childhood family, friends, and familiar places. Big changes can be overwhelming, but I adapted through courage, focus, faith, and commitment to personal success. New schools, teachers, and friends meant a focused effort to interact while letting go of my old way of life. More changes followed, as my mother remarried and I gained a supportive stepfather. I found that changes can be welcome, and now my stepdad assumes the role left vacant by my biological father. He supports me in every aspect of my life and ensures I have everything I need. Still, more changes were to come as we decided to move to the United States to strengthen family bonds.

New beginnings are never easy, but as my family and I chase the American Dream, I have found that a positive attitude combined with a willingness to adapt and work hard will pave the way for success. My mother and my stepdad work together in our family’s nail salon seven days a week, nonstop to maintain our daily life. Watching their example motivates me to strive even more, inspires my strong work ethic, and allows me to put my heart and soul into the classroom, where I commit extra hours to study English to integrate to our new culture and to help build a strong family business where customer service is central. The responsibility of being a translator for my family, walking them through every step of an important document, and helping them navigate life is my motivation. At an early age, every step I take emphasizes how my character, built through willingness to adapt and to work hard, will be the foundation for success in college, career, and life.

Having so much responsibility in my childhood taught me the importance of diligence and strengthened my character to become a successful person. The challenges I faced, all the sacrifices that my family went through, which influenced my desire, have helped me find a way to build a better life for myself and discover my purpose. Faith, family, an ironclad work effort, and perseverance are the cornerstones for my success, and I am ready for the challenges of college and career.

"Why do you like that kid's toy so much?"

My mom's question caught me off guard as I glanced at my scooter propped against the wall. But to me, the scooter was a vessel for airborne tricks, spontaneous adventures that unite friends, and pushing our limits.

In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic hit, closing all skateparks and shutting me and my friends indoors — destroying my community.

Two splintered, dicey ramps later, I found out: recklessly improvising a curved-takeoff with a rusty saw might look flashy, but does not hold up.

Swallowing my pride — and a considerable amount of sawdust — I decided to try again – NASA engineer-style. This time, I sketched a blueprint full of detailed measurements before hauling my mom’s car to Home-Depot. I hunted down 2x4s for the ramp’s inner-supports, and plywood for the ramp faces. Many hours later in my garage, a robust kicker ramp with “N-A-S-A” spray-painted on it lay before me.

I finally experienced the thrill of flying through the air again – I invited a few buddies over to share it with. That Saturday afternoon, I did a couple new tricks, a Briflip and a triple tailwhip, and also pushed Jason to try a double tailwhip, a trick he’d never done.

“The technique is just like a normal tailwhip, just spin it more desperately,” I coached.

When he landed it, I screamed louder than he did.

But how to level up the ante? I proposed a contest: who could pull off the silliest tricks or poses mid-air? Kyson won with a Swan to triple “Ye-Ye,” (a trick he invented) which had us all on the ground. While my humble 18-inch tall ramp may not compare to the grand structures of quarter-pipes and spines the neighboring skateparks offer, I was proud of creating something that could last, reuniting me and my friends to ride together.

While it might seem silly, ramp-building taught me to balance meticulous planning and reckless improvisation, which I’ve applied to other areas of my life, such as founding my high school’s Anthropology Club.

Having no such club before, I wanted to bring together students who were passionate about anthropology to study this field together, rather than in isolation. Initially, I threw together detailed lecture-style presentations, but was met with blank stares.

A few Ted Talks later, I realized I had to channel my ramp-building spirit to rile up the kids.

During our next lesson, the projector flashed a wide-eyed gorilla. I asked, “Why do some animals have eyes on the sides of their heads, while humans have eyes on their front?”

A few giggled. A first stab came, “Because humans need to see things that are really far away.”

I nudged them closer to the answer. “Picture where our ancient ancestors might have hung-out.” A monkey swinging on a tree appeared on-screen.

“Better depth perception!” Naomi chimed.

Setting up engaging activities to stimulate students had them coming back a month later, eagerly explaining how they remembered retinal disparity on their last AP Psychology test from my demonstration of the paper tube illusion, where students roll-up a piece of paper and look through it with one eye while holding their hand next to the tube, making a hole seemingly appear in their palm.

Whether I'm crafting a Superman-worthy kicker ramp, or designing a lesson that gets kids excitedly flying in the air, I’ve learned the process remains the same: attention to detail and a dash of creativity. Through trial and error, a meticulous 'ramp-building' mindset, by balancing meticulous planning and spontaneity, I’m able to succeed in my ambitions. In college, I'm excited to apply this 'ramp-building' philosophy to new challenges like sparking curiosity for anthropology with my roommates and bringing them together for spontaneous Friday night get-togethers. I’ll continue to build my way step-by-step to my dreams.

As the clouds settled in the sky, snow streamed down to the earth. On a winter morning, as I stepped into the backyard, the snow crumbled beneath my feet while falling flakes adorned my hair with crystals. The snow encapsulating my world seemed to whisper meaning through its beauty.

For most, visual snow translates to seeing snow, but my snow is another kind, a grainy old television with sparks—like at the ends of fireworks—that scurry across my field of vision.

I first noticed this phenomenon during the pandemic when I saw a flurry of grain on the ceiling. I had no idea where it came from—whether from endless screen time or a dormant gene wired to turn on. Afterward, I bombarded Google with question after question: What are these light particles? Where did they come from? The algorithm seemed to memorize my frantic queries, plastering false ads about health and medicine onto my screen to exploit my desire for answers.

Soon, I learned that visual snow might be a product of my brain fabricating illusions. When I tried communicating this phenomenon to my parents, the neurologist, and the ophthalmologist, they didn’t know how to respond to my obscure descriptions. If visual snow only lived in my mind, if neither those around me nor medical tests could confirm its existence, how could others understand it?

After a seemingly endless battle to translate my experience to others along different perceptual lines, I discovered storytelling, where art and words could compensate for my vision.

During a summer workshop for a creative nonfiction course, my five classmates, whom I had known for only one week, would read four years of my life in just six pages. I built this essay upon days of research on visual stimuli and Gottfried Leibniz. I worked obsessively over the project, highlighting every detail relevant to my final takeaway.

As we engaged with each other's personal stories, there was an air of respect and understanding, for each one of us were sharing our vulnerabilities. Their discussions on my essay revealed to me that they grasped my work's essence. One of my classmates commented that her ignorance of visual snow had dissolved by the end of my essay. Many experiences are left unspoken, as people live along their unique lines. But at this moment, our lines intersected.

Since then, I haven’t wanted any person to feel invisible. In wondering about my own condition and the lives of others, I found that people’s experiences are susceptible to misinterpretation, so I wrote another story, hoping to teach what I learned.

As I walked to the podium for a public reading, my fictional vignette paralleled my struggle with visual snow and how humans contend with the vagaries of life. I conveyed the alienation of the “other,” the misinterpretation of experiences, and the power of stories to unify the human experience. A few of my audience members expressed how my story resonated with them, touching on the complexity of dementia and inspiring wonder. Their feedback strengthened my belief that storytelling has the power to bridge gulfs in perception and build understanding between people.

As I went down one rabbit hole after another, I was fascinated by the various subjects that debunked my past assumptions. What I have come to value is the flexibility of thought and diverse experiences to foster greater understanding.

My art and words help me share different worlds across perceptual borders. Whether telling students’ stories in the yearbook or tutoring elementary school students in math, I will continue fostering connections between diverse groups of people through empathy.

Just as the snow is complex in its dual representations of cold isolation and magical transformation, so are the intricacies of knowledge and experience.

Dissonance is, for me, a catalyst, pushing me further down the inextricably bound path of curiosity and creativity.

My goal has become clear: to make the invisible seen and valuable.

Flayed skin. Ruptured inside. Over-ripe flesh. CPR could not save the dying cherry tomatoes! Left on the shelves to rot…they were undesirable. I grabbed the box of decimated flesh, ready to throw out another hundred.

Squeaking onto the freshly waxed linoleum, I saw Mrs. Tran, who impatiently tapped her foot as I approached. “No tomatoes again, huh?” she teased. As I dropped the box into the trash, I watched a few burst on impact and grimaced. Why should patients lose out on cherry tomatoes filled with Vitamin A, C, iron, and chock-full of potassium, especially when they need it the most?

As a volunteer at Hartford Hospital, I was supposed to nourish geriatric patients, diabetics, and the malnourished, but we were not upholding our end of the bargain.

The problem? Shipping time. While the firm onions or the tightly packed jalapenos could endure the ride from the farms in big cardboard boxes, the delicate cherry tomatoes, constantly bouncing around, succumbed to near-fatal injuries.

I could no longer sit idly by, allowing Mrs. Tran not to receive the best care possible. At the end of my shift one night, I paced back and forth (well, as much as I could in the supply closet) and plotted. It was not until I bumped my knee on the bucket of PVC pipes (the third time) that it finally popped into my head. I immediately got to work.

I had found the spot for my makeshift garden on the rooftop and began poking thick holes into the walls of the plastic pipes, snuggling cups with tomato seeds inside. It became my special place, tending to them each day for two weeks. But…there were only dying seedlings. The soil’s dry texture suffocated the poor seedlings, silently killing the plant’s root size and water intake. Ending their misery, I remembered the words of my ninth-grade science teacher, Ms. Highland, who plotted pea plants with us in plastic bags. She had proven soil is not necessary, just proper nutrition. It was simple hydroponics!

I scoured the internet to understand which minerals and nutrients nourished tomatoes the most. I watched podcasts, YouTube videos, and content from my grandma’s gardening Facebook group. Finally, I found the ingredients to make Mrs. Tran proud: Epsom salt and calcium for nutrients, limestone to balance the pH, and manure for its high NO₂ concentration. Sourcing the ingredients from the greenhouse, I placed the thick combined paste in each small cup and desperately hoped. The results showed themselves in two months when I bore the fruits of my labor (yes, tomatoes are fruit!) and tasted my sweet victory.

Sitting in the cold, misty office with a basket of my love, I offered it to anyone who dared walk through the doors.
