Bombarded with my pleading, all accepted, placing the plump fruit in their mouths while their eyes lightened up joyfully. I’d urge them to take as many as they wanted while filling their cart with farm-fresh eggs, whole-fat milk, lean ground meat, and anything their hearts desired.

As I began to wipe down the tables and pack away the leftover produce, I noticed one single glistening cherry tomato at the bottom of the basket. It was the last one. I couldn’t help myself and popped it into my mouth. The sharp umami flavor flooded my taste buds, and tears stung my eyes. I felt overwhelmed knowing I had brought solace to Mrs. Tran.

Now, I am entering a new season and have new seeds I hope to plant. No one should be left without the barest necessities, the juiciest tomatoes, or the kindest of companions. I feel I have been planted to bring warmth to others through food, and see myself creating gardens to serve communities bereft of such joys. Through biological sciences, we can innovate hydroponics to make sustainable farming all the more efficient, just one little tomato at a time.

“My little sister almost drowned here.” I pointed at the fresh water spring with a heavy metal grate over it.

“Damn, that sucks!” My friend was now clearly interested in the rest of the story.

“She fell in head first.”

“Do you remember it?”

“Well… no, I was like five when it happened. My dad told me,“ I reluctantly admitted.

It was my fourteenth time visiting my mom’s hometown in rural Japan, but for Mitchell, his first time abroad.

We arrived late at my grandmother’s house and fell straight onto futons, exhausted from traveling almost twenty hours straight. After a couple hours rest, jetlag struck.

I remembered what my family used to do: the drowsy walks to the nearby convenience store with my parents and sister at four am, grabbing some melon bread, skipping rocks on the seashore, and watching the sunrise.

“Let’s go on a walk!” I grabbed Mitchell, leading him to the nearby 7-Eleven.

From the store, our walk led us back to the coast. We stood there nibbling on the melon bread, taking in the sunrise over Toyama Bay. I taught Mitchell some useful Japanese phrases, we skipped rocks, and talked plans for the next two weeks.

I felt a pleasant warmth as I watched my friend smile. Sharing this small part of my past made it feel new again.

The next day, I showed Mitchell around Kurobe. As we walked, I shared stories of the lazy summer days that I’d spent there as a kid.

At the playground next to the old temple, I told him about playing endless rounds of tag with the neighborhood kids, the air thick with laughter and the hum of cicadas flooding back into my mind.

We kept walking, jumping over little canals filled with water running from the rice fields. And as I took a left, I spotted a freshwater spring.

This was the setting for the dramatic tale of my little sister almost drowning.

As I finished up the family legend, I realized this place was different now. The monkey bars were streaked with rust, and the swings, long removed. My neighborhood elementary school was quieter, with fewer children in its classrooms. Yet, in sharing these places with my friend, I was able to rediscover their meaning.

Watching Mitchell in these moments – his laughter while skipping rocks, delight at the taste of melon bread, and surprise at the absurd challenges on local TV game shows – helped me realize that these experiences weren’t just about nostalgia. I dove into my memories, searching for the best bits. Were they just funny or were they something that I actually cared about? Worth telling my friend? Worth walking to? I would dissect each one, finding fragments to tell stories from my many past visits. Gluing them together, I would carefully present them. Did I get back confusion or laughter? Each time, I reached back into my mind to find a different fragment or perhaps a new story. Each question from my friend, reshaping the story in my mind until it became something entirely new.

In sharing these pieces of my past with Mitchell, I began to understand myself in ways I never had before. I saw my own experiences with fresh clarity through the simple act of choosing what to share and how to tell it.

As the crickets began their nightly chorus and the Tateyama mountains in the background faded into twilight, I understood that these memories weren’t just mine anymore. They had changed into something richer, something my friend and I now carried together.

The hiss of batter hitting hot oil, the sweet smell of powdered sugar—these were the sounds and scents of my teenage years.

When Dad lost his job, we struggled financially, so he started working the light show at Bristol Speedway to keep us afloat. Every winter, for the next nine years, he’d be gone for 52 nights, enduring long hours and returning exhausted but hopeful.

Most winters, Dad became almost unrecognizable: Saving every dollar possible for us rather than spending money on food for himself, he’d return with a slimmer face and clothes hanging looser on his body.

When my school went virtual during the early stages of COVID-19, I took the opportunity to be with my father. I helped tie down our appliances in the food trailer and packed my suitcase.

My father fist-bumped me in tradition as we set our five-hour journey. "Son, it's just the boys!"

As we neared Bristol Motor Speedway, my heart raced with excitement. After unloading and setting up the trailer, we moved into our tiny apartment across the street. I unpacked in my new room, joining my dad later for chicken wings on the counter.

The next morning, I learned my first lesson—no Mom, no breakfast. We rushed to buy supplies and prepare for opening night. By dusk, my nerves were peaking. Our first customer ordered—"fried Oreos and a funnel cake"—and I went to work. The heat from the fryer made me sweat as the smells of grease and sugar filled the air. Handing over my first order, I saw the customer’s smile and felt a surge of pride.

The days became a routine: long hours spent frying, serving, and running errands. We worked 8-9 hours on weekdays, and on weekends, it stretched to 12. Every spare moment was spent prepping, cleaning, or counting sales, trying to beat last year’s numbers. I had to keep up with school, too—logging in from a small table in the corner of the trailer to attend Zoom lectures, I’d squeeze in assignments between rushes.

My feet throbbed by the end of each day, and homesickness crept in. My dad must have seen it, because halfway through the show, he said, “Son, you don’t have to stay. A kid your age shouldn’t be working this hard.” For a moment, I wanted to accept. But I couldn’t imagine leaving him to face the long hours alone. I chose to stay.

When the season finally ended, we broke down the setup, packed the trailer, and prepared to head home. I was filled with a sense of accomplishment. Dad turned to me and said, “I’m proud of you, son. For 52 nights, you put in the hours without complaint.” On the drive home, I realized that what had been a few hard weeks for me was something my father had endured every winter for years.

I now juggle the demands of running my food truck while pursuing my education and planning for the future, just as I once stood in that trailer alongside him, balancing customer orders and school assignments. Whether it’s designing a menu or building relationships with local suppliers, I draw on the resilience and resourcefulness I learned during those winters at the Speedway.

These lessons extend beyond the trailer. As DECA president, I mentor students in entrepreneurship, sharing the skills and mindset I’ve gained over the years. I encourage them to see challenges as stepping stones, just as my father showed me. The food truck taught me that hard work and collaboration can create lasting impact, whether in business or the community. Looking ahead, I am inspired to explore sustainable and ethical entrepreneurship, not just for profit but for purpose. My journey with Charli Jay’s Food Truck has been more than a job—it has been a testament to the power of perseverance and the importance of uplifting others along the way.

Growing up as a lone programmer in [Xizhou], a city more familiar with coal dust than coding, I was an isolated node in a network that I would eventually help create.

Since my parents divorced when I was four, I've lived with my father's family. For much of my childhood, he'd return home after midnight. Often drunk, he'd pull me away from my computer, regardless of whether I was solving a programming challenge or playing Command and Conquer. To him, both were distractions to my studies and bad for my eyesight. At my mom's monthly visit, when she discovered that I secretly journeyed to the province's biggest bookstore 100 miles away for a book on Computing, another argument broke out in the already shattered family reunion, followed by an old-fashioned "physical education" for my reckless "irrelevant pursuits."

Things started to change after I won first place in the provincial informatics contest. Surprised, my parents started receiving calls from coaches and recruiters. As they made a collective effort to understand my academic path, before and forward, they started consulting with friends, relatives, educational experts, and me to learn that C++ is a programming language - not a grade - and which countries have the best CS PhD opportunities, despite never having college degrees themselves. That year, as we celebrated my birthday together, my parents gifted me a MacBook. But more than a computer, I re-gained my once-lost family connection.

"You do that, I WILL quit." My co-chair, [JC], vehemently objected when I proposed flexible scheduling for the [X-CUP]. Since we founded the competitive programming competition two years ago, it has gained a large global audience, making fixed contest scheduling a nightmare across all time zones. Yet, having gone through the Chinese Olympiad of Informatics system myself, I understood the sense of ritualistic experience [JC] aimed to preserve. So, after sharing my personal experience of USACO's more inviting format, we reached a compromise: a ten-slot schedule to balance both communal formality and logistical convenience, a format never seen before but welcomed by over 1000 [X-CUP] community members hailing from all continents. Now, our [X-CUP] is running smoothly in its third season, with international participation doubled. [JC], still my co-chair, has become my research collaborator and a close friend in life.

In [Aksu], [Nubia], the call to prayers punctually interrupted the training for the national teams. [Nour], the only female team member, expressed concerns about balancing religious duties with her workload. Wanting to hear more unvoiced opinions like [Nour's], as the acting coach for many teams from the Middle Eastern and North African regions, I initiated and moderated the Roundtable Consultation (RC) sessions, where students from [Libya] and [Saudi] also echoed [Nour's] words. Experienced in scheduling, I reorganized the training and mock tests to minimize conflicts with Islamic prayer times. Hopefully, someday, the [COC] committee will accommodate a lunchtime (and Dhuhr prayer) break in its official schedule. Mashallah (As God willed). Trusted by the [Nubian] team to cast their national vote at the [COC] general assembly, as an atheist and a foreigner, I had never felt so close to a community I once thought so different from my own.

Returning to my hometown, [Xizhou], after these experiences, I no longer saw isolation but opportunity. Sharing my journey with my middle school's new competitive programming team and learning from leaders at the newly founded local high-tech park, I realized to build meaningful human connections, whether with divorced parents, an online programming community, or those whose beliefs might differ from mine, I must first seek to understand before being understood, letting humility form the bridge between cultures, motives, and even opposing opinions - a mindset I will carry into college and life beyond.

Bippo was almost home when he noticed two soldiers following him—one dressed in a blue uniform and the other in yellow. I saw them chasing Bippo. I tried to save him but the blue soldier captured him just a step away from his front door. He was my last hope.

It was time to accept that I lost my almost predictable Ludo win. Well, there is no real Bippo (it was the last red Ludo piece I had). The front door was the box before the Ludo board's home column. The blue soldier that engulfed my red piece and my Ludo fate for the night belonged to my mom, the ultimate Ludo champion of our household. Ludo nights in my home were intense—a four-colored battleground where we fought with our soldiers for the ultimate title.

With each six-roll of the dice, one of the soldiers was released from the barracks, ready to fight. The key is to predict opponents’ moves cautiously without letting them know yours, strategizing every move of the game. All the critical thinking I developed by inspecting each box to build a roadmap went beyond the board game to make an actual cat Uber for Toby.

My neighbor adopted Toby, a stray cat from an animal shelter after it met with a severe road accident. The accident left one of Toby’s forelimbs paralyzed. Seeing Toby’s condition, I intended to help. Initially, I thought of designing a support for its leg, a crutch. Though it sounded perfect in my head and I spent weeks building it, it was not even close to a practical solution. Through multiple trials and errors, I finally managed to make a customized resin tray, screwed in wheels, and added a cushion on top. Toby could sit on it and push itself slowly with one of its hindlimbs (Toby’s cat Uber). I knew I did not disappoint myself with this month-long project when my neighbor sent me videos of Toby going to bed all by itself sitting on that tray.

Ludo is the epitome of adaptability and patience. Even when I need a six to win the game or survive another piece but the dice roll down to one, I should act according to the situation. Similarly, my patience and ability to handle situations are reflected in my Model United Nations Journey. Hours of Reuters reports, news articles, YouTube videos of press conferences, analyzing the UN charter, and countless clicks verifying ‘I am a human’ enabled me to write a position paper and 4 pages of handwritten speech. Besides, the Continuous Crisis Committee was one of my most preferred committees to choose from. It not only tested my knowledge of the national and foreign policies of my assigned country but also to come up with continuous solutions to crises in the committee.

At the end of the Model UN conference is a game of Ludo. Each country and ally represents a team of color, fighting to establish their point in the committee. The trophy here is to pass the drafted solution in favor of the country. However, what I enjoy is the fact that everyone, despite the arguments, as a form of sportsmanship enjoys after the conference networking and building beautiful friendships. Just the way my family sits at the dinner table laughing at the match we just played.

Ludo was beyond the pieces and winning for me. It helped me to have a beautiful family bond and also to develop various skills that I would not have mastered in any other way. From the sound of rolling the dice to the relief of letting a piece enter the home column, the thrill, and challenges guided me to be a better problem solver. I intend to use the skills I have learned and insights I have gained to face real-life challenges, outside the world of Ludo with resilience, patience, and strategically calculated steps.

My dad loves making bets.

Growing up, he’d constantly challenge me to wager on anything: if my favorite batter would get a hit, the number of red lights driving to school, or how long my mom and sister's night out would last. While I relied on gut feelings, he’d mastered probabilities, meaning I often lost — big time. I’d later learn I admired his analytical approach to choosing a side. However, growing up, all I knew was his ability to win seemed like magic. I wanted to know the feeling of predicting the future like he did, but as I racked up losses, I doubted myself and began skittishly folding my hands. As our relationship’s fabric grew strained, I felt our interactions becoming forced.

I needed certainty. So, I searched for a deterministic outlet. After trying Investing Club, which I deemed too unpredictable, my dad showed me a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket video. Inspired by SpaceX’s innovative landing boosters, I decided to bet on myself through a personal engineering project: I’d launch and land a thrust-vectoring model rocket!

I worked tirelessly, but my seventh-grade summer flew by without a rocket flying up. I’d walk nervously to the launch site, only to get my hopes crushed after my control system slammed my work into the ground. Dad often said, “Failure is crucial to success; keep trying!” I feigned a smile, but his sympathy was no roadmap forward. After one particularly bad launch, I told him I didn’t know how to interpret his advice; how could I get closer to success by simply failing?

In response, he smiled wisely and gifted me one of his favorite books: Annie Duke's Thinking in Bets. Duke emphasized life is a game of probabilities influenced by skill and chance. She argued that true learning doesn't come from merely experiencing events but from actively analyzing the decisions and other factors that lead to them. Her perspective revealed how my dad had approached his bets all along. Instead of passively enduring failures, he proactively analyzed outcomes to guide his next move. Duke's insights empowered me to transform my engineering approach from hopeful trial-and-error to purposeful analysis of my rocket's performance.

The key? Data. I added an SD card to record over 18,000 data points per flight, enabling me to pinpoint problems instead of guessing. I boldly iterated and launched, knowing failures would yield more data. After four years, I became the first person to land any rocket without throttling, which landed me an internship at SpaceX! The first person I told? My dad.

Even with my successes in rocketry, I didn’t immediately become a decision-making maestro like my dad. My new perspective did, however, reassure me that even failed bets would indeed help me improve, and my dad and I resumed our wagers. As I stopped worrying about immediate outcomes, my relationship with my dad became effortless again. Like he had, I followed Duke’s advice and proactively emphasized improving my decision-making process, eventually feeling confident in my choices. Finally, I understood my dad’s advice from my failed rocket launches.

Applying what I’ve learned through my dad has given me the confidence to take more bets in other areas of my life, too. For example, after seeing examples of beautiful Chinese character etymology, I decided to leave my comfortable Spanish class and try Mandarin in high school. When my grades dropped, I didn't panic. Instead, I took a step back and analyzed how to improve. After scheduling weekly meetings with Mr. Zhou to refine my pronunciation, I won the sophomore Chinese award! My journey with Mandarin highlighted that listening intently to others is analogous to my rocket’s flight data.

In college, I intend to pursue engineering. While I might hesitate to play poker against my dad, applying his improvement-oriented framework to my pursuits has given me the confidence to innovate and continue to take on exciting challenges headfirst.

I am a seasoned veteran in monster hunting, but I don’t search for cryptids in the Himalayas or UFOs in Nevada, but rather for legends in retail stores across the country: I hunt for Pokémon Cards. My calendar’s plastered with trainer box release dates, my spreadsheets track the market sentiment of cards on my wishlist, and the local Target knows me as the scourge of Aisle 3.

But it's not just those like me who search for legends. As hype builds outside of the Pokémon community, the cards no longer belong to those of us who chase the myth out of passion, but rather out of profit. Scalpers arrive, ready to sell the legend at a price as inflated as Snorlax after a buffet. Returning home from DECA competitions or science fairs, I’d see a $50 card shoot up to $125 in that week.

I couldn’t watch as the cards that supported my entire childhood became yet another vehicle of profit for others, and I definitely knew my wallet wasn’t ready for it. Because of that, I tried to predict which cards would become a target of interest before any scalping happened. At first, I tried tracking trends manually, but my mind was led astray by anything shiny or holofoiled. Even after trying a statistical analysis of which Pokémon had high scalping probabilities (Charizard won), many cards still acted in defiance to my ranking. And so, in another attempt to thwart resellers, I began working on the project that would end up being my Pokémon Magnum Opus: An AI model that could predict the most valuable/popular cards of any box release.

I originally envisioned a model that could interpret images of the cards, but it quickly became clear that a low-parameter machine learning model couldn’t really decipher the intricacies of their designs accurately. Instead, I pivoted to a web-scraping approach. I scoured sites like tcgplayer.com for details like ‘Attack Power’ and ‘Rarity’, feeding these attributes into a Naive Bayes model. After training, cards like “Rayquaza VMAX (Alternate Art Secret)” became high potential cards, while cards like “Oddish 4/147 Burning Shadows Regular” were quietly dropped by the algorithm.

The first model iterations already showed promise, identifying the obvious patterns, such as knowing that Alternate Art and Holo cards were far more enticing than their regular forms. What surprised me though, was that my model also started to find patterns that I didn’t even see myself, such as how cards with playable moves for the competitive Pokémon scene were often more valuable, even if they weren’t flashy. It was as if my AI could peek into the collective subconscious of the Pokémon community, noticing hidden gems I’d never seen. For me, what I made was more than a financial tool, but something that helped me take back my agency as a monster hunter, as I knew I wouldn’t be at the mercy of scalpers whose behavior I could predict.

Whether it’s applying the machine learning skills I learned through medical research to Pokémon cards, or studying behavioral psychology to improve traditional social health programs, life is about finding the luster in the mundane. At college, I’m eager to build on my love for uncovering hidden patterns and share it with others—not just in Pokémon cards, but in the broader world. I’m excited to bring this mindset to my next adventure, and who knows—maybe I’ll even inspire a few others to see that luster, whether it’s a piece of cardboard with a dragon on it or a new outlook on the world.

My favorite childhood memory is waking up as early as my mom to make our family’s favorite breakfast – crepes. The ones filled not only with meat and mushrooms but also with the love my mom poured into them, as she sang a magical melody, handing each one over for me to fill. A warm, comforting smell of crepes drifted from the kitchen, curling through the hallway, wrapping our home in a scent that felt as warm and familiar as a hug. Little did I know that those mornings would turn into nothing but fragments of my childhood memory.

It was now my own responsibility to take care of my three meals a day and endure all the life challenges that came with living independently as a nine-year-old. It happened without warning. I didn’t fully understand why my parents had to leave, only that in our family of five, even with two parents working, there wasn’t enough to support us all.

After that morning, I lived with my grandparents. They did everything to make me smile, but they knew the little boy I was before was missing. Beyond my own worries about school and grades, I found myself grappling with emotions I didn’t fully understand. Every time my friends asked me about where my parents went, I had the same automatic response: “I don’t know.” It was hurtful to admit that my parents had to be immigrants in an unfamiliar country while seeing my friends getting picked up by their parents after school. Watching my friends hop into their parents’ cars, I’d hear the soft hum of engines fading down the road, which made me want to feel their happiness. I would repeatedly ask myself if I was not worthy of having my parents present in my life. I also wanted my parents to cheer me up at my boxing competitions and during the award ceremonies at math and science Olympiads.

People around me noticed how my smile faded and my eyes lost their spark. Every time my friends’ parents offered me a ride home, I would accept it without a second thought, closing my eyes to imagine, just for a second, that they were my parents. I still remember how I’d promise God that I would be the most well-behaved child if He brought my parents back. But it never happened.

For the next five years, I only heard my parents’ voices ten times – twice a year. By skipping lunch and saving the allowance my parents would send, I was able to make a call on special moments. Hearing them wish me “Happy Birthday” was my biggest birthday present. It put more of a smile on my face than a birthday cake or blowing out a candle.

I slowly began getting used to the life without my parents and mending my own tears, but I kept my emotions locked away in my mind so no one would worry about me. Always having to stand up for myself against the bullies, cooking steamed rice for my empty stomach for the fifth day in a row, and doing my homework and self-checking it for grammar mistakes were constant reminders that now I was on my own; I grew up way too soon.

As my parents’ presence grew in my life, I still feel like an outsider when listening to my friends say they wish they could just go back to when they were little kids; but for me, it was the roughest times that taught me to be on my own. My parents' presence is what my soul yearned for the most as a child, but I thank their former absence for shaping who I am today. Reuniting with them after five years was truly comforting. Although my dad no longer remembered my favorite color or my favorite ice cream flavor, my mom’s crepes were just as incredible as in my childhood.

My 15th birthday began like every other lockdown day—quiet, uneventful, and tinged with monotony. The mahjong tiles sat untouched, the Zoom lesson ended with muted goodbyes, and I wondered how long friendships could survive in a pixelated world.

Then, a notification broke the silence.

“[Name], I made you a gift!” Min, a fellow Robotics Club member, had sent a hyperlink. Curious, I clicked it. My speakers erupted in an off-key yet exuberant rendition of “Happy Birthday,” looping endlessly. On-screen, a 3D-rendered cake emerged, topped with strawberries and crowned with “Happy Birthday, [Name]!” in playful cursive that dissolved into colorful confetti. Delightfully excessive, it was Min’s cheeky way of saying, “I’m not there, but I can still mildly annoy you.” I couldn’t stop laughing.

Min and I had drifted apart during the lockdown, our friendship reduced to sporadic texts and half-hearted emojis. Yet, here she was, creating something uniquely personal—a thoughtful gesture that reminded me I was seen and valued.

Her effort sparked more than gratitude—it inspired action. Determined to reciprocate, I decided to create a gift just as meaningful for her birthday four months later. At the time, our club was abuzz with Nethack, a roguelike game featuring Sokoban-inspired puzzles. Intrigued, I resolved to design a Sokoban game as her birthday surprise.

The task was daunting. I had never coded a game before, and the intricate logic required for player movement and puzzle mechanics felt overwhelming. But Min’s creativity emboldened me to try. I scoured Nethack’s open-source code, pored over tutorials, and taught myself to program real-time gameplay in C++. Debugging became my nightly ritual—equal parts frustration and triumph.

“Why won’t this execute?” I’d mutter to my laptop at 1 a.m., only to whoop with joy when I finally fixed the issue. Between classes, robotics projects, and peer support sessions, I spent long days refining puzzles to strike the perfect balance between challenge and fun.

When I sent Min the game, her excitement made every late-night coding session worthwhile. “This is amazing!” she exclaimed, sharing screenshots of her progress as she solved each level. Her joy crystallized a realization: technology isn’t just about functionality—it’s about connection. It bridges distances, turning isolation into shared moments of laughter and understanding.

This realization reshaped how I viewed programming. Beyond solving technical problems, it became a way to nurture relationships and spark meaningful interactions. Motivated by this perspective, I began creating projects to bring my friends closer, blending humor and creativity to strengthen our bonds.

One of my favorite creations was a Telegram bot that let us play multiplayer card games like Bridge, sparking lively debates reminiscent of our pre-lockdown game nights. Another was a trivia quiz bot that delivered sarcastic commentary for wrong answers, drawing both groans and laughter. I even built a Secret Hitler rating tracker to quantify each player’s “sneakiness” in the social deduction game—much to the amusement of our group’s resident trickster.

My most meaningful project, however, was helping a friend develop a bot to track eating habits for a service-learning initiative. Though unfamiliar with Google Apps Script, I dove into tutorials, learned the language, and delivered a functional tool. The project earned us a $100 grant, but more importantly, it demonstrated how technology could empower and connect people in practical ways.

These projects weren’t just coding exercises—they were acts of care that reminded me of the resilience of human connection. While physical proximity might fade, the bonds nurtured through shared creativity can endure. Friendships are rarely effortless; they require attention and thoughtfulness. Min’s 3D cake wasn’t just a whimsical gift; it transformed how I view technology, relationships, and creativity. It reminded me that even the simplest gestures can ripple outward and create profound impact.

At college, I’ll carry this spirit forward, blending technology with human connection, and push the boundaries of what’s possible. I aim to design solutions that connect and inspire, showing that in an increasingly digital world, creativity and thoughtfulness remain profoundly human.

"Beyond what has been shared in your application what do you think makes you a good candidate for the University of Californi?” (350 words max)

The first time I picked up a calligraphy brush, my hands trembled, still bearing the pain inflicted by my father’s abuse. With each stroke, I felt calmer and happier, calligraphy soon becoming a recluse each night.

As I adorned my school assignments with calligraphed headers, my classmates and teachers took notice, requesting my calligraphy for posters and custom cards. My work gained traction among student organizations, giving me a renewed sense of connection and increased confidence in my abilities. After countless pages full of calligraphy, I commissioned my work, donating proceeds to organizations like RAINN and ASCA that support CSA survivors.

My most significant project was my collaboration with a local women’s shelter. I often volunteered there as a child caretaker. When I first visited, the walls seemed bare and lackluster. I wanted to add life and beauty to the blank walls. So, I offered to create large canvases full of positive and supportive messages–helping others find comfort amid their struggles. I added turquoise accents to the canvases in order to match the soothing white and turquoise theme of the shelter. As I adjusted the canvases, the center owner walked in.

“Beautiful,” she gasped, “You really turned this place around.”

In that moment, I realized art was not just about beautifying a room; it was about fostering healing and creating a sense of community for those in need.

What makes me a strong candidate for admission to UC is my resilience and my commitment to utilizing art as advocacy. I plan to collaborate with the National Alliance on Mental Illness, using my skills to raise awareness about abuse and mental health with calligraphy workshops and awareness campaigns across campus. Using my artistic abilities, I want to create comforting spaces, forming connections and creating calming environments for others–just like how my art did for me. In a world that often seeks to silence the voices of the abused, my advocacy at UC and beyond will serve as a testament to their strength and resilience, turning every letter into a resounding declaration against silence.

I spent four hours in the operating room, donning a surgical mask, hand gloves, safety goggles over my -5.5 prescription glasses, and an apron. My gloves turned red as I drilled a hole right through the center of the paw.

It turned out just as I imagined: a red paw-shaped keycap made from epoxy-resin for the control key of my keyboard. I am a self-proclaimed epoxy resin artist, and the abandoned community room on our rooftop is my operation theater, where I uncontrollably spend hours performing artistic surgeries and dissecting art scraps to make new art.

It all began as an experiment when I used epoxy resin to fix one of my most treasured possessions: the key to my pocket money locker. I carefully superglued the key I accidentally broke, took air-drying clay, and pressed the key to make a mold. I poured the resin mixture and waited two days until it was ready. I sanded the resin key to match the original one and tried unlocking the locker. IT WORKED! (after multiple attempts) Every resin project I worked on afterward was beyond art: it polished the combination of my creativity with functionality.

Over the years of mixing resin and hardener in a 2:1 ratio, I found a way to blend my love for animals with my art.

It started when my neighbor adopted Toby, a stray cat from an animal shelter after it met with a severe road accident. The accident left one of Toby’s forelimbs paralyzed. Seeing Toby’s condition, I had an idea for a project. Initially, I thought of designing a support for its leg, a crutch. Though it sounded perfect in my head and I spent weeks building it, it was not even close to a practical solution. Through multiple trial-and-error, I finally managed to make a customized resin tray, screwed in wheels, and added a cushion on top. Toby could sit on it and push itself slowly with one of its hindlimbs (Toby’s cat Uber). I knew I did not disappoint myself with this month-long project when my neighbor sent me videos of Toby going to bed all by itself sitting on that tray. I eventually had the opportunity to sell my creations- resin pendants, cup holders, and pet collars to raise funds for an animal shelter nearby and I could combine my love for creating art with a pawrfect purpose.

The resin mixture solidifies when poured into a mold. Just the way, my interest in breaking mental health stereotypes transformed into a rock-solid commitment over the years.

I have always struggled to relate to the societal standards set regarding mental health, neglecting maternal mental health, overlooking academic or workplace stress, or enforcing people to fit into a certain behavioral standard. To address this, I made small efforts to understand the importance of mental health and educate my classmates through open-ended discussions and various initiatives. Arranging meditation sessions for 117 participants in my college with an instructor through a newly established meditation club provided a sense of accomplishment I will cherish for life. Additionally, my experience working in the backend operations of a mental health organization allowed me to connect with a community of passionate mental health advocates. The joy of gifting my team custom-made Mental-Health-Matters resin keychains on international suicide prevention day as a token of appreciation reflected my journey towards a cause I value.

Resin art unfolded a realm of possibilities blending my interests with every step of creating art. Through this craft, I have performed art surgeries, calculated measurements, and failed in multiple perfectly thought attempts. It even taught me the biggest lesson of my life: the art of letting go. I drifted apart eventually when I started learning about microplastics and the effects of improper disposal of resin products. However, this journey has been one of learning and transformation— solidifying the resin I mold and the values I hold.

Jason slams headfirst out of the portal, his helmet the only thing keeping him from eating concrete. He lets himself lie there for just a moment, then pushes himself up and swears as he takes in—

My fingers stilled on the keyboard as I shuffled through scenarios in my mind. Where had the portal thrown him: an alternate past? A world where he didn’t meet Batman, or die? A universe where he and his family existed only in comic books?

When I began writing fanfiction, I had eyes only for my favorite characters. Hoping to spend more time with them, I sent them into situations and interactions that would’ve been impossible in canon, gradually expanding their worlds and stories and carefully engineering each event to reveal new pieces of their personalities.

But as I drew new threads in the complex web that made up each character, I gradually realized that my pure imagination was far from the only thing guiding them—I was also taking inspiration from my own real-life experiences. Though the characters live in worlds vastly different from my own, with unexplained magic or incredible feats of science, our emotions and motivations—the things that make us human—are fundamentally the same. Jason Todd’s uncertainty facing the unknown, Kaeya Alberich’s complicated relationship with his brother, Henry Strauss’s desperate desire for acceptance—I’ve felt the same things, albeit on a smaller scale, walking through my school gates on the first day of ninth grade or bickering with my sock-stealing sister. And as each character grew and changed, I learned alongside them: keeping levelheaded in the face of uncertainty; staying persistent in frustrating situations; being less self-conscious around others. The day I gave my first bio lesson to a room of distracted elementary schoolers, I tamped down my nerves and stayed calm while I tried to explain cell organelles; at the end of the lesson, one parent admired how patient I was. When my piano teacher told me once again that my Beethoven wasn’t quite emotional enough, I resisted the urge to sprawl onto the floor and give up; instead, I persevered, placing my hands back on the keys once more. As I helped a reluctant patient shuffle around the ICU for exercise, I wracked my brain for a way to make him smile and ended up dramatically narrating the entire walk as an adventure, telling myself not to be embarrassed when we passed by nurses and staff; it was worth it when he thanks me at the end of the walk. Ultimately, my stories have become not just doors to other worlds, but wells from which I can draw inspiration to help determine the type of person who I want to be.

Unlike the fictional characters that I write about, I don’t have an authorial hand guiding me along a predetermined path; all I can do is learn from the lessons each of my characters face as I forge my own way. As Jason uses his new start to unleash his inner nerd, devoting himself to his studies like he’d never had the chance to before, I double down on my efforts to finish my chem project before midnight. While Kaeya takes the first tentative steps towards reconciliation with his brother, I vow to stop bickering with my sister and let her use the Spotify… sometimes. Before I nervously strike up a conversation with the girl who sits next to me in psych, I remind myself that it hadn’t been until Henry finally stepped outside his familiar, but isolating, apartment that he had finally met friends who truly saw who he was. As every character I’ve journeyed alongside gradually finds their way to a happy ending, I close my eyes and prepare to weave a new story: a narrative characterized by curiosity, perseverance, and creativity—and most importantly, one of my own.

Standing before the oven, I watched the rows of eclairs bake, their dough rising as beads of condensation trickled down the glass. My heart raced with anticipation, my mind filled with the image of my mother’s delighted smile. Her love for eclairs made them the perfect treat for Mother’s Day, and I was determined to give her something special. I’d carefully measured the ingredients and piped the batter with precision, yet a flicker of doubt remained. Would these eclairs finally work, or would they deflate like all my previous attempts?

Baking has always been my creative outlet, a natural evolution from the crafting projects of my childhood. Back then, I spent weekends surrounded by colored paper and glue, transforming scraps into homemade treasures. Over time, my tools shifted to whisks and mixing bowls, but one thing remained constant: my need to make the most of whatever materials I had. Baking came with its own set of challenges, particularly the cost of ingredients, which forced me to adapt recipes and innovate with what was available in the kitchen. This resourcefulness became my hallmark as I learned to substitute ingredients and adjust measurements.

My first baking success was a cheesecake I made after spotting a recipe on the back of a cream cheese packet. That triumph opened the door to a world of possibilities—tarts, macarons, mochi, tiramisu—and I baked for every occasion: Christmas, birthdays, or simply a lazy Sunday afternoon. With every new creation, my confidence grew. So when Mother’s Day approached, I was ready for a new challenge: eclairs. I naively assumed they’d be as straightforward as my other confections.

I couldn’t have been more wrong. Batch after batch emerged from the oven, only to collapse moments later. I meticulously followed the recipe—ensuring the dough formed the perfect triangular drip from the spatula and timing the bake down to the second—but the puffiness I needed remained elusive. Frustrated but unwilling to admit defeat, I put eclairs aside, returning to chiffon cakes and other desserts I’d mastered. Yet the thought of my failed eclairs lingered like an unfinished story, urging me to try again.

Months later, I resolved to conquer the elusive pastry. This time, I approached the challenge scientifically, experimenting with ingredient ratios, tweaking baking temperatures, and documenting every attempt. Each failure revealed a new insight, and eventually, I succeeded. I pulled a tray of golden, perfectly puffed eclairs from the oven for the first time.

When New Year’s Day came, I decided to push my limits even further. For a family gathering, I planned to make six desserts, including scones, Mont Blanc, and, of course, eclairs. To pull it off, I meticulously scheduled every step, prepping key elements the day before and starting early on the big day. Most of the desserts came together smoothly, but when it was time for the eclairs, I felt the familiar tension return. Drawing on my earlier experiments, I worked with precision, piping and baking each batch with care. When I finally opened the oven door, I was greeted by the sight of tall, golden eclairs. This time, they were perfect.

While my family enjoyed the array of desserts I’d made, I realized that my baking journey wasn’t just about creating treats. It was about persistence in the face of failure, resourcefulness when resources were limited, and the ability to adapt when things didn’t go as planned. These lessons have shaped me far beyond the kitchen.

I still find myself standing in front of the oven, waiting for that first glimpse of success—or failure. Whether the recipe turns out perfectly or crumbles at my fingertips, I know the process is where the magic lies. As I try new recipes and refine old ones, I’ve come to see failure not as an endpoint but as the necessary heat that helps me rise.

Open the fridge. Take out an egg. To most, it’s just breakfast waiting to happen. But when your every-morning routine of frying eggs reflects your thought process, you know you’re on the right path to getting a Nobel Prize.

It begins whole and untouched, waiting to be recognized for its potential. As someone with Level 2 Autism Spectrum Disorder, while others accepted formulas and theories, I saw them as an egg in the refrigerator. I found joy in questioning them, peeling back layers to uncover overlooked possibilities. Just as cracking an egg, my unconventional approach to problem-solving allowed me to redefine challenges.

At 15, during a national math competition, while others used calculus, I visualized the optimization problem as a tessellation, revealing a solution with half the steps. The judges’ skepticism turned to enthusiasm as I explained how geometric symmetry simplified the problem. This taught me: breaking the shell of convention reveals brilliance.

After the crack of the shell, the transformation begins when an egg meets the frying pan—with patience, it solidifies into something entirely new. At Ushiba Lab, its established signal processing methods faltered, but I proposed adapting a machine learning model from speech recognition to uncover individualized brainwave patterns. Watching the system’s performance solidify felt like seeing an egg transform on low heat—patience and innovation working together. At Princeton, with my skills in spike sorting, I hope to join the Buschman Lab’s investigation of how neural stimulation can treat mental and neural diseases. I will inspire my lab teammates to challenge assumptions and explore the untested to create similarly transformative breakthroughs.

As the egg firms up, seasoning enhances its flavor. In my work at Matsumoto Lab, when the existing model failed to capture the behavioral data, I seasoned computational modeling with a bold cross-disciplinary connection between combinatorics and the Markov Chain Monte Carlo model. Initially dismissed by the graduate students as an odd pairing, this idea led to a 40% efficiency improvement in our model. At Princeton, with the Mellon Mays Undergraduate Fellowship, I hope to continue this process of discovery in Professor Jonathan Pillow’s lab, where neuroscience, machine learning, and mathematical modeling converge.

The egg’s journey ends on a plate, transformed into a power source. Our ideas, too, once cracked open and thoughtfully cooked, can nourish and inspire not just ourselves, but everyone at the table—like my more accessible mathematical approach, precise signal processing method, and accelerated computational model. I imagine Princeton’s early-morning residential discussions as intellectual kitchens, where students from diverse backgrounds challenge established norms in cognitive science, neuroengineering, and computational modeling, blend perspectives, and take bold risks, transforming ideas into a nourishing breakfast—while also cooking together fried eggs.

So, open the fridge. Take out an egg. Let’s see what we can create together.

For me, it’s noise that makes a community, with all its myriad of different people, opinions, and voices.

It can be heated discussions on the intersection of game theory and psychology in my Advanced Math & CS Club. The classroom jammed full of people standing, perched on window sills, seated on the floor, sweltering under the Shenzhen summer heat in the AC-less room, all ready to join in the debate for how the “pirate game” can be explained by decision-making psychology instead of combinatorics.

Or perhaps it’s my partner Lys’ shouts of excitement after he wins with a lucky three-bomb hand at Chinese Poker. The crowd of 30+ normally quiet and reserved students erupting at Lys’ ridiculous luck and demanding an additional double-point round after the final match of “Who Runs Quick” Chinese Poker Tournament.

It’s also Ruiwei’s off-tune rendition of “We Are All Heroes” and Zihan feeling himself during his electrifying guitar solo of “Numb Stars” at my open mic music festival for special needs children. The newly savvy performers shouting, drumming, and running around the music stage with no reservations, unbound by their deafness, self-enclosure, or lag in development.

I’m proud to be a part of communities of noise (although sometimes it gets hectic). Growing up in a family where heated voices perpetually filled dinner conversations, I’m conditioned by the chatter of family debates over the reason why China’s soccer team is so horrible to my Sister’s passionate demands to pass over the chicken wings before I ate it all. Whether it's founding my school’s nosiest Math & CS Club, hosting chaotic weekly Chinese Poker meet-ups, or organizing a loud and lively open mic for young disabled performers as the President of my highschool’s longest-standing charity club, I aspire to be a noise maker – to create opportunities where people can gather, connect, and express.

For me, noise is home, and at the University of California, I can’t wait to make some.

My dad loves making a bet. Growing up, I always wagered against him.

Whether it was predicting if his favorite batter would get a hit, the chances of a flush on a river card, or even the length of my mom and sister's girls' night out, he had mastered the art of probabilities. Naturally, I often lost our gambles – big time. These losses made me fear taking bets, so I tried my hand at engineering, a field I’d seen as more deterministic. Inspired by SpaceX, I set myself a challenge: launch and land a thrust-vectoring rocket.

I worked tirelessly towards a landing, but my seventh-grade summer flew by without a rocket flying up. Despite my original impression, engineering certainly seemed risky. I’d go to the launch site, unsure of how my rocket would perform, only to leave heartbroken after my control system slammed my work into the ground. My parents told me that these malfunctions were crucial to success and I should keep trying until it worked. I appreciated their sympathy but didn’t understand how I got any closer to success by failing. I saw their consolation as a clichéd saying that lacked real-world truth, leaving me unsure what to do next.

That's when my dad gifted me Annie Duke's Thinking in Bets. As a poker player, Duke emphasized that life is a game of probabilities influenced by both skill and chance. She argued that true learning doesn't come from merely experiencing events but from actively analyzing the decisions and factors leading to those outcomes. Her perspective was a revelation. I realized that instead of passively enduring failures, I needed to investigate their underlying causes proactively. Duke's insights motivated me to shift my focus toward understanding every aspect of my rocket's performance, transforming my engineering approach from hopeful trial-and-error to purposeful analysis.

The key? Data. My first change to my rocket included adding an SD card to my rocket’s circuit board. With over 18,000 data points per launch, I could pinpoint problems instead of guessing. Knowing any failures would just lead to more data, I boldly iterated and returned to the launch site. After four years of work, I became the first person to land any rocket without throttling, which also landed me a SpaceX internship.

Having practiced risk-taking when building my rocket, I felt empowered to explore other interests without worrying about adverse outcomes. Going into high school, I decided to leave my comfortable Spanish class and try Mandarin after seeing examples of beautiful Chinese character etymology, such as how characters like yue (moon) evolved from ancient crescent moon pictographs. When my grades dropped, I didn't panic. Instead, I took a step back and analyzed what I could improve. I sought my teacher’s help and discovered that my tones needed work. After scheduling weekly meetings to refine my pronunciation, I won the sophomore Chinese award! On the soccer field, I listened to my coaches’ advice and worked on my positioning skills and shooting power, eventually making the starting lineup for the first time. Now, as a proctor in my dormitory, I frequently seek feedback from new students to see how I can improve the dorm.

These moments showed me that listening intently to others—teachers, coaches, peers, or authors like Annie Duke—is just as valuable as my rocket’s flight data. I’ve learned I can only make good decisions for myself and the communities I belong to once I have heard many voices.

Life doesn’t always go perfectly. I’ve often heard that failing is essential for growth, but I’ve realized that it’s only the first step. For me, progress comes from seeking advice and engaging with the people around me. Although I still might hesitate to play poker against my dad, applying this understanding to my life has given me the confidence to take more bets. With enough time, I might just win a few!

Although I speak three languages, I communicate best using numbers. On my TikTok account, 'Calc.Corner', I speak to a global audience through the universal dialect of mathematics.

When I posted my first video, I had never expected anyone other than my friends to see it. This all changed when a video of me explaining limits to an audio from the movie "Mean Girls" unexpectedly went viral.

Since then, I have perfected a meticulous process of engagement optimization. I choose trending audios, replicate viral videos, experiment with ad copy and hashtags, and utilize strategic marketing techniques. I keep a spreadsheet full of performance metrics to document my approaches to both math problems and marketing.

I have cultivated over 9,200 followers and 500,000 likes by blending my love for problem-solving, graphic design, and marketing through videos that transform once-daunting problems—from Algebra 1 to multivariable calculus—into approachable solutions.

The process begins with research and trend observation, allowing me to select mathematical concepts that resonate with my audience. During AP season, I focus on integral review, ensuring my content is inclusive to all learning styles. By exploring trig identities, u-substitution, and integration by parts, I discover the beauty in diverse problem-solving approaches.

Visual storytelling supports the technical aspects, appealing to visual learners. I use Canva to create clean layouts that guide viewers and enhance comprehension.

I am glad I can express my love for math while demystifying complex topics. By making my content relatable and relevant to teens worldwide, I inspire more math enthusiasts each day.

A sharp voice broke the stillness of the night. My mother clutched my hand, her trembling fingers betraying her calm. “We’re going to visit nani [grandmother] in Delhi,” she whispered. But the hurried packing and muffled urgency—I knew this wasn’t a visit. Fleeing creditors’ threats after my father’s business collapse wasn’t a choice; it was survival.

Eight years ago, “asylum seeker” was a distant phrase. Overnight, it became my identity—a heavy cloak that obscured the life I knew and forced me to redefine myself.

We landed in Boston with nothing but suitcases and hope, cramming eight people into my uncle’s two-room apartment. Privacy vanished, and nights rotated between couch corners like musical chairs. The smell of reheated lentils lingered, a reminder of our shrinking resources. I missed school—not just math problems, but the routine and belonging it brought. Days blurred into a monotonous haze. When my uncle’s responsibilities grew, we became homeless. Shelters, borrowed couches, and temporary accommodations blurred into one relentless stretch of survival. While my parents navigated asylum paperwork, I took on household duties: cooking meals, scrubbing counters, and rationing supplies. At ten, I found stability in small victories—stretching ingredients, saving shampoo, shielding myself from fear with borrowed textbooks and makeshift math challenges, and bringing order to chaos. In survival, I found strength.

Still, I craved purpose. Rummaging through my cousin’s belongings, I uncovered an old computer. Its flickering screen and sticky keys didn’t matter—it worked. Clicking through its unfamiliar interface, I stumbled upon Codecademy. At first, it was just a way to pass time, but soon, it became my obsession. Hours blurred into nights as I taught myself to code. My first project—a Scratch game with a pixelated cat chasing a mouse—was clunky, but it was mine. Amid chaos, coding gave me something rare: the power to build, control, and fix.

That stability shattered when my mother fell ill with Lyme disease. Without health insurance, professional therapy was out of reach. I watched her struggle through YouTube tutorials, each hesitant, pained movement a reminder of how much we’d lost—and how survival was once again an issue. Watching her struggle, I realized—I wasn’t powerless.

Coding, once my escape, became my solution. A video on pose estimation sparked an idea: Therapose, a virtual physical therapist for people like my mom. Developing it was grueling—debugging hundreds of lines of code, integrating pose-estimation models into Swift, and testing features late into the night. At 2 AM one night, after hours of failure, I fixed a motion-tracking issue. Exhausted but elated, I ran to show my mom. When she completed her first exercise without pain, her smile erased months of frustration.

Therapose soon grew beyond my mother’s needs, reaching 257 seniors across six rehabilitation clinics. Local news outlets shared its story, and suddenly, I was no longer the outsider. Presenting Therapose before Congress, I realized it wasn’t just code—it was a bridge to equitable care. Zainab Farah, one of the seniors who used Therapose, captured its impact perfectly: “After my hip replacement, Therapose helped me regain the joy of tending my garden. You’ve given me my independence back.” Her words reminded me that resilience isn’t just enduring hardships—it’s transforming them into opportunities for others.

“Asylum seeker” is no longer just a phrase—it’s who I am. Coding became my refuge, my voice, and my way forward, transforming chaos into opportunity and resilience into innovation. Today, I’m not just a seeker of safety—I’m a seeker of knowledge, a coder with a cause, and a future computer scientist shaping a more equitable world.

I blankly stared at the glass skull in front of me, losing myself in its empty eyes. With interconnected sutures and crystallized teeth, the vitreous matter smiled at me, absorbing my attention and provoking my thoughts. How could such a simple object perfectly convey the complexity of death and the unknown? I didn’t know, but I was determined to find out.

The next day, I visited Westside Hospital in search of answers. I had been volunteering there for seven weeks. Initially, I signed up because of my passion for medicine and learning through novel experiences, but I found my days filled more with repetitive tasks and a lot of free time to think. As I was walking the halls, I overheard two nurses complaining about room 527. Curious, I went to investigate. Upon entering the room, I saw an older, stern-looking man sitting semi-upright in Fowler’s position, glaring at me fiercely. I asked if he needed anything, but he coldly responded “No”, demanding that I leave. I complied, but the loneliness in his eyes beckoned to me.

The following day, I came back to speak with the patient, whom I’ll call John. He was recovering from a myocardial infarction and rarely had visitors since he was a widower and his only daughter was away at college. I made it a point to stop by room 527, John’s room, every day. Two sentences turned into five, and five sentences into long conversations as we started bonding over common ground. John talked about being a professional bodybuilder in his 20s and how the tremendous discipline and effort needed to maintain a competitive physique, along with his desire to be the best, shaped his being. I shared my own experiences, including my achievements in health informatics at HOSA leadership conferences driven by my resolve to succeed. Every day, we worked on sudoku over a cup of coffee—black with two sugars for John, and a latte for me.

Each story John shared peeled back layers of his loneliness and taught me valuable lessons. Over time, I realized this and understood the true value of my seemingly small actions. By simply exchanging words, I was partaking in the purest form of humanity and leaving a substantial impact on someone. I finally knew my calling—to help the silently suffering in any way I could, even through small acts of kindness, motivated by a drive to make a difference. The once melancholic man was now smiling with each conversation. This filled me with joy, and I began to talk to other patients, hoping to brighten their day and learn from them. I started applying this new outlook to other aspects of my life: seeking a deeper understanding of scientific topics like biology and finding ways I could use them to create real-world change, and recovery.

One afternoon, I stopped by John’s room, and he told me that he was being discharged soon. He thanked me for everything, saying I was the reason he was able to endure for so long and that I reminded him of his daughter, a caring soul who always selflessly helped others. I thanked him too for his stories that showed me the importance of diligence and always striving for greatness. That is when I decided to carry John’s lessons with me, recognizing that even the simplest interactions can have profound effects, similar to the glass skull. I resolved to become a physician who not only treats the illness but also the person, truly listening to and understanding all my patients.

I returned home with John’s words engraved in my soul. In my room, I gazed at the skull, now a fitting reflection of myself—the death of my old perspective filled with uncertainty and the rebirth of a new me, fueled by a clear purpose. It smiled at me again with its blank face, and this time I warmly smiled back.

Cross-legged on an old, Persian carpet resting my arms on a Takkaya, cardamom tea filled my senses as my uncle Ahmed leaned forward, adjusted his shemagh, and in an animated voice: “The golden age wasn’t just luck, it came from Abbasids merging Greek, Persian, and Indian ideas—making something uniquely their own.”

I grew up in my grandfather’s Jummah gatherings every Friday as he’d invite theoretical physicists, historians, and poets alike. I didn’t understand most of it at the time—sometimes they compared Al Farabi’s Madinat AlFadilah to Plato’s Republic; other times, it was how our digital revolution may land some countries into a Orwellian-type dystopia. But at 12, cradling my tea and nodding along, I felt like a revolutionary thinker drawn in by their erudition—a Master Oogway in the making.

Yet something always used to bug me. Jummahs brimmed with talk of authenticity; Thoreau’s call to “suck the marrow out of life” wasn’t foreign to them. Embrace curiosity, they’d say—but only through books and theories, it seemed. I wanted more. Nietzsche hiked the Alps, Diogenes lived in a barrel—each living their ideas as fully as they wrote them. I wanted to do the same: to try and fail, to create my own lore, to live my philosophy.

So I bought a ticket to Turkey, kissed my mom goodbye, and headed straight toward my destiny! I swear this made sense to me at the time, but it was every bit as extreme as it sounds. Three weeks of scaling the rocky trails of Cappadocia, bunking in hostels that seemed allergic to hot water, and seeing more greenery than this sand-dweller had ever known, 16-year-old me returned a new man—or, more accurately, one with a solid case of food poisoning. It wasn’t the grand revelation I’d envisioned. Out of all my lofty expectations, what stayed with me the most was playing my guitar around a campfire with friends, my new speed tent-pitching skills, and the fact I learned to solve a Rubik’s cube just to race a Hungarian friend I’d made. I realized just as life shouldn’t be all theoretical, grand existential talk, it also shouldn’t only be crazy, life-altering adventures. Instead, there’s a balance—an appreciation for those bigger questions and ideas, but also fulfillment through smaller, more tangible pursuits.

So during the next four-hour drive to a Kishta in the desert, I spent the first hour jaw dropped, trying to wrap my mind around Cantor’s ideas on countable vs uncountable infinities while discussing them with my grandfather. By the second hour, I was gazing into the dunes that spilled endlessly only to be contrasted with grand, weathered mountains of Madinah in the horizon. In a weird way, I felt the same smallness and awe at the universe both discussing my grandpa and staring at those sands I’ve always called home.

But eventually, I took out my notebook and switched to solving my own Olympiad problems. Sure, Cantor may have broken our understanding of infinity in the 1940s, but transforming that recursive number theory problem into a graph where the nodes were prime numbers, that was one hell of a trick. My trick—and one I’ll always be proud of.

For me, fulfillment lies in these small acts of creation, where curiosity meets my own ingenuity. It’s why I choose to learn how to kickflip despite my mother’s reluctance and try so hard to reach 1800 on Chess.com. But it’s also why I lose myself re-reading a Borges short story and can’t wait to visit home and join another Jummah. It’s not about choosing between the grand and the grounded—it’s about living both.

I’ve made a habit of diving into a new skill, reading about a new theory, or exploring a new problem whenever curiosity strikes. So while I doubt I’ll solve a Millennium problem or start a modern-transcendentalist movement anytime soon, I’ll keep seeking balance between ideas and experiences, failing and learning. And I’ll try to harbor mini-Jummahs during meals, classes, and late-night study sessions.

I’ll become a guitarist who skateboards, a mathematician who has too many hobbies, and, most importantly, a learner who never stops exploring.

Humans, I hypothesized, were walking contradictions—emotions driving them to illogical extremes while they pretended at control. My father’s abandonment at birth, my mother’s absence while she worked in Japan, and my caretaker’s indifferences and selfishness in Korea all taught me that to trust another person was to invite disappointment.

Most people wouldn’t remember first meeting their mother, but I do. My mother and I reunited at Narita Airport when I was five after my mother decided she was financially ready to raise me. I didn’t know how to hug her back, so I stood stiff, clutching the plastic bag of Korean snacks my caretaker had packed for the flight. We were strangers—only bound by blood.

Life afterward did little to disprove my hypothesis. As my stepfather's Pachinko addiction left us in poverty, my mother’s marriage collapsed. Depression crept into my mother. And in this, her undereducation became a deep symbol of how life had carved its marks into her. Bills, written in hiragana and kanji, piled up on the table, left for me to navigate. “You shouldn’t have to do this,” she said once apologetically with a quiet shame. I didn’t respond; I just kept reading.

I sought solace in logic: numbers didn’t neglect, codes didn’t betray. Yet there was one anomaly I couldn’t ignore. Every year, at the Tanabata sky lantern festival, my mother and I would watch warm, golden lanterns rise into the night. I had spent years researching “depression,” and yet, I could never find a way to reach her. But in that fleeting moment, light could reach her. She showed her smile—rare as a supernova. On the night of Tanabata when I was 11, for the first time, I saw the connection. Sitting beneath the glow of a thousand lanterns, the idea for Hikari was born: a program that would send my mother a glowing message every night at 9pm, reminding her, “You’re not alone.”

The execution wasn’t simple. Programming had always been my sanctuary, but the Scratch tutorials I’d followed before were child’s play compared to the CS50 lectures. Conditionals and loops twisted in my brain like double helixes, but worse was the language barrier—English. I printed out lecture transcripts, spending hours deciphering them with a burrowed Oxford dictionary. My ancient Fujitsu laptop also suffered; it groaned with every program I tried to compile that the “restart” button became my closest ally. But I refused to give up.

The first time the message appeared, I watched from the doorway, holding my breath. Her fingers brushed the screen. Then, a smile appeared on her face. I saw the wall around her heart begin to crack.

Later that week, my mother also began eating dinner with me again, and one night, when I reminded her to eat the vegetables, she laughed. “When did you become such a parent?” she teased. “Around the time you stopped acting like one,” I shot back, grinning. It felt good to joke. It felt even better to hear her laugh. But there is a measure of guilt when I see her smile. Eyes narrowing, corners of the mouth turning up—I was still learning myself.

I shared Hikari to my peers, and one day, a boy pulled me aside to thank me. “Your app reminded me to breathe when I really needed it,” he said. I smiled. “That’s the thing about computers—they never forget to care.” If a simple light could spark hope in my community, what could we achieve with the right tools in the hands of many? My goal now was clear: to develop innovative technologies that could address mental health on a global scale.

As a scientist and engineer now, I approach life with curiosity and compassion. I still debug systems, but I’ve also learned to embrace their contradictions. After all, even the most intricate algorithms—like humans—are beautifully imperfect, thriving not in spite of their flaws, but because of them.

We cruised across the famous Mumbai Sea Link, the city’s skyline glimmering with lights as the world outside slowed down. Every month, often on a Sunday evening, my parents, my younger brother, and I would announce, “Let’s go for a drive.” It didn’t matter where we went—sometimes to a coffee shop on the outskirts of the city, other times to a quiet beach we hadn’t visited in years. These drives became our ritual. I’d ask, “What have you accomplished this month? What do you hope to do next?” The answers, ranging from anecdotes to reflections, became resets, offering valuable lessons that would carry us forward in both that moment and in our lives.

Before these drives, I often felt a sense of nervousness and anxiety about what the month ahead held. But afterward, I was always filled with a sense of calm and fulfillment, as if each drive had cleared the path for what was to come. They shaped me by encouraging introspection, inspiring ideas, and fostering creativity in unexpected ways, each journey leaving behind lessons that would guide me, both personally and professionally.

A constant during these drives were my father’s casually woven narratives on economics, stocks, and financial planning. He highlighted the transformative power of compounding and described how the right investment strategy leads to financial stability. These lessons inspired me to help blue-collared workers struggling with financial security across the city. Building on the principle of saving early, I created Bachat hi Aadhaar (Pathway to Saving), a financial literacy movement that empowers gig workers and young professionals to channel part of their earnings into a meaningful corpus for the future. I also applied these principles to my own finances. Carefully following my father’s guidance, I grew my small investment portfolio, securing a 63% return over the last 12 months.

The lessons didn’t end there. These drives evolved into my personal incubator for ideas. One evening, as my mother vented about the constant flood of bills from her trading business—sometimes as many as thirty a day—I recognized an opportunity. Her frustration sparked a concept that could simplify the process. Drawing inspiration from her, I developed BillSense, a system that extracted handwritten dates and invoice numbers from bill images and automatically sorted them into an Excel sheet. What had once been an overwhelming mountain of paperwork was transformed into a streamlined, manageable database. What began as a small challenge blossomed into a solution that alleviated my family’s burden and underscored how technology can address tangible, everyday problems. The drives, with their open-ended conversations and moments of quiet reflection, provided the perfect space for such insights to take shape—turning routine frustrations into creative breakthroughs that might have otherwise been buried beneath the weight of daily life.

These drives brought more than lessons; they fostered connection. They helped me grow closer to my younger brother. What started as brief, sometimes tense exchanges gradually evolved into meaningful conversations about our goals and academics. After understanding his struggles with ADHD and schoolwork, I began tutoring him in science and economics. Finding techniques that worked for him took effort, but the results paid off. From being able to focus for only 15 minutes at a time, he eventually built his ability to sit for two-hour stretches, significantly improving his confidence and grades.

Not all takeaways came from insightful conversations though; some lessons arrived in subtler forms. Watching Mumbai’s maddening traffic jams, accompanied by the honking of frustrated drivers squeezing through every sliver of space, taught me resilience and patience.

Navigating offbeat paths and taking unplanned detours convinced me that exploration is often half the fun of meeting a goal.

Taking off at 6 a.m. for a Starbucks 150 km away instead of one near our house, in pouring rain, reminded me that it’s okay not to have a determined destination for every journey.

Perhaps the most important thing these drives gave me was a bond with my family—a thread that ties us together, giving me strength in knowing that, no matter the road, we’d navigate the path together.

Anxiously plugs in the power adapter, check! 
Rushes to turn on Yamaha keyboard, check! 
Sits upright and double-checks hand placement, check!

“Derin, turn to page 45, today you will be playing “Wonderful Words of Life” by Philip Bliss,” says Uncle.

Oh no... not page 45! The difficult pieces were usually found in the last pages of the book. I barely managed to play “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.” How am I meant to play this?

Whispers of Wisdom. It was precisely 6:00 am on a bitterly cold morning. I had just got dressed for elementary school. As my mother tells me my “Rice Krispies” breakfast is ready, I eagerly dash off to the dining table. Little did I know that would be my last breakfast in that house. As I clench my fist on the metal door handle, I am met by the harsh voices of people trying to evict my family from our home. In less than 3 hours, my first home was scattered over the compound—from the furniture to the clothes to my toys. Though internally overwhelmed, I hear my older brother Diran whisper to me some words of wisdom, “Let’s be strong for Mom and Dad.” This, I carried from that day onward.

I stared at the music sheet trying to decipher the black p’s and d’s hovering all over. I struggled to play with both hands. My right hand was my best, as I am right-handed; however, playing both left and right hands felt like my arms were on fire. Despite this, I pushed myself to play the first few notes: F - F - G - A - C - C - A - G - F, and when I heard the vibrant echoes of “Sing them over again to me,” filling the room, I was determined to embrace the challenging notes ahead.

The Embrace of New Perspectives. I wasn't enthusiastic about the new house my family moved into. It's like we traded a Maserati sports car for an old Peugeot vehicle. I had to adjust to the idea of living in the same compound with different families. Getting used to the “2 am cries” from baby Kayla and fending off little Johnny's attempts to infiltrate the house were not so easy. Don’t even get me started with the fact that I had to live in a smaller space with my three older brothers, and anything called privacy was completely obliterated. I complained, got frustrated, and even contemplated the idea of running away. It wasn't until that fateful night our cooking gas finished that I started to appreciate having neighbors. When my mother voiced out her problem, Jossy (the flat 1 neighbor) lent her gas cylinder to us, so we could finish preparing dinner. This unusual kindness helped me to truly embrace new perspectives. Kayla’s cries taught me patience. Johnny’s adventurous and playful energy reminded me to find joy amid change. The smaller space was a blessing in disguise as I was able to connect with my family on a deeper level.

As I played, those notes I once dreaded soon became familiar patterns. I felt the rhythms of growth as the melodies smoothly connected. I had made the jump from the first to the final line, and with each note, I found new meaning in the hymn's lyrics.

"Wonderful Words of Life?" I carry them with me as my guiding principles through life’s obstacles. "Let Me More of Their Beauty See?" As I set out to begin my college journey, I hope to experience the whispers of “You got this!” from future friends, embrace new perspectives in new communities, and add more wonderful words to my life.

My right and left hand, once on fire, are now in unison. As I play the final verses: “Beautiful words, wonderful words, wonderful words of life,” I am filled with a sense of accomplishment.

“Derin, I'm impressed," says Uncle. “Now to page 46.”

Oh no…not page 46!

Its flesh thick and glistening while it stretches its arm: plump, green, and swollen. Small but vibrantly alive, as if whispering, “Take me home." There was something about it, seemingly pulsing with energy. And before I knew it, I was carrying my first succulent home. It was no easy task. The watering, soil change, and meticulous care of succulents intimidated me. I had never owned a plant. Plant care was like raising a child. The continuous waiting seemed frustrating; the time commitment overwhelming. But gradually, I shifted away from ticking hours and slipping days. I developed a routine of plopping onto my blue gardening stool and tending to my ever-slow-growing succulent adoptees.

While my plant children took up my evenings after school, I’d often let case studies and statistics take up my weekends: analyzing economic problems and pitching solutions—my interwoven hobbies for economics and the environment.

The prospects of a biogas start-up to generate affordable electricity for Nigeria. Similar to my country, Malaysia, governmental policies and revenue streams revealed the towering market barriers within the industry.
