Yet, knowing that biogas could potentially help children in Nigeria to no longer worry about reading in a dark room or having gas to cook their favorite meal, I felt compelled to solve this case. But no one had ever set up a successful biogas company in Nigeria. We couldn't figure out how to keep it afloat for even a few months. The hopes of a brighter Nigeria seemed distant. I questioned if I even had the economic acumen. But in an unexpected way, my journey into succulent care urged me on. I had started forcing myself to be patient and persistent. My endeavor in nature emboldened my academic one. I was careful not to overwater or overfertilize; I waited for months. I continued my hunt across the web for a feasible biogas operation model, going through piles of documents. Using tools like the Ansoff Matrix and Pareto’s principle, my team and I assessed price competition, product differentiation, and governmental support for optimal pricing. We consulted research papers on biogas plant size and production for days to figure out how to exploit economies of scale. The biogas dilemma slowly then presented its solution: diversifying revenue streams into biofuel and composts through a Circular Economy model.

My two interests have created a synergy—like Adam Smith’s invisible hand in the forces of supply and demand. Every day that passed as I watched my succulents slowly grow seemed to fuel me when I worked on my case solutions: I immersed myself in the world of scarcity, choice, and opportunity costs. Laptop fully charged and ready to research. I’m on my gardening stool most evenings and my laptop most weekends. My succulents have almost filled up my porch; and my team’s case solution of diversification eventually won the competition out of 1,800 participants.

However, the future of biogas, like many others, is still vague and uncertain. But most importantly, the intersection of these two disciplines has taught me that growth is tender and fragile, embracing patience and organic change. It also reflected the greater intersection between economic interests and environmental impact. By propagating new succulents from fallen leaves, I’m no longer afraid of daunting economic problems, but rather I feel emboldened to turn them into solutions. This case and many others will only mark the beginning of my journey to draw on both disciplines to work towards sustainable development, or, as Kate Raworth would call it, the doughnut.

The tears wouldn’t stop. I desperately tried to keep myself composed, but it only got worse as they blurred my vision. I abruptly stopped crying and waited for the tears to fall onto my desk. Once my vision cleared, the objects that caused my emotional turmoil once again stared back at me. The small papers containing math problems with one word at the top - KUMON. Holding the tears back, I took my pencil and worked through another day of completing my packets.

As a ten-year-old, my situation felt like a modern retelling of Sisyphus, the Greek myth of the man condemned to roll a boulder up a mountain as a punishment in the underworld. Whenever he approached the top of the mountain, the boulder would roll back down, erasing his hard work. However, my boulder was replaced with Kumon packets, completing them only to do it again the next day, for the rest of my life.

Perhaps the metaphor I made for myself was the reason my jealousy would spark whenever I went into the center to turn in my work. I’d see the teenagers at the front grading papers, seeming much more peaceful than I was. I’d aspire to be like them one day, free from my shackles. Four years later, that’s exactly what I did.

As I walked into the center on the first day of work, nostalgia hit me, serving as a reminder of the impact this place had on me still. This wave soon stilled with the thought of working at a place I once resented. Holding the red pen, I felt a sense of pride, as if I had crossed to the other side of the Kumon experience. Instead of a struggling student, I was now holding a key to helping others.

Over time, my perspective of Kumon transformed as my role shifted from grader to teaching assistant. This new position is when I was faced with the challenges of my role: communicating effectively, addressing parents, and managing schedules. When a parent voiced concerns about their child’s slow progress, I could relate to the issues and felt compelled to help. By breaking the lessons into manageable portions and working patiently, I saw steady improvement over the weeks. The parents showed me gratitude, which made me recognize the importance of adaptability and problem-solving skills. At this moment, I felt I had learned more now than I did as a student.

During springtime my freshman year, my friend invited me to accompany her to a DECA meeting. Not knowing much about it, I agreed. As I listened to discussions about the principles of business, I was struck by how closely they mirrored the skills I applied at Kumon. Topics about customer relations, communication, and adaptability shifted my perspective as I realized my time at Kumon didn’t only help me to educate but taught me to navigate real-life situations. Inspired, I joined DECA my sophomore year, where I found success and uncovered my passion for the business field. This action led me to increase my involvement in more business-related activities and solidified my decision to major in the subject.

I walked into work as usual on Tuesday afternoon. I picked up a red pen, sat at my desk, and routinely started to grade papers. A groan of frustration caught my attention as I looked to the source. It was a girl, around nine years old, glaring at her Kumon packet. She reminded me of my younger self, caught in something that felt like a never-ending struggle. But this time, instead of pushing the boulder, I was helping her push hers. As I guided her through the problems, I glanced at the Kumon sign at the wall and reflected on how far I’ve come. Kumon, which had once felt like an endless punishment, was now the foundation of my passion and future.

"Do you think you can still believe in God after losing someone dear to you?” I asked my neighbor, mourning his wife lost to COVID. Wiping the tears from his face, he replied, “Why not? Everything happens because He wills it.” I was struck by his response. We’d both endured painful losses, yet our reactions couldn’t have been more divergent. While I felt anger and betrayal, he mourned with a calm acceptance that left me questioning my own stance.

Growing up in a family of faith, belief in God was as natural to me as breathing. My days were filled with rituals, devotional songs, and tales of gods and heroes from my grandfather. I even memorized long passages from the Ramayana under his guidance. Yet, my prayers, especially those filled with childlike hopes for family unity and protection, never felt tested… until January 1, 2018.

On that day, while vacationing in Rajasthan, my parents received a fateful call: my grandfather had passed away. They didn’t reveal the whole truth immediately; instead, they said his health was critical. For the entire eight-hour drive home, I silently repeated “Om Namah Shivaya,” desperately hoping that God would intervene and preserve his life. But when we arrived, I learned he had already departed. For the first time, I felt betrayed by God. Why hadn’t my prayers worked when I needed them most? From that moment, doubt began to take root, blossoming into a quiet rebellion.

Over time, as I distanced myself from rituals, I came to realize how much of my faith was grounded not in genuine belief but in fear… of ghosts, societal expectations, and a comfort in routine. The devotion I’d once thought was profound turned out to be mere habit. Years of observance hadn’t made me a believer; a single moment of despair had transformed me into an agnostic. I refused to engage in rituals and shunned religious discussions, seeing my skepticism as a protective shield against the heartache that faith had seemingly wrought.

Then, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the world felt plunged into chaos. Death and uncertainty became daily realities, and my father, working in a high-risk area, ventured out each day. Yet, remarkably, our family never contracted the virus. I couldn’t dismiss it as mere luck; statistically, it felt improbable. For two years, despite daily exposure and interactions with many infected individuals, we remained untouched, even as one in four people in the country tested positive. My parents attributed our health to divine will, a perspective I initially resisted. In my search for answers, I spoke with individuals who, like my neighbor, had endured loss yet clung to their beliefs with an enigmatic calm acceptance. How could I ignore the peace it bestowed upon them when that same belief had once felt like betrayal to me?

This confrontation led me to recognize how faith provides solace amid life’s many unknowns. If our safety during a pandemic was indeed God’s will, then perhaps so was my grandfather’s passing. Revisiting Hindu teachings on karma and samsara, the continuous cycle of birth, death, and rebirth, I began to view his departure as part of a larger journey rather than a finite loss. In Hindu thought, each life serves as a step toward greater spiritual understanding. Recognizing this, my grief softened, allowing me to honor my grandfather’s memory not as an ending but as part of our shared spiritual path.

I am learning to find peace not in complete answers but in humble acceptance of life’s mysteries. Walking a path that embraces both science and spirituality, I am comforted by the notion that there may be a balance beyond my understanding, something that bestows purpose upon both our joys and sorrows. In this synthesis of past beliefs and newfound insights, I am slowly cultivating a faith that welcomes life’s uncertainties with quiet resilience, knowing that sometimes, one must take a leap of faith.

Sitting at the kitchen table, the fresh scent of steamed dumplings fills the air as I indifferently prod my food with chopsticks. “Just one more bite,” my grandma begs, holding a dumpling up to my mouth. I reluctantly comply. She grabs another. “One last bite,” she promises for the fifth time. Pestering me, she continues her antics until I completely clean my plate. This all too familiar situation would happen nearly every night to me as a kid because of one problem: I suck at eating.

Hunger is a faint, muted feeling for me. I have struggled with this unfortunate fact for my whole life. I simply don’t eat enough, but I want to gain weight. However, I have virtually zero appetite. Completely unfazed, I sometimes skip meals without even noticing. What’s more, eating enough food takes a conscious effort. My habit is to eat only the bare minimum to get through the day. If I try to force down more food, my brain tells me I’ve had enough, leading to lots of gagging. What feels like a simple, effortless task for others is a hurdle for me. When I don’t eat, I lash out at others, have no energy, and lack the motivation for school, friends, or anything else. When my mom calls me for dinner, I groan instead of rushing to the dinner table. I see eating as an inconvenience, a chore. In the back of my mind, I knew this mindset wasn’t healthy, but I brushed it off anyway.

However, one night while rallying with my brother at the tennis courts, my mind suddenly turned hazy and my vision blurred. My arms and legs turned to jelly. I felt my legs give out, and the next moment, my back hit the ground, the overhead lights glaring over me. I remembered that I skipped dinner that night. Lying on the ground, the harsh reality hit me: pretending everything was okay was no longer an option. Something had to change, but I had no idea where to start. Then, I heard my grandma’s familiar words echoing inside my head: “just one more bite.” It struck me. Change didn’t have to happen all at once. It can happen in small, deliberate steps.

I started with one seemingly insignificant change – a Yoplait yogurt before bed. That was it. But that yogurt was a promise to myself to work towards a healthier life. As I got more comfortable, I stacked on more adjustments like doubling school lunches, exercising more, tracking calories, and gulping down protein shakes. Whether it was big or small, day by day, I pushed myself to make any improvement I could, even in times when it felt impossible. Throughout this process, I slowly began conditioning myself to eat more, push forward, and grow stronger.

Through my ongoing internal battle, I’ve learned that any problem can be tackled by breaking it down into small, manageable steps, whether it’s eating, schoolwork, or life in general. A complex dynamics problem in physics can be broken down into Newton's Second Law equations, vector components, and a free-body diagram. A challenging musical piece can be broken down into basic notes, rhythms, and articulations by starting slowly and gradually increasing the tempo. As a section leader in marching band, I guide and lead others by breaking down and demonstrating concepts step by step. Like an integral in calculus, I’ve realized that even though each tiny component may seem unimportant, they are integral to constructing a larger whole.

Today, I still have a long journey to a healthier life, but looking back, I’m proud of every protein shake chugged, dumbbell lifted, and Taco Bell burrito eaten to bring me to where I am today. Although there will be daunting challenges in my life that are hard to swallow, I’ve learned how to break them down into small, bite-sized pieces.

And every day, I’ll take one more bite.

Growing up in an immigrant family, I witnessed my parents working tirelessly in a new country to provide me with a better life and education. They woke up early, came home late, and faced countless challenges with language barriers, all in the hope of creating opportunities for me. Seeing their sacrifices made me realize that hundreds of thousands of families in California face similar struggles. I decided to support my community, which led me to join the Parent Education Program at my school.

The Parent Education Program is a free initiative by the Visa Club at the Dream Center, which aims to help parents improve their English and better adapt to life in the U.S. Our efforts in the community have earned our Dream Center the California Golden Bell award. For the past two years, I’ve served as a bilingual student assistant, helping to translate and provide guidance on everyday issues. We teach parents about civil rights and assist with life challenges they may encounter. We also offer childcare to make it easier for them to attend. This experience has helped me refine my communication skills as I translate in class and connect with parents by sharing life experiences. I’ve also gained insights into the challenges of adulthood, taking note of issues I might face in the future.

Building relationships with the parents, I often hear about their struggles. Many open up about work challenges or life problems that they keep hidden from their children, not wanting to add pressure to their families. Hearing these stories reminded me of my parents, it was a moment of growth.

One day, my mother was involved in a car accident. It was a hard time to go through, but I was able to put my translation skills and knowledge of civil rights to use. I was so grateful that my experiences gave me the ability to help her navigate the insurance and legal processes, ensuring she received fair treatment.

These experiences made me proud of my ability to make a difference, both for my family and my community.

One of the most challenging experiences in my life began with starting a 3D modeling club at my high school. My friend and I noticed there wasn’t a club for 3D printing, we saw an opportunity to build a community for others who shared our interest. Establishing an entirely new club with no prior experience was tough, However, the biggest challenges surfaced only after we had set everything up.

Some of the other club leaders had previous leadership experience, and as a new president, I was open to every suggestion. One person was very direct in pointing out what he saw as my lack of contribution and responsibility. I appreciated his honesty and worked hard to address his feedback, making every effort to improve. Despite my efforts to communicate more effectively with this person, he remained negative towards my work during the general meeting, purposely trying to trigger my feelings.

At first, I took his criticism to heart, reacting emotionally. His public negativity during general meetings left me feeling defensive, and it was difficult not to let my feelings take over. It took me a while to realize that this was a valuable lesson, but rather than giving up, I took my experience as an opportunity to become a stronger leader. I took advantage of their judgment and adjusted my mindset. I started proactively seeking feedback from other team members and gathering input on each activity to help us connect and collaborate more effectively. I also established clear team objectives and roles to help align everyone’s efforts and give directions. This approach not only helped me rebuild my confidence but also fostered a more supportive team environment.

Ultimately, this experience taught me that effective leadership is a balance of listening to others while also trusting my judgment. I learned a better understanding of behaviors that trigger reactions from me and I feel stronger about how I regulate my emotions during difficult experiences. This process helped me develop a deeper understanding of myself and showed me the importance of building relationships founded on open communication and mutual respect.

In my sophomore year, a teacher recommended me for a tutoring position, but I doubted my abilities. Until I met a tutor in my English class whose patience and kindness helped me through many difficult times. Inspired by her, I accepted a second recommendation my junior year and decided to become a tutor, hoping to help others as she had helped me.

At first, I assumed tutoring would be simple, but I quickly realized it was more challenging than expected. Initially, I relied on basic skills from my training, but I soon learned that a personalized approach was essential for effective communication.

One student caught my attention because he often stimmed quietly during class. Thinking he might be nervous, I gently tried involving him in group activities. However, he remained distant and reserved, even with the teacher. Over time, I observed his interest in drawing and complimented his artwork. For the first time, he made eye contact, though he stayed silent, so I decided to give him space, not wanting to overwhelm him. A few days later, I grouped him with other tutees to discuss the project, but they did not want to talk. Feeling discouraged, I unintentionally showed my disappointment, which caused them to start a brief conversation. Even though their conversation ended quickly, it was still an encouraging sign. Gradually, my efforts finally paid off. I went up to this tutee and slowly started a conversation about a drawing topic he was interested in. Then a lovely conversation began and ended with both of us smiling sweetly.

Tutoring taught me to understand each student’s unique strengths, creating a comfortable learning environment. This role helped me develop communication and adaptability skills while showing me the impact of small kindnesses. I hope my support inspires my tutees to succeed and shine on their path.

“FORE LEFT!” A golf ball is quickly driving to the people on the left side of the greens within a shout, but I can’t see. During the summer golf practice, my shot nearly hit the crowd in the frontier, leaving me with a fear of potentially injuring the audience in the future. I decided to take my path to overcome that fear. I created a plan.

First, I centered on understanding my abilities through focused practice during the summer. Once school began, I balanced between the demands of schoolwork and my extracurricular responsibilities. I scheduled practice almost every day on the golf range. The efforts that I put in rewarded me with a great sense of predictability of balls. I can easily recognize how far the ball will go by the way I grip the club, the movement of the backswing, and the angle of my downswing, which indicate whether a shot is good or bad. However, I understand that being complacent about it won’t help me manage unexpected events on the course.

I started to learn how to control the direction of the ball. After understanding the angle of the clubface would determine the ball’s path, I started intense, dedicated practice focusing on this aspect. I kept adjusting my position and changing swing angles to judge different effects. I analyze my stance and improve its accuracy. I recorded myself and reviewed the video over and over, I asked for advice from teammates and trained with a private coach to find out the best move for me. Additionally, I practiced visualizing crowds during my sessions—Whenever I thought the ball might land in that direction I mentally shouted “Fore”. This repeated practice helped me gain better control of the ball’s trajectory. I found my success satisfying.

I realized this process by which I solve academic and personal challenges is much the same way, just as I focused on addressing my weaknesses to overcome academic challenges. Finally, I next stepped on the course again. I wasn't afraid of those unpredictable factors anymore, my efforts gave me the ability to succeed in every game.

Stepping into the UK at the age of eight felt like being thrust into a foreign world. 10,000 kilometres from my home in Macau, with little grasp of English, I was timid and reserved, unsure of how to navigate the challenges that lay ahead. However, determined to make the most of this new environment, I joined the school football team. The biting winds and piercing cold—completely alien to me—did little to discourage my determination. Each session became a test of my resilience, a constant reminder of the unfamiliar world I was learning to navigate both on and off the pitch, and I was determined to push through it.

As I grew more comfortable, my passion for football deepened. I was no longer just showing up for practice—I was striving to master the game. I spent hours watching YouTube videos of skill moves like stepovers, La Croquetta, and the Cruyff turn. My role models weren’t just players; they were tacticians and thinkers, adapting their play to any situation, constantly thinking ahead to outmanoeuvre their opponents. I practised these moves obsessively, determined to perfect them. This meticulous approach to learning mirrored the same curiosity and drive that fueled my academic interests. Football became a way for me to problem-solve, analyse, and seek improvement. Soon, I began taking on more responsibility on the field, encouraging my teammates so that the team functioned as a dynamic, finely-tuned unit. The shy, hesitant boy was slowly becoming a leader.

Football also brought me together with Felix, my polar opposite. With his blonde hair and British upbringing, Felix was everything I wasn’t—outgoing, boisterous, and deeply rooted in British culture. Yet, despite these differences, we bonded over our shared love for the game. His world of roast dinners and Sunday church stood in stark contrast to my world of dumplings and red lanterns. Our friendship showed me that differences don’t divide—they enrich. It kindled a curiosity to learn more about the cultures that shaped people and the shared experiences that bridge the gap between us.

Felix was the one who introduced me to Fantasy Premier League (FPL), and together, we joined a league with other students. Our conversations about player transfers and strategies became a platform for me to open up, not just about football but also about my life and my thoughts. The deeper we dived into FPL, the more confident I became in sharing my thoughts, whether it was debating who the best player was to buy for the upcoming game or discussing our opinions on the new Marvel movie.

My interest in STEM unexpectedly developed roots in the strategic mindset I developed through FPL. My competitiveness and meticulous nature found a new outlet. I would spend weeks researching players, analysing statistics, and creating intricate plans to better my opponents. The game was like a puzzle, and I constantly broke it down, searching for ways to stay ahead. However, occasionally rushing into decisions often led to mistakes, and I quickly realised the value of patience in achieving success.

This lesson translated to my growing interest in STEM. Just as I honed my strategies in FPL, I began applying the same problem-solving and analytical mindset to my academic pursuits, particularly in STEM subjects. With this newfound approach, I finished in the top ten thousand out of ten million managers that season, reflecting my adaptability and foresight.

Beyond the football field, FPL gave me access to a global community. I connected with players from places as far-reaching as Ghana and Australia, each with their own stories and cultural perspectives. These interactions fueled my curiosity to learn about people’s lives and traditions. This desire to connect and explore inspired me to volunteer with organisations like Edulit and Gamelan. With Edulit, I organised various writing competitions for children in Ghana, aiming to develop their skills and ignite their curiosity and passion for learning. My work with Gamelan immersed me in Javanese music, where I led and guided primary school kids in mastering traditional pieces. I also introduced them to the rich cultural history and significance of the Gamelan, helping them appreciate the deeper connection between music and heritage.

Football wasn’t just a game for me—it became a metaphor for how I approach life. The ability to adapt and think critically cultivated through the football sessions, the problem-solving skills I developed in FPL, and the teamwork I embraced on the field all shaped my identity. My passion for problem-solving and comprehending perplexing concepts in STEM mirrored the analytical mindset I cultivated through football and FPL. Whether it was tackling a challenge in a robotics competition or collaborating on a science project, I approached each task with curiosity and determination.

With a scalpel quivering in my right hand and a magnifying glass squeezed tightly in my left, one thought screamed louder than the rest: There is absolutely NO WAY I'm going to touch the gross, slimy creatures wiggling before my eyes. Notoriously capable of making even the strongest of stomachs churn, these creatures were the renowned *Dugesia tigrina*–freshwater brown planaria. While hundreds of years of stem cell research hailed these tiny flatworms for their extraordinary regenerative abilities, my naive freshman self felt nothing but disgust towards the squirming *Platyhelminthes* before me.

Despite my revulsion, I quickly came to terms with my choices: cut the flatworms or fail the class. Like any other nerd caught in such an abominable predicament, I forced myself to swallow back the nausea bubbling in my stomach and prepared to bisect the gelatinous creature in my petri dish. Holding my breath, I lowered my trembling scalpel to its gooey body, and, with a grimace on my face, I made the cut. To my amazement, the two independent segments survived and suddenly scrambled away from one another. At that moment, I observed with awe a trait in my planaria I had yet to develop: resilience. A simple worm, barbarically separated by the cruel bearer of a scalpel, flourished and harmoniously formed two new creatures. These flatworms sparked a quality that would follow me throughout high school: a deep-seated adoration for scientific experimentation.

Two long years later, I found myself staring down at the same *Dugesia tigrina*, but this time under vastly different circumstances. Surrounded by a chaotic labyrinth of electric circuits and coiled wires, I was knee-deep in my research project working with electrical stimulation. Through many tedious trials and frustrating failures, I found that success was more elusive than worms wiggling away from trouble–I accidentally electrocuted over 300 of my critters through my fieldwork. But with time, I learned how to navigate my research expedition. Whether that meant hauling my experiment home over winter break–much to my mother's dismay–or binge-watching biology lectures until 2 a.m., I forged a way, like my worms, to persevere. More importantly, I discovered a valuable lesson through my voyage: I learned to rely on myself. The quirky determination I once admired in my resilient flatworms began to twist into my identity, supporting me with the same strength as my indomitable planaria.

The following year, I mentored a freshman, reminiscent of my younger self, through her first foray into research. I watched with nostalgia as her curiosity cemented into confidence while trying to nurture her growing enthusiasm for experimentation. Guiding her through the successes and failures of the scientific world mirrored my own growth as I traversed the delicate balance between leadership and patience. Together, we soared through our state-level competition and tackled nationals side-by-side. And while the accolades and prize money we won were exhilarating, nothing could match the initial catalyst for curiosity my *Dugesia tigrina* ignited. As time progressed, I expanded my research horizons and continued taking younger students under my wing, hoping to kindle in them the same electric passion a tiny flatworm once fired in me.

When I think back to the young, wide-eyed girl who first entered that research classroom, I'm astonished at how a simple worm triggered such a substantial transformation within me. In the end, it's not just the experiments, the mentorship, or even the countless hours spent in the lab that define my story—it's the resilience that I cultivated within myself and passed on to my own students. My peculiar creatures taught me that even the smallest cuts can spark regrowth and that setbacks can fuel strength. Although it sounds silly, I proudly owe my journey, my growth, and my passion to those resilient flatworms all those years ago. Patiently awaiting a single sacrificial cut, my unrelenting *Dugesia tigrina* unknowingly molded the very core of who I am today.

Jump Serve

I leaped, eyes focused on the ball soaring above, ready to nail a perfect jump serve. Fwip, the sound of my fingers grazing the waxy striped ball as it fell lifelessly a few feet in front of me. Feeling my cheeks heat up, I frowned and tried again, throwing every ounce of my strength into the swing. This time, it shot straight into the net. It’d been a few weeks since I decided to master my jump serve, but despite the long hours and max power I put in, I was trapped in a cycle of failure that had me lost at what to do.

Maybe I should just stick to my regular serves. After all, it wasn't bad. No, I thought. I really wanted to step up my serve for my next tournament. But not at the rate I was currently going about it. So, I turned to my coach for more advice, hoping for a breakthrough. He stuck out three fingers. The key to a good jump serve? Target, timing, and strength, and a balance between these three things would only come with dedicated practices. The advice was simple, but it made me realize my faults. I had been too focused on strength, disregarding the other factors. With this realization in mind, I felt a new sense of determination well up, and a new training plan came to mind.

That weekend, I looked for a training harness for practicing jump serves, and once I got it, I put it to use immediately. Every spare moment, after finishing my homework during school days or weekends when my parents went out hiking, I brought my ball and harness to the backyard to practice serving. Sometimes, I’d call my volleyball friends out to the rocky pavement in front of their house for serve-receive drill to better my overall coordination and timing. Over and over again, I chanted the mantra in my mind: target, timing, strength. For each serve, I took a mental note of how far the ball landed from my preset target and adjusted my throw to be higher or lower, and swung harder or lighter, experimenting with timing and force. Slowly, my toss became controlled, my approach rhythmical, and my swing timed perfectly to feel the ball’s rough texture on my palm. The ball started to accurately hit the targets I aimed at, with precision that improved after each swing.

Till today, I still recall vividly the sound of my palm hitting the ball and the ball echoing through the gym at the next tournament as I jump served and the cheers from my teammate as I watched the ball sail gracefully over the net, bouncing off the court from the arms of the other team’s receivers.

As I continued to train, that mantra spread beyond volleyball, becoming a central part in my academic life. With my heavy load of AP and honors level courses, I needed a good strategy to juggle deadlines, especially with group projects. When our group presentation on GMOs was initially assigned, we were quite overwhelmed. After a few meetings ending with our heads in our hands, I brought up the idea of splitting the seemingly daunting task into smaller sections, where each member would work on the assigned section following an agreed timeline for researching, drafting, revising and rehearsing. After delivering a well-put together presentation that garnered applause from the whole class, I was more confident that I would be able to navigate my school work by setting the right target, timeline and effort.

As I step into the next chapter of my life, I’ll always remember these three principles. While I may not know what challenges I could face in college, I know I won’t be blindly swinging around. Target, timing and strength will lead my way, showing me a path through whatever my next jump serve might be.

### Student Essay

“A naughty child will become calm in life, and a calm child the opposite,” my grandfather mused, attempting to allay my mother’s wrath. I had just been caught painting over my popcorn-white bedroom ceiling to recreate The Lion King, complete with utterly vague animals I’d fashioned from finger paint, the ladder wobbling as I worked. I dismissively laughed, chalking up his tender words to parental overconfidence. Still, they lingered—like the paint smudges on my hand that would not come off—a riddle I’d spend years unraveling.

As a child, I made my makeshift home in the timeout corner: knees huddled, eyes darting. Why? Probably because I called someone an “angry bird”, or leapt atop a rickety desk to launch a paper airplane.

Somehow, I also found the time for bursts of brilliance. I composed poetry, built a recycling tool to become a finalist in a sustainability competition, and reached state for a kid's movie-making competition. A month after my principal scolded me for taking my friend’s behavior points, I was congratulated for bursts of creativity I had all but forgotten about.

I would soon find a new home: cardboard boxes. I moved almost yearly, from California to Texas, Illinois to New York. My family perfected the rhythm of moving—my mother collected pots, my father packed, and I taped. Without roots, my once mischievous creativity turned inward. I grew cloistered, hesitant to build friendships or pursue my beautiful and random passions.

High school became a quiet backdrop, but gradually, I found new sparks. While my hands never darted across my walls again, I found meaning in debating the world’s issues and immersing myself in the rich tapestry of the past.

Just as I began to feel a sense of home, life dealt another blow. My father’s DWI charge shattered years of my family’s hard-fought progress. It began with a desperate night I never forgot. My mother paced the kitchen, her face stricken with worry, as I continuously refreshed his location, watching, as his dot remained agonizingly still. Hours ticked in dreading silence. Finally, at 3:30 a.m., we found out.

In the immediate weeks, my mother, disillusioned, threatened to leave to my Alzheimer-stricken grandfather and ailing grandmother, leaving my father and I to pick up the pieces. My father, sinking into depression, lay in a hopelessly blank stupor.

Amid this turmoil, I discovered my stoicism, a resilience forged by years of solitude. Night after night was painstakingly spent mediating the painful fights that erupted. I’d sit with my father, fighting for him to talk about his court case and the work problems he lost the energy to address. Neither of us had been good at expressing our feelings, but gradually, I watched him lower the walls that divided my family. Slowly, my home became whole. I came to realize that life wouldn’t wait, and I couldn’t afford to let the opportunities I had slip away.

Five months later, driving home from a difficult soccer tournament loss, my father turned off the engine. The silence hung in the misty morning for a moment. Then, he spoke, his voice steady, but soft.

“Our family was on the brink of collapse,” he admitted. “But through your determination, you pulled us back. Use that strength—channel it into every tackle, every pass.”

He couldn’t have known how profoundly his acknowledgment touched me, how it justified my struggle for peace at home and my newfound pursuit of life.

My grandfather’s riddle—naughtiness and calmness—revealed itself as a paradoxical balance. Life demands both: the fearless audacity of my childhood, which drives me to chase the impossible, and the resilience I cultivated that built the maturity to save my family.

In solving my life’s mystery, I found my home. And it’s in that home, imperfect yet ever-growing, that I’m ready to take my next leap.

**Flickers**

After completing just one flip on the mat, my heart races like I had just run two marathons back to back. Flips are easy, but my diagnosis of Atrial Septal Defect with Arrhythmia (or “Heart Flickers,” as my mom called it) looms over me, reminding me to play it safe and get off the mat. Nightmares of my heart exploding mid-routine terrify me, and I tearfully ask my mother about giving up gymnastics. Together, we research my condition, understanding that I can continue with gymnastics, but need to keep it more casual. I feel like a victim of my diagnosis, an invisible barrier limiting the extent to which I can follow my interests. Suddenly, my stubborn side prevails, and I decide to continue training in gymnastics.

At thirteen, during a check-up, my doctor tells me my heart has healed. My parents are thrilled, but I feel calm, wondering if anything actually changed and if my flickers are anything more than an annoying metaphor for any obstacle. I return to gymnastics and hold nothing back. I see myself in the reflection of the gym mirror five hours a day, five days a week. Revisiting my four-minute routine hundreds of times made each musical art movement a clockwork motion, turning melody into mere mechanics. My team functions like gears in a clock, with everyone memorizing their part perfectly. With each launch during rehearsal, soaring ten meters into the air, my back ages by a decade. I pant and sweat, without remembering my heart. After the long journey of injuries, in 2023, our team won a world championship. I want my heart to see how far I got without the uncertainty of its flickers.

Maybe I would have survived my world championship preparation years before, but a lack of specific implications about my diagnosis left room for fear to take over. To spare others this fear and uncertainty, I consult my former doctors for an ambitious project: partner with peers under my former doctors’ guidance, developing dAIgnosis, an AI diagnostic tool to catch the subtleties in medical data that could shorten the wait for life-saving diagnoses. Building the AI tool proves as challenging as training for my gymnastics routines, each piece requiring focused attention to reach perfect synchronization. I work with peers from my school, researching the process. My genius friend, Timur, with whom I develop and train the AI. Data scientists collect medical books and real patients’ cases. Other teammates consult financial professionals to build a business plan. Like gymnastic training for perfection, we train our AI on thousands of real cases. In weekly sessions, we refine the algorithms, each adjustment like a precise movement to avoid falling. Eventually, our model, used in over thirty hospitals across Kazakhstan, reaches an impressive 95.7% accuracy rate, and hundreds of patients receive timely answers and diagnoses.

After our initial success, I envision broader applications. I discussed scaling the tool to improve hospital efficiency and reach the audience in the sorts hall - the whole country. My next trick in this performance is to pitch integrating this tool to the National Database in Kazakhstan to spread it further, even to other neighboring nations in Central Asia. When studying abroad in the future, I look forward to more experiences and collaborations that will inspire me to contribute further to the medical field and community well-being. After each meeting and refinement, I make to dAIgnosis, I return to the mat, where gymnastics helps me process ideas and push my limits. I love my heart. While I may not punish it as hard as I did during my gymnastics training, I am grateful for how it taught me to overcome my limitations and find ways to help others surpass theirs. I am grateful for how my “flicker” taught me that obstacles are quiet invitations to explore my own strengths.

The hiss of batter hitting hot oil, the sweet smell of powdered sugar—these were the sounds and scents of my teenage years.

When Dad lost his job, we struggled, so Dad started working the winter light show at Bristol Speedway to keep us afloat. Every winter, for the next nine years, he’d be gone for 52 nights, enduring long hours and returning exhausted but hopeful.

Most winters, Dad would become almost unrecognizable. His face slimmer and clothes hanging looser on his body, he was saving every dollar possible for us rather than spending money on food for himself.

When my school went virtual due to the early stages of COVID-19, I took the opportunity to be with my father. I helped tie down all of our appliances in the food trailer and packed my suitcase.

My father fistbumped me in tradition as we set our five-hour journey. "Son, it's just the boys!"

As we neared Bristol Motor Speedway, my heart raced with excitement. After unloading and setting up the trailer, we moved into our tiny apartment across the street. I unpacked in my new room, joining my dad later for chicken wings on the counter.

The next morning, I learned my first lesson—no Mom, no breakfast. We rushed to buy supplies and prepare for opening night, and by dusk, my nerves were peaking. Our first customer ordered: "fried Oreos and a funnel cake", and I went to work. The heat from the fryer made me sweat, and the smells of grease and sugar filled the air. Handing over my first order, I saw the customer’s smile and felt a surge of pride.

The days became a routine: long hours spent frying, serving, and running errands. We worked 8-9 hours on weekdays, and on weekends, it stretched to 12. Every spare moment was spent prepping, cleaning, or counting sales, trying to beat last year’s numbers. I had to keep up with school, too—attending Zoom lectures during breaks, logging in from a small table in the corner of the trailer. I’d squeeze in assignments between rushes, knowing there was little time to waste.

It wasn’t easy. My feet throbbed by the end of each day, and homesickness crept in, making me crave the comforts of home. My dad must have seen it, because halfway through the show, he said, “Son, you don’t have to stay. A kid your age shouldn’t be working this hard.” For a moment, I wanted to accept. But I couldn’t imagine leaving him to face the long hours alone. I chose to stay, even as exhaustion took its toll.

When the season finally ended, we broke down the setup, packed the trailer, and prepared to head home. I was filled with a sense of accomplishment as we closed that chapter together. My father turned to me with a look of pride, saying, “I’m proud of you, son. For 52 nights, you put in the hours without complaint.”

On the drive home, I realized that what had been a few hard weeks for me was something my father had endured every winter for nine years. His resilience and sacrifices taught me the true meaning of hard work and family.

My dad has since ended his annual sojourn to the Tennessee light show, but the lessons I learned under those bright lights stay with me as an adult. The business acumen I’d picked up calculating our profits and talking to customers with my dad helps me every day, as I now own and operate my own food truck. I have shared these lessons with other students as president of my DECA chapter, mentoring students in entrepreneurship and business skills. I hope to pay forward the gifts my father’s hard work gave me by supporting students facing challenges, showing them, as my father showed me, that perseverance and sacrifice create opportunities, and using the lessons I’ve learned while running my food truck to help them realize their potential.

Growing up in a world where girls couldn’t walk the streets freely, I dreamed of something far beyond my surroundings. I dreamed of walking on the moon, of seeing the universe up close. When the Taliban took control of Afghanistan, everything changed. As a girl, even stepping outside became dangerous, and I was left waiting for a passport and visa to escape. Yet, my determination to continue my education only grew stronger because I knew it was the key to building the future I wanted. My dream of studying the stars became a source of strength during these hard times.

In 2018, my friend Razieh and I were introduced to ideas we had never considered before—our teacher spoke of the vastness of the universe and humanity’s journey to the moon. It sparked a curiosity in us to learn more about space, even with the limitations we faced. We joined a small astronomy group in Kabul, where we visited schools and showed students, especially girls, the wonders of the universe. I’ll never forget the looks of awe on their faces when they looked through a telescope for the first time. It reminded me how powerful education is and why it’s worth fighting for.

Tracking a meteor shower with basic equipment taught me how to be resourceful and think outside the box. Even in a volatile environment, I developed problem-solving skills, patience, and focus—qualities I’m eager to bring to George Washington University. I’m excited about the opportunity to study planetary systems and to collaborate with others who share my passion for space.

As Afghanistan’s situation worsened, I lost contact with Razieh, and my dream of pursuing astronomy felt uncertain. But my commitment to education stayed strong. Eventually, I left Afghanistan and made my way to the United States, beginning a new chapter with renewed hope.

I am drawn to George Washington University for its emphasis on space exploration and astrophysics. The chance to study phenomena like gamma-ray bursts and black hole formation with faculty like Dr. Sylvain Guiriec—whose work aligns with my goals—would be an incredible opportunity. GWU’s collaborative environment and cutting-edge facilities will deepen my understanding of space and allow me to contribute to important research.

At GWU, I plan to continue my studies in astronomy and use my experiences to help other Afghan girls and refugees. I want to show them that, despite the obstacles they face, education is a pathway to a brighter future. I hope to inspire them to follow their own dreams, just as I once dreamed of walking on the moon. With GWU’s strong planetary science program and connections to NASA, I’m excited to join a community that shares my passion and to work alongside others advancing our knowledge of the universe.

Through my education and advocacy, I want to prove that resilience and learning can overcome any barrier. At GWU, I look forward to growing academically and helping others realize their potential and chase their dreams.

**The roar of airplanes enveloped me as I clutched an abacus, its beads worn smooth from anxious fiddling. At five years old, the bustle of Narita Airport overwhelmed me. The air smelled different—cleaner, crisper, with a hint of sweetness. My heart pounded as I scanned the sea of adults.**

**Then I saw her. Standing apart, her gaze fixed on me. She approached slowly and knelt. Her hands were calloused and rough, like the cracked earth of the Korean village where I’d been passed from one indifferent caretaker to another. She reached out and brushed my cheek. “Are you my mother?” I whispered, the word foreign on my tongue. She nodded.**

**A year later, I navigated the labyrinth of a Japanese elementary school. “Garlic girl!” my classmates sneered, their taunts sharp as thrown chalk. I counted the fifty tiles on the floor to anchor myself as laughter echoed around me. My refuge was the computer lab, where I spent hours creating animations with Scratch, finding comfort in a world I could control.**

**At home, silence filled the air. Mother sat by the window, staring out as if seeking something lost. The scent of stale tea and uneaten rice lingered. I learned about her sacrifices—caring for disabled sisters while scraping horse feces–and a husband who disappeared after my birth, leaving her in the arms of a man whose love for Pachinko drained what little we had.**

**One evening when I was eleven, I heard her familiar sobbing from the kitchen.**

**I crept closer, finding her hunched over the table. That day was different. Helplessness gnawed at me—I couldn’t stand by anymore.**

**“I need to do something,” I whispered to myself. Using technology, my solace, sparked hope.**

**I retreated to my room, heart pounding. My mind flashed to my Scratch projects, but I knew this required more. Searching online, I found CS50. People warned it would be challenging, but I was undeterred.**

**I took a deep breath and clicked “Enroll.”**

**The weeks that followed were a decoding of codes as well as English. I grappled with loops, conditionals, and prepositional phrases. I hit roadblocks constantly that left me frustrated. My old laptop crashed frequently; I spent hours in the library for a reliable computer. Yet each small victory—a successfully executed line of code, a bug fixed—fueled my resolve.**

**Slowly, I crafted a simple Python program. It would send a message—“You’re not alone”—to my mother’s phone every evening at 9 p.m., when she seemed most distant. Accompanied by a soft glow on her screen, like a digital lantern, I called it “Hikari”—a small beacon of comfort.**

**The first time the message appeared, I watched from the doorway, holding my breath. Her fingers brushed the screen, her eyes softening. I felt a crack in the wall she’d built around her heart.**

**The success of “Hikari” ignited me. Realizing technology could illuminate the darkness of mental health struggles, I started a mental health tech club at school, creating a safe space for students to share and innovate. Delving into neuroscience, I reviewed and developed neurofeedback treatments for mental illnesses. Moreover, in pursuit of a deep understanding of the human brain waves, in Ushiba lab, I work on a project analyzing the innate characteristics of the brainwaves that may subconsciously influence our behaviors. I will continue this pursuit at university, aiming to develop accessible biotechnologies that address mental health issues on a global scale.**

**One evening, my mother approached me with a handmade paper lantern, its gentle glow mirroring “Hikari.” She held it out to me, her hands still rough, but her eyes the softest. “Thank you,” she whispered. Emotion welled within me, warmth chasing away the chill of the past. She was reaching back across the bridge I’d built.**

**Now, every evening, we share tea and laughter. With just the two of us, we’ve built a family overflowing with love and hope.**

I had nearly burned my house down.

A rambunctious rattling could be heard by anyone in a ten-mile radius; meanwhile, I was blasting Ariana Grande, confused as to why water stopped coming out of the nozzle. After taking my headphones off and tracing the noise to my backyard, I found an overheated power washing engine. Regret for my carelessness set in; the engine could’ve exploded or started a fire. Despite this, I had been power washing my house all day, and I was looking forward to finishing what I had started. “It’s almost nighttime; just leave it,” my dad insisted. I was drenched in water and nearly turning to ice, yet I could not let it go. A tenacious fire had lit inside of me. I didn’t know where to start to fix the engine, but my mind was hard set on trying. So, I began scouring Google for common issues and watched four hours of YouTube to learn how to replace gaskets. Using spare parts, I spent the next day repairing the engine. Throughout the process, my dad thought I was foolish and said, “You are too stubborn for your own good.”

Just as I couldn’t walk away from the engine, I’ve found the same stubborn fire burning in my pursuit of knowledge. In AP Chemistry, I couldn’t grasp entropy and its role in our universe at first. I understood what I needed to succeed in the class, but for me, it’s a matter of visualizing and explaining everything that occurs, leaving no gaps in my understanding of how something works. I desired to comprehend the bigger picture of entropy’s uses and why the Gibbs free energy equation worked. Through hours of research, I did everything in my power to create a complete visualization of the concept until I could see the role of microstates of entropy in my mind.

So, yes, I am stubborn. It’s a core part of my being, my form of intrinsic motivation. It’s part of the way I operate, and it shines through in anything I do. It helps me move past failures and stride through my lows because I can keep my eyes on the prize and be too stubborn to let it go.

Nevertheless, being stubborn can burn you in ways I had to put out. In my anatomy class, Karen was one of my top competitors, although she likely didn’t pay me any attention. She was a year younger than me, and yet, she was always on top of her game. I, on the other hand, repeatedly made small errors, with perfection perpetually out of grasp. Fueled by my stubborn nature, I aimed to be the best and competed with her in my head, ignited by her unwavering excellence. However, it took hours of reflection, delving deep into the heart of the issue, to recognize that my once-bright flame of confidence had dimmed, leaving me in a cycle of burnout. Now, I realized I needed to refocus my efforts. My stubbornness had focused on competitiveness, while instead I should’ve been stubborn about bettering myself. Without the weight of rivalry, I began to learn from my mistakes and collaborate openly with peers, adopting a more confident and motivated approach to learning. Embracing my new mindset, I reignited my desire to acquire knowledge, leading to my success in the class. Self-awareness had allowed me to once again harness my stubbornness to my advantage.

Stubbornness is the engine that fuels my passion—a passion for both learning and helping others. Learning anatomy compelled me to pursue medicine to fulfill both passions. This tenacity fuels my relentless pursuit of solutions, ensuring I leave no stone unturned in understanding and healing. As with the engine, I will be too stubborn to not give a patient my full effort, knowing that there is always a possibility that there is hope.

I see each of us as a sphere of light, starting as a soft, pure white. As I interact with others, I adjust my light to match their spectrum, creating shades of empathy, resilience, and curiosity. This adaptability has been essential, especially growing up in Mongolia, a country rich in traditions like Mahayana Buddhism—a philosophy close to my heart but often ignored by my generation.

Mongolian Buddhism is more than faith; it’s woven into our history, art, and values. My grandfather would tell me stories of ancient lamas meditating on compassion, teaching that true strength lies in conquering inner battles. “Defeating all enemies begins within,” he’d say, explaining that compassion is as vital as courage. This heritage has influenced how I view myself and my goals, even as I navigate a modern world that often seems detached from these principles.

My journey has sometimes felt like a ship navigating the vast Gobi Desert—seeking purpose and connection in an unexpected landscape. When I was rejected from sports clubs at school, I felt out of place, like that ship. But when I noticed a small, overlooked poster for a coding club in the hallway, I sensed a chance to chart a new path. Though I became the only member, learning alone under the guidance of an eccentric IT teacher, that coding room became my sanctuary, a place where my purpose started to come into focus.

As I developed my first project, an astronomy learning game, I wanted to share it with my peers. But presenting it to my classmates was a harsh reminder of how a new idea can feel out of place, much like a ship in the desert. Their disinterest stung, but the teachings of my culture taught me resilience. Over time, I realized that my efforts, even if imperfect, reflected the endurance and adaptability of my ancestors.

Later, at a coding academy, I saw a classmate sitting alone, struggling. His isolation mirrored my own past experiences, and the teachings of compassion urged me to help. I shared my project with him, and in return, his feedback strengthened my resolve and deepened our connection. The experience reminded me that, as much as I might feel like a ship misplaced, compassion and collaboration are like an oasis—unexpected but transformative.

Creating a social app to connect people later brought these lessons full circle. The app was celebrated, and that same classmate reached out to congratulate me, saying my kindness had inspired him. In that moment, I felt a deeper connection to my heritage, to the principles of Mahayana Buddhism that had shaped my journey. Just as my grandfather’s stories of lamas in meditation grounded me, this experience reminded me that connection and compassion can carry us, even in the most unlikely places.

My sphere, though white at its core, now glows with colors from my culture, resilience, and empathy. I want to continue charting new paths, like a ship crossing the Gobi—defying the limits of place and expectation. And as I journey onward, I hope to share this light with others, bridging the old with the new, preserving compassion in a way that resonates in our modern world.

If I can inspire others to embrace kindness and resilience, then each step in this journey, each hue in my sphere, will fulfill its purpose.

The bowstring thrums against my cheek as I draw back, the arrow’s tip locked on the distant yellow X. My heartbeat hammers, but my hands remain steady. It’s the final shot—a tie, the entire tournament hinging on this moment. I feel my coach’s gaze pinning me in place and the clock ticking down the seconds. One shot to clinch first place, one chance to prove that every dawn and weekend practice has led me to gold. I exhale, releasing the tension, and let the arrow free. For a mere millisecond, the world holds its breath.

Archery teaches that you compete only with yourself. Each missed shot becomes a lesson I must shed, leaving only the next arrow within my control. At 70 meters, the target is a blurred dot; all I stand on is my focus and confidence that the arrow will reach it. The archer’s philosophy states that one is the bow, arrow, and target, all at once. I have woven this idea into the way I carry through my own life.

I am the bow, the steady force anchoring each shot. At the Summer Science Program, I had to draw on this strength constantly, tested in every way. After a 40-hour journey, I arrived, only to be met with a deep sense of isolation that compounded with the unexpected loss of my grandfather during my stay. Grief hung over me during long study nights, where I battled exhaustion and the pressure to excel in a new, demanding environment. But the bow is engineered to bend and endure tension. I recalibrated, knowing that university, halfway across the world, will ask the same of me. My summer was deeply rewarding, and through its challenges, it gave me a quiet resilience, teaching me to hold steady even in times of loss and change.

I am the arrow, darting forward with purpose. Organizing TEDx Youth tested me like no other event before—balancing it with SSP and school was a challenge, but doing it all in Russian made it even harder. Translating scripts and drafting outreach emails in a language I haven’t used professionally felt like drawing a bow with shaky hands. But I kept aiming forward. Watching our volunteer team pressed with determination, and inspired by speakers I had long admired, rekindled my commitment to management and service. Like an arrow mid-flight, I had to trust that each uncomfortable moment was guiding me closer to my target—empowering my generation to be the future Kyrgyzstan deserves.

I am the target, the measure of progress that reveals where I stand and where I need to adjust. Similarly, I am the big sister my siblings try to hit—sometimes literally—but more often by following my lead. I see it when they pick up my vocabulary or "borrow" my clothes, attempting to keep up in their own way. Being their target means I’m there to celebrate each math homework conquered, every soccer goal scored, and all those times they look for me after a tough day. They remind me that progress isn’t just about moving forward; it’s about being patient, even through setbacks. With every little victory we share, I realize that my own growth is grounded in being there for them, someone to draw strength from, no matter how many tries it takes.

The world sharpens back into focus. I watch as the arrow lands—straight to the blue ring. I finish in second place. There is a moment of stillness, I feel the weight of what could have been; but just as quickly, the familiar calm returns. I know the values I gained have not escaped with that final arrow. While I didn’t clinch first place, true victory lies in the lessons I’ve learned on the range. Wherever life leads, I will hold steady, forge ahead, and keep aiming—embodying the bow, the arrow, and the target.

The sweltering summer heat radiated through my balcony screen, warming my back as the cool air from my fridge brushed against my front. Scanning my fridge, I found my ingredients: brown eggs, shiitake mushrooms, and cherry tomatoes. Today will be the day!

After chopping the fillings, I cracked the eggs into my white porcelain bowl–no shell in sight! Triumphantly, I seasoned and whisked the eggs before heating oil in a pan.

~

I stirred with my chopsticks, watching as the center of the egg mixture began to set into fluffy, cloud-like folds. Just as I shimmied my chopsticks underneath, I felt the weight shift. Oh no! I’ve torn the egg!

Spotting a solution, I tilted the pan, letting the uncooked egg fill the tear–a trick learned from past mishaps. As I watched the tear mend, I arranged quartered tomatoes and diced mushrooms I’d prepared on the untorn side. Then, I lifted the omelet with my chopsticks and folded it in half.

~

As I bit into the omelet, I smiled–I did it! Though not Michelin-star quality or Instagram-worthy, I created, through effort and practice, an omelet I could call my own. More importantly, it was tasty!

***

“What’s my next move?” I asked, holding up the cube to Eddy.

“Let me see.” Eddy examined the cube. “Line up one of the centers first.”

I rotated the cube until the center squares of the red face lined up vertically.

“This red and blue edge,” he continued, pointing at the cube, “needs to go to the left.”

I paused, making sense of the idea.

“So, memorize these steps: right, up, left, down.”

I mirrored his steps as he spoke–right, up, left, down–then paused, reversing and redoing the sequence to ingrain it in my memory.

“Next, turn to the blue face,” Eddy prompted.

I followed.

“Left, up, right, down.”

As I followed along, the red and blue edge slid into place. Shocked, I repeated the steps, back and forth, until I began to make sense of the moves.

With growing excitement, I tackled the remaining three edges, repeating the same eight steps–and their inverse when needed–to align each edge, ultimately solving the second layer.

***

Buh-dum.

“Oh come on!” Noah’s shoulders dropped. “We were so close!”

“Yeah, these measures need work.” I sighed, feeling the pressure of tomorrow’s recital.

“How about this,” I suggested, determined to find a solution. “Let’s both count the beat.”

I demonstrated my part, counting as I went.

“Let's try together,” Noah responded, raising his hands to the keys.

“One, two, three, four… B-dum.”

“Better!” I exclaimed. “Let's try again!”

With each repetition, our timing improved. The counting felt awkward initially, but gradually, we started to get the hang of it.

“One, two, three, four… Dum.”

~

At last, it was recital day. Despite rehearsing that morning, my stomach fluttered as I entered the dimly lit church.

As Mr. Cayres delivered his opening remarks, Noah and I sat together, discussing the music before agreeing to silently mouth the beat during the performance. After Mr. Cayres finished, we handed our score to Jeff, our page-turner, and approached the piano.

~

During our performance, we matched each other’s rhythm. Occasionally, we slipped up, but we recovered, drawing on our preparation to continue. Before long, we reached the end.

One, two, three, four…

Duuummmmmm!

A success! The G major chord rang out in perfect unison.

To me, success isn’t about perfection but rather finding joy in the process. Through my experiences, I’ve learned that this process requires resilience, curiosity, and openness. Whether I’m debugging a project, exploring finance on my blog, or listening to the stories of seniors I meet while volunteering, each moment contributes to my development as a learner, collaborator, and individual. As I turn to the next chapter, I’ll carry this mindset, prepared for every challenge and opportunity, knowing that the journey will be as enriching as the destination.

Tick, tick, tick, tick. I listen intently to the rhythmic sounds of the metronome as my father guides me through the four-count measures. I learned the discipline of adhering to a rhythm and consistency thanks to this steady, regular tempo. Back then, as I sat next to my father at the piano bench, time was a tool for learning music—a pattern that I would ultimately apply to hone my skills through consistent practice.

Beep…beep…beep… A decade later, I’m still sitting beside my dad, only this time in the ICU. This rhythm was different. Time wasn’t something I felt like I had too much of. It was precious, fleeting. My perception of time changed as the metronome's steady tempo gave way to the unpredictable beats of a weakening heart. I watched the once-reliable beats wane as I sat next to my father. What had seemed like an abundance of time now slipped through my fingers like grains of sand. Reflecting on the fleeting nature of life and the importance of making each moment count, I wish I had expressed my love and gratitude more, my thoughts plagued with regret. As I watch my dad in a medically induced coma tethered to an oxygen tube, IVs, and a balloon pump to support his waning heartbeat, time now teaches me of the fragile nature of life, reminding me of the mortality and vulnerability of someone I saw as invincible as a child. Usually, time embodies life moving forward. Now, it felt like a countdown.

Beeeeeeeep. The sharp sound of a flatline cuts through the noise of life. Somehow, when I wasn’t paying attention, time ran out. Time was no longer predictable, it was erratic; it loomed like a reminder of our mortality and left no time for preparation. It’s all so sudden. I can almost hear the world stop and my reality collapse in the jarring sound that signifies the end, and it feels like a cruel joke. One buzzing, unbroken line. A sharp, continuous sound fills the ambulance, unchanging and final. What I hear instead is wasted time, unrealized potential, dreams extinguished, and words left unsaid. It’s a sound that necessitates urgency—to live, connect, and make each moment count before it fades away in the blink of an eye. This time, I wasn’t sitting beside my dad.

Buzzzzzzzz. Clear! Thump… thump…thump… Time was merciful to me. I am lucky to be given a second chance to learn from my mistakes and finally say everything I left unsaid, the words written in smudged ink now more tangible than ever. This second chance at life was a precious gift, one that I vowed to honor by living each day with renewed purpose and intention. Now, as I sit beside my dad, I’m acutely aware of the ticking clock and the weight of the time I've been given, using my time to honor his.

Tick…tock…tick…tock…Each familiar tick represents not just the seconds slipping by but the urgency to make my time on this earth meaningful—to create, connect, and leave a lasting impact on the world. I channel this newfound sense of urgency into pursuing my political, social, and academic ambitions with unwavering determination, driven by a deep desire to make meaningful contributions to society through social reform and academic research. As I reflect on the fragility of life and the finality of time, I am reminded of the importance of living each day with intention and purpose. Whether it is pursuing my passions, nurturing my relationships, or striving to make a positive difference in the world, I am determined to make every second count. The rhythmic flow of the clock mirrors the urgency of life itself—a precious gift that we can never have enough of but one that we must strive to make count. It challenges me to prioritize what truly matters. How I choose to spend the time I have is the true measure of my life's worth. I strive to cherish every moment with my father, to express my love and gratitude more openly, and to savor the preciousness of our time together. When my own time runs out, I hope that my contributions to society will continue to resonate long after I'm gone, and that I will be remembered not just by the people I love but by the impact I leave behind. I choose to make the time I have meaningful and ask myself daily, "What do I wish to be remembered by?”

**My favorite symphony is played in 81 keys. While most instruments can play notes from A through G, mine can express every character in the world.**

When an injury sidelined me from playing soccer, I searched tirelessly for a new form of expression. When I stumbled across an online keyboard-building community, I became enchanted by videos where creators transformed mundane machines into masterful instruments. They infused keyboards with a delicate human touch; the resonance of every sound test echoed through my bones.

What began as a simple inquiry turned into months of research. I compiled full spreadsheets of different cases, plates, switches, stabilizers, and keycaps. To me, the switches were the center and essence of the keyboard. Their distinct sound signature, price, pros, and cons formed the foundation of my research. Out of the hundreds, I found my favorite: the Gateron KS-3X1. Capable of resonating deep tones, it was perfect for my dream “thocky” keyboard.

My anticipation grew with every handpicked piece that I screwed into place. I meticulously brushed each switch with Krytox for a smooth buttery feel. As I fitted the final part, my fingers were already poised above the keys, ready to play.

*clack-clack-clack.*

I’m silent as hollow pinging fills the air. I type again.

With every sharp clack, each more jarring than the last, my excitement crumbles. Perplexed, I looked back inside.

I layered masking tape onto the PCB, sealing the air pockets. There goes the pings. Yet each key fails the test. Then, I carefully inserted 2 mm wide strips of bandaid into the stabilizers, padding the rattling metal-on-plastic impact. The sound signature softened, now more subtle and complex. Still, not quite right. I packed in foam to absorb higher pitches. A pitter-patter of rain now soothed my ears. The rhythm of keystrokes melded together with the case’s dark shade like rainfall with the night sky, a perfect harmony of calm that tranquilized my senses.

When I crafted the rich stabilizers, the thick PCBs, and dense foam, I gave each component the freedom to rework the sound. The components that I had once left in the background didn’t overwhelm the switch’s melody; they enhanced it.

Captivated by crafting harmony, I founded my non-profit, Keyselect, to create custom keyboards for others. I designed mood boards and specialized concepts for my clients. Hours past midnight, I stayed up filming and editing videos of these keyboards for YouTube, emulating the cinematic style that I had fallen in love with in my own keyboard journey. I felt a need to show my viewers that fixing their keyboards can be as simple as using a bandaid and some tape.

My keyboards were perfected through meticulous experimentation. This mindset of continuously creating with a willingness to fail until I succeeded refined how I approached soccer. From a lost soul with an injured adductor muscle, I became a curious one, finding new ways to integrate myself with the team. I started with setting up drills during practice. The next week, I started film analysis and studying managers like Hansi Flick. I delved into the world of tactics, bringing new ideas and fervent callouts to every game. I fell in love with coaching when I began conducting the FSA FC Juniors. The sideline where I had once felt trapped became where I was truly in my element. When I let go of rigid structure, Jackson played with more creativity. As I modeled team play in practice, Yosef learned to harness his flair. Individualism didn’t hinder teamwork; instead, it enhanced our versatility.

Just as each key in my favorite symphony expresses something unique, each player adds a vital tone to a flowing team harmony. Whenever my injuries flare or whenever I’m put through stormy times, I will think of my 81 keys as I start to tap my feet to the rhythm of the rain.

Maybe it was due to the post-homecoming euphoria, but as the clock struck nine, I thought that a 360-degree spinning roundhouse kick in socks would be a perfect way to end the night. Spoiler: it wasn’t. One second I was gracefully mid-spin, and the next, I was face-planting straight into concrete—teeth-first.

Thirty minutes (and many ice packs) later, I was seated in a dental chair at GreenRoot Endodontics, staring into the harsh light overhead, while my parents paced anxiously by the door, my mom clutching her purse like it held the cure. After completing a thorough examination, my dentist gave us good news: I had made it just in time to avoid permanent damage, and the procedure would be relatively risk-free.

Over the next few months, I visited GreenRoot three more times. While most people dread the dentist, I found myself looking forward to each visit. Not because of the goodies they gave out (Colgate toothpaste wasn't exactly thrilling), but because each week presented an opportunity to learn. Fascinated by the array of whirring tools and the precision of the dentist’s hands, I wanted to know everything. I found myself asking questions like, “What’s that for?” and “Can I try?” (the answer was always no).

What I didn’t learn from my dentist, I took upon myself to study. Fueled by a sense of post-traumatic curiosity, I took to Google with my queries and found out that the treatment I had was a Cvek pulpotomy, which is a fancy term for “saving the nerve without going full root canal.” With this knowledge and the self-proclaimed title of “dental detective,” I began searching for novel ways to care for my teeth post-procedure. Rummaging through my mom’s seasoning-drawer, I found turmeric, a unique spice with anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties ideal for resisting gum-swelling and infection. Sensing its potential, I dove into studies on turmeric’s ability to manage oral submucous fibrosis, exploring how curcumin’s modulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines could offer patients a less-invasive alternative—soon becoming the youngest-ever to publish in the Santa Clara Dental Society Journal. Already hooked on the promise of unconventional dental treatments, I continued writing boundary-pushing papers, branching into laser-activated stem-cell therapy and beyond.

However, I felt like something was missing. My research, in theory, was sound, but without the practical experience to back up my ideas, I felt like a chef with a cookbook, but no kitchen. So, I took the leap and began an internship back at GreenRoot. I found myself adjusting the headrest for a sweet elderly patient with trembling hands and a stiff neck, holding the suction-tip for a small child whose wide blue eyes betrayed her growing panic, and offering reassurance to a nervous young man whose back stiffened at the sound of a MidMark handpiece (though, to be honest, I was probably more nervous than he was). Knowing, firsthand, the fear that comes with sitting in that dental chair allowed me to form deeper connections with patients. I had realized the key factor missing from my research: empathy.

While my studies were valuable, without understanding patients’ experiences, I risked reducing a real person to mere data points. Empathy allowed me to see how these non-invasive natural treatments could ease not just physical pain, but also the anxiety that comes with dental procedures—a reminder to me that innovation without humanity is like a perfect set of teeth without a smile.

Looking back, my not-so-graceful tumble into dentistry has transformed into something far more meaningful. Now, whether I’m mentoring students at UP-Next Scientists or supporting communities through OSAAT, I leverage empathy to balance innovation with human connection. In college, I plan on continuing to pursue human-centered research initiatives that elevate my dental research into real-world impact. This work keeps me grounded (in my case, quite literally!) and while I may have fallen face-first into this field, I’m pretty sure I’ve landed exactly where I'm supposed to be.

I once believed with absolute certainty that teasing was cancerous. I thought that compassion alone brings people up, making us stronger; teasing only tears us down. With this conviction, I adopted a strict “no teasing” policy in my professional and school life, even plastering kindness posters across the walls. I felt proud. But in my personal life, my friends and I teased each other constantly—almost religiously—and I started feeling like a walking contradiction. I didn’t understand how these two factions of myself could coexist.
