It became clearer while playing pickleball with my friend Truman. He wanted to get better, but his swings were so… enthusiastic that I questioned his desire to keep the ball within the stratosphere. I jokingly suggested we switch to a tennis court and started sending him “Tennis for Beginners” videos. He laughed, but his grin said, “Challenge accepted”. Soon, he was bingeing pickleball videos and even joined a club, promising, “Alright, lil bro, you’ll see me next time—just wait.” One night, Truman and I played late under the court lights. A few minutes in, he smashed the ball past me. Right into my court. Our eyes lit up; I ran over, hugged him, and we jumped up and down, screaming with joy. “Yooo, your trolls actually worked,” he exclaimed. Thus, The Subtle Art of Teasing was born.

It’s an encrypted love language that only works with mutual trust, the beauty being in its reciprocity. One time, I’d preached my "unbeatable" Connect 4 strategy to my math class, only to be mercilessly 6-0’d soon after. Truman lovingly calls it the “Defenestration of Prab,” and I'm grateful for these regular humility checks—they keep me on my toes and remind me there’s always room to grow. This back-and-forth dance is like our little unspoken challenge, nudging us past our perceived limits. It’s never about mocking struggles people can’t control; it’s an inside-jokey way of showing that I see their strengths and weaknesses and that I’m here to help them reach their potential. Without it, pushing people to improve can come across as superiority, leading to choosing the easier way out: shallow praise and quiet criticism. When we can laugh at our shortcomings or stumbles, they lose their ability to intimidate, making failure a comfortable, expected part of growth.

My seemingly airtight theory was soon tested. I was spectating an Entrepreneurship Club pitch competition when one of our members froze mid-presentation. The ensuing silence was painful. I could see it painted red on her face—how tough it must’ve felt, especially knowing how much she cared about perfecting it. I considered my next words carefully. I could lightly tease her to push her to do better next time. No. There’s no point in teasing someone who’s already down, no matter how well-intentioned. I could ignore what happened and move on—better, but I knew we’d all be silently acknowledging it and letting her stew in it alone, a clear zero-sum game. Finally, I quipped, “Well, that was a solid dress rehearsal!” Her wrinkled face slowly relaxed into a smile, then a laugh, as she playfully smacked my shoulder. By addressing the elephant in the room, I helped her quickly regain her confidence to crush the next round. It’s so easy to let small mistakes feel like heavy, personal failures. But I’ve found careful humor can lighten this weight—poking fun at situations, not people, to turn daunting solo battles into shared journeys.

In the end, I learned my two halves can coexist when rooted in genuine care. I look forward to refining this art in college, where I’ll grow as much from late-night banter as from lectures. It’ll mean embracing teasing enough to laugh with my friends over our failures while respecting its limitations to know when humor should give way to empathy—my fittingly subtle approach to the balance between challenge and compassion that defines the resilient community I seek to build.

For 359 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes, I was imprisoned behind a fuzzy, 7 by 4.5 inch wall of non-woven fabric.

When Covid-19 mask mandates were lifted on March 7, 2022, thousands of high schoolers celebrated around the state. I was NOT one of those students. “Why do you still wear that wretched thing?” I was often asked. I would quickly respond, “You can never be too careful.”

But the truth? I wasn’t worried about the global disease ravaging the world, I was petrified that I failed to meet people’s expectations of what I looked like. Mirrors were my enemy. I refused to look at my face in the bathroom for more than 5 seconds, already convinced that I was ugly. What had started with scooping up quick spoonfuls of my favorite kimchi fried rice at lunch under my mask between furtive glances turned to skipping my meals entirely. But I knew, I couldn’t keep up my act all four years of high school. I sought change.

My opportunity came in sophomore year, my second year of confinement. What was this profound key to my mental restraints? The answer was algae. Whether it was by calling local Korean seafood restaurants like Bada Story to source fresh Ulva or building make-shift terrariums to simulate a real ocean environment, I actively tried to break the social barriers I had set for myself. I spent 20 minutes before school, taking on the task of polluting our algae samples to test whether algae affected their pH. It was a task that required me to remove my mask, and strangely, when I did, I relieved the past 395 days’ pent up anxiety. What remained was a confidence that only grew when I presented my findings at the Student Research Symposium. Met with “Congratulations!” from my classmates, I realized that what didn’t matter was my appearance. What I had to say served a much more important purpose.

I desperately strived to utilize this newfound confidence in my actions. I found my calling at my church as a TA to supervise a class of 8 first graders during service. My class was assigned to sit in the first row. But, a wide-eyed student named Andrew, tugged at my shirt, beckoning for me to sit with him in row 8. When I asked him why he didn’t want to sit in the front, he would just firmly shake his head “no”. In our class meetings when I would exclaim “WOW ANDREW. AMAZING DRAWINGS!” he would giggle but wouldn’t say a word. I realized, like me, he lacked self-confidence. I made it my goal to get him in the front row, confident enough to find his voice.

Every week I asked him different questions like “How was school?” or “Do you like your teachers?” I noted each result similar to the process I had implemented in the lab. But no matter what I asked, he would only reply with a head nod and a shrug. I devoted my Saturday nights before service scouring the internet's resources until I found one post on Reddit under the thread R/NoStupidQuestions. It was literally meant for me. “Treat them like an adult” it read. Skeptical, I put my findings to use the following week in a rubber duck rescue balancing activity:

“Andrew, what if you put all the ducks on the right side of the sticks?”
”Then they would all fall over!” he laughed.

Now, Andrew’s laughter is heard regularly both in the class and in the front row of the service. Through Andrew, I found a new passion. If I am asked whether I still wear a mask, I would respond that I do. But now I don’t wear a physical mask, I wear a smile, determined to help others like me move to the front row.

Zzzt, zzzt… crackle, crunch.

The paper shredder roared to life as I fed in another handful of sheets. My parents insisted I pitch in, but I could easily imagine a hundred more exciting ways to spend my time.

During the summers, I helped out at my parents’ office, scanning exam forms into the computer and shredding the papers once I was done. The quiet hum of the shredder became the soundtrack to my thoughts, prompting me to reflect on the past few years. I recalled the awkwardness of freshman year, the thrill of sprinting in my first track meet, and the quiet strength I discovered while working late nights on my AP Seminar papers.

Crunch, clank, stop. I snapped back to reality—the shredder had jammed. As I had done many times before, I probed and untangled the mess. Little did I know that these moments of problem-solving were honing my skills and inspiring me to apply my analytical abilities to other intellectual pursuits.

I fully embraced the challenge of biology, psychology, and statistics, diving into each subject to understand the problems we were tackling. At the same time, I immersed myself in macroeconomics and U.S. government, terrified at the thought of presentations, but eager to confront these challenges head-on.

As the paper shredder hummed back to life, I found myself wondering, "Why are they even using paper exam forms?" It was in this question that I learned the office wasn’t fully utilizing their electronic medical records (EMR) system, primarily due to dissatisfaction with its functionality. I dedicated myself to identifying the gaps in their EMR system, customizing templates, and creating new fields that streamlined their workflow and added much-needed detail. This led to a complete transformation of their entire process.

With each sheet of paper shredded, I discovered not just their potential for growth, but my own. In those quiet moments, I gained a deeper understanding of myself—my curiosity sparked, and my desire to problem-solve blossomed.

The sun dipped low as Aditya revved his new motorcycle, laughter echoing down the quiet street.

"This is freedom!" he shouted, his eyes gleaming joyfully.

I stood on the curb, thrilled to see my cousin—my best friend—embracing life beyond his textbooks.

Weeks later, that motorcycle became the silent witness to tragedy. Aditya lost control on a secluded road, crashing into a hidden ditch. Fatally injured and with his phone destroyed, he was trapped, unable to call for help, his newfound freedom cruelly stripped away.

"Aditya is gone."

My mom's trembling voice broke the news; the ground vanished beneath me. The word “freedom” now echoed differently in my mind, no longer a symbol of joy but a haunting reminder of a loss.

Grief settled heavily in Aditya's home. His parents drifted like ghosts through rooms that once echoed with laughter. Unable to bear their sorrow or my helplessness, I had to act. I showed up one afternoon with groceries and cooked Aditya's favorite meals. The scent of cardamom and ginger brought back memories of happier times. As we scrubbed dishes, we laughed, wept, and shared stories of his laugh and boundless dreams.

Supporting them honored his memory and helped me heal. But a nagging question remained: Was this enough? As I helped Aditya's parents navigate their grief, the thought he might have survived if he'd been able to call for help consumed me. How many others were silenced in critical moments? Though I couldn't save Aditya, I could prevent others from facing the same fate. Determined to turn my grief into action, I created CantSpeak—an organization designed to ensure no one is left voiceless when it matters most.

Making CantSpeak a reality required resilience, learning, and teamwork. With no technical background, I dove into coding basics, dissecting open-source projects, and posting on forums like TechRepublic for help. I went to hackathons to connect with experienced programmers. Slowly, a team formed: school peers, college students, and mentors guiding us through the technical hurdles. Late nights huddled over laptops became our norm, yet doubt still lingered.

Juggling school work, basketball, and CantSpeak was draining. Nights blurred as I returned home exhausted. Questions plagued me: Even if I succeeded, did this idea truly matter? At times, these thoughts made me want to give up.

Just as doubt began to overshadow hope, an unexpected email illuminated my inbox one evening. It was from Jamie, a mother whose son had narrowly survived a severe car accident.

"If emergency services had arrived an instant later, I might've lost him." Through her research on emergency accident prevention, she discovered CantSpeak.

"You don't know the impact you're making," she said.

Her words reignited my determination, affirming that CantSpeak could save countless lives.
CantSpeak is currently more than a prototype design; it symbolizes the transformation from tragedy to hope, from helplessness to action. The journey hasn't been easy—technical setbacks, funding challenges, moments of self-doubt—but each obstacle has taught me invaluable lessons in discipline, leadership, and the power of perseverance. Motivated by its potential, I envision expanding CantSpeak beyond transportation safety, adapting it for use in schools and universities to enhance security and protect more lives.

Looking back, I've come a long way since losing Aditya. I've turned pain into purpose, discovering unknown strengths. Taking every opportunity to make a difference shows my gratitude, and I tackle each task with determination, no matter the challenge. I honor Aditya's memory by continuing to grow and hope to prevent others from enduring similar loss.

I've redefined what freedom means to me. It's not just the thrill of chasing horizons but the assurance that someone will support you if you falter. Freedom is living life fully, unburdened by preventable fears. Aditya's legacy has taught me that while we cannot change the past, we have the power to shape the future—a future where freedom is safeguarded by our collective compassion and care for one another.

I don’t want to do anything today. I glanced towards the corner of the monitor. 4:35 PM. Half of my Sunday had disappeared and I hadn’t done anything productive. Where did all the time go? I decided to inspect my never-ending list of tabs open in search of an answer.

I quickly skipped through my work-related tabs: Gmail, a to-do list, summer work, robotics planning, SAT prep, recommendation letter forms, and the Common App. So far, these were pretty standard for any high school student.

My YouTube playlist for music was next. It was paused, with music videos and channels of artists I liked branching off of it. These videos then led to searches for sheet music on MuseScore, looking for the music I liked. In one of these searches, I was looking for reference material to arrange a piano concerto from a rhythm game. Oh right, I still need to rearrange that one part of the original concerto for the strings section to transition into the woodwind soli in my Sasoribi arrangement. I then came up on some tabs about music theory and chord progressions. I was trying to understand where the emotion came from in the music I listened to, in hopes to apply the same ideas in my compositions and arrangements. This included my Hookpad tab, where I was trying out chord progressions. I couldn’t help but take another listen to what I was experimenting with. I should try seeing if I can utilize the III or iv chord I was learning about earlier. But I stopped myself and kept looking through my tabs.

The next group of tabs were dedicated to figuring out how to quickly set custom video speeds. I had the Jump Cutter extension page open, an extension that would speed up silent parts of videos, along with an old lecture recording from my AI Capstone course to test it on. I had Stack Overflow questions about using JavaScript for adjusting video speed and pitch open, along with an official Genshin soundtrack video to test out my custom-coded bookmarklets. Shoot, I forgot to send my friend the bookmarklet code. I quickly paste over the code to my friend and move on.

I then came across some of my previous writing assignments I enjoyed from AP Lang. They were left open after I was talking with a friend about what makes a class enjoyable. The first tab was an essay where I wrote about why people do good. For this assignment, we got to research and write about any topic, so I took the opportunity to look into a challenging philosophical topic that interested me. Despite not being sure if I would be able to find an answer at all, I was able to come to a satisfying conclusion. “People do good to somehow matter in this massive world.” The next tab was an assignment involving a writing process that included 30-minute outside observation sessions, leading me to write about the importance of slowing down and taking a break. You know what, maybe I should follow my own advice. I put on my headphones with my music playlist shuffled and let my mind breathe for a while.

I don’t want to do anything today. I just woke up on a late Saturday morning but I’m ready to go back to sleep. I have three tests on Monday, along with college applications to complete. Maybe I’ll start with studying for the Physics test, since applying the harder integrals for center of mass problems were interesting to solve. I keep trying to envision a plan for the rest of the day, unsure of how productive I’d actually be. Perhaps I should abandon this fragile definition of productivity I keep chasing altogether. Regardless, I’ll keep pursuing a better understanding of myself and the world. After all, I must understand before I can know how to matter.

My cracked screwdriver would expose me as a fake handyman.

As I wrestle with curtain rods and faux blinds, I glance down at the vertical pressure ridges indented in my palms as sweat trickles down my temples. With loose nails scattered on the floor, I reflect on how much I've always enjoyed working with my hands. Yet, becoming a handyman was never on my bucket list.

Surprisingly, this foreign routine of simplicity—measure, label, drill—became a process I savored as each piece fit seamlessly together. Through these adventures, I transformed my laundry room into a workshop station, diving into the world of craftsmanship. There, I recovered leftover art materials, repurposing colorful rubber hands and fixing them into U-shaped anchors (a fake wrench) to tighten bolts while fixing furniture. Amid wobbly installations, and in some cases sprained ankles, every wrist rotation was an effort toward optimal precision and flawless alignment.

This was the vision that I never wanted to lose focus on.

***

Three years ago, I strolled into my grandmother’s living room and noticed her struggling to lift herself off the couch, her hand trembling. Involuntarily. Months later, the devastating diagnosis came: Parkinson's Disease. As I looked at my grandmother's still-strong body, I couldn't believe the words. What was Parkinson’s disease? What did dopamine deficiency even mean?

I applied my fixing skills. Seeking expert advice, I contacted neurologists who urged the importance of dietary changes. Although my grandmother is one of the sweetest people I know, she is an unbelievably picky eater who stays true to her African dishes. Scavenging online forums for diet plans, I pinned up a weekly schedule of high-fiber and antioxidant-rich meals, crafting ways to fuse these nutritious foods with our traditional Ghanaian cuisine. Despite my cooking skills being on a journey of its own, my days were spent alternating between oats and a fruit bowl and cooked yams with tomato stews.

With diet changes and the addition of daily walks after school to help maintain her mobility, I saw more scenery in town than ever before. Yet, this wasn't enough. My grandmother’s hands quivered with a new intensity. Her cane, now, became an extension of her arm as she shuffled slowly across the sidewalks.

After school, I folded sketch papers into identical squares to hold my origami lessons. Every Tuesday and Thursday at five PM, I taught my grandmother inside reverse, squash, and swivel folds to turn these one-dimensional flat pieces of printer paper into soaring jets, springing frogs, and flappable cranes. In maneuvering my fingers, I created cardboard NBA rims, sizable enough to host basketball tournaments in her living room. Despite my spectacular track record of defeat, our makeshift tournaments gradually grew her steps steadier, though her fingers trembled slightly. Her hands launched the ball into the basket with a smile endlessly stretching across her face (It was also the first time I saw her try to dunk!).

***

A month later, after a stroll home, my grandmother, shaking slightly, stops. She holds my shoulder, and says “At first, when I got diagnosed, I didn't know what would happen. But then, you showed up almost every day to support me through my pain. Thank you for everything you have done, you have made me a healthier person now.”

I stared across the distance of the street, struggling to keep my tears from falling onto my face. As she held onto my shoulder, I sniffled and continued straight on our path home.

In the world we live in today, It is easy to think that being a handyman is just about household renovations, but when Grandma got sick, I realized that the real value rests not in the flawless completion of tasks, but in the heartfelt adventures of empathy and care. Moving forward, I am ready to fix the objective questions I can and look for ways to create bonds and nuance in life's less pliable corners.

“The Robot Burned Down in Colorado’s Marshall Fire.”

My stomach dropped when I heard the news. With less than a month until the competition, everyone was quiet at the next team meeting. Then, a teammate said, “There’s no way we can make it.” Others nodded.

“No way.”

The phrase hit me. On one hand, I understood the team, feeling just as daunted: finding substitute parts, manufacturing components, and rebuilding seemed impossible given the time frame. But I sought to find a way forward–everyone on the team put in months of work, and I didn’t want anyone to feel like it was wasted.

Still, I was nervous; as team captain, I aimed to guide the team, but with the robot gone, the plan I had for the month was now obsolete. For the first time this season, and when the team was looking at me, I was truly at a loss. Though I could sense the reason everyone was so nervous: they just didn't know where to start. So I pushed past my hesitation to avoid worrying the team and took action. Breaking through the silence, I grabbed the whiteboard and started writing to-do items: 3D-print the frame brackets, machine the polycarbonate bumper, drill the side panels, and so on. To be honest, I didn’t know what reaction I was expecting. But when teammates started throwing out suggestions, I noted how a first step could set things in motion. With this subtle shift, I thought if the team saw tangible progress, hope would reignite.

So, right after the meeting, I got to work. Every day, I’d come home from school, using everything from a Dremel to a soldering iron to piece together progress. When the team returned and saw the robot coming together, morale soared to a level it hadn’t been at in days; everyone shuffled around, collaborating in the cramped living room. I recognized what I was doing was working, so I continued, striving to show the team we could do it. As I built, hours blurred together, the ticking clock constantly reminding me of time running out. 6 PM. Then 11 PM. Up to 2:36 AM, the last time I recall. After that, everything went black–nothing but the faint hum of the 3D printer. Exhaustion hit: my hands ached and my eyes felt heavy. I had fallen asleep beside the robot. Lying there, I doubted if I could sustain the effort, contemplating why I was doing this. I wanted to inspire the team through action that a comeback was possible. Yet, beneath it all, was fear. Fear of seeing their smiles turn to frowns if we came to the competition with nothing but a pile of parts. I pressed on.

It was the competition’s eve. The team worked for hours, giving their all, but the robot’s software was incomplete. As everyone was packing up, one teammate stayed. “If you’re staying, I’ll stay too,” he said. That moment meant everything–from it and the way the team rallied as a whole, I realized my efforts to motivate truly paid off.

The competition went great: we won, but what I remember most is carrying the robot into the venue and seeing the team excitedly huddling together, when just a month ago morale was doubtful. I realized the key to leadership is jumping in, taking the first step to create a stream of momentum. I’ve applied this principle, whether in group projects or the competitive programming club I help lead, where students often hesitate to partake in a contest. I’ve encouraged several students to participate by joining in myself, so they know they aren’t alone. As I move on, I’m confident the determination and leadership I learned will continue to prove invaluable–whether fostering communities or starting new ventures. Even so, I’ll always remember that first robot, reforged from the ashes, a reminder of where a single step can lead.

I have no major setback. Or at least that's what I thought trying to come up with an idea for this essay. Every single draft was scratched out with the same excuse of not being unique enough. Whenever I look for inspiration, I stare at my ideas with shame. How can I talk about my own setbacks when there are people around the world who have gone through way more unfortunate situations? It didn't seem fair.

As application season started to come along, I decided to reuse last year's essay. I just needed to add some finishing touches and re-read it a couple of times to make sure there were no mistakes, and then it hit me, the guilt. That same guilt made me hesitant to submit the essay. None of my problems felt worthy enough to talk about.

"You're not the only one who went through this" is what always coursed through my mind writing this essay. Whether I was talking about my problems with obesity and anorexia, or about my uncertainty of applying abroad; I never felt confident in myself to present those problems as "major setbacks".

In case you didn't notice, that was my major setback, overthinking every situation, downplaying every problem, and getting rid of every idea for not being unique enough. I couldn't help but look at the people around me, disregarding everything I did to the point that I simply faded out. In essence, having low self-esteem.

It was never easy coming to this conclusion; looking back, I now see how this low self-esteem seeped into different aspects of my life. I made it to the national level in coding competitions, and all I did was compare this achievement to my classmates around me. They competed in those same competitions but internationally. The guilt would, once again, creep in; my success felt insignificant compared to theirs, making me question whether it was worth sharing. This constant comparison made it difficult to take pride in my accomplishments, only reinforcing the cycle of self-doubt.

One of the hardest parts about facing this setback has to be the perfectionism that comes with it. It's as if every story, every experience, needed to reach some invisible standard before it even felt worth sharing. This constant need for things to feel exceptional kept me from accepting my experiences for what they were—imperfect but still meaningful. It's only recently that I've started to understand that real growth doesn't come from chasing perfection but from learning to see the value in each moment, however small.

I can't say that I completely overcame this setback, but I am confident that I am on the right track to do so. The hardest part of any change is taking the first step, and this essay is my first step. Writing it hasn't removed the doubts, but it's given me a clearer sense of the patterns that keep me stuck. Acknowledging these tendencies in myself is uncomfortable, and I don't expect them to disappear overnight. Yet, even as these feelings linger, putting my experiences into words has allowed me to see the value in my journey and take a small step toward accepting my challenges without needing them to be more impressive.

Though my setback may not be the kind you read about in inspiring memoirs, it has shaped who I am today. Recognizing my tendency to overthink and doubt myself has been an important step in learning to value my experiences. I may not have all the answers, but I'm beginning to understand that setbacks come in many forms, and what matters most is how I choose to grow from them. By learning to see the worth in my own story, I'm preparing myself, slowly but surely, to face future challenges with resilience and confidence. And with each moment of acceptance, I'm reminded that growth often lies in the quiet courage to keep moving forward.

The wad of tissues clung to my fingers as I brushed them across my little sister’s tear-streaked face. Around us, the walls trembled with my father’s roars and my mother’s weary responses. The feuds were constant, and my father regularly ripped my mother’s credit cards and car keys from her grasp. His crippling dominance made me cower in silence.

However, as a child, something anchored me despite the chaos at home. At school, I sat cross-legged on the polka-dot carpet, flipping through pictures of polluted water and books about recycling. I was set ablaze with an urge for environmental stewardship.

In high school, I collected silvery wrappers during trash cleanups for my school’s Envirothon club, feeling fulfillment as I admired our collective efforts. During junior year, I collaborated with a few club members to replace the school’s plastic water bottles with canned water. My emails to the school’s finance board and the town’s police chief were rewarded with their approval, and we finalized our presentation. Victory was within reach…

Until Mr. S. He was the school’s food director: our most crucial stakeholder.

“Compostable utensils—not enough. Meatless Mondays—still not enough! I’ve done plenty to ‘be sustainable,’ don’t ya think?”

He refused to cooperate, pushing our explanations aside. With the project on the brink of collapse, somberness brimmed the air. Mr. S reminded me of my father—an intense, power-wielding figure. Nonetheless, my desire for a plastic-free school fueled my persistence. As I stole glances at him, I saw not a nemesis but a sweat-soaked leader sparking positivity in the kitchen. I conferred with my teammates to refine our approach for our final meeting with him.

“We wanted to thank you, Mr. S,” I said. We’d come to understand that his frustration lay not with the project itself but with the lack of acknowledgment for his efforts. My teammates chimed in after me, and our gratitude softened his scowl. After discussing his concerns about the profit margin, he promised us a response by the end of the week.

We erupted into cheers at his approving email. In April, we presented the seven-month effort to the town’s Select Board. Our policy was considered and, in July, passed. At the start of the school year, plastic waste dropped by 70%.

Seeing Mr. S as a collaborator rather than an intimidating presence opened me to his viewpoints, allowing my visions to be fulfilled without unresolved conflicts. With this triumph, I felt comfortable outgrowing my hushed persona.

Gradually, my new outlook reshaped my home life. While my mother lay exhausted after arguments, I allocated chores among myself and my siblings. As for my father, I started to realize the loneliness in his solitary meals and how his face brightened whenever I greeted him. Although awkward at first, I accompanied his hikes and massaged his knotted muscles, sharing heart-to-hearts about his burdens. My father’s agitation seemed eased by our conversations, and his outbursts grew sparse.

Now, radiant laughter fills our home more than ever before. On rainy days, the five of us partake in lively card games and spear crab meat onto toothpicks to make sanjeok. Meanwhile, I continue working towards environmental solutions. This past year, I collaborated with other high schoolers to produce sustainable heparin, diving into hour-long discussions to design bacterial genomes.

Our environmental realities aren’t perfect yet, nor is my family. However, recognizing where rapport meets resolve empowers me to overcome barriers of intimidation and transform my communities. The young girl reading on the carpet still lives within me, but now I’m not just a dreamer: I commit to my visions. Having witnessed the fulfillment of possibilities that were once beyond my imagination, I am driven to continue traversing the pressing matters I hold dear and engage with the Mr. S’s I will encounter.

I can’t wait to meet them—who knows what beautiful realities we could create together?

I shook with fear as my opponent pressed aggressively forward. “Halt!” 15 to 7–I lost again. Each scoreboard seemed to agree: my fencing score couldn’t pass 10. After 9 straight losses this season, my blade couldn’t bear my frustration anymore. I watched in horror as a broken piece of my blade clattered to the ground.

I picked up the broken piece. Wires ran down the dip of the blade, resembling a river valley and running into the covered tip. I’d examined bike gears and remodeled unicycles, and I saw potential inside the blade. My frustration turned into excitement.

Borrowing a screwdriver, I took out two tip screws the size of sesame seeds along with the weapon tip. Peering into the barrel, I let two nested springs fall into my hand. Then, the fun began! I experimented with different configurations: I noticed the large and small springs worked together to adjust the sensitivity of touches. The timing, angles, and distance of a touch started to make sense. I was immersed, even forgetting to watch the finals.

I had protected the face value of my weapon only to find its intrinsic value after deconstructing it and recognizing my power to innovate. From the 10th event onward, I found cohesiveness in my fencing strategy, and scoreboards showed decisive victories.

* * *

Months later, I rose from bed at 3:00 one dark June morning to take a call with Eric, an expert from Artinis Medical Systems in The Netherlands. Over an hour later and the gray glow of dawn approaching, I only had the same, tired response: there is no affordable brain monitoring solution outside of labs.

Undeterred, the summer before my sophomore year, I dove into hundreds of research papers on topics from brain signal principles to brain dysfunction digital biomarkers. Sparked by work from Prof. Murthy’s lab, I streamlined my democratization goal into affordability, wearability, and accuracy of brain monitoring devices in non-lab settings.

To reduce cost, I went down a less traveled path by designing an unheard of 3-D helmet, housing and assembling electronic components. Instead of eating pumpkin pie on Thanksgiving, I spent it prototyping to cut down weight, rebalance for better wear, and find a home for my Wi-Fi module. After more than 300 hours of trial and error, my helmet could be worn on a unicycle and collect EEG and fNIRs brain signals, all within $300.

In my quest to achieve accuracy, I did 50+ ablation tests to rule out low signal-to-noise regions. I still remember the thrill the first time my computer captured a live set of my own frontal lobe’s brain signals!

Eventually, combining my helmet prototype with a novel cross-informed algorithm, I created the NeuroHAT system, moving one step closer to allowing stroke patients to monitor their brain health at home.

* * *

When facing obstacles, whether in fencing, research, or something entirely unrelated, I take a similar approach: breaking down perceived restrictions and forging my own path. I started to fence with purpose, even beating a 2024 USA Olympian in a bout! I approached my research hypothesis by looking beyond industry norms, obtaining a provisional patent for NeuroHAT. In college, I’ll continue to innovate through collaborating with experts while remembering: the power of deconstruction can unlock new paths to innovation.

A few manuscripts of old, withered philosophers may have very well saved millions of lives.

Al-Ma'mun, an Abbasid caliph, was signing a peace treaty with the Byzantine Empire. His main ask though? Books—not the lands of Armenia or control over the eastern trade routes, but books. Manuscripts of Plato and Aristotle, Ptolemy and Galen—philosophy, science, even theology. For Al-Ma'mun, knowledge wasn’t just foundational; it was as crucial as land and wealth.

These were the stories my grandfather raised me with; I grew up overhearing his Jummah gatherings every Friday as he’d invite theoretical physicists, historians, and poets alike. From discussing parallels between Al-Mutanabbi’s Journey of Desire and Plato’s Phaedrus in grappling with ambition’s burden to debating the influence of Euclid's Elements on the very foundations of geometry, these discussions always inspired me.

Between these gatherings, 3Blue1Brown Youtube videos, and my grandfather’s library, I decided to become a mathematician. Yet something always used to bug me. These gatherings brimmed with talk of authenticity; Thoreau’s call to “suck the marrow out of life” wasn’t foreign to them. Embrace curiosity, they’d say—but only through books and theories, it seemed. I wanted more. Nietzsche hiked the Alps, Diogenes lived in a barrel—each living their ideas as fully as they wrote them. I wanted to do the same: to experiment, to try, to fail, to create my own lore, to live my own philosophy.

So I bought a ticket to Turkey, kissed my mom goodbye, and headed straight toward my destiny! (Drastic, I know, but it seemed to make sense at the time.)

Three weeks of scaling the rocky trails of Cappadocia, bunking in hostels that seemed allergic to hot water, and seeing more greenery than this sand-dweller had ever known, 16-year-old me returned a new man—or, more accurately, one with a solid case of food poisoning. It wasn’t the grand realization I’d envisioned. Out of all my lofty expectations, what stayed with me the most was playing my guitar around a campfire with friends, honing my tent-pitching skills, and learning to solve a Rubik’s cube just to race a Hungarian friend I’d made.

I realized just as life shouldn’t be all theoretical, grand existential talk, it also shouldn’t only be crazy, life-altering adventures. Instead, there’s a balance—an appreciation for those bigger questions and ideas, but also fulfillment through smaller, more tangible pursuits.

I returned to the same corner desk in my grandfather’s library, but this time I set aside books on naturalism and intuitionism—debates on whether math is discovered or invented—and turned my attention to my own Olympiad problems. I drew out the diagram: the circumcircle, excircle, and orthocenter of a triangle are all placed. Somehow, I was supposed to prove a relation between the two centers of the circles and the midpoint of a random line. So, I used my new favorite weapon in the arsenal: complex bashing. Six hours, some 20+ pages filled with algebra, and a defeated question later: I learned that complex bashing doesn’t go well with more than one circle.

Still, it was fulfilling because I wasn’t just reading about someone else’s journey or watching Don Quixote make missteps in idealistic quests. This time, the trials, the lessons, were mine.

I’ve made a habit of diving into a new skill, picking up a new book, or exploring a new problem whenever curiosity strikes. The Jummah gatherings are still a big part of my life; only now, I get to contribute more and more. While I doubt I’ll solve a Millennium problem or start a philosophical movement anytime soon, I’ll keep seeking that balance between ideas and experiences, learning and sharing at mini-Jummahs during meals, in classes, or even over late-night study sessions. I’ll become a mathematician who skateboards, a musician who reads Dostoevsky, and, most importantly, a learner who never stops exploring.

Where I grew up, a princess named after a fruit is heir to a throne usurped by a tyrannical dinosaur, all while a pair of Italian plumbers save the day. As a child, this was one of many realms I explored. I’d soar through the Pokémon world on Charizard or stop Ganondorf from kidnapping Zelda.

A little bit of context – I grew up in the world of video games. They provided me an escape from everyday life–ultimately, however, once I played a game through, I had to face reality again, something I didn’t want to do. I found a way to prolong my connection to these fantastical realms for as long as possible.

I scoured the internet to boost my games’ replayability until I stumbled upon a Reddit post about custom firmware — a term that sounded straight out of my dad’s conference calls. A Redditor described how custom firmware can enhance consoles and personalize the gaming experience. It seemed too good to be true, as all it needed was an SD card. One quick trip to my dad’s office drawer, and I was ready.

Loading the necessary files onto the SD card should have been easy, however, each console has its own way of making life difficult. From squinting at the DS’s ancient screen or pleading with the Wii remote as I navigated the home screen, each device threw a new curveball. The biggest hurdle came when I learned I needed Python scripts to keep my gadgets from self-destructing. So, instead of becoming the Pokémon champion or kicking Koopa butt, I was learning Python. I was miserable – but determined.

I typed away, facing error after error, with silly syntax mistakes crashing programs completely. After weeks of trial and error (and learning that spacing is crucial), I taught myself basic Python. Successfully implementing it on my first device showed me how determination can yield amazing results.

Although I initially started learning how to code to immerse myself in the digital world, the resourcefulness I learned spurred me to take notice of the physical world around me and see what else I could try to solve.

Today’s environmental challenges can feel as complex as custom firmware once did, but just like I learned from others then, I felt driven to inform my peers about the issues we face. The summer before my senior year, I co-founded the Real Earth podcast. The central mission was to make fighting climate change more digestible. I focused on aspects like rising temperatures, unpredictable weather, and extinction chaos—and explained what steps a high schooler could take in their daily lives. By interviewing environmental activists, I’ve learned that solutions can be fruitful if we collaborate and actively listen.

Being an active listener was further emphasized as my school’s Model UN club president. My fellow leaders often gravitated towards teaching eager middle schoolers ready to absorb new information. Working with experienced high schoolers offered a different and challenging perspective. It involved advising to the extent of criticizing your close friends. Most resisted my advice on being a delegate believing they knew it all. I would spend hours lecturing them about committee strategies – but it only further agitated them.

I knew I had to take a different angle. As a mentor and leader, my goal was to unlock potential. Instead of talking at my friends, I talked to them. I’d ask them to self-evaluate their performance at each conference. By listening, I tailored specific plans for each person and developed helpful workshops. I learned that patience and listening can take a leader farther than trying to dominate a space.

Where I grew up isn’t real, but it shaped my reality. My love for video games no longer serves as an escape; instead, it pushed me to enact real-world change. I find my home now not in digital landscapes, but in my activism, thought leadership, and work towards social justice.

I once believed there were patterns to everything. If I could just decipher them, maybe I could make sense of this unpredictable world. I began with simple things—a pencil, a notebook, the sweetness of Kashi-pan on nights that were too quiet to bear. Powdered sugar dusted across the pages filled with numbers and graphs, each calculation offering a hint of calm.

In Korea, I was passed from one caregiver’s hands to another, tasting neglect in every shade. Moving to Japan at 5 even deepened my isolation. I was the “garlic girl” with the wrong accent, buried in numbers while classmates bonded over anime. My father drifted through Pachinko, while my mother’s voice flared sharp and clipped in arguments with her sisters about heartbreaking illusions.

At eleven, I discovered that my father wasn’t my real father. My biological father, a Japanese stranger, had left after my first breath. Desperate for something—anything—to stitch together this hole in my heart, I searched through every drawer, only to find emptiness, the whisper of Kashi-pan crumbs, and a growing pile of fractured trust. Yet, I clung to the one thing that couldn’t abandon me: my mind. I began to wonder if the very calculations that grounded me could also give me the power to change something real.

One night, I reached for my Kokuyo Campus notebook from the growing stack I kept for hours of equations. I began tracking my mother’s moods: “c” for her mood, “a” for the time, “b” for hours since her last call with my aunts. I could see the rhythm emerging. One day, I said, “Mama, you seem happier around 7pm after tea.” She didn’t say a word, but the next evening, she had her tea—at 7.

Seeing her drink felt like a victory, a hint I could ease her burden. But it wasn’t enough. Reading about how affirmation and light affects mood on the internet, an idea began to grow. “Hikari” became my quiet labor of love. Night after night, I taught myself programming with CS50. The finished app sent a message to my mother’s phone—phrases like “Let go, it’s ok”—accompanied by a warm, soft light on the screen every 7pm. Each message glowed softly, creating a cocoon of calm around my mother.

“Hikari” showed me how technology could soothe minds in turmoil. This set my heart burning to devote every piece of passion I had for confronting mental health challenges with technological innovations. I threw myself into the world of neuroscience and engineering, each late night study a testament. Now, in the lab, I develop EEG systems that confront silent wars of anorexia and build models to ease the suffocating cognitive fatigue that haunts countless individuals.

I stand against the silent suffering and the stigma that buries countless voices, determined to illuminate the shadows where pain hides. Each pain reminds me of my mother. Each line of code is another bridge toward understanding those waiting to be heard.

One late night in the lab, my phone buzzed. At exactly 7pm, a rare message from my mother appeared: “Thank you for ‘Hikari.’ I still play it.” Attached was a photo of her smiling, holding a real paper lantern that glowed softly against the evening sky. Somehow, she had transformed the light on her phone into something tangible, something she could hold close—a light she had made her own. The sight made me smile, though my eyes stung with tears. In the background, I could almost hear the familiar sound of her pouring tea.

That smile is my guiding light, reminding me that life isn’t a flawless equation or a perfect pattern, like I used to believe. Instead, beauty often hides in imperfections. And perhaps that’s why I savor the memory of Kashi-pan, powdered sugar and all. In the end, it wasn’t perfection I sought, but the quiet strength in discovering light amid chaos—like the gentle glow of Hikari.

He saw a different world overlaid onto his, one whose foundations collapsed along with its inhabitants, who had been wandering the fractured land until they saw him, rushing towards him either to attack or become a maundering mess. The protagonist later found this world to be the past of his, a different time rather than a different place. I readjust my lens and see the story I made for what it was, LEGO.

I saw the world through that lens of stories, seeing glimpses of tropes and cliches—the concept of a shadow-world is not new, that twist ending commonly follows the shadow world, and the protagonist was named Bob. Despite this, the lens I saw through remained its own blind spot. My mind needed the shift of refraction.

I looked through the foggy window. It was hard to see through, but sounds of rain had made it clear. I had to walk outside to check, and once I did, my suspicions were confirmed. Lying in the bushes was my broken machine.

I found it funny that as soon as I began working on an irrigation system for my home, the winter had started, and the rain began to fall. A week of work had been destroyed by the heavy rain, with nerves of wires spread across the leaves of the bushes below. Even though the events surrounding my machine were more ironic than its parts, I saw that it fulfilled the trope effortlessly: Boy makes machine, Boy loses machine, Boy rebuilds machine.

But as funny as it was to think of it that way at the time, it also served to make me realize my real eyes, the lens. Then, like forced plot progression, I was reminded of Isaac Asimov’s Foundation and its concept of psychohistory—the prediction of large-scale trends using statistical analysis. Excited at the prospect, I decided that I could use the lens qualitatively for what psychohistory did quantitatively.

Yet, while this had sounded reasonably attainable, I found fault in my work; I couldn’t predict people, lunch, or even my own actions the next day—wearing socks and sandals when I had predicted crocs.

I gave myself my final chance in the game of assassins during the Saudi Research Science Institute. I sat down at the coffee table, took a sip of my hot chocolate, and surveyed my target. Assuming they believed they were being watched, I attempted to know their plan. At that moment, I took the role of Detective Dahoomy, and my mission, though unordinary for a detective, was simple: kill, and don’t get killed.

One of my fellows approached me; he told me he wishes to ally—his story checked out, and swiftly, so did my target. The game of assassins was brutal; likewise was my fellow, who betrayed me with little hesitation.

Bitter that psychohistory and my lens had failed me, I returned to my room to continue my project at the time. I couldn’t focus; I tried to write down what I understood about psychohistory and the lens, finding incoherent jumbles of thought. Concluding that without a concrete foundation to build upon, my ideas of psychohistory and lens had crumbled under their own weight of complexity—truly, I had lost the plot.

Taking a break and returning to my work, I couldn’t stop seeing my machine learning model do the same I had done; it attempted to look for the patterns in flame emissions in much the same philosophy as I had looked for patterns in life’s routines, but where it succeeded—99.6% accuracy no less—I had failed. Coated by the sheen of perspective, I let the lens become a mirror to self-reflect. Without a basis, whether it be statistical or philosophical, I could not expect my lens, let alone psychohistory, to work. Psychohistory itself, even when fictional, had been founded on statistical mathematics. I chose to do the same.

*THUD* I winced in pain as my knuckles were smashed against the tabletop. Little did I know I’d be voluntarily exposing myself to that torturous experience countless times in the coming years and enjoying it too.

I was arm-wrestling with my friends and lost to all of them. I knew that each match had ended before it even began. I could barely even get a grip on their hands. Frustrated, I searched for arm-wrestling techniques online and was surprised to discover it was a professional sport with its own strategies and competitions.

At 5’7” and weighing only 89 lbs, I was severely underweight. Gaining mass was challenging and uncomfortable; every meal felt like a battle against my own body. Eating beyond my appetite was painful, and I often felt sick. However, my desire to excel at arm-wrestling gave me a purpose to endure the discomfort. I learned discipline by setting a diet plan to meet my nutritional goals, researching calorie-dense foods, and timing my meals carefully. I even found myself trying to sneak Sukkari dates into class under the desk so my teacher wouldn’t notice to hit my daily fiber intake. Over time, as I reached 135 lbs and became healthier, I felt a newfound confidence in my body.

Arm-wrestling became an unexpected social catalyst in my life. When I attended my first international Olympiad in tenth grade, I knew no one and found it intimidating to connect with others. Challenging students to a friendly match of arm-wrestling became the perfect icebreaker. People were intrigued that arm-wrestling was a professional sport, and our matches led to discussions about techniques, training methods, and eventually personal stories and ambitions. Each match turned into a friendship, bridging gaps and sparking conversations with people I wouldn't have met otherwise.

As my enthusiasm grew, I wanted to pursue the sport seriously. With no arm-wrestling clubs in Saudi Arabia, I searched for opportunities elsewhere and found a tournament in Bahrain. Convincing my brother to drive me wasn't easy; it took hours of persuasion and promises. There, I met competitors from diverse backgrounds, each with unique techniques and perspectives. The atmosphere was filled with spectators screaming the names of their friends to cheer them on. In a moment of excitement, I started talking to the participants, exchanging our expertise to build each other up. Arm-wrestling became more than just competition to me—it was a window into other cultures and a way to connect on a deeper level. Interacting with people from different nationalities and hearing different strategies and philosophies deepened my appreciation for diversity. The experience ignited in me a desire to bring this sense of community back home.

Recognizing arm-wrestling's impact on my life, I decided to build a local community to share this experience with others. I, along with my friends, started a Saudi Arabian arm-wrestling network, connecting enthusiasts of all levels. We shared strategies, supported each other's growth, and organized meet-ups, making the sport a collective experience. We created a community centered around the progress of even the weakest members, so that everyone could reach their fullest potential.

My interest in arm-wrestling was a surprise to everyone, including myself. During my scholarship foundation year in the US, I used my first stipend to buy a professional arm-wrestling table to bond with my cohort, teaching them correct technique, and getting ready for future tournaments. While it’s true that I did fall in love with the competitiveness aspect of arm-wrestling, it’s the relationships it helped me build that I’ll cherish.

In the future, I'm eager to bring this spirit of connection and collaboration to new environments. Whether it's through arm-wrestling or other pursuits, I hope to continue building communities, fostering friendships, and breaking down barriers. Arm-wrestling started as a simple curiosity but evolved into a lifelong passion that has shaped who I am today.

Being your older brother has always been more than just a role—it’s a blend of protector, coach, and sometimes co-conspirator. Now, as I prepare for college, I feel the weight of leaving you behind, hoping I’ve left a path strong enough for you to find your own way.

I still remember the day we met. You were this squirming bundle swaddled in a pink blanket almost as big as you, and all I wanted was to hold you. I begged Mom, who finally relented, and as fate would have it, you slipped out of my arms faster than Dad, running for his favorite cheesecake in the fridge. Maybe that's where your wild side started—or perhaps I’d planted the seed for a lifetime of "organized chaos" in our adventures together.

Years passed, and it became less about physically holding you and more about teaching, guiding, and maybe nudging you. Together, we took on everything from building elaborate pillow forts to baking that birthday cake for Mom (which, let's face it, looked more like a chemistry experiment gone wrong). And I'd bet good money that no one else could have turned our living room into a concert venue for the worst karaoke performances of "Last Friday Night" by Katy Perry you'll ever hear. It wasn't about nailing the high notes but finding our voices, off-key and all.

One of the most important lessons I wanted to pass on was resilience. I started my first business—a pickleball brand—as much for you as for me. It wasn't just about seeing if I could turn a passion into profit but showing you that taking risks can pay off, even if the road is bumpy. Later, I took over our family's food truck, diving headfirst into the world of flavors, customer complaints, and long hours of sizzling grills. I wanted to show you that success isn't about getting everything right on the first try. It's about picking up the pieces when things fall apart and knowing there's always another shot, another idea, another day to try again.

I'll never forget that one time I took the blame for something I didn't do—wasting Mom's shampoo in a "science experiment"—just to keep you from facing her wrath. Mom never found out, and the truth stayed hidden, but that moment taught me something valuable: sometimes being a big brother means shouldering the blame, even if it's not deserved, because keeping you safe mattered more. Now, as I head off to college, I realize I can't always be there to catch you. That's one of the hardest parts of this journey—knowing I can't be your shield forever.

However, there's beauty in letting go; this is where growth comes in. When I started different projects—real estate school, entrepreneurship, even the food truck—I was scared of failing, terrified of disappointing everyone who believed in me. But over time, I learned that fear is part of the process, and instead of trying to bury it, I could use it. Building a brand, helping run a business, learning the ins and outs of investments—each one taught me that mistakes aren't setbacks; they're essential steps. Growth isn't about achieving something spectacular; it's about learning to adapt, embrace both triumphs and failures, and come back stronger each time.

As I leave for college, I'll be cheering you on from afar, proud of every stumble and every triumph. No matter what challenges come your way, remember you have someone who believes in you wholeheartedly, someone who's walked the road ahead and is waiting for you to catch up. Sometimes, life feels overwhelming, but don't shy away from the chaos. Embrace it, make it your own, and surpass even my wildest dreams. I love you.

It’s interesting that most physicists credit the start of the universe and of time to a Big Bang because I feel as if the start of mine began with a Big Fizzle. Two of them.

See, my mother was divorced twice. And each time, my world was left empty and chaotic. Divorce turned nights of laughter, jumbled Mahjong tiles, and sharing peeled grapefruit into ones of bitter feud and heartbreak. When my sister refused to accept a stepfather, arguments escalated into broken doors and police visits, shattering our family.

***

“Liar!”

My stepfather had just brought home a dog. A cheerful grin stretched across his face from ear to ear as his boisterous but uncoordinated tango with the dog revealed his excitement.

“Liar!”, my sister repeated. “First you lie to my face that you don’t smoke, and now you bring home a dog with no warning? How dare you!”

I could see tears well up in my mother’s eyes as my stepfather wiped the joyful expression off of his face. He had been trying to quit, and in his efforts to bring us together, he had taken us on multiple vacations, introducing us to a new family favorite, Popeyes (which he funnily pronounced as “Pot Pies”), along the way. My mother’s furrowed brows indicated an internal dialogue between sister and step-father, but ultimately daughter had won: less than two months later, he was gone, along with the dog.

***

I’m ashamed to admit that for a long time, I wasn’t fully cognizant of my mother’s struggles. I was bitter that I had been denied a normal childhood, and in my foolishness, I blamed my mom for it. Pierced by the stabbing glares of my sister, I masked the problems of our family using my social life, fostering new connections with friends rather than mending the ones within my family.

But as mom and sister argued, as my mother worked herself to exhaustion to support her two kids amidst navigating heartbreak, unable to fathom the energy to bring food to the table, I realized I was wrong to do so. It pained me to see my mother’s dreams for our family fall apart, to see her less frequently in the living room as she retreated behind closed doors.

The least I could do was to honor her sacrifices by studying physics, a topic she would painstakingly attempt to explain to me at a young age, but starting from zero was not easy. Only after encouragement from my mother did I find my resolve. After all, she had done it herself; after immigrating to a new land, struggling with an unfaithful husband, and failing to reestablish a complete family, she still worked tirelessly for us. Who was I to back down from a setback?

As I opened my textbook to chapter one, I began to fill sheets of blank paper, problem by problem. Sheets of scribbled equations turned into stacks of manuscripts, and late nights scouring the depths of Physics Stack Exchange while my mother toiled away on the floor below me transformed physics into not just an intellectual pursuit but one of atonement and sacrifice as well. Eventually, I finished that textbook, cover to cover, and I had a large stack of papers to show for it.

***

It was May. I had attended the Physics Olympiad a month prior, and I had just received my results. Exiting school, I found my way into my mom’s car. She had been waiting for me.

As she turned to me, I could see her crooked smile, wrinkles, and gray streaks creeping up her hair. With a quiver of solace in her voice she tells me, “I’m proud of you, son.” I realized then that what I had done in the past year was what my mother had done for me in the past twenty, and for that, I was filled with eternal gratitude.

”Something is wrong with your daughter” I heard the doctor telling my parents. The room felt like I'm trapped in a morgue freezer. A huge machine stood there shining white and black blurry images my younger self didn't make sense of. “Wrong” I thought to myself. What could possibly be wrong with the sister my parents promised whom I would play with?

Setting Off on Familiar Tracks

Life throughout my childhood felt like an unpredictable train ride, stopping at specific yet unscheduled stations, only to depart suddenly, abandoning everything in the previous stop without any warning. Vayan, my sister, was born with a rare condition called Fanconi Anemia which is an abnormal genetic disorder affecting bone marrow. During this time, my parents and I were living in America for them to complete their studies. I vividly remember the day of her birth: the sky was dark with rain pouring on the way to the flower shop as if a sign to my young, slow-witted mind that today was going to shape my journey’s trajectory. When we arrived at the hospital, with the flowers still in my hand, my eyes widened as I saw that my first sibling looked different than I had imagined her to be. Even though my parents were smiling radiantly, I could still feel the anxiousness hovering in the room like the day of the ultrasound.

The Last Platform

From the United States, flying back to the farthest northern part of Saudi Arabia where Tabuk is located, and finally arriving in Riyadh, I reached what was supposed to be the last destination of my migration. When my sister’s doctor approved our request to move, my parents thought it was best that we came back to Saudi Arabia, our homeland. As the years passed, changing from one hospital to another, my sister’s condition eventually entered a state of stability. Little did I know, the page had turned but I was still reading the same chapter. “We have to go to the hospital now!” It was my mom screaming at the top of her lungs with a shake of panic in her voice. I jolted as I stood up, spilling the juice in my hand and bolted through the hallway to find my whole family surrounding my sister. Within that moment of chaos, I had my epiphany. I realized that reality needed not be what was happening, but rather what I made of it. I accepted that I couldn’t influence the unexpected turns and challenges that shaped my life, thus I learned to foster and nurture a growth mindset by exploring different hobbies to keep myself busy. The hobbies that took me to another world -my imagination- were arts and craft and drawing. I hoped to influence my sister with the hobbies I picked up, so after her return from the hospital I made drawings of things she often observed, like colorful flowers and a sunny sky with clouds. I adorned her room with these paintings to ease her solitude and admire the things she enjoyed seeing.

Boarding: Destination Unknown

For many of us, the unknown is scary because we have an inherent desire to control every aspect of our lives. In cases such as mine however, this is nearly impossible. Realizing that my parents’ full focus would always be on my sister, I learned the importance of using my intellect and experience to develop creative ways when approaching problems. In other words, I am shaped by my profound love for my family, especially my sister. I have seen and experienced what is needed to persevere in difficult times and my adaption, tenacity and resilience skills are what will ultimately shape my future. As I look to embark on a new journey, I fear not that the destination is not listed on my ticket. Rather, it is the journey which excites me the most about my endless train ride.

**The sun bore down mercilessly on the crowd of mortals…**

Exhausted by the summer heat, I begged my parents to stop at an ice cream stand instead of continuing our journey to Space Mountain. Upon arrival, however, the line seemed endless, proof we were all just a part of a hive mind. While wearily waiting in the swelter, a glimpse of light caught my eye. I separated from the herd, drawn to the glow until I reached a peculiar glass entity on a shelf staring at me with empty eyes. I examined it closely: with interconnected sutures and crystallized teeth, the object smiled at me. I raised the vitreous matter to my eyes and peered through it; as if contracting metamorphopsia, I viewed warped images of a mirrored reality. Dazed, I snapped back to the present, purchased the item, and hurried back to my family.

That night, I studied the object again in bed. While observing this symbol of mortality and the inexorable end, I pondered about the alloter, the spinner, and the inevitable. I probed my existence with the scalpel of my mind and questioned the life I’ve lived. Who am I?, I wondered. Was I merely a lost lamb meandering toward the heartless butcher? Drowning in myself, I turned to the world for help, only to be met with the suffering of the poor, sick, and oppressed. Desperate to escape these dreadful thoughts, I turned my back to the glass being and surrendered to the gentle embrace of sleep.

Days later, I returned home and resumed volunteering at Westside Hospital, where I relished being surrounded by medicine and learning from new experiences; however, the memory of that night still haunted me. Struggling to shake those lingering thoughts, I wandered the halls when I overheard two nurses discussing how troublesome room 527 was. Curious, I immediately went to investigate. Upon entering the room, I saw an older, stern-looking man in Fowler’s position glaring at me fiercely. I asked if he needed anything, and he coldly responded no, demanding that I leave. I complied, but the loneliness in his eyes beckoned to me.

The next day, I came back to speak with the man, whom I’ll call John. He was recovering from a myocardial infarction and rarely had visitors since he was a widower and his only daughter was away at college. I started talking with John daily, and over time he was no longer the problematic room 527 but instead a man with a life full of stories. He loved Sudoku, had his coffee with exactly two sugars, and had been a professional bodybuilder in his 20s. Each story he shared peeled back layers of his loneliness and taught me the importance of human connection.

Some time passed, and our conversations became a cherished ritual. One afternoon, I brought him a cup of coffee. We were talking when John told me he was being discharged soon. The once melancholic man began happily thanking me for everything, saying I was the reason he was able to endure for so long and that I reminded him of his daughter, a caring soul who always selflessly helped others. Listening to John, I found the answers I had been searching for. My mind, once dark with uncertainty, illuminated with purpose. I realized who I truly was—someone who existed to help all those silently suffering and make a difference through my passion for medicine and discovery.

That day, I returned home with John’s words engraved in my soul. I laid on my bed, gazing at the catalyst: the glass skull. Now, the skull was a reflection of myself—the death of my old perspective and the rebirth of me. A reminder of the past and a promise of the future, this crystal skull was a part of my being. It smiled at me again with its blank face, but this time I warmly smiled back.

It's December 13, 1981. General Wojciech Jaruzelski of the Communist Party has declared martial law in Poland, fearing that the Solidarity movement would end the Polish Communist regime, which could trigger a Soviet invasion. The streets in Gdansk, Poland, are tense. My grandfather stood with thousands, fighting for freedom. Poland was at war again, but this time with itself.

My grandfather told me the Solidarity story when I was 11 years old. He had worked in the Gdansk shipyards when intellectuals and trade union workers came together to create the Solidarity movement. The story of Solidarity’s fight against the Polish Communist Party stayed with me. I suffer from Mastocytosis, a rare cell disorder in which mast cells that usually protect the body from allergens and bacteria mutate, causing a constant allergic response. I began to picture the Polish Communist Party as my Mastocytosis, launching a battle within my body. When Mastocytosis strikes me with a reaction, it restricts and rations my abilities—holding me captive in my room until the Communist Mastocytosis decides to give back my abilities—just as my grandparents were rationed in basic needs like food. But I refuse to let the Communist Mastocytosis dictate my life.

I needed to create a battle plan to manage my Mastocytosis. I had to figure out what was triggering my allergic reactions and avoid relying on my EpiPen to resolve them. Like Lech Walesa, the shipyard strike leader, he learned that the best way to strike against the regime was from within the shipyard, not outside, to avoid the disastrous strike of 1970. I needed to find the root cause. When conducting research about the disease, I found that there was not much information available; even some allergists did not have enough information about it. So, I started a medical journal to document every reaction I had. I noted if I had eaten a certain food, if the weather was too hot, or if I was hit during physical activities. Every detail was written down to help me avoid future allergic reactions. I shared this information with my doctor back in Germany to find the root cause of my allergic reactions, which provided him with great insight. and I even volunteered to show my body to the University of Tübingen for research. As I went through this process, I became fascinated with researching solutions. Watching the researchers diligently conduct their work, I realized how much strategic planning was involved, much like the meticulous organization of the Solidarity movement.

The oppression faced by both my grandparents and me has shaped my perspective. The fight to end Communism or to overcome chronic illness requires great planning, determination, and knowledge. Understanding the complexities of your enemy will lead to victory. I want to be part of a team that is as significant as my grandfather's fight for the freedom of Poland—by curing a rare disease. As a Cellular and Molecular Biologist, I will gain great insight into my enemy: the Communist Mastocytosis. Specifically, I hope to utilize cutting-edge research tools to investigate what causes this disease and explore novel treatments that improve patients' quality of life. I envision a world where individuals with disorders like mine can lead fuller, unrestricted lives, just as Poland emerged from oppression to thrive.

Years ago, I made a virtual friend in a world built from blocks and pixels. Our conversations began with Minecraft strategy—how to defend a fortress or gather resources—but quickly turned into something deeper. One night, mid-battle, his voice cut out, then returned. “Mom pulled the plug again,” he said, his words shaky. “It’s not just the Wi-Fi. Things with my mom… they’re bad.”

I didn’t know what to say. Sometimes, there aren’t any words. But I wanted to be there for him, and I hoped that being there was enough. In this virtual world, I felt like I belonged. At school, though, I drifted through hallways like a shadow, slipping into conversations just long enough to nod and smile, before disappearing again. In person, I was guarded and careful. How was it that I could open up to voices in my headset but not to the people right beside me?

That night, Reese opened up more, talking about how his parents were constantly fighting. I just listened. We kept playing, and I stayed on through the pauses, offering what little comfort I could. Somehow, his openness cracked something in me, making me wonder if silence was as strong as I’d always believed. I was raised by my Chinese dad and Korean mom to believe that strength meant silence, that keeping everything inside made you strong. But deep down, I resisted. I wanted to be seen, and I wanted others to feel seen too. I wanted to take the risk of reaching out, even if no one responded.

I started texting my school friends, hoping someone would answer. Most didn’t, and the silence cut deep. But I kept trying, and one day, I decided to take a bigger risk: “Doheny Beach this weekend?” It was an invitation, carrying more weight than I could explain. To my surprise, a few people replied, and those responses led to a beach day.

We met by the shore, volleyballs bouncing across the sand. We laughed, and for a while, the salty air lifted the stress of the week. But as the sun dipped, so did our easy smiles. In the fading light, I found the courage to open up. “I bombed my physics lab,” I admitted, grinding my heel into the sand. Tom, sitting next to me, barely spoke. “I haven’t slept in days,” he said, exhaustion heavy in his voice. I didn’t say anything. I just put my hand on his shoulder, grounding him. We didn’t need to say a word; just knowing we weren’t carrying our burdens alone was enough. I realized that connection is something you build in those quiet moments, in the spaces between words. Sometimes, words aren’t even necessary.

I carried that lesson with me as a Peer Pal for Vincent, a shy second grader who reminded me of myself—quiet, guarded, slipping through the cracks. At first, our meetings were awkward: a lot of silence, a lot of fidgeting. For weeks, I didn’t push; I was just there. One day, noticing Vincent watching other kids play soccer, I brought a soccer ball, and we kicked it around in silence. Over the next few weeks, he started to relax. Eventually, other kids joined in, and he started laughing. By the time the bell rang, he was talking and smiling—no longer on the outside looking in. For Vincent, laughing and playing together was the connection he needed to break out of his isolation. He just needed someone beside him to take that first step.

Now, I understand that the power of opening up isn’t just for me. In a world where so many hide behind “I’m fine,” especially in Asian cultures like mine, sometimes the strongest thing we can do is let ourselves be seen. And just like in Minecraft, sometimes words don’t even matter. Connection, I’ve learned, is something we build—block by block, silence by silence.

At five, I dreamed of becoming king of Saudi Arabia, like a Monopoly player aiming for Boardwalk. I wanted to control everything—the board, the outcome, my future. But soon, I realized not every space was within reach. Instead of controlling everything, I had to find my own spaces to lead and create opportunities.

My childhood began with optimism, like the first roll of the dice. But life soon forced me to adapt. Constantly moving between countries, I was often the new kid, struggling with language and hesitant to make friends. Dreading the move back to Saudi Arabia in 6th grade, I feared losing the friends I’d worked hard to make. I told myself I’d make new friends, but I underestimated the language barrier. When I learned my new school would be Arabic-only, I felt trapped, unable to understand or connect, like landing in Monopoly jail. People referred to me only as “The American,” and I felt increasingly isolated.

To cope, I turned to the internet. Anime forums became my escape, where I connected freely, without language barriers. But as my online hours piled up, I found myself drifting away from real life. I knew I needed something productive to help me bridge cultures and connect with others meaningfully. I began searching for something to identify with. Then, the Monopoly gameboard popped into my mind—I was rolling the dice to find my next “investment.” This gave me a clear goal, so I persisted, searching for ideas.

My breakthrough came with business. After exploring politics, science, and IT, I discovered my passion for entrepreneurship through the idea of combining my interests—like anime—with a successful endeavor. Business became my universal language, making conversation feel natural and giving me confidence. Inspired by “Truedream,” an online friend from an anime forum who simply messaged “cryptocurrency,” I dove into research. I was fascinated by its potential for decentralization, transparency, and global accessibility. Soon, I realized I needed capital to start. With a $10 loan from my father, I started flipping video games.

It wasn’t easy. Early on, I was scammed by someone impersonating a reputable seller. After sending them money, they blocked me on all platforms. I contacted the bank to resolve it, but the seller reappeared only to send my IP address, threatening to “SWAT” me. At 14, this was terrifying, but it taught me about risk management and the importance of caution online. Each transaction was a step toward confidence—my own Boardwalk moment.

When I returned to the U.S. for my junior year, I was the new kid again, but this time it felt different. Hearing others discuss cryptocurrency, I joined in, leading to a friendship where Mahdi told me, “[Name], it feels like we’ve known each other for years.” I was overjoyed. In that moment, I couldn’t help but reflect on how far I’d come. The me from 6th grade would never have taken the initiative to start a conversation, let alone build friendships without barriers. Business had given me confidence, allowing me to reach out, share my interests, and build genuine connections. What once felt like a painful struggle had become a thrilling opportunity to connect.

I’m not a finished product. I still grapple with shyness and trust, remnants of my early struggles. This journey isn’t about becoming a hero but about learning to grow and connect. I believe college will be the ideal place to continue this journey, surrounded by people with shared aspirations who value collaboration and self-improvement.

As I roll the dice for this next chapter, I’m excited to see where I land.

The newest addition to my map collection is one of Hong Kong. However, it holds more than just geographies and landmarks.
