Unlike the other maps I’ve gathered, each capturing places in precise detail, this one represents a piece of myself. It’s a map of my creation, born from my interpretation of the city rather than rigid coordinates. This map is not about perfection or functionality; instead, it marks my journey toward understanding and owning my identity, blending creativity and precision, freedom and structure.

Maps, similar to the mapmaker, are laden with contradictions. The meticulous precision required in mapmaking has to grapple with the reality that a map is, ultimately, just a diagram. A map’s dormancy contrasts with the dynamic place it aims to capture. Correspondingly, my identity oscillates between artist and scientist. While the scientist in me carefully sets scales and contours, the artist adds distinctive, vibrant hues.

My mapmaking began as a spontaneous habit—quick sketches in my red diary, linking restaurants to visitor hotspots. Just as my sketches evolved into maps, the densely integrated characteristics of a place unwilling to be captured by a mere sketch, mapmaking coalesced my different identities, each too precious to discard. Instead of serving as mere tools of navigation, maps became my mirrors for self-discovery. Instead of choosing between artist and scientist, I carved out a new path—one where they coexisted.

The map of Hong Kong began with the scientist in me: intent on capturing the city’s vivid geographies—its waters, mountains, and streets. Focused on painstaking rigor, the scientist resisted the artist, eager to put pen to paper, instead reaching out to the Chinese Society of Geodesy Photogrammetry and Cartography, consulting governmental archives, existing maps, and my own field notes. Each layer of detail grounded me in scientific certainty. Armed with this technical foundation, the artist in me stirs, ready to infuse color into facts, balancing accuracy and expression.

For that reason, my room transforms—mats laid out, furniture pushed aside—and the artist’s work can begin. Here, the pair’s dynamic collaboration unfolds: had the artist worked alone, a scale would have felt unnecessary: “My instincts will never fail me!” If the scientist held command, precision would rule unchallenged.

The compromise—a precise yet unconventional 1:38,461 scale—balanced intuition and accuracy. From those calculations, a grid of intersecting longitudes and latitudes breaks down the impossible into manageable steps. As the scientist’s research found their place on the canvas—Repulse Bay, the Hong Kong aviary, and Causeway Bay—the artist’s hues gave them life. Each pen stroke transformed blank paper into meaning.

Yet, even though the map appears “complete,” it remains unfinished. Just as Hong Kong is constantly evolving, my own journey fuels ongoing change in each work I create. Lifeless is the map without my personal colors—for I, like these maps, am a work in progress, continually exploring and redefining myself.

Since Hong Kong, maps of Macau, Shanghai, and Nanjing, among others, have joined my growing collection, each conjuring memories and sparking deeper reflections on my motivations for cartography. While my desire for an artistic outlet rooted in scientific precision remains steadfast, it’s the blend of art and science that drives me, encouraging an embrace of my most authentic self. Each mapmaking journey sparks curiosity into uncharted lands along with further exploration of the self.

This appreciation of diversity extends to other aspects of my identity: by redesigning my signature to feature both my English and Chinese names, I’ve blended my cultural and linguistic backgrounds; in music, I’ve combined creative improvisation with structured discipline. Embracing these layers of identity and perspective fuels my pursuit of new experiences, celebrating diversity in myself and others. Unlike the maps I grew up with, there’s no “X” marking treasure on my maps; that’s simply the way it is on the path to self-discovery. And while an entire landscape of possibility may seem daunting, I’ve come to see “unfinished” as an invitation to keep growing.

I'm sorry, [Name], but you failed Biology.

I don't remember much after that. I could only focus on that one word I've become all too familiar with: failed.

As I walked to the car, tears blurred my vision. My whole life, I wanted to prove my mother wrong; I wanted to show her I wasn't the failure she thought I was and that I wasn't a mistake. I was ashamed to walk in public carrying the bruises she left, but even worse, I hated the way I saw the world through her words.

***

The buzz of conversation and the noises of paper bags opening filled the Chick-fil-A, where we were seated at a table for ten meant initially for four.

"Anyone feel like sharing their testimony today?" Our Youth Group leader, David, glanced around.

I joined the youth group two years after my failure; a chore implemented by my father soon became a reservoir of hope that I so desperately needed to heal.

In the past months, they'd all shared their testimonies; I was envious of their courage; simply thinking about my past was exhausting and filled me with terror. I wasn't used to a group of boys being so vulnerable about the divorce of their parents, alcohol abuse, or even drug overdose.

So when everyone looked at me, I felt like I was being rooted for.

"My mother always told me she hated me…" I began.

Each word spoken felt like a step onto pins and needles. It seemed like I paused every other sentence, but after my third abrupt stop, I felt David's hand on my back. I didn't think much of it, but soon, almost every member joined in. It took me two hours to share my story, and it's been the most challenging thing I have had to do thus far in my life. However, each hand placed on my shoulder was another push to finally cross the finish line in a race I've been driving for 16 years.

Afterward, the other group members didn't say much; they simply hugged me. Coming from a household where I was constantly neglected, being embraced by ten other students who were struggling as much as me brought me a feeling of peace. David and the other students, telling me it wasn't my fault, lifted a weight off my shoulders that never seemed to stop growing heavier. I felt uncomfortable, but I also finally felt that my trauma wasn't something to run from but something to embrace and challenge.

I was raised a certain way my whole life. I was told I would never amount to anything, and every mistake I made led to ridicule and beatings. However, it's much easier to forget about bruises as they heal, but words stick. Merely hearing the word failure made me choke up. I began to take a new perspective; instead of crying myself to sleep and wishing for a different life, I finally saw failure as crucial to my development. Every day, I would look at myself in the mirror and tell myself I would encounter failure that day. From getting a question wrong when being called upon to not making a starting roster, I understood that failure was the first step to improve, and now, I don't shy away when I encounter these moments but instead ask for help. I've become obsessed with improvement, and my familiarity with failure—once enough to bring me to tears—has become my greatest source of inspiration.

***

I choose to see the abuse inflicted by my mother as a blessing instead of a curse. What she did was meant for evil, but what I can do with it can lead to so much better. I hope to create a community where I can foster the hope and love that was instilled by ten other individuals and make a space where others who weren't as fortunate as myself can grow and heal.

As I stare at the mountains of discarded sourdough starter, failed loaves, and scattered dustings of flour throughout my kitchen, a single question stares back at me: “How could three simple ingredients produce such drastic failures?”

My obsession began with a blog titled “The Perfect Sourdough Bread Recipe.” Seeing how combining just flour, salt, and water could produce a beautiful loaf astonished me. Easy enough, I figured, right? Wrong. On my first attempt: a tasteless, grainy loaf; on my fifth: unevenly scattered air pockets; and on my seventh: a rock-hard crust and so much tang my mouth puckered—a product far from the golden-brown, perfectly crusted sour loaf of my dreams. Week after week, the supposedly simple process continued to yield unpredictable variations of a failed loaf.

Perhaps the “No-Knead dough” method would work—it did not. The autolyse method seemed promising, yet that didn’t work either. Between new recipes and more failed loaves, I realized how passively I had approached mastering bread-making, seeking simple solutions through new recipes and waiting for tips and tricks to come my way rather than seeking them out myself.

Instead of making further attempts at new recipes, I shifted my focus to seeking the details within the steps of the bread-making process. In researching the fermentation process, I learned that an 8°F difference in the temperature of my water was the cause of my overly sour loaf. Achieving the balanced, piquant flavor that I had long yearned for ignited a newfound drive for seeking out the small details. Scoring the loaf just 3 millimeters too deep causes it to collapse, neglecting to add extra water to account for humidity creates a gummy texture, and creating too much surface tension on the dough's outer layer could weaken the gluten structure. It was hard to believe that such small adjustments could result in such drastically different results, providing solutions to the problems that countless attempts and new recipes had failed to solve. After eight months, two 50-pound bags of flour, and five pounds of salt, I finally mastered the art of sourdough.

Through unlocking the secrets of sourdough, I gained more than just a delectable loaf. I realized that what seem like small, insignificant details in bread-making are anything but; they are the essential ingredients that infuse beauty into the final loaf.

The small details became far more than the answer to perfecting my loaf. I began to approach every aspect of my life seeking opportunities to identify small details. As I adjusted the temperature of my water by 8°F, my attention to the slight adjustments of the shifts of my body weight, body position, and tucking my feet enabled me to finally master doing my backflip. Seeking the small details in my interactions with my peers has shaped my inordinate perceptiveness, helping me understand people in distinctive ways. Supporting my sister grieving the loss of a friend, my keen awareness of her subtle emotional cues allowed me to grasp her needs and offer her a safe and comfortable space to feel heard. From seizing chances to share a smile with my teammates as a gesture of encouragement to uncovering shared interests that draw me closer to others, I find that these seemingly small details are, in fact, the threads that weave the beauty of my interactions.

So now, as I stare into the world of wonders that lie ahead of me, a new question stares back at me: “Where are the small details I have yet to discover?” From flour to loaf, my journey of seeking subtle differences continues: not just in the kitchen, but also in every endeavor I pursue.

Buttery popcorn crackling, teenagers in choruses of laughter: the cinema concession stand was bustling. My four-year-old self stood on tippy-toes at the counter. 
“One red licorice for me and one black for my mom, please.”
“Sorry, we’re all out of red. Is two packs of black ok?”
Later, while the pre-movie ads played, I opened my licorice pack with skepticism—it was nothing like my usual, sweetly-fragrant, cherry-red twists. As I bit in, an acrid taste burst over my tongue. Yet, in fighting through the initial bitterness, I relished the sweet, herbal flavor beneath.

Since then, there are now two people in The Licorice Society (my mother and I, but we can round up to 2.7 if you count my brothers’ unenthusiastic participation). From music festivals in France, to friends scattered across the country at my online school, to international peers I encountered at writing workshops, responses to my affinity for black licorice’s acquired taste have ranged from gagging to side-eying to, memorably, telling me how a man died from eating too much of it.

Nevertheless, black licorice shows me that just because something is bitter on the surface doesn’t mean it is underneath. This much-maligned candy, a taste I’ve acquired to the point where I can hardly imagine how anyone wouldn’t enjoy it, reminds me to approach everything I do with the fully-fledged desire to embrace every part of it, from beginning to end.

This desire to go deep has shown up in every literal and metaphorical rabbit-hole I go down, from fostering my beloved bunnies to ruminating on Marxism and Panopticism for months. Every time, just like the deliciousness at the end of the black licorice tunnel, I’ve found another enticing door to open, another mesmerizing window to climb through. While it may be surprising when I explain to others how rabbits introduced me to neuroscience, or David Foster Wallace got me writing cognitive poetics, these connections bubbling under the surface give me endless joy.

Take the aforementioned rabbits. When I adopted my first pet bunnies during the pandemic, researching how to take care of them taught me how frequently rabbits are surrendered to shelters. My heart broke imagining their suffering, and I began brainstorming ways I could help—enter rabbit fostering! As I partnered with animal rescues to host adopt-a-rabbit-thons, I met a woman whose daughter attended online school, irrevocably transforming my ability to take agency not only over rabbits’ well-being, but also my own. Once I had the opportunity to choose classes for myself and go down even more rabbit-holes, ranging from neuroscience to astrobiology to creative writing, I fell in love with the way each of these disciplines strives to understand the same questions—the nature of our universe, what makes us human—from different angles. In this way, I’ve seen firsthand, time and time again, that just because something starts out bitter, that doesn’t mean there isn’t still value beneath the surface.

When I throw myself wholeheartedly into one area, whether candy or rabbits or critical theory, I inevitably find something new within it—something I never could have expected or imagined, that might seem completely unrelated, but that takes me down a wholly new path that I want to continue tracing until I reach their ends. The beauty is that there are no ends—just endless concentric circles, looping into one another. In tangents, in Venn diagrams, in nine-hour conversations with classmates, and in the endless complexity of black licorice, this is where I find myself.

That is why, as a student, I cannot limit myself to just English, or psychology, or science, or linguistics, but rather feel driven to expose myself to as many of them as possible: because I know that in pursuing each of them, I will discover the unending interdisciplinary connections between them and find my way back to the critical theories that connect them all.

What does it take to “extinguish” a burning desire to change the world?

Having been a Keystonian for 10 years, Keystone has been my world.

For the past 17 years of my life, whether it’s when my classmates complained about a teacher, when the assessments are too crammed, when our class was being too loud in a public area and needed a public apology, or when people were lying on their beds in 102℉ during Covid trying to meet project deadlines, I have always been the one to stand up and speak. Because I am a darer, I felt the sense of urge and obligation to join student council and make a bigger change.

Making a difference seemed like a simple formula to me—trace the cause, remove it, done. Fully charged with confidence and the desire to change, I made the promise to “find where the voices come from and return solutions” in my first election. With that beautiful promise, I got elected.

However, it didn’t take long for me to realize that the equation I pictured didn’t work out the way I thought it would. For a suggestion as simple as offering floss in the cafeteria, the student council negotiated with our supervisor for 2 hours straight, drafted plans from the rationale to the replenishment schedule, sent 5 follow-up emails across two months, and in the end received a “No. I think it is not suitable.”

The pain of typing in “unfortunately, this cannot be done” in public responses to student suggestions had become normal, yet when I think of the unseen efforts behind this brief statement, it still stings. To land on this conclusion, I have become used to answering “I have a meeting” every other afternoon when being asked of my after-school plan; when my roommate yawned and said “Finally, I can sleep!” in relief at countless midnights, I have to click open proposal documents and the student council chat where messages continue popping up.

When I unintentionally eavesdropped on a peer complaining, “literally, every response starts with ‘unfortunately’. What’s the point of having student council?” in the corridor the other day, I really felt wronged.

Is that what we get in return? The whole point of me doing this is to make life better for them, how dare they blame back on us for not doing anything? What’s the point of doing all this if all I get out of it is a cold rejection and unthoughtful denials to my efforts? Was I wrong in thinking that I can actually change their lives? Am I wrong in attempting to change? Should I stop doing this altogether?

Yet when I walked to lunch in anger and confusion that day, I can’t help but notice that things aren’t that bad. I see people comfortably throwing their backpacks into the cubbies that we proposed, people walking into the cafeteria with a glimpse of pleasant surprise on their face for seeing the dish they voted for, and people relaxedly throwing themselves onto the beanbags in the library as they came back from lunch—a behavior we unbanned.

It is exactly those moments of frustration that make every tiny achievement very worth cherishing and celebrating.

When our head of school thanked the student council for bringing student voice to their attention on the stage of the high school assembly, it finally feels like our efforts are seen and leading up to a better world. The school has started to seek student voices. It is our efforts that seemed futile that incubated their attention. We started it, and I feel so proud.

Seeing scattered pieces of evidence proving I did bring some changes to our school life, I can now contain my burning desire to change with a reality that extinguished this flame. Even if I didn’t actualize the utopia I had in mind, it’s better than nothing.

Recognizing the limitations in reality, I will still picture one and another ideal picture and work towards it. I am a pragmatic idealist.

In my re-election in the second year, I brought this understanding with me: “I want to make changes in this pragmatic fashion and not promise the sun and moon when that is not possible.”

I will bring this perspective forward with me as I step into a greater world.

The hunt for buried treasure has never really stopped. Ships with black flags, gold chests, and cryptic maps have simply turned into cars, GPS, and mysterious containers tucked away in plain sight.

As a timid Asian-American kid growing up in the mountains of Pennsylvania, I was the last person you’d imagine on a treasure hunt. I’m no pirate, but I do hunt for buried treasure through geocaching—a global game where people hide and seek “caches” left by others. Every day, thousands of “treasure hunters” set off on quests, following only coordinates and instincts. The thrill lies as much in the search as in the find.

Intrigued by the idea of following maps and exploring hidden places, I signed up for a local geocaching event with friends, tackling low-difficulty hunts rated one or two stars. My approach was straightforward: follow the map, check landmarks, and enjoy each discovery, however small. I knew that somewhere, people had hidden caches—maybe a container of tiny toys or quirky notes. Yet, as weeks passed, I craved something bigger—a challenge that would test my problem-solving skills and resilience.

Then, one day, I received a notification that seemed to answer this call: Near you: Difficulty 5.0, Terrain 5.0, Hidden on 4/19/2012. A five-star cache, left unfound for nearly a decade, was geocaching’s ultimate prize. Without hesitation, I rallied a few friends, convinced we could conquer the challenge.

We set off, our enthusiasm high, thinking it would be a day like any other. But soon, we realized why this cache remained undiscovered. The mountains tested every ounce of energy we had, and we were in over our heads. Within an hour, the terrain turned our journey into an ordeal—mud claimed my sneakers, thorny branches tore at our arms, and fatigue set in. Each step forward felt like a battle. Our map was spotty, and dense shrubs blurred any clear path. Four hours later, exhausted and unsure, my friends wanted to quit. But something in me refused to let go.

In that moment, I remembered my grandmother’s words: “Every thorn on your path sharpens you for something greater.” Her wisdom felt like a guide, a reminder that adversity often requires the endurance to keep going. Inspired, I gathered my friends, suggesting we divide tasks: some would stick to the GPS coordinates, while others scouted landmarks further out. This new approach gave us momentum. Step by step, we pushed forward, my grandmother’s words echoing in my mind. Finally, after another hour of focused searching, we found it—a rusted tin box tucked under a rock, filled with odds and ends from geocachers past. But the real prize was in our journey—the teamwork, the resilience, and the shared triumph of overcoming something we hadn’t thought possible.

That experience changed my approach to challenges. Inspired, I returned to the Smoky Mountains a week later, determined to leave my own legacy in a five-star geocache. Inside, I placed a handwritten poem by my grandmother about resilience, leaving a piece of her wisdom for the next adventurer. By sharing her words, I hoped to inspire someone else to press forward through their own challenges, just as her words had done for me.

Since then, geocaching has been more than a hobby—it’s become a way to test limits and embrace setbacks. Each new search builds my confidence and teaches me to adapt and work with others. Whether collaborating on a school project, strategizing on the basketball court, or tackling a public speaking challenge, I approach everything with a “treasure-hunter” mindset. Rather than giving up at the first sign of trouble, I break down the problem, devise a plan, and lean on others’ strengths to help. In every part of my life, I find myself using the resilience geocaching has taught me. It reminds me that even in the face of obstacles, I can keep going.

Geocaching has become my personal rite of passage, showing me that real treasure lies not in the finds but in the journey to discover them. Now, as I look toward college, I’m excited to bring this mindset with me. I want to dive into new fields and embrace challenges that might seem insurmountable at first. I know that even if I stumble or get lost, every obstacle I encounter will simply be another piece of the adventure.

Entering my first escape room, my heart was pounding and my palms were clammy. But as I immersed myself in the plot and the dilemma came to life, my nervousness dissipated. A sense of urgency overtook me, and I became hyper-aware of anything out of the ordinary. A slightly crooked painting could indicate a hidden object behind it. The rhythmic flickering of a set of lights might reveal the combination to a locked safe. I was Sherlock Holmes, piecing together the clues, and every solved puzzle felt like a massive breakthrough.

Despite our efforts, my family and I were unable to escape in time. During the ride home, my dad, frustrated with the result, vented, “I don’t understand why anyone likes torturing themselves with these foolish, impossible rooms.” But sitting in the backseat, I was captivated, busy replaying the experience in my head and trying to figure out the puzzles we failed to solve.

That’s what I love most about escape rooms: the struggle. The puzzles that make a room memorable aren’t the ones I figure out quickly—it’s the ones my friends and I spend what feels like an eternity unraveling. A mysterious glass box with six seemingly random numbered spheres. An incomplete chess board: a white bishop, knight, rook, and queen surrounded by a sea of black. In those moments, I am inspired the most—each test of ingenuity pushing me to decipher its truth and exercise my creativity. To me, escape rooms are not just about solving puzzles. They’re roller coasters of experimentation, failure, and redemption as I learn from my mistakes.

As time passed, however, I noticed that the satisfaction I gained from completing each room was becoming increasingly fleeting. While I found the process of deciphering clues intoxicating, I lacked a sense of purpose. I began to strive for this missing piece—to create a tangible impact.

The first time I played my clarinet at Kaiser Roseville Hospital, I felt nervous, unsure of the reception I would get. Sheltering behind the music stand, I imagined myself practicing at home as I played through Rosé’s 32 Etudes, a book of standard clarinet repertoire. As the sounds echoed through the hallways and people slowly gravitated towards me, I felt encouraged. Yet when I finished a piece, there was little recognition; the patients were preoccupied, listlessly staring off into space.

Although initially frustrated with my inability to connect with them, I viewed this setback as a personal challenge, much like a particularly complex escape room puzzle. What could I do to unlock the doors to their emotions? How could I help alleviate their discomfort, even for a moment? I began altering my approach, experimenting with different styles of music. Rather than hiding, I started reaching out and taking song requests to sight-read. Throughout each week, I spent hours learning more recognizable, lively tunes. And every Saturday morning, armed with my new repertoire, I made it my mission to communicate with patients through my music. When I performed Elgar’s Salut d’Amour, I played with the intent to soothe and was rewarded with relaxed sighs from the audience. Monti’s upbeat Csárdás garnered head nods and foot taps as the rhythm flowed. These subtle signs let me know I was reaching them, and I experienced a newfound sense of fulfillment.

Every escape room adventure brings plot twists that force me to adapt, fighting through struggle and uncertainty. As I gradually piece together the clues to my own story, I’ve come to realize that in many ways, these challenges mirror those I personally face. In my real-life escape room, I’m drawn to the experiences most meaningful to me—where the successes are measured not by ostentatious awards or first place trophies, but by appreciative smiles, words of gratitude, and, most importantly, effort.

Our kitchen belted out a rich, savory fragrance that served as a warm hug to my senses; it carried notes of crispy, toasted potato and a hint of smoky salt. Seven-year-old me waited eagerly at the dinner table for my fix. Pan-fried and culturally prepared, my mom’s Peruvian-style fries are symbolic of my family’s heritage. In the same way my mom’s cooking sustained me physically, my Peruvian heritage has nourished me intellectually and culturally, fundamentally shaping my perspective on the world.

Though unexpected, the source of my mom’s fries jump-started my interest in science by being the star of my first ever experiment in 7th grade. Let me explain: out of pure curiosity, I calculated how many potatoes needed to charge a phone—around 250-300 if you were wondering. This project, which took me to the state science fair, helped me intuitively see how scientific principles are manifested in the natural world. I had the chance to apply this integrative perspective and apply mathematical principles to real-world challenges on the math team. Explaining concepts to my younger teammates—such as determining the angle formed when light reflects on a mirror—gave me the chance to be a teacher, and also to share the excitement of seeing transcendent beauty in otherwise mundane happenings. Seeing the world as a symphony of tangential lines and quadratic curves, each geometric line complementing the other, feels like a super power, one I’m eager to share with others.

While Peruvian potatoes jump-started my love of the scientific world, my Peruvian heritage has shown me how to appreciate the varied influences that shape our reality. I find that my mixed background has helped me see how many identities exist within people. I saw this in action last summer, when I worked with a diverse and brilliant group of peers conducting research into the regulation of the BMP10 gene and its effects on Alzheimer’s. Everyone’s input was critical. Keshavan’s work with mental illness served as the foundation for our research. After studying correlations between heart arrhythmias and the onset of Alzheimer’s, I advocated for further study of the potential connection. Alongside Minjun’s statistical prowess and Paige’s argument assembly, I integrated our ideas into our final product. Tracing the influences in my own cultural background has helped me see and weave together different perspectives, and I’m proud that here it led to our second place at the annual GIDAS research conference.

Lastly, the natural environment in my beloved country of Peru never fails to capture my imagination and inspire feelings of reflection and humility. When I visit the beautiful sun-baked country, I feel an intense spark as if I was meeting a long-lost brother for the first time. My mornings there are quiet: I sit in my grandma’s backyard and notice the dew on the plants, the chirp of the birds, the flourishing ecosystem within her single avocado tree. I obsess over the history of the region, go to museums to learn about the Incas, and talk to locals, all in an effort to connect the past to what I see in the world today. Nature serves as a connection to my cultural identity: I see my own backyard at home in Chicago as a portal transporting me to my memory of hiking Machu Picchu with my grandfather. This perspective on nature and the past is the foundation of my humility.

We all find nourishment in different places. While I can trace many parts of my identity back to my family’s home country, I also see myself in the people and passions I surround myself with in my home city of Chicago. Whether it’s cooking picarones with my siblings or summiting the great Machu Picchu, I see my creativity and humility reflected in those I love. My hope is to bring all of my identities—Peruvian-American, scientist, big brother, and many more—to my college community to help nourish, inspire, and connect with others.

A tiny monkey lives in the jungle of my brain. He swings from dendrite to dendrite, darting across my mind’s gears and cogs at his whim. Like a mad scientist, he watches in awe as glowing orbs roll in, pulsing like tiny batteries, each representing a separate thought. As the monkey plugs these balls into a central socket, the room lights up and gears whir to life, converting my thoughts into actions and emotions.

Constantly chasing these bright, playful orbs, he leads me to explore curiosities and sometimes go off-task, like uncovering what “chess-boxing” is on YouTube. Realizing his supreme control over my decision-making, I ventured into my brain to see his work in real-time. Suddenly, a new orb rolled in, vivid and alive—a thought I just had in class…

******

Damage, damage, damage. I continued to see the same word at least ten more times while studying Autism-Spectrum-Disorder (ASD) and Attention-Deficit-Hyperactivity-Disorder (ADHD) in my psychology textbook. But the monkey in my mind latched onto one question: why were these conditions so drenched in negativity? As he eagerly plugged in this idea, even brighter thoughts started flooding my mind. Suddenly, I was consumed by curiosity.

I plunged into my school library, diving further into the physiology and diagnostics of these conditions. As the monkey frantically stacked up the ever-growing pile of orbs, I started noticing a troubling pattern—terms like “unempathetic” and “socially disruptive” felt more judgmental than descriptive. Medical descriptions felt eerily… subjective. As the monkey pulled me deeper and deeper down this rabbit-hole, I started to become more and more aware of how these labels seeped into my daily perceptions.

While volunteering at the Animal Assisted Happiness (AAH) farm, a nonprofit offering therapeutic outdoor animal experiences, I noticed a young boy with ASD holding a frozen water-bottle near my favorite bunny, Alfie. A twinge of worry crept in—I’d just read that kids with ASD might struggle with empathy, and here he was, close to Alfie with that ice-cold water. But then, in a spout of compassion, the boy gently pressed the bottle against Alfie’s fur, cooling him from the heat of the day. The monkey froze mid-swing, watching intently as the boy’s wordless act of care shattered every textbook assumption I’d ever embarrassingly internalized.

Awakened, the monkey scampered up to a mental gear, sending it spinning wildly, jolting me out of my narrow mindset that ASD only manifested negative behaviors. The child was expressing empathy, just not in the traditional, vocal way. Feeling deep shame, I felt compelled to apply my fresh perspective on ASD through scientific research at UCSB.

I was initially assigned to study a population of mice displaying “harmful” behaviors similar to those seen in ASD. However, recalling my library studies, I noticed a clear bias in my research: hyper-focus in neurodivergent individuals was only portrayed as a self-damaging “obsession,” not a potential vessel for increased passion or care. I hoped to be the researcher who revealed the profound insights hidden beyond this narrow, negative perspective.

The monkey, drawing on this idea, meticulously arranged orbs in new patterns as I reframed my research approach. Inspired by the boy I met at AAH, I shifted my focus from the harmful effects of excessive self-grooming in mice to exploring the positive aspects of grooming by measuring how often and gently parents groom their young.

Through this lens, I discovered that ASD-mice groomed their young significantly more frequently and gently, proving to myself how limited my understanding of neurodivergence once was. Empathy isn’t a one-size-fits-all concept; it’s as subtle, surprising, and complex as any science I could study.

*****

This monkey—guide and disruptor—taught me that curiosity is powerful, especially when paired with openness. I was once proud to contribute to research that “helped the vulnerable,” unaware that my work was fueling the stereotypes and stigma I wanted to break. That realization was heartbreaking.

Heading to college, I'll actively pursue the unexpected, fostering empathy and diversity within my classes and research labs. Empathy can reveal truths that no label can sincerely capture, and I’m excited to uncover those insights in science and people alike (with my monkey friend, of course!).

Maybe, along the way, I’ll let him enjoy all the NFL highlights he wants.

Slipping across the newly polished wooden floor, I sprinted up the stairs to my grandfather’s study. He greeted me with a confident smile, letting me inject a round of his insulin. Sure, it was risky, but what could make a 75-year-old surgeon more proud than to teach his grandson to practice medicine? Exhilarated after shakily administering the shot, I rushed to re-cap the sharp 2-inch needle. Suddenly, I felt a shock in my left palm, watching a stream of thick dark-red blood roll down my finger. I had stabbed myself. The abrupt pain quickly flooded my thoughts with disappointment and embarrassment. Hopelessly vulnerable to my failure, I was no longer the perfect grandson. My grandfather brushed it off, but I couldn’t. My confidence shattered, I faltered whenever I crossed paths with dangerous risks. So, in the haven of quarantine, I buried my face in my screen, embracing the safety within isolation.

Returning to the bustling hallways as a freshman when “in-person school” trickled back, I experienced a trembling fear of social interaction, as if every word I spoke became a sharp needle stinging back at me. “Don’t try it and flop,” I kept telling myself while keeping my head down until the bell finally rang.

As I struggled to regain confidence, my worried parents sat me with the club brochure, pushing me to choose just one. Rushing to get it over with, I chose one I had heard the most about: Speech-and-Debate. I reluctantly showed up for practice, mortified. Frozen at the podium, I muttered fragments of phrases, preparing for countless laughing needles to sting me as a crowd of unwavering eyes seemed to pierce my being. When the timer mercifully rang, I rushed to sit back down, trying to remember each embarrassing word, until I realized the audience had already moved on to the next speaker, and I somehow even got a thumbs-up from a stranger: I was scared for nothing! As I came to my senses, I began analyzing each argument I constructed: had I really called “high-speed” rail SLOWER than rush-hour traffic?? Was no one going to call me out for such an obvious mistake?

My first effort gave me incredible but short-lived fuel. It was always a tireless battle against my clumsy tongue and its endless “Uhm”s. Fortunately, my captain’s heartening (and scary) pep-talks, and my teammates’ cheeky teasing about my mistakes gradually washed away the fear. Win or lose, I returned to practices every week until debate became routine. I debated my mirror about the burdens of student loans, radar in the Arctic, or if the chicken came before the egg, gradually gaining speed and eloquence. By the tenth tournament, I still felt vulnerable to the potential failure of every argument, but the rush-prep, the jitter on stage, and the gratification of a round win kept driving me forward. In retrospect, I am proud of all the mistakes that I bravely faced and I learned that risks shouldn’t be feared, but embraced.

No longer afraid of needles or conversations, I returned to my grandfather with renewed courage. I delivered grandpa’s shots skillfully, careful to not make the same mistake. His smile reassured me as before, but now, I had confidence in myself, too. I now openly welcome new experiences; I aspire to explore the risky opportunities as they help me grow. I parasailed over the Florida Keys, tried out for the basketball team, and even dissected a shark!

I’m proud to be captain of our debate team, where I dabble as both mentor and student, and share my embarrassments to help my peers overcome their fears of public speaking, just as I did. Guiding others has taught me that everyone has a uniquely powerful voice that deserves to be heard. I can deliberate the opportunities in my future endeavors with an open-minded perspective and choose my next quest for growth, embracing the uncertainty each step of the way.

The map of Hong Kong began with the scientist in me: a command to systematically capture the vivid details of Hong Kong’s geographies—its waters, mountains, and streets. The scientist dives into research, ignoring the impatient artist dying to put pen to paper. Keen on meticulous rigor, the scientist reached out to the Chinese Society of Geodesy Photogrammetry and Cartography to learn about cartography and its methods. He pours over governmental websites, existing maps, geographic information, and personal field notes. Armed with the technical foundation established by the scientist, the artist can finally start.

For that reason, my room transforms—mats laid out, furniture pushed aside, and the artist’s work can begin. Soon, the pair’s collaborative efforts will transpire. Had the artist embarked on this endeavor alone, a scale would have been deemed unnecessary: “My instincts will never fail me!” Had the scientist also worked independently, a precise scale would have been needed: “All maps have a perfect scale!” An uneasy compromise saw an unconventionally “perfect” 1:38461 scale implemented. The scientist’s long hours finally paid off as locations from his research found their correspondence on the canvas, pinpointing places of memories: Repulse Bay, the Hong Kong aviary, and Causeway Bay, among others. After bouts of triangulation, topological calculations, and contouring, a locus of points in the set of “coastline of Hong Kong” forms. With each stroke of the pen, the unconquerable blankness of the paper lights up, a map complete.

Yet, even though the map appears “complete,” it remains “unfinished.” Just as Hong Kong is a city in constant evolution, my never-ending exploration fuels continuous change in my maps. Lifeless is the map without my personal colors.

Since Hong Kong, maps of Macau, Shanghai, and Nanjing, among others, have entered the ever-growing collection. Just as they conjure memories of past times, they also invite reflections upon my motivations for mapmaking. My inherent craving for an artistic outlet rooted in the depiction of physical spaces is steadfast. Yet, what drives me the most is mapmaking’s harmonious coalescence of scientist and artist, encouraging me to embrace the entirety of my authentic self. That appreciation of diversity extends to other aspects of my identity: by redesigning my signature, which now features my English and Chinese names, I’ve integrated my different cultural and linguistic backgrounds; through my music, I fused creative improvisation with disciplined structures. In embracing my various identities, perspectives, and values, I empower myself to seek new experiences and celebrate diversity in myself and others. Contrary to the maps I’d grown up playing with, no “X” marks the “treasure” at the final destination; that’s simply the way it is on the path to self-discovery. Although undeniably daunting, I find in “unfinished” an invitation for growth.

I watched, horrified, as my army was pulverized, lying misshapen in a pool of red. My once pristine, sharp-edged deck of Bicycle cards now sat paint-splattered and victim to a stray slap in a vicious game of Egyptian War. While they didn’t fight in every battle, those 52 cards were valiant soldiers in my latest conquest: unite COSMOS.

In the summer after junior year, I spent a month at UCLA, where I faced a peculiar challenge: I didn’t know anyone. With no one to talk to and no classes on the first day, I was incredibly bored. Luckily, I had prepared for this by bringing my trusty army: my deck of cards. Heading into the dorm room lounge on the first evening, I was ready to quell my boredom and unfamiliarity.

Sitting in the lounge with the two new friends I’d made earlier, we tried to figure out what game to play. Poker? No, I didn’t know it well enough. Blackjack? No, we thought it was too boring.

“Egyptian War?” Sumedh suggested

“What’s that?” Lawrence and I both asked.

As I listened to Sumedh describing the rules of Egyptian War, I realized that I knew the game, just by a different name: Egyptian Ratslap. Maybe if we both enjoyed the same card game, we had a lot more in common. Despite the game's simplicity (all you had to do was slap cards), Sumedh embarrassed us, winning game after game. Still, I racked up wins in my own way. The walls of unfamiliarity quickly fell as we all learned about each other’s interests. Sumedh and I bonded over our love for the Golden State Warriors (he branded me a traitor to the Lakers). Meanwhile, Lawrence explained his botanical journaling, which he even taught me how to do later in the week.

While I no longer had to worry about having friends, many people in my cluster were still homesick and anxious, sticking to themselves as everyone else found groups or friends. Attempting to bring people together, I organized card games in the lounge. Finding different people with their cards and unique games, we sat around the lounge teaching others the games we enjoyed the most. From Poker to Rummy, the lounge buzzed with dozens of people duking it out in their card game of choice.

At my table, I was engaged in deadly (to my deck) games of Egyptian War. Stung by my humiliation at the hands of Sumedh, I was mastering my craft and plotting my revenge. I set my cards in the lounge every night and played whoever I could. Sometimes, I won dominantly against a roller coaster enthusiast from Pasadena who taught me all about “dive loops” and “ride ops,” and sometimes my experimental strategies failed against an avid fisherman from San Francisco who built robots to help him in his adventures.

As the weeks flew by in a flurry, my skills and friendships grew stronger. Even as we moved on to research as complex as “see card hit card” was simple, I ensured that our group took breaks to play cards to play cards and build camaraderie. In the camp's final days, I rematched Sumedh, and all my training finally paid off. I finally bested my foe. After a month of tiring war, my army could finally rest. I’d become the victor of the dorms.

The victory at COSMOS was just the first step in the overall fight that defines my life. Reaching my hand out to those without a voice and helping them find one goes beyond just cards. Looking forward, I aspire to help create a world where everyone can share and understand ideas in open dialogue. Climate change is backed by exorbitant research and scientific understanding, yet the voices of dissenters still ring loud. Effective communication of ideas is vital to global change, as everyone is together in the fight.

I hope that my deck of cards and I can continue our conquests. As I turn towards college, it’s time I began preparing to become the best card game player in college.

I froze, horrified, as my grandfather waved enthusiastically.

“Haohao (my nickname), I’m here!” he called, beaming.

Grandpa flew in from China just a few weeks prior. With time in the afternoon, he developed a ritual of walking me home from the bus. Wearing a worn wool sweater and covering his head with a brown scally cap, he greeted me everyday with heavily accented Mandarin.

Embarrassed that I was to be seen with an old Chinese man who constantly repeated the same outfit, I came to dread these walks home.

This time, however, I was horrified. My friends, already amused by his appearance, cast looks of judgment at my grandpa now holding a bright pink umbrella.

Today was worse than usual; it was raining. Standing in his usual spot, he held an obnoxiously pink umbrella. As my busmates filed past, a few stifled giggles, while others shot me amused glances.

Tired of the daily humiliation, I leapt from the bus, berating my grandpa for his “ridiculous” umbrella, ignoring his explanation that it was the only one he could find.

We walked home in silence.

It was only after I’d taken off my shoes that I noticed Grandpa was completely drenched; strands of hair hung limply from his head, and his sweater was now two shades darker. He wasn’t lying- that umbrella was the only one he could find, and he’d chosen to cover me instead of himself.

Seeing the water drip from his thin, battered body, I realized that I’d been too harsh. He was doing his best. I could only watch as he trudged slowly upstairs to take a shower. Later, when I checked on his condition, he simply said, “I’m fine. I’m here for you."

Despite my initial reluctance, Grandpa proved to be someone I could count on. By walking with me each day, he gave me his presence, which, for a little boy struggling with loneliness, mattered more than I knew. His consistency made his moment of self-sacrifice that much more impactful.

I began to understand that love is more than grand gestures; it’s about understanding others' needs and being present for them, no matter the circumstances.

Having broken the ice between us, me and Grandpa began to talk regularly on our walks home. I learned the reason behind his simple wardrobe- raised during Mao’s cultural revolution and one of seven brothers, he was taught to save whatever money he could for his family. Through his recounted stories of boyhood, I grew a deep appreciation for his selflessness.

A few months later, he moved back to China, and I walked alone again. But that’s not to say that my heart became empty; it was still full from the care he showed me.

The summer before my Junior year, I signed up for a Christian outreach camp named Joshua Generation. Headquartered in Philadelphia, its mission is to spread the gospel, support local churches, and serve the surrounding communities. My participation meant 8+ hours of work each day in grueling 100 degree heat.

Walking down the streets of Philly, I remember feeling lost in a foreign city. Remembering my grandfather, however, I knew I needed to take initiative. That week, I successfully participated in a local food drive, helped organize a block party for young children, and prayed over a drug-addled man, who smiled sweetly with open ears.

Closer to home, I’ve learned how to be present for friends and family alike. I’m a wealth of SAT knowledge to underclassmen, a leader to the youth at church, and a motivator to my little sister, who is starting to develop her passions in music and art.

Now, I rarely see my grandfather outside of the occasional Facetime. But I know that, over 10 thousand kilometers away, he’s proud of my growth.

If I ever see an opportunity to extend myself, I’ll show up, perhaps with a pink umbrella in hand.

My blue hydrangea macrophylla had the same life cycle as my parents’ marriage. In the wet spring, things mostly took care of themselves. During the summer, more of an effort was needed to ensure the blue petals flourished. When fall came around, we got lazy with the watering, and by winter I noticed the once-strong stems were now brittle and lifeless. The leaves' edges curled, and my parents separated.

We were in Richmond, VA, there were no kids were my age in the neighborhood. It was only me, my parents, my newborn sister Sara, and my seemingly dead hydrangea.

Before I could get a new one, my mom took my sister and me on, what she called, a vacation to my grandparents’ in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The weather in Saudi was harsh, with no clear sense of spring or fall. You couldn’t grow hydrangeas. Instead, there was my grandma’s mint. She put it with shahi (tea), lemonade, and seemingly every other aspect of my life — mirroring mint's rapid and aggressive root system, I saw the new family dynamic unfold.

In Tabuk, my neighborhood consisted of 24 first cousins and 12 aunts and uncles, all of whom felt like strangers. The sudden appearance of those excessive roots made me feel outcasted and simultaneously grew me closer to my mom and sister.

Soon enough, I discovered the reason behind our move was my father’s abusive nature towards my mom. As uprooted as I felt, I knew I had to keep my sanity for my sister. My mother and I agreed she deserves a relationship with her father, and so does he. During this time, I often felt torn between anger and responsibility as if I had to grow up faster than I was ready for.

I grew to control my emotions when he guilted me for not calling him "enough," telling me I would go to hell for my disobedience. Yet, I maintained contact for my sister. I was always in the middle of that relationship, helping my sister understand that despite his flaws he still cared about her and helping him understand that she needed space and time to trust him again.

Through years of carefully tending to the nuances of our interactions, and many heartfelt conversations with my father, he grew gentler.

When it came to taking care of myself, I found solace amidst the soft hum of nature in my grandma’s garden, where jasmine vines hung over the walls and a weathered swing swayed gently in the breeze. There, Fatimah, my grandmother, taught me how to care for the plants just as I had been caring for my family—delicate pruning, balancing sunlight, water, and, of course, patience. Those moments in the garden were ours alone, a refuge from my role as the family mediator.

In learning to take care of the garden, I started to realize that tending to myself created space for me to better tend to my family. The garden became my mirror; as I nurtured it, I nurtured myself. Slowly, I began to feel less like a weed and more like a mint leaf in the garden of my family, reconnecting with them one blossom at a time. My uncles Ahmed and Abdulaziz challenged my introverted nature. They invited me to join their friends in the mashab, where I played FIFA and debated political issues despite being much younger than them.

My connections even deepened with my newborn cousin Mohammed. His constant crying was impossible to ignore, but it gave me an idea. His cries reminded me of how I kept alarms for watering my plants. From there, I researched moisture sensors, microcontrollers, and tutorials for the XIAO ESP32S3. Soon, I created a “crying plant” alarm. When the soil dries out, it plays Mohammed’s cries non-stop, ensuring I stay as attentive to my plants as I am to my family.

Two months ago, I propagated those same mint plants, and what sentimental values they carry, to Philadelphia, placing them by my living room window along with the crying plant alarm. Whenever I glance at it, I’m reminded of how far I’ve come and how strong my roots are, stretching from Mohammed to Sara to Fatimah. Each grounding me in my past while allowing me to flourish in new adventures to come. Heck, maybe next, I'll try to give the hydrangea another shot.

Ever since I was little, the journey back to China was something I dreaded. The seemingly endless plane ride, the airport security that always forced me to leave something behind, the times my family couldn't sit together – all of it made me miserable. Yet, despite the exhaustion and discomfort, the thought of reuniting with my family kept me going. The moment I saw my uncle waiting for us, I was reminded of the warmth and love that awaited me.

As far back as I can remember, I’ve always wanted things to be quick and easy. Whether it was taking long tests, dealing with faulty equipment, enduring long car rides, or waiting in line for my favorite ride, I despised any activity that demanded patience. Cooking, unless it involved a microwave, was not for me. I craved instant gratification, despising anything that required a long wait.

When COVID-19 hit, at first, I was relieved. No more arduous trips to China. But as the days turned into weeks and then months, the house grew lonely. I made no effort to reach out to people, and slowly, I lost connections. The isolation was stifling.

Then, my grandpa passed away. I was overwhelmed with regret for all the lost opportunities to bond with him, simply because I had dreaded the journey. Time was slipping through my fingers, and I wasn't making the most of it. It had been years since I last visited China, and with the pandemic, I hadn't reached out to others. I lost the chance to indulge in my grandpa's wisdom and company because of my reluctance to endure the journey. My grief and self-loathing isolated me further, pushing me into a dark place where I barely interacted with my parents. I bottled up my emotions, refusing to share my pain with anyone.

But then, Rosie came over. A family friend, she was always like a sister to me. We used to talk about everything, but after I moved to a different school district, we’ve been separated since. We met up for the first time in a long time to celebrate her entering college. During the sleepover we had like old times, she noticed how withdrawn I had become. She forced me into a conversation, deeply concerned about my mental health. Unable to keep it in any longer, I exploded, sharing all my grief, my regret over my grandpa, and my self-hatred. I feared judgment, but instead, she hugged me. The weight lifted off my shoulders. It felt good to be vulnerable, to take the time to understand my feelings and share them with someone else.

Back on the plane, I still hated the long hours. But instead of dreading the lack of instant gratification, I looked forward to the journey because it meant reuniting with people who cared about me. Life is full of opportunities to invest in our well-being. I realized that true investment isn't about instant relief but about understanding others, their emotions, and their unique perspectives.

Now, when I get off the plane and meet my family, I embrace the long car rides and the conversations that come with them. The lighthearted chats and the deep, emotional ones where our perspectives clash and blend into something new. I no longer shy away from these hard conversations. Instead, I welcome them, knowing that they are the key to understanding and growth. Through these interactions, I have learned that investing time in others is worth every moment. It shapes us, strengthens our bonds, and enriches our lives in ways that instant gratification never could.

Not every kid can say their mom swapped her professional attire for a superhero cape. But that’s my mom—an electrical engineer who traded a promising telecom career for a messy kitchen and daily homework battles.

Growing up, I marveled at the contrast between my mom’s upbringing in India and my own, split between India and the U.S. While I thrived with information at my fingertips, my mom grew up in Indore, a small town where computers were a luxury and quality education was limited. Yet she pushed through these challenges, navigating a male-dominated field, earning her degree, and establishing herself as an engineer. Before stepping away from her career, she determined network coverage in telecom and taught engineering students—roles that demonstrated her ability to break barriers and share her knowledge.

As the aroma of cardamom and cloves filled the kitchen, I realized my mom’s sacrifices went far beyond her career; they had quietly shaped the person I was becoming. My mom’s decision to leave her career wasn’t just about staying home with us—it showed me that success is measured by the impact we make. I’ve spent my life learning how to live by that lesson. Watching her blend our Indian culture with the modern world of coding and problem-solving, I’ve developed my own path—teaching myself to code, tutoring others, and pursuing challenges that allow me to embody her resilience and compassion.

Inspired by my mom’s resilience, I decided to take on a new challenge—teaching myself how to code. I started with Java and Python, but what I initially thought would be a straightforward journey turned into hours of debugging and frustration as I explored data structures and Object Oriented programming. Like my mom, I learned that pushing through these obstacles is where the real growth happens. Each time I solve a bug or finish a programming project, I’m reminded that success isn’t about ease—it’s about staying with the process, no matter how tough.

Inspired by her selflessness, I decided to extend my learning beyond myself by helping others through tutoring. One of my most rewarding experiences was teaching middle schoolers to code. I worked with a student struggling with conditional statements, and seeing their face light up when they finally ‘got it’ reminded me of the power of patience and support. Through these moments, I’ve learned that leadership isn’t just about what you know—it’s about helping others grow and finding joy in their success.

Resilience became a constant theme when I faced a particularly challenging AP Physics unit last year. I spent countless late nights trying to solve complex problems, often feeling overwhelmed. Frustration set in, but I pushed through, drawing on her determination and not stopping until I mastered everything from Gauss’s Law to capacitor equations. That experience reminded me that success comes from persistence, and it has fueled my desire to face even bigger challenges in the future.

Through coding, tutoring, and overcoming challenges, I’ve embraced the resilience, compassion, and creativity my mom showed me. I’ve learned that success isn’t measured by achievements but by the lives we touch. As I move forward, I’m committed to using my skills to uplift others—whether solving problems through code or mentoring future students. My mom’s example has set the foundation for who I am and who I strive to be. Every time I catch the scent of paneer curry from our kitchen, I’m reminded of her strength, her lessons, and the path she’s helped me carve for myself.

My mom truly is a superhero—not for the career she gave up, but for the love, strength, and unwavering support she provides our family. Her resilience drives me to push through challenges, knowing that true strength lies in helping others grow. As I continue my journey, whether through coding or running, or mentoring, her invaluable lessons will remain at the core of who I am and who I strive to become.

“You should never play that bad with a swing that good.” My coach's words stung, but I had been thinking the same thing and knew what he said was true. I had just shot an 86 at the Optimist Qualifier Tournament, on a course I carded a 72 the week before. Frustrated at my tournament play, I began losing interest in practice and competitions. I needed to find a way to improve and redevelop my confidence in my golf game.

For years I had used a “brute force” algorithm to develop my swing. I bunkered down, going through every possible swing thought and pattern. I wore a hole in my hitting mat, eroded the grips on my clubs, and deeply calloused my hands. On course, I approached problems like writing code. I accounted for every variable - wind, slope, lie - but still, I was failing to unlock my potential when it mattered most. I needed another way to improve.

Determined to develop better on-course strategies, I turned to the study of golf course architecture. I spent hours reading The Anatomy of a Golf Course by Tom Doak, watching videos from the Fried Egg, and studying renowned courses. Fascinated and inspired, I set off to design holes of my own. I scribbled at the end of tests, in my free time, and in my mind’s eye. I experimented with the rolling greens of MacKenzie, the strategic designs of Dye, and the minimalism of Maxwell. However, my sampling of different design philosophies turned the courses I drew into Frankenstein’s Monsters: sets of mismatched golf holes without the soul of a great course. Similarly, while I now understood the architectural concepts, I could not fit them into my game when I was on the course.

I went back to the drawing board, now approaching my designs as a jazz saxophonist. Gone were the designs built with logic gates and if-else statements. Instead, I composed runs that had the laid-back feel of “You’re A Weaver Of Dreams” by Cannonball Adderly or the frantic cadence of “Giant Steps” by John Coltrane, holes that flowed from tee to green. When arranging a 9-hole course to surround the range where I work, I let the land guide me like I was improvising over a II-V-I chord progression. Becoming looser with my game allowed me to adjust when necessary, and implement strategies that flowed naturally rather than following a rigid plan.

By melding my scientific and creative interests, I began to see each hole from the architect’s perspective. I saw the purpose of each carefully placed bunker and how each break in the green affected the entire hole’s strategy. With this new perspective, I started making better decisions, playing smarter golf, and ending more rounds on a high note. I combined the tools I had already developed - rote learning and analytical thinking - with artistry to finally put together tournament rounds in line with my ability.

My new multifaceted approach gave me the insight to tackle problems with creative, on-the-fly solutions. I splattered paint across the Science NHS banner? No worries, we’ll just splatter more and give the sign a little extra pop. A talented freshman is disappointed he didn’t get the solo? Let’s rewrite it so we can each play part of it. These experiences helped me realize that there is one underlying reason I love golf, STEM, and jazz: all provide opportunities for improvisation, whether I’m shaping a shot around a tree, ripping through a lick in the middle of a solo, or making a model car out of bottle caps and pencils. However, my improvisational skills are synergistically stronger when I utilize facets from all of my interests.

Knowing I can use lessons from my varied interests has given me the confidence to take a swing at anything. So whether I undertake a new research project or join an unfamiliar club, I’m prepared to dive into college head-first.

*How do I keep myself useful when I’m not medically trained?*

With only a few patients that morning, I quickly finished wiping down every dermatology exam room. "Six hours to kill," I thought. Grabbing a pamphlet about skin cancer, I wandered the halls, looking for a quiet room to do some light reading.

In the hallway, I bumped into E.J., the clinic tech, juggling a stack of glove boxes. Stuffing the pamphlet in my pocket, I gathered the precarious containers and helped restock patient rooms. A few minutes later, I stumbled upon Nurse Stephanie stapling a box of patient appointment sheets. Following her gestures to the space beside her, I grabbed a stapler, matching her pace. After we finished, I saw Dr. Soong behind me, sorting info pamphlets. Wordlessly, I stepped over and started stacking them into tidy piles.

For the rest of my volunteering term, I began recognizing the countless unseen tasks that keep the clinic’s rhythm alive. Quietly, I’d slip in to finish those jobs without prompting. And now, guiding our newest volunteer Param, I zero in on those simple tasks that lighten the mental load.

***

*How do I weave my piano into Erin’s violin and Igrainne’s cello?*

As a soloist, the metronome’s mechanical march had always served me well. But now, sitting next to two other musicians, my trusty metronome failed me. In each run, the melody stumbled, timing fractured. I was too early, Igrainne’s offbeat, and Erin’s violin barely kept up. Silence hung heavily after each failure.

Remembering my weeks with the All-State Orchestra, I composed another solution. Instead of metronomes, non-verbal cues orchestrated our string section’s success. Sometimes, the solo violinist raised an eyebrow; other times, the violist lightly breathed towards the conductor. Soon, the orchestra sounded like one.

Next to Erin and Igrainne, I flourished an invisible baton, playing mini maestro for our trio. Lifting my hands above the keys, my chin shot towards Erin who mirrored the nod to Igrainne.

Through countless rehearsals, we learned to breathe as one, like the voices of a well-tuned choir. On performance day, our trust carried our trio’s instincts, sharing a heartbeat which pulsed beneath each note.

***

*How do you teach a 6-year-old about craters without boring a 16-year-old?*

The script under the demo cart said: “Define an asteroid,” followed by a monologue of scientific jargon. Clearly, the script wasn’t prepared for Lisa and Raymond. Lisa toyed with the Earth’s surface, represented by a bucket of tan industrial sand while her teen brother Raymond stared blankly. Both were deeply uninterested.

As awkwardness loomed, I tossed the script. “Let’s all make fists,” I proposed. Clenching my hand, I softly hit the sand, forming a small indent. “Your turn!” Lisa and Raymond enthusiastically pummeled their fists down, forging their own craters.

Despite having the smallest hands, Lisa carved the biggest pit. Gently, I explained the relationship between impact and speed to Lisa as we changed up how fast we hit the sand. Then, I referred to Newton’s laws with Raymond, describing the relationship between force and impact. Soon, we were experimenting with different objects and speeds, each crater representing a unique moment of discovery.

~~~

Classrooms are all around us—at a dermatology clinic, between three chairs in a music room, and even in a bucket of sand. It exists in the shared experiences of the unseen, unspoken, and unscripted.

At the clinic, I found value in the mundane. In the practice room, we learned to trust our non-verbal cues: tossing back heads or breathing before downbeats. And between the grains of industrial sand, Lisa and Raymond dug their own craters, making each impact a new realization.

Though my college ID will read “Undergraduate,” I’ll be both a student and a teacher. Whether in the small chores, the silent rhythms, or the sparks of curiosity, I’ll learn from every moment and leave my mark through shared breakthroughs.

Sometimes boredom sparks brilliant inventions. Modern ideas like ironing board mirrors, pizza scissors, or the football chair all started with just a quirky idea! My proudest creation was also born out of boredom. When COVID hit, being stuck at home, I began to write a story for my YouTube channel. I wanted to convey my story visually, through video games. Inspired by popular games such as Minecraft and Rainbow Six Siege, I put my ideas into action. That goal set me down a path that influences me to this day.

An avid history nerd, I had read about Alan Turing and felt inspired by him as he created the world’s first rudimentary computer from scratch. I thought, if he could bring his dream to life, I could do the same—bring my story to life through a game. I researched and found the best free basic video game engine, “Unity,” to use. I had no formal coding education; however, I had four very important resources to help me on my mission: YouTube, Udemy, my determination, and a lot of snacks. After many late nights of watching videos and scouring the internet, I took the dive.

It was frustrating at first because I had no one to ask for help. “There must be help I could get online. No way am I the first coder!” I combed the internet and found an interactive “Unity” chat group on Discord, dedicated to newcomers learning to code. I felt empowered, picked the brains of developers, and gained useful insight and inspiration for coding my simple game.

Sunday morning was my favorite day of the week—family get-togethers, eating and chatting over delicious steaming dim sum. “What’s the latest with you, [Name]?” asked grandpa. “I am coding my first video game!” That sparked an unexpected conversation. My aunt, a child speech therapist, often remarked that constant engagement with video games can worsen speech delays in children with developmental issues. That’s when the light bulb turned on. What if I repurposed my basic game to help them enjoy their therapy sessions and improve their speech delays? “What a fantastic idea! Can you do that for me?” I had never seen my aunt so excited. We spent the day discussing the challenges her patients faced. Armed with that knowledge, I repurposed my game immediately.

The premise of the game is simple: a child navigates a small capsule, avoiding spinning obstacles and running into walls to find a blue box. Each time the box is found, they move to the next level. There were multiple levels to keep the child engaged, each progressively more challenging with faster-spinning obstacles. The goal was to enhance the child’s hand-eye coordination and condition the brain through repetitive action. My aunt explained that the right video games enhance motor functions and help with speech patterns. I did not fully understand the science behind that, but if non-overstimulating video games help, that would be a win! She loved the design—simple but challenging—and suggested features: an option for an aerial view, a pad to stand on, and avoiding sounds to prevent confusion. The game was complete. She guides them through saying things like “see, red spinners” or “the green wall,” helping kids remember what they see and repeat words. An idea to a tool! The game is now also used by her friend, another speech therapist.

Whether working on my video game or writing skills, I realized my abilities can be useful for positive change. Just like Alan Turing did eighty years ago, I believe that in the right hands, the technology at our disposal can be used for good.

We worked in unison: Cut stalks. Gather bunches. Feed bunches into a grinder. Sieve debris from rice grains. Weigh harvested rice. Collect samples of rice grains for moisture content. Repeat. Following this system produced more than rice grains; it sparked a synergy that drove our entire team as we toiled in the heart of a Javanese rice paddy. After three hours, the team of 17 felt like family. Despite our differences — military soldiers, government officials, professors, and even me, a high school student — we were united by a shared goal: discovering why Indonesia struggles to produce enough rice, its staple diet, to feed the world’s fourth largest population of 250 million people.

I found myself on this team due to my interest in solving global food challenges. After experimenting with Eco-Enzymes, a multipurpose liquid derived from organic waste that could enhance photosynthesis, I felt a spark of hope as it gave me the opportunity to be a part of the growing movement toward green practices in food systems. Armed with a determination to understand the root of this issue, I sought out the opportunity to research with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI).

After multiple days of calling and no one answering, I drove to the office to meet Dr. Herta, IRRI’s liaison scientist, who was due to leave in two days to conduct field research, collecting data for Layanan Konsultasi Padi, a web platform which aims to help farmers manage their fertilizer use more economically and sustainably. She invited me to join her on a lengthy overnight research trip and despite being the only team member without a high school diploma, I formed powerful bonds huddled over maps during briefings, bumping along dirt roads to the paddies, or knee-deep in grains under the blazing sun.

The farmers and I collided at the crossroads of tradition and modernity. Their deep-rooted faith in maximizing fertilizer usage clashed with my science-backed perspective. In our conversations, I offered them a glimpse into my generation’s approach: precision hydroponics and tailored nutrient plans, instead of the old “more is more” mentality.

As I worked with the local farmers and my research delegation, I learned to see the rice fields that stretched endlessly to the horizon, a vast, open-air laboratory beyond the confines of my classroom. The tiny granules, that I grind the rice into taught me a lesson in biology: the extrapolation of data revealing the effect of nitrogen and phosphorus on plant growth. Experiencing the toil of working in the field – the grittiness of soil on my hands, and the weight of carrying harvests – made me realize that community is the very foundation of a successful food system. To thrive, food requires the rich amalgamation of ideas, the reconciliation of tradition and modernity, and the collective efforts shared by a united goal.

Stepping out of the rice fields and back into the classroom, I carry the farmer’s lessons into my work as a scientist. My trip to the fields motivated me to further enhance my Eco-Enzyme research, a symbol of the reconciliation between passion for the environment and pushing for innovation. Learning from the struggles for the farmers, I replicated the stress conditions that caused farmers’ yields to decrease, allowing me to find an impactful discovery on how Eco-Enzymes can maintain an accelerated rate of growth in plants, even under these challenging conditions.

I flourish in finding ways to integrate as much diversity in the ideas I present, finding harmony between seemingly contradictory values. As a scientist, environmentalist, and altruist, I combine innovation, environmental consciousness, and heritage to become a catalyst in propelling our food systems on a path of progress.

**Break-Through**

“Halt!” 15 to 7, I lost again. It’s the 9th event of the season, and each scoreboard seems to agree that my score can’t pass 10. My skin crawls at the feeling of my sweaty fencing gear, which felt protective at first but became clumsy and restrictive; my glove severing the connection to my blade. Worse, I broke one of my two blades. Despite my careful protection, buying bright yellow sheaths, half my weapons were gone.

As I walked off the strip, I picked up the broken blade and could see wires running down the broken piece. I enjoy making small gadgets, from 3D printed toothbrush holders to remodeling unicycles, but I had never yet dared to work on my valued weapon. Borrowing a screwdriver, I unscrew two sesame-seed-sized tip screws, which bounce onto the desk with the button tip. I peer into the barrel and let two nested springs fall into my hand. I played with different configurations: the smaller spring contacts wires to complete a circuit, signaling a touch; the larger spring acts as a pressure threshold. Immersed, I even forgot to watch the final.

Since I broke my blade, I started understanding the timing, angle, and distance of a touch with the context of its inner mechanics, and set up attacks with confidence. I broke through on the 10th event, and was nationally ranked in two months.

***

My alarm rings at 3:00 am in June. I had a call with Eric, an expert from Artinis Medical in Europe. I was disappointed, getting the same answers after 10+ conversations like this: in brain monitoring, we have to trade-off between temporal and spatial resolutions, and useful resolutions can only be achieved in a lab/clinic setting.

Are there any other possibilities? Are we researching brain monitoring and hoping someday to use it at home? The entire summer before my sophomore year, I dove into research papers, designing 6 versions of helmet housing, testing electrodes allocation, and running 50+ ablation tests. Eventually, I blazed my own path utilizing multimodalities and creating a cross-informed algorithm, moving one step closer towards democratizing routine brain-wellness monitoring.

***

It’s 8:30 am on a summer morning at Hillview library. I’m there to co-host a summer camp for underserved middle schoolers. By 8:35, my phone pings: Ketan has COVID, and Alice is heading to a family emergency. Making matters worse, the projector doesn’t work. Thirty-odd pairs of expectant eyes are on me now, I feel I am losing control of the classroom, and my confidence begins to crumble.

Our 3-person team regrouped virtually. How can I engage students with only one teacher and no prepared slides? Drawing experience from our own collaboration, we pivot from one-person lectures to collaborative activities. Ketan and Alice become remote support, messaging me activity plans as I moderate the discussion. Students design marketing strategies, mock negotiations, and brainstorm for profit margin improvement. Ideas fly, and students discuss fervently. During a revenue plateau discussion, I encourage a shy student to share. He points out how leveraging algorithms for advertisement could enlarge the pie.
