Campers start discussing his concept as our whiteboard brainstorm grows like a detective’s corkboard. By noon, several thought leaders emerged from our classroom. As I recap with my team at lunch, we all laughed: “It is not a bad thing to lose control”.

As I’ve grown up, each unfolding year has revealed a different part of me that is still scared of breaking a weapon, confined by well-accepted experts' opinions, or holding on to the typical leader role. With each deconstruction, persistent trial and error, and lecture-turned-interaction, my perception of restrictions breaks, and I break through. I started to fence with purpose (even beating a 2024 USA Olympian in a bout!), exploring science frontiers along less-traveled roads (filing a patent for my project), and leading with the goal of empowering others (stepping back from the spotlight).

My road to fulfillment starts here. Personal growth and community contribution are two key commitments that I have grown to live by and seek. Allow me to paint you a picture of who I am and the future I envision for myself through the inspiring influences in my life.

Growing up, my parents’ relentless pursuit of their goals and perseverance in the face of challenges deeply influenced me. My father began his career as an army engineer. He then resigned to follow his entrepreneurial dream, where he managed to build a successful construction business in Egypt. Similarly, after a 15-year corporate career in multinationals, my mother decided to establish her own coaching firm to pursue her passion for supporting individuals and teams to maximize their potential. Watching them reinvent themselves taught me the value of ambition, personal growth, resilience, and the rewards of chasing dreams. My uncle’s educational journey in the U.S. also inspires me. Leaving Egypt at 17, he earned his undergraduate and postgraduate degrees from prestigious U.S. universities, eventually becoming one of the youngest partners at a top private equity firm in New York. The growth mindset I witnessed in my family drives me to explore new challenges and to persevere to reach personal fulfilment.

Personally, I have developed a strong passion for technology. I thrive on troubleshooting, investigating patterns, and figuring out how things work. Since the age of eight, I have always been the go-to person, at home or school, for computer or phone-related technical support. I enjoy looking at matters from different perspectives and finding new ways to do things. For instance, during my final math project last year, I discovered a technologically efficient way to animate images in Desmos through experimentation. I later shared this method with my classmates, and my teacher was impressed by how effective it was. I found this incredibly rewarding. I am now seeking an education in the US, where resources in technology and innovation are unmatched to further develop my skills and ability to think creatively and to collaborate with like-minded peers to find solutions to big problems.

On a social level, I like to build genuine relationships that cross boundaries. My mother’s humanistic worldview has deeply influenced me. Through her life experiences, which include living and studying in the U.K. and the U.S. for years, she taught me to accept others without judgment, to be compassionate, and to always make others feel valued regardless of their differences. My positive outlook on life helps uplift myself and others in the face of adversity, pushing us towards a better tomorrow. In group projects at school, I learned to recognize others’ talents, capitalize on team diversity, and ensure we collaborate to get the best outcome. In the coming years, I look forward to widening my social network, getting exposed to different cultures, and growing through interactions with the university’s diverse student body.

Born and raised in Cairo, I learned the value of community contribution early in life. My grandparents displayed this through decades of work in public service. My grandfather was a surgeon who was dedicated to treating the poor in public hospitals, and my grandmother built an extensive career working with special needs children. At an early age, I felt the need to donate large sums of my savings to the poor in our community. In 2023, I interned at the Mersal Charity Foundation, where I learned about fundraising and nonprofit management. I trust that my university degree will equip me with the knowledge and resources that allow me to make a meaningful impact on underprivileged communities in Egypt and beyond.

With these goals in mind, I am determined to give education my all, as it is the most critical stepping stone towards everything I want to achieve in life: becoming the best version of myself to reach my highest potential and making a lasting impact on the community.

It was the 3rd Monday of July. My 2-week summer vacation was over, and we were all exchanging goodbyes. As I entered the airport van, the humid summer air clinging to my skin, I bent down as my grandma whispered in my ear, “Remember to take care of yourself. Everything is going to work out in the end. I believe in you.”

Why did I, a 14-year-old boy, have to sacrifice so much for my dad? Why did I have to move to a foreign country? Wasn’t it supposed to be the other way around? Shouldn’t he be the one giving up his dreams for mine? Words caught in my throat as I hugged her, my mind racing with all the things I wanted to say but couldn't.

Despite countless explanations from my parents, I never truly understood why we had to move to Portugal. My frustration festered, and I directed all my spite toward my father. I constantly complained, convinced that his selfish decision had destroyed my future. And it genuinely felt that way. Everything felt lost.

One night, on the car ride home from a nearby restaurant, my parents began to argue. The sudden noise jolted me awake, but I pretended to be asleep, squeezing my eyes shut. Their voices escalated, filling the small space of the car with tension so thick I could almost feel it pressing down on me. My mother’s voice, usually calm and soothing, was now sharp, slicing through the air with frustration. “You promised me things would be different here,” she said, her voice cracking. “It’s still the same—if not worse.”

My father spoke in a guarded, somewhat desperate tone. “I’m doing this for all of us, not just for myself! This move was supposed to be a fresh start.”

That night, I was awake processing what I'd heard. My parents, who I had assumed were fine, were carrying their own burdens. As the oldest child, I should have been helping them, supporting them in this difficult time, but instead, I had only added to their troubles. A wave of guilt and embarrassment washed over me as I recognized how immature I had been.

Desperate to make amends, I researched, "How to make parents happy?" I spent weeks cutting, chopping, and burning vegetables while my parents were at work. I wanted to surprise them with a meal that would melt away the tension. When I showed them my first edible meal, my dad's eye became glossy, and my mom's shoulders rolled back into her seat.

"Thank you."

I found peace in simple tasks such as washing the dishes, helping my brother with homework, running to get groceries, and taking out the garbage. I wanted to ease my family's burden in any way and doing small, insignificant tasks seemed to be the only way I could help. The work was tedious, but my family's look of weary gratitude filled me with pride.

My efforts were finally working, and our unusually quiet dinners had finally returned to normal, with my parents sharing stories of what they learned from new Portuguese locals they met and my brother eagerly chiming in with tales from his school day. Everyone seemed to be slowly adjusting, becoming more and more accustomed to life here.

I realized that my brief actions of supporting my family were what my dad had been doing for my entire life. I was too caught up in bolstering my ego, neglecting my family. I’ve always been ambitious for success, but I've been sacrificing this ambition for my personal values. As I enter college, I’ve become wary of what true success is. I’ve realized I need to improve myself, not only with selfish ambition but with the ones closest to me.

Brightly flashing on the screen, I saw my name and was pulled back to third grade—creating my first Roblox account, FaceTiming friends, and playing our favorite games. It was my first hackathon, and despite my passion for programming, a paralyzing fear that I didn’t belong lingered. Unfamiliar technical jargon permeated the air as seasoned teams discussed APIs to make their projects compatible with VR headsets they'd won previously. Yet there I was, at the podium, accepting the Best Execution Award at AstroHacks.

With junior year over and a hackathon win under my belt, I returned to my summer job at the Academy of Technology, Art, and Music (ATAM), where I bring my love for coding to middle school students. One student aspired to recreate a bandit attack from One Piece, his favorite anime game. Guiding him through the mathematical dot product to calculate collisions, a technique I used in my own horror game inspired by The Backrooms, I remembered the impostor syndrome I faced at my first hackathon. Frustrated by bugs from missed capitalizations in LuaU, Roblox's language, he shoved his keyboard aside, saying he’d rather play games than make them. When it finally worked, his face lit up as he showed his friends. Seeing his transformation, I became determined to make learning accessible and turn the intimidating process of coding into something collaborative, creative, and fun.

I realized the best way to inspire excitement for programming was by creating a collaborative hackathon centered around teamwork and community—right in my hometown. Determined to address the isolation I felt at my first hackathon, I designed an event inspired by ATAM's wacky science days, where we’d blast music and dive into fun, collaborative projects like 3D printing our own model rockets. I wanted participants working together on engaging challenges, sparking innovation beyond solo competition.

Initially, I underestimated the complexity: venues were expensive and hard to find. After months of calling, I secured a local church, but the cost exhausted my resources. At a crossroads—proceeding with limited means or delaying to gather funds—I felt a wave of disappointment. I reached out to Hack Club, a nonprofit network of like-minded hackers, and realized I had the support of the hacking community, renewing my determination.

A Hack Club advisor suggested postponing the hackathon to ensure success rather than risk compromising due to limited resources. Not willing to give up, I've worked with my school's booster club to raise $500 in funds, registered the project as a non-profit with the Hack Club, and reached out to Hack Club-affiliated companies to secure merchandise and prizes for the event.

Reflecting on the joy of collaboration, I’ve learned that programming is more than just writing code; it’s a tool for building community. Whether guiding students at ATAM or organizing a hackathon, I’m committed to creating spaces where anyone can collaborate without impostor syndrome. Looking ahead, I’m excited to organize more hackathons, fostering inclusive spaces that turn isolation into collaboration, where creativity thrives and ideas take flight.

My heart was palpitating as I nervously glanced at the school gate and then back at my textbook. As the clock struck five, the lights went out, and the room was pitch black. Under the cover of darkness, I entered the stuffy classroom to secretly teach 21st century skills to twenty-seven girls from my neighborhood, aged 13 to 17. My eyes stayed glued to the gate, shivering with fear that the Taliban, who banned education for all girls, might catch us. For the last year and a half, I’ve lived in fear, knowing I could be tortured and lose my educational opportunities if discovered.

While I worried about the girls’ future, my parents feared for my safety. I felt guilty because it was my first time standing against their wishes, advocating for the girls’ right to education. Remembering the times we sang songs, played games, and held movie shows motivated me to organize hands-on lessons despite my parents’ objections. For example, during a lesson on Treasure Hunt, when the girls seemed tired, I arranged a Treasure Hunt Game. They acted as treasure hunters, bringing the lesson to life. During vacations, I also hosted United World College Scholarship editing sessions, checking grammar and offering comments. Six girls were shortlisted for interviews.

My father always said, “Education is the key to success and personal growth.” He taught me that if I wanted to improve life for myself and others, I must prioritize education. Knowing that my female peers were denied this right and often pushed into marriage, I continued working in risky ways, even starting lessons before 5:00 PM to allow extra time. We communicated via WhatsApp and Telegram, but half could not afford the internet. I spent a third of my salary, $60, on their internet for two months. In-person schooling was impossible, and online education was inaccessible, so I approached school principals in Dashte Barchi for help. When they couldn’t assist, my friend Abigail and I started a GoFundMe, reaching out on LinkedIn and Facebook. Although I feared exposure, we raised $1,362 to cover the girls’ monthly internet fees.

With the internet covered, girls like Maryam and Zinab could catch up with online courses. Seeing these changes, I felt immense happiness. Yes, the fear of Taliban exposure initially consumed me, but now it pushes me to be strong and continue this educational quest. Recalling the joyous tears of the girls after graduating from an English course with me inspires me to continue, possibly helping more than another 27 girls who are deprived of education. I no longer let fear define my future.

I strive to ensure that education is a right for all Afghans and for everyone, regardless of age, gender, or race. In college, I will continue to strengthen this belief. Neither reality nor danger prevents me from doing what I believe is right. After seeing all twenty-seven girls navigate constant obstacles, I am proud of us.

I have two names: [Name] and عبد الملك. They’re pronounced almost the same, but they represent two distinct worlds—one belonging to a black sheep in Texas, the other to a foreigner in Saudi Arabia. Growing up as the only Saudi Arabian student in a Texas school of 400, I couldn't hide my differences—my name, my accent, my skin color. Even in Saudi Arabia, the place I thought was home, I was met with the same sense of isolation, marked by my Texan mannerisms and American accent. I was caught between two worlds and cultures. As a result, I often asked myself: Who am I?

One of my earliest memories is the first day of first grade. The teacher read out the names of all the new students—“Sarah, Michael, Aaron.” Then she paused, squinting at the paper in front of her. “Abduu–Abdoolmaleek,” she stammered, sounding unsure. I sunk into my chair, reluctantly raising my hand. I looked around the classroom, filled with bright pictures and colorful furniture, and couldn’t help but notice the other kids staring at me. My face grew warm, my palms grew sweaty, and I shrank even further, waiting for their curious eyes to move elsewhere.

Over time, though, I slowly acclimated. Instead of eating my lunch alone, I found myself sharing it with friends, explaining to them what a samboosa was. What had once been a source of anxiety became a way to socialize. My differences became conversation starters—be it my name or food. I realized that being different didn’t have to mean feeling isolated; instead, it could be a way to connect with others.

When I moved back to Saudi Arabia, I thought I’d finally be home—a place where my name was familiar, where my accent wouldn’t turn heads. I imagined seamlessly reconnecting with my culture and finally feeling like I belonged. But reality hit hard at the first family gathering. Determined to fit in, I proudly decided to wear a shemagh, the traditional Saudi scarf worn on the head. I wrapped it confidently, convinced I had nailed it.

As I walked into the bustling room, the air thick with the aroma of Arabic coffee and the sound of laughter, I felt a brief sense of relief. For a moment, I thought I had finally blended in—until my uncle’s booming laughter broke through the noise.

“You’re wearing it backwards!” he exclaimed, pointing at my shemagh. I froze as all eyes turned toward me. My stomach dropped, and heat rushed to my face. I awkwardly tried to fix it, but it was too late. The atmosphere had shifted, giving me the same eerie feeling I once felt in Texas.

But this time, I was prepared. My time in Texas had made me more resilient and adaptable. It taught me that being different didn’t have to be a disadvantage; it could be an asset. Instead of retreating in embarrassment, I laughed along with my family. I began telling stories of Texas and the cultural differences I’d experienced. Just as I had done in Texas, I embraced my uniqueness and found myself, once again, bridging two worlds.

Rather than choosing between them, I embraced both. I am both [Name] and عبد الملك, a blend of two worlds, which has shaped me into who I am today—someone who thrives on experiencing different cultures and ideas. In addition, it has allowed me to excel academically by allowing me to represent my school as head of the student council and providing me the resolve to pursue new opportunities like being accepted into Saudi Aramco’s College Preparatory and Scholarship program.

As I look ahead, I carry the best of both worlds. Now, I can say with pride: I am the Saudi with the heart of a Texan!

I wished I was a book. I wished I could communicate with people without speaking and people could understand me without asking. These were my thoughts growing up, when talking to strangers overflowed my mind with uneasy thoughts. It wasn’t like I never tried to face it. I signed up for a summer camp on congressional debate and attended a year-long weekly public speaking class, but these classes rarely included application-based speaking exercises. So when the time came, my nerves never failed to show up.

In one more attempt, I joined the Speech & Debate club at my school. It offered a platform that encouraged everyone to voice their opinions and speak freely, free of criticism. Yes, it was still in front of strangers, but I convinced myself that comfort begins with unfamiliarity, which starts with taking risks.

8:58 AM: I sat waiting for The Grey Matter Online Invitational - my first debate tournament - to begin. The comforts of my house - my cushy rolling chair and scenic window view - helped ease some of my anxiety as I clicked the mouse to unmute, beginning the narration of my team’s starting argument: why increased federal regulation of cryptocurrency transactions would produce more harm than benefits.

As I spoke, my brain fired away with nagging thoughts and worst-case scenarios: Was I talking too softly? Would I run out of time? Short preparation times forced me to constantly dig for the right words in my mind. The long speech time, however, had me glancing at the stopwatch every few seconds, hoping for the timer to reach zero.

“That was great, [Name],” my partner complimented me as I reached the end. I smiled, knowing this positive energy was crucial in fueling my upcoming speeches. Similarly, whenever I sensed Sumedh’s nerves, I reassured him, whether it was wishing him luck before speeches or unleashing waves of compliments afterward. Simultaneously, we built a strong foundation of trust, relying on each other to prepare speeches and take notes throughout the debate.

Sure, I ran out of time on a speech and stuttered through countless sentences in others. But it was at this moment that I realized I was capable of speaking endlessly in front of strangers. Even when the rounds did not go as planned, I found contentment in valuing what the opponents did well and absorbing the judges’ constructive critiques: risks were simply opportunities to learn.

In this way, my confidence gradually grew after each debate tournament. I was eager to immerse myself in intriguing debate topics, browsing through endless resources until I paired every argument with an indestructible counter-argument. Rather than reading off a script, I aimed to express a dynamic story that could resonate with the audience by using vocal inflections and hand gestures. My creative self was also brought out, whether it was running unique cases or developing rebuttal exercises with my partner to practice improvisation skills.

What resonated with me the most in debate, however, was guiding others to navigate similar hurdles I jumped through. Attending weekly middle school coaching events that my school’s Speech & Debate organized, I felt a sense of purpose, contributing to the same community that had escorted me out of my comfort zone. Besides walking through methods I used to communicate speeches effectively, I also planned activities for students to implement these skills through mini-debate tournaments and speech improvisation challenges. But it was the gratitude and smiles from the students that motivated me to keep coaching.

Debate has taught me not to fear speaking up, but to look forward to it. The impacts have extended beyond debate: You can see me directing players on the soccer pitch or leading club meetings in my school’s classrooms. Most importantly, I’m no longer afraid to take risks. Sure, I may still get nervous before giving speeches in the soccer huddle or introducing the Science Olympiad club to a packed room. But when I start speaking, the anxiety vanishes as I understand that risks are merely paths to new chapters.

My parents are Indian, yet I was born Vietnamese. As a result of being raised in an Indian household in a suburb in Ho Chi Minh City, I was left estranged from my roots. I could never claim to be Indian nor Vietnamese and so began the pursuit of my “real” identity.

“Một, Hai, Ba, Dzô!” echoed before beer glasses clinked. Familiar with this tradition, 9-year-old me still smiled in awe. By this time, I was fluent in Vietnamese thanks to the hundreds of hours I’d spent with Dad’s friends.

Especially Uncle Hai. He became my translator. He taught me how to distinguish dừa (coconut) from đưa (give) – the difference lying in the slight shift of tongue. He entertained my endless questions, however silly, about why the sky was blue, why the food was kept in the middle of the table for everyone to share and God’s existence. My favorite answer was to why everyone was drinking. He would always say, ‘Ary oi, look at the smiles. Hear the laughter. It’s about being together, not drinking.’ I was always overcome with warmth in those moments. I finally felt at home. A feeling I continued to crave as I grew older. While business brought about these gatherings, it was true friends that my Dad always walked away with. And over time, I found a friend in each one of them too. What enamored me was the ability for these initially manufactured bonds to blossom into real friendships that endured through thick and thin.

For most of my childhood, I assumed I was Vietnamese, but my passport jarringly said otherwise. Worse, my friend Khang would always taunt me, ‘You’ve never spent any time in India, how can you call yourself Indian?’ My mom, barely seeing any similarities between mine and her childhood, began spending her evenings with me flipping through Hindi textbooks she used for my sister. Ever since, I’d find myself tinkering in my room with sticky notes haphazardly stuck across my walls after school. Each representing new values learned from watching Pramod Bhatija or from reading Unacademy’s Indian traditions. I even went on stakeouts at Diwali and Independence Day parties (without binoculars of course), observing what, from the outside, made one more Indian.

Through this, I grouped being Indian into four main categories: food, clothes, greetings, and language. Clothes were a search away: a kurta pajama worked best. I refused to give up pesto gnocchi and struggled with Hindi. As for the greetings, Mom gave me the lay of the land: gently placing my hands together, instructing me to say ‘Namaste’ before touching a person's feet. “It’s how you show respect to your elders,” she explained.

Yet, I still felt confined to a mold not fit for me. I wanted out.

Discouraged, I confided in my Nani. She taught me an essential life skill: making chai. As she demonstrated the creation of the foam, pouring the hot mixture from pot to pot, she said, “Beta, it’s not about the tea, your clothes or your broken Hindi. It’s your warmth and how you make those around you feel.” It was then that I realized I didn’t need to conform to one culture. My identity wasn’t defined by my possessions, lack of language, or even affinity for pasta. It was the values I rooted myself in - the kindness, respect, and an openness to explore where I came from.

Flying back home, I reflected on Nani’s words. I realized my fixation on what I lacked only left me out of place. I made a promise - to embrace my differences, as a product of two cultures, and to accept others as they are too. Just like Nani and Uncle Hai did. And in that acceptance, I found it. I found belonging within myself, and a place for me in this melting pot of a world - and I hope to offer the same to others.

At 12 years old, my proudest moment was destroying my family’s business.

Or at least, that’s what I imagined. How dare they take away my Roblox privileges, I thought. My solution: to siphon customers and bankrupt Wing Yum Chinese Restaurant. While a shy kid, my younger mind was only filled with ambition. Claiming territory at an empty table, [Name]’s Store was born. I rummaged through my backpack, finding various pencils to sell, one of which was my dearly, beloved blueberry Smencil; On a folded notecard, I charged customers 50 more cents. But the most prized item of all was a shiny remote-control helicopter, though it lacked a controller. I boldly priced it at $12.99, a trick I had learned from my parents' menu. In a few hours, however, I was shut down by my own rival, my dad.

Going into freshman year, I worked at the same restaurant I once competed with. Carrying the same reckless attitude, I struggled to find patience on slower days. As I sat on a wooden stool, waiting for customers to enter, I could not help but imagine all the time wasted I could have used to complete SBC objectives on Fifa or edit Fortnite montages with friends. Envious of my friends who were able to stay at home, I desperately hoped for a way out.

Despite my lack of interest, I kept going to work each day, slowly progressing my kitchen knowledge. With each responsibility- peeling strings off snow peas, deveining shrimp, and chopping baby bella mushrooms- I began to develop an appreciation for my parent’s business. Handing out small containers of duck sauce, I met a retired England coach in which we debated about a replacement for Erik Ten Hag. While chopping carrots, a biker in a Harley-Davidson jacket noticed and taught me “middle-finger front, index and ring fingers back”. What I thought as futile work ultimately affected society as a whole, being able to provide food while also developing meaningful relationships with customers. 
Craving to serve more customers, I imagined myself in my dad’s worn Nike Metcons, flipping chicken, broccoli and lo mein effortlessly. "You want to cook lo mein, [Name]?” My dad laughs. “Show me you can fry rice first, then we will talk about lo mein”. 
Glancing at the tickets tucked on the kitchen countertop, beef fried rice and wonton soup caught my attention. Throwing in the beef too fast, hot oil snapped onto the back of my hand, making me flinch, but I pushed through. Pouring the wonton soup next, a splash hit my arm, the heat stinging instantly. My grip loosened from the burn of the metal dipper. As my palm instinctively lets go, I am left with numb, painful fingertips. Yet, as I packed up the order and handed it to the customer, throwing in a couple extra fortune cookies, his smile outweighed the temporary sting. “Thank you boss!” He waved at me as he exited the restaurant. As the night winds down, I take off my apron, stained with grease and soy sauce, and hang it on the hook by the kitchen door. I glance over at my mom and dad, veterans of countless Friday night rushes, their faces calm but tired. I could not help but crack a little smile.

Today, I engage in new responsibilities at the restaurant, eager yet patient to help grow the business. As I meticulously navigate the walk-in refrigerator, I take note that egg rolls and scallops need to be restocked, applying basic principles of supply and demand. When my dad taught me the proper way to hold a chinese cleaver, pinching the steel with my thumb, pointer and middle finger, I introduced him to GrubHub and DoorDash, increasing our sales steadily. Leveraging the negotiation skills developed from buying Abercrombie crewnecks on Depop, I whittled down prices on deli containers and oyster pails with different suppliers.

As the motors whirred over pounding rain, I let out a silent prayer. In the dim light of my basement, Exo—a brain-controlled exoskeleton designed to help stroke survivors regain hand movement—clenched into a fist. It was Exo’s first spark of life. Months later, Exo's joints contracted again, this time in Delaware, where we were pitching it at the Diamond Challenge.

I FaceTimed my dad to share Exo's progress. "Okay, remind me...what does it do?" he asked. I dove into Exo's ability to interpret brain signals, translating intent into motion for rehabilitation. Before I could finish, he interrupted, "What's the real point?" I paused, surprised—wasn't it obvious?

"Never mind," I sighed, "Text me when you land." I hung up frustrated, knowing my dad, the resident skeptic, could never just nod his head.

I pushed his misgivings aside and returned to reciting our pitch for the umpteenth time, moonlight spilling through the hotel curtains. But with each pitch, instead of feeling reassured, something gnawed at me: Why hadn’t my dad understood it? Hoping for fresh insight, I grabbed my notes and headed into the hall.

Soon enough, I was running around the hotel, begging any unlucky hotel staff for a few minutes of their time. Eventually, I stumbled upon the hotel concierge, who happened to have studied human biology. After going through our pitch, his reaction confirmed my growing fear. He nodded along blankly, impressed, but not comprehending Exo’s significance. Not only did my dad not understand Exo, but a biology graduate didn’t either. Maybe my dad wasn't just being skeptical.

With only hours before the morning ceremony, I knew we had to make a change. In my excitement over Exo's technical marvels, I’d lost sight of what mattered most—the people it could help. I thought back to my conversation with my dad; our brain-controlled exoskeleton had to connect with people like him. They needed to understand Exo’s real purpose. I wanted my dad, the concierge, and every listener to picture that profound moment when a stroke patient slowly clenches their fist again.

Invigorated, I rushed back to our hotel room. Drawing on my debate experience, I knew we needed more than facts—we needed a story that would resonate. By sunrise, surrounded by empty coffee cups, I’d transformed the pitch. Instead of technical specs, we opened with a question: What would it feel like to move your hand for the first time in years? From there, we shared stories of lives Exo could change, even creating visuals mapping a patient’s journey from helplessness to hope. Our pitch now presented more than a device; it painted a vision of what Exo could mean for someone desperate to regain control.

Walking into the room of judges, I felt certain this pitch would leave no doubts. By the time we walked onto the stage to collect first place, it was clear they felt the same. But to me, the accolade wasn’t as important as seeing my dad nod, comprehension etched onto his face, as we wrapped up our pitch.

As the caffeine rush faded, I reflected on the risk we'd taken in pivoting away from technical details—it taught me that true persuasion lies in making people feel a story and connecting with them. Since the Diamond Challenge, this lesson has shaped how I communicate. When my little brother struggles with his science homework, I find myself transforming abstract concepts into stories he can visualize—turning electrons into race cars zooming around a track, their energy levels like different lanes. His eyes light up with the same understanding I saw in my dad's.

Whether I'm tackling global challenges or sharing my latest idea on FaceTime with my Dad, I'll carry forward this power to connect, turning innovation into stories that ignite understanding and bring ideas to life.

*Just put it in The Box.* I stared at the “For Sale” sign outside of my home, minimizing my childhood to merchandise. The Box was not real, but it might as well have been. It was where I harbored everything I did not want to feel—fear, confusion, failure. I built The Box in third grade when I overheard my parents discussing moving cities; a minuscule shift that felt enormous to me. I stored the confusing emotions in neatly sealed mental compartments, labeled "For Later."

The Box offered easy solutions to everything. A bad grade? Into The Box. A missed opportunity? Sealed away. It worked for me, but how do you compartmentalize someone else’s struggles?

“Do you ever just feel like giving up?" My best friend confided in me one night in sixth grade, sharing how overwhelmed she felt after failing a math test. The Box could contain my emotions, but I could feel the plastic beginning to bend, unable to hold hers. Instead of turning away, I listened, offered to study with her, and made sure she didn’t feel alone. Maybe The Box did have its limitations.

The catalyst for truly questioning The Box’s power came as COVID restrictions relaxed. Eager to support more people like my best friend, I found YouthLine; a teen crisis helpline. Typically, I would have labeled this “Too Intense” and stashed it away. Instead, I kept their pamphlet, not forgetting their mission—an uncharacteristic move for me. Four months and two interviews later, I spent my fifteenth birthday learning crisis intervention at YouthLine. Holding onto that brochure marked the first crack in The Box's bending walls.

At YouthLine, I guided peers through struggles I once buried within my mental walls. With each call, a realization settled in—growth comes from the very confrontation I had avoided. That understanding was tested one night with a familiar ring, triggering a practiced composure: "Hey! This is Avni with YouthLine. What's your name?" After a long silence, a trembling voice responded: "I'm holding a knife." For three hours, I guided the caller through their pain until we found a fragile thread of hope: a love for poetry, a dream to become an author. With this hope, I persuaded her to put the knife away.

After the call ended, a puzzling sentence lingered: "I called four other lines before you." Who did she call? Why didn't they help? How many don’t make it to a fifth call? Instinctively, I wanted to label these as "Unsolvable" and lock them away—but I stubbornly kept the lid of The Box sealed.

I was left to solve what felt “impossible”: the gaps in mental health resources, the fact that someone had to try four times before finding help. Motivated to foster change, I joined the campaign of Congresswoman Andrea Salinas, a fierce advocate for mental health reform; someone who wanted to ensure that it only takes one call. My work on her campaign—canvassing and engaging with voters—wasn’t about politics; it was personal. Every conversation became a chance to advocate for better mental health support, and to dismantle the walls of The Box.

There were days when endless canvassing amounted to nothing more than a sequence of polite, superficial exchanges. The old me might have labeled this "Too Difficult" and retreated, but today, The Box no longer offered refuge. Accepting the status quo was not an option.

I now understand that The Box was no sanctuary, but a prison. It kept me from pain, but also from growth. YouthLine taught me that progress begins with facing our fears. The calls, the silences—they taught me that avoiding discomfort only deepens its roots. Through my work with Congresswoman Salinas, I have learned that impactful change is accomplished through firm directness. The Box has diminished to a shadow of its former self, and I have moved beyond its confines, addressing discomfort and embracing challenges.

**Student's Essay:**

Joseph—clad in matching Paw Patrol shoes and a shirt—picked up the abandoned controller, placed the robot on a table, and began experimenting.

THUD.

“Ahhh!” he exclaimed. “I hurted it! It's injewred,” he said, cradling the dented frame in his small hands.

“It's okay,” I said, gently straightening the bent metal. “See? All better!” Joseph wiped his nose with his sleeve as his gaze softened. In his hands, the robot wasn’t just metal and wires. It was alive. To him, its ultrasonic sensors were eyes, the bent metal frame was an injury, and its beeps expressions of emotion. Among all the kids at Haven House (a child development center where I was interning), only Joseph showed any interest in the robot. Perhaps, if I viewed the robot with Joseph’s imagination, I could inspire the others to see beyond its bolts and screws, showing them science isn’t intimidating—it’s alive and full of magic.

Channeling my childhood obsession with American Ninja warrior, I transformed Haven House classroom carpet into a treacherous terrain for the robot to conquer: bridges made from stacked books, winding paths outlined by crayons, and towering obstacles built from wooden blocks. Now, the kids marveled, itching for a chance to wield the controller. Moving to the child-sized lunch tables, I explained how circuitry controlled the robot, which they had named “Sparky” after Dariella’s dog (for their similar clumsiness). Capitalizing on their intrigue, I showed them how to use Snap Circuits to make simple contraptions out of colorful components that snap together. Soon, whirring helicopters spun to life from small plastic discs and red LEDs turned into rushing ambulances; the circuit boards became playgrounds for their imagination.

Inspired by my time at the Haven House, I organized a robotics camp for middle schoolers. After months of planning and training volunteers, the first day finally arrived; the kids filled in, sitting on worn stools atop the polished concrete floor of my school's workshop.

A student named Alex stood apart from the buzzing group, buried in his sketchbook, hoodie up and earbuds in. "Those are some impressive drawings," I remarked. "Thanks," he mumbled. "What if we bring one of your characters to life using robotics?" His eyes widened, revealing a flicker of excitement. Together, we selected one of his sketches to animate—a small, spider-like creature. We commandeered the demo robot and transformed it, forming spindly wire legs, a segmented cardboard body, and glinting foil eyes. As we worked, he shared glimpses of himself—parts that seemed tucked away, now surfacing.

After a week of building their robots, the kids were ready for the final showdown. In a series of two minute battles, they raced their robots to collect as many ping-pong balls as possible. As the robots battled on the field—a patchwork of reused 2-by-4s—I imitated the bravado of an MMA announcer: “LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, IN THE RED CORNER, WEIGHING IN AT 2.5 POUNDS OF PURE METAL.” Amidst the chaos, Alex crouched beside a struggling team. “Try angling the sensor down a bit,” he suggested. They adjusted it and the bot jerked forward, met by a wave of cheers and high-fives. No longer holding back, Alex embraced the freedom to lead, imagine, and celebrate each success with newfound confidence.

As a lifelong math nerd, I used to measure my success by numbers: test scores, competition rankings, workshop attendees. Now when I measure success, I count different things: laughing with classmates, meeting new people at robotics competitions, and watching a child’s eyes light up as their creation comes to life. I’ve realized that what truly drives me is building meaningful relationships and creating spaces where everyone—whether in a classroom, robotics camp, or beyond—feels they belong. In college, I will continue encouraging curiosity, imagination, and problem-solving as a way to connect with others, where technology becomes a bridge rather than a barrier, and where every 'injewred' robot is an opportunity to create connection.

The school bell rings, and I quickly stuff my math worksheet into my backpack. I need to get home before my house turns into chaos. Just a few weeks ago, my life flipped upside down. My dad’s job was falling apart, and so was he.

Every day, I came home to the sound of shouting, banging on the walls. It was unbearable. All I wanted was to finish my math problems. I didn’t know then what was upsetting him, all I knew was I had to stop him from breaking the walls and distracting me from my homework.

So, I became the mediator, therapist, and parent. I put on a smile, greeted him kindly, and reminded him of what was good in life. I reassured him there was a brighter future ahead. After an hour or two of comforting words, I’d collapse in my room, staring at my math problems. But before I could focus, it was my mom’s turn to vent.

I understood she was the one being yelled at. It must’ve been exhausting, but I couldn’t help thinking, did she not realize I had work to do too?

“No, Mom, Dad didn’t mean what he said,” I’d repeat, using what I learned from behavior research online. “He’s just upset and needs an outlet.”

But my mom wasn’t as well-versed in psychology as I was. So, once again, I’d put on my nice face, encourage her to go to her room, and finally, after separating them both, I’d dive into my homework.

I loved math, but I couldn’t make sense of the way my teacher explained it. My parents, being immigrants who spoke little English, couldn’t help either. I bet they didn’t even know what PEMDAS meant. So, I relied on my best friend: the internet. Unlike my classmates who might look up answers, I refused to cheat. Instead, I searched for explanations, watched lectures, and solved problems myself. There are things you just have to figure out alone.

By the time I finished, the sun had long disappeared. But my night wasn’t over. I still needed to research ways to help my dad. I didn’t know how much longer I could keep doing this without breaking down myself. So, I dove into studying his symptoms—depression, anger management, childhood trauma. My thirst for understanding kept me up late into the night, often until 2 a.m., my mind full of new knowledge.

My sleepless nights introduced me to the captivating world of human interactions: sociology. What began as a quest to understand my dad evolved into an obsession with understanding people—why they act the way they do, how society shapes them, and how trauma and mental health play a role in shaping lives. The more I learned, the more I realized how interconnected we all are.

Years later, and things are stable now. My dad’s job recovered, and the shouting has stopped. We don’t talk about those tough times anymore. But my curiosity about sociology never faded. What began as a desperate attempt to save my family led me down a path of discovery that I hope never ends.

My mind raced like the intricate motions of a butterfly knife. Each thought flipped open, sliced into another, rolled over edges, lingering for a moment, before snapping shut, eager to spin again. As I poised myself for a new trick, I paused on the knife’s edge — I just discovered a new fundamental law of the universe. Well, not one that wins Nobel Prizes or even applies to most people, but one that defines me: I am always moving.

Whether it’s my hands fidgeting with scraps of paper or thoughts racing down winding trails, this need for motion—the blend of hands and mind always busy—has been a constant. I used to resent it though. It meant distracted thought-spirals during a critical test, teachers telling me to “sit properly,” and friends half-joking that I was “somewhere on the spectrum.”

But one day, I saw a butterfly knife in a video game, and it was mesmerizing. The precise, rhythmic motion was the kind of movement I wanted to learn — an expression of control in chaos. I began learning not just butterfly knives, but many other hobbies that allowed me to move my hands: penspinning, flipping a coin on my fingers, cardistry, and begleri, a Greek skill toy of two beads on the ends of a string. These small hobbies brought balance back to the equation, splitting the constant between my hands and mind.

While searching for a new balisong trick, a video labeled “852 HZ” caught my eye. Intrigued, I clicked play, and within minutes, the internal monologue that had been running inside my head for years died. And while I’d often wished for that silence, now that it had arrived, I panicked. My movement no longer summed to the constant. My universal law was broken. I craved that familiar rhythm, realizing in that moment how much this law was a part of me.

The need to move my hands brought balisongs, belgeri, and all my other random hobbies I adore, and the constant thought fueled my curiosity of topics, from keyboards to particle physics. I created my own unique keyboard PCB, diving into Ergogen and KiCad, spending countless nights on YouTube tutorials. My early attempts were clunky, circuits as useful as cardboard with holes punched for switches. Yet, I persevered, with my thought driven curiosity stronger than the sting of failure (or maybe that was my hands getting zapped yet again). My constancy was my ultimate companion, pushing my curiosity to its bounds. Accepting failure as the path to growth, it eventually led to success: completing my unique split Steno PCB!

My “law” also shapes my social world, driving friends a little crazy with random interjections that lead us into labyrinths of thought. 'You guys ever think about quarks?' I blurted out randomly during a group study session. Textbooks forgotten, we spent the afternoon Googling Cherenkov radiation and making sense of equations about pion decay. Our Google Docs were as messy as the particle showers from collisions in the Large Hadron Collider, wrapping our minds around subatomic chaos. Seeing how all my friends loved this experience, I decided that these core memories were more valuable than a moment of anxiety over social norms. I stopped caring which side of the equation I would reside on, and accepted this law with all of the downsides, as it would drive me to new places. In fact, I now actively look for ways to use my universal law to make connections and memories with others. From introducing them to balisongs or random conversations about AI evolution, I hope to continue my constancy with all the new people I can meet at college.

So now, when I see three pens on my friends desk, and am curious of what their clicks feel and sound like, I don't hesitate to check. And when they laugh at my randomness, I laugh along with them, knowing the randomness was unapologetically me.

“Jason, *please* pay attention!” Exasperated, I stared expectantly at the restless first-grader. He swiveled toward me mid-pencil playfight, pouting defiantly.

Suddenly, he flung his finger at the open page. “Ewww, they kiss!”

“The picture is showing how much Mama Bear loves her baby,” I replied, straining to contain my irritation. “Doesn’t your mom kiss you goodnight?” Jason shook his head vehemently. I exhaled skeptically. “Come on, Jason.”

Jason’s brows furrowed and fists clenched, his face a brewing storm. Beside him, his best friend peered at me nervously. “He doesn’t have a mom.”

I blinked, frozen, as Jason furiously shoved the traitor. What had I done? Guilt crashed through the silence.

“I’m sorry, Jason. Can I give you a hug?”

Jason hesitated, eyeing me with guarded anticipation. Then he nodded. Although his arms wrapped tentatively around me, I felt a stab of regret at how obliviously I’d slipped into assumptions about his behavior.

As a high school freshman volunteering at an elementary school, I was still a student in more ways than one. In my readiness to chalk up students’ unruliness to apathy, I’d become ignorant of the nuances of their behaviors. In my own elementary years, I’d proudly identified as a puzzle fanatic – in fact, I got glasses in first grade from poring over scattered pieces and brainteaser collections for hours on end (and my dad’s near-sighted genes certainly didn’t help). But in my haste to fit together bits of information, I’d overlooked how incomplete they were: Jason’s fitfulness wasn’t merely to seek attention, and his blurted answers weren’t merely to disregard classroom rules. I began to recognize that understanding wasn’t a matter of simply putting together objective facts and drawing logical, rational conclusions.

Mid-sophomore year, my usual lunchtime snack offers were suddenly met with unfamiliar outbursts of impatience from my closest friend Gigi. The edge in her voice was unsettling, but when she asked to eat lunch in the guidance office, I walked there with her, stashing coconut cracker packets and lychee jellies in my locker in case there might be a day when she would want them again.

The weeks of uncertainty and silence dragged. Finally, Gigi accepted a package of cookies from me and smiled. She’d been grappling with grief over her dad’s terminal illness, she confessed, adding, “Thank you for being here for me, even when I was too worried to tell you.”

Still, I couldn’t help feeling relieved to be able to tie Gigi’s moments of abnormality to a tangible explanation, a clear external influence. But when I started a new year of volunteering at the elementary school, I lost touch with the reasoned, unambiguous answers that I’d uncovered about Jason and Gigi, and that had always been achievable in my riddles. When a half-folded paper box fluttered from Paola’s fingers as she clawed at her swollen eyes, I was helplessly unaware of the source of her tantrum despite my best efforts to decipher her mumbled syllables with my meticulously-studied textbook Spanish. Instead, I let her cling to my hand as we went out to recess and challenged her, “Race me to the fence!” As we collapsed on the asphalt, giddy and giggling, I said, “Remind me to teach you how to make an origami butterfly next time.”

Her tear-stained cheeks beamed. “¿Me lo prometes?” (You promise?)

Now, as I graduate, I’ve made a promise to myself: to accept that there will always be a missing piece in the picture others present to me, and to strive to understand others through both empathy and humility. Jason, Gigi, and Paola weren’t problems I could fix or puzzles I could solve. They were stories I had to learn to listen to. Because when I hear the laughter of six-year-olds who squirm in their seats, I discover the true meaning of compassion.

Grabbing another handful of popcorn, my eyes were glued to the TV as I watched Dom Toretto’s crew save the day with their heroics, risking their lives to retrieve a microprocessor chip from a dangerous mercenary group. To me, Fast & Furious 6 is more than an action-packed thriller. It’s an example of people using their talents not for personal gain, but for the greater purpose of helping people. The chip demonstrates how technology can be destructive if we don't ensure that it is used correctly. The crew conveyed to me that it is our responsibility to ensure that technology is used safely. The movie taught me that significance comes from something deeper than wealth or fame--from using our talents to make a positive impact.

Watching this movie as a young child, my exposure to the impacts of technology did not mean much to me back then. But as I grew older, I started to gain more exposure to the technology field through my father and his work as a cybersecurity engineer. While my initial interest in the technology field was sparked by the movie, I was able to expand on that through the work of my father.

I started taking computer science classes in high school as a way to build my knowledge. I built my coding skills and gained a solid foundation in computer fundamentals, but my biggest leap into the field came through my internship. Here, I went through a variety of different fields in tech ranging from networks to cybersecurity to software development. While these topics did interest me, none of them quite resonated with me.

That was until I was introduced to artificial intelligence. Initially, it seemed like an interesting concept, but not feasible to work on. However, as I dove deeper into AI, I realized that it is already all around us. My aunt being targeted by a scam call exposed me to AI’s misuse. She received a call from someone claiming to be our local police department urging her to send money. She was aware that this was likely a scam call until the scammers impersonated someone from her community by talking to her in her native language. The scammers were able to leverage language processing AI to make their scam more believable. This incident gave me first-hand experience on malicious AI use.

This encounter inspired me to gain a better understanding of how we can prevent AI from being used in harmful ways. Preventing AI from becoming misused intrigued me, compelling me to investigate how it can be regulated to ensure that it is used safely and responsibly. My research and internship enabled me to understand the technicalities of AI as well as its ethical implications. As my grasp on AI expanded, so did my views on my future--where I have a role in shaping the direction of AI, promoting its ethical use and steering its development.

This is where I found my sense of significance: being able to positively impact lives across the world by harnessing the potential of AI. Working on AI isn’t just a career path, but a way for me to take my core values of fairness and innovation and apply them to my life. In Fast & Furious 6, the crew had a sense of significance because they were able to prevent the chip from being used to wreak havoc on the world. In a similar way, I have uncovered my true purpose in channeling AI to build a better future. Through the ethical innovation of AI, it will be my mission to advance the responsible and impactful use of AI. I aspire to take advantage of AI by leveraging it to tackle challenges that impact society in order to promote innovation in the field and empower my community.

I felt like I was being set up for my own embarrassing highlight film. “Guess who got the 500?!” My friend rushed into the swim locker room, staring at me. He had to be joking. But there it was, my name scribbled on the 500-lineup. I’m a sprinter, but distance swimming isn’t my strength. To make matters worse, we were facing our biggest rivals. Coach must have made a mistake!

An inescapable knot of anxiety mounted inside me as race day loomed. Would I be lapped? Or worse, collapse from exhaustion before completing 20 laps? When race day came, I made my peace: I’ll try my hardest, even if it meant risking embarrassment and failing catastrophically.

Race day. I dove into the frigid water. My arms stiffened with each lap and my lungs craved oxygen. I swam and swam, with a mounting sense of doubt. When I felt depleted, my teammates’ cheers erupted, cueing my sprint to the finish. Lunging to stop the clock, everything faded: the pain, the four swimmers trailing me, and the realization that I hit my fastest 500 – nothing mattered except that I had gone beyond what I thought was possible.

Finishing the 500 didn’t make me a distance swimmer, but it motivated me to step beyond my comfort zone, something I’ve since taken outside of the pool. On a whim, I decided to compete in a coding competition as a first-time coder. As the hours passed, I struggled to program my game-play asset, even as others launched code at unimaginable speeds. I pushed past my doubts and remembered those moments in the pool. When my asset was used in the final program, I wanted to stretch myself even more: today, I’m the Business Liaison, working with two other students to host our own hackathon.

I’ve spent the past 2 months cold-calling venue and sponsor leads, facing possible rejection with each call. From fielding questions about our turnout to our financial viability, I felt discouraged after our third rejection call. Remembering the resilience I learned in the pool, I persisted. Calls later, I negotiated a well-priced lease for an all-day space near my school, as well as two sponsorships to start us off. Last year’s coder couldn’t have imagined organizing a hackathon. This year’s coder is determined.

The mentality of diving head-first into new challenges has really changed me. Now, in other areas of my life – whether I’m tutoring my math student or teaching a new swimmer how to navigate the pounding ocean waves – I never let any of my students give up due to self-doubt. Instead, I push them to take a chance, just like I push myself.

This season at swim practice, I heard those familiar words again: “Guess who got the 500?!” This time, it wasn’t aimed at me. A younger teammate anxiously rushed in. It was his turn to swim the 500. I offered reassuring words: “I know it’s stressful, but break it up in your mind. And as long as you try, you got this.” Words I could share, knowing I did it too.

In my next chapter, I’ll continue to embrace my discomfort and try all the new things I can. Maybe I’ll try field hockey or a study-abroad program in Korea. Maybe I’ll intern at an investment bank or study big data or AI for business, even if they feel out of my current skill set. For me, there is only one path forward – to dive right in, no matter the depth.

The scent of fabric dye and cardboard lingered as I stood behind the counter, counting coins and watching customers come and go. While my classmates were playing soccer or tag, I helped my mother keep our small business afloat. Although I did not fully understand my mother’s words, “This is the hard labor you'll face if you don’t study,” stuck with me. They knew better than anyone else the true importance of education as they barely even completed high school. Flash forward to 8th grade, I was finally set “free”. We finally had enough money to hire an employee to cover for me. I could start pursuing things I had wanted to do my whole life, or so I thought.

The next day, I outlined everything I wanted to do. After hours of dreaming about the endless possibilities, I looked back at the list.

It was completely EMPTY.

What do I even want to pursue in life?

What even are my true passions?

I tirelessly researched sports, academic interests, and recreating hobbies around me, but nothing clicked—not that there were many options available to begin with. I lived on a remote island in Portugal, stranded from where all the “fun stuff” was. I blamed the island for limiting my growth.

In 9th grade, my parents sent me to study in the United States. Where else would it be better to set me “free” than the land of freedom itself?

Was I finally unchained from all the restraints of my home?

A blunt answer would be NO.

I crashed into a new environment, sleeping under the roof of people I barely knew. Even 6-year-old children spoke English better than I did.

Boundless opportunities I once could only dream of surrounded me, calling out to me, yet I froze.

Covid-19 forced me to return home.

I was defeated and lost once again.

I started reflecting on my time in the United States, dwelling on all the regrets I had left behind. I could not shake the feeling that I had let fear hold me back. That is when I stumbled upon the book that encapsulated everything I felt and brought me clarity that I was lacking—“The Midnight Library” by Maith Haig. The mysterious library is filled with stories of the what-ifs that tormented the leading character—Nora Seed. Like her, I was haunted by the cycle of regret, constantly contemplating all the paths I could have taken instead.

As I lived vicariously through Nora Seed’s life, I slowly began to understand that freedom was not just about escaping the island or responsibilities from home. Ultimate freedom comes from within. It was all about the strength to face adversity, learn from successes and failures, and prevail. Instead of lingering for the perfect opportunity to come by, I started creating them myself.

I formed the Asian Culture Club. Even though we initially had a small number of members, it was still so fulfilling to reconnect to this mystifying culture and introduce it to more people. It was something to be proud of and has fueled me to go the extra mile. I took graphic design courses to develop appealing posters to promote events and fundraisers.

I began helping younger students in my community with academics and exploring their passions. These kids overflowed with desire and dreams that ignited my blaze to push even harder. After each session, I felt so accomplished. I was becoming the person they needed, just as I was becoming the person I needed as a kid.

My main goal was to make an impact on my community.

It was apparent then that it was not the environment restricting me but my fear of taking the first step. This time, I am ready to return to the United States to tackle all the challenges fearlessly and prove myself with this new mindset and contribute meaningfully to my future community.

“That was a trumpet of disdain… Sorry, you dour imp!” My sister, who was about to reprimand me for farting, rolled her eyes at my wordplay instead. She was used to her rambunctious little brother, an elementary school student who viewed communication as a game of Tetris. With English as my mother tongue, I aimed to get the highest score by deploying complex words and verbose turns of phrase in rapid-fire succession. Later, I began to embellish my attempt at sparkling wordplay with philosophical and political wit, forming a (self-described) potent mixture of zaniness and dry humor.

But if I felt like Superman in English, I was meek Clark Kent when conversing in Korean. I’d grown up in Hong Kong before moving to Korea at age six, attending international schools and using English at home all my life. When I tried to speak Korean, my luminescent ideas went dim in translation, leaving me in a Vantablack abyss. Worse still, my struggles seemed to embarrass or annoy Korean taxi drivers or store clerks—why does a Korean in Korea not speak the language? I was a strange creature in two stages of life at once: a soaring butterfly in English, but a weak, immobile pupa in Korean. I reacted by compensating for my inferiority in one language by hyper-focusing on the other. What did I need Korean for anyway?

My maternal grandma, however, had unlimited patience for my halting Korean. As she cooked in her cramped kitchen, she plied me with tasty morsels and told stories—in Korean—about how she’d learned to cook from her mother. She persisted even when I struggled to understand, and her passion and affection allowed me to grasp the culture and history behind what I was eating.

“Shinheng-ah, songpyeon… Sweet. Hot, care the mouth,” she said one day in splintered English, handing me rice cakes. My heart swelled. She’d somehow brushed up on words she might have learned 40-some years ago in school just to communicate with me. My pompous “master of words” mentality should have been bothered by her awkward pronunciation and turn of phrase, the way I was embarrassed by my own Korean. But it no longer mattered. I was touched by her effort and dearly wanted to understand her.

Grandma’s kitchen became a fun laboratory then—a setting for experiments in imperfect Korean or English that created a conversation while we prepared food together. I learned to infer words by reading her tone and facial expressions. We often burst into laughter at our mutual clumsiness, but both knew we earnestly wanted and tried to understand each other.

I realized then that words become meaningful not because of our linguistic prowess, but rather our will to cross a divide. The pupa evolved; I proudly embraced my own country and its language, growing more confident, free, and inspired to learn what I’d previously rejected.

This realization has made me a resilient, investigative student with a passion for debating, which in turn has provided me with skills to understand and embrace various perspectives and adroitly navigate social and political discourse. It’s even helped me find unexpected validity in positions I would once set aside as nonsense. In one debate competition, I almost exclaimed to the rebutting opponent, “You’re right!” I’m proud of my ability to seek out understanding amid conflict or division.

Thanks to my grandma, my Vantablack abyss morphed into a joyful lab of learning, simply through a genuine will to understand what I’d once deride as “incomprehensible” or “not my thing.” My Korean identity was restored to me, and I gained the confidence to venture forth on new quests. I still enjoy impacting my community (and my long-suffering sister) with witticisms and wordplay. But I know my most valuable tool is my mindset and drive for inquisitive exploration, both undaunted and even made stronger by any initial lack of understanding.

I have a twin—54 years my senior. Sharing the same birthday, May 20, we were bound by more than blood; it was fate, driving through life together in a “car” we built side by side. It’s my father. Known for his love of nicknames, he called my sister Zulya “Pulya” (Bullet) and Botagoz “Botan,” while I affectionately dubbed him “Twather.”

Each journey with Twather held memories that taught me more than words could. When our car broke down, he showed me how to fix an engine running on fumes, turning problem into a victory. When the sun blinded us, he turned a mesh shirt into a sunshade. Despite our age difference, we were like twins, learning from each other. I still laugh at the time he insisted we were watching a recorded Golovkin fight, only to realize it was live. With him, it always felt like our journey was just beginning.

But on January 12th at 13:35, our journey took an unexpected turn. I received a message from my cousin: "May his soul rest in peace." My calls to my sisters went unanswered, and when I finally got through, my sister told me to pack my things. Walking through the snow, my tears fell like crumbling flakes. Twather, my co-pilot, was gone, leaving me to take the wheel alone.

The “car” we had built over 15 years, filled with love and memories, seemed to collapse, parts scattered like fragments of my heart. As everything scattered, it felt like my journey was shrouded in fog and dust. I was haunted by not speaking to him one last time. In my grief, I searched for anything that could bridge the distance and found a letter I’d written to him in 2022. In it, I apologized for my immaturity and promised to take responsibility for the family. The final words—“I love you, Dad”—brought me both tears, comfort. That letter became my navigator, guiding me as I began to rebuild.

I wrote another letter, now filled with gratitude, recounting memories like the time he accidentally gave me vodka instead of water. I left it at his grave, feeling certain he’d read it. As I walked away, I smiled, knowing he was with me. That smile became the foundation of my “car.”

Still steering through the fog, I met my mentor, Askhat Abzhanov, at “Zhana Urpak” camp. His words, "After many miles, even the most vibrant car paint starts to fade under layers of dust," reminded me that it was my turn to wipe away those layers and make my car shine brighter. I realized my engine was fueled by helping others. Returning to “Zhana Urpak” not as a mentee but a mentor, I met a 16-year-old named Zhanel who felt disconnected from her father. Through brief conversations, I helped her find value in their relationship. On the last day, I saw her crying on the phone, talking to her dad. In helping her, I found pieces of my car.

Thinking I could rebuild alone, I soon learned the importance of community. I joined a volunteer project to clean up Astana’s ecosystem. One day, an older man praised our work, saying, “Thank you for caring for this city. I’ve watched you coming back here day after day. Even when no one else was watching, you didn’t give up. It’s rare to see such commitment—you’re a true hero.” His words reminded me of my father, inspiring me to keep going. I felt my father watching over me, his love coming through in my actions.

The community’s support became the wheels of my journey, wiping away fog and dust on the way. What began as a bond with my father has grown into a broader mission. TW, which once stood for “Twather,” now represents “Together We.” Everything I’ve experienced has shaped who I am, and I know TW will keep driving the journey forward, creating a lasting impact on the community.

Flayed skin. Ruptured inside. Over-ripe flesh. CPR could not save the dying cherry tomatoes! Left on the shelves to rot…they were undesirable. Some like their tomatoes in sauce, others in salad, but nobody likes them bruised.

As a volunteer at Hartford Hospital’s Food4Health program, I am dedicated to nourishing those who need it the most: geriatric patients, diabetics, and the malnourished. Why should they lose out on cherry tomatoes filled with Vitamin A, C, iron, and chock-full of potassium?

The problem with our cherry tomatoes was shipping time. While the firm onions or the tightly packed jalapenos could endure the ride from the farms in big cardboard boxes, the delicate cherry tomatoes, constantly bouncing around, succumbed to near-fatal injuries by the time they arrived.

As we wasted hundreds of decimated tomatoes each week, I felt a pang of guilt in my stomach. I knew I needed to do something to bring the plethora of tomato nutrients to our patients. An idea crept into my thoughts when I saw PVC pipes, buckets, and seeds all in the same dirty closet.

I had found the spot for my makeshift garden. The rooftop promised me the highest yield of tomatoes. I started poking thick holes in the walls of the plastic pipes and nestled small cups containing a plotted tomato seed snuggly inside. After two weeks of diligent care, there were only dying seedlings. The soil’s dry texture had suffocated the poor seedlings, silently killing the plant’s root size and water intake. At this time I remembered the words of my ninth-grade science teacher Ms. Highland, who plotted pea plants with us in plastic bags to prove soil is not necessary, just proper nutrition, formally dubbed hydroponics.

I scoured the internet for a solution, aiming to understand which specific minerals and nutrients nourished tomatoes the most. I watched podcasts from Garden Talk with Mr. Grow It, YouTube videos from The Millennial Gardener, and random gardening videos suitable for my grandma's Facebook feed. After much research, I found the ingredients to make Food4Health proud of our cherry tomatoes again. Epsom salt and calcium for nutrients, limestone to balance the pH, and manure for its high NO₂ concentration. Sourcing the ingredients from the greenhouse, I placed the thick combined paste in each small cup and desperately hoped. The results showed themselves in two months when I bore the fruits of my labor (yes, tomatoes are fruit!) and tasted my sweet victory.

Sitting in the cold, misty office with a basket of my love, I offered them to anyone who dared walk through the doors. Bombarded with my pleading, all accepted, placing the plump fruit in their mouths while their eyes lightened up joyfully. I would urge them to take as many as they wanted while filling their cart with farm-fresh eggs, whole-fat milk, lean ground meat, and anything their hearts desired.

Trying my own treasures, I was delighted at the sharp umami flavor. A single tear rolled down my cheek, but I knew it was more about the satisfaction I brought to our patients than my own.

As the tomato harvesting continued, I searched for new ways to give back. I began tutoring underserved in Chicago and met Amira, a 7-year-old Pakistani immigrant living with her single mom on the south side of Chicago. It was profound to watch Amira bloom from failing to spell becuz to completing the Magic Tree House series. Her laughs after spelling a new word or finishing a book reminded me of the pleasant warmth I felt watching the patients eat ripe cherry tomatoes.

Entering a new season brings new seeds I hope to plant. I want to create community gardens on campus to build and nourish the student community through food and nutrition. I often think back to my garden of cherry tomatoes to remember the start of my unquenchable thirst to give.

It’s 9 p.m. on Tuesday. Baking will take four hours, but I proceed anyway. With practiced efficiency, I grab the eggs, flour, sugar, honey, oil, salt, and yeast, ready to make midnight challah.

With the ingredients out, I wait for the yeast to bubble before beginning to mix everything together. I first baked challah with my Bubbe, and ever since then I’ve sought to make the perfect loaf. I take each loaf as a learning opportunity to improve the next one. I learn everything I can about the bread, from watching videos such as BenGingi’s on Youtube, to testing out whether olive or canola oil was better, to observing how each tiny change affected the final product. Because of this, my recipe has gotten better and better each time. I love this aspect of challah – learning what works and what doesn’t, while also being able to be creative and create something from scratch each time. But it isn’t just in baking challah where I love to learn. From researching about Napoleon’s Marshals, to engaging in dialogue through the philosophy discussion group I started with my English teacher and a few friends, I love learning new things and, most of all, sharing that with others and exchanging ideas.

After kneading, I let the dough rise, and an hour and a half later, I see that my dough has now expanded to fill nearly the entire bowl. Now comes the most complex part: braiding. This gives the loaf its final shape, determining how beautiful the loaf will be. As I divide the dough into strands and begin to fold them together, I’m reminded of the three braids of my own identity: my Jewish heritage, my Black identity, and my family having a long history of military service. Each of these three parts of my identity has taught me something.

After braiding, I proudly send a picture of the loaf to Bubbe before baking the bread. Thirty minutes later the hot air from the oven hits my face as I take my creation out of the oven. The next morning the smell of the challah is still in the air as I pack the challah as I get ready for school. Of all of the steps of baking the challah this final one is my favorite: sharing. To me, eating challah is a joyful experience that brings everyone together. I share the challah at lunch, and everyone gathers around to tear off a piece. I love seeing the excitement on people’s faces when they eat the challah, and the challah also brings together a community where we have discussions and exchange viewpoints. Whether it’s discussing philosophy or modern politics, the challah fosters a space where a diverse range of opinions can be shared. To me this is what makes sharing the bread so special.

As I leave school for the day, I start to think about what changes I can make to create an even better loaf next time. In college and beyond, I hope to continue to bake challah to share something that’s important to me, while also making people’s lives a little bit more tasty.

A tiny monkey lives in the jungle of my brain. He swings from dendrite to dendrite, darting across my mind’s gears and cogs at his whim, but he truly finds the most joy in a small control room. Like a mad scientist, he watches in awe as glowing orbs roll in, pulsing like tiny batteries, each representing a separate thought. As the monkey plugs these balls into a central socket, the room lights up and gears whir to life, converting my thoughts into actions and emotions.

There’s just one problem: he hates the dull, dimly lit orbs that power me through boring tasks; instead, he’s constantly chasing after the bright, fun ones that lead me to search for “chess-boxing” on YouTube, even when I have an assignment due the next day. Realizing the monkey’s control over my decisions, I ventured into my brain’s control room to see how he steered my choices in real-time. As an orb rolled in, vivid and alive, I leaned closer—it was a thought I’d just had in class…

******

Damage, damage, damage, damage. I continued to see the same word ten more times while reading about Autism-Spectrum-Disorder (ASD) and Attention-Deficit-Hyperactivity-Disorder (ADHD) in my psychology textbook. The glimmering orb blazed with a question: why did these conditions carry such a negative weight? Part of me wanted to file them away as mere cognitive impairments in preparation for my final exam next week. But the meddling monkey wasn’t satisfied. I could see the spark in his gaze as he lifted up the orb—he was itching to chase this thought down.

I crept further into the room, witnessing him plug in the orb, oblivious to my presence. But something odd struck me: when he plugged it in, even brighter ones started to flow in. Suddenly, I was consumed by curiosity. In the days that followed, I dived into my school library, exploring the physiology and diagnostics of these conditions. Yet, unsettling phrases like “socially disruptive” and “unempathetic” started to stand out more and more. Medical descriptions felt eerily… subjective. I glanced back at the monkey, who was now frantically plugging an exponentially growing pile of orbs. I felt myself being pulled deeper down a rabbit hole of discovery, to the point where my thoughts became intimately intertwined with my real-life experiences.

One afternoon, while volunteering at the Animal Assisted Happiness farm, I noticed a boy with ASD holding a frozen water bottle near my favorite bunny, Alfie. A twinge of worry crept in—I’d just read that kids with ASD might struggle with empathy, and here he was, close to Alfie with that ice-cold water. But then, in a spout of compassion, he gently pressed the bottle against Alfie’s fur, cooling him from the heat. My heart lifted, and I embarrassingly realized firsthand the effect of those labels I’d been studying.

Just as relief washed over me, the monkey scampered up and leaped onto a gear, running frantically like a hamster on a wheel, sending it spinning wildly. In that moment, an epiphany ignited within me: the child wasn’t expressing empathy in the typical, vocal way. His empathy was purely physical—a non-traditional, silent way of expressing compassion. Previously, I had been geared to assume that the child could only commit negative behaviors.
