But the monkey’s frantic spin jolted me out of these rigid notions, revealing that neurodivergence could lead to positive traits, just in an unorthodox way.

This realization accompanied me during a study I conducted at UCSB, where I examined a mice population that exhibited behaviors similar to those seen in ASD, such as marble-burying and excessive grooming—both labeled as “obsessive” and “harmful.” Previously, I would not have batted an eye; I once took pride in conducting research solely to achieve significant results. However, now, I felt a pull toward something greater—a desire to break free from traditional thinking.

Motivated by the child at AAH, I proposed to my professor that we examine physical forms of empathy. To my excitement, she agreed. We found that the mice displayed remarkable empathy, grooming their young with extraordinary care—a striking contrast to the negative traits past studies often fixated on!

******

As I watched the monkey take a well-deserved break from his long adventure, I realized that he might not be so bad after all. His constant chase of bright ideas led me to seek the "why" behind everything. As I head to college, I’ll balance focus with spontaneity, knowing even my wildest impulses can lead to discovery. Together, we'll challenge the belief that disorders are only negative, focusing on strengths rather than deficits in order to reveal insights overlooked by a purely negative perspective. And maybe, in return, I'll let the monkey enjoy all the NFL highlights he wants.

"Hel-loo, me na-me es Peei Heng Ni; I come-China." Little giggles ensued. "Your name is Pee?" My entire class erupted in fits of laughter. The teacher quickly stopped the students. However, my classmates' laughter stung in my heart. I was raised by my illiterate grandmother and had just emigrated from a small town in China while my mom was studying in the USA after divorce. I only knew some essentials and pleasantries, like "Hello" and "Thank you," along with the alphabet, due to my lack of English learning experience. My mom was busy with her PhD dissertation and job searching. Only my illiterate grandmother took care of me, and I had to take my grandmother to grocery stores routinely and deal with the payment at 6.

After that fateful morning in Mr. Leon's first-grade class, some students called me “Pee” instead of my name daily, and some bullies asked me for money during recess; if I forgot to bring money with me that day, they would kick me in my legs. I had to lie to my mom to ask for money and give them to the bullies. I first realized the necessity of literacy and tried to learn English by myself. So, every night, I took it upon myself to study past 8 pm with a website called ReadingEggs. With fun lessons from Sam, The Ant, ReadingEggs taught me how to pronounce sight words and how to write a sentence using games.

At the end of the semester, I received the "Most Improved" award, along with the teacher's congratulations. The improvement I was able to make in my language skills through my hard work helped me to find a voice when it came to dealing with bullies. Reporting to teachers and our principal didn't help, but I was eager to do something, anything, to elicit a change. One day after math class, I saw Drew crying after Kim mocked him for getting a D on the recent long division test. Seeing this opportunity, I told Kim to leave Drew alone, or I would snitch on her. After a short argument with Kim, I offered to help tutor him at lunch. Drew quickly became one of my first friends at school after I helped him study and improve his math skills. Drew's grade went from a D to a B, and he was so excited and hugged me after the grade was posted. After I made several friends, the unfriendly buddies stopped calling me 'Pee' and asked for money from me.

My desire to help others extended beyond the walls of my school and onto the screens of computers around the world. My friend Elvis accidentally clicked on an IP grab link on Discord, and people started threatening to dox him and cyberbullying him with his address as a threat. This inspired my friend Samuel and me to try to help those with data breaches. However, as we sent multiple emails to others, we quickly realized our method's failure, and many of our messages ended up in spam mail and went unread. After reading through online forums and Reddit, we decided to make a website called Dataleaks.us using JavaScript and PHP to educate people on what to do after their information is leaked. Dataleaks.us is programmed to send business-level emails to those whose information has been compromised. We sent over 1.6 million emails and collected over 100 million pieces of data, providing crucial support to those who have been hacked, had their identity stolen, or cyberbullied. My work preventing all types of bullies continues, with Dataleaks.us now sending over 50,000 emails daily to assist those in need.

From struggling with language in a new classroom to advocating for others and creating Dataleaks.us, my journey has been one of resilience and courage. I hope to use my code skills to start an interactive doxxing awareness education website to help victims.

Of all my possessions, blank, white paper is my most valuable. This is no understatement. For someone who can’t seem to stick to one thing, the last thing I would do is pick a favorite. But the empty canvas of paper feels especially fitting because for a long time, I had no idea what I wanted to do or who I wanted to be, evident by the dreadful silence which followed the what do you want to be?’s at my family’s monthly social get-togethers. Today, though, when someone asks me what my thing is, I can confidently tell them that it is physics. Whether it is in the school library, under the watchful eye of a “no lunch” sign, or at a football game dressed in my mandatory marching band uniform with a trusty pad and pencil, my friends will attest that I am always scribbling away at a new physics puzzle on an unmarked sheet of paper.

It’s interesting that most physicists credit the start of the universe and of time to a Big Bang because I feel as if the start of mine began with a Big Fizzle. Two of them.

See, my mother was divorced twice. And each time, my world was left empty and chaotic. Divorce turned nights of laughter, jumbled Mahjong tiles, and sharing peeled grapefruit into nights of bitter feud and heartbreak. When my sister refused to accept a stepfather, arguments escalated into broken doors and police visits, shattering our family.

The truth is, I’ve always wanted to do everything. At five, I knew I would be the future president. At the time, the artificed smile on my uncle’s face was all that I needed to confirm my suspicion. When that dream fizzled out, art took its place, and eventually little league baseball, magic tricks, competitive video games, saber fencing, and olympiad mathematics had pumped their way through my system as well. But as mom and sister argued, as my mother worked herself to exhaustion to support her two kids whilst navigating heartbreak, unable to fathom the energy to bring food to the table, I realized that my scattered interests were no less futile than a scattered family. Disgruntled at the disarray of sibling and parental conflict, I forced myself to start anew, from an untouched canvas.

But it wasn’t easy. Torn between my old passions and the fear of starting from scratch, I questioned my new path. Was I right to abandon robotics and push math aside to study physics? Would pursuing this new direction leave me behind as my peers advanced? Only after encouragement from my mother did I find my resolve. After all, she had done it herself; after immigrating to a new land, navigating the struggles of an unfaithful husband, and failing to reestablish a complete family, she still worked tirelessly for us. Who was I to back down from a setback?

As I opened my textbook to chapter one, I began to fill sheets of blank paper, problem by problem. Sheets of scribbled equations turned into stacks of manuscripts, and late nights scouring the depths of Physics Stack Exchange while my mother toiled away on the floor below me transformed physics to not just an intellectual pursuit but an act of gratitude and sacrifice as well. Eventually, I finished that textbook, cover to cover, and I had a large stack of papers to show for it.

Today, I continue my work with the hope of earning a spot on the U.S. Physics Team. Call me crazy if you will, but at the very least when asked the question: what do you want to be? I have an answer, and I am certain my mind will not blank.

The monotony of life. Fighting tooth and nail, people desperately try to force their way out of this brutal cage. However, I am the opposite. I invited this frowned-upon concept into my life with open arms in the form of a capsule, two eggs, and three Brazil nuts.

I examine the capsule in hand, taking in the smooth surface and delicate exterior. Last year, I went to get bloodwork done at my local clinic. I had no specific condition in mind to get checked; I had it done mostly out of sheer curiosity. The ecstatic feeling of seeing the results was overwhelming.

When the bloodwork results came back, my parents yelled for me to come downstairs. Hands sweaty, heart racing, I rushed downstairs. There were no abnormal findings, but I was slightly deficient in vitamin D. I wasn’t completely taken off guard by this, given the stringent circumstances in which it is obtained. Also, because it was done in winter, the test may not even have been fully accurate. It was not a big issue. However, I had this nagging feeling in the back of my mind.

I went back upstairs and fired up my computer. The clicking of the keys pierced through the silent room. Whether it was scrolling online blogs or meticulously examining research papers with little understanding, my eyes were glued, and my fingers strained. There was really no end goal, just a flood of euphoria. After exhausting the written resources, I proceeded to delve into YouTube. One simple search prompted me to scour through numerous videos. After accumulating whatever knowledge I could obtain and a blue-light-induced headache, I decided it was best for me to supplement.

Vitamin D, a fat-soluble vitamin, is best taken with dietary fat.

Consuming eggs and Brazil nuts can help fulfill this requirement. The eggs are cooked in vitamin K2-rich butter (Vitamin K2 and vitamin D work together). Occasionally, I put a little too much in the pan, causing it to splatter everywhere. This sizzling mess didn’t always happen, though.

“Why are you always so tired?” My mom exclaimed. It was a struggle for me to keep my eyes open, let alone respond. Mornings were the worst for me. Even with adequate sleep and nutritious meals, I struggled to pinpoint the cause of this fatigue. I then decided to try a dietary intervention with the help of medical professionals online, like Dr. Anthony Chaffee and Dr. Matthew Nagra, well-known advocates for carnivorous and vegan diets, respectively.

I soon learned that eating too many carbohydrates at once can raise blood sugar levels too high, which can lead to a sudden ‘crash’ in energy and an onset of fatigue.

Figuring the lower sugar content of bananas may help, I switched them out for apples, but it didn’t work. Instead of tinkering around with my current breakfast options, I decided to switch it up completely. If this worked, I was about to put a big dent in my old views of optimal diets. Growing up, fats and cholesterol were vilified. Whether it be from some article online or the insights of a family member, there weren’t two sides; therefore, there was no need to probe further. When I talked to my parents about this new meal I was going to try, they thought it was a pretty funny joke. Everything I read and heard said I would feel the opposite.

I did indeed feel the opposite. My eyes didn’t feel like they were going to close any second. The persistent yawning stopped, and the brain fog went away almost immediately. I tried this exact same meal plan for the next few days while sleeping the same amount each night to make sure it wasn’t a coincidence.

However, this didn’t stop at the end of those few days. Eventually, I fully embraced the three eggs, two Brazil nuts, and the vitamin D capsule with open arms.

“[Name]!” My teacher’s eyes narrowed in scrutiny, clearly aware of my daydreaming. “Do you have any questions?”

I stopped incessantly tapping the end of my cracked mechanical pencil on the desk. “Yeah, actually. How did they come up with the Law of Sines? And, why?”

He grumbled, stacking his notes and clearing his desk. “You don’t need to know that for the test.” I sighed, a familiar weight settling.

Thoughts of Michael, my old friend and study-buddy, resurfaced. I remembered his zeal and the inspiring ardor with which he lived, all taken from him so abruptly. Could this be part of what he felt? How heavy did the weight become?

***

The walls of the tutoring classroom offered a place of solace, allowing me to help instead of requiring help. As I assisted my students in isolating y or combining x terms, I saw Bogan fidgeting in his seat, eyes scrunched, hands cupping his cheeks. When I asked him what he was confused about, he expressed a similar concern to my own: “What’s the point of all this?”

It was like hearing myself speak. I smiled.

“Let’s take a step back,” I said, “What problem do you think someone had in order to come up with this?” A moment passed before his eyes lit up as a smile curled his mouth. We began formulating possible uses of the coordinate system and lines, from recovering lost ships to mapping military strikes.

As the year progressed, Bogan began sharing his new perspective with his classmates, imploring them to see that math exists beyond the numbers.

***

When the summer came around, I shifted my focus to All in AI. However, teaching at our yearly summer camp was intense: I had to do more than just instruct math problems; I had to teach entirely new concepts from scratch.

My lessons started out rough. Drawn-out rambling about the downsides of having too accurate of a model put half of the class of middle and high schoolers to sleep while the others feigned interest. Jargon like underfitting, overfitting, and noise rang through the library walls with no one on the receiving end. I finished diagramming the process of creating a machine learning model before sending them off to do a more engaging activity. The Google Teachable Machines they created seemed to reinvigorate everyone after suffering the dullness of my lecture.

As the camp worked towards eliminating error from their models, I was approached by Keanu, a timid, quiet rising 8th grader. He made brief eye contact with me before sheepishly looking back at the ground, fidgeting with the zipper of his gray jacket. “The stuff you said about machine learning predicting cancer was really cool. I feel like I can maybe change the world!”

A smile gripped my face. I thought back to Bogan and the successes he had in math after changing his perspective on math.

***

Nowadays, I often think about Michael. He took his own life, weighed down by the constant stress of school. “School” was the only reason he gave for committing suicide.

Being his dedicated “homework buddy,” I always wondered if I ever did enough to alleviate the pressure he endured with school. If I helped him see his math as a fascinating world of possibility rather than another assignment to complete, would he have taken his life still, or would he have faced the weight of the world with more determination? If I could have replaced academic concern with zeal, would things be different?

Unfortunately, I’ll never know. Instead, I take the lessons from Bogan and Keanu to approach learning how it should be taught. My next machine learning lecture will spark more discussion and encourage more active thought. Throughout my summer camps and into college, I hope to foster curiosity that breaks the chains of academic pressure. Everything becomes a little more exciting when you start solving for “why,” not “y.”

“Bellacist. b-e-l-l-a-c-i-s-t.” This was the word that would lead to me losing the Northern California East Bay Regional spelling bee. I was only in fifth grade, but I learned valuable lessons from that journey that I have carried into high school.

First, I immediately learned that the correct spelling of the word is “bellicist,” or one who advocates for war. The root of the word was not “bella” as in beautiful but rather “belli” as in war. In preparation for this rigorous competition, I was determined to master as many words as possible. In addition to reviewing the 1,100 language-specific words given by Scripps that I had studied in the previous year’s competition, I had printed out the 10,000 most high-yield words and spent three hours a day studying word patterns that would help me memorize. For example, the schwa sound as found in this word is one of the most common traps in the systematic memorization of word roots and language patterns.

This analytical approach to learning has propelled my learning of other algorithms such as learning how to solve the Rubik’s cube in nearly thirty seconds, but especially in my learning of mathematics. Beginning in the summer of eighth grade, I self-taught Algebra I and accelerated through Geometry, Algebra II w/ Trig, and Precalculus by the end of my freshman year. Math became my guide through challenges and has opened new doors both inside and outside the classroom. My favorite moments in math are when I have the chance to explain a new concept, such as the squeeze theorem, to my peers. This led me to be selected for a teaching assistant internship through UC Berkeley’s Academic Talent Development Program (ATDP).

Math also opened my eyes to the world of data science. I quickly fell in love with data science after taking an introductory course at ATDP where I explored how to clean data and applied text mining techniques to evaluate Yelp reviews for business entities. I dove deeper with Wharton’s Global Youth Data Science Academy summer program where I used R to create and test the accuracy of many different prediction models. For the group final project, we analyzed what factors would have the biggest protective impact on earthquake preparedness, such as fear and anxiety. Through these experiences, I see how my love for math and statistics creates opportunities for me to positively impact my community through education and data science.

Additionally, I learned that perhaps it is fitting that I missed the word “bellicist" since it is the opposite of “pacifist,” one who advocates for peace. In fourth grade, I was elected at school as a peacemaker. As the eldest of three siblings, I am often the peacemaker of the family. For example, I notice the moments between my siblings to see which one is an instigator to sneak a toe into the personal space of the other and which one is an overreactor who responds by throwing their entire body back at the other. I am also a lifeguard who needs to keep calm in possible life-threatening situations like watching over a child with a seizure disorder in the pool. And even in tennis, my coach would often delegate me to help resolve the conflicts between teammates. It is no wonder I missed the spelling of ‘bellicist’ as I reflect on my peacemaking nature.

What I think I learned the most in participating in the fifth grade spelling bee was how much I enjoy tackling challenges, solving difficult problems with persistence in an algorithmic and systematic way, as well as how to apply this skill to life’s more global challenges. Through my experiences, I am learning that making significant and impactful contributions in life is more about ambition, perseverance, and character than it is about being the smartest.

When sailors get lost at sea without navigation, they have one last resort: follow the Northern Star. Polaris, a star that leads you home, symbolizes comfort and unwavering direction. For centuries, it has been a beacon, a constant in life's stormy seas. Life’s journey can be exhilarating, but when overwhelmed, where do we turn for solace?

Since childhood, my roots in Fuzhou, China, have been my Polaris. It's a place of vibrant lanterns, bustling towns with tales of warriors, and rich cuisine. This city is my identity and my home. But at five, my firm roots were uprooted. Moving to New York was bewildering. I was surrounded by children who didn’t understand my words, who cast confused looks at my grandmother’s shuijiao (dumplings). I felt different and alone. My Polaris seemed to dim as I struggled with language and identity.

As days passed, I withdrew into myself. I watched my peers form friendships while I yearned silently. That was until Meika joined me at lunch. Her presence was a beacon of hope. From a different culture, she didn’t shy away from my broken English and encouraged me to embrace my new surroundings.

Meika loved butterflies, once telling me: “Butterflies don’t stay in one place. To become beautiful, they must leave their cocoons.” Her words struck a chord. Like a caterpillar, I learned to embrace change. With her help, I saw beyond cultural differences and appreciated New York’s rich diversity.

Moving again to Maryland felt different; I was braver, shedding the cocoon of my comfort zone. Each move left a piece of home in my heart. I realized we are meant to grow and travel, and I had learned to navigate change with courage. In the end, my Polaris always shined brightly. No matter where I go, I know where my home is.

"Reeses," the barista called out, placing a Matcha Latte on the counter with a scribble in black marker. I stepped forward, smiling as I retrieved my matcha latte. They spelled my name wrong again.

My name is Risus—pronounced like the candy. Though a ubiquitous conversation starter, this quirky privilege felt more like a curse than a blessing. Awkward roll calls, painful introductions, "sweet nicknames"—I never liked the attention tied to such a title. Finally, I pledged to shed this sugary persona for good.

Yet after seven years as Risus, I hesitated to change. First, I turned back to the name I'd left behind: "Box, uhm... Box-wan?" My birth name, Boxuan, buried since age ten, resurfaces only on legal documents and family reunions. Realizing my neglect, I sat with my family during the Mid-Autumn Festival. As I savored the mooncakes, I learned my name's meaning: "Bo" means knowledge, "Xuan" signifies dignity—the characters chosen by my grandparents were part of something greater, my heritage. Ironically, as a proud advocate of Chinese culture, I had abandoned my own name. Thus, I became Boxuan again. Instead of introducing myself as Risus, I corrected people's pronunciation; instead of suppressing my real name, I embraced it. Risus, I concluded, was merely an ugly mark of assimilation.

But something didn’t feel quite right.

As I strolled through the halls, a hollow feeling lingered. With each confused remark, my initial label of Risus became weaker. I didn’t understand: hadn't I already embraced my true self? Why do I still feel foreign? Seeking answers, I turned to friends. Enze chose his legal name, Jerry preferred his nickname, and Kyle used both—they each had a heartfelt reason, yet none fit me. Then I looked to stories. Gogol in The Namesake is inspiring, but unlike him, Risus was my choice. Amy Tan expresses her culture eloquently through writing, but I felt worlds away from such articulation. The more I searched, the more conflicted I became. Finally, I was done. Names are social labels, but ultimately, they belong to me. So instead of seeking validation, I asked myself: What does Risus mean to me?

As a 12-year-old fresh off the plane from China, I was terrified of what lay ahead. Given the rare chance to choose my own name, I scrolled past the 'Michaels' and 'Davids' until Risus caught my eye—not for its resemblance to the candy (which I hadn’t even realized), but for its meaning. Simple yet elegant, Risus meant “The One Who Is Laughter.” At that moment, amidst all the uncertainty, I made a promise to keep laughing, no matter what.

And I did. When Jerry came out sobbing after the literature test, I told him an unfunny joke about how he resembles a ghost archetype; while side-eyeing me, his mood lifted. Before the nerve-wracking district race, I proposed that we entrap the other team in a giant man-made circle; despite not being a realistic plan, it helped ease off the butterfly in our stomachs. On Christmas Eve, when my dad was rushed to the ER with appendicitis, I was left alone with my 4-year-old brother. Despite not even knowing what to do myself, I first comforted my little brother with a smile and a game of “Reymann Legend.” The meaning of "Risus"—laughter—remains as much a part of me as Boxuan. To abandon Boxuan is like to abandon part of myself, but the same could be said about Risus. If I wasn’t ashamed of Boxuan, why should I be ashamed of Risus? A name is just a name in the end – but my names are not.

Pushing the door open at Humble Grounds, it seemed that nothing had changed. As I ordered another Matcha Latte, the barista once again asked for my name. However, this time, I am neither just Boxuan nor just Risus. I am proudly both.

Moving from Ukraine to a Massachusetts boarding school in 9th grade, I found myself surrounded by a dizzying array of cultures—Chinese, Korean, Mexican, German, Indian. Eager to expand my perspective, I joined the International Student Alliance.

Twice a week in the dining hall, my friends and I gathered in the top-right corner, creating fusion dishes like spicy curry on sweet varenyky. As we blended flavors, we blended ideas too. We’d tackle questions about the world—climate change, education access—no problem felt too big. Inspired by the innovative solutions we developed together, I decided to start a podcast, interviewing people from around the world to address a topic I’m passionate about—mental health stigma. Interviewing people—from an Afghan refugee to a psychologist in Turkey—I realized that the main barrier to mental health acceptance is a lack of education. I now wanted to find the solution. Collaborating with individuals from around the world, I led an initiative to translate mental health resources to make them more accessible and, reaching out to individuals from different communities, I partnered with underfunded schools to integrate mental health curriculums. Through collaboration, I was able to take my first steps in addressing mental health stigma. With the resources at Johns Hopkins, I am eager to take the next.

Collaboration and a culture of research that foster new ideas and solutions to pressing issues excite me about Johns Hopkins. I’m deeply interested in psychology and am eager to engage in undergraduate research on mental health. I would be thrilled to work in the Papadakis Lab under Dr. Alison Papadakis, where fascinating research on co-rumination and its links to depression and anxiety is underway. Having worked with kids around the globe, I’ve seen how poor mental health affects individuals across all backgrounds, and I hope to collaborate with fellow Blue Jays to develop impactful solutions for the mental health challenges facing future generations. With Hopkins’ resources for research and emphasis on collaboration, aligning with my passion for mental health, I know it’s the ideal place to deepen my understanding of the world while creating change within it.

The cold metal of the chair bit into my skin as I sat trembling in the Taliban detention cell. Two meals a day—if I could keep them down—were the only breaks from the barrage of questions.

“How dare you defy the Supreme Leader’s law?” they roared. But, I wondered, how could a simple desire to learn threaten an entire regime?

I remember the morning the Taliban stormed our city. My siblings lost their jobs serving the previous government overnight. The following evening, Baba clasped his hands at dinner and said: “We have no choice, [Name]. You’re the only one who can keep us afloat now.” For my family’s well-being, I sacrificed something precious: my schooling.

My once-uninterrupted 1,368-hour Pomodoro streak at Khan Academy gave way to the daily grind of tracking my earnings at a shoe factory. Every time I passed the school, a pang of loss hit me, but I choked back my despair. I wanted to find my way back into the world of learning. And I couldn’t stand by while my female friends were condemned to lives of submission. Something had to be done.

So I revived a once-abandoned academy with Sharif, Omid, and Fahim, my high school peers, to covertly homeschool girls. Textbooks were concealed under religious covers. Before the city woke to threaten our learning, the students crept to the academy. They snuck back during calls to prayer.

Inevitably, as the number of students grew to 300, we were caught. As the Taliban interrogated me, I couldn’t stop thinking about our female students who would no longer be able to learn – including Layla, who told me she aimed to become the Minister of Technology and fearlessly provide free education to all her sisters.

Eight days later, a truck dropped me somewhere near our mahala. Barefoot, I limped home. Knock, knock. Mom screamed my name, and before she reached the "n" in [Name], she pulled me into the tightest hug, tears streaming down our faces. I felt a heavy weight in my arms as she fainted. For the first time in my life, I saw my 80-year-old father cry.

After four terrifying months, I returned to school for my final exams. Girls my age didn’t. Then came the news that broke me – Layla had taken her own life by ingesting acid. Layla, whose hands were decorated with hennas of algebra and physics formulae, would never become our technology minister.

As 1000 days without girls’ education approached, I decided to try again. For Layla. During the day, I translated Khan Academy lessons into Persian and hosted Zoom tutoring sessions for girls. At night my mind drifted to the soldier’s last words: “You may go, but we've seized your home documents—disobey again, and your family will be homeless." I kept my voice low while tutoring, knowing my parents would stop me if they found out.

After 15 months of relentless work, I began sharing our resources online. I taught myself web development through trial and error and crafted my encrypted archive website. Using funds from a bake sale I organized with my mom, I bought DVDs and collaborated with local drivers to deliver them to places where the word "education" had become no more than a whisper.

We began in underground darkness, planting the seeds of education where it was most forbidden. Every attempt to cut down the tree of knowledge we wished to cultivate only birthed new, stronger roots. We lost Layla, but her legacy lives on. I see it in the twelve girls who began recording their mastered subjects to educate fellow Afghans.

After our make-shift school was shut down, I felt like we had failed. But now I know we succeeded just by trying. After all, success isn't reserved for the final chapter of our veiled books; I feel it during every whispered lesson, every risk taken, and every sprout born from darkness.

In West Houston, beside a little mall where roads I-10 and 99 cross, there stands a small restaurant named Freddy’s that has the best burgers in the world. When I lived in Texas, my joy was to go there on weekends or after a long day of football practice.

Consisting of a juicy smash patty, onions, special sauce, and three-inch pickles that always find a way to fall off, Freddy’s burgers were made simply. My hungry eyes always fixed on the teenagers at the grill, cranking what I hoped to be an endless supply of burgers. I thought Freddy’s would be with me forever.

Then, when I was ten years old, I had to move back to Japan. I was anxious about starting a new life, but even more devastated to leave behind my home and my precious burgers.

After returning to Japan, my cravings for Freddy's hit almost immediately. From trying teriyaki chicken burgers and even my forceful homemade burgers, I did everything I could just to have another taste of my past. But it was shocking how bad they tasted.

The patties weren't as juicy, the buns weren't as crispy, and most of all, the pickles were lacking their primal flavor. Freddy’s occupied a special spot in my heart, not only because of their deliciousness but also their connection to my life in America.

It wasn’t until six years later that I started to question my desires. I was having dinner at a conveyor-belt sushi restaurant in Tokyo with a friend from Australia. He mentioned how jealous he was that I had access to good, cheap sushi.

This struck me. My mind rushed back to something I'd long forgotten: how much I craved Japanese food when I lived in Houston. My family and I traveled several hours just to visit a “real” ramen restaurant run by a Japanese chef. Once we moved back to Japan, I eagerly anticipated the weekend when we would eat out to enjoy how good the food was again.

There’s a Japanese phrase: nai mono nedari, "to beg for things you don’t have”. It took a casual comment at a sub-par sushi chain for me to understand how trapped I was in my own feelings of nai mono nedari. Whether I was in Texas or Japan, what I wanted most was always what I couldn't get.

Although I can no longer take in the vast Texas skies, or rejoice in the genuine southern hospitality, I came to notice the more profound things surrounding me now: the mesmerizing scenery of Mt. Fuji I see everyday, or the respectful and calming demeanor of Japanese people.

What I had in the past or what I want in the future is not as important as what I have now—not just food, but the environment I’m in, the people in my life, and what I have within me. I learned to cherish every moment, to embrace, to savor, and to live in the present because there might not be another day to taste the pickles that slip out of my burger.

Despite my aims of living in the present, I'm eager to explore what lies ahead. As I also dream of becoming a flag football Olympian, my perspective about what it means to achieve my goals has changed. I know that true joy of learning comes not from grades and numbers, but from the knowledge and relationships gained through the process. I'm still an ambitious and driven individual, but I no longer feel the disappointment of nostalgia. Instead, I’ve learned to appreciate the special things I have now and value every step along my journey.

Now, I’ll cherish every bite of the Japanese food I have, knowing my next Freddy’s awaits me. From here on, I'll make sure nothing goes to waste: whether it’s a burger or life more broadly. I’ll treasure the time I have to enjoy it.

The newly fallen ethereal snow has become a sheep graveyard. The white wool fades even whiter, blending in the snow, making it hard to spot. Each winter, millions of sheep die of starvation and the bitter bite of the Mongolian cold breeze—this is called Dzud.

For nomadic herders, their herd is their entire net worth. If so, dzud is like the Earth committing arson to thousands of Mongolian people’s life-savings every winter. I briefly remember my childhood in the countryside, witnessing my friends sinking deep under the snowfall. Even though I didn’t understand as a child, the bigger problem was the financial burden the herders faced in the spring.

When farmers' crops are destroyed, insurance compensates them. But that's not the case for the nomadic herders in Dzud. I thought to myself. How come no herders held financial protection for their sheep herds? Like at least an insurance?

However, the current livestock insurance offers to insure the herd by the region to split the damage and compensation. This meant herders might receive nothing, even if they lost their entire herd to Dzud. Dumb, right?

It was designed as “index-based insurance” because the trust between insurance providers and herders was somewhat unstable. The insurance providers couldn’t tell if the herder was lying or not, and herders couldn’t tell if the insurer was overcharging.

Just as I was thinking about that, a pair of dots connected in my brain. The time I waited eagerly for the J.P. Morgan financial reports to be released and the hours I spent researching Dogecoin’s blockchain transactions gave me an idea.

Blockchain is like a digital notebook: Everyone has the same copy that updates together, preventing secret changes or cheating. My idea was to let the nomadic households act as notebooks/blocks and verify each other’s information on the proven trustworthy chain.

Blockchainifying the sheep. I know it sounds weird. But the strange thing is that the local university trusted my proposal for the project, and after some convincing (a lot), they decided to adopt and develop the idea.

The sheer number of problems that occurred made me realize why no one has done it before. There is a lack of data about the herds and the dzud. Convincing the conservative herders for a new idea and, most interestingly, navigating through the bureaucracy of the government agencies was like hell.

After several trips and thousands of kilometers commuting to the Altai Mountain ranges and the Khuvsgul taiga, we made progress, gathering data directly from herders.

My main role was to connect foreign blockchain developers to national government agencies for the necessary information and access. Not that it was a technically challenging job, but thanks to that, I became fluent in “bureaucratese,” a language full of words that meant “maybe someday,” where every simple request required at least three stamps and a signature from someone who was “out of office.”

But finally, this winter, we will do a test trial on a small group of nomadic households in Arkhangai province. A total of over 4000 sheep will be blockchain-insured through our system soon.

No other country is facing Dzud the way we are. Instead of hoping that a magical fairy will come up and help us, we can count only on ourselves. My hope is that the integration of technology and financial instruments filled with innovation could alleviate the nomadic culture that is slowly fading away.

This pursuit, to me, is about protecting the soul of Mongolia. I hope to be at the forefront of this transition from the past to the future, ensuring that our culture survives the bitter winters and the rapidly evolving world.

My interest in history was foundational to my academic journey, evolving over time and eventually leading me to international relations. My love of history started in middle school when my parents took me and my older sister on dozens of trips over three summers, all centered around the American Revolution. In Philadelphia, I found Independence Hall fascinating. I admired the living history actors at Fort Ticonderoga and Colonial Williamsburg and wanted to become one myself. Shortly after, I began volunteering at the Nathan Hale Homestead. I loved learning about the cultural history and customs practiced in rural early America. Although volunteering at this museum had taught me much, I wanted to learn about colonial history on a broader scale. Because of this, I turned to library books and documentaries. I began to learn everything I could about colonial history and was especially intrigued by settler-native conflicts such as King Philip’s War and the Anglo-Powhatan War. In addition, my parents took me on field trips to museums such as the Pequot Museum and Colonial Jamestown. No matter how I learned, I was fascinated by colonial America’s early history. At twelve, my interest shifted from early American to Polish history. While on a Boy Scout camping trip, I listened to a group of older boys talk about Germany in World War II. They discussed how Germany was so successful in the early years of the war and used the invasion of Poland as an example. They said that Poland was unsophisticated and technologically backward compared to Germany. The boys claimed Poland’s cavalry army resorted to charging German panzers with sabers and criticized Poland’s leadership for wasting lives resisting inevitable defeat. This upset me, as I disagreed that resisting subjugation was ‘foolish.’ With this thinking, our country would never have revolted against England in 1775! Initially, I felt embarrassed that my Polish ancestors seemed so dumb fighting the German army. But I began to doubt this label of ineptitude, as it reminded me of the anti-Polish stereotypes my machinist grandfather faced, silently haunted by slurs like ‘dumb Polack.’ Determined, I wanted to prove that the Polish did not fit the label of stupidity applied to them. I started learning about Poland’s tenuous situation at the heart of Europe over the centuries—from its partition to the Second World War and beyond. Daily, I broadened my geopolitical understanding of Polish and European history with hours of reading and watching documentaries. Additionally, I read dozens of books about Poland’s history, my favorite being Applebaum’s ‘Poland 1939.’ From this book, I learned that Josef Goebbels’ Nazi Propaganda Ministry created the story of riders charging tanks to minimize Poland’s war contribution and depict them as primitive and incompetent. This myth began at Krojanty, where Polish cavalry surprise-attacked infantry and retreated once German armored cars arrived. Unfortunately, this Nazi rhetoric is still unknowingly espoused. Germany’s military was bigger and more modernized than Poland's, yet the Polish fought bravely for their freedom. France and Britain misled Poland with promises of substantial military support. Poland’s ‘Plan West’ tried to stall the German invasion to support a Western invasion of Germany that never came. While Poland was the topic that first interested me in geopolitics, my AP European and US History classes opened my eyes to the history of US intervention and diplomacy abroad. This interested me in post-WWII American geopolitics, particularly its interactions with Russia, Vietnam, and Iraq. I love history. I am interested in the evolving geopolitical stage and the combination of conflict and diplomacy that shapes it. I want to learn about America’s geopolitical situation by studying international relations. I plan to apply to law school and study international law, using this knowledge at the US State Department. I want to help make the world more peaceful by learning from past misconceptions, truths, and mistakes. I hope to use what I learn at your school to do that.

Sitting center-stage, my hands shield my eyes from the audience. Scribbling over sudokus in elementary school and reciting pi at my fifth-grade talent show, I found a hunger for training my brain. By middle school, this passion evolved into participating in memory competitions. I was thrilled by the complexity of memorizing new forms of information.

As a memory athlete, my fascination with organizing information through systems formed my second home: my memory palace. In my head, my house is segmented into fifty marked locations. While memorizing, I transform the abstract data—words, cards, names, digits, and people—into images to place at each locus. During recall, my mind traverses through my palace to decode each image.

However, my journey took on a personal significance as I witnessed my grandmother’s dementia progress. Through her growing silence, memorization became a means of reclaiming control over a biological function that slipped away from her. While I can’t recall what I ate for breakfast two mornings ago, much less barcode-scan strings of digits, I was determined to prove that my normal brain didn’t limit my ceiling.

I strived to surpass my foundational strategies, tailoring them to my strengths. Experimenting with audio in my palace offered nothing but a headache, yet bizarre images that interacted with their surroundings appeared more vivid and proved significantly more memorable. The image of a “tall man” in my palace—originally a six-foot figure—became a living colossus, his elongated head piercing the foyer ceiling. These subtle adjustments propelled my progress forward.

Remembering my grandmother’s battle, I wondered how my practice modifying memorization techniques could apply to memory loss. My research into cognitive training revealed that the same techniques I employed in competitions had been adapted into training programs. Over six months, I partnered with professors involved in memory research, blending insights from memory training studies and my experience as a memory athlete. We developed training sessions incorporating a variety of cognitive exercises that I could facilitate at assisted living centers.

As I volunteered, I realized that, like myself, each senior had unique cognitive strengths. Louise Higginbotham was no exception—a 68-year-old woman with cascading silver curls that framed her face and an endless supply of winding stories. Initially, I introduced body parts as loci for participants’ memory palaces, but Louise struggled to distinguish the apple on her ankle from the grape on her knee. She'd scrunch her eyes with her lips pressed tight, yet the images remained tangled.

Sensing her frustration, I recognized that I needed to adjust her memory techniques. Sharing my own journey adapting methods, I turned to her favorite story topic: her old job at the local church. I asked if she could retrace her morning commute. Without hesitation, she articulated every detail: passing the bakery on Cedar Street, the winding road flanked by pine trees, and the sneaky pothole by the park. Once we anchored her memory palace along the route, everything clicked; her fruit salad became an unclouded journey.

Following my grandmother’s decline, crafting memorization strategies reassured me of control over my cognitive future. Mastering these same techniques, memory training has empowered Louise to reclaim her aging process. Though in opposite stages of our lives, exchanging our stories, bridged my tall man and her winding road to reveal a shared journey. I’ve learned to value the diverse experiences of others, gaining wisdom from unique connections found through their narratives. For me, memory training has adopted a new meaning: keeping our stories alive. Through cognitive science, I’ll continue preserving memory, protecting the connections that weave together our identities.

How do you teach a 6-year-old about moon craters without boring a 16-year-old?

The script under the demo cart said: “Define an asteroid,” followed by a paragraph of scientific jargon. Clearly, the script wasn’t prepared for Lisa and Raymond. Lisa toyed with the Earth’s surface, represented by a pile of sand, while her teenage brother, Raymond, stared blankly. Both were deeply uninterested.

I always find the feeling of a half-full backpack odd. Perhaps it’s the sensation of items shifting around in the thin-canvassed bag that puts me on edge. Or maybe it’s my logical brain resisting the thought of carrying a few small things in a bag meant for more. This concept of unfilled space suggests untapped potential, wasted opportunity, and disappointment. I’ve searched for ways to fill those gaps, to alleviate the discomfort of emptiness. The sad truth is that I can seldom find enough necessary items to fill the bag to its fullest capacity. This feeling of emptiness lingered not just in my backpack but in more significant areas of my life. Yet over time, I came to realize that I can only fill my bag so much on my own. Before I could understand that, however, moments in my life changed my mindset. Some of life's most valuable moments aren’t about completely filling the “bag.”

My much younger self “fixed” the illogical dilemma with an even more irrational solution. I remember the frantic rush of grabbing whatever I could cram into my fabric knapsack as if sheer volume could fix the empty feeling. I resorted to textbooks I’d never use in class, folders to organize nothing, a change of clothes I didn’t need, and… socks? Turns out, 10-year-old [Name] was more of a quantity-over-quality guy when it came to packing. I figured out that if I packed enough socks to fill a model of “Sockramento, Calfafornia,” I could fill up my backpack. As ridiculous as it sounds, it balanced out the unease I felt.

And then, just like the socks in my bag, the small gestures of recognition from people around me started to fill a different kind of emptiness. I hadn’t realized there were cracks in my emotional stability after actions from others began to smooth them over. A compliment from a teammate after a rough practice, a friend pointing out that I seemed quieter than usual, or a peer asking if I had gotten a haircut. These moments weren’t grand, they were like those socks, minute and easy to overlook, but somehow they brought a necessary element to my life.

When I enrolled in a psychology class at my local high school as a homeschooler, just to join the district’s tennis team, I was introduced to Bandura’s social learning theory and Adler’s focus on social connectedness. This allowed me to realize that no matter how carefully I packed my own “bag,” there were always spaces I couldn’t fill by myself. The most valuable parts I still remember come not from what I carry or do myself but from what others pour in.

Only when I look back, can I see that my feelings of being half-filled weren’t anything to fix by cramming in more activities. Small but meaningful contributions from others were what replenished me day-to-day. Gratitude seeps in when you start noticing a smile, a brief but thoughtful check-in, or a quiet understanding in a shared glance. Those are the things that fill my bag, not by carrying more stuff, but with something much more valuable: acknowledgment. And so, as I’ve learned how important recognition is through others, I strive to notice others. I’ve always excelled in reading subtle details—a person sitting alone, a moment of discomfort in someone’s eyes, a pause in someone’s usual chatter. Because of others pouring into me, I strive to act on these realizations, to help fill their emotional packages in ways that they might not even realize they need.

Life isn’t about cramming every space with things—it’s about finding the right things. And sometimes, the most important parts are the ones given to you by someone else.

Since I was four, I drew what I wanted to draw. Disney princesses and Powerpuff Girls made their way from TV screens to paper. I loved that I could make them tangible and carry them everywhere. My creativity spilled onto our white walls; rocks, shells, even lightbulbs became my canvases. These eventually became the subjects of seven-layered acrylic paintings that experimented with perspective, depth, composition, rule-of-thirds, shades, and color changes. I loved that I could interpret these tangible objects from a distance as my hands transformed silent sketches into brisk brushstrokes soothingly filling up my canvas.

Some might say I have the Midas touch, but instead of turning things into gold, I transform them into wonders. With my “magic hands,” I put imagination on paper and bring objects to life, fixing our food waste disposer and soldering our circuit board.

But despite my Midas touch there was one thing I couldn't fix:

My mom's cancer.

One afternoon, my brother and mom left hurriedly for his soccer match, accidentally leaving a report on our kitchen table.

Like Sleeping Beauty drawn to the spinning wheel, I touched the paper.

Five centimeters.

My mind went blank. Tumor. 5 cm. Google.

I quickly deleted my search history. My heart stopped, exhausted from frantically pounding. I was paralyzed by the weight of the news—news that had already taken away my grandmother three years ago.

Days with my mom hospitalized were cold, matte, and shapeless—my artwork, an echo of emotions I struggled to express. Papers wrinkled with blue tears as gray hues dominated, while charcoal became my medium of choice, capturing stark contrasts between dark and light. They seemed to say that I’m not okay. In my drawings, I was barefoot on a bison. My self-portraits featured mirror reflections of hands gripping my heavy head with tentacles unfurling from my back.

With my sister in college, my dad away on frequent business trips, and my mom bedridden, everything changed. I was no longer simply the engineer to fix things or an artist to beautify; I became the head of the household, even as a middle child. I stepped into my mom’s role: vacuuming, tracing imaginary grids; doing laundry, playing with chemical compositions; and washing dishes, in a systematic color arrangement. My artistic skills found new expression in packing lunch boxes for me and my brother, using food as my paint.

I visited my mom every day. Squeezing my hand with her right and an IV stand on her left, she walked me through the artwork-filled hallway outside her room.

"I found a lot of comfort in seeing these paintings," she said quietly.

As her eyes traced painted roofs and flowers, I watched them glisten for the first time since the fight for life began—her smile no longer held secrets. What seemed like simple brushstrokes held the power to transport her beyond the sterile walls and beeping machines.

At home, I lifted my favorite No. 12 Velvetouch acrylic brush to create a cozy house with a serene garden. Home. This piece now hangs in the very hallway where my mom gave my life an extra dimension. Art allowed her to dream of a future beyond those walls and make it back home. I continue to fill up hospital hallways with my art while keeping my hands busy sewing compression pads specially geared for cancer patients.

These small acts became my way of staying connected, sending my love across the distance, and hopefully bringing them joy through the drawings and DVDs of the latest DreamWorks movies I sent.

During my most recent visit, I stood in awe as we completed the final touches on the house. Together, we transformed misfortune into narratives that anchored us and filled our hearts with renewed hope. From that small, crumbling playhouse to our newly rebuilt home, I’ve come to understand the profound importance of environments that invite relaxation, foster companionship, and promote ease. My journey has evolved from simple play into a dedicated mission—to be the person who helps others unwind, enjoy a meal, or watch a film without the fear of a roof collapsing above them.

As an online student, my world revolves around my desk, with most connections happening through a screen. However, my most meaningful connections have flourished beyond it.

I've always been drawn to the shadows. As a child, I'd squint at the spaces between streetlights, convinced that magic occurred there, just beyond illumination. This fascination followed me into adolescence, where I discovered science fiction, reveling in its mysterious cloak. Authors like Ursula K. Le Guin and Mary Shelley became my guides, showing me how to probe the darkness without dispelling it entirely.

Two centuries ago at Lake Geneva, Mary Shelley, in the company of accomplished male writers several years her senior, was spurred by a dare to tell a ghost story—a story that would become Frankenstein. What was initially a middle school literary obsession soon became a reference in my own science, embodying the balance between mystery’s allure and the illuminating force of knowledge.

It was this delicate balance I tried to maintain when I joined a bioengineering competition at UC Berkeley with my school’s science team during my freshman year. Our challenge: congenital pulmonary stenosis—a condition where infant hearts labored against their own anatomy, valves narrowed by nature's capricious hand.

I listened to my teammates discuss current treatments, each of which meant a lifetime tethered to the operating table for the patient, a Promethean punishment for the crime of being born with a faulty heart. The upperclassmen traded polysyllabic terms, their expertise a constant reminder of my novice status. In our desperation to find a solution, the prevailing attitude was a collective shrug that seemed to say: this is simply the best we can do. Despite everyone’s resignation, I was determined to be the person who didn’t simply shrug.

Driven by this determination, I dove into scientific literature. Cardiology journals became my bedtime reading, tissue-engineering papers my lunchtime companions. But my preparation went beyond reading. As I experimented with the prototype, using computer-aided-design (CAD) software I'd taught myself in stolen moments between classes, I thought about Mary Shelley. She, too, had dared to imagine a world where the boundaries between known and unknown, between life and death, were not immutable. Her creature wasn't a triumph of illumination, but a reminder of the mysteries that persist even in our most ambitious creations.

The solution began to take shape in my mind: a heart valve that wasn't just a mechanical fix, but a collaboration between man and machine. I envisioned a device that would grow throughout the recipient’s lifetime, providing a crucial element for pediatric patients while having innocuous effects on adults. While explaining my proposal, I saw my teammates’ initial skepticism give way to cautious interest. Leveraging the CAD program I’d taught myself in the days prior, I led our team in modeling blood flow through stress distribution and fluid dynamics—each iteration was a balancing act—too rigid, and the valve wouldn't adapt; too flexible, and it risked failure under pressure. I created spreadsheets comparing tensile strengths and inflammatory responses, turning our desk into a command center for a five-person bioengineering division.

The day of the competition came with little fanfare. We didn't win that year. But when one of the judges, a UCSF cardiothoracic surgeon, approached me and said, "I'm sold," I felt a surge of vindication. His recognition was more than a consolation prize. It gave me confidence that I was on the right path, proving that innovation thrives when we embrace mystery, regardless of experience or academic background.

As a first-generation college applicant and aspiring engineer, I carry with me the lesson of that long-ago summer in Lake Geneva—a reminder that innovation knows no pedigree. We live in an age desperate to deny magic, to unravel every thread of mystery. But in our quest to illuminate every shadow, we risk losing the very magic that drives innovation. As I move forward in my studies and career, I aim to craft systems that bridge the divide between humanity and technology. Like Shelley, I believe that true innovation thrives not in erasing the shadows but in daring to explore the mysteries they hold, always seeking what lies just beyond the edge of light.

After every journey, my father would come home and tuck away his precious earnings—hours of labor distilled into something small yet invaluable. Some struggled with marching, their uncertainty reflected in awkward steps, but I knew better than to dismiss them. Instead, I encouraged them, just as my father had saved those bags, understanding that their worth would shine with patience and care. I brought the upperclassmen in on this mission, turning our fragmented section into a unified whole, one high five at a time.

As weeks turned into months, our unity grew. Spirit day after spirit day, the once uncertain recruits became confident, driven individuals. And then came the 50th Annual First Flag Festival—my first festival as an officer. We stood, waiting, tension threading through our veins. A whistle pierced the air, and we marched. Our music, our movement—it all flowed effortlessly. Holes that once marred our formation were now filled with vibrant sound. The adrenaline surged as we stepped off the field, knowing we had given it everything.

The results came in: we won every single caption for the first time in our band's history. Surrounded by shouts of joy, I looked at my section and felt an overwhelming gratitude for each person, regardless of where they began. We were like those plastic bags—ordinary, maybe even overlooked, until we discovered our purpose. Together, we created something far greater than the sum of our parts: something beautiful, meaningful, and deeply ours.

Growing up, I heard stories from my parents about how they came to the U.S., giving me an impression of immigration as a hard road to a better life. I listened to my parents reminisce about how they would avoid the checkout in the supermarket and struggle to talk to their colleagues at work. While their process of immigrating was easy from a legal standpoint, thanks to the work visas they obtained due to their CS degrees, they struggled for many years to integrate into the nation and society due to language barriers. My parents’ stories about moving to six different states while dealing with a foreign language and culture filled me with awe, making me view them as role models, journeymen who had thrived in a new land. Looking up to my parents so early in my life, I took great interest in their work. Seeing the large monitors filled with colorful letters that I could not understand filled me with wonder, looking like magical enchantments to my young eyes. I wanted to follow in their footsteps by doing something that would make them proud. From the moment I got old enough to use a keyboard, I spent my free time soaking up knowledge about simple coding through tutorials on Python and Java Leetcode problems, joining my local robotics team, and designing simple online text-based adventures. I immensely enjoyed learning programming for these projects above. Even with the projects themselves being essentially simple with parameters defined from the beginning, the linear process and the clear end goal allowed me to keep my motivation high. When I returned to school at the start of 11th grade, my friends created my school’s Model United Nations, which I quickly joined for fun. Initially, I did not expect it to be meaningful, but MUN enabled me to debate in UN committees through the lens of a diplomat representing the people of an entire country, entering a world of diplomacy I never could have on my own. In my research on Rwanda for my first conference, I learned how the Rwandan genocide caused the economy and food security to collapse, creating a terrible refugee crisis that the world largely ignored. What I discovered in my research for Rwanda and other countries at the conferences I attended opened my eyes to how immigrants and refugees worldwide struggle not just with access to essential resources but also with being able to voice their needs on a global stage. As I opened my eyes to everything happening worldwide, I started to reflect more on my family's story. My parents’ struggles paled in comparison to what others had to face, but their struggles in language were genuine, and I saw that as an entryway through which I could get involved. Learning more about the linguistic and cultural barriers immigrants face, I thought about how I could help, being no stranger to the story of trying to navigate a new and unfamiliar environment without a strong command of its predominant language. Soon after, I was grateful to join an internship at GLOW Action, an organization that helps refugees worldwide struggling with language barriers, food insecurity, and access to healthcare. At GLOW, I combine my passion for programming with my desire to amplify the voices of immigrants by developing an AI chatbot with numerous prompts and languages, including Spanish, Russian, and Arabic, granting refugees and immigrants from all across the globe the ability to communicate more effectively within their newfound communities. Unlike before, I could finally contribute towards something bigger than me, the large-scale, multifaceted, real-world issue that immigration is. In designing and implementing these programs with GLOW, I have grown from creating personal projects for my enjoyment and benefit to stepping up for people worldwide. Sometimes, I think back to my parents and all they did to provide me with a better life. I am proud to have followed in their footsteps and worked hard for a better future, but I am also proud to have made my own path, helping to give immigrants a voice and realize their dreams.

It’s 9 p.m. on Tuesday. Baking will take four hours, but I proceed anyway. With a practiced efficiency, I grab the eggs, flour, sugar, honey, oil, salt, and yeast and place them on the counter. I heat up some water and stir the yeast and sugar. There’s no turning back now.

I first tried challah at my Bubbe’s house. Growing up, I was very close to my grandparents–my Bubbe and Zadie–who helped raise me while my mom was deployed to Iraq. Being Jewish, challah was significant to my Bubbe. Recently, I’ve been making my own challah as a way of connecting with my heritage. I still remember the first time I made the bread on my own. I wanted to make a great loaf and make my Bubbe proud. At the start, my recipe was okay, but I knew I wanted to make a loaf as good as my Bubbe’s Bubbe’s which I had heard stories of. By experimenting each time, from researching online to observing how different changes affected the bread, my recipe has gotten better and better. I love this aspect of making the bread–learning what works and what doesn’t–while also being able to be creative and make something completely from scratch.

Now that I have the ingredients out, I measure each ingredient carefully and combine them together. Then I begin kneading the loaf, a critical step in the process as it determines how fluffy the end result will be. My arms tire as I knead for what feels like an eternity, until the sticky dough starts to smooth out and I place it back into the bowl to rise.

As the dough rises, I head upstairs to my room. My curiosity extends to more than just improving my challah recipe. While waiting on the dough, I’ll watch a few interesting philosophy videos before getting out Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics to prepare for the philosophy discussion group I started with my English teacher and a few other students. But it isn’t just learning that I love – it’s also exchanging ideas with others and figuring out why people think what they think. Whether it’s reading Aristotle, independently researching about Napoleon’s Marshals, or debating contemporary politics, a large part of my joy in learning new things is sharing that with others.

Back in the kitchen, my dough has now expanded to fill nearly the entire bowl. Now comes the most complex part: braiding. Often, I’ll call my Bubbe and Zadie as I form six strands, pinch their ends, and begin to braid. Like a braided loaf, my identity is interwoven. I’m both Black and Jewish, and it has often been hard to fully identify with one part of my identity. While I’m connected to my Jewish heritage thanks to my Bubbe and by baking the challah, I didn’t grow up religious and so it has been hard to claim that identity fully. Similarly, I’m connected to my Black identity through my family and cultural experiences, but it’s sometimes been hard for me to explicitly identify with that side of me on the basis of my appearance. In this sense, my identity is something that I’m continually figuring out. Finally, after I’m done braiding, I give my dough an egg wash, let it rise again, and place it in the oven. The smell of the warm bread is heavenly, and it fills the whole house. Just 30 minutes later, the loaf is complete.

The next morning, I pack the bread as I get ready for school. Of all the steps, the final one is my favorite: sharing. To me, eating challah is a joyful experience that brings people together. I bring my challah to the Jewish Culture Club, where everyone tears off a piece. I then share the bread with the rest of my friends. Everyone’s excited, and I’m sometimes offered suggestions for improvements, which I’ll incorporate into my ever-improving recipe.

I was on an intense treasure hunt, frantically searching for myself. My parents finished eating, unfazed, while I scoured. A wave of relief washed over me as I found and started to sort the round mustard seeds into piles from my rice, elevating them onto their own space. From the mild potato curry I cherished as a kid, to my current obsession with spicy mango pickle, the subtle but constant ingredient in the dishes always remained. Every seed I consume travels from my stomach to my mind, marking each moment of my existence. At last, they were in their prospective group: red, violet, and black.

Red: These seeds are mild and undercooked. Carrying memories of my childhood I dream of reliving. What I relished most wasn’t materialistic; it was playing hide n’ seek at Costco and accidentally eating a glow stick at outdoor school. But above all, singing was my biggest source of joy, whether I was screaming out to One Direction’s entire discography or immersing myself into the rhythms of Carnatic music. Like the seeds, my voice was unpolished and full of untapped potential. Lunch always filled me with excitement, having no doubt my favorite ingredient would always be present. In the quiet cafeteria, I subconsciously sang, ready to dig in as the tune drifted through the air, but was instead met with judgemental stares that quickly erupted into laughter. My throat tightened as I shut my lunchbox and parts of myself while the red seeds crumbled, planting a tree which feared judgment.

Violet: These seeds are mellow and constantly evolving. My freshman year, I was still surrounded by fault finders, hidden under their overpowering lentils. Stepping outside my comfort zone while risking failure was my deepest fear. But I knew I couldn’t keep my voice hidden forever. At last, days stopped blending together when a Carnatic singing workshop flyer caught my attention– an opportunity to sing in front of others. Singing had always been something I only shared with my teacher, but this was about being heard. After being overlooked all this time, I’ve finally been given the chance to rise. The first few days, I felt like a hidden seed again as I sang in public, feeling everyone’s eyes on me, searching for flaws. Nervousness overtook me as my mind went blank, the melody slipping away. My voice cracked as I rushed through the rest. But I kept pushing, refusing to get trapped again. Unexpectedly, it was the memories contained of the red seeds– the moments I was laughed at– that brought me closer to the surface. It shouldn’t keep planting seeds of fear in my mind. The voices of others cannot hold more power than mine. I closed my eyes and stopped thinking about everyone else and more about how I felt in the moment. With that mindset, by the time of my performance, the tree of judgment withered as I reclaimed my voice.

Black: These seeds are impactful and full of flavor. Through performing, I didn’t just learn how to sing better– I found an even greater purpose: helping others overcome the same fears that were holding me back. Teaching Carnatic music, I saw my reflection in one student. Opening up about her complicated relationship with singing after getting teased during a talent show, struggling to embrace her love. Her passion was overshadowed by mockery, just how I buried my voice. I guided her to reconnect with music, reminding her that imperfections help us grow. With each lesson, her voice grew stronger, and so did mine, feeling a new tree taking root– one of confidence.

With that, I savored the very last black mustard seed, realizing I had come in a full circle. No matter the size, shape, or color, it deserves to be on a surface.

Placed, photo taken, published. As I proficiently linked the latest magnet I acquired from my recent trip to my travel blog using NFC tools, my attention rested on my collection of magnets on the display wall. Tasmania, Sri Lanka, Hawaii, Hokkaido—each magnet encapsulates a memory, a fragment of my journey through different parts of the world. While browsing through the magnets, I realized they reflect milestones of my growth, each one a marker of adventure, resilience, and self-discovery.

My gaze turns to the small turtle magnet given to me by Gerard, our local driver in Sri Lanka. Gerard guided us through the winding roads of tea plantations and Hindu temples along the sun-soaked southeastern coastline. During our long car rides, he eagerly learned Chinese, hoping to enhance his business. I became his teacher, patiently explaining phrases like "chi fan" (eat) and "gong xi fa cai" (may wealth be with you) during traffic jams and meals at local restaurants. His determination to overcome a language barrier inspired me. Before I left Sri Lanka, he gifted me the turtle magnet, symbolizing our bond. Later, when Sri Lanka faced an economic crisis, our friendship offered me a unique lens through which to understand global economics. As I studied AP Macroeconomics and Microeconomics, I kept thinking about Gerard and how his struggle was more than an economics lesson. I researched Sri Lankan consumption data on Kaggle and explored trade policies in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan to grasp the crisis's impact. As I studied, I kept thinking about Gerard and his struggle. This experience deepened my understanding of our interconnected world, revealing how economic data is more than numbers but the realities of everyday life.

The Taipei 101 magnet I brought back from Taiwan represents a cross-cultural interaction. I remember sitting in a restaurant with my father, snapping at him in impatience. A nearby waitress gently reminded me, “You shouldn’t talk to your parents like that.” Her tone was soft yet firm. Her words were delivered in Mandarin with a distinctly Taiwanese accent. Initially embarrassed, I then realized how language, culture, and behavior interconnect, as the unique accent made me appreciate the different charms across cultures. Later in the trip, I visited Eslite Bookstore and bought a history book in traditional Chinese characters. The narrative differed significantly from what I had been taught, revealing that history is multifaceted and often depends on perspective. This experience encouraged me to seek new viewpoints and question the knowledge I had taken for granted. These cultural nuances prepared me for more diverse experiences later on.

The magnet of Heaven Lake from Paektu Mountain was a place I never witnessed. During my trip, I waited two days to see the lake, only to have the weather halt my efforts. Amidst the sighing and angry tourists, my initial discontent was gradually quelled, as I realized that crafting the ideal plan doesn’t always guarantee success. The magnet, featuring an image of this unobserved lake, now serves as a reminder that even well-laid plans can go awry. This experience inspired me and instilled a sense of independence, especially when I began solo trips around China at the age of 16. These journeys required not only time and money management but also data analysis for geography, weather, and transportation. Despite encountering similar situations, I embraced the experience itself, learning to adapt and appreciate the journey rather than just the destination.

What appears as a simple souvenir collection is something much more profound. Each magnet embodies a valuable lesson learned. Traveling, listening, learning, cherishing the moment - this has shaped my identity as someone who never denies an opportunity for personal growth. As I look at each magnet, I see a clear, visual timeline of my development. Among all of the pieces scattered on the wall, there is a noticeable empty space, a reminder that my journey has not yet come to an end.

It was the beginning of winter, and New York City's Union Square Subway Station was especially busy. Home for the Christmas holiday, I set out to sing for an audience of strangers for the first time. I had been singing since I was seven, and I believed it was time to push myself to share what I had spent so long cultivating.

A nauseating nervousness overcame me as I got my equipment ready. A sea of commuters surged around me. As I connected the microphone to the speaker, I still could not decide what to sing—Charlie Puth or Jay Chou. Instinctively, Charlie Puth, the mainstream American artist, seemed the better choice, but my fear of an imperfect performance moved me to choose Jay Chou. The Chinese lyrics would mask any flaws for my American audience.

As I sang, Jay Chou's lyrics took me home. Emboldened by this sense of comfort, I turned up the volume like I had in the privacy of my dorm room. A woman paused and leaned against the wall. Wearing an elegant white jacket with her hair in a neat bun, she swayed to the rhythm, eyes closed, face serene. After the third song, she walked up to me. Unsure what to expect, my heart tightened.

"These songs are so beautiful," she said with a soft yet genuine eagerness. "Even though I can't understand the lyrics, the melodies are extremely touching." She pulled out a twenty-dollar bill, a bag of chips, and a soda. "This is all I have, but your voice and melodies deserve much more."

Encouraged by the woman's kindness, I decided to take a leap. Even though my peers had previously expressed mixed feelings about my compositions, calling them not hip-hop nor mandopop enough, I began to sing a song “No One to Confide in” I had written when the weight of the loneliness of being in a country far from my family had begun to feel overwhelming. A Dominican couple approached me, their expressions soft as they enjoyed the melody. Their quiet appreciation reminded me that my music did not need to fit a genre—it simply needed to connect.

"Could we share a song with you?" The couple asked, approaching with a smile. I searched for the Spanish title they requested and played their song. Pulsating beats filled the station. Their energy was contagious. Despite not knowing any of the words, I could not help but ad-lib and join them. Huddled together around a single microphone, the December wind whisked away the forgotten lyrics and imperfect pitches, leaving in its wake our shared moment of joy.

In embracing the music of my homeland, I found the strength to share my authentic voice; in sharing my voice, I bonded with other humans regardless of our differences. Music became a means of connecting with others, a doorway to those who would have otherwise remained strangers. I strove to remember that as the seasons changed.

Emboldened by my subway experience, I decided to put on a small concert to raise money for teenagers' mental health in rural areas of China while I was home last summer. As the prelude of “No One to Confide in” filled the concert hall as it had filled the Union Square Subway Station so many months ago, people started to point at me excitedly. Inviting them up with a smile, they rushed onto the stage, forming a tight arc around me. Fifteen of us bounced together to the beat, bodies moving in sync as I sang the line:

"There are too many worries, but I have no one to confide in."

The lyric spoke of isolation, but in that moment, the weight of loneliness dissolved. Instead of being alone, the music made us one. We were a single pulse, united by sound, no longer solitary but bound together.

All I was missing was his iconic, tweed deerstalker hat, tobacco pipe, and magnifying glass. Entering my first escape room with my family, my mind was racing, palms sweaty.
