But as I immersed myself in the plot and the dilemma came to life, the nervousness dissipated. A sense of urgency overtook me, and I became hyper-aware of anything out of the ordinary. A slightly crooked painting may indicate something was hidden behind it. The rhythmic flickering of a set of lights could reveal the combination to a locked safe. I was Sherlock Holmes, piecing together the clues, and every puzzle solved felt like the breakthrough of a lifetime.

Despite our efforts, we were unable to escape in time. During the ride home, my dad, frustrated with the result, said, “I don’t understand why anyone likes torturing themselves with these stupid, impossible rooms.” But sitting in the backseat, I was captivated, busy replaying the experience in my head and trying to figure out the puzzles we weren’t able to solve.

The thing I love the most about escape rooms is the struggle. The puzzles that make a room memorable are not the ones I figure out quickly. They are the ones where my friends and I spend what feels like an eternity unraveling. A mysterious glass box with six seemingly random, numbered spheres. An incomplete chess board with four white pieces–bishop, knight, rook, and queen–surrounded by a sea of black. It is in those moments when I’m most inspired–each test of ingenuity forcing me to decipher its truth in creative ways. While I’m always happy when we complete a room successfully, I’ve actually grown to prefer it when the opposite occurs. That way I know I have been challenged to the fullest.

To me, escape rooms are more than just a collection of puzzles. They represent a portal into the unknown. A place where I’m constantly searching for answers and not always sure of the path forward. It’s not a comfortable feeling–not being certain of oneself. A younger version of me would never have voluntarily put himself in such a scenario. But as I have matured, I’ve begun to embrace the “not knowing.” Whether it’s exploring a new computer language or discovering how to play the oboe, the lessons I’ve gained from experimenting and failing are often more valuable than the solutions themselves.

Ironically, escape rooms have also given me a greater appreciation for my real-life experiences. Over time, I eventually began noticing that although I found deciphering the final clues intoxicating, any satisfaction I gained from completing a room successfully was fleeting. I was missing a sense of purpose. On the other hand, through my real-life achievements, I’m able to witness a tangible change in the world around me. Whether it be on one friend, my family, or entire communities, the positive influence I have the ability to impart differentiates the superficiality of escape rooms from my personal experiences.

The first time I played my clarinet at Kaiser Roseville Hospital, this sense of meaning struck me. Performing as a soloist among strangers, I felt nervous, unsure of the reception I would get. But as the sounds echoed through the hallways, I noticed people slowly gravitating towards me. Yet there was little applause after I finished a piece–they were preoccupied with more serious matters. I knew I couldn’t cure their illnesses, but their subtle head nods, foot taps, and relaxed sighs let me know that I was temporarily putting them at ease.

During every escape room adventure—where the unexpected becomes expected—I encounter many surprises. Plot twists that force me to adapt as I fight through the struggle and uncertainty. I’ve come to realize that in many ways, this is no different than the real-life challenges I face as I slowly piece together the clues to my own story. In my real-life escape room, I’m drawn to the experience’s most meaningful to me—where the successes are measured not by ostentatious awards or first place trophies, but by appreciative smiles and words of gratitude.

“School 58 News” influenced me far too much for a school news channel. Its namesake, started by the administration, had posted about students’ volleyball victories and exceptional USE scores. When the parody appeared, the anonymously run “rogue news channel,” it took the school by storm, sparing no one with its absurd, yet cleverly referential stories. I was captivated. Over the months that followed, the channel inspired me to question and to ignite change, to unite and to lead. I pored over every word, seeming just as captivated as my peers. Little did they know, I was the one fueling the fire from the shadows—I was the infamous founder.

It was the end of summer, and I was getting ready to stomach yet another year devoted to the Unified State Exam (USE), the national final exam and the single determinant of college admissions. I had moved from California at the age of ten, expecting the same array of opportunities I'd enjoyed back in San Francisco, only to find that the educational climate was as bleak as the urban tundra outside. “The purpose of school,” my math teacher summed it up, “is to study for the USE. Real learning begins in college.” However, the USE wasn’t the only burden.

Enter the “Important Conversations”: government-mandated propaganda lessons, targeting students from the first grade and up – our very own "Two Minutes Hate” from Orwell’s 1984, stretched to an hour for good measure. One day, as the cheerful robotic drone from the classroom TV informed us that “dying for the Motherland” was in fact “not scary” (and, evidently, something to strive towards), we decided that if we had to swallow their nonsense, we might as well dish out our own; at least it’d be entertaining. Luckily, the prime material for our stories swaggered through the halls every day.

For years we had cracked jokes about the “230”s – the school's muscle-bound disciplinarians named after their lair, room 230, a place so lavish it made most palaces look modest. With shimmering bald scalps, Herculean physiques, gold chains that could anchor ships, and a talent for delivering harsh reality checks, the men were perfect.

Our sleepless nights editing, rewriting, rephrasing soon began to pay off. After posting about how the skinny, cigar-smoking security guard Valera was gifted a new titanium baton (the last one, we claimed, had gotten bent during some 'educational encounters'), the channel exploded– soon, even the administration and 230s themselves became subscribers.

Our success only stoked my drive to create my own opportunities. As our subscriber count blew past 300, I forgot the USE entirely. Refusing to allow my curiosity to be stifled, I started pursuing my own education on online platforms like MITOpenCourseWare and KhanAcademy, deep diving into my favorite subjects like algorithmics and hardware design. Our small apartment lacked space for a lab, so I took a screwdriver to my dad’s closet – dismantling shelves and all – to make room for my first computational server and 3D printer. His socks and shirts found their new home in a plastic bag, but progress waits for no wardrobe.

My newfound skills materialized into gadgets aplenty—and sometimes unintended explosions and outages (sorry, Mom). After gathering some dedicated students, we started work on our channel’s most ambitious project yet: PavelKombat – a multiplayer game based on the popular game “HamsterKombat” – where players tap Pavel Sergeevich, the 230s' own colossus, to earn crypto. The complexity of the game was no match for our squad, with each member taking on key tasks.

This was a different “School 58 News”. As our masterpiece nears 400 subscribers (⅔ of our student count!) and PavelKombat nearing release, I've realized that the barren educational climate was the perfect breeding ground for creativity and change. Who knew that when life gives you "Important Conversations" praising senseless wars, the best response is to start more important conversations - preferably involving code, engineering, and the occasional dismantled closet.

“Guess who got the 500?!” my friend asked, rushing into the swim locker room. He had to be joking. But he wasn’t.

Seeing my name scribbled on the 500-lineup felt like I was being set up for my own embarrassing highlight film. I’m a sprinter. I swim 100s. Distance swimming wasn’t my strength, and to make matters worse, this race was against our biggest rivals. Why did Coach put me in this race? What if I burned out before the last lap? What if I forgot what lap I was on? I was immediately overcome with anxiety.

T-minus 3 days until the race. I thought of everything possible to avoid the 500. I could fake sickness, my mom could schedule a doctor's appointment, or I could not show up. T-minus 2 days until race time. Okay, so I’ll do the race. But what if I got lapped and did terribly? T-minus 1 day until the race. I decided to go through with the race and try my best—even if I embarrassed myself, I’d still complete the race successfully. I sat on this for a few days but ultimately decided to push past my fear of failure. Race day. I did it. I didn’t win, and maybe I still sped out too fast, but I powered through the last lap, ultimately beating out 8 other swimmers, and, in the process, I learned how to push through and do things that otherwise seemed impossible.

The 500 didn’t convince me to be a distance swimmer, but it did motivate me to step out of my comfort zone, something I’ve since taken outside of the pool, too. Last year, I decided to compete in my first coding competition as a total coding amateur. Over the course of the day, I struggled with both coding and web design, but I took this as a personal challenge—to push myself out of my comfort zone. My experience swimming the 500 made it a lot easier for me to push through and complete the competition. Fast forward to today. I’m the Business Liaison working with two other high school students to host our own hackathon. I’ve spent the past 2 months cold-calling potential venues and sponsors, facing possible rejection with each call. Despite my nerves about what questions they might ask or how I should respond. With each call, I was berated with questions, “What’s the expected turnout?”, “Why should we support you?” “How does this benefit us?” while I struggled to answer, I recalled my notes and preparations, eventually securing a venue and sponsors. Now, with over 30 signups, we’re excited for the event to begin on December 14.

This season, one day at practice, I heard the same, “Guess who got the 500?!” I turned around, but this time, it wasn’t aimed at me. A younger teammate rushed in with a look of worry on his face; It was his turn to swim the 500. I walked up to him and said, “I know how it feels; it's daunting and stressful, but you’ll do fine. You’re a good swimmer, and as long as you put in effort, you’ll do good.”

In other areas of my life—whether I’m tutoring one of my math students, helping a young kindergartener read his first chapter book, or teaching a young swimmer how to navigate the pounding ocean waves in junior lifeguards—I now never let any of the kids I mentor give up because of self-doubt or fear of failure. That’s the standard I set for them, and I want to always lead by example.

In my next chapter, I won’t shy away from uncomfortable situations but rather embrace them. Maybe I’ll play volleyball, try horseback riding, or even participate in a study-abroad program in Korea. Maybe I’ll pursue a challenging internship that seems beyond my current skill set, like doing investment banking. I’ve realized that I can miss out and lose opportunities if I let my fear take over. And I’ve decided not to let that happen and to instead always dive right in.

**The Endless Train Ride**

After traveling across the United States, flying back to the farthest northern part of Saudi Arabia where Tabuk is located, and finally arriving in Riyadh, I reached what was supposed to be the last destination of my migration. Only for an unexpected event to occur. Due to many aspects, my whole childhood felt like a train ride stopping at specific locations for a while and leaving for the next stop, leaving behind everything at the previous stop without any warning. Although hardships arose, I had to adapt to the different environments and make the most out of these ever-changing situations. Soon thereafter, independence emerged when I was obliged to understand my specific needs.

My sister Vayan was born with a rare condition called Fanconi Anemia which is an abnormal genetic disorder affecting bone marrow. During this time, my parents and I were living in America for them to complete their studies. I vividly remember the day of her birth; the sky was dark with rain pouring on the way to the flower shop as if a sign to my young, slow-witted mind that today was going to be the turning point of my whole life. When we arrived at the hospital, with the flowers still in my hand, my eyes widened as I saw that my first sibling looked different than I had imagined her to be. Even though my parents were smiling from ear to ear, I could still feel the anxiousness hovering in the room. I felt the pressure on my shoulders as the weight of responsibility for making my sister feel comfortable in her surroundings rapidly increased.

As the years passed, changing from one hospital to another, my sister’s condition eventually entered a state of stability. Over these years, I realized that since my parent’s full focus would always be on my sister, I shouldn't be a burden to them. Rather, I should depend totally on myself regarding all affairs, whether it was about school or even tying my own shoelaces. Moreover, my parents always praised me for being a quick learner, yet they were unaware of the source of this trait. When my sister’s doctor approved our request to move, my parents thought it was best that we came back to Saudi Arabia, their homeland. After staying in Tabuk for one year, we then moved to Riyadh. Riyadh was the city I felt most at ease in, probably because my mother’s family lived nearby and the city was huge with a busy, distracting environment.

However, this ease didn't last long. It was a Friday morning at my aunt’s house. I was watching TV peacefully as a shout emerged from a familiar voice: “We have to go to the hospital now!”. It was my mom screaming at the top of her lungs with a shake of panic in her voice along with the screaming. I jolted as I stood up, spilling the juice in my hand and bolted through the hallway to find my whole family surrounding my sister with drops of sweat sliding down their faces. It was then revealed that my sister had a new problem concerning her health and my parents were obliged to travel back to her hospital in America the next day. I thought our lives would finally be normal, but history began to repeat itself, just as it was in the beginning. I found myself alone once more, but this time was different as I consciously worked on developing my own sense of individuality.

My sister's condition impacted all of us, not just herself. Whenever she weakened, our family weakened with her as a whole. As of today, my sister is living a great life where she has accomplished the so-called impossible. My childhood hurdles led me to develop adaptation, responsibility, and independence. These qualities define me now, and I aim to enhance them further moving forward.

Sometimes the price of admission is a punch in the mouth. I was fourteen when I was invited to see an older schoolmate perform at The Crunch House, a grimy punk club just outside of the city. I stood alone against a sticky wall when a tall man with a short beard pressed a beer into my hand. It was unsettling—not just because of the satanic graffiti, the moshing, or the beer in my hand—but because this scene embodied everything I wanted but felt I couldn’t join.

I envied the free self-expression of those in the mosh pit as they threw their bodies around with reckless abandon. I saw freedom, community, and creative collaboration, but I avoided joining in, convinced that those who were carefree were actually being careless. I was out of place and afraid to get hurt. I was scared to pay the price of admission. I called my dad to come pick me up.

It took me over a year to build the courage to attend another show. This time, I had a plan. I invited my boyfriend Leo and my sibling Esther to a house show. Together, we stared down the tornado of Carhartt jackets, dyed hair, and flailing fists. Again, I stood paralyzed, feeling self-conscious and scared of getting hurt. With Leo and Esther behind me, I sought the resolve to lead us all into the tempest.

It had been a rough school year—learning jazz guitar from scratch because my teacher resigned, teaching myself geometry because teachers kept quitting, coping with “dysregulated” schoolmates, fights, lockdowns, tone-deaf SEL lessons, burnt-out teachers, oversized classes, and all manner of post-pandemic high school nonsense. Each school challenge felt like a punch I couldn’t avoid. At the edge of the pit, I was ready to exercise my choice. Stepping into the chaos was about me embracing the moment on my terms.

Pause. Inhale. Brace.

I pressed into the pit. I swirled in a cacophony of sweat and noise and I dissolved. I paid the price of admission, I took the punch in the mouth, and I was renewed. I was carefree. High school stress lifted. Moving in unison with this community was cathartic. All at once, I took space and yielded space. We danced through the night like a single organism, vulnerable and safe, together in the pit.

Today, I don’t just attend shows. I lead bands, sometimes sharing the stage with those same musicians I first saw at The Crunch House, and I record, engineer, produce, and publish music for local young musicians. My background in the arts has instilled a ‘rising tide lifts all boats’ mentality—when a player succeeds, the band succeeds; when the band succeeds, everybody wins.

Recently, I helped a new local folk artist, Leon Armstrong, bring his voice to life and publish his first works. He just started his first year of college and now carries with him the art we created together. Knowing I helped him achieve this gives me great satisfaction and further inspires me.

In my role as a producer, fellow musician, and mentor, I encouraged him to take his first steps into new territory. Into the pit. While some of my support came in the form of physical resources I’ve collected, most of it came from the creative resources I’ve cultivated. I was sensitive to Leon’s free self-expression—the very kind I once envied at The Crunch House and now nurture in others like him. More assured now, I balance attuning myself to an artist’s voice with integrating my own ideas. I am obsessed with building walls of sound—something crunchy and comforting, a mosh pit of noise that becomes a cocoon for something precious, beautiful, and delicate to emerge. And for those future collaborators with the courage to step up, I offer a punch in the mouth.

We worked in unison: Cut stalks. Gather bunches. Feed bunches into a grinder. Sieve debris from rice grains. Weigh harvested rice. Collect samples of rice grains for moisture content. Repeat. Following this system produced more than rice grains; it produced a synergy driving our entire team toiling together in the heart of a Javanese rice paddy. By the time the first break occurred, the team of 17 felt like family. Never mind that we were a diverse team of military soldiers, government officials, university professors, science researchers, rice farmers, and me, a high school student. We were bound by our shared interest: to discover why Indonesia cannot produce enough rice to feed the world’s fourth largest population of 250 million.

I found myself on this team due to my interest in plant science. After experimenting with Eco-Enzymes, a multipurpose liquid derived from organic waste that could recover plants, I felt a spark of hope as it gave me the opportunity to be a part of the growing movement toward sustainable practices in food systems. I sought to understand the problem more deeply, and I figured the only way I could understand my country’s difficulties in producing the staple diet of rice was by gathering research from the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI).

After multiple days of calling and no one answering, I drove to the office to meet Dr. Herta, the liaison scientist, who was going to leave in two days to conduct field research. She invited me to join her, and our initial bonding spread to all of the team members as I met each one during briefings, rides to the paddies, and in the fields.

Though young, I found myself capable of holding my own with the team as we approach agriculture differently: tradition vs modernity. Many of the farmers clung to the traditional belief that more fertilizer meant a higher yield and that chemical fertilizers are the best. Sharing my experiences with how the youth approached agriculture: using hydroponics and regulated fertilizer use specific to their needs rather than simply using more, helped to expand their knowledge of agriculture.

As I worked with the farmers, I learned to see the rice fields that stretch as far as the horizon as a vast laboratory unbound by the walls of my classroom. The tiny granules that I grind the rice into taught me a lesson in biology, the extrapolation of data revealing the effect of nitrogen and phosphorus on plant growth. Experiencing the toil of working in the field – the grittiness of soil on my hands, and the weight of carrying harvests – allowed me to recognize the enormous effort required to create a thriving environment for crops and made me realize that the very foundations of what made a successful food system was community: the rich amalgamation of ideas, the reconciliation of tradition and modernity and the collective efforts shared by a united goal.

As I step outside of the rice fields and back into the classroom, I embody what I learned there into my day-to-day life whether I am in a lab or a conference. Replicating the stress conditions that caused farmers’ yields to decrease allowed me to discover how Eco-Enzymes helped plants maintain an accelerated rate of growth, even under these challenging conditions. Moreover, the strong cultural ties held by the farmers helped me to formulate solutions that push for progress whilst still encouraging the local community to embrace their traditions. I plan to continue finding ways to integrate as much diversity in the ideas I present in spite of their seemingly contradicting natures. As a scientist, environmentalist, and altruist, I combine innovation, environmental consciousness and heritage to become a catalyst in propelling our food systems on a path of progress.

A map of Hong Kong is the newest addition to my family’s collection of maps. Although far from being the only map of Hong Kong in our collection, just shy of a hundred strong, it is much unlike the rest. It cannot fold into a neat rectangle, nor does it document Hong Kong in painstaking exactness. Instead, it was a map of my own: ownership by creation.

Mapmaking started as an intuitive habit—quick diagrams in my red diary, linking visitor hotspots to restaurants to hotels of different places I visited. These diagrams soon evolved into maps, the densely integrated characteristics of a place unwilling to be captured by a mere sketch.

Maps, like my understanding of myself, are full of contradictions. The very scrupulousness that is integral to mapmaking has to grapple with the reality that a map is, in essence, still a diagram. The dormancy of any map is at odds with the dynamic place attempts to represent. Just as maps blend precision with creativity, the mapmaker’s identity oscillates between an artist and a scientist. Initially, anguish and confusion came from the two seemingly contradictory identities within me. Much to my discontent, my only outlets for artistic expression during high school became quick doodles. Mapmaking became a testament to the coexistence of the scientist and the artist within me.

The map of Hong Kong started with the scientist in me: a command to capture the vivid details of Hong Kong’s geographies systematically: its waters, mountains, and streets. The scientist dives into research, ignoring the impatient artist dying to put pen to paper. Accustomed to the almost mandatory learning process of immaculate research, the scientist reached out to the Chinese Society of Geodesy Photogrammetry and Cartography to learn about the science of cartography and its methods. The scientist pours over governmental websites, existing maps, geographic information, and his own field notes. Armed with the technical foundation established by the scientist, the artist can finally start.

For that reason, my room transforms—mats laid out, furniture pushed aside, the pair’s cooperation can begin. Had the artist embarked on this endeavor alone, a scale would have been deemed unnecessary: “My instincts will never fail me!” Had the scientist also worked independently, a precise scale would have been needed: “All maps have a perfect scale!” An uneasy compromise saw a 1:38461 scale implemented (instead of the 1:[multiple of 1000] scales of “perfect” maps). Those long hours of research finally paid off when the locations from the scientist’s research found their correspondence on the canvas, pinpointing places of memories: Repulse Bay, the Hong Kong aviary, and Causeway Bay, among others. After bouts of triangulation, topological calculations, and contour lines, a locus of point in the set of “coastline of Hong Kong” forms. With each stroke of the pen, the unconquerable blankness of the paper lit up, a map complete.

Yet, even as the map appears “complete,” with all the features you’d expect from a map (minus the sea of minuscule labels), it remains “unfinished.” Lifeless is the map without my personal colors. My map is still uniquely mine to choose and discover.

Many maps made by yours truly have entered that ever-growing map collection since. Just as they conjure memories of past times, they also invite reflections upon my motivations for mapmaking. My inherent craving for an artistic outlet rooted in the mental organization of physical spaces is still there. Its harmonious coalescence of the seemingly inherent paradoxes of the scientist-artist complex within me encourages me to embrace my authentic self. I’ve reconciled my different identities in many other aspects: through my signature, I’ve integrated my different cultural and linguistic backgrounds; through my music, I fused creative improvisation with disciplined structures. By embracing these dualities, I empower my authentic self to pursue new experiences and embrace diversity. Although no “X” marks the “treasure” at the final destination of my maps, that is the way it is on the path to self-discovery.

Bathed in warm sunlight, I faced the computer screen with a daunting blank music sheet before me. This morning, against a backdrop of breakfast and free-spirited birdsong, I announced my intention to quit five-year-long piano lessons to pursue my own compositions.

Surprisingly, my parents agreed. Now, for the first time, I’ve stepped away from a structured path, and it’s overwhelming. Doubt crept in – was this the right decision? But I know that by deciphering a new way to enjoy music, my aspirations might carry me beyond the limits of lessons and repetition.

Slowly, I forget my worries. I hum softly to myself, experimenting with melodies, motif by motif, the notes swiftly dancing toward me, as if orchestrated by an unseen angel, gradually coming together. My mouse glides across the staff line, capturing the scene in musical notation. The melody started to take shape.

Months later, I find myself staring at another blank computer screen with empty coding space. Accepted into a six-week STEM project to build machine learning models predicting mental health outcomes, I had no experience with machine learning and only basic knowledge of Python. Immersed in the harsh glow of the monitor, I felt that familiar pang of doubt. How can I survive? Taking a deep breath to steel myself, I remind myself: “Machine learning is the future. So instead of wondering if I’ll fail, I should ask, ‘What if I succeed?’”

For the first two weeks, I spent hours grappling with machine learning algorithms, researching mental health studies, and following tutorials on installation and using Jupyter Notebook. Whenever I hit a snag, I tried to find the answer for myself. I felt too shy to ask my teammates, convinced I should know what they knew since we started at the same time.

The deadline approached, and the data felt overwhelming, with more than fifty variables to choose from for the models. Gathering my courage, I walked through the maze-like computer server room to find Eric, one of my teammates.

We were delighted to meet each other: I had made little progress with my code, whereas he was a Python expert trapped in a fruitless struggle over which variables to choose for the model. I shared my research findings on mental health, and he showed me data-cleaning Python tricks. Together, we broke down the complex symphony into manageable movements: data cleaning and re-categorization, model setup, results analysis, and model comparison. Piece by piece, the project took shape.

Before the deadline, we managed to implement three models for prediction. More importantly, by admitting that I didn’t know everything and seeking help from teammates, I opened myself up to a wealth of learning I hadn’t anticipated.

Each challenge we faced became a note in our collaborative score, our efforts harmonized like two melodies merging into one powerful symphony of knowledge and experience, transcending individual efforts toward a crescendo of success.

A year after that first sunny morning, I performed my composition, “Establishment,” with the bright lights of Vienna’s historic Ehrbar Hall washing over me. My piece concluded with the rhythmic pulse of a train. Like a train, I keep moving forward; unlike a train, I don’t stay on pre-designed tracks. Composing music has taught me a lot of solitary confidence and self-discovery, but the idea exchange in STEM projects was equally refreshing. Both were necessary and valuable to my growth.

Facing uncertainty is the only certainty. As I prepare for college, I look forward to more blank pages - some in libraries, where I’ll explore how machine learning can accelerate drug discovery; others in labs, collaborating on treatments for autism; and some in clubs, where I might fuse classical music with robotics. The journey of growth — whether through self-creativity or collaboration with other nonconformist thinkers — begins with a single, courageous mark.

"Just put it in The Box," I muttered, gripping the worn edge of my desk. It was late, but I stared blankly at the unfinished project due the next day. My mind was elsewhere, seeking refuge in the familiar place I had created years ago. The Box wasn't real, but it might as well have been. It was where I packed away everything I did not want to feel—anxiety, confusion, failure. I created The Box in elementary school after being told I would be switching schools, a tiny shift in the world that felt massive to me then. Each confusing emotion got packed away, labeled "For Later." Stored in neatly sealed mental compartments.

The Box was the easiest answer to everything. A bad grade? Into The Box. A missed opportunity? Sealed away. It worked—for me, but how do you compartmentalize someone else’s struggles?

"Do you ever feel like everything's just… too much?" a close friend asked one afternoon in seventh grade. She shared how overwhelmed she felt at school. It was the first time someone had confided in me like that. I was not prepared for this, yet I could not turn away. The Box had changed, its walls bending to feelings I could not ignore. I felt an urge to step outside of my internal world and be there for her.

Two years later, I discovered YouthLine, a teen crisis line, at the Beaverton volunteer fair. I was exploring opportunities to reconnect with my community as COVID restrictions eased. At fourteen, I was too young to join, and usually, I would label this "Too Intense" and put it in my Box. But instead, I held on to their pamphlet, not forgetting their mission. Something inside me had shifted. Four months and two interviews later, I spent my fifteenth birthday learning crisis intervention at YouthLine. I could not have imagined then how that small act—holding on to that pamphlet—would be the first crack in the walls of The Box.

At YouthLine, I began guiding others through the struggles I had once buried deep within The Box. With every "thank you" from a contact, a deeper realization settled in—growth comes from the very confrontation I had avoided.

That understanding was soon tested with a familiar chime—a sound echoing through my headset, triggering a practiced composure: "Hey! This is Avni with YouthLine. What's your name?" Silence. "Can you hear me alright?" After a moment, a soft yet resolute voice responded: "I'm holding a knife."

For nearly three hours, I guided the caller through their pain and guilt. I had handled difficult contacts before, but this one was different. One sentence lingered: "I called four other lines before you." Who did she call? Why didn't they answer? Instinctively, I wanted to label these "Unsolvable Problems" and tuck them away—but the lid of The Box remained stubbornly sealed.

It was not just about searching for answers anymore—it was about confronting the more profound issues they represented, one that required action beyond YouthLine. That drive for change led me to Congresswoman Andrea Salinas, a champion of mental health reform. Joining her campaign was not a political move—it was my push to solve the unsolvable. I was ready to tear down The Box and confront realities I once avoided. I was determined to create change rather than simply accept things as they were.

I see now that The Box was no sanctuary—it was a prison. It kept me from pain, but it also kept me from growth. YouthLine taught me that true progress begins with facing what we dread. The calls, the silences—they showed me that avoiding pain only deepens its roots. And in joining Congresswoman Salinas's campaign, I learned that change does not happen in isolation. I no longer retreat into the walls of The Box. I live beyond them, embracing purpose and action.

At my aunt's house for our usual weekend visit, I couldn’t take my eyes off her bulky 2000s-era laptop on the kitchen table. She mentioned paying a few hundred dollars for a Costco subscription “promotion.” I briefly scanned the email, noting the 200% size text and the suspicious sender address paired with an urgent "PAY NOW” message– all signs of a phishing scam. A wave of frustration flooded me. I failed to protect my aunt from the bugs that leeched her retirement savings.

Many of my Cantonese-speaking elderly relatives likely could not differentiate a scam from legitimate bank or services emails, particularly with their limited English proficiency. Staying current with ever-evolving online threats is a challenge, and for them, it was twice as hard. They are vulnerable not because of their age, but their lack of awareness of these scamming methods.

I analyzed examples of these scams and poured over anti-scam forums. Later, I shared my quest with family and friends, collecting 50+ examples from their inboxes. Many scams were obvious but others were so effectively disguised that I embarrassingly became a victim of a test phishing email at my summer internship.

Knowing that these "ah-sooks" (uncles) and "ah-pohs" (aunties) were already experienced with watching online videos, evident from the many YouTube videos they often talked about, I created Cantonese videos that were a combination of advice and walkthroughs of scams I had collected. I used short and simple scripts to guide them through visual examples, and recruited my parents for some complex translations of tech lingo. I shared these videos with my aunt and grandparents, and they circulated them in their many Whatsapp groups within the elderly community. Many replied stating the videos were genuinely helpful, others sent thank you messages. My grandparents felt more protected online. My aunt even told me I had helped regain her trust with emails.

In raising awareness about these scams, there was no way for me to squash all these scamming bugs alone. Rather, I equipped potential victims with their own flyswatters, just as I similarly guided my peers in identifying and squashing literal bugs in their code.

Through this experience, I realized that as much as "community" involvement often centers around volunteering at events to help strangers with food, clothing, or other needs, when I saw needs in my own family and sought to meet them it led to ripples of impact in the community as well. Valuing the impact I had on the elderly Cantonese-speaking community, my senses were tuned to look for more ways to foster access and equity in technology.

I had another opportunity this summer to foster awareness and access as I worked with my local city on a simulation project for a planned zoo. Although the plan had been officially announced, many in the community were not aware of the project’s scope and the awesome proposed design of a vivid and modern zoo.

As our team tirelessly detailed the 3D model and scripted prototype showcases, I raised the concern that this form of interactive simulation would be too complicated for some children and elderly people to use. They were the ones who were least likely to have seen the limited press releases about the current design of the zoo. To address that, I created a film that envisioned the proposed zoo in all its 3D ray-traced glory. When my film was played at a city hall meeting, applause erupted in the crowd. As I left the city hall, a family came out to thank me for making them aware of the zoo project.

Experiences like these remind me that joy comes in forms other than personal achievements. I find deep satisfaction in ensuring that everyone gets access to the safety and opportunities they deserve. I hope to continue using my skills to serve and care for those who are often ignored or under-resourced in society.

The sweltering summer morning heat radiated through the screen of my balcony, warming my back, while the cool air from my fridge brushed against my front. Scanning my fridge, I found what I needed: three brown eggs, a piece of green onion, a half clove of garlic, and three cherry tomatoes. Today, I thought, will be the day!

I grabbed my flower-adorned bowl, pulled out my cutting board, and started chopping. I quartered the cherry tomatoes, minced the garlic, and chopped the green onion.

After cracking the eggs into the bowl – no shell! – I added garlic, soy sauce, salt, and pepper. I heated the oil in a pan and waited.

***

After a while, I poured the egg mixture inside and watched as the outer portions began to set. Grabbing my chopsticks, I began to lift the egg off the pan, when a crack on the top left portion developed.

Oh no! I thought.

However, I realized that there was a fix to this. I tilted the pan to allow some of the uncooked egg mixture inside to spill over, mending the crack. Afterward, I placed the tomatoes and green onion on the left half of the omelet. I shimmied my chopsticks underneath the right side of the omelet and flipped it over.

***

As I bit into the omelet, a smile spread across my face. At last, I succeeded in making an omelet! Though not perfect or picturesque, it was tasty – and it was mine.

***

Buh-dum.

“Oh come on!” Noah exclaimed, frustration creeping into his voice. “We were so close!”

“Yeah, these last few bars need work.” I sighed, the recital was just a day away.

“How about this,” I suggested. “Let’s both mouth the beat as we play. Like this.” I flipped back to the last page of our duet and demonstrated, starting on the second-to-last bar.

“Hmm, let’s try that together,” Noah said, lifting his hands to the keys.

One, two, three, four… Bu-dum.

“Hmm… better!” I said, feeling a spark of optimism. “Let’s do it again!”

One, two, three, four… Buh-dum.

One, two, three, four… Bdum.

One, two, three, four… Dum.

We exchanged glances, smiles spreading across our faces. Finally, we had it.

***

At last, it was the day of the recital. We had rehearsed the challenging section earlier that morning, but I still felt a wave of nerves wash over me as I entered the dimly lit church.

As Noah and I reviewed our music one last time, we heard Mr. Cayre’s voice echo through the hall as he made introductory remarks for the recital.

We stood up, handing our music over to Jeff, our page-turner. We gave each other a quick nod of good luck and walked towards the piano.

***

As we performed the piece, we matched each other’s rhythm. Occasionally, my fingers slipped; occasionally, Noah’s fingers slipped. But regardless, we carried on, and, before we knew it, found ourselves at the end.

A glance; a nod.

One, two, three, four…

Duumm!

The G major chord rang out, and we smiled.

***

Success is not about perfection, but rather resilience and growth. Whether it’s salvaging a torn omelet or playing in sync with my duet partner, I’ve learned to find value and joy in the process, which I’ll take with me for the rest of my life.

Flayed skin. Ruptured inside. Over-ripe flesh. CPR could not save the dying cherry tomato! Left on the shelves to rot…they were undesirable. Some people like their tomatoes in sauce, some like them raw in salads, but nobody likes them bruised.

At Food4Health, an organization run by The Hartford Hospital, where I volunteer, we promise to get nutrients to the people who need them. Geriatric patients, diabetics, and the malnourished can all pick the produce they choose at no charge. Why should all these people lose out on cherry tomatoes filled with Vitamin A, C, iron, and chock-full of potassium?

The problem with our cherry tomato supply was how long it took to ship. While the firm onions or the tightly packed jalapenos could endure the ride from the farms in big cardboard boxes, the delicate cherry tomatoes, constantly bouncing around, succumbed to their injuries by the time they arrived.

An idea crept into my thoughts when I saw PVC pipes, buckets, and seeds all in the same dirty closet.

I had found the spot for my makeshift garden. The rooftop promised me the highest yield of tomatoes. I started poking thick holes on the walls of the plastic pipes, and placed small cups containing a plotted tomato seed. After two weeks of diligent care, my eyes only saw dying seedlings instead. The soil turned out to be the silent killer-inhibiting the plant's root size, subsequently limiting the water intake. At this time I remembered the words of my ninth-grade science teacher Ms. Highland, who plotted pea plants with us in plastic bags to prove that soil is not necessary, just proper nutrition, formally dubbed hydroponics.

I scoured the internet for a solution. I watched podcasts from Garden Talk with Mr. Grow It, YouTube videos from The Millennial Gardener, and random gardening videos suitable for my grandma's facebook feed. After much research, I found the ingredients to make Food4Health proud of our cherry tomatoes again. Epsom salt and calcium for nutrients, limestone to balance the pH, and manure for its high NO₂ concentration. I found these items in the greenhouse, lying in a dusty plastic crate. The results showed themselves in two months when I bore the fruits of my labor (yes, tomatoes are fruit!) and tasted my sweet victory.

Sitting in the cold, misty office with a basket of my love, I offered them to anyone who dared walk through the doors. Bombarded with my pleading, all accepted, placing the plump fruit in their mouths while their eyes lightened up joyfully. I would urge them to take as many as they wanted while filling their cart with farm-fresh eggs, whole-fat milk, lean ground meat, and anything their hearts desired.

I would be lying if I said the epitome of this experience was the sharp, umami flavor of the tomatoes. It was not. Seeing people come in bruised and firm up with joy brought me immense satisfaction as their lips softened into a ripe smile after trying my cherry tomatoes.

This feeling gave me a high that I pursued to no avail until I discovered Tutoring Chicago, an organization aimed at providing brighter futures for the underserved children in Chicago. I started tutoring Amira, a 7-year-old Pakistani immigrant living with her single mom on the south side of Chicago. I oversaw her journey from being unable to spell becuz to completing the Magic Tree House series. Her laughs after spelling a new word or finishing a book reminded me of the joy associated with eating a perfectly ripe cherry tomato.

I often think back to my garden of cherry tomatoes to remember the start of my unquenchable thirst to give. While I am allowed to become a bystander to the philosophies I care about, I opt to create a two-way street of love, build meaningful connections, and chase a goal paying little attention to the struggles that come on the way.

When my mom came home with her breast cancer diagnosis, my first instinct was panic. Throughout my life, I had always relied on her strength to guide me, but this sudden shift in positions before the start of my junior year felt as if it was the end of the world. Only now, as I look back on this trying time, I understand that this experience was the push I needed to break free from my dependence on others.

My mother had always been my beacon of virtue, but seeing her break down as she clutched her diagnosis made me realize that it was now my responsibility to provide for her. As a result, I felt a sense of duty to support my family as much as possible during the course of her treatments.

Coming from a family of only three people, with my dad working, I realized just how much my mother sacrificed on a daily basis. Not even the first day passed before I had scrambled home after practice, made dinner, only to find that I had completely forgotten to study for a test the next morning. Day in, day out, the absolute mess I made of these first couple of weeks of my mother’s treatment only served to help me fully recognize my dependence on her. During this period, I felt such a sense of helplessness that there seemed to be no way I would be able to handle the responsibility given to me. Errands like the prospect of having to pay for my own credit card bills seemed insurmountable, causing me to stare at piles of paperwork and assignments, wondering if I would ever be able to finish it all.

However, with each small success, whether it be a scheduled appointment or another day without a disaster, I gradually adapted to the shift in responsibilities. The independence I gained from supporting my family began to feel ever more empowering. As the days went on, this independence allowed for me to come to the realization that I no longer needed my parents' help with every little thing in my life. Eventually, my perspective shifted, the positive nature I buried for so long because of my stress began to show itself again. I was able to organize my time effectively, with the chores becoming a way of contributing to my moms recovery. Each doctor’s visit and pharmacy run became a small victory in my mother’s battle, a step forward in both her journey and my personal growth.

Despite all the difficulties, my mothers treatment concluded quickly, and through it I had found independence and maturity in myself that I never knew I had. Though, looking back, there was never a risk of losing my mother, her illness became a monumental influence on my self-development. A year later, I find that it's important to spend as much time with her and my family as possible. Whether it is waking up just slightly earlier to cook a quick breakfast or going to a park so that she can get some fresh air, every extra task checked off becomes a testament to the importance of not only relying on myself but also being a source of strength for others. Even though my mom has returned to being a guiding force in my life, I now take ownership over both minor and major decisions in my life. The tasks that had seemed so tedious before now act as motivation to stay positive and cherish what I have, acutely aware of how fast life can change. Going into junior year, there was always the assumption that it would be my most difficult year of high school. However, through my experiences, it became the most rewarding year of my life, as it marked a personal transition into accepting the responsibilities that adulthood brings.

“I’m not letting you race this Saturday because you don’t show enough emotion.”

Coach Barb’s words stung me as I sat beside her during practice, contemplating the year and a half I’d spent coxing.

Did I throw myself too far out of my comfort zone? I’m someone who would rather spend a day reading the “Tiny Love Stories” section of the New York Times than scream my head off at Six Flags with my friends. After Coach Barb’s criticism, I wondered: Did I really have the potential to be a good coxswain given my naturally quiet disposition?

I reminded myself why I’d joined crew in the first place: it was to escape the swim team, but more importantly, I wanted to develop my assertiveness, and above all, courage, both through my voice and actions.

So, for the remainder of the fall, I asked my friends for suggestions after each practice. As soon as I opened myself up to more criticism, Sylvania mentioned she wanted me to be harsher when talking to her and to tell her what place we were in, while Ophelia asked for an incentive/threat during a race. So the next week, I told them that they would have to row a grueling 2k in practice if they slacked.

As winter term began, I practiced talking in front of a mirror and yelling at my obliging family, incorporating the suggestions from my rowers. I made a mental list of every area I wanted to work on, such as using an expanded vocal range when talking, timing my words with each stroke, and using my choir experience to crescendo during heated moments. Watching Youtube videos of coxswains slowly became my favorite procrastination strategy. I would also repeatedly listen to my friends’ favorite coxswain recordings, including one where the coxswain repeatedly yelled, “Let’s get to nationals!” and described the team getting on a plane to Sarasota.

When springtime came and Coach Barb and I met to discuss my coxswain recording during practice, she remarked, “I love how you got so excited during that last hundred. None of the other coxswains showed this much emotion while rowing.” I beamed, knowing that all the pain and toil these months had been worth it.

In addition to helping me (literally) find my voice, being a coxswain has helped me grow in my ability to bring individuals together.

As I start my senior season in the fall, I confidently articulate my expectations for the rowers as they row around the lake. As we start the race, I tell them the story of a stroke: “Reach out and catch, lock the blade in, and drive with your legs. Use your lats to keep your body forward. Then swing your body, then arms, and relax out of the finish.” I emphasize ratio and relaxing on the recovery every few strokes while urging them to swing and suspend, reminding them of their favorite “butt-off-the-seat drill.” While encroaching upon a boat ahead of us, I would yell, “Oh my gosh, I’m at the bow of Izzy’s boat! Now I’m at Emily! Now Sarah!” Finally, as we push towards the finish line, I culminate with the line I had rehearsed repeatedly - in the mirror to myself, and shouting to my parents’ after dinner as practice: “Last 10 here! Come on, guys!! Jump HERE and drive!”

And one day after a power piece, Coach Barb once again remarked, “[Name], you had them flowing together so well out there!” I know that the momentum that I helped build in the boat will carry me through college and beyond.

I hate the letter “S.” Or so I thought; see, in my life, “S” stands for soup. Always served following dinner, the mixture of bones, meat, and ingredients I can’t even begin to distinguish has been persistently praised by my mom for its ability to cure anything and everything. Sore throat? Soup. Broken leg? Probably still soup. I am almost certain that if I ever get into a car accident, my mom will come running frantically with, you guessed it, soup. Helpful, I know. Yet, despite everything, I’ve never had the same tolerance for my watery rivals. However, built on decades of tradition––or so I’ve been told––our family has always had dinner with soup. I, unlike my mom, am not fond of these traditions.

So, I tried to break free.

But how? How could I give her a reason to abandon, what was to her, the elixir of life? I thought back to all my hours researching cancer treatments for my dad: I learned best, not when I knew the solution, but when I sought out the process myself. If I could understand soup, I could create a much better alternative.

So, I turned to what I knew best: the web. Scavenging again across platforms like Quora, PubMed, YouTube, and even Reddit, I was no longer grappling with tradition but science. Instead, I devoted hours exploring recipes, studying how ginseng and radish—much like my mom and I—clash and cancel each other out. I became dumbfounded at how traditional cooking methods like decoction extracted essential vitamins from seeds and leaves and infused them into soups. I even found out my mom still uses the same wok and pot she first bought in America—now a concern of mine. But surrounded by papers and websites that all seemed to oppose my stand, I began to piece together the looming truth that I had tried to avoid all along: I had no reason to reject soup.

But yet, to solve my problem, I just had to simply watch.

Instead of taking action, I periodically took notes. In those recipes, ingredients, and techniques, my mom’s dedication taught me what Google simply couldn’t. As I paid more attention than ever before, one ingredient began to stand out: soy sauce, and by association, sodium. Scrambling back to my research, it all made sense. My mom’s unwavering recipes could be the culprit to hypertension—a condition that has also persisted in my family for decades. Surely a coincidence…

But simply telling my mom wouldn’t be enough. She needed confirmation to believe it, and after a couple of weeks of bothering her for “checkups”, I gave her one. I spent those weekday nights in classes training to become an EMT and many more practicing to take a blood pressure. After all, I already lost one to health, I couldn’t risk losing the other. And from reading all those studies, papers, and experiments, I sought out to design my own. Armed with my stethoscope, cuff, naive optimism, and weeks of tracking, the results were hard to ignore. The two-week intervals she would stay off soup were correlated to a much lower blood pressure.

Over time, our arguments over other traditions have become the hallmark of our household, transforming ordinary dinners into battlegrounds. One by one, this created a tradition itself. It was in these moments that I realized it was never about who was right or wrong—that was never the point. For her, soup was the only tether back to her humble beginnings in Shenzhen— the place she had left for more opportunities. For me, an challenge that has left me with a love for learning. We’ve worked together to alter the recipes, less oil here, more scallions there, using more research to spearhead these efforts. Today, we still drink soup—albeit a lot less often—and as I’ve learned, tradition and science aren’t all that different.

I am the number one loser. Despite countless hours of practicing volleyball spikes in the scorching sun, or all the meet-ups at the dirty local KFC to develop the perfect business plan for a contest, I’ve always found myself in second place—a silver medalist in a world ruled by gold—a Silver Boy.

In college admissions, gold naturally takes the spotlight. Spotless and shiny, it catches the eyes of onlookers and goes promptly to the highest bidder. In a market looking for gold, my silver never seemed to sell all that well. Even if my soccer team worked twice as hard, our efforts weren’t enough to beat the older, more experienced team. If I studied Japanese for 12 hours a day, I could never reach that acclaimed first place in the school ranking.

Yet, just like silver requires time and care to shine, I began to see that failure wasn’t the end—it was just a refining process. My silver wasn’t flawed, it just hadn’t reached its shiniest potential.

Frustration isn’t a barrier; it’s like a silver wire, conducting energy toward improvement.

With my silver-connected engine, I entered my “Silver Years.” High School was unforgettable in many ways. I moved from Brazil to Japan, learned Japanese in one year, fundraised for Ukrainian students fleeing the war, and even led a team to win a themed research contest. Some gold started popping up, and I didn’t feel dull, unpolished silver anymore; I began to feel more like a 1:1 scale silver Pietà from Michelangelo.

Even as I polished my skills, setbacks still blotted my progress—after all, silver is always prone to oxidation. In junior year, my volleyball team went undefeated until the final, where the strong serves of the opponent team completely obliterated us. Or when my friends and I spent hours at that KFC inhaling fried chicken air, conceptualizing, preparing logistics, and coding an app for a virtual cafeteria for my school as part of our business contest project. If we won, we would receive the budget to finalize our idea, but our hopes were cut short when another team had a better idea and won the competition.

I took my silver medals and got to work. I practiced volleyball with college students every Friday night, honing powerful serves and quick spikes. This training arc allowed me to improve and rise victorious in the tournament in my senior year, even being elected the championship MVP by other people participating. Additionally, the same friends who spent several weekends at that KFC and I conducted our own Hot Dog Kiosk, where we used Joey Chestnut’s and SDGs’ (Sustainable Development Goals) principles to sell vegetarian hot dogs to help our planet and reduce CO2 emissions. We sold out in two days. Those same silver medals turned from failures to learnings. Maybe silver isn’t so bad after all.

I now write this essay as a silver medalist. Last year, due to financial reasons, I couldn’t go to college. I realize now that these adversities come into our lives to teach us what we must learn, and I am ready to take the next step in my education. I spent this last year improving myself, exploring the world, receiving college grants and even getting a job at the airport to save money for college. From the fall of 2025, I hope to share all my crazy adventures with all my peers.

I may not have an internship with the president, but I assure you I will give it all to shake their hand one day. I may not be a New York Times best-seller, but I am determined to write as many books as I need until I get it right.

In a world ruled by gold, I choose to be myself—the Silver Boy.

The moment they announced my name as the winner felt like fiction. It was my first hackathon, and the world's edges had gone blurry. The room was full of seasoned hackers, each seemingly brimming with confidence and experience. Despite my passion for programming, there lingered a paralyzing fear that I didn’t belong here. Throughout the day, I overheard wisps of technical jargon permeating the air, making me feel like I was in the middle of a NASA space launch. I doubted my code was good enough. Yet, here I was, standing at the winner's podium, taking photos and accepting my prize at the AstroHacks Hackathon for Best Execution.

After winning, I returned to the Academy of Technology, Art, and Music (ATAM), where I work as an instructor to guide middle school students on coding projects. One student asked me how to recreate a bandit attack from his favorite anime, One Piece, in Roblox Studio. So, I walked him through the process of using the mathematical dot product of vectors to calculate collisions, a technique that I use in my own projects, such as when I created a zombie attack for a horror game.

Helping him navigate this challenge reminded me of the struggles I faced at my first hackathon and how essential it is to foster learning through a collaborative environment. I realized how daunting the steep learning curve of programming can be when you're a beginner without a community. I wanted to make learning accessible and transform the intimidating process of computers into something collaborative, creative, and fun.

I knew the best way to make others excited about programming would be through a collaborative hackathon. Unlike individual projects at ATAM, hackathons bring people together to tackle unique and fun challenges, fostering creative problem-solving and exposing students to diverse ideas and approaches. This collaborative environment builds confidence, helps students learn from each other, and sparks innovation in ways that isolated work often can't. Inspired by this, I decided to organize my own hackathon.

Initially, I underestimated how complex the process would be: venues were challenging to come by and expensive, dwarfing the funds I had raised so far. Eventually, I secured a local church as a venue, but the cost exhausted nearly all of my resources. This left me at a crossroads: either proceed with limited resources or delay the event to allow more time to gather the necessary funds. I felt a wave of disappointment wash over me, but I quickly realized that I had the support of the hacking community to help my hackathon succeed.

I consulted with an advisor from the Hack Club, who told me that postponing would allow me to ensure the event's success rather than risk compromising it due to a lack of resources. I knew postponing the hackathon would be worth it. Since then, I've been working with my school's booster club to raise funds, registered as a non-profit with the Hack Club Foundation to access additional sponsorships, and reached out to Hack Club-affiliated companies to secure merchandise and prizes for the event. The entire process—each call, each email—has been a lesson in patience and persistence, but the revamped website, booster club funding, and support from the hacking community have made me unexplainably excited. I even told the students at ATAM, and they are just as excited as I am. Coding needs to be more accessible to people from all walks of life because it is individual creativity that will effect the most meaningful change.

Whether working on my own coding projects, guiding students at ATAM, or collaborating to create an inclusive hackathon, I've learned that programming is more than just writing code: it's a tool for creative expression and creating community. As I move forward, I'm more determined than ever to help others transform fear and isolation into excitement and opportunity, fostering an environment where they can bring their ideas to life.

Mic check... Mic check. Welcome back to Carreira na Real, the podcast where we dive into the minds of entrepreneurs and economists, uncovering the stories behind their success. But today, I’m flipping the script. Instead of asking the questions, I’m here to share my own story – one that began not in a classroom, but on a hot soccer field in Miami.

“Gollllll! Great job, Leo!” My dad’s voice rang out as I scored the winning goal. The rush of victory filled me, the same rush I’d felt for years. But in a heartbeat—literally—everything changed. The cheers faded, a sharp pain shot through my chest, and suddenly, the game, my triumph, didn’t matter.

I made my way to my mom, gasping, “Mom, my chest hurts.” Her eyes widened as she felt my racing heart, and before I knew it, we were in the hospital. The last thing I saw was the monitor flashing “248 BPM” before everything went black.

I was just 11 years old, new to Florida, and barely spoke English. Yet, in those uncertain days, kindness transcended language. My teammates, kids I had only met, visited me in the hospital. The real victory wasn't on the field – it was in the hearts that showed up for me. They proved that community isn’t built on words—it’s built on taking action, inclusion, and solidarity.

In my current projects, these values remain core to everything I do. As Student Council President, I learned that initiative is essential to success in leadership. One of the biggest challenges was addressing widespread complaints about the snack bar. So, I created a Google Form to gather feedback from the entire student body, ensuring everyone’s voice was heard. This not only solved the issue but reinforced the importance of action and inclusivity. However, my initiative in StuCo goes beyond just problem-solving. I also invented the fan-favorite event, the Interclasses – a futsal class competition that brings the entire school together to cheer for their teams, fostering school spirit and unity.

But again, community isn’t just about action – it requires inclusion. In Student Council, I prioritize making sure every officer, regardless of the grade, feels involved. I lead meetings through questions, ensuring even shy members have a voice.

One of my most memorable experiences was during the 7th grade fun night, where I met Pedro. He stood alone, visibly shy. I approached him, and although he seemed uncomfortable at first when I asked about his interests and goals, he soon began to open up. After a meaningful 20-minute conversation, Pedro felt comfortable enough to join the others. Later, he thanked me for our talk, turning what began as a simple act of inclusion into a moment that fostered a new friendship.

The final pillar is solidarity, which I embraced through my work in the National Honor Society. In my project, I chose to focus on an often-overlooked issue: menstrual equity. My mom mentioned how many girls miss school because they lack access to menstrual products, and that insight inspired me to take action. We not only organized a donation drive but also worked to educate the community about this issue. As a result, we collected over 1,100 menstruation products, creating 126 kits for women in Paraisópolis, São Paulo. This experience taught me that solidarity isn’t just about giving – it’s also about educating and empowering others to make a difference.

My chest healed, but the lessons stayed in my heart. Life, much like business, throws unexpected challenges, but it’s how we respond to them that defines who we are. Whether it’s organizing a futsal tournament, resolving issues in Student Council, or fighting for menstruation equity, I’ve learned that true leadership is about taking action, inclusion, and solidarity. These are the same principles that guide the entrepreneurs and leaders I interview on Carreira na Real – those who transform setbacks into opportunities, who understand that success isn't just personal, it's collective.

I know all the languages! or at least that's what I thought. I grew up in a household where my mother spoke to me in an eastern accent, my father used words unique to the western region, and I mixed these accents into flawless sentences that everyone understood. This unique blend of accents served a rhythmic sound that made me feel at home. I often extended this feeling wherever I went through Arabic accents. But everything changed when I moved from a national school to an international one in middle school.

On my first day, I was approached by a group of students. They burst into laughter when I introduced myself: “Me name is [Name].” Later, my instinct to write equations in Arabic numerals from right to left during math class drew confused looks from my classmates. During lunch, the walls of language blocked me as I tried to interact with others. By the end of the day, the language specialists called me in, clearly as helpless as I was: I couldn't explain myself, and even the after-school English classes felt impossible. School made me feel like a foreigner: isolated, disconnected, and desperate for the sense of belonging I had once taken for granted.

Determined to change, I took upon myself to learn English by switching my entertaining sources to english. I first started by removing Arabic subtitles when watching TV shows and replacing my book collection of the “Diary of a Wimpy Kid” with the English version. By the second week, I began to understand conversations in class. I felt a glimmer of hope when I fully understood a story our teacher read out loud. But when it came to answering questions in math, fear gripped me. I knew the answers but couldn't raise my hand, afraid of being laughed at for my broken English. Although ideas were clear to me, framing it into understandable English sentences was seemingly impossible.

I realized that merely switching sources of entertainment to improve my English was not enough, and I hesitated to express it. This realization drove me to face my fear: speaking english. I sat in front, my fingers gripping the desk, ready to participate. The teacher asked a question; my hands shot up, though fear swirls through my hands. “The answer is…” my voice sutters, though I still fight. Although my sentence was broken, the teacher nodded as I got the correct answer. This became my routine. With each week passing by, my words began to flow, and fear started to fade away.

Everything was going well until I was faced with my biggest fear: history class final presentation. We had to summarize a chapter for the entire class period. Struggling with formulating short sentences, it felt impossible. So I decided to memorize a script. But when I stood in front of the class, I froze. Unabling to recall the script, I decided to improvise. I expected laughter, but as I moved from slide to slide, no one laughed; they were showing interest. When I finished, the class erupted in applause. For the first time in school, I felt at home. A week later, the teacher announced the grades for the presentation. I knew I had done well, but I still didn’t expect a high score. As he went through the names one by one, I anxiously waited for mine. Finally, he said, “[Name] Alhussaini, 99/100.” It was the highest score in the class.

My grandmother’s door creaking open at 5 a.m. filled me with dread. I silently raced to change my soaked sheets before anyone noticed. For years, mornings started this way and evenings ended with no water after 4 pm. While others rode bikes, I tried mastering dry bed sheets—it took me almost 14 years. A doctor’s consult for severe headaches revealed dehydration and stress. Not drinking enough water was leading to headaches, and stress and anxiety were causing my bedwetting.

This revelation hit me hard. Bedwetting went from an unexplainable physical challenge to the stress of meeting expectations. I was often told what to wear, how to behave, and even what I should aspire to. My parents held on to traditions such as making me wear bangles and a bindi every day, symbols I did not resonate with. My self-expression was suffocated. I understood that it was not simply about keeping my sheets dry—I was attempting to meet expectations that did not align with who I was.

Deciding to face my challenges by slowly pushing back was my turning point. Communicating to my parents that wearing bangles and a bindi every day made me uncomfortable was a difficult conversation, marred further by initial misunderstandings. It taught me to express my feelings calmly and empathetically. We reached a compromise: I would wear them to family gatherings and occasions, but not daily. My voice was heard for the first time.

As I grew aware of how stress shaped my actions, I started observing it in others. While volunteering at the Rural Development Trust school to teach English to blind students from grades 6-10, I met children struggling with their fears. Most came from backgrounds associated with poverty or disability and were trapped between tradition and unrealistic aspirations shaped by exaggerated cinema. Latha, one of my mentees, had a sharp mind and a quiet determination. She confided in me about her dream to study law, but her parents, challenged with raising a blind child in a traditional village, decided that she would not even finish school. Latha’s disappointment reminded me of my helplessness when others decided what I could or could not achieve. I proposed introducing a screen-reading software to help students like Latha study independently. Subsequently, I helped Latha use it confidently. Watching her overcome her hesitation proved that leadership is more than solving problems—it’s about empowering others to believe in their abilities. I saw a reflection of my own journey. Helping her grow gave me a deeper understanding of the impact that compassionate leadership can have.

Persevering to have my perspective heard taught me that nothing was insurmountable. Basketball seemed that way when I was 14. My sudden interest in basketball was driven by the stubborn determination that helped me overcome bedwetting. If I could conquer that, why not a sport? Surprisingly, I found teamwork easier than anticipated given my habit of struggling alone. Everyone’s goals aligned: improvement, contribution, and victory. By focusing on steady improvement and teamwork, we grew and medalled at the ISSO Cup. It was the collective effort and upliftment that led to our success, a lesson that mirrored my own personal growth. This was not a big breakthrough cinematic moment but the result of quiet hours spent piecing things together.

Overcoming bedwetting taught me that addressing the root of a challenge—whether fear, anxiety, or doubt—can spark change. This reshaped how I navigate challenges, helping me understand both myself and others better. I no longer live in fear of what I cannot control and now seek to help others find their own strength. My journey from a passive observer of my life to an active contributor in the lives of others became the foundation for my growth. What I learned in overcoming bedwetting became the bedrock for my success, and I’m determined to use this compassionate leadership to drive change in the communities I serve.

My mind raced like the intricate motions of a butterfly knife. It flipped open one thought, sliced into another, rolled, lingering on a final thought before snapping shut, eager to spin again. But before I started another trick, I paused and thought, coming to the realization that I discovered a new fundamental law of the universe. Not one that wins Nobel Prizes or even applies to most people, but one that defines me: I am always moving.

Whether it’s my hands fidgeting with a random scrap of paper or thoughts racing through my mind, it was always true that adding the movement in my hands and mind will always sum to some positive constant. But I hated this part of myself back then, because it was always defined by distracted thought spirals during a critical test, teachers telling me to “sit properly,” and friends telling me I'm “somewhere on the spectrum.” So I fought it at first, keeping it all in my mind.

But one day, I saw a butterfly knife in a video game, and it was mesmerizing. The precise, rhythmic motion made me want to learn it myself. I began learning not just butterfly knives, but many other hobbies that allowed me to move my hands. Penspinning, flipping a coin on my fingers, cardistry, and begleri, a Greek skill toy made up of 2 beads on the ends of a string. These small hobbies brought balance back to the equation as the constant was split again between my hands and mind.

As I was searching for a new balisong trick video, a different video caught my eye. “852 HZ” with the caption “Did the internal monologue go silent for you too?” Curious, I clicked play, and after a minute, I was surrounded by a silence I’d never felt. The internal monologue that had been running inside my head for years had stopped. Yet despite the silence I thought I craved, I started freaking out. My movement no longer summed to the constant. My universal law was broken. And as I panicked in silence, I realized how much this law was a part of me.

While my need to move my hands brought balisongs, belgeri, and all my other random hobbies I adore into my life, the constant thought fueled my curiosity of new topics. I remembered how the tinkering aspect of my movement led me to turn keyboards into a true obsession after I stumbled across a forum about custom mechanical keyboards. Then limited by the designs of other people, my constant thought drove my curiosity to create my own unique keyboard PCB, diving into Ergogen and KiCad, and spending countless nights on YouTube tutorials and documentations learning each step to eventually successfully create a unique split Steno pcb. I remembered a funny scene between me and my friends from math competitions. 'You guys ever think about quarks?' I blurted out randomly during a group study session. After some laughs and a little bit of discussion, they were interested as well. We spent afternoons Googling Cherenkov radiation and making sense of equations about pion decay. We'd chaotically collaborate on Google Docs to note down all the different topics, trying to wrap our minds around subatomic chaos. Working on particle physics with my friends wasn’t just about the concepts; it taught me to embrace different perspectives, and approach each challenge as a team. And additionally, it showed me how expressing this aspect of myself could lead to valuable moments or even grow into a project like this. So as I tried desperately to revive the voice in my head, I decided I would stop caring which side of the equation I would reside on and accept this law with all of the downsides so it could continue to drive me to new places.

So now, when I see 3 pens on my friend's desk, and am curious of what their clicks feel and sound like, I don't hesitate to check. And when they laugh at the randomness of my actions, I laugh along with them knowing the randomness was not a bad thing, but was unapologetically me.

Forty-four kneads later, the mixture of flour, water, and salt comes together to form a smooth, elastic dough. Now, I’ll let the dough rise and then bake it at 450°F.

It all started with the YouTube video “The Perfect Sourdough Bread Recipe.” I was astonished to see how combining just flour, salt, and water could produce such a beautiful loaf. Easy enough, I figured, right? Wrong. On my third attempt: a flavorless, grainy loaf; on my fifth: unevenly scattered air pockets; and on my seventh: an impenetrable crust, and so much tang my mouth puckered—a product far from the beautiful loaf of my dreams. Week after week, the supposed simplicity of the process continued to yield unpredictable variations of a failed loaf.

In a bid to solve my failed attempts, I searched dozens of cookbooks, blogs, and videos. Perhaps the “No Knead Sourdough” would work—it did not. The autolyse method seemed promising, yet that didn’t work either. The simplicity I found in the step-by-step recipes of cookies, cakes, and brownies through my journey was nowhere to be found. Sourdough was my greatest rival, and what I learned to be full of opportunities for missteps and a deceivingly simple process layered with complexities.

When dozens of new recipes failed, I shifted my focus from seeking new recipes to using my failures to understand the breadmaking process.
