The pungent sour flavor I loathed guided me to explore the intricacies of the fermentation process. It turns out, not using colder temperatures of water to adjust for the humidity of my environment will cause my dough to over-ferment. The persistent gummy texture of my bread prompted me to investigate shaping a boule. It turns out, creating too much surface tension by pulling the outer layer of my dough too tight compromises the gluten structure, resulting in a flat, rock-hard lump.

By seeking an understanding of my failures, I gained an understanding of the small details hidden in the layers of complexity within my bread, fitting them together like a puzzle. As I worked my way through two 50 pound bags of 00 flour mountains of discarded starter, and, of course, more failures in which I used as a guiding light to discern the subtleties of the breadmaking process, at last, I mastered the art of sourdough.

Through unlocking sourdough’s secrets, I gained more than just bread. My quest to fix my sourdough made me realize that the answers didn’t lie in seeking the easy solutions, hoping to quickly solve the innumerable issues of my sourdough, but in embracing the failures, which revealed the subtle differences intertwined in the layers of complexity of the breadmaking process.

Much like adjusting the recipe for the right outcome, I embraced each failed grant proposal at Finclusion as a chance to seek the nuances of our proposal to improve upon, whether through quantifying our need statement or conducting interviews with past participants to exhibit our progress. To correct my speech impediment, I practiced, failed, and reflected on until I achieved the accurate pronunciation for the first time. Then, I practiced hundreds of more times, embracing each failure as an opportunity to identify subtle differences in my pronunciation to improve upon, until I ultimately tested out of the speech therapy program. As a tutor, I find the subtleties to adapt my teaching style to. Here’s a refined version of your sentence. When a student struggles to grasp a concept, I ask questions and analyze their responses to understand how I can adapt subtle details of my teaching style to adapt to my student’s learning needs.

As I continue to share my constantly improving golden brown-crusted sourdough with others, I look forward to seeing where the subtle differences bread has ingrained in me will take me.

“Jason, *please* pay attention!” Exasperated, I stared expectantly at the restless first-grader. He swiveled toward me, his face contorted into a defiant pout. Suddenly, he flung his finger at the open page, yelping, “*Ewww*, they *kiss*!”

“The picture’s showing how much Mama Bear loves her baby,” I replied, straining to contain my irritation. “Doesn’t your mom kiss you goodnight?” Jason shook his head vehemently. “She hugs you, then?”

Jason’s face was a brewing storm. Beside him, his best friend whispered, “He doesn’t have a mom.”

I blinked, frozen, as Jason furiously shoved the traitor. Guilt crashed through the silence.

“I’m sorry, Jason. Can I give you a hug?”

Jason hesitated, watching me with guarded anticipation. Then he nodded. He stood stiffly, until slowly, I felt him hug me back. Despite the wind seeping through the classroom window, the hint of warmth in his eyes warmed me, too.

As a high school freshman volunteering at an elementary school, I was still a student in more ways than one. I hadn’t realized how easily I defaulted to assumptions, chalking up students’ misbehavior to pure carelessness. As Jason’s fitfulness began to transform into a bold hand that shot up during class, I began to notice and question other motives I’d previously taken for granted. Rereading lines under the auditorium’s half-dimmed lights, I pondered whether *Clue*’s Mrs. White was driven to violence by pure mercilessness or past scars (although admittedly, killing five ex-husbands was a little extreme). Unsettled by uncharacteristic fits of impatience from my closest friend, I walked her to lunch in the guidance office when she wanted space, even before she confessed to grappling with grief over her dad’s terminal illness.

Still, I struggled to accept that I simply couldn’t understand every hidden struggle. I often felt insufficient; I yearned to offer more than guidance for pronouncing unfamiliar words to my students and silent nods of sympathy to my friends. In my own elementary years, I’d proudly identified as a puzzle fanatic – in fact, I got glasses in first grade from poring over scattered pieces and brainteaser collections for hours on end (and my dad’s near-sighted genes certainly didn’t help). But volunteering at the elementary school made me realize – first with frustration, then with resignation, and ultimately with appreciation – that no matter how much patient observation I tried to apply, the people I cared about weren’t logic riddles to be deciphered or problems to be fixed. When a half-folded paper box fluttered from Paola’s fingers as she clawed at her swollen eyes, I was painfully unaware of the cause of her tantrum despite my best efforts to decipher her mumbled syllables with my meticulously-studied textbook Spanish. Instead, I let her cling to my hand as we went out to recess and challenged her, “Race me to the fence!” As we collapsed on the asphalt, giddy and giggling, I said, “Remind me to teach you how to make an origami butterfly next time.”

Her eyes lit up, tear streaks still glistening on her now-beaming cheeks. “*¿Me lo prometes?*” [You promise?]

Now, as I graduate from both my high school and the elementary school I’ve come to call my own, I’ve made a promise to myself: to carry my commitment to compassion alongside my newfound awareness that even the best intentions may be flawed. Yes, I’ll always love learning by dissecting the overlap between my sociology project and our current English text with my teachers between periods, or by accidentally brute-forcing a math problem before I realize the more elegant solution. But I’ve discovered that perhaps my favorite way to learn is in the company of six-year-olds who squirm in their seat and teach me what it means to love.

**What do a dermatologist clinic, a music practice room, and a science cart have in common? For me, they’re all real-life classrooms—spaces to truly learn.**

~~~

**The Dermatology Clinic** 
So, what now? With few patients that morning, Param and I finished wiping down every exam room, leaving little to do. “It’s a two-week volunteer gig,” I sighed, “so I guess we’re chilling.” But looking around, silent chairs stared back. “Where’s everyone else?” 
Getting up, I walked around, bumping into E.J., the clinic tech, juggling a stack of gloveboxes. Gathering the fallen boxes, I helped restock patient rooms. Afterwards, I saw the nurse, Stephanie, stapling patient appointment sheets. Without a word, I grabbed a stapler and matched her rhythm, stacking completed papers beside her. Misplacing even one page could make patients wait 30+ minutes. I reflected; what other behind-the-scenes work keeps operations running smoothly? Behind me, Dr. Soong was sorting info pamphlets, so I stepped over and started stacking scattered flyers into tidy piles. 
Even Param joined, helping with paperwork or discarding expired syringes! For the next two weeks, empty chairs reminded us to value the mundane. After all, no one’s always telling us the next step.

**The Music Practice Room** 
How do I synchronize my piano solo with violin and cello accompaniments from Erin and Igrainne? Years of practicing solo taught me the value of flicking on a metronome. 
But now, in a cramped, windowless practice room, the metronome’s steady beat was futile. Our individual interpretations of tempo dissonated when confined to a mechanical tick. 
Recalling my time at All-State Orchestra, I composed a solution. As principal cellist, I coordinated eight cellists, weaving our playing into melodies led by the principal violinist or violists. Here, subtle non-verbal cues, rather than metronomes, became our true guide. Sometimes, the solo violinist raised an eyebrow; other times, the violist lightly breathed towards us cellists. This was just the strings; I’m curious how the conductor coordinates the entire orchestra! 
I took up the imaginary baton as “mini conductor” for our trio. Lifting my hands above the keys, my chin shot towards Erin who mirrored the nod to Igrainne. 
With each rehearsal, we grew attuned to everyone’s cues, learning to anticipate and respond seamlessly. On performance day, the pulse resonated at the end of each phrase, keeping our harmony in sync.

**The Science Center** 
How do you teach a 6-year-old about moon craters without boring a 16-year-old? Following the script taped to the cart, I “defined an asteroid.” Unsurprisingly, Lisa toyed with the Earth’s surface (a bucket of industrial sand) while her older brother Raymond blankly stared, both clearly uninterested. As awkwardness loomed, I abandoned my script. “Let’s all make fists,” I proposed. Clenching my hand, I softly hit the sand. “Your turn!” They enthusiastically pummeled their fists down, forging their own craters. 
Despite her small hands, Lisa made the biggest crater. I was amazed by her crater’s size, wondering if it was like the cosmic collisions that shaped Earth! Gently, I explained the relationship between impact and speed. Soon, we were experimenting with different objects and velocities, carving all sorts of craters, each holding a personalized story.

~~~

At first glance, a dermatology clinic, a music practice room, and a bucket of sand might seem an odd trio. 
Yet, in the clinic, my actions unknowingly taught Param, pushing us to help wherever we could. We synced our performance by teaching each other our cues: tossing my head back or breathing before the downbeat. Working with sand as Earth’s surface, Lisa and Raymond forged their own craters, making each impact a new discovery. These moments taught me that teaching isn’t confined to classrooms—it happens through shared experiences of the unspoken, unexpected, and unscripted. Although it’ll read “Undergraduate” on my college ID, I’ll still be a teacher, uncovering lessons from every encounter and shaping the world around me, one shared insight at a time.

In May of 2024, my first love took, and shattered my tender heart into a billion pieces. He wrote to me: “Dear [Name], we know you have many choices in your job search and we are humbled you considered an opportunity with In-N-Out Burger. We wanted to reach out and let you know that, unfortunately, we won’t be moving forward with your application at this time.” What pained me most was that on that fateful day, there was so much more I wanted to say than what I had rehearsed. If I was given another chance, the interview may go as follows.

Tell me about yourself. 
My name is [Name] and I’m a senior at Palo Alto High School. I’ve wanted to work here for as long as I can remember for two simple reasons. One, the burgers are phenomenal. Two, I want to represent a company that shares my core values: “respect, honesty, and integrity.”

In my sophomore year of high school, my figure skating team had our bake sale debut in the merciless public park. I spoke to a middle aged lady in athleisure, and I could sense her eyes taking small bites of our cookie tray as we chatted about the goals I had for the team. Then her curiosity brought her to the sole question I had been dreading the whole day: what rink do you guys practice at? The truth was, we had not yet raised enough money to get on ice. It was simple, yet the words tangled and knotted before leaving my mouth a perfectly packaged lie. Now she believed that our team had gone to Solar4America Ice. “I’ve been there!” she replied. I had sacrificed honesty for the sake of a shallowly good impression and another dollar to our pockets.

Weeks later in the grocery store parking lot, I was reminded of my little fib by a man selling gorgeous big red strawberries to shoppers. I bought a small green plastic bin of them and rushed home, only to uncover that beneath the vibrant red facade the strawberries had molded. Initially I felt cheated, but I realized the strawberry man and I were not so different after all. We were both liars. I rummaged through my thoughts hoping to find some justification only to find a crumpled printout of George Washington.

This behavior wasn’t right, and certainly wasn't the behavior of the person I wanted to be in the world. I was so fixated on fundraising that I lost sight of why I chose bake sales in the first place. I could have run an online GoFundMe or social media campaign, but physical bake sales provided something the others couldn’t: the opportunity to show up, be seen, and connect with our local community. I realized that I cared deeply to build a team that I was proud of, which couldn’t be true if it stood on a foundation of distrust. It is important to me to live a life where I have without a doubt had a positive impact on the world, yet easy to lose sight of what a real life of respect, honesty, and integrity truly means. Doing good is not only an end goal, but the compilation of small actions we make every day.

At the movie theater last month, I offered to assist the lone custodian cleaning the ridiculous carpet of buttery popcorn. At the ice rink last week, I took time out of practice to assume my new title– Coach [Name]– teaching aspiring skaters how to do a two-foot-spin. At In-N-Out, I’ll make crispy fries, creamy shake, and juicy burgers with a smile, improving the quality of life for all people one fry at a time.

Maybe with this story I would have landed the job. I just wish I had told In-N-Out I could work weekdays.

I marched into Macy’s, eyes wide at the endless rows of shirts, pants, and sweaters, wondering if the store layout was scientifically designed to overwhelm. Teenagers usually outgrow their clothes as high school progresses, but it was junior year, and everything from my middle school wardrobe still fit. Up until then, my attire had been carefully curated by my mom from the illustrious clearance racks of Costco, all from the "Kids’ Section." As much as I appreciated Costco’s unbeatable discounts, it was downright embarrassing to walk into class wearing striped Adidas joggers while my peers sported straight-fit Levis. But after browsing through countless racks, I found it: a powder-blue North Face hoodie, my first piece of men’s apparel.

Once home, I slipped the sweater on with excitement, but my heart immediately sank. The sleeves drooped past my hands, and the hem hung awkwardly loose around my waist. Am I really an “adult” if even an extra small doesn’t fit? It wasn’t just about the hoodie, but about fitting into a world that seemed determined to leave me behind. I felt the same shame when my friends teased me for being 5’4”, when my doctor noted I was dangerously underweight, or when I realized I was the only one in my friend group who had to shave regularly. In a world where masculinity was defined by muscle mass and height, I felt inadequate, trapped by expectations I couldn’t meet.

That’s what started my (admittedly one-sided) war with corporate America’s mass standardization of apparel. Who decided that adulthood is measured in sweater sizes? Are these categories just a capitalist trap that promises growth but leaves you swimming in oversized sweaters (and insecurities), all neatly packaged in shrink-wrapped labels?

So, after digging out the North Face sweater from the depths of my closet, I plunged into the world of tailoring. I grabbed my mom's dusty Singer sewing machine from the attic, and over the next few weeks, spent afternoons reading through the manual and consulting YouTube. Carefully measuring the sleeves and waist seams by an inch, I ran the bulky cotton fabric under the needle, using a triangular zigzag stitch to allow subtle stretch without awkward bunching. Then, I folded in the sleeves, scrunched the fabric around my waist, and tucked in the hem so it didn’t hang awkwardly.

Next came the hard part, a thirty-minute pep talk in front of the mirror, where I finally mustered the courage to wear the sweater to school. Walking nervously through classes, I received a couple of “that’s clean” and “drip’s crazy!!” (colloquial, albeit reassuring, Gen Z terms).

Say what you will about a teenager’s newfound fashion habits, but it cemented adaptation as a core part of my character. My interests, like that sweater, don’t always fit right away, but I’ve learned to roll up my sleeves and make it work. Nowadays, I dedicate an hour each afternoon to playing basketball with my sister (and our dog, who loves chasing the ball) in an attempt to bulk up my stature. I’m still a klutz on the court, tripping over my feet more often than I dribble the ball, but it’s not about mastering the game, it’s about finding my own fit. In my intellectual pursuits, I began embracing challenges that felt uncomfortable. That’s why I took on Chinese as an Indian student; it was like wearing an oversized sweater, awkward and challenging, but I dove in, practicing stroke order each night to exhaustion. Whether it’s trying new hobbies like mixing music, launching kickflips at the skatepark, or dancing in front of hundreds of people, I’ve learned to embrace the uncomfortable.

So no, I still haven’t “grown” into that North Face sweater yet. But as I move forward, I’m ready to adapt to new academic challenges, navigate different cultures, and even try out new styles and unexpected places to ultimately create – not wait for – my own fit.

I'm sorry, [Name], you almost did it but failed Biology.

I don't remember much after that; something about summer school. I could only focus on that one word I've become all too familiar with: Failed.

As I walked to the car, tears blurred my vision. My whole life, I wanted to prove my mother wrong; I wanted to show her I wasn't the failure she thought I was and that I wasn't a mistake, but it seemed like no matter how hard I tried, I couldn't escape the abuse I suffered for years. I was ashamed to walk in public carrying the bruises she left, but even worse, I hated the way I saw the world through her words.

After summer school one day, I entered the office for my weekly meeting with the Vice Principal; I waited outside the closed door and overheard two voices arguing. I recognized a voice belonging to Ms. Germain, my summer school teacher.

"I don't know what's happened to him; it's like he's lost all interest in life. He used to be so vibrant. No one knows what's wrong with him; I feel powerless watching him do this to himself."

While every other teacher seemed to have given up, there she was—the one person I thought I burdened every day with my silence and cold demeanor—actually believing in me.

That day, I faced a hard truth. I believed I was alone and had given up on myself. However, seeing the compassion of a teacher who didn't understand my situation but was still fighting for me made me realize that maybe there was a point.

***

We often sat silently for the first 30 minutes, a regular but unnerving ritual. The quiet brought a sense of peace, but beneath it, anxiety churned, making me despise it. Dr. Perez eventually broke the quiet, suggesting we walk by the river despite recent storms leaving destruction in their wake.

Dr. Perez began talking about trauma; for the past four months, she tried to discuss my mother's abuse, but I always deflected. However, this time, she didn't continuously ask me questions but instead one. Do you feel at fault?

Without giving me time to answer, she continued, "A storm passed by. You've been in a few throughout your life. It's broken you just like it's torn down these trees. Do you think it's the tree's fault?" Sometimes, things happen in our lives, but it doesn't mean we are to blame for the damage.

Unfortunately, this anecdote didn't magically fix my mindset, but it did begin a line of questioning that challenged my belief that everything my mother told me was the truth.

***

The buzz of conversation and the noises of paper bags opening filled the Chick-fil-A, where we were seated at a table for ten meant initially for four.

"Anyone feel like sharing their testimony today?" Our Youth Group leader, David, glanced around.

I’d joined the youth group only four months prior, motivated by my desire to find people who would help me grow and deal with my trauma. In the past months, they’d all shared their testimonies; I wasn't used to a group of boys being so vulnerable about their trauma. So when everyone looked at me, I felt like I was being rooted for.

“My mother always told me she hated me…” I began.

On average, many students can share each meeting. I took up the whole two hours, but I wasn't ashamed. Afterward, the other group members didn’t say much; they simply hugged me. Coming from a household where I was constantly neglected, being embraced by ten other students who were struggling as much as me brought me a feeling of peace. I felt uncomfortable, but I also finally felt that my trauma wasn't something to run from but something to embrace and challenge.

***

Through these experiences I have come to the realization that community isn’t tangible; it is not a goal to be achieved but a gift to be received. I thought I was born to be an example of what not to be, but now I remind myself daily that we are meant to be in a community; I found people who will catch me when I fall and pick me up even when I don’t want to get up. The care given to me by random strangers was something I always failed to find in my family: Community.

**Why do you like that kid's toy so much?**

My mom's question caught me off guard as I glanced at my scooter leaning against the wall. I was seventeen, way past the age when most outgrow their "toys." To me, it represented endless possibilities—not just tricks, but bringing friends together and pushing limits.

When COVID-19 hit, closing skateparks and isolating us, my solution was to build my own ramp. How hard could it be?

After failing twice, I learned that improvising with a rusty saw doesn't work. Adopting a NASA-like approach, I sketched detailed blueprints and gathered materials. Hours later, a robust kicker ramp, proudly labeled “N-A-S-A,” stood ready.

I relished flying through the air but missed friends. So, I invited them over to ride. I landed new tricks and motivated Jason to try a double tailwhip. When he succeeded, we all celebrated. We even created a fun contest for silly tricks, fostering camaraderie.

Building the ramp taught me meticulous planning over rash decisions—a skill I applied to starting the Anthropology Club at school. Initially, I used lecture-style presentations, but realized interactive sessions engaged students better.

During a lesson on eyes, I asked, “Why do some animals have eyes on the sides, while ours are front-facing?” After guiding them with hints, Naomi answered correctly. In another session on bipedalism, I turned it into a quiz-competition. Ethan's realization about energy conservation showed me the impact of this approach.

By applying a meticulous mindset, I've achieved lasting results, whether creating a ramp or designing engaging lessons. Bringing people together—whether watching a trick or understanding evolution—drives me. I'm eager to apply this philosophy to new challenges, building step-by-step to my dreams.

Oh! I could have won that chess game if I went C6. No, focus [Name]. THINK. An invisible rabbit chased by a hunter, both moving a mile per step. Could the hunter ensure he's within a 100-mile radius after a billion moves? Four hours passed on the math olympiad team selection test and all I had to show were 3 crumpled scratch papers, half an idea, and a poorly drawn kakashi doodle.

I blundered. But this time it wasn’t just a rook I lost—it was my spot on the team. I just couldn’t focus, the second I wasn’t doing ten things at once my chest would seize up like a gordian knot.

But this blunder was one that outweighed my anxieties, because no matter how stressful moderating custody schedules debates between my parents was, at least I had a math problem to dive deep into, a chess game to analyze, or a riff I could play on my trusty, old Martin. Yet, that didn’t seem to be the case anymore.

I dived into Wikipedia articles on dopaminergic pathways, neuroplasticity, and the default mode network, trying to understand why my brain seemed so intent on running from stillness. Turns out, I was being cognitively overloaded—gaming, cubing, even skateboarding. My tendency to multitask was slowly corrupting my hobbies from passionate, fulfilling journeys to mind numbing distractions by using them to run from my problems. My passions were at stake, and I had to act.

I deleted TikTok, limited Instagram to visiting the webpage, and bought Digital Minimalism by Cal Newport. Everyday, after Fajr prayer, I’d open the shutters, close the door, and sink into my leather Churchill chair, journaling about the most recent anxiety-inducing event. This stillness was new, and my body resisted it. Brushing my teeth without music had my eyes jumping between the red toothpaste cap and the dust between the tiles. “Single-tasking” was a mental workout that left me feeling bored. And playing my guitar, my mind longed for the comfort of The Office in the background.

Rationally, I knew why—for years, guitar had been a way to drown my anxiety about the next familial “negotiation”, and when that wasn’t enough, a comforting sitcom would bury the leftovers. My mind tried to trick me: multitasking saves more time for real work later. But feeling my chest tighten after a single John Mayer riff, when I used to spend all-nighters with painful, calloused fingers, showed me how much my attention span had shortened. It wasn’t just about losing focus; it was losing crucial activities that had satisfied my curiosity, kept me learning, and most importantly gave me a sense of purpose and accomplishment.

Day after day, with every hour of silence I chose to embrace, that knot around my chest slowly loosened now when I cubed, it was to improve my times by learning new algorithms. When I played Valorant, it was to analyze my mistakes afterwards and improve. And when I saw a math problem, my creativity could roam free as each new question sparked another. It wasn’t just solving a problem; it was about exploring original ideas to new problems, marveling at this poetry of logical steps.

I spent uninterrupted hours analyzing why constructing the Sharky-Devil point worked, why harmonic ratio approaches fell short, burning through reams of scratch paper trying the problems I found on YouTube videos just like I did as a younger, carefree middle schooler. I was regaining the focus that allowed me to appreciate the journey of understanding the problem at hand.

When I pick up the guitar now, it isn’t to drown out frustration or lingering doubts—but to express them. I bend slow blues notes in A minor when I feel uneasy, or run up and down the mixolydian when I’m energetic. I may have lost my passions to the noise before, but I won’t again. Whether I’m buried in real analysis problem sets or preparing for [specific club per school] tryouts, I’ll lean on my passions to ground me. I’ll choose my joy intentionally.

At age ten, I wasn’t just playing games on my phone—I was seeing the world through them.

The game that caught my attention was “Snake.” In it, the player’s snake grows longer with every apple it eats; but as it grows, space becomes scarce and the game becomes more challenging. I initially liked the game’s intensity, but as time passed, my vision evolved and I began looking into its inner workings.

In "Snake," the apples are easy to spot, glowing right in front of you. But in life, growth opportunities aren’t as clear. I initially thought staying busy was the key to growth, so I filled my days with school, hobbies, and eventually my first business: a tutoring company. I believed that if I kept moving—kept expanding—I’d find those elusive "apples" leading to success. But my first company failed, and that failure made me pause and reflect.

For the first time, I wasn’t just reacting to the world around me; I was contemplating it. Why hadn’t things worked out? Was I focused on the right goals? Was I truly listening to myself and the needs of my community? I realized that in my rush to grow, I hadn’t considered the deeper purpose behind my efforts.

That’s when I decided to start again, but with clearer focus. My second company, Accompany Communities, wasn’t just about business—it was about creating meaningful connections. As I took on more leadership roles both in and outside of school, I became more aware of different types of community engagement. In some communities, people only had vertical relationships with leadership. In others, members formed strong horizontal relationships, working together, building friendships, and helping one another in daily life. Over time, I learned that what distinguished these communities was empathy.

I wanted to help local service businesses in Santiago build stronger, more empathetic horizontal relationships within their clients. By building and marketing personalized online community platforms where the business owners could make posts, interact with the members, build and upload courses, host meetings, and encourage engagement, I helped them scale and reach hundreds of new people—and enabled them to build relationships and meet new friends. This wasn’t just a strategy—it was an extension of what I had come to understand about growth and connection. People thrive when they feel supported and are part of something bigger than themselves. I had learned this through my own experiences and wanted my business to reflect those values.

As I worked on Accompany Communities, I felt a shift. Instead of being driven by external goals, I began listening more—to myself, the people I was working with, and the needs of the community. I realized that true growth isn’t about adding more, but about deepening connections. Through the company, I partnered with local business leaders in Santiago; ran advertisements on social media; appeared in radio and TV programs; and signed agreements with three Latin American schools. This happened not because I was pushing it forward, but because I was paying attention. I learned that progress comes from empathy, from understanding others, and from creating spaces where everyone can grow together.

Like the game "Snake," life presents constant challenges, but unlike the game, there’s no limit to how much space we can create for others—and for ourselves—when we lead with empathy and purpose. My first failure taught me the value of reflection, and my second venture showed me that success isn’t about expanding reach but about making space for others to grow alongside you. Behind the game’s facade lay infinite opportunities, brilliant people to meet, and a tail that has room to grow as long as it wants.

A sharp, erratic ticking sound jerks me awake. I glance at my phone: 3:15 a.m. I roll over, hoping to drift back to sleep, but the disjointed clatter continues. I sit up, scanning the room, and my eyes land on the perpetrator—my old, reliable desk clock. Frozen hands, but still ticking. This clock, a gift from my grandfather, has always been a comforting presence, a quiet companion through countless late-night study sessions and sleepless nights. But tonight, its familiar rhythm has betrayed me, replaced by a chaotic rattle that refuses to let me rest.

I squinted with distortion at the clock, nostalgia and frustration meticulously blending inside my sleep-deprived brain. How could something so small, so ordinary, suddenly tilt the axis of my universe like this? I try to ignore it, turning over in bed, stuffing my ears with pillows, but it keeps ticking—stubbornly.

The next morning, still groggy, I stare at the clock in the light of day. Its silence feels unnatural now. The ticking had always been present, steady and comforting. I wasn’t ready to let it go. I’ve always been the kind of person who can’t leave things broken: whether it’s a relationship, a project, or an old clock. I knew I had to fix it. There was no other way.

I spent the next week submerged in the process of repair. I carefully pried the back open, revealing its labyrinth of gears and springs. At first, I thought it would be easy—just a matter of realigning some pieces, maybe tightening a screw here or there. But the deeper I went, the more complicated it was for me to come above the surface. Gears slipped, springs popped out of place, and each time I reassembled it, another part malfunctioned. The frustration gnawed at me.

Yet, through this process, I began to see the clock in a new light. It wasn’t just a machine anymore, it was a puzzle, a challenge. Every time I put it back together and it didn’t work, I learned something new. I studied tutorials: the gears broke; I consulted forums: ended up with an expanded spring. I even visited a repair shop for advice, but nothing seemed to fully restore the clock’s quiet perfection.

Each failure was frustrating, but I couldn’t give up. I realized that this wasn’t just about the clock, it was about my approach to problems. I’ve always prided myself on finding solutions, but this clock was teaching me that not everything is easily fixable. Some things require patience. Some things require persistence. And sometimes, things remain imperfect, and that’s okay.

Finally, after countless attempts of my rivalry with the ticking box, I put the clock back together one last time. It ticked—irregularly, faintly, but it ticked. The hands still didn’t move, and the chime was silent, but I felt a strange sense of peace. I didn’t need it to be perfect anymore. The process had been enough. The clock, in all of its imperfection, had taught me more than a fully functioning one ever could.

Now, as I sit at my desk, the clock still manages to tick faintly. It no longer wakes me at odd hours or serves its original purpose of presence, but I can’t find myself to dispose of it. I realized, lying in bed on the night of January 12, 2023, that I missed the sound of it when it was broken, its imperfections reminded me of the journey, the hours spent tinkering, failing, and learning. I’m not sure if I’ll ever fully repair it. But maybe, I don’t need to.

BEEP! BEEP! BEEP! The sound of the clock alarm starts to abruptly wake me up. Waking up faster than at any other moment, and my consciousness begins to remind me why I'm on my feet so quickly. Today is the day, but not the ordinary day; I take my final physics exams.

Everything that I need is already prepared: suit, ID, pen. A quick look in the mirror and the last sentence from my mom (after a lucky kick in the butt): "You are ready."

I didn't even notice, but I'm already in high school. My friends seem focused on the common goal—getting the best score, which will determine university.

Finally, sit spectaculum incipere. The sound of the turning paper was perfectly in tune, like that of a big orchestra, and everyone was concentrated to the limit.

First question - kinematics. I did it faster than a jet flying during the opening ceremony of the Super Bowl. The caffeine from RedBull, which I drank earlier, starts to kick in. What's next? Dynamics. It's an easy one, too. Astronomy, electrostatics, waves, basics of relativity and quantum mechanics. Pages flip so fast, I can't even tell how long I'm doing my exam. Everything seems so easy and familiar to me...

BEEP! BEEP! BEEP! The sound of the clock alarm wakes me up. Looking outside from my window, I can see the breathtaking landscape of the Oder River. Today is my day. I will be able to see the results of my final physics exam.

First glance of the paper... 57%... Everyone congratulated me; that's an excellent score. It's enough to get into Jagiellonian University (the most renowned university in Poland). BUT. Were hundreds of hours of learning in class and at home worth it? Did I do everything I could do? Am I satisfied? No…

I sat and started to think. Does this score really define who I am? Can someone tell my story by looking at this result? No. Then, what is the true definition of a person? Well, it's their story. In a world where we see everyday that someone has won a Nobel Prize or an Oscar, got their PhD as a teenager, or broke world records in some sport. We can feel disappointed about our lives. We work so hard, try new things, and think outside the box, but we don't get our desired results or even recognition of all the things we have done in our lives. But Lord of the Rings isn't so popular because of the ending. It's popular because we can experience the journey from the Shire to Mordor, all the people Frodo meets, and every obstacle the characters must overcome leads us to the grand finale. We don't enjoy the result; we appreciate the adventure. Yet, we don't perceive our lives that way.

We are motivated to see good points on the test results, huge salaries, gold medals, and a high social status. We tend to forget how much work the leaders and record-breakers had to do to achieve success. As Usain Bolt said: "I trained four years to run nine seconds." I discovered that my high school odyssey wasn't just my final exam. It was every day meeting with my friends, developing my social skills and academic knowledge, every pause before the test where I taught them, all their help offered for me, every time we went out to a restaurant for the afternoon and every exciting conversation with my teachers. Those are the things that define me, not the score on the exam.

I wish that more teenagers would look at our lives this way. The outcome of our goals isn't the primary purpose of living. Once, A$AP Rocky rapped, "My life is like a movie; they should film me through it." This line should apply to everyone.

Red for heroes, white for cowards.

Four decades ago, my Great Uncle Ming “returned” home in a white urn—a glaring anomaly in a village awash with red. Executed by a Chinese general for refusing to fire on Vietnamese civilians, Uncle Ming became a Ghost-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named, a figure whispered about in fear and silence. As a child, I watched Grandma’s face harden at even the faintest mention of his name and mistook her silence for shame.

When she passed away, I unearthed the hidden urn nestled in her bottom drawer, buried beneath a trove of photographs. The edges of those images bore the marks of her longing—small, soft impressions shaped like thumbs, remnants of a love profound but painful.

A wave of guilt washed over me as I traced those impressions. I had never grasped the depth of her grief, the weight of the shame imposed by a world that had forgotten both her and Uncle Ming. I had failed to defend her against the oblivion that swallowed their stories.

I kept that box of memories beside my desk, a silent testament to our family's hidden history.

Then came February 24, 2022.

News broke of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine: 130,000 casualties. 250,000. 380,820. Amid the chaos, the world clamored for clarity—“Who’s winning?”

I sat at my desk, the weight of Grandma’s box pressing down on me.

Who were the Ukrainian individuals simplified into those staggering numbers? Would their stories dissolve into obscurity like Uncle Ming’s? I felt a fierce urge to rescue the narratives of those forgotten by history—if not for Grandma, then for the people of Ukraine. Thus began my quest to enter the war-torn country.

Two years later, after navigating a labyrinth of visa applications and customs scrutiny, I finally stepped into Kyiv. I immersed myself in conversations with locals, recording every story that unfolded. I listened to harrowing accounts of soldiers enduring brutal beatings in Russian prisons and documented the destruction of churches, flagrant violations of international humanitarian law. I was right—buried stories were everywhere, lurking in every alley and corner, numerous beyond my imagination.

Yet the weight of my differences from the Ukrainian locals started to press upon me. Each time my faulty translator left me gesturing in desperation or my ignorance of local customs led to faux pas, the chasm between us felt insurmountable. I questioned my right to tell their stories, especially in light of whispers about China’s alignment with Russia.

A week into my stay, while I cooked varenyky with Lesya, she spoke of her son Andriy—a war hero, she said. Their family had received bouquets and medals. Yet, as I surveyed her home, I saw no signs of those honors.

“He died by suicide, two days after the commendation,” Lesya answered my unasked question. Her knuckles turned white as she gripped the spatula.

In that moment, the title “hero” crumbled under the weight of grief and heartache.

As I leaned in to embrace Lesya, my doubts evaporated.

Ukrainian. Chinese. Hero. Coward. The labels felt hollow, irrelevant. The stark divisions imposed on us dissolved. There was only our shared humanity—our collective struggles, fears, and dreams for peace and harmony.

Back in China, I printed the stories I had gathered and organized a charity exhibition to fund rebuilding efforts in Ukraine. Although some viewers turned away, indifferent or skeptical, more others were drawn in. I watched as they paused to absorb each individual story. Their expressions shifted from light curiosity to solemnity, and one by one, they bent down to sign donation forms. The personal narratives bridged hearts across political divides.

There are no heroes in a war. All our stories are too fractured for the legends of victory; the people we love are too bruised for medals acclaiming valor. When our authentic, fragile stories are heard, transcending national boundaries through our shared humanity, we can join hands in solidarity and reconciliation.

It started with my legs turning numb—like they went for a vacation without notifying me. By the time I was lying on that sterile white hospital bed, it was clear this wasn't just a cramp. Apparently, I had hit a one-in-a-million jackpot called Acute Myelitis. I thought of being special, but this wasn't exactly what I had in mind. The doctor mentioned a one-third chance that I could recover. Well, proud winner of a 'Mega-rare Illness,' I should be excited at this humungous 33% possibility of walking again—or I could settle for the reassuring flipside - excelling in wheelchair racing or Hopscotch.

But I hated wheelchairs or Hopscotch, so I gave every grit to fight for that deceivingly hopeful one-third chance. Right out of the ICU, I threw myself into a new "enrichment program": three-hour IV drips treatment morning sessions, followed by gruelling six-hour afternoon rehabs. Stretching, bending, electro-stimulating... Every day, my legs turned to jelly, the floor turned wet. On exhausted nights, I dreamt of simply admitting to being a limp poet like William Henley. Yet the next morning, I felt ashamed of myself, muttering, "... master of my fate... captain of my soul..." through my clenched teeth. So I kept going, for six months, 6 days a week, maxed at the doctor's permitted intensity.

Then, I ran again.

**

With my unbalanced moves (due to a permanently damaged spinal cord), I thought I had beaten the one-third odd at being "normal" until I went back onto the soccer field. Despite my limping motions and awkward dribbles, I could still somehow cut, break and goal, easily, but too easily. Although imbued with goodwill and compassion, the cheerings shattered my ego. No matter how hard I worked at rehab, I had been stamped as a "person with disabilities," involuntarily commanding "politeness" more than real competitiveness from everyone, even in contact sports.

For several weeks, my tears soaked the pillows wetter than the rehab floor, but thankfully, I found refuge in a sport where my skills wouldn't be assumptively judged by my appearance - APEX Legends.

To regain my lost pride, I entered my new rehab program with mice and keyboards, not for my upper limbs but for my crumbled aspirations. Hundreds of hours of aim practice at Kovaak (FPS training platform) to bake recoil patterns into muscle memory, dissecting professional match playlists, noting down their playstyles, decision-making and even warm-up routines. Soon, my 40-page notebook was bulging with scribbled notes and diagrams- breakdowns of team plans, statistics of ring changes, colour-coded drop zones heatmaps ... Within four seasons, my team rose from beginner to a global top 750 tier. In 2022, this amateur team, from four countries, speaking five different languages, and with a 50ms cross-boarder lag disadvantage, qualified as one of the 30 teams for the Regional Pro League, playing against legendary players with big sponsors. After rounds of knock-offs, VKG Aono, once my idol player, typed out "Good Game" ("GG"), congratulating our victory against his team, lifting us to the 10th in the entire Asia-Pacific region, amongst its ten million player base...

Top ten out of ten million, that's "one in a million".

**

Reading up to now, maybe you have forgotten about my leg problems, a measly inconvenience brought by a one-in-a-million unlikely mishap.

If so, that's good because, whether for this essay or my life, there are many more exciting things to remember, rather than dwelling on a second-class recovery from a rare disease. The excitement of writing poetry, the elegance of my femtosecond laser control algorithm, or the improvised balancing pose I on skateboards, and, of course, my Apex trophies. At the gate of entering college, I look forward to treading many more rocky roads with my limping legs, and a held high head.

If life gives me a lemon, I'd throw it right back, wearing my "ONE IN A MILLION" badge with pride, no slack.

Despite the looming threat of missing my flight, I left my mother’s side to investigate what was being reported.

“The latest semiconductor shortages have spread beyond consumer electronics,” the reporter announced. “The latest victims? Credit cards. COVID-19 has resulted in credit card shortages due to microprocessors being back-ordered for months.”

Despite all the tech news I’d been reading recently, I hadn’t considered how shortages could extend beyond smartphones to something as unexpected as credit cards. Glancing around, I noticed how much of the world around me—TVs, vending machines, even the plane I was about to board—relied on semiconductors. As I hurriedly boarded, it struck me how something as small as a microprocessor could have such a profound global impact. This moment sparked a new curiosity, prompting me to probe further.

When I got home, I began researching semiconductors and their shortages before the pandemic. One revelatory article examined the geopolitics of the semiconductor trade, and I was fascinated by how US reliance on Taiwanese semiconductors helped protect Taiwan from Chinese invasion. I started to grasp just how much nations prioritized technology for their own strategic interests.

Clearly, countries cared about the value of technology. But a question lingered: why didn’t people care?

Lying in bed that night, I thought of one word: care. I realized how often, as Gen Z, we take technology for granted because it's so deeply embedded into our lives, rarely stopping to appreciate its complexity. This led me to a new goal: sharing these realizations with my peers.

At first, I wasn’t sure how to convey such complex concepts to people my age, many of whom seemed relatively uninvolved. I began by leading discussions on semiconductor fundamentals at my school’s STEM club, where I knew my peers would have some foundational knowledge.

One time, a student unexpectedly brought up the ethical implications of semiconductors in environmental and military contexts. Recognizing the topic’s complexity, I encouraged everyone to share their thoughts, without injecting my opinion. This sparked a passionate discourse with stances all over the spectrum. Creating such an open environment where diverse viewpoints could flourish became something I wanted to replicate in the future.

This drive to share knowledge extended beyond the STEM world when I joined Oregon Model UN as a leader. As VP, I facilitated debates on semiconductor issues, merging technological perspectives with others' geopolitical insights. For example, I learned from a student delegate representing Japan how countries are reshoring chip production to mitigate supply risks and strengthen national security. Engaging in these discussions not only deepened my understanding but demonstrated the impact I could have on others: improving their absorbance of new ideas.

More recently, I’ve shifted my focus to the future. After connecting with Professor Teuscher from Portland State University to explore machine learning and semiconductors, I also began developing my teaching and presentation skills. While listening to him explain next-generation computing models, I observed how he transformed us, students, from passive listeners into active collaborators. Despite having limited prior knowledge, my experience at the lab has shown me the power of active mentorship, even with complex subjects.

While technology is often treated as a backdrop to our lives, I now view it as a powerful catalyst, demanding our attention. But it wasn’t enough for only me to see that. As I became aware of the barriers of complexity that prevent others from fully engaging with technology, my focus shifted. My passion for technology evolved into a desire to help others share in that excitement. Whether in a lab, classroom, or lecture hall, I’ve realized what brings me joy is being surrounded by people who care deeply about their fields of study and passions—and I’m here to create that.

"I did it!"

I finally restored the generator. Instantly, Chief Mercedes's window flew open with a big smile.

But quickly, his face turned into a panic.

"Baek! Look! The generator is smoking!"

I swiftly turned with fearful doubt, mindlessly observing the swirling white smoke. The blazing heat soon melted my frozen hand, and I promptly turned off the generator. Immediately, a single thought raced past my mind—three months of effort had just blown to smoke.

Since the beginning, I knew rebuilding the mission-essential 15kW generator was no simple task. This was one of the two generators that lit up the field exercise, and my task was essential to keeping the training going. With our mission readiness dropping daily, the pressure of getting it done grew as our mission depended on it.

Beyond the technical challenges, the pressure weighed heavily on me. As the only generator technician, I felt responsible for our mission's success. Failure wasn't just a matter of broken equipment but of the entire team's failure and, worse, a halted operation.

Thinking I could grasp a solution, I dug through the piles of shabby manuals every day. Day after day, the burden became heavier as the solution was nowhere to be found.

Even when I hesitated, my teammates' faith kept me going. Every day, I felt their trust, and I couldn't let them down. Their faith gave me the strength to continue, even in the moment of doubt.

So I couldn't give up.

With no visible solution, I began inspecting each part closer. At first, I thought this was another failure; everything seemed intact on the surface, and I felt like I had fallen into an endless loop. No matter how much I tried, the generator wouldn't run.

Then, deep inside, I found a burnt wire plugged into the wrong terminal.

The weight of my mistake punched me hard. Yet, I knew this could be the breakthrough I had been waiting for. Unfortunately, the burn had already spread to the generator's other components. Now, I had no choice but to replace the entire harness.

As I began placing wires carefully, I realized every wire was essential for its function. It wasn't just about replacing the wires anymore. It was about understanding the whole system, where every part counted on each other. With a new perspective, I again started precisely connecting each wire to the spot.

Then, I turned the switch once again.

As if time itself had been stuck, waiting for this moment, everything slowed. After a short anticipated silence, a loud sound echoed through the extensive motor pool. Our generator finally returned to life. Soon, I woke up to the familiar sound of my teammates' voices behind me.

I looked back.

I saw the waves of cheers that had supported me throughout this grueling process. Their faith ignited something within me as they stood beside me.

Indeed, I was never alone.

Our teammates' trust was refined as the generator powered our new missions in the field. In just days, I observed how the pace and atmosphere changed. The entire process wasn't just fixing a generator but earning trust through persistence and resilience. The success proved our team's ability to perform crucial operations when it mattered the most.

Trust isn't built through success. It is constructed through resilience and persistence, even in the face of failures. My teammates' faith pushed me forward when my confidence was lost, reminding me that I could do more than I believed. By persevering through each setback, I earned their trust and learned to trust myself. I will carry this lesson with my heart, knowing that challenges are not obstacles but new opportunities to grow.

As I face future challenges, whether in college or beyond, I’ll rely on trust and resilience to guide me through.

Piracy didn't cease to exist when ships gave way to cars. Rowdy parrots, razor-sharp hooks, and gold chests just assumed the form of flashlights, GPSes, and mysterious containers.

As a timid Asian-American boy growing up in the mountains of Pennsylvania, I was the last person you'd expect to be interested in swashbuckling adventures. That soon changed when I discovered geocaching—an endless worldwide treasure hunt where people hide and seek containers called "caches." Every day, thousands of "treasure hunters" go on quests rated in difficulty between one and five stars for items left behind and posted by other hunters. Whether it's a vibrating scalp massager or a pack of ten Ken Barbie dolls, geocachers never know what they'll find at the end of a quest.

Intrigued by the opportunity to decipher maps and search unfamiliar territory, I immediately signed up for a local geocaching event with a few friends. I started with low difficulty one- and two-star geocaching hunts. My approach to geocaching was simple: find the treasure and replace it with something of equal value, even if the treasure is less than desirable (like animal-butt magnets in a Chipotle parking lot). More importantly, I enjoyed the adventure of traversing state lines, roaming amusement parks, and hiking forests.

After uprooting nearly every beginner cache in the local area, I rose the "cor-pirate" ladder and went on higher difficulty quests. On my first three-star geocache, I accidentally contracted poison ivy all over my legs—all for some old Magic School Bus books. A couple of weeks later, I upped my swashbuckling antics and rummaged through a vile sewer to look for an expert four-star geocache, which turned out to contain a rare 1973 baseball card of Willie Mays! My experiences became more meaningful, exciting, and memorable as I took more risks.

A few months later, before heading out for a hike in the Smoky Mountains, a message popped up on my geocaching watchlist: "Near you: Difficulty 5.0, Terrain 5.0, Hidden on 4/19/2012". A 5-star cache was the last piece of the puzzle I needed to reach the pinnacle of geocaching.

I set my eyes on the ultimate treasure.

It didn't take long for me to realize why this geocache hadn't been found in a decade. Through four hours of searching, I stumbled through mud, fell face-first in a stream, and crawled through dense shrubbery. In the end, the quest was worth it because I found an antique 1930s one-dollar bill!

I also seized this opportunity to hide my own five-star geocache. Before my grandmother passed away, she wrote a heartfelt poem that inspired me to become a more community-oriented person and always look out for others. It was time to spread the love, so I took that poem my grandmother left and placed it in that same geocache 6,000 feet above sea level in the Smoky Mountains. I hoped for another geocaching pirate to stumble across not only a unique treasure but also a unique part of me.

I won't stop at 5-stars to parlay adventures into treasures. As a go-getter, I have a deep-rooted enthusiasm for embracing new challenges and stepping outside my comfort zone. Whether it be aneurysm research, public speaking, or geocaching, I face every obstacle head-on with determination and courage.

Not only has geocaching helped to build my confidence and taught me valuable teamwork skills, but it has also introduced me to countless other “treasure hunters” worldwide, each with their unique stories and experiences. While I do enjoy finding a valuable cache, it’s the geocaching community that is truly priceless. I don’t know what treasures lie hidden in the geocaches of the future, but I can’t wait to find out.

Geocaching isn't only my hobby; it has been my rite of passage. And for now, yo-ho-ho, it's time for another adventure!

My family’s prized possession is a decade-old shoe rack. Walk into our garage and the first thing you’ll see is this organized holder, one section allocated to each family member. The first pair, standing out against faded silver drywall, are my Yeezy Belugas.

The Belugas are a dull gray, contrasting the eminent bright orange stripe stitched across the side. This neon orange isn’t just a pop of color—the vibrant hues remind me of the Indian flag and its principles that guide me in an increasingly diverse world. This diversity is evident at my local mosque, where every member brings a unique interpretation of Islam. The contrast between my sneakers and kurta pajama often draws curious looks from the other congregants. Their skeptical glances suggest an incongruity between my modern shoes and age-old conventions, and I occasionally find myself lost at this intersection where the great expectations of the traditional and contemporary converge.

This meeting point seems challenging, but it also empowers me to embrace both worlds confidently; ironically, when I hang my head in momentary dejection, I’m reminded of the very flag that inspires my identity. My own saffron stripe encapsulates the strength of my heritage, the white the balance I strive for while navigating between my customs. Whether reciting Arabic verses barefoot or playing Frank Ocean on guitar with my Belugas, I connect past and present, bridging cultures to build harmony. As I take a step forward in my Belugas, I realize I also mirror the growth represented by the flag’s green stripe. This growth doesn’t just shape my journey; it also deepens my connection with my culture and community—a connection embodied by my pair of Mono Ices.

The worn soles and faded color of my Mono Ices outline a map of the places I’ve been and the connections I’ve built. They’ve glided across polished tiles of math team banquets with my friends. They’ve traversed the driveway where my family and I play badminton together. They’ve slid across the repurposed fields where I play cricket.

But the most impactful terrain they’ve tread is the floor of Hoover Crescent Clinic.

While volunteering at the clinic, I saw firsthand the impact of healthcare disparities and the efforts grassroots initiatives take against them. Crescent provides free care to the uninsured, contributing critical health care and building stronger links with every interaction. My time logging patient information allows me to see the direct benefits of such initiatives, and my conversations with a diverse array of patients give me the power to nourish our relationships. By connecting science with compassion, each day at the clinic gives me a chance to give back to the same network that taught me, each patient interaction an opportunity to practice the cultural respect I’ve cultivated. My experiences applying empathy, understanding, and knowledge to aid the clinic—traits whose effects are etched into the shoe’s fibers—remind me of the values I’ll carry to college and beyond.

As I prepare for college, I unbox a third pair for my collection: the San Francisco Dunks. This sneaker’s chief feature is a familiar-colored tie-dye pattern that’s only visible once the shoe has aged. This vibrant swirl of color reminds me of old and new yet again—but this time, I observe a blend of my past and future. I see myself using the principles of the Indian flag’s colors to bring cultural awareness through an Indian-American student group and employing the unity and resilience I’ve learned through the clinic to address healthcare disparities in other facilities. Whether deepening my connection to my roots, battling inequality, or embracing new challenges, I know each step will continue to shape my shoes and myself, one forward step at a time.

“You see P? Without nori the musubi can’t be complete,” my mom explained to 6-year-old me, as she guided my hands to a sheet of nori, wrapping it tight around a uniform stack of rice and spam, “Just like how I wouldn't be complete without you!”

This was our tradition. Every weekend we would stand at the kitchen counter, our hands sticky with teriyaki, bits of furikake sprinkled throughout our clothes, and my cheeks burning from the wide smile stretched across my face that I could never seem to get rid of.

***

In the beginning of freshman year, I joined multiple clubs—excited at the promise of fundraising, discussions on diversity, and supporting a greater cause—but soon noticed a large disconnect between the number of “welcome to our club!” emails in my inbox and their actual presence on campus. Seeking to bridge the divide, my best friend and I founded our own club revolving around the one thing I could rely on for connection: spam musubi. Through the sales of thousands of spam musubis, reach4 kindness has been able to raise over $4000 for Lucile Packard Children’s Cancer Research. The opportunity to create such a large impact while sharing my love of musubi, a huge part of my childhood, with my peers has proved to me over and over that musubi is a vessel for connection.

***

But somewhere, as middle turned to high school and my schedule became jam-packed from 8 am to 8 pm with AP classes, varsity basketball and softball, tutoring, and volunteering, I lost my passion for making musubi. What used to be a tradition bringing her and me together, began to feel like a chore. My actions, which I knew were impactful on a greater scale, felt empty.

It's 9 pm on a Tuesday—the night before our fundraiser—and my eyes and shoulders droop from an exhausting 12-hour day. The will to make 200 musubi ceases to exist in my mind.

***

I eventually look up at my mom, who had joined me sometime in the past 4 hours, and we lock burning eyes from the salt of sweat and spam. She holds up a misshapen musubi, so disfigured it’s threatening to fall apart, and we devolve into hysterical giggles. I reach out and split it into two, extending a half to her. The salty, sweet, and savory flavor blooms in my mouth as we indulge in the treat together. Being here—joy spread across our faces and musubi in hand—is so reminiscent of us making musubi before the act of it was buried in my overflowing plate.

As we toiled away in the dark of night to create small squares of heaven that forever encapsulated our memories in its flavor, it was all too clear that musubi was never about me at all. It always has been and always will be a dish defined by the people I share it with. A staple for my mom and me to bond over, a meal to be shared between teammates, a fundraiser foundation that connects us to something greater, and a reminder to follow through and appreciate those who have followed through for me.

***

This “musubi” mindset has allowed me to form strong relationships with those around me and acts as a constant reminder to nurture those commitments. On the basketball team, I have helped cultivate a team environment where our genuine love and support for each other translates to our play on the court, making every win a greater victory and every loss a bit more bearable. As a tutor, I have seen how being a constant and simply walking through concepts can lead to exponential growth in young kids.

I will continue to form these “musubis” in my life—striving to make connections stronger than the nori that wraps the musubi tight and even deeper than the giant vats of white rice that have filled my childhood.

“Hey [Name], I’m over here! Not outside?”

I saw Zidan and Max, the two of the eighth-graders I was coaching, squirm in their seats. I ignored their antics and continued to plow through the ideals of capitalism. I was focused on achieving the timeline.

It had been two weeks since I had started coaching them for the upcoming city-wide junior debate; it was time to test them. “AI for school homework” was the prompt, hopeful that this topic would ring a bell.

After an argument towards an opposition point, Daveen, the soft-spoken 8th grader, went blank. He looked at his friends, then towards me, looking lost. By the third round, Zidan’s responses lasted 30 seconds out of his 4-minute quota and then he stopped. I groaned in my head. They hadn’t mastered any of the topics I had painstakingly covered.

A practice debate spar was in two days, and Mr. Matt, my debate coach, was going to watch. I started panicking, worried that my teams were not ready. It was like sending them out to an MMA title fight unprepared. I thought everything was under control, having sped through the topics, but my doubts had only begun.

I broke out in a cold sweat.

That afternoon, I stared at my laptop. I needed something, so I quickly typed “Effective teaching, 10 tips” and started jotting down notes; “raising your voice”, “attractive visual presentations”.

Two days later, armed with my newfound knowledge, I met the team. Speaking louder and going through my PowerPoint quickly, I was confident that they would be able to master the debate material.

Yet, an hour later, as I turned to them, I was faced with a yawning [Name].

My heart sank.

Dejected, I went home. Laying down facing my wall, I focused on a picture of me with my old team. A faint memory surfaced as I recalled Mr. Matt calling out to me, asking my opinion on diplomacy, followed by back and forth discussions between me and my teammates.

The following week, I rehashed my previous topics and asked Zidan, “Black Markets, is that illegal if it exists because of war?” He nervously explained that black markets at night, during war, were acceptable. His teammates nodded in hollow agreement.

A wave of despair took hold of me.

I felt frustrated that all my efforts would not be enough to save my little platoon from doom.

The next day, walking the school halls, I overheard Leo, a 9th grader, excitedly discussing the Flying Dutchman. I stood there wondering how their coach, Johan, inspired his team. I pushed my pride aside to attain insight. Johan laughed and said, “I make it fun” and explained his unorthodox methods to keep his team engaged—teacher-student debates, 30 seconds per speaker.

During the next session, I switched to rapid-fire debates, rotated the team members every 10 minutes using a spinning wheel, and limited the teams to a 5-minute prep time for each debate. No more daydreaming, everyone was busy scribbling arguments and discussing at lightspeed; their auras present, I was optimistic.

Finally, it was the awards ceremony. I nervously stood in a corner. Then I saw my team name. Daveen excitedly ran up to me and said, “Hey kak, look at all our medals!” His gold medals gleamed back at me brimming with fulfillment. I’ve never felt more proud that I was finally able to transform my students into the A team.

I realized my fixed mindset—I believed that everyone could be helped the same way. With my new growth mindset, I have evolved my knowledge not just from independence but from asking others and by being open to trying new things. Going forward, I’ve realized I will never have the answer from the start, but I’m finally open to collaborate, inquire, and experience new ideas. Only through continuous inquiry and collaboration can innovation and creativity thrive.

I’ll never forget the sight of my grandfather with a pink umbrella. Strange, to be sure, but more importantly, embarrassing. As the bus screeched to a halt, I found myself in a critical dilemma: walk home alone in the rain or risk being made fun of by the other kids?

Brown wool sweater, shiny bald spot, with hands folded behind back. That was Grandpa’s signature look. Recently arrived from China, he’d given himself the task of greeting me at the bus stop, where he drew no shortage of judgmental glances. I’d done my best to feign ignorance.

This time, however, I was terrified. My friends were already amused by his appearance, and he wasn't doing himself any favors by holding such an obnoxious umbrella.

Resentment building, I leapt from the bus, berating him for his choice of appendage. His desperate explanation was that he’d taken the only umbrella he could find.

We walked home in silence.

It was only after I’d taken off my shoes that I noticed Grandpa was drenched; strands of hair hung limply from his head, and his sweater was now more black than brown. He wasn’t lying- the umbrella I held was the only one he could find, and he’d chosen to cover me instead of himself.

Seeing the water drip from his thin, battered body, I realized that I’d been too harsh. He was doing his best.

Grandpa is exactly sixty-one years older than me. As old Chinese people like to say, he’s eaten more salt than I have rice. This, paired with the fact that he was from a different country, meant no shortage of barriers in our day to day interactions: he didn’t understand why I loved to program or play video games, and I didn’t know any of the Chinese proverbs he liked to use.

Despite this, he proved himself to be someone I can count on, his presence at the bus stop undeterred by the elements of circumstance. We managed to build a connection amid our misunderstandings through his simple yet meaningful act of love.

“Be like him,” I told myself. I carried his kindness forward, starting from its source. My grandfather loved to talk, but my family, too busy with work and errands, rarely had ears to listen. Seeing this, I decided to give him a piece of my time. Shutting off the TV and putting my phone away, I let him know that he commanded my undivided attention. The result was a barrage of his finest memories: boyhood, raising my father, and even meeting me for the first time.

I can’t say I enjoyed it all, but it was a good conversation. I even learned a thing or two about Chinese.

Five years later, I took my curiosities to Taiwan, volunteering at an English camp. My bilingualism was handy in bridging the gap between local coworkers and visiting Americans who had trouble understanding each other. What I was most excited about, however, was being able to directly influence young and impressionable minds: twenty second graders. I’m proud to say that, through being attentive and a cheery presence, I was able to reach beyond our cultural differences to make the week I had with them truly special. Their smiles became badges of honor.

In a world where people are increasingly suspicious of each other, the strings that tie society together seem more and more strained. It’s everywhere: surveys showing division in the United States, cancel culture in popular media, as well as a general attitude of disdain between kids my age, who’ve grown to both hate and fear diversity. In college, I hope to use my resources to reverse this trend; I want people to know the powers that lie beyond these surface-level differences.

Love doesn’t require understanding, and it doesn’t always have to come at a cost. The key lies in taking the extra step. Reaching out, or maybe just being present.

I am a bad big brother. Growing up, I was a very self reserved boy that was very shy. Unlike me, my brother was always bright and never failed to bring smiles on people’s faces. While my brother expressed his feelings thoroughly, I was very conscious when it came to expressing myself. Most of the time, I always tried to keep my cool and look “mature”. This attitude of mine continued into my teenage years. I called anything I couldn’t do, or was scared to do, “cringe” and showed my dislike for it.

This toxic trait of mine soon started to affect me. There were multiple times I felt like I couldn’t control my anger. Although I never let it out, the anger and hate I felt just didn’t cool down. I had so much hate on me that I didn’t even like myself. This is when I started to binge eat every night. I ate so much junk food at night that in the morning my face would always be bloated.

Everyday, I spent hours and hours on my phone and it led me to unconsciously compare myself to people on the internet, which led to envy and hate. On the internet, there were so many great people my age: people who became millionaires in their teenage years, people that had my dream physique, talented athletes who were already set up for their future, etc. However, I was just living in a loop everyday: wake-up, go to school, play video games, binge eat, sleep, repeat.

My hatred was also expressed towards my brother. Each time my brother would try to do something new that I haven’t done or tell me about the cool things his friends had done, I would call it childish and worthless. However, deep down I was just envious. At that time, I felt like accepting meant losing and showing how weak I was.

One day, an old friend of mine texted me. It had been years since we had talked. He was my best friend who moved to another country a few years ago. He had told me the hardships he had been going through and how he overcame them. For hours and hours, he and I were just talking about what has been going through our lives. And throughout those hours, I felt so small against his maturity and positivity. Although he was a year younger than me, the way he viewed the world seemed like he was years older than me. He truly inspired me to want to become a happier and better person, and this made me want to do the same for my brother. I wanted to be someone my brother can be inspired from. I wanted to be the reliable and wise big brother I haven’t been.

To become a better influence to my brother, I realized I first needed to become a happier person. I set goals for myself which were quite simple but very impactful. I made it a hobby to be honest with myself and seek growth. If someone accomplished something, I made sure to praise them. If I felt envious towards someone, I accepted those emotions and asked for their advice. As time passed, I began to feel much happier and began to have a clearer thought for my future. And now I am on my next journey to become a pilot.

3.141592653589 793238462643… each digit floating through my mind like the inked bygone pages of myself, seemingly random but bound by a higher order. These tiny decimals of a number escape my mouth in an exhale, 348 of them. Intrinsic and inexhaustible they are fun to say. The strain of the day, drained away by the life of pi.

…383279502884… the digits echo as I continue my recitation. They grow longer, more complex to derive, harder to keep in order. I can do hard things. The pages of my journal flutter as I flip through them. A dull thud and sharp pain scream through the stadium as I crumbled to the mat. My landing awry, right patella grossly jutting sideways, audience hovered as I waited five hours for the ambulance. Elite gymnast status gone in an instant, my identity lost.

…197169399375… focusing, the persistence of pi tumbles out— wrong. I conquer doubts to begin anew. Searching for my purpose, my truth; constructing the puzzle that is me. Sprawled atop my mattress under strings of multi-colored LEDs, I lay my truth on naked paper whispering as I write, I am here…I am enough. Fortuitously, Donna's Dream found homes for my many, sparkly leotards and I began again. Using my sudden availability to donate with Donna, leaving inky remnants of myself like through a looking glass, my past captured— reminders. I’ll look at the blue smeared, sacred pages and think of where I began and the digits I have yet to recite.

…105820974944… pi and I race onward with renewed spirit. I’m a regular now at the shelter where there is no audience, only humanity. Earning trust from the asylum-seekers, I leave a little of my soul each week; I think of Bruno in The Boy in the Striped Pajamas and wonder why we all can’t see so rightly. Mental agony from the injustice of it all stains my hand like childhood scars painted— blue. I accept the challenge and quietly get on with it.

…592307816406… intensely persistent, strands of pi grow longer. Listening to their stories, giving a pair of size 14 trainers to an ebony distance runner refugee in his identifying flip-flops, sharing soulful smiles with a new Iranian friend receiving her hard-won right-to-remain status. Daily deviations, in which the journal is necessary and the ink smears; I find the pieces of my puzzle. Peace washes over me, comforting me in the reminder that these stains are eternal. Peace is hearing “Good afternoon Tuli, are you fine?” in smiling, broken English, a comfort and an honour. Digits of pi lineup definitively. A numerical arpeggio when my pen tip dimples the page and words flow before me. My story, more privileged than my refugee friends’ but encouraged by their courage; I offer pen to paper my bravery, ‘I am [Name], I am unstoppable’. Blue swirls of plans and dreams for future days populate my journal, cohabiting symbiotically with grit and humility from lessons of the past. It fills me with hope, but sometimes fear, that there are infinite more digits, infinite more stories to be told.

…286208998628… the allure of memorizing pi lies in its mystery, its refusal to be fully finished or understood. Yet there is order in this sometimes disordered space. When it seems garbled, it reliably carries on further, to infinity. My journal tells a similar story, not always elegant but always with a resolve that is my very own. Gingerly, then excitedly making unanticipated and novel choices in my personal and civic life, making human connections, building truth, determined to find my own destination. Determination is my journal I fill out and cross out, ink poetically soaking into my hand’s edge. These connections, like tiny decimals, push me to take more chances, to connect more deeply, and cherish more fully, to keep on going—infinitely…034825342117…

“So which way is it?” The sun was setting quickly, and we were nowhere near camp. We came to a halt in the middle of the tall pine forest, and my crew stared blankly at me, waiting for an answer. It was day six of my Boy Scouts wilderness backpacking trek, and I was in charge of navigating. The trail had split into two paths. My plastic compass pointed to the right, but my digital compass pointed to the left. Hiding my uneasiness, I took a deep breath and set foot on the left trail, hoping I was making the right decision.

After an hour of climbing hills and crossing streams, we stumbled upon a serene, shimmering lake. However, my heart sank when I checked the map and realized Crater Lake was on the wrong trail.
