In a wave of embarrassment, I turned to face my crew, leading them on the shameful walk back towards the correct trail with a heavy heart.

Even after the trek was over, I remained troubled about the incident. Why did two compasses at the same location point in different directions? The plastic compass was correct, but why was the digital compass wrong? The blunder shouldn’t have happened, and I couldn’t stop thinking about that.

I discovered that digital compasses take raw data from Earth’s magnetic field and convert it into accurate data. I was convinced that the one I used on the trek didn’t convert the data properly, as it had pointed me in the wrong direction. Motivated to solve this anomaly, I embarked on a journey to create a novel algorithm that could accurately convert any raw data set into accurate data. After months' worth of researching compasses and writing code, I developed the algorithm. I then presented it to a professor who specializes in magnetology, anticipating praise. However, the professor’s feedback was purely critical. “This isn’t going to work, Andy,” he bluntly stated. “The output data from your algorithm may as well be another set of raw data — it’s not accurate at all.” If I had gone on the trail with that algorithm, I would’ve most definitely been led off a cliff to my demise.

I kept pushing forward, though. I wasn’t going to let the discouraging comments deter me from reaching my goal. Step by step, I slowly revised my algorithm. The noise variable was added to stabilize the compass needle’s movement. The effects of bias were taken into consideration, ensuring that the compass wouldn’t lead me astray into nearby trees. Months of continuous learning and persistent revisions marked my journey. I talked with the professor again and comprehensively tested my algorithm using both real-world data and computer simulations. The algorithm proved to be remarkably accurate, surpassing the professor’s expectations.

What I realized from coding a new algorithm is that it’s much like hiking with an inaccurate compass; the process is filled with uncertainties. One cannot expect the code to compile perfectly the first time, just like one cannot expect to always trek through the correct path. We cannot traverse through the wilderness without challenges; hence the “wild” in “wilderness.” However, what we can do is appreciate the challenge, because that’s what makes the journey all the more special. An inaccurate compass brought me down the wrong path; but, it presented me with an opportunity to stop faulty compasses altogether. In the future, I don’t know where my journeys will take me. But, I do know one thing: I will push through every obstacle with unwavering determination.

The next time I went hiking with my crew, I brought along my prototype compass which used my algorithm. And, once again, we reached a part where the trail split into two different directions. “Which way?” they asked. I looked at the map, and then my compass. I walked in the direction the compass pointed, but this time with full confidence that we’d be going the correct way.

Not every kid can say their mom swapped her professional attire for a superhero cape. But that’s my mom—an electrical engineer who traded a promising telecom career for a messy kitchen and daily homework battles.

Growing up, I often marveled at the contrast between my mom’s upbringing in India and my own, split between India and the US. While I thrived in a large city with access to information at my fingertips, my mom grew up in a small town where computers were a luxury and quality education was limited. In school, I could research any topic with a few keystrokes, but my mom had to wait days to find the right book. Yet she pushed through these challenges and navigated a male-dominated field, earning her degree and establishing herself as an engineer. Before stepping away from her career, she worked on determining network coverage in telecom and taught engineering students—roles that demonstrated her ability to break barriers and share her knowledge.

After my sister was born, my mom made a choice that once confused me: leaving her career in telecommunications. Why give up a job that brought respect and income to stay home with us? It wasn’t until I grew older that I understood the depth of her sacrifice. My mom didn’t just leave her career; she traded it for a commitment to giving my sister and me a well-rounded upbringing. Her ability to stay at home was only possible thanks to my dad, who continued working to support our family. Together, they ensured we celebrated our cultural traditions—dancing at Garbas during Navratri or lighting fireworks for Diwali—while also encouraging academic success and supporting our passions.

Her selflessness allowed me to explore my interests with freedom. I’ve pursued coding with the same sense of adventure my mom showed in her career: teaching myself languages like Java and Python and tutoring others through volunteer work. Her sacrifices have inspired me to give back, whether I’m helping middle schoolers learn to code or assisting classmates with tough problems. Like my mom, I see value not only in what I achieve but in how I help others grow.

Even with her busy schedule, my mom still finds time for her hobbies. I often see her painting beautiful landscapes—her calm amidst the chaos. These moments remind me how she balances maintaining her identity while always putting our needs first. Sometimes, I feel guilty about the sacrifices she’s made. I see the exhaustion in her eyes after a long day, yet she always finds the energy to ask about my day, cheer me on at races, or review calculus problems with me. Her resilience constantly redefines my understanding of success.

My mom has created a life for us rich in experiences and encouragement—far more valuable than any corporate title. Her success isn’t tied to material wealth but to the impact she has on our lives. Whether she’s helping me with homework or emphasizing the importance of empathy, these values have shaped my approach to life. I strive to embody her spirit of compassion in everything I do, whether solving coding problems or pushing through a tough race.

When I sense the aroma of paneer curry mixed with cardamom, cloves, and peppers wafting from the kitchen I’m brought back to my mom’s story. Her journey reminds me that worth isn’t measured by a paycheck or title but by the impact you make. Like her, I’ve learned that fulfillment comes from the unspoken virtues of compassion, resilience, and creativity. Whether it’s tutoring middle schoolers in coding or pushing through a tough run, I know that achievement isn’t solely about results—it’s about the effort you put in and the people you uplift along the way.

My mom truly is a superhero—not for the career she gave up, but for the love, strength, and unwavering support she gives to our family every day.

Sing, O Muse, of the bond of a family that brought creativity and individuality upon me!

Like my favorite Greek and Latin poets Homer and Virgil, I call to my Muse who is not a deity, but instead, my father, a software engineer by trade but an artist at heart. This lesson I learned through him can be summed up in a quote by the Roman historian Livy: “Many things which are naturally difficult are solved by ingenuity.”

It all began during quarantine when my dad and I found ourselves desperate to escape our boredom. One afternoon, we rummaged through several forgotten boxes in the garage and stumbled upon a half-empty storage box filled with beads and tools he had once used to craft jewelry for my mom. Suddenly inspired, he taught me the basics of jewelry making. As I threaded the delicate beads through string, my father became my first Muse. My skills improved, and our designs diverged. He liked to make matching jewelry sets with a bolder look, while I found myself focusing on the intricacies of bead wiring and weaving for bracelets. My pieces featured smaller beads, forcing me to become patient when a glass seed bead escaped my fingers and disappeared on the floor. While one bracelet could take weeks to complete, the final product always makes the time and precision worth the wait.

Soon after, I became inspired by my dad’s portrait photography studio in the basement, leading me to take a photography class. My teacher had us experiment with the basics of the camera, letting us play around with shutter speeds, aperture, and more, but the pandemic pressured me to photograph places, not people, leaving my photos empty. When I asked my friends to model for me, they awkwardly posed in front of my camera, unsure of what they should do. Dejected by the shoot, I turned to my dad for advice about his ability to easily comfort others around his intimidating lens. While doing portraits of a girl in my neighborhood, I quickly adapted to her bubbly personality by casually talking with her and cracking “dad-jokes” in order to capture that same energy with my camera. Eventually, I applied these conversational-photography skills at various Latin events as Virginia Junior Classical League (VJCL) Historian. As an elected state officer for Classics, it was helpful creating an engaging conversation before asking permission to take a photo. I always focused on making others comfortable with my presence, whether that be the more academic or joyful side of Classics conventions. I smiled as I snapped students jumping for joy while competing in spirit contests, huddling around a table practicing Latin verb tenses, and singing karaoke in togas.

One of my most ambitious projects as Historian was creating a scrapbook themed around Livy’s quote on ingenuity. I embraced the challenge with my dad’s support as I prototyped the back-booking of my scrapbook. For the cover, I airbrushed a wooden plate with a purple galaxy that was splashed with gold stars, the colors symbolizing Roman royalty. With my dad’s guidance, I carefully drilled holes to form the constellation Auriga, known for its association with ingenuity. Then, we threaded star-shaped beads through the holes, illuminating them with fairy lights. For the past few months, I have been working tirelessly on the scrapbook, often staying up until midnight to perfect each spread with the placement of a photo I took or to create a Roman-inspired beaded bookmark attached to the cover. Each project I’ve done with my dad, including others like creating color-recognizing AI or 3D prints, instilled me with a mindset of ingenuity. As I embark on new projects with him before heading off to college, I’m proud to carry forward his excitement to experiment and create. My father’s support sings to me with creativity and curiosity as I aspire to continue cultivating these values as a future engineer.

As my mother taught me, starting the coffee roasting process on low heat is more than a cooking tip; it’s a ritual deeply embedded in our culture. In my Ethiopian home, coffee isn’t just a drink– it’s a gathering, an invitation to share stories, time, and hospitality. The scent alone transports me to countless moments: the crackling of charcoal as my mother shook the pan to prevent the beans from burning, her gentle reminders in Amharic to “give it a quick shake.” Coffee has always grounded us in daily rituals, weaving generations together.

Roasting coffee is a slow process, with each stage building layers of flavor. For me, the first stage– when the beans turn a soft golden brown– symbolizes my childhood: rich in experience, patient in pace, and unforgettable. As Mortimer Adler said, “Time spent savoring the flavor of tradition deepens our intellectual and personal connection to the past.” These moments with my family sipping coffee taught me patience, attention to detail, and community– values that shaped my academic pursuits.

Yet, as I grew older, these cherished rituals began to fade under modern pressures. Economic challenges forced families like mine to work multiple jobs, disrupting the gatherings that once united us. My grandparents, once regular visitors, now struggle to maintain their farm, hit by rising costs. A recent holiday felt incomplete when my cousin couldn’t attend due to a lack of access to critical data that could have improved his farm’s output. His absence– like an under-roasted bean– left a bitter note in what was once a beloved tradition.

This moment was a turning point for me: I realized the transformative power of technology and data in preserving not just livelihoods but also the traditions that bind us. During my internship at Development Sovereignty Group (DSG), I saw how Ethiopian farmers, like my family, struggled without data to optimize their crop yields. Many planted crops unsuited to their soil, leading to wasted resources and missed opportunities. At DSG, I developed web tools that automated climate inputs and integrated machine learning models for yield prediction, bridging the gap between tradition and modern necessity.

This experience mirrored lessons I had learned from roasting coffee: precision, patience, and layering knowledge are essential. As Ray Kurzweil said, “Technology is a process of continuous layering of intelligence,” much like roasting. Just as a skilled hand keeps beans from burning, technology can empower farmers to make informed decisions. At DSG, I saw that technology could not only boost efficiency but also restore balance to communities, freeing up time for traditions that sustain us. Driven to learn more, I explored the intersection of technology and agriculture. A Case Western University study highlighted how AI is helping farmers adapt to changing climate conditions with precision. This distinction becomes central to my vision of how progress and heritage can coexist.

This realization solidified my goal: to use computer science as a bridge between tradition and innovation. Just as coffee roasting balances heritage with modern techniques, my work seeks to preserve cultural customs while embracing technological advancements. The tools I developed at DSG showed me how technology can bring people together, empowering them with data to make better decisions. Armed with this knowledge, farmers can achieve higher yields with fewer resources, freeing them to spend more time on what matters most– sharing moments with loved ones. By providing farmers with reliable data, I hope to free up the precious time needed for life’s most meaningful moments– like sitting around a table with loved ones, sharing stories, and savoring the aroma of freshly roasted coffee.

Looking ahead, I am drawn to Case Western Reserve University for its interdisciplinary approach, particularly in artificial intelligence, data management, and machine learning. These fields align perfectly with my aspirations, providing me with the expertise to develop sustainable, tech-driven solutions to real-world challenges.

I gripped the cold handle of the metal seat, staring at the door where my mom had disappeared minutes ago. The hallways were too quiet, too empty. Each second that passed by, my mind raced through every possibility, until I finally heard her footsteps returning, each one heavier than the last.

“It’s positive.”

I sat in silence and disbelief. Nothing felt real. I wanted to scream, but nothing came out. How could something I’d been dreading for days still manage to shatter me? A week later, my biggest fear came true: it took my mother too.

The smell of disinfectant filled every corner of our house. The dining table, once furnished with empty Cheetos packets, was now cluttered with boxes of masks and bottles of sanitizer. For the first time, I was fully dependent on myself. Even my allergies, which my mom always had the cure for, worsened. Without her kadha, a simple yet powerful drink she made, my body started giving up in ways I had never seen before.

But more than my allergies, it was my dad who scared me. He’d been fighting this battle just as hard as mom had, but unlike her, his condition wasn’t improving. He wasn’t just physically weak—he was losing hope.

That’s when I realized how much he needed something to hold onto, a reminder that I was always with him. The more I pushed myself to do things I assumed were beyond me, like reaching my fitness goals or ironing my clothes without burning myself, the more it seemed to lift his spirits. It made me think of the one thing that had always comforted me—the kadha. If I could make it, something I’d never thought I could do without mom, maybe it could give him the strength to keep going.

The first attempt, like all first times, was horrible. I boiled the water for too long, put in seven extra tulsi leaves, and even learnt the hard way that haldi isn’t just used as a hair mask. But I didn’t stop. I couldn’t. The fear and hesitation slowly simmered away with every stir, every new try, until the kitchen no longer felt like an intimidating place, but a space where I found strength I didn’t know I had.

Each time I prepared the kadha, I focused on fixing the little things—cutting the ginger just right or grinding enough black pepper to avoid burning my throat. It was my way of channeling all the uncertainty into something tangible, an escape from all the chaos around me.

After countless tweaks, I finally got it right. With a steady hand, I poured my creation into a cup. I could feel the steam rising, fogging up my glasses. I closed my eyes and took a sip; it tasted exactly how my mother’s did: bitter, but comforting. I immediately sent a fleet of minute-long time lapses to my dad, sharing every detail of my journey.

The next morning, during our daily calls, I noticed a change in him. His face lit up when he watched the videos, and the way he smiled seemed different—like he had found a spark again. His subtle nod of approval told me what words couldn’t: my efforts were helping. Each time I challenged myself, I felt like I was moving both of us forward, one small victory at a time.

The mindset I built in that kitchen is the same force that pushes me today: the drive to give my all in everything I do. The lessons I learned weren’t just about crafting a perfect remedy; they were about doing what I thought I couldn’t do and refusing to accept less than my best. Now, every time I step into a new challenge, I think back to that first sip of kadha. It didn’t just taste bitter—it tasted like perseverance, like strength. And that’s a taste I never want to lose.

I carefully place my high-precision tweezers around the covers of a miniature book and slowly slide it onto a shelf. A final nudge to align it just so, and I sit back to survey the miniature library forming amid the scattered pieces of discarded paper and wood on my bedroom floor.

My bedroom has two large bookshelves that are “human” size. Over the years, the books themselves have changed multiple times. These days, most are mysteries, true crime, and crime-fiction novels. Spooky and deranged stories I love to get lost in. Scattered among them are also several more “serious” books, mostly on psychology, the brain, and behavioral science.

If you look more closely though, you will notice that some books on my shelves are not books at all, but rather miniature bookends with mystery worlds inside them. A potions shop, a detective’s office, a library, a crime scene …

These are the worlds I create from scratch—miniature universes where attention to detail transforms the ordinary into something entirely new. From a distance, they appear as simple, small-scale models. But, when you look closer, they come to life. You can see the names of exotic spices on bottles in a tiny kitchen, or titles of books no larger than a grain of rice. Every element has a specific role, placed with precision and purpose to contribute to a bigger picture.

In between my projects, I often flipped through Netter’s Neuroscience Coloring Book, immersing myself in another mysterious world – one that is ruled by the complex functions of the brain. As I read about the brain's scientific functions, I began connecting the parts I was learning about with the process of building my models. For example, the cerebellum, responsible for fine motor skills, oversees the precision I need to glue each tiny element in place. Meanwhile, the parietal lobe, which helps us understand spatial relationships, helps me carefully maneuver my giant fingers across the miniature spaces I furnish. And the prefrontal cortex, the executive part of the brain, helps me strategize which steps to take next as I map out each scene.

With each new miniature bookend added to my shelves, these connections help me develop more patience, creativity, and attention to detail–skills that I apply outside of my hobby. For example, after truly enjoying my AP Biology class during junior year, I requested to be my teacher’s aide during senior year. The job often requires patience to complete many tedious, repeatable tasks. I use creative analogies to help my freshmen colleagues remember some of the more confusing concepts. Finally, I apply my attention to detail with everyday tasks at the lab, for example, when prepping solutions for diffusion labs or pre-grading post-lab reports for my teacher.

What began as a simple hobby of crafting miniature worlds in my bedroom has over time transformed into a deeper understanding of the skills I will need to explore my more academic interests. Having an opportunity to translate these skills into hands-on experiences in my school’s bio lab has strengthened my desire to study neuroscience in college. I plan to actively seek opportunities to participate in research projects on how the various brain functions affect human behavior. I believe that being able to effectively collaborate with others, work independently, and patiently sift through detailed data will help me be a productive student and undergraduate researcher.

For each of my miniatures, hundreds of tiniest pieces – with their unique colors, shapes, and details – come together to form intricate and life-like scenes. For my college experience, I hope to bring in my own experiences, skills, and perspectives to contribute, in small part, to a vibrant and rich college community.

My sister and I aggressively scramble the jade tiles while my angkong (grandpa) and ama (grandma) sit quietly, waiting for us to organize the game of mahjong. Each click-clack cut through the suffocating silence, a silence I had grown used to over the years.

Unfamiliar with my grandparents’ ancestral Lannang-ue, a rapidly-declining spoken-only Filipino-Chinese dialect, I remained complacent using my school-taught English. Our superficial exchanges—restricted by my painfully limited vocabulary of ‘thank-you’s’ and ‘how-are-you’s’—isolated me from both my family and heritage.

As the world grew quiet during the pandemic, the silence between our generations became more pronounced. I was forced to confront the fact that I was a passive observer to Lannang-ue’s silent extinction.

I began to fill the silences of our mahjong games with overflowing questions. When I asked my angkong about escaping Post-Revolution China, I learned about WW2’s far-reaching effects on Chinese families during 1940s Manila. Listening to my ama relaying their epic love story, I discovered the term ‘kai-shao,’ the practice of parents introducing their children to potential partners—a tradition that persists in many Filipino-Chinese households today.

The once-distant figures sitting across the table transformed into my angkong and my ama—living embodiments of anecdotes and histories I was just beginning to understand.

Spurred by the outpouring passion my grandparents expressed while sharing their stories, I engaged with and listened to more native voices within my local Lannang-ue community. By interviewing elementary school-teachers and fervent churchgoers, I was struck by the people’s sense of resignation, paralyzed by the academic prioritization of Mandarin and prevalence of English in social media discourse. As I reflected on the loss of this dialect, a sense of urgency and responsibility began to stir within me: what if I built a web-based translator to help revive it?

In early 2022, I started compiling frequently-used words in conversations to compose the translator's database. I then reached out to my fluent-speaking relatives, recording them as they articulated the lists of words. I’d pester them on weekends, couch-surfing between my grandparent’s living room and my aunt’s single-roomed condominium.

After collecting the audio files, I noted their romanizations and set the rules for the translator’s standardized orthography. From my uncle's crisp, clear syllables to my ama's nasalized yet precise speech, each recording brought the words of Lannang-ue to life. Hearing their variety of accents and articulations, I realized how much I’d failed to appreciate the voices that raised me. Within silence held possibility—a space where unheard stories, voices, and perspectives reside, waiting to be shared.

Two years after embarking on this initiative, I find myself presenting my translator at the Lannang-ue Symposium. Scanning the room and noticing school principals’ gentle smiles and the tears in my parents’ eyes at the mention of my deepening bond with Ama and Angkong, I was reminded that only through our collective voices and dedication could this project and the community that comes with it become a reality.

Over the three-day conference, I engaged with individuals from varied backgrounds and careers, from aspiring filmmakers to prominent social activists, learning about Lannang-ue dubbing in Filipino movies and traditional Lannang-ue calligraphy. The more I asked and listened, the more I learned that silence was nowhere to be found. Through it all, I recognized that the impact of preserving a language goes beyond words: it fosters relations and safeguards identities, ensuring that no one’s story is forgotten.

The silence between me and my grandparents was never just an absence of sound. It is emblematic of a larger, historical silencing—one that prioritizes certain languages and knowledge while drowning others out. In a world where diverse voices are stifled by indifference, I’m determined to uncover the mysteries of those around me from family, acquaintances, to strangers and empower them to express their truths. No matter where I am, or who I’m with, or what language we speak, I vow that the world I live in will never fall silent.

The First Technology Challenge, my first event in 10th grade, marked the beginning of both my high school journey and my experience in competitive robotics. For four months, we learned how to build a robot from various parts, but it was challenging to implement the predetermined functions smoothly. I connected a claw to the robot’s servo, but it couldn’t fully grip. During the automatic phase, the robot’s four wheels did not travel equal distances, making it impossible to stop at an exact location. Time was running out, and we had to upload a video of the robot’s performance. After over 30 exhausting rehearsals with countless mistakes, we submitted the video. Unsurprisingly, we did not win the prize we had hoped for.

From a young age, I have been passionate about robot design and construction. This trial dealt me a heavy blow. The memory of the last game haunted my dreams for some time. After reviewing every detail of our preparation, I realized that inadequate preparation, lack of experience, and limited tools were key factors in our failure. Additionally, our reluctance to refine and polish our design and operational skills only compounded our mistakes, reinforcing the challenges we faced throughout the process.

After careful analysis, I resolved to rebuild my team and compete once more. However, my parents strongly opposed my decision, citing insufficient funds and my heavy school workload. Undeterred, we secretly developed our robot design, but we struggled to find a training location. To secure a suitable space, I scoured the internet, sent hundreds of emails to various organizations, and publicized our project among those around me. Eventually, we secured a meeting room at a local company to continue our work. With renewed determination, we meticulously crafted our robot, aiming to avoid the mistakes and shortcomings of our previous experience. Excited and confident, we arrived at the National Qualifier competition in Shanghai.

In the same venue and competition, I felt nervous yet determined to seek revenge. Reviewing our 15-page engineering portfolio, I gathered all our efforts and encouraged my teammates to collaborate closely. Ultimately, our hard work paid off, and we proudly secured first place, earning a spot in the National Finals.

This small success earned my parents’ praise, but I soon faced a new challenge. On the last day of registration, four team members withdrew, leaving just three of us for the next round. I began to doubt whether I should continue fighting in the final round. Fortunately, the other two firmly believed we could win an award at the national competition. Motivated by their enthusiasm, I spent the entire night recruiting new members. To rebuild our team’s confidence, I personally spoke with each individual and passionately introduced our plan.

The final training sessions were intense and challenging. I embraced the unique strengths of each team member and boldly used carbon fiber to reduce weight, reconstructing our robot to better suit the competition field. Additionally, I focused on promoting our team and project to attract the attention of judges and the audience. Ultimately, we earned first place in the Motivational Award.

I was exhausted but deeply satisfied. I proved myself, stepping out of my comfort zone and achieving significant growth in leadership and teamwork while gaining valuable insights about life. I learned that trying, challenging myself, changing, and ultimately succeeding are vital. Failure is not an obstacle but a catalyst for my continued refinement.

My book lied to me.

Seven years ago, I picked it up from the bookstore. But it wasn't the typical "Wings of Fire" or "Percy Jackson" adventure I used to read. This book had big, black, bold letters written on the cover, saying: "How to Beat Your Dad at Chess." In the following days, I buried myself in the book, memorizing every trap and checkmate pattern there was. Finally, I was ready. With a bishop in one hand and the book in the other, I challenge my Dad to a game of chess, determined to beat him for the first time ever. But as the moves unfolded, I realized something: the book had lied to me. I, in fact, could not beat my Dad.

I had learned something important that day: that there were no shortcuts, no single book that would magically help me beat my Dad. So, I kept reading. "Silman Complete Endgame Course" and "The Art of the Middle Game" became my companions. They revealed how much there was to learn on this tiny 8x8 board. The more I played, the more question arose: "If two bishops could checkmate a lone king, why couldn't two knights do the same? They're worth the same points, after all." As I got better, I would find the answers to these questions. Yet, the mystery and intricacy of this game would continue to intrigue me.

Eventually, I joined a local chess academy near my house. Being the only amateur in a room full of competitive players was intimidating. While the other players cruised through the chess puzzles set by our coach, I struggled to process even the simplest ones. The matches I played against my classmates felt like those with my Dad: hopeless. There was Lucas, whose aggressive style always broke through my defenses; Ava, the cunning fox who set traps like her notorious "poison pawns," which I fell for more times than I'd like to admit; and Marcus, whose slow, positional plays gradually suffocated my pieces.

There were countless moments when I felt like quitting, but to walk away would mean giving up on my goal of beating my Dad. Long after classes were over, I remained behind, running through strategies with my coach. I took home puzzles, filling my evenings with diagrams and pieces. Nights were spent staring at my computer screen, trying to outmaneuver other online players. After two years of relentless practice, I was finally ready.

At the age of 12, I took down the reigning champion of my house: Dad.

Chess was more than just beating my Dad, though. While the goal motivated me to start, the community, support, and friendship were what kept me going during these two years at the academy.

Wanting to share my knowledge and this sense of community, I founded a chess club at my school. Initially, the club struggled. The numbers were low, and I did not know how to teach middle school students. Through continuous breaktime promotional campaigns, flyers posted around the campus, and mimicking teaching techniques from Ms. Claire, my club began to flourish with over 20 students each session. Though creating lesson plans and hosting intra-tournaments took hours to prepare, seeing my students' eyes light up when solving a puzzle and watching them grow into formidable players was truly rewarding.

Now, the book "How to Beat Your Dad at Chess" lies on a shelf somewhere, covered in dust. I don't need it anymore; I could easily beat my Dad blindfolded! But the real lesson wasn't in beating him; it was the journey. Improvement doesn't come from shortcuts or quick fixes but from perseverance, community, and a love for learning. Whether on the chessboard, in the robotics lab, or while training AI models, there is always more to discover, learn, and achieve.

The moment they announced my name as the winner felt like fiction; it felt like the world's edges had gone blurry. I was standing in a room full of seasoned hackers, each seemingly more confident than I was. My heart pounded like a drum out of sync: no steady, predictable beat, just a sense of unease and instability. Despite my passion for programming, with my first hackathon, there lingered a paralyzing fear of not belonging. Throughout the day, I wondered if my code was good enough as I overheard others finalizing their projects, wisps of technical jargon coloring the air, making me feel like I was in the middle of a NASA space launch. Yet, here I was, standing at the winner's podium, taking photos and accepting my prize.

This was my first hackathon, and it opened my eyes to a steep learning curve that often intimidates beginners. At that moment, I realized how daunting programming could be when you're isolated. This experience made me worry for others who feel the same fear I did. I wanted to make learning accessible, to transform the intimidating process of computers into something collaborative, creative, and fun.

Creativity has always been the core of my programming journey. I once spent weeks recreating a grappling hook movement from the anime Attack on Titan for a video game. To capture the fluid, realistic motion, I used a linearly interpolated sinusoid function for the grappling hook and meticulously adjusted the player's camera settings to match the chaotic yet controlled feel that I was attempting to emulate. Each challenge pushed me to think outside the box, and seeing the final project work perfectly was incredibly satisfying. These moments of creativity and problem-solving are what drives my love for programming. However, until the hackathon, I had yet to realize the true significance of collaboration. As a counselor at a tech camp called ATAM, I collaborate with students by helping them design their own projects. I witness the spark of excitement when they are finally able to bring their ideas to life. Recently, a student asked me how to recreate an attack from the anime One Piece. Helping him navigate this challenge reminded me of the struggles I faced at my first hackathon: it is essential to foster learning through a collaborative environment.

I knew the best way to make others excited about programming would be through a collaborative hackathon. And so I've embarked on the ambitious journey of organizing my own. Initially, I underestimated how complex the process would be. After contacting several local venues for weeks, I finally secured a space at a nearby church, but the cost for a single day was $500—an amount that would exhaust all the funding I had raised so far. This left me at a crossroads: either proceed with limited resources or delay the event to allow more time to gather the necessary funds. I felt a wave of disappointment wash over me.

I consulted with an advisor from the Hack Club, a community of like-minded hackers, and I knew postponing the hackathon would be worth the wait. Since then, I've been working closely with my school's booster club to raise more funds. I have registered as a non-profit with the Hack Club Foundation to access additional sponsorships. I've also reached out to companies affiliated with Hack Club to secure merchandise and prizes for the event. The entire process—each call, each email—has been a lesson in patience and persistence.

Whether working on solo projects, guiding students at ATAM, or collaborating to create an inclusive hackathon, I've learned that programming is more than just writing code. It's a tool for creative expression and collaboration. As I move forward, I'm more determined than ever to share this realization with others, transforming fear and isolation into excitement and opportunity for students everywhere to bring their ideas to life.

“What if they don’t accept me for who I am? Will they see me as a fraud, someone trying to act smart?” Millions of thoughts rushed through my head as I struggled to present my new sprouting identity in front of my friends. The battle between authenticity and acceptance was relentless. Then, by capitulating to an easier route, I wore a fake mask and pretended to be someone I was not. At this moment, my thoughts threw me back to the beginning of my self-improvement journey.

The best thing about a mirror is that it holds you accountable by being direct and brutal. It speaks the truth that one needs to hear. I would roll out of bed, stumble towards the mirror, and look at myself. Procrastination, being out of shape, and lacking energy are all reflections in the mirror. I was around 136 pounds then, undoubtedly underweight for a 6-foot individual. I sighed before turning away from the mirror, knowing I desperately needed change. I started by reading. To become the best version of myself, I have to start by changing my mindset. Just like a plant can’t bloom if its roots are damaged. After reading my first self-improvement book, Seven Habits of Highly Effective People, I no longer underestimated the power accumulated by small habits. So, I started with a simple task every morning: 10 minutes of reading. Completing this “small” task allows me to carry this pride and proceed the day with more significant tasks.

At the age of 16, this tiny habit embarked on the beginning of my self-improvement journey. It was never simply because I was eager to become the best version of myself, but more importantly, because I could be my authentic self whenever I immersed myself in those activities. The non-negotiable daily routine was each practice—Stoicism, weightlifting, cold showers, meditation, and reading self-improvement books. I found solace in conversations with ancient Stoic philosophers by reading their writings imparted throughout generations. It was never an easy journey. This “difference” was amplified as none of my classmates were interested in self-improvement.

Our teacher asked the class to discuss something that influenced our lives one day. Excitement engulfed my mind as I was passionate about how Stoicism changed me. I confidently walked up to the front of the class, and suddenly, the confidence disappeared like an extinguished candle. While others talked about sports and outfits, my heart raced at how people would alienate me if I talked about philosophy. My face appeared to blush, and without consciousness, I spoke about social media falteringly. My heart sank with every sentence, knowing I was betraying my true self in exchange for acceptance from my classmates. My classmates nodded, but deep down, I knew they were responding to a version of me that didn’t exist. Despite their positive reaction, the immense weight of wearing this mask rested on my shoulder for the entire night. I failed to apply the values of Stoicism I internalized—principles of courage, control, and wisdom—when I needed them most. I stumbled back towards the accountability mirror. The two options were evident from the mirror reflections: I could either continue to wear this mask or start being my authentic self regardless of how others perceived me. The things within my control became more evident: my values, actions, and how I respond to the people around me.

At that exact moment, the idea of Stoic Virtue was born; I decided to create an Instagram account, not to seek external validation but to integrate ancient wisdom into my life. Through meticulously crafted reels, I combined cinematic clips with texts that conveyed Stoic wisdom. This time, I chose not to focus on things not within my control, such as likes or followers. As I reflect on this lonely journey, I now see this disconnection and loneliness as never a burden but an opportunity to practice the virtues I embody and become my authentic self.

I blew away a rebellious strand of hair, trying—and failing—to keep it from blocking my vision as I placed down the diya, carefully trying not to ruin the surrounding rangoli designs. I got up, stood next to my mum and looked at the masterpiece we had created. It was my favorite time of year: Diwali.

Growing up, my parents never failed to remind me of my heritage, one that survived constant relocation. I was born in the UAE to Indian immigrant parents, raised in England, moved regularly within the Middle East, and yet, each Hindu festival was celebrated in the grandest ways: my mother and I drew rangoli outside our front door, lit diyas around the house and polished the silver murtis. Each time we moved, I carried the weight of my heritage - one that contrasted starkly with my surroundings.

Starting afresh in each new country felt like repeating the same cycle. Classmates chatted in unfamiliar languages and cafeteria food had names I couldn't pronounce. I watched others find their places through shared cultural similarities. I felt out of place. So, I pushed away my heritage, trying to force myself to fit in. Rather than fast during Diwali, I began to fast alongside my new friends during Ramadan. I was excited to find a new community, but I was scared too. Would my parents be mad? Who am I if not my mothers daughter, kneeling beside her and drawing rangoli on our doorstep? Is this the right choice?

When I struggled to remember the words during our pooja, or prayer, at Diwali, I realized I had made the wrong choice. I felt embarrassed. My mother reminded me of the words, and I finished the prayer.

I had forgotten my Indian roots, my favorite traditions, to make space for newer ones to form. Now, rather than rejecting my culture, I have learnt to share it. After moving to boarding school, I use the opportunity to teach others about Diwali and Ramadan, and celebrate with them - starting new traditions, but not forgetting old ones. We celebrate every festival together, from having colorful water fights for Holi to playing dreidel at Hanukkah. My friends and I share a bond not made of cultural similarity, but instead of understanding and appreciation; as a result, I have learned that light holds important symbolism in many cultures: Diwali diyas, menorah on Hanukkah and Christmas advent candles. Yet, living so far from home forced my peers to leave behind their traditions, not having the appropriate artifacts to celebrate them. I wanted to fix this. So I started a foundation, Lumière, with my two closest friends. I handcrafted candles specific to each tradition, providing students at my school an accessible way to reconnect with their heritage. We stocked nutmeg advent candle sets, olive oil menorahs, and lotus-shaped diyas. I watched as my peers opened up and shared their beautiful traditions with each other.

Observing the impact we made, I expanded Lumière’s outreach and decided to donate our proceeds towards funding education in underprivileged areas. After pitching to local businesses, we acquired partnerships and currently stock our candles at three boutiques in Oxford. Our efforts were celebrated when we were named finalists for the Wings of Hope Award (WOHAA), an honor recognized by the House of Lords. We also received the title for ‘Most Entrepreneurial Project: WOHAA 2024’ from London Business School. I am proud to say that as of this year, we have funded the education of four young girls in India. I am grateful to be a small part of the reason why another community is able to learn and take interest in the world, using their knowledge to unite others.

While initially, conformity had motivated me to explore cultures besides my own, I hope to keep doing so, continuing to unite my community in a way that is uniquely me. I am not scared to relocate for university, because I know that wherever I end up I will find purpose in sharing my traditions and starting new ones.

**Essay:**

Trying to bottle a storm: unpredictable, chaotic, and impossible to control. This is what packing our home felt like. Zollikon, Switzerland has always been the most beautiful place on earth in my eyes. The thought of going away filled me with dread, and I tried delaying the goodbyes as much as I could. Terrified, I was certain that my life was going to change for the worst. On the verge of tears, I thought of a friend's perspective-shifting advice: “This will be a great adventure."

My first adventure was enrolling at my new school. As I sat in the uncomfortable chairs of the new auditorium, I was overwhelmed with fear as I recognized no one. While they were happy, chatting excitedly, laughing with relief as they reunited with their friends, I continued to feel excluded, a deep ache of loneliness creeping in, because connections were blooming around me while I was isolated.

As I slowly began to realize that I had to take the initiative to become part of this new community, I brought up the courage to ask the people around me to play a simple game of catch. When they agreed, I felt a sense of relief and joy to have made a first connection. Leaving that game of catch, thoughts started racing through my head: these people were open, nice, and shared my interests. Happiness, belief, and belonging - within reach. I couldn’t help but think that this had the potential to turn out fine.

I feverishly thought about further possibilities to get in contact and pushed myself to try them out. Looking back, the game-changing idea, in terms of conveying a real sense of community, was to organize a study group. When my classmates got overwhelmed (especially in math and physics), we would sit together for hours in my house to explain and revise but also to laugh and chat. The more I branched out, the more integrated I became.

I now am certain that what I had initially thought to be a catastrophe that would cause a deadly storm, has been one of the most valuable challenges to overcome. It has created an understanding of my character that has shaped me into who I am. I have grown beyond myself, into someone who learns from others, benefits his community, and sees the positives in change.

As I turn toward the future on the college campus, this experience will be a blueprint for using my curiosity and for confidently exploring diverse challenges. I can cope with novelty and seize opportunities resulting in pushing my boundaries. I can integrate myself and others into a team of students, creating good spirit and thus laying a foundation for a successful community.

At College, I am particularly drawn to cutting-edge research on Tariff Negotiation and Trade Agreements. I am fascinated about how these economic policies can create change on a global scale, and I am thrilled for the opportunity to share this with others because it is crucial for tackling issues like poverty. I envision creating a club on campus to foster a sense of community, kinship, and support with students who are also passionate about this. It will be intimidating to do this in yet another new area, but I will take a leap, engage with others, and learn from new perspectives to make this successful.

The confrontation with novelty and the method I developed to overcome my struggles will help me venture further into the fascinating topic of economic policies, contact other researchers, and thus fuel change for the better by teaching others about these policies that will reduce poverty and improve life for everyone around the world. Because of these personal changes, the frightened boy from Switzerland can aspire to improve life for others around the world.

The harmonium mocked me, demanding answers I didn’t have. My guru’s words—“Just feel it”—echoed, taunting my instinct for control. Feel it? No. Music had rules, and I was supposed to follow them.

After years of memorizing every note and phrase of Hindustani raags, my guru asked me to try the vistar—an untethered improvisation. I waited for the right notes to come, but they didn’t. Every part of me clung to what I knew: patterns, rules, and structure. None of which could save me.

This tendency began when I first got a Rubik’s cube. It was simple: twists and turns led to either success or failure, forward or backward. No surprises. It became my lens for understanding the world—a method to the madness.

The lens fogged when my parents announced we were moving. Amidst the mayhem, I needed control. I turned to the cube, spinning its colored faces over and over, finding comfort in the precision of each solution. But now, it couldn’t solve the looming uncertainty. Using the objectivity of formulas as my guide, I started detailing blueprints for all aspects of life to stay afloat amidst uncertainties. These rules were my buoy. By high school, they guided me through academics, dieting, music, and even social interactions. If something could be broken into steps, I could manage it. Control was my constant.

It had its limits, however. When my sister left for college, I realized I lost something I hadn’t fully appreciated—our spontaneous conversations. I tried to fill the silence by fitting calls with her into my structured routine, but loneliness wasn't on the clock. The more I clung to control, the more life slipped through my fingers. The world I tried to organize had begun to feel cold and mechanical.

In my attempt to control my life, I lost the human touch—which didn’t fit a set solution. Relationships, creativity, self-discovery—they needed the vistar—messiness, imperfection, unpredictability. What once felt like discomfort now beckoned me toward the harmonium—not with answers but with freedom to explore. I stopped waiting for the "right" notes, and just played. The music that spilled out wasn’t perfect, but it was mine. For the first time, I stopped playing music and started feeling it. The harmonium sang with something raw, something I couldn’t predict—and I loved it.

I started small, weaving vistars into the memorized phrases of each raag, creating a unique composition each time. Structure—like a neatly wrapped gift—gave shape and purpose. But vistar, the ribbon, added life, balancing order with creativity. Gradually, spontaneity seeped into other parts of my life.

In my role as a life insurance intern, the meticulousness of policy calculations felt reassuring. However, the fundamentals of insurance lie in human connection. We speak with clients at two significant moments: when purchasing a policy, and later, on the worst day of their life.

Sitting across from someone in their darkest moment, structure faded. What remained were the unscripted moments—the pauses, the ache in their voices as they searched for words. There was no formula for these interactions. Instead, I focused on what I could offer: a quiet, listening ear. Structure and improvisation were not opposites but companions. Policies offered security, but trust and comfort were born in unplanned, human moments.

Beauty isn't solely hidden within order and perfection. It thrives in the spaces in between—the moments where I let go, allowing life to surprise me. The Rubik’s cube still sits on my desk, but it no longer symbolizes control. Instead, it serves as a reminder that life, like its twists and turns, rarely follows a set pattern. Each time I solve the cube, I let go of the path that got me there, instead focusing on what I can control while embracing the uncertainty of a new solution. Spontaneity is no longer something I resist; instead, I welcome it. I’ve learned to sing with it, creating harmony, one vistar at a time.

When I watched my meticulously crafted rebellion against the Trojan authority unfold under my feet, entropy felt like gold. After all, I was the mastermind. But entropy doesn’t feel all that nice when I’m no longer in the driver’s seat.

Chaos, shouting, and anger were what the first meeting to plan the South Bay Model UN conference had devolved into—entropy, in its purest form. And, “leading” it all, was me. With my every attempt to subdue the masses drowned out by the cacophony of their voices, a flicker of doubt crossed my mind.

You see, I’ve always liked the idea of clean, neat categories—like in personality types. In 6th grade, I was typed as an ISFP. One of the 16 personality types from the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, the letters in ISFP stand for Introvert Sensing Feeling Perceiving. I had never resonated with any descriptor so vividly.

In career, ISFPs are free-spirited designers, artists, and creatives.

ISFPs are not natural leaders. Those were the extroverts, the “E”s. To top it off, the “power delegate,” the embodiment of the ideal in Model UN is synonymous with “E.” So when I joined the Model UN club in freshman year, I often found that my introverted “I” stuck out rather awkwardly in a room full of those extroverted “E”s.

Nor are ISFPs scientists. In the cold and uncompromising realm of science and equations, my Feeling, my “F,” struggled to find its place among Thinkers, “T”s. In an activity in my freshman year Java class, my teacher had everyone take the personality test, referencing a ranking of the personality types most likely to succeed in different fields. ISFP was ranked last in every quantitative field. Ouch.

This was simply the natural order of the world—or so I thought.

Literary analysis threw a wrench in my carefully constructed worldview. In my junior year Honors American Literature (HamLit) class, I analyzed Gene Luen Yang’s “American Born Chinese,” a graphic novel following Chinese-American Jin Wang’s struggle to overcome the forced assimilation of his cultural identity in an environment that refused to acknowledge it. Analyzing “American Born Chinese,” I found, was surprisingly methodical. A claim, evidence, and a line of reasoning. A class, a function, and an if-else block. A problem, a business solution, and a value proposition. It seemed impossible: literature, a field I had always associated so deeply with the humanities—with “F”—could simultaneously be “T” too. Clearly, those “clean-cut” categories weren’t so clean after all.

I’d always believed that you had to fit a specific archetype to succeed in different disciplines, that my ISFP meant that I couldn’t pursue my passions. But I’ve come to realize that the premise of putting personality in clean-cut categories is flawed—after all, my existence is the very antithesis to the one-dimensional “I” and “E,” “F” and “T” binary. Even if I could define a million binaries that could somehow represent every single identity that shapes my personality, it can only describe the person I am in the present—not the person I will be tomorrow.

Embracing chaos has led me to a new understanding of entropy: the infinite possibilities in my future. I am an artist, researcher, diplomat, entrepreneur, mentor, leader, and everything in between—a chaotic mishmash of identities that shape my identity. I’m not what people call a “power delegate,” nor do I want to be one. Rejecting conventional definitions of success has allowed me to pave my own path—to define for myself what it means to succeed in Model UN and STEM.

That moment of doubt that flickered across my mind is now no more than a fleeting instance, a flickering shadow of my previous worldview. I’m back in front of the Zoom meeting on my laptop screen, with a strange sense of clarity amidst the chaos. This is entropy—it’s where I thrive.

“Jason, please pay attention!” I sighed for the sixth time in fifteen minutes, setting the book down in my lap. The restless first-grader’s head swiveled in my direction, breaking his riveted gaze out the window, but his round face was contorted into a defiant pout. His classmates tittered as I watched him expectantly. Finally, he huffed, folding his arms as he turned toward my chair.

But before I could continue, Jason flung his finger at the open page, his eyes scrunched and tongue stuck out in a disgusted expression. “Ewww, they kiss!” he cried, repulsed.

“This picture is just showing us how much Mama Bear loves her baby,” I replied, straining to contain my bubbling frustration. “Doesn’t your mom kiss you good night?”

Jason shook his head vehemently, frowning with an intense ferocity. I stared, half-confused and half-incredulous. “She must at least hug you, right?”

The only response to my question was the ticking of the wall clock. Jason’s face was a clouded storm, his brows furrowed and lips pressed tightly together. Finally, his best friend, the boy beside him, quietly murmured, “Jason doesn’t have a mom.”

I blinked, frozen, as Jason furiously shoved his friend. His dark eyes suddenly welled with tears that glittered under the classroom’s too-bright lights. In that moment, I was all too aware of not just the guilt knotting my throat, but of the place in my heart that I had taken for granted simply because I had never thought that it could have been empty. A new silence stretched, but the tension was no longer from my prior irritation.

“I’m sorry, Jason. Can I give you a hug?”

Jason hesitated, watching me with guarded anticipation. Then he nodded. He stood stiffly in the embrace, awkwardly unsure of how to respond, until slowly, I felt him hug me back. As the tiny feathery bits of dust, illuminated by the afternoon sun, settled on the damp beads on his eyelashes, I felt a hint of warmth in his eyes, and it warmed me, too.

After three years of volunteering at this elementary school, I’d thought that compassion and cultural sensitivity simply meant being able to form connections despite our wide differences in backgrounds. But that day, I was reminded of how easily I could still default to assumptions. I had forgotten that there was more nuance than I could see in the hidden battles people were fighting and in the help they truly needed. What Jason needed wasn’t my quickness to react to a presumption that he was intentionally being disruptive for attention, but my recognition that my interpretations of his actions couldn’t account for the parts of him that I did not yet understand.

Later that spring, my best friend’s dad passed away. At first, I was unsettled by her occasional flares of uncharacteristic impatience and avoidance. But as I tried to comprehend the loss she was grappling with, I knew that I could only carefully avoid pressuring her into talking about her feelings or assuming what grieving was supposed to look like. I was careful not to overstep when I knew that I could not relate to, understand, and address her pain the way that others in her support systems could, even though I still tried. Through hugs that held both apologies and understanding, our friendship grew stronger even when it was unspoken.

After all, good intentions, even towards those we care most about, might not always offer support in the ways we expect.

What do a dermatologist clinic, a music practice room, and a science cart have in common? For me, they all became real-life classrooms—spaces where we can truly learn.

The Dermatologist:
So, what now? Param and I had cleaned all the exam rooms as there weren’t many patients. “It’s only a two-week volunteer gig,” I sighed, “so I guess we’re chilling.” Then I looked around: “Wait—why’s there so many empty chairs… where’s everyone else?” 
Lifting myself, I walked around and bumped into EJ, a clinic tech, juggling a stack of gloveboxes. Gathering the fallen boxes, I joined him to help refill rooms out of gloveboxes. Closing the cabinet to the last room, I saw the nurse, Stephanie, stapling patient appointment sheets together. Without a word, I grabbed a stapler and matched her rhythm, stacking the finished sheets beside her. Behind me, Dr. Soong was busy sorting pamphlets, so I stepped over and started stacking the scattered flyers into neat piles. 
Even Param joined in on the action! Apart from sanitizing the used exam rooms, these mundane tasks were on lockdown between us two. Through the next two weeks, the empty chairs became a familiar sight.

The Music Practice Room:
How do I synchronize my piano solo with Erin’s and Igrainne’s violin and cello accompaniment? From years of solo practicing, the “correct” solution was to slap on the metronome to our playing. 
But now, stuffed in a cramped practice room, the steady beat of the metronome would be of no help. Our individual interpretations of tempo or minute changes in dynamics of ensemble playing couldn’t be constrained by a mechanical tick. 
Then, I recalled my time as principal cellist with the All-State Orchestra. Along with performing, I had eight other cellists to lead and coordinate with the other sections. There, it wasn’t our sheet music or metronome that guided us. It was the subtle cues of non-verbal communication. Sometimes, it was an eyebrow raised from the solo violinist; other times, it was a subtle breath towards the violist. 
Recycling this concept, I used my independence to become a mini conductor for our trio. Lifting my hands above the keys, my chin shot up towards Erin who would then mirror the nod to Igrainne. This pulse would continue at the end of each phrase, keeping the harmony together.

The Science Center:
How do you teach a 6-year-old about moon craters without boring a 16-year-old? Following the volunteer script under my science cart, I “defined an asteroid and its impact on the moon.” Unsurprisingly, Lisa played with the demo sand while her older brother Raymond stared at the wall. 
As the awkwardness loomed, I abandoned my script. “Let’s all make a fist,” I proposed. Clenching my hand, I softly hit the sand. “Your turn!” They each pummeled their fists down to make craters, each of a different size. 
Despite my big hands, Lisa’s crater was bigger. Gently, I explained the importance of impact speed, and soon, we were experimenting with different objects, sizes, and speeds, creating all sorts of craters.

At first glance, a dermatology clinic, a musical practice room, and a science cart may seem like classrooms at the opposite ends of a school. Yet, I unknowingly taught Param in the dermatology clinic, as my actions pushed us both to help wherever we could. We synced our performance with the trio by teaching each other our unique cues. At the science cart, Lisa and Raymond truly learned about craters through a personalized, interactive lesson. These moments taught me that the art of teaching isn’t confined to classrooms or textbooks—it happens in the shared experiences of the unspoken, unexpected, and unscripted. Although it’ll say “Student” on my college ID card, I’ll still be a teacher, finding lessons in every interaction and sharing them with those around me.

She’s caught me again. I bolt, and Mrs. McKay pleads, “Wait!” as my little legs pump ridiculously fast in order to escape the horrifying ordeal of being photographed. Thankfully, Mom has come to pick me up from kindergarten – my grabby hands reach out as I hide behind her, using her legs as a shield. I was overwhelmed with discomfort, uneasy with the eyes upon me.

It wasn’t until a decade later, during the pandemic, when reading "A Short History of Nearly Everything" by Bill Bryson completely changed my introverted tendencies – it captivated me with questions. What am I made of? How was the universe created? What is the meaning of life? This made me recognize the miracle of my existence; the odds of any one of us being born are estimated to be 1 in 400 trillion. How crazy is that? What was I doing, shying away from social interaction? My life was too precious to waste worrying about small talk, awkward pauses, and cameras.

With this realization, I managed to introspect, branch out, and overcome my insecurities. The most transformative step in my journey came on a Monday in French class my freshman year. In the middle of past tense conjugations, my class partner turned to me suddenly, asking, “Are you the [Name] that wants to join speech and debate?” I learned she was the club captain, and that their first meeting would be that afternoon.

Joining the club was intimidating to no end – as the only freshman in a team full of juniors, having no previous experience, I felt like a rock being chucked into a peaceful puddle, disrupting the surface tension and creating ripples in the team dynamic. Even worse, our debate team was a shallow pond compared to the vast ocean of experienced teams outside our town. At tournaments, we were often known as the only team from Tucson – making us easy prey for the merciless Phoenix teams.

Hamilton High butchered me, leaving me bleeding out on the podium as I scrambled to salvage my case. Arcadia poked holes into every argument I designed until I was grasping onto the edge of my chair in hopes that I wouldn’t burst into tears.

And yet, just when I began to lose hope again, shrinking down to hide, my eyes caught on a poster in the classroom: a breathtaking image of the Earth from outer space, surrounded by an infinite sea of black. I suddenly remembered those revelations from quarantine – those mind-boggling statistics that had yanked me out of my comfort zone in the first place. What a funny world. Here I was, on the verge of tears, standing on a floating rock, arguing with other Homo sapiens about cryptocurrency in a high school classroom in the middle of the Southwest desert. Liberated by this image, I straightened my back and opened up my shoulders. The trembles in my voice ceased, and the crackles in my throat cleared up as I rose above my fear of public speaking, transcending above those many humiliating defeats I had suffered.

Throughout the years, I navigated many losses, learning that in debate, it is not solely the argument that wins; it is also the confidence you project to the judge that influences the final decision. My relentless pursuit of self-improvement paid off when I eventually won my first debate. This wasn't just a victory in a competition – it was a personal triumph over the shy girl I once was, hiding behind my mother’s legs. Stepping out from the shadows of comfort and security, I have begun to accustom my eyes to the light as I tackle the challenges in life, with the help of Bill Bryson, French class, and a poster of our beautiful planet Earth.

Time moves slowly in Kunming, Yunnan's Spring City. Leisurely living prevails here. In the afternoons, elderly people play chess and practice Tai Chi in the park, their faces relaxed and free of anxiety. Nearby, children laugh as they play.

Most Kunming residents hold steady jobs, earning a modest yet sufficient income to support their families. Generations have lived this way. But I always felt something was missing.

As a child, I meticulously sorted every penny my parents gave me, storing it in different areas of my room. I feared the money would run out without any future accumulation.

I wanted more than just a peaceful existence.

During elementary school, I stumbled upon "Rich Dad, Poor Dad" in the library. The line "The eyes see reality, while the heart sees vision" struck me powerfully as I read it in one night. The next day, beneath the campus cherry tree, I watched my classmates rush to class while I plotted ways to increase my pocket money.

Everything became a financial lesson. I saw business potential in selling second-hand textbooks, offering tutoring, or running errands. This was my “financial enlightenment.” My notebooks were filled not just with class notes but also financial calculations—customer acquisition costs for 7-Eleven or Starbucks' EBITDA. At the back of my journal, I scribbled business ideas: a food marketplace app, a drone delivery service, an eco-friendlier way to grow cabbage. I analyzed the unit economics of each, pondering how to best deploy $1000 if I were to start my business.

During the summer break of Grade 7, I worked part-time at a supermarket, earning 1,000 yuan in two months. Instead of spending it, I tried stock investment. I spent two weeks studying JD.com's financial statements, analyzing its quick ratio, debt-to-asset ratio, and other indicators. I also considered the government's e-commerce policy and the Fed's interest rate hike. My fingers trembled when I clicked "Buy." I monitored my investment regularly, assessing the reasons behind each price fluctuation. Three months later, my investment tripled.

Two years later, when I moved to Canada and shared my investment experiences in Economics class, my classmates were astonished. "Investment? Don’t only the rich play that?" one said. "It's more practical to focus on our studies and find good jobs," another echoed.

At that moment, I realized there was a significant lack of financial literacy both in Kunming and Canada. I co-founded the first "Finance Club" at school with like-minded friends. Our weekly meetings shared investment knowledge and discussed economic news. Once, a member, Matthew, shared his family's struggles with inflation, sparking a heated discussion. Many students faced similar issues, such as managing pocket money and protecting college funds from inflation.

Our club shifted focus to practical problems. I designed courses to teach members financial management in everyday scenarios. Six months later, Matthew reported that he saved a medical reserve fund and earned enough investment income to cover a month's worth of his father's medical expenses. The club's membership tripled, and our discussions became more lively. We analyzed how the Middle East crisis affects gas expenses and studied the impact of Canada's new immigration policy on international students' rental choices.

This summer, I returned to Kunming. Having been part of the fast-paced, high-stakes business world, I realized as I watched the peaceful teahouse patrons sip their tea, that this calmness is another form of freedom. For me, financial knowledge is not only about making money but about the freedom to choose one's path. In the future, I hope to leverage financial education to empower others with this same freedom of choice.

“Are you wearing makeup or are your eye bags actually real?”

A classmate asked me this after we had finished senior picture day. My school has a tradition in which the seniors take silly, fun photos instead of typical “nice” photos for the yearbook. Rather than seeing button-up shirts and dresses, you’ll find a gym full of neon pink wigs, Groucho glasses, and Halloween hazmat suits. I didn’t go all-out like some, but made sure to join in, wearing a cowboy hat my Uncle Joe had given to me and a stick-on beard that I wore for a fifth-grade history project.

But my eye bags? Those are all too real–a physical manifestation of imbalance in my life. And although I laughed it off, this question was a punch to the gut. Actually, it was more than that. It was an uppercut by Mike Tyson himself, and I was the lucky soul on the other end of it.

These dreaded eye bags weren’t formed overnight. They had been developed layer by layer, and I certainly knew they were there. But that day prompted me to realize that these eye bags are more than shadows on my face–they are a testament to years of restless nights and sleep deprivation; a testament to the relentless pursuit of growth.

On the wrestling mat, I fought off yawns in between sprints. Oh, to lay down a pillow, snuggle up under a blanket, and doze off to the sound of Coach's whistle. Alas, I had to drag myself home to shower before I’d be eaten alive by the mat fungi. These small moments underpinned a greater issue.

From physics to the choir room; from the football field to driving my brother, I was wearing thin. Hectic as it was, it didn’t matter. Nothing could beat the feeling of making a great tackle, or finally solving the total resistance of a combination circuit that has way too many in-line and parallel resistors. The way the tennis ball slingshots off my racket, or finally understanding Solzhenitsyn’s philosophies on national pride and the desire to break free from oppression has always fueled my drive to push beyond what’s comfortable. My goal throughout high school has always been the type of personal growth that is earned through mastering new challenges. This drives me to excel in life and, paradoxically, is the genesis of my imbalance.

Outside of academics and extracurriculars, I was juggling individual relationships with family, friends, and a new girlfriend. Each of these pursuits had brought me joy, but also meant my eye bags’ unwelcome residence.

After years of toughing it out by myself with no change, I decided to move to the dreaded final option–turning towards others. For months, my mom had been telling me to buy a planner, even providing one. I thought that something so simple wouldn’t help, and I ignored her. However, my picture day made me realize that her advice was ineluctable. As I began mapping out my days, the pieces slowly began falling into place. I was doing more than simply writing down homework due dates and tournament times–I was taking control of my chaotic schedule and, for the first time, prioritizing my health and well-being. I began working more closely with my teachers to manage my workload, too. Accepting others’ help didn’t make me any weaker; rather, it strengthened me, taking weight off my shoulders.

I understand that I don’t have to navigate everything alone. Authentic people and support in my life will always be there for me; I’ve learned to look around and see my family, my friends, and my teachers. While the eye bags dissipate with each passing day, the hard-earned lessons remain. And by the time you see me on Yale’s campus, my face devoid of shadows will reflect my life devoid of imbalance, ready to support my classmates just as others helped me.

I rush to the door as my mom’s car pulls away, disappearing around the corner before I even have a chance to wave goodbye. My brother, eighteen years old, had already moved off to college. My dad, who was still trying to secure a job, was in the basement studying and preparing for interviews. It was a typical summer morning for eight-year-old me. And that meant a typical day of wandering outside, then dinner, then going to sleep as my parents fretted over various bills and paperwork.

I had to learn to make do with entertaining myself, which often led to endless questions. Why does my bicycle balance when I pedal but not when I stay still? Why does the small Lego fire truck move faster than the bigger one when I push it?

Getting Internet access at the age of ten allowed me to explore new freedoms. I entered a whole new world, and within a minute’s search, I could discover angular momentum and mass on YouTube. Browsing online forums like Stack Exchange, I devoured posts discussing Fourier series, refraction, and relativity. These concepts involved math and intuition I didn’t quite understand yet, but I was captivated by physics from the start.

Soon, my math and science skills caught up with my curiosity. With the symbols and formulas I’d learn with each lesson, I could now model how fast a ball falls or the torque behind turning a door. The gravitational pull and orbits of entire planets could, with elegance, be summarized into a few succinct equations. But physics was much more than just formulas; it was a way to explain the world around me.

Flipping through the old Java books on my dad’s shelves, I was immediately fascinated by programming. After much frustration, a “Hello World” blinked onto my screen. I was hit with a sudden realization: if physics is about interpreting the natural world, then programming was my way to construct the laws of my own imagination. Over the next few weeks, my fingers tapped away, creating Connect4 games and chemical equation balancers. As my coding skills grew alongside my newfound physics knowledge, I created collision simulators and robot lift programs to bring the concepts I’d learned to life.

Having the ability to create in the virtual world created yet another desire within me. I desired not just to learn for myself but also to share my interests with my peers so that they could appreciate the beauty of physics and programming, too. Whether demonstrating air pressure rockets, teaching servo system coding, or simply explaining a math concept, my cumulated years of experience allowed me to express my passions with a renewed sense of clarity and precision.

Surprisingly, my curiosity to understand the physical world shaped me into a natural teacher. As I organized lessons for elementary schoolers, the detailed way in which I had learned to see the world manifested itself in how I organized my lessons. Sentences, after all, were just patterns of words. And cross multiplying, though daunting at first, was simple once the core logic of setting fractions equal was understood.

But with each “aha!” moment, I gradually realized something else: I was connecting with not just the other coordinators and tutors; I was also connecting with the kids. As I guided them through the jungles of geometry, I saw smiles across their faces as I clarified concepts in a way an eight-year-old could easily understand and bonded with them over shared school struggles.

And even then, I couldn’t help but think back to those quiet mornings when I watched my mom’s car pull away around the corner. Just like me, these kids were navigating their own paths, searching for answers to their endless questions. Now, as I created and helped others, I realized I was also reflecting on my own journey—piecing together things one at a time, just as I had always done, but this time not alone.

The surf’s smashing sound is jarring, yet the steady melody is comforting. I’m drawn to the water. I go there for tranquility. I only lived in homes near water, including a canal, ocean, bay, river, and sound. My life’s ebb and flow is analogous to currents. Turbulent times turned calm. I persevered despite difficulties. I navigated my way on a journey to strength and understanding. Living a lifetime by water, and the reason for that, shaped me.

My father’s naval aviation career landed me in different locations and sent him around the world for many months. The bulk of my childhood, he was deployed.

Stressors related to this adversely affected me. People know my dad as a successful fighter pilot who completed combat missions and led thousands in roles of increasing responsibility.
