However, I saw turmoil. I witnessed his emotions fluctuate like an ocean swell particularly when he returned home after months away. He used harsh words and his short temper erupted in moments of pressure. I felt uneasy as I experienced his turbulent temperament. Still, I mourned my father's leave, scared he wouldn’t return. The sadness faded as deployment days passed and my mother provided a secure feeling for my sisters and I.

We made colored paper chains adding a link for each day of the deployment. My older sister and I meticulously painted a colorful welcome home banner that stretched across our deck. I remember the excitement around homecoming. My sisters and I wore hot pink noise canceling headphones smiling and waving small American flags while jets in formation roared overhead returning from months away. I ran to my dad with excitement as he stepped out of the jet in his green flight suit.

Like the ocean, I experienced high and low points in Navy life. Among the best times: trips to places like Disney World as a gift from my dad after our reunions. One of those significantly impacted me. A SeaWorld visit inspired my dream to work in the marine world. I stared in awe as I watched whales and trainers interact. I began to envision myself in that realm.

The vacation moved me to learn about marine environments. In middle school, I joined a hydroponics club and cared for axolotls in a science classroom. I was selected as part of a student group to participate in the Chesapeake Bay Foundation Smith Island Education Program, where I spent a weekend learning about watermen and the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem. My science curiosity grew, motivating me to apply to my rigorous Math and Science Academy.

I plunged into papers on marine life, such as dolphins in captivity and ocean climate effects on sea turtles. However, my academic performance didn’t always go swimmingly. My endurance tanked, particularly early in high school. The COVID quarantine during eighth grade washed away my study habits. I froze under pressure as my dad preached perfection, a vital quality in his profession. I failed to complete assignments and lacked the effort needed to earn As in my difficult classes. My grades plummeted.

Dissatisfied, I changed my direction, turning to teachers for extra help, surrounding myself with supportive friends, and talking to my dad about my concerns. I felt encouraged and slowly steered away from my listlessness. “Happy thoughts.” The words my mother once whispered to me when I had awoken from bad dreams echoed in my head through it all.

One constant remained through my ups and downs: my attraction to water for clarity and calmness. I found peace paddleboarding along my backyard canal, swimming in the ocean, and savoring sunsets by the Chesapeake Bay. These moments strengthened my focus to achieve aspirations, including to pursue studies to address environmental challenges.

I want to help maintain the habitats I enjoy. I will encounter smooth sailing and rough seas on this voyage, but, having learned from my struggles, the path of persistence will overcome barriers.

As I walked into the library, my palms were sweating and my legs were trembling. I was heading to my AP seminar presentation, and although I’d spent a week practicing, I felt unprepared. From the moment I stood before the class, everything began to unravel. I fumbled through my opening lines—my voice was shaky and barely comprehensible. When the teacher began to ask questions, my heart pounded so loudly that I could hardly focus on what she was saying. The answers I had memorized vanished from my brain, and I stood there humiliated. As I walked out of the room, the weight of the embarrassment destroyed me.

That night, I reflected on the lingering embarrassment and knew something had to change. I’ve always felt hindered by a fear of speaking to others, whether in public or one-on-one conversations. My first instinct was to turn to the internet for answers. I searched YouTube for tips on public speaking, but the content didn’t address my problem. However, this information gap helped me realize that my fear came from deeper insecurities. I was afraid of being judged for my mistakes and how I looked in others’ eyes. After hours of research and reflection, I encountered an unexpected piece of advice recurring in the videos: go to the gym. Even though I was unsure how working out could build confidence, I decided to try it.

After a few months in the gym, I noticed subtle changes in myself. I didn’t wake up daily with a rush of confidence, but each week brought small improvements. I set achievable goals, like increasing my bench press weight and mastering my form. Each accomplishment encouraged me to step outside my comfort zone in other areas of my life, such as starting conversations with new classmates and maintaining eye contact—challenges that once felt intimidating. It wasn’t always easy, however; some days I would revert to keeping my head down and avoiding small talk. However, with each workout, the small changes began to accumulate. The awkward moments in the gym—trying new exercises or dropping weights—taught me to worry less about others’ opinions. As I grew more confident in those situations, I found it easier to interact with people without fear of judgment.

This newfound confidence started to extend beyond school and the gym. When I first started volunteering at Habitat for Humanity, I was only there to complete my tasks and go home. But as weeks went by, I began engaging more with the customers and fellow volunteers. One day, I encountered a machine I didn’t know how to use. Normally, I would have felt too embarrassed to ask for help, but I approached the older volunteers instead. These little changes were a result of new confidence, and each change further boosted my confidence in turn. This reinforced the lesson I learned from working out: small changes can have an immense impact on personal growth.

Towards the end of junior year, I decided I wanted to study finance. The fast-paced and challenging environment of the major intrigued me, and, after reading about what it takes to succeed in the field, I noticed that the same principles that helped me conquer my insecurities—hard work, patience, and consistency—will help me navigate through a finance major as well. These same principles will also guide me on my way toward that career: I now have the confidence to actively engage in classroom activities, build strong connections with my peers, and embrace the many academic challenges that will come my way.

Looking back, that presentation wasn’t a failure but a turning point. Working out pushed me to take control of the things about which I felt most insecure and develop confidence I never thought possible. Whether in the gym, the classroom, or my future career, I know how to approach challenges with determination and a focus on small, daily improvements. I’m confident that the discipline and perseverance I’ve gained from this journey will guide me and help me succeed in college and beyond.

“Yep, like [Name] Lee.” A Chinese kid growing up with the name “[Name],” I often drew comparisons to the martial artist. This wasn’t an accident. My father wanted to name me after [Name] Lee, while my mother preferred Jackie Chan. In a creative compromise, I was born [Name] Jack Ruan.

Courtesy of my parents, I grew up immersed in kung fu cinema. In addition to the flashy technique, I came to appreciate [Name] Lee's signature belief: “Be water, my friend.” Just as water ebbs and flows through unpredictable currents, I learned to attune and acclimate as my own life’s river faced rocky terrain. Worried about layoffs at my father’s work or navigating new schools as one of the few Asian students in my class, I held steadfast to this faith in Lee’s anchor––reminding myself that when shaped by life’s turbulent waters, adapt by becoming water itself.

In my freshman year, I joined our school’s tennis team. Early in the season, though, we stumbled upon an unfortunate pattern. On match days, we’d often hear “Today’s boy's tennis game is canceled.” And after, our coach would follow with the expected: “No bus.” Of course, I was usually disappointed––but beyond that, I was also confused. How did this happen so frequently?

The answer was simple: years of legislative negligence plummeted Arizona to 49th in the nation for per-student funding. This meant extracurricular programs across the valley, like sports, were left neglected by an eroded education budget. Like before, I felt compelled to adapt.

My teammates and I hosted free tennis lessons for students, hoping to create a community of enough dedicated tennis players that schools would see the need to fully fund our programs. This grew into neighborhood equipment drives and community tournaments, and I felt proud knowing that I again found a way to react productively to my circumstances.

Yet, the scope of this issue was far greater. As I met more and more students throughout the state, I heard stories of campuses only capable of operating four-day weeks and many kids relying on school lunches as their main meals. The consequences of inadequate funding were pervasive. This time, perhaps simply adapting wouldn’t be enough.

Just as Lee tells us that water can “flow,” in the same breath, he explains it can also “crash.” Like a forceful river, being water doesn’t only mean following the flow of the stream, but also eroding away and shaping the banks that guide its movement. I was unsure that my understanding of water was complete. While before I had hoped for decision-makers to change their minds, I was beginning to see the importance of taking active roles in changing it ourselves.

I learned to be water in new ways: guiding students in community lessons became facilitating meetings with state officials, and soliciting donations for equipment drives became soliciting support for local school board members. The issues facing Arizona students aren’t just boulders in the river to navigate around, they’re challenges we need to confront head-on with active engagement. Whether it be lobbying in support of increased public school funding with local nonprofits, or traveling hundreds of miles across the state to advocate for Career and Technical Education, my ability to “be water” is continually informed by the potential to both shape and be shaped––to actively participate in dialogue.

As I continue to reflect on my place in the world, I hold Lee’s mantra as a reminder to understand the need to both adapt and advocate. Water can be a tranquil stream, but it can also be a roaring tsunami. Be water. But don’t forget that water can flood, reshape, and even transform the landscape. Flow, yes—but when needed, crash.

As I slowly turned the key through the rusted knob and stepped in, I peered around the familiar surroundings. I began the opening process, booting up the system, and flicking on the lights. While sprinkling a handful of pellets for our remarkable parrot fish that has fought to survive for nearly 8 years, I couldn’t help but reflect on the obstacles I’ve overcome, each one making me stronger, similar to the fish.

Like most immigrants, my parents moved from China when they were hardly adults. Without university degrees and essential skills, there was no other option but to establish a restaurant, knowing the long hours required. But they had one thing that nobody could steal: hope for a prosperous future. After many failed attempts but always persevering, they finally settled in a quaint town, that I’m proud to call my second home.

Ever since I was 5 years old, I’ve been helping them run the business, starting with straightforward duties like sweeping the floors and bringing dishes in. Fast forward to now, I’ve continued on to becoming the manager. I operate the entire front end of our restaurant. All human interaction falls onto my shoulders. I’m entrusted with processing payment transactions, packing orders, and managing our online websites. My job has been consequential for our family, saving them the expense of having to hire an external manager. With already years of experience under my belt, I thought I was ready for anything.

Unfortunately, tragedy hit when we were least expecting it. About a year ago at the start of a promising summer, news broke about my now deceased grandfather’s terminal illness. We didn’t know what to do. I knew my mom had to spend as much time as she could with him, but she was hesitant on departing, as the restaurant was our sole income. She did everything except for the cooking. My dad didn’t understand English fluently, so he was incapable of opening the restaurant without her. In this disheartening moment, I knew my mom needed me, so I was willing to take up the responsibility of running the restaurant, even though I was fearful. She was gone for more than a month, and the entire time I oversaw everything.

A week following her departure, I resolved a conflict with my first unsatisfied customer alone. He claimed that we allegedly forgot one of his items, but I concluded that there were no containers absent. Confusedly, I questioned if he skipped anything. Enraged and all sensibleness lost, he began to forcefully insist that he did not overlook anything on his list. As swiftly as I could, I made every effort to douse the fire before it even sparked. I approached him patiently, and offered him two simple options of how we could proceed: he could take the order as is, or our staff would be more than willing to prepare the missing item. Once I noticed he was visibly composed again, I took his payment information and charged the new total. Before, I was uncertain of how to act if I was confronted by this predicament, but it taught me how to address a situation like this.

My eyes opened after witnessing this first hand, and made me better adapted to withstand any future curveballs. When I someday leave home, the experiences and lessons I have acquired from our restaurant will never wane. It is truly a rare experience, growing up in a restaurant with many regulars commenting on how big you’ve grown, or rushing to do your homework as you’re carrying heaping plates of food to waiting tables. Even though I resented having to work from a young age for so many years, I cannot deny the jump start it gave me to boost my career in business. So just like the fish, my past will continue to guide me through unknown waters ahead.

“Hey dad, did you know that particles can sometimes ‘entangle’ and influence each other no matter the distance between them? Changing one changes the other and scientists can’t explain it.”

“Oh, are you referring to the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox? Yeah, it’s a mind-blowing phenomenon.”

“Honestly, I’m not 100% confident in its validity. Could you try convincing me?”

~~~

During my sophomore year, I’d satisfy my “learn something new every day” quota by scouring the web for juicy new physics concepts to soak up. I made a lot of physics friends that year: 3Blue1Brown, Zach Star, and a bunch of professors named David (Morin, Griffiths, Kaiser). However, the most important friend I made was my dad. When he moved 300 miles away during 5th grade, we began drifting apart. Even when he returned in high school, he felt more like a cohabitant than a parent. Still, I was determined to bridge that gap. Vulnerably vomiting our emotions felt uncomfortable, but I wondered if our mutual love of physics could spark discussion. I began finding a new topic to discuss every day during dinner–some conversations were serious and philosophical, but others were silly and absurd, allowing us to discover new sides of one another. After a few months, awkwardness melted away as curiosity and understanding replaced it.

One day, wanting to know him better, I asked why he studied biophysics. He explained that he chose biophysics over pure physics because “theory can't save a life.” His choice was cemented after his mother passed from cancer. When auntie passed from the same illness, I thought critically about the impact I wanted to make.

I began approaching physics differently. Instead of keeping it theoretical, I wanted to apply my knowledge to something tangible. I wanted to know why detection technology had failed auntie and was shocked to learn about its limitations. Even mammograms, which are more accurate than MRIs or ultrasounds, miss one in eight breast cancers. Could I do something to fix this? During my research, I found papers from NIH and the University of Waterloo who utilized quantum computing to improve detection. Motivated by their work, I took part in a quantum computing internship where I tested models that could hasten the development of quantum technologies and be applied to cancer screening or drug discovery. And every evening as I come home brimming with excitement, I’d share my findings with dad who intently listened.

The discussions made me realize that physics was a common language dad and I used to unfurl our relationship and aspirations. I began speaking this language to build bridges with others. Through Girls in Quantum, I befriended Sophia, a girl who lives in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. I introduced myself in broken Google-Translated German, both of us nervously laughing at my awkward attempts. However, we found a common language in physics, our hands flying as we debated how to optimize quantum circuits, troubleshoot decoherence errors, and approach algorithm design. Soon, our conversations traveled outside the technical realm. We voiced our uncertainties as girls in quantum–how I was one of only four female researchers on the entire floor during my internship and how she rarely found community in her classes full of guys. We found solace in one another and would stay up late or wake up early to talk to each other due to differing time zones. She showed me that the beauty of quantum lies not only in its revolutionary applications but also in its ability to unite people across different worlds in a shared pursuit of understanding.

A few weeks ago, dad and I returned to a familiar topic: The Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paradox. I used to be skeptical, but today I’ve been convinced that it may be true. No matter the physical or emotional distance that may have existed, physics has acted as an entangling thread that mends my barriers with others. Using this philosophy, I will continue to foster new relationships and memories while sharing my faith with my future community.

The intricately woven kimonos, well-dressed hair, and gentle complexion of the dolls were simply breathtaking. They were placed on a pedestal-like display, with soft red velvet beneath them. For the time being, they would stay inside a Japanese residence house open for all visitors to see.

I silently admired them from behind my local museum’s Japanese garden activity cart, glancing from my origami fold to the display repeatedly. This cycle, however, was quickly interrupted.

“What are those creepy-lookin’ dolls for?”

A tall visitor with hazel-colored hair and icy blue eyes broke the calm silence, and I explained to him that they were Hinamatsuri dolls representative of Girl’s day in Japan. Such a question was not the first of its kind, as many seemed unconscious of the cultural significance the floor they treaded upon and the buildings they quickly passed possessed.

This question was going to be the last of its kind, however, as I was determined to enhance the cultural awareness of my local community.

My proposed whiteboard stands were approved, and other volunteers and I began writing snippets of relevant information about both the Japanese residence at the garden and important aspects of Japanese history. I quickly learned that my excitement to share did not translate into excitement to learn however, as visitors did not bother to read what we wrote. Instead, they remained detached and disinterested.

Nonetheless, seeing as origami was the main attention grabber at our cart, I worked with the other volunteers to add more visual and participatory activities.

Origami lotuses soon turned into more complex folds like kimonos and samurai helmets, each accompanied with a brief discussion of Japanese fashion and the Edo period. The whiteboards became filled with colorful diagrams illustrating festivals occurring that week. As more shifts passed, we even introduced Ikebana (the art of flower arrangement), tatami weaving, and other events as both activities for visitors and presentations for volunteers and program advisors.

Larger crowds began to form, and through our discussions I even learned aspects of Japanese culture and history that I had not known before!

During my junior summer, I published a children’s book titled A Bowl of Blessings about a little girl named [Name] celebrating both Japanese New Year’s and self love. I had found that the intersection of illustration and the written word knew no bounds, and I continue to hope that this book will provide an entertaining yet educational experience for children of all interests.

The journey did not end there though. I sought out ways to fold traditions into my high school community, and decided to use the fact that I was the only Japanese girl in my grade to my advantage.

To understand more, I worked with other cabinet members to have a Fashion and Design Club meeting specifically on traditional attire. We drew clothes important to us, and shared it. Emily informed us why traditional Chinese dresses were most commonly red and Fiona explained why her father had to wear a Scottish kilt during his wedding. They made me confident in openly displaying what I once had thought of suppressing, and it only made me more fascinated with the interconnectedness of tradition and identity.

Now, instead of just hearing about these beautiful stories, I have been able to experience them too. Grace taught me how to play the drums in the Korean art of Pungmul Nori, Sasha invited me to eat dinner with her Indian family during Diwali, and Helene taught me how to make Turkish Delight!

I currently not only celebrate Hinamatsuri, I celebrate the many cultures in my diverse community, and the fact that the key to cultural education lies in loving the little details.

Origami paper, no matter how it is folded, can always fold back into its original shape. Similarly, we have the power to create change while preserving what makes us… us. What change can I fold in a world of immeasurable possibility? I’m finding out.

12-year-old me screamed in terror as my trembling hand caressed my face. 
Pomegranates used to be my favorite fruit—until I became allergic to them. I picked up the spherical fruit with its thick, red skin and began digging in. It was just as delicious as the last time I ate it. But unlike last time, the next morning I woke up with hives and rashes all over my body. I learned I had somehow developed an allergy to pomegranates. 
How could something I loved so much become something I couldn’t have? 
That same helplessness struck me again, only this time it wasn’t just some fruit—I was faced with losing someone I loved.
14-year-old me had always thought my family would be by my side forever. But like pomegranates, a person I cherish deeply was slipping through my fingers before I was ready to let go.
My grandpa’s lung cancer diagnosis crashed over me. I held onto the hope that things would improve, that some wishes might come true. But two weeks later, he was diagnosed with colon cancer, and the minuscule hope I had was slowly replaced by fear. Even so, I stayed by his side. I didn’t want to waste what could be the last few months I had with him.
One evening, he asked me about a pill he was prescribed. The label read “Oxycodone.” The jumble of letters meant nothing to me then, but my grandpa, aware of my interest in medicine, smiled and joked, “You’ll have to tell me what these pills do someday.” His words, though lighthearted, sparked a determination in me to become someone he could depend on. 
16-year-old me, during the summer of 2024, interned at a pain management center to take steps toward that goal. On July 8th, I finally learned what oxycodone did—it relieved pain. Although its primary purpose is to reduce discomfort, I witnessed its darker side: patients constantly begging for refills, struggling with dependency and side effects. Oxycodone, much like the pomegranates I once loved, had a dual nature—it could provide relief and comfort, yet also cause great harm. On the bus ride home, I reflected on how much pain my grandpa had endured, always masking it with a smile, protecting us from his battle. That realization stuck with me. I wanted to help lessen that burden for others, offering not just knowledge, but also care and understanding.
After long months of treatment, my grandpa finally recovered. He came home, and that night, he told me how much he appreciated me standing by him through it all. At that moment, I realized I did not want to be just the little girl in the family, the girl they protect from harsh realities. I wanted to be the daughter they could rely on, the granddaughter they could come to with their worries. I wanted to be the person my grandpa did not have.
Freshly, 17-year-old me realized time, like the sweet taste of pomegranates, is precious. Just as we must peel away the tough layers of the bright red fruit to reach its sweetness, life, too, demands we face challenges. But the rewards are worth the effort. My allergies won’t magically disappear and my hardships won’t vanish in the blink of an eye. But, with time, my allergies may fade, and similarly, my challenges will improve as well. Making a difference doesn’t always mean grand gestures; it's about being there when it matters most. And that’s the kind of person I want to become, someone who can leave a meaningful impact on the people I care about.

On a chilly September morning, I stretched on damp planks, straining to dip an oxygen probe into the pond as my Environmental Science friends gripped my ankles. The pier was just tall enough that no one’s arms reached the water without such a maneuver. I then ventured onto rocks for the turbidity measurement. With Mrs. Girardi’s lesson in mind—that the water closest to the shore was not representative of the whole pond—I inched further down to collect the perfect sample but felt water collecting in my shoes. My friends laughed as my sneakers squeaked embarrassingly with each step. As motivated as we were, our inexperience made field research challenging.

On our next pond expedition, we lugged a pile of green rubber supplies from Mrs. Girardi’s trunk, appreciating her thoughtfulness in providing the right equipment. This time, we evaluated the ecosystem’s well-being by measuring the biodiversity of macroinvertebrates as a more thorough approach to ecosystem health. Every detail mattered for sample collection, from adjusting galoshes and tightening waders to differentiating mayflies and dragonfly nymphs. Recalling Mrs. Girardi’s lesson about depth, now with the right equipment, I waded into the water and felt accomplished in reaching new depths. I concluded with excitement that the pond was healthy, inspiring me to actively engage in our community’s environmental stewardship.

Mrs. Girardi's thoughtful support helped me achieve more ambitious goals in and out of the classroom. She taught me that the right equipment is essential for good science, and a positive attitude is key to effective leadership. As a freshman on varsity soccer, I believed competitiveness was everything. Although this mindset helped me make the team, it wouldn’t help us build a community. I remembered how Mrs. Girardi strove to reduce stress and tension by understanding our pressures during busy times to accommodate our best learning. Following her example, I built connections to bring out the best in others. On bus rides to games, I led my teammates in visualizing their ideal run or cross, and on the rides home, I celebrated wins and highlighted improvements despite a loss. At the end of that junior season, my team elected me captain and crowned me with the “fun captain” regalia: the Freaky Hat, my most prized piece of equipment. This deflated yellow and white soccer ball is decorated with inspirational notes left by captains of the past two decades. It reminds me to balance my drive with positivity and how I can improve community through connection and thoughtfulness.

I take Mrs. Girardi's lessons about environmental science and community leadership home as I tend to my parents' lawn. Since my parents grew up in Soviet bloc housing, lawn care did not come naturally. Therefore, as soon as my feet could reach the pedals of the ride-on mower, I took over the responsibility. Through Mrs. Girardi’s hands-on experiments, I became fascinated with biodiversity and ecosystem health. I began to avoid pesticides and herbicides that harm native species, so my lawn was no longer a monoculture. I skipped mowing in May for the pollinators and whenever I saw a new litter of cottontail rabbits. Before the season’s first soccer game, my family helped me host a spaghetti dinner for my team on our lawn. Redirecting watermelon rinds into our new compost bin filled me with joy at being able to use our resources to come together as a community.

This August, I entered Mrs. Girardi’s classroom as a teaching assistant, eager to help this year’s class explore. When my soccer season ends, I’ll write my own note on the Freaky Hat and crown the next “fun captain” to model the importance of positivity in leadership. As my high school years come to a close, I look forward to wading into new, deeper lakes of college life, carrying Mrs. Girardi’s lessons of optimistic leadership and environmental stewardship.

The sliding doors of the library part with a whisper, ushering me into a world where time bends and reality expands. The soft hum of air conditioning mingles with the rustle of turning pages, a symphony of anticipation that stirs within me. My fingers dance across spines of books, each touch a potential doorway to new discoveries. Here, amidst towering shelves and hidden nooks, I feel most alive, most myself—a seeker of truths both universal and deeply personal.

I pause at the comic section, my hand hovering over Batman: The Long Halloween. It's an old friend, yet each visit reveals new secrets. As I flip through the pages, Gotham's shadows seem to deepen, and Batman's moral dilemmas sharpen into focus. The Caped Crusader's world of blurred lines between right and wrong mirrors my own internal debates. I find myself pondering: How do we navigate decisions when the path isn't clear? How do we weigh intentions against consequences? Batman's resilience isn't in his gadgets or fists, but in his mind—a lesson that resonates as I face my challenges. This comic isn’t just entertainment—it's a springboard launching me into deeper waters of thought.

My quest for understanding pulls me deeper into the library's labyrinth. In the science section, The Underworld by Susan Casey beckons with its dark allure. As I immerse myself in its pages, the abyssal plains of the ocean materialize before me. Bioluminescent creatures dance in the darkness, thriving where others fear to tread. Their adaptability reminds me of my own journey from a small, private middle school to a bustling high school. Those first days felt like plunging into frigid, unfamiliar waters – overwhelming and disorienting. But like those deep-sea denizens, I learned to navigate the currents of conversation and the pressure of new expectations. Each day, I found my footing a little more, until the once-alien environment became my new normal.

Yuval Noah Harari's Sapiens catches my eye next, its pages a tapestry of human history. As I trace our species' journey from prehistoric savannas to modern cities, I see echoes of that epic tale in my own life. The same relentless curiosity and inventive spirit that pushed early humans to craft tools and build societies fuels me as I tackle my own obstacles. Whether I'm grappling on the mat or navigating academic challenges, I tap into that primal instinct to learn, to adapt, and to push beyond what I thought was possible. Through this connection with our shared past, I see that every challenge is part of a larger journey of growth—both for humanity and for myself.

In the technology section, Quantum Supremacy by Michio Kaku pulls me into the bizarre realm of quantum mechanics. The pages buzz with the potential of quantum computing, each paragraph a window into a world where certainty dissolves into probability. It's a far cry from my former obsession with perfection and rigid plans. Yet as I delve deeper, I find a strange comfort in the uncertainty. Like a quantum particle existing in multiple states, I too am learning to embrace the complexity of my potential – scientist, writer, athlete, each path simultaneously possible until observed.

As I leave, my backpack heavy with books, my mind feels paradoxically lighter. The library isn't just a repository of knowledge; it's a gymnasium for my intellect, each visit a workout that leaves me stronger, more flexible in thought. With every book, every idea encountered, I peel back another layer of understanding–of the world, and of myself. I step out into the sunlight, the warmth of the day blending with the warmth of my newfound insights. I’m not just carrying knowledge in my backpack, but also a renewed sense of purpose. Armed with these ideas, I’m eager to apply them, ready to sketch new possibilities on the canvas of my life, knowing that every discovery propels me forward in my journey of growth and self-discovery.

Our bodies don’t always fight for us. Sometimes, they wage invisible wars.

When I was eleven years old, a doctor visit for minor bleeding turned into a life-altering diagnosis: Ulcerative Colitis, a chronic Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) with no known cure. Affecting less than 0.7% of the U.S. population, IBD cases have been increasing by 133% among children. Within a year, I could no longer play tennis, attend karate classes, or participate in debate, and my days were full of frequent, hour-long bathroom breaks, colonoscopies, and endless blood and stool tests, all while balancing the demands of high school.

The steroids prescribed were only a band-aid for a gaping wound, and after years of unsuccessful treatments, my doctor recommended biologics—the final option before a colectomy. Hesitant due to its extreme side effects, we delayed as much as possible. With no clear solution, I embarked on a quest to find an alternative through online research and support groups. Trusting in medicine, I resorted to a holistic approach by modulating the microbiome, healing the mucosal layer, and controlling inflammation through conventional medicine.

The kitchen became my laboratory, and I became my experiment. I channeled my frustration into research: publications, clinical trials, alternative medicine, and various IBD diets. One study that caught my attention was Maria Chiara Mentella’s “Nutrition, IBD, and Gut Microbiota: A Review,” shedding light on the connection between diet, genetics, and gut health. Dr. Allan Desmond’s work on plant-based diets and Breaking the Vicious Cycle by Elaine Gottschall further amplified my determination. With support from my parents, my two-week journey of a juice-only diet tested my resolve but ultimately calmed the flare-ups, allowing me to slowly engage in my passions again. I regained the ability to be social, as I was always too ashamed to be around others while experiencing flare-ups. I rejoined the NHS and took an active role in organizing fundraising and voluntary engagement events.

After six years of discipline, the long-awaited diagnosis finally arrived: clinical remission. My strict adherence finally paid off, and the happiness I thought we had lost slowly returned to me and my family. My body was no longer a foe: all it needed was a deeper understanding of the mind and the recalibration of the “second brain” - the microbiome.

Having nearly lost my large intestine, my journey became a source of motivation for many in the support groups, resonating with their struggles and empowering them to reclaim their confidence in their battles. My diet plans and regimen even became a reference for others. I’ve learned that, with perseverance, even the most complex challenges can be solved, and I intend to channel this mindset into solving the difficult problems I’ll inevitably encounter in college and beyond. In the future, I will be guided by this mindset, applying advanced medical research and innovative technologies to solve patients’ complex healthcare challenges, never giving up on finding solutions, even when it seems impossible.

My inner John Stewart was on the verge of the most important interview of his life. As I hurried up the steps, my heart pounded frantically. I felt how I imagined Socrates must have as he prepared to drink the famous cup of hemlock that ended his life but immortalized his principles. I felt like Neo facing the horrendous choice between the comfortable blue pill and the unknowable plunge of the red. Just hours ago I consulted a team of advisors–my friends. They all agreed: this was the only path.

At the top of the steps, I paused to catch my breath. I rounded the corner and saw her. I battened down the hatches and delivered the opening line as coolly as I could: “Hey, are you free to get ice cream with me at Sweet Cream’s this Friday?”

The interview lasted about five seconds. By the end of it, I was firmly confined to the friend zone, and my first shot at high school romance was an abject failure. And yet, I somehow found the process of confronting my fear exhilarating. I started to master the art of the interview as a serious endeavor, less because I wanted to overcome my romantic mishap and more because I felt driven to understand the people around me.

By the summer before my senior year, I was an old hand at interviews, and I had long since embraced the fact that many people don’t want to be interviewed by an acne-riddled high schooler. I had also realized that I could handle rejection like a champ. Pressing on, I interviewed every willing interviewee I found remotely interesting, from prison wardens in Connecticut to professors of medieval cuisine. Each interview made me more eager to learn about people’s worlds.

I started understanding my curiosity more consciously when I interviewed a Buddhist monk in Singapore. My main goal was to understand the interreligious dynamics of the tiny red dot we both call home. He poured hot water into a teapot, waited silently, and then poured tea into our cups. No religion, he explained, has a monopoly on truth. We are each like a blind man touching the trunk of an elephant and claiming we are touching a snake.

Although I’d heard the old parable of the elephant many times, it struck home like never before. His perspective on the power of a free forum for faiths of all kinds resonated with the work I pursued. Subconsciously, I had felt trapped in the narrow perspective of my senses and the environment that shaped me. The microphone had become the skeleton key that unlocked the world. As I listened to the monk, I realized that my journey would never end: I had interviewed Buddhists, Christians, and Muslims, but there were also Hindus, Jains, agnostics, and universalists, not to mention the sects within each faith. And this was just religion.

My “imaginary microphone” often swaps out for a pen or a cello; yet the stories I encounter still reverberate in my approach to life. Whether I’m researching the bioethics of infant organ donation or checking in with the freshmen in my dorm, I tether myself to the humanity of each moment. I make sure that the routine of checking on my dorm’s freshmen is paired with five-minute conversations about how tough physics class can get, and in these moments, my friends’ stories become my entire world (and not just because physics is a tough subject).

When I feel like I’m touching only the snake, I follow the inkling that pushes me to search for the full elephant. In my advocacy for the formerly incarcerated, I capture and share the stories that slip through the cracks of 24-hour news cycles by stepping foot into police centers, stories that demand more than just surface-level attention. In doing so, the conversations my “microphone” has absorbed never die—they continue to shape how I navigate life’s quirks, constantly seeking to understand more fully, always reaching for the elephant beyond the trunk.

My mom has carried a miniature champagne bottle in her backpack all summer, waiting for my big moment. Now I am on the final hole of a US Junior Amateur qualifier, two under par and needing a miracle from the trees to advance to the biggest tournament in junior golf.

The fragrance of the soft pine straw underfoot is no comfort as I analyze my ball’s lie. Peering through the small window of pines to the green, I run through my options. Thinking about my computer science class, I approach this problem like I’m writing code. I account for every variable - wind, slope, lie - and plug them into my script. If I create an elegant solution, my program should run flawlessly. After crossing my fingers over the “Golf Pride” writing on my grip, I make my swing, and - “thwack!” - watch my ball rocket into a bunker. The bright red “AssertionError” message found in Colab flashes across my mind.

For years I tried to avoid such failures by using a brute force algorithm. I bunkered down to perfect my swing, going through every possible swing pattern and thought. I wore a hole in my hitting mat, eroded the grips on my clubs, and deeply calloused my hands. Strangers began complimenting my swing, and my tournament finishes rose from the bottoms of fields to the top third. However, my fixation on mechanical perfection led to major disappointments. After I shot an 86 in one tournament, my coach commented “You should never play that bad with a swing that good”. Frustrated, I lost interest in practice and tournaments. Midway through rounds, I often found myself thinking “How am I going to choke this time?” I felt like my golf game had plateaued, and searching for a diversion or another way to improve (or maybe both), I dove into golf course architecture.

I spent hours reading The Anatomy of a Golf Course by Tom Doak, watching videos from the Fried Egg, and studying renowned courses. I learned about golf’s schools of design (strategic, penal, and heroic), green contouring, bunker and hazard placement, risk/reward opportunities, hole templates (my favorite is the Redan), and course routing. On a great course, all of these elements come together to create a cohesive and exciting experience. Inspired, I set off to design holes of my own. I scribbled at the end of tests, in my free time, and in my mind’s eye. I experimented with the rolling greens of MacKenzie, the strategic designs of Dye, and the minimalism of Maxwell. However, instead of helping my designs, my sampling of different philosophies turned my creations into Frankenstein’s Monsters of golf holes.

I went back to the drawing board, now approaching my designs as a jazz musician. Gone were the designs built with logic gates and if-else statements. Instead, I composed runs that had the laid-back feel of “You’re A Weaver Of Dreams” by Cannonball Adderly or the frantic cadence of “Giant Steps” by John Coltrane, holes that flowed from tee to green. When arranging a 9-hole course to surround the range where I work, I let the land guide me like I was improvising over a II-V-I chord progression.

I began to see each hole from the architect’s perspective. My view expanded from the club in my hand to the course as a whole. I saw the purpose of each carefully placed bunker, and how each break in the green affected the entire hole’s strategy. This experience helped me realize that there is one underlying reason I love golf, jazz, and STEM: all provide opportunities for improvisation. Now I see mistakes not as failures but as opportunities to improvise, and I am less afraid to take risks. This reframed thinking is more important to my future than any single success.

So it’s fine that the miniature champagne remains unopened in my mom’s backpack. For now.

“Now approaching Fremont. This is a Daly City bound train.” The distinct sound of the BART announcement with the rumble of the incoming train fills my ears as I stand on the platform. Stepping into the train, I sit down on the familiar blue seat and open my phone to a map that contains one goal: go to every San Francisco district library displayed.

My love for libraries started when I was young. Every summer, my mother would take my sisters and me to the local library in lieu of our anti-air conditioning house. Originally, I was upset, what was there to do? For days I would lounge around in a bean bag chair thinking about when I could go home. However, as I wandered around absentmindedly for the 5th time, I stumbled upon a summer reading challenge where students read books to earn prizes. Drawn in by the appeal of winning new toys, I randomly picked up several books to read. My want for prizes turned into a thirst for knowledge—I began to eagerly flip through pages of comics and novels of any genre and length just to learn about anything and everything. As I started to take advantage of what the library had to offer, my journey didn't just end on the bookshelves.

In a small study room, I practiced the art of Chinese calligraphy, using a brush pen and liquid ink to craft each and every stroke of “新年快乐.” Within the auditorium, I watched with delight as ribbons and fans twirled across the stage to perform classical folk dances. And as the day ended, I unwrapped candies while watching the infamous dragon dance with loud drums beating in the background. Unable to experience the elaborate traditional festivals held for Chinese New Year’s in Guangzhou, I turned to the library to let me be one with my culture.

When I became entranced by the transformations of houses on “Property Brothers," I had the urge to make something with my own two hands. Marching into the library, I sat in hour-long workshops on Saturday afternoons learning how to construct paper into origami figures while mastering the delicate art of popsicle houses.

Even today, I head back to the library to finish dozens of assignments, making use of the textbooks and study rooms until closing time. Sometimes, I head back to sit and read at the place where it all started: my bean bag chair.

Circling back to my San Francisco library adventures, I wanted to give back to the place that provided me with accessible, free, and endless knowledge: libraries. In the San Francisco Main Public Library, I help host speaker events with individuals from a number of backgrounds and fields, inspiring youth across the San Francisco Bay Area. Within hackathons, I help create opportunities for students to interact with one another to design and brainstorm, reminiscent of the reading challenges I once participated in. In the Excelsior library, I lug a box of laptops to teach workshops on experimenting with interactive electronics to an Intro to Game Coding course. Guiding students in Cantonese, I watch as they marvel with joy at the running code segments similar to my excitement years ago. When they ask me when I’ll be back, I make a mental note to schedule another workshop next month.

In the Marina library, I plan the Intro to AI course for the eager Excelsior kids. Continuing to brainstorm ideas to give back to each library, I jot down notes of each library’s different characteristics to accommodate them. Whether that be through hosting interactive workshops or just helping out in any way, I aim to give back to my first teacher and second home. Libraries helped me craft my first few chapters and as I continue to assist with theirs, I make sure their stories are heard and recognized for years to come.

I woke up at 5am. It was a dim morning before the summer leading into 10th grade. He was already downstairs eating something that smelled like apple cinnamon oatmeal. I descended, prepared a bowl, and sat with my dad. I tried to eat, but the thought of what was coming up made every bite harder to swallow. In thirty-five minutes would be my first ever programming contest.

Eventually, I was in my room staring at the countdown for the competition. Days ago, I knew nothing about this, and seeing the nearly ten thousand participants, I felt intimidated. For the past four years I poured myself into robotics—it was what I knew well. This was different. I’d be a complete beginner again, and that thought made me hesitate. Yet, I wanted to see what the competition would hold. So as the timer ticked down I bundled my nerves and clicked the little ‘enter contest’ button.

In two hours, the competition was over. It felt strange. I ended up near the bottom of the standings, but It felt surprisingly good. I couldn’t pinpoint exactly why, whether it was the sudden focus I got or the adrenaline of seeing the green ‘Accepted’ message after solving my first problem. I decided to continue throughout the summer, practicing hours per day and attending countless competitions. But it wasn’t just smooth sailing. When things were going well, smaller hiccups didn’t worry me—but they stacked up. So when I’d find myself not understanding an algorithm or a new concept, they all rushed out in one quick burst, fueling a spiral of doubt. I’d sit there late into the night, trying to figure out, debating with myself about why I was doing this, investing so much time into something that I wasn’t sure would pay off. And as I moved towards more complicated problems, these feelings were only heightened. I recognized just how much more there was to learn, keeping the thought of returning to robotics, the familiar ground built over years of experience, lingering in my mind. Yet, when I’d wake up the following morning, I was determined to continue. When I pushed past the discomfort, I saw myself genuinely enjoying the blend of creativity and logic required, eager to learn more. So, I continued up to the present day where I look at my placements near the top of the standings, remembering that first contest with a smile. I realized that if I hadn’t stepped beyond what felt comfortable, I would have missed out on something I’ve truly come to love.

While I have since grown confident in my own abilities, I often spot students in the club I lead, hesitant to try out a competition—just like I was years ago. So, as my dad did for me during that first contest, I participate in competitions alongside them so they know they are not alone. Doing this can sometimes be hard, as they are looking to me for guidance and I seek to provide support. But in these moments I remind myself why I do it: to help them grow past familiarity. And from the ever increasing amount of participation I see from students, that I accomplish.

Over the years, I’ve found that it is crucial to push beyond comfort to explore new opportunities. Those moments of internal pressure are foundational to growth. I’ve used this skill in other experiences, from investing, to asking questions, and even to physical activities. And I know that as I move on, opportunities will only keep expanding, whether it be in unfamiliar communities, new technologies, or business ventures. Just as before, I will need to confront uncertainty to pursue them, but I know that now, I can do that. Sometimes, I think back to that dim 5 am morning, half an hour before my first competition, if I would still take the leap. The answer is yes. Every single time.

The sound of an explosive pop echoed through the halls of my house. It wasn’t a balloon or a prank; it was the battery powering my Parkinson’s project, now lighting my room on fire.

The source of inspiration for the project is not what you'd expect. I do not have a family member with Parkinson’s and was not even watching someone’s hand tremor. It was the nozzle on my 3D printer, immediately responding to every slight movement of the structure. That day, I wondered, "can a cup do this for hand tremors?"

Hours of brainstorming designs, building, and iterating followed. I took inspiration from camera gimbals to design a motorized joint on the handle and learned about PID controllers and Kalman filters to program it. But this initial excitement was soon met with a series of setbacks, and the progress between iterations was beginning to blur. I felt like a surfer overcoming a wave as he paddles out only to have the next push him closer to shore.

Then I heard the pop.

Upon finding my dirty clothes next to the outlet in flames, I sprinted to the other end of my house, nervously recalling the fire extinguisher lecture my mom had given a few weeks prior. While I was able to put it out, these flames consumed a lot of my excitement towards the project along with my dirty khakis next to the outlet. I felt like the world was telling me this thing shouldn’t exist, and for a moment, I almost believed it.

A couple weeks later, I met with Chris, a Parkinson's patient who is also the president of the local Parkinson’s support group, and after spending over an hour discussing his story, I learned that around 30% of the members forgo a beer at their monthly social gatherings at the pub because drinking from a normal cup is such a nightmare. He told me that, while not necessarily life-changing, this cup could remove a lot of stress involved in these patients’ daily lives.

I left that meeting with a reinvigorated motivation for the project, and a clear understanding of the source of my growing apathy towards it.

My parents are both social workers, and a love—no, a need to help people not only dictates the way they treat people in daily interactions, but also what they do for a living. Like them, I need to know that what I am doing is truly helping someone, even if it is in a small way, and this meeting helped me see why this thing needs to exist.

So, I brainstormed, built, and iterated again—this time with a renewed vision, and helpful insight from Chris. He told me about the way vibration from motorcycle handles eases his hand tremors. Research agreed with him, so I added 5 vibration motors to the handle. I changed the battery to one that doesn’t violently explode when overcharged and upgraded the motor to better handle the weight of the water. And now, having a working prototype, I am not only excited for the ways this cup is going to help people, but also grateful for the lessons its taught me.

I will never stop creating things that lift people up because knowing my work brings a little more ease or joy into someone’s life—even if it simply removing the stress involved in a fun social gathering at the pub—is what lights my fire. This project taught me that setbacks, even fiery ones, are inevitable, and while I am not excited for them, I know that by remembering my vision there aren’t many I can’t overcome. That is who I am, and in college, I’ll continue to embrace these challenges knowing that every fire I overcome brings me a little closer to making a meaningful difference in people’s lives.

“If forcing patients to undergo life-saving treatment against their will is unethical, then isn’t saving someone from a speeding car also unethical?”

I nibbled on a piece of kiwi as I hugged my stuffed pig closer and pondered this year’s moral dilemma at the International Ethics Olympiad. As I chewed and scribbled down the word “intention,” I remembered sitting in the same spot back in ninth grade. I’ll never forget listening to the Hamilton soundtrack non-stop as I flipped through The Federalist Papers, Common Sense, and Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, where the lyrics of “You’ll Be Back” perfectly complemented the principle behind liberty. Or the time when I combed through the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, learning about Virtue Ethics, Nozick’s Entitlement Theory, and Rawls’ Veil of Ignorance. Just because.

Back then, my fascination with philosophy and politics was limited to my bedroom, where my ceramic doll stared down at me late into the night. One night, as I was discussing Aristotle with a fellow debater Calvin over Discord, he recommended I try the Canadian Ethics Olympiad, which he described as “debate, but nicer, and you can bring more friends.” Wanting to enhance my debate abilities, I messaged my friend Emily and we quickly formed a team of three for the upcoming Ethics Olympiad. Over a few weeks, our Discord chat turned into a vault of philosophy resources, inside jokes, and SpongeBob GIFs. To prepare for the competition, I shared Crash Course videos for us to listen to on our commute and introduced a buzzer-style game to test our fluency with ethical theories. We had late-night YouTube watch parties of documentaries to understand topics relating to the competition’s cases: brain drain, historical statues, or Helena (the art display where fish were blended like smoothies). As my teammate Emily had trouble grasping the Veil of Ignorance, I related the concept to her favorite subject, math, attempting to explain the theory through the probability of flipping a die.

In the next few years, the Veil of Ignorance crawled into the margins of my case notes and the list of questions new teammates had. Listed as team captain on the competition roster in grade 11, I modified our training plan to focus on refining how we answered questions from judges or criticisms from our opponents. We grilled each other on our arguments, where one person would present the case and the rest of the team asked clarification questions or follow-up questions and brought up examples to challenge their stance. During breaks, I initiated rounds of "Gartic Phone," where our wacky drawings grew into inside jokes of our cases on sharing, the politics of sports, and “evil race” in fiction.

As a competitive debater, I have spent the past few years planning lessons, activities, and resources for new debaters while using my knowledge and experience from the Ethics Olympiad to make debate less intimidating. Economics and international relations are digestible because I recreated my Ethics Olympiad resource vault for debate—“Sunday Spec” teaches debaters how to approach knowledge-heavy motions. Like the games I created for the Ethics Olympiad, we play lighting rounds of “Debatable” where debaters speak about pop culture or humorous topics to familiarize themselves with impromptu speaking.

Many believe that philosophy is flowery language spoken with cigarettes over coffee, but instead, it is about shared experiences and new ideas. Philosophy is in everything, from pondering the latest novel in English, teaching the newest history lesson for volunteering, or reviewing anatomy flashcards for HOSA. In college, studying philosophy means connecting with the world around me—gaining new perspectives and exploring diverse academic interests. In a world driven by collaboration and new ideas, I hope to use philosophy to help others find a voice and explore others’ stories—to be a person who can lead, learn, and inspire.

“Your father and I are lucky we even made it to middle school. You know we just had a few communal pencils because we couldn’t afford our own?” my mom recounts for the second time this week. As a daughter of immigrant parents, I can’t even count the times I’ve heard about the blood, sweat, and tears put into my parents’ education.

I developed a habit of zoning out during these conversations, dismissing the topic as an outdated issue that wasn’t pressing today, especially not in first-world America. My mother, however, continued to insist that I listen. After enough times going through this routine, I was finally convinced to quickly Google “education inequality today”. Much to my surprise, I learned that students in my own county struggled with the same affordability issues that my parents once faced. I felt immediate guilt for being so dismissive of my parents’ experience, yet also anger that such inequality persists today. Horrified that my neighbors couldn’t afford school supplies while I lived in oblivion right next door, I asked my mom what would’ve alleviated the burden of educational poverty as a child. Hearing her simple response of access to school supplies, I decided students in my community would never have to tell the same story to their future children.

No longer approaching my job at Kumon, a children’s tutoring center, simply as work experience and pocket money, I started taking extra shifts, commuting between two Kumon locations and fervently tutoring geometry and grammar to help marginalized students access basic educational necessities. After finally completing my fourth week of extra tutoring, I stopped to make a purchase at Staples on the way home from the night’s shift. I filled each backpack with the freshly acquired pencils and notebooks, adding a handwritten note to each wishing students luck on the new school year. After meticulously checking over the packages, I placed them in my trunk for the next morning’s three-hour solo trip to greet my new students.

Three small pairs of arms suddenly wrapped around me. I had just met the classroom of kindergarten students at Compton’s 95th street Elementary, greeting them with the backpacks I had tutored 20+ hours to create. Sarah, a 4-year-old girl with beaded braids and a toothy grin, was the first in line, eager to swap her grocery bag for a brand new backpack. Embracing each new student that came my way, I imagined my mother’s reaction had she received these supplies as children, envisioning her classic teary smile. Immediately, I was invigorated to broaden my impact.

Through dozens of emails, DM’s, and calls, I established Youth for Our People, an organization fighting educational poverty in the US, opening chapters across four states. Through YFOP, I’ve gifted hundreds of students educational resources that my parents could only dream of as kids.

Weeks after a delivery, Kimberly, a kindergarten teacher in North Alabama, reached out: “One student with separation anxiety read eight of the books you delivered with his mom before she left; your donation has helped exponentially and our families are beyond grateful.” I’ve even embraced my mom’s habits, nagging teachers for updates on their students at least monthly. With each backpack I assemble, I fight to heal my parents’ inner child, allowing my mom’s persistence at the dinner table to finally pay off. I’ve been touched by the impact my work has had on the primary school level, now preparing to expand YFOP to higher education by fundraising for my peers who may lack resources available to others. I hope to use my college campus as a launching point into new communities in areas local to my future school. Plus, now my mom and I have a new tradition: whenever she brings up her singular pencil, I take one from my pile for YFOP and hand it to her.

My sister was glaring straight at the road amidst an uncomfortable silence. Her senior night volleyball game had just ended in a narrow overtime loss by two points after she dove to save the ball and missed.

I began replaying the last moments of that game in my head. The ball was coming right at me, and fear pierced my body; the ball she dove for had actually been in front of me. She’d sacrificed herself to save me from having to carry the mistake myself. Guilt and comfort washed over me, knowing she’d given up her own moment for me. She’d been the reason I even played volleyball.

I recognized that my sister prioritized me a lot. From taking me and my friends to Starbucks after school to allowing me to talk to her about anything—from school to our home lives—in the car, she’d been putting my needs above hers. “You know that ball was actually in front of me right,” I said as we turned into our driveway. “I know,” she responded. I felt assured, knowing that, like always, she had been intentionally looking out for me.

Wanting her to see our car rides as a supportive environment too, I began to treat our once mundane car rides as a foundation to build our relationship. Finding joy became all that mattered to us. Whether we were rushing out of our house at 6:30 to grab an energy drink before school or rushing out of school to pick up our favorite smoothies before practice started, we kept our days exciting through these drives.

After my sister left for college, I knew things were going to change, not the least of which was me driving my brother around. He’d always been more laid-back, whereas I’m more proactive; we’d never had much in common—just like my sister and me before she started driving me. I took this as an opportunity to look for connection, just as my sister had once offered me.

The first day, Noah Kahan blasted through the car speakers and my brother let out a huge sigh because he thinks his music taste is better than mine. I was annoyed, but remembering how my sister would sacrifice her own plans to drive me around, I handed him aux. As we drove together more, he started confiding in me. One night, he asked me to take him to ask a girl to Homecoming. As we approached her driveway, I could tell his nerves were starting to get to him; he then asked me to continue driving around so he could listen to some music and calm himself. I happily complied, as I remembered my sister would always allow me to rant to her in the car until I composed myself. I realized all our quiet drives to school with his music playing in the background had built a simple silence, where we only needed each other’s presence to connect and bond. Just like how I managed to shift the silence with my sister into understanding, I learned how to create a comfortable silence with my brother, becoming a person he could count on.

Now, when my sister comes home from college, I appreciate our car rides together. Whether we’re driving five minutes to Downtown Chandler for a quick breakfast or driving an hour to a flea market, I appreciate those moments more than I ever did before she left. From seeing the sacrifices my sister made for me to creating comfortable silence with my brother, all those unstructured moments of time dedicated to being together have built the closest relationships in my life. Besides loving my siblings, these relationships have made me a better friend to others, where I’ve learned how to step out of my own experiences and recognize silence as the weight of emotions. In college, whether or not I have a car, I will forge even stronger bonds by creating conversations and comfortable silence in any space to create an environment for understanding and connection in the stillness.

Where were they?

Were they still painting the skies with their flights? Could they have been navigating through the shadows of the leaves? Had these miners already breathed life into their underground kingdoms? My imagination kept stinging me, but not even in my wildest dreams did I think that one of the tiniest creatures on Earth would teach me one of life’s biggest lessons.

Hidden from any peer judgment, during my pre-junior year vacation, I could finally dedicate myself to my secret fascination: ants. At 7:45 AM, watched only by the trees, I set out into the woods near my house. As the tropical breeze tickled me, I documented in my notebook the harmony between humidity and moderate temperatures (quite the task when failing to dodge branches). Those rare conditions, especially during the final days of the mating season of Camponotus rufipes, blessed me with the best chance I ever had of spotting my first queen ant—it was a one-shot opportunity.

The stakes were high, but I was ready. My backpack was filled with glass flasks, gloves, and gentle scooching papers. I also didn’t leave behind my lucky green shirt (yes, I relied on every means necessary).

Where were they?

By 12:30 PM, sweat slid down my skin as the rising temperatures melted my dreams into illusions. Good thing my friends weren’t watching—they certainly would’ve judged me…

Wait! What was that? A queen? My squinting radars identified a trail of working ants—false alarm. But wait! Behind one ant came another, and another, and another. Soon, a massive army marched between the tree roots. Held hostage by the spectacle, I knelt in admiration, observing their tiny legs lead me to a mysterious destination.

In an inst-ant, a section from my eternally-in-progress "[Name]’s Personal Economics Exploration” Word file crossed my mind. I sprinted back to my room and started my computer. I scrutinized its 94 pages, searching for the notes those ants reminded me of.

Where were they?

Not microeconomics, not developmental economics, not finance… A-ha! Resting in the behavioral economics section were my annotations on economist Alan Kirman's ant model.

Kirman's model illustrates how individuals are influenced by social interactions (and random events) and can, thus, exhibit large-scale herding behavior. For presumably most ants, herding means an artistic, coordinated work. However, for others, it might mean a mindless tagging along. Caught in the swarm of life, I realized those insects were the ant-pitome of humanity.

Flashbacks flooded my mind. Loud parties I forced myself into. Luxurious shoes I didn’t need but bought. Rushed lunches I barely tasted. All to not be left behind. All just to be part of the “all.”
Whenever I failed to find my friends during recess, I always asked:

Where were they?

That day, those ants indirectly taught me that curiosity gives me the courage to be free. The same curiosity leading me through my academic and field explorations could further release my potential and authenticity. And it did.

I began raising my hand more in class, wearing clothes that made me comfortable, and even singing (terribly) during study breaks in the library. From presenting my admiration for ants in a Theory of Knowledge project to finding unapologetically genuine people, I found the herd I want to be part of. It is the artistic, coordinated herding from the woods.

Today, genuity is one of my utmost priorities. At the university, I want to connect with people who are passionate about their unique interests so we can listen and learn from each other. However, I also found clarity in solitude’s peace. I discovered that I didn’t need to chase after every crowd to feel fulfilled; walking a different path takes courage and often leads to those redefining their routes.

Where are they?

In the end, I didn’t find the queen ants.

In the end, I began painting the skies with my own flight.

“How do you say this in English?” is something I found myself asking people often as a little girl. Czech and Spanish were the only languages that filled my household and the only ones I ever knew until I started school. I vividly remember being in a classroom, surrounded by other students’ laughter and conversations. This language was all foreign to me, and I soon recognized it to be English. Frustration and exclusion filled my young mind as I started my educational journey. As I grew older, I purposely went through uncomfortable social situations just to learn English on my own. This led me to become the person I am—confident.

My parents—having recently moved to the United States before having me, were unfamiliar with the English language. Teaching myself was the hardest obstacle to overcome because my peers would often look down on me since I couldn't communicate with them. Starting school made me realize how different I was from kids my age; they all came from English-speaking households and all had a unique connection with each other. I would try to make friends, but it was very difficult because they couldn't understand me. Little kids' patience is not the best, so my stuttered and slurred speech would annoy the other kids and they would walk away before I could complete a sentence.

Being made fun of extinguished my self-esteem in a classroom setting. Whenever the teacher would ask a question or ask for volunteers to read something out loud, I would pray that I wouldn't get called on. This affected my confidence tremendously not only in the classroom but also when it came to conversing with people.

Despite the challenges, there was one teacher who gave me confidence to speak out and gain a sense of belonging. When I was in kindergarten, this teacher made sure to give me support and be a friend to me when I needed it most. The next school year, I had the confidence to speak out, raise my hand in class, and start conversations with new people. As the years went on, my skills developed more and more. The person I am now draws on the need to be confident throughout school and my everyday life.

Naturally, I've utilized my skills to get myself through differently challenging circumstances in school. One example of this is when I was diagnosed with ADHD. All throughout my school career, classes felt too fast, making it hard to keep up. This heavily impacted my abilities to achieve my expectations for myself. After getting diagnosed during my junior year, I recognized my challenge, and I was able to address it. My determination in my academics improved, and I felt more comfortable seeking help. Although speaking English is no longer an obstacle, high school still came with its own impediments. I was able to use the skills I learned as a young child to thrive.

From the start of my educational experience, I have had to develop important skills at an early age. Developing perseverance, flexible thinking, and confidence have allowed me to overcome a language barrier and undiagnosed ADHD. College and life after will come with its own set of barriers, but I know I am equipped to handle them.

A cold sunset I watched. The dim red and yellow sun rays hit my window. The strong wind turbulences hit the trees in our field. Broken branches fell on the dirt and rocks. The animals ran away to their shelters, but I stayed, watching. A beast, lurking from a distance, silently observed my ten-year-old self, waiting for the right moment to consume my essence. As the sun sank lower, the creature stepped closer. I was a child scared of monsters under my bed, but now, a real one was preparing an attack.

The night came. No light could be seen anywhere. All sounds stopped. My last hopes dwindled. The monster manipulated the shining strands of my existence's fabric. The victory was his, and my happiness was the trophy. It was the start of six years of depression.

The seeds of my depression sprouted with sudden feelings of numbness and emptiness. I hated myself for it. My parents believed it was just a phase that would pass. I tried convincing myself it was all in my head, but I couldn’t. The concept of psychological health was unknown and refuted by my community.

No help was offered. The same words were repeated every time: "Pray to God, and He will help you." But the pain only intensified. I was left alone all day, with thoughts screaming louder. I withdrew from all social activities and became obsessed with sanitizing everything, unable to tolerate any imperfection. Joy was absent, no matter the situation. All I wanted was an escape from these relentless nightmares.

What is the point of a life where no help is given, no happiness is enjoyed, and no thoughtful concern is offered? I was afraid to share my struggle with anyone other than my parents. So, I determined to face them independently.

Three months later, a warm sunset I watched. The sun rested at the end of a long, empty road. Rain softly fell from the sky. An overwhelming happiness, unlike anything I had ever felt, washed over me. A moment of epiphany came over me as if I had solved a puzzle without knowing. I realized that stress had been at the root of all my problems. So, I began learning how to face anxiety.

After seven long months, I finally triumphed, defeating the inner monster that once consumed my entire existence. My own transformation had just begun. Now, I had a reason to challenge myself, enjoy life, and contribute to my community. With this newfound purpose, I took the biggest step of my life: I applied for Mawhiba’s gifted students' program. In 9th grade, through Mawhiba, I transitioned from a public school with no English curriculum to an American curriculum school that provided a wide range of advanced classes for gifted students.

I had to learn an entirely new language to understand what was happening around me. Overwhelmed, I doubted whether I could succeed in such an environment. Using what I learned to defeat anxiety, I began outlining the steps I needed to understand English.

I worked tirelessly, studying for at least five hours each day to prepare for my first English quiz. I expected to get an A+, as I had in my previous public school. Instead, I got a D. It was devastating to feel so far behind my peers. But I didn’t give up. I sought help from my friends and learned everything I needed to succeed.

Since then, I've been driven to help others who struggled like I did. I began offering free tutoring sessions to anyone in need, and through that, I became friends with nearly everyone at my school. I also co-founded two online communities, each with over 2,000 members, to share resources, offer support, and help people meet new friends.

I’ve grown to cherish every sunset. Everything fades, but with each sunset, there's the promise of a sunrise—another chance, another beginning.

“Vamos, vamos, sí se puede!” I cheered as I eagerly watched men of all ages race past with sweat dotting their shirts. I sat on the grass eating arroz con pollo from the food truck while absorbing the game. I remember the joy of hanging out at these neighborhood pickup soccer games with my dual-language school classmates in the cultural-melting-pot neighborhood where I was raised across the river from New York City. On those sidelines, I was indoctrinated into the 4 billion fanbase of the most popular sport in the world.

Adrenaline rushed through me as I flew down the field with the ball at my feet. During a game, with the coach on the sideline, I had freedom to be creative. I weaved around opponents, passing the ball to my friends. The energy of the team working as one and the connection to the community that celebrated players drew me in. Soccer became a passion woven into my identity. At boarding school, soccer kept me tethered to the community back home and provided an instant connection for new friendships. I sought to grow in the game that meant so much to me through hours spent alone on the field perfecting my skills.

Until my dreams began spiraling downward. In the third game of my junior year, my team was behind, when the ball got free and, naturally, I attacked at full speed to gain possession. I collided hard with an opponent. Our feet tangled, each reaching for the ball, my ankle twisted and I lost balance. I fell awkwardly landing on my right wrist when I heard a crack. I simultaneously twisted my ankle and broke my arm. Realizing I would be sidelined, my heart was broken too. I supported my team as best I could from the bench. With the cast removed and replaced with a brace, I was approved to play, but warned that the brace might affect my body movement. The very next game, I tore my ACL. I was out for the rest of the season. Now my heart was broken and ripped from my chest.

My recovery was frustratingly slow. I pushed through physical therapy after school and hit the gym in the mornings.
