As injuries began to derail my aspiration to continue competitive soccer, I was overcome with fear of failure. If I couldn’t play, would I lose my identity and friends, and let my family down? I evaluated my options and made the courageous decision to leave yet another community behind and switch boarding schools for a top soccer program, while committing to an additional year of high school.

The training at the new school provided renewed optimism. I followed a strict diet and exercise regimen and the trainer declared me one of the fittest on the team. Yet despite my discipline, old injuries resurfaced and my body continued to betray me. Injuries take both a physical and mental toll on an athlete. I found myself torn between two worlds: my passion for soccer and the limitations of my body. It was just as painful to pivot on my ankles as it was to pivot to a new future without competitive soccer, although an inevitable decision.

Reinventing my identity has involved self-reflection and exploring new interests. I recently traveled to Colombia to visit the family who helped raise me. There I saw soccer again for its community-building gap-bridging ability. My athletic days are not over; I have accepted my limitations and am finding new sports that do not stress my injuries. I am also using my love of sports to raise awareness of the importance of psychological coaching of athletes through community outreach programs.

My passion for soccer sparked me to persevere in the face of setbacks and my injuries taught me resilience. I gained the confidence to tackle these obstacles. Yet it is equally important to have the courage to reflect and pivot. As I look towards the challenges that lie ahead in college, I take with me the lessons of perseverance, courage and resilience to guide me in this next chapter.

In Florida, I saw school library shelves go empty, as science, history and the truth of people’s lives were labeled indoctrination. House Bill 1467 required all school books to be reviewed, with no books approved in advance. Entire libraries, often built by teachers over decades, were hidden or emptied. Teachers, threatened with loss of credentials and even felonies, took down posters of civil rights leaders and rainbows, and put away their family photos if their family had LGBTQIA+ members. My family chose to leave, because, as my mother put it, “For us, Connecticut is warmer than Florida.”

The library in my own mind is sprawling, and slightly disorganized, with a staff consisting of a couple humans, a troop of raccoons, and some crows bustling around. Moving to Connecticut was the third time I’ve had to change high schools. Each time I got better at reorganizing as I brought in the sometimes heavy stacks of new materials.

Some of the library’s shelves contain more order than entropy. In the smooth leather-bound hardcovers on calculus, I expect a neat and exact answer found at the end of a clear and logical path. If a book describes a method like Riemann’s sums, which approximates an answer, the next chapter is almost always about an exact solution, such as integrals. So when I showed up to class last year prepared for elegant calculus, learning about series that do not have an exact solution was incredibly frustrating.

In other areas of the library, inaccuracy and imperfection are welcomed. In the aisles dedicated to sewing, I run through the rows with loose pattern pieces flopping out of their folder, instruction manuals bookmarked with scrap fabric, and overflowing bins of half-worked ideas. When making a pair of pants recently, I indulged in the following: not pinning or tracing certain pattern pieces, not topstitching or putting a button above the zipper, and at a certain point completely ignoring the instructions. The waistband is held together with hope, but I wear them with pride and a tightly fastened belt.

While these sections are very different, being me is not a negotiation between different competing factions. I am myself when I take care to write plus c after every general integral, and I am myself when I tear a chunk of fabric off a scrapped prototype to show a friend. I have energy for creative chaos, and energy for precision and refinement. I am the most proud of projects that involve both. Color makes 3D graphs readable and math turns flat fabric into curves.

Developing a more complete view of the world involves combining disciplines and listening to a variety of perspectives. In Connecticut, I am working on another kind of library. One that is typed in archival ink on acid free paper, and stored in a climate controlled underground vault (a more accessible version will also be shared to the wider world online). As a research assistant on the LGBTQIA+ Oral History Project for the town of Ridgefield, I’ve interviewed people who work in the visual arts, medicine, and comedy, who have watched Ridgefield go from somewhere they weren't comfortable being themselves into the welcoming place it is today. Their stories illustrate the impact of policy. They describe the joy and security they feel living in a town dotted with rainbow welcome signs while married to who they love. Having listened to people who have witnessed this progress, and seen the effort my community has put into making sure these stories are preserved, I feel more hopeful in humanity’s capacity to expand to love the people around us.

My high school path has taught me that I am temporary, and though the bonds I make can fall apart, be replaced, or reform, life continues. When other people have library collections that are very different from my own, I recognize that it isn’t a threat to my identity, it is an opportunity to gain perspective. I am still discovering the edges, smudges, and curves in the lenses I see the world through. Navigating the confusion and discomfort of complex situations is familiar. Knowing that mistakes and change are a part of learning makes me more prepared to study science and engineering. Because innovation and exploration are not solitary activities, I look forward to working with others. I plan to expand libraries, and innovate (some elegant something).

As a kid raised by my grandmother, I used to believe she had superpowers. She knew how to cook every dish in the world and gave wonderful massages. However, as a typical traditional Chinese family, her habits seemed to differ from those of the other members of my family. She often spoke on the phone in languages I could not understand and sometimes invited foreign strangers to our house.

The relationship I used to share with my grandmother gradually deteriorated as I got older because of the growing differences in our lifestyles. I couldn't match the cultural differences between her and my community, so I naturally started to estrange from her internally.

One evening, as she was preparing dishes for the Mid-Autumn Festival, I finally asked about her memories from when she was young and the stories behind all the skills she had learned. As she shared her stories with me, I began to understand what life was like for her as an immigrant during that time, and I slowly realized that her "superpowers" all seem to have been honed through experiences from different cultures. The super-strength of her massages comes from a job she took when she emigrated to England, and her unconventional cooking style stems from the experiences as a young Chinese Indonesian girl living in Indonesia. At that point, my grandmother to me was really the true hero with superpowers.

After learning a lot from my grandmother, I realized that I had the opportunity to share this spirit with others in my community. Thus, I joined a school organization to help promote its international culture. Throughout the events, I was able to engage with families to answer their questions about the school and its diverse environment. Outside of my community, I thought of children who, like me, may not know about lifestyles outside of their own without exposure and information. For this reason, I founded a community service club, which hosted trips to teach children at elementary schools in remote areas. During our time at the schools, we hosted venues that taught children about cultures in different regions worldwide. For instance, we collaborated with students to create presentations on countries like Thailand and Japan, and I was able to introduce children who had never experienced Indonesian food to recipes I learned from my grandmother.

During that time, I noticed a child who looked different. Despite speaking Chinese, he appeared to have a foreign face. I was told by other students that he is from an ethnic minority in China, but few of his friends seemed to really know his background. With a tentative attitude, I invited him to introduce his stories. Surprisingly, he showed great confidence and described the beauty of his hometown to us. At that moment, his unique charm reminded me of my grandmother. At the same time, other students showed great interest, as if they couldn't wait to get to meet this classmate again. Since my goal was to inspire their curiosity so they can expect more from the world ahead, after seeing their eyes as if they had discovered a new continent, I really felt the impact of diversity. It taught me the importance of being open to new things.

Throughout my childhood with my grandmother, staying curious and accepting diversity is the most important knowledge that I learned from her. The power of curiosity leads me to the path of finding the answer to every question. Whether it is meeting new people or diving into new areas of study, the urge to explore different aspects pushes me to become successful. Thus, my passion for helping communities will continue as I move on to the next chapter. By using my strength to provide a better worldview for others, I can deeply resonate with how my grandmother brought her spirit to me.

Freddy's

In west Houston, beside a little mall where roads I-10 and 99 cross, stands a small restaurant named Freddy’s that has the best burgers in the world. When I lived in Texas, my joy was to go there on weekends, or after a long day of practice.

Consisting of a juicy smash patty, onions, special sauce, and 3-inch pickles that always find a way to fall off, Freddy’s burgers were made simple. On the grill, teenagers cranked out as many orders as they could. My eyes were fixed on their swift movements, eager to taste the food that I loved. I thought Freddy’s would be with me forever.

When I was ten years old, I had to move back to Japan. I was anxious about starting a new life, but even more devastated to leave behind my home and my precious burgers.

After returning to Japan, my cravings for Freddy's hit almost immediately. I visited as many restaurants in Japan as possible, hoping to have another taste of my past.

I went to many popular eateries, but they all fell short of what I yearned for. Freddy’s burgers occupied a special spot in my heart, not only because of their deliciousness but also their connection to my life in America.

It wasn’t until six years later, at a conveyor-belt sushi restaurant in Tokyo station that I started to question my desires. One night, when having dinner with a friend from Australia, he mentioned how jealous he was that I had access to good, cheap sushi.

This struck me. I remembered how much I craved Japanese food when I lived in Houston. My family and I even traveled several hours just to visit a “real” ramen restaurant run by a Japanese chef. Once we moved back to Japan, we ate out every weekend because of how good it was to eat the food again.

I came to understand that whether I was in Texas or Japan, what I wanted most was always what I couldn't get. There’s a Japanese phrase: nai mono nedari, "to beg for things you don’t have”. In the end, it took a casual comment at a sub-par sushi chain for me to understand how trapped I was in my own feelings of nai mono nedari.

Before leaving the US, I received a parting gift: a framed message that read, “What lies behind us & what lies ahead of us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.” At first, it sounded like a simple motivational phrase. However, since realizing how affected I’d been by my craving for things I no longer had, I’ve found a deeper appreciation and understanding of the meaning behind this message. What I had in the past or what I want in the future is not as important as what I have now—not just food, but the environment I’m in, the people in my life, and what I have within me. I learned to cherish every moment, to embrace, to savor, and to live in the present because there might not be another day to taste the pickles that slip out of my burger.

Now, as I look ahead to entering university, working towards becoming a flag football Olympian, and continuing my search for the next Freddy’s, my perspective about what it means to achieve my goals has changed. I'm still an ambitious and driven individual, but I no longer feel disappointed when I can’t have the things missing from my life. Instead, I’ve learned to appreciate the special things I have now and value every step along my journey.

I’ll cherish every bite of the Japanese food I have now and the American food that awaits me. I won’t do it just for the joy, but to make sure nothing goes to waste: whether it’s a burger or life more broadly, I’ll treasure the time I have to enjoy it.

A map of Hong Kong is the newest addition to my family’s ever-growing collection of maps. Although far from being the only map of Hong Kong in a collection, just shy of a hundred strong, it is much unlike the rest; it cannot fold into a neat rectangle. Nor does it document Hong Kong in painstaking exactness. It was a map of my own: ownership by creation.

Mapmaking started as an intuitive habit—quick diagrams in my red diary, linking visitor hotspots to restaurants to hotels. These diagrams soon evolved into maps, the numerously integrated characteristics of a place unwilling to be captured by a mere sketch.

Maps, it seems, exist in contradiction to themselves, their identities always in flux. The very scrupulousness that is integral to mapmaking has to grapple with the reality that a map, is, in essence, still a diagram. The dormancy of any map is at odds with the dynamic place it attempts to represent. Meanwhile, as a mapmaker, I also find my identity oscillating between an artist and a scientist. But less like a perpetual tug-of-war between precision and creativity, between details and clarity, between facts and feelings, mapmaking is a collaboration, a testament to the coexistence of the scientist and the artist, however fraught that collaboration may seem to feel sometimes.

The map of Hong Kong started with the scientist in me: a command to systematically translate the details of an experience into a structured visual medium. Striving to capture every intricate detail, the scientist dives into research, ignoring the impatient artist dying to put pen to paper. Accustomed to the almost mandatory learning process of immaculate research, the scientist reached out to the Chinese Society of Geodesy Photogrammetry and Cartography via me, learning all about the science of cartography and its methods. The scientist immediately gets to work, pouring over governmental websites, existing maps, geographic information, and his own field notes. Armed with a comprehensive understanding of the project, the artist can finally start.

As my room witnesses profound changes—the floor donning a new carpet, the usual occupants discreetly shuffling off to the sides, leaving the center for new occupants—the pair’s cooperation begins. Had the artist embarked on this endeavor alone, a scale would have been deemed unnecessary: “My instincts will never fail me!” Had the scientist also worked independently, a precise scale would have been needed: “All maps have a perfect scale!” An uneasy compromise saw a less-than-ideal scale implemented.

As the scientist arranges and rearranges numbers, exacting out the dimensions, the artist lays down the grids of intersecting longitudes and latitudes according to those calculations. Those hours of research finally paid off when the locations from the scientist’s research found their correspondence on the canvas, pinpointing important parts of the map. From those pinpoints, the scientist loses himself again in a mix of triangulation, topological calculations, and contour lines.

The map, in its current manifestation, is merely a locus of points, all with the commonality of being in the set “coastline of Hong Kong.” Lifeless is the map without my personal colors. The artist now steps in. Not only does the map receive a slew of new colors, but a path also begins to take shape. It is a path retracing the connection between the past and the present, as well as connecting places to memories: Repulse Bay, the Hong Kong aviary, Causeway Bay, among others. Any geographic map will display possible paths, some even going as far as to show every single street and road there is, but my own path is still uniquely mine to choose and discover. And with that, this map, a testament to the uniqueness of my own journeys but also a reminder of the power of the harmonious coalescence of the seemingly inherent paradoxes of the complex scientist-artist complex within me, is finished.

I could feel the worry growing inside me. It was another day getting ready for swim practice when my friend rushed into the locker room, looking straight at me, asking, “Guess who got the 500?!” He had to be joking. Every swimmer knows the 500 is the worst race to get assigned.

Seeing my name scribbled on the 500-lineup felt like I was being set up for my own embarrassing highlight film. I’m a sprinter. I swim 100s. The 500 is the longest race for high schoolers, and it meant an additional 16 laps! Distance swimming wasn’t my strength, and to make matters worse, we competed against our biggest rivals. Why did Coach put me in this race? What if I burned out before the last lap? What if I forgot what lap I was on? I was immediately overcome with anxiety.

As race day approached, I thought of everything possible to avoid the 500. I could fake sickness, mom could schedule a doctor's appointment, or I could just not show up. I sat on this for a few days but ultimately decided to push past my fear of failure. And when race day came, I did it. I didn’t win, and maybe I still sped out too fast, but I did better than I expected and, in the process, learned some lessons about myself.

Am I now a distance swimmer? Not necessarily, but this race reminded me to step out of my comfort zone and not be so afraid of failing. Last year, I decided to compete in my first coding competition as a non-computer science wiz. Fast forward to today. I’m working as the “business liaison” with two others to host our own hackathon. I cold-called potential venues and sponsors, facing possible rejection with each call, nervous about what questions they might ask or how I should respond. However, I embraced the unfamiliar and ultimately successfully negotiated a venue contract and identified sponsors. I can take college-level business classes and present bold business proposals in my Entrepreneurship class. I can go on a 10-day Europe trip without my family, knowing everything won’t always go smoothly, but still feel I can learn more by trying my own approaches. It’s now easier to push past thoughts of failure because I know it’s not just about the win and that a “failure” can also be an opportunity to pivot and discover something better.

Just last month, I was back in the locker room when a younger teammate rushed in with a look of worry on his face; It was his turn to swim the 500. Back when I was facing his same doubts, admittedly, I also considered finding a way out. Ultimately, however, I didn’t want to set a bad example as an upper-classman. In other areas of my life -- whether I’m tutoring one of my math students, helping a young kindergartener read his first chapter book, or teaching a young swimmer how to navigate the pounding ocean waves -- I would never let one of my kids give up because of self-doubt or fear of failure. That was the standard I set for my own kids, and I wanted to lead by example even then. I told my teammate about my prior situation and to be on one lap at a time. He decided not to quit, and I made sure to cheer him on during the meet.

In my next chapter, I won’t shy away from uncomfortable situations and instead plan to embrace them. Maybe I’ll play a sport I’ve never tried or participated in a study-abroad program in a country I’ve never seen. Maybe I’ll pursue a challenging internship that seems beyond my current skill set. I’ve realized that I can miss out and lose opportunities if I let my fear take over. And I’ve decided not to let that happen and to instead always dive right in.

In Vietnam, the grading system goes from 10 to 1. In the United States, the letter graded system told a different story. Getting picked up from preschool on my dad’s motorbike, I proudly flaunted my 10/10 paper to my father. Jumping off the motorbike, I ran to my mom as I relished both their praises. Relocating from Vietnam to Florida turned my life completely upside down. The letters were different, the grading system was from A to F; English had no accents like Vietnamese did. My name Thư now became Thu. I was able to speak some English by 2nd grade, however for the first time in my life, I became a below-average student. Accordingly, I grew used to seeing mostly S for satisfactory and C’s. My performance was at its lowest in 7th grade – it felt like I had hit rock bottom. But that took a turn in the second semester.

The change began with my creative writing teacher, with her attentive brown eyes and candid teaching style. She was brutally honest, and she never beat around the bush. On a sunny day, when she took us out to the courtyard for some air. I trudged behind class staring at my phone. Unexpectedly, a hand tapped my shoulder, I looked up to see my teacher, she asked me, “are you going to repeat the grade?” My face burned with shame but my tan skin hid my embarrassment. I had no response for her, although I knew my grades were below par, my other teachers hadn’t pointed it out so bluntly.

I wanted a resolve, a solution to where I could feel proud of my grades. I started making adjustments to my life. I wasn’t just learning how to improve my grades, I was learning how to communicate and when to ask for help. Little by little, I saw my grade going up from single digits to the tens. Over the span of several weeks, I ensured that I turned in my work on time and completed each assignment thoroughly. With consistency and hard work my grades ascended. I had straight As on my report card by the end of the school year, something that I had never achieved before.

I was ready to confront my next challenge, enrolling in rigorous courses. Mrs. Collins became my English teacher, her once-threatening eyes transformed into sources of encouragement. At the beginning of the semester, she nominated me as Student of the Month. The same teacher who’s frankness once made me feel embarrassed, now commemorated my achievement. We rejoiced over my awkwardly posed photo in a bright red “Student of the Month” shirt.

This journey not only changed my academic life; it reshaped my social life as well. My family became proud of me – not just for my grades, but for the increased effort I put into everything I did. By actively participating in class, I developed friendships and teachers became more approachable. My academic progression rewarded me with lifelong friendships, newfound confidence, and strong relationships with my teacher.

The American letter-based grading system taught me that true growth comes from commitment and perseverance. Among the years where I was unable to give my best, I felt helpless. However, constructive criticism in combination with a rigorous academic schedule, I became organized, motivated, and developed lifelong relationships. College marks my next chapter where I can utilize what I have learned and face challenges with the tenacity that has gotten me to this point.

My younger sister often reminds me, usually mockingly, that my favorite joke is “What is the opposite of down? Up. Out? In. A house? Not a house.” I was only three years old when I made it up, but ever since I’ve been fascinated by the concept of opposites, especially how we balance their existence in our minds and bodies.

Early in high school, I struggled with finding balance in my relationship with food. When sitting at a neighborhood restaurant in ninth grade, a close friend, who happens to be thin, kindly ordered pizzas for the table when the waiter arrived, but I whispered, “I’ll just have the salad—no croutons, dressing on the side, please.” For years, I wrestled with my weight. I spent countless hours watching “What I Eat in a Day” videos on YouTube, hoping to find a secret formula for becoming fit. But nothing changed until I stopped focusing on restrictions and embraced a new philosophy: the 80/20 rule. 80% of my diet became whole, balanced meals, leaving the other 20% for flexibility. Over time, I transformed from struggling to run around the block and having minimal arm strength to training for a half-marathon and doing 40 push-ups. Yet, I wanted this balance to benefit others too. In the summer before 11th grade, I co-founded a non-profit that encourages others to enjoy the benefits of caring for one’s mind and body through fitness events and educational resources. I also developed a fascination with metabolism, trying to better understand our bodies’ subconscious forces that make the opposing goals of losing and gaining weight so difficult to achieve.

While I achieved balance in physical health through structure and flexibility, music became my intellectual and creative challenge. Studying the music of composers like Chopin and Rachmaninov, I choose a piece and, after hours of practice, turn it into something that, hopefully, resembles the composer’s intentions; analyzing music theory and history reveals patterns and a methodology to approach each piece. I then explored the antithesis of classical piano: jazz, which felt like stepping off a tightrope and onto a surfboard for the first time. My peers and I savor the unpredictability of capricious key and time signature changes so much that we improvise our own jazz arrangements outside of class and perform for our schoolmates. Jazz and classical music now harmoniously exist within me, and I have become a more versatile and creative musician by exploring both genres.

The intriguing nature of opposites extends beyond our bodies, music, and the English language. In middle school, I sought a way to expand my understanding of fundamental complements through another language entirely. For five years, I explored ways to immerse myself in French language and culture: I created a French music playlist, watched English Netflix with French captions and vice versa, changed my entire phone to French, and practiced the language in France and Quebec. But I was still far from fluent. I wondered if I even had a talent for languages until, at the end of junior year, I gathered a group of French enthusiasts interested in self-studying for the 2025 AP exam to meet or call weekly and speak only in French. These sessions have been meaningful because I've come to see language beyond rote memorization—appreciating differences in pronunciation, phrasing, and derivation shape opposites and complexities that make fluency so valuable for connecting with others.

Through these experiences, I've learned that the tension between the opposites I encounter does not require restricting myself to one extreme or delicately balancing both. Instead, I can use that tension as a powerful force to propel my growth and build communities of those who do the same. I now cherish the temporary imbalance of the push and pull between my frustration and fulfillment, structure and spontaneity.

I’ve been thinking towards the future ever since I was 5 years old at the bank with my mom, pestering her with complaints in my high pitched voice that “we’ve been here to long,” “I’m bored,” and the question that started my quest of never-ending thirst: “Why are we even here? What's the point of putting our money into a bank account,” to which she responded to little me by teaching me the captivating concept that is interest: the financial return account holders receive from banks for depositing funds or the much simpler, child version I got digest: “when we put money in the bank account, they give us extra money in return the longer we have it in there.”

As I grew older, thoughts like: “my grandma’s health is going to worsen in the future so I need to learn more medical vocabulary words in Spanish in order communicate with her more effectively” and “I need to start cooking more so I can sustain myself when I move out” constantly flooded my mind, encompassing my life. My mindset also aided in little things like scheduling my day but also during my downtime, when I utilized it to contribute to my passion — attempting to predict stock market performance, curating budgets for imaginary scenarios, and speculating what shark tank products will actually achieve financial success.

But in the middle of Sophomore year, I was unable to use my special skill. My mom gained the courage to move us out of an emotionally abusive household after over eight years of psychological torture. I didn’t know we were moving until it was in motion and when I found out, even though I was overcome with immense relief, I still had worried thoughts of how adjusting is going to be so tough and “how am I going to adapt to living with so many people (my grandma, aunt, and dog)” because I wasn’t prepared.

I was able to fall into a routine in my new home: schoolwork, taking care of my grandma and dog when needed, and indulging in my passion, without freaking out if something came up at the last minute or I “wasn’t prepared”. Despite my preconceived notions about how difficult life was going to be after moving, it was as if a weight lifted off my shoulders. In my new environment, I challenged myself to talk to new people and get closer to those who were already by my side. With this strong support system I built, I felt encouraged to take courses the next year over the topics I had been enamored by for so many years such as Principles of Business, Marketing, and Finance, Financial Literacy, and Business Law.

Finding a balance between future and present can prove difficult, especially when looking towards the future can benefit me so much; however, unexpected obstacles and variables are always prominent in real life and while I can’t always be prepared for them, I can allow myself to adapt to it. I’m still learning this, but it helps this lesson can be incorporated into my everyday life through my passion for economics.

Sitting at the piano, bathed in warm sunlight, I faced the daunting blank sheet before me. This morning, against a backdrop of free-spirited birdsong, I announced my intention of quitting five-year piano lessons to instead pursue my own musical compositions.

To my surprise, my parents agreed. Now, for the first time, I’m stepping away from a structured path, and it’s overwhelming. I feel doubt trying to creep in–have I made the right decision? I know that by deciphering a new way to enjoy music, my aspirations might carry me far beyond the limits of lessons and repetitions.

Slowly, I start to forget my worries. I hum softly to myself, experimenting with melodies, motif by motif, the notes swiftly dancing toward me, as if orchestrated by an unseen angel, gradually coming together. The melody takes shape; my pen glides across the staff paper, capturing the scene in musical notation.

That familiar feeling of teetering on the edge of the unknown resurfaced this past summer, when I applied to a six-week STEM project to build machine learning models predicting mental health outcomes. I had no experience with machine learning and only basic knowledge of Python, but I knew machine learning is the future. Instead of wondering if I would fail, I asked myself: “What if I succeed?”

The first two weeks were overwhelming. I spent hours grappling with algorithms and tutorials. When I ran into a question, I tried to find the answer for myself. I felt too shy to ask my teammates, thinking I should know what they know as we start at the same time. The deadline approached and the data was overwhelming with more than fifty variables to choose for the models. I walked through the maze-like computer server room to find one of my teammates.

We were delighted to meet each other: I had made little progress with my code, whereas he was a Python expert who had been fruitlessly battling with which variables to choose for the model. I shared my research findings on mental health, and he showed me data-cleaning Python tricks. After the discussion, we decided on the setup of a composite for the dependent variables, and re-categorized the rest of the 50 variables to streamline model building based on research results. Together, we broke down the complex project into small chunks: data cleaning, model setup, results analysis, and model comparison. Piece by piece, the project took shape.

Before the deadline, we managed to implement three models for prediction. More importantly, I learned to embrace the power of collaboration to navigate uncertainty. By admitting that I didn’t know everything and seeking help from my teammates, I opened myself up to a faster learning path I hadn’t anticipated. Composing music had taught me a lot about solitary confidence and self-discovery, but the collaboration and idea exchange in group STEM projects are equally refreshing. Both are necessary and valuable to my growth. Like a train, I keep moving forward; unlike a train, I don’t stay on pre-designed tracks.

Facing uncertainty is the only certainty. As I begin college, I envision myself living and working alongside other nonconformist thinkers in a crucible of innovation. In this environment, I'll grow, contribute, and prove that another way isn't just possible—it’s essential.

A year later, I performed my composition, Establishment, at Vienna’s historic Ehrbar Hall. I couldn’t discern my parents’ beaming faces through the bright lights washing over me. As I put my fingers on the keys, I knew it was their faith in me that had given me the courage. My piece concluded with the rhythmic 'clickety-clack' of a train, symbolizing my ongoing journey toward embracing uncertainty with hope and determination. I was proud of myself for taking this leap into the unknown.

Like many upbringings of a true Angeleno, my childhood took place at the top of the Griffith Observatory hiking trail. Scaling the steep inclines and brushing past the shrubbery as twilight deepened into night, the brightest of stars began to reveal themselves to the world. It was during these hikes my passion for the stars ignited; countless stars illuminated my journey. Stars were my companions, guiding my thoughts with their faint glow from reconciling friendships to debugging asteroid simulation codes for observations made from the Pohl Observatory.

On my nightstand sits a cherished star projector gift from my mom. When facing the anxiety of not fitting in, I would find solace in the sprawling stars. During the school retreat to Joshua Tree, as I watched drones of kids pulling into the bus loading area in luxury cars I wondered if I would ever share anything in common with my peers. The blazing sun melted away my hopes of finding common ground; girls pulled out designer sunglasses to shield their eyes and chatted about their lavish summer vacations. The first night after countless futile ice breakers, we partook in star gazing in silence. As we all lay there, under the same sky, I realized regardless of wealth we all have the same opportunity to reach for the stars. Despite the fact I was thrown into a different realm, I knew I could come across connection over status. I was determined to forge a path forward. The starlight became a constant companion. The stars stood by me as I turned my fears into resilience and embraced the value of inclusion, learning to find my place and support others along the way.

Carved into the side of a tree swaying in my front yard is the constellation of Leo: evidence for my love of art. One day, as Lindsay admired Van Gogh's Starry Night, she remarked, "I feel like I can sense Van Gogh's breath." This sparked my curiosity: could we really feel the breath of Van Gogh? I began my experiment, exhaling into a rubber glove to measure my breath's volume. I calculated the total air Van Gogh would have breathed and estimated the number of molecules in his breath with Avogadro's number. After that, through various chemical and statistical calculations, I discovered that Van Gogh's breath still lingers in significant amounts today. I realized that not only was I breathing his breath, but I might also be enveloped by his artistic spirit. My illustration of stars became intertwined with Van Gogh’s artistic spirit. I was pulled into the swirling stars of his world, encased between the tension of artistic delicacy and the complexity of reality.

A childhood photo album my parents put together adorned with a celestial theme reminds me of my family. When my mom was contemplating whether to take the GED, I decided it was my turn to support her. I became her teacher. Together we jumped from question to question, conquering every topic. On the day of her math exam, I reminded her of what she used to tell me the morning of my math competitions: “Does passing truly matter? Challenge matters." During her test, I flipped through nostalgic memories, reflecting on how my family has supported each other–through math competitions and my first disastrous attempt at baking macarons. As the pages turned, I recognized that the challenge my mother and I faced together was the true reward.

Throughout my life, stars have brought me joy, peace, and courage. Just like the lattice of stars I admired during those twilight hikes, I will illuminate a path not only for me but for others who ponder about the universe. Yet unlike the majority of stars, I won't just fizzle out following the perceived predestined path of someone who grew up with hardship, but I’ll go supernova pushing against the boundaries that were once placed upon me.

I’d love to smell rain, curry fish-balls, and humid concrete. Engrossed in the power of scent, I'm a fragrance connoisseur, caught in the dance between the top, middle, and base notes of life. Let me introduce you to a few from my collection.

Le Labo’s Bigarade 18.

The middle notes of lily flower pull me back to my grandpa's cramped, humid apartment in Hong Kong, reminiscent of summer days alongside him. I helped him file stacks of ancient documents, a task stolen from him as age weathered his body. Surrounded by vases of well-kept lilies, I tediously checked over 30,000 papers for an orange stamp indicating its date. He sat in his wheelchair, handing me paper after paper, narrating childhood stories as rain pitter-pattered outside. I distinctly remember fragrant lily flowers and even while squatting on dirt-cheap pink stools sweating profusely – it wasn’t discomfort I remembered – it was his patience and quiet persistence. Though, isn’t that how fragrances work? The deeper notes are the ones that stay.

Maison Margiela’s Coffee Break.

My leg shivered, pulse racing, as I stared at the chessboard, paralyzed. The pressure—my parents’ bragging, my grandpa’s expectations—was suffocating. Fear gripped me, not just of losing but of failing them. Reaching for my bottle of Coffee Break, I spritzed my collarbone. The warm notes of cappuccino and lavender hugged me, reminding me of MoonGoat Cafe, where I first learned to play chess over sweet-scented coffee and Louis Armstrong’s scatting. Coffee Break was a reminder – a reminder to breathe, to balance my drive for excellence with peace. Losing didn’t define me. What mattered was how I faced the pressure and how I could use it to grow. Wearing Coffee Break, I returned to the game ready to play my heart out.

Xerjoff Torino22

Sitting at my desk staring at my dim screen, I had a total of zero orders placed.

In 2022, I started a fragrance business, driven by my curiosity of the story behind one’s perfume. My first sale, Afternoon Swim, was sold to a close friend who had just quit swimming to take care of his mom. Helping him reconnect with his passion was the beginning of a fragrance community, and I found like-minded connoisseurs by sharing my love locally.

Transitioning online was challenging. The lack of personal connection and community frustrated me. Among a sea of fragrance e-stores, I felt like an outsider, someone “un-cut for business”. Doubt crept in. Was this just another failed attempt at entrepreneurship? DJing, crocheting – fragrances would soon join the list.

But fragrances weren’t just a “business” to me. Torino22 helped me meet my best friend in AP Biology, when he noticed Torino22 and asked for fragrance recommendations. Cedrat Boise reminds me of baking mooncakes with my mom. French Riviera, a trail of sunscreen and seasalt. They’re not just “businesses.” They’re doors that turned shy kids into baking rivals and kayaking buddies. Fragrances foster connections, transforming the mundane into the memorable.

I realized I wanted to bring those connections to my work. I spent that night redesigning my marketing strategy, adding personal anecdotes to every product, emphasizing the story behind each fragrance. I ended up with over 400 fragrances listed – each with a unique story.

The next morning, a barrage of notifications woke me up. 25 new orders had been placed overnight. Soon, it was 60 orders per day.

My Fragrance(s)

My fragrances have shown me that life, its challenges, and its commemorations aren’t fixed. They’re fluid, shaped and reshaped by its wearer. We’re all blends of moments, ever-changing, forced to grow, yearning to transform. You ask me what I’m wearing, and I pause. Fragrances suck me into a world where time blurs; it's hard to explain. I’m not just wearing a scent; I'm wearing a memory, a part of me still unfolding. Today, it’s light and airy – like me. Tomorrow, it could be dark and bold – also like me.

A tiny monkey lives in the jungle of my brain. He swings from dendrite to dendrite, darting across my mind’s gears and cogs at his whim, but he truly finds the most joy in a small control room at the center. Like a mad scientist, he watches in awe as glowing orbs roll in, pulsing like tiny batteries, each representing a separate thought. As he plugs these balls into a central socket, the room lights up and gears whir to life, converting my thoughts into actions and emotions.

There’s just one problem: he hates the dull, dimly lit orbs that power me through boring tasks; instead, he’s constantly chasing after the bright, fun ones that lead me to search for “chess-boxing” on YouTube, even when I have an assignment due the next day. And when it comes to my shyness, he’s even more devious. Just as I’m about to offer a potential improvement to the usual approach of my football coach’s drill, the monkey swipes the thought, leaving me silent and frustrated. Recognizing that my procrastination and diffidence are at the mercy of this mischievous creature, I’ve set out to track him down. The first step was crossing the threshold into the space he called home…

I ventured into the sprawling maze of my mind’s neurons, marveling at the electricity pulsing like flashes of lightning. Suddenly, I caught a glimpse of the monkey. He paused with a curious glint in his eye, head tilted in playful inquisition. I started after him, but his limitless energy carried me deeper.

I continued the chase for what seemed like hours, getting closer with each step. However, just as I got within arm’s reach, the monkey scampered up and leaped onto a gear. He started running in place, like a hamster on a wheel, sending the gears spinning wildly. These frantic spins, I realized, are what spark my sudden, impulsive adventures—a random urge to hike Rancho San Antonio at dawn or the decision to make a wasabi-cream-cheese and honey-banana-pickle toast at midnight. Unlike the orbs of thought that guided most of my actions, these impulses felt innate and thoughtless, adding an element of surprise to my day-to-day life, which is typically rife with schedules and to-do lists.

The monkey then climbed up to the terminal of my brainstem. As I looked up, I came face-to-face with a large box labeled in bold letters: “CONTROL ROOM.”

“Subtle, huh?”

I slowly crept into the room and saw him curiously observing an orb, oblivious to my presence. As expected, that little rascal was only plugging in the brightest balls, leaving the dull ones to decay. But something odd struck me: when he plugged in a bright orb, even brighter ones started to flow in. I remembered my time studying organic chemistry and how encountering one niche, intriguing topic would lead me down a rabbit hole of even brighter ideas. Was this annoying monkey the reason behind my curiosity?

I took a step towards the monkey, but my foot suddenly landed on a tiny, crinkled banana-flavored Hi-Chew wrapper. Thrilled to discover someone else who enjoyed this unfairly hated flavor as much as me, I couldn’t help but grin. The monkey, startled, jumped back and dropped one of the orbs. As it rolled towards my feet, I picked it up, observing the thought inside it.

“Huh? I guess we both like thinking about the inherent impossibility of Marty McFly’s time travel.”

The monkey’s frightened face quickly brightened, eyes widening as he nodded in excited agreement.

“Why don’t we plug this one in together?”

As I handed him the orb, we both gripped the sphere, our hands—well, my hand and his tiny paw—pushing it into the socket. We watched in awe as the gears churned while my brain worked its magic.

“I forgot to ask. What’s your name?”

For the first time, he spoke, smiling,

"My name is [Name] Rane."

The air was thick with the scent of Mr. Sketch Scented Markers and the thrill of adventure, transporting me to a world where anything was possible—one that would shape my journey with origami.

Back then, origami was simply my favorite pastime—a way to conjure entire worlds by transforming a plain sheet of paper into everything from delicate butterflies to the bold heroes, like Captain Awesome, in my stories. I was mesmerized by these endless possibilities, losing myself for hours in the elaborate folds of each piece.

Eventually, what started as innocent fun evolved into a way to connect with others. I began crafting origami bouquets and vividly remember the joy they brought others, especially my best friend, Ana Laura. Witnessing her awe blossom into a wide smile when I gifted her a vibrant bouquet of tulips and lilies revealed to me the delight these intricate artworks could bring.

Soon, I found myself creating more bouquets, with the hope that everyone could appreciate the beauty in something as deceptively effortless as creased paper. Thus, Mooki Bloom was born, a small business offering origami bouquets, but more importantly, a way to share that sense of wonder, one handmade petal at a time. Origami was something I already loved, and now I had discovered a way to let that joy bud in the hearts of others.

As Mooki Bloom flourished, I recognized its potential went far beyond inducing glee—it also had the power to cultivate community and assist those in need.

Around late April of 2024, floods were sweeping South America, displacing nearly 500,000 residents in southern Brazil. My best friend's hometown was ravaged, with entire houses nearly submerged under water. Realizing these floods were due to excessive carbon emissions made my blood boil. I couldn’t help but resent the fact that countries near the equator, like Brazil, were bearing the brunt of global warming’s effects, even though the nations most responsible for the damage remained largely untouched. Amidst this frustration, all I could think about was innocent people suffering, and how I desperately wanted to help them rebuild what was lost.

Moved by their tragedy, I founded Petals for Peace, a non-profit organization with a mission to provide humanitarian assistance to people in crisis on a transnational scale. Initially dedicated to animal welfare, we promptly shifted our focus to the devastating floods in Brazil. Together with Ana Laura’s family, we raised awareness about the so-called ‘natural’ disaster, collected donations for displaced families, and collaborated with Mantena Global Care to amplify our impact.

I was deeply touched witnessing my community come together to provide relief to those in need, aiding countless lives. As our presentation unfolded, I saw the sea of faces transform—empowered, inspired, and ready to spark change. Soon, groups formed, each crafting a different artwork to be sold, while sharing dreams of a brighter future, and bonding through the universal language of origami, one that communicates through creases rather than words.

The impact we made was awe-inspiring, and we quickly set our sights on new volunteer projects. United in our mission, we rallied together in protest for a ceasefire between Palestine and Israel, marching resolutely down Palestine Way and Gould Avenue. During that protest, we were more than a gathering; we were family, woven by our unwavering hope for a just world.

It was in these moments, I understood that, compassion, when paired with action, has the power to ripple through communities and beyond borders, as we ultimately fundraised over $350 for families affected by the floods in Brazil and $320 for Gaza aid, advocated for a Palestine-Israel ceasefire at several protests, and secured over $340 to feed impoverished women and children in my nearby area of Paterson.

At college, I envision myself making origami flowers at Earth Day events with my peers in environmental engineering, fundraising for water filtration system prototypes in disaster-stricken areas while demonstrating the centrality of creativity to our course of study. Captain Awesome’s heroic spirit, sense of adventure, possibility, and creativity has continued to guide me, but they have now evolved into something greater. Each fold isn’t just about playful creation anymore; it’s about transforming creativity into community, and weaving together those who share a vision of a healed world. Just like the heroes of my childhood, my mission has grown—to inspire, unite, and use art as a bridge to engineer meaningful change in the world around me.

At ten years old, I was the CEO of a game company. At least, that’s what it felt like to me. With my fuzzy purple notebook in hand, I would spend hours scribbling down game ideas, organizing movie nights on a silly mouse game called Transformice, and assigning my friends leadership roles within my company. I didn’t know what it meant to be a game developer or a CEO, but I knew one thing: I wanted to lead. My friends and I would hold mock meetings, brainstorm ideas, and even decide roles through rock-paper-scissors (though I frown upon nepotism now). My plans, drawn out neatly in my notebook, gave me a sense of purpose, a way to create a world of my own.

But as I grew older, the power I felt with that notebook in hand began to slip away. The world around me told a different story. “You’re just a kid.” “You’re a girl; you wouldn’t understand.” The voices around me weren’t just loud; they were constant. I grew up hearing racist, homophobic, and sexist ideas, especially from people close to me. My parents often made demeaning comments about others, whether it was mocking someone for their weight or making sweeping generalizations about different races. I never believed those things. In fact, I fought back, sometimes fiercely, even if it meant crying the whole way home from dinner parties where such comments were casually thrown around. But each fight, each argument chipped away at me. They acted as though my voice didn’t matter—as though I didn’t understand the real world. Slowly, my confidence waned. The person who once led her friends with certainty, planning events and games with enthusiasm, began to retreat. I had always believed in fairness and equality, but I started to doubt whether I had any right to speak up about those values. As a girl, I was told I was “less than.” As a child, I was told I was too naive. These words took root, and I felt the power I had in fourth grade fade away.

It wasn’t until years later that I began to reclaim my voice. The words that had diminished me couldn’t hold me down forever. I realized that leadership wasn’t just about assigning roles or organizing events. It was about something deeper: giving others a voice, especially those who feel unheard. My early drive to lead, while fueled by the excitement of a childhood game, was actually an early expression of something more meaningful—a desire to create spaces where everyone can contribute, no matter their age, gender, or background.

Years later, I still carry with me the lessons from that fourth-grade CEO: a determination to lead with both confidence and compassion. My childhood dream of running a company has evolved into a more grounded ambition, one where leadership means elevating not just myself but others, and where every voice—including my own—has a place.

As the scent of incense filled the air, our Diwali ritual began with my Grandpa Vinaya placing Tilak on my forehead, a mark of spiritual protection and devotion. Then, as I felt my grandpa’s rough, wrinkled hands wrap the coarse thread of a Kalava bracelet around my wrist, I felt spiritually tied to every ancestor before me. Next was a puja, where all of my family sat in a circle for a self-paced meditation. Yet, after about 10 minutes, I opened my eyes to find only my grandpa and me left in the circle. He looked disappointed and said, “Diwali is meant to be a time of reflection, not just a social event.” As he started to stand up and put his shoes back on, I told him that I wanted to stay. A sly smile crept up on his lips, and we continued our practice.

For the next two hours, he guided me through chants of Vedic hymns, silent reflection, and breath-focused meditations. As we practiced, waves of relaxation and calm swept over me, quieting my restless thoughts. This meditation opened my eyes to a profound aspect of my culture, and it became something that I wanted to explore further.

As I practiced on my own in high school, I aimed not only to master the techniques but also to learn the principles that guided each meditation. During this exploratory phase, I meditated daily. One afternoon, as I sat under a mighty oak tree at the Chicago Botanic Garden, I wondered: How would society change if everyone could access this level of inner peace and harmony?

This idea inspired me to work towards becoming a Certified Meditation Practitioner. After attending a meditation retreat in Sedona, Arizona guided by mindfulness experts, I earned the distinction, and it became one of my proudest accomplishments. With newfound confidence, I began teaching meditation to peers at school. For example, to offer support before exams, I volunteered to lead breathing exercises in classes, and also guided my golf team in meditation before games. I became known as “Zen [Name].”

During the summer of my junior year, I had the opportunity to deliver a speech about meditation to a large group of peers, teachers, and family. On the night of the event, I sat backstage frantically reviewing my script for the 1,000th time, when I noticed my grandpa walk in. He brought a red Jaipur rug, a scented candle, and a thin cotton bracelet, recreating the puja ritual we do together. He took my script and said, “Remember, [Name], meditation isn’t just about the words; it’s about the heart behind it. Speak with love, and you’ll light the way for others.” We then sat and meditated together, up until the final moment when it was time for me to present.

In my talk, I explored the paradox of our advanced minds struggling with mental well-being and presented mindfulness as a solution.

My voice brimmed with purpose.

After a warm reception from the crowd, I saw my grandpa dawn the largest smile I’d ever seen, realizing that I’d made him proud.

When I play two truths and a lie, people are often shocked to learn that I'm a quarter Indian, given I have tan white skin and dirty blonde hair. Yet, a hidden part of my identity emerged when I chose to share the benefits of meditation with my community. Whether I’m leading an auditorium into relaxation or calming a friend before a test, I aim to promote an environment where personal growth is cultivated. I not only expect the best of myself in every situation, but also encourage others to reach their full potential. I now understand that our cultural rituals are not just about tradition; they’re about fostering connection—between generations, cultures, and the essence of who we are.

I nervously stepped into classroom 201. The teacher started class and asked us to introduce ourselves. After seven other students, it was my turn; I began, "Hel-loo, me na-me es Peei Heng Ni; I come-China." "Your name is Pee?" Laughter erupted as I said my introduction, which had the worst pronunciation ever and a Chinese accent. The teacher quickly stopped the students from continuing. However, it was too late. My classmates' laughter stung in my heart; their snickering resonated deep within me. The echoing sounds validated what I already felt: I did not belong.

I had just immigrated from China, and I needed more than a few weeks to learn a new language, especially with the conflicting similarities between pinyin and the alphabet. My mom only taught me the basics of English, like "Hello" and "Thank you," along with the alphabet, due to her working towards a PhD degree and job search. But after that painful day at school, I knew I was far from literate. My mom was too busy to help me study, so I took it upon myself to study past 8 pm with children's books, dictionaries, and the Internet. Every night, I sat on my bed, cross-referencing definitions, learning to pronounce unfamiliar sounds, and matching words to classwork. I used a learning website called ReadingEggs daily, which perfectly suited my needs. It helped me break down complex words and taught me how to speak with fun lessons from Sam, the Ant.

One evening, my mom walked into my room while I was studying and said softly, 'Good job, son. I am very proud of you.' Those words were like a beacon of hope. At the end of the semester, I received the "Most Improved" award, along with the teacher's congratulations. These moments of encouragement have left an important mark on me, reinforcing the belief that hard work never betrays you.

My mom's busyness helped me refocus my thoughts and realize that I have to deal with bullies myself. Reporting to the principals doesn't work, so I decided to help other students and be kind to them by teaching them math. One day after math class, I saw Drew crying after Kim mocked him for getting a D on the recent long division test. Seeing this opportunity, I told Kim to leave Drew alone, or I would snitch on her. After a short argument with Kim, I offered to help tutor him at lunch. Drew quickly became one of my first friends at school after I helped him study and improve his math skills. Drew's grade went from a D to a B, and he said to me, "Thank you so much; you're such a great friend." After I made several friends, the unfriendly buddies chose other people to bully. After self-learning mathematics at Khan Academy, I helped my classmates with math and received invaluable friendships.

My desire to help others extended beyond the walls of my school. My friend Elvis accidentally clicked on an IP grab link on Discord, and people started threatening to doxx him and cyberbullying him with his address as a threat. This inspired me and my friends to create a free website to educate people on what to do after their information is leaked. This website is programmed to filter out sensitive information being sold on hacking forums and automatically sends emails to those affected. We sent over 1.6 million emails and collected over 100 million pieces of data, providing crucial support to those who have been hacked, had their identity stolen, or cyberbullied. My work preventing bullies continues, with the website now sending over 50,000 emails daily to assist those in need.

Balancing my schoolwork with taking care of my younger siblings has helped me become more responsible and persistent. I've learned that by facing challenges head-on and finding ways to help others, I can continue to grow and contribute in meaningful ways.

When I was much younger, I relentlessly asked my dad to walk with me almost daily to the local park. I would play wood chips or tag with other kids, but consistently I was always drawn to the adjoining basketball court. A varied group of teenagers or adults playing 5-on-5 with the intensity of last night’s NBA game on television. How was I the only one watching this great playground game? I saw large men who looked like they just got off an 8-hour shift playing with a 5’2” teenager fast as a bullet making amazing plays. I saw a dad cheering on his kid and others waiting patiently on the sidelines to substitute into the game. What I picked up on importantly, were people of all ages and abilities, coming together and playing together as an amazing team. There was no scheduled time for this game, yet it happened consistently. And I realized I could play that game too, with them, even though I wasn’t the fastest player or best dribbler. I could still be a part of this game and everyone was welcome. That’s where my love of basketball started at a young age.

All through my middle school years, with my playground days in mind, I played with my whole heart on the basketball team for my small school. Going into 7th grade, I had practiced religiously in my driveway with my friend every day in hopes of making the “A” team. I was overcome with joy and had a fantastic bonding experience with my classmates. I set my sights on the high school basketball team. The transition from a middle school class of under 50 to a freshmen high school class of over 600 was difficult, but did not deter my determination to play basketball. I went to optional early practices every week at five in the morning. I practiced more than I ever thought I could and spent even more time studying plays. Then the heartbreaking news came that I had not made the team.

I was very disappointed for a bit, but decided to find a new way to play basketball. I saved up for a gym membership at a local fitness center where some classmates gathered to play basketball. This membership became a big part of my life and led me to improving my nutrition and overall health. I ate better and exercised daily. I became much stronger physically and mentally. And I found the joy of my playground days experience, where the pick-up basketball games at this gym brought together a diverse group of community. I formed new friendships from my own school and neighboring schools and other mentoring adults. We played only for the love of the game.

Throughout my years of playing basketball, I have gained more confidence in working with every type of person, plus a good mindset that setbacks are okay. I have also learned that finding what you love to do is a great journey. And gratefully, I have had the privilege to journey to other countries. Thanks to my dad having been born in Spain and my mother’s family being all Irish, my travels have taken me to playgrounds abroad. The games were still being played there with the same heart and soul. And the love of basketball it seems can be a universal language. A global perspective and an inclusive community is important to me in my studies and future plans in business. I realize childhood utopias will be hard to replicate, but the playground lessons learned will be in my heart forever. I look forward to becoming an important part of a new community, learning how to become a stronger better player and getting into the new game of college and playing on a new team with my heart, soul and kindness.

I lacked the confidence to play Chinese songs in my dorm shower. As a Chinese international student, I was uncertain whether my homeland's music would resonate with my peers. Instead, I streamed Spotify's "Best of the Year" playlist and was relieved when my American friends complimented my music, making me feel closer to being part of the group. As soon as I was alone in my room, however, I switched back to my favorite Chinese artist, the iconic Jay Chou.

Walking to my dorm’s bathroom, I knew a decision awaited me. While others might have described it as insignificant, to me, the choice was monumental. Would I take the safe route and stream something popular, eager for the approval of my American friends? Once there, my finger, as if by instinct, pressed on Spotify’s “Best of the Year” playlist. In my room, though, I would switch back to my favorite Chinese artist, Jay Chou, and think of home.

*

That night, New York City's Union Square Subway Station was especially busy. Home for the Christmas holiday, I set out to sing for an audience of strangers for the first time. I had been singing since I was seven and believed it was time to push myself to share what I had spent so long cultivating.

A nauseating nervousness overcame me as I got my equipment ready. A diverse mix of people and cultures passed by in front of me. As I connected the microphone to the speaker, I still could not decide what to sing—Charlie Puth or Jay Chou. Instinctively, Charlie Puth, the mainstream American artist, seemed the better choice, but my fear of an imperfect performance provoked me to choose Jay Chou. The Chinese lyrics would mask any flaws for my American audience.

Jay Chou's lyrics took me home, emboldening me to turn up the volume like I did in the privacy of my dorm room. A woman paused and leaned against the wall. Wearing an elegant white jacket with her hair in a neat bun, she swayed to the rhythm, eyes closed, face serene. After the third song, she walked up to me. Unsure what to expect, my heart tightened.

"These songs are so beautiful," she said with a soft yet genuine eagerness. "Even though I can't understand the lyrics, the melodies are extremely touching." She pulled out a twenty-dollar bill, a bag of chips, and a soda. "This is all I have, but your voice and melodies deserve much more."

Although my peers had expressed mixed feelings about my compositions, calling it not "hip-hop" nor "mandopop" enough, the woman's kindness encouraged me, and I decided to leap. I played a song I wrote about my solitude and mental health struggles. A Dominican couple approached me, their expressions soft as they enjoyed the melody. Their quiet appreciation reminded me that my music did not need to fit a genre—it simply needed to connect.

"Could we share a song with you?" The couple asked, approaching with a smile. I searched for the Spanish title they requested and played their song. Pulsating beats filled the station. Their energy was contagious. Despite not knowing any of the words, I could not help but ad-lib and join them. Huddled together around a single microphone, the December wind whisked away the forgotten lyrics and imperfect pitches, leaving in its wake our shared moment of joy.

*

In embracing my music, I found the strength to share my voice; in sharing my voice, I bonded with other humans regardless of our differences. Music became a means of connecting with others, a doorway to those who would have otherwise remained strangers, and I strove to remember that as the seasons changed. At my summer concert, as the prelude to the last song I had written began, people started to point at me excitedly. Inviting them up with a smile, they rushed onto the stage, forming a tight arc around me. Fifteen of us bounced together to the beat, bodies moving in sync as I sang. Then came the line:

There are too many worries, but I have no one to confide in.

The lyric spoke of isolation, but in that moment, the weight of loneliness dissolved. Instead of being alone, the music pulled us together. We were a single pulse, united by sound, no longer solitary but bound together.

Light broke through the glass beads, bursting across the looping sheen of metal in an ever-shifting scatter of vibrant blue hues. I smiled to myself. When I clipped the trailing end of the necklace, the sound of metal hitting my desk was sharp and satisfying. This piece was done, and I couldn’t have been happier.

…until I tried to stand and nearly fell over, my leg having fallen asleep in the four hours I’d spent hunched forward, utterly engrossed in my task.

I have always been an obsessive creator. My first fixation was slime: although I lacked the two main ingredients, PVA glue and borax, I refused to let this challenge hinder me. Instead, I experimented with soap, peel-off face masks, and cornstarch—anything I could find in the house—in a hunt for an alternative recipe. With each DIY project I tackled, my room overflowed with self-made trinkets, from paper flower bouquets to mini-cardboard vending machines.

My creative thirst was insatiable, and in my search for my next creative pursuit, I discovered a jewelry-making guidebook at the library. As I flipped each page of stunning designs, I was entranced by the endless possibilities for pairing beads and gems and by the graceful curves of wire wrapping.

For one of my first pieces, I handcrafted matching bracelets for my sisters. When I expanded my reach and began gifting my pieces to friends, I was struck with a thought: “What if I could turn this into a business, sharing my passion for creation with people across the globe?”

Soon enough, this entrepreneurial spark ignited into a burning passion. I took every opportunity to immerse myself in the world of business, spending hours listening to podcasts from inspiring entrepreneurs and taking free online marketing courses through edX. In the meantime, I carefully saved up every dollar I earned from art commissions and poured them into launching my own handmade jewelry business.

Each piece I make begins from scrawled sketches in my notebook. With a clear vision in mind, I reach for the basket on my shelf, where my sturdy pliers are nestled among my collection of colorful beads and delicate resin charms. After looping the final wire, I slip the accessories into a tiny pouch and gently tuck it into a box, along with a handwritten note that expresses my sincere gratitude to each customer.

One morning, I received a message from a girl who had been following my jewelry business since its beginning. As I read her words, my heart shattered and swelled at once. She opened up about how she had been battling an eating disorder for months, but wearing one of my jewelry pieces made her feel a glimmer of confidence, and gave her a sense of comfort that she hadn’t felt in a long time.

To think that something I crafted myself could impact someone in such a way made tears well up in my eyes. Throughout my business journey, my focus had always been on creating the most aesthetic designs, but I never fully considered the potential I had to empower others through my craft. Her message shifted my perspective: I want to create beauty while also uplifting others. Through sewing stuffed animals for hospitalized children, organizing community art projects, and guiding young hands through their first projects, I see my younger self reflected in their wide eyes as new passions blossom.

From my earliest eccentric endeavors to now running my own jewelry business, I’ve grown from not only finding joy in creation but also in the beauty of connecting with others through my work. As I continue to forge genuine links between creativity and compassion, I am determined to illuminate the brilliance within each of us.

I was born in a place where the volcano Teide, mountains and valleys meet the gleaming Atlantic. The island of Tenerife, in the Spanish archipelago of the Canary Islands, ingrained its volcanic energy into me when I took my first breath. But at the age of six, this energy began to ebb away. Things didn’t feel quite right: I was skinny, and constantly lacking appetite and energy. Worried, my parents sought answers, only to be told nothing was wrong. Naturally, they were unconvinced and days later, we were on a plane to Mumbai, seeking another opinion.

I was in the city of chaos: the cacophony of a million cars cutting through the vibrant marketplaces. This was my grandfather’s home, where he introduced me to the horse carriages, locally known as Victorias. These horses exuded a grandeur, with heads held high and regal poise. I was intrigued. They were a fortuitous distraction to the impending diagnosis. Though awe-inspired by them, there was an unknowable fear that held me back from approaching them. Yet, unbothered by my exclamations and cries, in a riding arena near our hotel, my grandad hoisted me onto a stately black horse.

Pulses traveled to my throat, but then, adrenaline seeped in too. I loved the sensation of freedom, and my heart performed backflips – I was entirely attuned to the animal. Unwittingly, my grandfather had sparked an unexpected passion; it invigorated the hidden, dormant energy within me. The day arrived and they explained that I had a condition similar to Addison’s where my body was unable to produce cortisol. While the solution was very manageable, I still didn’t know how or what to feel except defeat, but I found that horse riding was my liberation, my source of energy.

After our trip, when I returned back home to Tenerife, I started horse jumping at a local stable – I loved soaring over the jumps; mid-air I was unrestrained, unstoppable, and the fire in my belly grew. Sometimes I fell, with grit in my mouth and the sharp sting of failure. Yet, every fall strengthened my determination. I’d spit out the grit, remount and persist until I succeeded. Curious, I switched to dressage at ‘Pura Vida’ stables. When the piaffe wasn’t elegant enough, when the flying changes weren’t fluid enough, or when my half-passes weren’t lateral enough, I had to repeat them several times until they were perfect, until I had prowess. While the sport required resilience and dedication, with my horse, Linaje, by my side, we created a dynamic synergy and reveled in the challenge.

As I have learned in my science lessons, energy cannot be created or destroyed, it can only be transformed and transferred: the illuminating vigor I regained has led me to help children with disabilities in England. I met children with autism, Down syndrome, ADHD, and Tourette’s at a riding association. Tugging at their mothers’ arms, they did not want to mount the horses. Sensing the fear, I smiled at them reassuringly, and explained how much fun they would have. Once on their horses, I taught them riding techniques and how to communicate effectively, moving as a single entity. They grew taller in their saddles, gaining connections to the horses, with their giggles echoing in the arena. They found catharsis and solace in these beings, just as I had.

I am experiencing a ‘Pura Vida’ – a full life. One where I have revitalized my birth energy and have been able to transform it into a catalyst for meaningful change. After all, energy is contagious, and I am determined to continue passing it on.

I was exposed to Bangla and Arabic before I heard a word of English. Then, Math taught me what English couldn't: to utilize language.

*****

An outsider would be surprised to see me riding my bike on the cracked pavement of one of the most dangerous cities in New Jersey: Paterson.

I approached the Bengali-owned corner store. I push the glass doors. A warm aroma of tandoori-masala packets permeates the air. I ask for a cup of "pani" instead of "water."

This same “dangerous” neighborhood doesn’t just feel nostalgic. It feels like home.

What Paterson couldn't do, however, was break the language barrier. No amount of asking for “pani” could’ve accustomed me to the intricacies of speaking the English language.

*****

English was my fourth language; mathematics was my third. My accent was the culprit behind the infamous "My name is Salman and my pavreet color is biolet" on the first day of fifth grade.

"Your name is Thalman?"

"No, my name is Salman."

“Thalman?”

“No, Salman.”

I was shocked to learn I also had a lisp. My confidence was shattered in seconds. Unable to speak English without being self-conscious, I sought refuge in the only language that carried no accent, no judgment, no reminder that I was different: mathematics. In mathematics, regardless of what equation I use to describe a line, the line will never be mistaken for something different the way my name was mistaken as "Thalman."

*****

Independent study of Mathematics in Quarantine advanced my love for numbers. What started as graphing y=x, slowly transformed into graphing the layout of my path to Engineering in High School.

Sophomore year, my physics teacher, Dr. Sloane, articulated, "Mathematics teaches you how to hammer a nail, but what good are nails unless you use them to build a house." Until that moment, I understood math as a shelter from society. Upon reflecting on Dr. Sloane’s words, however, I realized my fascination with applying mathematics to model the real world could help me make real improvements in my community.

I began working on improving my school's classrooms, plagued with disposable wipe packets.

Three peers of mine and I invented a reusable wipes mechanism, GreenClean, to fix the issue at hand. Conducting calculus-based optimization techniques and creating regression models, I utilized math to optimize GreenClean’s dimensions and maximize its efficiency in managing E. Coli growth.

Witnessing the benefits of applying math made me feel valuable, and that would only be enhanced when I was confronted with one of the most important engineering challenges of my life: the floating farms of Bangladesh.

*****

August 22, 2024—it was one of Bangladesh’s worst monsoon seasons. I was heading to my aunt's house, and the tides covered the muddy brick-paths.

“How do people live here, boro abbu?” I asked my dad’s eldest brother.

“They’re farmers of floating farms.” Farms designed to stay afloat as water levels rise.

Well, now the "floating" farms were sinking, and my mind raced with ideas about differentiation and Archimedes' principle to fix it. The cultural experience and resilience of the Bangladeshi people led to the innovation of these farms to begin with, teaching me that for every problem there is a way to engineer a solution: perhaps this time the problem may need someone experienced with applied mathematics.

Being a Bangladeshi-American born in the Middle East has allowed me to experience situations from Paterson’s cracked pavements to Bangladesh’s flooding. Although I initially thought math was a means of seclusion, I’ve learned if I want to fully demonstrate mathematical ability, I must connect with those around me—now a bit easier as I developed a more “American” accent and the ability to pronounce “s.”

Through math I can serve the greater purpose of improving my community.
