Looking forward, I want to collaborate with people of different strengths and backgrounds, ultimately engineering a better future: from improving Bangladesh’s farms to Paterson’s poverty.

“I want to get out.”

After being sexually assaulted by her deskmate in middle school, Sarah’s mother told her, “Harassment is just typical boy behavior.” But for three years, she had been stalked, threatened, and physically violated in a way that made me feel both disgusted and heartbroken.

In early 2024, Sarah visited To-Listen, a teen-focused online support platform I’d built to offer companionship to peers facing struggles alone. After studying with Fudan University’s Professor Wang and learning about patient-centered therapy (PCT), I knew the facts I needed to be a good companion – when dealing with trauma, PCT theory recommended I be a non-judgmental listener, offering only attentive comments and questions. However, as I listened to my young visitor describe behaviors not just unlawful but wrong, my gut tightened. I couldn’t help but feel compelled to tell her that none of it was her fault.

Given the exam culture in China, I believed most questions had a solid solution, which gave me a sense of control I craved. In Psychology, it led me to not just readings of PCT, but Robert Salvin’s group interaction theories in educational psychology, and pushed me to develop a four-step “hello–affirm–inquiry–listen” companionship and support template. Yet, in Sarah’s case, every textbook response was met with silence. I tried encouraging Sarah to “seek support from others,” but this wasn’t an option for her. Her conservative Northern Chinese town blamed her for her overreaction and dismissed her assaulter’s actions as childish misbehavior.

After five days of constant conversation, Sarah was not healed, but she told me she felt better. Theories like maintaining respect were useful, but I also recognized the profound lack of understanding she faced. Through relevant criminal laws, sexual assault recourses, and hugging emojis, I tried to affirm that her feelings were justified. I knew my contributions were somewhat insignificant compared to the severity of Sarah’s situation, but seeing her replies grow longer and more confident, I felt proud of myself.

At the same time, I was humbled, and disappointed too. Sarah’s story exposed the dreadful gap between theory and reality, while simultaneously raising questions about the efficacy of the platform I’d spent hundreds of hours building over the past year.

In the following months, I began seeing reflections of Sarah in every peer I met, each requiring an approach to support beyond standard theoretical responses. I was forced and inspired to modify the four-step companionship template I’d used to train my team, holding group meetings and WeChat discussions reintroducing the template as not always having to be followed. The change was initially received with confusion and discomfort. But seeing volunteers like Leander’s formulaic responses slowly turn into genuine back-and-forth conversations filled my heart with warmth.

There were smaller steps, too. In interviews with Sam, a teen of Inner Mongolia’s GeLao ethnic minority facing cyberbullying, I learned how GeLao culture was more open to disclosing personal struggles compared to Han culture, and how support could be even more listening-focused as a result.

Of course, self-doubt still arises sometimes. My team aren’t licensed therapists. While there are crises that feel out of our control, we try our best to offer support, realizing that in our technologically advancing but socially distancing society, young adults may need not only professional support but also companionship and community.

Sarah, Leander, and Sam have taught me that while there are principles to help others heal, there is no true textbook for compassion. Even though helping someone belong can sometimes feel like an impossible challenge – especially across cultures and distances – this doesn’t mean we should give up. In fact, it means we must work even harder to develop the necessary flexibility and mindfulness to help others through their darkest moments. As I approach college and beyond, I commit to always carrying the adaptive spirit with me.

When it comes to physics, most think about gravity or momentum. However, I think of Gaussian surfaces–any closed surface used for measuring field lines in a certain region. And when I say “any surface,” I do mean “any surface”! It doesn’t matter if it's a cylinder around an electric wire or an imaginary sphere around an ice cream scoop. Anything imaginable can be made into a Gaussian surface. On top of being a lifesaver in tackling electromagnetism problems, these surfaces have taught me valuable lessons to apply to life.

Just as there’s freedom in creating Gaussian surfaces, I find joy in being able to freely explore my intellectual curiosities outside of the classroom. One night as I scrolled on my phone before bed, I fell down the notorious “Wikipedia rabbithole.” Before I knew it, I was reading an article about the Japanese Yamauchi clan. Fascinated by the samurai family’s pivotal role in the founding of Mitsubishi, I later wrote a history paper on the relationship between the Japanese feudal system and the nation’s industrial revolution. Meanwhile, I reinforce my long-standing love for FC Barcelona by studying Catalan (263-day streak on Duolingo – and counting!). By doing so, I aim to uncover the club’s rich cultural nuances. Like Gaussian surfaces, my identity is defined by freedom – the freedom to be curious and expand my academic horizons to uncover interests.

Yet, choosing a Gaussian surface isn’t all freedom. Applying a Gaussian surface involves a surface integral with a vector dot product – which, in English, means things can get messy with the wrong surfaces. This also applies to life, where calculated choices are crucial. When I founded a string quartet with my friends, I advocated for a more relaxed organizational structure, believing that creativity thrives best in a loosely-structured environment. Mishaps emerged – jumbled programs, lost music, the full experience! Recognizing our mistakes, my friends and I created stricter rehearsal routines. By implementing score studies and drilling rhythm and intonation, we weren’t confined, but instead able to play better, tighter and more creatively. Admittedly, we still occasionally lose our music – we’re only human! Yet our new approach has led us to performances at state conferences and universities. The need to carefully select Gaussian surfaces reminds me that in life, rigid frameworks are necessary. While they may seem restrictive, they can channel our energies in productive directions, empowering creativity to flourish.

Did you know that no matter how much Gaussian surfaces differ in shape, they will share key properties if they contain the same charge? Similarly, I derive joy from finding the metaphorical charge that links different people together. While volunteering to teach math at my church, one student named Jude was always struggling to focus. He reminded me of my younger 5th grade self, when I had similar problems sitting still. Back then, my teacher was supportive, giving me “Secrets of Mental Math”, a book filled with fun tricks I would use to impress friends. Seeing myself in Jude, I handed him a copy of that book. Reading through a section about magic squares, his eyes lit up as he exclaimed, “These are so cool!” From that point on, he would regularly come to me to ask about a formula he read about or a math video he watched, becoming my most engaged student. At the end of the day, a love for discovery unites all us math minds! Finding common “charges” like this lets me connect to people like Jude, who may otherwise seem different.

Gaussian surfaces are known for their extraordinary versatility in electromagnetism problems. Yet, the real-life values they comport are just as universal. Looking ahead to college, I will apply these lessons by trusting my curiosity to guide me in and out of class, balancing freedom and order in student organizations, and finding common threads between people while volunteering. While I’m sure I’ll continue studying Gaussian surfaces in the lab, they’ll be just as important in my day-to-day activities!

It was 1:15 am on competition day, and our rocket’s prized flight computer lay broken in my hands. I looked with bleary eyes towards a dishearteningly blank screen- crucial wires on our flight computer had snapped, and I had 45 minutes to fix them before our test flight.

After a minute of stunned silence, I began scrounging the car for the limited materials we had: candy (of course), spare wire, super glue, electrical tape, and a dead soldering iron.

Impossible, rattled in my brain:

42 minutes.

I tried to carefully braid the broken wires together to repair the circuit: No luck. The strands broke off into shards between my fingers. I tried electrical tape: but it’s traction wasn’t enough to hold them together. So I coated the connection in super glue, smiling as a pull on each side revealed it gave plenty of strength to force the ends together.
But plugging our board into our computer revealed a critical mistake: the thin glue had created an invisible layer between the ends, blocking current to our motor instead of enabling it. Waves of frustration followed suit as that same wall of null inputs laughed in my face.

Great, now I had two problems: a severed connection protected by indestructible glue.

23 minutes. Impossible.

I grabbed some Skittles and paced the lot. How was I going to clear the glue? I remembered worrying about our glue evaporating under the rockets' flames…

My eyes wandered to our soldering iron, slowly a picture began to form: the extreme heat from the iron could vaporize the glue! But without power it was useless, we needed an outlet, fast.

Nearly dropping my phone, I frantically navigated Google Maps until I found it: A lone gas station amidst our sea of fields.

***

10 minutes.

The station's door chimes flung to life as I shouldered my way inside, clumsily cupping materials to my chest as I searched for an outlet, while my friends dispelled the owner's confusion through extra Skittle purchases.

Rounding the corner I saw it: an outlet. I clumsily plugged the iron in and crafted a shoddy makeshift desk of plastic displays and milk cartons as it heated.

8 minutes.

Holding my breath against the fumes, I tapped the hot iron to the glue, a beaming smile blooming across my face as it dissolved into thin white vapor. With the ends exposed, I fed metal wire with my left index and middle finger, precariously pinching the board with the rest. The metal melted, welled up, and set to connect the ends. I exhaled.
Heart pounding, I looked towards the screen, hoping for anything but that blank monitor. The team watched over my shoulder.

2 minutes.

250, 245, 240. The whirr of gears washed over me as our air brakes’ motors sprung to life, my eyes welled up amidst our cheers as we all pounded our fists in celebration.

***

Impossible. It’s been a word for insurmountable ambitions, a discouraging, whispering fear of failure. But why should it? Rocketry has taught me that what’s impossible is relative to you, and that once insurmountable tasks can become routine skills. Really, that whisper of failure should be embraced, because every challenging martial arts kick, head-scratching physics problem, or overwhelming circuit failure is just a determined night of failures away from being beaten.
As I begin my college journey, I seek a path to strengthen myself for the world’s impossible challenges: to create machines that explore, inspire and cure.
Of course, our big world is more complicated than rocketry, but I’ve realized that the mindset of perseverance and innovation that’s given me success is now what I resolve to become: a student pushing themselves to fail, grow, overcome, and repeat.

There were no more board games left to play. My uncle Andrew pulled out his phone to access his list of random questions and thoughts. “Would it be ethical to give emotions, such as pain and suffering, to AI consciousness? What about love and joy?” he looked up from his phone and at all of us expectantly. My siblings and cousins stared back with blank expressions. I replied with a question right back, “How can we tell if AI really feels those emotions? And how can we tell if people really feel those emotions?” He paused and considered my question. This is where our game started, a game where we would ask each other various philosophical questions, such as this one, to propel our conversation forward.

These questions would often branch off into separate conversations, and we would end up talking about human nature, ethics, morality, and paradoxes for hours. There seemed to always be just one more idea that I thought of, one more question I needed to ask before ending the game. By the end of every conversation and game, I felt fulfilled and enlightened. I eventually created my own list of questions and prompts to kick-start conversations myself. My list and notes continue to grow from day to day, recording my train of thought.

I noticed myself becoming more reflective and appreciative of my experiences in life, as well as understanding my own self. During one of our games, I was reminded of a phrase that had stuck with me since the day I heard it: Cogito ergo sum. I think, therefore, I am. René Descartes had meant that he could not doubt his existence, as doubting it in the first place proves he exists. Before I had understood its full meaning, I interpreted it a different way. I saw what I had learned from this game with my uncle. My thinking defines who I am. It was through these conversations that I discovered that a large part of my identity is defined by my desire to think deeply and to connect with other people by communicating.

Despite having been known as “the quiet kid” for most of my academic life, I found that communication is the best way I connect with people. Being social was always a weaker skill of mine, and I would avoid talking to people. However, as I’ve matured, I’ve discovered that communication, and the deep connections that form as a result of it, is something I love. As a result, I often search for interesting ideas or topics that can spark a conversation. Exchanging ideas, considering different perspectives, and the excitement of having thought-provoking conversations are what make me lose track of time. With my uncle’s game, I began welcoming my most authentic self and understanding parts of who I am. This has allowed me to interact with the people around me better. I now accept talking to others in a natural and authentic way instead of avoiding them.

I continue to learn and understand more about myself every day by reflecting on these discussions. I believe that this game of asking philosophical questions for hours and hours on end contributed to my ability to think deeply in this way. I discovered that my passion lies in learning, thinking, and experiencing shared understanding, and that it is in these moments of being lost in thought and conversation that I feel most alive.

As a child, I spent most of my summer afternoons playing pretend with my father in my grandma’s manicured backyard. I was always Woody, and my dad was Buzz Lightyear. Grandma was Andy, the person who brought us both into the world, and who gave us such joy. But on May 20, 2022, she passed.

In just three months, overgrown grass and my father’s countless cigarette butts replaced the laughter that once filled grandma’s backyard. Losing her left an invisible wound on my father’s heart. Before my grandmother’s passing, I attended a mental health convocation that introduced me to behavioral psychology. I didn’t see its relevance then, but witnessing my father’s grief changed that. To try to help my father heal, I began with what I’d learned in the convocation—stages of grief. Through hours of research on Google Scholar, I broke each stage down into distinct pathways of acceptance, expression, and connection. In after-school sessions with my school counselor, I studied narrative therapy—reframing stories to foster healing. Combining these insights, I crafted what I named a 'grief support loop.’ Each week-long loop involved storytelling to externalize grief, role reversals to reshape the narratives, and creating new stories to help dad look forward. Now that I had a strategy, I needed my father to see how his grief was affecting his loved ones, so I modeled vulnerability by opening up first.

I stood there, voice shaking. "Every time you shut yourself in that cloud of smoke, I feel like I am losing you. Confront your pain—for me—please."

At first, my dad resisted. But I have a feeling he saw something in my face that day that made him want to change for the better. That moment set the grief support loop into motion. Progress was slow. Nevertheless, loop by loop, as my father began to rediscover his happiness, I found mine. From my father’s journey, I’ve realized that no matter how broken someone seems, there’s always a path to reach them if you’re willing to walk beside them—step by step, story by story. I wanted to be that person that walked beside real people with raw stories in communities where the stigma around mental health was greatest. That's why I chose to host mental health workshops in developing countries.

I spent weeks preparing my workshop, but when I presented, the kids fidgeted and yawned. Realizing I needed to adapt, I started sharing relatable stories and reframing them—such as turning the fear of disappointing parents into the understanding that parents value their children regardless of their achievements. Slowly, the kids started listening. To keep their attention, I adapted again. I asked the class how they handled stress. A teacher broke the silence by sharing how prayer helps him when he’s anxious. His honest vulnerability opened the dialogue. One boy talked about how his grandmother helps him with exam stress. Another proudly announced that soccer was his therapy. The teacher later confided that those who spoke up were already managing their mental health well, while the students who most needed support remained silent.

Coming from a culture that stigmatizes mental health, I knew few would seek traditional therapy, but most wouldn't refuse a free app. With my school psychologist’s help, I developed an AI chatbot that creates personalized grief-support loops just as I had done for my father and checks in regularly to ensure users stay on track. After months of training the chatbot on terabytes of data on narrative therapy, the grief-support-loop structure, and cultural idiosyncrasies, I shared the web app with the teacher. He called me a month later and said, "Several kids have used the app weekly. I just wanted to thank you for giving them this lifeline."

As I move forward into college, I want to continue my work with mental health in my pursuit of becoming a practicing psychiatrist. As I grow, I’m ready to help others process their stories, navigating the plot twists of their lives, until they too can move to infinity and beyond.

My eyes dart back and forth with anticipation, as I struggle to find the corresponding section to the puzzle piece I have in hand. Relieved, I finally see the complementary edges and click the piece into place, creating a harmonious connection on a surface otherwise filled with unique puzzle pieces.

Born in the UAE to Indian immigrant parents, raised in England, and relocating regularly within the Middle East, my life reflects an assortment of puzzle pieces. But, my parents never failed to remind me of my heritage growing up. Each festival was celebrated in the grandest ways: my mother drew rangoli outside our front door, time was given to polishing the silver murtis, and effort put into lighting diyas, hoping their flame would last. As my father’s job uprooted us to a new country every few years, I carried the weight of my heritage with me - one that often contrasted starkly with my surroundings. The nuances of my upbringing interest my peers, but for me, they serve as a constant reminder of my differences.

Starting afresh at each new school and country felt like repeating the same cycle. Classmates chatted in unfamiliar languages and cafeteria food had names I couldn't pronounce. Struggling to fit into pre-existing friend groups, I watched as others clicked, finding their places through shared cultural similarities. I felt out of place - a piece unfit for an ever-changing puzzle. Not wanting to not be left behind, I found myself pushing away my identity in futile attempts to force myself to fit in. Rather than fast during Diwali, I began to fast alongside my new friends during Ramadan. I molded myself into the illusion of a piece I thought would fit in seamlessly with my peers.

It was when I first struggled to remember the words during our pooja, or prayer, at Diwali that I realized I was neglecting my Indian roots in a desperate attempt to make space for newer ones to form. Over time, my sense of self had blurred, like a puzzle piece whose jagged edges had gone dull, no longer able to click into place.

Rather than focusing on fitting into others’ puzzles, I decided to concentrate on piecing together my own. After moving to boarding school, I use the opportunity to teach others about Diwali and Ramadan, and celebrate with them - starting new traditions, but not forgetting old ones. My friends and I share a bond not made of cultural similarity, but instead of understanding and appreciation; as a result, I have learned that lighting a diya on Diwali, preserving a menorah’s flames on Hanukkah and burning Christmas advent candles each use light to symbolize hope and unity. Yet, living so far from home forced my friends to leave behind their traditions. I wanted to fix this. So, I started a foundation, Lumière, with my two closest friends. I handcrafted candles specific to each tradition, providing the students at our school a way to reconnect with their heritage. We stocked nutmeg advent candle sets, olive oil menorahs, and lotus-shaped diyas. Soon enough, I decided to expand Lumière’s outreach. We worked with three local businesses in our community to stock our candles for others to purchase. By collaborating with Wings of Hope, a program dedicated to youth involvement in fundraising for access to education, we raised enough money to send four young girls in India to secondary school. Uniting my community helped me to spread hope to those who need it most.

Accepting my identity, rather than suppressing it, has not only shaped who I am but also allowed me to help others embrace their unique backgrounds. I understand that amongst a thousand unique puzzle pieces, the only way to make a truly harmonious connection is to accept each other's different shapes, hues and edges. I admire the beauty of my unique puzzle piece, one that continues to evolve as I grow and learn.

The bell rang for recess, but for some reason I didn’t feel like running out the door onto the field to play soccer with my friends. I was stuck in my seat reading a book called Percy Jackson and the Lightning Thief. The book amazed me by weaving mythology into what seemed like a regular young adult novel. The monstrous minotaur seemed so real I could imagine it being in front of me and the battle with Ares showcased what it meant to have the power of an Olympian god. Rick Riordan had drawn me into the world of mythology, and I was desperate to learn more about it. This curiosity led me to the Kane Chronicles for Egyptian mythology and Magnus Chase for Norse mythology. I was fascinated by how different cultures interpreted their gods.

This was the beginning of a ten-year journey, my own Odyssey. When I study mythology, I feel inspired. Although mythology is fun to learn about because of the stories and characters, it has also changed my worldview. Mythology is a representation of the human experience.

I read stories of Odysseus using his cunning and resourcefulness to escape the island of the Cyclops, avoid the sirens’ allure, and defeat his wife’s suitors. I was inspired by Horus fighting against Set to avenge his father. Rama, the avatar of Vishnu, fighting against the demon Ravana showed bravery and courage. The story of Nuwa using stones to fill the ocean one by one represented perseverance and hard work.

I am the Medusa mythology exam coordinator in my school’s Mythology Club. We create and play Kahoots about mythology trivia, do tarot readings using mythology themed cards, and discuss content for the exam. It is a 40-question multiple choice test that covers topics of Greek mythology from Apollo to Zeus. I lead discussions and analysis of readings from Homer, Ovid, Hesiod, and more. Being able to teach and discuss mythology gives a greater purpose to learning mythology than for my own entertainment.

Even more fulfilling than my knowledge about the stories themselves was applying mythology to my worldview. One of the most impactful lessons I have learned is overcoming fear by stepping out of my comfort zone. My voice used to shake and stutter whenever I spoke in front of people. In spite of this, I was inspired by how Hercules lived through danger and never faltered. I learned to throw myself into situations such as giving speeches in front of audiences and taking the fear head on. I used my speaking skills to earn leadership roles in clubs such as mythology, DECA, and chess. I make more friendships and communicate in a clearer manner, helping me both within and outside of the classroom.

During a club discussion about the Iliad, I answered a friend’s praise of Achilles with my claim that Hector was more heroic. Defending my argument and making another one made me feel like Hector, first parrying a slash with my thick shield and then launching my spear back. I realized that being able to express myself fully was not only beneficial, but fun and fulfilling.

In my school we have poetry out loud where people recite poetry. Usually people do short poems, but this year, I plan to recite a passage from the Iliad or Poetic Edda. Whether I’m a rhapsode reciting Homer or a bard singing of the Muses, I want to spread my love for mythology.

Ever since my first Percy Jackson book, mythology has shaped my character and provided me with new ways to understand the world. Going forward, I plan to continue learning about myself through mythology by teaching these amazing stories and starting a Mythology Club in college. I will always cherish the stories that taught me how to bring out the most human part of me and I hope to inspire others in the same way.

“Unmonitored fish populations can destroy our ecosystems.”

Shocked, I leaned back in my chair while staring at this quote. It described how domestic goldfish and koi dumped in local ponds could lay hundreds of thousands of eggs per year, reproducing at a rate that could wipe out native species.

Earlier that overcast Saturday, while walking to tennis practice, I passed a stormwater pond and noticed small red dots moving below the surface. My shoes sank into the damp soil as I curiously stepped forward to get a better look; to my surprise, the dots were goldfish. Immediately, I became confused—after all, these species certainly weren’t native to Washington.

Given the fact that pet fish had been part of my life for over 12 years, I naturally wanted to get to the bottom of the situation, which led me to this shocking local news article. Determined to remedy the issue, I returned to the pond with a net and trap in hand. Catching a few goldfish, I felt their slimy bodies in my grasp as I transferred them to a bucket. While excited about my success, after a few hours, I realized the pond was too big—this wouldn’t make a difference.

Seeking more answers, I started contemplating why fish would be dumped in the first place. By scrolling through countless articles, forums, and videos, the picture became clear. Sharing my alarm, many emphasized how the problem was rooted in pet owners who opted to release unwanted fish in nature as a humane way to get rid of them.

Naturally, as a fish enthusiast, I thought of a solution: I could adopt and rehome these unwanted fish. Eager to get started, I ordered the necessary aquarium supplies: tanks, heaters, aerators, substrates, sponge filters, and live plants. Then, I started posting pictures of my setup on Craigslist to promote my free adoption service.

Within the first week, I already got four responses. With the first adoption at 30 miles away, doubts crept in—what if he didn’t show up, what if the fish was not healthy—but excitement quickly overtook them. Billy, a middle-aged man in a white hoodie, introduced me to the 20-gallon tank and its inhabitants—50 plecos in various colors and a few guppies and snails. After moving the tank together to my trunk, with a mixture of gratitude and anxiety in his voice, Billy told me how he’d been worrying about what to do with his fish in the midst of his upcoming move.

As the species in the tanks grew, so did my pride in the work, leading me to expand my scope. Through an article, I realized that fish shops often gave away fish they couldn’t sell. After calling all fish stores within 30 miles, one PetCo said they had a fish that needed rehoming quickly. Ultimately, I helped three nearby stores offload such fish.

With a business mindset shaped by past ventures, like selling my paintings and generating income from YouTube, it felt natural to start distributing my adopted fish for profit while keeping my stock flowing. This journey provided me with hands-on experience in real-world situations, allowing me to practice marketing strategies, develop negotiation tactics, and refine sales techniques.

In time, these skills translated into my service with Seattle Friends. At school club fairs, I used marketing expertise to recruit new members; when spearheading a ski camp, I negotiated a 25% discount on equipment and a free practice area; during a fundraiser at Google, I applied sales skills to raise $5,000 with a team together.

Since that Gloomy Saturday at the pond, I’ve adopted 200+ fish and made $1,500+ revenue with 50%+ gross margins, all to help stop more “red dots” from being released into local ponds. In college, I hope to apply my studies to explore new ways to use my entrepreneurial drive to make a positive impact, even beyond my local ecosystem.

We’re a potluck kind of home. With the holidays, and the odd weekend, come slabs of pork belly, bathroom deep cleans, and a scattered flock of guests. The ritual is the same. Once the dessert spread–sunflower seeds and red bean porridge–is served to the adults, us kids are left to fend for ourselves.

Upstairs, the game room awaits. Tasked with entertaining everyone here, I raid our closet of knickknacks. With the range of ten year olds to teenagers comes heightened pressure–no settling for Apples to Apples. For the quiet siblings in the corner, I pull out Connect 4. For the energetic middle schoolers, I supply pool noodles.

Between the remaining teens though, the awkwardness is still palpable. My tried-and-true remedy? A game of Spoons. As the round progresses, the tension soon dissolves into intense scrambling, finger-pointing, and laughter. By the end of the night, our silverware drawer is nearly empty–everyone has joined in.

The joy I find through games has shaped how I tackle challenges. It’s the same thrill of devising a winning strategy that drives me to formulate elegant proofs. The satisfaction of fitting in the final puzzle piece fuels my hunt for the perfect synonym. And while I argue for my innocence in a game of Mafia, I also defend Amy March’s strength of character in class.

Above all, though, games bring people together–a feeling of community that I craved in high school. Although I cherished the academic freedom of my homeschooling education, I often feared that I was missing out. I felt like I was blindly searching for a sense of belonging—that I needed to mold myself into a perfect, confident leader to invite people into my world.

Despite this nagging feeling, I sought the courage to reach out to others. Slowly, I realized that community did not come naturally. I had the tools to foster meaningful connections with others, but my fear had blinded me into waiting for someone else to provide them. As I intentionally pushed away from my comfort zone, I formed new spaces for people to come together.

When I first decided to launch a school newspaper at my homeschool co-op, most didn’t care. Students were already uninterested in school events, and even more disconnected from each other. Determined nevertheless, I gathered a staff of five. Sure, it may have taken silly flyers and too many sweet treats, but I was ecstatic.

Beginning with monthly interviews and birthday calendars, students like me that had previously felt insignificant started to become involved. Those I once passed with a brief smile became the very people and stories we sought to highlight. Throughout this process, I also became close with my team, many of whom possessed incredibly diverse talents. During our meetings, I discovered how to fold an origami jumping frog, lose a hand in slapjack, and complete an NYT mini crossword in under ten seconds.

Although I spent many late nights at the printer, it was all worth it. I saw the pride in a mother’s eyes as her daughter’s artwork was featured front page. I heard the excitement of a second-grade class when they held the end-of-school edition they had created themselves. I read the heartfelt stories of students brave enough to share their voices. With each edition and every typo, The Miscellany brought people together.

I have come to realize that leading a community is not about being the most entertaining host at the potluck, or the smartest student in the classroom. True leadership is about being a connector. It is finding common ground between strangers. It is understanding who needs the pool noodles or the Connect 4. It is recognizing those who feel alone through my own fears.

As I leave the familiar soon, I no longer fear missing out. Armed with a deck of cards and a handful of spoons, I will forge on relentlessly in search of new connections.

Sitting on the sand at Doheny Beach, the ocean’s rhythm feels familiar. Each wave rolls in like a memory—some crashing violently, others gently nudging me. Just as the waves reshape the shore, my experiences have reshaped me.

A wave pulls me back to the board, the Maclaurin series twisting into confusion. My chest tightens—if I can’t grasp this, maybe I’m not cut out for it. But I refused to walk away. That night, I sat at my desk, replaying tutorials, solving problem after problem. Each wrong answer chipped away at my confidence, but I kept going, determined to find the logic in the chaos. There was no sudden breakthrough—just a slow, deliberate process. As hours passed, factorials and powers of x began to align, revealing connections I hadn’t noticed. I realized solving complex problems wasn’t about instant clarity—it was about persistence, breaking each part down until understanding emerged. After a quiz, my teacher recognized my progress and asked me to help classmates. As I guided them, their frustration softened into comprehension. In helping them, I not only deepened my understanding but found fulfillment in guiding others to their own breakthroughs.

A gentle wave rolls me back to this beach, just a month ago, when I finally let go of the loneliness I’d carried for years. Growing up, I thought strength meant handling everything alone, like my stoic parents. Over time, that isolation weighed on me, leaving me disconnected and overwhelmed. After a brutal week of exams, I broke down and texted my friends: “Doheny Beach?” They came without hesitation. We played volleyball, but as the sun set, something deeper shifted. I hesitated, feeling my chest tighten, then finally admitted to Tom, “I feel so stressed.” To my surprise, he confessed, “I haven’t slept in days.” In that moment, an emotional barrier shattered. I realized true strength wasn’t about carrying the weight alone, but in releasing it. For the first time, I felt unburdened and connected—no longer isolated. Since then, I’ve focused on building those connections—more beach outings, studying with friends, and volunteering with friends. Opening up has created a community for me, and I want to do that for others.

A third crashing wave hit me, stirring a deep shift in my understanding of intention and impact. Days earlier, my friend Aiden had challenged my beliefs in a heated debate about Mr. Beast’s philanthropy. I argued it was wrong to turn suffering into entertainment, but his question lingered: “Does it matter if a homeless man gets a house?” His words cut deep. I had always followed deontological morality—believing that doing the right thing mattered more than the result. But as I poured salt into my mother’s water softener and saw the gratitude in her eyes—her back spared from pain, her cracked skin being soothed—I began to see things differently. This simple task, one I often resented, suddenly felt like more than just duty. Was my help valuable because I cared, or because it truly eased her suffering? That moment unraveled my rigid beliefs. I realized that consequentialism—the outcomes—mattered just as much as intention. Now, I’m driven to act with both empathy and purpose, proactively seeking ways, however small, to make a real difference.

These reflections fuel my commitment to creating technology that empowers others. As a Team Leader at my local food pantry, I’ve witnessed families struggle, and handing out food feels like a temporary solution to a much deeper issue. I aspire to develop financial tools—microloan platforms, educational apps—that give people control over their futures and break cycles of poverty.

Sitting by the ocean, I reflect on how deeply these moments have shaped me. I’ve learned that perseverance requires patience, that true strength is built through shared vulnerability, and that morality is a balance of intention and impact. Brushing off the sand as I stand, I’m not waiting for easy answers—I’m forging my own path, ready to turn challenges into solutions that make a lasting difference.

Leaning into the mirror, I brush strokes of thick, green paint across my face, contorting my youthful features to resemble a terrifying hag. I widen my eyes in the reflection, marveling at my transformation into the Wicked Witch. The spotlight beams on my viridescent skin as I clench my broom, a scowl masking my nerves. Dorothy splashes me with water. I scream and thrash as I’m lowered into the pit: “Noooo!! I’m melting, I’m melting!!”

Initially, I was not thrilled about playing an ugly villain. However, standing in her shoes, I embraced the role and saw her as mourning the death of her sister, murdered by Dorothy. With this unorthodox perspective, I conveyed a more nuanced story to the audience and revealed how powerful female roles are often misunderstood as villainous.

But these unjust caricatures of women extend far beyond fairy tales. In 2016, I watched Hillary Clinton on TV, perplexed and angry as she faced both overt and subtle sexism for the same assertive traits that are praised in men. In a related, yet different, manifestation of systemic sexism, I watched my mother, a single mom, struggle to balance a full-time job with raising two kids due to insufficient childcare.

Motivated by a deep sense of protectiveness toward my mom and a desire to empower women, I channeled the boldness I’d gained from portraying strong female characters in theater into other areas where women remain underrepresented, creating Leadership for Women, the first female and career-oriented club on campus. I secured speakers including U.S. Congresswoman Grace Meng and LAPD Deputy Chief Ruby Flores to share their powerful journeys. Through their inspiring stories of being the lone female voice in a room full of men, I facilitated guidance and inspiration for girls to understand how to pursue leadership positions in a male-dominated world.

These inspiring conversations introduced me to a new avenue: utilizing public policy to address gender inequality. Determined to find an outlet where I could put forth actual legislation, I searched deeper into school bulletins and newsletters and eventually found Youth and Government (YNG), a national YMCA program with a mock legislature that presented actionable bills to the state and national government. After being elected as a delegate for the Sacramento conference to present a bill, I thoroughly researched legislative approaches to something personal: childcare. I was resolved to propose a public-private partnership where corporations would receive tax credits for offering onsite and offsite childcare to employees, a bill that could have aided my mother.

As the Bill came up for vote, I knew it could cross Governor Newsom’s desk. Despite my unease, I drew from my mother’s resilience. Standing firmly at the podium, I glanced towards the table of all-older-male panelists and faced an auditorium full of 87 people. I spoke with conviction, but when my bill did not pass due to "practical concerns," I felt misunderstood—like the Wicked Witch—by an audience who did not grasp the issue or its impact on millions of working women. While self-reflecting, I realized diversity is essential in voting. This frustration fueled me at National Conferences, as I scrambled from building to building in business attire, handing out badges and encouraging girls to pre-register to vote, spreading the value of not only the youth voice but the female voice. I was unsure if my efforts were truly influencing anyone until I spoke with Anya, who will now be the first girl in her family to vote! I was filled with pride when our grassroots efforts led to the announcement of 89% of conference attendees being pre-registered.

In college, I want to expand and share the impact of Leadership for Women with my classmates by introducing my personal mentors to a new network and launching a voter registration initiative. Playing the Wicked Witch emboldened me to defy stereotypes both on stage and in real life. Though the Wicked Witch may have melted, her fierceness endures in me.

When I was appointed the class monitor, the "highest-ranking officer" in my class, I saw myself as the glorified gatekeeper of order. Even when perpetrators were my friends, I would mercilessly call them out. However, my self-esteem quickly crumbled as the rest of the class alienated me, and self-directed study sessions became chaotic.

Therefore, when the entire city was trapped at home during the 2022 Shanghai lockdown, I felt relieved. There was no need to maintain classroom order—turning off the camera and muting the microphone was enough. But more serious problems soon emerged. With 26 million people suddenly confined to their homes, even basic life essentials, including food, became a logistical disaster.

Then, the residents at our building started a grassroots movement of posting links in WeChat groups to share grocery sources with logistical clearance. Each link was then submerged by hundreds of anxious replies—

"I want 2!"

"How much?"

"Reserve some for room 801, please! There are kids and elderly!"

"Where's the egg link?! I can't find it anymore!"
...

Hoping to do my part in re-establishing order, I enlisted myself in the team of volunteers to disinfect, separate, and deliver orders to residents' doorsteps. Like the WeChat group, the first volunteer Zoom meeting was a ruleless chaos. With everybody talking over each other, the topic flipped from who's making a profit to debating whether coffee and ice cream are "life essentials." Still recovering from my painful experience managing the classroom, I listened quietly and wrote down a few useful minutes.

After the meeting ended with an abrupt call for PCR testing downstairs, I checked my minutes and realized some sort of order had arisen:

"Profiting is allowed but not encouraged,"

"Organize WeChat links,"

"Give priority to the elderly."
...

Familiar with tools like online shared documents and coding, I knew exactly how to implement these ideas. Within two hours after my PCR test, I automated a form titled "Consolidated Grocery Orders." It was soon posted in the WeChat group notice, which is a central place for all rules and announcements. "Thanks to our volunteer [Name], we have a consolidated form," followed by a link and a long list of thumbs-up emojis.

Encouraged, I further refined the form, adding automation to prioritize families with elderly members. With minor hiccups at first, soon, hundreds of submissions turned from "logged" to "paid for" and eventually "delivered." 200 families successfully received life essentials with the help of 20 volunteers and the form.

Soon, similar documents with emergency contacts and baby item exchanges began circulating online. During the 68 days of lockdown, I witnessed how rigidly imposed rules could nearly crumble a prosperous society while committed communities could bring it back to life.

Entering high school, Economics helped me understand the effects of failed policies like the Great Leap Forward and Prohibition—well-intentioned but disconnected from reality. Studying machine learning also taught me that even computers, which I once saw as loyal to logic, learn by iterating through mistakes. I realized that rules must evolve and adapt to circumstances—they are not absolute.

After volunteering at a local animal shelter, I rallied a group of classmates to address the growing stray cat population on campus. Starting our first meeting without an appointed leader felt reminiscent of my earlier volunteer experience—chaotic and without direction. However, amidst the chatter, we agreed to use the TNR (trap, neuter, release) approach. Over 18 months, we established a set of guidelines collaboratively: using authentic cat photos over cartoons for marketing, designating a bookkeeper with a transparent ledger, and automating data logging—all built on a community consensus.

The best rules are spontaneous—grounded in reality, shaped by consensus, and filled with mutual respect. These rules do not alienate people; they bring people together.

My parents say the objects I engage with will one day speak for me, bearing witness to the good and bad experiences I've had with them, and reflecting the marks I leave behind—profound or subtle. This thought brings me comfort.

As an online high school student, my world revolves around my desk. Though I live in a constant home base, it transforms daily—yesterday an art studio, today a study hub. But three objects have a permanent home on this desk. These items have stood the test of time, anchoring every version of me and my ever-changing space.

First, nestled under my desk is a small Japanese foldable table. On this, I traced my earliest words under my mom’s careful guidance and later wrestled with math problems. Now, it’s the space where I help my sister conquer her b’s and d’s and my brothers tackle PEMDAS. This table has seen my growth from learner to teacher.

I’ve gained confidence tutoring children like six-year-old Sarah, who now scrunches her nose less at fractions, and eight-year-old Ahmed, whose sighs over the Arabic alphabet have evolved into cheers. When I doubt my tactics, I glance at my little table. Its crooked back leg yet sturdy presence reminds me how patience and good intentions nurtured my growth. By extending those same virtues to others, I can also be a sturdy presence for them.

Next, on the far right of my desk rests a purple basket filled to the brim with my homemade cards. Each card began as a blank sheet, presenting a daunting challenge to my creativity, easily stifled by fears of mistakes and unmet expectations. Though not every card turned out as planned, I learned to adapt—transforming smears into vibrant streamers or uneven letters into playful balloons. Eventually, I was crowned my family’s go-to designer, crafting cards around their interests. A pop-up fried chicken card welcomed my dad home from Indonesia. A 3D pocket card filled with intricately folded paper chili peppers, each holding a special note, wished my mom a happy birthday.

Each card has witnessed the triumph of trial and error, shaped by my sweating palms and colored fingers. As I dig through them, I am reminded of how mistakes can birth something unique. This basket cradles a trove of memories and a testimony to creative experiments.

Lastly, hanging elegantly on the side of my desk is my green badminton racket, its leather-wrapped handle worn from countless family matches. Unfortunately, overlooked amid late-night study sessions, I rarely paused to appreciate its charm.

But nudged by my mom, I began playing for short periods between assignments. Slowly, I stretched those rounds longer, hesitant yet hopeful, letting progress unfold. One afternoon, I spotted a new neighbor peeking through the fence. Although I planned on getting back to my assignment, I waved him over, inviting him to join. His shy grip on the racket melted into a beaming smile. Now, I happily teach him every week.

My racket bears witness to the breaks I take from my studies, reminding me that I’ll discover unexpected opportunities if I give those breaks a chance. Just as I balance on my back leg for a winning badminton shot, I’ve learned to find that same balance off the court.

These 3 objects remind me of the mark I want to leave in this world. I hope my wooden table testifies to the patience I have learned and taught. I pray my cards speak of my journey of turning mistakes into beauty. I trust my racket shares the strength I’ve gained from embracing balance in my studious life.

I know beyond my desk, I’ll discover more objects that spark memories and inspire growth. Through every person I meet and challenges I face, I’ll let these items silently anchor the worlds I explore. I want to feel proud of what my objects say about me. This thought brings me comfort.

Sharp and synced flicks of my uncle’s thumb and pointer on a paintbrush of a single strand of squirrel hair were able to create elephants, peacocks, gods, flowers with microscopic intricacy. Crouching on my knees while hovering over his elbows and scrutinizing each stroke filled my childhood days.

Intrigued, I tried my hand at it. My art came out as you’d expect for a kid whose cursive v’s looked like u’s—canvases peppered with smudges, extra lines, and disproportionate shapes. My family lovingly mocked them, but I delighted in thinking of my oversized, misshapen lily pads as rocket launchpads.

Following those curiosities to see where they lead – without the pressure of a predetermined outcome – became a struggle amid repetitive worksheets and Zoom meetings when remote learning emerged as a reality in eighth grade. Searching for that familiar flutter, I found competition math.

I could find the sum of the first 100 integers in 100 seconds by the symmetry in pairing the numbers forwards and backwards. After devouring a textbook on probability & statistics, I revisited the problem and realized it was also equivalent to choosing 2 elements from a set of 101. Exploring by making such polar connections always fired me up.

The problems were maddeningly difficult, often featuring math I’d never even learned. But I loved it. My notebooks filled with crossed-out, reworked diagrams. For the ones I still needed help with, I turned to Discord, where I'd connect with mathletes online. Asking many for tiny hints individually, I also unlocked different ways to approach the same problem. It directly translated into how I played around on my own – each problem feeling like a spiral staircase. Much slower than a straight one, but with deep exploration, far more fulfilling. Something seemed to be a Law-of-Cosines application? Wait—extend a line, and Ceva’s Theorem could swoop in too! Thriving on this mindset, I’ve self-learned from the ground up.

When quarantine restrictions were lifted, I desperately wanted to show others the power of embracing, rather than stifling, their boundless energy and curiosity. The chance to volunteer at NYC’s National Museum of Math sucked me in. Here, I’ve gotten to interact with many different types of visitors - from those just learning to count on their fingers to others who’d presented at top AI conferences. Each conversation presents its own unique opportunity to rework and improvise new explanations on-the-spot and show theoretical math within visible reality.

One particular exhibit, the square-wheeled tricycle, is consistently a hit. Visitors sit on a tricycle whose wheels are squares and ride along undulating curves that rise and fall. What seemingly promises to be a scarily bumpy ride was, in fact, perfectly smooth! The magic lies in the power of catenary curves which, when aligned with right angles whose sides match the arc length, make for flawlessly smooth rides.

Sometimes, I direct people to walk heel-to-toe along the curves to feel the hidden patterns. Other times, I even nudge the tricycle off its red-marked path, revealing how it won't budge—thanks to the underlying math.

Visitors were always taken aback, eagerly requesting an explanation. But it was when a young boy, José, asked, “Could pentagon or hexagon wheels also work?” that I felt truly fulfilled. I saw myself in José, driven by curiosity. Even moreso, I transitioned to the giving end, not just directing him to competition math but also constantly dropping hints through Discord to different solution paths for problems he got stuck on. Sparking these moments of discovery in others and exploring them through long discussions made the exhausting two-hour commute entirely worth it.

The very thing many others see as flaws or eccentricities is where I’m most inspired. That overarching restlessness of what more? and what else? urges me to tackle challenges with many unconventional routes. It’ll continue to drive me to create spaces where each new conversation, algorithm, and data point reveal unexpected lines and shapes that shine unique perspectives and discussions. I’ll always be in the pursuit of the beauty that lies on and off the canvas, one rocket-launching lily pad at a time.

I grew up with contradictions. I swung aggressively on monkey bars with my brother and his friends after school, but was mesmerized by the peace of the piano and the challenge of Sudoku during nighttime. Though a lively child growing up in Shanghai, I did not feel belonging enough to express this liveliness at boarding school. At home, I was told to respect authority without question and examine my own faults when things went awry, but teachers seemed to reward kids who spoke out freely and challenged order.

Navigating these contradictions sometimes felt like a game of tug-of-war with me in the middle. I developed habits of imitating others and code-switching as these became my only ways of reconciling two worlds.

I noticed that the subtle sway in Kate’s elbows gave her a confident stride, and began to add a slight sway to my own arms. I noticed that Rick could command respect at the Harkness table, and began pausing in between my own sentences. I noticed that Henry could work through hours of homework without pause, and I chided myself for needing breaks and child-like fun. I noticed the accolades Catherine stacked up for her singular, well-discovered passion for computer science, and I wished I were her.

I was losing my ground. During the day, my skin felt stiff, every movement and reaction orchestrated, the concept of being myself more and more distant. At night, fatigue consumed me as I lay, disenchanted, staring at the ceiling. Feeling burnout from chasing perceived success and confidence, I focused on what I had control over: gratitude.

I grew an appreciation for the blend of contradictions that make me me. The contrasting environments I’ve been part of have created tension in finding my own beliefs, yes, but just as nothing in the world is ever black and white, just as Sudoku's perplexity makes it amusing to me, navigating contradictions has given me color.

While Rick possesses a charismatic sureness of his beliefs, I’m still developing my opinions and possess a greater love for spicy viewpoints. Additionally, the child-like instincts I envied Henry for lacking, coupled with the diverse environments I’ve been exposed to, allow me to build bridges. At lunch, where friend groups sit divided by gender and race on opposite sides of a long table, I initiate and facilitate cross-table conversations. By asking others questions about themselves and making jokes equally hilarious to all genders and races, I bring an air of child-like enthusiasm no one can deny.

While I was envious that Catherine found her singular fascination in computer science early, staying true to seemingly opposite passions—an appreciation for ineffable human subtleties and an evidence-based way of navigating the world—led me to neuroscience. Immersing myself in a neuroimaging lab this summer, I sought out a quick, reliable, and equitable method for diagnosing Multiple Sclerosis. I found purpose sifting through large amounts of data to uncover actionable steps for alleviating brain disease. I left my internship aching for more research opportunities to seek cures for Alzheimer’s and answers regarding 21st-century happiness.

I will continue to seek, rather than suppress, this desire to experience fulfillment through various forms. In our student-led band The Disciples, we play around with instrument-switching, not because it means we’re weaker on our own, but because a comprehensive understanding of different instruments helps us listen for each other and gain intentionality during our playing. The power produced by the sharing of our complex understanding transcends, touching the hearts of others.

The human experience is about tackling contradictions. In our world full of contradictions, society chases categorization and labeling. I chase gratitude. Owing my colors to the contradictions I navigated, I span across instruments, across lunch tables, across cultures, and across disciplines.

Poshmark and my shelf have one thing in common: they're full of used shoes. The difference? Nothing on my shelf is for sale. Instead, it's home to my basketball shoes from 7th grade—destroyed—and my 9th-grade tennis shoes—somehow even more beat up. Unlike most shelf decorations, shoes are like memory books for me. Each pair reminds me of the values that shape who I am. The following pairs are still in use and represent the core of who I've become.

House Slippers

Soft and unmarred, my house slippers are part of my cherished Sunday morning routine. Every Sunday, I bring my mom's coffee from the kitchen island to her seat—a small gesture that holds immense meaning. My mom's neurodegenerative condition (cerebellar degenerative atrophy) means she does not move, think, or talk as swiftly as she once did. After breakfast, I help her walk downstairs to help her with physical therapy. In these shoes, I have identified needs, like installing a railing for the front steps and grab bars for her shower. My routine in these shoes has shifted over the years—more pauses, more careful steps. I've learned to be patient, not just physically but emotionally. These slow mornings taught me how to listen beyond words—how to sense the tight grip of her hand on mine when she's struggling or the way she leans less on me on her stronger days.

Dress Shoes

Roughly twice a month, I lace up my black leather dress shoes—the soles worn smooth from early Saturday mornings spent guiding my Model UN team to conferences in NYC. Once inside my competition room one morning, I spot Abi, a freshman, nervously fidgeting with her notes as she did on the subway. Her wide eyes darted around the room, searching for reassurance. I remember that trembling, apprehensive feeling all too well. "I don't think I can do this," she whispered, barely audible. Leaning in, I said, "You do not need to be perfect—just be clear." Her hand trembled as she looked at me, unsure. I slid my annotated notes toward her. "Use these. If you believe what you say, they will too." She nodded and rose slowly. Her first words wavered, but by the third sentence, she commanded the room, her voice steady and her argument sharp. In these stiff shoes, I've realized that leadership isn't just about physically guiding someone through public transport, from the LIRR to Penn Station; It's about creating an emotional runway for their confidence—like Abi's—to take off and soar.

Sneakers

My sneakers crease 100 times a minute when I learn. My top speed happens in the library, tucked into the corner table by the window, my right leg bouncing as I devour submissions for my international trade essay competition. With my sneakers tapping the ground (quietly, I promise), I lean forward, absorbing my peers' approaches to global issues I had not considered. I had craved these insights for months, and now, I'm finally feasting. One particular essay stood out—it explored how local economies in sub-Saharan Africa could thrive through micro-loans and import substitution policies. I was so intrigued by this essay that I shared it with my economics teacher, who had agreed to adjudicate the winning entry. He wanted me to share this with our class in some way, so I started a socratic discussion. Growing up in a household with several political views, I discovered that understanding begins with curiosity. In these shoes, I have carried that truth beyond my home, never turning down the chance to engage with new angles, no matter how unfamiliar.

These experiences—the empathy I've gained in my house slippers, the leadership I've practiced in my dress shoes, and the curiosity that has creased my sneakers—will guide how I walk on campus.

Amidst my usual bus ride to awkwardly maneuvering an overflowing backpack to avoid my friends’ faces as I squeezed through the aisle, I noticed an unusual figure waiting for me. Brown wool sweater, brown scally cap. Hair on the sides of his head wholly insufficient in concealing a shiny bald spot. The other kids gave only a strange look as they strolled in their respective directions, but I recognized the man: my grandfather, who had recently arrived from China.

He told me that he’d like to join me on my walk home. Slightly annoyed, I had no choice but to allow it. We were quite the eye-catching duo that day: a little Chinese kid in misfit Nike clothes followed by an old Chinese man whose wardrobe reminisced of the 70s. Already a bit of an outcast in a mostly white school, I knew that being seen with my old Asian grandfather didn’t do me any favors.

He came again the next day, and the next after that, not seeming to notice the judgment he’d garner every time the bus arrived. I, for one, was indignant. Desperate to save face in front of my peers, I prayed everyday that I’d arrive to find his usual spot empty, but it never happened.

One day, he showed up with a little girl’s umbrella.

It was pouring rain. I hadn’t expected to see him there at all, but like always, he was standing near the street corner. Same old clothes, same stooped gait, with a bright pink umbrella that belonged to my little sister. Suddenly, I found myself debating whether I wanted to get off the bus at all. No way was I getting under that ugly thing.

Realizing that I didn’t have a choice, I decided to face my challenge headstrong, stomping angrily toward the place where Grandpa stood. Ignoring his wide smile, I challenged him immediately, berating him, asking him why he felt the need to pick such an audacious umbrella. He tried desperately to explain that he’d taken the only one he could find.

We were silent for the rest of the walk.

It was only when we got back that I noticed Grandpa was completely wet; strands of hair hung limply from his head, and his clothes were two shades darker than usual. He wasn’t lying- the umbrella I held was the only one he could find, and he’d chosen to cover me instead of himself.

Seeing the water drip from his old, battered body, I realized that I’d been too harsh. He was doing his best.

Grandpa and I came from two different worlds. He didn’t know of my vanities, and I was too young to understand his intent. However, he taught me how to love beyond the limits of age and culture. By walking with me each day, he promised me a piece of himself, which, for a little boy struggling with loneliness, mattered more than I knew.

Five years later, I’m starting to appreciate his brilliance. With neither the ability to read minds nor the wisdom that comes with advanced age, I know that I can’t possibly expect to understand the full human experience. As a brother, son, and friend, I find myself powerless in others’ struggles all too often.

However, I do know the power of simply being there, offering a piece of myself. Sometimes, it takes real commitment—like when I stayed up all night to help a friend through a tough breakup. Other times, it’s as simple as sitting quietly beside my little sister as she tackles a challenging math question. Either way, I’m sending the same message: I may not have the answers, but I’m here with you.

Violated by my mind's psychological mechanisms, I knelt down on the rugged floor. My mind was a haze and I could barely stand as a weakness enveloped my body. The living room was circulating as I tried to grab ahold of the nearest table. I hadn't eaten much that day - nothing unusual for me - but now, it had caught up to me in the worst possible way. I was on the brink of passing out.

As I sat down, trying to steady myself, my parents’ concerned faces hovered over me. They had warned me for years about my picky eating habits. The constant nagging of how surviving on bread, fruit juice, and an occasional bland meal with rice isn't sustainable was pounded into my mind. At that moment I realized my negligence had become too strong. My parents were right. It wasn't just about disliking certain foods anymore; it was affecting my health. I was nutritionally deprived and the effects were undeniable.

Growing up I was notorious for turning down meals. I had an immense list of foods I wouldn't touch - anything with a strong smell, unfamiliar texture, or even a hint of sourness was out of the question. My biggest enemies among them all were onions. The mere sight of those slimy, pungent, tear-inducing intruders was enough to destroy my whole appetite. In my mom's freshly made biryani, a bite into an onion or even a pepper hidden within the brown rice would lead me to abandon the dish for weeks. Eventually, even family gatherings became sources of nervousness as I felt like an outsider for avoiding foods that others enjoyed without a second thought. I was hiding, living in a bubble of comfort food. After the near-fainting incident, the doctor sternly said I needed to incorporate a greater diet. In my mind, the changes felt far more urgent and profound.

It wasn't easy. Every new meal and every new ingredient felt like a hostile force against my body. I needed to start small to combat this weakness so I turned towards the books. If I learned how each ingredient functioned within its little ecosystem maybe I would be more enticed to give it a try. I became intrigued as I discovered how garlic provides acidity, how herbs like thyme add an earthy depth, and the way onions add a layer of sweetness to a dish. Now I had to apply my knowledge into the kitchen.

While starting I was making simplistic dishes following certain recipes I found online. Slowly I became more confident and started straying away from these confining recipes. I began to explore different vegetables and different spices trying to figure out the perfect fusion between them. After countless trials of paprika, cumin, and turmeric into eggplant stew, I created this exotic dish that my parents enjoyed and which I loved. I was eating onions, peppers, eggplants, and all sorts of spices - an event I would never have envisioned myself in before. What was once my battleground turned into my personal laboratory, where I mixed, tasted, and developed flavors I had once sternly rejected. It was a place of infinite exploration and my health had never been better.

In every dish, each ingredient withholds a certain character. Ignoring such elements removes you from possible experiences of growth and happiness. You need to put your best effort into intaking as much as you possibly can. In doing so you remove any possible limiting factors to reveal your true self. Whether it is cracking down on an impossible calculus problem, assisting someone who’s getting a root canal, or even figuring out how to put a smile on a kid's face in the hospital, I approach challenges with the same mindset I developed during my picky eating endeavor. I analyze, obsess, then perfect. Subsequently, I try to find my next grand endeavor.

An invisible rabbit chased by a hunter, both moving a mile a step. Could the hunter ensure he’s within a 100-mile radius after a billion moves? The problem was absurd yet exhilarating—the kind that made my fingers twitch and my mind race. With four hours left on the math Olympiad team selection test, my brain buzzed with possibilities—construction, strong induction... definitely but no, no. I could have won that chess game if I went C6 yesterday. No, focus Mohammad. THINK.

I blundered. But this time it wasn’t just a Rook or a Queen I lost—it was my spot on the math Olympiad team. I just couldn’t focus, my mind was constantly on the run from silence. The second I wasn’t doing ten things at once, anxiety gripped my chest like a Gordian knot, tightening with every moment of stillness, and the only way to loosen it was to stay busy—constantly. But this blunder was one that outweighed my anxieties, because no matter how hard the familial problems outside my control were, at least, at least I had my passions.

I dived into Wikipedia articles on dopaminergic pathways, neuroplasticity, and even the default mode network, trying to understand why my brain seemed so intent on running from stillness. Turns out, I was being cognitively overloaded—gaming, cubing, even skateboarding. Too many tasks flooded my brain at once, making it impossible to focus on any of them. My devices and hobbies were tools, avenues to grow, but ones that had revolted with my multitasking tendency leading the charge. I had to keep them in check. I deleted TikTok, limited Instagram to the website, and bought Walden by Thoreau and Deep Work by Cal Newport. And so everyday, after Fajr prayer, I’d open the shutters, close the door, and sink into my leather Churchill chair as I started writing about any problem that might add to my anxiety. But this stillness was new, and my body resisted it. Brushing my teeth without music had my eyes jumping between the red toothpaste cap and the dust between the tiles. “Single-tasking” was a mental workout: even while playing my guitar, my mind longed for the comfort of The Office in the background.

Rationally, I knew why—for years, guitar had been a way to drown the anxiousness, and when that wasn’t enough, a comforting sitcom would bury the leftovers. My mind tried to trick me: It’s productive. Multitasking saves more time for real work later. But feeling my chest tighten after a single John Mayer riff, when I used to spend all-nighters with painful, calloused fingers, showed me how far my attention span had fallen. It wasn’t just about losing focus; it was like I had lost a part of myself. So I pushed through. Day after day, that knot around my chest slowly loosened with every hour of silence I chose to embrace. I was beginning to live intentionally.

I started to solve “boring” problems I’d seen the solutions to before, but now I would dig deeper—analyzing why constructing the Sharky-Devil point worked, why harmonic ratio approaches fell short, and truly trying the problems I found on YouTube videos just like I did as a younger, carefree kid. Four hours between Dhuhr and Asr prayers would slip by, and I’d still be focused on a single geometry problem—tracing lines, testing different constructions, and questioning every instinct. I was regaining the focus that allowed me to appreciate the beauty of math.

When I pick up the guitar now, it isn’t to drown out the frustration or lingering doubts—but to express them. I bend slow blues notes in A minor when I feel uneasy, or run up and down the mixolydian when I’m energetic. What were once distractions now anchor me. Valorant isn’t just a game to kill time anymore; it’s where my friends and I compete every Saturday, feeling the nerves of a 1v5 clutch or the shared realization about the Cypher who always flanks. It’s no longer just about winning, but about growing as a player and teammate, finding fulfillment in the strategies we build together.

**Essay:**

“Why do you look so weird?” Ryan cackled as he spun in his swivel chair. “Light skin, small eyes, and Dumbo ears?” The other students broke out in laughter. Even at just ten, I remember feeling exposed. And I recall how from that moment, I feared being noticed. So, instead of speaking up, I chose to be silent. I forfeited my voice.

I spent much of the next few years alone in the library. Amidst the aisles of books, cooling AC, and bean bag chairs, I found sanctuary in my books. Always, I gravitated towards the history section. Reading about famous battles, intriguing treaties, and conspiracy theories, I was immersed in fascinating new worlds. I imagined myself joining the fight to expose government exploitation of Hispanic people under the Bracero work program; I envisioned myself rallying against the unresponsiveness to hate crimes towards Asian Americans during the immigration acts. Key historical figures quickly became my friends – Ida B Wells, Fred Korematsu – friends who never judged me for who I was.

Inspired by my heroes who had fought against systemic adversity, discrimination, and socio-economic divides, I joined Mr. Shah’s after school public speaking class. From learning voice inflections, tone, and breath of speech to hand motions, gestures, eye contact, and posture, I rinsed and repeated the lessons that Mr. Shah taught me along with my other peers. Although I was a soft-spoken kid ridden with fear, I practiced every day, working to improve my voice inflections, tone, and breath, and my eye contact, and posture. With every passing session, I found myself speaking more freely and confidently, engaging in high-level discussions and debates, arguing for topics that I cared about just like my heroes of the past had.

With a newfound power, I raised my hand more in class, joined the school speech and debate team, and even volunteered first for group projects. I also felt a responsibility to follow in my heroes' footsteps to utilize my powers to help others discover and utilize their own voices, especially those from marginalized communities.

To help others find their voice as I had, I created Youth Prose Scholars. Just like Mr. Shah had once taught me, I worked with students to develop public speaking and conversational skills while improving argumentative and critical thinking. With the students most influenced by my lessons, I pushed them further by encouraging them to apply for local OC debate tournaments, the most prestigious in Southern California.

After the success of our flagship YPS program, I wanted to expand into marginalized communities. I have other like-minded friends from different regions across the U.S to pass down the self-curated curriculum I developed to communities in their vicinity. To further educate our growing community, I created newsletters spotlighting the growing issue of low funding for public education across the US and the pressing need for environmental advocacy and political socialization. I was so fortunate to lead an international team who raised the bar on developing student voices and holistic education, especially for minority students.

Seeing how much work there was left to be done on a policy level, though, I started working with Representative Dave Min to analyze the work in public education and student access to resources in local Southern California and abroad. I engaged in discussions on the repercussions of childhood education reformation, analyzing how issues like racial inequities in politics affected student outcomes, and evaluating methods to uplift voices of other local AAPI leaders like Derek Tran through canvassing and political outreach.

Little did I know, my fifth-grade bully would set me on the most unexpected journey. For many years I would have been afraid to face him, but now, someday I hope we meet again. If we do, I’ll offer a smile and a friendly handshake. “If not for you,” I might say, “I might never be where I am today. So, thank you.”

As I deftly manoeuvre my knight into position, I feel a surge of confidence: this could be it. My grandfather, watching intently, arches an eyebrow and smirks, as if he knows something I don’t. I take a deep breath as he playfully sacrifices his bishop, leaving his king vulnerable. I leap from my seat and declare checkmate for the first time. "Hey, you’re getting better at this!" he chuckles, his eyes sparkling with pride. I giggle, eyes glossy.

The screech of our landline snaps me back to reality. My grandfather was gone, the funeral complete, and that moment existed in memory. Witnessing someone so full of life vanish sparked a fear of death I couldn’t shake. The idea that every achievement I'd celebrated could dissolve into the vast unknown jolted me. My family tried to help in their ways; my mom turned to rituals for comfort while my dad drove through long, silent stretches, each mile heavy with unspoken fears. I awkwardly voiced my fear to friends, scrolling through Quora late into the night, searching for comfort in others' stories. Each conversation deepened the void, making me feel like my fear was mine alone. As I searched for answers, 'thanatophobia' appeared on the screen, an intense fear of death—a label for the shadows lurking in my mind.

Then came a Saturday morning, bright with promise, when my mom suggested, “How about joining me at work today?” A few hours later, I trailed behind her at the hospital, watching her try to convince yet another patient that Dolo 650 wasn’t a miracle cure for every ailment under the sun. Suddenly, a nurse slipped in with urgency in her voice: “Doctor, the delivery room is ready.”

The brisk walk from the bustling patient hall to the hushed delivery room was a blur. As I stood silently, my mom made a horizontal incision on the woman’s belly, revealing layers of purple skin. A moment later, the baby's piercing cry burst forth, filling the room with raw, life-affirming energy that reverberated in my chest, illuminating a truth I had long overlooked: death is a door to new lives, each with the potential to create newfound joy and memories. I felt overwhelming gratitude for the emptiness in my head, a quiet space that allowed me to appreciate life’s fragility.

In that instant, I realized life is a series of fleeting moments—a cry in the delivery room, a gentle word on a long car ride, a shared memory with a loved one. Each moment ripples outward in ways we can’t always see. It was then that my grandfather’s impact began to reveal itself.
