His cancer hospital was not just a building; it was a lifeline for hundreds, a chance to fight for more time and hold onto loved ones a little longer. Witnessing how cancer could strip away moments we take for granted ignited a fire in me. I wanted to help others cling to their moments, to extend their time to create memories that this cruel disease often threatened to steal.

Thus, Susankalp was born. It became my way of channeling everything this phase taught me into tangible action. Through Susankalp, I reached hundreds of young girls, educating them about menstrual hygiene and raising awareness of precancerous traits. This initiative became my way of touching lives, giving people a chance to hold on a little longer and create memories that time could never erase.

If there’s one thing I’ve learned through this, it’s that we’re all bound by the delicate threads of life and death. Every moment is a ripple that can touch lives far beyond our own. I’m committed to spending my life illuminating those moments we often let slip by, creating ripples of hope in a world that craves connection. If I’m lucky, my efforts will one day become part of someone else's story, just as my grandfather’s has become part of mine.

The instructor’s commanding voice echoed through the dojo.

“Five!”

My body ached. Sweat dripped down from my brow as my chest reached the floor.

“Four!”

My legs tremored vigorously. My knuckles were bruised, redder than anything.

“Three!”

I was at my breaking point.

“Two!”

But at the same time, at that moment…

“One!”

I enjoyed it more than anything. My black belt in taekwondo proves that very statement. But in order to show you how I got into that very room, we need to go back.

My mom likes to say that, one day, while walking down the street holding my hand, she saw two buildings. One was an arcade place, the other a dojo. An idea popped into her head. Out of the blue, she asked “Of the two, which do you like?”

Maybe it was the synchronized kicking, the powerful yells that accompanied each snap of the fist, or the cool nunchucks I saw inside the dojo that piqued my curiosity. This instant connection I felt led to my walking through those fateful glass doors. My taekwondo journey had begun. There was just one unique challenge:

My feet.

At birth, I was diagnosed with clubfoot, a congenital disease characterized by the inward twisting of the feet. My case was uniquely severe. Over 8 years, along with casting and bracing, I required a tendon transfer – an operation that would rearrange the tendons in my feet to correct the growth process.

Both before and after my surgery, I struggled in taekwondo. From the beginning, I was lacking in balance, coordination, and strength compared to other kids. There are countless times I lost every sparring match, failed a kick, or was unable to break the wooden board. So, so many times I failed when the rest succeeded. Thus, I needed to try twice as hard as the next kid. Hyper analyzing each muscle movement proved insurmountably difficult. I felt the need to quit. Yet I didn’t; I refused to. Because, from early on, I had unlocked a remarkable power within myself: the ability to find success in failure. As the instructor would yell at us, as my feet ached, as I was ready to give up, I would feel a greater sense of purpose to do the opposite. Success and failure became two sides of the same coin for me.

Every exercise and kick gave me a sense of purpose. They never got easier, but I got better and better. In a local tournament, I won five gold medals and one silver. The next year, at 11 years old, I passed the black belt test. As I held my belt high, my chin in the air, standing tall on my feet, I saw how far I’d come. From a kid with a debilitating disease to a martial art master.

In life, I consistently demonstrated an ability to overcome obstacles, beyond my challenges with clubfoot and taekwondo. Be it involving myself in volunteering, community service, school, or in research, my unbreakable mentality was critical in such achievements.

The statement – “My black belt in taekwondo” – is a reflection of my journey and a signifier of the future. I dream of a future where I can help more sick kids just like my young self. To work day and night to solve their medical problems. To see the joy when a kid can finally walk without a crutch to depend upon. To turn failure into success.

Chicago, Illinois, Summer 2014

My grandmother slides me last week’s The Daily Herald. Tenderly, she takes my hand, guiding me through folding my first origami tray. Later, we’ll fill these makeshift boxes with our snacktime sunflower seeds.

During these quiet summer mornings, I’ve learned how to meticulously repurpose old sheets of newspaper into beautiful keepsakes. The Chicago Tribune becomes flower vases to preserve my mother’s precious lilies. The Sun-Times transforms into a photo frame, capturing our Thanksgiving dinners, a rare moment with the whole family together.

“Polanyeyouyong,” she’d say to me. Even scraps have their value.

*****

During the school year, I jump out of bed at 5am, just in time to start my virtual Applied Digital Literacy lessons for the Kenyan students of Dawamu High School.

In the outskirts of Nairobi, Grand had the passion, but no opportunity, for computer hardware. He stays after each class as I teach him how to squeeze every bit of value out of his dilapidated laptop, from refining its display resolution to reconfiguring its cooling system. Through trial and error, we discover how even the most outdated technology can be revitalized with a little ingenuity and teamwork.

Realizing the potential of second-hand technology, I crease and flatten scrap cardboard from the school cafeteria, assembling drop-off boxes to collect hundreds more used laptops and electrical devices to send to disadvantaged high schools around the world. Repairing the damaged screens of old Kindles and Chromebooks, I breathe new life into these discarded devices, nursing them back into the catalysts for learning they once were. Shipping a donated driver to the Dawamu school to fix Grand’s defective webcam, I finally can see the face behind the voice that had been my constant companion over the last year, and in that moment, all the miles between us seem to disappear.

*****
Alongside tutoring students in Kenya each morning, I spend my afternoons reaching out to churches across the Chicago area to create an intramural sports league inclusive of everyone, regardless of their beliefs.

Every Friday in the spring, I lead twenty-something high schoolers, many of whom have never been to church prior to my invitation, in preparation for our grass volleyball tournament. Coaching with an open-door policy, I come to practice meeting more and more people each week. Seeing an opportunity to strengthen and solidify our team spirit, I decided to ditch the impersonal online jersey order and instead share some tie-dye techniques of my own.

The day before the tournament, we take over my backyard. We spend the evening squirting old t-shirts senseless with our own unique design. While their days accompanying a belted cardigan are long gone, these ratty clothes find new life as multicolored jerseys and headbands.

Looking back now, I can’t even remember how many games we won the next day—all I picture is a day full of colors, laughter, and friendships that will last a lifetime.

*****

This league now not only includes dozens more churches from all across Chicago, but has also grown to be year-round—basketball in the winter, volleyball in the spring. Grand now spends his weekends running a free computer repair clinic for his neighbors, completing the cycle to teach his own group of computer newbies. And though my late grandmother’s origami lessons were rooted in traumatic memories of poverty, reuse was an expression of familial love to her, one I now share each morning with my eight-year-old brother Matthew as we fold paper trays in our dining room.

All of these lessons were not just tutorials on the value of saving, but also celebrations of resourcefulness and creativity. Each is a treasured memory reflected in a deepened relationship with not just one individual, but the community around me. With an eye for value and a heart for others, I will continue to embrace every opportunity to uplift and inspire those around me, one scrap at a time.

“Your mother and I are lucky we even made it to middle school. You know we just had a few communal pencils because we couldn’t afford our own?” my dad recounts for the second time this week. As a daughter of immigrant parents, the blood, sweat, and tears put into my parents’ education remain a favorite topic of theirs to discuss with me.

My habit of zoning out from these conversations became a familiar routine each time the subject was brought up, dismissing it as an outdated issue that wasn’t as pressing today, especially not in first-world America. However, as my parents insisted that I listen, I was finally convinced to quickly Google education inequality in the US. Much to my surprise, I learned that even students in my own county struggled with the same affordability issues as my parents once faced.

***

“Hey [Name], would you mind giving me some extra shifts?” I receive a silent wave back from my boss, signaling his acknowledgement. Although I previously took my job at Kumon simply for work experience and pocket money, I finally had a true cause. I began commuting between two Kumon locations in order to work more hours, fervently tutoring Kumon students on advanced subjects such as geometry or grammar with the goal of helping less fortunate students access basic educational necessities.

Invigorated after finally completing 4 weeks of extra tutoring, I made my first purchase from Staples on the way home from that night’s shift. I rationed an array of pencils, notebooks, and more into each backpack, also handwriting a note for each student wishing them luck on the school year. After meticulously checking over the packages, I placed them in my trunk for the next morning’s three-hour solo trip.

***

Three small pairs of arms suddenly wrapped around me. I had just met the classroom of kindergarten students at Compton’s 95th street Elementary, greeting them with the backpacks I had tutored 20+ hours to create. Sarah, a 4-year-old girl with beaded braids and a toothy grin, was the first in line, eager to swap her previous grocery bag for a brand-new backpack. Sarah was the first to run over to me, embracing me in the first of many hugs I would receive that day. Embracing each new student that came my way, I became increasingly motivated to broaden my impact by recruiting peers from other areas to join my cause.

Through dozens of emails, DMs, and calls, I established Youth for Our People, opening chapters across four states. Through YFOP, I’ve gifted hundreds of students educational resources that my parents could only dream of as kids.

***

Weeks after a delivery, Kimberly, a kindergarten teacher in North Alabama, reached out: “One student with separation anxiety read about eight of the books with his mom this morning before she left; your donation has helped exponentially and our families are beyond grateful.” I felt beyond touched, never having imagined the scope of my own work achieving its impact.

YFOP has given me a deeper appreciation for my own unhindered access to education, helping me realize that I can impact students beyond my own community. Yet my ambition is not exclusive to the outside world– with each backpack I assemble, I fight to heal my parents’ inner child, hoping they see their own reflections within students I aid. In college, I aim to expand YFOP to secondary and higher education, aiding students of all levels in accessing educational resources in order to maximize their academic potential, an impact I hope to extend to my future home on a college campus.

“We’re alive ‘cause we are not alone
We run for roses” - NMIXX “Run for Roses”.

I’ve come close to death many times in my life.

As everyone is more familiar with than need be, people come and go. Friends turn into acquaintances, and acquaintances turn into familiar figures… into longing memories. Family is supposed to be forever, but being left behind incites the greatest feeling of loneliness—of death. No person ever escapes death; through accident, time, or a metaphorical sense of death through loneliness, and yet, we continue to survive; we continue to seek something greater, to run for roses.

“Cheese!!!” 12-year-old me exclaimed, smiling wide and hugging my then-best friend. 6th-grade graduation was a beautiful moment, the end to an amazing first chapter of my schooling journey. Even so, with each photo I took, and each friend I greeted with a smile, more tears left my eyes, a deep sadness pooling inside. My life might as well have ended at that graduation. After 6th grade, I was registered to go to a middle school where none of my friends at the time were enrolled. At that point, in my mind, I was truly alone. The truth of the matter though was that my sister and parents were walking me to the car, leading me to the next chapter of my life.

Years later, as I stared down the 12-page Google doc, an inexplicable urge to slam my desk brewed. This couldn’t be happening, not again. At the end of the document read one last message from my former friend, “I’m sorry guys”. I can’t remember exactly what went on between my friend and his girlfriend, but one thing I know for certain, is I had lost once again. I had, for all intents and purposes, died, and it wasn’t any easier the second time. Despite all the troubles I had in my once tight-knit circle, a Discord message popped up at the bottom of my screen, reading “LoL in 5?” Nothing could have put a smile on my face faster.

I just saw him yesterday. Was he waiting for me? I still had so much to say; so much I didn’t know how to say. Sitting hunched over in my seat adding salt to my pho broth was not my proudest moment, but weeping felt natural. Surrounded by my aunts and uncles, I looked up to see red noses, puffy eyes, and… smiles? Something wasn’t sitting right. Now wasn’t time for happy stories; for smiles. My grandfather just passed, and his family, his own sons and daughters, were smiling? I couldn’t help but struggle to choke out the words “How can you smile right now?” Idle chatter stopped, and all of a sudden, everything made sense. “How could we cry right now? It’d make him sad.” So sure, he wasn’t here with us, but I wasn’t so alone, was I? Not in spirit; not in my heart. Not with my family, friends, and grandpa behind me.

So maybe my “death” was exaggerated; maybe I was a little blind to my surroundings, but who hasn’t been? It was hard, after all, to look around and realize everyone I needed was right there. Sure I lost friends, but snipping the bud left room for beautiful flowers. I lost family, but who says they lost sight of me. How could I ever be dead with the love surrounding me keeping my heart pumping? With those who matter by my side, I fully intend to make the most of my future. I see drifting apart from friends and losing loved ones all as a part of being alive, but carrying their love is enough for me to shoot for the stars. Enough to find success; to run for the roses that I know they would want me to reach, and do something they would be proud of with their love.

A silent burden.

These are the words I once used to describe my time chauffeuring my little brother. Red lights blurred into stop signs, and the patchy asphalt roads seemed never-ending. I would find myself hoping the traffic would clear, ready to escape the monotonous routine of an exhausting role.

One afternoon, as I was surveying the sea of traffic at a red light, the rapid motion of my brother’s thumb against his fingerprint-covered iPhone momentarily caught my gaze. Shorts flashed across his screen briefly, the audio faintly detectable through his blasting earbuds. At home, I would notice the pattern repeat with the TV, ending with his Chromebook before bed.

This realization took me back to 8th grade, when online school during COVID pulled me into a cycle of social media and video games, leaving me isolated with a difficult addiction starting in 9th grade. Seeing my brother walk a similar path alarmed me; I didn’t want him to struggle with the same sense of isolation that once impacted me.

Determined to make a change, I dove into research, scouring Google late at night for solutions to social media addiction. Studies showing how constant scrolling could rewire the brain scared, yet simultaneously fascinated me; from the thinning of the prefrontal cortex to the ability to read emotions dulling over time. The subtle ways YouTube pulled us in with tailored recommendations, while Instagram pushed dopamine-triggering visuals, became a puzzle I obsessed over not just solving, but re-engineering.

Eager to put my research into action, his initial skepticism halted me. Countless promises his current homepage would not be damaged finally wore him down. That evening, we jumped to work, armed with his phone and Chromebook at our dining table; dissecting his feed, and analyzing creators he followed like puzzle pieces. I taught him how to "like" with intention, and how to save only posts that added genuine value. Each refresh of the screen felt like a small victory as we chipped away at the noise that once dominated his homepage. We threw out mindless videos and hunted for new creators that sparked his curiosity (though we kept some Minecraft Youtubers at his insistence). By midnight, we were satisfied with his social media page, which now reflected the content he wanted over what the algorithms fed him.

As these regulations became a reality, our car rides changed over time. One day it was a battleground for friendly debates, my brother challenging me on whether Drake’s introspective lyrics or Kendrick’s raw storytelling reigned supreme. I learned of his lifetime devotion to the silhouette of Air Forces, while I argued the timeless appeal of Jordan 1s. When we weren’t debating, we shared stories. I’d confess being stuck on mastering a piano melody for weeks, and he’d counter with his admittance of a failed gym lift.

As time passed, the impact of our new adventures gradually spread to new corners of my life. My father’s forehead lines faded as we laughed about his childhood memories over ritual evening chess games. My mother’s stress over her father’s health slowly subsided as the scent of biryani filled our kitchen, and my grandfather and I shared stories over simmering pots.

I realized the adventures with my brother were paid; simply in a currency I wasn’t familiar with.

I am relentlessly grateful for car rides with my younger brother, as they showed me our daily routines are our greatest place for growth; the predictable moments in our lives are chances for us to alter their meaning over time. Our quests serve as an invaluable blueprint for transforming a predictable routine into unpredictable moments of enjoyment. I’ve learned to spot “car rides” everywhere now. As I move to the next stages of my life, I look forward to seeking the meaning of every moment.

I take pride in knowing they will never be a “silent burden.”

I had been humbled. Put in my place by, of all creatures on this Earth, a grumpy little rat who'd trade my left kidney for a frozen pea if given the opportunity.

Amidst my everyday chores at Irvine Nature Center as a devoted intern... brushing away the poop pellets in the guinea pig enclosure whilst they squeaked indignantly at me, speaking gently to the disgruntled box turtles as I treated them for shell rot....She was always lurking in the back corner of the Animal Care Room.

Casper was one of the rats we were fostering while her owner was overseas. Testy and skittish (but with the tiny brain of a beeswax polished coconut and her stupidly adorable looks), I and the other staff members would often catch her staring at nothing. On days when she didn't seem like a cryptic prophet burdened with knowledge of the universe, she jumped at the slightest sounds and touch, making a snack out of our fingers (and her poor sister, Peach's rear end).

To the naked eye, it was obvious that Casper was albino. However, the lack of pigment that comes with albinism also affects vision. After running a few tests (mostly consisting of us waving our hands in front of her face and getting no response), we realized that this was certainly the case with our little diva.

Casper struggled with vision impairment, if not complete blindness.

That was when it began to click. Casper wasn't aggressive because she was inherently mean...but because she was frightened. It was no wonder she jumped at sudden, loud noises, no wonder she never liked being grabbed or picked up without warning...to her? That was the equivalent of being snatched up by a possible predator. Who wouldn't fight back in her situation?

She just wanted to feel safe, and she, like any creature - big or small, 'insignificant' or not - deserved to feel safe. I wanted to become what nobody else had managed to become for her yet. A protector.

I was advised against investing too much time into this little 'project' of mine. After all, when I began working with them, Peach and Casper didn't have much longer before their owner came to pick them up. Plus, bonding with such an aggressive personality would cost me plenty of precious time (not to mention a whole box of my beloved Ninja Turtle Band-Aids).

But if Casper taught me anything? It was that the most rewarding experiences don't always come easy.

As we began to work together, we developed our own little 'system' after a few weeks. During my lunch break, for about 30 minutes per workday, I would sit quietly in front of her cage, only speaking in a whisper. I tapped the cage door three times in a row, the vibrations letting her know that I was approaching and that I was going to let her out.

The most tedious part was helping her gain the courage to step up onto my hand. Instead of grabbing her suddenly, as I had done before, I wanted her to feel as though she had control in the situation.

She wasn't sure what to do first. One foot, run to the back of the cage... come back, two feet, good girl, treat. It was new and scary for both of us (she had never befriended a human before, nor had I ever befriended a rat).

The day I became the first person to hold her without gloves, to have her willingly step up onto my hand whilst giving me kisses in the form of gentle licks... well...

I had been humbled. Put in my place by, of all creatures on this Earth, a tenacious little rat who taught me the value of patience and tenderness better than any human I had ever met.

The electrodes on my father’s freshly-shaved abdomen transmitted an undulating waveform onto my screen. I leaned over, connecting him to my creation—a patchwork of transistors, microcontrollers, and circuit boards, all powered by a 9-volt battery.

The device I was testing was supposed to trigger contractions in his stomach muscles using transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation—big words that mean gently shocking the skin. If it worked, I’d be closer to addressing a disease that affects 2% of the world. But for six days, the lines on my screen stubbornly showed me the same thing: nothing.

The idea, now hanging by a thread, got its genesis on my patio. While researching gastrointestinal issues I stumbled upon gastroparesis. Patients waiting for their stomachs to digest food endure chronic discomfort, but treatments are invasive and expensive. I was convinced I could build something better: an affordable, non-invasive device that could drastically improve the quality of life for millions.

This desire to find a human-centered solution was a departure from my earlier work. Past projects focused on machine learning for tissue analysis and arrhythmia detection—significant, but without human connection. I wanted a way to directly improve lives. It became clear that my next step wasn’t about refining algorithms, but about chasing the chance to impact daily life. And with that realization, my focus sharpened.

However, my path was riddled with obstacles. Validating the device required human testing, which is expensive and required informed consent, amongst countless other legalities. Fortunately, my mom, dad, and brother were free, “consented,” and unlikely to sue me. So, I zapped my family.

By day seven, my optimism had worn thin. Still, I connected the electrodes, tweaked the settings, and watched the same lifeless data flash across the screen. As usual, I pressed ‘enter,’ bracing for disappointment as the LEDs flickered in a familiar rhythm. My computer triggered the electrical pulse, perfectly coordinated to the tissue and nerve composition. I expected hours of tedium. Then, something unexpected happened.

On my monitor, I saw clear, undeniable spikes in stomach contractions. My dad, still in his chair, remained oblivious. But on my screen, the proof was clear. The undulations, the ones I’d come to dread, were replaced by sharp, unmistakable peaks—peaks of success.

Sharing my results with other researchers earned me a spot in a Harvard Medical School lab, where I’m developing an advanced version of my device. It’s a small, robotic pill, as easy to swallow as a vitamin but as powerful as surgery. Once in the small intestine, it records and stimulates electrical signals, offering a non-invasive treatment for gastrointestinal disorders.

At Harvard, the evaluation environment was starkly different. Instead of my father, who happily retired from his role as a 170-pound guinea pig, I moved on to a 400-pound pig. The sterile hum of machines, the acrid smell of cauterized flesh, and the cold precision of surgical instruments replaced the familiar warmth of my living room. Still, I felt a strange déjà vu.

Although 3,110 miles from home, the experimental procedures were similar. With the pill already in the intestine, I adhered its electrodes to the tissue. I monitored the sluggish waves on the screen, still waiting for the moment of truth. The setting had changed, but the process—including the nervous focus—had not.

My transcontinental exploration of the gut has taught me that science doesn’t care where it unfolds. The beauty of bootstrap science is that it transcends environments. While million-dollar experiments that win Nobel Prizes are inspiring, there’s equal potential in Isaac Newton waiting for an apple to hit him on the head.

To me, what matters is the drive to pursue solutions that improve society, regardless of the setting. Turning a sketch on my patio to a clinically viable device, I’ve learned firsthand that a 9-volt battery, consenting parents and a little ingenuity are all you need to start creating solutions that advance science and touch lives.

“My body is my enemy,” I often thought as it waged an invisible war.

At eleven, a routine check-up led to a life-changing diagnosis: Ulcerative Colitis, a chronic Inflammatory Bowel Disease with no cure. Initially, we dismissed the diagnosis because my symptoms were mild. However, my life soon revolved around medications, flare-ups, and hospital visits, while juggling school and enduring severe pain. Steroids provided only temporary relief, leading to the daunting suggestion of biologics—our last option before surgery. Each bathroom trip chipped away at my hope, pushing me toward a more holistic approach.

The kitchen became my laboratory as I immersed myself in research: reviewing studies, clinical trials, and alternative diets. Maria Chiara Mentella’s work on diet and gut health, and Dr. Allan Desmond’s studies on plant-based diets, fueled my determination. My experiments began with a challenging two-week juice-only diet, and I gradually transitioned through various structured plans like the IBD-AID and Modified Specific Carbohydrate Diet. Consulting with nutritionists and IBD specialists nationwide, I remained committed despite early failures, focusing on anti-inflammatory and microbiome-healing foods.

After six years of steadfast discipline, I achieved clinical remission. My journey taught me that complex problems don’t have simple solutions, but perseverance and thoughtful analysis lead to victory. This experience not only healed my body but also shaped my mindset.

Returning to my social and academic life, I applied this resilience beyond health. Joining community initiatives, I advocated for nutritional awareness, sharing my insights to aid others in their journeys. This narrative of perseverance and research-driven solutions reflects my dedication to solving complex challenges through a holistic lens, preparing me for a career in medicine where I aspire to explore the intricacies of the gut microbiome and its impacts.

This journey illuminated that confronting adversity with determination transforms challenges into opportunities for growth—a mindset I carry forward as I step into a future of medical exploration and discovery.

“[Name], I don’t want to lose you to the Math/Science Department.”

Mr. Fokken’s words lingered as I turned away from his office, my back facing three years of dedication in the Music Department. “But, if you do leave, remember this: In STEM, a lot of things are yes or no, right or wrong, 1 or 0. But in music, correctness is a spectrum.” As a naive freshman, I thought, “so what?”

Turns out, this reminder would redefine me in music and STEM.

The Practice Room:

How do I synchronize my piano solo with the violin and cello’s parallel scales? From years of soloistic practicing, the “correct” solution was to slap on the metronome to our playing. Here, however, my independence clashed with my peers who usually played in groups. I thought of a similar situation: 8 cellists each trying to sync with the other strings. In that case, I as the principal chair had to not only worry about my own playing but also non-verbal communication between the other principal chairs. Sometimes it was an eyebrow raise from the more soloistic violinist; other times it was a subtle breath towards the violist. Recycling this concept, I used my independence to become a mini conductor for our trio. When it was my turn to solo, I’d shoot a glance towards the violinist whose orchestral experience could easily pass it to the cellist. At the end of each phrase, this pulse would continue, keeping the harmony together.

Now, rather than only pivoting on my own skills in group efforts, I always try to improvise a strategy where everyone can use their strengths to form a cohesive result. For example, in the lab, rather than just using excel (my trusty data-crunching sidekick) for data presentation, I’ll try to draw easy to read flow charts or talk through pathways depending on whoever is working with me.

The Science Center:

How do you teach a 6-year-old about the moon craters without boring a 16-year-old? The script I had on hand told me to “define an asteroid and its impact on the moon.” So, I lectured. Unsurprisingly, the toddler just played with the demo sand while his older brother stared at the wall. As the awkwardness loomed, I paused as I was about to pick up the two marbles. Abandoning my rehearsed script, I confidently said “Let’s all make a fist.” Clenching my hand, I softly hit the sand. “Your turn!” They each pummeled their fists down to make craters, each of a different size. Despite my big hands, my crater was still smaller than the toddler’s. I asked, “Why is that?” The older brother, intrigued, started to explain the importance of impact speed. Soon, we experimented with different objects, sizes and speeds, creating all sorts of craters. By setting aside the script, I had opened a door to hundreds of ways of facilitating the program, each for its own unique recipient.

Motivated to share these possibilities, as a Teen Leader, I make sure to tailor each lesson for newcoming volunteers to their own strengths. For example, I guided Terrence, an incoming volunteer who was more on the shy end like me, to make meaningful 1-to-1 connections with guests. As for his brother Eric who was more outgoing, we challenged ourselves by doing demos for field trips with dozens of kids.

All my life, I’ve always strived for improvement—self-improvement. But when it comes to working with others, rigid solutions never fit perfectly. That said, even the best solutions don’t fit perfectly. My trio struggled with technically difficult sections which ultimately relied on solo metronome practice. As a science volunteer, we must still define the demo’s facilitation and goals. However, once more people are inevitably involved, those independent solutions might not work anymore. And, as I transition into college, I want to continue improvising harmony through chaos, combing through solutions until I find one that works with everyone.

I've always been drawn to the shadows. As a child, I'd squint at the spaces between streetlights, convinced that the real magic happened just beyond the reach of illumination. This fascination followed me into adolescence, where I discovered science fiction—not as an escape, but as a flashlight. Authors like Ursula K. Le Guin and Mary Shelly became my guides, showing me how to probe the darkness without dispelling it entirely.

Two centuries ago at Lake Geneva, Mary Shelley, in the company of accomplished male writers several years her senior, was spurred by a dare to tell a ghost story—a story that would become Frankenstein. What was at first just a middle school literary obsession soon became a text I brought into my own science, embodying the balance between the allure of the unknown and the pursuit of knowledge.

It was this delicate balance I tried to maintain when I joined a bioengineering competition at UC Berkeley with my school’s science team during my freshman year. Our challenge: congenital pulmonary stenosis – a condition where infant hearts labored against their own anatomy, valves narrowed by nature's capricious hand. Around me, upperclassmen traded polysyllabic terms, their expertise a constant reminder of my novice status.

I listened to my teammates discuss current treatments, each of which meant a lifetime tethered to the operating table for the patient, a Promethean punishment for the crime of being born with a faulty heart. In our desperation to find a solution, the prevailing attitude seemed to be one of resignation, a collective shrug that seemed to say: this was simply the best we could do. I was determined to be the person who didn’t simply shrug.

Driven by this determination, I dove into scientific literature. Cardiology journals became my bedtime reading, tissue-engineering papers my lunchtime companions. But my preparation went beyond reading. As I experimented with the prototype, using computer-aided-design (CAD) software I'd taught myself in stolen moments between classes, I thought about Mary Shelley. She, too, had dared to imagine a world where the boundaries between known and unknown, between life and death, were not immutable. Her creature wasn't a triumph of illumination, but a reminder of the mysteries that persist even in our most ambitious creations.

The solution began to take shape in my mind: a heart valve that wasn't just a mechanical fix, but a collaboration between man and machine. I envisioned a device that would grow throughout the recipient’s lifetime, providing a crucial element for pediatric patients while having innocuous effects on adults. While explaining my proposal, I saw my teammates’ initial skepticism give way to cautious interest. Leveraging the CAD program I had taught myself in the days prior, I led our team in refining the design, exploring stress distribution and fluid dynamics. We used computational fluid dynamics simulations to model blood flow through various valve designs, noticing that each iteration was a balancing act—too rigid, and the valve wouldn't adapt; too flexible, and it risked failure under pressure. I created spreadsheets comparing tensile strengths and inflammatory responses, turning our desk into a command center for a five-person bioengineering division.

The day of the competition came with little fanfare. We didn't win that year. But when one of the judges, a UCSF cardiothoracic surgeon, came up to me and said, "I'm sold," I felt a surge of vindication. His recognition was more than a consolation prize. It gave me confidence that I was on the right path, proving that innovation thrives when we embrace mystery, regardless of experience or academic background.

As a first-generation college applicant and aspiring engineer, I carry with me the lesson of that long-ago summer in Lake Geneva – a reminder that innovation knows no pedigree. We live in an age desperate to deny magic, to unravel every thread of mystery. But in our quest to illuminate every shadow, we risk losing the very magic that drives innovation. In my future studies and career, I envision developing systems that seamlessly interface between humanity and technology, bridging the gap between shadows and light, always ready to explore what lies just beyond our reach.

The traditional example of the butterfly effect is the flap of a butterfly’s wings causing a hurricane. My own butterfly effect started with a bike ride. A few years ago, I was looking for more ways to train for cross country, and I settled on biking. It was a logical conclusion: I could introduce variety into my training schedule, go easy on my muscles to avoid injury, and I had a fantastic bike, complete with a bell in the shape of a marshmallow. In addition to designing a training regimen, I was motivated by a desire to escape. I entered the summer wanting nothing more than to be somewhere else, bitter about the fact that my small and sequestered hometown placed the world out of my reach. So starting in May, I biked on Mondays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, and after a few weeks, I started biking by my friends’ houses to say hello. When I told them why I was riding, some of them asked to join to socialize and train for their own sports, and a group formed - the butterfly effect took place.

As the time spent biking turned from weeks to months, my friends and I unearthed a treasure trove. First was the Greek restaurant with walls covered in colorful drapes and landscape paintings and shelves full of baskets of beaded bracelets that customers could buy. Next was the antique store with a terrifying hidden room dedicated to old dolls. However, our ultimate discovery was a pond hidden in the woods behind a skate park. I was still insistent that I was missing out, but it only strengthened my determination to explore. When I began to see my city in a different light, it shocked me. For all my frustration, it had never occurred to me that I didn’t need to go somewhere else to experience the world. I just needed to look outside.

And look outside I did. Wanting to share my passion for learning, I organized study sessions with my classmates at Panera, and wanting to meet new people with new perspectives, I joined speech and debate. My eagerness to improve and meet the rest of the people competing in my district led me to a week long camp the summer after my second competition year. I devoured every learning opportunity that the camp provided and practiced until I had dreams about doing drills. Meanwhile, the courage that I had built years ago to explore the uncharted outskirts of my city helped me foster and maintain connections with the intimidatingly talented people attending with me. My decision to go on a bike ride had now led to some of my favorite memories, and to some of my lifelong friends. Eventually, I even got to travel more, and that desire has not faded. However, I know that I will enjoy every new place and experience more than I would have if I hadn’t discovered my home first.

Just as a butterfly can cause a hurricane, bike rides that were intended to be exercise can change someone’s life. Even after my friends and I got too busy to bike together, the recollections of deep conversations while skipping stones and fixing broken bike gears on the side of the road are a source of happiness and nostalgia for us. The rides were also, on one hand, a catalyst that deepened my curiosity of what the future has to offer and my desire to explore it. I’ve always loved to learn, but these experiences showed me the true excitement of discovering where my decisions lead. On the other hand, they were a source of an invaluable sense of perspective. I know, without a doubt, that I want to explore. However, I can also be content with where my life is, because I know that no matter what, I will find my way to where I’m supposed to be.

As I walked into the library, my palms were sweating and my legs were trembling, ready to collapse at any moment. I was heading to my AP seminar presentation, and although I spent a week practicing, I felt uncharacteristically unprepared. From the moment I stood before the class, everything began to unravel. I fumbled through my opening lines; my voice was shaky and barely comprehensible. When the teacher began asking questions, my heart pounded so loudly that I could hardly focus on what she was saying. The answers I had memorized vanished, and I stood there humiliated. As I walked out of the room, the weight of the embarrassment destroyed me.

The night after the presentation, I took a moment to really reflect on myself. I’ve always felt hindered by a fear of speaking to others, whether it was public speaking, or engaging in a one-on-one conversation with someone I didn’t know. The embarrassment from earlier lingered into the night—I knew something had to change. My first instinct was to turn to the internet for answers. I went to YouTube and looked up “how to speak more confidently in public.” I came across a lot of content, but none seemed to cover my problem. However, this information gap helped me uncover something. My fear came from deeper insecurities. I wasn’t just afraid of speaking. I was afraid of what people would think about me if I made a mistake. I was afraid of how I looked in others’ eyes. After hours of research and reflection, I encountered an unexpected recurring piece of advice in the videos: go to the gym. I didn’t understand how working out could help build my confidence, but I decided to try it.

After a few months in the gym, I began noticing subtle changes in myself. I didn’t wake up every day with a rush of confidence, but each week brought small improvements. I began to hold my head higher, and holding eye contact didn’t seem so daunting. At school, I found myself making conversations with classmates I had never spoken to before–something that usually was intimidating. However, it wasn’t always easy. Some days I would default back to keeping my head down and avoiding small talk when it didn’t seem convenient. But with each workout, the small changes started to add up.

This newfound confidence started to extend beyond school and the gym. When I first started volunteering at Habitat of Humanity, I was only there to complete my tasks and go home. But as weeks went by, I began engaging more with the customers and fellow volunteers. One day, I encountered a machine I didn’t know how to use. Normally, I would have felt too embarrassed to ask for help, but I approached the older volunteers instead. These little changes in how I would act boosted my confidence. I noticed that each time I set a small goal to step outside my comfort zone, my confidence grew a little more. This reinforced the lesson I learned from working out: small changes can have an immense impact on personal growth.

Towards the end of junior year, I decided I wanted to study finance. The fast-paced and challenging environment of the major intrigued me. The same principles that helped me conquer my insecurities will help me navigate through a finance major as well. Additionally, my newfound confidence will help me engage in classroom activities, build strong connections with my peers, and embrace the many academic challenges that will come my way.

Looking back, that presentation wasn’t a failure but a turning point. Working out pushed me to take control of the things about which I felt most insecure and develop confidence I never thought possible. Whether in the gym, the classroom, or my future career, I know how to approach challenges with determination and a focus on small, daily improvements. The discipline and perseverance I’ve gained from this journey will guide me and help me succeed in college and beyond.

Every May, the bushes across my boarding house slowly fill up with bloomed peonies. Their bright pink petals are a joyful proclamation of the arrival of summer. I am drawn to the flower I was named after, the “king of flowers” in Chinese culture, because of its unyielding spirit and restorative properties.

My name has always been a source of discomfort for me. I resented how teachers often mispronounced it, and its peculiarity made me stand out in my early adolescent years. But it wasn’t until I found myself at a new boarding school in Sevenoaks, England, a staggering 9,532km from home, that I truly despised it.

Like a bee in a field devoid of flowers, I felt lost in classes and clubs. Instead of being a peony, I just wanted to blend in with the roses. Hailing from different cultures and having no idea how to relate to each other, I found myself experiencing a whirlwind of discomfort sharing a room with five other girls.

My roommate, Alex, who was from Romania, often spoke in her native language, using words like "scuze" and "nu inteleg." I found myself staring back at her, completely clueless about what she meant. However, one late night, I returned to our room to find Alex visibly upset. It was then that she confided in me about the challenges of navigating and adapting to this new environment. Drawing inspiration from the resilient qualities of the peony, I reminded her that discomfort often presents an opportunity for growth and learning.

As I engaged with my Romanian roommate, I not only learned about the rich cultural traditions of her homeland, such as the Martisor festival, but also got to taste traditional dishes like Ciobor. To my surprise, I found striking similarities between Ciobor and the Cantonese-style Oxtail Borscht I grew up with. Late-night conversations with my roommate became moments of solace, fostering a sense of belonging and warmth. Through these exchanges, I learned the value of overcoming discomfort with curiosity and the rewards of perseverance in the face of fear.

A few years later, I found myself utilizing the properties of the peony flower once again. This time, on a much bigger stage: the London Olympic Pool. Under the torrential downpour, tensions had flared up among my teammates over relay orders. In an effort to diffuse the conflict, I turned to the calming properties of the [Name]. I lightened the mood by making a lighthearted joke about our swim caps, and then I pointed out Anjola's impressive split, suggesting that she take the lead in the upcoming relay. Recognizing Amelia's exceptional endurance in the 400 IM, I proposed that she take the 4th place spot. After taking everyone's input into consideration, we finally reached a consensus with just 2 minutes to spare. Five minutes later, we made history by clinching the Bath and Otter Cup, standing united as a team. Once again, the [Name] flower had worked its magic.

Regardless of the superstitions that plague me or the fears that haunt me, I believe in my power and heritage to make others feel empowered, heard, and healed. These new and different ideas about belonging and understanding, and skills about adapting and persevering, are the soil that has enabled me to foster an environment of support and acceptance of diverse perspectives and knowledge everywhere I go. The opportunity to join different communities in sports, culture, and arts in college will only expand my ability to think with open-mindedness and my knowledge of the power of healing and empowerment.

In July, my dad visited me at school, and I pointed out a peony I saw. He insisted it was a rose. In fact, it is a Paeonia lactiflora hybrid: a [Name] Rose Mix. Scarcely showing the first signs of sprouting, its determination promises a breathtaking flower once its individual loosely folded petals come together, surrounding the bud.

“If you could define your life in one word, what would it be,” my 11th-grade French Teacher asked.

“Change.”

Uprooted frequently growing up, I navigated the uncertainty of new beginnings; each move became an opportunity to learn resilience and adaptation. Strong friendships were my foundation.

My earliest memory of Lucas was a violent embrace when, as toddlers, I hugged him so tightly that we both tumbled to the ground. As each other’s first friends, we never expected anything from each other except ourselves. One year, I remember breaking the sword from his knight costume just before trick-or-treating. Fear consumed me as I confessed. But he simply smiled and said, "It's okay."

The comfort I felt from our time together helped me understand the value of empathy and kindness. As a leader in my school’s senior band and music program, I aspired to share this insight with others. Whether it be staying a couple of hours after Wind Ensemble to help Sihan with his solo or waking up at 6:00 to set up chairs for Symphonic Band, I always kept Lucas in mind.

In grade four, our family moved closer to my ailing grandparents. On my first day at school, I saw Eddie sitting alone, mustered the courage to introduce myself, and we quickly bonded over Pokémon. Growing up, I struggled academically because of anxiety and waning confidence. One day, however, after another painful science class, Eddie asked me if I needed help. He answered my questions about why animals only eat certain foods and what happens to those without predators. He gave up his recess to help me understand and explained in accessible ways my teacher had not.

Eddie showed me that I was capable of succeeding if only removed from the pressured environment of the classroom. Ever since, I’ve been motivated to create a community where people can receive the same support. Now, when I see students thriving in my free tutoring program, I feel fulfilled having paid Eddie’s goodwill forward.

On my first day at a new high school, I remember hearing a booming voice from the corner of my English class. Nelson was loud, assertive, and everything else I wasn’t. That’s why the first time I saw his vulnerable side was so memorable. He had received a bad mark on his English test and broke down, opening up to me about the pressure he was feeling from his parents and himself. I comforted him, reminding him that we can only give our best and that it’s okay if we’re not always perfect.

During our time together, I’ve seen Nelson slowly let go of his performance-oriented values of self-worth and how it’s helped his effervescent smile return. Throughout my life, I’d always focused on learning from others, but Nelson helped me realize I also had something to give. As I progressed throughout high school, our friendship gave me newfound confidence to meet other people, encouraging me to support others as a Captain of our debate team and leader on our school’s fencing team and wellness council.

My life has been filled with transitions—new schools, new experiences, and new friends. I used to worry I was losing people every time I moved rather than seeing it as an opportunity to add new layers that could enrich my previous relationships.

In college, I look forward to joining a new community in Public Policy where I can meet like-minded individuals passionate about combating social issues. In this new environment, I will use the kindness I learned from Lucas, the support I received from Eddie, the confidence I gained from Nelson, and my own learnings to create new relationships. I no longer fear change, I look forward to it!

Sitting center-stage, my hands form a visor to shield my eyes from the audience. Six sheets rest before me, filled with intimate details of fictional strangers; birthdays, favorite foods, and addresses wait to be absorbed into memory. Soon, the judge will collect the papers and ask me a question about the face on the TV. The beet-haired man with freckles splashed across his cheeks stares at me from the screen. *Is that Samuel or Sebastian?*

Progressing from memorizing pi to participating in memory competitions, I found a hunger for training my brain. However, this passion became far more personal as I watched my grandmother fade away. Her growing silence marked her peaceful retreat as her memories succumbed to dementia. Memorization became a way to shape a biologically determined function that she lost control of. I can neither barcode-scan strings of digits nor recall what I ate for breakfast two mornings ago; achieving abnormal feats with a normal brain proved to myself that my ceiling wasn’t limited.

As a memory athlete, my fascination with organizing information through systems formed my second home: my memory palace. In my head, my house is segmented into fifty marked locations. While memorizing, I streamline the data—words, cards, names, digits, and people—into images to place at each locus. Then, during recall, my mind saunters through my palace to decode each image.

Advancing in competitive memory pushed me to refine my foundational techniques. I initially experimented with audio in my palace, but it left me with a headache-inducing cacophony impossible to decode. However, I found the more bizarre the image was, the better I could visualize and retain it. An image of a “tall male” in my palace transformed from a six-foot man to a living colossus, his elongated head jutting through the foyer ceiling.

Remembering my grandmother’s battle, I wondered how my practice creating memory techniques could relate to memory loss. After researching cognitive training, I found that the same principles I employed in competitions were developed into training programs; my knowledge could be applied to prevent memory decline. Over six months, I worked with professors involved in memory research. We combined insights from memory training studies and my experience as a memory athlete to tailor weekly training sessions. We incorporated a variety of cognitive exercises focused on memory and reasoning that suited seniors in assisted living.

As I volunteered, I quickly learned that each senior had unique strengths like me. Louise Higginbotham was no exception—a 68-year-old woman with silver curls that framed her face and an endless supply of meandering stories. Initially, I introduced body parts as locations for participants’ memory palaces, but Louise struggled to differentiate the apple on her ankle from the grape on her knee. She'd scrunch her eyes with her lips pressed tight, yet the two remained jumbled.

Sensing her frustration, I realized I needed to adjust her memory techniques just as I had adapted my own. I turned to her favorite story topic—her job at the local church. I asked if she remembered her morning drive. Without hesitation, she recalled every detail: passing the bakery on Cedar Street, the winding road flanked by pine trees, and the sneaky pothole by the park. Once we anchored her memory palace along the route, everything clicked; her fruit salad became an unclouded journey.

Witnessing dementia steal my grandma’s vibrant smile revealed the painful truths of memory. Watching Louise relive her youth displayed memory’s heartwarming joys. Understanding the mind has offered me a space for gaining emotional reflection and empathy while fostering meaningful connections. Though in opposite stages of our lives, Louise and I have shared a common path. I discovered how learning from each other through our differences holds the power to shape both of our journeys. During her next never-ending story, hopefully she’ll teach me how to make my morning waffles unforgettable. Maybe then, I’ll remember what I ate for breakfast.

I shake my head, tapping my right thumb sideways on my chest. “I’m fine.” As a hearing-impaired person, my grandmother’s voice goes unheard—something she has dealt with her whole life. Her eyes soften, and she signs back, “Okay,” calling me in for a tight hug.

Despite this barrier, I’ve always been close to my grandmother. During my first year at the Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy, I was tasked with giving a speech about somebody close to me. Of course, I chose to talk about her.

But as I made my way to the front of the class, my legs quivered, the microphone slipping in my sweaty grip. The expectant gazes of the audience pierced through me as I opened my mouth, only to hear my voice emerge as a feeble whisper. Later at lunch, my friend thrust a vibrant flier into my hands, the bold letters TALENT, representing our entrepreneurship club, offering a glimmer of hope.

TALENT challenged me to identify a problem faced by my community. Thinking about my grandmother, an idea came to mind. I raised my hand and shared, “What if there was a Google Translate for sign language?” My idea was met positively, but some students questioned the feasibility, “Is that even possible?” I admitted that I didn’t know, but decided to try anyway.

I called it SignAll. With my background in app development, I excitedly began building my first prototype. However, initial versions of our AI struggled, “thank you” was read as “banana.” Although perhaps suitable for primates (or minions), this wouldn’t suffice for humans. Bringing on some friends, we spent hours refining code, debugging errors, and reading research papers, hoping to find a solution.

After realizing our initial approach wasn’t effective, I contacted our local sign language school for advice. Seeing their expressive signing, I found our missing ingredient. Our algorithm was missing facial expressions—nuances critical to the understanding of sign language. Incorporating these non-verbal cues into our algorithm was a breakthrough.

Powered by this new approach, SignAll evolved from a concept to a working translator. I knew who our first user had to be. As I handed my grandmother the first demo, her eyes gleamed with excitement. I saw the smile on her face grow as the app worked—her voice was finally heard.

As we grew, SignAll received feedback from thousands worldwide, excited to join our beta program. From fast-food companies up to special dating apps, we heard from businesses who wanted to use SignAll to reach their customers. This helped me realize the full impact of what I had built: not just an app with innovative technology, but a bridge for people who had long been excluded from conversations. My experience with SignAll reaffirmed my belief that technology should serve not only as a convenience, but as a tool to help people find their voice.

Ironically, in building SignAll, I discovered a voice of my own. Whether I was presenting it to the ASL community, pitching on international platforms like the Taco Bell Ambition Accelerator, or simply working as a tutor, each experience strengthened my voice. Now, I speak confidently, eager to share my passion.

With this growing desire to give back, I founded a branch of the Young Coder’s Initiative (YCI). At YCI, I helped teach the same technologies behind SignAll to over 100 underprivileged middle schoolers across Chicagoland, guiding them to find their unique voices through code.

Looking ahead to college, I’m eager to bring the same passion for problem-solving to new challenges. Whether working in the lab, leading service initiatives, or rallying my peers at football games, I want to foster a sense of community and help others find their own voice—just as SignAll helped me find mine.

Participating in the world’s longest raft race gave me unexpected insights that reshaped my understanding of what success truly means. The Great Amazon River Raft Race is a competition that pushes participants beyond their limits. With only a self-built raft and four paddles, we faced the unpredictability of the Amazon River for 111 miles over three days. After two years of preparation, I was committed to completing the race.

On our first day, we reached the checkpoint as planned. However, on the second day, our raft began sinking when a porous log started absorbing water. This setback affected me deeply, and I pushed myself and my team to turn the situation around. Thirteen hours passed, daylight faded, and the fear of not reaching the checkpoint before being towed tormented me. With just one mile to go and my teammates losing hope, I found the strength to row alone for another 20 minutes. But it wasn’t enough, and the rescue boat eventually came to tow us. Despite my reluctance, my teammates and the race officials persuaded me to accept the help. As we were towed, I noticed my muscles cramping and my hands bleeding.

That night, I realized I had pushed my teammates too hard.

The following day, sore muscles and blistered hands felt insignificant compared to my emotional burden. We gathered for an honest conversation, and I sincerely apologized for the previous day's intensity. My teammates, without resentment, encouraged me to focus on the next rafting day, and I was determined not to let it happen again.

Driven to change and rebuild team unity, I lost interest in our final race position. For the first time in more than eight years in varsity sports, I let go of a results-oriented mentality. I decided to dedicate my last-day efforts to supporting my teammates.

As the day progressed, we battled through accumulated soreness and the sinking raft. However, the mutual support we gave each other allowed us to harness our remaining energy with every stroke. As I rowed, I felt a sense of unity that made all negativity and pain fade. We were truly a team. With thirty minutes of daylight left, we reached the checkpoint in last place, but I felt triumphant and proud. Reflecting on my feelings, I realized they stemmed from my shift in mentality. It was the effort and collaboration that filled me with satisfaction.

I learned that in life, your raft may inevitably sink, preventing you from achieving desired results. However, true success is no longer defined by outcomes, but by maximizing personal input, teamwork, and valuing everyone’s contributions. Now, I am free from anxiety and pressure regarding results, not only in sports but academically as well. I prioritize communication and healthy collaboration over any outcome.

7 years old, colored a deep shade of blue, about 1 meter tall and 2 meters wide, my bookshelf is perhaps my most treasured possession. It is the most honest representation of my life’s journey. When I look at it, I don’t just see paperbacks and hardcovers, I see the story of my own growth, told through the stories of others.

Like Santiago in The Alchemist, I am an explorer. We were sitting in the candlelit courtyard of the 500-year-old city palace in Udaipur, Rajasthan. The mood was undeniably electric as we were waiting, yet a hint of skepticism lingered in the back of my mind, echoing the disappointments of previous performances my mom had dubbed “unforgettable”.

As the first dancers emerged, my skepticism quickly faded. The vibrant colors of their costumes glimmered in the candlelight, and I watched in awe as the women twirled gracefully, balancing up to ten pots atop their headsenchanting. I was mesmerized by the fluidity of their motions, the way each dancer seemed to float, their movements precise and enchanting as the rhythm of the accompanying music pulsed in the air.

In that moment, I felt an overwhelming sense of pride was over me. I was a shy Indian kid, always afraid to say my name and self-conscious of my accent. The performance connected me to my roots in a way I had never anticipated, reminding me of my rich cultural heritage I was hesitant to embrace. When I flew back home to Abu Dhabi, I made it my mission to learn as much as possible about Indian history. From astronomy-obsessed Rajput kings to grandiose Mughal emperors to the independence struggle, I pored over every detail of my ancestry, never again afraid to embrace it.

Flash forward

Like Aza in Turtles All the Way Down, I was anxious. It was two days until my photography exam, and I had a grand total of zero ideas for my final project. “Just think, you idiot” I muttered to myself, pacing around my bedroom, desperately trying to brainstorm ideas. “I should’ve taken my camera to Udaipur” I think, regretfully. Going to the desert would take too long, architectural shots felt cliché, and landscapes were uninspired. The stress overcame me, and the all too familiar feeling of crushing pressure on my chest returned. I started spiraling, my brain running through all possible outcomes of the test, hyper analyzing my surroundings, each breath labored. My mind was rushing through a million thoughts, and to cool down, I went to get a glass of water, hoping a change of scene would bring clarity.

Then an idea hit me.

My head cleared, and I felt an odd sense of calm. I grabbed a pan from the kitchen and filled it with water. I set up the pan and my tripod on the kitchen counter. Then, using a pipette, I painstakingly squeezed out a drop of water on the pan, snapping photos in quick succession, hoping to capture the perfect splash. I started experimenting with food coloring and soda, adjusting my angles and camera settings with each shot. Anxiety forgotten and in a flow state, I took over 1000 photos that day, creating a collage of splashes as my submission for the exam. Through photography, I learned how to turn overwhelming pressure into focus, and how to conquer the chaos in my mind.

As I look toward the next chapter, college, I look at the empty space on my bookshelf and feel a sense of excitement. That space is a symbol of the books I haven’t read yet, the knowledge I have yet to gain, and the stories I haven’t experienced. I hope it will serve as a token of my life’s journey for my children or grandchildren, a reminder of the stories that have shaped me.

In Florida, I saw school library shelves go empty, as science, history and truth was labeled indoctrination. Teachers were silenced by fear of legal attack, removing family pictures from their desks, posters from their walls, and libraries from classroom shelves. My family chose to leave, because, as my mother put it, “Connecticut is warmer than Florida.”

The library in my own mind is sprawling, and slightly disorganized, with a staff consisting of a couple humans, a troop of raccoons, and some crows bustling about. Moving to Connecticut was the third time I’ve had to change high schools, and each time I got better at reorganizing to bring in the sometimes heavy stacks of new materials.

Some of the library’s shelves contain more order than entropy. In the smooth leather-bound hardcovers on calculus I expect a neat and exact answer found at the end of a clear and logical path. Methods that only approximate like limits or Riemann’s sums are usually replaced with something exact like derivatives and solvable integrals. So when I showed up last year prepared for elegant calculus, learning about things such as series that I cannot find the exact solution for was infuriating.

At other times I can enjoy being inaccurate and imperfect. I sew, and I delight in running through the aisles of loose pattern pieces, instruction manuals bookmarked with scrap fabric, and overflowing bins of half-worked ideas. When making a pair of pants recently, I indulged in the following: not pinning or tracing certain pattern pieces, not topstitching or putting a button above the zipper, and at a certain point completely ignoring the instructions. The waistband is held together with hope, but I wear them with pride and a tightly fastened belt.

I am myself when l take care to write plus c after every general integral and I am myself when I tear a chunk of fabric off a scrapped prototype to show a friend. Color makes 3D graphs readable and math turns flat fabric into curves. These different sections coexist and improve each other.

Finding a more complete view of the world involves combining disciplines and listening to a variety of perspectives, which is why in Connecticut, I am working to add to a library. As a research assistant on the LGBTQIA+ Oral History Project for the town of Ridgefield I have interviewed people who saw Ridgefield become more inclusive over the years. Without their stories on the shelves, the impact of regressive policies would be hard for many to understand. Having heard their stories I feel more hopeful about humans, our ability to change our minds, and our capacity expand to love the people around us.

While I am excited to dive into new volumes, I know being exposed to unfamiliar things can be confusing and uncomfortable. My high school path has taught me that I am temporary, and though the bonds I make can fall apart, be replaced, or reform, life continues. Understanding that mistakes and change are a part of learning makes me feel more prepared to study science and engineering. I do not know exactly where these interests will lead me, and I am still discovering the edges, smudges, and curves in the lenses I see the world through. In this next chapter I hope to develop my interests into understanding and skills needed to support others.

Twice per day at the bustling border checkpoint, a dozen kindergarteners with identical bowlcuts waddled like ducklings between home in Shenzhen and school in Hong Kong. The duckling in front–raising her voice to guide the rest through security guards as she stood on tiptoe to hand her ID to the custom's officer–was me.

I was born in 2007, a decade after the “handover” of Hong Kong to Chinese control. Despite our Hong Kong IDs and neutral position, cross-border students symbolized the encroachment of the mainland, and tensions elevated after the announcement of the controversial extradition bill. One day, a schoolmate told me I had become one of the targets of a cyber manhunt due to my bicultural identity. Peers stared at me strangely afterwards, and even my best friends avoided me at school.

During the pandemic, travel restrictions forced me to end my cross-border lifestyle and live alone in a Hong Kong subdivided flat; otherwise, I would have to spend four years studying online. “NAHH FAM!!” was the first thing I shouted out when I opened the door. Hellish stench, stained yellow bedsheets, moldy walls, and litter everywhere… There wasn’t even room for a desk. My bed was just a single mattress on top of two cardboard pallets.

Trevor Noah’s memoir was my closest friend throughout those dreadful nights. Despite being “born a crime” as biracial under South African apartheid, he showed that he was capable of bridging the gap between two distinct tribes/cultures. "I was like a chameleon," he wrote.

Maybe, so was I. I thought of the skills I learned thanks to my special identity: independence, trilingualism, even the vigor to wake up at the crack of dawn to get to school on time. I had always been made to feel like an outsider, but perhaps I never needed to “fit in” to my environment. I could shine as myself.

I spent the next two weeks refreshing the stinky flat that caged me. Then, I set out to film documentaries on other chameleons, starting with my cross-border peers then queer migrant workers. As I volunteered with cross-border families, joined line dances and even the wedding of a lesbian migrant couple, their unique ways of navigating conflicting perspectives truly struck me.

On the day I premiered my documentary on the school stage, I realized the confusion I'd grown up with was the catalyst for my journey of self-exploration.

These days, when I see another flock of students crossing the border in cheongsam, bringing 100 years of Hong Kong culture back to Shenzhen, I feel a quiet sense of hope. I believe cross-borders are the future, intimately familiar with the needs of both cultures and capable of mending strife through our multifaceted experiences. Borders are not so difficult to cross. You put one foot in front of the other.

“I want to get out.” Sarah wrote.

Sexually assaulted by her deskmate for three years in middle school, my young visitor's mother told her, “Harassment was just typical adolescent boy behavior.” Molested, stalked, and forced against her will in ways I cannot put into words, Sarah sought a community that would not dismiss her experiences as her mother pungently had.

In early 2024, Sarah visited my teen-focused online support platform, To-Listen. I knew the facts I needed to be a good companion – when dealing with trauma, the PCT client-centered support theory I had spent the previous summer studying indicated that I should listen passively, offering only attentive comments and light questions. However, faced with descriptions of behaviors so unlawful and unjust, I felt compelled to tell her that what happened wasn’t her fault.

Throughout my life, I aspired to get as close to the standard “textbook” answer in every school examination. Knowing that every question had a “perfect” solution gave me a sense of control I craved. I found comfort in the Central Limit Theorem and Schrödinger’s Wave Equation, which dictated that probability gave our world a fixed answer. In the field of Psychology, it led me to readings of PCT, Robert Salvin’s theories on educational psychology, and the development of a four-step “hello–affirm–inquiry–listen” companionship and support template.

Yet, in Sarah’s case, every textbook response seemed inadequate. I thought back to my middle school mental health classes, and how the case studies on the whiteboard encouraged sexual harassment victims to “seek support from others.” I gave the same encouragement to Sarah, but asking for support wasn’t an option for her. The boy’s actions were dismissed as childish misbehavior by the conservative culture of her small Northern Chinese town.

After five days of conversation, Sarah was not healed but better. I still followed theories like maintaining respect and confidentiality, but I also recognized the profound lack of understanding she faced. Through laws, sexual assault recourses, and hugging emojis, I tried to affirm that her feelings were justified. I knew my contributions were somewhat insignificant compared to the severity of Sarah’s situation, but seeing her replies grow longer and more confident, I felt proud of myself.

Yet, I was also deeply humbled, even uncomfortable. Sarah’s story exposed the tremendous gap between the theories I had wholeheartedly followed and the complexities of reality. It also raised questions about the efficacy and legitimacy of the platform I had dedicated myself to building for the past year.

In the next months, support for every peer I met required going beyond the standard theoretical response. I was forced and inspired to modify the four-step theoretical companionship template I had been using to train my team of companion-supporters, reintroducing it at a whole group meeting as an adaptable guideline that no longer has to be always followed. The change was initially confusing and discomforting. But seeing STEM-student volunteers like Leander’s initially formulaic, rigid responses slowly turn into genuine back-and-forth conversations filled my heart with warmth.

Our transition also exposed the cultural and regional nuances that exist across China. In interviews with Sam, a teen of Inner Mongolia’s GeLao ethnic minority facing cyberbullying, I discovered how GeLao culture was more open to disclosing personal struggles compared to Han culture, and how support could be more listening-focused as a result. In analyzing the geographical distribution of our visitors, I discovered that in a sample of 120 teens, 77% were from land-locked provinces like Guizhou with more conservative cultures relating to mental health struggles, and how support should hold a more encouraging and reassuring attitude.

Of course, self-doubt still arises from time to time. My team are not even adults, much less licensed therapists. But we try our best to offer a safe space of support, realizing that in our technologically advancing but socially distancing society, young adults may need not only medical or professional support but also companionship and community.

Every day brings new questions and challenges. As a child, I believed the right answer was the textbook solution, but today, I realize that life is too complex for fixed answers. As I approach college and beyond, I commit to always carrying the adaptive spirit instilled in me by the peers I met and the stories I heard.

At 12, while folding the corner of my notebook, I discovered a new fundamental law of the universe. Not one that wins Nobel Prizes or even applies to most people, but one that would come to define a large aspect of myself. I am always moving. Whether fidgeting with my hands or racing through thoughts in my mind, it was always true that adding the movement in my hands and mind will always sum to some positive constant. But I hated this part of myself because to me, it was defined by being unable to focus on a test because a word sent me down a winding train of thought, teachers telling me to sit properly because I was rocking in my chair, and my friends telling me I'm “somewhere on the spectrum”. So I fought it. If the movement needed to sum to some constant, I’ll let it all be in my mind, so nobody can see it.

I fell in love with butterfly knives when I first saw them in a game. It was mesmerizing to see as such a simple mechanism creates an infinite number of complex precise movements, each with their own beauty. And when I learned, it brought balance back to the equation as the constant was split again between my hands and mind. I began learning not just butterfly knives, but many other hobbies that allowed me to move my hands. Penspinning, flipping a coin on my fingers, and begleri. I even picked up cardistry after I was embarrassed that I didn't know how to do a bridge shuffle in AP Bio during an evolution lab using cards. These small hobbies gave me a way to move in a way I wasn’t embarrassed about.

As I sit in my room, I come across a video. “852 HZ” with the caption “Did the internal monologue go silent for you too?” I watch it out of curiosity. The loud high pitch sound runs for a whole minute and then it stops. I never understood what deafening silence meant until now. Time seemed to stop as the whole world stood still. The internal monologue that had been running inside my head for years had stopped. Yet despite the silence I thought I craved, I started freaking out. My movement no longer summed to the constant and the world was ending like a universal law had actually been broken. And as I panicked in silence, I realized how much this law was a part of me.

The need to move introduced me to butterfly knives, begleri and all the other hobbies I adore, sending me down deep rabbit holes for each one. Each worn page corner I fidgeted with in class symbolized my unique mind. And the need for thoughts drove the curiosity that I value as every time my train of thought reached unknown, I went online searching for answers. Random thoughts about the makeup of protons lead me to teaming up with my old friends from math competitions to learn about particle physics. Curiosity about the limits of keyboard building sent me learning Ergogen and KiCad to design my own unique keyboard PCB.
