So as I tried desperately to revive the voice in my head, I decided I would stop caring which side of the equation I would side on and accept this law with all of the downsides so it could continue to drive me to new places.

So now, when I see 3 pens on my friends desk, and am curious of what their clicks feel and sound like, I don't hesitate to check. And when they laugh at the randomness of my actions, I laugh along with them knowing the randomness was not a bad thing, but was unapologetically me.

**Essay:**

The free-spirited chirping of a bird outside my window contrasted sharply with the repetitive scales I was practicing. After six years of piano lessons, I was about to tell my mom I wanted to quit.

"Mom, I'd like to stop piano lessons," I said. The silence that followed felt unbearable. Quickly, I added, "I've built a solid foundation in music theory. I'm going to try composing my own pieces instead."

To my surprise and relief, they agreed. Now, it was time to decipher a new way to enjoy music.

Sitting at the piano, bathed in warm sunlight, I faced the daunting blank sheet before me. Doubt crept in—had I made the right decision? For the first time, I was stepping away from a structured path, and it was overwhelming.

Slowly, I started to forget my worries. I hummed softly to myself, experimenting with melodies, motif by motif, the notes swiftly dancing toward me, as if orchestrated by an unseen angel, gradually coming together.

A year later, I performed my composition, Establishment, in Vienna’s historic Ehrbar Hall. The bright lights washing over me, I couldn’t discern my parents’ beaming faces amid the crowd. Putting my fingers on the keys, I reminded myself: they were proud of me. The piece concluded with the rhythmic 'clickety-clack' of a train, symbolizing my ongoing journey toward embracing uncertainty with hope and determination. I was proud of myself for taking this leap into the unknown.

That familiar feeling of unease from the uncertainty resurfaced the summer after my junior year when I was accepted to a six-week STEM project to build machine learning models for mental health prediction. I had no experience with machine learning and only a basic understanding of Python. Instead of wondering if I would fail, I asked myself: “What if I win?”

The first two weeks were overwhelming. I spent hours grappling with algorithms and tutorials. When I ran into a question, I tried to find the answer for myself. I was hesitant to check with my teammates.

As the deadline approached, I realized I hadn’t started coding yet. Walking through the maze of the computer server room in front of the lab, I decided, “No, I shouldn’t work alone,” and hurried to my teammates.

The data was overwhelming, with more than fifty variables to choose for the models. Fortunately, one teammate was a Python expert and was battling with what variables to choose. I shared my research findings on mental health, and he showed me data cleaning Python tricks. We set up a composite for the dependent variable and categorized the rest of the 50 variables into 10 buckets to facilitate model building based on research results. Together, we broke down the complex project into small chunks: data cleaning, model setup, results analysis, and model comparison. Piece by piece, the project took shape.

Before the deadline, we implemented three models for prediction. More importantly, I learned to embrace the power of collaboration as a means to navigate uncertainty. By admitting that I didn’t know everything and seeking help from my teammates and professor, I opened myself up to a faster learning path I hadn’t anticipated.

Facing uncertainty is the only certainty. As I begin college, I envision immersing myself in a crucible of innovation with nonconformist thinkers. Whether exploring new concepts in the library, collaborating on medical treatments in labs, or fusing classical music with robotics in clubs, I'll be surrounded by minds challenging the status quo. Here, ideas will collide, collaboration will thrive, and unconventional innovation will flourish. Together, we'll turn the impossible into possible, paving the way for transformative discoveries. In this environment, I'll grow, contribute, and prove that another way isn't just possible—it's essential.

My summer kick-off was with sweaty palms and butterflies.

I anxiously awaited the email from the 2024 Simons Summer Research Program. As I opened it, the first few words were enough to eject me from my chair like Tom Cruise from a fighter jet. I did not have any parachutes, but my excitement was real.

I had a whole summer for my “what ifs.”

From morning pipetting to culturing cells and asking all the questions in between, I started to marathon my way through science. I threw myself into literature reviews and experiments for pancreatic cancer research. All-nighters became the norm, and each discovery felt more thrilling than the last. However, eventually, the dark crescents under my eyes caught up to me.

I desperately needed a break, and a casual game of pickup basketball with the other Simons interns was a perfect escape. Our game quickly intensified into Game 7 of the NBA finals: during a particularly spirited play, my friend went up for a contested rebound, but something was off when he landed.

“Are elbows supposed to bend that way?”

At a glance, I realized his injury was serious and required aid. No one was in sight, so I asked my friends to bring the t-shirt I had worn at the gym. I folded it to fit his arm, tied it securely, and gently pulled his arm to his chest to prevent movement. We helped him up and headed to the hospital, which was fortunately nearby. Five hours later, seeing him emerge with a brace on his arm, a sense of relief washed over me. We laughed at the absurdity, and headed back.

Even after leaving the ER, that night's events stayed with me. The relief I felt after the situation was only brief, but it was the faces in the waiting room that left a lasting impact. The anxiety in the room was palpable—children crying, families whispering, and patients quietly enduring their pain. Fear was etched on many faces, and the hurried footsteps of doctors and quick exchanges between nurses only added to the tension.

The emotions ran deep. Fear wasn’t just about physical pain, but the uncertainty of the future and the dread of losing a loved one. I confronted human vulnerability, a fear that extended far beyond the present and into the unknown ahead.

Seeing the anxious faces of those awaiting news reminded me of the tension I felt while waiting for lab results. The frustration of a failed experiment or the impatience of awaiting results paled in comparison to the helplessness people felt in the ER. These were people who could do nothing more but hope.

Yet, in the midst of fear, I saw people holding on to hope—thanking doctors, exchanging smiles, and offering prayers. Even when faced with the unknown, they found solace in hope. This taught me a crucial lesson: in life, much like in the lab, setbacks are inevitable, but what matters is how we respond to uncertainty and keep moving forward.

That summer became more than just research; it was a lesson in resilience. In my pancreatic cancer project, experiments didn’t always go as planned, but like in the ER, I learned to face uncertainty with strength. Resilience isn’t just about enduring setbacks; it’s about finding growth and learning through them. Even when things didn’t go as expected, I saw them as chances to adapt and learn.

The setbacks I faced, both in the lab and in life, taught me to find growth in those moments and keep moving forward. True progress, in science or life, comes from navigating uncertainty with determination and hope. My resilience and adaptability from this experience will guide me through my academic and research pursuits in college. When faced with uncertain results or challenges, I will always seek opportunities to learn and find better solutions– I will always welcome more sweaty palms and butterflies.

Plant, Swing, Invert

The official raised the yellow flag indicating I only had 15 seconds left to jump. Everything else faded away – the buzzing crowd, distant noises, and my coaches’ expectations. I tightened my grip on the unfamiliar pole vault pole, the tape feeling foreign as the powdery chalk settled into every groove of my skin. It was my first time using this pole, and uncertainty flickered in my mind. I lined up my foot at the mark I measured, repositioned my grip, and concentrated on the moment. The bar was set at 14'6", more than double my height. I knew there was no room for hesitation; I had to go for it.

Coming into the regional track meet of my sophomore year, I had a record of 13'6", and at 5'6", 135 pounds, I was going to be one of the smallest competitors. I was proud of my season, but compared to past state qualifying heights, it was nowhere near. Overhearing my parents discussing arrangements for me to stay with my grandparents while they went to state for my sister got into my head – I questioned my ability to perform. Still, after dropping out my freshman year due to an injury, I wanted to prove myself.

Arriving at regionals, I was filled with nerves as only two people from each region could qualify to state, but with an extremely talented senior present, it left one spot open. As warmups started, I saw the fierce competition I had only heard about. The meet soon began, and as the bar kept moving up, I realized it wasn't about outjumping the competition; it was about outlasting them. The competition was grueling, going for hours, and after clearing 14'3" and shocking everyone, even myself, I knew I had a chance. This excitement was short-lived, as my only remaining competitor cleared the bar moments after. We both missed the following height, and all I could do next was wait. Standing by my coach, I held my breath, every muscle tensed. Time seemed to stop as the official looked up from the results. I was in.

Having qualified for the state meet, the motivation to prove that I could perform at that level drove me to train harder. Being one of the lowest-seeded competitors, I knew I would need to outperform athletes with far more experience and better records, so I pushed myself to my limits. I spent long hours training after school, staying after club practices doing Bubkas and plyos to improve my take-off and invert.

The state meet was supposed to be a grand experience – the reward for all my hard work and determination – but reality didn't take long to set in. As I came to the runway for my last attempt at 14'6", I signaled to the crowd to clap for me as I attempted a new personal best. From all my hard training and the energy from the crowd, I knew I could clear the bar, so I ran down the runway knowing this was it, but as I reached up, my hand slipped.

How could one fail to hold onto the pole, I thought.

Watching the meet come to an end I came to my senses. This moment was just a step forward toward my future success in this sport. Having let the expectations of my parents and coaches affect my self-view and ultimately my performance was a mistake. Even if I didn't do as well as I wanted to, I was still incredibly proud.

Packing up my poles after the meet, I saw all the disappointed athletes around me and realized that one pole vault jump isn’t decisive of one's success; it's an opportunity to reflect on the past and see how far you’ve made it, not what others see.

I proudly celebrate the festival “Hyena-Missouri.” At least, according to nine-year-old Miranda, who stood folding paper lotuses at my local museum’s Japanese garden activity cart. The actual pronunciation is Hinamatsuri, which is Girls Day in Japan. I froze mid-origami fold as I shifted my gaze to her.

“Is this your first time hearing of Hinamatsuri?”

With a nod of her head, I realized how little of Japanese culture is known to many of those in my local community.

I explained to her what it was as my mind retraced to freshman year when I wore a kimono to commemorate a family event. My wooden geta had clicked through the school hallways as I became subject to judgmental stares and passed by unintelligible whispers. Being the only Japanese girl in my grade was difficult to get used to, and I had entertained the thought of hiding my differences from others.

However, my infrangible ties to the culture prevented me from doing so. Instead, I attempted to find new ways of showing the public the beauty of learning different traditions.

My endeavors started off small. Having used bright pink paper for a while at the cart, I brought from home traditional Origami paper. We originally only folded lilies, lily pads, and lotuses, so I taught the visitors and other volunteers how to fold kimonos, samurai helmets, butterflies, and more. Integrating a whiteboard stand into the cart program where we drew people and objects for festivals occurring at the time was another one of my ventures.

I watched the interactions at the cart, one that was once barely noticed by passersby, evolve into a bustling location for discussions of the history of Ikebana (art of flower arranging) and the materials used to create a tatami (traditional flooring).

As we got busier, it seemed many of the visiting kids wanted to see and understand more about the Japanese activity cart. I felt an intense excitement, and going into the summer before my senior year, I made it my passion project to complete the first children’s book of five (as there are five primary Japanese seasonal festivals to cover). How should I illustrate the meaning of the story effectively? What can I do to make it engaging?

So, for six hours every day I planned. Drawing scenes, researching publishing companies, and finding the dimensions they could print their books filled my every moment.

The story was about a little girl named [Name], who describes what her family does for New Years and grows to understand the value of self-love. Just like [Name], my grandmother is a vital part of my New Years. I had called her and asked her to detail the affectionately honed recipe, and now it is my book’s special last page.

After getting the first printed version, I hurried to read it aloud to a friend’s little brother. Throughout the reading, he sat deadly still, wide eyes tracing the lines on each page. My heart thumped loudly as I asked what he thought.

“I want to pound mochi!! Will you make me Ozoni?”

Surprised that he earnestly wanted to keep the book, I felt more encouraged to share it with others community-wide. After copywriting and publishing this project, I am working with the museum to sell it in their gift shop and have it accessible at the Japanese garden activities cart.

Now, I not only celebrate Hinamatsuri and other festivities. As my journey continues, I celebrate the power of the spoken and written word, the acceptance of various cultures in a diverse community, and the fact that the key to cultural education lies in loving the little details.

Origami paper, no matter how it is folded, can always fold back into its original shape. Just like the human race; We have the power to create change while preserving what makes us… us. What change can I fold in a world of immeasurable possibility? I’m finding out.

Sometimes we all just need to jump in a lake.

Last February, ninety-two of my classmates, teachers, and school staff rallied to take a leap into a pond near my school. Though our excitement for the Polar Plunge was unlike anything that happened all semester, I scarcely observed as much delight when I announced the big jump to my school two weeks earlier.

I was shivering in anticipation that Monday. One corny speech and a hype video later, I scanned the crowd to judge my school’s reaction.

But I could see only bewilderment in front of me. It turns out that not many people are willing to jump into a lake of freezing cold water for fun. My friends were even less interested in the Polar Plunge’s themed attire, groundhogs for Groundhog Day.

It was dispiriting to see the occasion that I had championed through my school’s administration just ignored. The Polar Plunge was intended to be fun for us. Instead, I saw only my peer’s reactions in scrunched faces and discerning eyebrows. I heard a whisper of “Why would I want to do that?” Everything I had done to attract more thrill-seekers had the opposite effect.

I think that teenagers are all too unwilling to embarrass ourselves by doing weird things. When I was a freshman, I was so sensitive to how I blended in–or didn’t–with the rest of my high school friends. As a new student, I felt like I had to anticipate every move that my new freshman friends made. How they acted and what they thought of that person and what was acceptable to talk about. Frankly, it was exhausting. I only realized sophomore year that my friends–and anyone in my classes, on my soccer team, at church–-would appreciate me for me more if I was unique in the way I dressed, spoke, and my sense of humor.

And that included the Polar Plunge. I enjoy the thrill of fun, a wacky adventure, doing something weird because it’s funny. I wanted to jump into freezing cold water because it would bring other people with me. For once, I didn’t let my enthusiasm hide. I kept asking my friends, people I walked with, and anyone who would listen. Are you going to take The Plunge? Will you be there? My little pet project, diverted at first by people’s indifference, began to grow. I refused to be, well, embarrassed, about having such excitement.

I left school the week of the Plunge with strep throat, and I was only able to return at lunch before the afternoon we jumped. So I had no way of knowing what I would return to. I hoped it would be good.

Because the Plunge wasn’t just about cannonballing into mind-numbingly cold water; it was about bringing our school together. The crowd that gathered pondside was buzzing with warmth on a clear blue February afternoon. We huddled like penguins around a small dock from which the plungers would jump. A fervor ran rampant through our mob as we rushed up with shouts to see the first daredevils plunge. I saw my friend Livi grab an old friend and a new one alike. The plungers leaped, shrieking at the kiss of the water. And the crowd went wild.

The Polar Plunge became an instant school tradition. We got our head of school, the new freshmen, and our beloved security guard Daywan to all jump. I witnessed plungers in both speedos and in costume–a Viking helmet, a tutu, and an inflatable flamingo floatie.

I never could have created the Plunge as a freshman. After transferring schools and upheaving my life, I would never have been able to speak directly with administrators or talk in front of the entire school. Now, I would have wanted to jump in the lake, but not if my friends weren’t.

But I had just seen how my spirit had caused so many underclassmen to take the leap of faith that I wished I could have made earlier. It was invigorating.

I think, also, that my school became more cohesive that day. We were emerging out of the shadow of the pandemic. Whether it was cheering for the plungers together, or jumping hand in hand, gathering for just one afternoon in camaraderie led to the strengthening of bonds. Maybe we all decided to embrace the awkwardness and take a leap of faith.

“Beep, beep, be—” The noise of my glucose monitor interrupted the discussion of "The Count of Monte Cristo," and I was desperate. It had already beeped twice, indicating my low glucose level, yet I stubbornly avoided drinking my juice. Fearing it would beep a third time, I placed my thumb on the “off” button.

As I felt eyes on me, my teacher asked who enjoyed the book. My hand shot up immediately—the revenge, drama, spite—I couldn’t resist. I was captivated by Dantès and the letter that falsely accused him of treason, stripping him of his identity and sealing his prison fate.

Noticing I was alone in my enthusiasm, I quickly lowered my hand. But my teacher noticed and asked why it resonated with me. An awkward freshman, I stared blankly; I wasn’t sure how it appealed to me personally. I left class half-flustered, half-curious...my juice still sloshing around in its box.

With the question in mind, I began reading through a new lens—searching for fragments of myself within the ink of an author’s imagination. Literature became a meditation, finding beauty in the reflexive nature of characters.

I was clearly connecting to their ink as I was searching for mine. But I was still stumped on Dantès.

A year into this habit, I received a call from family friends, concerned about their newly diagnosed 5-year-old daughter. Knowing I also had diabetes, they asked to meet. Questions swirled as I anticipated the day: Would I be lying by saying it’s “going to be okay” or radiating confidence I had not found myself? Pressure surged through my veins. Nevertheless, I accepted.

At the hospital, I stuttered even at "hello," but as the conversation unfolded, my words began to flow. I told her I enjoyed the questions from curious classmates about why I had a second “phone” that “beeps.” Switching the narrative helped. By telling her it was going to be okay, I felt at ease; by acting confident with my condition, I realized how good it felt.

Her little arms leaned into a hug after our conversation, and I let out a sob.

Realizing I wanted to become a role model for kids like Valeria, I picked up a book I had avoided since my diagnosis: "My Beloved World" by Sonia Sotomayor. The prologue started, and I traveled back in time: I was in our kitchen, hands trembling, parents screaming, just to get my first insulin shot. Sotomayor’s diabetic experiences made me feel seen; my own ink was starting to become clearer.

It then hit me. I understood why "The Count of Monte Cristo" resonated with me. I had found comfort in Dantès’ struggle to defy the label of traitor others had given him; his ambition to escape mirrored my need to belong. While I found consolation in Dantès, I found strength in Sonia. Just as she was scared to be vulnerable, I kept trying to blend in with my classmates.

Today, I find myself not only in ink but also in people—especially in those young patients I've impacted. They've motivated me to turn my authenticity into action by raising awareness for diabetes and co-founding T1DOSE. By organizing educational workshops and volunteering as a mentor, I've witnessed the growth of a resilient community through shared support.

In the process of answering a seemingly simple question, I discovered myself. I’ve realized there’s no need to fix my inner Dantès but to accept his racing thoughts and let them coexist with my courageous Sonia. At the end of the day, the Dantès in me still gets uneasy because of the beeps, but the Sonia in me breathes and lets the three beeps be.

I remember the moment I learned that my mom may never walk again. The realization struck like a gust of winter air: cold, shocking, and inescapable. She had been diagnosed with Cauda Equina Syndrome, brought on by stressful years as a teacher. Our once-bustling home moved at a slower rhythm defined by patience and perseverance.

With this change, I took on more household responsibilities: cooking meals, cleaning bathrooms, and grocery shopping. During one of our trips to Patel Brothers (our favorite Indian grocery store), I realized how much had changed. As I sprang across aisles, grabbing heavy produce that exceeded my mom’s new carrying weight limit, my mom watched me with a soft smile.

“Funny how you once sulked about coming here, and now you bring me along,” she remarked.

Our Patel trips became a stepping stone out of our slumps, as our car ride conversations grew from stunned silence to tender solace. In these exchanges, I discovered resilience in vulnerability. During the first car ride home from Patel, I hesitated before voicing my fears about the future. My mom, squeezing my hand, shared her feelings of hopelessness. Through these intimate moments of protected openness, our conversations brought us closer together as we found strength in our mutual feelings.

As we navigated the challenges of our new life together, I felt unexpectedly grateful. Grateful: I felt closer to my mom than ever. Grateful: my mom was still here. Grateful: the support from the community specifically the Cauda Equina Foundation (CEF). Their support groups provided critical information and resources offering a community of understanding individuals who shared our journey. CEF’s company of others who had experienced what she was going through and the sense of belonging that eased our burdens were the biggest resources for my mom. The new relationships formed through this challenge showed me that the world persisted through grace and empathy.

Experiencing the transformative power of community support through CEF, I was inspired to contribute to the flourishing of grace in the world leading me to the Teen Philanthropy Initiative. A program empowering students to engage in community service and philanthropy by providing them with the tools to make a meaningful impact, TPI explained how nonprofits, like CEF, channel resources into tangible support. Participating in TPI offered a unique opportunity to support local nonprofits by deciding which receive a grant. Reflecting on my mental health struggles with my mom’s surgery, I chose to review the NAMI-Dupage grant, a nonprofit focused on mental health advocacy. Visiting their facility for an onsite interview, I was introduced to the Teen Talk forum, an online safe space for teenagers to work through their mental health issues. During my interview, I met Leigh Nelson, the director at NAMI Dupage who had battled mental health problems herself. At first, I didn’t know how to respond to such a situation. However, recalling my mom’s first days after her surgery when she felt fear and depression, I remembered how much patience and empathy do for a person who is suffering. So I listened to her explain how the Teen Talk Forum space helps relieve mental health stressors by allowing people to talk about them. Little by little, we started to connect over our experiences and I saw a smile spread across Leigh’s face.

When I got to present my work at the Capstone ceremony in City Hall, I proudly handed Leigh a $750 grant funding the Teen Talk program. What began as a personal challenge catalyzed my growth, teaching me the impact of empathy and service. The once daunting silence in the car rides gave way to a symphony of support within my community and through my work with TPI and NAMI. Standing on the threshold of new beginnings, I am reminded of that first cold winter air realization - a journey not of isolation but of collective empowerment, where love and resilience shape each step forward.

Hue, Vietnam

“Season spring so fruitful,” my Dad frolicked and awed, pointing at a lonesome dandelion sticking out of a crack in the rocky path. His giggle as he inspected the spectacle was childish; I couldn’t help but smile.

Atlanta, Georgia

Crash. In a blink, the kitchen turned into a stained mess with bun rieu splatters all across our Vietnam family portrait; my dad, face twisted with anger, had smashed his plate. “To hell with this family.”

I blinked back tears, struggling to understand how the man who once marveled at dandelions in cracks had become so unrecognizable and explosive. I tried at-home therapy sessions, but even after years, I still suffocated under his unpredictable rage.

How could I connect with him again? I improvised to find answers. And over several years, I found them in rhythm.

Hoping to alleviate stress for both of us, I lugged home a six-foot-wide marimba, remembering that my Dad was fond of the T'rưng, a similar Vietnamese xylophone he listened to daily in Vietnam. “This thing so big,” my father remarked in Vietnamese, peeking his head into my practice room. He asked me to teach him Nam điệu, his favorite style of music.

Admittedly, my classical head had never improvised—let alone in Southern Vietnamese music. I tried teaching him through the unfamiliar notes, but when my attempt met his frustrated, “That’s not Nam điệu,” I decided to delve deep into music theory. After countless hours dissecting Southern Vietnamese music like “Đoản Ca Xuân” and Bobby McFerrin’s demonstration of pentatonic scales, I discovered that Nam điệu (Southern mode) mirrors the improvisation freedom of jazz blues. Yet, it strictly follows a simple five-note pentatonic scale that is rooted in our culture. Feeling like the Bach of South Vietnamese music, I reattempted to connect with my Dad using my newfound knowledge.

Months as our improv grew, note by note closer to the nostalgic style, my father began sharing snippets of his feelings. What started as just “work was tiring” eventually turned into confessions. “I’m sorry for my anger these years,” he broke a sad smile squeezing his frail hand on my shoulder. All these years in America–the shattered plates, the spewing hatred, the racking debts– my Dad cracked while trying to keep his stress from drowning me. But now, feeling his warm hug and words of guilt, I felt like we had found our way back to springtime.

I wouldn’t say my Dad is the same man who joyfully marveled at Dandelions in Vietnam, though he’s gotten better at controlling his emotions. Learning how to improvise in Southern Vietnamese music to reconnect with my Dad despite years of unsuccessful at-home therapy sessions made me realize that sometimes the answer doesn’t come so obvious the first time around. Sometimes, it’s about improvising around the unpredictable and coming up with creative solutions. When I’m missing penne for my Alfredo pasta, I whip out the rice steamer so my Mom who comes home at eight every day has a delectable dinner: Alfredo curry rice. When I forgot my props for the Key Club Georgia Governor election, I based my campaign on a banana I brought from home the same day (which, unfortunately, was a flop).

As I head into college, I’m ready to bring this spirit of improvisation with me. While I value careful planning, I’ve found that embracing spontaneity and working through the unexpected can uncover answers that structured paths might miss.

To my father, I forgive you for your outbursts. I know you try to keep stone-cold to protect me, but you know, even stone can crack under heavy storms. But just as dandelion can emerge from a crack, so too can beauty blossom from our most unexpected emotions. Con yeu Cha.

There I was again. Lost, alone, and above all, not understanding what a “verbe impératif” meant in this new school. While most of the kids at my new school spoke about how easy the homework was in French, I would eat my homecooked “arroz con pollo” beside the corner bookshelf to save myself from embarrassment. But my worry faded each time I heard Madame Guahirana’s soft voice say “Bonjour [Name]”. An immigrant from Mauritius, she seemed to know exactly what I was going through and devoted her time to helping me learn the language.

“How can this one be worth more?” I asked in one of our lunchtime private lessons.

“This one’s much bigger than that one”, I reiterated as I held up a dime and a nickel.

“Sometimes what is small in size is large in value” responded Madame Guihirana.

***

With a father working in another continent and a mother busy taking care of my younger sister, Madame Guahirana was where I’d turn to for support. In small ways, she would constantly push me to overcome the communication barriers I had with others. Whether it’d be by giving me my first pack of Pokemon cards I could trade to get over my shyness and talk with other kids or reminding me to put my gloves on in the winter, she would look out for me. Not only did Madame Guahirana help me learn how to use “conditionnel” verbs, but her relentless compassion cared for me when no one else had the time or patience.

***

In my sophomore year, I found myself in a familiar situation. Yet again, I had transferred schools. At Glenforest, in particular, it was common to see ESL students skipping class or getting in fights at lunch. Looking for ways to create a space where immigrants could be helped with their algebra homework or socialize with others led to the founding of the Newcomers Club.

Growing the club was difficult. Finding a balance between schoolwork, extracurriculars, calculating the socially optimum quantity of pumpkins for the Halloween pumpkin carving event, making sure we had the right amount of Graham crackers for the Cheesecake event, or coordinating with local banks to give workshops on financial literacy was demanding. But making sure the flyers of the pumpkin carving competition were in eight languages so everyone understood or the times I’d stay up well past midnight playing with the colors on Canva to create a post for our Instagram account was worth it.

In the gingerbread house-making event, I witnessed how the activity encouraged shy newcomers to surpass the language barrier and integrate into the community. Whether it be by discussing where the gummies should be placed or how much frosting should be used, this activity allowed students who fear rejection and suffer from the pain of leaving home to forget about their worries and simply bond with each other.

After three years of running this club, I can say that we have built the richest community – not in capital wealth but instead in diversity and tolerance. Along with the 150 active members and 600 school participants, we have built the richest community in the world – not in capital but in compassion. At Glenforest, you can be sure that the moment a newcomer walks through the door, they will be greeted with sincere kindness and thoughtfulness. It is through one Valentine’s Day card-making event at a time that the people new to our school feel more connected to our community.

My once prominent fear of hiding from social interactions to save myself from embarrassment is a feeling prominent in the minds of several newcomers. The feeling of rejection and not knowing how to become part of a community. At the Newcomers Club, I had the chance to witness how the events we hosted helped shy newcomers integrate into the community, one gummy at a time.

The sight of my father’s sneakers was irksome. The insipid carbon gray colorway, the frayed fabric edges which now sagged with fatigue and the cracked sole exposing the raggedy stitching beneath. I didn’t bother trying to make conversation with my father as he sat putting on his raggedy old shoes, figuring that I would get the habitual “hmm”, a sound which represented our estrangement. Amongst the chaos of making sure the dosa is crisp, my mother sentences me to a trip to the market with my father. My futile rebuttal goes unnoticed, so I resign to my fate.

During the car ride to the local super irvine, my father repeatedly dismissed my hopeful conversation-starters with his usual “hmmm.” Defeated, I gave up and let my observational nature take over. Yet amid the bustle of the supermarket, A bizarre scene caught my eye: My father meticulously examining mangoes.

At once, my mind was invaded by insatiable curiosity. Why was he so passionate about such a mundane task? The curiosity ate me up; I had to know more.

This curiosity pushed me to sit through painfully awkward drives, and ask questions even though his answers were often dry. I became an apprentice, learning the fundamental formulas of fruit picking: The webbing test, press test and smell test, which involve looking for the right amount of scarring, the perfect amount of give, and the sacred smell of ripeness. Every week, we traveled to the market together, where I would showcase my newfound skills, looking to earn his approval. Over time, our conversations began flowing freely – his “hmms” were increasingly replaced with “excellent”s and “try again”s…

“I’ve always wanted a garden of my own,” he once told me.

“Why not?”

“The soil may not respond well” he hesitated.

His words astonished me. I was touched, yet conflicted: I had never heard him talk about his wants before. Although I had grown up comfortably, fostering a willingness to chase wild desires, my father’s tough life experiences made him highly risk averse, explaining his fear of failure. Seeing his love for fruit inhibited by his subconscious vulnerabilities, I resolved to guide him to a fearless reality.

I spent mornings before school researching, scouring the joe gardner blog for easy plants to raise. I spent routine drives to the Orange County Table Tennis Academy listening to the gardening for everyone podcast. I spent my nighttime toiling among the bugs to measure the depth and nutrient supply of the soil. I spent hasty passing periods scribbling down my notes at the library, exhausting the plethora of basic gardening books. As rain would rock, my consistent efforts eroded my father's risk-averse outer layer. The blurry vision of creating a garden together was now becoming a clear reality as we stood marveling over our blank yard, plotting a future garden, a united smirk on our faces.

Observing him in the garden I watched him planting seeds, nurturing the soil, and relocating plants to ensure the garden’s flourishment. While observing him, I recalled where this journey began. I finally had an answer to my question – fruit was his vessel of communication. He advised through the fruit, he loved through the fruit, he was a father through the fruit. Amidst my epiphany, my attention shifted to his shoes once again. There was a medley of colors rising from the soil, penetrating into his shoes: The raspberry’s pink blush, the grape’s sour green, and the lemon’s complex yellow. My attention then turned to the laces. A stark contrast to the vibrant sole, the raggedy laces still chewed at me. I realized the profound impact of the past on shaping the present, how it can inhibit the creation of new opportunities and tear down excitement in every moment. Our relationship continues to grow by the agency of my relentless perseverance, and most days I can look past his raggedy shoelaces. Most Days.

As I write my name, 'Zheng [Name]', in Chinese, I carefully inscribe each stroke, shaping the characters with precise lines and delicate accents. In contrast, "Joyce" is sleek and simple, with each letter flowing smoothly into the next. Though my two names seem as different as night and day, both share the same meaning: joy.

I find joy through wonder as I face the unknown.

When I was seven, due to political factors, our Christian faith, and my parents’ ambitions, my family left behind our stable life in Shanghai for the untamed land of Texas, with new faces, customs, and language.

I find joy through determination as I overcome challenges.

As I entered high school, the events on my Google Calendar began to grow. Baby blue for orchestra rehearsals; cherry red for LEO Club Volunteering. To balance responsibilities with my sacred mornings, I kept to a 5 AM routine, studying while the world slept. Amid the stillness of murky mornings, I wrestled with math problems, experimenting with different approaches and learning from every misstep. My knowledge of mathematics deepened incrementally, and the insights I gained into each problem’s underlying ideas cultivated a sense of enchantment within me. I sought to explore math’s weird and wonderful ideas—from mind-bending spherical coordinates to the unique characteristics of Jacobian matrices. This led me to pursue opportunities like the Program for Research in Mathematics at A&M and college math courses beyond the limits of my high school. My determination drove me to train rigorously for the American Math Competitions, overcoming my previous lack of experience in competitive mathematics. Despite doubts from others and myself, the confidence I gained through struggling and the joy I found in maintaining determination keep me pushing forward.

I find joy through fulfillment as I help others grow.

Over the last four years, I’ve sought ways to give back. I saw joy trembling in the hands of a 4th-grade girl in pink Barbie jeans as she shyly accepted her first-place trophy at the 2023 Elementary Math Competition hosted by my high school Math Club. I caught joy in the eager grins of my Sunday School students as I brought Bible stories to life, sharing adventures of faith and love. In these moments of generosity, I find purpose in uplifting others. I experience a fleeting surge of pride when I reach a personal goal or some tangible achievement; but the joy I feel when I love selflessly, laugh openly, and offer support and kindness to those around me is unseen but lasts forever.

Each day brings me closer to understanding why my parents named me Zheng [Name], with “Xuan” symbolizing optimism and “Joyce” inscribing joy into my identity. I’m committed to carrying joy with me, embodying the virtues connotated by my names, and sharing it in every corner of my life.

A multicolor geometric sphere made of Post-it notes was forming between my friend's fingers. From across the classroom, I fixed my attention on her vibrant sphere with intricate folds. I scooched forward to catch a better glimpse, captivated by her ability to create a geometric sphere out of paper without glue or tape. I wondered how that was even possible.

On our first playdate, I noticed a half-finished sphere like the one I saw at school lying on her desk. My curiosity urged me to ask her how it was made, and she built one for me. She placed twelve sheets of six-by-six-inch origami paper before me and meticulously folded each into a triangular pattern. Using three segments of each triangular pattern, she wove the segments together using hidden flaps, creating four weaved segments. She then merged these four segments into one sphere with the same hidden flap technique without adhesives.

At first, I utterly failed to replicate my friend’s success, creating instead a jumbled mess of paper and my initial optimism. My brain struggled to conceptualize how to create an interconnected structure. Obsessed, I scoured YouTube for more geometric origami, discovering that my sphere was a Sonobe Octahedron, built using a technique called modular origami, where multiple sheets are folded into units and combined to form a 3D structure.

After watching countless videos, I began identifying unnecessary steps, allowing me to build figures quickly. My colorful stack of origami paper dwindled as my desk piled with creations. Following tips from my scrupulous research, I even persuaded my mom to buy expensive yet high-quality paper for my geometric figurines. I was excited as I could visualize the dynamics of modular structures and the design features that uniquely add up to assemble a unit.

I resumed this concept when I later learned calculus. At first, I struggled with integrals, which are used to find areas under curves. One night, while grappling through a particularly difficult problem, I had an epiphany — I realized I could apply my origami skills. Equipped with those skills, I was able to comprehend integrals by visualizing them as modular units that build up to form a whole. The following unit, I encountered using derivatives to optimize a 3D structure’s shape. Applying my skills with origami, I was able to simplify the process and find solutions more efficiently.

These mathematical concepts truly mirrored the modular origami technique. Drawing parallels between the two, I effortlessly grasped summation's utility in various ways, like identifying the relevance of inputs in a neural network —known as weighted sums—in my computer science classes.

As I continued my study of calculus, I encountered problems that used derivatives to optimize a 3D shape’s dimensions to maximize or minimize its volume or size. This brought to my mind how I would maximize the size of my origami sheets with specific folds without adding or subtracting anything from a singular sheet. In addition, when writing trigonometric proofs, I also found myself unconsciously reducing the steps, just as I had streamlined my origami-making process. Since there were no strict rules for structuring proofs, I focused on selecting theorems that maximally solved the proof in fewer steps. I became fascinated by my ability to naturally apply the concept of optimization, realizing how prevalent it is in my life.

Summation and optimization frequently converge in applied math to solve complex problems. The Taylor series, for instance, involves summation and, in some cases, optimization to approximate complex functions. It adds derivative terms and optimizes by linearizing a function at a particular point. Reflecting on these concepts, I realize summation and optimization have converged within me. They are part of a blend of traits that have made me curious, creative, analytical, resilient, and always willing to take risks after weighing potential outcomes.

The vision was blurred while my childish and veritable laughter filled the room. Three shapes were in the shadows but so familiar. Trying to reach, a desperate hand stretched out to hold the treasures that shaped me the most, saying…

“Grandma!” when you need a lesson from decades of wisdom. The unoiled hinges made a slow creaking sound, catching my attention. My grandmother opened a closet with a wrinkled but soft hand. A banknote and a clear jar that still smelled of cucumbers appeared in front of me. Despite the scarcity of money, she taught me my first lesson in finance - to save. She was always repeating her advice to avoid being an office clerk in economics, ironically because of her own career in the field. To this day, her collection of books inspires me to pursue a future in economics. So, she can say “I advised the opposite” in paradise.

“Dad!” when you need leading. During a harsh financial situation, my family moved to a suburb. Feeling the struggles and hoping to support, one night I sat at a shabby table and brainstormed ideas. The concept of an advertising banner stuck in my mind, and it seemed simple to implement and cost-effective. After my confident demonstration, Dad was the only one who looked with delight in his eyes. It was not due to my idea but rather due to the first particle of fire that led to a flash and flare-up. An immediate invitation to his desk, and I feel the smell of old paper - a 20-year-old diary he used to collect ideas. Dad hands it over, transmitting the entrepreneurial spirit. Suddenly, it feels like a beacon. Although the advertisement project did not work out, the seed of my obsession was planted. Whenever any business thought or innovation strikes me, the diary waits eagerly for my pure smile and excitement. Ideas, as granules of sand compose a beach, make up my area of freedom, where I can finally enter the flow state.

“Mom!” when you need someone you can trust. In the suburbs, the loud and comforting snores of my father stopped being a signal of safety because of his alcoholism and anger issues. As the family situation worsened, learning geography, mathematics, and financial literacy, which kindled my curiosity, became essential because no educational opportunities were provided. Some evening, I stumbled upon an application for a National School. After the test, selection process, and decisions, I got in. Joyful screams and congratulations from the family, but I was not as happy because I had to leave my mother without protection. Mother saw concern in my eyes. She held my hand and, with a soothing voice, elaborated the term of trust, demonstrating if it is a critical decision, you have to trust the surroundings. As always, my mother was right. Every day was like a fairy tale: ideal academic conditions, friendly students, and helpful teachers. Looking at my face in the first photo with the class, you can see that this was the first school where I was truly happy.

Family is the most, what shapes from the first breath until the last bits of soil over a buried coffin. Some can teach fundamentals of financial literacy, molding all the further paths I am still flowing into. During unexpected storms, inexperienced youth want to support, discovering their passions of entrepreneurial ideas from transmitted legacy, which are now transformed into solving business cases in competitions. Another member may arouse trust and independence in just a few sentences, leading to significant shifts in educational opportunities and changing my plans from pursuing a standard university degree in Kazakhstan to pushing myself and applying abroad with long-term goals. Gratefulness is the only word that comes up after all my journeys. Someday, I will influence people with something valuable as my Grandmother, Mother, and Father did to me.

A Band-Aid is more than just a piece of fabric. There’s the adhesive strip that clings even in the toughest moments, the pad that heals, and the outer packaging that conceals its potential. Little did I know that the countless Band-Aids I used to cover my blisters while playing soccer with boys would become a fitting metaphor for my experience.

At 11, I joined my first boys' soccer team. I had played casually with boys before, but this time was different—the stakes were higher, and the competition fierce. I remember the long, silent drive to La Cañada, my excitement slipping away as I saw heads turn and heard the whispers: “Why is there a girl here?” When practice began, I realized this wasn’t the soccer I was used to—it was faster, more technical, and much harder. I barely kept up, and felt ashamed, as if I embodied the stereotype of how a girl “should” play. But as I drove home, sweaty and teary, I knew one thing: I would be back. I had to prove to them—and to myself—that I could keep up.

After every practice, my dad and I dissected my performance. At first, I dreaded these talks, feeling like he focused too much on my mistakes. I thought he was just rubbing salt into my wounds. But soon I realized these conversations were like peeling off a Band-Aid—painful, but necessary to heal and grow. My dad wasn’t trying to lower my confidence; he wanted to help me improve. Slowly, I saw that his feedback was a way to prepare me for the next challenge. Before each practice, I’d write key "focus items" on the back of my hand to remind myself of what to work on, each new blister serving as proof of my determination to improve.

Practices were tough, not just physically but emotionally. When the coach said to grab a partner, the boys avoided me. I often ended up with the coach or a boy too slow to reach his friend. The isolation was palpable, and it made me hesitant to speak up on the field. I worried that if I demanded the ball or criticized a teammate, I’d make things worse. But over time, I realized that I wasn’t there to be liked—I was there to get better. Staying silent wouldn’t help me improve, and the more I stayed quiet, the more I isolated myself. Slowly, I found my voice, calling for the ball and asserting myself.

An unexpected turning point came during rondo, a simple warm-up game where players pass around a defender. In those brief moments, I bonded with my teammates. The casual conversations during this daily drill bridged the gap between us, and through this connection, I learned the value of speaking up, not just for myself but for the team. By speaking up in rondo, I built trust with my teammates, and I became more than just “the girl”—I was a valued player.

Reflecting on my journey, I see the parallels between my soccer experience and a Band-Aid. Like the adhesive that holds tight, I stuck with the team through discomfort and doubt. Like the pad that heals, I worked on my weaknesses and grew stronger. And like the packaging that hides the Band-Aid’s potential, I discovered my own strengths over time, even when they weren’t immediately visible.

This experience, playing soccer as the only girl on a boys' team, has shaped me in profound ways. It taught me to communicate, push through discomfort, and challenge stereotypes. It helped me understand that being different doesn’t make you weaker; it can make you stronger if you embrace it. As I look ahead to future challenges—whether in the job market or life in general—I know I’ll draw on this same resilience. I’m ready to face whatever comes my way, confident that I can heal, adapt, and thrive, just like the Band-Aids that have accompanied me throughout this journey.

I shivered, my heart caught in my throat, terrified that the Taliban, who banned education for all girls, might come and find me violating the law. My heart was palpitating, and I nervously glanced at the school gate, and then back at my textbook. As the clock struck five, the room went pitch black. Under the cover of darkness, I filed into the stuffy classroom to secretly repeat everything I had learned about 21st century skills to more than twenty girls from my neighborhood aged 14 to 17. Indeed, my eyes remained chained to the gate. For the last year and a half, I’ve lived in fear, knowing I would be tortured and lose my own opportunities for education if we were discovered.

While I worried about the girls’ future, my parents were afraid for my safety. I felt guilty because it was my first time I stood against my parents’ will: I advocated for the girls’ right to continue attending the crammed classroom. In fact, remembering our times singing songs, playing truth or dare, engaging in hopscotch, and having Thursday movie shows pushed me, despite my parent’s insistence, to spend hours organizing engaging lessons and activities to create a kinesthetic learning environment for the girls. For instance, during a particularly challenging reading unit about treasure hunt, I organized a Treasure Hunt Game. Students were tasked to immerse themselves in the roles of treasure hunters and seeking clues as if they were happening in real-time. During my vacation and holidays, I would host application editing sessions checking grammars, word choice, and supplementing comments for their United World College scholarship essays. An invaluable opportunity for the girls to study IB abroad. Amazing, I learned six were shortlisted for interviews.

I remember my father saying, “education is the key for success and personal growth.” He drilled into me that if I wanted to make a better life not only for myself but for others, I had to prioritize education. Knowing that my female learners were denied this right and pushed into marriage, I continued working in risky ways starting the classroom even earlier than 5:00 PM to have more time for each lesson. We could only contact each other through WhatsApp and Telegram, but half of the girls could not afford a connection. Therefore, I spent $60 one third of my salary to cover their internet fee for a few months. Because they couldn’t go to school and online education was not feasible for them, I talked to several principals in my region Dashte Barchi to see if they were inclined in donating. After learning, they were unable to help, I spoke to my friend Abigail. We opened a GoFundMe fundraising campaign and reached out to our friends, and others through LinkedIn and Facebook to help these girls pursue education online. Together, we raised $1,362 to cover the girls’ internet fees monthly.

But Money was not the only issue. In my evening classroom, Maryam and Zinab stayed calm and did not participate in the activities. Am I not doing enough? I asked myself for several times. Although the fear of exposure from Taliban initially consumed me, I now feel strong and thrilled because I added a new session on the weekend, on Fridays. Hence, I noticed Maryam shed her shyness and eagerly enter into discussions after our Friday stream of consciousness sessions to hearing Zinab become motivated through her own engagement. Although fear of punishment constantly consumed me, my heart is warmed seeing Maryam and Zinab rediscover their love of education.

I don’t let fear rule my future. I strive to someday ensure that education is not only a right for all Afghans, but for everyone regardless of age, gender or race. In college, I will continue to strengthen this belief. Reality and danger never prevent me from doing exactly what I believe is the right thing to do.

The cold metal of the chair bit into my skin as I sat, hands trembling, in the Taliban detention cell. Two meals a day—if I could keep them down—were the only breaks from the barrage of questions.

“How dare you defy the Supreme Leader’s law?” they roared. But, I wondered, how could a simple desire to learn threaten an entire regime?

I remember the morning the Taliban stormed our city. My siblings lost their government jobs overnight. The following evening, Baba clasped his hands at the dinner table and said: “We have no choice, [Name]. You’re the only one who can keep us afloat now.” I knew what his words meant.

My once-uninterrupted 1,368-hour Pomodoro streak at Khan Academy gave way to the daily grind of tracing my earnings at a shoe factory. Every time I passed the school, a pang of loss hit me, but I kept walking and choked back my despair. Meanwhile, I couldn’t stand by while my female friends, feeling suicidal, were condemned to lives of submission.

My peers and I revived a once-abandoned academy to covertly homeschool girls. I taught English and Math, integrating my Khan Academy insights into senior-grade lessons. Before the city woke, everyone rushed to the academy and left during the calls to prayer. At night, my mom and I baked Bolani to sell at the academy’s door. At our bake-sale stall, we monitored distant Taliban patrols so we could alert male instructors to flee through the back door. Textbooks were concealed under religious covers.

Inevitably, as our students grew, we were caught. As the Taliban interrogated me, I couldn’t stop thinking about our 300 female students who would no longer be able to learn – including Layla, who told me she aimed to become the Minister of Technology and provide free and fearless education to all her “virtual siblings”. Struggling to keep straight, I asked, "Why are you so afraid of educated girls?" A pin-drop silence followed. The soldier gripped his Kalashnikov tightly and spat, "You want some weaklings to rise above us?"

Eight days later, a truck dropped me somewhere near our mahala. Barefoot, I limped home. Knock, knock. Mom screamed my name, and before she reached the "n" in [Name], she pulled me into the tightest hug, tears streaming down our faces. I felt a heavy weight in my arms as she fainted. For the first time in my life, I saw my 80-year-old father cry.

After four terrifying months, I returned to school for my final exams. Girls my age didn’t. Then came the news that broke me – Layla had taken her own life by ingesting acid. Layla, with her hands decorated with hennas of algebra and physics formulae, would never become our technology minister.

As 1000 days without girls’ education approached, I decided to try again, for Layla. I translated Khan Academy lessons into Persian, reaching millions of Afghans. During the day, I hosted Zoom tutoring sessions for girls. At night, stationed on the landing, my mind often drifted to the soldier’s last words: “You may go, but we've seized your home documents—disobey again, and your family will be homeless." I kept my voice low, knowing my parents would stop me if they found out. Wrestling with technical terms with no Persian equivalents, I replayed videos countless times to craft analogies and coined new terms to simplify complex concepts.

After 15 months of relentless work, I began sharing our resources online. I taught myself web development through trial and error and crafted my encrypted archive website. Our lessons aired to thousands on Meraj TV. Using funds from our bake sale, I bought DVDs, collaborating with local drivers to deliver them to places where "education" had become no more than a whisper.

We began in underground darkness, planting the seeds of education where it was most forbidden. Every attempt to axe us down only spurred new roots. We lost Layla, but her legacy lives on in the twelve students who have begun recording their mastered subjects and educating their peers. In the face of fear and failure, I will persevere through every obstacle, determined to grow. After all, success isn't reserved for the final chapter of our veiled books; it's cultivated in every whispered lesson, every risk taken, and every sprout born from darkness.

The Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paradox suggests that it’s possible for two entangled particles to stay connected no matter the distance between them. Can people, like particles, do the same? I hoped so, but when dad moved away for work in the 5th grade, our family felt some disconnect. Like particles after measurement, our entanglement seemed to collapse into separate states.

Even after we reunited in high school, the years apart made Dad feel more like a coinhabitant than a parent. However, I began noticing Dad’s chemically callused hands and long days at the lab. While he silently carried our family on his shoulders, we gave him lukewarm welcomes. I wanted to be better–I wanted to connect with him. Vulnerably vomiting our emotions felt overwhelmingly uncomfortable, but I wondered if our mutual love of physics could spark meaningful conversations. I began testing my theory.

Every night, I’d come up to my dad with a new topic to discuss. Some days, our conversations would be serious and philosophical:

“Imagine you observe something incredibly frequently. It wouldn’t have enough time to change between observations so you technically ‘freeze’ it in time. This is called the Zeno Effect.”

“Woah…and this is real?”

“Yes! It’s been experimentally observed in quantum mechanics. It’s true in life too. It reminds us that if you overanalyze everything, you never really move forward,” dad smiled.

But some days, they’d just be silly:

“Dad, this pasta is so good. I’m gonna eat enough to become the mass of a black hole and warp time to eat it longer.”

Over the course of a few months, awkwardness melted away and curiosity and animation replaced it. Every question opened new pathways for conversation, and we began communicating the way I’d hoped we would. Still, I wanted to know dad deeper. I brainstormed how I could twist our conversations to be more personal. One day, I asked him why he majored in biophysics. What did he want to accomplish? He told me that in the past, he wanted to pursue pure physics, but “although theoretical questioning is important for inquiry, it can’t save a life.” He switched to biophysics because he’d wanted to apply physics to something tangible. When grandma passed from cancer, it cemented his decision. He told me that “maybe my research can prevent you from going through the same situation.”

I fell quiet. “Thanks, dad,” I whispered. Understanding his motivations made me feel closer to him than I ever had. I felt a wash of appreciation and resolve come over me. Dad inspired me to think critically about the impact I wanted to make. While creating a lecture for Physics Team, I opened a closet door to a Narnia of possibilities: Quantum Computing. With applications in everything from drug discovery to clean energy, I knew I’d found a special field of science. I sought an internship on the subject, and every evening I’d come home brimming with excitement as I shared my findings with Dad who intently listened. We were a positive feedback loop, fueling each other’s passion for learning while discovering more sides of one another.

These discussions made me realize that physics was a language used to unfurl our relationship. I began to speak this language to build bridges with others. Through Girls in Quantum, I befriended Sophia, a girl who lives in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. I introduced myself in broken Google-Translated German, but our conversations connected us. One of my proudest accomplishments is dragging my friend, a self-proclaimed “D1 physics hater,” to a physics Jeopardy activity I created that made her realize physics can be interesting (sometimes). In college, I’ll continue to learn and apply my knowledge to break new barriers. Still, every time I learn something interesting, my dad will be the first person I call and share it with. I know I'll be able to see that familiar spark in his eyes, even if it’s through the phone.

In the heart of Kabokweni’s bustling shantytown, surrounded by the rhythmic hum of life and the clatter of makeshift homes, I found a new purpose. At 17, I arrived with a suitcase full of art supplies, uninflated soccer balls, and a bold idea: to help South African elementary school children tap into their creativity. Standing on the dusty streets, corrugated iron shacks stretching into the horizon, I wondered if my plan was enough. Could art really make a difference here?

Growing up, art had always been my escape, a place where my imagination soared. I’d spend hours sketching and painting, turning the dining room into my personal studio—where no table, chair, or counter was safe from paint splatters. Art was my personal adventure, but I never imagined it could reach beyond my own world.

The kids, wide-eyed and curious, cautiously gathered as I handed out brushes, canvases, and soccer balls as the ultimate bribe. Tentative strokes quickly turned into bold expressions, their small hands bringing their inner worlds to life. In that moment, I realized art wasn’t just a hobby—it was a lifeline, a bridge, a voice for the unheard. Each brushstroke revealed their resilience, as they transformed their emotions into colors and shapes, reflecting the African philosophy of Umntu Ngumntu Ngabantu—I am because we are—a reminder of our interconnectedness and shared responsibility to uplift one another.

This resilience mirrored the stories I grew up with—my father, an immigrant from North Africa, and my grandparents from Central America, each forged their place in a new world. My grandfather, a hotel porter, carried the weight of other people’s stories while building his own. My grandmother, a bank teller in San Francisco’s Mission District, navigated an unfamiliar world without losing her sense of purpose. Like the children in Kabokweni, they faced uncertainty with courage, using creativity to build something meaningful in the face of adversity. Art, I realized, wasn’t just about creating images—it was a tool for turning obstacles into opportunity. Much like my family’s pursuit of the American Dream, it is in the space between risk and vision where true growth happens.

Seeing art as a catalyst for change, I began exploring its potential to address societal issues. At Brown University, I immersed myself in the Social Entrepreneurship program, blending creativity with problem-solving to tackle educational disparities, particularly those caused by the defunding of art programs. One evening, as I worked on my capstone project, doubts resurfaced: was art enough? I thought back to Kabokweni and the resilience those children had shown. A turning point came during a conversation with a classmate who, as a child, experienced homelessness. They shared how drawing—sometimes on scraps of paper—gave them a sense of freedom and hope. That exchange reminded me of art’s capacity to foster resilience and healing, even in adversity.

Beyond the classroom, I deepened my commitment to social change through volunteering with Shelter, Inc. Leading an art therapy class for individuals experiencing homelessness, I saw art give voice to emotions words couldn’t capture. One woman, in her 40s, who had endured years of domestic abuse and homelessness, began painting with hesitation, but her strokes soon grew bolder as she reclaimed her story. Each brushstroke became a testament to her resilience, a quiet transformation unfolding before my eyes.

Looking ahead, I envision a future painted with vibrant colors of change. Whether advocating for social justice or using art to challenge perceptions, I will always hold my paintbrush and purpose close. From the bustling alleys of Kabokweni to classrooms filled with new ideas, my journey has reinforced my belief in the transformative power of art, service, and social entrepreneurship. Umntu Ngumntu Ngabantu—I am because we are—drives me to uplift others, knowing my growth is intertwined with the communities I serve. Art didn’t just make a difference in Kabokweni—it transformed lives, mine included. As I step into the next chapter, I’m ready to make the invisible visible—one brushstroke, one story at a time.

“Mommy, why’d it stop flying?”

Before my innocent eyes, a symmetrical frame adorned with blue and white polka dots soared higher and higher, seemingly capable of touching the stars. The hand in control, belonging to a young, freckled boy near my age, fiercely sprinted through the beach sand. But then—lights out. The wind got the better of the string, and the kite settled to the ground. So close.

The kite and I share more than just that memory. Growing up, I’ve, too, often tried to 'soar' past my limits, desiring to live as if the future were already here. But unknowingly, I fell into the habit of rushing toward the destination without appreciating the lessons from the journey—like building a computer without knowing the parts’ purposes. Whenever someone attempted to help, I’d firmly reply, ‘I’ll handle it.’ In truth, ‘handling it’ meant ignoring the opinions of others, yet somehow managing to find my own way in the end. These shallow victories in my bubble instilled a false belief that no matter how high I flew, I didn’t even need a string.

Last summer, I had the opportunity to conduct neurobiology research at Stanford University. During the internship, I lived independently for the first time, detached from friends and family. Surely, I’d figure out living on my own—right? Or so I thought. Living on a tight budget brought unexpected challenges: sharing a home with older strangers, walking three miles to the BART station at 6:00 AM, and managing food and water on my own. It was the opposite of my previously sheltered life.

The first few days were manageable. While preparing meals, a woman just a few years older—whom I knew only by her room number (#5)—initiated a conversation. What began as casual talk soon evolved into sharing history about the area: how the neighborhood becomes sketchy after dusk. Her warnings didn’t cross my mind—once again, ‘I'll handle it.’ But one Friday evening, while returning home from the station, clashing noises startled me. A dark-cloaked figure stood among shattered glass behind me. I speed-walked home, noticing him following. As I rushed through the door—still shaken—a voice greeted me: 
“Is everything alright‽”

I vented to her about the encounter. In response, "Room 5" shared a similar story, but hers ended far worse: her necklace was stolen, and she was left with an indelible scar. I stopped and stared, unsure of what to say. “I guess you just got lucky,” she added before turning to leave.

Survivor’s guilt felt like a heavy weight on my shoulders. What if I, too, had lost something irreplaceable—perhaps my heritage chain? What if I, too, had been hurt? Being open-minded could’ve made the difference. It wasn’t easy, but I started accepting learning from those around me—from cooking hot pot with “Room 2” to hearing “Room 1’s” stories of escaping wartime Vietnam, I was exposed to new perspectives. Rather than confining myself to my room, I sought to be the initiator—bonding with new tenants by asking questions. For the first time, I saw life’s beauty through others’ lenses, discovering hidden lessons in their stories and experiences. I guess I’d underestimated the power of a string.

Even now, I still never shy away from chasing the unknown. But without proper support—like the perspectives gained over the summer—soaring past my limits remains a hypothetical dream, and it might even cause me to fall short. Lessons comprised of academics, experiences, and mentorships are the strands woven into the string, holding me steady whenever turbulence arises.

As I move into the next chapter of my life, whether leading higher-level research or pursuing entrepreneurship ventures, I won’t forget the importance of these strands. To fly high, I’ll need them for the unexpected. My drive to soar to new heights inspires me to learn and innovate, but first and foremost, I need grounding.

I’m ready for the next strands in my string.

Driving home from my sister’s senior night volleyball game, which we lost by two points in overtime after my sister dove to save the ball and missed, our usual conversation was replaced with an uncomfortable silence, my sister glaring straight at the road.

I began replaying the last moments of that game in my head. The ball was coming right at me, and a fear pierced my body; the ball she dove for had actually been in front of me. She’d sacrificed herself to save me from having to carry the mistake myself. A mix of guilt and comfort washed over me, knowing she’d given up her own moment for me. She’d been the reason I even played volleyball. I recognized that she tended to prioritize me a lot. From giving rides to my friends and me after school to allowing her car to be my place of trust and vulnerability, she’d been putting my needs above hers. “You know that ball was actually in front of me right,” I said as we turned into our driveway. “I know,” she responded.

From that time on, I no longer saw our car rides as mundane, seeing the confined spaces of that car as a foundation to build our relationship. Finding joy became all that mattered to us. Whether we were rushing out of our house at 6:30 to grab an energy drink before school or rushing out of school to pick up our favorite smoothies before practice started, we kept our days exciting through these drives.

After my sister left for college, I knew things were going to change, not the least of which was me driving my brother around. He’d always been more laid-back, whereas I’m more proactive; just like my sister and me before she started driving me, we’d never had much in common. I took this as an opportunity to look for connection, just as my sister had once offered me.

The first day, Noah Kahan blasted through the car speakers and my brother let out a huge sigh because he thinks his music taste is better than mine. I was annoyed, but remembering how my sister would sacrifice her own plans to drive me around; I handed him aux. As we drove together more, he started confiding in me. One night, he asked me to take him to ask a girl to Homecoming. “Can we just drive around a bit more and listen to some music before we pull into her house? I need to calm my nerves,” he asked. I realized all our quiet drives to school with his music playing in the background had built a simple silence, where we only needed each other’s presence to connect and bond. Just like how I managed to shift the silence with my sister, I learned how to create a comfortable silence with my brother, becoming a person he could confide in.

Now, when my sister comes home from college, I appreciate our car rides together. Whether we’re driving five minutes to Downtown Chandler for a quick breakfast or driving an hour to a flea market, I hold those moments close to my heart. From seeing the sacrifices my sister made for me to creating comfortable silence with my brother, all those unstructured moments of time dedicated to being together have built the closest relationships in my life. Besides loving my siblings, these relationships have made me a better friend to others, where I’ve learned how to step out of my own experiences and recognize silence as the weight of emotions, creating space for understanding and connection in the stillness. In college, whether or not I have a car, I plan to apply this mindset by continuing to step out of my own experiences and forge relationships that will stay with me for the rest of my life.

I grew up with contradictions. I swung aggressively on monkey bars with my brother and his friends after school, but was mesmerized by the peace of the piano and the challenge of Sudoku during nighttime. Summertime came and Mom advocated for the freedom of sleeping in, while Dad mandated 7am runs. Throughout middle school I felt a deep shame for how my brother dressed and acted, yet when other kids made comments, I defended him fiercely. Though a lively child growing up in Shanghai, I struggled to express this liveliness and feel valued at boarding school.

Navigating these contradictions sometimes felt like a game of tug-of-war with me in the middle. At home I was told to respect authority without question, but teachers seemed to reward kids who spoke out freely and challenged order. Whereas Dad lectured me to always examine my own fault when things went awry, school culture defined confidence as rejecting self-blame. Lawrenceville’s values seemed so foreign from those at home, at times it felt impossible to introduce others to systems of thinking ingrained in me; I would have to fit theirs. With Dad’s constant drillings, my predisposition to recognize strengths in others, and now the need to fit, I developed a habit of imitating others.

I noticed how Kate’s elbows bent at a slight angle as she walked around campus, and began to give my own arms a slight sway. I noticed that Rick could command respect at the Harkness table, and started adding pauses in between my own sentences. I noticed that Henry could work through hours of homework without pause, and I chided myself for an instinct to want child-like fun. I noticed the accolades Catherine stacked up for her singular, well-discovered passion for computer science, and I wished I were her.

I was losing my ground. The concept of being myself, of doing or saying what I felt in public, was becoming more and more distant. During the day, my skin felt stiff, every movement and expression orchestrated. At night, fatigue from imitating and code-switching consumed me as I lay, disenchanted, staring at the ceiling. Feeling burnout from chasing perceived success and confidence, I looked within. I practiced the controllable, emphasizing gratitude and opting for integrity. I lost the need to look to others for exemplary living and focused on my own adventure. In order to fly, I needed to first learn to fall.

Gradually, appreciation for my unique self grew, and habits compounded to a healthier outlook. Though contradictory environments I’ve been put through have created tension in finding my own beliefs, it has also been a gift. As navigating complexities allows our brains to make connections, a contradictory subconscious has complicated my thinking and opened my curiosity to different viewpoints. Bridge-building grew to be a favorite activity of mine. In chemistry class, where the tables are divided by gender and race, I initiate and facilitate cross-table conversations. By asking others questions about themselves and making jokes equally hilarious to all genders and races, I grasp the essence of the shared human experience and bring an air of child-like enthusiasm no one can deny.

Besides the ability to connect with a variety of people, I learned to channel my upbringing as a strength by appreciating, rather than criticizing, my diverse interests. While I was first envious of Catherine's singular passion for computer science, I now know I find joy in a variety of ways. I adore creative expression and ineffable human connection, but also navigate the world through an evidence-based lens.
