In our student-led band The Disciples, we play around with instrument-switching, not because it means we’re weaker on our own, but because a comprehensive understanding of different instruments helps us listen for each other and gain intentionality during our playing.

I span across categories, across tables, across instruments, and across disciplines.

Staring into the opaque lake to understand myself, I find muddy sticks and tar obscuring the essence of my soul. Like Sisyphus, I strenuously fought my boulders of trepidation, only for them to roll back down. Since eighth grade, I had been coerced into a cocoon of doubt. In class, I relished the feeling of being correct. In Calculus, I shot my hand up every time I knew the answer, flaunting my prowess toward my confused classmates. I would explain my solutions, attempting to sound smart, with little regard for their learning. However, during English my lips were sewn shut, as I was uncertain about the validity of my interpretation. When I dared to project my thoughts my voice unconsciously became shaky, as I feared judgment from my peers. During choir, I would suppress my vocals, fearing ridicule from the conductor. Upon arriving home, I would scurry to my room and find refuge in manga, detaching myself from my family. When the boulder of external validation became unbearable, my mind succumbed to Nihilism. Sympathizing with Nietzsche, I believed the material world was valueless and that religion was merely a figment of the imagination. Like him, I felt “God is dead”.

Observing the hollowness in my spirit, my dad asked me to join him at the temple at 4 AM next Sunday. Initially, I rejected his suggestion. Why would I let the absurdity of religion ruin my sleep? After a bit of begging, I reluctantly agreed. After an eerily dark and quiet ride where the roads remain dormant, we arrive at the Kalachandji Mandir.

Despite the vacant route, the parking lot was jam-packed. Upon entering, I observed the tranquil smile on everyone’s face. After making our way to the altar, we stood beside the devotees. One man slams the Mridangam; Another clashes Manjeera cymbals; a lady sings bhajans, and another plays the harmonium. On the other side of the altar, people of all backgrounds dress deities and cook prasadam. Every devotee performed a vital role, all unified by God. After hesitating, I began to sing in unison, free from any doubt. Eventually, I even started dancing without a care for how foolish I may have looked. After an exhilarating three hours, the aarti concluded, and we exited the altar. Before leaving, I was given a copy of the Bhagavad Gita on the way out. Rejuvenated by the devotees, I realized God was not dead. Entering home, I started crying, and the boiling tears melted my cold heart. My soul had been rejuvenated, and a root grew, puncturing my false ego and planting me in a newfound community. With fresh faith, I vowed to read a line from the Gita daily, integrating its insights.

Returning to school, I underwent a mental metamorphosis. Instead of being stifled by fear, I ebulliently voiced my opinions, hoping to enrich my English class. Instead of seeming snobbish, I sought to simplify mathematical concepts, eager to foster understanding. At home, I sang enthusiastically with my family, expressing our devotion to Krishna. I spoke to swamis at the temple, who deepened my knowledge of the Gita. Energized by these three roots, I broke out of my cocoon and permeated into my communities, ultimately finding refuge in religion by serving others, not By myself. Like the recursive swirls of galaxies and the Mandelbrot set, I realized that our lives are fractals, with our persona shaped by numerous similar experiences.

9/06/2024 marks my final moments with my grandmother. By her bedside, I spent a few long hours expressing my appreciation. Her expression remained calm, without regret or fear of death, for she had strived to serve our family consistently despite battling cancer for over thirteen years. I hope to capture this transcendental feeling on my deathbed.

Visiting the lake after three years, now as clear as my grandma’s soul, reflects a serene smile, for God had freed Sisyphus.

A zoo of paper animals bounced around in my backpack as I walked to school, my anticipation growing with each step. In the classroom, students excitedly laid out their treasures: stickers, worms on strings, fancy pencils, along with various other trinkets. I emptied my backpack, and soon my desk was filled with multicolored origami creations. Anxious yet hopeful, I waited to see how my paper animals would be received.

Not long after, laughter filled the room. My classmates formed cat and dog families, set sail with duck companions on boats, and competed to see whose frogs could leap the highest. This was part of a market activity in my second-grade economics class. Even a decade later, I can still vividly picture my friends happily playing. It was the first time my ideas and creations brought joy to a large group of people.

Throughout elementary school, I continued exploring creative ideas for fun and helping around the house by coming up with innovative solutions that I could be proud of, like building a display stand from Lego pieces when my mom needed one. In middle school, I enjoyed technical creations to help my family. A circuit design kit from my sister introduced me to the world of STEM, where I found myself captivated and my creations followed. Later, in return, I designed and created a custom digital alarm clock and proudly presented it to her as a special gift. When one of my dad’s friends missed my house while driving at night, I created a LED house number panel. When my dad helped hang the panel up, I felt an immense sense of family connection, realizing this project was more than just a technical achievement—it was my support and care for the people I love.

In high school, I’ve learned to tackle real problems with creative solutions. On my robotics team, I proposed a 360-degree spinning camera that let our robot shoot balls from any orientation without repositioning, improving speed and accuracy. However, space limitations caused the off-center camera to interfere with aiming dynamically for different robot positions. After days of building geometry simulations and incorporating trigonometry to program dynamic aiming offsets, I was thrilled to see the team’s excitement when our robot, at any random orientation, shot the target perfectly at the world championship. Many teams were impressed and approached us to learn more about our unique design. During competitions, when we encountered difficulties with data collection, I developed a scouting app with a flexible, reusable design that allowed non-programmers to easily adapt it each year as the challenge evolves. Recognizing that other teams might encounter similar challenges, I made the app open source, shared it with the FIRST Robotics community, and created instructional tutorials.

Last year, my mom was anxious about leaving our house empty during a family vacation. To ease her concerns, I designed and built an autonomous home security robot that could detect intruders and send alerts to a phone. This complex project involved mechanical and electrical design, control systems, and network communication. During development, I encountered numerous challenges, one of the most significant being the incompatibility of various open-source software packages with the robot’s components or with each other. The trial-and-error process of design and debugging was time-consuming, requiring patience and persistence as I searched for suitable packages and components. When the robot finally navigated its designed path around the house and successfully sent an alert, I felt a deep sense of accomplishment, knowing I had created something that would give my family peace of mind during our holidays.

My passion for exploration and problem solving has deepened as I continue to learn, design, and experiment with new ideas. In college, I look forward to connecting with other students and academic leaders who share my passion for STEM. My ultimate goal is to continue bringing joy and solutions to people’s lives through creativity.

“Who are you?” he asked.

“It’s me, Yeye. It’s your granddaughter,” I whispered.

I was raised by my grandparents, and my grandfather especially has been my beacon of light, instilling values and character in me. He would tell me stories about his days working as the pioneering group of telecommunication scientists in Shanghai. I remember his favorite tale, which was about how he used his expertise to develop telecommunication infrastructures in rural China, connecting communities that had long been isolated. He would always finish with, “Promise me, my girl. Study hard. Make a real difference in this world like me!” Looking back, I realize how heavy those words were as they are now reminders of my purpose: to be that agent of change.

Those were the good old times. As I left Shanghai for Singapore, the man who meant everything to me began to forget about the promises, my name, and soon, everything.

For years, I wondered if I had stayed, would dementia have never taken him from me like this? Could we have made more memories so he would take longer to forget? Witnessing his gradual loss of memory and identity made me experience the painful truth of how isolating and disorienting it can be when one’s independence is taken away. Inspired by this, I observed another community with comparable challenges: People With Intellectual Disabilities (PWIDs).

It began with volunteering at Singapore Special Olympics, where I joined athletes with disabilities in their training. Many have ADHD or autism, yet the way they darted across the field and played soccer was unrestrained by any notion of limitation. While society often defines PWIDs by their limitations, my interactions with them have shown me their strengths and capacity to experience the world differently.

As such, I founded my multinational project, "Project Little Heroes," for PWIDs. Starting from Singapore, I noticed a well-structured support system, contrasted with the more grassroots approach from neighboring countries. Such differences sparked my curiosity. Why not create a platform where countries can collaborate and share experiences?

However, when I reached out to Malaysian organizations, the silence that followed was deafening. Each unreturned email served as a call for me; I had to be the one to spark change. At 18, I flew to Malaysia, meeting beneficiaries face-to-face to share my vision and mission. These efforts came to fruition when we co-hosted with MINDS Penang for an overseas week-long volunteering program in 2022 that no one had thought possible.

Going beyond the region, I launched “Knowing Minds,” a video series aimed at changing the narrative around PWIDs. Many of the PWIDs struggled to express themselves verbally, yet their expressions and enthusiasm spoke volumes. I remember one boy, who couldn’t find the words to thank me after the video shoot, but his beaming smile and tight hug said more than words ever could. Furthermore, to grasp public perceptions of PWIDs, I took my camera to the bustling central business district, interviewing adults with myth-debunking questions. Many were surprised to learn that over 200 million people globally are diagnosed with PWIDs, admitting how little they knew. Through these authentic narratives, my videos creatively challenge stereotypes and bring much-needed awareness to the forefront. Moments like this keep me going, reminding me that my actions have sparked meaningful changes; I am one step closer to fulfilling my promise to my grandfather.

I recognize real changes demand sustainable solutions beyond what I have achieved. At university, I am excited to develop myself with the knowledge and platforms and expand the current scope and transform regional work into global projects. My goal is to create replicable self-sustaining models for PWIDs so they no longer rely solely on private donations. The path ahead is long, but I am ambitious, and one day, I will proudly tell my grandfather, “Yeye, I have made a difference in this world.”

Once I wished I were a book. I wished I could communicate with people without speaking and people could understand me without asking. Whether it was borrowing a pencil at school or joining a soccer pick-up game at the park, growing up I sometimes was overflowed with uneasy thoughts that crept up, playing out every possibility that could go wrong.

It wasn’t like I never tried to face it. I signed up for a summer camp on congressional debate and attended a year-long weekly public speaking class. But when the time came, the nerves of my anxious self never failed to arrive.

In a last ditch attempt, I saw the Speech & Debate club at my school as a chance to escape the anxiety. The first few meetings showed a world of havoc, where everyone competed to share viewpoints on controversial topics. Also, no one seemed bothered by what others thought; they were simply there to have fun. This is what I wanted. This is what I needed.

My mouth tensed up as I reached for the water on my desk. It was a brisk Saturday morning. No, I wasn’t about to watch Premier League soccer games - I was waiting for my first debate tournament: The Grey Matter Online Invitational. With the click of the mouse, I began narrating my team’s starting argument: Why increased federal regulation of cryptocurrency transactions would produce more harm than benefits.

Was I talking too softly? Would I finish it in time? Amidst my weeks’ preparation, my mind was still flooded with these thoughts as I stuttered my way through the end, “Thus my partner and I support the negation.” I scrambled for the mouse to mute myself and my heart took a gasp for air.

Then, it was another mental battlefield. Short preparation times forced me to constantly dig for the right words in my mind, until the ending sentence: “Thus, it is imperative for you to vote for the negation.” The judge’s smile gave me some comfort and relief, but my mind was replaying everything that went wrong.

With each passing round, the near-heart attacks I had gradually faded away as I noticed others fell into the same trenches - floundering, overtime, etc. Moreover, the scenarios of me breaking down mid-speech or judges laughing at me never happened. They were merely thoughts.

My shoulders loosened as the final round ended. I looked up. The bright yellow lights reflected off the blue painted walls in my room, masking the darkness outside. A full day of talking had left my throat dry and my overworked mind spinning around. But it was at this instance that I realized I was capable of speaking endlessly in front of strangers. Even when the rounds did not go as planned, I found content by valuing what the opponents did well and absorbing the judges’ constructive critiques, making these learning opportunities.

As each tournament passed, my confidence increased, eventually overpowering anxiety. I was eager to indulge in intriguing debate topics, stirring matching cards until I paired a counter-argument with every argument. Rather than reading off a script, I aimed to express a dynamic story that could reach into the audience’s deep memories. The most vivid images, however, are the smiles and relief I saw when coaching at my old middle school. Helping to navigate their ways through the same hurdles I jumped through brought me a sense of purpose and contribution to the same community that had escorted me.

Debate has guided me not to fear speaking up, but to look forward to it. The impacts have traveled outside of debate, whether it is directing teammates on soccer pitches or leading club meetings for Science Olympiad. Most importantly, I’m no longer afraid to take risks. Sure, I may get nervous sometimes to present my research project or math solutions in class. But when I start speaking, the anxiety vanishes as I understand that risks are merely paths to next chapters.

I scan the area and plot the clearest path on the track. The rope connecting me to Jing Yang tugs as we narrowly avoid a roadside trash can. We sense each other’s breath and enter our fourth mile. Just like every Sunday, I tell Jing Yang, my blind running companion, that we’re halfway there. I act as their eyes, yet they have taught me to “see” more than ever.

After hearing a podcast about the power of guide running, I couldn’t shake the feeling that I could use my passion for running to help others. On my runs with Jing, I find myself slowing down and controlling my speed, staying alert to any dangers for Jing while also savoring the experience. Now, on my solo runs, I keep Jing’s pace, and it reminds me I can shape my own path. It’s humbling to know that I can’t predict every twist in the path, but it’s also comforting. It’s okay not to have all the answers—just keep moving forward with an open heart, grateful for the lessons that come. Running grants me the power to grow in resilience and empathy, allowing me to discover the rich community hidden right before my eyes, forever changing my perspective.

I prefer spontaneous trail-making versus preset GPS routes. When I mindlessly follow the navigation, I only see the destination. Avoiding Google Maps pushes me to appreciate my surroundings, from the sounds of birds to the passing smiles of other runners. As a painter, this awareness offers endless inspiration. Abandoning the “preset route” granted me the freedom to blend Ukiyo-e techniques to create a Mucha-style manga portrait. It's become clear the openness and spontaneity I learned on the trail open endless possibilities.

To my left, a fellow runner gives a quick nod of encouragement; to my right, a group of early risers chat softly on a bench; straight ahead, a child waves as he bikes past. My experience with Jing demonstrated the value of human connections, leading me to seek out the History Enthusiasts Community online. Whether it’s a visitor bringing Portugal’s seafaring history to life by describing her tour of Lisbon’s Maritime Museum or a PhD in history discussing how climate factors drove the Mongol expansion, the community challenges my existing knowledge. Being accepted into this group fills me with gratitude and a sense of belonging. Growth happens fastest when you’re paying attention to the brilliance of the world around you, whether on the trail or beyond.

After I completed the Chicago Marathon, our grade director asked me, “Did you win the race?” The question echoed in my mind. When I started running, I wanted to win races, but things are different now. After running with blind runners, I realized running—like life—isn't about speed but perseverance. Running makes tutoring an extra AP Politics student feel as manageable as one more hill climb. For me, there is no finish line in life or in running. The journey ahead excites me, fueling my determination to keep going.

My four years of running enriched my life in ways I’m still discovering. As my physical endurance grows, I have also found emotional strength that I can carry into the future. College presents the physical challenge of a new living space with the emotional opportunity to connect with new people and grow together. I’m ready to support my new community past the hurdles of midterms and through the challenges of studio critiques, knowing lifelong friendships formed and knowledge gained are far more important than the diploma at the finish line.

Hearing my heart pound and my breath shorten is an antidote to the demands of school and the looming pressures of a career. In the immediate future, I hope to join the university running club and guide blind runners in the surrounding community, moving toward new joys, opportunities, and the endless possibilities that await in the trail ahead.

The sharp crack of the ping-pong ball rang out like a starter’s pistol. It ricocheted across the table, barely skimming the edge before flying past my paddle. I lunged, but my seventy-year-old opponent had already moved on to the next serve.

When I first walked into the community center, I imagined ping-pong would be an easy way to meet new people, maybe even impress a few with my reflexes. At 14, I was competitive and brimming with confidence—apparently too much.

My opponent, Mr. Liu, adjusted his stance, paddle at the ready. He wasn’t playing just to pass the time—this was his domain, and every movement he made was calculated, like a viper waiting to strike. As I flailed around the table like I was trying to swat a fly, I marveled at the way Mr. Liu positioned himself, the way he seemed to predict my moves before I even thought of them.

Another serve, another miss. The ball zipped past me before I even realized what had happened. I glanced over at the crowd—a few older men who had gathered to watch—and noticed their barely hidden smiles. I felt my cheeks flush when I lost the round.

Still, there was something humbling, almost meditative, about returning to the table each time, knowing I’d likely lose, but still desperate to get better. Mr. Liu wasn’t showing me any mercy. Every game threw something different at me, and each time I missed, I picked up on something new about my technique. Maybe my grip was too rigid, or perhaps I wasn’t adjusting properly to the spin on the ball. But the more I played, the more I learned patience with every shot, adapted to faster opponents, and celebrated even small improvements.

As I returned to the table day after day, I no longer chased the ball in a flurry of reflexes. I began to sense the rhythm of the game—my feet glided with intention, carrying me effortlessly into place as if I was in sync with the game’s flow. The frustration that once clouded my focus disappeared, replaced by a calm precision.

I still lost more often than I won, but the small victories became sweeter. I’d land a tricky shot here and there, and Mr. Liu would raise his eyebrows, impressed. One day, I won a single point off Mr. Liu’s famous backhand. It was a fleeting victory, but it meant so much to me. Just that one point told me my hard work had paid off.

By the time I was 17, competing against Mr. Liu no longer fazed me. He had become a close friend, and the lessons from our matches started to shape the rest of my life.

During my senior year, I faced an even scarier opponent—a macroeconomics test with a disappointing score. After the initial punch to the gut this dealt me, I realized that the disappointment felt the same as when I lost to Mr. Liu. All I needed to do was re-tie my shoes, wipe the paddle, and refocus.

The following week, I spent nearly every day in my teacher's room, asking questions about fiscal stimulus and inflation’s impact on investments. At night, I replayed the graphs from class, focusing on the shifting supply curves and the balance between inflation and unemployment. That next test, I felt the same calmness I did when I faced Mr. Liu for the 10th time. I knew exactly how to crush the test.

These small victories and failures have made me eager to tackle other challenges. On a college campus and beyond, I hope to tackle issues that matter to me, like reducing economic inequality through progressive tax reforms. So far, my ping-pong pursuits have impacted me and the small community of players in that gym, but I know that in college, I will apply these lessons to larger challenges—whether through collaborating on research to address global economic disparities or leading initiatives that drive social change.

This May, I found out I lost my best friend.

Immured within white construction barriers was Tom Lee; Sadly, the guitar store beneath where I lived had been torn apart overnight. Every now and then, you’d see a shop around the corner renounce itself to the same white walls, but I never imagined this affliction would finally reach me.

We had been inseparable for years. I’d spend hours there on free days, although he did have a particularly strict curfew at 8. Sure, there’s plenty of other branches, but this one was particularly special to me. This was the store that made me pick up the guitar.

Armed with YouTube tutorials, I spent weekends with the Epiphone he recommended, and whenever I finished learning a song, I’d head straight back to the store and play it on a fancier piece of equipment. But back then, I was a hopelessly introverted person; I swore public speaking was my kryptonite. Whenever I was there, I would conscientiously dial the amp’s volume to a level where I avoid irking any passers-by and publicly humiliating myself. My voice then, both in sound and spirit, was quiescently timid. But whenever I played the guitar for someone, I always walked away feeling a little proud and confident in myself.

Tom was the first to hear me brave through my scrappy renditions of ‘Sweet Child O Mine’ and ‘Back in Black’. I graduated through these ‘rites of passage’ songs and started playing more around the store; I could stay there for hours. Sometimes, he’d seemingly materialize into an employee, shoot me a “Good stuff, kid!”, and would start backing me with a blues progression as I soloed. I played, and he listened. In those times, I thought: Maybe I should try performing in front of people.

Gathering some of my mates, we took up our first lavish performance opportunity: a five-minute slot at lunch. Fortunately, our music tastes mostly aligned, and we crafted a glamourous 2-song setlist and prepped hard. Before the day, I had been doom-scrolling the horror stories from my idols describing their first gigs, succumbing to stage-fright or malfunctioning cables. Equipped with 57 different things that could go wrong in my mind, I skipped onto stage, plugged in my guitar, and looked into a sea of silence.

Then, the sticks clicked, the amp’s feedback turned on, and the song started. We musically melted into a cohesive smoothie, viscerally blending rhythms, timings, playing the soul of the songs frictionlessly. It was an intensifying crescendo of musicianship, orchestrated by the hours of rehearsal we’d put in; I had completely forgotten my expectation of a disaster. The minutes glided by, and the few kind souls that stayed past the first song clapped fervently (they were our friends). Still, they had connected with me, and I felt like I was floating. I wanted to keep on flying.

I realized something illuminatingly clear: To speak is, really, to perform, which in turn, is to ultimately connect with people. I buried my shyness and began to find ways to perform beyond music. At student council meetings, service projects, and lessons, I mustered the confidence to put forward ideas, interact more, volunteer after school, and eventually, to lead. Getting the hang of it, talking with people became less chore-like, but rather a chance to connect. Instead of just Tom, my audience is now everyone and I relish the opportunity to find these connections. Instead of choosing the right song or notes, I choose the right anecdote or joke to tell. Instead of keeping quiet, I choose to speak.

My shyness still lingers around, but I’ve learned to speak over it. And though Tom may be gone, what he gave me—confidence, hope, a voice with the courage to share it—stays with me always.

An inconspicuous sign was hung on the wall the following day: Store under renovation.

You bet I smiled hard.

The relentless Singapore sun blazes at 90 degrees. But I’m oblivious to the heat, my legs chugging as the howler monkey enclosure whizzes by. "Slow down!" my aunt calls, so we pause, breathless, marvel at giant pandas, then tiptoe past sleeping pygmy hippos. The sky shifts to amber, and we’re perched on plastic stools at my favorite street vendor. My mouth waters as my uncle shares a styrofoam container of culinary gold: Hainanese chicken rice.

We head home, and as night falls, in the soft glow of our apartment, true magic unfolds.

***

Evenings in Singapore transformed our coffee table into a fortress against every kid’s enemies: homework and broccoli. Amid playing cards and game pieces, there was only room for mischief, laughter, and my uncle’s victory antics. But the move to New Jersey in 2016 threw a wrench in these family game nights. Now, the magic was hidden behind nineteen hours squeezed into 32x18-inch seats through jolts of turbulence. Separated from familiar faces I loved, I sought comfort through a virtual solution.

After hours scouring the internet, I struck gold with Colonist.io, an online Settlers Of Catan platform. With its endless strategies, element of chance, and evolving nature, the game quickly became a family favorite. My aunt’s tortoise-paced play earned her the title “Sultan of Slow-Mo” and prompted us to set a fifteen-minute timer for her turns. Meanwhile, my uncle hoarded wheat like a dragon guarding riches, leading to comical fits when he lost half his precious stash. Laughing with my family, even through a screen, made the oceans between us a little bit smaller.

As our Catan calls continued into high school, I grew more grateful for my relatives’ support. Despite my busy schedule, my relatives always made time, even if it cost them sleep. Each game reminded me of Singapore—I could feel the heat, hear the howler monkeys, smell the street vendors, taste the Hainan cuisine.

Over time, I grew determined to emulate their example, and just like building roads to connect settlements in Catan, I sought to create bridges of connection between people outside of family.

Without my relatives’ regular calls, I manifested my determination in other settings, starting while working at Mega-V Day Camp. There, I noticed ten-year-old Marcus often alone with his Nintendo Switch, occasionally stealing glances at dodgeball games from afar. Wanting to create a new brick bridge, I joined him, at first just watching, then slowly inquiring about his game. He eventually gave in, passionately describing Link's perilous quest to defeat Ganondorf and restore his kingdom. I saw an opportunity. The gym became a battlefield with every throw and dodge an attack against Ganondorf's evil forces. It wasn't long until the Switch sat untouched.

Encouraged by the summer camp success, I strove to extend my road-building skills to my Coral Independent Research Team. One of my teammates stood out: Eshaan, a new 11th-grade student. His enthusiasm was clear, but he looked like a "deer in headlights" at the far end of the table during meetings. So, determined to connect with him, I asked about his classes and discovered the catalyst for another paved path: calculus. As we confronted the course together, his shyness gave way to animated discussions on integrals and Taylor series. Soon, his confidence blossomed, and our research meetings found the table's far end vacant.

***

As I prepare for the next four years, I carry with me the lessons learned from my family Catan nights. The board may change, and the dice may not always roll in my favor, but I know that true success lies in building bridges, not walls. Whether in Singapore or New Jersey, online or in real-life, the most rewarding victories are those shared with others.

And as I look to the victories, challenges, and opportunities of my college journey, I'm determined to keep expanding my network of settlements, one road at a time.

In a gently lit bar in downtown Birmingham, a boy touches the cold mouthpiece of his saxophone to his lips. He exhales and his fingers ripple across the keys, a rich tone cutting through the haze of cigarette smoke that swirls within the tavern. He holds the top note for a lingering moment, and then—the band drops in. The whipping articulation of drumsticks and shifting of dissonant piano chords join the soloist, who furrows his brow as he improvises bebop over cascading harmonies. His heart pounds with excitement. Some turn to listen, but the boy doesn’t notice: he is engulfed in the passion of the tune.

The next morning, the same boy sits at his desk. His bedroom is quiet except for the gentle clicking of fingers on a keyboard whose letters have faded with years of use. He has been writing a narrative for a few weeks about visiting his father’s rural village but is only halfway done—finding the right words has been tedious. The boy closes his eyes and tilts his head back, dreaming of the odor of fertilizer and the heat of the Hunan sun on his face. He exhales and brings his fingers back to the keyboard, meticulously transferring his memories of a Chinese summer onto the page.

Some days, I’m a jazz musician, playing in downtown jam sessions or for local corporate mixers. Other days, I’m a writer, authoring creative fiction, judicial statements, occasionally poetry. These two archetypes are distinct in form, one reckless and the other scrupulous, but they are fundamentally the same. Between the emotional spontaneity of jazz and the thoughtful diligence of writing, I’m still an artist at heart, composed of both passion and precision.

I am invigorated by the anarchy of jazz. The spiritual child of slaves in the deep South, Dixieland’s music was born from a mix of European harmony and African rhythm. And while my lived experiences are greatly unlike those of jazz’s storied ancestors, I find the same joyful freedom in the power to synthesize emotion and identity through purely improvisational music. Jazz at its very core resonates within US history—that we would rather compose our own harmony as a nation than perform the melodies of our predecessors. Indeed, as the first musician and American-born member of my family, I am inspired by this unprecedented music. Jazz is an empowering reminder that I am the sculptor of both my music and my legacy.

My creative self-expression isn’t limited to music though. Writing is improvisation in slow-motion: a careful, precise reflection of my psyche. The artistry of jazz is expressed in the moment, while writing is an introspective journey of many hours, but both are equally significant to me as outlets of self-expression. Whether it’s a financial report or an ode to Mounds chocolate bars, writing is my interpretation of the world, a blend of scholarship and identity. Literature is the very basis of our shared human experience—to not contribute would be an act of cowardice. I write to discover what I believe. I write both to celebrate and to criticize. I write to tell my own story.

I wish I could say that I love transcribing Coltrane or dissecting a feature from Harper’s in my free time, but it’s only half true. It’s the potential for creation that really electrifies me—on a midnight bandstand in downtown Birmingham or between dog-eared pages of my own prose. Whether it’s through songs or sentences, passionate improvisation or meticulous writing, composition allows me to fuse the scrapbook of who I’ve been and the blueprint of who I’ll become, to combine both mind and heart in my contributions to the world. I await the future with zeal: there’s much more to learn, to create, to become.

I expected Owen to share typical hardships: a sense of abandonment, identity confusion, or racial and cultural alienation. I was interviewing him for my Oral History Lab while working on a book that I published to help adoptees navigate through trauma—something I had never experienced myself. But Owen spoke calmly and confidently. “Being an adoptee helped me feel free,” he said. “It allowed me to disconnect from society’s expectations.”

His words caught me off guard.

How could adoption—something I assumed came with difficulty—give someone freedom? He explained that his adoption gave him a fresh start, free from inherited expectations. It allowed him to define himself on his own terms. I began to realize that I had been volunteering from a place of assumption, believing I knew what was best for the organization and the people I was helping. But Owen wasn’t asking for my sympathy or my solutions; he was living his own experience. This realization made me uncomfortable, as it forced me to confront my misguided belief that my role was to 'fix' things rather than learn from the people I was serving.

I questioned my reasons for volunteering. Was it really to help others, or just to feel better about myself? As I reflected more, I saw the bigger picture. I hadn’t just been helping others: I was looking for connection, for a community I could grow with.

This realization also shaped my role as President of the Korean Adoptee Family Foundation (KORAFF). I first learned about KORAFF through my aunt, who urged me to join. I was drawn in by their mission of spreading culture and traditions with adoptees, and how it allowed me to take action within such a marginalized and underscored community. What I learned from speaking with adoptees was their desire to know more about their history. Most of them had not visited their country of birth since arriving in the United States, so I decided to help Mrs. Chung (our founder) organize a fully funded trip for them. I worked with Starbucks, the Korean Embassy, Brown Bear Car wash, and the Korean local news station to raise funds, and collaborated with a Korean consultant to organize the travel details. We successfully covered airfare for forty adoptees, and hearing their stories of connecting with their homeland for the first time and discovering their origins was incredibly rewarding.

I wasn’t there to give solutions; I was there to share in the work and experiences. I understood that MY real purpose wasn’t about being SEEN as helpful, but about building a community where we could help EACH OTHER.

Owen’s story had also made me more curious about identity and belonging. I began reading adoption narratives, not as a researcher, but as someone who wanted to connect with these experiences. This new perspective shaped how I approached everything, from my academic work to my personal relationships. This perspective has fueled my interest in furthering my research on how affinity communities shape individual identities and collective belonging. I’m particularly interested in examining the social and political structures that impact marginalized groups, and I hope to expand my platform for sharing adoption narratives, fostering a space where adoptees can connect and advocate for greater visibility and support.

Owen helped me understand that my purpose wasn’t to help others; it was to build a community where we all help one another. I thought leadership was about guiding people, but I’ve learned to approach my role not from above but from walking alongside them as we all navigated our own paths.

As I deftly manoeuvre my knight into position, I feel a surge of confidence: this could be it. My grandfather, watching intently, arches an eyebrow and smirks, as if he knows something I don’t. I take a deep breath and make my move, only to be met with an unexpected grin as he playfully sacrifices his bishop, leaving his king vulnerable. I leap from my seat and declare checkmate for the first time. “Heyy, you’re getting better at this!” he chuckles, his eyes sparkling with pride. I giggle, eyes glossy, heart warmed.

The screechy handpicked sound of our home landline snaps me back to reality. My grandfather was gone, the funeral was done, and those moments now only existed in memory. The shock of seeing someone so full of life and energy simply vanish felt like a jolt to my core. The burn in my chest slowly deepens, the pit in my stomach making itself more pronounced, a constant reminder of the fear of death I can’t seem to shake. The idea that everyone I love could vanish, just as the body I've nurtured all my life fades away frightens me. Every achievement I've celebrated, every life I've touched — all dissolving into the vast, unending unknown. In my search for answers, “thanatophobia” emerges on the screen: an intense fear of death and the dying process, a label for the shadows lurking in my mind.

The constant ache of uncertainty seeped into my life, revealing the turmoil I had tried to hide. My family tried helping in their own ways; my mom turned to rituals, seeking comfort in tradition, while my dad drove me through long, silent stretches, each mile echoing the weight of unspoken fears. Yet, those moments felt like mere band-aids on a wound that ran deeper.

“How about joining me at work today?” my mom suggested one Saturday summer morning, her smile bright but weary. A few hours later, I found myself trailing behind her at the hospital, watching as she tried to convince yet another patient that Dolo 650 wasn’t the miracle cure for every ailment under the sun. Before she could say it a third time, a nurse slipped in, urgency in her voice, “Doctor, the delivery room is ready.”

A brisk walk carried me from the bustling hum of the patient hall into the hushed whispers of the delivery room. Time seemed to blur there. I watched, caught in a strange blend of horror and curiosity, as my mom made the horizontal incision on the woman’s belly, revealing layers of purple skin beneath. What felt like just a moment later, the baby's piercing cry echoed, bursting forth with a raw, life-affirming energy that reverberated in my chest. The smiles spreading across everyone’s faces illuminated a truth I had long overlooked: rather than an end, death is a door opening to new lives, each with the potential to create their own joy and memories, just as I had. As the baby’s cries filled the room, the whirlwind of chaotic thoughts that had plagued me gradually faded away, leaving my mind blissfully clear; in that moment, I felt an overwhelming gratitude for the emptiness in my head, a quiet space that allowed me to appreciate life’s fragility.

That day made me realize though, that perhaps life is just a series of small moments—a cry in the delivery room, a gentle word on a long car ride, a shared memory with a loved one—that ripple outwards in ways we can’t always see. As I look ahead, I no longer fear the emptiness that once haunted me; instead, I’m determined to fill it with moments that matter, both big and small. Maybe the true legacy we leave behind isn’t in our grand achievements, but in those fleeting, quiet connections that make us feel a little less alone. It’s something my grandfather showed me long before I even realised it—as he built a cancer hospital in Ongole, touching lives through acts that were as much about heart as they were about healing. Inspired by his example, I later began my own journey into cancer awareness, hoping to create ripples of change just like he did. And if I’m lucky, someday, my efforts might become a small part of someone else's story, just like my grandfather’s has become a part of mine.

Lemons, caffeine, and eucalyptus, each an engrossing scent. I'm a fragrance connoisseur, caught in the dance between the top, middle, and base notes of life. Let me introduce you to a few from my collection.

Le Labo’s Bigarade 18. Citrus, florals, a carefree childhood

The initial spray of Neroli and Bergamot are reminiscent of Park Lane’s Hotel Lobby. This memory quickly fades with the top notes, and the middle notes of lily flower pull me two streets down – back to my grandpa's small, humid apartment. The smell carries me to my summer days spent alongside my grandfather, rummaging through stacks of endless files, surrounded by vases of well-kept lily flowers. He tidied the chess pieces, the English textbooks, his flower growing magazines, showcasing his purpose: doing what he loved. Even though we sat on mini pink stools sweating profusely – it wasn’t discomfort I remembered – it was his patience and quiet persistence. Though, isn’t that how fragrances work? The deeper notes are the ones that stay.

Maison Margiela’s Coffee Break. 5:30 PM chess with cappuccinos

I resigned from my chess match and slammed my MacBook shut. The suffocating pressure for excellence, my parents’ bragging, my grandpa's pride in my achievements… Amidst it all, I began drifting away from chess, avoiding the game I once loved. I felt like a knot of anxiety tightening in my chest, the fear of losing crushing my heart.

Then I discovered the magic of Coffee Break. The voice of Louis Armstrong echoed in the background, the cappuccino and croissants in front of me drifting through scent. Coffee Break relieved me of this suffocating feeling as I envisioned the café atmosphere each time I spritzed it on and played chess. Falling in love with chess once more, I felt my knot disappear, no longer anxious to lose – flagging my opponent, blundering, and winning. Through Coffee Break, I reclaimed my passion, transforming anxiety into motivation and rediscovering the artistry of the game.

Xerjoff Torino22, a bold eucalyptus raspberry tea.

Sitting at my desk staring at my dim screen, I had a total of zero orders placed.

Driven by my curiosity of the story behind one’s perfume, I started a fragrance business. My first sale was local: Louis Vuitton Afternoon Swim, sold to a close friend who had just quit swimming to take care of his mom. Helping him reconnect with his passion was the beginning of a fragrance community. I found like-minded connoisseurs, obsessing over chemical compositions of fragrances at lunch.

However, transitioning online was challenging. The lack of personal connection, the lack of a community, it frustrated me. Among a sea of fragrance e-stores, I felt like an outsider, someone “not cut out for business”. Doubt crept in. Was this just another failed attempt at entrepreneurship? Chess tutoring, car detailing – fragrances would soon join the list.

But fragrances weren’t just a “business” to me. I found joy in picking a fragrance in the morning, receiving compliments, and complimenting others. Torino22 was the fragrance that helped me meet my best friend. That wasn't just “business.” If a picture is worth a thousand words, Torino22 is worth a million. It was a door that turned two shy kids into study-buddies, chess rivals, and brothers.

I then realized: I wasn’t just obsessed with fragrances. I was fascinated by transformation – both in others and in myself.

I spent that night redesigning my marketing strategy, adding personal anecdotes to every product to emphasize the story behind each fragrance. Torino22 - the story of my best friend. Cedrat Boise - baking with mom. I ended up with over 400 fragrances listed – each with a unique story.

The next morning, a barrage of notifications woke me up as 25 new orders were placed overnight. Soon, it was 60 orders per day.

My Fragrance(s)

My fragrances have shown me that life, its challenges, and its commemorations aren’t fixed. They’re fluid, shaped and reshaped by its wearer. We’re all blends of moments, ever-changing, forced to grow, yearning to transform. You ask me what I’m wearing, and I pause. Fragrances suck me into a world where time blurs; it's hard to explain. I’m not just wearing a scent; I'm wearing a memory, a part of me still unfolding. Today, it’s light and airy – like me. Tomorrow, it could be dark and bold – also like me.

A bulldozer was illegally driving down the road during the morning rush hour, and I drove one of the dozens of cars stuck behind it going 25mph in a 50. As my Honda Civic inched down the road, it shook slightly when its three occupants moved energetically in our seats to the dance break of one of our favorite songs. My two sisters and I knew we were going to be late for school that morning, but we could see the good in it. We appreciated that it meant more time to enjoy one of our few shared loves: Korean pop music, a.k.a. K-pop.

I still remember vividly how I fell in love with the genre. On a Sunday in January 2022, one of my younger sisters asked me to watch a music video with her: Permission to Dance by BTS. I watched in awe as 7 Korean men danced around the screen in wild-west-themed clothing and bold hair colors, singing an upbeat song in English about dancing and letting go of your worries. Immediately, I was captivated. I needed to learn their names, memorize their choreography, and experience their other songs.

After three years of dance class, I had only picked up a tiny fraction of BTS’s skill and charisma, but K-pop was expanding my music taste and my horizons. I started to learn about the people and customs of South Korea, a country halfway around the globe. I was fascinated by how strikingly different it was from the culture of Middle Tennessee. Discovering K-pop introduced me to a whole new side of the world that I had never considered before, both figuratively and literally.

The groovy, fun energy they embodied in Butter was contagious. I had caught that energy and now I wanted to share it with others. Up until that point, I had been too shy to discuss or display my dance skills outside of classes and group performances, but my love of K-pop finally overcame that shyness.

At my youth group’s camp talent show, I performed Butter to a crowd of about 400 friends and strangers. To combat my nerves over my first solo performance, I reminded myself K-pop idols, some of them as young as me, regularly deliver amazing performance to crowds much bigger than this one. When the familiar beats of the Butter intro began blasting from the speakers around me, my anxiety melted away as passion and muscle memory took over.

Not only was K-pop expanding my music taste, but it was expanding my horizons. I started to learn about the people and customs of South Korea, a country halfway around the globe. I was fascinated by how strikingly different it was from the culture of Middle Tennessee. Discovering K-pop introduced me to a whole new side of the world that I had never considered before, both figuratively and literally. I want to expand the world for other people and change the way they interact with it by teaching them English.

I scan the area and plot the openest path on the track. The rope connecting me to Jing Yang tugs as we narrowly avoid a roadside trash can. We sense each other’s breaths and enter our fourth mile. Just like every Sunday, I tell Jing Yang, my blind running companion, that we’re halfway there.

I act as their eyes, yet they have taught me to “see” more than ever. When I used to run alone, I’d often get excited and speed up uncontrollably. But with Jing, I slow down and control my speed, staying alert to any dangers for Jing while also savoring the experience. Now, on my solo runs, I do the same. As I run, each stride reminds me that I have the power to shape my own path, no matter how the Beijing I’ve run through has changed and will continue to change. Running grants me the power to grow in resilience and empathy, allowing me to discover the rich community hidden right before my eyes, forever changing my perspective.

I prefer spontaneous trail-making versus preset GPS routes. If I mindlessly follow the navigation, I only see the destination. Avoiding Google Maps pushes me to appreciate my surroundings more, from the sounds of birds to the passing smiles of other runners. As an artist, this awareness offers endless inspiration and allows me to blend techniques and styles freely, unconfined by rigid frameworks. It lets me merge ancient and modern elements into a single work, revealing new aspects of creativity. This mentality of spontaneous exploration in running opens up endless possibilities in art and life, where thinking and experimenting during the process matter more than simply reaching the final outcome.

To my left, a fellow runner gives a quick nod of encouragement; to my right, a group of early risers chat softly on a bench; straight ahead, a child waves as he bikes past. Awareness in this shared journey makes the city feel smaller and the run more meaningful. Because of my experience with Jing, I now value the human connections running brings over the solitude of running alone. It has also led me to seek out the History Enthusiasts Community—whether it’s an organizer encouraging me to present my research about the intellectuals’ figure in Chinese propaganda posters or a PhD in history discussing how climate factors drove the Mongol expansion, challenging my existing knowledge. Growth happens fastest when you’re paying attention to the brilliance of the world around you, whether on the trail or beyond.

After I completed the Chicago Marathon, our grade director asked me, “Did you win the race?” I paused, the question echoing in my mind. Winning? When I started running, my goal was simply to run faster and beat my opponents, but things are different now. After running with blind runners and interacting with others, I realized running—also life—aren’t just about speed. Running gives me the perseverance to climb one more hill or take on one more responsibility when tutoring AP Politics. For me, there is no finish line in life or in running. I just have to keep pushing.

From my four years of training, I began to appreciate the subtle ways running has enriched me in the world. As I’ve grown in my physical endurance, I have also found emotional strength that I can carry into college. It presents the physical challenge of a new living space with the emotional opportunity to connect with new people and grow together. I’m ready to push and support my new community up the hill of midterms or through the challenges of studio critiques, knowing lifelong friendships formed and knowledge gained are far more important than the diploma at the finish line.

Hearing my heart pound and my breath shorten is an antidote to the demands of school and the looming pressures of a future career. The more I run, the more I open myself up to the world around me. As I enter this next phase of my life, I hope to join the university running club and guide the blind runners in the surrounding community, moving toward new joys, opportunities, and the endless possibilities that await with companions.

“Chuva e Fogos” was my first hit song. Well, as big of a hit as it could have been for a four-year-old girl in Vinhedo, Brazil. Performed to a dedicated audience of about fifteen people, my magnum opus, which translates to “rain and fireworks,” debuted in my living room using my heroically run-down karaoke machine. Unfortunately, my smash hit was never shared past that private audience. While the performance didn’t lead to stardom, the essence of that song has reverberated throughout my life—not just through my family replaying the video, but as my unspoken language with the world.

Despite growing up in the superficially “silent” countryside, I never seemed to escape the loud Sertenajo music blasting from a nearby speaker. My life mirrored a continuous, melodic record scratch–subconsciously learning scales from my uncle’s guitar, perfecting the lyrics to “Chuva e Fogos” countless times, and spontaneous karaoke where everyone, regardless of talent, grabbed a microphone. That unfiltered togetherness introduced me to a world built on unapologetic authenticity, a place that taught me to revel in my free-spirit and vulnerability. Or, as my younger self would lyricize, to embrace both the ‘chuva’ and the ‘fogos.’

As I grew up, looking out my bedroom window became a habit as new graffiti murals transformed my community into an art gallery. Immersed in the inescapable presence of art and music, I realized how invaluable artistic expression really was. In my experience, art was priceless. However, before my neighborhood’s paintings could be finalized, my parents took the risk of moving to the United States, where my new canvas was completely blank. Though it was difficult for my eyes to adjust from a place of vibrance to one of seemingly monochromatic uniformity, what was hardest to comprehend was the idea that art now had a price tag, one we could not yet afford.

In navigating the unknown, I turned to what I knew best: writing music. Gradually, English words began weaving into my Portuguese lyrics, unconsciously dissolving the language barrier for my parents as my at-home concerts turned into nightly English lessons. With their growing proficiency in English, thanks to my translated verses, they found a way to repay me through my enrollment in ballet lessons.

I discovered a strange familiarity within the marley-wood floors, which held the same comforting spirit of authenticity now imbued with a sense of refined structure and discipline. ‘Yeshchyo raz’—a staple command from my ballet teacher that echoed over the accompanist, urging us to 'repeat.' Repeat. With every ‘yeshchyo raz,’ my attention to detail became instinctive. Even in the simplest plié, I activated every muscle, turning repetition into precision. What began as repeating steps within the mirrored studio walls evolved into a deep-rooted dedication to give my 100% effort in all I do.

I began desperately craving the comforting familiarity of these authentic spaces, so I shaped my life around them, meticulously structuring my days to maximize my time in those pursuits. I focused my honed discipline into a cyclical routine of classical piano lessons, musical rehearsals, voice-over auditions, and performances with the Arts Ballet Theatre of Florida's corps, each one a nostalgic portal back to where my karaoke machine once lived. Eventually, the unique pigments of my newfound sanctuaries slowly filled up my vacant canvas, shrinking the void of cultural absence with a fresh meaning.

My canvas may not be perfect, but I will continue blending, finding value in each unique hue that serves as a gateway to my self-expression. Though the presence of art in my new community has since grown, I thank its former absence for challenging me to find beauty in silence and monotony. In the end, a world that neglects authenticity is one that silences its own voice, and I am committed to continue amplifying my own and that of others through inclusive spaces that embrace both ‘chuva’ and ‘fogos.’

Every May, the bushes across my boarding house crowd with blossomed peonies, their bright pink petals a joyful proclamation of the arrival of summer. I am drawn to the flower I was named after, the “king of flowers” in Chinese culture, renowned for its exquisite beauty and unique intricacy.

My name had been a source of discomfort for me. I resented that teachers often mispronounced it, and its uncommonness made me stand out more than I wanted. But it was when I found myself at a new boarding school in Sevenoaks, a staggering 9,532km from home, that I truly despised it.

Like a bee in a field devoid of flowers, I felt lost in classes and clubs. Instead of being a peony, I just wanted to blend in with the roses.

On Easter of year 10, my dad and I embarked on a journey to the Keukenhof flower festival in Amsterdam. The festival was a magnificent display of an array of vibrant flowers in full bloom. I found it fascinating to observe the diverse and unique characteristics of each flower, yet they all thrived together harmoniously. During this visit, I came across the remarkable "1000-year-old [Name] Tree" from China, which struck a chord with me. I couldn't help but draw parallels between myself and the resilient nature of the tree and the flowers.

Initially, sharing a room with five other girls with distinct backgrounds and personalities made me uneasy. However, my Cantonese upbringing instilled in me a sense of discipline and resilience, which helped me embrace the opportunity to learn from others. Engaging with my Romanian roommate, I delved into the rich cultural traditions of her homeland, such as the Martisor festival and traditional dishes like Ciobor. Surprisingly, the culinary similarities between Ciobor and the Cantonese-style Oxtail Borscht I grew up drinking created a sense of connection.

Late-night conversations with my roommate became moments of solace, fostering a sense of belonging and warmth. Through these exchanges, I learned the value of overcoming discomfort with curiosity and the rewards of perseverance in the face of fear.

The London Olympic Pool was shrouded in a torrential downpour, the gloomy April sky serving as a backdrop to the tension that had flared up among my teammates over relay orders. In an effort to diffuse the conflict, I turned to the calming properties of the [Name]. I lightened the mood by making a lighthearted joke about our swim caps, and then I pointed out Anjola's impressive split, suggesting that she take the lead in the upcoming relay. Recognizing Amelia's exceptional endurance in the 400 IM, I proposed that she take the 4th place spot. After taking everyone's input into consideration, we finally reached a consensus with just 2 minutes to spare. Five minutes later, we made history by clinching the Bath and Otter Cup, standing united as a team. Once again, the [Name] flower had worked its magic.

Regardless of the superstitions that plague me or the fears that haunt me, I believe in my power and heritage to make others feel empowered, heard, and healed. These new and different ideas about belonging and understanding, and skills about adapting and persevering, are the soil that has enabled me to foster an environment of support and acceptance of diverse perspectives and knowledge everywhere I go. The opportunity to join different communities in sports, culture, and arts in college will only expand my ability to think with open-mindedness and my knowledge of the power of healing and empowerment.

In July, my dad visited me at school, and I pointed out a peony I saw. He insisted it was a rose. In fact, it is a Paeonia lactiflora hybrid: a [Name] Rose Mix. Scarcely showing the first signs of sprouting, its determination promises a breathtaking flower once its individual loosely folded petals come together, surrounding the bud.

“Vamos, vamos, sí se puede!” I was surrounded by faces painted yellow, blue and red resting on bodies wearing similarly colored fútbol kits. The aroma of saffron-flavored arroz con pollo filled the air. Cheers roared and then quieted in concentration. You might think I was at a soccer match in Colombia. Yet, this was a typical day in my childhood home, rich with Latin American culture. What is surprising about this scene, however, is that my family is not Latin American; we are eastern European and have been in America for generations.

I was born and raised in New Jersey in a neighborhood just across the Hudson River from New York City where the Statue of Liberty stands tall welcoming foreigners. This region of New Jersey is a melting pot of nationalities. It was here that my family met Alejandra, a Colombian immigrant, who sometimes lived with us but always cared for me. Alejandra gave me the gift of Latin culture weaved into my traditional American upbringing.

As a child, I was drawn to the Hispanic community that enveloped me. I loved the colorful food, energetic music, and the gathering of close-knit families that turned every occasion into a fiesta. I was warmly welcomed into these gatherings. Even though my English responses set me apart as an outsider, I hesitated to speak Spanish for fear of embarrassment. I vividly remember tagging along to a birthday party when, suddenly caught up in the celebration, Spanish words burst through my lips. I can’t recall what I said, but suddenly I felt empowered. It wasn’t that I had lacked the words; what I had lacked was confidence. Gaining the confidence to speak Spanish to native speakers was a struggle I had to work through. I learned that mistakes are part of growth, and the harshest critic is often ourselves. Overcoming this fear gave me the strength to tackle future obstacles.

In addition to the language, being exposed to Latin culture meant embracing their passion for soccer. In Latin America, soccer is not just a sport; it is an obsession. Soccer holds important historical, social, and cultural meaning for Colombians, and that tradition was being passed down to me. I joined a soccer club and quickly realized I needed to apply the same lessons learned through Spanish: embrace mistakes and keep practicing. With this mindset, I advanced to more competitive teams and soon matched the skill of those who were exposed to the sport since birth. Whether playing in competitive matches or community pickup games, soccer was part of my identity now, just as it had been for generations of people who bridged gaps sharing this common interest.

I felt the connection to my Colombian roots slipping away once at boarding school, so I clung to our shared passion for soccer. However, as the high school years went by, injuries started to derail my aspirations. I spent more time in physical therapy recovering from broken bones, torn ligaments, and ankle sprains than I spent on the soccer pitch. Fearful of losing out on my dream, I made the bold decision to switch boarding schools for one with a top soccer program and commit to an additional year of high school. I sacrificed graduating with my friends to reach my goal. However, in soccer as in life, sometimes the ball hits the back of the net and sometimes it goes wide. Despite my dedication, as the clock ticked down, my dream of playing college soccer slipped through my fingers.

Whether it is conquering my fear to speak Spanish or navigating an early end to my soccer career, these challenges have taught me the importance of possessing resilience and grit. Each setback grounded me to reflect on my goals and strengthened my resolve to succeed. Recently, I took a Global Studies course and traveled to Colombia, reigniting my passion for this culture. I aim to continue studying Spanish in college. I also worked at a Costa Rican-inspired restaurant and interned at a law firm to explore new interests. I am proud of the confidence I have gained through these experiences. As I look towards college and a potential career in international business or law, I carry with me the understanding that resilience and determination are the keys to pursuing my dreams.

**Essay:**

Packing our home felt like trying to bottle a storm: unpredictable, chaotic, and impossible to control. I sat on our black couch crying, my sister was shouting at my parents. The outlines of our living room blurred as my eyes filled with tears. The thought of leaving my school, my friends, my hobbies weighed on me like a rock. To me, Zollikon, Switzerland had always been the most beautiful place on earth. The thought of going away filled me with dread, as I tried delaying the goodbyes as much as I could. Terrified, worried, and anxious, I was certain that my life was going to change for the worst.

“This will be a great adventure.” On the verge of tears, sitting in the plane between the familiar and unfamiliar, I found myself thinking back to a conversation that deeply impacted me before our departure. In the midst of my despair during a period of uncertainty, introspection, and doubt, a friend of my mom offered me perspective-shifting advice: "this will be a great adventure." Over the next weeks, this idea, shared around their dining room table overlooking lake Zurich, gradually shifted my view from chaos, uncertainty, and loss to an opportunity for exploration and growth. The previously grey picture of leaving suddenly filled with color. Captivated by the idea that like an explorer, I could see a devastating situation as part of a journey, in which a variety of experiences and novelty were the basis of something worth striving for. Over the next weeks, I gained the ability to look forward to a new part of my adventure and the positive aspects of it that would be impossible to experience without curiosity for the unknown.

Sitting in one of the uncomfortable chairs in my new school’s auditorium, I was looking into entirely unfamiliar faces, overwhelmed by the fear of a challenge I had never faced before. It seemed as if everyone else knew each other from primary school and I was the outsider. When my name was called, I left the seat between my parents and walked to the front of the room to join my future classmates. Everyone seemed to be enjoying the moment, happy to be put into the same group as their friends. As they were celebrating, I was thinking about my friends in Switzerland. Sitting on the cold floor of our auditorium, a sense of loneliness overcame me. Even though, with the people around me, I had left behind parts of myself, as the adventure continues, I would have to find a different aspect of myself in these new people. During our first break, I asked them if I could join their game of catch.

Playing catch with my friends became a cherished memory symbolizing the bond that started in this friendly competition. With these people, I started building connections and sharing experiences. Taking a leap into new interactions has been a crucial opportunity for my personal development.

During my high school experience, when my heart starts beating faster and a feeling of anxiousness overcomes my body, I pause and reflect. Through my past experiences, I have created a compass, found a guiding star that guides me through new territories from which I can learn. Driven by curiosity, broadening my horizon, talking to people, reading about new concepts, and revising my opinions has been the basis for the person that is enriched by diversity that I want to shape myself into.

I now am certain that what I had initially thought to be a catastrophe that would cause a deadly storm, has been one of the most valuable challenges to overcome. It has created an understanding of my character that has shaped me into who I am. It has been the basis for the experience that has shaped my character.

Sitting on the same black couch, I intend to leave Germany like I did Switzerland. Now I feel more prepared and can contribute to campus: my search for connections with others and my diver’s interests. While it certainly would be easier to study at a local university, jumping into the cold water and taking the chance is what makes life amazing. Only in another environment can you meet new people and learn something new. Although still frightened, I am better equipped to continue the adventure. My experiences have brought me closer to the ideal adventurer. One who takes initiative. One who learns from others. One who benefits his community and one that sees the positives in change.

It is no surprise that Friday is most people's favorite day, and my Friday night anticipation of the weekend is no exception. I had just heard a familiar voice, a scream so sharp that the world immediately narrowed to just that sound. It was my mother. Like any other typical Friday evening, I was taking a nap. I couldn’t imagine what could have possibly happened to her, but I immediately ran out barefoot to find out.

She had placed her hand on the car door as she unpacked groceries from the car. In her haste and excitement to start the weekend, she had not properly engaged the parking brake. The car rolled back leisurely, causing the accident that left her hand trapped and bleeding profusely. I was only 12 years old and lacked maturity and knowledge in how to handle a situation like that let alone administer first aid. I felt petrified as I struggled to understand the situation.

The sight of my mother in agony and the ocean of blood that flooded the floor triggered an immense feeling of helplessness in me. Despite being a twelve-year-old, home alone with her distressed mother, I was well aware that I had to act quickly to save my mother’s life before I found myself as a maternal orphan. As barefoot as I had run out of my room, I ran to various neighbors seeking someone to take her to the hospital.

As she was taken for treatment, I was told to stay at home. That Friday night I found myself cleaning the garage floor full of blood instead of having our usual family dinner. I could not help but blame myself that if I had any knowledge about first aid, my mother would not have lost as much blood, and at that moment I got fuelled with an obsession of doing my best to make sure I would never be unable to help someone in need again. Over time, I was able to turn my childhood trauma into a driving force for personal growth by learning how to give first aid by joining the first aid club and practicing it at school, therefore overcoming the deep sense of powerlessness I carried around.

Coming from a developing country where the healthcare industry is still a work in progress, I became more motivated not to let the trauma from that Friday evening be the end of my dream but a driving force to immerse myself in medical technology as my way of being there for people in need, giving back to my community, and sustainably making the world a better place.

That dreadful day molded me into a resilient person, capable of overcoming obstacles and challenges with quick responsiveness and emotional resilience. I learned the importance of being prepared for emergencies, staying calm under pressure, and to not give up when faced with adversity. The accident also taught me how to move forward after a challenging period, and shaped my career aspirations and personal goals in very unimaginable ways.

As I look back, I am filled with gratitude for the lessons I learnt from that Friday night and the greater person it helped me become. Even though the road ahead might get challenging at times, I am confident that I now have the strength to make a positive impact in the world. I am proud to have conquered my fears and on the right path towards my dreams. I am fueled by a passion for excellence and look forward to Friday nights.

“You don’t know someone until you walk a mile in their shoes.”

I suggest you choose shoe #3. The first two aren’t suited for walking.

House Slippers 
Soft and unmarred, my house shoes are part of my cherished Sunday morning routine. The rich aroma of my mom's brewing coffee fills the air as she sits at the head of our kitchen table, awaiting her cup. Every Sunday, I bring her coffee from the kitchen island to her seat—a small gesture that holds immense meaning. My mom's neurodegenerative condition (cerebellar degenerative atrophy) means she doesn't move, think, or talk as swiftly as she once did. After breakfast, I help her walk downstairs to help her with physical therapy. As I have worn these shoes, I have developed a skill in identifying needs. This means doing research to install a railing for the front steps of our house. Getting shower grab bars. My routine in these shoes has shifted over the years—more pauses, more careful steps. I've learned to be patient, not just physically but emotionally. I am able to deepen my capacity for empathy and care.

Dress Shoes 
Roughly twice a month, I lace up my black dress shoes—the leather stiff, the soles worn smooth from countless early mornings. By 6:45 AM, I'm standing alone at Great Neck station, the cold concrete biting through the soles. As my Model UN club arrives, I catch a nervous glance from a freshman adjusting her tie too many times, and I see myself reflected in her—wide-eyed, unsure of where to step next. I guide her through the ticket machine, my fingers moving through the motions effortlessly now, no longer hesitant like they were in my first year. We board the train, and I settle the team into their seats, the once-overwhelming roar of the tracks now a familiar hum in my ears. I lean over, whispering strategies to jittery first-timers, reminding them to breathe before presenting their resolutions. When we step into the chaotic pulse of Penn Station, I scan the group, counting heads, moving automatically. Between subway stops, I brace myself against the pole, feet steady as others stumble with the train's jolts. I let them find their footing, offering a hand only when needed. The scuffs on these shoes tell a story—not just of miles walked, but of the delicate balance I've learned as a leader—knowing when to speak up and step back, letting others find their voice as I once found mine.

Everyday Shoes 
Scuffed, my white canvas shoes are the pair I wear every day—because I like getting them dirty. By 7:30 AM, my English teacher pulls at the seams of my argument, urging me to rethink everything. I dive in, reshaping my thesis until it’s airtight. By 10 AM, a marker squeaks against the board as I scribble furiously, determined to chase every equation to its end. By noon, a Socratic seminar rubs the soles with debate—an argument about Plato’s Republic scuffs one side, a rebuttal on justice marks the other. Each idea leaves its imprint, not just on my shoes, but on how I see the world. After class, I sift through essays submitted for my international trade competition. I love it—the fresh perspectives, the angles I didn’t anticipate. Did they approach the theory as I imagined, or take it somewhere new? Every essay opens a window into someone else’s mind. Throughout wearing this pair of shoes, I have seen the value of different perspectives. Everyone’s perspective is uniquely shaped in some way, and I am just hoping my shoes get painted with the ideas of everyone I interact with.

When I move into college, I’ll bring these 3 pairs of shoes with me.

Beneath the lightless moon where even the stars got tired of their vigil, Darkrai drifts. Born from darkness itself, this elusive Pokémon exists on the border of the real and the subconscious, feeding on the terror of those caught in its nightmares. Every Pokémon card captures a legend, and since 2020, I’ve been on the hunt for new legends. My calendar bears the marks of card box releases, my spreadsheets track the market activity of cards on my wishlist, and the local Target wonders when I would pull that elusive Greninja EX and single-handedly cut their revenues in half afterwards.

But legends don’t stay hidden for long. As hype builds outside of the pokémon community, the cards no longer belong to those of us who chase the myth for its story. Scalpers arrive, ready to sell the legend. Returning home from DECA competitions or Science fairs, I’d see a 50$ card shoot up to 125$ in the week I was gone.

I couldn’t keep letting cards slip through my fingers, so I needed to be able to predict which cards would be a target of interest with the highest possible degree of objectivity. At the time, I already found out that doing it myself wouldn’t cut it, because my thinking was flawed around my choice of selection; a colorful background influenced my mind far more than the market. To remove my biases from the equation, I began working on the project that would end up being my Pokémon Magnum Opus: An AI model that could predict the most valuable/popular cards of any given box release.

But, it was easier said than done. While I had hoped to use images of the cards themselves, the intricacies of their design—ranging from varied font styles to small, detailed artwork—proved too complex for a small machine learning model to interpret effectively. Instead, I pivoted to a web-scraping based approach. To replace pictures, I relied on scraping information from card sellers on tcgplayer.com and other sites from key words like ‘Attack’ and ‘Rarity’.

With a dataset in hand, I began feeding the data into a Naive Bayes model, teaching it to recognize patterns and see which cards would spike in value. “Rayquaza VMAX (Alternate Art Secret)” became a valued quantity, while cards like “Oddish 4/147 Burning Shadows Regular” were quietly dropped by the algorithm. The first model iterations already showed promise, identifying patterns that I expected it to see, such as knowing that Alternate Art and Holo cards were far more enticing than their regular forms.

What surprised me though, was that my model also started to find patterns that I didn’t even see myself, cards with playable moves that sounded strategic for the competitive pokemon scene also suddenly had increased value spikes.
