I had created a model that could even see the hidden gems I left unnoticed. What I had built at the time was more than just a financial tool, it gave insight into the collective unconscious of the pokémon community as a whole in the context of cards.

Whether it’s applying the machine learning skills learned through medical research to Pokémon cards, or studying philosophy to understand the ethic behind AI in healthcare, my life has become a fusion of the different pieces and skills that allow me to see the subtle luster in the mundane. At college, I’m eager to build on my love for uncovering hidden patterns and share it with others—not just in Pokémon cards, but in the broader world. In the same way my creation detected hidden Pokémon card values, I hope to apply my AI skills to identify early signs of Cardiac disease in Electrocardiograms, creating tools that could save lives. As a new chapter of my life unfolds, I aim to surpass my limits and grow out of my comfort zone to discover new frontiers and make new connections in my learning journey.

As a kid I was a relentless question machine—questions popped out faster than I could process them. Why does the universe keep expanding? How do airplanes fly? And, most puzzling of all, why do we never see baby pigeons? These questions fueled my insatiable curiosity, leading me to countless trips to the library where I had limitless access to ideas, experiences, and minds. But the real magic happened when I discovered coding.

Coding was a portal to worlds I could create with my own hands, a playground for my imagination. My first taste of this world came in 4th grade, when I stumbled upon Scratch, a block-based programming language. Scratch allowed me to create digital worlds complete with animated characters and special effects. Scratch was like a playground for my creativity, and I spent many hot summer days indoors tinkering with code and creating stories and games that had a similar unlimited nature as the books I devoured.

After spending a few years making projects with Scratch, I realized that computers were my true calling. So, I spent countless hours after school and on weekends teaching myself Python and Java programming to feed my curiosity. These were tools that allowed me to build something from scratch (haha, get it?) and see it come to life on my screen. I built games like Blackjack using Java where the user could play against the computer. Wanting to challenge myself even more, I also started taking part in weekly coding competitions on platforms such as CodeForces and LeetCode so I could sharpen my skills. The thrill of solving complex problems, creating detailed solutions, and seeing my code come to life fueled my passion.

I wanted to share this excitement with others, so I started tutoring middle school students on computer programming. I vividly remember one tutoring session where a student was struggling to understand if-else statements. We worked together to debug a simple Scratch program line by line and when the dog sprite on the screen finally barked “woof” when fed, the student’s eyes lit up with excitement. It was very rewarding to see the joy on his face watching the program run properly, and it also reminded me of my initial experiences with computer programming and why I still enjoy it so much.

Inspired by my positive experience tutoring, I decided to start helping my friends learn Java programming. During lunch, I would work through problems and I soon became the go-to guy whenever anyone had a bug in their code they couldn’t find or was having trouble understanding a data structure. Through these interactions, I not only strengthened my own knowledge of the subject, but also formed new friendships and gained confidence in expressing my ideas and sharing my knowledge.

Now that I’ve gained experience with Python and Java, I’m excited to apply what I’m learning in AP Statistics to create programs that provide practical insights. I’ve started exploring Python tools for data analysis, which allow me to visualize and interpret data. Whether it’s analyzing my running data to improve my times or developing programs to predict football outcomes, coding allows me to solve real-world problems while pursuing my passions. I see endless possibilities in applying these skills to real-world problems, from optimizing athletic performance to predicting outcomes in various fields. 
Looking ahead to college, I’m excited to dive into AI and Machine Learning, fields that will combine my interest in computers and statistics and allow me to tackle broader challenges in fields sports analytics and financial modeling. One of many questions that continues to swirl in my mind is: will my next project predict football outcomes, or help me run like the wind?

Paper plates flailed away from my arms when my hasty foot caught the corner of my high school’s hallway. As the discs and I graciously flew through the air, only one thought crossed my mind: I’m going to be late. I scrambled to collect the scattered treasures knowing they were key to the day’s success. Finally, I had made my way out of halls and into the winter sunlight only to be halted by a foreboding text notification. Great, I had forgotten the utensils. Murphy’s Law sure had its grasp on me that day; the holiday teacher luncheon I had planned for school was not turning out at all how I had hoped.

It had only been 2 months prior that planning for the luncheon had begun. Being appointed head-planner of said event was not a role I expected to receive in my first year of student government, but I took the opportunity in stride. Immediately gathering our team of three, I sternly eyed each soldier up and down, and with wrinkles furrowing the brow on my face… I asked them each what their favorite color was. Their faces lit up, and we discussed the niche hues and tints of colors near and dear to our hearts. Suddenly, creative ideas were flourishing just as the discussion of colors did; we were off to the races.

Myriads of posters spanned our office-space, each depicting multitudes of cultural holidays celebrated by the diverse student populous. The tasks at hand were not exclusively artistically driven, so I rolled up my cuffs and got to work: I called the caterer, filed paperwork for expenditures, and personally designed Rudolph themed cocoa jars – a pocketable treat for each staff member to take home. And yes, even our school’s beloved security guard received one. As the heat began to dissipate and monstrous lofty clouds rolled across the wintery skyscape, so too did the luncheon begin to roll around the corner. Confidence filled our minds as we checked, double checked, then triple checked the components necessary for a successful event. We had planned for the unpredictable, or so I thought.

Disaster struck on the morning of the event when I received messages from each member; Not a single one could attend. Turns out the unpredictable truly was unplannable. Was I able to pull off this event without the group chemistry we formed over the past months? Calmly, I texted trusted friends I made while in student council, and they were able to fill the open roles after the event started. All I had to do now was juggle my physics final and the workload of 3 others to set up the event. The scene is now set; my feet flutter across the floor as I navigate the halls scavenging for the utensils. I locate them, snatch them, and rush them to the event. Sweating profusely, I reach the luncheon location, and dash to set the tables. Thankfully, one of the fill-ins arrived early and set up our unset decorations. Against all odds, the luncheon was on.

Former staff poured into the building and, with good intentions, wanted to reorganize the setup. Giving these retirees the benefit of the doubt, they were used to being in charge. Managing them, my replacement team, current staff, and caterers proved challenging, but not impossible as the day proved so far. While everyone arrived, relief washed over me as everything fell into place.

More often than what I would like to admit, I fear the unknown. On the contrary, I would attribute myself to being adaptable. I was dealt unfavorable cards, but I played with what I had and as a result the staff did not notice the chaos behind the scenes. All they saw was the dedication, creativity, and love we poured into the event. That day the unknown did not conquer me, for I had conquered it.

I think of myself as a scarecrow; dull, mysterious, yet a necessity for the cultivation of those around me. While the farmer may be seen as the one driving growth, it's the scarecrow's presence that protects the delicate crops from harm. Though they may not till the soil, they are a quiet necessity, holding a vital role in the background of success.

“[Name], what is something you keep hidden from others?” 
I am a man of few words. I only felt the need to say something if I felt it was relevant or important to others. My friends, having known this, always told me that I was the best at poker. A calm poker face that betrayed nothing of the thoughts swirling beneath. Only the closest of my friends knew this “other” side of me. The eccentric side, doing strange dances and making random beatboxing noises to make my friends laugh. The caring side, comforting and listening to my friend after a grievous heartbreak. I never wanted to keep these faces hidden from others.

“[Name], would you like to work independently or in a group?” 
People always viewed me as the shy, quiet kid who rarely talked to anyone. Rather, I was the complete opposite. I enjoy the presence of others around me. Within group projects, I may have not been the best at small talk. However, I always took the time and effort to ensure the success of my group. Meeting up with my group, I found that each member was stressed on finding resources to gather information for our history presentation. Overnight, I spent hours of research finding quality sources and creating elaborate topics for them to delve into. Incorporating everything together, we secured the top presentation in our class.

“[Name], how come you never ask questions in class?” 
Being the self-conscious high schooler I was, I was always afraid to ask that one stupid question. They always say, “there is no such thing as a dumb question,” yet I never believed in that; I watched as another student asked how to derive a simple equation, followed by snickers that quietly filled the room. I believed the best questions given were the ones created among proper research and dedication, with no lackluster thought behind it. Confidently, I asked, "How does the concept of limits in calculus relate to real-world phenomena, and why are limits crucial in defining derivatives and integrals?" My teacher, being the math enthusiast she is, started diving deep into examples. Through the question itself, this solidified my own and my classmates' grasp of the subject while encouraging us to view mathematics as an interconnected system rather than isolated rules and formulas.

“Mr. [Name], how do I solve this looping error in Python?” 
I had students left and right asking for help on their programming projects. Programming has always been a solitary comfort zone. Being the teacher now, I constantly was put on the spot, the place where I never thought I belonged. Anxiety rushed through my head, terrified of saying something wrong or being judged by my students. However, the smallest actions I took began to chip away at my facade. The more I engaged with my students, answering questions and guiding projects, the more I realized that my passion for programming could bridge the social gap that I always struggled to form. I started to learn about the students around me, being the first to engage with students to ask about their day. I began asking students about their coding challenges, encouraging group discussions, and fostering a collaborative classroom environment. Teaching, once a source of dread, became the catalyst for my transformation into someone who could comfortably speak to others without hesitation but also fostering new futures ahead. Although my face may stay composed, the cracks of my actions were still there, revealing more than words ever could.

When I was younger, my favorite pastime was playing billiards with my family. Now, I enjoy a different kind of game: quantum billiards—a quantum mechanical system that mimics classical billiards. The particles are analogous to billiards balls except they move based on their wave functions versus applied force. From watching PBS Spacetime since childhood to now conducting research, quantum mechanics is an avocation in my life. Coincidentally, its “rulebook” parallels the various facets of my life.

Rule 1. Quantum Zeno Effect: when a quantum system is repeatedly measured in a way that effectively prevents it from evolving.

My face flushed as I missed another haphazardly thrown shot, highlighting the contrast between my amateur skills and the exceptional players on my 4th-grade basketball team. Each failed attempt only strengthened my sense of ineptitude. As I slung another destined-to-fail shot, the unexpected, yet satisfying, swoosh of the net as the ball fell through the hoop surprised me. High-fives from teammates and cheers from the audience gave me a glimmer of hope to reject my preconceptions and embrace my vision for improvement. The subsequent countless days spent perfecting my dribbling and shooting skills propelled me to the top of my house league. Yet, my key accomplishment wasn’t the newfound skills, but my perseverance and self-reflection as I stopped “measuring” myself against others to “evolve from my current state”.

Rule 2. Quantum particles can exist in multiple states or superpositions simultaneously until measured.

As a middle school debater, I believed my role was two-fold: advance our side and refute the opponent’s. As it turns out, argumentation is more nuanced. While debating about loosened medical patent protections, I argued for preventing pharmaceutical monopolies but my opponent countered with concerns of illegitimate drug circulation, compelling me to consider multi-faceted arguments and weigh both impacts to win the debate. In addition, my opponent’s heckles improved my adaptability and strengthened my extemporaneous responses. Ultimately, three years of immersive debating shifted my perspective from a black or white “state”, to a more nuanced view that considered a “simultaneous superposition” of ideas.

Rule 3. Quantization: certain properties can only take on discrete values rather than a continuous range.

Can a machine learn? Not in the traditional sense, but the pattern recognition capabilities sparked my excitement, prompting me (a freshman) to buy the most advanced machine learning (ML) textbook I could find—The Principles of Deep Learning Theory. Ever the rationalist, my dad advised against it, and after reading the first chapter—packed with random-number function distributions and Gaussian integrals—I appreciated his foresight. With his encouragement, I created a two-year plan for self-studying Python, Statistical modeling and advanced ML. I learned that successful execution of a plan required pragmatic, “discrete” steps rather than a vague, “continuous” notion of direction.

Rule 4. Particles take all possible paths from one point to another, and the probability of an outcome is derived from the sum of all possible paths.

Watching seminars as a NASA intern on quantum mechanics rekindled my life-long passion and prompted me to explore its intricacies through a science fair project. Despite the challenges I faced, the skills I gained from my past endeavors helped me overcome them. I used my goal-setting skills from ML to create a learning plan with incremental milestones. My multifaceted approach from debate allowed me to understand both the mathematical and spatial aspects of a qubit. Most importantly, my determination from basketball helped me to overcome the temptation to give up when the learning curve steepened because I knew I wouldn't make “the shot” unless I kept rebounding. My success was not just a result of my passion in quantum but a “sum of all my possible paths” in basketball, debate, and ML.

While the “probability” of success in my future endeavors is uncertain, I hope the future paths I take and traits I acquire will guide me to a positive outcome.

Every Sunday, I lead Jing Yang, a blind runner, on a run. I strictly control my pace and keep an eye on all possible dangers ahead. Connected by a rope, my teammate and I run along the park’s path. We perceive our surroundings as one and sense each other’s breaths.

I act as their eyes, yet they have taught me to “see” more than ever. When running alone, I often get excited and speed up uncontrollably. But with Jing, I slow down and control my speed, allowing me to care about everything around me. Afterward, on my solo runs, I start situating myself in my surroundings, geographically and temporally. As I run, each stride reminds me that I have the power to shape my own path, no matter how the city around me has changed and will change through the years. Running will forever influence the way I see the world, granting me the power to grow and find community through means I never before thought possible.

I prefer spontaneous trail-making preset GPS routes; If I mindlessly follow the navigation, I only see the destination. Avoiding Google Maps pushes me to appreciate my surroundings more, from the sounds of birds to the passing smiles of other runners. This mindset shift reminds me that running isn’t just about reaching the finish line but about noticing and enjoying the experience along the way. When I run, I am present. I engage fully not only with myself but also with the scenes and lives around me—the authentic experience of individual freedom.

To my left, a fellow runner gives a quick nod of encouragement; to my right, a group of early risers chat softly on a bench; straight ahead, a child waves as he bikes past. I wouldn’t miss out on these moments of connection. Awareness in this shared journey is what makes the city feel smaller and the run more meaningful. I’ve learned to seek out communities that challenge me in my everyday life—whether it’s a gallery pushing me to introduce my creative ideas to strangers or a PhD in history that encourages me to question my understanding of history through different countries’ perspectives. Running taught me that growth happens fastest when you’re surrounded by others striving for more, and I’ve carried that lesson with me beyond the trails.

After I completed the Chicago Marathon, our grade director asked me, “Did you win the race?” I paused the question echoing in my mind. Winning? When I started running, my goal was just to run faster and finish ahead, but things are different now. After running with blind runners and interacting with others, I realized it wasn’t just about speed. For me, it is a tool for mental clarity, a way to connect with others, and a test of inner strength. Now, I am still discovering new parts of myself with each mile, and the growth doesn’t end at the finish line.

From my four years of training, I began to appreciate the subtle ways in which running has reintroduced me to the world. As I’ve grown in my physical endurance, so too have I found emotional strength. I hope to carry this approach into college—whether it’s tackling difficult projects or exploring new communities. The race is but a celebration of the connections and discoveries one has found along the way, the relentless physical and emotional dedication poured into every training session. Much like college, late nights in the library and lifelong friendships matter far more than a diploma.

Hearing my heart pound and breath shorten is an antidote to unwinding from the demands of school and the looming pressures of a future career. It’s as if the more I run, the more I open myself up to the world around me, and by the time my feet stop, I’m moving toward new joys, opportunities, and the endless possibilities that await.

In middle school, I was obsessed with Love Nikki, an online battle royale of pixelated clothes. I was so serious about this extracurricular I joined a 16+ guild on Discord. Within a year, I became guild president, helping CrimsonMoon rise to #5 globally…until I was found to be only 13.

That’s when I joined Petite Designers, nervous and quite petite, where an elegant Ms. D taught kids to sew.

Within weeks, I was smitten with making real clothes and flooring that sewing pedal. Following Hurricane Dorian, Ms. D suggested we create dresses to donate to girls in Haiti. So we did! When I saw pictures of our Haitian sisters beaming like quasars wearing our (less-than-perfect) creations, I felt a flurry of butterflies burst in my stomach.

During the pandemic, I picked up Genshin Impact. Again, I was transfixed by the game’s virtual finery. Character Keqing caught my attention, flaunting a glimmering navy-blue cocktail dress, its deep heart-shaped neckline tapering into layered skirts adorned with butterfly wings.

Keqing’s Opulent Splendor needed to grace the real world, but a store-bought costume wouldn’t do it justice. Thus began my chef-d'œuvre.

But how doth one chef-d'œuvre when one hath limited resources, no pattern, and amateur skills?

After hours of perusing YouTube and four drafts, I sketched a bodice pattern, banking on geometry to match angles of sectioned patterns, general math to fit my design on my bodice circumference, and some eyeballing because of the mystifying neckline.

I overheated my phone scrutinizing the Gamesfashionarchive rendering of the skirts, but it didn’t differentiate among their perplexing layers. I had to take some artistic liberty. Measurements proved risky in waist circumference multiplications for the fractionally-pleated skirts. In the end, I stitched together a right-slanted circle skirt, left-slanted half-pleated skirt, pannier-lookalikes, and crescents of butterfly pinions. Speaking of butterfly wings -- in an admittedly extemporaneous move, I improvised by staggering tulle carved from an old rainbow-colored tutu.

The literal blood, sweat, and tears shed made finishing this 80+ hour dress more than opulent to me. This splendor was priceless. Embarrassment, pride, and gratification flooded over me earning Fashion Club’s best-dressed award, at each “I love your fit!”, and “IT TURNED OUT SO STUNNING.”

While I felt emboldened to make the virtual into reality, I remembered those butterflies in sewing for others. So in 2023, I joined SewPowerful, a nonprofit that provides Zambian girls with purses and hygiene supplies for them to stay in school while menstruating. Within a month, I chartered Sunshine Sewing, SewPowerful’s South Florida chapter and youngest member base.

While other SewPowerful chapters utilized email lists, FaceBook advertisements, and Nextdoor, I resolved to modernize for the teenage force. Capitalizing off existing large clubs, I pioneered collaborations with the Key Clubs I preside over as Lieutenant Governor. In my Slime and Service Social, I left home with packages of cardstock and stationery and returned with hundreds of loving cards for our Zambian sisters. I formed partnerships with other clubs for fabric drives and purse making. I also improved the purse making process by pre-cutting the fabric so members can just enjoy sewing.

Ever since, my favorite way to spend Sunday afternoons is hosting group sewing sessions. There we are, teenagers around tables. Beside me, Sonia stitches, Enya photographs, and Alexa cuts. Aside from (still) flooring that pedal, I’m the sewing mentor, frozen-yogurt treat chauffeur, and the joker to lighten the room.

What started as a rebellious passion for fashion has evolved into a means to dare myself intellectually and creatively while serving a cause I believe in.

I’d like to think of my days with Mrs. D as when I was just a caterpillar, and truthfully, today I still feel like I’m emerging from my cocoon. I know I’m not the most graceful lepidoptera out there. But even still, sapphire skies brighten and ambrosial flowers bloom as I glide in spires, assembling more butterflies to fly with me in a kaleidoscope of colors, wings all exquisitely unique. Along the way, we bestow pollen and empower others to serve with sewing.

As I enter college and beyond, I’ll take my needles, threads, and sewing machine with me. And if you ever dare challenge Love Nikki user 101183545, you’d best bring your A-game!

As I leaned back in my chair, craving a much-needed stretch, a freakish sight nearly sent me toppling: the figure to my right was no longer my best friend but a pale, human blueberry. Wide-eyed, I rushed to Ryan’s side as soon as the bell rang, shaking him from his self-induced stupor. “What’s wrong? Are you okay?” I blurted. Gasping for air, he shook his head depressingly. “I was holding my breath so I wouldn’t fall asleep. But no matter what I do, I can’t focus or learn anything in this class!”

He made a valid point: though our teacher was undoubtedly well-versed in math, his teaching methods didn’t always align with everyone’s needs. Typically a good student, I often found my own eyes wandering to the clock during class, my mind calculating when the hands would align to release us. I even had to do extra research at home from time to time to keep my grades up.

As several days went by, I noticed Ryan’s stress levels rising. Considering him as a brother, I felt a strong urge to somehow help him. So, I offered to tutor him one afternoon. Of course, I was no Einstein in math (despite the worrisome presence of a few gray hairs on my head), but I was pretty confident that I could mentor him with what I had learned in class and from countless hours of independent study. After all, how hard could it be?

The first meeting went smoothly—or so I thought. I removed as many distractions from our study area as I could and eagerly tried to pour everything I knew about the subject into Ryan. Afterwards, I was quite pleased with myself. That wasn’t too shabby for someone without much teaching experience!

However, the results did not speak for themselves.

“Thanks a lot, your lessons actually put me to sleep faster than my old bedtime stories!” Ryan’s brutal review quickly wiped the smug grin off my face. How could I have possibly messed up? I had put in so much time and effort into making what I thought was a quality tutoring session, only for it to fall flat. With the weight of my overconfidence sinking in, I winced at my initial arrogance in offering to tutor—yeah, that aged well. Determined to redeem myself, I tried to keep an open mind as I replayed the call in my head. It didn’t take long before I embarrassingly realized my over-exuberance dominated our discussion. I had been so focused on making sure that I covered everything in the unit that I neglected how Ryan was actually processing it all. If I wanted the math concepts to really hit home, I had to keep him consistently engaged.

For the next few days, I experimented with various instructive techniques I researched online. As I gained a better understanding of Ryan’s learning style, I adapted my old lesson plan, incorporating new practice problems inspired by our late night pickleball duels and catchy mnemonics for complex formulas. Most importantly, I included time to work through questions after each of my explanations so the topics truly registered in his mind.

Our next study session, to my delight, yielded far better customer satisfaction than the first. Not letting my newfound success get to my head, I took Ryan’s critiques to heart and tried to hone my skills for future lessons. As our after-school meetings continued, I observed Ryan’s self-esteem slowly healing along with his test scores; his happiness was immensely gratifying and strengthened my own resolve. Now, as I lean back in my chair, I feel very relieved to see my best friend back in full vibrance and the possibility of having to perform CPR no longer looming over my head.

Watching the sun dip into the horizon, listening to the rhythmic rolling waves hit the shore, I feel at peace. The ocean has always reflected my inner world—both my dreams and struggles. Each wave feels like a lesson: some gentle and patient, others crashing with force, reshaping the sand. Over time, I’ve come to realize that, like the waves, every experience—whether soothing or overwhelming—has the power to shape me.

One of these shaping moments came during a frustrating afternoon in calculus. I stared at the board, feeling a knot of frustration tighten in my chest. The Maclaurin series sprawled across the page, but every formula blurred as my mind spun in circles. My classmates’ pencils scratched away, but mine hovered, motionless. It felt like I was sinking into a hole I couldn’t climb out of. What am I missing? My heart raced, and for a moment, the thought crept in: I just wasn’t getting it. I exhaled slowly, letting the tension ease. Time stood still. I started small, breaking the formulas into pieces. Patterns emerged—the powers of x, the repetition of terms. The chaos unraveled. In that moment, I realized that patience and perseverance, not force, were the keys to overcoming even the hardest challenges.

That lesson came back to me during a particularly stressful week of exams. A simple text from a friend— “Beach?”—was all it took to remind me how much I needed a break. Thirty minutes later, we were driving toward the coast, windows down, the smell of saltwater filling the car. As soon as my feet hit the sand, it was like a weight had lifted. I spent the afternoon diving for volleyballs and laughing until our stomachs hurt. Later, as we sat in a circle eating sandwiches, Tom vented about a failed exam while Mark talked about his painful Crohn’s disease flare up. In those moments, I realized how much belonging meant to me. Surrounded by friends who understood what I was going through, I felt lighter. It hit me that shared experiences, like waves, wash away the weight of our burdens, making the connection between us even stronger.

Another important lesson came from a debate I had with my friends Aiden and Jay about Mr. Beast’s philanthropy videos. I argued that using people’s hardships for views felt wrong, even if the result was good. Aiden, grounded in consequentialism—the belief that outcomes matter more than intentions—challenged me, saying, “Does it really matter if a homeless person gets a home?” His point made sense logically, but I still felt uneasy. Later that week, while helping my mom with her water softener to ease her eczema, it clicked. What had once been just a chore had become a way for me to show care. That’s when I really understood deontology—the idea that why we do something matters just as much as what we achieve. Helping my mom wasn’t just about the outcome of relief—it was about the love behind it. I learned that real empathy isn’t about grand gestures, but the quiet, consistent ways we show up for those we care about.

As I sit here watching the waves tonight, I’m reminded of how these lessons have shaped me. Serving in a community where financial insecurity was common inspired me to tackle the root causes of their challenges. Learning and using computer science and AI—not just for the intellectual challenge, but I want to FinTech tools that give people more freedom, helping them live without the constant worry of economic stress.

Just as the ocean shapes the shore, these experiences have shaped my aspirations. The lessons I’ve learned—patience, connection, and quiet care—will guide me as I work to create technology that empowers people, helping them navigate life’s challenges, much like the waves continually reshape the shore.

“Guys, does anyone have an extra phone charger?” 
“What if we all get seasick?”
 “Are we there yet?” 
Sighing, I turn my head and look out the window of our van at the vibrant blue ocean, with doubts slowly creeping into my mind. I’d been excited when I got the opportunity to attend Seabase High Adventure, a Boy Scout experience of living on a sailboat while exploring coastal environments. But when people were already complaining during the car ride there, I began to worry.

The sun's orange glow painted the afternoon sky as we slowly motored behind Rodriguez Key, our anchorage for the night. After we grilled and devoured burgers for dinner, our Captain, Chuck, brought out an old conch horn from his cabin. Flattening my chin, I took a deep breath and buzzed my lips against the small opening at the end of a conch. The conch produced a resonant tone, echoing through the afternoon sky. Astounded by the huge sound, I called over my other scouts, encouraging them to give the conch a try. One by one, our crew began taking turns, playing the conch into the setting sun. Afterwards, crew members who’d been seasick and gloomy were now talking excitedly preparing for the next few days “Donut Reef is gonna be sick!” “Can we explore one of the islands?”

The next morning, as the grubmaster, I dipped slices of bread into a mixture of milk, eggs, and cinnamon. While we sat around our cabin table eating breakfast, I realized our crew had become stronger, no longer having sullen looks, but relaxed and laughing. The resonant call of the conch horn became a symbol of our newfound unity, reminding us that sometimes, the simplest joys can forge the strongest connections.

I wanted to continue bringing people together. With encouragement from adult leaders, I ran for and won the position of Senior Patrol Leader. The following fall, I led our troop on our annual backpacking trip, tackling a 10-mile loop with almost 2000 feet of elevation gain for 6 miles straight. Checking our line, I noticed two newer scouts starting to fall behind, looking increasingly exhausted. I remembered the breakdowns I had on my first outing as a scout. I wanted our troop to feel comfortable and safe. So during our next water break, I joined the newer scouts and checked they were drinking enough water while getting rest. I set a slower pace and after we finally reached our campsite, I assured them that the next day would be much easier. The next morning they were looking forward to the day's hike and excited about future adventures.

With a desire to lead and find community, I turned to the clarinet for new opportunities. With few wind players to choose from in my school’s chamber music society, I orchestrated a Bach duet between the clarinet and the saxophone for a performance at a senior living home. But because the clarinet and saxophone are in different keys, we couldn’t mesh the sounds of our instruments together. Realizing that our pitches would continue to clash, I decided to make a change. I suggested to my saxophonist the idea of transcribing and transposing a piano piece, explaining how this could probably make our sounds mesh together better. Although our performance wasn’t perfect, the duet sounded fantastic. I felt joy watching the seniors brighten as they listened to our performances.

Whether I’m bringing my crew together on Seabase, looking out for new members in a community, or leading musical duets, I’ve discovered how as a new leader, I can bring cohesion and unity to my peers. I’ve built a community and memories that I’ll never be able to replace in the process, and I hope to do the same in college.

**Why Major Essay for Georgia Tech**

The pungent smell of formaldehyde hits my nose as I eagerly prepare for my freshman biology dissection lab. With both my parents holding PhDs in biology and often discussing scientific research, I was excited to delve deeper into a world I had only heard about. As I carefully slit the outside of the earthworm, spreading open the skin using T-pins and labeling the pharynx and intestines of the worm, I felt like a proper scientist.

As I progressed through school, I was determined to deepen my knowledge of biology. In AP Biology, despite my shaking hands, I loved using pipettes to load DNA samples into a gel tray for gel electrophoresis. I was fascinated by everything from cellular communication in fungi to microscopic views of protozoa flagella. Emerging from the pandemic and reading the weekly CDC news updates, I realized the importance of epidemiological data analysis and the power of AI and machine learning in combating infectious diseases.

At Georgia Tech, I plan to pursue a Bachelor’s in Biology and apply to the BSBIO/MSBINF program to become a bioinformatician, developing new computational genomic approaches to address public health challenges. Through student organizations like the Tri-Beta Biological Honors Society and Bioinformatics @ GT, I will be able to apply knowledge from rigorous courses such as BIOS 4150 Genomics & Applied Bioinformatics and BIOS 3451 Cell & Molecular Biology Lab to analyze microbial genome sequences and identify genomic variations that cause infections. Outside of class, I’d love to become a research assistant with Professor King Jordan at the Jordan Lab, working on cutting-edge approaches for molecular epidemiology to prevent future pandemics. Georgia Tech will best prepare me as a biologist and then a bioinformatician, ready to tackle public health challenges of the future.

“My granddaughter [Name] won the science fair today!” My grandmother squealed with pride as she told me about her granddaughter [Name]’s accomplishments. She was referencing the latest sketch on her blanket, a young girl holding up an award for the most creative project at her school’s science fair. The thing is, I am that granddaughter, [Name].

The gentle sweep of a finger across a plush blanket can open up a world of art. As the microfibers bend to my touch, light moves across the surface, revealing intricate patterns and scenes—a girl dancing Bharatnatyam, a birthday cake with candles forming the number “10,” a girl holding an award at her tennis competitions. This art form, known as blanket doodling, was my way of communicating with my grandmother.

Although both my parents are Indian, India's linguistic diversity meant my heritage was split between two languages: Tamil from my mother's side and Kannada from my father's. Growing up, I learned to speak Tamil and only understood Kannada, which connected me more closely with my maternal grandparents. However, I never stopped finding ways to relate to my paternal grandparents, especially my Paati (grandmother in Tamil). Every summer, I visited India or Paati would come to the US. Although I couldn't speak Kannada, we found other ways to express love. Her masala-filled biryani and the fruits she'd bring while I studied spoke volumes about her affection for me.

Paati introduced me to blanket doodling when I was barely old enough to hold a pencil. During my stays, she'd leave surprises on my bed—a garden one day, a rainforest the next, or a group of playful monkeys. Initially, I showed little interest, but over time, it became my passion. When I was six, Paati was diagnosed with Alzheimer's. It began with forgetting small things but quickly progressed to the point where she couldn't recognize her own son. The language barrier exacerbated the communication challenges her condition posed.

As I grew better at creating complex designs, Paati was losing her ability to read. Yet, even in her twilight years, she never lost her love for blanket doodling. When she could no longer draw for me, I began creating them for her. I turned to these drawings as my primary communication method with her, showing her my day’s highlights or if I was having a bad day.

Paati has been gone for many years, but through our shared love of blanket doodling, she has stayed with me. This experience taught me the power of non-verbal communication and the importance of finding creative ways to connect across generational and cultural divides. I’ve carried this lesson into other parts of my life. When I teach Bharatnatyam remotely to underserved children who don’t speak English, I modify my lessons to connect them to the dance through rhythm rather than words. I hope to apply this lesson in academic collaborations, community service, and personal relationships. Just as I found a way to communicate with Paati, I aim to bridge gaps wherever I go. Like the art of blanket doodling we honed together, I've learned that the most profound connections often come from the simplest moments—enriching our lives truly.

Every Sunday, I lead the blind runner on a run. I strictly control my pace and keep an eye on all possible dangers ahead. Their complete trust in me is a great responsibility, honor, and joy—the joy of connection. Connected by a rope, my teammate and I run along the park’s path. This is joint navigation: we perceive our surroundings as one and sense each other’s breaths, moving in sync, forming our answers to “Where are we?” and “How do we get to where we want to go?” This is mutual guidance; I might be guiding him to the destination, but he is guiding me to the perception, thought, and exploration during the journey.

I act as their eyes, yet they have taught me to “see” more than ever. When running alone, I often get excited and speed up uncontrolled, only focusing on the running data on my watch and enduring physical pain. But with them, the sense of responsibility forced me to learn to slow down and control my speed, which naturally suppressed my excitement and allowed me to care about everything around me. Afterward, on my solo runs, I start situating myself in my surroundings, geographically and temporally.

Running past timeworn stone slabs on the Forbidden City, I wonder whether people centuries ago walked the same paths, overwhelmed by the same never-ending deadlines. Arriving at the CBD with towering skyscrapers, I imagine myself as one of the busy but accomplished professionals who work here, questioning whether the heavy burden of work one day would stop me from my daily runs. Sometimes, these unknown uncertainties of my imagined future make me afraid. However, I find solace in knowing that while I can’t control the sweeping changes of the future, I can control the steps I take in the present. Each stride reminds me that I have the power to shape my own path, no matter how the city around me has changed and will change through the years.

In this conscious exploration, I like deciding which turn to take just as I come to an intersection. Let’s arrive at the destination based on spontaneous impressions rather than preset GPS routes. I enjoy having complete control over decisions — to me, that means being aware of everything around me. If I mindlessly follow the navigation, I only see the destination. When I run, I am present. I engage fully not only with myself but also with the scenes and lives around me—the authentic experience of individual freedom.

To my left is a beautiful old tree with an orange cat resting on its branches; to my right, the solemn and quiet gate of an ancient temple; straight ahead, the sun slowly rises. I wouldn’t miss out on so much beauty that surrounds me. Awareness in this free exploration does the trick. I’d like to think that I am waking them up to this beauty when I say “good morning” to the old man walking his dog alone, the police on duty, and the tourists and “you got this” to fellow runners, sometimes we speed up tacitly together for a sprint, pushing each other to breakthroughs. Through running, I connect with the people in this city, which could sometimes seem too big for genuine connections. Even though I run alone, I know I am not; I belong to a larger community.

After I completed the Chicago Marathon, our grade director asked me, “Did you win the race?” I was unsure how to respond; most people who run marathons do not compete to be the first to cross the finish line. It’s always about the journey; every runner knows that. That’s a shared understanding in our community.

From my four years of training, I realized that the real marathon isn’t the race itself but the training that comes before it. The race is but a celebration of what is possible, a culmination of the relentless dedication poured into every training session. Hearing my heart pound and my breath shorten is an antidote to unwinding from the demands of school and the looming pressures of a future career. It’s as if the faster I run, the further my worries are behind me, and by the time my feet stop, I will have shaken them all off, ready to embrace the future with open arms.

“Don’t throw that away!” My mom shrieked as I stood by the trash can, dirty takeout container in hand.

“We can use that to hold the oil!”

I sighed, inched towards the sink, rinsed out the container, then stacked it alongside the dozen others that lined our countertop.

As the daughter of two Chinese parents who have saved every plastic grocery bag ever, the concept of frugality flows through my veins. To this day, we still have sixty glass Costco tiramisu cups we bought six years ago (my mom uses them for sauces; wrapped in aluminum foil, with two alligator clips from an old arduino kit, and a magnet, I made them into capacitors!)

These moments with my family taught me that no matter how insignificant an item may seem, with a little bit of ingenuity, even seemingly useless objects can find a new life. Finding solutions using the skills and objects I already possessed became an important part of my life—a custom Wordle game I made for my friends in Google Sheets, or the file server made out of an old Raspberry Pi for my mom.

Last winter, my crafting skills were put to the ultimate test at Wonderland, a hackathon themed around the idea of limitations, where the goal was to create something that could be experienced by all the attendees using a randomized box of items.

Ivannah, Gary, and I opened our box to discover a giant water jug, a party balloon, some rope, and a roll of packing tape.

We were stumped.

Racking my brain I piped up,

“Why don’t we just throw out anything we can think of making? How about…”

“How about we make an animatronic?”

“How about we make a whack-a-mole game?”

“How about we make an arcade punching bag?”

After generating a list of outlandish-seeming ideas, we ranked each one based on feasibility, uniqueness, and enjoyability. We wanted to create something that everyone would have fun using during the showcase, knowing that many teams would be frazzled from coding all night, we ultimately decided to roll with the arcade punching bag machine—a lighthearted way for everyone to punch out their frustrations.

Knowing Ivanna had a knack for using materials she found lying around, I suggested she begin suspending the balloon and given Gary’s interest in Physics, I asked him to draw up a schematic of our creation. I focused on coding a method to track the balloon after it was punched to calculate the player’s score.

After searching through online forums, I followed a Youtube tutorial to create an object tracking system with Python libraries. Staying up until 6 am to get our code running, our makeshift arcade game machine was finished!

As people swung by our booth, we enthusiastically invited them to give our machine their best shot. Ivannah, Gary, and I fist pumped the air whenever someone managed to max out the machine, happily handing out brightly colored completion certificates. Someone even complimented us on our project’s concept, joking that it was a great way to destress. It was wonderful seeing something so silly bring someone so much joy.

Over the years, I’ve built everything from a file server for my mother to mini-keyboards with my sister and joke websites with my friends. But the creations I’m proudest of are the ones made out of everyday objects, that spark joy, and got me to imagine something new along the way.

I want to construct a world where people aren’t just cognizant of the items we buy, but actively repurpose them to better reflect their own personal and artistic values. Whether that be the tiramisu-cups-turned-sauce-containers, or a-giant-water-jug-turned-punching bag, everyone (and everything) deserves a second life! Just like my mom’s piles of takeout containers, I’ve come to realize the joys of resourcefulness, knowing that I’ve made someone’s day better with items that might have otherwise been overlooked.

When I stepped into my first calculus classroom, I was horrified that all the rumors were true – this course would be the hardest class I’d ever taken. Integrals, derivatives, and theorems swam in my head like a dizzying hurricane, and many late nights were spent wondering how such a cruel world could invent calculus to torment students.

A key component to my eventual success was my teacher, Mrs. Bithi. When teaching she was ruthlessly fast, but without her organization and discipline, we never would have covered the entire curriculum in time. She had a reputation for piling on homework and grilling students, which terrified me, but only because of all this practice did I master calculus.

Her tough-love approach did not make her popular with every student, but she was unfazed, and it ultimately gave her class such a high pass rate. She didn’t care about being liked so much as students succeeding, which was a noble prerogative and amazed me as an introverted people-pleaser. In a way, Mrs. Bithi showed me how trivial being well-received is in comparison to being yourself.

But I don’t want to give the idea that she was a wild tyrant. In fact, Mrs. Bithi was one of the kindest teachers I ever had.

One night, my restaurant job had me stay late and I came home to a mountain of homework waiting for me. The next day, I trudged into class sleep-deprived and completely bombed a quiz. The material had been basic calculus, yet I still failed horrifically. Too shocked to move, I sat immobilized in my seat and just sobbed uncontrollably.

When I finally handed in my quiz, vision still clouded by tears, I was surprised that Mrs. Bithi didn’t chastise me but instead pulled me into a hug. Knowing the kind of student I was, she knew this score was out of the ordinary, let me retake the quiz, and told me I shouldn’t let one bad grade bring me down. Her empathy and understanding gave me a push of confidence to keep pursuing higher-level math.

Though in class she was seen as intimidating, during office hours she was always willing to work through a tricky problem. Mrs. Bithi’s model of unfailing patience has taught me how much more effective a teacher is when armed with not just fierce determination, but also tireless kindness.

I’ve had many days where the pressure of all my commitments makes me high-strung, but when I can’t handle things anymore I remind myself of Mrs. Bithi’s stoicism. This mindset has helped me manage those days where I’m rushing straight from eight hours of school, to hour-long theater rehearsals, to five-hour shifts at work, all while fitting in homework and extracurriculars.

As a worship team leader for my youth group, I’ve been ready to explode with exasperation countless times when half the team cancels the night before or shows up without looking at the music. But when I think of all Mrs. Bithi endured as a teacher for her students, managing the team suddenly seems manageable.

This year, when I stepped into my multi-variable calculus class, I knew it was because of Mrs. Bithi that I wasn’t scared, but ready to face math’s new challenges. One day, I hope to possess Mrs. Bithi’s enduring sweetness and to touch the lives of others as much as she has touched mine.

Low-hanging trees sheltered the park from the summer rays of Shanghai as I pondered my moves. Locals gathered around, taking turns playing, curious to see an outsider play their game. I grew up playing weiqi, named “Go” in English, a traditional Chinese strategy game played on a 19 by 19 grid. Each player secures territory by surrounding space by placing pebbles as a wall. The complexity of the strategy, despite the simplicity of the game, fascinated me.

Whenever I would return from Shanghai to Dallas, I would struggle to find weiqi players. My mother was busy raising me alone; besides, I had far surpassed her skill. In school, few had even heard of Go, and when combined with my initial reclusiveness, I could not find a weiqi partner.

Yet, crossing the Pacific gave life to the pebbles. One day in the library, I found two opponents seated across from each other as I had seen countless times before. However, their stones took up ornate forms of soldiers and royalty. Chess, they called it.

I’d heard of chess before, but like those who played it, it was different, foreign. Even more than asking others to play my game, I was hesitant to play theirs. I envisioned either getting ignored for lack of skill, or worse, mocked. Yet, that day’s display demonstrated delicate, beautiful strategies built upon simple mechanics: semblances that brought me comfort, enough for me to swallow my reluctance and step outside my shell.

To my surprise, they were willing not just to play, but also to teach. I already knew the basics, but they introduced me to opening theory, almost identical to josekis in Go. With my interest sparked, I referenced online tutorials and borrowed books covering all aspects of the game, finding more similarities to Go than I ever expected. For instance, while territory does not directly win you the game, extra space leads to advantageous positions.

My transition from Go to chess was more to me than simply finding a new game; it also served as my bridge between the two cultures I struggled to reconcile. On one end was my conventional mother, raising me to follow the traditions and societal expectations of her homeland. On the other hand, I had to observe others and learn the expectations of American society without guidance: I didn’t dare ask what trending slang meant and could only learn via inference. Yet when I finally understood the terminology, new ones would become popular. This largely contributed to my feelings of isolation, as I struggled to connect with others, with whom I lacked commonalities.

With chess, however, I finally found a way to expand my social horizons. After chemistry class one day, someone I had met while playing chess asked me if I could tutor him. We went to the library to answer his questions by explaining confusing concepts in a new light. When his questions were resolved, someone else I didn’t know asked my friend if he had time for a game of Magic: The Gathering. Intrigued, I learned the game, tying strings of friendship between me and his friends who shared this hobby. Before, I would rush home after school, finding peace away from societal pressures. Now, I would ecstatically linger with the friends I made. Even outside the game of Magic, I was included in everyday conversations ranging from pop culture to schoolwork. Finally, I was accepted, not just for a hobby, but for friendship as a whole.

Just as my friends taught me American culture, I taught them my culture with them as well: weiqi. The black-and-white pieces showed the division between yin and yang. The nine star points were the constellations of the sky, and the square board was the map of the world. As I dusted off the panel, it appeared larger than in my memory, as if the world had expanded—at least, my world had.

I sprinted to our backyard as fast as my legs would take me. Just as my brother had described to me, my dad’s koi pond appeared remarkably unsettling. The surface of the 6,000-gallon body of water was murky, and the water was tinted an unusual green. The fifty-three koi fish that resided there were all at the surface, desperately gasping for air. To make matters worse, my dad had just gone out on a business trip the night before and was unavailable to address the situation. It hit me that if I didn’t act immediately, the fish would die.

I realized quickly that the waterfall that supplied filtered water back into the pond was completely arid. With the waterfall malfunctioning, the water of the pond would remain stale, without any new supply of oxygen. In the filter pit, I discovered that one of the main pumps that supplied the waterfall was inert. Acting swiftly, I disconnected the power and disassembled the pump. I realized that the impeller was missing several of its blades and had partially detached from the axle it was mounted on. It was clear that it would have to be replaced, and so I ran over to the shed housing the spare parts. Upon obtaining the new part and replacing the damaged one, reassembled the pump and started the power back up. Slowly but surely, the waterfall began to flow again. Over the next few hours, the pond’s water began to clear up, and the fish returned to their regular behavior.

As an aspiring engineer, the ability to react quickly to time-constrained situations would be crucial in many high pressure scenarios that would come my way. The koi pond demonstrated a significant instance of rapid problem-solving skills, and I would continue to use this kind of thinking in future endeavors.

A few months after I rescued my dad’s koi, disaster struck at the FTC robotics World Championship. As we removed our robot from the field following a qualification match with a frightfully violent collision, it was apparent that something was terribly wrong with our robot’s linear slide. The full extent of the problem was revealed when I returned to our pit and tested our robot. Though its movement was fine, I noticed that the linear slide would no longer return to the original starting position when we retracted it.

Panic set in among the team at the idea that we could no longer compete in this championship that we had been working towards for months. Not long after, a moderator came up to our pit and requested that we be on the field in five minutes. Five minutes? There was no way we could possibly finish our robot in five minutes.

In that moment, I put my own fears aside and focused solely on solving the problem at hand. For the sake of expediency, I opted for a makeshift solution that would need replacing later. I resourcefully used some surgical tubing and small beams to attach the end of our linear slide to the servomotor we had assigned to our drone launcher. After some quick adjustments and a single test, we were now able to control the retraction of the slide. As we moved the robot onto the field, I reflected on how remaining collected and promptly reacting had provided us the coveted chance to contend in the competition once again. I felt proud to be a reliable asset who my teammates could depend on.

Eager to take on many additional engineering challenges in college, I look forward to honing my dexterity and mechanical skills to further equip myself to diagnose problems accurately and grow my abilities for solving them. By continuing to employ quick-thinking, I hope to harness the ability to complete various goals and projects in engineering and other fields. Even with intense deadline pressure, I find engineering exhilarating.

I was in first grade when I started to learn Kuchipudi, an Indian classical dance form with roots in Southern India. My mother was my driver to the lessons, both literally and figuratively. To this day, I remember my first performance with the same joy I felt on that day. It was at an outdoor multicultural festival by a lake—I can still feel the crisp fall wind on my face.

However, my love for dance was slowly drained by the harsh words of critique from my guru. One day, I would hear effusive praise; another day, "You're useless" or "You’re hopeless." The occasional affirmation was not enough for me to ignore the pain of humiliation. Every class, I collected her insults like puzzle pieces.

When the puzzle was completed six years later, I told my mother I was done with Kuchipudi. The statement broke her, but I did not want to be convinced to give it another chance. Months passed, yet a sense of emptiness gnawed at me.

Late one night, I opened the door to my mother sitting alone in her bedroom. There she was, watching my first dance performance, tears silently falling down her face. Was it because of the joy of seeing her little girl dance out her own childhood dream, or the lament that she would never be able to see me dance again? The very same night, I went down a rabbit-hole of my dance videos and felt a deep longing to dance again. Did I not love Kuchipudi enough to get past hurtful words? Time had mellowed the sting of criticism and resurfaced the joy I had forgotten.

I took the time to understand from my mother how Kuchipudi is taught in traditional settings. I realized that what my guru said to all of her students in frustration was not intended to be taken the way I took them. My guru and I come from different cultural contexts. What must have felt to her as casual teacher-student interaction came across as personal jabs. Her harsh words may have stemmed from passion—a desire to push me to get better, try harder—not a desire to hurt. I thought about my guru’s own learning environment and the conditions under which she taught now, working a demanding day job yet spending her valuable evenings teaching her students. Seeing the lack of Kuchipudi schools in our area, she started her dance school purely out of a desire to pass on the tradition. My path forward became clear; I did not want to regret leaving this core part of myself unexplored.

“Amma, I want to dance again. And I want to continue with the same guru. I do not expect her to change but I have.” My mother smiled gently. "I am so glad you decided not to throw away your gift."

When I asked my guru to take me back under her wing, she accepted me with an expression that told me she knew I would always come back. She said “I always felt that you were born to be a dancer. I was only pushing you because I thought that was the way to make you better.”

As a child, I couldn’t defend myself from carelessly cruel words. Now, that which shields me from those words also reminds me to be measured in my interactions. Whether I am explaining a problem to my student for the third time or speaking to the same barista who always asks me to spell out my name, my words and actions reflect understanding. I tell the younger students in the dance school not to let any words break them down so they do not make the same mistake I did.

Finally, I convinced my mother to fulfill her childhood dream of dancing at the age of fifty-eight. It really is never too late.

When people bring up physics, most think about gravity or momentum. However, I think of Gaussian surfaces—any closed surface used to measure how field lines are entering or leaving a certain region. And when I say “any surface,” I do mean “any surface.” Whether physically practical like a cylinder around a current-carrying wire or something more abstract like a sphere around an ice cream scoop, there’s a Gaussian surface to be found. Not only are these surfaces a godsend when doing electromagnetism problems in physics, they have taught me valuable lessons that I have applied to life.

Just as there’s freedom in selecting a Gaussian surface, I find a lot of joy being able to freely explore my intellectual curiosities in order to uncover unique perspectives. One time, while delving down the notorious “Wikipedia rabbithole,” I came across an article about the Japanese Yamauchi clan. Fascinated by the samurai family’s pivotal role in the founding of Mitsubishi, I wrote a history paper on the relationship between the Japanese feudal system and the nation’s industrial revolution. Meanwhile, outside the classroom, I reinforce my long-standing love for FC Barcelona by studying Catalan (258 days on Duolingo – and counting!), hoping to better understand the rich cultural and historical nuances of the club and its supporters. Like Gaussian surfaces, my identity is defined by freedom — the freedom to be curious, allowing me to find outlets of expression through interesting new ideas.

However, the freedom inherent in choosing a Gaussian surface can be misleading at times. Applying a Gaussian surface requires using a surface integral with a vector dot product—which, in English, means things can get messy if the wrong surfaces are chosen. This applies to life as well, where calculated choices are crucial. When I founded a string quartet with my friends, I advocated a more relaxed organizational structure, believing that creativity thrives best in freedom. This caused a couple performance mishaps — jumbled programs, lost music, the full experience! Recognizing that we had to rethink our approach if we were going to mature as musicians, my friends and I created stricter rehearsal routines. By incorporating score studies, listening to professional performances, and drilling rhythm and intonation, we were not confined, but instead able to improve and even be invited to perform at state conferences and universities. Moments like these teach me to value trade-offs between freedom and meticulous decision-making, helping prevent unnecessary chaos and allowing me to dismantle challenges efficiently.

Did you know that no matter how much two Gaussian surfaces differ in shape, the laws of physics guarantee that they will share unexpected key properties as long as they contain the same charge? Along a similar vein, I derive joy from finding the metaphorical charge that links different people together. While volunteering to teach math at my local church, I had one student named Jude who was always restless and struggled to focus. He reminded me of my younger self in my 5th grade math class, where I had similar problems. However, my teacher, Mr. Perinotti, was always supportive — he made me excited to learn, especially by giving me “Secrets of Mental Math”, a book filled with fun tricks which I would use to impress friends. Seeing myself in Jude, I handed him my tattered copy of that book. As he flipped through the pages, I saw a spark ignite in his eyes, reminding me how shared experiences can help bridge gaps with others. Experiences like this continue to inspire me to seek out and nurture meaningful connections.

Gaussian surfaces are known for their extraordinary versatility, being used to solve many types of problems in electromagnetism. However, the values they comport are just as universal. Looking ahead to college, I hope to apply these lessons by trusting my creativity to guide me through my future courses in abstract math, where the freedom to explore new ideas is crucial to understanding; fostering order by demonstrating confident leadership in student organizations such as chamber music groups or quiz bowl teams; and finding common threads between people by volunteering at community, even if it’s something simple like tutoring at local schools or helping keep our environment clean.

When they announced the results, my hands trembled slightly, my breath quickened, and a familiar tightness gripped my chest.

I’d just presented LessonGPT, an app that generates lesson plans in under 30 seconds, at the DigiCode-Ed Challenge. Despite being called “impressive” by EdTech professionals, I still lost. Three months earlier, I’d survived a near-death car crash – I still remembered the sounds of glass shattering and tires screeching vividly – that left me determined to make every moment count. Losing this hackathon reignited my fear of dying without accomplishing anything meaningful.

As a high-functioning internet addict, I coped by drowning myself in YouTube. While I scrolled lying in bed that evening, I stumbled upon a Crash Course video on Existentialism. Intrigued – clearly “existentialism” was related to existential dread – I watched the video and later binge-watched their entire Philosophy course. To get more context on existentialism, I also read “At the Existentialist Cafe” by Sarah Bakewell, which described its history and main tenets.

Raised in a competitive Indian culture, I'd been conditioned to prioritize winning over everything. But existentialism taught me I didn’t have to meet others’ expectations of constant victory. Balancing this admittedly antisocial idea with utilitarianism, I found a new purpose: helping others.

This realization led me to nervously visit my vice principal’s office to present LessonGPT (I thought it would reduce my teachers’ workload). As I showed him a demo, he smiled and said he loved the app. The tight knot in my stomach now unraveled, giving way to a flutter of excitement. He immediately called our school’s technology head, and we planned to launch the app as a surprise on Teachers’ Day.

That summer, I attended regular Zoom meetings with my school’s senior leadership team, leaning forward in my chair and furiously scribbling notes as they shared feedback on my app. With each piece of constructive criticism, I felt a renewed sense of purpose, diving back into the code not just to improve my app, but also so that it would actually serve those who would use it.

A week after the final Zoom meeting on August 27th, towards the end of the Teachers’ Day assembly, I was invited into the spotlight to demo the app (its interface is shown below).

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
 Lesson Information Input Fields:
 Subject: ___
 Topic/Unit: ___
 … (Printing Error: Can’t mention all input fields; limited to 650 words) 
 [ Generate Lesson Plan ]
––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

I demonstrated the app to teachers, filling out the input fields and generating a lesson plan. Within 30 seconds, it produced a well-formatted plan matching our school's template, complete with four class activities, homework, URLs for class resources, and even sample exam questions. The presentation ended with applause that echoed against the auditorium’s high ceilings. Seeing the gratefulness, I felt a warm glow spreading through my chest — a sensation much more potent and lasting than the fleeting shine of any trophy or the superficial glimmer of fame.

However, 2 months later, I woke up to a text from my mom sharing an article about my app in Gulf News. As I read the article, pride swelled in my heart, my breath hitched and I grinned. The superficial glimmer of fame caught onto me. But wait, hadn't I just embraced utilitarian existentialism? I realized life philosophies aren’t formed in a day: they’re a constant internal struggle that requires perseverance, patience, and a lot of self-awareness.

I'm gradually learning to prioritize an intrinsic motivation to help others, seeing technology as a tool for positive impact — not prestige. At college, I'll study computer science to improve my ability to develop more useful tech products (some ideas I have to include a habit tracker generator for self-help books and an AI college essay editor for low-income students), and I’ll use the startup incubators there not only for revenue but to also increase the number of people I can impact.

Like almost all upbringings of a true Angeleno, my childhood took place at the top of the Griffith Observatory hiking trail. Scaling the steep inclines and brushing past the shrubbery, as twilight deepened into night, the brightest of stars began to reveal themselves to the world. It was at that very moment my passion for the stars ignited; countless stars illuminated my journey.

“Let's play together”
An ancient folder riddled with rainbow stars dating to my elementary days sits on my bookshelf. A blue star still stuck to the top corner shined brightest. One sunny southern Californian afternoon, I noticed a girl sitting alone being teased by a group of kids. Despite the fact I would catch the attention of bullies, I gathered my courage and pushed through the crowd and invited her to go learn cartwheels in the field. As the days went on, the teasing faded and a lifelong friendship was born. "Thank you, [Name]!" That day Ada gifted me a shiny blue star sticker. Although I received this sticker to mark her appreciation, my determination to help others only grew with it: on Saturdays, I would come up with practice plans on my way to help coach middle school volleyball players. Despite the fact that this sticker slowly deteriorates, the memories it holds still shine bright.

“Sure, I’ll try”
Zipped away in my battered pencil case lies a five-sided star marker, a reminder of my early love for art, sparked by my mother drawing Disney princesses for me. Known as “the art girl,” I helped classmates and volunteered for a poster and placard advocating for affordable housing, channeling my emotions into each project. Art became my escape, a means to process the complexities of my reality. Inspired by the world around me, I delved deeper into still life art. I became engulfed in the explanations of the artistic shapes within the environment. From there, I started exploring physics and astronomy, deepening my fascination with the universe. This shift helped me understand not only the beauty of creation but also the intricate systems that govern our world.

“Can I make it?”
On my nightstand sits a cherished gift from my mom: a starry night projection light that calms my mind and reminds me of my family. When she started studying for her GED, I became her teacher, guiding her through problem-solving. On the day of her math exam, I turned on the projection light to calm my nerves, reflecting on how my family has always supported each other—through math competitions and my first disastrous attempt at baking macarons. When facing the anxiety of not fitting in, having been pushed into a universe of unfathomable wealth after being a part of such a different reality, I would find solace in the sprawling stars. The kids sharing my same uniform had a particular glow: one that only the richest possessed. Yet, I was determined to forge a path forward. The starlight became a constant companion, guiding me through my fears and watching as I transformed them into courage. The stars stood by me as I turned my fears into resilience and embraced the value of inclusion, learning to find my place and support others along the way.

“I can find a way”
Nearby, fossilized to the ceiling of my room, glow-in-the-dark stars dimly illuminate the night, sparking curiosity since middle school. Gazing at those eerie green specks, I found inspiration in the seemingly ordinary. As a child, I often overthought small quarrels with friends, like losing sleep over an animal eraser dispute with Ada. Late at night, these stars were my companions, guiding my thoughts from reconciling friendships to debugging asteroid simulation codes for observations made from the Pohl Observatory. Even the most far-fetched ideas were guided by their faint glow, always leading me toward new discoveries and solutions.

As my foot throbs from tapping and sweat trickles down my forehead, I patiently wait for my teacher to take roll. Three minutes feels like an eternity; my heart jumps into my throat as I tremble in fear. “Ty-reek…Tear-ik?” my teacher calls forth, as my classmates grin. I raise my hand and bashfully mumble my acquiescence as my face gushes red in embarrassment. I wondered how I would be able to show confidence to the world when the mere thought of my name brought such apprehension.

“The sea is behind you, and the enemy is in front of you,” my young ears hear as my little heart bursts with pride. These words echo through my mind as I recall my mom telling why me she named me after a great Muslim leader who ordered his army to burn their ships after they landed in Spain. I found it odd that my mom, whose life has been rooted by values of Christianity and American customs, chose this name. Growing up in a blue-color family, things were sometimes wrought with hardship—my mom recalls the shame she felt using food stamps. Nevertheless, she has taught me that being half-American can mean nights ignited with fireworks, complemented with hot-dogs, potato chips, and smores around the fire on the 4th of July, and late Christmas nights, decorating cookies while listening to silver bells and patiently waiting by the tree. My name is a testament to my ability to serve and treasure what I believe is a part of my identity.

Although it was my American mom who chose my name, it is my Lebanese dad who calls my name with the voice of my ancestors. I can hear him calling my name now, my eyes weary as he wakes me for Suhoor. As we eat our yogurt and dates together, he recounts his childhood, having only “dry bread” and “boiled bath water” during Ramadan amidst the civil war in Beirut. My dad has always been a survivor and fought to make a name for himself. As an immigrant, he was subject to persecution for his accent—the very accent I love to hear. Yet, he persisted along his path. As sunset approaches, I hear the call to prayer, and I join my dad for Iftar. I sense the warm hue emitted from the Adhan as my mouth waters, eager to start eating. Later, as we have tea and namoura, I reflect on my dad’s immigration considering what it means to be a Muslim. I parallel his patience, perseverance, and willingness, to that of fasting – the wait is enduring and toilsome, but there is hope.

My name means “star of piercing brightness” in Arabic. I believe that my experiences played out in my upbringing provide the light and vibrance instilled in the star. From my mom’s compassion and my dad’s determination, my identity is composed of various traditions that make it rich in complexity. From counting down the time on New Year’s Eve, to praying in the Mosque on the day of Eid, my encounters of the distinct fruits which my cultures bestow define my identity and fulfill the luminescence in my name.

As these experiences amass, my lens of the world enriches as I expose myself to the beauties of the unique identities that define us. I often witness people struggling to communicate because of perceived differences, when really it is internal insecurities surfacing, pulling them to a place of silence, complacency and, possibly, hostility. I perceive others with an empathetic lens and understand that names do not suggest an absolute but can be a backstory to so much more.

Now placid, grateful, I sit in my seat and patiently wait for my teacher to call my name. “T-[Name]?” she says. “Here” I humbly exclaim as my identity courses through my blood and fill my mind with content.

“Do not let him get between you and the door.” My purple-gloved hands were covered in the nauseating smell of cleaning solution as I turned to face the charge nurse who had just warned me of the potential danger of entering Room 408. It was as if cleaning hospital rooms in unsightly grey scrubs all summer as a rising senior was not challenging enough. All around me, nurses and doctors swirled about the floor without missing a beat; for them, this was just another day on the East Wing; for me, it was my introduction to Environmental Services (EVS) as an intern at a teaching hospital, feeling woefully unprepared for what lay in front of me.

A wary “Environmental Serv-” came out of my mouth just as a blaring alarm sounded to alert seemingly everyone within a 100-mile radius that the door to Room 408 was ajar. Upon entering, I was met by “Bob,” a man of average stature with salt-and-pepper hair and tan hospital socks hanging halfway off his feet. He greeted me with a gentle smile and seemed to welcome my presence by moving to the side of his room so I could begin cleaning. Bob’s eyes tracked my movements as I swept up an astounding number of crumbs, picked up the remnants of a dismantled potted plant, and mopped up an impressive amount of urine from under his bed.
