His nurse informed me that he was a “permanent resident of Dartmouth Hitchcock for the foreseeable future.” Although Bob was nonspeaking, as the weeks passed, he seemed to anticipate our regular but brief interactions that began with a mutual smile and always ended with him pressed up against the door, laughing, smiling, and waving at me while his breath fogged up the window.

Bob was the most memorable patient I interacted with, and no matter what condition I found his room in, I felt like I restored a piece of his dignity when I cleaned it. As the weeks passed, I became more comfortable with my role with EVS, simply by doing the work, developing friendships with the EVS employees, and taking stock of the interactions I was having with patients like Bob. I also realized that my role with EVS gave me the opportunity to interact with people at very vulnerable and difficult times in their lives. Some patients shared pieces of their life stories with me, and others asked me questions about my own. None of them seemed to view my work as menial as I initially did.

I was admittedly very confused when I received my internship schedule and discovered that I would be spending a significant part of my time with EVS. Would I be planting trees or helping to reduce waste? A quick Google search clarified this for me, as did my many early mornings on the job. EVS headquarters is hidden away in the bowels of the hospital, where few employees dare to go. The dimly lit corridors and unadorned ‘Environmental Services’ sign are in stark contrast to the colorful hallways, beautifully framed artwork, and blooming plants that greet doctors, nurses, and patients each day. This distinction mirrors the sometimes tense interactions I observed between the doctors, nurses, and EVS staff, with neither seeming to acknowledge the presence of the other.

As the daughter of a surgeon, I floated undetected between these two worlds, one of privilege that I had grown accustomed to and the other where I became invisible to many by donning my EVS scrubs, moving from room to room while methodically following cleaning protocols. Each day, after changing into my business casual attire for the Urology Clinic or Pathology Lab, I left the EVS world but took with me a lesson in humility, deep appreciation for unseen workers, and gratitude for all the patients who took the time to give me a glimpse into their own lives.

I can picture Mom’s worried face. After six years of piano practice, I’m about to tell her I want to quit. My heart pounds as I walk up to my parents. “I’d like to stop piano lessons,” I say, my voice quiet and uncertain.

That morning, I had listened enviously to a bird cheerfully singing outside while practicing a piece I’d played countless times. “Why can’t I create my own melody instead of repeating someone else’s?” I wondered while listening to the bird's free-spirited song.

“Can I not practice piano?” The pause that follows feels unbearable. I quickly add, “I’ve built a solid foundation in music theory.” Then, a more determined tone: “I’m going to try composing my own songs instead.” The fear of disappointing them lingers in the air. To my surprise, they agreed. Relief. Now it is time to find a new way to enjoy music.

For the first time, I’m stepping away from a structured path, and it’s overwhelming. I sit at the piano, the blank sheet music in front of me seeming like an impossible challenge. For minutes, I wonder if I’ve made the right decision. Slowly, I start to forget my worries. I experiment with melodies mortif by mortif, hum softly to myself, notes dance swiftly toward me orchestrated by an unseen angel, gradually come together. A year later, I performed my composition, Establishment, in the historic Ehrbar Hall in Vienna. The bright lights washed over me, a slight tremor coursed through my hands, I couldn’t discern my parent’s beaming faces amid the crowd, but I reminded myself: they were proud of me – and I was proud of myself for taking this leap into the unknown.

During junior year, as I delved into the materials for Academic Decathlon with the theme of Technology and Humanity, realizing how crucial technology would be in transforming every aspect of our lives—including chemistry, my area of interest. I was accepted into a six-week STEM project using machine learning project to predicting mental health situations this summer. That familiar feeling of unease from the uncertainty resurfaced. I had no experience with machine learning and only a basic understanding of Python. But I asked myself: “what if I succeed?”

The first two weeks were overwhelming. I spent hours trying to understand algorithms and tutorials. When ran into a question, I tried to find answer on myself. The deadline is approaching, quickly I realized that I shouldn’t work alone, I reached out to my other two teammates. The data is overwhelming with more than fifty variables to choose for the models. We divided tasks, sharing the research result, Python tricks, deciding on setup of a composite for the dependent variable, and categorizing rest of 50 variables into 10 bucket to facilitate model setup. Together, we broke down the complex project into small chunks, data cleaning, model setup, results analysis, and model comparison. Piece by piece, the project took shape.

Before the deadline, we managed to implement three models for prediction. More importantly, I learned to embrace uncertainty and power of collaboration as a strength. By admitting that I didn’t know everything and seeking help from my teammates and professor, I opened myself up to learning and growing in ways I hadn’t anticipated. Even when I feel uncomfortable, it can still lead to meaningful growth.

As I look toward college, I'm both excited and nervous about new challenges, whether it's joining an AI club, exploring music composition, or tackling a chemistry research topic. I know I'll face many uncertainties, but I aspire for the opportunity to learn from talented classmates and passionate professors who will guide me on this journey.

Facing the unknown is known, I'm learning to see it as an opportunity for growth. I ended my composition 'Establishment' with the rhythmic sound of a train—the 'clickety-clack' that represents my ongoing journey toward embracing uncertainty with hope and determination.

On a hazy night in November, I met Mr. Ba, an old man from my church, for the first time in the Birmingham hospital. He had been living with a brain tumor, and I had offered to give his wife a ride home. As I turned off the lights in his barren room, I felt a loneliness heavier than the night fog settle. I wondered if solitude called his fear to attention.

As his wife and I walked to my car, I thought of the many other patients like him. I knew I couldn't help all those people single-handedly, but perhaps the compassion of a hundred high schoolers could. That night, I began planning a club to fill patients’ rooms with cards or gifts, so, even in solitude, they wouldn’t feel so alone.

With a three-week deadline, I launched a Christmas donation to the Birmingham hospital.

By December 11th, I recruited most of the people in my classes and more during lunch and rallied 100 members for our new club. I only had one week to organize and execute a full-fledged drive. Trusting the strength in numbers, I directed my officers to seek donations from school clubs they had connections with, specifically targeting those closely tied to classroom activities. Teachers even accepted our proposal to offer bonus points to incentivize contributions. On December 18th, I drove to the Birmingham hospital with $3,000 in gifts packed in my car. I felt proud of our efforts–but I was too late. Mr. Ba had passed. I never gave him the gifts. I never had a conversation with him again.

After the donation drives, I set up a card-writing event for a smaller cancer center whose patients did not receive as much from the community. However, the event didn’t unfold the way I had hoped. The idea was to connect with people who felt forgotten, but what resulted were hastily written messages from distracted students, devoid of the sincerity I had envisioned. It dawned on me that for many patients, receiving another generic card might feel more obligatory than heartfelt. The realization weighed on me, but it also sparked something new.

I wanted to give something meaningful to the patients while inspiring students to serve with compassion. This led to the formation of the pen pal initiative, but getting it off the ground had setbacks. I couldn’t reach the oncology center by phone, so I went in person to ask for a partnership. I also had to ensure HIPAA compliance to protect patient privacy. After sending flyers to the center, we received no responses for over a week. Concerned, I emailed the director with suggestions like having doctors inform patients directly. The director admitted the flyers hadn't been put up yet but accepted the suggestions. Despite these challenges, the initiative became a success. I carefully paired students with patients, guiding them toward ongoing, meaningful exchanges based on shared interests and empathy. Encouraged by this progress, we expanded the program to include patients at Children’s of Alabama, further extending our impact.

What began as a few hastily written words transformed into something greater: relationships that patients could look forward to, and students could learn from. I’ll never forget how “get well” scribbles and bags of cardboard-encased gifts grew into moments of listening, understanding, and offering a piece of oneself. I’ll never forget how silence in a dark hospital in Birmingham grew into a thousand streams of conversation that flow from the one I never had with Mr. Ba. As I move forward into college, I hope to grow that thousand into a million–and to find new ways to bring people together to create meaningful connections.

Watching oblique waves ripple across the screen, shifting faster than my eyes could follow, I was glued to the monitor, lost in rhythm, when suddenly the thousand-twenty-four-second neural recording cut to black.

“You got all that? It's pretty simple really,” Prashant remarked casually, jogging off to his next meeting. Perplexed, I gazed at the monitor, where a notification in a vibrant green font read: “Recording Analyzed, Media Exported.”

Murphy’s Law–the unwelcome storm cloud on a sunny day. Anything that can go wrong will go wrong; although not scientific, it’s ironically synonymous with academia. I was stuck in the corner of the laboratory, contemplating Murphy’s Law while tinkering with the analysis software, attempting to retrace Prashant’s magic as an avalanche of errors flooded my screen: “This recording has different streams than the previous file.” After hours of experimentation, seemingly trying every possible permutation and combination, I was still trapped in an inescapable vortex, having only analyzed one of the thirty neural recordings—the lone triumph? The same one Prashant had analyzed in his demonstration hours earlier.

That night, I lay awake, distraught by the day’s failure. Technical terms like “Cutoff Frequency,” “Channel Maps,” and “Spike rate analyzer” swirled through my subconscious mind. Despite the mixed emotions, I was cautiously optimistic that with Prashant’s guidance, I’d adopt his magical touch. But when I arrived at the graduate lounge early the following day, eager for answers, all that greeted me was an empty chair–and the sinking realization that I was on my own.

As I sat there, staring at the empty seat where Prashant should have been, a thought began to crystalize: Panta Rhei, translating to “everything flows.” Coined by Heraclitus, it speaks to the constant state of imbalance in the universe, where change is the only certainty in a world filled with uncertainties. The Fall of Blockbuster? The Tragic Case of Yahoo? The byproduct of unwillingness to adapt: Heraclitus’s principle in action. All alone, I had to pivot, adjust to this newfound change in circumstance, and make headway myself.

Returning to the laboratory, I scoured manuals, online blogs like Research Gate, and outdated literature. I was soon lost, traversing through a never-ending intellectual labyrinth, with each breakthrough only revealing underlying layers of complexity. By noon, I had made no progress, with nothing to show for but piles of half-read manuscripts. However, these half-read fragments were all I needed. Much like the neurons I was measuring, which responded to electrical stimuli by discharging signals, I, too, was systematically eliminating sources of error, meticulously implementing each strategy I’d read. And finally, after hours of trial and error, the puzzle piece clicked into place with a lone glimmer of hope: Green notification of triumph, “Recording Analyzed, Media Exported.”

The first domino had fallen, and the momentum had shifted in my favor for the first time. Soon, the second and third recordings were analyzed. As the dominos spiraled, my monitor lit up with green notifications of success as I analyzed all thirty recordings.

When Prashant returned the following day, he remarked, “All too easy for you, huh?” With a wry smile, I responded, “Felt like a warm-up,” (Though I did wonder what Prashant considered “hard”) reflecting on the sleep-deprived nights and the roller coaster of emotions I’d been through.

Throughout that summer, I continued experimenting, recording, and analyzing neural data. I even formulated my manual, which I dubbed the Flux State–a beginner's guide to the basics of neural data analysis. But at times, I encountered roadblocks beyond trial and error, beyond Panta Rhei, where critical thinking wasn’t enough. In some cases, I was the annoying intern emailing Prashant late at night asking for assistance. Still, through this all, I found it thrilling to scour an infinitely deep well of knowledge for a solution and learn from my vastly experienced colleagues to charter a new frontier where innovation is fostered through adaption.

I could feel the familiar thrill as the propellers spun up, the same excitement I always got when something I’d built came to life. I started my engineering journey thinking that it had always been about taking an idea from my mind and turning it into something real and impressive. That’s what drove me. I was obsessed with building things that looked cool and worked well enough to show off and impress people. But that day, my mindset was about to catch up with me. It was two days before the final round of Codeavour, an international AI competition. My team had spent months working on a search-and-rescue drone, combining parts from past projects with new AI software my friends had developed. I was responsible for ensuring the drone‘s hardware and flight systems while they worked on the AI detection system.

But I’d been reckless. I knew that one of the motors had been vibrating strangely during earlier tests, a warning sign that I should have addressed. Well, I didn’t think much about it; after all, I was busy soldering and attaching batteries so our team could brag about our drone’s flight endurance. If that wasn’t enough for the poor motor, I decided to add an arm to carry a first aid kit which will be dropped automatically upon the detection of someone in need of help. Together, we had created something that I was sure would blow the judges away.

When the drone lifted off, my excitement surged—it was finally happening. But then, just as quickly, that excitement turned to dread, after flying for 10 minutes autonomously following our programmed search and rescue pattern, the motor failed at 120 meters, and the drone began to spiral out of control. I could only watch as it plummeted toward the ground, taking with it not just months of work, but my overconfidence. I realized, with a sinking feeling, that I had made the same mistake I’d made so many times before: focusing on the outcome, not the process.

This crash hit me hard, but it also sparked a fundamental change in my mindset. My obsession with the end result—impressing people with something that looked cool—had blinded me to the importance of the details, of the process itself. I had ignored the warning signs, overburdened the motor, and pushed ahead recklessly, all because I was too focused on the final performance rather than ensuring everything was functioning perfectly.

This failure forced me to confront a truth I had long resisted: engineering isn’t just about flashy creations; it’s about precision, patience, and thinking through every detail. I realized that while I had been innovative, innovation without careful execution was reckless. That crash marked a turning point in how I approached my projects. Since then, I’ve become more methodical, focusing on the process over the outcome, balancing creativity with discipline, and ensuring that my excitement to innovate never overshadows the importance of precision. This shift has made me a more resilient problem-solver, grounded in the understanding that true innovation lies in mastering the details.

I applied this mindset to my next project: leading younger coding club members in designing self-cleaning solar panels. This time, we prioritized durability over showy features, constantly asking ourselves, "What could go wrong, and how can we prevent it?" After months of testing, the panels began generating clean energy without any issues. I also mentored new members of the robotics team, teaching them the importance of precision and patience. Watching them embrace these concepts and grow as engineers has been more rewarding than any project I’ve completed.

Now, I know true success comes from creating reliable, lasting solutions that solve real-world problems. As I look toward college, I’m eager to continue learning, collaborating, and building technologies that make a meaningful impact—slowly, carefully, and with every detail in mind.

Each jagged crack, each busted joint, whispered of danger lurking beneath. If I kept my eyes on the flagstones, I could avoid these fissures, avoiding everything else, too. One foot in front of the other, my eyes darting between the breaks of each cement square, I move swiftly and silently, ignoring the hidden fractures that threaten to engulf me. 
***
As the youngest of four, I was the quiet one. The soothing strains of a gentle Buddhist melody are drowned out by my eldest sister’s latest rendition of Für Elise. My brother kicks and screams as our mother attempts to strap on his asthma mask. Another sister dribbles a basketball on the stone foyer. I remain silent.

The obvious chaos of my siblings is nothing in comparison to the emotional chaos bubbling under the surface, threatening to erupt. It’s 1:00 AM on a sweltering summer night in the Bronx and just a floor below, my mom’s voice pierces the air with takeout orders as she deftly works the fryer at our restaurant. It’s rare to see her without her sauce-stained navy Yankee's cap, and although she stands beside me she feels even further away than she does when the layers of wood and drywall separate us.

How do you tell an eight-year-old that the weight of his parents’ immigrant dream and the heavy [blocks] of familial piety were slowly shattering his mother? You don’t. In many families like mine, this heaviness is passed from parent to child, silently for generations. Until the weight becomes unbearable and it slips, it hits the ground. It causes tectonic plates to shift, small cracks deepening into craters, growing so vast that they reveal an abyss of darkness below.

The most vivid memory of my absent father is of him pushing my siblings away from the ambulance that was transporting my mother. Headlights drown out the red and white lights that dance around my feet as my Spiderman Skechers hit the pavement one foot in front of the other. My siblings and I have arrived. The sterile scent of antiseptic envelops us as we enter a room with a faint beeping.

“You wait right there, sweetheart” commands a nurse, forcing a smile. A blue curtain stretches across the room deepening the chasm of confusion and fear. Once again, I am separated from my mom. Fragmented voices drift through the fabric, asking questions I can't bear to hear. “Did you know about these… attempts?” and “Any prior attempts at self-harm?” My dad sits in silence, unable to offer any insight…
***
Even though my involvement with the Society to Prevent Teen Suicide(SPTS) has enabled me to detect suicide warning signs, back then, I was ignorant. I now know my mother was silently crying for help and exhibiting behaviors that a trained eye could have easily detected. I vowed to learn more about mental health issues and spread awareness among my peers many of whom surely have family members who also struggle with anxiety, depression, and isolation.

Freshman year, I joined Active Minds, our school’s mental health club. My mission was simple: to ensure that others wouldn't have to shoulder their struggles alone. Soon my mission became grander: I sought to dig deeper, guiding others to see past the layers of drywall and wood and even beyond the facades of normalcy.

Wanting to educate younger children on mental issues, I led a Mental Health Awareness Day, teaching the warning signs and behaviors at a local elementary school. I wanted these children to know that their concerns deserve to be heard.

One foot in front of the other, I walk along the sidewalk, no longer feeling the need to avoid the cracks. The strides I take are bigger and more confident than before and remind me of my mother's journey back to the Light. I plan to stride confidently on campus, eager to continue this outreach in college, as I hopefully inspire a more supportive and empathetic community.

Stepping into the jungle of middle schoolers in a junior high school cafeteria, I was confident that this would be straightforward since I’ve worked with kids of all ages before, so I expected this camp would be a short five-day event.

My carefree plan was quickly crashed on the first day. Many kids were too afraid to even talk to us coaches, let alone give speeches. One girl, Sarah, stood out in particular. She’d rather watch her phone than socializing, and when spoken to her eyes shifted around nervously.

Although feeling frustrated, I had no complaint. I was just like them when I joined my first speech camp four years. On the first day, when the coach asked us to give a speech on any topic we liked, I remember my heart bucked wildly, my legs shook like a leaf, and I indeed would have rather dropped dead instead of humiliating myself for so many ogling eyes. But later I found the camp was pretty fun. The coaches and campers were very kind and encouraging. I made friends, and discovered my passion in Interp, a masterclass in storytelling and performance. The piece I performed was about an Asian immigrant of losing her culture, which allowed me to explore my own Asian American identity. Every line and interaction of the role has an echo in my own heart, and analyzing the emotions and motives of the character helped me work through my own complex knot of emotions. Making people laugh and cry and feel through performing was a much stronger motivator than the fear of embarrassment.

Realizing this was probably the first speech camp for these kids, I felt like helping them to have fun while nurturing their interest in speech. First, I needed good teaching materials that suited their learning level. The teaching materials provided by the management did not suit them. Therefore I decided to develop my own teaching curriculum. Every day, I came early and stayed after to create my own lessons and organize materials. In the class, I constantly acknowledged that yes, acting was scary and vulnerable, but also noted that at the camp, everyone was doing it with you and no judgment from coaches or peers would be accepted.

Gradually everyone fell into acting at their own comfort levels. While others were ready to commit their every fiber to their characters, Sarah was up for simply reciting the script and I appreciated her bravery to try regardless. Through every step out of her shell, I was there cheering her on and helping her grow comfortable in front of a crowd.

On the last day of the camp it’s a blast to see the students demonstrating enthusiasm and spirit in each of their three-minute performance. It’s rewarding to see they were encouraging and applausing for each other and having fun together. When they walked out, they were chattering about joining Speech and Debate Club when school started. I even heard Sarah saying that as well.

When the last kid skipped away into her parent's car, I couldn’t believe that in just a few short days I was able to turn things around and help over 20 students overcome their fears of public speaking. I never thought that my little help could make others to recognize their potential and empower them to improve. If I could empower others, I could empower myself, too. This experience gave me courage to do what was previously unimaginable to me. I began starring in my school’s theater productions and leading discussions on women’s issues as chair member in my school’s She’s The First chapter. At college, I will continue to involve myself in helping my community and improving myself.

One summer, when my family was discussing vacation ideas, I pridefully defended my plan to drive a few hours North to Salem, Massachusetts. In 2nd grade, I wrote that my favorite movie was Dark Shadows on an “All About Me” worksheet (a low-quality movie starring Johnny Depp about a 175-year-old vampire who rises from the dead and wreaks havoc on his 21st-century relatives). I don’t believe that's what Mrs. Magee expected. More recently, I built a bookshelf in the shape of a coffin, because who wouldn't want that as bedroom ornamentation? Shoutout to my Dad who passed down his skills as a carpenter. Every birthday I can expect to open an envelope with tickets to a haunted house tucked inside. I am currently reading a book written by a forensic anthropologist that describes her story of discovering the horrors of the 1992 Rwandan genocide through human remains found in grave sites. My fascination with the dark has always been a facet of my identity. Things that would make the average person cringe draw me closer like a moth to a streetlight. The dark intrigues me, I find it to be descriptive of the true human experience. Despite this, I would not describe myself as “emo” or goth. The macabre is simply an intellectual and entertaining interest of mine. Horror movies, for example, are a lens that I can use to explore human nature or simply appreciate the beauty that comes with low-lit scenes accompanied by Bernard Herrman. My strongest interest goes further than ghost stories and Michael Meyers. Death, grief, and the real dark sides of life are what will keep my head in a book for hours. The macabre is about finding beauty in the strange and uncanny. There's a certain thrill that comes along with exploring topics most people would shy away from; whether it's uncovering the Rwandan genocide or discussing the complexities of people suffering from anti-social personality disorder. I share my passion for the macabre with the world as often as possible. I raised funds for historic restoration by curating a gothic Halloween feast at a 17th-century Hotel and Tavern in my hometown; it’s rumored to have a few non-living residents roaming the halls. Similarly, I’ve turned my high school into Trick-or-Treat Street for the past 3 years, a free event for elementary-aged students. My interest has helped me understand and embrace the full spectrum of life. Darkness and death are inevitable, natural, and in an odd way, poetic. I never understood the purpose of taboo-ifying anything, let alone one of the only things all beings are promised: death. Though it may not be the most conventional passion, I still choose to embrace the macabre as an essential part of truly living.

For years, I looked down at the ground when I walked. I did so not out of shyness, but out of wonder. In each new canvas of land my feet explored, my eyes feasted on the soil, fixating on the colony of ants transporting breadcrumbs or the white-speckled wildflowers sprouting from the pavement. By eight years old, my habit of analyzing and absorbing my surroundings transformed me into a human GPS who could remember routes better than my parents. At fifteen, being observant proved beneficial as a leader; I initiated events taking into account my club members’ opinions by listening to and applying their feedback.

As an explorer of my surroundings, volunteering at Chesterbrook Senior Residences during my sophomore year placed me in a completely uncharted land. My first assignment whisked me into the unfamiliar biome of the exercise room, where I would perform a daily "sittercise" routine with the residents. Thoughts such as, “What if the 50-year age gap severed our connections?” and, “What if, as my volunteer coordinator warned, the residents say offensive and outdated words?” plagued my mind. But as I slinked away to the back row, I decided to observe the details around me - this time, my observation skills would help me discover possible connections.

Soon, a group of residents surrounded me, playfully criticizing my weak performance. I awkwardly joked back, unaccustomed to their humor. The residents responded with perplexed glances - most had trouble hearing close conversations. How could I connect with them if we could not communicate?

With the residents, I couldn’t passively scan my surroundings or engage in surface-level communication. Instead, I needed to unearth deeper ways to connect. I scoured the internet to understand the activity that connected us, learning that sittercise improved flexibility and strengthened joints. Watching other instructors on YouTube helped me uncover new moves. I made a mind map, crafting personalized exercises for each resident according to their health and capabilities. I designed equipment moves for Julia, the most athletic resident. For Evelyn, who used a wheelchair and couldn’t reach her toes, I invented alternative upper-body exercises.

One day, halfway through our routine, our sittercise DVD suddenly glitched. When disappointed faces multiplied, I knew I had to improvise. Drawing on my newly acquired knowledge, I led a live routine, incorporating music and moves like an upper-body "breaststroke pull" inspired by my swimming experience. I unearthed songs the residents knew and loved, like "It's Raining Men" and "Rhythm of the Rain," with arm raises becoming our dance moves. By the end, my squad unanimously declared it the best session yet. I was in the middle of the room now, chatting and laughing at the residents' jokes.

After my volunteer experience ended, I sought ways to expand our connections. Knowing the residents’ love for music and engaging with the younger generation, I started bringing the Musicians Association club to perform. Debbie, a longtime attendee, eagerly rallies other residents when we arrive. My classmates, propelled by the residents' bravos and claps, flourished with newfound expression as they performed.

All those times I marveled at the ants and flowers around me, I never realized that these invaluable treasures existed because of the vital networks of trails and roots beneath the surface. I discovered that social connections, too, are sustained by the hidden networks of supporting and uplifting one another. I learned how to dig through communication barriers and age gaps to discover the genuine connections cultivated through shared activities like music and sittercise.

Today, although I’ve corrected my dangerous habit of not looking ahead when walking, I still keenly observe my surroundings. However, I’ve learned that simply observing is not enough to truly understand others. I need to actively unearth these connections. Equipped with empathy, curiosity, and attentiveness, I’ll be prepared to seek out more genuine connections that lie beneath the surface, waiting for me to be unearthed.

It was just a few weeks after my 18th birthday, the ink on my "adult" card barely dry, when my mom dropped a bombshell. We were in the living room, just chatting, when she told me the man I'd always called Dad, my biggest supporter, wasn't actually my biological father. She explained that I was conceived through a sperm donor.

My brain short-circuited. Confusion, anger, sadness – it all hit me at once. My world had been flipped upside down. It felt like someone had pressed pause on my life, leaving me stuck in limbo. And I was trying to figure out who I even was.

Once I could process it, Mom explained how she and Dad had always wanted a child, but things weren't working out. So, they chose to use a sperm bank, and that's where I came in.

This whole thing forced me to rethink what family truly means. Growing up, I thought it was all about blood, but now I wasn't so sure. If my dad wasn't "really" my dad, then what did that make us? It was hard to comprehend. I even started Googling sperm donors, DNA, and everything related, desperately trying to make sense of it all.

But then I thought about all our memories. Dad taught me to throw a baseball, being at every game, cheering me on even when I struck out. He always had my back. Even though my parents aren't together anymore, he's still a huge part of my life.

I realized family isn't just about genes. It's about the people who love you, raise you, and shape you. It's about shared experiences, inside jokes, and unconditional support. Sure, my family tree might have a detour, a branch that started in a sperm bank, but that doesn't change the love and support I have.

This experience taught me that life throws curveballs, and sometimes you just have to roll with it. It also showed me how strong love can be and how different families are formed. I'm grateful for my parents and their choices.

As I enter adulthood, I'm filled with gratitude for the extraordinary love that brought me into this world – the love between my parents and their desire to have a child. I am a testament to the unlimited possibilities that arise when love and determination intertwine. My story celebrates the diverse ways families are formed, a reminder that true sense of family lies not in shared DNA but in the enduring power of love.

One grand pause. Two bars of woodwind flourish. Three beats carefully counted before I placed the bow on the strings under the gleaming lights. Without a moment to spare a glance into the hall, I immersed myself into my violin performance as the soloist. First, I played a gentle melody, and then a vibrant crescendo. Next, I traversed the complex arpeggios before I prepared myself for the final, intricate passage.

Please. I tell myself as I lift my bow for the next note. Please work this time. But it was no use. The tremor in my left hand ignited through my body like wildfire. In a split second, the melody faltered, and my confidence collapsed. I opened my eyes to the realization that my condition had once again overshadowed my performance.

Ever since I was young, I loved playing the violin. However, my body had other plans. Throughout middle school I had developed a subtle tremor in my left hand, that snowballed into a blinding tension each time I played the violin. After a visit to my pediatrician, the ailment was diagnosed: functional tremor.

Functional tremor is characterized by uncontrollable shaking when performing a certain activity. The underlying cause is the nervous system rather than the brain— “a software problem and not a hardware problem” as my pediatrician described it. Though the condition can be mitigated with a regiment of exercises, functional tremor was essentially incurable. And a year after diagnosis, my tremor had only intensified, making it clear that I could not longer play the violin.

But I never gave up. During that time, I was assigned a project in my engineering class. The directions for the project were broad—design and manufacture a medical device that includes specific components.

While researching what kind of device to design, I came across a walking device for individuals with tremors in their legs due to Parkinson's disease. The device emitted lasers, creating a visual cue for individuals with Parkinson's to alter the neuropathway used to move their legs. Miraculously, this device allowed them to do what they once believed was impossible for them– walk. As I read the results of the experiment in awe, a thought popped into my mind. What if I could ‘walk’ again too?

Thus, I began to design a glove. First, I researched which muscle groups in the hand were affected. Next, I built a glove with a built-in metronome and LED lights, providing both audible and visual cues to help zero in on the affected muscle groups. Additionally, I integrated flex sensors to detect the tremor’s intensity, enabling my computer to monitor progress.

Finally, after weeks of preparation, my glove’s design was completed. And in one final test, I wore the glove to test its effectiveness. I started with my hand open on the upbeat. Then– for the ultimate test, I bent each finger down to my palm on the downbeat. One. Two. Three beats and release.

I did it. It worked! After several repetitions, my movement felt smooth, and I was amazed: the tremor was gone. Even if it was a small step, I could finally play the violin again.

Though only partially successful, the project laid the foundation for reclaiming my life. This journey not only strengthened my resolve to beat functional tremor but also fueled my passion for innovation. By blending my love for music and engineering, I discovered a way to overcome a personal challenge and, in doing so, opened a door to help others facing similar obstacles.

In fourth grade, a friend recommended the Percy Jackson series. But I couldn’t stop there – I was fascinated by how different cultures interpreted different gods, a curiosity which led me to the Kane Chronicles for Egyptian mythology and Magnus Chase for Norse mythology. This was the beginning of a ten-year journey, my own Odyssey.

In middle school, I heard about the Medusa Mythology Exam. I finally had a place to use all of my knowledge and I received the gold medal award. In high school, I became the myth exam coordinator in my school’s Mythology Club. One of my favorite activities is creating and playing Kahoots about mythology.

One time, a student asked why the hundred-handed Hecatoncheires became the prison guards of Tartarus. I referenced a passage from one of the sources we were reading by Hesiod, Theogony. I explained that it all went back to the Titanomachy, the war between the Titans and Olympians. The Titans were children of Gaia that ruled the world. Although the Hecatoncheires were also children of Gaia, they joined the side of the Gods because the Titans were harsh rulers. Being able to easily provide an explanation to others really made it feel like there was more to mythology than for my own entertainment.

But even more fulfilling than having more knowledge about the stories themselves was applying mythology to my worldview. Over the summer, I read a book called A Short Story of Myth by Karen Armstrong. It inspired the idea that mythology was important not just because it was entertaining, but because it shows us how people in every time period understood their world.

When I study mythology, I feel powerful. I believe that to study mythology is to study the purpose and meaning of life. Mythology is a representation of the human experience.

A common motif is a hero entering the underworld, symbolizing death, and then leaving the underworld, showing rebirth. He undergoes a metamorphosis and gains a new understanding of the world. We are changed after going through an unfamiliar ordeal or experience.

Even in movies and books today, you can find examples of the archetypes of early myths. Outside the magical realms of fiction and fantasy, we embody certain archetypes in our daily lives. This is because these archetypes are based on basic characteristics of people that hold true even in different times.

In the past, religion and mythology gave people a reason for everything. In the first dawn of the hunter-gatherers, there was the belief that the gods helped the harvest, as well as hunting gods that assisted with the kill. Today’s modern religions are similar in that they give people a reason for existence.

I had a conversation with my friend Jibran about the validity of religions. Before, I was a skeptic because religion was not linked to actual historical events. I didn’t believe that Jesus performed miracles or that Muhammad rose to heaven, the same way I didn’t believe that Zeus was throwing lightning bolts or that the Sun was driven in a chariot by Helios.

However, Jibran talked about how things didn’t have to exactly happen for people to believe in an idea. For example, the story of the Buddha achieving enlightenment and understanding suffering was just a story, but it was able to convey a message of trying to detach from desires. I realized that a way to look at myths or religious stories was that they were sending a metaphorical message, as opposed to a literal one.

Because modern religions are taken as literal by some believers and I disagreed with that, I thought that their purpose as a whole was invalid. The same way ancient Greeks believed that praying to Poseidon led to a good voyage, people today could believe in Jesus for his compassion and kindness. Even though science obviously disagrees with the facts in the stories, getting the exact details wasn’t the point. This idea influenced my worldview. I no longer have a solely scientific perspective. I take into account a desire to understand things through different ways including mythology.

As I walked into the library, my palms were sweating and my legs felt like they were about to collapse. I was on my way to my AP seminar presentation, and even though I had spent a week practicing, I felt completely unprepared. The presentation went horribly. When I stood before the class, everything went downhill. I fumbled through my opening lines; my voice was shaky and barely comprehensible. When the teacher began asking questions, my heart pounded so loudly that I could barely focus on what she was saying. The answers that I had memorized completely vanished, and I stood there humiliated. As I walked out of the room, the weight of the embarrassment hit me. I knew something had to change.

The night after the presentation, I took a long look in the mirror. I’ve always felt hindered by a fear of speaking to others. Whether it was making a presentation in front of the class, or starting a one-on-one conversation with someone I didn’t know. My first instinct was to turn to the internet for answers. I went to YouTube and looked up “how to be more confident in public.” I came across a lot of content, but I realized that my fear of speaking was from more than just being in public. It came from deeper insecurities. I wasn’t just afraid of speaking. I was scared of what people would think about me if I messed up and what people thought I looked like while I was doing something. After hours of research, I encountered a current theme in the videos: going to the gym. At first, I didn’t understand how working out could help build my confidence, but I decided to try it.

After a few months, I realized that going to the gym had boosted my confidence. With each achievement I made, I felt more comfortable in social settings, finding it easier to make friends and interact with people without feeling nervous. Before I started going to the gym, I often kept my head down, always focusing on my phone, and avoiding eye contact as much as possible when speaking to others. But once I started to train, my confidence grew. I began to stand taller and felt more confident when looking people in the eye. I started to care less about what people thought, and more focused on my progress.

As the year went on, I realized that my growth extended beyond just my physical appearance. I learned the value of discipline and how setting goals could apply to all aspects of life. I began to apply this mindset in other areas, like volunteering at Habitat for Humanity. This allowed me to meet new people and portray my new confidence. I made a goal each week to assist one person- whether they were an employee or customer. This helped me not only use the confidence I had from the gym but my confidence also grew because I was exposing myself to new people and social situations.

Towards the end of my junior year, I started to think about what I wanted to study in college. I decided that I wanted to study finance. The fast-paced and competitive environment of the major intrigued me. The same principles that helped me succeed in the gym, consistency, determination, and patience, will be very important as I navigate through a finance major. In addition, my newfound confidence will help me engage more in classroom activities, build strong connections with my peers and professors, and embrace any academic challenges I come across.

Looking back, that presentation wasn’t a failure but a turning point. Working out pushed me to take control of the things I felt most insecure about and develop confidence I never thought possible. Whether in the gym, the classroom, or my future career, I know how to approach challenges with determination and a focus on small, daily improvements. The discipline and perseverance I’ve gained from this journey will guide me as I take on challenges in college and beyond. As I prepare to major in finance, I’m committed to applying these principles to my academic journey, knowing that the consistent effort and self-discipline I’ve developed will help me succeed.

“I want to get out.”

Sarah visited my teen-focused online support platform, To-Listen, in early 2024. Sexually assaulted by her deskmate for three years in middle school, my young visitor was told by her mother that harassment was just “typical adolescent boy behavior.” She was molested, secretly followed, and forced against her will in ways I cannot put into words.

I knew the facts I needed to support Sarah—when dealing with trauma, Robert Salvin’s companionship theory indicated that I should be a passive listener, only to make attentive comments. But in the face of an act so unlawful and unjust, I couldn’t resist the urge to tell her that what happened wasn’t her fault, to do something beyond responding passively.

I had spent my entire adolescent life trying to get as close to the standard “textbook” answer in every examination I had taken at school. It gave me a sense of control and safety, knowing that every question had a “perfect” solution. Yet, in Sarah’s case, every textbook response seemed to fall short. I thought back to my middle school mental health classes, and how the case studies on the whiteboard encouraged sexual harassment victims to “seek support from others.” I gave the same encouragement to Sarah, but asking for support wasn’t an option for her. What the boy committed was stigmatized and dismissed by the conservative culture of her small Northern Chinese town as child play.

After five days of conversation, Sarah thanked me with a string of emojis. I had still followed theory, like not fixating on the specifics of the assault. But I also learned the complete lack of understanding Sarah received—and through laws, sexual assault recourses, and hugging emojis, I tried my best to be an unwavering affirmer that the fears and injustices she felt were completely justified. I knew what I contributed was insignificant compared to the severity of Sarah’s situation, but seeing her replies become longer and more confident, I still felt proud of myself.

I was also deeply humbled and discomforted, though. Sarah’s real-life story exposed the tremendous gap between the theories I had wholeheartedly followed my whole life and the complexities of reality. It also called into question the efficacy and legitimacy of the platform I had poured my heart into building for the past year.

In the next months, I started noticing hints of Sarah in every peer I met, each of their situations demanding an adaptive approach to support beyond the standard theoretical response. I was forced and inspired to modify the four-step “hello–affirm–support–listen” theoretical companionship template I had been using to train my team of companion-supporter volunteers, reintroducing it as an adaptable guideline instead of a fixed solution. The change was initially confusing and discomforting. But seeing STEM student volunteers like Leander’s initially formulaic, rigid responses slowly turn into genuine back-and-forth conversations filled my heart with warmth.

There were smaller steps, too. In interviews with Sam, a teen of GeLao ethnic minority from Inner Mongolia who was facing cyberbullying, I discovered how the culture there was more open to speaking up about personal struggles compared to Han culture, and how support could be more listening-focused as a result.

Of course, self-doubt still arises from time to time. My team are not licensed therapists. We are not even adults. But we try our best to listen, to offer a safe space of support and not advice, realizing that in a modern society that is advancing technologically but growing apart as humans, young adults may need not just medical or professional support but also companionship and community.

Every day, new questions and challenges inevitably arise in life. As a child, I believed the appropriate answer was the textbook solution, but today, I realize that life is too complex to hold a fixed answer. As I approach college and beyond, I commit to always bringing the adaptive spirit instilled in me by the peers I met and the stories I heard. From co-organizing a music festival for children with special needs using extra loudspeakers to pronounce their initially shy voices, to implementing a double point round in my Chinese Poker tournament when scores were close, I aspire to answer life’s challenges not by following the textbook solution but by rewriting it based on the unique context of the situation with nuance, compassion, and love.

My sister and I aggressively scramble the jade tiles while my angkong (grandpa) and ama (grandma) sit quietly, waiting for us to organize the game of mahjong. Each click-clack cut through the suffocating silence.

The notable absence of conversation and laughter was something I had been accustomed to growing up. Unfamiliar with my grandparent’s ancestral Lannang-ue, a spoken-only Filipino-Chinese dialect, I hid behind the comfort of my school-learned English. Our surface-level exchanges—restricted by my painfully limited vocabulary of ‘thank-you’s’ and ‘how-are-you’s’—isolated me from both my family and heritage.

Yet as the world grew quiet during the pandemic, the silence between us became more pronounced. Before long, I confronted the fact that the rapidly-diminishing usage of Lannang-ue had kept me from learning the language, turning me into a passive observer to its extinction.

Determined to bridge the gap between us, I filled the silences of our mahjong games with overflowing questions. When I asked my angkong about escaping Post-Revolution China, I learned about WW2’s far-reaching effects on Chinese families during 1940s Manila. Listening to my ama relaying their epic love story, I discovered the term ‘kai-shao,’ the practice of parents introducing their children to potential partners—a tradition that persists in many Filipino-Chinese households today.

The once distant figures sitting across the mahjong table transformed into my angkong and my ama—living embodiments of anecdotes and histories I was just beginning to understand.

Spurred by the outpouring of love and passion my grandparents expressed while sharing their stories, I began listening and engaging to the other voices within my local Lannang-ue community. While interviewing native speakers, from school-teachers to church members, I was instantly struck by their shared experiences witnessing Lannang-ue’s slow death, catalyzed by the academic prioritization of Mandarin and Western social media. Slowly, a new idea emerged: what if I built a web-based translator to revive the dialect?

In the summer of 2022, I started compiling thousands of frequently-used words to compose the translator's database. I then reached out to fluent-speaking relatives, recording them as they articulated the lists of words. I’d continue pestering them on weekends, couch surfing between my grandparent’s living room and my aunt’s single-roomed condominium.

Once I completed collecting the audio files, I noted their romanizations and established the rules for the standardized orthography to be displayed as the translator’s output. From my uncle's crisp, clear syllables to my ama's soft yet precise speech, each recording brought the words to life. Upon hearing the variety of accents and articulations, I realized how much I’d failed to appreciate the voices that raised me. Within silence was possibility, unique perspectives and stories left untold.

Leading a panel discussion at the Lannang-ue Symposium to present my translator, I was touched by the school principals’ gentle smiles and the tears in my parents’ eyes. Their support reminded me that sustainable transformations can only be made possible through collective effort and cooperation.

Over the three-day conference, instead of the usual suspects, I spoke with individuals that I’d idolized from a distance: John Chua, an aspiring filmmaker who explores the often-overlooked narratives of the Filipino-Chinese community and Theresa See, a prominent social-activist that has long worked for the social integration of the ethnic Chinese minority to mainstream Philippine society. The more I asked and listened, the more I realized that silence was nowhere to be found.

As we engaged in community discussions and grassroots activities on Lannang-ue dubbing in Filipino songs and traditional calligraphy, I learned that the impact of preserving a language goes beyond words: it fosters relations and safeguards identities, ensuring that no one’s story is forgotten.

My mission extends beyond merely filling and uncovering the voices beneath the silence. I aim to shatter that silence altogether by nurturing open dialogue and amplifying the marginalized. In a world where narratives are often stifled by indifference, I’ll cultivate an environment that empowers diverse voices to express their truths. No-matter-where-I-am,-or-who-I’m-with,-or-what-language-we-speak,-I-vow-that-the-world-I-live-in-will-never-fall-silent.

“[Name]! Pablo’s ready! Could you get the code ready for Thursday?”

“What? But it’s Tuesday!” I panicked. Pablo is the name of our robot. This would be at least a two-week job, and I had my schedule already packed.

“Gordon and Nicole just got the robot together. HKIS said the only day they can do is Friday, and they’re the only team willing to practice with us noobs,” Ryan, our captain, explained. “I’m sorry - we’ve been begging for school funding forever. The parts just came through last week..”

I sprinted to the lab, where a weary Gordon, his eye bags heavy with fatigue, passed me the robot and its hastily assembled engineering notebook. The only thing keeping me from completely freaking out was that I'd already roughed out most of the code without testing.

Leaning against a metal pole in the crowded subway crossing Hong Kong Island, I digested the sketches of half-baked claw designs mingled with illegible performance logs. I sketched out a rapid development timeline, allocating precise blocks for coding Pablo's autonomous functions and rigorous testing of each subsystem.

I sacrificed lunches to optimize the code, wolfed down snacks during compile times, and stayed in the lab until I heard the security guy’s bellows. On Thursday afternoon, surrounded by my team and coach, Pablo blazed through its final diagnostic routine.

Packing up for the next day’s match, Ryan shuffled over to me and gave me a fist bump. After the frenzied coding and testing marathons, the gaps in our knowledge sharing became obvious to me and the team. We overhauled our engineering notebook into a telegraph line between the teams, where everyone could access the status and decisions of the other teammates. No matter how tired we were, we concluded each day by adding our rationale, decisions, and reflections in the notebook.

At the Hong Kong tournament, our fledgling team clawed its way to the semifinals. We came home with a touch of dismay, but began contemplating how to improve for the new season. A week later, we discovered our engineering notebook—that tome of technical tears and triumphs—had charmed the judges into awarding us the Excellence Award.

As the new school year started, we soon noticed something interesting. The robotics lab was expanding, with upgraded workspace.

The 3D printer and a shiny new laser cutter in the upgraded workspace caught the eyes of my eight budding scientists from the new branch of my ethical hacking club – we are incorporating computers into physics and math. These tools had opened a world of possibilities for our team. When someone half-jokingly proposed building a submarine, initial laughter quickly gave way to serious consideration. We realized we could use these tools to create a submarine model as an educational prop for the physics lab, built entirely from scratch. This would help concretize many challenging physics concepts, demystifying topics that often intimidate some peers.

I swiftly developed an initial proposal and a feasible plan. I approached the principal with a request for $4,000 in funding, which she found our proposal reasonable and promptly approved. Of course, I created a space on GitHub where each of us could contribute, adding our rationale, decisions, and reflections to the project notebook, just like the engineering notebook of the robotics team.

Just two years ago, we had barely managed to scrape together eight engineers for our robotics team from a school of future doctors and lawyers. However, this year, the robotics team became the most sought-after club, with 80 students applying for just 20 spots in the tryouts. I knew they would, like me, experience the exhilaration of transforming a concept into tangible reality after overcoming numerous challenges and uncertainties.

Rather than fixating on these unknowns, we're anchoring ourselves to what we can control. Our engineering notebook, once a mundane requirement, has evolved into a key success factor. By focusing on the tangible 'doing' - prototyping, testing, refining - we're laying a robust foundation. This methodical approach, honed during our robotics seasons, is our compass. It may not guarantee immediate success, but it's steering us toward long-term growth and innovation, both in college and beyond.

And building that, I'd say, is more important than any machine.

“It’s my win,” he triumphed. For someone who didn’t speak English just two months ago, I was surprised at my grandpa’s growing level of skill. Trailing behind by 150 points in our final game, I made one last ditch effort. “Karyotype! That’s 71 points for me!”

At the beginning of June, I had decided to teach my grandpa English to overcome our language barrier. Starting with my personal favorites, we watched films like No Country for Old Men and Inside Out. We then tried workbooks, but I could not speak Korean well enough to teach English, and in my opinion, it was too boring. After 2 weeks of trial and error in my lessons, Scrabble became our game of choice. Unfortunately, he had never even heard of Scrabble.

After researching for a weekend on Youtube and scouring countless Reddit posts, I came up with our own, personalized version of Scrabble. I created a list of 100 words, our own Scrabble dictionary, each translated so grandpa could understand. Then, I spent one weekend repurposing wood chips to substitute as blank tiles, creating new tiles with each of the words from my list. Finally, using the old, checkered dining table as our board, we could begin playing.

Playing one game after dinner became our nightly ritual. In our first game, I won by more than 200 points. Feeling confident, we went into the next game. This time, with a little more focus and effort required, I won by 150 points. After this cycle continued for a few weeks, he was beating me by 100 points each game. Aiming to not get outdone, I also began to improve, listening to Scrabble tips on my drive to school, playing games on Scrabble.com in my freetime, and playing with friends and family. Where I taught my grandfather English and board games, he taught me community and risk-taking.

Surprisingly, you can learn a lot about a person from Scrabble. When I tutored students in Korean and Math, Scrabble became my signature method of introduction. The awkward silence of a first meeting soon becomes filled with frustration and laughter as we’d argue if words like “Qanat” were real or if “Zwieback” was really 78 points. In our games, we challenged more words than a skeptic in a debate (where we would need a Google search to stop arguing). Even as a shy, introverted person, I began to look forward to meeting more people.

Community doesn’t always look like big gatherings or grand gestures, it can look like two people, huddled over a board game, slowly learning how to understand one another. From each game, I’ve also realized that while a connection to my community requires communication, true interconnectedness also requires empathy, inquiry, and a little bit of strategy. Whether I’m mentoring younger students in Korean and English, or slicing cross sections of samples in my research, I’ve used my realizations throughout my life.

While I didn’t notice at first, each game was a small way of opening up to each other and learning to embrace failure. Like the risky words I would use in Scrabble, I’ve also started to pursue other risks in my life, like trying to learn how to play the piano to play music at our next family gathering, or running every morning in the hopes of completing a marathon in the future (Boston Marathon, here I come!). While we don’t continue our nightly games anymore, we both learned more than words on a board—we shared stories, laughs, frustrations, and eventually, our wins. We weren’t just two people playing a game anymore, we were two people building a community that I continue to share.

I’ve wondered why Scrabble has become so important to me, who once saw it as a challenge to find meaning in every word I played, and I think I’ve found it: To find connections, one letter at a time.

There I was, my hand hovering over the table, my heart pounding, and my mind racing through each possibility.

It’s over, I thought, already imagining Kevin pouncing on the material and time advantages I had handed him. As he took my knight with his pawn, I found myself admitting, “I resign,” and shaking his hand. After the game, Kevin moved my queen to H5 and pointed out a counterplay he had been worried about. I shook my head, realizing I had been so fixated on taking back a useless pawn that I had overlooked other opportunities to counterattack.

I asked if we could continue the game for fun, and he agreed. We resumed our battle as if I hadn’t prematurely resigned. I played more boldly, freed from worrying about possible consequences. Move by move, I squeezed him, patiently waiting for him to slip up as he defended. It wasn’t long before he blundered a piece, and I swiftly finished the game. I left that day feeling a surprising sense of satisfaction, even though I had officially lost.

Instead of walking away frustrated, I felt compelled to ask my opponent to review the game—an opportunity to uncover strategies I had missed and grow from my mistakes. I joined the local chess club, Chaturanga, a diverse group with members ranging from 1st graders to 85-year-olds. The club met in a cozy church, where warm wood-paneled floors echoed with quiet conversations and the soft clatter of chess pieces. During their weekly tournaments, I embraced my new practice of reviewing games with my opponents, which brought me closer to everyone, especially Kevin. Our similar ratings often had us playing against each other in most tournaments, and we became frenemies, both eyeing the $100 cash prize at each event. One time in the final round, we agreed to open with the worst two moves: h4 and h5, challenging ourselves to adapt to this terrible position.

Setting aside our rivalry, I brought together Kevin and two of my school friends to form a team for the 9-12 state tournament. Afterward, we donated the trophy to Chaturunga, where it inspired younger kids to form their own team for the next state tournament. To help them prepare, I encouraged them to arrive 30 minutes early for our weekly tournaments, where Kevin and I reviewed their games from the previous week. The week before the state tournament, we held a bughouse match, where teammates could give each other pieces to place anywhere on the board. Kevin teamed up with two of the kids against me and the other two kids, creating balanced teams. I remember laughing and yelling at my teammates to get me a knight while they yelled back that they were about to get checkmated. Their state tournament went exceptionally well; they took first place. Each time I walked through the K-6 section after my game ended, I smiled with pride seeing my fellow Chaturangans win and felt especially glad to see them continue coming early each week.

Reflecting on my chess journey, I realize that time around the game has deepened my appreciation for it, reducing stress over outcomes and improving my skills. I have adopted this perspective in my various pursuits in and out of school, from tennis and cultural clubs to biology class. I thrive on the diversity of my schedule, much like the vibrant Chaturanga chess club. Whether playing the deciding match for our tennis team, organizing a fundraiser to sell 300 onigiri, or exploring the Krebs cycle, I focus on enjoying the activity rather than the results. Just as every piece in chess plays a role and collaboration of the pieces is essential to strategy, working with others beyond the chessboard—learning from and teaching them—enhances my experience in my endeavors.

When you think it’s the end, that’s the perfect time to counterattack.

The show started late, but my adrenaline made it feel like the day had just begun. Sitting in the front row, I was pulled to the edge of my seat as Nasheet Waits, a renowned jazz drummer, performed with his trio of famed artists. It was an eye-opening experience to see so closely how such accomplished musicians collaborate, spontaneously coming up with new ideas. The longer I watched, the more questions I had, and once the show ended, I saw the chance to approach him. I asked Mr. Waits why he works with the particular musicians in his ensemble, and he replied “They always show me more than I could see myself.”

At first, music didn't make me think. It was like reading a textbook without analyzing the information, rather than just skimming the words. I could play Chopin and Bach, but that’s all I saw music for—an experience for the individual. Once satisfied with how I played a piece, it was time to move to the next. After all, what could my young self have to say about creating art?

Consequently, I didn’t truly enjoy playing my instrument, and instead saw piano lessons as a chore forced by my parents. My ears felt fatigued from hearing the same piece being practiced repeatedly. Just when I thought it was time to drop Beethoven and pick up basketball, my perspective was changed.

Enrolling into a performing arts high school, I became close friends with a trumpet player, Victor, a grade above. We frequently spent time in and out of school playing jazz with older musicians, learning from their relatable experiences. Furthermore, It was the first time my mind began to think critically about music, and I felt a new drive to pursue it. Together, our joy for jazz was ignited and we began looking for more opportunities to grow. As we got older, Victor started a music club that gave free assistance to young students, so we traveled weekly to the local public middle school. In the beginning, it was easy to get lost in the cacophony of instruments, and hard to have great patience with so many energetic kids. However, as we returned every week, I felt that I had gained a greater understanding of how to guide the students. I shared my enthusiasm for music in a format that they enjoyed, and through this I learned not only how to be a better teacher but a better musician as well. This was the next step, I thought, as I continued to find comfort in a routine of creating music with my friends. However, life moved on, and so did my closest friends as they entered college.

I felt left behind, as the music’s vibrant color had gone. Nonetheless, I was given new opportunities such as leading the club Victor had once started and sought to put my effort into something beyond personal musical pursuits. As a president, I searched for ways to expand the club’s reach, finding other schools requesting assistance. I formed new relationships and encouraged others to join and help out these public institutions. My interest in music grew back, but not how I expected it to. What I once saw as setbacks were only moments that challenged how I felt, giving me a greater perspective.

I now realize that what helped me rediscover my joy for music was not my persistence to keep practicing, but the feelings of satisfaction in leading initiatives I am passionate about. Teaching people from different backgrounds across the 4th largest city in the U.S. has taught me the importance of being mindful and inspired by various ways of thinking. I am excited to keep pursuing music as I take the next step into college, but I see that the interactions I encounter with people across the world help me reach my long-term goals in the future.

I was ready.

Ready to Stargaze with my brand new pair of HD military-grade binoculars. I had arrived at the Connecticut Star Party, a gathering of astronomers from all over America, nestled in the hills of rural Connecticut. I imagined myself impressing everyone with my gear. But as I pulled into the campground—a vast meadow resting on the peak of a hill—I froze. Before me stretched a sea of telescopes which dwarfed my binoculars in every way. Some telescopes were over nine feet tall, some were complex computerized systems. Suddenly, my binoculars didn’t seem so impressive. I felt insignificant, like a small particle, barely noticed in the vastness of space.

The campers gathered in the dining hall to hear a lecture, but my mind was elsewhere. The astronomical jargon floated past me; all I could focus on was the upcoming raffle. The prizes ranged from shirts and hats to the grand prize of a SkyQuest XT6 Telescope. I barely heard the smaller prizes being given away. My hands were slick with sweat as the tension mounted with every draw. My heart was thumping just like I was back at the starting line of a varsity cross-country race. I jittered nervously as the host dug his hand into the ticket jar, with my fate within his grasp. At that moment, that telescope was all I ever wanted.

And then—it happened. My number was called. I had won!

While I relished the euphoria of winning the raffle, I soon realized that my emotions were rather mixed. Even though I got what I wished for, I hadn’t anticipated that it would come with a sixty-page operating manual, and an unexpectedly complex set-up process. I gathered the courage to ask for help from the other experienced astronomers, and slowly we worked to assemble every piece and focus every lens. When I just asked for help, the astronomers were eager to lend a helping hand. Mr. Jeff from NJ gave me a Barlow lens that had an increased magnification. And Mr. Mark from MA helped me see the Andromeda galaxy for the first time! A few others encouraged me to join the Westport Astronomical Society(WAS). Thanks to WAS, I got the opportunity to connect with astronomy professors and NASA researchers. Through these connections, I started a research position with data analysis on asteroid occultations. I thought the telescope would only give me a better view of the stars, but it opened a universe of new opportunities.

Once a shy kid, I was caught up in my own world of stargazing, but the telescopic moment changed all that. At school, I hosted public stargazing nights bringing out everyone’s love for astronomy. People of differing interest levels had the opportunity to view the wonders of the night sky. The sparkle in their eyes after seeing Saturn and its rings for the first time made all my efforts worth it. Our school’s astronomy club became a melting pot of space nerds, thanks to my telescopic moment. People in my school looked forward to my monthly write-ups on astronomical events. Even during the bone-chilling nights of December, my school showed up for my “S’mores & Showers Night” where we watched the Geminids meteor shower decorate the sky. Working with astronomers and engaging with the wider community on many events made me more outgoing and socially active.

In retrospect, that cold night on top of the mountains changed the mere hobby of a freshman into a deeper connection to his purpose in space. Just like a nebula birthing new stars, it opened up the stars inside me. Now, I continue to look out for stars inside myself and in others. Just like me, everyone just needs their telescopic moment to find their own north star. At the end of the day, we are nothing but space dust, trying to find our way back to the stars. I am no different.

As I stepped through the doorway of my home, the frigid reality struck me like a gust of winter air: my mother may never walk again. Diagnosed with Cauda Equina Syndrome, a condition brought on by years of stress as a dedicated teacher, my mom had emergency surgery, casting a shadow over our family. Her once vibrant presence was now confined to the limitations of her surgery, unable to lift anything heavier than five pounds and relearning to walk. Our home, once bustling with energy, now moved to a slower rhythm, as we adjusted to a routine defined by patience and perseverance.

With the once-familiar rhythm of life seemingly lost, I took on new responsibilities with my mom such as cooking. Each shared moment in the kitchen became a stepping stone out of our slumps, as conversations grew from silence to solace. In these exchanges, I discovered resilience in vulnerability and strength in connection. Through our stronger bond, I realized that life, although altered, would persist with grace and empathy.

As my mom and I navigated these challenges, I found myself deeply grateful for the compassion that formed the bedrock of our resilience. This gratitude sparked curiosity about how compassion extends beyond personal relationships into the wider world. I first thought of nonprofits as the embodiment of this human instinct to support one another. Intrigued by how these organizations operate on donations while driving change, I joined the Teen Philanthropy Initiative (TPI). Through TPI, I learned about the economics and business models of nonprofits, gaining insight into how they balance financial stability with their mission to help others.

Through TPI, I gained a deeper appreciation for how nonprofits can channel compassion into tangible support for communities. Participating in TPI offered me a unique opportunity to connect theory with practice. As part of the program, we had to interview nonprofits that had applied for grants. Reflecting on my own mental health struggles with my mom’s surgery, I chose to interview NAMI Dupage, a nonprofit focused on mental health advocacy. Visiting their facility for an onsite interview, I was introduced to their Teen Talk program, which offers teens a safe space to talk to other teens and share challenges and stressors. This initiative mirrored the essence of the compassionate conversations I valued at home. The connection between my personal journey and NAMI Dupage’s mission fueled my desire to advocate for their cause, recognizing the transformative power of compassionate support both in personal and community settings.

Through my involvement with NAMI Dupage, I saw firsthand the profound impact of their Teen Talk program and was determined to support their mission. Utilizing the skills I gained from TPI, I took on the challenge of securing a grant to further their efforts. After thorough research and preparation, I successfully advocated for NAMI Dupage, securing a $750 grant to help expand their resources.

The culmination of this effort was the capstone ceremony, where I had the opportunity to present the grant. Standing before the mayor and community leaders, I delivered a speech that conveyed not only statistics but also the stories of lives changed by NAMI Dupage's work. It was a moment of immense pride and accomplishment, knowing that my advocacy could contribute to such meaningful change. This experience reinforced my belief in the power of community support and the impact of dedicated advocacy.

Reflecting on this journey, the shock of my mom’s condition transformed into an understanding of community service. What began as a personal challenge catalyzed my growth, teaching me the impact of empathy and service. The once daunting silence gave way to a symphony of support within my family and through my work with TPI and NAMI. Today, as I stand on the threshold of new beginnings, I am reminded of that first realization at our doorway—a journey not of isolation, but of collective empowerment, where love and resilience shape each step forward.

Ctrl-C + Ctrl-V: copying and pasting the success of others into my life’s goals.
Esc: escaping from my problems.
Ctrl-Z: undo.
My life can be described with keyboard shortcuts.

Amidst quarantine year, I created a blog named Ctrl-Z. Blogging became my outlet – from an improvised Python probability game to my high school goals, I would share my passions, aspirations, and frustrations. Initially a name harboring no significance, Ctrl-Z is now suffused with personal meaning.

Growing up as the only child of an immigrant household, I was constantly compared. I gave up easily – When I got hurt trying my first serve, I quit tennis. After my hands froze over the keys during a recital, I quit piano. Hoping to surpass expectations through talent, I gave up my passions. I feared failure.

At first, coding was the same – when my code flashed a syntax error, I X’d out of the window. Frustrated, I powered the computer off. But that night, as I tried to sleep, I couldn’t stop thinking about Lightbot, the robot I had programmed to solve a maze. Why couldn’t it reach the exit? I rose from my bed. Though it pained me to see the error, I scanned my code furtively. There! A misplaced semicolon. With a couple keystrokes, Lightbot moved. The next time Lightbot got stuck, I only felt mild confusion before returning to my code. Exploring Python, C, and countless data structures years later, I encountered bugs of all kinds. From mistakenly using reference copies while simulating Minesweeper to incurring infinite recursion in graph traversal, or having the wrong algorithm, I pushed through discomfort.
