Slowly, instead of frustration, I found enjoyment in debugging.

The most frustrating error I’ve encountered took three days to fix. My junior year, as I watched classmates stress over our Calculus BC midterm due to a lack of review material, I had the idea to create an AI-powered calculus question generator. I dreamed of bringing my app to my school and perhaps the entire district. Instead, I watched in horror as the AI spit out gibberish, cryptic JSON files and old Latin texts flooding my app. In search of a solution, I pored over countless lines of code with just my desk lamp and a monster energy, scouring StackOverflow and Youtube late into the AMs. Just when it seemed there was no hope for my app, I found an error in the AI configuration. The app wasn’t perfect, but as I watched my classmates use it to study integration the next day, I was proud. From my odd idea, I had created something my friends could appreciate.

My change of mindset helps me empathize with peers who fear failure as I used to. During my time at Governor’s School, I was given further perspective on overcoming fear. Through shared love of music, I made a good friend, Nam, just a year younger than me.

“I don’t get these proofs,” he sighed. “I was never really good at math… why did I choose this class?”

Suddenly, I was reminded of how I had felt the same. Undertaking the role of mentor, I helped him practice proofs late into the night, watching concepts solidify in his mind. Before Nam presented his final project on the fourth dimension, he smiled.

“I’m glad I chose math."

As his words echoed in my mind, I came to a realization. We had formed a connection, from the nights we sang karaoke to Flowers In May and each painstaking proof. I had assumed that the fear of failure was mine only, but it connects me to others.

Once, I dreamt of a life without challenges. Now, I look forward to every single one. Once, I bristled at a small error preventing my robot from moving. Now, I love late nights debugging complex algorithms.

Once, Ctrl-Z represented my desire to undo failure. Now, it is a story of growth.

Each mile back to Rhode Island stretched longer than the last, the landscape blurring past the droning bus window. Tired and dejected, I pondered what I was going to do now. We were shockingly knocked out of the USA Hockey Nationals in the first round, although we were a favorite to win.

I left home when I was 15 to pursue a dream of earning an NCAA D1 hockey scholarship. In my junior year of high school, I was on a partial scholarship living in a small dorm room with three other teammates. For the past seven months, we woke up at 6:00 a.m. to train and go to classes. After the school day ended at 2:00 p.m., we were on the ice for two hours of practice, then in the weight room at 4:00 p.m. We had film reviews at 5:00 p.m., concluding each day with evening study hall and lights out at 10:00 pm. Now, abruptly my season was over. What could I do for the remainder of the school year to fill all that previously occupied time?

I discussed the issue with some of my teammates. At first, we offered profound suggestions, like buying a thrift shop couch to watch TV or play more baseball. I suggested that we could teach the local kids how to skate. At first, my friends laughed it off, but I insisted it could be fun. After a little convincing, we started brainstorming.

The first hurdle was getting the rink to give us an ice slot. Cost was a significant issue, depending on the time, a one-hour ice slot could cost $500-700 dollars. I met with the rink manager and he gave us ice three times a week for May. The next obstacle was equipment but after rummaging through forgotten storage rooms and some donations we had an assortment of skates and helmets.

We already had a relationship mentoring kids from the community elementary school. I contacted the principal, who was receptive to our initiative. We developed a plan to incorporate our learn to skate class in their after-school program. We quickly had twenty young kids sign up. The next challenge was convincing the parents to let their kids participate in a program run by 16-year-olds.

We entered the rink with nervous excitement on the first day. I wish I could say that the day was a smashing success. While I had anticipated that they would have trouble staying up on the ice, it surprised me when they had trouble just walking in skates. As the month progressed, I could see the kids become more and more confident on the ice.

Seeing the joy on the kids’ faces skating for the first time was rewarding. The skill that I had spent years of my life working on, I could finally help others begin to learn. Several of the kids compared the experience of being on skates to learning how to swim or how to ride a bike, initially difficult and scary, but then liberating. At the time, the experience felt like a success. We created a win-win situation. We filled our free time productively helping others and had fun.

It wasn’t until I left school senior year to play Junior Hockey that I realized how special it was that we taught those twenty kids how to ice skate. My friends and I were from across the United States and four countries, and we are now widely dispersed, but for that brief period in that old rink in Rhode Island, we were together creating a positive impact. The disappointment of the loss was outweighed by the feeling of helping other people. This experience taught me how we can teach and help others in our community. Rather than just being focused on achieving things independently, I want to share my skills and experiences with others.

Arriving in Macau from Taipa Ferry Terminal, I am welcomed in two of the official languages of Macau: Portuguese and Chinese, an odd mix unique to Macau. The recoil of the ferry docking urges me to wrap up my diary entry detailing the snippets of Portuguese I’ve learned—“saída” for exit, “chegadas” for arrival, and “terminal” for terminal. I sign off with my cursive signature, “frank”.

My name always felt jarring to me. I’ve grown accustomed to dropping the tones of my Chinese last name to ease the juxtaposition of the second-tone “Wáng” with the flat uniformity of “[Name].” Consequently, the signature that I’ve adopted always felt off, retaining only my English identity. My thoughts followed me as I hastily closed my diary, hurrying off the ferry.

To the casual tourist, Macau is “the Las Vegas of the east,” “small Portugal,” or “land of egg-tarts.” To me, it was a linguistic wonderland. Beyond all the luxury and glamour of the casinos lies a historical enclave unveiling the nuclear fusion of a cultural exchange that has taken place there. As such, I was there on a mission to learn more about the languages born from this cultural exchange but also to reconcile my internal cultural clashes.

Typed into Google translate, “Amochâi” yields no results. Yet, Amochâi is both an affectionate greeting and a loving moniker—“darling” would be its counterpart in English. To the meticulously attentive speaker of both Portuguese and Cantonese, that explanation is enough to elicit an “Oh!” “Amochâi” derives from the Portuguese word for love, “amor”, and the Cantonese suffix for a loved one, 仔, pronounced zái.

Imagine my pleasant surprise when finding out that the linguistic marvel born out of the subtle synthesis of culture that is “Amochâi” was not an individual occurrence. In fact, there is an entire collection of words like it that constitutes Macanese Patois, or Patuá, a creole formed from the interaction of speakers of languages as distinct as Portuguese and Cantonese in the melting pot that is Macau.

During my two days in Macau, the pages of my diary filled up, absorbing all that I’ve learned. Regrettably, I did not experience the Macau Literary Festival in Patuá, watch a play in Patuá by a Macanese theater group, or see the Patuá exhibit at the University of Macau.

Despite my setback, I was not one to give up on a mission. My diary bears the mark of fervent research and insatiable curiosity. Questions about how language contact forms creoles, how morphosyntactic structures preserve and change through language evolution, and the relationship between language and personal identity guided my way forward, bringing me to interact with linguistics professors, watch online courses, and conduct research of my own. Above all, Patuá showed me that in a multicultural world, the extraordinary is found in the mixing of identities, cultures, and languages.

I see myself finishing the mission I’ve started, back on the streets of Macau in the future, but as a linguist, there to study and preserve the beauty of Patuá. But for now, it is my signature and identity that has witnessed a subtle Patuá-induced change.

Behold my evolving map of the self, a testimony to embracing openness, a reconciliation of different cultures:

It starts with a graceful sweep of the pen, looping up and down, to create an “f” in equilibrium, sleek in shape but strong in disposition. The pen then levels off, delineating the rest of my name with the loops and curls of “…rank.” Then, with a sudden speed, the “tail” of the “k” rises up as another character begins to take shape. Two crescents with the sharpest of angles trace out the Chinese character for my last name, “王” in cursive, ending in a sleek horizontal line. In one smooth, fluid pen motion, twirling and dancing on the paper, the trail of ink paints out me, in all my juxtaposed glory.

The sharp crack of the ping-pong ball rang out like a starter’s pistol. It ricocheted across the table, barely skimming the edge before flying past my paddle, its faded red rubber slick with sweat and worn from countless matches. I lunged, but my seventy-year-old opponent had already moved on to the next serve. Sweat dripped down my forehead as I wiped it away with the back of my hand, trying to regain my composure. This wasn’t going as I had imagined.

When I first walked into the community center, I imagined ping-pong would be an easy way to meet new people, maybe even impress a few with my quick reflexes. At 14, I was competitive and brimming with confidence—perhaps too much. After all, how hard could it be to play against seniors in their sixties and seventies? Yet, there I was, gasping for breath, completely outplayed by players who treated ping-pong with the precision of a serious sport. My ego, however, hadn’t signed up for this reality check.

My opponent, Mr. Liu, adjusted his stance, paddle at the ready. He wasn’t playing just to pass the time—this was his domain, and every movement he made was deliberate. I couldn’t help but admire the way he positioned himself, the way he seemed to predict my moves before I even thought of them. Meanwhile, I was all energy and no finesse, flailing around the table like I was trying to swat a fly.

Another serve, another miss. The ball zipped past me before I even realised what had happened. I glanced over at the crowd—a few older men who had gathered to watch—and noticed their barely hidden smiles. Instead of feeling embarrassed, I found myself laughing inside. Everyone starts somewhere, right?

There was something humbling, almost meditative, about returning to the table each time, knowing I’d likely lose, but still wanting to get better. Mr. Liu wasn’t showing me any mercy, and oddly enough, I appreciated that. Every game threw something different at me, and each time I missed, I picked up on something new about how I was playing or what I needed to change. Maybe my grip was too rigid, or perhaps I wasn’t adjusting properly to the spin on the ball, causing my returns to go off target. But the more I played, the more I realised it wasn’t just about getting better at ping-pong—I was learning patience with every tricky shot, adapting to faster opponents, and celebrating even the smallest improvements.

As I returned to the table day after day, I no longer chased the ball in a flurry of reflexes. I began to sense the rhythm of the game—the way the ball curved with each spin, the way the paddle felt as I controlled the angle. I learned to anticipate its trajectory, reading the subtle shifts in my opponent’s movements. My feet glided with intention, carrying me effortlessly into place, as if I was in sync with the flow of the game. The frustration that once clouded my focus disappeared, replaced by a calm precision.

I still lost more often than I won, but the small victories became sweeter. I’d land a tricky shot here and there, and Mr. Liu would raise his eyebrows, impressed. One day, I won a single point off Mr. Liu’s famous backhand. It was a fleeting victory, but it symbolized so much more. Just one point, yet it felt like a quiet triumph, one that only I could fully appreciate.

With each game, the small victories grew more meaningful. The lessons I learned—patience, resilience, and adaptability—extended beyond ping-pong. Whether facing challenges in academics, relationships, or personal growth, I approach them like those matches: aware I might stumble, but embracing the chance to learn and improve. That mindset has shaped who I strive to be, and it's what I hope to bring to a college campus.

“ARE YOU A GIRL?”, Ishansh asked as I exited the painting classroom. It was not the first time I was faced with this question and it wouldn't be the last, as I was the only boy who had chosen to study the humanities in our school. This path is considered ‘inappropriate’ for boys in Indian society. Many male students thought that I was ‘insane,’ but I persisted with my choice. I see this choice as an opportunity to be an example for future male students and break the irrational societal norm–boys are ‘born’ for STEM.

It feels rewarding to study with my new (girl)friends, and political science, which not only opened me to John Locke’s idea of Tabula Rasa, Immanuel Kant’s Theory of Human Dignity, John Rawls’ Theory of Justice, etc. but also but also transformed me into a leader from classroom discussions to the entire school. It was a novel social shift, and I adapted to this new environment by forming new bonds.

This choice not only reshaped my academic path but also enabled me to connect deeply with my peers. Every Friday night and weekend (SPOILER ALERT! No parties are on the agenda), I would organise group calls on WhatsApp for my friends to help them clear their last-moment doubts before our test days on Mondays. With a book in hand and a phone in the other, I became their pseudo-teacher for political science, psychology, and economics, and answered their every question. These group calls made me confident and solidified my knowledge. And most importantly each time I saw my friends’ confidence grow, I realised that helping them succeed brought me just as much fulfilment as my own achievements.

After a long day of studying and games, at night, I have a habit of deep introspection. As I lie in bed cocooned in a blanket, my mind fills with thoughts, replaying the day's events. I silently question my actions, reflecting on what I did right or how I could have handled situations better. Because of these beautiful introspective nights, some of the embarrassing moments of my childhood are still kept alive in my memory, and I keep on learning from my past mistakes.

As I study political science, I want to explore the relevance of political theories in the contemporary world and the role played by political institutions in modernising society, while forming timeless bonds at college that I, and most importantly, my future friends will remember throughout their lives. Reflecting on my journey, I’ve learned the importance of following my own path and in college I want to help others along theirs. Through introspection I have learned the importance of critical thinking, and I hope to instil courage and confidence in my friends using my experience as a tutor. I aspire to leverage my U.S. education to bring meaningful reforms to my home country where they are truly needed. That’s the kind of person I hope to be.

My dad came home that day at 3 a.m., reeking of alcohol, the smell so suffocating it felt like it seeped into the very walls. It was a visceral reaction, a learned defense against the chaos that accompanied it. I could hear him stumbling through the house, as I left him behind the wooden door of my room. Slamming was too risky, so I let it hover just enough for the latch to almost click, before it made a sound. Headphones charged, music queued — I turned to dance. Athletics never came naturally to me. Ball sports, in particular, were a cruel joke thanks to my poor coordination, but dance was different. Dance became my rebellion. I cranked the volume to its max, letting the notes pour down my ears into my limbs. Each beat was a rebellion, as the rhythm coursed through my movements out of anguish, joy, and pain.

That room door might’ve been tightly shut, but my dad’s presence was always lurking somewhere just beyond it, although he was hardly ever home. On the rare occasions I saw him, I had to deal with his overworked rage, the rage from the burden of being a husband, an only son, and a father. His anger was unpredictable; it was never the same thing that set him off, whether I forgot to pull down the curtains to keep the so-called “perverted old men” watching me from ten stories below or if I didn’t wake up at 5 a.m. to greet him with a precise ninety-degree bow before he left for work every day.

There seemed to be a missing connection -- the type of connection my friends had when they spent weekends with both their parents, while I stayed behind with a parent. They’d return to school bubbling over with stories about family dinners where their parents bickered over the best recipe or the yearly family camping trips during the break.

I only understood its meaning through the nights I spent dancing alone in my bedroom. Dancing had become an oddly comforting escape for me, yet it carried a bittersweet weight that I couldn’t quite shake off. I often find myself wondering why chaos seems to be woven into the very fabric of my life, why I must carve out moments of joy within the confines of a stifling space.

I may not have been the best dancer, but I had learned to wipe my tears and appreciate the value in each unique movement. The same sense of understanding deepened as I began teaching dance to the orphans at the local child center. These children had already endured more hardship in their young lives than anyone had, and many of them carried weights of life most couldn’t relate to. But in the studio, there were no labels like "orphan" or "abandoned” -- there were only dancers. My experience of growing up alone single-handedly by my mom became the reason I saw pieces of myself in them.

As I stood before those eager faces, I was reminded that true strength does not lie in perfect execution but rather in the ability to envision the possibilities each movement holds for the future. Amid the beauty of growth lies the reality of lessons learned through adversity, and I learned how to mend my mom’s tears even before mine and stand up for her in the same situation. Each misstep carries a lesson, and I embrace these lessons as opportunities for positivity and growth.

There’s something potently ordinary about tragedy. In my case, the 13.8mm disc was especially monotonous.

After I’d squinted at one sign too many or lost sight of yet another golf ball, my parents dragged me to the optician. The verdict? I needed contacts. Suddenly I began to regret going—perhaps ignorance really was bliss when it came to eyesight. Since I had never even been able to put in eye-drops, I blurted, ‘I can’t wear these.’ ‘Nonsense’, he said, ‘everyone can.’

Back home, I set to work, in an anxious flurry. Contacts ended up everywhere except where they should—from the sink to my shirt. If I could not hold my eyelid open, was my existence merely predetermined? Inability to subdue my subconscious reflex flew in the face of all my conceptions of meritocracy—I was not, in fact, getting out what I was putting in, although I suppose I wasn’t even putting them in, in the first place. I had always been coordinated: why were my neurons failing me now? The petty convictions that had so far buoyed me along with relative ease had instantaneously vanished. No longer would my single knotted laces stay tied, or my socks always find their match. My confidence had hung on such trivialities; without them, I felt monstrous.

These contacts had demeaned me, without even looking me in the eye—not least because I couldn’t really see. Yet, I began to feel emboldened—only a full-scale mobilisation could remedy my pride and my vision. My concurrent reading of Bonhoeffer, claiming that God’s will is only visible in the moment of action, only heightened my impulses.

Drafting all my resources—a bottle of anti-bac, my father’s finest shaving mirror, and my father himself—I stepped up to the mirror for my moment of reckoning.

On only the second try, the contacts just slipped in. Although I had no idea how to get them out, I ran around the house in clear-sighted victory.

With my -0.75 prescription, I was transformed into a visionary—not just in the sense of seeing street signs more clearly. I became a self-ordained St. Paul of Contacts. My letter to the Romans came in the form of ineedhelputtinginmycontacts.co.uk.

At school, my friend Timothy was complaining that he had lost his glasses and couldn’t see from the back of the class. ‘Why don’t you just wear contacts?’ I asked smugly. The suggestion alone seemed to dissolve him into an anxious heap. Seeing this, I began to relive my own traumatic memories. Yet, I suddenly saw it all through a different lens, one that underscored a broader, lifelong pattern of hesitation, instilled by a fear of failure, which had deprived me of that carefree daring I craved. From not asking that carefully formulated question to the Philippines ambassador to never trying Brussels sprouts, I saw a string of opportunities missed through sheer avoidance. No more! Beating the contacts had, symbolically, broken this cycle: I was a new man.

With apostolic confidence, I messaged Timothy ‘fear not’, along with a link to the website which housed my greatest tips and countless YouTube tutorials. Next day, I brought in a pack of contacts, and we got to work. Admittedly, my zeal may not have had the backing of the Holy Spirit, as there was a fair bit of struggling, and I spent rather a long time shining my phone torch in his eye to see if they were actually in. Soon enough, however, his fears evaporated, much like mine. My first disciple.

Experiencing our success prompted me to try more things—milk before the cereal, then public speaking—in a series of trials against my timidity. Success or failure, I began to see clearly, both literally and in life, discovering myself anew by challenging my (often illogical) limits. As people from around the world view the website every day, they’re giving me confidence that failure is not so tragic after all.

2014. A decade ago, I left everything – my home, my friends, my family – to study in Singapore. It was a new start for me. And also a new beginning for my grandpa.

At first, it was little things – forgetting where he placed his glasses or the details of our address. The day I left, he insisted on coming to the airport. I can still picture him with those loving eyes at the departure door. He hugged me tightly and said, "Study hard, my girl, and go make a real difference in this world."

Looking back, I realize how heavy those words truly were. I didn’t see it then, the way he repeated his goodbye just way too many times. All I knew was I must not disappoint him, just as he had always believed I would. As I flew off, the man who meant everything to me began to forget my departure, then my voice, and soon enough...

“Who are you?”

became our conversation starter every time I called. A question that stung more each time I heard it. I would force a smile, trying to blink away the tears, not wanting him to feel my pain and gently remind him,

“It’s me, Yeye. It’s your granddaughter.”

There’s this sharp pang of guilt, like a wound that never heals. I wonder if I had stayed, would dementia have never taken him from me like this? Could I have made more memories with him so it would take longer for him to forget everything? These thoughts have haunted me for years, replaying in my mind over and over.

As I grow older, this pain has driven me to channel that love into the way I interact with the world, as I constantly strive to carry the weight of his hopes with me – be that agent of change.

I commit myself to serving the overlooked and giving a voice to the forgotten. I feel the sense of mission on me, one that pushes me to effect real changes. Whether I am spending time with the elderly, tutoring children with incarcerated parents, or working with people with intellectual disabilities (PWIDs), I carry that same love, empathy, and gratitude he taught me since I was a kid.

This conviction, especially when it comes to PWIDs, drives me even further. While society often defines them by their limitations, I see their capacity to love, to laugh, and to experience the world differently. As such, I founded my own multinational community project, "Project Little Heroes," serving PWIDs in both Singapore and Malaysia.

I envisioned a platform where cooperation could thrive, organizations could learn from one another, and benefit from shared experiences. There were moments when plans fell through, but I persevered, determined to make this a success and deliver tangible improvements. At 19, I led the team in building long-lasting partnerships that no one had thought possible.

This is just a start, I told myself. I want to change the existing narrative surrounding PWIDs. Drawing on my skills in photography and video editing, I started creating a video series that aimed to highlight their uniqueness, which garnered thousands of views online. It was a truly humbling experience. Many of the PWIDs struggled to express themselves verbally, yet their expressions and enthusiasm spoke volumes. I remember one boy, who couldn’t find the words to thank me after the photoshoot, but his beaming smile and tight hug said more than words ever could. It keeps me going, reminding me of my presence in the bigger world.

2024. As I welcome another new chapter in my life, getting ready for a new start in University, I carry with me the values and character that have shaped who I am today. Each step forward brings me closer to fulfilling the promise I made to my grandpa – to become an agent of change and a leader of tomorrow.

My Family’s Cult

About a year back, my family joined a cult; the ‘Sunday Irodori’ cult. “Irodori” is a Japanese term that means “to color”, it is also my family’s favorite ritual spot. Located in the quiet charms of Singapore’s historical district, dining at this eatery has gradually become a regular Sunday routine for us.

Dad secures the earliest dining slot available, proudly explaining this is to avoid the lunch crowd. Upon arriving, I wheel grandma past the entrance drapes and through the restaurant, navigating the maze of tables and chairs. We usually take an empty table deep in the restaurant. I pull out a seat from its neatly arranged position and on a count of three, mother and I assist grandma from her wheelchair onto the seat. As part of my family ritual, we each grab a cup of freshly brewed cappuccino from the machine situated at the far corner of the restaurant. Of course, we grab an extra cup for grandma before commencing our Sunday Irodori.

As the dimly lit lamps punctuate the otherwise gloomy dining hall, I could see grandma’s profile against the light. Her face is edged with lines and creases; her eyes struggle to sparkle and her dark irises are surrounded by a veil of milky white that hints at the onset of age.

Grandma was brought up during the Japanese occupation of Singapore in the second World War. I had read all about it during history classes. Babies on bayonets. The wretched smell of dead bodies piled on top of one another. The blood, the diseases, the screams of mothers and their children. Death; thousands of deaths. I can see these memories edged into the weary eyes of grandma as she scans across the restaurant.

At first, she notices the Japanese paintings on the walls of the restaurant. I try to imagine myself in her shoes. I wonder what they remind her of? Perhaps they look like the paintings she saw in school as a kid. They often depict people or landscapes crafted by elegant brushstrokes. People say paintings have a scent; though I suppose they are not referring to the stench of blood and dust.

Then, she turns to the dishes in front of her. Under a similar warm light, she would have been seated on a wooden chair like the ones we are sitting on now. While the waiters serve fresh dishes to our table, her table was likely filled with whatever scraps her parents could gather and steal. This usually consisted of plain rice with the occasional treat of a few sweet potatoes. Oh, and did I mention that she had to share this with 10 other family members?

The occasional calls of the chefs echo out like punctuating commands given by Japanese patrol guards. Did her fingers tremble when she heard the sounds of a soldier’s heavy boots? Was she filled with a sense of vengeance or helplessness? Did she grasp her lost relatives so hard that she left marks of despair on their deceased bodies?

The truth is, every time she sets foot in this restaurant, the past whispers in her ears, louder than the present. It isn’t the food that unsettles her, but what it represents - remnants of a time when soldiers marched through her streets and devastated her world. It is never easy, but she takes a bite anyway. Gradually, the tension in her body eases. As she digs into lunch with the rest of us, I can see a warm smile soften the fatigue edged into her face. It always does.

As lunch comes to an end, dad gestures politely for a waiter and picks up the tab for us. Today, our lunch is paid for by my parents. But I know that for every Sunday Irodori that has passed or is yet to come, its true price has been paid long ago by grandma.

I move covertly, rummaging through my arsenal, positioned for attack. I lay eyes on my target: a woman sprawled across the grass, deeply immersed in the bounded pages before her. Amidst the bustling scene of NYC, framed by the towering green giants that make up Central Park, she instead seeks refuge in the world that lies at her fingertips.

Armed with my weapon, my camera, I prepare to shoot. I wonder, where does she escape to? What is her story? Swiftly capturing the transient moment with my lens, this woman no longer becomes a stranger, but rather an addition to my photo album of human experiences. My gallery of characters grows as she joins the wide-eyed museumgoers who marvel at the Exploratorium’s CLOUD sculpture and the eclectic street performer whose impressive headstand attracts a crowd of tourists.

As I explore places, familiar and foreign, I often find myself scanning for candid moments: authentic expressions that act as windows into another person’s narrative. I don’t use my lens to merely document the radiant light of a summer day or the clean lines of modern architecture, but rather to understand, observe, and connect with my ultimate inspiration — people.

We pass countless faces every day - hazy silhouettes that fade into the background while we remain in the limelight. With each photo I take, I challenge myself to break this cycle, refocus my frame, and acknowledge the diverse range of perspectives that reside behind every unfamiliar face. This outlook extends beyond my creative endeavors, shaping how I view the world through my personal lens as well.

I belong to many circles: my family, school, TEDx club, and research community, each one offering me the opportunity to observe life from a different vantage point. However, volunteering at Peer-1-on-1 to provide companionship to children who have neurodevelopmental disorders has been especially transformative.

When I first met Aaron, an intelligent 13-year-old boy who faces severe social anxiety, I struggled to connect with him due to his unwillingness to speak. Communication had always meant one thing to me - the exchange of words. How could I help him if he wouldn’t open up? But with time, I realized that there were other ways to learn from him.

I began to notice the way his eyes widened at the sight of eight-legged organisms and the look of satisfaction on his face when stomping on the dried leaves of an autumn day, revealing his appreciation for nature’s unconventional beauty. His hesitant stare every time he marches a bishop onto the battleground that is our chess board displays his thorough and analytical nature, while the sour grimace on his face when his peers rise to a clamor indicates that he desires a quiet space to compose himself.

These small, silent cues became my aperture into Aaron’s world. His experience became part of my own. I began to understand his struggle to connect with others and his visible discomfort in social situations. But simply empathizing with him wasn’t enough. I needed to take action, to find a way to bridge his unique frame of reference with the larger world.

I raised my concerns to the director of our nonprofit branch, and from there, I led the development of a Generative AI-powered AAC (Augmentative Alternative Communication) app. The app anticipates what someone might want to say, drastically reducing the effort required to communicate by offering personalized options, going beyond the limitations of traditional AAC devices.

Whether through photography, engineering, or connecting with others, observation has been my greatest asset. It’s the foundation of the scientific method and, to me, the most important step. Without observing those around us, it is impossible to create with meaning. Observation has allowed me to grow as a person and solve problems, both human and technological. But I’ve learned that to observe isn’t enough. After all, the most impactful images are not those I capture, but those I create.

5, 10, 15, 20, 25…

As the minute hand of the clock spirals forward, a memory runs into the past. Looking back, my mind always rewinds to a time of my life when things were different: symmetry, order, perfection. The three cornerstones of an 8-year-old me’s life – one who would get mad if a single grain of rice was persistently out of place on my plate or if wrinkles in clothing demanded ironing again. It was an obsession – with discipline, order, and etiquette. School supplies had to be organized by color, size, and type. Each class had its designated color, folder, and notebook in matching hues, with each notebook and pen neatly placed in my backpack.

But life has a way of unraveling even the most perfectly folded shirts.

With a record of thirteen moves, I was no longer just managing chaos in my physical environment, but in my social and mental world as well. The cardboard boxes, rolls of packing tape, and moving trucks never respected my seemliness, as unpacking always involved missing and deranged belongings. Each move shattered the neat world I had created for myself, and slowly, control became less of an option. My once meticulous habits that I had relied on could only take me so far. Navigating through the uncertainty of unfamiliar places, I started to find beauty in the very thing that used to terrify me: chaos.

By my eighth move, I had earned the role of editor-in-chief for the school’s newsletter team, where my writing ability thrived. However, I was caught off guard by the series of interviews I had to conduct as part of the role. Being naturally introverted, I had always felt comfortable keeping to myself; I dreaded each one of them, debating whether to get them over with as soon as possible or to delay them, hoping for cancellation. But deep down, I knew my responsibility—the position came with tasks I had to complete, no matter how uncomfortable they made me. These experiences helped me realize that meeting people, building connections, and reaching out to others is not just a necessity - it’s a source of growth.

Even on move thirteen, I’m not perfect. Change doesn’t happen overnight. I still have days where I retreat into my meticulous tendencies and social interaction feels like a challenge. But now, I know how to navigate through them. Spontaneity and social connection have led to internships and job opportunities I never imagined. They have allowed me to shadow doctors from multiple specialties and help students in the field of STEM. As an Academy Ambassador for Biomedical Sciences, I’ve had the chance to teach prospective freshmen about the brilliant things my academy has to offer. I was even given the opportunity to perform independent dissections of snakes and minks to present to students, where I enjoyed sharing my passion for medicine.

Taking spontaneous risks—like joining clubs, applying for internships, and conducting interviews—pushed me beyond my boundaries as I learned that growth doesn’t come from staying in your bubble of order; it’s born from the chaos of new interactions and experiences. It was through these constant transitions—new homes, new schools, and new social circles—that I began to embrace what I now call "organized chaos." A grotesque paragon of my most feared idea, mixed in with something I had lived by my whole life. It forced me to give up my compulsive tenacities to breathe, to become adaptable, flexible, and spontaneous. It was this Frankenstein-like creature dwelling in my mind that fished for opportunities, grinning as it watched me transform. It flipped a switch, this parasite – bringing me out of this constricted hallway of compulsion to this flourishing garden of fluidity. A fluidity that has guided me through high school and will continue to guide me through college and life.

I carefully place my high-precision tweezers around the covers of a miniature book, a quarter inch in height, and slowly place it on a bookshelf. I adjust it to be just so, sit back, and take in the miniature library taking shape among the pieces of discarded paper and wood on my bedroom floor.

My bedroom has two large bookshelves that are normal, “human” size. Over the years, the books themselves have changed multiple times. These days, most are mysteries, true crime, and crime fiction novels. Spooky and deranged stories I love to get lost in. Look closer though, and you will see that some books on my shelves are not books at all, but rather miniature bookends with mystery worlds inside of them.

A potions shop, a detective’s office, a library, a crime scene …

These are the worlds that I get to create. Ones that from a distance seem so small as not to include any detail. Yet, when you put your face close to them, you can see the universe within, including titles of minuscule books or newspapers, or the names of exotic spices on the bottles in a tiny kitchen. Each tiny piece has its designated spot, a role to play in the “bigger” picture.

I love the process of completing each model. Sitting on my floor for hours, the pieces are spread out across my room as they gradually take over my personal space. The physical act of building something is exhilarating.

I recognize the time and effort spent on these mini projects could be put somewhere else. But there is something soothing in this process, as you focus on one specific aspect of the build at a time. There is also freedom in being able to switch from item to item when things become too tedious or boring. The mini credenza is giving you trouble? Perfectly fine! Just move on to the assembly of the shelf.

Among the books on my “real” shelves is “Netter’s Neuroscience Coloring Book”. Open it on any page and on the left you will see detailed scientific descriptions of the various parts of the human nervous system, including the brain. On the right, there will be a large intricate picture you get to color.

As I go through the pages, I see connections to my book nooks. There is the cerebellum which helps with precise hand movements and coordination, like when I glue each small piece to the wall, each needs to be precisely in the right spot, otherwise, the rest won’t fit. The parietal lobe helps with understanding spatial relationships, like figuring out how my tiny pots and pans fit in the miniature kitchen. There is also the big executive part of the brain, the prefrontal cortex, which I use when planning which part of a project to tackle next. Its frontal lobe controls creative thinking, such as deciding which miniature books I want to show in my mini libraries, as the details are so refined that each book looks like an exact copy of a real one scaled down. Finally, there are also parts of my brain that I think could use some help. My models require a lot of patience, but I am not the most patient person and often switch between projects when I get bored. I blame my anterior cingulate cortex, which should do a better job helping me maintain focus and manage frustration.

Building my miniatures is my escape. It was one of many new hobbies I tried early in the pandemic. But, unlike embroidery or 3D puzzles, my book nooks are here to stay. With each new one, my thoughts slow down and my body relaxes. But while it feels calm and quiet, I know that there is quite a lot of action in the various nooks of my brain.

“Now that you can cook for yourself, you’re ready for college,” my mom teases, as her eyes focus on the steaming bowl of ramen I just made. To her, it is a sign I won’t go hungry. To me, it’s something more, a reflection of myself, my community, and the experiences that have shaped me.

Ramen is one dish I learned to cook purely to satisfy an immediate craving. It has evolved over time, starting from ingredients chosen based on what I thought I needed. But through the years, I began to understand that ramen, like life, is enriched by more than just basic ingredients. It thrives on flavor, depth, and variety. And what used to be just a meal for myself has steadily nourished others along the way.

The hiss and sizzle of boiling water signals it’s time to make my ramen. Steam rises as I pull out the perfectly square-shaped noodles, crispy and intertwined. Each noodle represents the people who have shaped me. My grandmother, resilient and unbreakable at age 106, is like the firm noodles holding everything together. The curly noodles are my friends, weaving in and out, adding texture and spontaneity. My communities - school, basketball, mentors, and church are countless strands of noodles that form a network of support, trust, and growth. Together, these noodles lay the foundation, yet they are just the beginning of the bowl’s flavor.

Beyond the noodles, the broth represents the experiences that have seasoned my life. Early on, the broth was a simple miso base, flavored by childhood lessons and the comforts of familiarity. As I encountered new challenges, the broth deepened, becoming more complex. Spices reflect failed dreams of making the NBA, while triumphs like launching a patent pending startup to reduce chronic disease add richness. There is sweetness from infectious smiles of foster children I chaperone at the annual carnival, and bitterness from the moment my mom was diagnosed with stage three colon cancer. Together, these intricate flavors meld into a broth that tells my story.

In my earlier years, ramen was a dish meant only for me, focused on what I needed to feel nourished. But life, much like ramen, is not meant to be enjoyed alone. As my noodles intertwined with the lives of others, I realized I was serving more than just myself. This shift led me to engage deeply with my community by joining Challenge Success, a program at Stanford University to improve student well-being, collective belonging and classroom engagement where I piloted a school-wide Sleep Campaign, focus groups, and student shadow days to enhance overall student life on campus.

Meanwhile, the ingredients and ramen toppings I gathered over time as experiences broadened my empathy for underrepresented and marginalized communities. Through difficult discussions with my peers, I discovered that giving students a platform to express their voices benefits everyone. I listened to frustrations over inequality and financial struggles. Inspired by afternoons spent with teammates in a neighborhood very different from mine, I created a mentoring group for first gen students to help navigate the pursuit of a college education. What once nourished me alone now fuels my desire to share, give back, and support others.

I see the bowl before me, evolved and seasoned through every person I’ve met and every experience I’ve encountered. A sprinkle of green onions brings insight, while the umami of seaweed reflects wisdom I’ve gained. I approach life’s ramen knowing it is constantly evolving, and my bowl is far from finished. Whether leading student start-ups, promoting financial literacy, or innovating at the intersection of finance and social good, my journey has shown me that the true richness of life, like ramen, comes not just from the ingredients, but from sharing the bowl with others.

I feel my mom’s proud eyes on me as I dig into a heaping pile of noodles and I chuckle to myself. Mom is right again. I am ready for college and I won’t go hungry. But more importantly, I am ready to ensure those around me won’t either.

The bars were oscillating frantically, each fluctuation quicker than the rhythm of my heartbeat. I was captivated by the vibrant greens and reds climbing and falling across my Dad’s laptop screen. “What does all this mean?” I whispered, my nine-year-old eyes wide with wonder. He smiled and pointed his finger towards them. “These bars represent the value of currencies of different countries,” he explained. As I unraveled the causes for their shift — interest rates, geopolitics, monetary policies… — while shadowing my Dad’s work over the coming weeks, my interest in global affairs started to pique. The spark in intellectual curiosity and the gradual realization that the contours on our map do not entirely separate us made me want to learn more about the world we live in; and so I developed a habit of reading and watching documentaries, the research methodology my Dad imparted on me.

Daily engagement with scientific findings and global media was pivotal in allowing me to grasp the world’s complexities that I couldn’t be exposed to by cocooning myself in an easy life in Singapore. It made me desire something more, to make a difference in the world greater than myself. Witnessing the global upheaval and suffering caused by the coronavirus, I felt compelled to contribute to finding a solution. I coupled the analytical skills I honed from solving science and math problems at school with my knowledge of financial markets to identify companies that could make a difference. After days of scouring platforms like Finviz and analyzing intricate company details — such as debt-to-equity ratios and institutional transactions — I focused on Ocugen Inc (NASDAQ: OCGN). Using my Dad’s Interactive Brokers account, I placed an order for shares of OCGN at US$0.21/share with part of my pocket money saved over the years. A few weeks later, as I was scrolling through Yahoo Finance, my eyes widened as I read the headlines “Ocugen and Bharat Biotech to Co-Develop COVAXIN™…”. The share price had skyrocketed within hours in the pre-market session; in a week, my investment had quadrupled. In hindsight, my spiritual ideology of Karma, rooted in my Indian heritage, gave profound meaning to this experience. Over the years, whiling away in opinion pieces and Oxford Union debates, I developed nuanced perspectives to connect the dots on national and international affairs. It allowed me to engender personal thoughts on them, drawing parallels to my community. One evening, I sat at the dinner table after a lecture on social equity at school. The aroma of Appam and vegetable stew filled the air. Amidst the clinching of plates, I asked my Mom: Did you hear about the discrimination in panchayat elections affecting scheduled castes and tribes in Kerala? Her words reaffirmed my belief that healthy discourses are needed to combat and mitigate endemic challenges. Spurring such occasional conversations - simultaneously applying and honing my research skills - with my friends and family for us to canvass over became a way for me to champion the causes I believed in as little ways as I could.

I see the unification of my intellectual and philosophical endeavors contingent for me to make tangible impacts on society. In delving into advanced algorithms like the consensus protocol during my course on Blockchain and Cryptocurrency, I was inclined to inquire: do traditional notions of central authority professed by Thomas Hobbes still hold? What’s the environmental implications of such technology?

Binging through Shark Tank episodes, my entrepreneurial spirit ignites, and I'm urged to answer my own philosophical questions through novel solutions, rooting organically from my experiences. I believe the insatiable curiosity I have cultivated to traverse through the niche and illuminate new realms within the cosmos of mind can achieve this - guided by the research methodology my Dad instilled in me from a young age.

I’d love to smell like petrichor (smell of rain), mixed with curry fish-balls. Engrossed in the power of scent, I am a fragrance connoisseur, caught in the dance between the top, middle, and base notes of fragrances.

Le Labo’s Bigarade 18. 
The Neroli and Bergamot notes whirl me away to the hotel lobby, the cool stream of AC blasting relief on my sticky neck and fogged-up glasses. This memory quickly fades with the top notes, and the middle notes of lily flower pull me two streets down – back to my grandpa's small, humid apartment. The smell carries me to my summer days spent alongside my grandfather, surrounded by colorful vases filled with lily flowers. We sat on dirt-cheap pink stools sweating profusely – but it wasn’t discomfort I remembered – it was his patience and quiet persistence. Though, Isn’t that how fragrances work? The deeper notes are the ones that stay.

Maison Margiela’s Coffee Break 
Sitting in a corner booth of my favorite cafe, the warm notes of coffee and lavender hugged me, but the anxiety I felt was impossible to shake. While my friends confidently breezed through assignments, I stared at my notes, suffocated by expectations – mine, my parents’, my grandpa – like I was an imposter, pretending to keep up. Coffee Break became my lifeline in these moments, grounding me during the quiet, invisible battles that I fought every day, and although I wanted to give up, I didn't. Coffee Break revealed the solace and control that a fragrance can bring.

Louis Vuitton Afternoon Swim

What’s the significance of one's fragrance? Is it a gift from a first love? When I meet someone new, I always imagine the story behind their perfume. This curiosity drove me to start a fragrance business, initially selling to friends and locals. My first major sale was a bottle of Louis Vuitton Afternoon Swim, sold to a close friend who had just quit swimming to take care of his mom. Helping him reconnect with his passion reminded me that my business could form a tight knit community. 
Transitioning online was challenging. Orders trickled in slowly, and doubt crept in. Was this just another failed attempt at entrepreneurship? I remembered sitting at my desk, the faint aroma of Coffee Break lingering in the air – ironic, considering how far I felt from my goal. What had calmed me was now my only source of comfort as I started at my dim screen. I remembered my grandfather’s lessons: patience and persistence. He never let a setback define him, and I wouldn’t either. I spent that night redesigning my marketing strategy, adding personal anecdotes to every product description to emphasize the story behind each fragrance. It was risky and time consuming, but I was willing to try. Finally, the orders began coming in. Within months, I began generating thousands of dollars a month, sharing fragrances reminiscent of Mount Everest or springtime playgrounds. I found satisfaction in helping others embrace their identity through scent. They revealed that I was building a community where a perfume held immense value – if a picture is worth a thousand words, a fragrance is worth a million. Each bottle was a tool for transformation and expression, no words needed. 
I wasn’t just obsessed with fragrances; I was fascinated by transformation – both in others and in myself.

My Fragrance(s) 
Fragrances have shown me that life, its challenges, and its commemorations aren’t fixed. They’re fluid, shaped and reshaped by its wearer. We’re all blends of moments, ever-changing, forced to grow, yearning to transform. You ask me what I’m wearing, and I pause. Fragrances suck me into a world where time blurs; it's hard to explain. I’m not just wearing a scent; I'm wearing a memory, a part of me still unfolding. Today, it’s light and airy – like me. Tomorrow, it could be dark and bold – also like me.

An invisible rabbit, moving a mile each step. Could a blind hunter ensure that he’s within a 100-mile radius after a billion moves? The problem was absurd, exhilarating—the kind that made my fingers twitch and mind race. Four hours left on the math Olympiad team selection test, and my brain buzzed with possibilities—construction, strong induction... definitely but no, No. Yesterday. I could’ve won that chess game if I went C6. No, focus [Name]. THINK.

I blundered. It wasn’t Rook or a Queen I lost—it was my spot on the team. Four hours passed and all I had to show were crumpled scratch papers with half an idea and a poorly drawn Kakashi doodle. I just couldn’t focus, my mind constantly on the run from one monster—silence.

I was one hell of a runner. From friend to peer to stranger, I’d passionately explain why only higher-dimensional tic-tac-toe made sense, or pull an all-nighter helping with a research paper. Babbling about abstract math theories or diving into someone else’s struggles—it didn’t matter, as long as I stayed distracted, I wasn’t stuck between two turbulent worlds. For those moments, I was escaping.

But the more I tried to escape, the worse it got. My mind adapted: solving a problem alone couldn’t keep the silence at bay. I needed music, a YouTube video, and maybe even a barrage of TikTok—anything to avoid being alone with my thoughts. It was suffocating. I was running on autopilot, bouncing from one distraction to another, but never finding peace. Something had to give.

So, I deleted TikTok, abandoned Instagram, and found myself reading *Walden* by Thoreau and *Deep Work* by Cal Newport. From a serial multitasker, I became a plain old ‘single-tasker.’ It was chest-tightening at first—my instincts itched for my phone, my eyes flitted between the guitar on my wall and the game PC on my desk, and every few seconds, I’d wonder if Danny was the Gossip Girl. But no, I forced myself to brush my teeth in silence, shower in silence, eat breakfast in, you guessed it,… silence. All that quiet turned my high walls of problems into mountains I could finally climb.

So, I climbed. Each time I resisted the urge to distract myself, I pushed a little further. Two weeks in, I was comfortable enough in silence—so one by one, I reintroduced everything that used to distract me. Mindlessly strumming a guitar while watching a movie turned into hours hunched over it, fingers sore and calluses building as I tried to nail a quarter-tone bend. Casual chess matches I’d played with a podcast in the background transformed into intense games where I could finally savor each move. And most importantly, math became a beauty I could focus on and truly appreciate again.

Gradually, silence wasn’t just about confronting myself—it became space to listen. Helping others was no longer a distraction. I realized how often I’d ramble just to fill the air, only half-hearing their stories. But as the noise in my head quieted, I started to share my passions rather than unload my anxieties. Teaching Abd Al Sallam about Cyclotomic Polynomials and Primitive Roots had me grinning watching him share the fascination I once did. Showing Dana how to play *Twinkle Twinkle Little Star* on the ukulele reminded me of my own beginnings and most importantly, being present meant seeing my friends slowly open up and trust me with their fears and struggles (no murders, I promise).

So, while on the outside many might see me as the same exact math-guitar-chess-cubing-too-many-hobbies nerd, rediscovering my focus changed those distractions into anchors, enabling me to reflect on who I am. The guitar stopped being a prop to fill an empty space and became an extension of myself—each note bending to mirror my moods, from the delicate to the dissonant. Chess wasn’t just an obsession to stave off boredom; it became a quiet challenge where I’d test myself, savoring each game for its own sake. And math? Math was more than a mental workout—it became my language again. Problems weren’t just solutions to be boxed away, but puzzles to play with, to savor, and—most importantly—to share.

And that scary italic silence? We have hour-long dates every day—now my best friend.

The chaos theory in finance posits that small changes can lead to unpredictable, large-scale effects in the market. As it turns out, this theory applies to life as well—something I discovered at 16 when my doctor uttered words that sent my world spinning: "Your testicle hasn't descended, and you're sixteen?"

My stomach tightened as I processed this information. How could I have been unaware of something so fundamental about my own body? In my Sikh-Hindu family, discretion and modesty are revered virtues. While these values foster respect and dignity, they also created an unintended barrier to open discussions about personal health. This cultural reticence inadvertently obscured a serious medical issue in my case.

As the weight of this realization settled, I found myself grappling with a profound question: Do I really control my own destiny? Just as the stock market can plummet due to unforeseen circumstances, my health had taken an unexpected turn. Yet, I knew that even in volatile markets, there are ways to mitigate risk and maximize potential gains.

Weighing the risks and potential rewards, I made the decision to undergo surgery—my first major health choice. My parents, initially hesitant to discuss the issue, eventually supported my decision after I presented them with a well-researched argument, much like pitching an investment strategy.

Six weeks later, I lay on the operating table, surrounded by sterile white walls and the sharp scent of antiseptic. As the surgical team corrected nature's developmental error, I couldn't help but draw parallels to the careful maneuvering required in financial markets. Just as surgeons must navigate delicate tissues, investors must carefully navigate market fluctuations.

Post-surgery, I approached my recovery with the same diligence I apply to managing our school's $25,000 investment fund. I researched and implemented a nutrition plan to support healing, monitored my progress daily, and gradually increased my physical activity—all while keeping a keen eye on potential complications, much like watching for market downturns.

This experience sparked an interest in other areas where I could take control, particularly in securing my future. I became passionately involved in our school's Student Investment Fund, where we analyze market trends, assess risk, and make investment decisions. Managing this portfolio taught me that while we can't control market fluctuations, we can make informed decisions to optimize our position.

As I delved deeper into the world of finance, I noticed a troubling parallel to my health experience. Just as my family's modesty had kept me in the dark about my health, many in my predominantly Latino community lacked access to crucial financial knowledge. Determined to bridge this gap, I launched financial literacy workshops at my local community center.

During one of these workshops, while explaining credit scores, an unexpected moment occurred. An adult chaperone in the back, who had been quietly observing, suddenly leaned forward and started speaking rapidly in Spanish. With my limited Spanish, I understood one word she kept repeating: "importante." She was telling the kids that this information was crucial, explaining how credit scores impact everything from loans to housing in their community.

The room's atmosphere shifted instantly. Students who had been passively listening suddenly reached for their notebooks, pens poised to catch every detail. Their wandering eyes now focused intently on me. In that moment, I understood how knowledge could transform one's reality, much like how understanding market trends can transform an investment strategy.

This experience taught me that while we can't control everything in life—be it our health or the financial markets—we always carry some level of power within us. Just as I had taken charge of my health when no one else could, I was now helping others take charge of their financial futures.

As I look towards college and beyond, this realization fuels my passion to pursue a path where I can continue to empower others through education and community development. I'm ready for whatever descends in my future, confident in my ability to face these challenges—whether they're related to health, wealth, or the unpredictable nature of life itself.

Trying to ease the tightness in my chest, I rubbed my sweaty hands on my pencil skirt. Finally, the tournament director finished naming the competitors advancing to speech finals. Whistles and whoops became static as I realized she would never say “[Name] Li.”

When I read stories of anti-Asian hate crimes during the COVID-19 pandemic, I felt the victims’ pain without anybody assaulting me. However, I couldn’t feel surprised. I considered my childhood: my shocked friend exclaiming, “You’re Chinese? I thought you were normal!”, my karate partner making me pronounce my “R”s and then saying, “But people like you can’t do that.” As I considered others’ stories and my own, I felt so wounded that staying silent was suffocating. But before I spoke out, I needed to know more. I poured over history papers and old news articles. Discovering xenophobic laws and lynchings horrified me, but knowing that I had to dig through 19th-century news archives to find this history was almost worse. We could never change our future without learning our past.

Speaking in a conservative Christian league, I often heard uncomfortable “oh”s when I told people about my speech. Some advised me to lighten it up, but I wasn’t just fighting for other Asian Americans; I was fighting for my childhood self. I could never disappoint her by watering down my advocacy.

When I put so much of myself into this speech but never reached finals, I couldn’t help wondering—did anyone even hear me? Still, certain that my name would someday be called, I strove on. Yet now, once again, sobs strangled my chest. Then, my friend pulled me into a tight hug. More and more of my friends embraced me and strangely, the more love I felt, the more violent my weeping grew.

Driving home from the tournament, I remembered an interaction with a judge. “My friend was moved to tears by your speech,” she told me. I remembered another judge saying my speech impacted her more than I could ever know. Maybe it only touched a few people, but those moments still mattered. Those judges, listening to me, felt the passion I felt. My friends, showing love to me, felt the heartbreak I felt. Through their feeling, they helped me feel heard.

I often resented the people uncomfortable with my speech. When they expressed misgivings, I shuttered my ears and heart. But how could I then expect them to listen to me? My own fermenting bitterness taught me that close-mindedness encourages antagonism, not persuasion. Whenever resentment festered, I forced myself to imagine experiences that forged these people’s perspectives. Maybe they adopted their beliefs to cope with grief from a loss. Maybe if I experienced their lives, I’d be standing right by their side. They weren’t “others” to attack; they had just lived other lives to understand. Finally, I felt peace. The following season, I wrote a speech on the necessity of empathetic listening. I hope those touched can find peace like I did, both with themselves and others.

Although speaking on Asian-American discrimination came with many tears, those who supported me taught me to help others feel loved and heard. I remember stroking my friend’s hair as she cried into my shoulders. If we understand each other’s emotions, we can create a world where people heal. So, I will continue holding my classmates through their struggles. I remember conversing with a classmate for hours as we worked through our polar opposite beliefs. If we understand each other’s perspectives, we can create a world where we encourage change instead of echo chambers. I never could have grown into that person without each disappointment shaping my ability to empathize with others.

On a chilly September morning, I stretched on damp planks, straining to dip an oxygen probe into the pond as my Environmental Science friends gripped my ankles. The pier was just tall enough that nobody’s arms reached the water without such a maneuver. Mrs. Girardi taught us that the water closest to the shore was not representative of the whole pond. I then ventured onto rocks and trampled wet leaves. I squatted and inched further down to perform the turbidity measurement with the best possible technique of reaching as far and deep from the shore as possible. Collecting the perfect sample, made water collect in my shoes. My friends laughed as my sneakers squeaked with each step. As motivated as we were, our inexperience made field research challenging.

On our next pond expedition, we evaluated the ecosystem’s well-being by measuring the biodiversity of macroinvertebrates as a more thorough approach to ecosystem health. We carried a pile of green rubber equipment from Mrs. Girardi’s trunk, appreciating her thoughtfulness in providing the essentials. Every minor detail counted for sample collection, from how we adjusted galoshes and tightened waders to how we differentiated mayflies and dragonfly nymphs. Recalling her lesson about depth, now with the right equipment, I went further into the water than I ever could before. I concluded with excitement that the pond was healthy, which led me to a greater appreciation of my community’s environmental stewardship practices.

Mrs. Girardi's thoughtful support with the right equipment helps students reach our most ambitious goals. This lesson extended beyond the classroom, as I wasn’t this considerate early in high school. As a freshman on varsity soccer, I believed that competitiveness was everything. Although this mindset helped me make the team, it wouldn’t help us make a community. I remembered how Mrs. Girardi strove to reduce stress and tension in her classroom by asking students about the pressures we faced through busy times to accommodate our best learning. Following her example, I built connections to bring out the best in others. I led my teammates through visualization of their best plays and lightened the mood with humor. At the end of that junior season, my team elected me captain and crowned me with the “fun captain” regalia: the Freaky Hat, my most prized piece of equipment. This deflated yellow and white soccer ball is decorated with inspirational notes left by captains of the past two decades. It reminds me to balance my drive with positivity and how I can improve community through connection and thoughtfulness.

Mrs. Girardi’s lessons apply to my choices outside of school. Since my parents grew up in Soviet bloc housing, lawn care did not come naturally. Therefore, as soon as my feet could reach the pedals of the ride-on mower, I took over the responsibility. Through Mrs. Girardi’s hands-on experiments with our local ecosystem, I became fascinated with my community’s responsibility to our environment. I began to avoid pesticides and herbicides that harm native species, so my lawn was no longer a monoculture. I skipped mowing in May for the pollinators and whenever I saw a new litter of cottontail rabbits. Before the season’s first soccer game, my family helped me host a spaghetti dinner for my team on our lawn. Directing watermelon rinds into our new compost bin filled me with joy at being able to use our resources to come together as a community.

This August I entered Mrs. Girardi’s classroom as a teaching assistant, eager to help this year’s class explore. When my soccer season ends, I’ll write my own note on the Freaky Hat and crown the next “fun captain” as a way to model the importance of positivity in leadership. As my time in high school comes to a close, I look forward to wading my galoshes into new, deeper lakes of college life while carrying Mrs. Girardi’s lessons of optimism.

The cold headwind bites through my thin jacket as my bike picks up speed. Shivering, I resist the tantalizing desire to turn back towards the warm bed I left not too long ago and keep riding on. After another hour of climbing, I leave the forested valley behind and arrive at the summit of the Fichtelberg, soaking in the warmth of the sun’s rays. The rolling hills I am riding through are picturesque, but like many things in Eastern Germany, there are darker undertones present. Hidden below the hills are Soviet-era mines where forced laborers once mined for the ore used to create Stalin’s nuclear arsenal. Standing on the summit that day, I found myself torn between viewing my home state of Saxony through the beautiful landscapes on the surface or the dark history below.

Days later, I encountered a German proverb that gave me the solution. Die Hoffnung stirbt zuletzt. Hope is the last to die. I decided to acknowledge Saxony’s dark history but focus on the resilience of the inhabitants, to think of the warm summit ahead when I am still in the frigid valley. My success comes from hope.

300 miles in 24 hours. That was the dream. I trained for two years, working my way up from 100 to 200-mile rides. I read books on ultracycling and researched optimal nutrition, learning that real food like home-made Nutella sandwiches (my personal favorite!) beats energy gels long-term. I enthusiastically planned out an optimal route for minimizing wind exposure and maximizing safety and access to water. Through trial-and-error, I settled on 14.2 miles per hour as the magic average speed to avoid overexertion but still make good headway.

226 miles in, I realized that I forgot to account for one factor: drowsiness. My bloodshot eyes told the whole story- no amount of caffeine would keep me from nodding off. My zeal for success giving in to my better judgement, I decided to stop of my own accord rather than hit the asphalt in a moment of microsleep. I failed, but I learned the importance of having a solid plan-and to start 24-hour adventures at an ungodly hour of the morning to avoid riding through a full night. My success comes from careful planning and learning through failure.

I cannot keep riding. Eighteen hours in, the combination of tired legs, chafing from the saddle, and doubt over whether my goal is truly attainable is causing me to lose the war I declared against myself. Legs shaking, I reach for the bowl of rice on the table next to me. It was a final gift from my mother to me before she went to bed for the night, accompanied by a word of encouragement. My cracked mouth slowly musters a smile thinking of her kindness, and the pedals start moving again. I pick up my phone to check the time, and my cousin Joni grins at me through my phone wallpaper as our ten-year-old selves build a Gravitrax marble run. Suddenly, the bike seems to be moving by itself. The final miles were not easy, but I was not riding alone. With an invisible push from the people that believe in me, my bike and I danced in tandem up the virtual mountain road for the twenty-third and final time. After almost twenty grueling hours, a virtual Everesting 10k – 32,800 feet of elevation gain in a singular ride on the home trainer– was done. My success comes from my support network.

Through my 2012 Ridley Excalibur road bike, I have explored my mental and physical limits, but also formed a toolkit for fixing any flat tire or broken derailleur that life throws at me. As I ride on to college and adulthood, I will take with me my toolkit of an intricate plan, a healthy dose of optimism, and a dependable support network.

As I skipped around the living room when I was seven on Christmas Eve, singing Jingle Bells, something caught my foot and I fell, slamming my lip into the ground. I immediately cried out in pain as my mom rushed to my side. Knowing the stakes, she did a magic trick for me. She told me to close my eyes and wait. Moments later, I opened my eyes to see a glass of banana milk and a piece of homemade banana bread on the table. Those tears soon turned into glittering stars—and as I enjoyed this yummy treat, the pain seemingly melted away. Bananas truly are a happy fruit. This was the first time I learned that food has the magic to heal.

Since then, my curiosity and passion for food has only grown. I’ve tried various dishes from different places. Whether it’s burritos from Montecristo Taqueria in Berkeley, or spicy tuna rice plate from Oori on Solano Avenue, every new food I try is an opportunity to learn about another country’s cultures.

As a massive foodie, I never miss an opportunity to explore something new. Last year, during a cultural exchange program in Taiwan, I had a chance to visit Raohe Night Market in Taipei. As I walked through crowded and noisy streets filled with various aromas, something suddenly pierced my nose. The scent was funky and unfamiliar. It was stinky tofu, a Taiwanese snack known for its extremely smelly yet unusually delicious taste.

Curious as to whether it tasted as bad as it smelled, I ordered a plate. As soon as I was handed the dish, the courage I had just summoned was extinguished by that daunting smell. I held my breath and took a bite as my hands trembled. To my surprise, it was juicy and flavorful, tender on the inside but crunchy on the outside. The drizzled garlic soy sauce covered everything in a umami/savory blanket. While the smell was not very pleasant, the taste was unique and fascinating.

Early this year, I was sitting on a bar stool in a famous Japanese restaurant in Berkeley named Kirala. As I watched the chef, I couldn’t help but notice the dedication he had in preparing food. Carefully and precisely slicing hundred dollar cuts of tuna, hand kneading the rice attentively to form it into the perfect shape, he made every piece of sushi like this was his last chance. That heartfelt focus wasn’t only to assure dish quality for customers, but also for true passion for his job. I was deeply touched and inspired by the craftsmanship in his work and how hard he goes after his passions. That same hard work motivated me to pursue my passions to this day.

While crucial for survival, food has had a far deeper meaning for me and has transformed me into a better person. From my mom’s various cooking experiences (both failures and successes) that are fueled by empathy for others, I have learned to show love and care to people by offering a drink or snacks when they are down. I learned that don’t easily judge things or people by the surface from Stinky tofu. Finally, food has taught me the importance of commitment to my passions, as was shown by that sushi chef in Berkeley.

Nowadays, you can often find me at new restaurants, trying out dishes I’ve never heard of. You might find me at the supermarket, looking for the interesting snacks that I’ll be addicted to, or absolutely hate. Either way, with every food adventure comes a new learning experience for me.

Rows of gray metal boxes and tarnished blue roll-up doors. Trees branches swallow old billboards, power lines crisscross the sky. Another lot of metal boxes and green-roll-up doors, the entrance covered by overgrown bushes. More trees, and mismatched mailboxes jutting out. Self-storage facilities / rows of metal boxes and roll-up doors line my road to school, but for years, the monotony of their existence never gave me a reason to think twice about them. They were nothing more than a blur of rust and concrete, meant to keep things out of sight.

One night during dinner, my dad mentioned that the old self-storage facility down the road was up for sale. What was just a throwaway remark for my family became an idea I couldn’t shake. Despite being rather mundane utilities, storages were still necessities. Sleek climate-controlled storages were constantly built to meet growing demand, but the unmaintained, rudimentary rows of metal boxes and roll-up doors held the same potential. Driving to school the next few weeks, I imagined an opportunity to transform the neglected facility down the road into a thriving business.

But after weeks of convincing, my parents were hesitant. They deeply appreciated what they saw as the backbone of America: small, community businesses and local leadership. Yet, they saw entrepreneurship as a door closed to them, and something for my generation, the first-born Americans, to walk through. I was determined to continue exploring the world of self-storage ownership, learning about firsthand successes in tweets and Reddit posts. I began hunting for other storage facilities that existed only on Google Street View, and after cold-calling dozens of numbers from LLC filings, I reached Jimmy. He hadn’t tended to his storage in years, and it devolved into a long-abandoned lot of overgrown bushes and peeling paint.

Over the next few weeks, we mapped out every aspect of the business, from nearby occupancy rates to the water flow during a storm, even discussing whether the neighbor’s septic tank posed any threats. Everything was checking out, and my parents realized this could be the path towards their version of the American Dream, but the leap still seemed enormous. That’s when I reminded them of their own journey — they had taken an even greater leap leaving everything behind to move to the United States. They came here seeking opportunity; now, it was time to create one.

After investing in the facility, my weekends, while different from my friends’, became a way to bond with my parents. The storage became our workshop each weekend, and each task was its own puzzle piece. I started each day with a checklist in hand: Which doors were jammed? How many springs needed to be replaced? What was their diameter and wind direction? What I once saw as a simple construction separating two worlds revealed itself as an intricate collection of bolts and cables. Throughout the day, pulling weeds turned into competitions and forgotten items from old units were hidden treasures, but each clear pathway and spotless unit completed the next piece of the puzzle.

A few months in, the facility was unrecognizable. I spoke to neighbors and fellow small business owners, spreading the word that the once-forgotten corner of town had been revived, now open for business.
