Hearing the astonishment in their tone, I remembered that, while this was now my passion and livelihood, I too had ignored it for years. It had always been right in front of our eyes, yet we refused to see the potential. Simply by opening my eyes to a new form of opportunity, I turned an abandoned lot into a thriving business: today, we have about a hundred happy customers who rely on us to offer a safe home for their belongings.

On my drive to school, I no longer see storage facilities, or any small businesses, as just utilities. Instead, I recognize the hard-working, driven entrepreneurs who breathe life into even the simple necessities. In my future, I will continue observing the world with an open mind, and seeing value in the simple or mundane, even in the forgotten corners of town. The real value lies not necessarily in building new doors, but learning to open the ones we never thought to unlock.

Just like that, all my hard-earned money was gone. Worst of all? It was none other than my parents who had taken it all away.

My early elementary school days were spent at the SAFE after-school program, where I would spend 3-6PM in a lunchroom with a handful of other kids and a basket of old art supplies. With little to entertain ourselves, the first-come-first-serve basket would be our only escape from boredom. To avoid the fight for the two dozen packs of markers, I turned to origami, the Japanese art of paper folding. My favorite creation? The ninja star—a parody of the samurai’s shuriken.

Even without color, heads turned when my first star took flight across the lunchroom. Soon enough, other students began asking for one of their own. Sensing an opportunity, I turned my new hobby into a business: basic stars for 25 cents, multicolored ones for 50, and giant ones for a dollar. With demand skyrocketing, class time became covert origami ops, recess rivaled business hours on Wall Street, and by day’s end, I would leave feeling like Richie Rich with jingling pockets full of quarters.

One evening, my mom discovered my stash—a shoebox stuffed with shiny coins and crumpled bills. When I proudly presented how I got all that money, I expected a boatload of praise. Instead, my mom questioned what I was doing, “why do you need to sell them, why not just give them out for free?”

She explained to me how my profits were just wasting away in the shoebox, but the actual enjoyment I felt was not from the money, but rather from bringing joy to my classmates.

I didn’t fully understand her, but I reluctantly followed my mom’s advice. During the next recess, I attempted to return everyone’s money, doing my best to remember each sale. Whatever remained, I donated to our school’s fundraiser, where the winning class would earn a pizza party. Safe to say, with paper flying and pizza in their hands, ninja stars had brought my classmates together in a way that I didn’t expect—maybe my mom was right.

Years later, while packing for my transfer to the Illinois Math and Science Academy, I stumbled upon an old container filled with Post-It notes and a handful of leftover ninja stars. This nostalgic find brought me back to the pizza party at Sycamore Trails.

The true meaning of what my mom had tried to tell me years ago finally hit me. The value isn’t in what you make, but how what you create moves through others, transforming innovation into shared connection. The ninja stars weren't just intricate paper designs—they were catalysts for connection, creativity, and shared experiences.

This spirit pushed me into the world of social entrepreneurship, inspiring SignAll, an AI-powered sign language translation platform aiming to bridge massive communication barriers faced by the ASL community. Working on SignAll reignited the same excitement I felt when making ninja stars—code replacing paper and machine learning algorithms taking the place of folds. Through SignAll, I connected with thousands of people from the global sign language community who revealed how our technology could transform their daily lives. This potential for meaningful impact has driven me further than any technological advancement that we make. Their gratitude and experiences fuel my motivation, pushing me to work even harder.

Looking toward college, I am eager to continue leveraging technology for ethical solutions that address real-world challenges. Whether it be through ninja stars or apps, I will foster community by engaging shared purpose and connection through meaningful innovation. And who knows—maybe there will be a pizza party or two along the way.

A gentle nudge of my fingertips frees me from land, and I’m off. As I glide across the glassy surface of the Connecticut River, the wind ruffles my hair and carries the fresh scent of pines lining the shore. I feel a familiar sense of peace wash over me. Atop a slender racing shell, I tune into the rhythmic plunking of my blades. As usually happens when I row through this pristine passageway between the hills of Vermont and New Hampshire, my mind begins to clear.

I scan my surroundings for nothing in particular while taking in everything—a red-winged blackbird perched on a reed, a grove of lotus flowers in a protected cove, the echoing croak of a bullfrog. The sight of a path above the banks reminds me of my hand in creating opportunities for others to feel what I do in this moment. A volunteer trail builder, I have spent years expanding access to our environment and opening up spaces that bring this serenity to others. I’ve also come to rely on the outdoors for health and creativity. On this sun-filled afternoon, I happen to need inspiration for an upcoming essay on Romanticism.

The distant call of a loon offers an answer, evoking my favorite piece of music, “The Lark Ascending,” and planting an idea. Could I argue that Ralph Vaughan Williams's “pastoral romance” embodies the ideals of the Romantic movement? Based on a poem by George Meredith, it depicts a songbird’s “silver chain of sound” uplifting humanity with a soothing improvisatory melody. After another school day amidst the constant buzz of technology, I am struck by the timeless relevance of the poet’s message of nature as an antidote to the clanking of industrial noise. My paper’s thesis takes form.

Winding through this waterway, I feel attuned to the impact of my upbringing in a place where time feels slow and limitless. As a child, exploring outside was routine—collecting acorns and rocks, constructing forts in the woods, pitching a tent beneath the stars. Now, I understand what consciously draws me here, where my mind resets and my body recharges. That’s why I am determined to do my part to protect public lands. More than a mere pastime, shifting boulders and constructing bridges over wetlands is deeply rewarding. While cutting brush or laying waterbars, I imagine a happy hiker one day walking where I worked. Faced with a mountain of gravel to spread, I am undaunted and grateful that I can open up this world to those venturing into the wild in a wheelchair. A life without the joy of these surroundings is unimaginable.

A bend in the river brings the dock into view. Back on land, I wipe down the boat, feeling energized by my excursion. Over dinner, I mention to my family that I know firsthand what the Romantic poets recognized about our vital need for harmony with the living world. My outdoor pursuits have not only shaped my values—mindfulness, health, a commitment to service—they have deepened my curiosity about the intersections of philosophy, science, and the human experience. I am intrigued by the biological foundations of my experiences. Going forward, I’m eager to understand the science behind “Attention Restoration Theory,” which explains how the activities I regularly seek replenish our cognitive resources by resting the brain. Like the writings of Oliver Sacks on the benefits of gardens for his neurology patients, this concept suggests that in our fast-paced world, connecting with nature is not just pleasant, but truly beneficial to our health.

Endless opportunities lie just across my doorstep. Going forward, I hope to discover new terrain with my classmates and to explore insights in science on the effect of these activities on cognitive processes. After this day on the water, I am refreshed and focused for the writing ahead, fascinated by Romanticism and the modern science that confirms what I have felt all my life.

For most, a bed is a place of rest. For me, it was a battlefield. From the time I could form an argument, my bed became the site of an ongoing war between two opposing forces: “Curiosity, Intellect, and Freedom” (better known as CIF Squad) versus Order and Structure - my enemy - OS SQUAD. One side was driven by my insatiable hunger for discovery, the other firmly backed by my parents, who insisted that a made bed was the first step toward a productive day.

The CIF Squad—my team—had been dominant since fifth grade. It all started when I read Murder on the Orient Express, eagerly turning pages on my bed, constantly trying to outsmart Agatha Christie, never anticipating that all the passengers were guilty. Christie didn’t just reveal the solution; she revealed the thrill of intellectual pursuit, igniting my lifelong love for detective stories and the pursuit of truth. From that point on, my bed ceased to be a place for sleep and transformed into a sanctuary for unfiltered curiosity.

My floral patterned sheets and pillows became collateral damage in my nightly battles with new ideas. I would fall asleep in a fortress of scattered books and notes, my bed a canvas for whatever intellectual pursuit currently gripped me. One week, chess pieces would be strewn about as I tried perfecting the Scandinavian Opening; another, pages of Warren Buffet’s “Margin of Safety” equation would lie crumpled beside me, as I analysed whether Albemarle Corp. was a good stock to invest in. My mind was forever whirring, plotting its next move. The CIF Squad thrived in the chaos.

But the OS Squad, led by my parents, viewed this battlefield differently. To them, a neat bed symbolized a neat mind. “If you don’t make your bed,” my mother warned each morning, “you won’t leave this house.” The logic seemed flawed to me. Could a made bed truly symbolize clarity? To me, chaos was the birthplace of creativity. The messy pillows, the scattered chess pieces, the unfinished equations—they were evidence of thought in motion.

Then, one morning, everything changed. It was the day of my GCSE computing exam, and my room, predictably, was in disarray. Hundreds of flashcards of pseudocode, hand-drawn flowcharts, and A4 sheets were strewn across every surface, chronicling weeks of preparation. As I skimmed through my notes one last time, panic set in: I hadn’t mastered binary-to-denary conversion. I searched through the piles of paper, trying to make sense of the formulas, but it was too late. I left the house hoping that topic wouldn’t appear on the exam, but it did. I stared at the question in defeat.

In that moment, I recognized the first flaw in my system. The chaos I had once celebrated had betrayed me. My inability to impose order on my thoughts had left a crucial gap in my knowledge. That morning, I realized that intellectual freedom without structure was incomplete. My curiosity had led me to many discoveries, but it had also blinded me to my weaknesses. I had been too busy exploring to notice that some of my knowledge was shaky.

That day, I made a choice. I decided to invite the OS Squad onto the battlefield—not to give up my creative freedom, but to harness it. I started with a simple act: I made my bed. Not because I finally believed in the OS Squad’s mission, but because I saw value in their approach. A made bed became the foundation for a new kind of intellectual exploration—one that respected both freedom and discipline.

As I began to balance curiosity with structure, I found that my thoughts flowed more freely. My bed, once a symbol of opposition, became a space of harmony, where order amplified creativity rather than stifling it. The CIF and OS Squads, once adversaries, were now allies.

This lesson of balance is one I will carry with me to university. As I step into a new environment, where intellectual challenges will be greater and opportunities for exploration endless, I understand that curiosity needs a framework. The pursuit of knowledge demands both the freedom to explore and the structure to guide those explorations.

My bed, once a battlefield, is now a symbol of growth. The battles I fought over tangled sheets and misplaced pillows weren’t just about tidiness; they were about learning how to make space for my ideas. As I prepare to leave for university, I know that this new chapter will require the same balance: the ability to bring order to the chaos of new experiences, while still allowing room for curiosity to roam free.

I’ll be making my bed—this time, for myself.

Standing at an impressive five feet and six inches, weighing in the 0.16 percentile at an imposing ninety-seven pounds, and sporting a whopping seventy-five-pound bench press personal record that could probably rival Arnold Schwarzenegger’s, I’ve always felt the need to supplement my Herculean physical capabilities with a strong mind. To me, a strong mind required strong opinions, so I developed an obsession for finding a right answer to everything.

The trolley problem was one of the dilemmas that I came across in my search for correct answers, and after having wrestled with it alone in my room for nearly an hour, I firmly believed that I had successfully beat the gray area out of it. The unquestionable, indisputable, undeniable answer was to let the train run along its original path, letting the group of five die. Pulling the lever would mean actively choosing to kill the one person on the other track, and nobody should have the right to play God and decide who lives and who dies.

So when Rishi asked about the trolley problem during a drive to breakfast one morning, I proudly presented this explanation of the unquestionable, indisputable, undeniable answer. But my passengers disagreed—they claimed that the priority should be to save as many lives as possible. I could sense my position starting to waver as they elaborated, and I felt increasingly uncomfortable. I hated ambiguity. I was so hell-bent on forming firm views and defending them because—writing from experience—it’s incredibly easy to be forgotten in group settings with a physical presence as insignificant as mine, and I believed that asserting myself mentally was the only way that I could avoid being overlooked. Therefore, as soon as I could feel my certainty slipping away, I doubled down on my stance, initiating a stubborn back-and-forth argument that achieved nothing other than killing everybody else’s desire to continue conversing.

The train wreck (pun intended) of a discussion was still on my mind when I came home that day. Scrolling through various Quora forums, I was astounded at the absence of any consensus answer. For every post supporting my idea that pulling the lever would be an act of murder, there was another that called this perspective selfish, insisting that the decision should be based on the greater good rather than the individual’s conscience. This was the first time that I had attempted to tackle a dilemma by processing other opinions rather than fighting the problem in solitude, and seeing such a split between the people of Quora forced me to recognize that the correct answer I was in pursuit of didn’t really exist. I wasn’t right, but I wasn’t wrong either; rather, there was inherent complexity in the problem because fundamental moral values inevitably vary among different people. I had always failed to understand this because I believed it would be at odds with my emphasis on being opinionated, but the people of Quora seemed to embrace ambiguity without forsaking their own ideas. This was important—they used their strong convictions with the goal of providing insight and understanding into different perspectives, rather than simply bashing each other in the fruitless endeavor of looking for a singular correct answer.

Having resigned from my fight against gray areas, I strive to emulate the people of Quora in my transition to a college community colored by people from all over the globe. I look forward to contributing to discussions in classes, dorms, and dining halls by continuing to take pride in voicing my beliefs, while simultaneously learning from these conversations by applying my newfound appreciation for complexity to allow new understandings of diverse perspectives to coexist with those beliefs. I’m eager to sit at a table and chat with someone who would pull the lever, then walk out of the dining hall still in disagreement, but with the intricate understanding that both of us are equally correct and incorrect.

I had no idea that a fictional character would change my life forever.

As I made my way to the audition for a place in the All Region 24 Orchestra, I suddenly found myself shaking, not being able to hold and drink the warm water that my mother gave to me without dropping it over my white dress shirt and black tie. “Can you drive slower, amma,” I would ask her as if it would help my nervousness fade away. My hands shook during the audition, and my mind raced faster than the notes. Before I knew it, I walked out of that audition room, the sting of disappointment following me throughout the mustering hallway filled with sounds of outstanding performances from all directions.

I walked through the front doors of my house with slumped shoulders, every note from the audition replaying in my mind. It felt as if I'd lost not just an audition, but my confidence and passion for music altogether. As I climbed up the stairs, each step heavier than the last, my brother Varun called out, pulling me from the fog of despair. “Come watch this,” he said, switching on the TV. Reluctantly, I sat down, unaware that the show he’d chosen - one I’d always ignored - would soon shift my entire perspective.

As the screen lit up with vivid colors and spirited music, I was immediately entrenched as I saw young Pokemon trainer Ash Ketchum and his partner, Pikachu, facing off against the world’s best with Varun sitting by my side, a silent promise I wasn’t in this journey alone. As I watched Ash’s hopes crumble in a hard-fought battle, it felt eerily similar to my own defeat that day. His heartache mirrored the disappointment that had weighed on me since my audition. But what struck me wasn’t the loss - it was how Ash got back up, dusted himself off, and, with a smile, promised to try again. Varun glanced at me, with a knowing smile on his face. “See, it's not about the loss, but how you handle it.”

With Ash’s resilience in mind, I approached my next audition differently. Everyday brought new frustrations - missed notes, sore fingers, and endless hours of repetitive practice. I recorded myself daily, forcing myself to confront the rusty, unenchanting ‘screeches’ grieving from my tattered instrument. Late nights blurred into early mornings, as I practiced half-awake from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m. Through diligent practice, I ultimately was selected and given the opportunity to play the pieces that I’ve always dreamed of playing such as Vivaldi’s La Stravaganza and Beethoven’s A Song of Joy. Varun’s simple act of sharing that episode of Pokemon did more than entertain me; it instilled in me a lifelong lesson of resilience.

As I stand on the precipice of college life with Ash’s lesson etched in my heart, I am ready to embrace the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead. As I strive to become an orthopedic specialist, I know the journey will not be without its hurdles - long nights studying, difficult surgeries, and inevitable setbacks. Like Ash, I want to inspire others to view setbacks as stepping stones. At school, I’ve begun mentoring younger musicians who struggle with performance anxiety, sharing my story of resilience and encouraging them to keep going. A memorable moment was helping Aditya, a freshman who was struggling with an audition by reassuring him success isn’t without its failures. Seeing his face light up after his selection, I realized how powerful these morals can be. I plan to expand this mentorship to freshmen and other students by speaking every morning to the school of an inspirational quote to start their day as well as establishing podcasts open for any student. By sharing the lessons I’ve learned, I hope to build a community where perseverance is celebrated, and no challenge feels too big to overcome.

Players kept it simple: “Are you blind?!” The coaches got creative: “Check your voicemail, ref; you missed every call!” The parents managed to utilize a certain four-letter word as a noun, verb, and adjective, hurling the profanity over the plexiglass boards. Eleven years in the sport had toughened me against hockey sticks and rubber stones. But words? In all their various forms, the words hurt.

It was my fourth game as a referee, and I had blown another call, this time leading to a game-altering goal. I decided to stall in my dressing room and allow the angry masses to dissipate before making my walk of shame to the parking lot. This meant I had a few moments to commiserate with my referee partner. Usually, it would be something cliché about growing thicker skin or not being paid enough. But this time my partner Mark surprised me. “[Name], the words hurt less once they’re less true. Don’t get discouraged; get better.”

I went home and pulled up the game’s replay on LiveBarn. Though a highlight reel to some squirt’s remote grandparent, the video footage was, for me, a comedy of errors. I watched the play unfold, seeing how I had missed multiple calls because of poor positioning. I cringed, seeing how I hesitated to call a tripping penalty, only definitively blowing my whistle once pressured by the uproar that thundered from the bleachers above.

I resolved to fix these errors in the next two games, and the mistakes I committed in games five and six, I corrected in games seven and eight, and so on. I also asked Mark for tips on maintaining positioning and sightlines, and I got myself into mid-season form, hustling to the red and blue lines in order to see and make the correct calls. By the end of the season, I was hitting all the right notes with my whistle. I was enjoying my work, and the insults had lost their sting. Mark’s prophecy was fulfilled.

In my second year, only twelve of us level-one referees returned; the other twenty-three had quit, citing verbal abuse as the reason. I was intent on solving this problem. We referees are authorized to suspend and eject unruly players, but doing so just escalated hostilities, perpetuating the endless barrage of slander directed towards us.

I took a different approach – the handshake. Having participated in 355 post-game handshake lines as a player, I knew the impossibility of asking a competitor to share a fist-bump with the enemy, especially just seconds after the ceasefire. So, I pondered, what if we reversed the sequence? Would starting with something friendly make it psychologically incongruous to then be mean and nasty?

I began the next few games by extending a simple handshake and smile to each of the coaches. The early results were promising. Calls were still under dispute, but instead of spitting vitriol or muttering snide comments, coaches addressed me by name and made respectful appeals. So I doubled down. More handshakes, more smiles, more humanizing. I began showing up early to games, seeking out every coach, player, and parent. I offered my open hand, saying to them, “I’m [Name] Oh, your referee for today. I love this game of hockey, and I’m going to give it my very best to make the game safe, fun, and fair.” And without asking for it, I got their best in return.

Today, I’m a level-three referee, and I’m often paired with newer referees who feel unmotivated and unappreciated. I tell them what Mark once told me. I encourage them to stay strong, learn, and get better, and I pass on my humble learnings:

First, find yourself a Mark. You’ll always have a grandparent or friend who can show you the easy way out. Find yourself someone who will lead you to the hard way back in.

Second, be patient with yourself. The whistle is your instrument, and it takes time to learn how to play it.

And third, shake a lot of hands. Shake every hand you can, and let them know who you are.

As I watched my father’s smoky silhouette in the backyard, I could hear my 8-year-old self whisper urgently, "We have to catch up. Andy won’t wait." Grandma was our Andy. My father, with his best Buzz Lightyear voice, reassured me, "We’ll catch Andy and be his favorites again." Back then, no matter how dedicated we were to our role, unlike Woody and Buzz, we never really believed that Andy would leave us. It all seemed so perfect—until the day we lost her.

As my father gently caressed my grandmother’s hand with his calloused fingers, I watched her eyelids softly rest. In just three months, overgrown grass and my father’s countless cigarette butts replaced the laughter that once filled our backyard. What happened to the man who could be Buzz Lightyear to my Woody and Jackson Storm to my McQueen, all in the same day, just to transform back into my father by sundown? The physical loss of my grandmother left an invisible wound on my father’s mental health. Determined to ease his pain, I was seized by one question: How could I sew an invisible wound?

To find the answer, I delved into behavioral psychology, creating a list of methods for healing grief. I deconstructed stages of mourning into smaller, more digestible parts to form pathways of acceptance, expression, and connection. I learned about the brain and heart, the tangible affecting the intangible. Using what I have learned and repurposing the core principles of narrative therapy, I crafted a 'grief support loop' for my father’s experience. With a strategy developed, I now had to take the most important step. I knew that my father would only want help if he understood how his way of coping with grief was impacting his loved ones. So, I sat him down and modeled vulnerability by opening up first.

I stood there, voice shaking. "Every time you yelled at Mom or shut yourself in that cloud of smoke, I felt like I was losing you too."

His response was tight, distant. "Did you forget..." he knew I understood the reason for his pain, "I just… I just cannot talk about her now."

I looked at him, the silence between us suffocating, but I held my ground. "I know it's hard, Dad. I don’t want to force you to confront your feelings. Let’s just talk about stories we recall."

He stared at the floor for what felt like forever, then slowly nodded, his voice barely above a whisper. "Okay. Let's try."

That moment set the grief support loop into motion.

STEP 1: Storytelling Sessions 
Schedule: Twice a week. 
Goal: Help my father externalize his grief. 
Activity: I asked him to retell memories of his mother through Buzz’s perspective.

STEP 2: Role Reversals 
Schedule: Twice a week. 
Goal: Help my father transform his pain into a manageable narrative. 
Activity: I played Buzz; my father played Andy, directing the scenes.

STEP 3: Creating New Narratives 
Schedule: Twice a week. 
Goal: Help my father honor his mother’s memory while moving forward. 
Activity: We created new stories without Andy.

Each cycle lasted a week. There was guilt in every story I helped him rewrite. The memories, the emotions — I still felt pain for myself. Progress was slow. Nevertheless, cycle by cycle, as my father began to rediscover his happiness, I found mine. I wanted to mend invisible wounds beyond those in my backyard. And so, as schools invited me to speak, I learned to tailor the mental health workshops, be that through integrating interactive activities or creating safe spaces for open discussions, to the unique stories that made up the audience.

Ultimately, what I’ve realized is simple: no matter how broken someone seems, there’s always a path to reach them if you’re willing to walk beside them—step by step, story by story. As I move forward, I’m ready to help others process their stories, navigating the plot twists of their lives, until they too can move to infinity and beyond.

“I’m not letting you race this Saturday because you don’t show enough emotion.”

Coach Barb’s words stung as I contemplated the year and a half I’d spent coxing during practice.

For reference, I’m someone who’d rather spend a day reading the “Tiny Love Stories” section of the NYTimes than scream my head off at Six Flags with my friends.

So, I wondered: did I really have the potential to be a great coxswain given my naturally quiet disposition?

I reminded myself why I’d joined crew in the first place. Yes, it was to escape the swim team (they have to get up at 6 a.m., but we don’t), but more importantly, I wanted to develop my initiative, and above all, courage.

So, for the remainder of the fall, I asked my friends for suggestions after each practice. As soon as I opened myself to more feedback, Sylvania mentioned she wanted me to be harsher with my critiques, while Ophelia asked for some external motivation during a race. Which is why the next week, I told them that they would all have to row a grueling 2k in practice if they slacked.

As winter began, I made a mental list of every area I wanted to work on, such as expanding my vocal range, timing my words with each stroke, and using my choir experience to crescendo during heated moments.

YouTube videos of coxswains slowly became my new favorite procrastination strategy. I’d also listen to fellow coxswains and my friends’ favorite coxswain recordings on car rides, including one where the coxswain repeatedly yelled, “Let’s get on a plane to nationals!” Each video became a learning opportunity for me to address each of my weak points.

When springtime came and Coach Barb heard my latest coxswain recording, she took me aside again. But this time, she said, “I love how excited you got during that last hundred. None of the other coxswains showed this much emotion while rowing.”

***

“Check your email, [Name]–Ms. Green said you’re conducting today!”

My jaw dropped as I read the email. Did I have zero experience? Yes. But was I going to seize this opportunity nonetheless? Also yes.

That afternoon, I scurried to the chorus room and quickly got to work with my fellow chorists. I had trouble holding and ending the last note, and it took me half a dozen attempts to give a soft, clean, cutoff. But eventually, we got there!

When I got home, I shut myself in my bedroom and searched for video tutorials for choral conducting on – you guessed it – YouTube. I learned how the shape of my hands, the speed at which they move, and the arc of my rebound are all crucial to communicating my interpretation of the song.

A few weeks before we started to rehearse ‘Omnia Sol’, I took the sheet music and listened to six Spotify recordings of the songs on repeat while studying the annotations from the sheet music. As I documented the minute differences in each interpretation, I noticed that one version had a decrescendo in the climax while another version got louder instead! Wild!

***

At first glance, rowing and conducting a choir don’t seem to have much in common, but I believe both have helped me grow tremendously, not just as an individual, but also in terms of my ability to bring people together. Whether we’re rowing in sync or singing on beat, harmony stems from proactivity.

But this belief isn’t something that I just apply to crew and choir – whether I’m investigating the role of endogenous retroviruses in a cancer lab with fellow researchers or singing for Alzheimer’s patients in a hospital, I’ll strive to be a leader who drives and unifies the people I serve. In college, I want to keep stepping up in daunting situations but also prepare myself for these challenges through endless learning.

**The Sahara Desert — My Imagination**

You’re standing in the middle of the Sahara desert. You pick up a singular piece of sand. The sun blazes overhead, casting long shadows across the endless expanse of golden dunes. You’re trapped. Every 1 million years, you pick up a single grain of sand. You’re stuck in the desert until you pick up all of the sand. Every single piece. And suddenly, the realization hits you: the time you’ll spend in the desert is a mere millisecond compared to eternity.

*****

**Some Highway Exit Off I-485**

A homeless man in tattered clothes desperately holds up a sign: seeking human kindness. 
“Don’t make eye contact,” my father warns sternly. “He’s not your problem.”
But why, I wonder as I anxiously try to avoid the man’s gaze. 
Deep down, a tingling sense of guilt kindles a spark.

*****

My life can be summed up by perplexing conundrums. Pursue happiness, or pursue money? Live for others, or live for myself? As my father made abundantly clear, the answer is money and self.

But I pondered, and the tiny spark inside of me fanned into a flame.

*****

**My room, July 2022**

A 16 year old boy stumbles across a poem that will change his life forever and ultimately, lead to his death:

“Only one life,
Twill soon be past;
Only what’s done
For Christ will last.”
— C.T. Studd

The Sahara Desert became a prolific part of my life after I read Studd’s profound words. The conundrum of life suddenly became perfectly clear, yet frightening: you get a millisecond to make a difference for eternity. Thus, shouldn’t we take every chance we get to make an impact with our lives?

I died the night I read that poem. My old self was crucified along with his selfish ambition and in his place arose a new man. The fanning flame inside of me erupted into an all-consuming zeal to make my life count. Life was no longer about me or my worthless pursuits. Now, it was all about others.

At first, I turned to my church. While my contributions there are important, I realized impact doesn’t need to come through an organization. In fact, what really quenches my thirst are the acts that nobody sees.

*****

**A Red Light At a Traffic Stop**

I’m sitting in his car when Rickie, my youth counselor, rolls down his window and hands two dollars to a homeless person. It seems insignificant, but for the first time in my life, I looked at a homeless person.

I didn’t know it then, and neither did Rickie, but that moment revealed to me how I can make an eternal difference. Because from that day on, I also started keeping cash in my car.

*****

**The Sahara Desert — Right Now**

In a journey that was supposed to take me to a college campus, I somehow find myself in the Sahara Desert again. I’m trapped. But this time, it’s different. I look up at the sun and I see a blazing spark. I bend down and pick up a grain of sand. But it's no longer sand. It’s a grain of knowledge, kindness, and love. I take a look around the desert and let the exploration begin.

Suddenly, I feel a tap on my shoulder and I turn around to face a young girl — visibly broken. Her eyes are sunken and she's lost. All around, the cactus stare and the tumbleweed tumble, in a state of indifference. But I have compassion. I look in her eyes and hand her a singular piece of sand. Immediately, the desert disappears and I’m back home.

**The Sahara Desert - 100 Years In The Future**

I’m actually dead now, but as I look down on the young girl (now an old woman on the brink of death) and see the good that she has done through her life, I smile and rest. Mission accomplished.

Quiet. I always found comfort in quiet. While other children shrieked around the playground, I enjoyed solitary play with my dolls and calm pretend tea parties with my parents.

November 6th, 2008 – my little brother Max was born and the peaceful solitude of my only-child days was shattered. While I enjoyed quietly brushing my doll's hair for hours, Max screamed in frustration after only one or two puzzle attempts. Though I was assured crying toddlers were normal, I suspected Max was different. Every tantrum seemed more intense, each day filled with more and more tears.

Being in public with Max was especially hard. At the grocery store, other shoppers turned their carts while we shopped for milk and bread with a screaming child in tow. Walking down the street, families avoided eye contact so they didn’t have to encounter Max. Each venture outside filled me with apprehension and shame.

I felt responsible for protecting Max, shielding him from the judgmental glares of others. When we learned the correct terminology - a “mood disorder” - I spent hours each day filling my iPad with rudimentary Google research. I learned that the main cause of Max’s tantrums was his inability to express his feelings. So, I taught Max how to manage his frustrations, validating the intensity of his feelings while also modeling appropriate reactions. We practiced relaxation practices like deep breathing, expression techniques by using words to convey wishes, and self-soothing strategies like playing with fidgets. As the years passed, I learned terms like cognitive behavioral therapy and emotion-focused coping mechanisms, now understanding the science behind his treatment. And along the way, I learned how to adjust to having a sibling who had mental health issues, having my quiet life turned into a circus.

As I learned to read Max’s cues, I started to notice the Maxes in my class - kids who sat alone at lunch, struggled with their schoolwork, or went simply unnoticed. I began sharing my lunch with Theo, who had autism, tutoring Chloe through science, and teaching Michele how to dance. Every day, I made it my intention to share my friendship with one more new person, my effort to make everyone feel that they had at least one friend.

Though Max started to grow out of his tantrums, he faced other challenges. He was never invited to birthday parties or play dates. No friends' names were mentioned after school and he often came home without a smile. It hurt to see him so alone, just because he couldn’t pick up social cues or solve 2+2 as quickly as others. I began to also see the detrimental effects it had on him – how he started to backtrack, lashing out and screaming every day.

Soon, I started an anti-bullying Instagram page, speaking about Max’s experiences with bullying. I posted about bullying and noninclusive environments and how they affect people’s mental health. Offline, I taught Max how to listen to others instead of always speaking, how to strike up a conversation at lunch, and how to be patient and take turns on the playground. And as my account gained traction, Max also found his confidence, making friends with other kids just as special as him. After each school release, he now ran home with a smile, eager to tell me about his adventures with Lorenzo and Nico.

By helping Max grow, I grew too. I learned the importance of a good support system, the value of inclusivity, and every person’s capacity for empathy. Today, I look forward to each grocery store visit with Max. Instead of tantrums, we share conversations about what we’re feeling and happily rank our favorite snacks. Judgmental sneers are replaced with smiles and waves. I’ll always treasure my only child days. But through Max, I found not just the joy of a sibling but the power of kindness.

“What’s a ching-chong doing here?” Samantha spat as she glared at me, the only Asian person in the room.

I bit my tongue and reminded myself that Samantha wasn’t a normal 8-year-old. In fact, that was why I’d chosen to spend my Friday night at the Orange County Rescue Mission, a homeless shelter.

I was there for Bot-AZ, a program I’d founded to expand robotics education in disadvantaged communities. The ability to innovate and collaborate through robotics has fostered my passion for engineering, one I hoped to spread that night.

I’d been so excited to bring Bot-AZ to OCRM, that I’d spent the previous summer planning the perfect 90-minute workshop. We’d start with a brief, but riveting presentation on VEX robotics programs, followed by a 40-minute clawbot driving challenge, and 40 more minutes of programming brain teasers!

However, when I showed off pictures of my award-winning robots, the kids just blinked and yawned. One student, Carlos, sulked in the back (more interested in picking his nose than in what I had to say). Another boy, Mark, rolled his eyes and asked to use the bathroom. Fifteen. Times.

But I was determined to flip their mindsets.

Realizing that I had to change my approach, I cut my presentation short and pulled out two clawbots.

“Who thinks they can drive a robot through these obstacles the fastest?” I said, pointing to a maze of cones.

“WE get to drive them?!” exclaimed Samantha, her sassy disinterest replaced by eager curiosity.

“Yup, and you guys will be competing against each other.” I announced, watching wicked, enthusiastic grins spread across the students’ faces.

***
“WOW! 39 seconds! That’s a new record!” I high-fived Mark and showed him my stopwatch. 
“YESSSS!” yelled Mark, pumping his fist in the air.

Yet as he bolted to scribble down his name in big, red letters on the whiteboard, I noticed that Carlos still refused to leave his corner.

So, during the programming challenge, I grabbed a laptop and sat down next to him. He shot me a judgemental look, probably thinking “GO AWAY!! Can’t this girl take a hint??”.
Determined to get another 180 that night, I asked Carlos, “We know how to make the robot go forward…how do you think we can make it go backwards?”

“Just reverse the block. Duh.” Carlos mumbled, battling the curious smile creeping across his face.

By 8:00 PM, Carlos had become one of Bot-AZ’s biggest fans. In fact, he even teared up when we told him it was time to go (a problem I resolved by giving everyone Dum-Dums). 
And as I waved goodbye to the rest of the students, Linda, one of the parents, approached me with a kind smile.

“You know, most of the people here at the OC Rescue Mission have been in and out of jail. We’ve all struggled with addiction, homelessness, broken families. And I just wanted to thank you for giving our kids this opportunity.”

***
I want to flip the narrative that robots are elements of some distant future. Robots are present and impactful in our society, from the robotic servers zipping through Korean barbeque restaurants to the rehabilitation devices humming in labs. And by flipping society’s perspective on robotics, I hope to also flip the idea of who can be an engineer.

To me, an engineer looks like Carlos with his quiet curiosity, Mark with his energetic competitiveness, and even Samantha with her—let’s just say—fierce confidence.
Because as I’ve grown, I’ve seen my own perspective on engineering flip.

An engineer’s job is to create, but my dreams don’t end with creating something tangible.
I hope to create a world that welcomes innovation with open arms. 
A world where robotic rehabilitation ventures outside the lab and into homes. 
A world where every student is given the chance to dream as big as I have.
And, hey.

If I can dream it, I can do it.

Swoosh, long strips of pasta swished through the metal machine as I twisted the handle. This pasta maker, standing prominently on the front cover of my recipe journal, was a relic from my New Jersey home. My story unfolded from there, stretching, adapting, and taking shape among different cultures.

After relocating to Hong Kong and then Shanghai, I learned to make noodles, pasta’s Asian counterpart, at cooking lessons from my new school and quickly added some basic noodle-making techniques to my recipe book. Despite my Chinese heritage, I overheard people quite a few times calling me a banana (yellow on the outside, white inside) or a gweilo (literal meaning, a foreign devil).

Starting high school in England during the pandemic was equally challenging. In addition to adjusting to life in a boarding house, I was greeted with slurs or insults on the streets for bringing the “Chink virus.” When I explained my American identity, my classmates looked at me quizzically because I was not the blue-eyed, blonde-haired type they expected. In my recipe book, I drew noodles shaped like question marks.

Troubled by my identity, cooking, and making noodles in particular, provided a mental escape. The tactile experience of working with the dough was calming, easing the nervousness I felt. I spent hours tinkering with various flour types, water content, and salt concentrations in the noodle dough. At that time I was also tackling the BiangBiang noodles, a variety often found in Northwestern China, and I failed multiple times to pull the dough into long, thick, belt-shaped strips. Soaking the dough in oil overnight proved useful, making it much more resistant to breaking. I jotted down this line in my recipe book: patience; you need extra dose of patience.

In the beginning, making noodles served as an emotional outlet. Later, as my recipe book accompanied me in the exploration of my evolving identity, it stood for lessons learned as to how adaptable and resilient people could become from the kneading of life.

As I grew bolder in my cooking skills, I improvised on the fly. I tried adding butter to spicy garlic noodles and created a fusion of Chinese and Western flavors that wowed the palates of my family and friends. I replaced the hot chili sauce on the BiangBiang noodles with Provolone cheese melts, making it another delicious encounter between the Western and the East. Through these culinary adventures, I discovered what really set noodles and pasta apart was the added ingredients and the processing methods. Both were essentially flour at heart.

Appreciating our common bond of humanity made me more compassionate and empathetic towards people who are different from me, be it skin color, cultural heritage, or socioeconomic status.

To entertain my elderly residents of the town, I gave up lunch breaks and weekends to play cello solo or in quartets. For young pupils who could not afford tutors, I taught them STEM subjects in primary science club and found for the first time teaching was more rewarding than learning. In donating clothing and books to organizations in Hong Kong that help the domestic helpers, I tried to bring some comfort to these women who left their home and children behind to earn a living.

As dough needs time to release its gluten, I discovered that identity, like noodles, can be versatile and strengthened with time and experience.

The various chapters of my recipe book have taught me to appreciate the diversity of human experience and respect the uniqueness in each individual. These qualities will help me bridge differences, foster understanding, and promote collaboration within my future communities at college and beyond.

When I start college in America next year, it will be like returning home after a long journey. This time, I am confident to add a new chapter to my recipe book and confident that America is big enough to embrace all that I bring.

My mom got her PhD when she turned 35. She had worked in teaching universities and relocated to an R1 school in 2017. She divorced twice, remarried in 2017, and had two more new babies. She got 20 awards in five years, including the Distinguished Paper Award for the best security conference. She also delivered a presentation at the most prestigious meeting for all PIs -the NSF biennial SaTC PI meeting in 2024. She is managing a 20-person team, but the dark side for me is that she has no time to talk with me. I have registered in five schools and had challenges finding fixed friends in school. I am the one who got bullied because of my race and poor English. One boy told me to go back to China, and one boy asked me for money to avoid being kicked. I always remember the first day at a new school.

I nervously stepped into the classroom 211. The teacher started class and asked us to introduce ourselves. After seven other students, it was my turn; I began, "Hel-loo, me na-me es Peei Heng Ni; I come-China." "Your name is Pee?" Laughter erupted as I said my introduction, which had the worst pronunciation ever and a Chinese accent. The teacher quickly stopped the students from continuing. However, it was too late. My classmates' laughter stung in my heart, their snickering resonated deep within me.

I had only immigrated from China just a few weeks before school started. My mom only taught me the basics of English, like "Hello," "Thank you," and "You're welcome." But after that painful day at school, I knew I was far from literate. My mom was too busy to help me study, so I took it upon myself to study past 8 pm with children's books, dictionaries, and the Internet. Every night, I sat on my bed, cross-referencing definitions, learning to pronounce unfamiliar sounds, and matching words to classwork. One evening, my mom walked into my room while I was studying and said softly, 'Good job, son. I am very proud of you.' Those words were like a beacon of hope. I got the 'Most Improved' award at the end of that semester. These moments of encouragement have left an important mark on me, reinforcing the belief that hard work never betrays you.

Since my mom was too busy and negligent to me, I had to handle the student's bullying issue by myself. I first tried to report them to principals, but sadly, it did not work and made me more lonely. I chose to help other students and be kind to them by teaching them math. After I made several friends, the unfriendly buddies chose other people to bully. By helping my classmates with mathematics, I received invaluable friendships.

My desire to help others extended beyond the walls of my school. I created a free website to educate people on what to do after their sensitive information is leaked. This website, equipped with a program that filters out sensitive information being sold on hacking forums and automatically sends emails to those affected, has made a significant impact. To date, it has sent over 1.6 million emails and collected over 100 million pieces of data, providing crucial support to those who have been hacked. My work in this field continues, with the website now sending over 50,000 emails daily to assist those in need.

I am sensitive to what is happening in the world by building a free website to check whether AI-generated texts are misinformation/fake or not. Also, I investigated the pager and walkie-talkie explosion events in my class project. Sensitivity to the world's trends/needs will inspire good research after submitting one paper to the ACM FSE conference.

I am diligent in pursuing my academic success after taking care of my younger sister and brother. I enjoy learning as a life-long learner.

As I passed the sick or injured departing the trail by donkey, I knew the thousands of steps ahead of me would be life-changing. Known as “wa waca” to the porters who paved our way, I persisted in spirit and body as the youngest hiker on the Inca trail that summer. Through the calm nights and daily challenges, it is only here that I document the 7,972 feet of inner growth that makes me who I am today.

On the trail at age 6, I faced 8 to 11-hour hikes daily as I struggled to maintain the excitement I had so clearly begun my journey with. Perceiving the path as unimaginably long seemed greater than anything I could accomplish. However, as time passed, I began to learn my strength. A task that seemed far beyond my capabilities was conquered one step at a time. In the mountains faced today, I have earned confidence. I know that a positive attitude and persistence can accomplish even the most lofty goals. As we slept in tents and struggled through hot, mosquito-infested days, the reality of a 96-hour hike became apparent. I needed to become an expert in flexibility and grit. I no longer ruminated on discomfort or exhaustion but welcomed these things as a byproduct of my slow success. This mindset has made me an expert in overcoming obstacles and has grown my flexibility and grit to this day.

While some say that joy is found in the journey, not the destination, I’d add that the people beside you make all the difference. On the third day, my family and I embarked on the infamous Dead Woman’s Pass, which reached the highest point on the trail. As we climbed the 6,000 stairs and 4,000 feet, I began to have surging headaches, and yet we could not stop until we had overcome the mountain. I relied heavily on my family for altitude medication along with physical and emotional support as we climbed. Just as we passed the summit, I felt the energy of youth return to me. However, as I remembered the incline, I understood how I would not be where I was without my family’s support. I turned around and joined my Mema (Grandma) and Papo(Grandpa) at the back of the line, supporting them in a tedious trek over rocks and boulders. These obstacles taught me how to contribute meaningfully to group and individual goals, be vulnerable and lean on others, and the value of self-sacrifice for another. I highly value group settings, continually aiming to make the journey of others optimistic by establishing trust and connection along the way.

I recall my Papo and I cheering our victory one evening and slipping away to explore the path ahead. Our giggling, sweaty faces peeked around the mountain and dreamed of what lay in store for tomorrow. Today, I feel rooted in gratitude for where I am while also looking forward to the future. While some wait for others to lead, I take the first step toward the next checkpoint. My curiosity pushes me to be an innovative, inquisitive learner. I hunger for the unknown, and as I dive deeper into concepts, I am persistent and steadfast in my pursuit of knowledge.

The Peruvian mountains left me with memorable images of beauty, as well as inner strength, excitement for life, and the desire to help others. I will eagerly bring to my next journey a drive to keep exploring, my inquisitive mind, my gratitude for the moment and fellow travelers, and my inner leader, persistence, and grit. I know what lies ahead will be beautiful.

Slumping on the bed, gasping for air, I begged, “Mom, give me the sleeping pills– I can’t tolerate this anymore.” In that moment, I would have given anything for just one deep breath.

Since birth, I have struggled with asthma, but by age 10, it seemed to vanish. At 15, this problem surged back as a consequence of Delhi’s escalating pollution. Walking at night through the streets of Lajpat, deadlifting 40kg at gym, and most heartbreakingly, playing as libero in volleyball, all ended abruptly. Although my friends were supportive, I soon felt them drift away. Each wave—whether crippling asthma, weight gain, or estrangement from friends—pushed me deeper into the abyss.

Growing up, I saw my mom worshiping God daily. One afternoon, curious while stuck at home during volleyball practice, I probed her, “Why all this formality?” She replied, “It relieves me, knowing someone’s there in tough times.” Intrigued by her answer, I began exploring spirituality. I started visiting the temple—melodic chants of Lord Krishna and fragrant incense curling through the air, grew my confidence. This newfound strength motivated me to confront my biggest challenge: asthma.

I began my journey by practicing breathing exercises from YouTube. Initially, I struggled—even holding breath for longer than ten seconds felt like drowning in slow motion. Gradually, I saw progress with my lung capacity; I could hold my breath for 10 seconds, then 15, and eventually reached 30 seconds. I began daily visits at DDA Park, starting with 100 meters of walking and steadily extending the distance. While I adapted to walking, running was much harder; when I started running, I felt the shortness of breath, fast heartbeats, and sometimes even fainting. Therefore, to make my body immune from these hurdles, I increased my meditation and exercise routine and made the toughest decision: sacrifice eating Momos.

Despite my endeavors, I was inconsistent. The pressure to excel in trigonometry and geometry in school seemed overwhelming. Each time I made progress, I’d slip back into frustration and guilt over schoolwork. I was angry at myself, wondering, “What’s the point if I’m failing at both?” In those moments, I leaned extensively towards spirituality: meditation became my way of finding stillness in the chaos.

One day, I noticed a child playing volleyball alone, propped up by a tree. I approached him and asked why. He confided that his skill inadequacies led to his exclusion from the school team. The fact that he is playing even after being excluded from the team made me see myself in him. Thus, I started teaching him volleyball after finishing my running sessions. With each technique we practiced, his joy ignited a spark within me, pushing me to remain consistent for two continuous years.

Having initially been barely able to run 100 meters, I never imagined competing in a 10 km marathon and getting acknowledgment from the state government. As I was near the finishing line, the crowd faded away—it was just me, with the memories of my battle with asthma.

This journey gave me a lesson in creativity and innovation. Whether it was solving coding problems in hackathons or organizing school events on a low budget, I found every obstacle as an invitation to innovate. From inventing special breathing exercises to devising ways to teach volleyball with limited physical ability, my adversities made me think out of the box. I realized that creativity was not confined to art or science: rather finding unconventional solutions to problems life throws at you.

Equipped with these experiences, I look forward to receiving more invitations for innovation in research, volleyball, and service of humanity at college.

I navigated through hutong alleyways, searching for sugary tangren figurines, on the lookout for remnants of my Beijing childhood.

Amidst once-familiar streets, I spotted her—an inconspicuous street vendor with a small styrofoam stand displaying finely spun figurines of bunnies and puppies, their glossy sugar surfaces sparkling in the summer sun. When she noticed my interest, her face lit up. She eagerly explained that her maltose was made fresh every morning and even offered to let me blow into the straw. I savored this moment, a connection to a Beijing I feared was lost forever.

I pointed to my zodiac sign, the golden pig, and watched in awe as her calloused fingers deftly shaped the hot sugar paste into a piglet. Her fingers smooth from years of burns, she quickly inserted a straw into its belly, twisting up a tiny tail as the body puffed into shape. I attempted to explain how, in the U.S., crafts like this are considered artisanal treasures. But I stumbled over the words in my rusty dialect, unsure from years of underuse. I had become a foreigner in my hometown.

She didn’t judge though. Instead, she smiled and patiently corrected my erhuayin, the distinctive "er" sound, recognizing the effort in my fading Beijing accent.

—

The aroma of braised abalone wafted through the air as I entered the estate of Master Wei, a former state banquet chef. I carefully bowed and seated myself as I gazed around the siheyuan, the courtyard house enclosed by intricately carved wooden eaves and red pillars, a stark contrast to the bustling Beijing modernity beyond its walls.

Master Wei’s hands trembled as he spoke about historical traditions and culinary trends. I caught every other word—cutlery, diversified development, simmering. For those I couldn’t, I stealthily turned to my phone under the table. Old Chinese expressions and chef jargon swept into my brain. Master Wei smiled as he watched my desperate translations into Baidu. I still struggled to understand, but his smile said more than words could. As the night continued, I felt more connected to both worlds.

Before we left, Master Wei dipped his hands in his teacup and shook mine. I was taken aback. A washing of hands before a significant action signifies respect and purity. In that handshake, he recognized my effort to engage with my roots, even when the language felt distant.

—

More than ordinary changes quietly revealed themselves at the family dinner table. Eryilaolao’s hair, once salt-and-pepper, was now completely white. These changes, barely noticeable day by day, reminded me of the years I'd been away from my great-aunt. Had I changed just as drastically in her eyes?

As I drank in each wrinkle, I realized that each detail was an opportunity to reconnect. “Remember when I ran around during New Year celebrations?” I asked, watching her eyes twinkle. As we exchanged stories, she laughed, reminiscing about my childhood and sharing tales of her adventures. Her laughter reminded me that while time passed, our bond was always there, under the surface, waiting to be rekindled. I pinky-promised to stay connected through video calls, bridging the gap between the person I had become and the roots I had left behind.

—

I walked away from the vendor, clutching my little sugar pig. I departed Master Wei’s courtyard house, speechless after our handshake. I left dinner with my great-aunt, eager for our next WeChat catchup call.

Weeks later, boarding my flight back to Los Angeles, I knew my time in Beijing had done more than reconnect me to my childhood. Each farewell was not an ending but a new beginning, teaching me how to carry my lessons forward while embracing the person I am becoming. And, like the tangren in my hand, I will carry these moments with me: sweet, lasting, and full of meaning.

I’m an everyday rapper.

Well, kind of. My ‘rap’ doesn’t have much musicality to it. Instead of an album of songs, I have a OneDrive folder of PowerPoint presentations that should be slowed down by 20%. So, while others might call me a ‘speedtalker,’ I prefer ‘expeditious expounder.’

While I’m not as fast as Eminem (yet!), I still passionately articulate my favorite topics. As a true crime fanatic who just completed a 2.5-month group research project on how CNNs could help solve burglary mysteries, I was excited to present our findings to Congresswoman Kim Schrier. But, there was one problem: our prepared presentation was 10 minutes, yet Congresswoman Schrier could only stay for 5. So, I picked up the pace. With verses like, “wehadtoaugmentimagestoartificallygeneratemoredata-,” I rhythmically wove together key parts of our presentation while not omitting any crucial information.

“That was awesome,” Congresswoman Schrier said with a smile as we ended right at 5 minutes. “So much work explained so quickly.”

While walking out, a groupmate chimed, “The way you condensed the CNN layers slide was insane! I thought we’d run overtime.” I grinned, knowing that was exactly my goal. But it wasn’t rattling at the speed of light that did it. Like how many admire Eminem’s lyricism and cadence, my intentional word choice and energetic tone (perfected with a dash of speed) let me effectively communicate my key ideas, even while constrained by time.

Beyond expediency, my conversation style evokes new ideas, leading to iterations that otherwise may not have emerged. While calling my design team and brainstorming merchandise for the Mustang Math Tournament, verses flowed, ideas interweaved, and the energy in the call spiked as one suggestion followed the other – a standard meeting mimicking a rap battle. As I pitched a bizarre idea: “Imagine a Google Snake-esque theme,” excitement buzzed. “Ooh! We could color the snake into pigpen letters,” someone eagerly proposed. “Yeah! And the apples could be the dots in pigpen,” I bounced back.

Each new, unique concept only added to the collective discussion, pushing us towards our goal: a collaboratively designed competitor t-shirt. But more importantly, like how released rap songs are products of hours of lyric writing, beat experimentation, and recording, our shirt represented hours of back-and-forth brainstorming, tens of preliminary sketches, and endless rounds of feedback; a perfect representation of our combined efforts.

Still, even the best rappers know the power of a pause. Silence allows us to hear other voices, and I wanted to tap into that power. Sitting in my Key Club advisor’s room, I was jabbering about how marketing for our yard sale could be improved when I noticed a freshman, Anoushka, was silent. As someone who feared speaking up, I asked her what we could do better next year.

Although surprised by the call-out, Anoushka quickly took the floor, proposing we start donation collections months earlier – an idea we hope to put to action. Preetika then jumped in, suggesting we directly reach out to staff about donating. As I sat back, my heart swelled listening to initially timid members liven the room with fresh ideas.

Listening is as valuable as sharing. Giving everyone the stage to speak is incredibly important, as hearing varying perspectives not only lets us learn from how other thinks, but also creates a melting pot of brilliant ideas – a combination of all our bests. But, like how Dr. Dre’s support for Eminem helped him become one of the most influential hip-hop artists, sometimes it takes is a bit of encouragement to unlock a cascade of imaginative proposals. So, whenever I see a nervous kid itching to speak, I ask: “Hey! What are your thoughts on this?”

Being an expeditious expounder encourages me to approach knowledge similarly, allowing me to quickly but confidently piece together creative ideas. Intertwining my interests in computer science with environmental sciences, I’ll explain the risks of the depleting ozone layer to my peers, rapping through my presentation on my proposed prediction model. But now, I’ll also be listening. I’ll listen to the suggestions of my professors and peers as they note how my model could be made more efficiently. After all, the beauty of rap doesn’t exist solely in its creation, but in appreciating and sharing it with others.

One of my earliest memories begins with me sitting in the backseat of my dad’s car, twiddling my thumbs as he drove me home from school. My father is a man of few words—quiet, strict, and deliberate. He speaks only when he feels the weight of his lessons demands attention.

“Learn not to regret,” he would say, his eyes fixed on the road ahead. “Dawn still comes, even if you break the neck of a rooster.” To my five-year-old ears, these words felt distant and frankly confusing. I sat there in silence, staring at his broad back, trying to make sense of them. I felt a gap between us. I’d often watch through the window as my friends were embraced by their young fathers, showered with affection, while mine offered wisdom through proverbs instead of warm hugs. His words felt like riddles, not expressions of love.

Yet, I’ve learned to cherish those moments. His words became the fragile thread that linked us, something I brought with me when I moved to Irvine with my mom and sister, while he stayed in Korea for work. Here, I took on an unfamiliar role—helping my family in his absence. I would make dinner with my mom, support my sister, and sit in the living room where my dad’s empty chair remained as a reminder of how far away he felt. Staring out into the quiet woods of Meadowlark Park, I would mutter, “The dawn still comes,” reflecting on my dad’s words. As an older father, his approach to parenting was to make sure I’d be okay even if he wasn’t there. Better than okay, maybe. Sometimes, I’d hear his voice guiding me, instructing me as I encountered yet another new experience.

When I attended my first court proceeding, I watched as a boy, barely older than me, stood trembling before the judge. The courtroom was cold and intimidating; it was clear he was overwhelmed by the formality of the judicial system. Looking at him, I didn’t see a defendant pleading his innocence or guilt–he was lost, uncertain of what would come next. That moment has stuck with me. I recognized a problem: the system is too rigid, too distant from the people it’s meant to serve, especially for youth who needed guidance, not just punishment.

I didn’t know it then, but something larger was working through my mind. The proverbs my father taught me—“Character matters more than success,” “Dawn still comes”—echoed in my thoughts. I realized my father hadn’t just been teaching me how to survive life’s difficulties; he had been teaching me how to lead others through them.

His words were with me when I founded a youth court in Orange County to guide young people in ways that felt less intimidating than the rigid systems around them. It is designed to rehabilitate, to offer second chances, and help others understand their potential, much like my father’s teachings have done for me.

This summer, I visited my father in Korea and we went for a drive. This time, I sat in the front seat beside him. “I’m using your lessons to guide others now,” I told him, “just like you prepared me to.” My dad only nodded. He said he was proud of my work. I was no longer a child, he said, but a young man capable of teaching others life’s deeper truths.

As my father once said, “The nail that sticks out gets hammered down.” For a long time, I thought this meant I should blend in, and avoid drawing attention to myself. But now I understand. I am destined to be the nail that sticks out—not to be hammered down, but to create change. Through my work as a future lawyer and sociologist, I hope to lift others up, just as my father once did for me.

Every day at the bustling border checkpoint, a dozen kindergarteners waddled like ducklings from Shenzhen homes to Hong Kong schools, drowning in the crowd of merchants. The duckling in front, raising its voice to guide the rest through security guards and count each head, but having to stand on tiptoe just to hand its ID to the customer officer, was me.

This has been my daily routine as a cross-border student since I was 5. However, when I first arrived at kindergarten in Hong Kong, my Mandarin accent alienated me. My peers refused to talk to me, leaving little [Name] shuttling between crowds. I was clueless about Hong Kong culture. I was confused.

Middle school brought a shift. The landmark political movement struck in 2019. Like a cockroach, I hid silently. Though I admired the senior students’ resolve, staging sit-down protests and forming human chains filled me with insecurity. For in that moment, cross-borders, despite our Hong Kong ID, symbolized the repugnant encroachment of the mainland. One evening, I received a screenshot in a secret discord group chat – it had my name, ID number, and home address. It’s called cyber manhunt, Google said. People stared at me with strange gazes, my best friends walked away from me at school. I felt despised.

The pandemic only made it worse. After having online lessons for 2 years, I moved to live alone in a scruffy, second-hand Hong Kong flat that my parents rented abruptly. “Hell NO!” was the first thing I shouted when I opened the door hauling 4 suitcases and a guitar up to the fourth floor alone. Yellowed sheets stained with an unidentified liquid, landfill-like floor, prison-like windows, and pungent stench of rotten meat: a standard subdivided flat in Hong Kong. HELL NO. The night I moved in, I was a cockroach again. I revulsed my identity.

Trevor Noah’s words were my only friend back in the nights I spent on the cardboard bed. Despite being “born a crime” as a mixed-race child under apartheid, he showed that he was capable of mediating between Xhosa and Zulu. I was like a chameleon, he said. Maybe…So was I. I thought of my ability to speak two languages and connect with two different cultures because of this special identity. I had been made to be an outsider in both Hong Kong and Shenzhen, but I never realized that the power to belong had always been within my grasp.

The next morning, I equipped myself with mask and gloves, packed up the litter on the floor, ordered materials to make my own bed and desk… I turned that filthy house into a place where I no longer felt nauseated. Although I struggled for 32 minutes to kill 2 huge flying cockroaches and 42 minutes hauling the chemically-polluted bedsheet to the nearest garbage station, the moment I collapsed on the floor with a sweaty shirt and dusty hands was the moment I realized I was strong enough to change despite facing challenges.

Over the past years, I’ve been honing my ability to change and make changes. I am not exceptionally capable nor brave. When I interviewed cross-border students and queer migrant workers for the documentaries, I stammered to ask deep questions that hurt them; when I first presented my idea to connect the queer youths in GBA, I lost my words when no one approved it. But I would still explain Hong Kong’s history to my Shenzhen fellows while sharing tales of Shenzhen’s growth with my Hong Kong friends. I never stopped trying to make a difference, just like the time I transformed my awful apartment alone. Like a chameleon, I learned to blend in, not to hide, but to navigate and connect.

I once asked my mother, “Why did you make me so different?” In response, she showed photographs of me introducing Hong Kong to Shenzhen students as a tour guide, sharing international insights I gained from Hong Kong schools to my mainland friends, and premiering my cross-border documentary in both places.

I was raised in confusion, but I grew through the confusion. Even if I am not sure about my identity, I am sure about the journey I’ve been through and the lessons I’ve learned. I became a bridge between two places that rarely saw eye to eye. I embrace the power to shape my surroundings, my communities, and ultimately, society as a chameleon. Just like that young duckling leading the way: she ain’t more exceptional than the others, but she will still resolutely step to the front, guiding the way for herself and others.

It’s not so difficult to cross. You put one foot in front of the other.

“Guys, does anyone have an extra phone charger?” “What if we all get seasick?” “Are we there yet?” Sighing, I turn my head and look out the window of our van at the vibrant blue ocean, with doubts slowly creeping into my mind. The summer of my freshman year, I got the opportunity to attend Seabase High Adventure, a unique Boy Scout experience of living on a sailboat while exploring coastal environments. Although my crew was all in the same troop, I was worried about how well we could mesh together in such a tight new space with people already complaining about the car ride there.

The sun's orange glow paints the afternoon sky as we slowly motor behind Rodriguez Key, our anchorage for the night. After we grilled and devoured burgers for dinner, our Captain, Chuck, brought out an old conch horn from his cabin. Flattening my chin, I took a deep breath and buzzed my lips against the small opening at the end of a conch. The conch produces a resonant tone, echoing through the afternoon sky. Astounded by the huge sound, I called over my other scouts, encouraging them to give the conch a try. One by one, our crew began taking turns, playing the conch into the setting sun. Crew members who were seasick and gloomy on the first day were now talking excitedly preparing for the next few days.

The next morning after our conch playing, as the grubmaster, I dipped slices of bread into a mixture of milk, eggs, and cinnamon. While we sat around our cabin table eating breakfast, I realized our crew had become stronger, no longer worrying about personality differences.

My experience of bringing together my peers on the sailboat pushed me to continue to do the same with others. With encouragement from adult leaders, I ran for the position of Senior Patrol Leader.

As the SPL next fall, I led our troop on our annual backpacking trip, tackling a 10-mile loop with almost 2000 feet of elevation gain for 6 miles straight. As I looked at our line, I noticed the two newer scouts on the trip starting to fall behind, looking increasingly exhausted. I remembered the breakdowns I had on my first outing as a scout. I wanted to feel comfortable and safe in our troop. So during our next water break, I joined the newer scouts and checked up on them, making sure they were drinking enough water while getting rest. I set a slower pace and after we finally reached our campsite, I assured them that the next day would be much easier. The next morning as I checked in with them, they were looking forward to the day's hike and excited about future adventures.

Inspired by Scouting, I decided to try taking a leadership role in clarinet. With few wind players to choose from in my school’s chamber music society, I decided to orchestrate a duet between the clarinet and the saxophone. But because the clarinet and saxophone are in different keys, we couldn’t mesh the sounds of our instruments together. Realizing that their pitches would continue to clash, I transcribed a piano duet into both of our keys. Although our performance wasn't perfect on the day of the recital at a senior living home, the duet sounded fantastic and the seniors applauded all the performers. I felt joy watching the seniors brighten as they listened to our performances. Through music, I learned to apply leadership in scouts to different experiences.

Through scouting, I’ve developed crucial skills that have helped me grow as a person. Whether I’m bringing my crew together on Seabase, looking out for new members in a community, or leading musical duets, I’ve strived to apply these leadership lessons to help others. I’ve built a community and memories I’ll never be able to replace, and I hope to do the same in college.

I was in love. Everyday, as I approached the dumbbell rack, there was no better sight than seeing the dumbbells sitting on their little U-shaped holders, lined up in a satisfying, perfect numerical order. Scanning across, I could recall the humbling experiences associated with the seemingly insignificant 5’s to the authority I felt clenching 120 pounds in each hand; each weight had imparted its own unique lesson over the past four years of my life.

As a freshman walking into the gym for the first time over winter break, the dumbbell rack felt overwhelming and foreign. Fear of injury, self-consciousness about my form, and a severe muscle imbalance constantly plagued my mind. I could barely curl 5 pounds with my left arm while comfortably lifting 15s with my right. Trying to hide the disparity, I stuck with the 15s, only completing actual reps with my right. Unsurprisingly, weeks passed with minimal progress, but gradually, I began to realize I was surrounded by people striving to improve themselves–people who would help rather than judge. As my fear of being seen with the 5’s faded, I found true strength not in what I lifted, but embracing where I started.

After a year of consistent check-ins on my LA Fitness calendar, I progressed to the 30s. There was just one problem: the 30-pound dumbbells were the most popular in the gym, rarely ever sitting on the rack. Often, I was left with two options: waiting or asking for them. If I chose the former, I waited, sinking comfortably into the bench and drifting into my own little realm—envisioning the chicken potstickers I was planning to make for my parents (and myself) or pondering the deeper meaning of the Metallica playing in my AirPods—only loosely shifting back to reality when my partner Daniel urged me to grab the newly available 30s.
