Enlightened by these moments of patience and boredom, I learned to find tranquility and value in each ripple of thought passing through my mind.

The latter approach—asking—was the one I used to shy away from, but I began to view the dumbbell rack as a place to break that barrier. When I first asked my now good friend Rick—the big guy that was twice my age, covered in tattoos, and had biceps twice the size of my head—how many sets he had left with the 30s, my fears began to fade. Gradually, confidence came more naturally and seeped into my everyday life. I found the courage to explore the depths of my curiosity, raising my hand to ask Mr. Lee about integrating polar functions and figuring out how long the A.C. would take to cool my car using Newton’s Law of Cooling—though my estimates never seemed quite accurate during the California summer.

A few years later, hitting the 80s for shoulder press had become just another natural part of my routine. After finishing my sets, I enjoyed lingering by the dumbbell rack, taking in the people around me: the mentors who had guided me from the start and friends I’d see there almost everyday. But it was the freshman on my school’s soccer team that always brought a smile to my face, reminding me of where I had been just a few years ago. Just as my seniors had been there for me, I strove to be available to them, always happy to offer a spot and get them excited.

To me, the dumbbell rack was more than just a collection of rubber and metal; the battles I had with each weight marked my growth and change over the past four years. Yet, one thing has remained constant: the dumbbell rack’s endless demand for more, fueling my urge to lift heavier objects. Through commitment and consistency, I aim to inspire and foster a community defined by steady improvement and ambition—just like the dumbbell rack.

“I’ll pray for you.” The last week of school came a little early to me in my sophomore year. Teachers, friends, and even people I did not know came up to me with letters, hugs, and prayers. It was one of the hardest, and also the warmest, goodbyes I had experienced.

In September of 2022, something started to twitch in the corner of my left eye. Once. Twice. I rubbed my eyes to see if it would go away. No matter how much I rubbed my eyes and blinked, the cloud-like spot was still there. Had I not gotten enough sleep? I kept it to myself, hoping it would soon go away. It bothered me, but I shoved my worries to the side and finished my homework. I had no idea what the consequences would be.

Weeks went by, and the symptoms began to worsen. After finally going to a doctor, I was told I had White Dot Syndrome. More specifically, I had what is called Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy. It often happens to young healthy females and there is no known cure yet. The doctors prescribed steroids, and splitting headaches followed. From acing all the exams to having difficulty in reading a paragraph, it only took a couple of weeks; my life had completely changed.

I flew back home at the end of October. I was excited to see my parents, and was hoping to feel safe and relaxed at home. However, things did not flow as I envisioned. Harsh words from my family crushed me, and, all of a sudden, my joy to be home turned into anguished bitterness.

How can this be? My friends and teachers were crying and praying for me, but why were my parents indifferent about how I was doing? Did they even care? I was fine, or I was able to pretend to be fine, before my parents stabbed me with a dagger in the heart.

I was miserable, but nobody understood why. I was dying everyday, wondering about the purpose of living day to day. There were no reasons for me to smile or hope for a brighter tomorrow. It was one of those hopeless nights when I heard my mom’s confession. All the nights I was in sorrow and grief, she also was going through agony. My mom, in fact, was just another stereotypical tough Asian parent who wanted to be strong in front of me. She cried and cried at church, and my illness was well-known to everyone through her tears. She prayed and prayed that I would stay strong and brave in the long ways ahead of me. That is when I started to realize what I had forgotten when I lived for myself. The kindness, gentleness, and love that was constantly poured out to me by so many different people were buried in my memory. My grandma, grandpa, aunt, uncle, and, most importantly, my parents were treated as if they were in my way as I lived self-centered. I inwardly disrespected and ignored their love for me. Yes, I deserved to be partially blind. I deserved all the misery, and now it was time to go back to who I really was before the world changed me.

Now I truly understand that it is “better to be blind and see with your heart, than to have two good eyes and see nothing.” It cost me an eye to acknowledge the love from my family. I learned it the hard way, but I believe someday, with the overflowing love that was poured upon me, I will be able to share the love I received. Maybe I will have the power to soften the hearts of the stubborn, make the blind see, and deaf to hear like the selfish Sophomore girl who I used to be.

Chestnut hunting has an unofficial handbook. Growing up, I spent countless autumn afternoons at the local park with my family, scouring for fallen chestnuts from the grove of trees above. As a veteran chestnut hunter, I am compelled to share my lessons learned in the form of my Three Golden Rules of Chestnut Hunting (and beyond!).

Rule #1: Location, Location, Location 
The chestnut field is a dynamic environment. Not all areas of the chestnut field are made equal. Therefore, to find the most viable area for a given day, I must put my observational skills to use. Is the wind going to blow the falling chestnuts east or west? Which trees have the most ripe chestnuts? (the ones with brown burrs—green burrs mean unripe chestnuts).

My ability to analyze situations not only helps me collect more chestnuts but also creates ways for me to share my passions with others. When my school introduced “Viking Block,” a 30-minute free period in the middle of the day, I noticed an opportunity to start pop-up concerts around the school with a keyboard and a few friends. From whimsical Studio Ghibli songs to Bohemian Rhapsody, we created an atmosphere where everyone found something they liked. I find fulfillment in spreading joy to others, which is made possible by my ability to be observant.

Rule #2: Keep Your Eyes Up! 
Rather than waiting for a chestnut to fall near me, I relentlessly pace around the area, actively searching for fallen chestnuts. My biggest tip? As I scan the ground before me, I always keep my gaze focused on the area ten feet ahead, rather than at my feet.

It seems counterintuitive at first. Why would I purposefully ignore the chestnuts right in front of me? The answer lies in being able to effectively scour a much larger area. I may miss a few chestnuts at my feet, and that's okay. In the long run, looking ahead ultimately results in me spotting much more chestnuts.

However, “focusing ten feet ahead” extends to far more than just chestnut hunting. In life, it taught me to look beyond short-term failures and setbacks. Whether it's starting my own economics team at school or learning to sing despite my lack of natural talent, Rule #2 gave me the grit and patience to continuously chase growth and learning over immediate results. No matter how uncomfortable or counterintuitive it feels, I keep my eyes up.

Rule #3: It Isn’t a Competition 
My family isn’t the only one who knows about our chestnut spot, and so we are often joined by fellow chestnut hunters—parents tugging along their children, grandpas and grandmas in wide-brim hats, and even the occasional teenager.

At first, I had a complicated relationship with Rule #3. Growing up as an avid tennis player, I had always seen competition as a zero-sum game, where one person’s victory meant another’s loss. I viewed other chestnut hunters in the same light: as rivals rather than companions.

Things changed when I saw the interactions around me. My family set the example for me to follow, whether it’s my grandpa exchanging his chestnut recipes with strangers or my little sister spending her time picking up chestnuts for an elderly man so he wouldn’t need to bend down. When we got home, I noticed that while their bags had less chestnuts than mine, they looked much happier. Seeing their joy made me realize how narrow my previous mindset was. By focusing on results, I missed out on the happiness from sharing my experience with others.

Slowly, this change carried over to other aspects of my life. Nowadays, my fiercest tennis rivals are also my closest practice partners and friends. Above all, I hope to bring this collaborative attitude to all communities I’m a part of. Because as long as we know where to look, we can all walk home with a bag full of delicious chestnuts.

“17 chimes, for 17 victims…” I strike the chimes in my 17-note solo of “Forever and Always, A Reflection.” My heart rate slows to match the serene melody, calming my turbulent memories. To my right, a reporter narrates the NBC 5th anniversary feature dedicated to the lives lost on February 14th, 2018 at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School.

I call Parkland, Florida home. On that day, I hid inside a dark bathroom with my classmates for four hours. We huddled together, uncertain and terrified by actions driven by hatred, stemming from feelings of exclusion.

In the aftermath, I struggled with painful migraines that forced me to quarantine in pitch-black rooms to avoid excess stimulation. I tried countless headache medications, but still the debilitating pain pounded my head like a drum. Advil or Tylenol never worked. Instead, music became my medicine.

I was initially hesitant about joining percussion, fearing it would bring more chaos to my mind. But after enduring such a traumatic experience, I was desperate to find community at my new middle school. Trying something new seemed daunting, but the focus it demanded gradually distracted my mind. With each exercise and new technique I learned, the throbbing of my head slowed from unbearable to manageable to entirely unnoticeable. Before I knew it, every rehearsal brought waves of relief, and I realized that music had unexpectedly evolved into my haven.

Now, a headache strikes on the bus to school in the morning? I throw on my headphones, losing myself in the groovy sounds of Michael Jackson’s “Thriller,” part of our halftime show track. A stressful school day filled with important tests and after-school math practices? I escape to the band room to improvise a beat with friends, who join in playing cowbells, saxophones, and piano. Every note melts away the tension in my shoulders and relaxes my breathing.

I harness the soothing sounds of the band room in other areas of my life. Prior to the Boston University RISE research symposium, I tapped on my chest to the melodic “Queen” tenor drum feature to calm my nerves before presenting in front of a crowd gathered around my poster. During a playoff game against the Nova Titans, I led a pulsing chant and a bleacher-rattling stomp to energize my volleyball teammates before we clinched our victory. These musical rituals have calmed, centered, and guided me towards greater confidence and stronger leadership.

When selected to be the percussion section leader as a sophomore, I was nervous about being the youngest leader in the band, especially because of Logan and Dougie, two friends with special needs. Logan and Dougie both face challenges with the precise timing required for percussion and fitting in with the band. To ensure they are included and prepared, I dedicate extra time after rehearsals to review their parts. During concerts, I use subtle taps on their backs to help them stay on tempo. Though I must juggle my own responsibilities while assisting them during performances, I embrace their trust and listen as their rhythms align harmoniously with the ensemble.

“It’s Time to Unleash the FURY!!!” After every performance, I huddle the team to recognize members who displayed showmanship and passion by asking them to lead our “Silent Sam” chant. When I ask Logan and Dougie to take the lead, their proud smiles mirror my own, reflecting their growth as drummers, newfound confidence, and a sense of belonging in the band. I hope my efforts at inclusion can prevent the feelings of isolation that drive school shootings like the one my classmates and I survived.

The boom of the bass drum. The crash of the cymbals. These sounds aren’t a cacophony of random percussive noises, but rather a symphony of connectivity and emotion that feels like home. Through every beat and note I play, I endeavor to inspire and promote empathy and acceptance; in myself, in my audience, and in my community.

The oboe is a bridge that holds together the pyramid within the band, connecting the earthy roots of sound with the airy heights of music. Its tonal quality ranges from the tuba’s depth to the flute’s breathiness. But with the ability to both blend and stand out, it’s difficult to find a balance. My mistake was that I was unable to embrace the parts of it that made it most special.

Within a year of playing, I had already fallen in love with the instrument, but for the wrong reasons. Its warmth and roundness made it easy to hide among the flutes and clarinets. As the pandemic hit, my desire to hide deepened. Every Friday, we submitted recordings of our playing, and without the safety of the full band around me, I felt vulnerable. I started to cringe at the oboe’s squawky and buzzing sound, thinking that I should aim to sound more like a clarinet. As a result, it became a habit to point the bell of my oboe straight to the ground, clamp the opening of the reed shut with my mouth, and press my elbows tightly to my sides. It was as if I was playing defensively. Still, whenever someone asked me about my interests, playing the oboe was the first thing that came out of my mouth.

I hadn’t even noticed how small my sound had become, even after the pandemic. During a band jury one day, my director commented, “Your tone is beautiful, but you don’t have to hide when you play.” His advice resonated with me, but I couldn’t find the courage to fully explore the versatility of the instrument. I began listening to the oboists beside me in my bands and orchestras. It seemed that while they weren’t fixated on sounding a specific way, that was what made both their solos and their contributions to the band most interesting. Through playing alongside oboists with a variety of styles, I realized that finding your own sound isn’t about perfection, but about embracing what makes you unique.

One night, my school had a band concert that all my old music instructors attended. I even spotted my brother cheering me on from the audience. Having just been accepted into the All-Region ensemble as first chair oboe, I was more excited than usual for the concert. Throughout the performance, I felt free to focus on my phrasing and musicality without worrying about how my sound was perceived by others. On the downbeat of my solo, I shocked myself with the clarity and boldness of my sound. I had finally understood what it means to make music.

As I’ve found my courage as a musician, I’ve also found it in other aspects of my life. I’m able to fully trust in myself and my abilities, because that’s what makes my contributions to the world most special. Just as I found the courage to embrace my own unique sound, I want to help others find their voice–whether it’s through tutoring refugee children or working with autistic children. I used to be scared to make mistakes, to seem less than perfect. This should never have to be a worry or insecurity for other people. Although the main goals in the programs I lead are to tutor English and to support children with autism, I want them to be much more than that. There is so much personality in the students I work with, and I want to encourage them to be comfortable expressing themselves.

The little girl who picked up the oboe six years ago simply thought it sounded nice, not knowing how much of an impact it would have on her. If she saw me now, she would be proud of my music, my voice, and my courage.

Like glass shards falling under dawn, sparkling dresses shimmered under the ballroom’s warm lights, contrasted by neutral suits. Music permeated the crowd, and I could hear the monotonous buzz of voltage coursing through the speakers. Normally, I would’ve been excited by the audio setup and windowed golf course poised for my adventure. But tonight, I was engulfed by a different energy: being in a close moment with people who clicked with me and intimately pushed me to just do. I was excited because I knew I had found my people again.

A year ago, I would’ve enjoyed prom with my two friends. The ones who equally loved nerding over physics while crossing 60ft-high train trestles at night, and who connected with me so deeply they pushed me beyond comfort like no others. But after a family tragedy delved my closest friend into depression, his emotional disparity prevented us from connecting like before, and our group dissolved. I lost my people.

Having retained that archetypal close friend group my whole life, I was desolate, yet became determined to find my people again. I wistfully followed an innate desire to uncover others’ interests, getting to know those tablemates and nearby lunch eaters better—but I couldn’t make things intimate. No matter how sociable I appeared, the courage needed to reach out and deeply connect wasn’t there. I was trapped in my glass cage; I could speak to everyone, yet couldn’t grasp them beyond superficiality.

Months later, April came bearing prom.

Going alone was a testament to my comfort zone I wouldn’t let it have. This time, a willpower came from the realization that my unique path into this situation required an equally unique one out. I wasn’t taking the path of least resistance; I was asking that lunch group. For days, I grappled with my emotions, feeling a sense of fear and excitement. Pacing, I repeatedly weighed the exhilarating notion of organizing the best outing for the group juxtaposed with the harrowing outcomes of exploring my social vitality.

What if my request ruins these nascent connections?
Do I risk the only ones I feel remotely with?
How would I react?
What made my people before?

Realizing occupying my headspace with imaginary perspectives and exhaustive lists of negatives wouldn’t work, I pivoted. Every lunch from then, I revealed a little more about myself to that new group; my pets, my adventures, my music. In class, I became open about my situation to some. At home, I talked with my mom more to feel her natural support. Online, I embarrassingly searched if my social ideas were weird. Slowly, I chipped away my comfort zone with real scenarios and determination, like a sculptor on his prized project—weaving a social safety net for both me and them. Then, weeks later, I capitalized on a newfound confidence and just did. I asked, and went with them.

But prom only bolstered my determination.

After, I consistently pursued things that gave me that distinct feeling of fear and excitement, because now I knew I was doing something right. I joined that out-of-school robotics team regardless of the strangers, traveled alone more to experience my adventures with new liberation, and joined Link Crew, as I now took pride in being the catalyst of breaking comfort zones and helping others find their people. Ensuring the freshmen had those close connections and the timeless lesson of going beyond comfort was, and remains, incredibly important to me. Because by breaking my comfort zone after losing my people, I truly understood the indispensability of having them; how important the push to pursue those opportunities we get from our most intimate connections is—and how important it is we take them. As I stood in the ballroom, the glass shards of my cage falling, this revelation saturated me. I didn’t have a date, but I still felt loved; the party was the least important thing to me.

**Endless Opportunities, or Just a Coin Flip?**

That is the question of this highest-stakes environment. Back in 2021, when the GameStop stock craze was at its highest, it seemed like trading was essentially a money printer. I wanted in, so I begged my mom for permission to open a trading account. When she eventually agreed, I eagerly invested my yardwork income into companies that I liked, only to watch their value plummet as the craze faded.

It wasn't until April 2023 that the spark for trading reignited. On the way to Science Bowl Nationals, I watched as my friend scanned through stocks, while asking our physics teacher for his opinions. He then showed me his current returns, prompting me to check mine. To my despair, half of my money had vanished!

That summer, I was determined to change red to green. I decided to give trading another shot. Aside from the bioinformatics research program I was involved with, I devoted all my time to learning the fundamentals of the market as I worked to finance this hobby. I sought advice from my physics teacher—in my eyes, the epitome of a successful trader—reading his suggested books and adopting a similar strategy.

As my understanding grew, I realized that trading was a mixture of everything I loved and an application of everything I learned. The concepts and behavioral studies I had analyzed in psychology were evident in finance, with confounding variables shrouding relationships and emotions plaguing irrational financial decisions. The governments, wars, and recessions I had analyzed in history were all being used by analysts to predict the future. The interconnectedness was beautiful—whether it be history and psychology influencing a market correction after the pandemic (and destroying my first investments), or physics and math in the Monte Carlo simulation—it all inspired me to keep on learning.

Yet no matter how much love I showed it, the relationship was one-sided: my balance continued to dwindle. Still, this only fueled my desire to work harder. I did not want trading to become a money-eating hobby; I wanted it to be a job. I analyzed daily news, read books, reread those books, and reflected on my mistakes. Soon, I connected it all back to psychology class: my emotions ruined my judgment. I began to wonder: why don't I let my computer do all the thinking for me? The programming skills I learned during my bioinformatics research could revolutionize my trading approach. The plan was simple: code an algorithm that would eliminate my emotional trading—an algorithm designed to overcome my flaws.

However, the execution was extremely difficult. I spent every moment I had, whether during school transitions or pulling all-nighters, wrapping my head around computational finance. I spent days scouring forums and watching tutorials to troubleshoot my code. Eventually, those grueling efforts paid off. Now, it takes minutes to scan stocks without emotions obfuscating my judgment. And with my newfound time, I dedicate it to learning more advanced concepts in finance and coding them into Python. This year, I wrote my IB Extended Essay over Modern Portfolio Theory and my Mathematics Internal Assessment over analyzing technical indicators. I co-founded and now lead my school's stock club, where we learn the principles of trading and participate in the Wharton Investment Competition. Although small, our club was the first step into the financial world in a school focused on STEM.

It wasn't just the money that mattered, but the field as a whole. I finally discovered something to be passionate about—something I had struggled to be before. Learning about the stock market also made me realize that no matter how successful I am, the curiosity of learning will never be fulfilled. Like the stock market, the path life takes is unknown. But just as I’ve learned to adapt my trading strategy, I’ve learned to embrace life’s uncertainties, using them as fuel to shape my journey.

**Things I Wanted to Say But Never Did**

by Monica Murphy, vanilla yogurt, purple nail polish, and a promise from my sister Brooke that she would walk to school every day. My Notes App is full of my lists and musings. It is full of me.

12/24/23. “I spotted a worm in the Baccalà”! Whispering the news to my grandmother Mo about the intruder in her signature fish delicacy, Baccalà, was not an option. Her hearing aids stood little chance against the 25 family members who had gathered to savor the Feast of the Seven Fishes dinner, an Italian tradition she has hosted for 30 years. My Notes App would undoubtedly assist me with discreetly communicating the news to her. I was wrong. The time between holding up my phone for Mo to read my note and her exclaiming, “[Name], there’s a worm in the Baccalà?! Oh, come on!” was almost indiscernible. All eyes turned toward me. Mo declared she would simply extract the worm, problem solved, while everyone else insisted that the Baccalà be relegated to the garbage bin. Bets were waged on how quickly we would fall ill if we partook in the fish (from one hour to as long as ten days), and to my relief, everyone was laughing, including Mo. With the assistance of Google, I discovered that the worm was, in all probability, an Anisakid Nematode, a parasite that could indeed ruin our Christmas. Mo and I promptly discarded the Baccalà, and I hold the distinct honor of being my family’s de facto ‘worm spotter’.

4/24/24. “Quiz, the evolution of the heart, form fits function, and maintaining homeostasis.” I spent the evening engrossed in my Anatomy and Physiology (A&P) textbook. What my A&P class had not prepared me for was having an amputated foot placed in front of me while I was gathering specimens in the Pathology Lab during my summer internship. As I reached out to feel the foot through the yellow plastic bag, I couldn’t help but notice that it was still warm; I started to shiver and felt profoundly sad for the person who had just lost a part of themselves. I learned that the amputation was the result of osteosarcoma, a rare type of bone cancer. In all fairness to my A&P teacher, I don’t think anyone could have equipped me for this encounter, just as I imagine the person who is now an amputee could not possibly have been prepared for their amputation. How could they have been? I spent about 280 hours at my internship, and the few minutes that I spent with an amputated foot were the most grounding ones.

6/7/24. *Da Vinci Code* by Dan Brown was added to a running list of 19 novels that I will devour well past midnight. Without a doubt, I credit *The Hunger Games* with sparking my passion for reading; I adore the unconventional plot and the iconic characters (oh, how I admire the fierce Katniss Everdeen!). When I was 14, Mo and my Aunt Pam, captivated by my growing book collection, began asking me for recommendations. I was thrilled that two adults I loved and admired wanted a glimpse into my literary world. I found that sharing a title, while efficient, was not enough to convey how much a novel meant to me, so I began composing short reviews in my Notes App to share with them. At the very top of my recommendations stood a masterpiece, *All the Bright Places*, by Jennifer Niven. “From love and grief to finding oneself and maturing…”, I crafted my review, hoping they would find this novel as spectacular as I did.

I like to think that the ins and outs of my Notes App are like a convoluted autobiography that I carry around in my pocket. My 145 Notes and counting are a piece of my past and a peek into my future as I figure out my path and my purpose. My Notes beautifully capture my thoughts as they move around my head like clouds passing through a clear blue sky, thoughts that I can easily edit and update. As far as Brooke’s Note goes, she has kept her promise.

Kyiv, the city I was born and raised, it is a capital of beautiful Ukraine instilled such meaningful memories that I hold very dear with me. Everything changed when my dad passed away in a car accident when I was almost three. From that moment feeling the weight of all the heightened emotions around me I grew up. I was forced too. I understood what death meant at 3 years old, that my family wasn’t excluded from having people taken. But at a young age it gave me a huge appreciation for life. Not long after the death my mom was back working, as she was now the only source of income in our family. Leaving me with my Babushka in our apartment in Kyiv I was doing more tasks on my own than before, and at such a young age that was confusing to me, I was looking for certain help that wasn’t there. But my babushka would say to me “те, що нас не вбиває, робить нас сильнішими” (what is not going to kill us, makes us stronger), that has stuck with me ever since. While my mom had been working in the airline business, she received a better job offer, but this job was in United States, New York. This meant we had to leave everything and everyone behind, my grandma, friends, and everyone that we have ever known. All of this just to move to a different country at five years old. That move changed my whole life. I had to learn a new language, culture, and more all over again and I didn’t even know it. Having the confidence and independence that my grandma and mom had instilled in me from a young age and from everything that I had experienced really helped me thrive. I had to navigate kindergarten with only three days left and without knowing how to speak English. I had to use the help and knowledge of my peers and teachers around me. With the help and support of everyone I was able to thrive and find my way through kindergarten and through the rest of school seamlessly. I was speaking English perfectly by second grade, you would never know that I was born in Ukraine. I had never felt like an outsider, never been bullied for my language, being accepted all throughout school made me feel whole and validated. If I hadn’t felt like it before I definitely felt like I fit in now more than ever. But having the confidence and validation at school didn’t stop me from having the embarrassment of financial struggles, having to move apartments every couple of months because my mom was still the only source of income for us. I wanted to put a fake face on for every single person that I saw because nobody knew the truth about me or my life except that I moved here from Ukraine. My mom’s commitment to keep thriving and eventually get a better job for herself and a stable home for us really set an example for me that helped me build myself up as a person. Being able to go through experiences that I never imagined that I would have to go through in my life at a young age really built my confidence and instilled it in me till this day. It has caused me to have a different outlook on life and realize that anything can change at the snap of a finger. Growing up in America and seeing this war unfolding in Ukraine recently has caused me to hold every connection that I have with my home very closely with me. The struggles that my relatives and friends in Ukraine are now going through have become a reminder of what my life could’ve been like if my mom had never gotten that job offer here.

“The point of a timed free-write is to jot down whatever comes to mind, to let the words guide you to an open door and for you to enter it,” my writing instructor Ms. K advised. Yet here I was, my fingers stiff on the keyboard, my Google Doc barebone, and my mind far from any opening door. I was still down a hallway, stuck in a mess of mixed thoughts: Can I even call myself a writer? Will I have to share my work? I really hope not. “2 minutes left!” This wasn’t a normal case of writer’s block.

Since I was 7, Mama deemed me as “The Storymaker” of the family. A prolific writing machine, I sewed tales from all universes. A-clown-gone-psycho-but-teams-up-with-an-orthiniologist-romance? Finished. Prince-turns-into-rabid-dog-and-then-runs-off-to-live-on-a-remote-island-with-a-colony-of-cows-sci-fi? An in-progress. With a yellow fat Ticonderoga pencil pressed against my meaty hand and the other holding down a slip of loose-leaf paper, I was creatively unstoppable.

However, as I grew older, the urge for creation became twisted in its purpose. Fantastical worlds began to close off, words started to carry a waxy film of superficiality, and Ticonderoga pencils and loose-leaf paper became solely keyboards and screens. Soon enough, accolades and medals began to wall off my imagination—I was stuck in the sole world of merit and competition. When work was not awarded, I questioned whether I could ever live up to the title “writer.” Hiding my poetry and short stories, ashamed that they were never written to ‘standard,’ became my way of masking this insecurity.

Eventually, after several free writes, generative exercises, and many 'I don’t really wanna share’s', Ms. K took heed of my struggles. “[Name]!” she called out as I was leaving workshop. “Before you head out, I think you need this.” She slipped me a note and smiled. Inside, in sprawled handwriting, she wrote: “We are all here to speak to each other through our words. We are not here to be perfect.” At first, this mindset was easy to grasp but difficult to permeate into my actions. But perhaps it was the cinematic fashion of the note or my YOLO philosophy that made its meaning stick with me. Over that week, with some hesitation, I began to raise my hand alongside my peers when it came time to read our free writes. It felt scary, almost too intimate, but as I continued to share my writing, I could feel all these teenage hearts beating as one. No one was judging, no one was comparing. We were all somewhat bonded by the ability to simply share a figment of our internal selves. By the end of the following week, I was leaning forward in my chair, not worried about when I would have to share next, but excited and curious about how my words could blend into the minds and works of others.

Several months later, I eagerly reintroduced a schoolwide literary magazine at Cary Academy and tried my hardest to spread Ms. K’s mantra. With a seemingly immense lackluster of writers in our community, I recounted how having any form of space to elevate your writing completely flipped my mindset on what it means to be a writer. My concern for perfection diluted my perspective, leading me to view writing with a formulaic and stringent mindset—that there was only one right way to write. But, as I advise those thinking of submitting to the Lit Mag, there is no one way to write—it is a tool of self-expression and a craft intimate to some aspect of you. That year, we unearthed not only the many hidden gem-of-a-writer students within Cary Academy but also the transformative power of a passionate community. After all, through the voices of others, I found my own—something that can never be replaced with a gold medal.

I’ve been singing for as long as I can remember. It has always been my escape, my joy, my sanctuary. In preschool, I would run around the house, belting out the tune to “My Little Sunshine” or whatever new nursery rhyme we had learned that day. Now, more than a decade later, not much has changed–I still fill the house with song, serenading my family daily. But along the way, singing also began to carry something unexpected: fear.

The hardest part is always the first note. There’s a split second of silence before the sound escapes when I find myself haunted by all that could go wrong. Scenes of missed notes and voice cracks played in my head, convincing me that silence was safer. In those moments, I am completely paralyzed, unable to move or make a sound, as the heavy pressure of perfection weighs on my shoulders.

My entire life, I let this fear rule me—not only on stage but also in many aspects of my life, sure that it was better to stay where it was comfortable and easy. The fear of hitting the wrong note, failing a class, and not living up to my standards kept me from stepping out of my comfort zone and trying new things. I feared a single mistake would expose my shortcomings and flaws that I didn’t want anyone to see.

However, the summer after ninth grade, something inside of me shifted. I realized how much I had let slip by because of my fear of failure. It wasn’t just the missed notes; it was also the missed opportunities–conversations left unstarted, interests left unexplored, and words left unsaid– all because I was scared of embarrassing myself and falling short.

I finally confronted that fear for the first time during tenth grade when I sang my first solo, Reflection from Mulan. I forced myself to sing, and as shaky as my voice was, I finally understood that the first note didn’t have to be perfect; I only had to sing it. Taking that first step started a long learning journey to trust myself and own my failures and imperfections.

This past summer, I took on a new challenge as a software development intern, getting my first glimpse of what a future in technology might look like. As a high school intern working alongside full-time employees–some with decades of experience–I knew it would be challenging. I was right. I struggled with imposter syndrome, questioning my abilities as I tried to keep up with tasks that felt out of range of my skills. I had to learn a new programming language, React JS, and decipher a robust base of already-built code. I found myself watching countless YouTube tutorials and searching for answers to my endless problems on Microsoft Bing.

Collaboration was another skill I had to grasp. I had to shift from working individually in class to collaborating with others in a team environment. I had to overcome my fear of asking for help, worried it would expose my weaknesses and lack of ability. But I quickly discovered that everyone—whether a professional in the industry for decades or a fellow intern—was always learning.

I realized that learning to code is a process and comparing yourself to others is only a way to waste time. It became clear to me that everyone learns at their own pace, and although I am not as experienced as others, that does not mean I can not succeed. When I embraced the challenge instead of shying away, I discovered that every mistake is an opportunity to improve, and I became more comfortable with being a beginner. Looking back, I am grateful that I did not give up because, with perseverance, time, and effort, I succeeded. Both experiences taught me that the first step—whether the first note or the first line of code—may be the hardest, but it’s also the most important.

The traditional example of the butterfly effect is the flap of a butterfly’s wings causing a hurricane, but my own butterfly effect started with a bike ride. A few years ago, I was looking for more ways to train for cross country, and I settled on biking. It was a logical conclusion: I could introduce variety into my training schedule, go easy on my muscles to avoid an injury, and I had a fantastic bike, complete with a bell in the shape of a marshmallow. I started going on bike rides two or three times a week in May, and after a few weeks, I started biking by my friends’ houses to say hello on a whim. I told them why I was biking, and some of them asked if they could come with me to train for their own sports and spend more time together, and a group quickly formed.

In accordance with the butterfly effect, the weekly rides would have a far larger impact than I initially expected. In addition to looking for ways to train for cross country, I entered the summer restless and wanting nothing more than to be somewhere else. I didn’t even have a specific destination in mind, I was simply desperate to escape my hometown, to meet new people, and to try new things, and was bitter at the fact that I knew there was so much to experience that I couldn’t reach.

When the time spent biking turned from weeks to months, and June passed and then July, my friends and I began to find restaurants, stores, and nature getaways that I had no idea existed. Despite this, my cynicism didn’t immediately end. I was still insistent that I was missing out, and it wasn’t until the new discoveries reached a truly astonishing number that I was forced to reconsider. It shocked me - for all my frustration, it had never occurred to me that I didn’t need to go somewhere else to experience the world. I just needed to look outside.

Those months forced me to grasp the important lesson of making the most of the opportunities available to me. It was a lesson learned through experience, and I applied it to every area of my life. In school, I began organized study groups to share my passions and make new friends. In my extracurricular activities, I branched out from cross country to join speech and debate. After my first year of competition, I sought out ways to perfect my skills and ended up at a summer camp that introduced me to some of the most wildly talented people that I’ve ever met, who are now my lifelong friends. Eventually, I even got to travel more, and that desire of mine has not faded. However, I know that I will enjoy every new place and experience more than I would have if I hadn’t discovered my own home first.

Just as a butterfly can cause a hurricane, a bike can change someone’s high school experience. Bike rides with my friends became more than the exercise that they were intended to be. On one hand, they were a catalyst that deepened my curiosity of what the future has to offer and my desire to explore it. I’ve always loved to learn, but these experiences showed me the true excitement of discovering what’s around me and seeing where my decisions lead. I know, without a doubt, that I want to explore. On the other hand, these experiences gave me an invaluable sense of perspective. I can be content with where my life is, because I know that no matter what happens, I will create priceless memories and find my way to where I’m supposed to be.

My mortal enemies are a blend of lines and curves. I’ve been at war with them for years.

I look up onto the battlefield of my notebook, where a tangled amalgamation of lines mock me - different shapes, some curvy and others straight, bold, or faint. Under them were messy chicken scratches, one of my attempts to replicate these ink-made creatures. These intricate combinations of brushstrokes, the words of Japanese, were supposed to define me. Yet I struggled to understand them.

My drill sergeant, Miss Ono from Japanese school, calls these “kanji”. I had to memorize up to 200 of them alongside their several pronunciations and meanings in a year; my enemies were countless. Trying to memorize everything planlessly felt like wandering through endless mazes. I needed to turn the tides.

What worked for me before? I filled a notebook with nothing but kanji, writing each repeatedly; my first offensive attack. While my writing improved, my memorization faltered. These messy blobs were more elusive than expected.

I journeyed further into the world of memory. Fingers flying across the keyboard, I scoured for memory improvement strategies. Surfing through articles and books that guided me through long-term potentiation, the multi-store theory, and the forgetting curve, I finally found the key to victory in neuroscientist Yuji Ikegaya’s publications. Tomorrow, I would put my secret weapon to use.

9:30 PM. Before my slumber, I opened my kanji workbook and inspected these symbols one last time for 20 minutes. With my adversaries fresh in mind, I slept.

5:50 AM. I woke up to a personalized kanji test I had left there yesterday: my secret weapon. Reviewing my kanji before sleep reinforced their neural connections, preventing them from being sorted out during NREM sleep. After 3 weeks of this routine, I saw my scores skyrocket and after a month, alongside a smile from Miss Ono, I finally saw that fabled 100. I had won the war.

Or so I thought.

While I was in Japan to meet my friend Kazuma, eager to show off my hard-earned Japanese, the words wouldn’t come out. I tried again, but the thoughts on the tip of my tongue froze. Although my thoughts were clear in English, my mind couldn’t connect the dots. What happened to all my efforts to learn Japanese?

Weeks passed, and something strange happened. Immersed in the language, I started picking up phrases naturally. It slowly sank in: true language learning was not about piling hours into memorizing characters but about engaging in the language. I had focused too hard on the battle and forgotten why I studied Japanese: to reconnect with my heritage.

I shifted focus to experiencing Japanese culture. Venturing to the Kanji Museum in Kyoto taught me that these kanji were composed of components with individual meanings, combining to form a whole; much like America, where people from diverse backgrounds unite to create meaningful communities.

I needed to share this with everyone. Two aching hands later, I had bylaws for my Japanese Culture Club, where students from different backgrounds like Evan from Singapore with a passion for Japanese pop, and Shotaro, a Japanese exchange student looking to reconnect with his home, could explore Japan’s deeper culture. Starting a Japanese tutoring business, I aimed to show that language can’t be mastered through textbooks but through human connection. Kanji were no longer my enemies; they were now my own soldiers, used as a force of unity between diverse cultures.

There is always something new to be learned that can change my perspective on what I think is the “correct” way of doing things, helping me raise a flexible mind towards different perspectives. Utilizing these unique perspectives, I could be the bridge between cultures. My goal is to make my kanji on campus life, drawing on people of different backgrounds and uniting us to form meaning. As just like kanji, we gain meaning together rather than apart.

In Florida, historical truths were being removed from textbooks. The truth of some students, parents, and teachers’ lives became unspoken. I switched from in-person to virtual school my sophomore year. The laws changed again that spring, prompting the College Board to threaten to pull some AP classes from the state. I saw school library shelves go empty.

The library in my own mind is sprawling, slightly disorganized, with a staff consisting of a couple of humans, a troop of raccoons, and some crows bustling about. I find the idea of growth through challenge strange. In the case of exercise, it makes sense, and plants need to be repotted to continue growing, but I do not know if who a person is changes in response to challenge. I have been to four different high schools, but I do not think changing schools four times has fundamentally changed me, although I might have a narrow definition of change. I think to be a different person means to have a new default for processing information. I might respond to the same situations differently having learned new things, but fundamentally the process through which I learn and apply information is the same.

That is not to say my perspective is the same; by some definitions I change my perspective several times a day. For example, when I go to math class, I expect a neat and exact answer found at the end of a clear and logical path. I especially love calculus where methods that only approximate, like limits or Riemann’s sums, are usually replaced with something exact like derivatives and solvable integrals. When I showed up last year prepared for elegant calculus, learning about things that I cannot find the exact solution for, like series and certain integrals, was infuriating.

At other times, I can enjoy being inaccurate and imperfect. I sew, and when making a pair of pants recently, I indulged in the following sins: not pinning or tracing certain pattern pieces, not topstitching the zipper, not putting a button above the zipper, and at a certain point completely ignoring the instructions. The waistband is held together with hope, but I wear them with pride and a tightly fastened belt.

I am myself when I take care to write +c after every general integral and when I rip a chunk of fabric off a failed prototype (if there is such a thing) to take to school so my friend can approve it.

Attending different high schools did give me practice changing perspective and a wider sampling of ideas. Having seen and been under different leadership styles has prompted me to start developing my own. So far I picked up: 1. Hold myself to the highest standard (Mr. Simmons), 2. Find people who fill gaps in my skillset (Ms. Gillespie), 3. Make sure everyone can understand the process (Mr. Torres). Exposure to different contexts has also enabled me to distinguish bureaucracy from logic and the natural laws of the universe. It also made uncomfortable situations familiar. Frequently not knowing things everybody around me knows has made it easier for me to admit when I am confused. It’s probably been good for me to learn -- through so many moves -- that I am temporary, and how even though the bonds I make can fall apart, be replaced, or reform, life continues.

I have grown to like the unknown and unfamiliar, and using what I find there to improve how I do things. That is why I enjoy science and engineering, where I can bridge the gaps or at least throw a flashlight down into new places. I do not know exactly where these interests will lead me, and I am still discovering the edges, smudges, and curves in the lenses I see the world through. I know I hope to be useful, and that in this next chapter I will develop understanding and skills to become a human worthy of being integrated in the systems that helped me grow back stronger.

I owe the first chapter of my walk with initiative to Mr. Ba, an old man from church who was terminally ill with brain cancer. On a hazy night in November, I met him for the first time to give his wife a ride home. As we left and turned the lights off, a loneliness heavier than masked the room. I do not reside in his mind. Yet, if I did, how terrified would I be to have only the voice of mortality to listen to?

Mr. Ba’s image burned bright in my memory as his wife and I walked to my car. While I had kept Mr. Ba company for a bit, there were so many others in that hospital. So many, yet I had so little resources.

Rain began to drip off our noses. Slick rocks skidded beneath my Converses. One pebble slid in a puddle, cascading into infinite ripples.

Life is a puddle, I thought.

Of course I couldn't help all those people single handedly, but the compassion of a hundred fellow high schoolers could. All I had to do was throw a pebble. I came home and began planning a club to send cards or trinkets to patients so they wouldn't be alone when the last laugh of their loved ones faded. With a three-week deadline, I launched a Christmas donation.

On December 4th, I knew squat about how clubs worked. On December 11th, I became founder of a full-fledged club with over 100 members. But I only had 7 days to organize and execute a drive. Faithful to the strength in numbers, I assigned my officers to ask for donations from other school clubs they had connections in, specifically targeting clubs that had strong ties to classroom activities and proposing offering bonus points to donors as an incentive. On a clear blue December 18th just one week later, our team donated over $3,000 in gifts to the hospital where Mr. Ba had stayed. The drive was a blitz…but I was late. Mr. Ba had passed. I never gave him the gifts. I never had a conversation with him again.

Mr. Ba lying alone in that dark room led me to start my club. His memory leads me to continue trying to spread a ray of light with it. I knew many were not as fortunate as he–cancer doesn’t discriminate between those with family, and those without. As a start, I set up a card-writing event for a smaller cancer center whose patients did not receive as much from the community. However, the card-writing event didn’t unfold the way I had hoped. While the idea was to connect with those who felt forgotten, what resulted were hastily written messages from distracted students, devoid of the sincerity I had envisioned. It dawned on me that for many patients, receiving another generic card might feel more obligatory than heartfelt. The realization weighed on me, but it also sparked something new.

Determined to make a real difference, I expanded our efforts into a pen pal initiative. This time, I wanted to create a deeper, more lasting impact—one built on genuine connection. It took effort, but I paired students with patients in a way that encouraged meaningful exchange. Instead of one-off cards, I guided students to engage in thoughtful, ongoing conversations, focusing on shared interests, mutual curiosity, and, most importantly, empathy.

What began as a few hastily written words transformed into something greater: relationships that patients could look forward to, and students could learn from. In bridging these connections, I found that just a single pebble thrown—or two—could foster a kind of empathy that transcends the classroom. It’s not just about writing cards or sending gifts; it’s about listening, understanding, and offering a piece of oneself. It’s about the thousand streams of conversation that flow from the one I never had with Mr. Ba.

“She yells at me and yells at me and yells at me. Unceasingly. She has a point, but over this, I cannot yield. Of course life is not black and white, but rigid truths like the universal freedom to pursue happiness should never be compromised.”

A rigid axiom, called into question by the most trivial of things: shoes.

In an eighty-degree house swaddled in the humidity of a southern summer, the only thing better than ice cream is the coolness of the hardwood floor seeping into your bare feet as you sing and leap in the safety of home. But it was a cultural thing–wearing shoes in the house. The patter of my bare feet slapping the floor was always chased by the yelling of my mom. “I’VE TOLD YOU THOUSANDS OF TIMES, WEAR YOUR SHOES, THE FLOOR IS DIRTY!” Her voice bounced across those spotless floors, colliding with that same patch of hardwood for the thousandth time. This stubborn wall of ours wasn’t always up, though–sometimes, it would lower, and I would ask her once again if she had any more reasons for wearing shoes on clean floors. Once her reasons were exhausted by my rebuttals and offerings of compromise, it would always end in “No. Just wear them.”

She was never willing to compromise. Amid the whispers of self-love and hard boundaries that flowed from the words of peers and the culture in mass media, I wrote that entry on May 3rd, 2022. There was truth in my words, and falsity in my interpretation. I saw the “freedom to pursue happiness” as synonymous with the prioritization of my own, an ideal that starkly contrasted the lack of joy in my heart after those heated arguments with my mother. I was to realize the truth in those words when I resolved to stop this Tom and Jerry episode from happening for the one-thousand-and-oneth time: give up the feeling of dancing on cool floors in hot summers. Give up my happiness.

Little did I know of the joy that comes from selflessness.

Mom’s ringing laugh from the jokes I tell her. Sweet cinnamon from the bread she and I baked together. The closeness of friendships developed with devoted listening. Joy spread from events dedicated to an old man with cancer.

Now that I grasp more of what the “happiness” I wrote of in my journal those years ago is, I stand by my statement on a more solid foundation…wearing shoes.

It was a rigid axiom, clarified by the most trivial of things.

Thank you, Mom. Like my shoes, I will pass this understanding on, to every place I go.

Class of 2025 Valedictorian Speech Final Draft: “Happiness is friendship. Happiness is staying true to the values we were taught as little kids, values that we since then have strayed from because we thought there was a better way. Happiness is forgiveness. Happiness is generosity. And happiness is found when you seek to make others happy.”

“Thank you… so much,” she sobbed, touched. Her hands trembled as she took the steaming chicken noodle soup from my hands, and placed it onto the thoughtfully assembled dining table. Her clothes ragged and disheveled. Her 11-month-old baby beside her, cooing in a battered stroller. That was when the tears formed. I desperately clawed for them to stop, but the joy from such a simple gesture exposed the pain behind a lovely smile.

As I walked home, that smile followed me. The suffering in her eyes, her frayed clothes, her innocent baby. I couldn’t believe these were the same people struggling four blocks from where I live. As I went to school, they would have to survive on the streets, begging for humanity; as I ate home-cooked meals, they would be scavenging for leftovers; as I slept soundly at night, they would be fending for themselves, seeking every second of sleep possible.

I decided in that moment: this mistreatment had to end. I couldn’t continue knowing people like her were surviving, while I, on the other hand, was living. I immediately brainstormed how I could support her. Trying to think of ways to help was a struggle at first. Then, it hit me: bridge my talent for origami and my passion for helping those in need. This revelation set off Petals for Peace.

Petals for Peace is my vision for a non-profit organization whose mission is to assist people in crisis. It first started with gifting origami bouquets to friends and family. The joy on their faces inspired me to share that delight with others. That led me to establish Mooki Bloom, where anyone can appreciate unique handcrafted origami flowers. The success of my small business compelled me to organize origami sales at CHS, with all of the money benefiting Mustang Ambassadors. The overwhelming support from these sales had me envisioning the impact I could have on others.

Around this time, floods were plaguing South America, displacing nearly 500,000 residents in southern Brazil. My best friends’ hometowns were in ruin, the floods nearly submerging entire houses underwater. I could not shun their cries for help. My best friends’ culture has left such a lasting mark on me: I have picked up Brazilian Portuguese, discovered how to brighten any space through vibrant music and dance, and realized that there is no such thing as too much steak. I have acclimated to Brazilian culture from an uplifting community, and I could not bear to see them suffer.

We swiftly launched a fundraiser for Brazil Flood Relief, sold Brazil-themed origami bouquets, raised awareness about the disaster, went door-to-door for donations, and gathered food and clothing for those affected. By the end, we collected over $350 and collected nearly 50 pounds of canned food and clothes, directly supporting the displaced families.

It was truly awe-inspiring. I witnessed my community come together to provide relief to those in need, touching countless lives. The impact we made was exhilarating, and we quickly set our sights on new volunteer projects. In no time, we raised over $320 for Gaza aid, advocated for a ceasefire at several protests, and secured over $340 to feed impoverished women and children.

Looking back, that first small act of handing a bowl of soup to a woman in need was the spark that ignited something much larger. Her gratitude mirrored in the tears that welled up in her eyes taught me a lesson I carried from that moment on: compassion, when paired with action, has the power to ripple through communities and beyond borders. Whether it was fundraising for families displaced by the floods in Brazil, or serving lunches to the needy, I realized that every effort, no matter how small, has the potential to change lives.

The pendulum swings left.

Looking in the mirror, I see my white mustache and precious uniform. I think I’m a super proud and well-dressed dictator. I finish the milk Mommy made for me and eat breakfast. Then, I head to my headquarters.

I’m seven. I’m the president of my class. I feel happy commanding people. I raise my voice a bit when they’re not on their desks before our teacher arrives. In our student times, each of them is my friend, and I am theirs.

The desolateness of a ruler without his people was devastating. My mother finding a new job in a different city caused my first exile. My best-president medal was packed and unpacked numerous times as we continually moved in and away. Until high school, I was the president again, sometimes the friend, and sometimes isolated; eventually, each shift was followed by the other, in an erratic order.

The pendulum swings right.

As an animal adapts, I tried to survive in chaotic habitats: school and home. Although I liked being a chameleon with dynamic colors, I sometimes yearned to be an ordinary, static creature, like a tree perhaps. Regardless, the predator was the same: irregularity.

My shield against the hunter was “constant”, so I decided to embrace math and physics: the most trusted endeavors.

I am fifteen. I do not enjoy the extra augmented mechanics summer course in freshman year. After three all-nighters studying physics, I decided it is not my thing–ultimately failed. However, the search for the constant keeps itself alive.

Ironically, it was a math project session that rekindled my interest in humanities and social sciences, fields full of inconsistency. Evaluating Carmichael Numbers, the non-prime numbers imitating the prime, I cast doubt on math. When our professor showed the “Incompleteness Theorem” of Gödel, I felt lost: the axioms on which math depends were unprovable, and pursuing math seemed like looking for a treasure with a broken compass. Therefore, my long-lasting journey of seeking certainty was devastatingly demolished. I decided to look for something completely different, even quite the opposite. I befriended the beast that haunted me through every move and school change: uncertainty.

I dug into the Black Swan incident to explore the ineffectiveness of inductive methods to reach certainty. I researched Turkey’s changing position between NATO and Russia under the scope of realism and liberalism, political theories that lack proof, unlike math. Whether it be an MUN conference, or a simple meeting on the boarding, I loved how different voices arose to strive with a common issue, creating harmony in disorder. My passion became to finish a task with the departed feeling of ignorance, knowing that each discovery revealed more unknowns to exist: little calves of the beast of uncertainty.

The openness to change, which causes others to be intimidated, is what drew me in; maybe because I had already found out certainty is unattainable.

I am seventeen. In this boarding philosophy camp, I am now responsible for cleaning the dishes left from dinner with Emir and an “abi”, a Turkish expression for “older brother”, whom I met a few days ago. Standing between them, I manage the single sink to distribute water evenly.

With some sweat, dirt, and tears, we finally finished the most compelling task. I went over to hang my apron.

I recognized a rectangular object between the swings of the pendulum: a mirror.

I see my apron. It is the same color as the uniform of a child-dictator I once knew ten years ago. Shiny buttons are replaced with stuck-on food residues. “Everything constantly changes”, I think. The Earth moves in space, continents shift, parents age, families move. I realize that it is just a dance: the synchronous rhythmic gestures of us. Together, in an ever-changing ballroom. I feel happy, dancing with people, an affection I will seek in college and beyond.

Thus, the pendulum turned into a metronome.

The 4-foot behemoth lay before us, an intricate landscape we spent hours trying to conquer. The seniors seated around the table watched quietly in anticipation, aching for the final moment of triumph. I glanced around, searching for who would land the final blow—but no one stepped up. The puzzle, one step away from perfection, was missing its final piece.

I revealed the bad news, only to be met with a wave of disappointed groans. These cries belonged to none other than the memory care residents of my local Brightview Senior Living community. Despite their disapproval, I looked at our creation in awe, reflecting on how I got to this point. Each piece, an essential part of the picture, reminded me of the residents who had shaped me.

I met Patricia the first time I volunteered at Brightview. Entering the memory care unit, Patricia always greeted me with a warm smile. During art nights, Patricia was my loyal assistant, looking out for those who needed help as I gave directions. On sunny days, we'd sit outside, discussing our dreams and sharing advice. Eventually, Patricia's dementia progressed and our heartfelt conversations came to an end, but her smile never faded away. Her look of gratitude always motivates me to keep going amidst the often chaotic environment of the memory care center.

Irene was the second resident I met. In all my time at Brightview, I've never seen Irene without her journal. She would jot down everything we did: the Scrabble games we battled over, the Jeopardy questions we answered, even the '70s music we sang along to. One day, I found her writing a letter to her grandchildren. Catching a glimpse of my interest, she handed me an envelope and introduced me to the art of letter writing. Handwritten letters let me communicate a personal touch that can't be found in a simple text message. With Irene's help, I wrote letters to my grandparents over the following weeks.

Of the residents at Brightview, Angie stood out the most. Her dementia was far more severe, marked by frequent mood swings and aimless wandering. More than once I had to break up her quarrels with other residents that started over seemingly nothing. Despite her mischief, Angie is always surrounded by family and other visitors. In one conversation with her son, I learned about Angie's past as an elementary school teacher, which explained her soft spot for children. Hearing her family's stories about her vibrant and charitable life revealed to me not only the sad reality of dementia, but also the lasting legacy she left behind through her family.

Nina was the only resident who shared my ethnic background. It was the first thing she mentioned when we met. Nina grew up in India, yet she hadn't gone back in decades, so an Indian was a rare sight for her. Although we've had the same conversation dozens of times, I'll never get tired of hearing about her experience as an army nurse while she wishes for my success as a future physician. After visiting India over winter break, I witnessed Nina tear up at the sight of the pictures I took in her hometown of Delhi.

The residents of Brightview are each individuals with their own stories, experiences, imperfections, and insights. My interactions with them have played an integral role in the person I am today. Patricia showed me the impact of having a smile and a positive attitude; Irene showed me how to slow down in an age that is fast-paced and digital; Angie taught me to cherish the ones closest to me; and Nina taught me to value my second home in India.

Despite the experience I've gained, my puzzle is still unfinished. As I embark on my journey in college and onwards, I will seek out new pieces, navigate uncharted perspectives, and forge lasting connections that shape my ever-changing and growing identity.

**New Me:**

What if success lies not in perfection, but in embracing our imperfections? My heart raced with the rhythmic clapping of my classmates—an exhilarating yet terrifying sound. In a world that often equates success with flawless performance, I found myself grappling with the pressure to be perfect. When I was chosen to perform alongside the talented sophomore Aybüke, I was shocked. Now, standing in the blinding spotlight, anxiety surged within me. What if I stumbled? Panic tightened its grip as I faced eager eyes. But as the music began, Aybüke’s confident smile anchored me. Her words backstage echoed in my mind: “It’s not about perfection—just believe in yourself.” With that, I let go of the pressure, stumbled through the first steps, and danced—not perfectly, but fully engaged.

**Discovery:**

“Are you free to host the debate tournament this year?” My teacher's words caught me off guard—I was still stewing over my rematch with Aybüke, who had won after I initially defeated her. Losing stung, but I was determined to reclaim my pride and become champion that year. Host? The title was usually given to the strongest speakers, and organizing felt daunting. Could I pass up this opportunity? I blurted, “Can I do both?”—still daydreaming about my debate showdown. Surprisingly, he agreed.

Years as my class’s lead speaker had prepared me, yet hosting felt like stepping onto a tightrope—thrilling yet precarious. I stumbled under expectations, trying to follow the rigid format of past tournaments. Chaos ensued as I balanced rules and kept the event lively. Then it hit me: stumbling through the chaos could help me find a new way. I suggested loosening the structure to energize the event, and Mr. Murat agreed!

With newfound freedom, I transformed the atmosphere. I added upbeat music, invited freshmen to the dance floor, and taught them a few moves that made everyone laugh. Watching them giggle as they attempted to twirl was priceless. My mission was to turn debate from a source of fear into something enjoyable. When students called me “abla,” meaning “older sister” in Turkish, it reinforced my belief in what I was doing.

**The Big One:**

“Can you believe it? We’re actually doing this!” I exclaimed as I put the final touches on the flyer for our Scrabble event—the first-ever student-led tournament at my school. It felt groundbreaking. Just as everything seemed to fall into place, a wave of anxiety hit. My teacher considered canceling the event due to funding issues. I stumbled—how could I tell the team, especially my eager freshmen, that this might not happen?

Managing 30 students, half freshmen, I wanted to protect their enthusiasm, so I kept the news to myself, sharing it only with a few close friends. Each time a freshman asked, “[Name] abla, when’s our next meeting?” their excitement renewed my determination. Yet behind the scenes, I scrambled over logistical and financial hurdles, reaching out for secret sponsorships to save the event. It wasn’t smooth, but navigating those stumbles led me to solutions that ultimately made the tournament possible.

As I prepare to step onto the college stage, I envision a vibrant community where curiosity and creativity thrive—a canvas for every voice to shine. My experiences hosting the debate tournament and organizing the Scrabble event have taught me that true leadership isn’t about perfection; it’s about creating an environment where everyone feels empowered to share their stories and take risks. Each stumble along the way has imparted a valuable lesson: success isn’t found in flawlessness but in the willingness to embrace our imperfections and learn from them. Imagine the friendships and creativity we could foster if we celebrated our missteps instead of fearing them. It’s perfectly fine to trip—as long as we keep dancing through it all.

My body's full of stretch marks, as my life's full of stress marks.

The first stretch mark appeared at the age of four, on my mom's belly. Every night, I rubbed lotion on indented streaks along mama's stomach and felt her insecurities as she hesitated before leaving the house. As a four-year-old, I couldn't tell why those marks made her uneasy, but I began to wonder - “if those stretch marks hadn't marred her skin - could she remain the confident woman in her old pictures?” The first stretch mark in my life, though not mine, was a stress mark in my perception of beauty - one shaped by patriarchal norms and objectification.

The second stretch mark came in abruptly during puberty - a red line etched into my arm - an uncanny monstrosity from childhood suddenly topped up and haunted my life. Panic, I tried to run. But how can I outrun the quiet distress of my mother? The next day, following the whole semester, I hid my arms in long-sleeved uniforms, refusing to participate in any activities exposing them. Even the school's bake sale, once my favorite, now became a painful reminder of the life I missed out on and my self-imposed isolation. The second stretch mark in my life - the first on my body - was a stress mark in my self-confidence.

The third stretch arrived on November 13rd 2021. That night, I watched Miss Universe for the first time in years and saw Anchilee Scott-Kemis - a woman of my size, catwalking confidently on the stage that orthodoxly extols model beauty standards. With her stretch marks visibly shown to the world, her advocacy for real size beauty shone through. For the first time, I saw beauty in what I've long believed to be flaws.

Over the following weeks, I paid closer attention to the bodies around me: the stretch marks on my mother's belly, the scars on my friend's leg, and the lines etched into the skin of strangers. In each mark, I saw stories of strength, survival, and beauty. One evening, I looked in the mirror, and finally saw myself for who I was: a unique individual with a body that had carried me through countless experiences. The stretch marks weren't flaws; they were part of me, a testament to my journey. With my courage fueled, I went to school wearing short-sleeves. Nothing changed visually, but something else changed completely. I was still the same person - a crinkle master, a hippie blog writer, a “mom-vibe” friend. But perhaps, I've conquered my monster.

In time, the color fades, as I've fully accepted my stretch mark. Regaining self-confidence and learning to embrace my imperfection wasn't easy, but the love and reassurance from the people around really pushed me forward. From being my own agent of changes, I grew into the community's changemaker, helping other women battle out their monsters. Starting with my mother, through pillow conversations and daily doses of support, we’ve worked together to conquer her insecurities, and she’s even begun changing her wardrobe—something I never thought I’d see. Beyond the thresholds of my home, I founded TEDxTPC - a women-led initiative encouraging women to believe in their values through inspirational stories of different female pioneers. Through hosting annual talk shows, I forge an inclusive platform for women to raise their voices and be unapologetic of themselves.

As our themes evolved from "Trailblazer" to "Subversion", I hope to challenge the preconceived labels the society imposes on women, not just through storytelling but also systematic changes. With university life unfolds, I aspire to contribute to pilot policies and initiatives enabling women to celebrate the beauty in our differences, creating a world where we are free to wear our stretch marks - both literal and metaphorical - as badges of honor.

These marks, once my stress marks, are now marks of resilience, self-acceptance, and my power to shape the world.

My aunt always said to me, “If you can’t eat spicy food, you’re missing out on the good stuff, the REAL good stuff.” My family is from Chengdu, a city in China famous for its unbearably spicy food, where people are often described as “wú là bù huān,” or unable to feel joy without spice. However, I could never tolerate it. The spice hurt, the flavor hurt, and most prominently, my mouth hurt. Ironically, though, I was not a stranger to pain.

Since the age of five, I fell into a routine: rolling my hair into a bun, fastening it with bobby pins, tying the ribbons on my worn-out pointe shoes. My left hand lays on the barre, feet turned out in first position, shoulders down, chin up. A deep breath, then the music begins. Plies, then tendus. Right leg, then left. Again and again. In my classical ballet training, with its endless repetition, the familiar burn rises in my muscles as I hold my á la seconde longer than I thought possible, the aching discomfort lingering in my body after hours of practice. As painful as that sounds, they became my signals of progress, allowing me to move freely across the stage, leaping and turning. Compared to my family, ballet was my version of spicy food, painful but joyful.

What’s more? Throughout my life, I have moved a few times between LA and Shanghai, each time more difficult than the last. There were two versions of me–but instead of double, it felt like whichever half that represented the location I was in, would constantly need to compensate for not being whole. When I returned to Shanghai for high school, my half would struggle to handle both the familiar and the unfamiliar. It was confusing, almost painful, like a part of me was out of sync with the world I once knew so closely. I had to flip my switch to Shanghai mode, adjusting to the layers of language, culture, and formality, desperately keeping a poker face to fend off interaction in my unprepared state. But shopping with my grandmother weekly, I practiced my spoken Chinese while navigating through the market and stands. Soon I was able to understand Chinese social media, seeking out articles and trends that allowed me to integrate into my Shanghai circle once again. Words from my peers’ slowly became comprehensible, allowing my true expressions to escape from that poker face of uneasiness. Though navigating through change was painful, adapting through the changes revealed to me the joyful truth. Shanghai and LA will always be my two homes, two halves that make up a whole. Again this was my version of spicy food.

I’m no stranger to pain. But at the Chinese New Year dinner table in Chengdu, I was a stranger. Every year I would distance myself from the table to completely spicy foods, and every year my family tried to convince me to try it. In the end, it wasn’t the heat that won me over but the stories behind them: Grandma Ma tofu, named after a famous woman, the cold beef dish honoring a sweet couple, and more. Moved by their stories, the fiery sting on my tongue was flushed out to surprise me with rich and complex layers of taste, far beyond just spice. Embracing the spice, I finally felt the joy of calling myself a true Chengdunese.

Now, I am no longer a stranger at my family’s dinner table either. After all of these experiences I realize my aunt was right, and not just about the food. The unknowns in my future may seem daunting, but like with spicy food, ballet, and moving, I’ve learned that facing discomfort shapes a stronger, more versatile version of myself. Now, my heart beats for the richness that lies beyond the initial pain, waiting to be discovered.

Red numbers blinked on the monitor.

0322 am: 88%

Delicately, 15-year-old me clipped the oximeter off. I reached for the bottle of isopropyl alcohol, its sharp scent mingling with my nervousness as I slathered its contents onto my flaking hands.

As my parents battled COVID-19, I took on the responsibility of caring for my grandmother. Every day was a learning curve - operating a Metered-Dose Inhaler (without spraying my face), deciphering the oncologist (he was spewing jargons) and getting pummeled by Dad over Facetime (I forgot to refrigerate insulin).
