Amidst the chaos that I was, my grandmother would chuckle in response. “Sorry, Ah-Ma. I know I’m not the most helpful…” I murmured in Mandarin. Frustration swelled over my inadequacies, but I couldn't help but smile through the bittersweetness.

Worldwide, the success rate of a coronary balloon angioplasty exceeds 95%. Yet, the entropy in our lives pays no heed to probabilities. I remember hearing the sigh of the ventilator. Saying goodbye. Grief, I learned, is the sudden hill in the middle of a long run. It leaves me gasping for air, demanding I slow down and acknowledge it.

“I'm glad you took care of Ah-Ma in her final weeks,” Dad expressed after life lost its color.

I returned a blank gaze. How could I count myself a caregiver?

The broken vow of responsibility became my constant companion, casting shadows of gray into my life. Daily obligations morphed into Sisyphean tasks. Drink this water. Learn the Krebs Cycle. Cross-country training. I felt paralyzed. Mangled.

Convinced I could outrun grief, I filled every hour with activities. The relentless pace served a temporary panacea, and it became clear I needed something more meaningful than packed schedules. Then, came the opportunity to volunteer: “Provide academic support for primary school students from underprivileged backgrounds.”

“Can you try this question, Grace?” I requested.

“NO!” Grace proclaimed, arms crossed defiantly over her chest. A stubborn pout formed on her lips, and she shifted her gaze toward the colorful jumble of toys.

I have to be more interesting than whatever was distracting her. I coughed.

“Let’s try something new. Algebra!” I offered.

“What?” Grace whipped her head around, her jet black eyes wide with confusion.

Gotcha.

A 9-year-old, who failed Mathematics, tackling Algebra? Some saw my decision a glaring oversight. Nonetheless, I sensed I was on the brink of a revelation. As I worked with Grace, I became acutely aware of her struggle with self-doubt. “I can’t!” She would conclude, a refrain ingrained in her – and in many of us. Yet, life’s terrain of trial and error can mold us into something profound.

As Grace’s confidence blossomed, I learned to navigate the landscape of my grief. Within our brokenness lies the potential for beauty and connection, service to others. It is this truth that can transform our grief into growth. Through volunteering, I caught glimpses of grins, flickers of defeat, demonstrations of grit. And 7 months later, Grace declared, “I can!” for the very first time.

My journey into ‘caregiving’ began with my grandmother, and it’s since evolved in unexpected ways. Whether it’s distributing welfare packs to migrant workers, offering emotional support to dialysis patients, or organizing fund-raisers to improve the learning facilities at Sambour Primary School in Cambodia, I strive to bring visibility to the disadvantaged.

In our final session, Grace surprised me with “the best ice-cream in the universe” and, alongside it, a note: Thank you for being my teacher.

Time does not necessarily heal the ache; it only teaches us how to adjust our stride and embrace the pace of life. It may feel impossible sometimes, but that’s where our shared humanity shines. Therefore, I trust that every twist in the path leads to valleys of flowers and glorious sunsets (and ice-creams). And so, the journey to uplift others continues.

On a quiet Saturday morning, the sun shed a glimpse of warmth on my piano, the only sound is the cheerful chirping of a bird outside. I’m supposed to practice a piece I’ve played countless times. Why can’t I create my own melody instead of repeating someone else’s, as I listen to the bird's free-spirited song?

I can picture mom’s worried face. After six years of piano practice, I’m about to tell her I want to quit. My heart pound as I walked up to my parents. “I’d like to stop piano lessons,” I said, my voice quiet and uncertain. The pause that follows feels unbearable. I quickly add, “I’ve built a solid foundation in music theory. Could I try composing my own songs instead?” The fear of disappointing them lingers in the air. To my surprise, they agreed. Now it is time to find a new way to enjoy music.

For the first time, I’m stepping away from a structured path, and it’s overwhelming. I sit at the piano for hours, the blank sheet music in front of me seems like an impossible challenge. I constantly wondering if I’ve made the right decision. Slowly, I start to forget those worries, I experiment with melodies note by note, hum softly to myself, and gradually the notes come together. A year later, I performed my award-winning piece, Establishment, in the historic Ehrbar Hall in Vienna. Now I have no regret on changing the course as I know taking a leap into the unknown, despite the fear, is part of the journey.

This mindset followed me into junior year. Many classmates registered for SAT prep camps. "[Name], would you like to join the SAT camp?" my mom asked. "No, mom. I prefer to prepare on my own." Understanding that the SAT was originally an aptitude test, I didn’t want to over-practice and lose sight of its purpose. Instead, I went directly to take several mock exams, analyzed my mistakes, summarized lessons learned to ensure I wouldn’t repeat errors. I know I might get blamed for not spending adequate time to prepare for my test, I may waste money to take test again and again, but I decided to move forward with my way of preparation.

This uncertainty surfaced again the summer after my junior year, when I decided to join a STEM project using machine learning to predict mental health situations. The decision filled me with unease. I had no experience with machine learning and only a basic understanding of Python. The thought of failing before I even began was intimidating, but I may not lose anything eventually, I told myself.

The first two weeks were overwhelming. I spent hours trying to understand algorithms and struggling through tutorials. Every time I hit a dead end, I questioned whether I was capable of finishing the project. Quickly I realized that I shouldn’t do it alone, reaching out to my other two teammates for discussion of what their understanding. I listed the questions we all have, and clarified with the professor. Together, we broke down the complex concepts, sought advice from graduate assistants, and piece by piece, the project started to take shape.

Before the deadline, we each successfully built three models to predict mental health conditions. But more importantly, I learned to embrace uncertainty as a strength. By admitting that I didn’t know everything, I opened myself up to learning and growing in ways I hadn’t anticipated. The experience taught me that even when I feel uncomfortable or risky, it can still lead to a meaningful growth.

It’s the willingness to step into uncertainty, to face the fear of failure head-on, and to keep moving forward despite the doubts. I see facing the unknown as a tool that drives my resilience.

I ended Establishment with the rhythmic sound of a train—the "clickety-clack" that is my steady steps toward uncertainty without fear.

The Rubik's cube taunted me. I sat there staring at it. It stared back. Each colorful square seemed to mock my efforts as I twisted and turned, trying to make sense of the puzzle. The challenge felt insurmountable, yet I couldn't tear myself away. The cube became a symbol of every obstacle I had ever faced—complex, confusing, and seemingly impossible to conquer. Determined to master it, I set an ambitious goal: to solve the Rubik's cube in under 15 seconds.

I dedicated countless hours to learning new algorithms and practicing relentlessly. The process was filled with challenges and moments of frustration. There were times when I felt stuck, unable to improve my time despite my best efforts. However, each setback only fueled my determination to succeed. Breaking down each step of the solution, analyzing my weaknesses, and continuously refining my technique gradually paid off. Achieving an average solve time of under 15 seconds became a reality.

This journey was not just about solving a puzzle faster; it was about developing a mindset of persistence and continuous improvement. The skills and lessons gained from cubing—patience, strategic thinking, and resilience—have influenced my approach to challenges in all aspects of my life, from academics to personal projects.

Leading the Math Team was like solving a tough puzzle—challenging, demanding, and rewarding. One competition stands out: we encountered a combinatorics problem that none of us had seen before. The room grew tense as the clock ticked, and frustration set in. When everyone wanted to give up, the rubric cube reminded me of all the times I was just a few moves away from solving it. Remembering the problem-solving skills I had learned from cubing, I suggested breaking the problem into smaller parts and approaching it from different angles. Slowly, things started to click, and when a teammate spotted a key pattern, we managed to solve the problem just in time. That moment reinforced how persistence and problem solving, both skills I had developed through cubing, were just as important in leadership as in solving any challenge. It wasn’t just about solving the problem—it was about guiding my team through a tough situation, boosting my confidence in handling challenges under pressure.

Research projects also benefited from the strategic thinking and problem-solving skills developed through speedcubing. As the pandemic unfolded, I wanted to explore how computer science could potentially assist in the fight against COVID-19. I took on a solo project using machine learning to help diagnose the virus from chest X-rays. Just like in cubing, I broke the project down into manageable steps—learning data preprocessing, model training, and troubleshooting technical glitches along the way. When I hit obstacles, I turned to Kaggle's example notebooks to guide me through specific challenges, learning from others’ solutions and applying them to my own model. The persistence I had honed through cubing kept me motivated as I worked through these challenges. Gradually, my efforts paid off, resulting in a model that could accurately detect COVID-19 cases and assess their severity. This experience not only deepened my understanding of AI but also reinforced the power of persistence and research in solving real-world problems.

Reflecting on that rainy afternoon with the Rubik's cube, it's clear how much that moment has shaped my future. The same determination and methodical approach that enabled me to solve the cube in under 15 seconds now empower me to tackle any future challenge. Whether pursuing computer science, contributing to research projects, or participating in extracurriculars, the resilience and strategic mindset developed through speedcubing will be foundational. Every twist and turn of the cube taught the value of patience, strategy, and perseverance. Just as I conquered the Rubik's cube, I am confident in my ability to navigate the complexities of college life. This journey has made me not just a faster cuber, but a stronger, more determined individual ready for the future.

A lot of people around me thought I was crazy; others urged me to be more realistic about my goals. I was told it was almost impossible to get into the national cricket team of India, a country of 1.4 billion where nearly every child dreams of becoming a professional cricketer. The numbers don’t lie - the probability was less than one in a million. However, I surmised, if everyone thought that way, no one would make it to the national team. Only those who truly believe they have a shot at achieving the nearly impossible have any chance of succeeding.

My parents often emphasized that achieving greatness in any field requires not only hard work and passion but also natural talent. I never liked that idea because it meant success was dependent on factors beyond my control. I saw that as a convenient excuse not to put in the requisite effort. I asked them, even if you’re right, isn’t it a better approach in life to believe that you can achieve anything with hard work and passion? They reluctantly acknowledged that may be a better way of navigating life’s challenges. Also, how do we know the limits of our talent unless we put it to the test?

With that sentiment, I set out to test the limits of my talent, as well as physical and mental endurance; not to mention the limits of parents’ patience. Over the last decade I have spent more waking hours training for and playing cricket than doing anything else. I’ve trained 4-6 hours a day each weekday and played matches for 10-20 hours on weekends. Nearly every vacation has been spent at a cricket academy. I have played with broken fingers, ligament tears, hamstring injuries and uprooted nails.

During Covid, when Hong Kong shuttered all sports facilities indefinitely, I wanted to go to India to continue my cricket training. My parents were firmly against letting me go three months before my IGCSE exams. Born and raised in small cities in India, neither played competitive sports growing up but understood the value of quality education through firsthand experience. Undeterred, I tried to convey my passion for cricket, crafted a detailed study plan, found IGCSE examination centers in India (in case I couldn't travel back in time), and promised to get straight As in IGCSE. None of it worked. I felt powerless in front of my unyielding parents. Finally, I stayed awake one whole night, making and plastering posters all over the house with messages urging them to support my cricket practice and send me to India. When they woke up the next morning and saw the posters it was probably the first time they fully appreciated the depth of my passion and dedication. A week later, I was on my first solo international journey from Mumbai to Bangalore via Doha and Mumbai. Given a raging global pandemic there were no direct flights from HK to India at that time.

The effort I put in earned me spots on the Hong Kong Men’s Under-16 and Under-19 cricket teams, but I have also realized that I was not improving at the pace needed to play for India. While I was disappointed, I also carry deep satisfaction knowing that I tested the limits of what I could achieve instead of surrendering to the notion that my goals were unattainable. My journey taught me invaluable lessons about teamwork, leadership, discipline, risk-taking, time management and prioritization.

Is it better to set audacious goals and fail in the attempt or to choose easy goals and succeed? For me, the adventure of striving for a difficult goal is far more enticing and enriching. The lessons learned from failure serve as foundational stones for tackling future challenges. In the next innings of my life I am looking forward to setting another audacious goal and willing to give my all to achieve it. In cricket, as in life, I'll always aim for the boundary. Because even if I miss, I'll have stretched myself further than any easily achieved goal could have done. And that, to me, is the true measure of success.

When my brother, who is 10 years older than me, returned from Lancaster University, I noticed something was off. During our trip to Japan, as our family strolled down the streets of Tokyo, he faded into the sea of unfamiliar faces. While my parents searched for him, my heart was racing: barraged with conflicting thoughts—fear, confusion, helplessness. I reminisced about the time when we jokingly turned each other’s lights off; there were no traces of that left. After hours of missed phone calls, he returned to our hotel, shrouded in complete silence.

Following the trip, an unspoken heaviness lingered within our household. “I’ve had enough!” I heard him yell, and then there was a slam. I ran from my room to the hallway, just in time to see my brother carrying his haphazardly packed suitcase out the front door while my parents stood, helpless. Every night onwards, my parents’ saddening conversations about my brother’s depression slipped through the cracks of their bedroom door as I leaned on it, lifelessly. However, perhaps driven by our past bond, he still allowed me to talk and visit him, igniting a period where I visited my brother every weekend, bringing snacks like his favorite Tom yum-flavored cup noodles, hoping to mend our family.

Driven to support him, I committed long hours to researching depression online. While my parents wanted me to view visiting him as a hangout, I knew they hoped I could aid his return to our family. The videos and blogs I researched were pivotal in understanding my brother throughout our conversations. It also exposed me to the anguish people go through as they journey through life.

"What if I can’t reach him? What if I make things worse?" I questioned myself. However, while these storms of thoughts clouded my head, I felt an unwavering resolve to keep trying.

I weaved subtle hints into our conversations that my family always welcomed him home, like “Mom and Dad still love you, y’know,” but he never budged. Each interaction, each game of FIFA 21 (where I always lost miserably), became a piece in the puzzle I was trying to solve. The excitement and laughter my brother and I had when he scored an overhead kick with Ronaldo in the dying minutes made me realize that someone who I once held on a pedestal is also just a human. It also taught me—even when you miss the goal, others are there to support you. Like stepping in for an injured player, I knew it was my turn to step up for my brother. These moments felt like I forged a new bond, and not just trying to mend something that was lost.

Four months after he moved out of the house, as his perspective gradually shifted through our interactions, it finally happened. At 2:00 pm, I received a text from my brother that I will never forget: “I love you.” As simple as that. Overwhelmed with joy, I immediately ran to my parents to tell them what had happened. Seeing the joy in their eyes was like an early birthday present!

As my brother returned home, the family dynamics that I yearned for began to take shape, allowing my brother to reconcile with my parents and steadily recover from his depression. The empty seat at the dining table, now filled, eased the tension that had weighed on my chest for so long.

The lessons I learned from FIFA—of persistence and always looking to score the winning goal—have transformed me to become someone who can mediate and ignite changes within my community. I hope to apply my ability as a conduit both inside and outside the campus setting, helping to create and restore meaningful relationships even through the adversities of life. This is where my identity is rooted—within compassion and connection.

Two A.M. The house was silent, save for the rhythmic rumble of snores in the adjacent rooms. Surrounding me was a fortress of pillows and quilts, so even if a wisp of wind intruded through the slit in my window, I would be warm and cozy. In the dark of my room, a cascade of colors flashed before me as I scrolled through YouTube on my laptop. Comfort–If I had to describe this scene in one word, that’d be it; yet lingering in the back of my head, an abstract emptiness still eats away at me. How? I had everything I could ask for—warmth, quiet, entertainment—but why do I still feel so hollow? As if on cue, my computer died without warning, leaving me in total darkness. Though I couldn’t see anything, I could imagine my tired, bag-laden eyes, staring back at me through the now-dark abyss of the computer screen.

***

Dirt. All I could see was dirt, and beyond that, more dirt. The clanging of cowbells and voices were so present, yet ever so distant. Shoes trampled all around me. A red one. Two neon ones. There was no rhythm in this chaos, no pattern to cling to for relief. My lungs seized as I gulped for air, arms flailing helplessly about.

That was my recollection of my first Cross country meet. Unlike my bed, there was no warmth–the sun scorched my back, almost evaporating my sweat as it rolled off my forehead. Silence and serenity were all but thrown out the window, and as for entertainment–well, maybe for the crowd, but as I scrambled up the hills I had to seriously contemplate why I even joined voluntary self-torture in the first place. Yet, as I limped across the finish line, I felt more alive than I had in months. The emptiness that had gnawed away at me in the dark solitude of my room was nowhere to be found; instead, there was a raw, undeniable connection to the present—a clarity that cut through the noise and pain, a comfort that I found through discomfort. As I’d come to understand, not every challenge is as clear-cut as a race. Outside the course, I faced a different kind of discomfort—one not physical, but equally demanding: communication.

***

Because English wasn’t my first language, expressing my thoughts aloud often left me in awkward silence. Words that worked in my head fell apart on my lips. In my quest to fix these gaffs, I joined my school newspaper, The Outlook, as a sports reporter.

My first post-game interview lasted all of three minutes; I ran through my list of scripted questions before awkwardly walking away. Salvaging my transcripts for a clue, I was astonished to find over forty filler words littering the exchange–practically three per sentence!. My close-ended questions gave the athlete no room to expand, either; all I had were “yes” or “no” answers. But each interview left me with a crucial lesson: through discomfort, I analyzed my mistakes and made progress, one talk at a time. Eventually, I shed the script and let conversations flow, turning each interview into a dialogue rather than an interrogation.

By senior year, I was the sports editor for The Outlook. But more than the title, it was the responsibility that mattered—guiding new staffers through their first interviews, just as I had stumbled through mine. I became the pacer for others, helping them navigate their own races and showing them that discomfort isn’t something to avoid, but to embrace.

***

Two A.M. The silence in my room mirrored the awkward silences that had plagued me for so long. This time, I welcomed it–no longer are they marks of complacency or badges of shame, but a testament to how far I’ve come in my journey to confront discomfort. Tomorrow is a new start, a new chance to break my own records.

On your marks. Get set. Go.

At the age of ten, I felt I was born to resist.

In the sweltering heat of a Babylon summer, a small desert town two hours from the capital, I engaged in a daily battle against forces that sought to uproot the fabric of my community. An ISIS bomb went off nearby, shattering the glass of my room. This was the town’s fifth car explosion that week. It targeted my school.

“Yalla [Name] – today you fight, understood?” my father mumbled to me as we walked to school. As I stepped through the main gate, a metallic smell engulfed my nostrils; my airways constricted, a typical asthma symptom.

Soon after class started, blasts echoed in the distance. Instinctively, I sprung into action: comforting my peers, and ensuring everyone was safe while teachers frantically called their families to check in on them. Questioning my thoughts, my father’s words echoed in my mind. Maybe he was right; perhaps violence could only be met with violence.

Although I have momentary lapses in my nonviolent conviction, I disagree with my father on the way I should resist. While my father contributes to the military efforts by donating aid and weapons, I embody combat resistance by joining the volunteer community in my town. This, at times, has caused disruptions in our household from endless conversations about our different political views to how rightful a certain militia is in their approach towards ending the ISIS invasion. Though I could not change his mind, we always ended our conversations with understanding.

Lunch talks are always heated for the simplest of conversations; Islamic vs Secular state, fighting terrorism, or even Shawarma vs Kebab. It was frightening seeing weapons in our house, then a big military truck, barely fitting in the narrow road leading to my house made me think again about my position in supporting nonviolence.

While resistance for my father looked like donating our 100-year-old family gun to the Resistance Forces against ISIS, for me, it looked like providing for my family in nonviolent ways. I started making the daily dangerous journey to Baghdad while working two jobs to support my family. At festivals, we sat near a cozy campfire playing the guitar and singing “Babar Fil”, a song we all used to listen to as children while organizing events and activities to train community people on essential skills such as peace-building, conflict-resolution, and organizing skills. The conversation we had about what we wanted to do when we grew up while surrounding the campfire was my first exposure to dialogue and communal bonds.

It is those moments around the campfire that remind me that nonviolence is the only way. When I try to talk to my father about this, he says the uneducated should be met with what they believe in, violence. His way of looking at the conflict is fueled by the eras of destruction we faced because of all who misleadingly promised a ‘safe country’.

At these difficult moments, the only way we can resolve them is by dialogue and conversation, we talk to identify problems and we work towards addressing them. This is challenging because of the mindset people have, each part believing the only way to resolve the conflict is to diminish the other, and by that killing what makes us humans; our ability to talk and understand each other.

To resist in college will be to utilize education as a tool to develop and empower communities to navigate crises effectively, whatever that means for each community, and support them. I will bring not only my deep commitment to the community but a profound reverence for nonviolence to these conversations, with empathy for those like my father, who are forced to believe violence is the only way.

I dream of safer communities, resistant to ideologies of destruction and terror, and resilient like me, a “lion of Mesopotamia” from a small town in Babylon.

Whenever life feels breathtaking, I always happen to know the right place to be at. With her hands moving like a ballerina across my back, each step relieves the tension of my body, guiding me towards complete relaxation. As a kid raised by my grandmother, I used to believe she had superpowers. She knew how to cook every dish in the world and gave wonderful massages. However, as a typical traditional Chinese family, her habits seem to differ from those of the other members of my family. She often spoke on the phone in languages I could not understand and sometimes invited foreign strangers to our house. I never seemed to question her as I was growing up, usually accepting her behaviors without much thought.

The relationship I used to share with my grandmother gradually deteriorated as I got older because of the growing differences in our lifestyles. I couldn't match the cultural differences between her and my community, so I naturally started to estrange from her internally. However, her actions stimulated my interest in learning more about the past experiences she has been through, which developed my curiosity about different cultural backgrounds. Her broad knowledge and adaptable skills left me wondering, "Who is this person that has been raising me for the past ten years?" I was excited to learn more about this woman and how she opened my eyes to a larger world.

One evening, as she was preparing dishes for the Mid-Autumn Festival, I finally asked about her past. As she shared her stories with me, I began to understand what life was like for her as an immigrant during that time, and I slowly realized that her "superpowers" all seem to have been honed through experiences from different cultures. The feeling of envy came to my mind, never thinking that a person's identity can hide multiple cultural backgrounds. My perception of my grandmother changed, as did my previous perception of cultural differences. I no longer see cultural differences as an excuse to drive people farther apart. Instead, it is the perfect tool to pull people closer together. At that point, my grandmother to me was really the hero with superpowers.

After learning a lot from my grandmother, I realized that many children in the countryside seem to also lack the understanding of diverse cultures like I did before. They seem to have a strong impression of their own country and are rarely curious about other cultures. For this reason, I founded a community service club, which hosted trips to teach children at elementary schools in remote areas. During our time at the schools, we hosted venues that taught children about cultures in different regions worldwide. My goal was to inspire their curiosity so they can expect more from the world ahead, and after seeing their eyes as if they had discovered a new continent, I really felt the impact of diversity. It taught me that being open to new things and learning about them is always better than locking myself in my comfort zone.

Throughout my childhood with my grandmother, staying curious and accepting diversity is the most important knowledge that I learned from her. Whether it is meeting new people or diving into new areas of study, the urge to explore different aspects pushes me to become successful. The power of curiosity leads me to the correct path of finding the answer to every hard question. Thus, I try to grasp every chance for me to deepen my experience and expand my worldview.

I’ve never believed in Santa. If he was real, I should’ve received a delivery from him by now. Mom claimed that presents were merely courtesies wrapped in shiny paper; instead of material gifts, I was raised on acts of service: magical conjurings of peeled longans on my desk when I arose from naps and unspoken understandings that entitled me to the last drumstick at dinner. As a child looking to expand my toy empire, I wanted to disagree, but with frequent reminders on how money comes from hard labor, I reluctantly withheld my rebuttal.

Labor looked like the torn hangnails on Mom’s hands from folding hundreds of pounds of laundry every day. Labor felt like the cracked skin on Dad’s fingertips due to overexposure to detergents and fabric softeners. The image of their worn hands grasped my heart with guilt whenever I dared to feel disappointed by the absence of presents under my imaginary Christmas tree.

***

When Dad's birthday approached in late July, I had no idea what to get him. Hand-written cards ended up buried in the basement, while homemade cakes were devoured by my sister and me (Mom said he couldn’t have any because of his high cholesterol). For Dad, practicality determined the value of a gift. Yet, when I asked him what he wanted, all he said was “You should take care of yourself before taking care of others.”

Out of a mixture of spite and determination to prove that I could do both, I spent the last summer tutoring middle schoolers. I answered a seemingly endless slew of questions like, “Is 1 a prime number?” (no), “Were you nervous like us when you took your SHSAT?” (yes), and “Can you make penne alla vodka?” (kind of). As I left camp with cash weighing down my jeans pocket, my heart lightened, relieved that for a while, I could skip the trimonthly dread of asking my parents for allowance. After budgeting for the school year, I scoured “Best Father Day Gifts!” articles until I landed on an item that resurfaced memories of gingerly applying a herbal-smelling pain relief balm on Dad’s back: a shiatsu massage pillow. It’s practical, perhaps dull, but just his taste.

Along with a bunch of bananas (potassium for the cramps), I delivered the pillow, reminiscing about the hours I spent researching musculoskeletal benefits and corroborating product reviews. The gift was simultaneously an act of service and a declaration that often, albeit silently, echoed across this house: “I love you.” As Dad gleamed with a smile that showed off his chipped front tooth, my vicarious happiness revealed the symbiotic beauty of gift-giving. The $24.99 transaction in my Chase account never failed to flood my heart with pride every time I logged in to see the deduction again.

Although the bananas have long been digested, the pillow now has a permanent spot on our living room couch. Dad’s unexpected attachment to it proved that my parents didn’t dislike gifts—they just never had the chance to receive them, having grown up poor and internalized the frugality needed to survive the financial crisis of China’s Cultural Revolution. Now that they’re fifty-years-young, I’ll claim the pleasure of buying them their very first presents.

***

My family still primarily shows affection through acts of service, but now I’m also our designated gift-giver. My exploration of the diverse expressions of love has made it clear that affection isn’t bound by any single cast. It was because of my parents’ altruistic love that I took a step back to understand their childhood that generationally shaped them, and in turn, myself. It was out of a symbiotic love for both my family and myself, that I took a step forward to initiate new traditions in our home that no one else could. And ultimately, I found balance in this transience, learning how to adjust my affection to resonate with the people that surround me.

My stomach churned as we approached the Air India gate in silence. I’d never play pickleball with my friends again. Never take AP Stats with Mr. Moser. Never lead the entrepreneurship club. Never study at an American college.

The country and the life I’d poured my heart into had rejected me. The long letter carried a clear message: leave or you will be deported. At first, India was a pleasant escape. Exploring temples, tea stalls, and packed movie theaters was a fun quest with my grandpa. However, its novelty quickly wore off as I realized this wasn't a vacation. This was my new life.

Barbells and bench presses became rice bags and pushups. My eyes welled up as I swiped through freshman-year pictures of my friends and my past life. The “J” key popped off my keyboard when I slammed my laptop in frustration after my online school couldn’t offer me a single course I wanted. The opportunities that my parents worked their whole lives to provide were gone.

Two months later, on a scorching hot August day, ten relatives and I crammed into a 7-seater for a trip to my dad’s native village. We pulled over near a bus stop for a break from the road. There, on the hot bench, laid a boney man wearing tattered rags. A sob escaped him, his body shaking rapidly. Then, silence. Immediately after, a scratchy laugh filled the air, sounding more like a scream.

Seeing the despair in his eyes left a knot in my stomach. It wasn’t my first time seeing a homeless person, but at that time, as I felt I was at the lowest point, I realized I couldn't imagine a fraction of his pain. Suddenly, my self-pity felt like a childish tantrum. I had the ability to improve my life and others’, but I was allowing my own sense of victimhood to hold me back from reaching my goals.

I decided to push myself to make the most of my circumstances. In the following weeks, I wrote nearly a hundred emails, finally connecting my online school with a non-profit providing AP courses. This partnership created a pathway to offer more advanced courses to all 4,000 students. Despite the grinding cycle of starting school at 6 P.M. and ending at 1 A.M., I found an odd support system. Two (slightly terrifying) gray lizards perched on my wall became my nightly companions - their unblinking eyes reminded me that I wasn’t alone.

As days passed, I often thought of the man on the bench and the fact that I did nothing to help him. Seeing him had motivated me to improve my own circumstance, but what had I done for him? One morning, I opened Android Studio and began building FoodShift - an app connecting organizations with excess food to homeless shelters. Inspired by its impact, I taught students at my uncle’s rural school how to build apps using just a smartphone. Becoming their Anna (big brother in Tamil) and watching their career goals switch from “cricket player” to “entrepreneur” taught me that true content comes when my efforts are tied to their success.

8 months later, when my visa interviewer asked what I’d done in India, I told her this story. Being forced back left me desperate to rekindle past joys and opportunities, but I soon realized this only leads to anger, self-pity, and inaction. My friends often ask what if I hadn’t returned, and while I know I would have found happiness, this lucky second chance has given me a greater sense of purpose. Now, I focus on ensuring that those who truly need opportunities can access them. As I type this, the missing “J” on my keyboard reminds me that life’s gaps and imperfections are where true growth occurs—that sometimes, it’s in the spaces where something is missing that we discover if we have the strength to fill them.

My life through elementary school can be boiled down to two words: “constantly in motion.” My parents and teachers never seemed to fall short of ideas determined to tame my restlessness. At school I was assigned a clearly nonsensical to an eight-year-old task of carrying a heavy load of books from one classroom to another. My pockets were loaded with fidget spinners and squishy balls. Heavy blanket at night and rigorous morning exercise became an integral part of my routine at home.

The only time my body seemed to be able to quiet down was when my mind became deeply engaged into high dopamine activities. JeremyShaferOrigami YouTube channel with his complex and quirky origami designs became my absolute favorite pastime. I could sit motionless for hours absorbed with experimenting. How thick should the paper be? How much force should I apply to each crease? How should I angle my hand? Inspired by the Aboriginal boomerangs of Australia, I designed my own origami boomerang and spent weeks perfecting my throw and tweaking the design until it could consistently fly back to me.

I was so eager to share my origami zeal with others that every student in my class soon acquired at least a basic grasp of origami folding. Some went on to become my origami buddies proudly boasting intricate designs and seeking advice with challenging pleats, creases and twists.

As my voice became deeper and my frontal lobe developed, my body became less restless, but my racing mind was a different story. During my sophomore year, unsure of my interests, I went on a spree of reading and self-discovery. I devoured volumes of books on topics that did not seem to have anything in common. Eager to deeper understand my cultural heritage, I became infatuated with twentieth century history which led to absorbing conversations at the dinner table with my parents about their childhood. Symphony for the City of the Dead with its vivid portrayal of horrors of depravity and starvation in the besieged Leningrad, taught me to combine the highly rational and deeply emotional. My violin concertos were no longer based on reason but rather on a moving outcry of my feelings. Exploration of philosophy led me to discover Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations and gave me a power to “strip away superfluous troubles” overpowering my judgment. As I fervently engaged in discussions with my classmates, I gradually trained my brain to slow down focusing on clear-mindedness and rationality. My brain was no longer racing on its own but seemed to embrace a cosmic perspective with others actively sharing and listening to my classmates’ ideas.

Reminiscing my childhood origami, I immersed myself in physics and math experiments. Estimating the volume of a cross section through building of the actual model with the several dozens of cardboard pieces and further validating the estimation using abstract math calculations pushed me to the next level in my journey of self-discovery. Ability to combine the sensory feeling of methodically cutting out the cardboard pieces and getting my hands busy with gluing the whole project together with a challenge of applying abstract concepts to substantiate the calculations, became a new stimulus for my craving brain.

Last year I returned to elementary school to teach advanced math and science topics. I am overtaken with joy every time the expression of confusion and struggle on the students’ faces surrenders to the expression of thirst and determination. My pockets remain filled with carefully folded paper cranes that I readily share when I recognize myself in another student.

Even though I can now claim a full victory over the control of my body, I am not sure whether I will ever be able to fully pacify my ravenous mind. One thing that I am certain though is that as I move through my life, I will always remain in a restless pursuit of new challenges on my path of self-discovery.

“Grace! Where are you!?” My voice cracked as I rubbed the salt out of my eyes, searching for a small, easily overlooked girl in a bathing suit. Grace was gone. After emerging from the surf and hidden amidst beachgoers and colorful tents, my little sister had taken a wrong turn and wandered down the opposite side of the beach, almost disappearing before being found a mile down the shore.

Grace was diagnosed with autism at the age of two. From that moment, the world seemed to shrink—doctors’ offices, speech therapy sessions, special education plans, a maze of charts and papers. In those early years, we circled each other cautiously. She didn’t know how to start a conversation with me. I wasn’t sure how to approach her.

As time passed, new responsibilities found their way into my life. “Remember, don’t open the door for anyone” became my parents’ routine parting call, entrusting me with her care while they were away. What started as a chore became an opportunity for sparks of connection and discovery. We transformed her verbal tics into humorous gibberish words with ten different variations (like guhgyosi, which had no meaning but made us laugh). On a Death Valley road trip, we named and added new Pokémon to the 800 official ones in her guidebook. My camera roll still has a photo of her holding zoo binoculars the wrong way around; concrete evidence of a bond I hadn’t expected to find.

In time, I took on a new responsibility of my own choosing. It started with answering her questions about Spanish and math homework, and before long, she’d burst through my door every week (bright orange “Avancemos!” workbook in hand), full of questions about conjugations and verb usage. Even on the days when I was drowning in schoolwork, I found myself pausing my studies to help her navigate inequalities and tenses. It wasn’t just about being an older sibling, but also giving her the confidence and understanding to stand on her own.

I taught her social cues: how to approach new friends, read the mood in a room, or recognize expressions. Even when progress was slow, I reminded myself of why I started—Grace’s potential, not her limitations—and that pushed me to try again. Like the pieces of a puzzle inching together, I saw her connect with the world outside, one cautious step at a time. Her trust filled me with gratitude.

I became her teacher, yes. But in return, she taught me how to let go of the past, to stop dwelling on mistakes, and that optimism for the future is its own form of resilience. Her ability to straighten a slouched, dejected posture into a giggling and bouncing bundle of energy amused and inspired me. Her drawings scattered all over the house reminded me that creativity isn’t done, but lived.

I learned to enjoy the mundane moments in life while concurrently pursuing excitement and adventure–to embrace but also escape monotony. Every lesson spilled over into other parts of my life: Teaching a four year old at the library syllable pronunciation techniques after 10 minutes of trial and error. Science Olympiad, where I found the thrill of competition, but also peace in the repetitive process of building, destroying, and rebuilding 7g balsa wood towers to hold 14kg. Research, where exploring exciting new topics and fields coincided with grueling hours of debugging code and testing algorithms.

She’s taught me that being unorthodox is just another way of being unique–that the most unexpected and unpolished moments also have the most depth. I want to bring this openness to new communities, because it's only at the edge of our limits that we can plant the seeds of greatest potential. And now, standing on this beach, my heart no longer pounds looking for a lost sister, but at the prospect of new unknowns, my eyes searching for the next lesson just over the horizon.

The sight of my father’s sneakers filled me with unspoken irritation. I hated all of it: The insipid carbon gray colorway, the frayed fabric edges which now sagged with fatigue and the cracked sole exposed the raggedy stitching beneath. He sat in a dim corner next to the wilting plants, lacing up his austere shoes. I didn’t bother making conversation since I figured I would get the habitual “hmmm”, the repetition of the sound estranged us.

Amongst the chaos of making sure the dosa is crisp, my mother sentences me to a trip to the market with my father. My futile rebuttal goes unnoticed, so I accept my fate.

During the car ride, my fierce conversation starters were taken down by his defense of “hmmms”, I gave up on making conversation. Upon arrival at the Super Irvine, I retreated to a corner and let my observational nature take over. An anomaly against the bustling atmosphere, I saw the unseen: My father meticulously examining mangoes.

At once, my mind was invaded with a barrage of insatiable curiosity. Why was he so passionate about such a mundane task? The curiosity ate me up, I had to know more.

This curiosity pushed me to sit through those painfully awkward drives, and ask questions even though his answers were often dry. I became a sort of apprentice, learning the fundamental formulas of the webbing test, press test and smell test. Our shared experiences created a newfound understanding: I learned to see the expression in his silence, the love in his actions and the unseen sacrifices he made. I learned to see the color in his sneakers…

“I’ve always wanted a garden of my own”
“Why not?”
“It's too much work”, “The soil may not respond well”.

I had never heard him talk about his wants, I was touched, yet conflicted. Although I grew up comfortably, fostering a riskier and dream-like mindset, my father’s tough life experiences made him highly risk-averse, explaining the barrage of excuses. I stood firmly against his views, yet understood his hesitation regarding taking a leap of faith – Wait, what’s stopping me from taking that leap of faith?

I spent early morning before school researching, scouring the internet for easy plants to raise. I spent my time after school, exhaustingly taking soil measurements, my hypothesis backed up by vague memories of Mr. Blair’s AP Environmental Science class. I spent my nighttime toiling among the bugs to measure the depth and nutrient supply of the soil. I spent hasty passing periods desperately scribbling down my notes at the library, exhausting the plethora of basic gardening books. As rain would rock, my consistent efforts eroded my father's risk-averse outer layer. My dedication created a new bond, allowing him to realize the vision of us building a garden; And after the presentation of a lifetime, there we were, marveling over our empty lawn which was soon to be our new garden.

Observing him in the garden I watched him planting seeds, nurture the soil, and relocate plants to ensure the success of the garden. While observing him, I recall where this journey began, I finally had an answer to my question – Fruit was his vessel of communication. He advised through the fruit, he loved through the fruit, he was a father through the fruit… Amidst my epiphany, my attention shifted to his shoes once again. There was a medley of colors rising from the soil, penetrating into his shoes: The raspberry’s pink blush, the grape’s sour green, and the lemon’s complex yellow. It penetrated into his soul. My attention then turned to the laces. A stark contrast to the vibrant sole, the raggedy laces still chewed at me. I acknowledge that we still have ways to go and join my father in the vast lush, where we harvest our fruit, a faint, united smirk on our faces.

A farm of paper animals bounced around in my backpack as I walked to school, my anticipation growing with each step. After what felt like hours, I finally reached the classroom, excited by the day’s possibilities. The desks were lined in neat rows, with students excitedly putting out the supplies they brought: stickers, worms on strings, fancy pencils, and other trinkets they found enjoyable. I found my desk and eagerly unloaded my backpack, multicolored origami creations quickly taking over the entire area. Anxious yet hopeful, I waited to see how my paper animals would fare in our lively classroom.

My desk’s new vibrant colors soon caught the attention of my classmates, who lined up in front of me and eagerly handed over their fake paper money in exchange for my paper animals. Not long after, the air was filled with laughter. They formed entire cat and dog families, set sail with duck companions on boats, and tapped on frogs to win leaping competitions. I was as excited as them and could not wait to plan my ambition for that night: making attractive origami models that have never been seen before.

This was a one-week market activity in my second-grade economics class. Even ten years later, I can still vividly imagine my friends happily playing with jumping frogs and wiggling caterpillars. This was the first time my ideas and original creations brought joy to a large group of people.

I have had different creative ideas since I was young, and I enjoy turning them into reality. When I was in kindergarten, I loved digging through recycling bins for cardboard, papers, bottles, and different shaped containers, turning the waste into new toys that I would treasure.

Throughout elementary school, I continued to make creative new toys for fun, like an imaginary future flying car combining Lego Technic and K’NEX pieces. Also, I enjoyed helping out around the house through innovative solutions, like building a display stand from Lego pieces when my mom needed one.

In middle school, my creations shifted as I developed a deeper interest in STEM. PCB and circuit design quickly became a common theme in my projects. After a reunion with my older sister, I created a custom alarm clock for her as a special gift. When one of my dad’s friends missed my house while driving at night, I created a house number LED panel. By designing and building an autonomous robot car complete with sensors to avoid obstacles, I learned more about self-driving cars. I created a website with tutorials and guides to share my experience with others who are interested to learn.

Now, in high school, I tackle real problems with creative solutions. To ease my family’s concerns about home safety on vacation, I built an autonomous security robot that could detect intruders and send alerts to a phone. On my robotics team, I proposed a 360-degree spinning camera design that enabled our robot to shoot balls from any angle. At the world championship with over 400 teams, our distinctive design drew significant attention. When our team struggled to collect data at competitions, I made a scouting app with a unique reusable design, saving time each year as the game changed. Recognizing that other teams might face the same challenges, I made the app open source and shared it with the FIRST Robotics community.

My passion for exploration and creativity has deepened as I develop new projects in a cycle of making and learning. As I prepare to enter college, my goal is to expand my knowledge, expecting to continue bringing joy and solutions to people’s lives through creativity.

The first 5 years of my life were spent in Jersey City, a bustling and vibrant city on the banks of the Hudson River. But at least once a year, my parents and I would visit my mother’s small town in Gujarat, India.

Although we were over 7,000 miles away, the surroundings still felt somewhat familiar–packed, busy streets with people going about their daily lives. I still remember the endless honks of motorcycles as people rushed to work in the mornings, the vendor selling fruits on the street corner, or the milk lady going from house to house selling fresh milk to customers. My grandfather owned a jewelry shop on one of these street corners. There, he and his brother would sit behind the counter all day and sell all kinds of precious jewelry–necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pennants.

During one particular visit to my mom’s hometown, I remember tagging with my grandpa daily. I would tell him to wake me up early in the morning right after he had gotten ready. I would then get ready and follow him to the shop. When we reached, my grandad always prayed for a good day at work and the shop officially opened for the day. I went behind the counter and at first, I was amazed at the different pieces of jewelry on display–the shiny diamond rings, the gold necklaces, and the silver bracelets. But after a few minutes of marveling at these stones, my grandad would give me a task to do–it was usually weighing new jewels and writing them down on a sheet of paper. Of course, I would wander off occasionally and not do my work, but more important was witnessing how my grandad and his brother sold a product. Whenever customers walked in, they would greet them and ask what they were looking for. This was followed by a patient process of examining and discussing the different pieces of jewelry and their different qualities. Through it all, there was always this sense of deep respect and patience for the customer that my grandad and his brother embodied. More times than not, a deal was reached, and the customers left happy.

At dusk, the shop would close and I would follow my grandad back home. As soon as we reached, my grandad would count the money made during the day and store it in his safe at home. We would relax, spend time with our family, and then wake up early the next day to do it all again.

When it came time for my parents and I to head back home to the States, I was somber since I would miss my grandad and his shop. I couldn’t wait to visit again and on the flight back home, all I could think about was my grandad’s shop and how invaluable the past few weeks had been. I had grown to have a decent enough idea of my grandad's business in my 5-year-old mind. But more than that, I had developed a robust interest in his store. It wasn’t about money or helping my grandad grow his business–I was too young to have any real sense of that. There was just something gratifying about having a customer walk in, talking to them about their needs, and being able to sell your own product to them in order to bring them joy.

My family and I kept visiting my mom’s hometown every year or two, and my interest and understanding of my grandad’s shop and business continued to grow. During my last trip a couple of years ago, my grandad surprised me with a gift from the shop–a silver bracelet. After an entire childhood of witnessing and (somewhat) helping my grandad and his brother run a successful jewelry shop, I got a memento from that very shop. The gift was more than just a piece of jewelry, it represented not only my family’s heritage but also an entire childhood of learning hard work, patience, customer service, and the resilience to run a business. I am still wearing this bracelet on my wrist as I type these very words, and I endeavor to take the values they represent and apply them to my future goals in the business world.

Here goes another two hours to kill. Such was the general agreement between many debaters as we sat stranded in our school’s empty courtyard. Bright flashes of phone and computer screens instantly filled the area, indicating that novice and varsity debaters alike were restarting their video game or completing their homework.

Unexpectedly losing our debate coach halfway through my sophomore year, practices had never been the same. We were left to our own devices, as our debate president was too occupied with college applications to point us in the right direction. This was a stark contrast to what debate was only a year earlier; we were constantly holding practice debates, receiving feedback, and preparing for tournaments all as one. Remembering the high-spirited, excitement-driven atmosphere of the distant past and being hurdled back to reality, I felt a tightening in my gut. The after school practices had become homework sessions.

Where was the passionate team I was once a part of?

We simply could not waste after school meetings in anticipation for the unlikely entrance of a new coach, and especially not in time for National Qualifiers. Keeping this in mind, I sat down at my desk and began devising. I scribbled down all the things that I had observed about our team’s behavior and activity, realizing that what we needed was an entertaining way to provide real-world practice to everyone.

Before I had fully become aware of it, thirty-nine pairs of eyes rested on me as I stood in front of the debate classroom. With the permission of the debate cabinet, I was in a position of command. The previous determination I had wavered as apprehension rushed through my veins. Who was I to lead? Why would they listen to me? Would they even like the plan I would lay before them? Prior to joining the debate team, I was never the talkative type. I would smile and silently listen to others discuss important issues, and only speak when prompted to. Even then, it was more an acquiescence than a want to share. But that was the past. I decided to no longer anticipate change from the sidelines, but rather be in the midst of it. Straightening my back and suppressing the obnoxiously loud thumping of my heart, I described my proposal.

Newer members would debate each other in their respective events, and those not debating would judge a round of an event they were not a part of. New members were thus given a chance to develop competing experience and older members were able to derive unique topic ideas they could integrate into their own contentions.

To my surprise members were open to it, and rounds soon began in the courtyard.

The system started off a bit shaky. However, we gradually adapted and even implemented more event-specific activities. Over time, voices grew assertive, hand gesticulations developed into second nature, and phones became increasingly rarer sights.

Seeing members eagerly jotting down notes after discovering a strong contention and hearing their laughter as they recalled entertaining rounds, I found it impossible not to smile. A team spirit was rekindled, and a passionate intensity for debate was on its return.

Time seemed to whiz by as we found ourselves waiting for awards at National Qualifiers a few months later. We left the tournament with top qualifiers in almost all debate events.

Soon after, I was elected Vice President of Competitions and varsity captain. Little could I have known that the power of words I learned through debate would enable me to contribute back to it. Much can come from little, and the potential impact a student like me can have on peers and my community continues to spark my desire for advocacy and inspiring change. I am so grateful to have had the support of the debate cabinet and other members, and I endeavor to form bonds and collectively materialize our words into actions larger than us. One debate practice at a time.

I have the power to bring whatever I can imagine into reality. Don’t believe me? Welcome to my world of 3d modeling, where I am the wizard, capable of infinite creation. Empowered by my magic wand, a computer 3d modeling software, nothing is too hard for me to conjure up. This time, my imagination leads me down the path of modeling a spaceship, one from the far future, one that can take a person wherever they want to go. 
With my wand I create the backdrop of my 3d modeled scene, the pitch black vacuum of space. Its dark expanse reminds me of when I close my eyes as I prepare myself to play a piano piece. Ever since second grade, piano has been my creative outlet, a way to express feelings that I could not put into words. Playing beautiful music with my own hands brought me immense joy; joy which I would then bring to others by performing recitals at local senior homes. Those long, painful hours into the night that I had spent perfecting my craft were worth it when a kind old man told me how my music made him feel young again, bringing him back to the days when he used to play piano for others - I enjoy bringing others the same joy through my hard work. 
Up next, the centerpiece, a futuristic spaceship, gets materialized into existence. However, only after going through at least ten different iterations of the model, each time thinking about what can be improved and made better, was I finally satisfied. This feeling wasn’t new to me. For two summers, I researched at a Georgia Tech robotics internship where I witnessed how robotic operations also iteratively improves through artificial intelligence. Like a real life wizard, I gave life to a robotic hand as I 3D modeled and printed the parts for it. A challenge was making sure that the modeled pieces that needed to be precisely assembled and were capable of functioning like a dexterous human hand, a new aspect of 3d modeling that I had never considered before. Armed with my passion for engineering, I then went on to participate in a summer camp at Princeton as I continued pushing the boundaries of my capabilities, much like space explorers pushing the boundaries of exploration. 
Putting the finishing touches on my creation, I 3D model the distant stars in the background, like an artist splattering white flecks of paint across a black canvas. During my early forays into 3d modeling, free online tutorials shone out of the dark to me like stars, helping me along my journey. I went on to pay it forward and help others in the same way the tutorials helped me. At my robotics internship, I helped my fellow high school interns understand artificial intelligence, coding and 3d modeling. This sense of collaboration followed me to the Princeton summer camp, where I brought my research team together and pushed forward through a difficult research topic thanks to my internship experience. Even at school, whether it be Latin, computer science, or SAT preparation, I continued to fulfill my role of constantly seeking out ways to help others succeed, just as I had learned to. Like a star cutting through the dark, I aspire to become a beacon of light for the people around me, lighting the way as they pushed forward in their own journey of learning. True success is not only about an individual’s achievement, but it's about lifting each other up to move forward as a whole. 
Having finally finished my creation, I hit the render button. A beautiful spaceship scene appears before my eyes. I am truly grateful to have discovered 3d modeling, where my talents and interests meet. In my scene the spaceship zooms forward, into the future, taking my imagination along with it, ready to create a better tomorrow for everyone through creativity, compassion, and just a bit of magic.

The Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paradox suggests that it’s possible for two entangled particles to always know the state of the other no matter the distance between them. Do you believe that we, like particles, can stay connected to others despite the distance between us? I hoped so, but the 300-mile distance between dad and the rest of the family caused some disconnect. As middle school progressed, dad and I talked less and less while I defaulted to telling mom my stories, secrets, and news.

Even after we were reunited during high school, the norm resisted change and Dad felt more like a co-inhabitant than a parent. The lack of structure in the idea of sitting down to “talk” made it feel overwhelmingly uncomfortable. Still, I knew one similarity we carried amidst our differences. We were bridged by ideas.

I decided to do some research. I knew our mutual love of physics could spark meaningful conversations–I just needed to find the right topic. Bingo.

“Dad, I’ve been reading an article that mentioned the Arrow of Time.” He looked up from his laptop. “It’s the idea that time has a direction and always points towards disorder.” I paused. “What exactly does that mean?”

“Ah,” he grinned, “that sounds like the idea of entropy,” he responded. “Systems naturally become increasingly chaotic unless energy is put in to maintain structure. It’s like how the crystalline structure of ice becomes chaotic when it melts into water.”

“Hm,” I pondered, “what are the implications of that? If the natural order is to progress towards chaos, isn’t that kind of pessimistic?”

“Well,” dad chuckled, “it does eventually lead to the heat death of the universe, but if the chemical complexity of the universe hadn’t increased those billions of years ago, life wouldn’t exist and we wouldn’t have the privilege of sitting here and having this conversation.”

I blinked. “Hmm, I didn’t consider it that way. That's interesting!”

It became a tradition of sorts. Every night at the dinner table, dad and I would talk about Maxwell’s Demon, the Zeno Effect, the relativistic Twin Paradox, and more. Slowly, the awkwardness melted away, replaced by a sense of genuine curiosity and animation. Each question opened a new pathway for conversation, and before I knew it, we were talking the way I’d always hoped we would. Curiously, one day I asked him, “Dad, why did you major in biophysics? We’ve talked about it philosophically, but how do the fields scientifically relate?”

Dad gently smiled and pushed up his glasses. “There’s actually a lot of practical ways to apply physics to solve biological problems like protein folding or neuron communication.” He took a sip of his drink. “Actually, I was sure I wanted to do pure physics when I was younger, but I wanted to explore health as well. I switched to biophysics and graduated, but after my mom passed from cancer, it cemented the fact that the switch was the right choice. Maybe I could prevent you from possibly going through the same situation.”

The table fell quiet. I felt like I was reading my dad’s story for the first time. He was a person with his own struggles and motivations. I was never close to grandma, but dad’s resolve stuck with me. It felt magnetic, and I dug deeper. Over my junior year summer, I took part in a Quantum Computing internship where I tested models that could hasten the development of quantum interaction simulations that could be applied to drug discovery. Every evening, I’d come home brimming with excitement, eager to share my findings with Dad who intently listened. Dad and I were a positive feedback loop, fueling each other’s passion for learning while discovering more sides of one another. I began carving my footprint next to his.

These discussions made me realize that physics wasn’t just a passion we shared; it was a language we spoke to understand each other and navigate our relationship. As I look ahead to college, I’m excited to learn more, not just for the sake of knowledge, but to build bridges of ideas with new people. I want this language to become universal. Still, every time I learn something interesting, my dad will still be the first person I call and share it with. I know I'll be able to see that spark in his eyes, even if it’s through the phone.

Flashes of red filled the studio as dozens of long silk fans snapped open and shut in perfect unison. It was a world of ancient elegance, where every movement carried millennia of Chinese tradition. Yet, entering that room felt both familiar and foreign. For three years, I battled with excruciating cramps due to an obstructed unicornuate uterus, pain that made dancing nearly impossible. Being in that studio for the first time in years, I wondered whether there was still a place for me and if I could reclaim the dancer I used to be.

Walking away might have been easier, but it meant abandoning a part of me. Chinese dance was never just an activity—it was a way to connect to my culture and be intimately bound up with my sense of self. But with my diagnosis, I knew I needed to adapt if I wanted to continue dancing. I researched new stretches to accommodate my symptoms and instituted a new diet to reduce inflammation. My evenings turned into a mix of back and leg stretches, my muscles howling as I forced my body into the middle splits and backbends. In the kitchen, I learned to modify my favorite dishes like mapo tofu and experimented with earwood mushrooms and ginger. Gradually, my flexibility and muscle memory returned; I found myself able to execute a front walkover with ease again.

But more than each backbend or front walkover, what I missed most was my girls. There was Sydney, always offering a pack of matcha Pocky sticks during breaks, her quiet way of bringing us together. Then there was Kaelyn, the first to arrive every practice, her afternoon Celsius fueling not only her own drive but also the group as she charged through each routine, her loud counts keeping us all in sync.

My new role became clear: I had to fill the gap left behind by the older girls who had gone off to college. I became the one to spot front walkovers when our teacher was busy, lead the counts at each rehearsal, and share my granola bars during breaks. As I assisted with the routines, I recognized my younger self in the new dancers' struggles with the fan shen—a vertical cartwheel with windmill-like arms—and their efforts to bring elegance to the choreography. To help, I began providing additional coaching.

From then on, Saturdays became our Saturdays. I demonstrated how to isolate different body parts, moving slowly and clearly to highlight the subtleties of the dance. “Notice how the movement of the fan can draw the eyes, while your posture and expression invite engagement,” I explained, emphasizing the harmony between artistry and connection. “Watch how my fingers lead the movement,” I said, as the younger dancers mimicked my actions, their eyes tracking their own fingertips. “Try to find your balance here,” as I gently arched their backs, and redirected their posture.

On recital days, I embraced another new role–that of makeup artist. I recalled the warmth of the older girls' hands who had carefully arranged my hair and perfected my makeup years prior. Their care made me feel loved and confident, even as one of the youngest on the team. After hours of self-practice, I learned how to draw a perfect winged eyeliner in under a minute, apply fake lashes in one go, and style a bun that stayed flawless through every performance.

Little by little, I saw their confidence build up; little by little, my void was filled. Through this journey, I rediscovered the dancer in me that I thought was lost forever. I also came to understand that Chinese dance transcends the stage, embodying the spirit of community and connection. Like the vibrant red fans that fill the studio, I strive to infuse my community with energy and joy too.

“I remember you by your scent.” It’s not something I’ll say out loud, but it’s true. Long after we’ve parted ways, the little things slip away – The fragrance you wore? In your presence, the room bloomed into something more.

What some might call a strange quirk has, over time, become the essence of who I am: a fragrance connoisseur. Every inhale is vivid – a place, a feeling, a person – caught in the dance between the top, middle, and base notes of fragrances.

It all started with a bottle of Le Labo’s Bigarade 18. Neroli and Bergamot whirled me away to the Park Lane Hong Kong hotel, the cool blast of AC blasting relief on my sticky neck and fogged-up glasses. But this memory fades quickly like the top notes, and the middle notes of lily flower pull me two streets down – back to my grandpa's small, humid apartment. The smell carries me to my summer days spent alongside my grandfather. We sat on dirt-cheap pink stools sweating profusely – but it wasn’t discomfort I remembered – it was the lessons of discipline, the stories of Mauritius, and the quiet admiration in sharing those moments with him. That scent, wrapped in sweat and homesickness, lingers around my wrists and neck whenever I spray on Bigarade 18.

From that first bottle, my fascination with fragrances exploded. Maison Margiela’s Coffee Break, for example, with its mix of coffee and lavender, reminds me of quiet mornings in cafes, trying to shake off the frustration of not being the “perfect” student. While my peers seemed to breeze through lessons, I struggled, barely keeping up. On my wrists, Coffee Break, a companion that grounded me when work felt overwhelming.

It was in those moments of challenge that my curiosity deepened. I wondered: what was the significance of one's fragrance? When I meet someone new, I always imagine the story behind the perfume they chose. Is it a gift from a first love? Does it remind them of a high in their life, or a struggling time of perseverance? This question grew into a desire to help others find the scents that reflect who they are.

This curiosity led me to start a fragrance business. Initially, I easily sold to friends and local customers, excited to share my passion. But when taking it online, I found myself in unfamiliar territory. Suddenly, the personal connections I thrived on felt distant, diluted by a pixelated screen. Sales were slow, marketing felt pointless, and I found myself doubting whether my passion could scale.

It was eerily familiar. Just like in school, where others seemed to excel with ease, I was left struggling. I had to put in extra effort, learning the ropes of digital marketing, navigating algorithms, and changing my perspective on failure. Each time I stumbled, I remembered my grandfather’s lessons: patience and persistence. Just as I had done academically, I refined my approach, adapting to new challenges.

Finally, I began generating thousands of dollars a month, using new capital, to reinvest back into fragrances. As my collection grew, so did my understanding of their power – not just to evoke memories, but to shape identities. Each bottle became a tool for transformation, a way for someone to tell their story or to protest against an atmosphere. A way for someone to express themselves without expressing a word.

I wasn’t just obsessed with fragrances; I was fascinated by transformation – both in others and in myself.

I kept growing my business, motivated by this epiphany. I found satisfaction in helping others embrace who they are through scent. My competitive side thrived as I expanded my customer base, but more importantly, I saw my contagious passion spreading, forming my own community.

You ask me what I’m wearing, and I pause. Fragrances suck me into a world where time blurs; it's hard to explain. I’m not just wearing a scent; I'm wearing a memory, a part of me still unfolding. Today, it’s light and airy – like me. Tomorrow, it could be dark and bold – also like me. Fragrances have shown me that life, its challenges, and its commemorations aren’t fixed. They’re fluid, shaped and reshaped by its wearer. From “not smart” to “intelligent” or “introvert” to “outgoing”, fragrances have taught me that life isn’t static. We’re all blends of moments, ever-changing, forced to grow, yearning to transform. And in my transformation, I’ve found not just my passion – but my purpose.

It’s 11 pm, and while watching Speed Chess Championships, I stumbled upon the bullet chess genius Andrew Tang, an American International Master dueling the greatest in history on the grandest stage, suffocating his far more skilled opponents with strikingly quick speed.

I was fascinated by his intensity: the way each piece’s value for taking space was maximized, the ‘shapes’ the board constructed, the way he played without thinking. Tang revealed to me the ecstasy of bullet chess, discovering the rush from both triumphing through chaotic positions and blundering swaths of games away. Through my thousands of repetitions, I ingrained the fundamentals of chess into my subconscious, and I had begun to play by what I intuitively ‘felt’ was good, not what I calculated, just like Tang did. I would spend hours learning weird opening moves like the Polish defense, letting me experience more strange positions, helping me understand these ‘shapes’ better. As I was elected as chess club vice president and won multiple chess tournaments, I only wanted to improve more. Because of Tang, I became enraptured not just by the balancing chaos and control of bullet chess, but foremost the confidence gained from its strategies becoming second nature – instinct.

Instinct or intuition seems like just a spark of activity: momentary ‘gut feeling’ for choosing a certain restaurant. But, I think it’s more like building a rocket ship – taking ages to become functional, but once complete, it can travel virtually anywhere. In essence, intuition catalyzes creative insight.

When I moved to Singapore, I discovered my school’s jazz band, getting my first taste of artistic freedom in music. Learning jazz felt foreign but rewarding, and I quickly became close friends with my bandmates. Through our hundreds of rehearsals and jam sessions at our guitarist Zi’s house, for the first time, I found a community that wanted to explore the same interests so deeply, becoming the tenor sax first chair, chamber group leader, and founder of our band “Tone Deaf”, performing at jazz clubs frequently. They taught me so much about teamwork and dynamic, nonverbal communication through times when we analyzed the rhythmic ambiguity of Amelie xoxo’s “the Earth”, or when we rehearsed the smooth phrasing of John Mayer’s “Slow Dancing in a Burning Room” for a prom performance, absorbing these musical qualities till I exercised them unconsciously and applying them to my own playing.

There was one time when the electricity shut down during a concert while I was soloing, causing immense confusion, as I had to continue improvising without my band. However, my fellow saxophonist Payam helped me maintain composure as he started to tap my shoulder to keep me on tempo, while my snap judgment told me to begin playing a wave of chromatic enclosures and Brecker licks, forming melodic ‘shapes’ like how I saw chess, to fill the void left behind by the muted rhythm section. Momentarily, my trained intuition blossomed and manifested itself in a display of imaginative expression. I realized how much I had grown as a musician, and more importantly became an intuitive thinker, because my community of jazzers helped me accomplish far more than I would’ve independently.

Biologically, intuition is a critical survival mechanism, but as I’ve come to embrace the eccentricities of intuition, I’m confident that I not only survive, but thrive, in the advent of the unknown.
