Without chess and jazz, I would’ve been blind to how impactful being true to my intuition can be, and I’m grateful for those that helped me make these realizations. In the face of the uncharted territory, I welcome with open arms the dangers of exploration and recognize how to synthesize new information and weaponize them for my creative endeavors. As I move to an unfamiliar environment to become an applied mathematician, my intuition will allow me to thrive by finding inventive ways to apply my knowledge, much like I’ve done so before.

My blue Hydrangea macrophylla had the same life cycle as my parents’ marriage. While I cared for the ailing plant, my parents were growing further apart in the background, and I always wondered if I could’ve stopped it. We were in Richmond, VA, no kids were my age in the neighborhood. It was only me, my parents, and my newborn sister.

In the wet spring things mostly took care themselves. Summer, with more effort watering, the pink petals caught the light and leaves began to lush. As the days shortened I got lazy and stopped watering them. Winter came, and I saw the once-strong stems were now brittle and lifeless. The leaves' edges curled, and my parents separated.

The summer before 3rd grade, we moved out with my mother to my grandparents’ in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The weather in Saudi was harsh, with no clear sense of spring or fall, you couldn’t grow Hydrangeas. But mint was what my grandma grew. She put it with shahi (tea), lemonade, and its rapid and aggressive root system represented the sudden change in our family dynamic.

Amidst 24 first cousins, 12 aunts and uncles, the sudden appearance of those excessive roots made me feel outcasted. My family were strangers to me, even my own grandparents. Still, I had to keep my sanity after finding out my father abused my mom for my sister's sake. She was too young to understand what was happening but when my father started visiting she grew too old without him. She couldn’t remember much of our life in Richmond—or my father. I watched her grow up without the memories I had, and the absence of those memories left her with a sense of estrangement from him.

It wasn’t any easier with my father’s temper. He was an emotional manipulator—twisting my words, guilting me for not calling him 'enough,' and even telling me I would go to hell for my disobedience, until I began to question my own priorities. I didn’t know how to reconcile that. I spent a lot of time (building their relationship through specifics over the years all while trying to keep her safe.)

When it came to taking care of myself, I found my solace amidst the soft hum of nature in my grandma’s garden in the backyard, where jasmine vines hung over the walls, and a weathered swing swayed gently in the breeze. There, my grandma was no longer a stranger, I knew Fatimah by heart. We would prune the jasmine together, carefully trim the mint, and she would tell me which plants needed more sunlight. It felt like those moments were ours alone, a refuge from the Arabic tutoring session I was in just hours before that.

For the next 7 years that was one of the only constants in my routine — one-hour studying Arabic, the next hour out in the sun pulling weeds or watering.

When we moved out to our own house, I was still adapting to the busy social and academic life of high school, and the potted basil on my office table was dying out.

As one leaf fell, another flourished; my aunt Arwa had a baby—Mohammed. When we visited I instantly adored him, but he was a loud baby. He cried the whole time his mother was out. I tried everything—humming songs, changing his diaper—but nothing worked. Finally, I thought he might be hungry (he was). As he calmed on my lap, I sat silently, wondering if a similar persistent alert could help care for houseplants—something harder to ignore than a phone alarm. Inspired, I created a 'crying plant' device using a XIAO ESP32S3 and a water sensor, which plays Mohammed’s cries when the soil is low on moisture, honoring him for giving me the idea.

Soon after, I propagated those same potted basil and mint plant in the rich, clay-filled soil of Philadelphia, placing them by my living room window at Penn. From there, I walk to Pottruck for my Jiu Jitsu lessons, where I pass by the Zelkova tree, its strong trunk standing tall, deeply rooted, and firmly anchored in the ground. With each session, it reminds me of how far I’ve come and how strong my roots are, stretching from Mohammed to Fatimah. I see myself grounded like that tree, building my discipline in challenging environments, whether learning German or rolling in Jiu Jitsu. The moment I step into my apartment, a sense of calm washes over me as I water my basil and mint, reconnecting with my family from thousands of miles away.

I always thought of myself as someone who was helping and giving back through volunteering and tutoring. I felt fulfilled about my role, confident that I was making a difference. Deep down, though, I took comfort in knowing their struggles weren’t mine. But a recent conversation with Owen sent me on a journey—an uncomfortable but ultimately freeing one—of self-discovery.

I was interviewing Owen for my Oral History Lab while working on a guidebook to help adoptees navigate through trauma—something I had never experienced myself. Writing about other people’s pain had been easy because I wasn’t connected to it. I felt secure, confident that I was doing good. But Owen wasn’t just another person with a story of struggle. He showed me how wrong my assumptions had been.

I expected him to share typical hardships. But Owen spoke calmly and confidently. “Being an adoptee helped me feel free,” he said. “It allowed me to disconnect from society’s expectations.” His words caught me off guard. How could adoption—something I assumed came with difficulty—give someone freedom? He explained that his adoption gave him a fresh start, free from inherited expectations. It allowed him to define himself on his own terms. As I listened, I realized I hadn’t truly been listening before. I had been volunteering like I was above it all, but Owen wasn’t asking me for help, and that made me uncomfortable. I realized my motivations weren’t really about helping others but about wanting to be seen as kind and selfless.

That realization stayed with me, and I began to question my reasons for volunteering. Was it really to help others, or just to feel better about myself?

Owen made me rethink how I viewed the people I worked with. They weren’t lesser than me but equals, and I had never allowed myself to see them that way. One day at the food bank, I had a conversation with a woman I had seen regularly. She told me about surviving domestic violence, and I realized she wasn’t just someone in need; she was someone with her own strength and resilience, someone I had overlooked.

As I reflected more, I saw the bigger picture. I hadn’t just been helping others. I was looking for connection, for a community I could grow with, though I hadn’t realized it.

This realization also shaped my role as President of the Korean Adoptee Family Foundation (KORAFF). Before, I thought leadership was about guiding people, but I learned to approach my role not from above, but from the side, walking alongside them as we all navigated our own paths. I wasn’t there to give solutions; I was there to share in the work and experiences. I started to understand that my real purpose wasn’t about being seen as helpful but about building a community where we could help each other.

Owen’s story also made me more curious about identity and belonging. I began reading adoption narratives, not as a researcher, but as someone who wanted to connect with these experiences. I started seeing my work not as a way to stand apart but as a way to learn and grow alongside others. This new perspective shaped how I approached everything, from my academic work to my personal relationships.

Now, when I talk to classmates or friends, I listen more closely. I don’t feel the need to speak just to fill the silence. I’ve learned that true freedom doesn’t come from helping others or standing above them. It comes from recognizing that we are all equals, that we all belong to the same community. Through that connection, I’ve found a new sense of purpose.

The power of storytelling isn’t just in the words. It’s in how those words change the way we see the world. Owen helped me understand that my purpose wasn’t to help others; it was to build a community where we all help one another. In that space, I’ve found real meaning and am ready to keep growing alongside others.

**Unlocking My Inner Adventurer**

Growing up, I was always the cautious kid, the one hesitant to try anything new or adventurous. I preferred the comfort of my room, surrounded by books that transported me to far-off places without leaving my chair. While my friends were out climbing trees or playing sports, I found my thrill in the fictional worlds of my favorite novels.

Everything changed the summer I turned sixteen. My parents gifted me a trip to a wilderness camp in the mountains. I was resistant at first, imagining all the ways I could fail at outdoor activities. But their insistence, coupled with my desire to break free from my self-imposed shell, led me to take a leap of faith.

Arriving at the camp, I was greeted by towering trees and the intimidating silhouettes of the mountains. The air was fresher and crisper than anything I had known. We were divided into small groups, each led by an experienced guide. My group was assigned to a series of challenges, from rock climbing to river rafting, each more daunting than the last.

The first activity was rock climbing. As I stood at the foot of the rocky wall, my heart pounded with the familiar rhythm of fear. “You’ve got this,” our guide reassured us, echoing words that felt foreign to my ears. With trembling hands, I began the ascent. Each hold, each step upward was a battle against my instincts to turn back. But with every meter conquered, I felt a rush of exhilaration I had never before experienced.

The river rafting challenge was next. The fear of being swept away by the current loomed large in my mind. Yet, as our group paddled in unison, a different feeling emerged. Bonding with my teammates under the open sky, navigating the powerful flow of the river, I discovered a newfound appreciation for teamwork and trust. Together, we laughed and cheered our way through the winding waters.

That summer was transformative. I learned that fear, while powerful, could be an ally rather than an obstacle. Each day brought new opportunities to push beyond my perceived limits, and with every challenge, my confidence grew. The adventurous spirit I had only read about seemed to awaken within me.

Returning home, I found the experience had left an indelible mark on my outlook. The world outside my window was no longer a realm to be feared but one to be explored with curiosity and courage. I started seeking out new experiences, joining a hiking club and volunteering for environmental clean-up projects.

The once reserved observer in me had evolved into someone eager to engage with the world. I realized that life’s adventures need not be limited to the pages of a book. My story is now one of transformation—a constant journey to embrace the unknown with an open heart and an adventurous spirit.

There I was, my hand hovering over the table, heart pounding, legs shaking, my mind racing through each possibility.

It’s over, I thought, already imagining Kevin pouncing on the material and time advantages I'd just handed him. As soon as he took my knight with his pawn, I found myself saying, “I resign,” and shaking hands. After the game, Kevin moved my queen to H5 and pointed out a counterplay that he had been worried about. I shook my head, realizing I had been so fixated on taking back a useless pawn that I overlooked other opportunities to counterattack.

I asked if we could continue the game for fun. He agreed and we played on as if I hadn’t prematurely resigned. I played more boldly, freed from worrying about possible consequences. Move by move, I put pressure on him, patiently waiting for him to slip up as he defended. It wasn’t long before he blundered a piece, and I swiftly finished out the game. I felt a surprising sense of satisfaction, even though I had officially lost.

Instead of walking away frustrated after a loss, I felt drawn to asking my opponent to review the game—an opportunity to uncover strategies I had missed. That discussion and practice game with Kevin helped me improve more than my usual routine of going home and grinding tactics in irritation of my mistake. Seeing how I played better in that practice game, I researched top players like Anand and Kramnik, known for staying calm under pressure so that I could play like that in real games. The main lesson I learned from my research was to become comfortable with tense situations by playing more often. I also discovered that frequent play helps grow an appreciation for the game itself, allowing me to worry less about the results. To put this into action, I signed up for the weekly tournaments at North Penn Chess Club.

At the club, reviewing the games with my opponents allowed me to become closer to many of the people there. There is Greg, the funniest old man, who always wears shirts with sayings like “I play chess therefore I exist.” He would play like a grandmaster the whole game, then blunder an easy mate in two and laugh about it with me afterward in the room across from the tournament hall. I also met a 6th grader named Alan, who’d often stay after tournaments to review his games with me or play practice matches. I loved these sessions because Alan would teach me creative gambits that he had found on YouTube. Kevin later became a key player on my team when I invited him and two other kids from my high school to form a club team for the K-12 state tournament.

My experiences playing chess have helped me gain the confidence to try new things and embrace the challenges that come with them like starting clubs/nonprofits that I am passionate about or finding a doctor to shadow. When my fundraisers or shadowing schedule doesn’t work out, chess has taught me it's not the end; it’s an opportunity to counterattack by targeting a more local audience for donations and adjusting my club schedules so I can align with the doctor's availability. The chess community has taught me more than my games did. Kevin helped me feel more comfortable asking people more experienced than me for help. Now when I cannot decode the dreadful textbook, I can easily ask Mr. Keagy to reexplain Thermodynamics (a Chemistry unit I struggled in). Greg and Alan showed me the value of searching for a laugh or a cool idea in challenges rather than treating them like hurdles.

In chess, every move opens countless new possibilities. I plan to seek those same opportunities in life by trying plenty of new things, whether it's one of Alan's gambits or starting a new medical practice.

A Band-Aid is more than just a piece of fabric. There’s the adhesive strip, and the pad, and the outer packaging. All these components embody my experience of playing on a boys’ soccer team.

I was 11 when I went to my first soccer practice with a boys’ team. I remember the silent, hour-long drive to La Cañada. Even though I had been looking forward to this practice for weeks, the moments leading up to it were still nerve wracking. As soon as I touched the grass, heads turned and whispers started. In the next two hours, I experienced a new form of soccer. It was faster, more technical, and clever in all the ways possible. I could barely keep up. I felt ashamed that to them I was a representation of what a typical girl played like. I drove home with a wet shirt–part sweat, part tears–knowing that wouldn’t be the last practice with the team. I had to prove to not only the team, but mostly to myself that I was capable of being just as good as the boys.

I spent my evenings training at the park, with my dad or by myself, on the days that I didn’t have practice. Each practice I would come home with blisters on my heels and the soles of my feet. Before every practice, I would tape up my feet in hopes to mask the pain, and at the end of the day, I would take off my socks to see my blood bleeding through the Band-Aids. Although the sight of my raw, peeling skin made me cringe in disgust, I felt a sense of accomplishment because it shows how much effort I put into each practice.

The actual technical part of boy’s soccer was not the only challenging part about playing on a boy’s team. During my first couple practices, I was quiet and shy. The outcome of those practices showed that being quiet was detrimental to my success on the team. If I didn’t talk, I didn’t get the ball, and if I didn’t get the ball, how could I possibly improve? This realization pushed me to be louder and more assertive. Before the start of practice, the players formed into circles to play rondo (a game of monkey in the middle where the players on the outside pass around the defenders in the middle). This somewhat frivolous game became the most invaluable means to my progression on the team. The 15 minutes of rondo a day improved my touch and my ability to play fast, but most of all, it gave me the opportunity to talk to my teammates. The simple act of conversing created a bond between the whole team. Part of soccer, and most importantly, in life, is to build relationships with the people you meet. This experience opened my eyes to the importance of relationships in success. No matter how uncomfortable I feel about meeting new people, this experience will always empower me to put my feelings aside and introduce myself to new people.

Being the only girl on a boys' soccer team can feel much like being a Band-Aid—I offered resilience by protecting my own passion for the game while absorbing the discomfort of being different. Just as a band-aid shields a wound and nurtures it back to strength, I guarded my love for the sport, quietly challenging boundaries, making room for myself to grow, as a player and as a person. And, like a Band-Aid, I had a purpose—I was there to help the team grow, showing that strength comes in all forms, regardless of expectations.

It was unusually quiet down on the street. I took in every detail, burning it into my memory. I looked at the street decorations that extended from the balconies of each apartment, the steps of the building, the gate, and the number on the wall. I looked down the narrow road once more, bathed in the soft orange glow of streetlamps, the cars still crowding the sides. I refused to leave my grandmother, the apartment, the neighborhood—I refused to leave this life. Soon I was in the car, headed off to the airport. This was my last goodbye, to this life, to my childhood.

I had left behind this little girl who, at the age of 5, would walk to the fiteer store nearby and to La Poire to get desserts and snacks. I left behind a girl who saved money all year so that in the summer she could go down to the shack at the end of her road to get a snack and ful with her sister for breakfast after their parents left for work. Sometimes she would spend the day at her grandma’s house, trying to catch Dora the Explorer on MBC3 at 7:30 am, staying until Totally Spies aired at 8 pm. The little girl who once refused to leave her Mimi’s house after a weekend visit, crawling by the shoe cupboard, crying. Why did they say it wouldn’t be forever when it is? Why was it that my childhood had to stop at 9 years old?

Arriving in America felt like landing on another planet. The streets were wider, quieter, and the air felt colder in more ways than one. The life I had left behind was an entire world away, but I quickly realized there was no turning back. I had to learn how to adapt to my new life. I started picking up the language first. It was difficult, and I went to school every day discouraged and feeling isolated from my peers with whom I was not able to communicate. I felt like an outcast.

Life at home was rough too. My parents were questioning the move—they missed their own parents, and the paperwork seemed never-ending. Our life in America was unstable, never knowing how long we would be able to stay here on a visa. Nevertheless, our family grew closer during this period of instability. Our presence in each other's lives was a constant. I grew up faster. At school, I was in charge of my own learning, reading a bunch of secondary grade books and excelling fast to ultimately not have to take the ESL class. I immersed myself in American culture and society. I wanted to learn the jokes and slang that Americans used, so I started watching movies in English and practicing with my peers.

My eagerness to find my place in this new society didn’t stop there. I reached out to get opportunities because I wanted to be present in my new environment. I joined clubs in middle school and continued that in high school. The more I gained confidence in myself, the more I was able to reflect that by being more present in my community. When I found my passion for neuroscience, I craved the opportunity to learn more and seek more. I reached out to multiple professors to see who I could shadow over the summer. I took this movement as a way to build myself again, focusing on creating my passions, aspirations, influences, and character all through the guidance of my family.

As I prepare for college, I’m eager to continue this journey of growth, bringing with me the resilience, independence, and empathy I developed along the way. I want to be an anchor for the students who find themselves in a similar position, supporting and including them as they navigate their own journey.

After three miles of forested hills and snaking backroads, the racecourse finally revealed an open sky. My eyes fixated on the race officials glowing brightly in the morning light, signaling my heavenly finish line—the end of this grueling cross-country race was in sight. Just as my breathing relaxed, my teammates screamed. “Let’s go, Josh, don’t let him beat you!” Snapped out of my brief nirvana, my eyes darted around. A glimpse of running shoes flashed in my peripheral vision, slowly gaining on me. Quickly accelerating, I pumped my arms and heaved my lungs for air. Rechecking my peripherals, the other runner relentlessly inched towards me. Only seconds away from the officials, my lungs burned, and my focus faltered. My competition had pushed forward, crossing the finish line as I trailed behind.

Later that night, the official competition results were published online. Scrolling through the list, I found my friends in the rankings: 12th, 35th, and 61st place. Continuing further down, I found myself listed 103rd. My lackluster commitment had always produced warning signs, but I never expected it to catch up with me. Yet, seeing my name so low on the official results, especially compared to my friends, stung deeply, and sobered my pride. Why was I skipping practices? My thoughts bled into academics, forming dark premonitions—how soon would my procrastination catch up to me? Completely unsatisfied, I decided to train on my first nighttime run.

Initially, nighttime running was spontaneous. Not only was it inconvenient, but it felt daunting in the dark. Yet, as cross-country ended and my schedule cleared, I became fully engaged. In my mind, no one else was running at night, so it felt redeeming. I also felt refreshed, focused, and renewed after my runs. As AP testing neared, the silence and serenity of my night runs cleared my mind and allowed for streamlined studying and efficient work. By the end of junior year, nighttime running had become my joyful routine.

Even as evening schoolwork halted over summer break, my academic passions manifested in a more personal form. Through research, I addressed a widespread sense of cultural homelessness that plagues the Korean-American community as a whole. After running, my nights would consist of interviewing peers and drafting findings, reconciling this intimate cultural affair. Furthermore, my nighttime routine expanded beyond myself and the track. Solo training evolved into group runs and dual jiu-jitsu practices. Applying research ideas to activity, I bonded with close friends and acquaintances—even those I had previously felt culturally disconnected from. With this, my nighttime routine became more than just training sessions—it was the impetus for my fondest high school and cultural memories, which are forever a part of who I am.

As a senior, my cross-country competitions are just as physically exhausting as before. Yet, they are also infinitely more satisfying. At the season opener, I accelerated past my friend, who previously ranked 61st, scoring five places above him. And although I am still far from reaching 35th or even 12th, every night, I inch closer to achieving my goals. Now, my rankings are no longer a reminder of lackluster training—they are a testament to the countless runs and improvements I’ve achieved.

By finding passion in nighttime running, my commitment and enjoyment in the sport have skyrocketed, and this passion has driven me towards success. In school, I also continue to apply this understanding. Through pursuing my academic interests, I have found renewed joy in learning. Every day, I look forward to attending my human geography and economics classes and studying the complexities of human interactions and our choices. By following my research passions, I have not only been able to find joy but also a greater sense of purpose. Whether in a race, in the classroom, or within my community, pursuing passion is paramount to achieving excellence, finding joy, and discovering purpose.

Imagine the aroma of a perfectly baked panettone, with its fluffy texture and iconic taste—an achievement that seemed nearly impossible when I couldn’t find the crucial ingredient: panettone essence.

It was December and the Christmas spirit was in the air. I always loved baking cakes, cookies and at least trying to make pastries, but this year Christmas spirit struck me differently. I wanted to make panettone, the classic Italian dessert that graces Brazilians Christmas banquets. Though I had never heard of anyone making it from scratch—our family always bought it from stores—I decided to take on this challenge. I spent all day looking for recipes, only to find they all needed panettone essence.

I scoured every store in the small town I live in, even in nearby cities, but I couldn't find it. How was I going to make panettone without panettone essence? That couldn't stop me, I googled for hours how to make it, but I didn't find a recipe; instead I found out what were the key ingredients.

And all of a sudden it was December 21st—officially panettone making day. I danced around the kitchen as I added in the flour, water and yeast, to conquer the perfect sponge. After it had risen, I threw in the egg yolks, butter, sugar and a tablespoon of honey. The time had come where I had to add the panettone essence. I embraced my inner mad scientist as I made my own essence. I squeezed orange juice into a small bowl, added some vanilla extract, finishing it with orange zest. I added my concoction to the sponge mix and kneaded it for roughly an hour; my arms were extremely sore, I could barely raise them. I let the dough rise for a while, rolled it into 3 small balls and put them in the oven.

After almost an hour, I took them out of the oven and they looked phenomenal. I couldn't wait to share them with my parents, grandparents, and my friend Andrea. I waited what seemed like hours for it to cool so I could cut a piece for my parents. Once it had cooled, I cut it and anxiously waited for them to taste it, and immediately asked for ratings, they gave it a ten, but I knew they had rated it that because I had made it.

That same night I ran to my mom to ask her to take me to my grandmother's house to give her one of my panettones. I gave her my panettone although she couldn't try it at the time I had brought it, but she gave me the same warm hug that she would usually give whenever I brought her baked goods. The joy and smile on her face, along with her barrels of laughs made me forget all the soreness in my arms.

Through baking I have found my purpose and love for serving others. Baking is more than mixing up ingredients and putting it into an oven; it's about the love and admiration you put into it. When my grandfather started cancer treatment earlier this year, I felt useless, so when he would go to the city where he did his treatments and would stay for weeks at a time, I would always make different types of cakes every week so he could take and eat as a snack or have for breakfast. He would sometimes even give me some advice and suggestions, like adding anise into my cornmeal cake. Baking is a way for me to feel connected to my grandfather while he is far.

Seeing my grandfather undergo cancer treatments, I have learned the value of life and how someone's routine can change in the matter of a second, but I have also learned the beauty of making someone smile, and how valuable a simple cake can be.

Sitting on the grass bank, fifteen anxious year nine students surround me. Having never met before, they’re about to start high school together in a couple of weeks. As a prefect, I've been thrust into the role of icebreaker over the next three days of outdoor bonding.

Softy, I hear Ethan tell Jack, “You don’t have to do it if you don’t want to,” Jack’s eyes fill with terror as he watches another student cross the high ropes course. Moments later Jack is shaking the entire way across the high rope course 5 meters up in the air, moving slower than everyone else. Inch by inch he completes the course and soon as his feet touch the ground his smile beams.

The next day on the military-styled course, Ethan hits his ankle on a log, Jack is quick to rush over to support him, offering his shoulder. They hobble together over the finish line.

3 days later on a gruelling hike to Rangitoto island’s summit, I remember Jack and Ethan’s kindness and encourage the students to support each other, explaining the end goal isn’t fitness but brotherhood. By the camp’s last day, fifteen strangers had become fifteen friends.

***

“It’s as simple as Greet, Serve and Close” my manager Simon says. It’s my first day and I’m learning the trade secrets in retail - the warm greeting and reassuring smile that keep customers engaged and happy. At the counter, Simon takes an immediate interest in every customer he meets, welcoming them with a fun story or even a joke. He remembers Paula who bought a shirt for her husband a few days ago, and James, who finally picked up that Ninja blender he had been eyeing for months.

In the afternoon, a customer walks in angrily with a fraying jersey demanding a refund. It’s three years old and clearly worn. Despite the thirty-day policy, to keep the customer happy Simon puts the refund through with a smile.

Simon always went above and beyond, able to build a sense of community with every conversation. Clocking out after my first week Simon’s words rang in my ears - “Regardless of what we sell, we must always serve”. I left excited and prepared for the new customers I would meet the following week.

***

It’s another beautiful summer Christmas. Blooming red Pōhutukawa known as the New Zealand Christmas trees line the golden sandy beach across the road. In our kitchen, my grandmother glides like a ballerina past haphazard pots, bowls, and stovetops. I can smell the glazed ham in the oven. The smoke rises from the barbeque whilst I dream about her classic macadamia ice cream in the fridge.

As is tradition I offer my helping hands. She passes on her tips and tricks. Instead of wasting the fat from the ham, we use it to make crackling. Everyone helps, preparing food, getting drinks, or setting up the outdoor table. Our traditional annual Christmas gets all generations involved. Later the feast blankets the table and she looks up proudly, knowing it will impress.

Every year her hospitality brings our family together for a banquet. For just a few hours, the phones are put down, the news turned off, and we feast, laugh, and tell stories. Love takes on many different forms, for my grandmother, it was the pride in her Christmas meal, her way of reminding us she cares.

***

My learning was never constrained by the four walls of the classroom. From a high ropes course to a department store checkout counter to my family’s Christmas table, I was privileged to grow under the kindness of others.

Through their examples, I’ve learned to always be encouraging, to build connections and a community with strangers, and to honour traditions that bring friends and family together. As I continue through college I'll endeavour to share that kindness wherever I may go, to give back to the people and communities that will shape and support me.

When I was in fourth grade, I earned the most traumatizing five dollars of my life.

Every semester, my weekend public speaking class hosted a game. The task? Talk for a minute without stopping, stumbling, or saying filler words. Succeed, and five dollars was yours.

I couldn’t breathe at the thought of playing. My first attempt, I hadn’t even gotten out an actual word before uttering a fateful "uhm."

One semester later, I stared into the sea of classmates, knees shaking erratically as I rambled about zebras and tigers. This time, I earned five dollars after painstaking rehearsals in my bedroom.

Now a senior, the game I dreaded years ago seems like a trivial feat. I still have nerves before presentations, but I also have strategies. Three rules on a slip of paper taped to my desk, a guide for every sweat (or tear) inducing battle in my speaking career.

The rulebook is as follows:

Rule #1: Plan. One of the most stressful speeches I’ve given was the AP Spanish cultural comparison speech. Knowing that Hispanic culture was a realm I was barely familiar with, I began culminating a laundry list of information months ahead. I traversed sites like “La Estrella de Panamá,” to learn about the annual Carnival with the mouthwatering churros. I started practicing daily with a friend. We karaoked to self-translated Taylor Swift songs and agreed to set our phones’ default language to Spanish.

When I nervously entered the speaking section of the AP exam, I felt like I had struck gold. Shining in black letters was a prompt that I knew exactly how to respond to.

My parents don’t share my enthusiasm for the Spanish Google Map instructions that blast through my car speakers, but planning for Spanish has remained a staple in my life. Now, I plan to help the Spanish-speaking seniors at volunteering events, the students at the local elementary schools.

Rule #2: Focus. I had a hard time embracing the idea of delivering, instead of talking. In essence, the way I recited words could matter more than the words themselves. After failing to advance at a local competition, I began thoroughly annotating my speech to emphasize certain words. Neon highlight– enunciate. Underlining– dramatic pause.

Up until the following tournament, I spent downtime trialing my embellished speech to walls and vending machines, focusing on how I really sounded. As the final round of competition arrived, I found myself face-to-face with three stoic judges.

There, I blossomed with pride every time I guilefully raised my pitch for a joke, eliciting smiles, or every time I rhythmically vocalized realities like: “the MORE people HEAR something, the MORE likely they’ll BELIEVE it,” gaining sympathetic nods.

Finally, rule #3: Finish. As a seasoned debater, I grew frustrated that parent judges never understood my arguments. However, this revelation dawned on me during debates about the military in the Baltics.

I knew nothing about the Baltics.

Amidst foreign, often convoluted arguments between high schoolers, I realized it would be smart to leave a memorable final impression on the judges. Thus, I crafted catchy lines to end each speech. For the Pro side, “Be PROactive, vote PRO,” and for the Con Side, “Don’t cause more CONflicts, vote CON.”

It didn’t matter how cheeky it was because it worked, as my biggest joy became seeing those lines copied onto my winning ballots.

As I move forward from the fears that vividly defined my childhood weekends, I value my communication with the Spanish-speaking students I tutor at the elementary school, the sweet judges listening quietly across the classroom, and the “clueless” parent judge who’s just excited to be there. While I no longer receive five dollars for every minute that I talk without fluency breaks, I’m always happy to put in my two cents to continue nurturing connections as I speak, planning, focusing, and finishing to the mantra permanently taped to my desk.

“Please report to the principal’s office immediately.”

My legs felt like lead as I forced myself down the hallway, my mind racing, ‘Where could things have gone wrong?’ I was the 4.0 GPA student who had her life planned from day one—never one to take risks, always doing what was expected. My goal had always been simple: be the perfect student—quiet, attentive, never stepping out of line.

But perfection came at a cost. Beneath my calm exterior was the constant pressure to maintain top grades and excel in violin. In the chaos of academic life, my boyfriend became my anchor, providing the stability I desperately craved. Slowly, though, the lines between us blurred. My boundaries—ones I thought were firm—began to shift. Yet, I stayed silent, watching from the sidelines as things spiraled. It took every ounce of courage to utter one word: stop. By then, I was already drowning, the blood dripping down my leg a physical reminder of the emotional wounds I couldn’t yet process.

Weeks later, I found myself sitting in the principal's office. When I heard the word “suspended,” my heart shattered. Three weeks. That’s how long I’d be gone. I blamed myself for not speaking up sooner, but another part of me felt betrayed by the school for not recognizing what I had experienced. When I returned, I had to face the whispers, the stares, and the isolation. My parents advised me to transfer, but I refused. Leaving would have felt like surrendering to the situation, like letting him win. Instead, I stayed—believing that if I could endure this, I could handle anything.

My therapist was my greatest advocate. She helped me find a voice I hadn’t yet realized I possessed. Her unwavering support gave me the courage to return to school, knowing that my story—my truth—mattered. And as I embraced this belief, it ignited something within me. I began to step into leadership roles, not for validation, but because I finally believed in my own inner strength. I soon emerged as the concertmaster of both my school’s senior orchestra and the Wichita Youth Symphony, bringing musicians of all skill levels together. The goal of giving opportunities to the marginalized began to manifest itself in all that I was involved in. I founded my own community initiative—Opportunity Vehicles—bringing opportunities to the homeless population, who often don’t get a second chance, and traveled to Vietnam as a delegate of the Congress of Future Medical Leaders in uniting a community of medical scholars and spreading awareness for health disparities.

Yet, through all this success, there was a quiet ache that lingered. I knew I wasn’t alone in my experience, that countless other girls had endured similar struggles. One day, I partnered with the Feminist Club, creating an anonymous online forum where students could share their struggles and find support in kind-hearted comments. As the comments popped up left and right, I locked my eyes on my computer, seeing similar narratives of girls who struggled to accept their parents’ disapproval of their significant other, to those going through intensive anxiety from test prep. It was a wake-up call, which led me to discover a deep sense of purpose – breaking the silence that too often isolates us.

As I look ahead to college and beyond, I know that I’ll continue shaping my world and myself. Ironically, as I reminisce, being suspended was one of the best things that ever happened to me.

It all made sense then, as to why my peers often applauded me for my cheerful energy, even when others were dwelling on their IB Diploma coursework. It was the same reason I felt compelled to advocate for the voices of the voiceless victims of sexual abuse and domestic violence within my community and instill words of strength in fellow victims – my voice had mattered.

**Chicago, Illinois, Summer 2014**

My grandmother slides me last week’s *The Daily Herald* across our dining table. Tenderly, she takes my hand, guiding me through folding my first origami tray, which we fill with our snacktime sunflower seeds.

During these quiet summer mornings, I’ve learned how to meticulously repurpose old sheets of newspaper into beautiful keepsakes, like molding the *Chicago Tribune* into flower vases to preserve my mother’s precious lilies.

“Polanyeyouyong,” she would tell me. Even scraps have their value.

Despite holding stinging memories of stitching together paper-thin clothes in the wintry cold, my nainai laughs as she directs my hand over each embroidered pattern on her quilt.

*****

During the academic year, I routinely wake up at 5am, just in time to give the high schoolers at Dawamu School their afternoon “Applied Digital Literacy” lessons.

Born and raised on the outskirts of Nairobi, Kenya, Grand didn’t have the opportunity to pursue his interest in computers. Staying after class, we squeeze every bit of value out of his dilapidated laptop, from refining its display resolution to reconfiguring its cooling system. Fixing Grand’s defective webcam by installing a new driver, I finally can see the face behind the voice that had been my constant companion over the last year, and in that moment, all the miles between us seem to disappear.

Following my grandmother's expert origami folding techniques, I crease and flatten scrap cardboard from routine school lunch shipments, assembling drop-off boxes to collect dozens more used laptops and electrical devices to send to schools around the world. Similar to my lessons with Grand, it warms my heart to guide volunteers each week in nursing old game consoles back to life for the children of our local libraries—”Wii-Serve Wednesdays,” we’d call them.

*****

“What a hoot!” Blenda hollers, after we spend the morning together with all the grandmas scrunching, banding, and squirting t-shirts senseless.

Blenda, hailing from Englewood, Chicago, is a two-time breast cancer survivor and caring grandmother, her only daughter also hospitalized by the disease. She taught me the perfect baking soda-to-vinegar ratio needed to create my own DIY fabric softener, so I thought I’d teach her a clothing hack of my own.

Prior to setting up for the Pink Divas and Gents Breast Cancer 5K, I invite Blenda and other grandmas to join me with some old white t-shirts and pink dye. While their days accompanying a belted cardigan are long gone, those ratty clothes can find new life as pink headbands and wristbands.

Sporting their newly upcycled gear, the grandmas groove and clap to the beat of “Stayin’ Alive.” As Blenda waves me over, welcoming me to their dance circle, I break into a tentative two-step. But when the others cheer me on, I spontaneously bust into The Carlton (or try to, at least)! Laughing uncontrollably, I stumble around the dance circle, seeing warm smiles and receiving warmer hugs from all my new grandmas.

*****

Looking back on my grandmother’s sewing lessons, I realize now that even if her handicrafts brought back traumatic memories of poverty, reuse was an expression of familial love to her – whether it was those old shirts for her siblings or quilting with me. I feel inspired to carry her lessons to our local libraries and 5Ks, because in the same way that the biggest treasure we gained from our time together was our deepened relationship, I am so grateful to have built new treasured families in the communities around me.

Grand now spends his weekends running a free computer repair clinic for his neighbors. Blenda now runs her own “Dye-namic Creations” class at her local YMCA. They both honor my late grandmother’s dedication to others. I still fold these paper trays in my dining room each morning; only now I do it with my seven-year-old brother Matthew. With an eye for value and a heart for others, I will continue to transform trash into treasure, just as she did with me.

Standing at the podium next to my opponent at my first debate tournament, I felt a knot tightening in my stomach. As I heard his speech, I knew this was going to be a tough ride with all sorts of twists and turns. After he finished speaking, I felt my soul leave my body.

I always thought pure talent would take me to being ranked first in my class. For a while, I gave little effort compared to my classmates because I could keep up academically without much effort. I soon discovered that talent alone is not enough to achieve ultimate success as my peers caught up and surpassed me.

This same hubris led me to try out for the debate team during my sophomore year in high school. I despised public speaking, but I was confident because I thought arguing so much with my friends and family over the years would be a solid foundation for debate. I had no idea who my competition was, but I believed nobody was good enough to beat me. The moment I heard my first opponent’s speech, I felt like somebody punched me in the liver. I was supposed to give a rebuttal and ask questions during cross-examination. Instead, I sat in my chair, paralyzed from realizing how unprepared I was. I finally decided to forfeit and made a hasty exit.

On my way back to join the rest of the team, my friends came over and asked how my round went. All I could say was, “I just got obliterated.” I re-evaluated myself as a student and a person. I had lived sixteen years without ever experiencing defeat as harshly as I had done moments ago. The sting of defeat served as a catalyst for personal growth, forcing me to confront my weaknesses. Once I understood that learning required humility, a fire ignited inside me. The process of reaching new heights began, and along the way, new perspectives contributed to my overcoming of defeat. Recognizing that everyone's approach to defeat is unique, I sought to understand diverse perspectives to shape my own. I consulted close friends on how to deal with gut wrenching moments like my debate experience. Previously, I never sought advice from my friends on how to handle intense defeats. However, after they reassured me that setbacks were a part of the journey to success, I began to look at setbacks as fueling rather than poisoning. I also consulted my debate coach for her insight. Smiling reassuringly, she informed me to be resilient and take advantage of my mistakes in times of defeat. To improve my persuasive skills, I sought the help of my debate teammates by engaging in regular debates with them. My friends, with their years of debate experience, clearly outperformed me during our practice rounds. Repeated losses to my teammates helped me overcome my arrogance. Whenever I underperformed during a debate, instead of letting my heart sink, I maintained my composure and shifted my focus to the subsequent one. Soon enough, I was able to perform to my expectations and secure a debate medal before I concluded my debate career.

Experiencing the consequences of defeat helped me to be more compassionate towards others. I learned to help classmates who struggled with the same arrogance I did by reminding them of the inevitability of defeat. I made sure that all the people close to me would have the tools to prevent themselves from facing the challenges I came across from my previous hubris. Learning the significance of humility will enable me to accept defeat more gracefully because even in disheartening moments of defeat, I will always be resilient enough to use it to provide for others in college and beyond.

The act of silencing a call—so simple, so innocent. Just a tap on the glaring red Decline button, and the world is muted.

I was lost in the vibrant world of my favorite dolls, their hair a riot of neon colors, each one a unique blend of gothic and glam. Attending the one and only, Monster High.

On the screen of my aunt’s phone, a teenage girl was performing a dramatic makeover on her Monster High dolls, transforming them with each snip and dye.

“Sister smiley face with hearts emoji” flashed across the screen; under her name, two glaring icons appeared: one red, one green.

Four times, I pressed the red icon. Four times, I silenced my aunt’s calls. Who cared? The dolls were undergoing their metamorphosis, turning from their everyday selves into something extra-extraordinary.

If only I knew those ignored calls would end up ringing for the rest of my life.

My family does not understand the concept of “inside voices.” Maybe it’s a West Indian thing, or maybe it’s just them, but later that day, amidst the cacophony, my name appeared—“It was [Name] who had my phone.”

Their conversation now caught my attention. My name didn’t often surface in conversations, especially not like this. Curiosity pulled me into the kitchen, where I sat quietly, trying to piece together their fragmented, overlapping words in Haitian-Creole, a language that wasn’t mine to fully understand.

“She didn’t answer..”

“Jesus, please.”

“She could’ve been dead.”

Huh? Me not answering the phone.. what?

The realization hit.

Me ignoring the phone almost—did—cost her life.

My aunt, the one whose calls I had just given no thought to, was now in the hospital, clinging to life.

She had just arrived in America, her English halting. Her husband had turned on her, his fists pounding relentlessly, forcing her to run for her life. She had called my aunt four times, desperate for help, desperate for a voice that could speak to the police on her behalf.

Four times, I pressed the red button.

And when the calls failed, when silence was all that answered her, he found her again. He finished what he started. It was her screams—harrowing and desperate—that finally pierced through the walls, the neighbors’ ears, and summoned the police.

If it were not for the hospital, my action did cost her life.

My heart skipped a beat. Guilt seeped in, heavy and suffocating. How could I have been so selfish?

My family never blamed me. Bringing the topic up as I got older, “You were just a kid,” they said. “You didn’t know.” But knowing that has never lessened the weight I carry. That simple act of silencing—a tap—forever etched in my memory as a reminder of the moment I chose myself over someone’s cry for help.

I joined cheerleading my senior year to relive the joy I felt in elementary and middle school. During one practice, an 8th grader was struggling with the routine, and the captain’s frustration escalated. Her words grew sharper, and I saw the younger girl shrink under the pressure, too scared to stand up to seniors.

I stepped forward and said, “You can’t speak to people however you feel like.”

The captain shot me a look that said I was crossing a line. For a moment, I worried she might lash out, but I couldn’t let that stop me. After a pause, she backed down, and practice continued.

Later, the 8th grader said, “Thanks… I didn’t know what to do.”

That moment wasn’t about grand gestures. It was about instinct—standing up for someone who can’t. For me, it’s about never letting anyone feel unseen or unheard again.

Decline. 
Once an end to something that never began, now a promise: infusing each choice with empathy and altruism.

Accept. 
A commitment to mindful responses, using each moment to avoid past mistakes and make choices that honor my resolve.

“ARE YOU A GIRL?”, Ishansh asked as I exited the painting classroom. It was not the first time I was faced with this question and it wouldn’t be the last as I had decided to be the only boy who chose to take the humanities stream in our school, a path which is considered to be appropriate only for girls according to Indian society. Many male students thought that I was ‘insane,’ but I persisted with my choice and saw this as an opportunity to be an example for future male students to break the irrational societal norm–boys are ‘born’ for STEM.

However, choosing humanities was a difficult choice; my male friends gave phone calls to me, preaching the importance of STEM for hours, and told me to ‘re-evaluate’ my decision. But I chose to be surrounded by girls. It feels rewarding to study with my new (girl)friends, and Political Science, which not only opened me to a new dimension of thinking: Feminism, but also transformed me into a leader from classroom discussions to leading the entire school.

It was a novel social shift, and I adapted to this new environment by forming new bonds.

Every Friday nights and weekends (SPOILER ALERT! No parties are on the agenda), I would organise group calls on WhatsApp for my friends to help them clear their last-moment doubts before our test days on Mondays. With a book in hand and a phone in the other, I became their pseudo-teacher for all the subjects and answered their every question. These group calls made me confident and solidified my knowledge. And, most importantly, I used my knowledge to help my friends gain confidence in their own abilities.

My mother often asks me, “If you spend your time helping your friends, then when will you do your own preparation?” My only answer to her, “I cannot say NO to them when they need me the most.”

During free periods, we transform the classroom into a gaming zone by pushing together tables and arranging chairs in a circle. Kanika deals her black-backed UNO cards like a pro. I, having forgotten how to play, sat between Prachita and Kanika, who guided me when I made mistakes. At first, I lost almost every round, but I quickly picked up the game's tactics and soon matched their skill.

I have a habit of introspection every night. As I lie in bed and cocoon myself with a blanket, my eyes closed and face towards the ceiling, black bubbles of thoughts start erupting, and I question every step that I take that day. I analyse my actions whether they were right or wrong, and if wrong, how I could have corrected them or how I could have responded to a situation differently. It’s like a silent conversation with myself. And because of these beautiful introspective nights some of the embarrassing moments of my childhood are still kept alive in my memory and never allow me to repeat my mistakes. But when I recall those blissful moments–standing up for my choice to study humanities and supporting my friends through tutoring, from which I’ve learned the importance of following my own path and helping others along theirs. Learning to play UNO in eleventh-grade, reminded me that learning has no age barrier and one should never feel shy to learn new things from others–it gives me inner peace. These little interactions are my world and bring me joy during stressful times.

At college, I want to form such timeless bonds that I, and most importantly, my future friends will remember throughout their lives. That's the kind of person I hope to be. I aspire to create more colourful relationships and memories that are invaluable and bring smiles to my friends’ faces even when they have left college, got a job, and walk with a stick in their hands.

Beneath the lightless moon where even the stars got tired of shining, Darkrai drifts through the dreams of the unwary. Born from darkness itself, this elusive Pokémon exists on the border of the real and the subconscious, feeding on the terror of those caught in its nightmares. Yet beneath its haunting gaze, there is a strange, hidden sorrow—Darkrai's nightmares are not made from malice, but an unavoidable curse. Every Pokémon card captures a legend, and since 2020, I've been on the hunt for new legends. My calendar bears the marks of card box releases, my spreadsheets track the market activity of cards on my wishlist, and my local Target wonders when I’ll pull that elusive Greninja EX and single-handedly cut their revenues in half afterwards.

For at least a couple of weeks, cards will hover at a reasonable price, but as hype builds outside of the Pokémon community, the vultures will come knocking. Scalpers take interest in the most popular cards and can double their market price overnight. It was becoming such a common occurrence returning from DECA competitions and Science fairs to see a new card that used to be 50$ escalate to 125$ in the time I was gone that I started dreading opening my spreadsheet after getting home.

I needed to be able to predict which cards would be a target of interest for third parties so I wouldn’t go broke every month buying rare cards. So, I began working on the project that would end up being my Pokémon Magnum Opus: An AI model that could predict the most valuable/popular cards of any given box release. I began by scraping the attributes, titles, and rarity ratings of every card from various releases, feeding the data into a Naive Bayes model to categorize between cards of interest and not of interest to third parties. I could now quantify the price surge potential of a card title like “Rayquaza VMAX (Alternate Art Secret)” against something more common like “Oddish 4/147 Burning Shadows Regular”. The first model iterations already showed promise, identifying patterns that I expected it to see, such as knowing that Alternate Art and Holo cards were far more enticing than their regular forms. However, my model also started to find patterns that I didn’t even see myself, such as how cards with playable moves that ‘sound’ good for the competitive Pokémon scene also increase in value significantly. I had created a model that could even see the hidden gems I left unnoticed, with roughly a 75% accuracy.

Whether it be applying the ML skills I learned through medical research to Pokémon cards, it’s the fusion of the different pieces and skills that comprise me that allows me to see some of the subtle luster in the everyday and the mundane. In the same way my model uncovered those occluded gems for card values, I’m passionate about expanding my reach of knowledge in a myriad of subjects to push my goals further in unexpected ways, from learning behavioral psychology to promote heart-healthy habits in the subconscious thinking of my peers, to philosophy to better understand how to make interpretable AI models for Cardiology. Combining present characteristics into new indicators is what the AI model was trying to carry out in terms of Pokémon cards, and I hope to do the same for the bigger picture: In bringing my experiences to campus, I’ll be able to help others find new pieces of themselves and create new skills out of what they already had.

I called for attention as I revealed the topic for our Model UN debate: Protecting the Rights of the LGBTQ+ Community. Launching into a summary of the issue, I took a moment to register a sudden disruption from one of the members. He loudly proclaimed his desire to represent a country opposing LGBTQ+ protections, his words laced with unflinching homophobia, not the diplomacy I had spent months trying to instill.

My short-lived excitement faded into disappointment, caught off guard by the blatant opposition of inherent human rights. Was I naive for trying to discuss this prevalent issue, knowing that hatred and intolerance could be so normalized?

I chose to reject my brief wave of self-doubt. Quickly searching the ILGA World Maps 2023 index, I changed his allocation to Malta— the top-ranked European country for legal rights and policies, instead. With one passive aggressive bang of the gavel, he begrudgingly accepted his position.

Throughout the next few days, I helped him with research, slowly watching as he reevaluated his predetermined beliefs the more educated on the issue he became. Continuing to introduce middle schoolers to social issues allowed me to realize my purpose: it allowed me to change perspectives.

My Indian heritage is the root of my identity, but being born and raised in Indonesia, I feared that my branches were growing further from their origin— away from my cultural background. Wanting to nurture the foundations of my being, I began exploring India’s history by immersing myself in the Burma campaign. I find that all my ancestors' efforts coalesce, forming an unwritten version of history that is starkly different from what a google search reveals. Initially, after surface-level research, I fell victim to the half-written truth, which led me to believe that the significance of the campaign was solely due to its success as a military operation. However, gradually, one book at a time, I was able to counter that widely held belief and pinpoint the greater outcome of the Burma campaign: it marked the transformation of a British Imperial Army into the thriving Modern Indian Army that ultimately won India’s independence from its British colonists. Today, I celebrate my ancestors’ fight through every struggle that has shaped our legacy, paying close attention to the realm of underrepresented stories that weave together to strengthen my cultural pride.

During our first trauma counseling session, I asked the employees at House of Diamonds to describe themselves in one word. Ririn chose "strong." Ririn reached her breaking point when her job threatened her motherhood. After being coerced into working at a sweatshop with exhausting 16-hour shifts, she was unable to identify the early signs of her baby’s illness.
Finding out about her child's health problems, she resigned from her job without hesitation. Life after was a struggle—paying off medical bills and nearly losing her home while navigating parenthood—but she continued to preserve through all the guilt and burdens she had accumulated. In her culture mental health struggles were labeled as a taboo and healing was seen as a linear path. Physically escaping exploitation and now working at an ethical business, she was convinced that naturally, her mental scars were bound to heal on their own. She suppressed each trauma-related symptom she faced, fearful that doing otherwise would weaken her resolve. Seeing how detrimental this false portrayal of recovery could be, I was determined to break the silent barriers barred by taboos and show her that vulnerability was strong. I discussed trauma symptoms that validated her feelings as a modern slavery survivor. I reassured her as she recalled the painful memories of her past during our conversations, helping her express complex emotions without shame and normalizing discussions about mental health. Throughout our sessions, she continued to celebrate her own growing strength, which had shifted in meaning—from concealment of pain to caring for the neglected scars of her past. By simply redefining a word, I understood the importance one perspective change can have on reshaping lives.

The sharp click-clack sound filled the air. My sister and I aggressively scrambled the jade tiles while my angkong (grandpa) and ama (grandma) passively waited for us to organize the game. The silence of our games—the absence of conversation and laughter—echoed across the living room.

Silence was not just an absence of sound, but an undeniable barrier between myself and a rich culture I had yet to embrace fully.

Growing up, I was unfamiliar with my grandparent’s ancestral Lannang-ue, a spoken-only Filipino-Chinese dialect. I hid behind the comfort of my school-learned English—the rapidly-diminishing usage of Lannang-ue prevented me from learning the language. Yet as the world grew quieter during the pandemic, the silence between us grew more noticeable. I realized that our surface-level exchanges —restricted by my painfully limited vocabulary of mere thank-you’s and how-are-you’s—isolated me from both my family and heritage.

Before long, I was forced to face the fact that I was witnessing the extinction of the Lannang-ue dialect. Disturbed, I embarked on my personal journey to unearth the voices of those who came before me. I began listening to the Lannang-ue conversations that characterize my dining table. As I tried to understand each thought and emotion, I learned to navigate the silence—filling it with overflowing questions.

As I asked my angkong about escaping Post-Revolution China, I learned about WW2’s far-reaching effects on Chinese families during 1940s Manila. Listening to my ama relaying their epic love story, I discovered the term ‘kai-shao,’ the practice of parents introducing their children to potential partners—a tradition that persists in many Filipino-Chinese households today.

As I filled the silence, the once distant grandparents sitting across me on the mahjong table transformed into my angkong and my ama. No longer were they just my grandparents, but representations of living stories and histories I was just beginning to understand.

The missed opportunities from failing to converse with my grandparents inspired me to listen to other voices within the Lannang-ue community. As I interviewed native speakers, from school-teachers to church members, I was struck by their shared experiences witnessing Lannang-ue’s slow death, catalyzed by the academic prioritization of Mandarin and Western social media. Hoping to address their concerns, I decided to build a web-based translator, Lannang Lingua, to help revive the dialect.

I first compiled thousands of frequently-used words to compose the translator's database. I proceeded to reach out to my fluent-speaking relatives and recorded them articulating the lists of words, spending weekends between my grandparent’s kitchen and my aunt’s single-roomed condominium.

During weekdays, I scribbled down the romanizations of the audio files and established the rules for the standardized orthography to be coded onto the program. From my uncle's crisp, clear syllables to my ama's soft yet precise speech, each recording brought the words to life. Upon hearing the variety of accents and articulations, I realized how much I’d failed to appreciate the stories that raised me.

Silence is not merely a void to be filled. Within silence was possibility, unique perspectives and stories left untold. As I uncovered the silence, I realized that I’d been overlooking the beauty in the dialect and speakers all along.

I not only hope to fill and uncover the silence, but break it by nurturing open dialogue. Leading a panel discussion at the Lannang-ue Symposium to present my translator, I was touched by the school principals’ gentle smiles and the tears in my parents’ eyes. Over the three-day conference, I fostered a community bigger than myself—I engaged with individuals from varied backgrounds and careers, as I learned about Lannang-ue dubbing in Filipino movies and traditional Lannang-ue calligraphy. I realized that the impact of preserving a language goes beyond words; it creates bonds and preserves identities, ensuring that no one’s story is forgotten.

I’ll always use my platform to share the truths of those who can’t speak for themselves, to create environments where diverse voices can be heard. As I seek out and embrace multicultural communities, I strive to keep the conversations alive. No matter where I am, or who I’m with, or what language we speak, I vow that the world will not fall silent.

My fascination with global markets began when I was first introduced to Forex trading by my Dad when I was 9 years old. How a change in interest rates in the US or EU can drastically change fiscal distributions around the world, to me, was something of awe and to be leveraged with the right skills and knowledge. The spark in intellectual curiosity and the gradual realization that the contours on our map do not entirely separate us made me want to learn more about the world we live in; and so, I developed a habit of reading and watching documentaries.

Daily engagement with scientific findings and global media was pivotal in allowing me to grasp the complexities of the world that I couldn’t be exposed to by cocooning myself in an easy life in Singapore. It made me desire something more, to make a difference in the world that is greater than myself. When the coronavirus hit and the global stock market was in rampant chaos with pharmaceuticals hurtling to create a vaccine to ameliorate the crisis, I coupled the analytical skills that I honed from solving science and maths problems at school with the tapestry of knowledge I built to bet on the next bull in the market. After days of scouring platforms like Finviz, analysing the intricate details of companies, such as their debt-to-equity ratio and institutional transactions, I concluded on Ocugen Inc (NASDAQ: OCGN). Using my Dad’s Interactive Brokers account I placed an order for shares of OCGN at US$0.21/share with part of my pocket money saved over the years. A few weeks later, as I was scrolling through Yahoo Finance, my eyes widened as I read the headlines “Ocugen and Bharat Biotech to Co-Develop COVAXIN™…”. The share price had skyrocketed within hours in the pre-market session, and in a week’s time, my investment had quadrupled. I was elated over my accomplishment and realized that much like Bobby Axelrod from “Billions”, I could turn calculated risks into rewarding successes. I plan to leverage this zest I have engendered for financial markets through supporting meaningful solutions to looming global challenges. I'm eager to contribute to or even initiate clubs related to this in college.

The intangible values that having nuanced world views entail are also something I cherish as a global citizen. Whiling away in opinion pieces and Oxford Union debates has been enriching. It allowed me to connect the dots on national and international affairs and engender personal thoughts on them, drawing parallels between the communities I'm part of. This was an avenue through which to connect with my family at the dinner table amidst my busy schedule in junior college. I would frequently spur conversation regarding social issues such as a lack of progressive values or caste-based inequality in my home state of Kerala in India for us to canvass over. At school, during General Paper lessons, I would proactively tap onto my perspectives to contribute to discussions. I would advocate for issues I believed in such as greater academic freedom or political plasticity.

I see the unification of my intellectual and philosophical endeavors contingent for me to make tangible impacts on society. During my course on Blockchain and cryptocurrency, Professor Andrew Wu expounded on the idea of the consensus protocol underlying the proof-of-work concept. It provoked me to question traditional notions of central authority to maintain order, as discussed by Thomas Hobbes. Decentralized blockchains indeed function efficiently as individuals form collective agreements for mutual benefits. But we also have to tread carefully over the ethical dilemmas of an emergent technology like this: high energy consumption by nodes or the prospect of illicit activities being funded under the radar of the government are very conspicuous issues. While binging through Shark Tank episodes, my entrepreneurial spirit ignites, and I'm driven to develop novel solutions to issues - organically from my experiences.

My fervent passion for exploring ideas beyond traditional boundaries is what defines me. The relentless drive I have to learn and develop inquiry through dialogues allows me to illuminate new realms within the cosmos of my mind. The insatiable curiosity I have cultivated to traverse through the niche and achieve enriching results is, in essence, what I subsist on.

My mom pulled my hair back and loosely folded it up. Although she acted indifferent, I knew she was bothered, “You’ll look like a boy.” Nonetheless, I yanked the scissors from her hand and embraced it: –chop, chop, chop. As I felt the hair falling, I realized the literal weight on my shoulders was disappearing.

I combed my fingers through my hair, but the strands stopped prematurely. Rather than black hair flowing down to my hips, only rough edges poking my neck remained. Despite this new “boy-ish” hairstyle, I felt more feminine and like my true self than ever before, though I couldn’t figure out why. That answer would arrive soon enough.

The freedom of embracing my true hairstyle was a catalyst for more diverse gender expressions. Before, it mainly consisted of t-shirts, some jeans, and athletic shorts. Those clothes aren’t particularly my style, but I was scared to try on different clothes to find it, as I always felt uncomfortable wearing generational hand-me-downs rooting from the fear of being judged. Now, I try clothing I haven’t even looked at in years and apply Pacinos Signature Line’s matte paste to my hair with courage. If I can change my hairstyle, why not embrace other expressions? Even when my friends advised me otherwise, I chose what I looked like. I felt free from the restraints of society and my mother. My life was mine to create, not for her to control.

Propelled by this confidence boost, I decided to take another leap during my junior year and host a singing show in front of a thousand-person audience at the Pioneer Theatre Guild, despite having no experience in acting or singing. I couldn’t help but think about how my legs wobbled even when presenting in front of others at a Zoom meeting, much less in-person. As I gathered more experience with public speaking, I initially tried out for fun and didn’t expect to receive the role. While the other female hosts searched for dresses, I searched for a suit. Stepping out into the hot lights for the first time, I swelled at the feeling of not just representing my true self, but also those in the audience who also wanted to take the stage. I can’t help but think of 9-year-old [Name]: someone who was trapped in skirts and tap dance shoes, and how I needed to be the role model she never had. Even though I can’t go back in time, I can influence my peers right now. I think of Valentina, who was struggling with choosing prom suits that fit women, and it made me feel overjoyed, having the opportunity to help others. Finally, I think I’ve begun to find my style.

Though each of these moments had their difficulties, each brings me one step closer to my true self. Perhaps the most surprising was from my mother. The lady who once scored my choices now began to pick out suits for me rather than dresses. Changing her decades-old opinion of female fashion recommitted me to my journey of influencing others by finding and expressing myself, a win-win for both sides.

I will challenge stereotypes and explore my identity in the future. As my appreciation for the changing society norms grows, I can’t wait to host “Laughter is One Cure” events, where I will perform improv and stand up to those in hospitals, where I know patients can experience life with a lighter note with live comedy, just like how I began my recovery from mental health issues by listening to stand up. Whether it’s Laughter is One Cure or the dining hall, I will always exist as my authentic self, whatever form that may take, and assist others along on the way of my journey.

Hot summer days spent in the small villages of Bamenda, Cameroon, were filled with a strong aroma. Created by the spinning of pots and the kneading of hands, the essence of the village’s mothers' and grandmothers' cooking would fill the air on hot Sundays, a perfectly imperfect mixture of spices and herbs. As links to the past, those dishes carry me forward.

Jollof rice, a quintessential African dish made from the simmering of tomatoes, onions, and peppers, adds a complex level of flavor, just as life experiences do to one's character. Track practices during the winter months would leave me drained, but these meals nourished and warmed me through the day. Each summer, my grandmother would travel to America, and together we would prepare Jollof rice in our kitchen. Reconnecting to my heritage, through the stories of my grandmother’s survival in our war-torn homeland in her youth, I felt a profound connection to a world that was distant yet deeply rooted in me. Conflicts of the ongoing Ambazonia War have left my second home ravaged, preventing me from reliving those cherished memories in the summers before. However, just like the Jollof rice we made, though far from its place of origin, I could still feel its essence through my grandmother’s insistence to advocate against the war. I, too, am a melting pot of experiences, simmering and evolving. My connection to my Cameroonian roots serves as one of my foundational ingredients. Each moment, like the heat of dried chilies, the sweetness of ripe tomatoes, or the richness of beef broth in Jollof rice, has added layers to my identity.

Suya, a popular street food made of spicy grilled meat often accompanied by a spicy dipping sauce, is more than just a culinary delight to me. As a shy child, I looked for outlets to eat away at my time. Always fond of the movies I’d see on the big screens I created my first Youtube video. With nothing but the Sharefactory editing software on my PS4, I spent days and nights creating my own miniature movies. Hours spent stitching together scenes, overlaying music, and aligning the subtitles to be just right. Though frustrating, looking at the finished project and uploading it for the world to see gave me enjoyment. The “world” being my mom. Looking back today, they were what you’d expect a video edited by a 7th grader to look like. Not as good as I remember. However, making these videos was one of the first interests I initiated that led me to develop an overarching passion for creation. Though I no longer made silly edits of myself. The process has seared into me like the deep grill marks on a steak. Finding a new tool for creation, coding was a never-ending open world. Seeing how my activity brightened me over the years, I decided to teach my brothers. As a method for me to develop my passion for creation, I hoped to teach others the intricacies of coding. Teaching others the love that I had for not just coding, but the ever-expanding world of technology developed a leader in me as I became more outspoken. Making me bold like the intensity of Suya spices, embracing my fondness for creation led me to step out of my comfort zone.

My journey required a perfect balance. Much like the ingredients for a high-quality dish, it required the right mix of embracing my core cultural identity. My Cameroonian heritage is the foundation of my character while my new experiences give flavor and meaning to my life. Through my journey, I have learned to blend this fusion, accepting those bitter flavors that contrast with the sweet. As I continue to move forward I aspire to add new ingredients dish to create that imperfect dish of the past.

“You are lazy but smart," said my mom to the 9-year-old me who would finish all the math practice questions in the first week of the semester so she could sleep more after school. I got through school with straight As while my friends studied for hours; I would put in less time but still achieved higher grades. To them, it seemed impressive and inspiring, but they didn’t know that this led me to become a bit… lazy.
