So I got addicted to the effortless excelling, while thoughts surged questioning my purpose in the vast world. Luckily, fate rescued me, as my school nominated me into a new realm: the Chemistry Olympiad.

After I joined the team, as the hands of the clock ticked away, I found myself completely absorbed in the intricacies of pH calculations. “Eight hours every day! How did I get myself into this? I am only thirteen,” I said to myself after the first camp. However, these hours turned into four years, during which I was immersed in intense, advanced training, solving numerous Chemistry Olympiad questions every day. I pushed the boundaries of my limitations through relentless practice. Each day, my performance improved, capturing the attention of my lecturer, who praised my quick thinking and creative solutions. Chemistry wasn’t just formulas and reactions anymore—it became a lens through which I began to see the world differently.

This journey didn’t just teach me chemistry; it helped me unravel pieces of myself. Traveling alone at a young age, I learned to carry the weight of responsibility for my time and actions, like balancing a chemical equation. For the first time, the lazy girl who breezed through school found something worth chasing—a passion that ignited when I first saw the spark of a magnesium ribbon burning in the lab.

However, my magnesium ribbon turned out to be short, and the reaction soon ended – the spark disappeared. Nothing lasts forever, and neither did my journey with the olympiad team. After winning a silver medal in 2023, I was eliminated, and the lazy girl returned to her old routine. For that girl, it felt like the end of the world, but what I didn't realize was that after the reaction ended, a white solid remained–my enduring passion for chemistry. Initially, I saw my elimination as a failure, a confession that I wasn’t good enough in chemistry. However, instead of letting this setback define me, I began to volunteer to help other students navigate through the world of chemistry.

Yet, something inside me felt incomplete. I didn’t want to be just an observer, I didn't want to be a catalyst; I wanted to be a part of the reaction. So, I joined a research center as a summer intern and returned to the lab to immerse myself in chemistry again. This time, I conducted research on uranium, the magnificent element I had always heard about from day one. The feeling of holding 5 ml of 10 ppm uranium for the first time was like holding the entire world in my hands–a moment where I felt the profound power and beauty of scientific discovery– in that yellow liquid.

Once again, I tried my luck in a research competition. And though I didn’t win the grand prize, I gained something far more valuable—a special award from the International Atomic Energy Agency to attend a training course on environmental radiation in Fukushima. This was more than a prize; it was a dream come true. The city that the once-lazy 9-year-old girl had only read about, a place that seemed impossible to reach, now welcomed me. This time, I was visiting not just as that curious little girl, but as an 18-year-old researcher, an award winner, a chemist, and the first author of a published paper, ready to stand in the same city as a nuclear plant and explore uncharted territories and make a difference in the world.

If there was a color that encompassed the entirety of my existence, it would be the color brown. Not just one shade in particular, but an array of different, brown-colored hues melted and woven together to become one cast.

My earliest memories consist of leaning on my tiptoes to peer over my younger sister’s mahogany crib. In this moment, at just three years old, I was exposed to a quality of affection that would shape me as the eldest daughter, and ventured to fulfill the responsibilities that inherently came with my position. As I matured, brown continued to follow me. Sitting at my wooden dinner table and light-ebony piano, familial discourse and my pastime of reimagining Chopin’s impromptus and Erroll Gardner’s ballads continually refined my self-awareness and creativity. I inevitably began to embody the essence that the color brown had elicited within my life, and, with each breath, gained a newfound independence.

And yet, I remember the hour that I felt brown had betrayed me. Noon arrived, and I could hear the whispers of my roti calling my name as I scoured to find my lunch box, which had been bent and shoved aside by other students in the kitchen of my school’s cafeteria. Once I found and unzipped it, I was interrupted by the ravenous marches of a fellow classmate. Allured by the cinnamon roll facing him within the vending machine, he asked if I’d buy it for him. “[Name], I know you have the money to buy it. It’s obvious that you have tutors to help you survive the honors track.” Tutors? What tutors? My mind raced, attempting to determine whether I should satisfy him with a response. “You’re so smart for someone so dark.” In an embarrassing stupor, I stood there. I no longer concentrated on my curry, but trying to balance the notion that the validity of my thoughts and expressions was, to others, determined by the shades of my complexion, rather than the quality of my knowledge. As I began to regain focus, I remembered a novel I’d read the week before - Alice Walker’s *In Search of Our Mothers’ Garden*.

It is an homage to my mothers and grandmothers, as she discusses the Black American women who were not allowed to reckon with their creative or literary gifts. Described as the tawny mules of the world, they dreamed dreams no one knew, and visions no one understood. Wandering in cedar fields in autumn or drawing the mother of Christ in brown charcoal on courthouse walls, I imagined them as intricate butterflies trapped in honey. As the images— the fields, charcoal, and honey—began to flood my mind, I realized that he was right. From the sacrifices of my mothers and grandmothers, to overcome the inherent inferiority that was assigned to our native culture, and continue to pull out of myself the intellect that they themselves weren't able to know.

My mother lived in the Jungle, a gang-ridden area of Los Angeles. She latched onto every ray of opportunity in an attempt to escape the poverty and perils of her surroundings, and she did. Although intruded upon in many ways, she passed down an essence that was given to her mother before her, and one that is cherished within me. I march with the creativity of my ancestors kept alive, the suppressed writers, instrumentalists and dreamers that were all once inspired by the color brown, and I proceeded to march out of the cafeteria.

Nearly two years from that encounter, I still feel reawakened. The event led me to my tutee, a young brown-skinned girl from Baltimore City who I hope to empower; similarly, I’ve returned to my ebony-piano and wooded Sepia dinner table with a new sense of spirit, allowing brown’s warmth and security to pervade me entirely. Guided by millennia of ancestral beauty, artistry, and tenacity – embracing my mother’s garden, I have found my own.

It was a story you’ve heard too many times. She had it all, she was happy, no one ever would’ve known. At the time, I didn't know what could be done, but I knew I didn't want it to happen to anyone I knew ever again. After my best friend’s sister died by suicide, I wondered what our school would do. Months passed, but it was almost taboo to talk about it. I began to search for reasons why a wealth of emotional well-being resources exist, but so little of it resonates with teens.

Digging through stacks of paper representing months of mental-health research, I found my laptop nestled alongside my cherished copy of Thoreau’s Walden and prepared for my Zoom with renowned sports psychologist Dr. Jonathan Fader. Dr. Fader had opened my eyes to a world where mental conditioning was more essential than physical conditioning. Once we’d discussed his strategies for performing to our highest potential, I dove into my most pressing question: “How can we equip my generation with the tools necessary to succeed?” During our conversation, Dr. Fader highlighted the importance of promoting mental resilience in schools and observed that I was the first student to approach him with an initiative for improving youth well-being. Ultimately, he agreed to join Chasing Excellence, the speaker series I’d founded to combat mental-health stigma. His support would propel the series further than I’d ever imagined.

Chasing Excellence began during a theology class assignment. Tasked with finding solutions for societal problems like censorship, I wondered how teens could be expected to generate responses to significant crises even adults can’t solve. However, after researching Amnesty International’s work and enlisting classmates to sign the “Free Saudi Arabia’s Voices of Change” petition demanding the release of free-speech activists, I learned that, when acting together, my generation can make a difference. I resolved to improve my own school, where I’d realized the need for mental-health support. When an injury sidelined me from lacrosse, I was struck by the impact of missing daily practice with my team—losing the camaraderie and structure was hard. I experienced firsthand how it is possible to feel alone even when surrounded by people, and how we often keep our personal struggles hidden.

Realizing that a school-wide assembly would help us prioritize time for self-care and reflection while preserving a safe anonymity, I developed Chasing Excellence to bring mental health out of the shadows. This format would serve much like Thoreau’s sanctuary in Walden. With the student council, I surveyed the student body to identify concerns—like the isolation AvaClaire felt when she was too embarrassed to seek help about her troubles surrounding her parent’s divorce. Tailoring the program to students’ needs, I set our series’ missions: (1) erasing the misconception that seeking help is weak, and (2) expanding access to immediate care without fear or embarrassment. After sending hundreds of advocacy emails—and negotiating expensive speaking fees—I was thrilled to have Dr. Fader launch the series. Following his powerful talk, I watched some seventh-graders approach him to express excitement over his techniques. Even AvaClaire felt strong enough to talk to him. It was a watershed moment, proof that students were bonding and opening up as I’d hoped. I signed more speakers—including Bailey Parnell, Brett Ledbetter, and Vanessa Van Edwards—who each strengthened our foundation for mental wellness, crucial to unlocking our full potential.

I’ve realized how Thoreau’s philosophy that every action should be meaningful relates to my own journey. I, too, aim to live deliberately, honoring my values, striving to support others, and leading by example. Seeing Chasing Excellence grow well past my greatest expectations has taught me that helping others flourish provides me with purpose and nourishes my spirit. Our speakers’ information has enlightened me--and I’m sure that it could have helped my best friend's sister. My hope is to pave the way so no one hides their struggles behind a smile ever again.

Bzzz Bzzz... a strange sound tugged me from a cozy dream while filling the room. Annoyance won, and the curtains were pulled back by a rapid movement of my hand. A small nest of bees, which settled near the window, saw all the beauty of my poker face. Since childhood, insects have been intimidating for me. Even so, the yellow workers tirelessly built the nest whether it was a thunderstorm or unbearable summer heat. No bee is idle, each one moves purposefully, ensuring safety and growth. It reminded me of something…

A bee that betrayed the expectations of the former queen. The unoiled hinges made a slow creaking sound, catching my attention. My grandmother opened a closet with a wrinkled but soft hand. A banknote and a clear jar that still smelled barely of cucumbers appeared in front of me. Despite the scarcity of money, she taught me my first lesson in finance - to save. She was always repeating her advice to avoid being an office clerk in economics, but ironically because of her own career in the field. To this day, her collection of books inspires me to pursue a future in economics. So, she can say “I advised the opposite” in paradise.

A bee with the perfect name. Father picks up the phone when it rings heavily, with a deep voice that mentions “[Name]”. Oh, it's me?! After my asking, Dad looks with confusion. The right time for learning the darkest secret that the family kept for 15 years: the legacy of my great-grandfather, Tolepbergen—a farmer who toiled in the fields to support the front during World War II. The small family business and I were both named by him. The earthiness of the name, “[Name],” which means hard-working farmer, suddenly feels like a beacon. The family did not even try to hide that they just forgot to explain it. Yet, the burden of honor history carries will be embraced by me.

A bee is learning his passion. During middle school, my family moved to a suburb due to a financial situation. Feeling the struggles and hoping to support, one night I sat at a shabby table and brainstormed ideas. The advertisement concept stuck in my mind, and it seemed simple and cost-effective. Although it did not work out, the seed of my obsession was planted. Whenever any business thought or innovation strikes me, the notebook waits eagerly for my pure smile and excitement. Ideas, as granules of sand compose a beach, make up my area of freedom.

A bee leaving mother-colony. In the suburbs, the loud and comforting snores of my father stopped being a signal of safety, because of his alcoholism and anger issues. As the family situation worsened, learning myself in subjects that kindled my curiosity was essential because no educational opportunities were provided. Some evening, I stumbled upon an application for a National School. After the test, selection process, and decisions I got in. Joyful screams and congratulations from the family, however I was not as happy because I had to leave my sister and mother without protection. Mother saw concern in my eyes. She held my hand and with a soothing voice elaborated the term of trust, demonstrating if it is a critical decision, you have to trust the surroundings. As always, my mother was right.

Any bees contribute to the colony in their own way. Some can teach how to collect honey, while others’ bravery inspires bees to carry on the legacy. During storms, inexperienced young bees want to support, discovering their passions, arousing trust and independence. Someday this colony will fade and a new one will begin a cycle again. Bees seem to be not as daunting as before so it is time for me to clean up after them because it is already the 3rd one near my window.

Memories. Etched deeply into the hippocampus of the brain, these threads of reality are beautifully woven together in an ever-growing mosaic that presents individuals with their unique characteristics defined by diverse experiences. They encompass divergent moments: instances of happiness, despondency, and vague childhood recollections. The power of memories has always intrigued me; they are fragments of our past but also influence decisions of our present and outcomes in the future. Its cousin, Nostalgia, however, puzzled me. It lurked mysteriously in its capacious cave, only emerging occasionally and unexpectedly to hand me a delicate strand of a bittersweet memory before scurrying back to its sanctuary. Clutching the strand, I couldn’t decide if I despised Nostalgia or secretly found solace in the feeling.

I was still contemplating an answer to this internal dispute years later after first learning about my dad’s stroke that had damaged his ability to speak clearly with concise words and language. I sat in the frigid hospital room that day, unable to comprehend the sudden change. It was as though my eyes deceived me as I observed him in the hospital bed; I noticed no difference in the face of the benevolent and intelligent man with whom I laughed and smiled every day.

My dad turned to me. His mouth was smiling in reassurance but I could distinctly recognize the dark cloud of confusion in his eyes as he tried to speak.

“[Name]?” he asked softly.

I merely smiled back, unable to offer words of comfort. I silently watched him struggle with something that was once so natural but now became a task requiring his full attention and effort.

Reminiscing memories of my dad before this day felt uncomfortable and distant. I could faintly remember waking up to the permeating fragrance of fresh chai while my mom fruitlessly badgered my dad to eat some biscuits. He would hastily refuse, announcing he was late, and rush to work. I guess this is what you would call Nostalgia. If this was it, then I detested it. It infuriated me to recall routines I experienced every day, yet could not appreciate before they were rudely snatched away. These trivial moments I took advantage of so easily became those I was desperate to witness again, even for one last time. If this was Nostalgia, it was cruel.

I remember waiting in my dad’s office lobby, eagerly anticipating to surprise him. When I finally caught a glimpse of him in the crowd, I pushed through the hustle of workers and sprinted delightedly into my dad’s warm embrace. It felt safe, even happy. If this was Nostalgia, I didn’t mind it. It comforted me to know that my parents and I once knew blissful happiness, though it proved to be short-lived. If this was Nostalgia, I would cradle it, protect it, and never let it escape my mind. 
Both instances are fair reminders that the individual I am today is who I was ten years ago, who I changed into the day of my dad’s stroke, and who I became subsequently. These were all the components of my mosaic. I could not hate them; they taught me valuable lessons I carry deep in my heart even today. Yet, I also could not love them unconditionally when I felt nothing but emptiness and pessimism in their presence.

I gradually realized this was the purpose of Nostalgia: he did not exist to be my friend or my enemy. He simply reminded me who I am today and how I reached this point. He was there to remind me that my mosaic would transform, expand, and even fracture, but it was all part of me.

So, thank you, Nostalgia. Thank you for reminding me of my humble roots, colorful experiences, and lessons learned. I will wander into your cave again, now drawn by the light of your wisdom, to observe my cherished memories weave an endless mosaic.

“Where does a cat go when it’s thirsty?”

Isla, one of my school’s first graders, asked me after I corrected misspelled words.

“Where?”

I squatted down to converse with her at eye-level.

“The cat-fe!”

She burst out laughing. I paused only a second before forcing chuckling sounds out of my teeth. In the energetic first grade with 23 kids, Mrs. Hovancik often asks me to keep an eye on Isla, who was diagnosed with autism and ADHD. Throwing tantrums when her scissors went missing, interrupting teachers, and redoing work repeatedly in her chucky handwriting, Isla was a challenging student. The more I got to know her, the more I found it difficult to divorce my sense of stability and self-worth from her moods. I’d find myself questioning my ability to communicate if she didn’t immediately respond to my requests and directions. One day, after she pushed my hand away shouting that she didn’t need help, the whole class witnessed me bolting from the room barely holding back tears of hurt. Cheap sympathy and fake laughter patient teacher’s aide profile. It was time to try another method.

I began looking past words, carefully observing Isla’s mood, reactions, and the context of those jokes, recording data like a researcher. As observations and reading inspired each other, I began reading books and articles like “The Autism Revolution” and “What I Wish People Knew About Autism”. I read firsthand accounts of living with autism, trying to understand how autistic individuals often focus on the intricate details of the world rather than seeing the whole picture like neurotypical individuals. I also decided on autism as my research focus in the Pioneer Research Program, an undergraduate-level academic research initiative for high school students. Here, we discussed important neurodiversity subtopics, such as the nuances of autism diagnosis and language development in autistic individuals, along with useful techniques for enhancing communication, like using visual schedules and telling social stories. My research connected with what I saw in Isla: humor was her way of easing confusion and expressing herself in ways that words could not.

Although research and abstract theory was helpful, observation took me further. When Isla couldn’t follow directions or it got too noisy in the classroom, she would repetitively shake her head and yell loudly—overstimulation I mistook for defiance. After she calmed down, a joke would be told to me as compensation. Whenever my attention was directed elsewhere, especially complimenting another kid, she would tell me a joke and ask for confirmation on whether it was good or not. In group or pair settings, she had trouble finding partners to work with due to her impatience. Wanting a partner, she would pull a classmate aside to convince them with her jokes. The more I observed Isla, the more I realized that laughter was her invitation into the world.

Through my observation, Isla began to understand me too. When I asked, “Why do you only tell me jokes?” She was quick to answer. “You hear them.” With time, our relationship became one of trust, rather than one of duty or obligation, freeing me from feeling the need to make her "happy" all the time. As I enter college and Isla transitions middle school and high school, we both have a lot to learn. However, because of her, my relationship to laughter—whether my own or others—has changed for the better. Every time a classmate laughs during our neurodiversity advocacy initiatives or at a punny joke related to Special Education, I’ll think of Isla and the many ways laughter connects us all. And while I hope to be forcing far fewer laughs in college, I will never forget the power of empathy and the immense joy behind so many moments with Isla, even if her jokes went over my head—they were still “pun-derful!”

In my childhood home in Cliffside Park, New Jersey, the pasta maker in our kitchen would churn out long, curly strands of pasta, softly swishing onto the wooden board below. My story unfolded like those pastas, stretching, adapting, and taking shape in different cultures.

My parents moved to Hong Kong when I was a child, following the 2009 financial crisis. I learnt how to make noodles, pasta’s Asian counterpart, during a cooking class at my new primary school. The noodle dough would start wet and sticky, resisting my attempts to shape it. Yet, with forceful kneading, it would eventually turn smooth and shiny. The tactile experience of working with the dough was calming, easing the nervousness I felt settling into an unfamiliar country.

Despite my love of noodles, I felt I was pasta lost in a noodle land. To me, distancing myself from the Chinese influence was my way to stay loyal to America. I refused to speak the local dialect, watched lots of American television shows, and only read English novels. When my family subsequently relocated to Shanghai, my feeling of alienation deepened.

Starting high school in England during the pandemic did not alleviate the sense of disconnection. Yet, this time I was the noodle in a pasta universe. I was greeted in the form of slurs or insults on the streets because I looked Chinese. When I tried to explain my American identity, my peers looked at me quizzically because I was not the blue-eyed, blonde-haired type they were expecting.

One scene from the movie Green Book struck a chord. Dr Shirley, an accomplished black pianist and a gay man in the 1960s, feeling rejected by both white and black communities, asked, “So, if I’m not black enough and if I’m not white enough and if I’m not man enough, then tell me, what am I?”

Like him, I often wondered, “Who am I? Who gets to be a true American?”

During these moments of inner turmoil, I found solace in my kitchen. In between cooking sessions, I spent a lot of time reading, particularly about American history. While I waited for my dough to relax and release its gluten, I read the stories about the Chinese Exclusion Act, WWII internment camps, and Brown v. Board of Education, which show that these heroic Americans did not belong to a single skin color.

I experimented with various flour types, water content, and salt concentrations in the dough, as well as varied boiling temperatures. Through these culinary adventures I discovered what really set noodles and pasta apart was the ingredients added and the processing methods. Both were essentially flour at heart.

I was also tackling the BiangBiang noodles at the time. After several failed attempts, I found that soaking the dough in oil overnight would make it much easier to pull and the dough more resistant to breaking. Patience is an essential ingredient in every exploration, much as dough need rest to relax and release gluten, and identity, like noodles, can be versatile and strengthened with time and experience.

Through sharing the noodles I made with friends, I come to build a community of support, which was crucial in this transformative process of self-discovery.

Over the years, I have grown more adaptable and resilient from the strong kneading of life and I have discovered that reconciling with my Chinese roots would not render me un-American.

The various ingredients of my tale have taught me to appreciate the diversity of human experience and respect the uniqueness in each individual. I am confident that these qualities will allow me to better serve my future community.

When I start college in America next year, it will be like returning home after a long journey. This time, I am prepared to bring both noodles and pasta to the table, confident that America is big enough to embrace all that I am.

Today, I’m wearing googly-eyed burgers and monochrome aliens.

I’m talking about my socks, of which I allegedly possess the world’s largest, funkiest, and most mismatched collection. Although a seemingly small component of my overall outfit, they’re impossible to miss. The practice of wearing my outlandish, distinctive socks has ultimately become a physical metaphor for my experience living with cerebral palsy (CP).

Growing up, I wore unattractive, knee-high white socks pulled back down over my orthotics. For a teenager, this turned heads for the wrong reasons. Now opting out of regular orthotics usage, I’ve spent the past few years rebelliously relishing my opportunity to turn heads for the right ones. Last year, when I scheduled a meeting with a school administrator to bring up an issue with elevator accessibility, I stumbled into the room and fell awkwardly (as I often do). A little shaken, I picked myself up and in that brief moment, she asked, “Do you like Friends?” She noticed that I was wearing a “Central Perk” sock. Beginning the meeting by discussing “The One with Rachel's Sister," my socks helped inspire a successful “elevator pitch.”

I started mismatching my socks amidst the chaos of my sophomore-year exam period. With little time to sort my laundry, I picked two green socks off the pile and rushed to my math assessment. Later, tapping my foot inside the testing room, I looked down and tarnished the unyielding silence with a liberating chuckle. I had smiley avocados on my left foot and geometric jellyfish on my right.

My socks’ uncanny oddity perfectly matches the misfit that I am; yes, they’re normal socks, but something is a little off. Although most physicians classify me as “high-functioning” – able to get from A to B on New York City public transport – I simultaneously struggle with everyday tasks like opening a can of tomato soup (I own a pair of Campbell’s socks). Despite knowing I’ve earned my place in most rooms, I often wonder if I truly belong. When I first entered high school, my peers seemed to each have at least one thing that set them apart. For most, it was incredible talent in music, sports, or academics. What I believed set me apart was inherently a disadvantage.

For this reason, I initially questioned my team’s decision to elect me as next year’s Varsity track captain. After all, how could their slowest runner lead a serious team? Well, I may finish last in every race at school, but I’m always first at practice. Training with this team, I have become para-national track champion in my own right. With passion and commitment, I bring together these solo athletes. Last season, I cheered so vigorously at an away meet, a teammate joked they would be able to hear me back at school.

Admittedly my socks are weird, curious, and bold, but these same descriptors can be applied to having CP and both remain things that make me who I am. Over the years, my frequent falls and surgeries have arranged themselves into a permanent pattern of scars as brilliant as the ones on my socks. Mirroring my jovial, whimsical socks, I remain easygoing and good-humored. Like when a police officer misdiagnosed my unconventional gait as my being under the influence, I lightheartedly took the opportunity to introduce him to CP.

My feet, the most flawed part of my body, are laden with calluses and deformed with formidable bunions, collapsed arches, and heels that have never hit the ground. And yet, my favorite garments highlight them as if people don’t already look at them enough. People used to ask about my orthotics, but now they ask about my socks.

In literature, juxtaposing two items in an oxymoron beautifies both. The same can be applied to my odd socks. Disjointed from the rest of my carefully curated outfit, their chaos synthesizes with my disability, seamlessly telling my story.

“Move one rock to another because underneath, a plant is trying to grow.” Having been that struggling plant myself—and still growing—I now choose to move as many rocks as I can.

My grandpa sat cross-legged, chanting “Um daari dudari duuri suuhai” in front of the Buddhist Goddess statues in our small yurt every morning. Her mantra soon woke my cousin and me. As we got out of bed, the cold hit us instantly. I grabbed my axe and rushed out to chop firewood. Each swing felt heavier at minus 30 degrees, the axe metal stinging my bare hands—no gloves, just grit. My cousin, too young to handle the axe, helped me by carrying the wood back to the yurt. No matter the weather, our winter routine was the same: chop wood, start a fire, and stay warm.

One day, a friend called me to see the unusual winter birth of a calf. Curious, I left the firewood behind and hurried to join her. When I returned, Grandpa raised his voice, asking, "Why didn’t you prepare the firewood?" I tried to explain, but my words felt hollow.

It was then that I noticed my cousin’s tiny hand as red and raw from a fresh wound. That’s when I realized she had tried to chop the wood herself. My heart sank. She told me she was fine as she tried to hold back her tears, but her strained expression said otherwise. My tears flowed as I remembered how difficult it was when I first learned to chop wood. I used to think “I wish I were a bear, able to hibernate through the cold without having to face the harshness of winter.” Even though I knew how tough it was, I left her with a task she wasn’t ready for. I understood not just the challenge, but the emotions it carried.

Though Grandpa’s voice was harsh when I returned, it softened as he comforted us. I understood that his morning mantras were his way of protecting us, even if he couldn’t help physically. Since that day, the responsibility of staying warm grew heavier over time. I spent hours chopping enough wood to last for days instead of doing it daily.

Eventually, Grandpa’s health forced us to live separately. Before we moved, my cousin gave me a handwritten letter that said, “You are the best sister”. The letter moved me deeply, bringing tears to my eyes and helping me find forgiveness for letting her chop wood in the past.

After we separated, I moved to the city to live with my parents and quickly adapted to conveniences like heated apartments. But, as I walked through the city streets, I saw protestors against residents burning coal and wood to stay warm, frustrated by the air pollution. It made me reflect on times when I had no choice but to chop wood to keep my family warm. Nearly 400,000 people still struggle with this due to limited resources, and most of them are children who face hardships quietly.

While protestors advocate for environmental justice, which is valid based on their experience, I chose to stand up strongly for the children who silently want to be bears, which is valid based on my experience. As I stood up, I’ve been involved in various efforts, from working on a project to build green pocket parks for families in neighborhoods where people burn coal to survive the winter to researching if brick can be used for heating homes.

The day I saw two kids happily playing in our green pocket park made me smile; this simple yet valuable joy made me realize that standing up for those children truly made children happier, but I was the one who was happier than everyone.

To move rocks for a happier winter and happier children, I am also the happiest.

A gentle nudge of my fingertips frees me from land, and I’m off. Gliding across the glassy surface of the Connecticut River, the wind ruffles my hair and carries the scent of pines lining the shore. I feel a familiar sense of serenity wash over me. Atop a slender racing shell for an afternoon row, I settle into a comfortable tempo, tuning into the rhythmic plunking of my blades. And, as usually happens when I thread through this pristine passageway between the hills of Vermont and New Hampshire, my mind begins to clear.

I scan my surroundings for nothing in particular while taking in everything—a red-winged blackbird perched on a reed, a grove of lotus flowers in a protected cove, the echoing croak of a bullfrog. My observations soon begin to merge with memories of the day. I replay a debate on the validity of skepticism with a friend. Feeling my oar resist the water, I think back to Physics class and wonder how force vectors affect my rowing stroke. Recalling English class, I seek inspiration for an upcoming essay on Romanticism.

The distant call of a loon offers an answer, evoking my favorite piece of music, “The Lark Ascending,” and planting an idea. Could I argue that Ralph Vaughan Williams's “pastoral romance” embodies the ideals of the Romantic movement? Based on a poem by George Meredith, it depicts a songbird’s “silver chain of sound” uplifting humanity with a soothing improvisatory melody. After a day amidst the constant buzz of technology, I immediately understand this message of nature as an antidote to the clanking of industrial noise. My paper’s thesis takes form.

Winding through this waterway where my thoughts flow freely from one subject to another, I reflect on the impact of my upbringing in a place where time feels slow and limitless. As a child, exploring outside was routine—collecting acorns and rocks, constructing forts in the woods, pitching a tent beneath the stars. Now, however, I understand what consciously draws me here, where I may stumble on a great idea or simply find joy in my surroundings. More than a mere pastime, I look forward to shifting boulders and constructing bridges over wetlands in my community. Even in such grueling work, I feel happiness. Whether I am on a solitary journey like today’s, out on the trails with other volunteers, or hiking atop Franconia Ridge with my sister and friends, these pursuits reset my mind.

A bend in the river brings the dock into view. Back on land, I wipe down the boat, feeling energized by my afternoon excursion and ready to take on my work at home and at school. Over dinner, I mention to my family that I know firsthand what the Romantic poets recognized about our vital need for harmony with the living world. My outdoor pursuits not only improve my productivity but also shape my values—thoughtfulness, health, a commitment to service—and deepen my curiosity about the intersections of philosophy, science, and the human experience. Going forward, I hope to explore the biological foundations of these connections. I am intrigued by “Attention Restoration Theory,” which explains how the activities I regularly seek out replenish our cognitive resources by resting the brain and engaging our involuntary attention, and by the writings of Oliver Sacks on the benefits of gardens for his neurology patients. This work suggests that in our fast-paced world, connecting with nature is more than just pleasant, it’s truly beneficial.

Endless opportunities lie just across my doorstep. I can admire the forest beyond my home, rest my feet in a meandering brook, or run down to the farmstand for vegetables; these simple acts calm and inspire me even in the most difficult times. And after this day on the water, I am refreshed and focused for the writing ahead, fascinated by Romanticism and the modern science that confirms what I have felt all my life.

“Mom, watch out! You’re gonna derail the Azusa!”

My mom narrowly missed the white engine barreling down the sloped track from the dining table to the floor.

Each new piece of track expanded my “landscape,” sprawling from the living room through the dining room, bedrooms, and across the entryway before looping back. Passengers on the miniature plastic trains waved goodbye as they disappeared into the kitchen.

Inevitably, trains derailed, leaving passengers stranded. I scrambled to redirect them, abandoning some on sidings while others raced ahead. With limited space and tracks, much like Tokyo, I focused on scheduling. I was determined to optimize the entire network; after all, I imagined passengers smiling as they made their connections seamlessly, without having to wait on crowded platforms or miss their trains. I experimented with configurations and wait times in a notebook. Even after putting the tracks away for dinner, I’d spend hours shifting pages like puzzle pieces, to fit together a clearer view of the network. Each adjustment felt like unlocking a secret—small tweaks could dramatically improve flow. Yet satisfying passengers at one station often disrupted others. I wasn’t sure how to optimize the system for everyone back then, but it sparked my determination to find out.

Today, my parents no longer have to worry about kicking over engines or tripping over tracks. Instead, graphs and simulations manifest my passion for modeling. The waving passengers exist only as numbers, but their presence is more important than ever. I revived my childhood project by creating a scheduling optimization model for the Tokyo Metro. As I sat back to marvel at my work, a voice questioned in my head.

“But what about the elderly who take more time between connections?”

Without data on individual Metro users, I used population demographics of the regions surrounding each station.

“And what happens if there’s a delay? If the connection times are too tight, more people will crowd the narrow platforms.”

I’d minimized waiting times, but my model faltered during disruptions. My analysis wasn’t wrong, but it wasn’t complete. Weeks or months later, I’d still be thinking about my model when riding the Metro myself or listening to friends and family recount their experiences. I kept refining it, adjusting for everything I could think of. But every time I felt close to a perfect solution, I was reminded that no model is ever truly 100% accurate: that’s what makes it a model. It’s this constant pursuit of an elusive ideal that drives me and keeps me excited about engineering.

Even so, data only told part of the story. One winter morning, I arrived at a platform swarming with commuters—my train was delayed. I pulled out my laptop and adjusted my interval scheduling models to simulate the disruption. I estimated 300,000 commuters across Tokyo were recondering their plans. Most of them probably didn’t realize the full scope of the delay. Seeing the crowd firsthand, I felt a new sense of purpose: my models weren’t just numbers—they were people, and I could help them feel less lost during chaotic commutes.

I took on more complex analysis projects, applying my skills to optimize evacuation routes in earthquake-prone areas. Witnessing the lack of infrastructure in rural regions after the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake, I identified facilities that could serve as shelters and shared my findings online for residents to view. Similar to train disruptions, I optimized networks for safety, striving to help families reach shelters in time.

Before I knew it, my mind became the most intricate network I had created. The toy tracks of my childhood sparked a lasting curiosity, evolving into a fascination with how small changes can lead to significant improvements. This mindset allows me to envision how modeling can be applied to enhance community resilience, especially in the wake of natural disasters like earthquakes.

Throughout my life, I’ve felt like a pair of trainer chopsticks, the ones they give to little kids. Not fully traditional, but a set of chopsticks all the same. You see, growing up as a second-gen, half-Korean girl in America initially left me feeling detached from my culture. But working to discover passions of my own, I have learned to embrace my identity for everything it contains. It didn’t happen in one day—it took a journey. And what better way to start this journey than with a home-cooked Korean meal?

The scent of freshly cooked galbi-jjim, a heavenly rich stew of braised beef, carrots, and chestnuts, wafts from my grandparents’ kitchen. A colorful display of banchan adorns the table, spanning from kimchi to dotori-muk (acorn jelly).

“Dinner!” I hear. “Coming, Meema and Jee!” I skip to my seat. Traditionally, you’re supposed to call your maternal grandparents Oehalmeoni and Oeharaboji, but my monolingual, 2-year-old self wasn’t going to try and pronounce all that. So I made up nicknames that were as short and sweet as the time it takes me to scarf down the food on my plate.

As I got older, I became more aware of the language barrier separating me from my grandparents. Their discussions with my mom were utter mysteries to my dad and me, and whenever I told a story, the tricky bits had to be translated. There was this growing divide between myself and my identity that I couldn’t shake. If I couldn’t speak the language, did I deserve to say that I’m Korean at all? But then I realized—there is so much culture packed into that one word. I just had to find it.

In 2017, I arrived in Seoul. There was something so breathtaking about stepping foot in another country—I stood in a state of reverie, lost in the most wonderful dream. It was a metropolis containing every part of Korean culture I could have ever dreamed of. Stunning skylines met with tranquil but elaborate palaces, and vibrant shopping districts met with food-filled street markets. I saw art in the intricate details of fans as I passed by market stalls, the perfection of lush, green burial mounds, and the details that made up shrines and hanoks (traditional houses). I explored museums and marveled over the representation the pieces conveyed and the tradition they embodied. My eyes were opened to the possibility that creativity holds. Finally, I understood what Korean meant. It wasn’t just language and looks. It was family, food, life, and art. Maybe I could belong after all.

As art is a universal language, I can communicate visually. I show my grandparents drawings that contain stories within each facial expression or scene, and they can understand them. I may not fit in some ways culturally, but I can through art and storytelling. Rather than looking at what I am missing in my culture, I see what I can add. In a subject without rules, I have the power to express myself however I want. I’ve always loved drawing characters and making up stories, and in doing so, I can welcome both my cultural and creative sides, the mosaic that makes me who I am. And in the future, I can merge them into something new. Maybe that will be through art programs when I study abroad. Or through opening a studio where people of all cultures and identities are welcome to express and embrace every part of themselves. To gain that creative mindset that thrives in their culture. Because I know I wouldn’t be the same without everything I’ve been through to forge my identity. I’d be a puzzle left incomplete, a night sky without its stars. I take pride in being half-Korean just as I do in being an artist. Now, I’d say I’m more like a pair of chopsticks with playful patterns—balancing tradition with my own creative expression. And with a balance like that, I know I’ve found the perfect harmony that makes me me.

Prepare for a TV show like no other! Watch each day transform into an episode as I embrace sitcom-esque plotlines and the character development within them. You’re just in time for the series finale, where we’re looking back on moments from the past four seasons of high school through my favorite TV trope: clip shows. So strap in as you experience witty one-liners, plots that sneak up on you, and roaring laugh tracks. Let’s roll it!

Season 1, Episode 1: Pilot. A new character is introduced and [Name] tries to break the ice. How will it go?

Trying to start a conversation with my cousin, someone nearly a decade older and who grew up in India, only results in awkward silence. Instead of more small talk, I pivot: “Do you want to play a game?” Pushing aside classics like Scrabble and Clue, I pull out what I’m looking for: the Indian board game Chowka Bhara. As we start playing, the awkward silence is replaced with laughter as we send each other's pieces back to start. She then introduces me to new rules, letting me understand her strategic thinking and a new way of playing the game. As rematches ensue, we trade tips and tricks as two different styles of play meld together into something new: a unique game that ties us together and constantly teaches us more about one another.

The pilot often sets up who the character strives to be, and this experience helped me understand how to start conversations that seed deeper connections.

Season 2, Episode 9: Breaking Boats. Coxing, regionals, and stomach bugs, oh my!

With my teammate hurling chunks into the water mid-race, the intensity we had practiced with now risks breaking our flow. As I ensure he is okay, a quick nod affirms we can finish this race. While it initially slows us down, my first step switches the focus away from raw power, eliminating the out-of-sync timing to get everyone on the same page. With everyone moving together, I then break down the steps of the stroke and make suggestions focusing on each part individually to recover from our misstep. Now in full swing, emphatic shouts of motivation serve as the final push over the finish line.

While season finales like to end at a close, this episode stands out by starting my journey of addressing unexpected team problems effectively and taking calculated risks as a leader.

Season 3, Episode 8: Awake In Anaheim. A science-project-gone-wrong storyline forces an unconventional solution as [Name]’s prototype stops working at DECA ICDC (cue audience gasp)!

With the potassium chloride leaking, my invention can no longer turn food waste into electricity and is condemned to read 0.00 on the voltmeter. As a hotel transforms into a laboratory, I pull up a bright multicolored periodic table (a callback to season 2’s AP Chemistry). Countless hours of research beforehand combines with an impromptu scouring of Google to find a solution that just might work. While attempting to find a similar chemical may seem as improbable as finding the original, one row above potassium was sodium. Asking employees for sodium chloride may have prompted weird looks, so I opted for its more common name–salt. With the would-have-been seasoning added to the setup, my invention begins working again.

Big-budget episodes feel like they have to be perfect, but rewatching this one reminds me that even when things go wrong, understanding my work at a deep level allows me to find solutions in any environment.

If you’ve enjoyed looking back on our first series, speak up! We’re so close to convincing producers to make the sequel. On-my-feet problem-solving is a cornerstone of the most popular episodes, and you can count on it to be a major part of our next project’s four seasons. With some luck, by the fall of 2025, this sequel will be dropping at a college campus near you.

“Your dad is not coming,” my mother whispered, her voice trembling, barely holding back tears. She collapsed into my grandmother’s arms, the buzz of the television fading into the background. My 5-year-old brain couldn’t process what I had heard. “Yes he is,” I said, my voice firm with confusion, as if stating a fact. It felt impossible, like she had misunderstood. But when I saw the tears pouring down my mother’s cheeks, reality slammed into me. Suddenly, my dreams were shattered, and hope abandoned me.

As I grew older, I felt the weight of uncertainty closing in. My mother’s worried glances at the growing stack of unpaid bills became a constant in our home, the quiet tension lingering in the air. Each glance reminded me that things weren’t improving, no matter how much I hoped. I had always saved my birthday money, watching it slowly accumulate, reaching $100, wondering if it would ever be enough. That hope began to feel hollow. One evening, while browsing YouTube, I stumbled upon a video about investing in the stock market. Skeptical but desperate for something within my control, I spent days diving into research, watching videos and reading articles late into the night, trying to absorb everything I could. The idea of making my $100 work for me became a lifeline.

My first dive into the stock market was a mix of excitement and nervous energy. Late at night, I sat at my desk, eyes glued to the screen, scrolling through articles and videos, trying to understand everything I could about AMC and GameStop stocks. As I watched them fluctuate wildly, my heart raced. When I finally hit "buy," my hands shook, the glow of the monitor reflecting my anticipation. The profits didn’t come all at once—it took days of anxious waiting, checking my phone constantly. When the profits started to trickle in, I could hardly believe it. I had made $300—more money than I had ever seen. My heart pounded as I grabbed my phone and bolted downstairs. “Mom, I did it!!!” I shouted, transferring the money online. “I can help.” Her expression—a mix of exhaustion and gratitude—hit me hard. Fueled by this success, I launched a small dropshipping business. Though it wasn’t a major success, the experience taught me the value of risk, reward, and perseverance.

Moving to South Carolina during my freshman year felt like stepping into an unfamiliar world. The slower pace, accents, and new faces were overwhelming, but I knew I had to adapt. After finishing my freshman year at a local school, I switched to online learning, in search of a higher education. During this time, I began creating educational TikTok videos. Initially, I focused on business, but I soon shifted to politics and current news, sparking thoughtful exchanges in my growing online community. This experience fueled my passion for building spaces where knowledge could thrive. When I returned to in-person learning in my junior year, I took this drive to my principal. “We need a space for free thinkers,” I said. That conversation started our school’s first debate club, where ideas turned into action.

Reflecting on my journey from the first stock I purchased to the creation of my school’s debate club, I’ve come to realize that hope is just the spark, but action is what fuels the fire. From navigating financial uncertainty to building spaces for free thinkers, I've seen the impact of resilience and initiative. In college, I plan to dive into creating spaces where ideas can thrive—whether by joining student government, leading debates, or organizing forums that challenge the status quo. I can already feel the energy of those future conversations, the kind that spark growth and push boundaries. Obstacles will come, but they don’t intimidate me. Instead, I embrace them as opportunities to grow, guided by lessons of resilience, initiative, and the belief that hope, combined with action, leads to results.

My mom pulled my hair back and loosely folded it up. Although she acted indifferent, I knew she was bothered, “You’ll look like a boy.” I yanked the scissors from her hand and embraced it: –chop, chop, chop. As I felt the hair falling, I realized the literal weight on my shoulders was disappearing.

I combed my fingers through my hair, but the strands stopped prematurely. Rather than black hair flowing down to my hips, only rough edges poking my neck remained. Yet, despite this new “boy-ish” hairstyle, I felt more feminine and like myself than ever before, though I couldn’t yet figure out why. That answer would arrive soon enough.

Embracing my true self in my hairstyle led me to change my wardrobe to fit myself. Before, it mainly consisted of t-shirts, some jeans, and athletic shorts. Those clothes aren’t particularly my style, but I was scared to try on different clothes to find it, as I always felt uncomfortable wearing generational hand-me-downs rooting from the fear of being judged. Through the haircut I felt that the joy of expressing myself outweighed the thoughts of being negatively looked upon. If I can change my hairstyle, why not other expressions?

After I began finding myself, I experimented with more diverse gender expressions, from wearing clothing I hadn’t even looked at in years, to applying Pacinos Signature Line’s matte paste to my hair. Though my mom stared at my hair like the devil sat on it, I realized that my joy came from my courage to be myself, for myself, and not for others. I felt free from the restraints of society and my mother. My life was mine to like, not for her to control.

Propelled by this confidence boost, I decided to take another leap during my junior year and host a singing show in front of a thousand-person audience at the Pioneer Theatre Guild, despite having no experience in acting or singing. While the other female hosts searched for dresses, I searched for a suit. Stepping out into the hot lights for the first time, I swelled at the feeling of not just representing my true self, but also those in the audience who also wanted to take the stage. I can’t help but think of 9-year-old [Name]: someone who was trapped in skirts and tap dance shoes & how I needed to be the role model she never had. Even though I can’t go back in time, I can influence my peers right now—some friends sought advice from me because of my style with suits. Finally, I think I’ve begun to find my style.

Though each of these moments had their difficulties, each brings me one step closer to my true self. Even my once scornful mother is finally beginning to pick out suits for me rather than dresses. When she laid out her suits as options to wear, I felt accepted and satisfied. I felt recommitted to my journey when I changed her opinions on female fashion that she had held for decades.

I will challenge stereotypes and explore my identity in the future. As my appreciation for the changing society norms grows, I can’t wait to host “Laughter is One Cure” events, where I will perform improv and stand up to those in hospitals, so that they receive medical treatment and laughter—two ways I believe that can heal—and be able to connect them with personal stories. I also want to continue to act as the advocate not only for suits, but for whatever others wish to try; I want to help lift up others' voices now that I’ve found mine. As I leave high school, I will exist as my authentic self, whatever form that may take, and lift up those around me as I do so.

“If you could define your life in one word, what would it be,” my 11th-grade French Teacher asked.

“Change,” I responded.

The change I’ve experienced through my friendships has provided the most influential and meaningful experiences in my life thus far.

Lucas was my first friend: the first person who liked me for me and nothing else. We never expected anything from each other except ourselves. One day, I nervously asked him if he wanted to start playing a new video game together. I didn’t know if he would like it, but he just said, “If you’re playing, that’s good enough for me!” Lucas has taught me that true friends don’t need an excuse to spend time and help each other; they do so unconditionally.

Now, when I meet new people, I always try my best to make them feel at ease and help out where I can. This ideology is what motivated me to start my non-profit tutoring organization, Aequitas Tutoring. I wanted to connect with other like-minded students and give back to the communities that have given us so much together.

In grade four, I met one of the kindest people I know: Eddie. After mustering up the courage to ask him if he liked Pokémon, our joined interests and similar personalities helped us become inseparable. Eddie always had my back, whether helping me with my math assignments or picking me to be on his basketball team. Over the years, he showed me true kindness and loyalty, and I couldn’t have been more grateful.

Eddie always encouraged and believed in me even when I didn’t believe in myself. Now that I’m older and in a similar position to support other students at my school, I always look for opportunities to share what I’ve learned with others. In the band, I assign solos to younger players and help them during sectionals; In the Wellness Council, I make sure everyone has a chance to share and implement their ideas; and in Fencing, I mentor new students and spend time building their confidence and skills.

Nelson was loud, assertive, and everything that I wasn’t. I never thought we would become good friends, but over time, he proved me wrong. One memorable day, as we were walking around my school quad, he suddenly shared how grateful he was for our friendship.

When I asked why, he said, “You’ve given me kindness and understanding I didn’t even know I needed. I will never forget that.” Although Nelson likely didn’t understand the significance of his words, at that moment, I finally recognized the impact I could have on others.

My life has been filled with transitions — new schools, new experiences, and a sea of new friends. Each farewell felt like I was starting a part of my life over from scratch, and I became more guarded because I didn’t know if my new relationships would endure. I was focused on myself and what I was gaining rather than what I could give to others. Nelson helped me realize that in relationships, people build off each other, and the insights we take away so often have enduring value in our lives.

Ultimately, I’ve learned that It’s not the places I’ve been but the people I’ve met that have impacted the person I am today. Although goodbyes are inevitable, the memories we make, the lessons we learn, and the influence we have are forever. I used to think I was losing a piece of myself every time I moved away, but now I know I was really adding new layers and growing as a person.

Equipped with this understanding, I openly embrace the change around me because, for the first time, I know that I am moving forward, not backward. In college, I am excited to join a new community with inspiring people, so we can grow, learn from each other and embrace the next chapter in our lives together.

“3, 2, 1… Contestants, open your packets!”

Papers shuffle, pens click, and I focus on the article in front of me. This is what I love—the thrill of turning research and preparation into strategy and creativity. This is Future Problem Solving (FPS).

FPS introduced me to a new mindset, helping me analyze global issues, predict outcomes, and design solutions. As I advanced in competitions, one thing became clear: technology was at the core, whether through AI or smart cities.

So, I looked up how to get started programming. When I learned my first line of code: (“Hello [Name]!”);, computer science bridged my love of problem solving to a career path through creativity and innovation. It was natural, and I fell in love with the world where I could create, innovate, and manipulate my own ideas into reality whether that was through developing a react application or using Pandas to manipulate datasets into neural networks to predict strokes.

Computer science is a natural extension of my mindset—breaking down complex problems, identifying patterns, and creating solutions. It shifted my perspective, showing me how challenges are interconnected systems that can be transformed through innovation.

What started as a love for FPS grew into passion for creating with purpose. The same desire to solve drives me today, but now I’ve brought it to a different realm. Whether I’m designing AI that classified images or creating a website that helps people learn, the essence is the same—it’s about making something from scratch, repetition, and new possibilities. The scenarios I once solved for have been replaced by real world applications, and every challenge brings a new opportunity to push what I can create. For me, computer science has never just been a career choice— but a natural evolution of who I’ve always been.

“Wake up,” My dad whispers. “We’re doing the Window Trail.”

I rub my eyes. Not again. Road-tripping across Texas with family and friends was fun, but hiking? Not really—especially after sitting on a cactus. To me, hiking was a chore, a battle with exhaustion, and I only went because my dad insisted.

After the hike, we gathered for dinner in an RV—the room sang with conversation, and we watched a slideshow of pictures from past trips. As photos passed of us at Badlands, Yosemite, Zion, and countless other national parks, I realized those hikes were my dad’s way of gifting us memories. Even if I didn’t love it yet, I’d seen incredible places and created lasting experiences with my family.

I didn’t enjoy hiking until our trip to Alaska. The untamed wilderness and natural rhythms awakened a new curiosity in me. I began to notice the stars, the birds' songs, and the spruce air. I discovered hiking wasn't a chore, but rather a journey to be savored.

There, for the first time, with my dad’s guidance, I began to take the lead on the trips. I took charge of our hikes, leading my family through the reserves of Alaska. I researched the trails, noting climb rate, difficulty, and exciting features. I mapped out our daily routes, leading the group through dense forest trails and pointing out wildlife like bald eagles circling above.

When we reached the Kenai mountains, I encouraged my family to take extra paths to see new views. I learned about Alaska’s history, how the fjords were carved by glaciers, and shared that with them as we drove down the Kenai Peninsula. On that trip, as I took his place, I understood why he took us to hundreds of trails—not just to show us nature, but rather, to show us ourselves. Each of our hikes was an experience; an experience designed to teach us resilience, patience, and teamwork, and teach us about our own strengths and limitations.

Now, it helps me to see parallels between the challenges of hiking my dad brought to me and daily life. Just as a hiker conquers obstacles and finds joy in journeys, not only do I approach every challenge with a sense of goals and an appreciation for the growth they provide, but also with the perspective that all problems, no matter how difficult, can reveal strengths I didn’t know I had.

When I’m programming and faced with a bug, I see each line of Java I have to go through as a step along a rocky path, each error resolved an incline I’ve completed. When I’m struggling with weights at the gym or losing a tennis match, I remind myself that every rep and point is a small victory—a step closer to my goal. Hiking has flipped a switch of mindfulness that connects to my daily life that I find nowhere else. Whether I’m deciding where to put my foot on a rocky trail or where to insert a line of code into a project, both activities engage the same problem-solving mindset, and each success brings me a sense of satisfaction.

After all these years, a tough hike, to me, is finally a source of strength, a reminder of the importance of perseverance. The experiences my dad gifted me have fueled my determination to tackle the challenges that lie ahead in college and beyond. Whether it’s tough coursework, finding internships, doing research, or anything else, I will be driven by the belief that perseverance will turn the hardest challenges into growth.

Each step on a trail, once heavy with fatigue, is now a gift, and as I take on the trails of life, I’ll never forget the paths I walked with my dad. And when my path becomes hard, I remember the lessons from Yosemite to the Everglades: even the most difficult parts can reveal the most amazing views, and every step forward is a chance to discover something new.

Be courteous in your manners.

Have a strong sense of justice.

Be responsible for your words and actions.

Respect one another.

This is the Dojo Kun of my dojo. It signifies the character we wish to develop in ourselves and promote in our fellow Karatekas (students of karate).

These simple yet profound principles are the foundation upon which I have built myself. However, when I began karate at just seven years old, I had no idea how it would significantly influence my life. It shaped my character and continues to guide my actions in my everyday existence.

My first time stepping into the dojo was an unforgettable experience. The sensei welcomed me, and I was told to remove my shoes and socks, a traditional Japanese sign of respect. Right after the sensei closed the door behind me, the students quickly arranged themselves by belt rank. The sensei walked to the front of the class, and instantly each student kneeled on the floor. The sensei recited the Dojo Kun in Japanese, and the class repeated in perfect unison. The order, respect, and discipline I witnessed mesmerized me. From that day, I knew I wanted to be part of this unique community. Over the next seven years, the dojo became my second home.

Under my sensei’s leadership, I stayed dedicated and consistent in karate. I rapidly advanced through the belt ranks, becoming one of the highest-ranking students in just a few years. Soon after, my sensei signed the dojo up for a nationwide tournament. Walking into the tournament with my classmates, I noticed they were terrified by the immense number of competitors. I decided to bring them to a spot under the bleachers and guided them through practice in hope of eliminating any unnecessary fear. My classmates thanked me after, saying I helped them to be more confident in themselves. Looking back, that experience shaped my leadership skills and deepened my sense of responsibility to others.

Throughout my years, the discipline, respect, and leadership I acquired extended far beyond the dojo. These qualities propelled me to be selected for an internship opportunity through the Technology Association of Georgia. The host company I was selected by was called Discover Dunwoody, a hospitality company with the mission to bring business and connectivity to the city of Dunwoody. Under the mentorship of the vice president of sales, I learned about the importance of communication and connectivity with others in the work environment. Harnessing the embedded values I learned from karate, I left a lasting impression on my mentor and the executive director who said I “exhibited a strong work ethic, a positive attitude, and a desire to learn and grow.”

Karate has also instilled in me dedication, consistency, and a deeper sense of responsibility to be my best self. I intuitively applied these traits in many areas of my life. I began playing piano when I was four, and while it was easy at first, the more challenging pieces required relentless practice. My karate training taught me persistence, which helped me approach the piano with the mindset that success comes from consistent effort. That same dedication carried over into weightlifting. In my sophomore year, I felt self-conscious about being skinny and weak. So, I committed to strength training, with guidance from my school's strength coach and classmates. I found a passion for fitness. Now, two years later, I am more confident in myself, both physically and mentally.

Looking back, I am extremely thankful for what karate taught me. The Dojo Kun's moral code remains a guiding force as I embark on new challenges, keeping the mindset to take everything as an opportunity to learn and grow. The discipline, respect, responsibility, and positive attitude ingrained in me are now essential to my identity, driving me to contribute positively to the community around me.

If Beethoven was a maestro conducting the heavens with his divine touch, I would be a bewildered duck waddling across the keys, quacking out discordant honks where symphonies should soar.

The piano has never been my forte.

Fruitless attempts to conjure magnificent symphonies result in my cat howling and running for the door in a desperate attempt to escape the horror that has fallen upon his ears. A string of notes must be played nearly a hundred times, much to the dismay of everyone in the vicinity, before it begins to resemble the melody its author intended. My electric keyboard provided some respite - it connected to a set of headphones, so that the melancholy chorus of notes that was intended to be the Beatles' Here Comes the Sun would be contained to my ears alone.

These musical (mis)adventures were my secret; the piano resting in the dimly lit corner of my theater classroom and I were strangers. As I watched my musically inclined peers sweep their hands across the piano, I felt as though I was playing with legos while they were crafting architectural drawings.

Nonetheless, I persisted. I tackled “Fur Elise” with vigor and pored over elementary piano books. My hands swept carefully from one set of notes to the next, each key changing the course of the song like rocks in a current, before I built into a crescendo and the music tumbled over a waterfall. Late nights, after studying mechanics, would be spent on the piano. My heavy eyelids begged me to fall asleep, but my fingers kept pressing down on yet another set of notes. My lack of talent would not deter me.

Over time, my pianistic pursuits taught me far more than just simple melodies; they’ve allowed me to find resonance in imperfection. While my piano skills were abysmal at best, I strove to be a maven in everything else. Each Data Science club meeting and workshop was met with days of preparation prior, every last detail accounted for. But when my club advisor ran into traffic the day of our largest workshop, I drew upon my symphonic struggles. As with the unconventional tune I had composed through a series of mistakes the night before, I embraced the meeting’s disharmony. I took control of the chaos and directed students to settle down against lockers in the corridor. The meeting took place in the hallway, incurring the attention of people passing by and becoming even more successful than I had initially envisioned.

Playing the piano was far more than a melodious pastime. It was an investment into failure, and growth through it. I found that through repetition, certain songs on the piano taught me more about pattern recognition than coding tutorials ever could. A particularly difficult Calculus lesson unraveled in my mind as I sat in front of my keyboard, playing notes again and again. The idea for a homeless medical screening event struck me when a collection of discordant partnerships I was struggling to unite finally connected into a beautiful melody.

The piano became a medium through which I balanced a desire for perfection and the pursuit of knowledge. Each wrong note played meant that the next rendition of the song had the capacity to be just slightly better, and through this, my mistakes were transmuted into ability.

With college on the horizon, I’m still afraid of pressing the wrong keys, both literally and metaphorically. But my journey with the piano isn’t about the notes - it’s about the music behind it. As I embark on a path to follow my passions in data science, I know that chaos and imperfection cannot deter me. And if an idea for a symphony consisting of a discordant collection of notes (that the very thought of would reduce Mozart to tears) strikes me in the middle of the night - I promise to connect headphones to my keyboard in the dorm.

The intricate system of circuits, gears, and sensors seamlessly harmonized, allowing the mechanical contraption to effortlessly glide across the floor. While this miniature robot fascinated me, Casey stared blankly, as if he couldn’t imagine anything more ordinary. Similarly, Sky gave the machine an uninterested glance, equally ambivalent to its wonders. Dejected, I switched to helping Dariella practice her handwriting.

As an intern at the Haven House, I served as a teacher's assistant for a classroom of 5-year-olds. Although I enjoyed simply interacting with the kids, I clung to the hope of sharing my passion for robotics with them, despite their initial indifference. After a while, another student, Joseph, picked up the abandoned controller and experimented with it on his own. THUD “Ahhh!” Joseph exclaimed. I whipped my head around, concerned he had somehow injured himself.

“I hurted it! It's injewred…” he said in a pained voice, stifling a sob.

“It's okay,” I soothed, gently bending the metal frame back into place. “All better!”

As we kept playing, I realized that Joseph saw the robot as alive––its ultrasonic sensors were eyes, its bent metal frame an injury, and its beeps expressions of emotion. Maybe if I played along, the rest of the kids would see what Joseph saw. The next day, I tried exactly that.

To spark their excitement, I transformed the colorful classroom carpet into a treacherous terrain for the robot to conquer—bridges made from stacked books, winding paths outlined by crayons, and towering obstacles built from wooden blocks. As I skillfully traversed the course, the kids itched for a chance to wield the controller. Moving to the tables, I explained how circuitry controlled the robot (which they had named “Sparky” after Dariella’s dog). I began teaching simple concepts of electricity, using the light switch to simulate day and night, bridging new concepts with our makeshift robo-world. Then, they learned how to use “Snap Circuits” to make simple contraptions out of colorful components that snap together. Soon, Helicopters spun to life from small plastic discs and red LEDs turned into ambulances; the circuit boards became a playground for their imagination.

Last summer, I organized a camp teaching middle-schoolers about robotics. Recalling my time at the Haven House, I realized I needed to start by connecting with them. Instead of the same old icebreaker questions like “what's your favorite hobby” or the classic, “share a fun fact about yourself” we broke the kids into small groups and played two truths and a lie.

In one group, Grant confidently shared, “I’ve climbed a mountain, I own three snakes, and I’ve never had a cavity.” The group quickly agreed that owning three snakes was a lie, only for Grant to flash a sly smile and reveal he actually did have three pet snakes, and laughter filled the room. By the end of the game, walls had broken down, and the kids were chatting like old friends.

***

After the structured matches of the summer camp competition ended, the kids swarmed the field, eager to ram their robots into each other's in an attempt to dominate. But amidst the carnage, there was collaboration too. A member of team “Rubber Bandits” helped the “Mediocre Mavericks” troubleshoot their robot, while kids exchanged high-fives after finally getting their code to work. Though this scene might be discounted as mayhem by some, I saw the beauty of connection through the chaos.

As a life-long math nerd, I used to measure my success by numbers: 20 kids at my summer camp, 10th place at my climbing competition, etc. While numbers may be important, I’ve learned to value something else: fist bumps with excited kids, cheers from late-night robotics breakthroughs, students feeling comfortable to open up to me. Now, I understand what truly drives me is building meaningful relationships and cultivating a sense of belonging. In college, and beyond, I will continue to encourage curiosity, imagination, and problem-solving as a means of connection.

I was blind once.

I sat, blind, in my 9th grade English class, reading The Ramayana. While discussing Indian culture, the topic of the caste system came up. A fellow classmate shared her unfortunate experiences with the issue, discussing how she had been mistreated in the past due to this. Immediately, alarm bells rang in my mind. Caste system? I thought, unaware of my own privilege. I’ve never experienced such prejudice! Therefore, it must not truly exist. These people are berating my country; I must defend it.

Thoughts swirled in my brain, fighting for a chance to make themselves known through the vessel that was my words. With little thought, I allowed them to escape, the vessel transforming into a directed weapon as they invalidated my classmate’s genuine experiences.

I lived in a haze of ignorance, unaware of the harsh reality of some aspects of my culture. My wake-up call was a trip to India in the summer before my junior year.

Once I arrived at the New Delhi airport, the drive to my family’s village began. As we crossed town roads, I remembered begging my parents to buy the colorful toys I saw outside when I was younger. Now as I opened my mature eyes, all I could notice were the desperate young children begging for us to purchase them.

Upon arriving at the house, I saw that my family living there employed a maid who did the household chores along with her two young daughters, who had dropped out of school to help their mother. Tired, I asked my mom, “Mama, where is the bedroom?” This simple sentence of English had caught the little girls’ attention. They had never left the village, so this piece of the outside world manifesting itself in my words piqued their curiosity.

For the remainder of my trip, I spent a great amount of time with the girls, who were exceptional minds. I taught them the basics of English, and they could formulate basic sentences by the end of the month.

When it came time for me to return to the United States, I wondered what would happen to them. There were so many children like them, full of undiscovered potential that would never be found because of systematic inequality. I realized that I could inspire change in many others’ lives, just as I did for the maid’s daughters.

After contacting a non-profit in Bihar, India, I met young women who went against social norms for their education.
