Inspired by their determination, I decided to volunteer daily as a remote English teacher and content curator. Though I enjoy teaching English, I felt the need to contribute in a way that was unique to my interests. So, I developed a website with an introductory course of the basics of computer science for underprivileged children. Catering to their needs, I made sure the course was accessible in regional languages. Over 2 months, I provided individual support to 7 children through online calls. Though social norms are difficult to change, one benefit that came from lower participation was I was able to provide more individualized support to the children that were interested. It was a learning curve to build a site while simultaneously developing course content, but after reaching these 7 children (and counting) that would otherwise never have received such an opportunity, the proof of my efforts was lit up on my phone screen.

“Thank you didi [sister]. Because of our online calls, my parents enrolled me in computer courses today. I want to be a teacher like you!”

As I re-read the choppy translated message from a student, I felt proud that I impacted lives for the better. I gained skills in communication and problem solving that I can apply to multiple aspects of my life. Most importantly, however, this experience awakened me to inequality, giving me sight in place of blindness.

“17 chimes, for 17 victims…” I strike the chimes in my 17-note solo of “Forever and Always, A Reflection,” my heart rate slowing to match the serene melody, bringing a sense of calm to my turbulent memories. To my right, a reporter narrates the NBC 5th anniversary feature dedicated to the lives lost on February 14th, 2018 at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School.

I call Parkland, Florida home. On that day, I was forced to hide inside a dark bathroom along with my classmates. We huddled together, uncertain and scared by actions driven by hatred, stemming from feelings of exclusion.

Music has helped me process that day and reconnect with my community. In the aftermath of the shooting, I struggled with painful migraines that forced me to quarantine in dark rooms to avoid excess stimulation. I tried countless headache medications, but the pain was so debilitating that I could feel my head pounding like a drum. Advil or Tylenol never worked. Instead, music became my medicine.

Although I was initially hesitant about joining percussion–fearing it would bring more chaos to my mind–the band room gradually evolved into my haven for relief. With each exercise and new technique I learned, the throbbing of my head slowed from unbearable to manageable to entirely unnoticeable.

Now, a headache strikes on the bus to school in the morning? I throw on my headphones, losing myself in Michael Jackson’s “Thriller,” part of our halftime show track. A stressful school day filled with important tests and after-school math practices? I escape to the band room to improvise a beat with friends, who join in playing cowbells, saxophones, and piano. Every note we play melts away the tension in my shoulders and relaxes my breathing.

The soothing sounds of the band room found their way into other areas of my life. Prior to the Boston University’s RISE research symposium, I harnessed the effect of tapping my chest to the “Queen” snare drum feature to calm my nerves before presenting in front of a crowd gathered around my poster. During the district playoff game against the Nova Titans, I led a pulsing chant and a bleacher-rattling stomp to energize my volleyball teammates before we clinched our victory. These small musical rituals have calmed me, centered me, and guided me towards greater confidence and stronger leadership.

When selected to be the percussion section leader as a sophomore, I was nervous about being the youngest leader in the band, especially because of Logan and Dougie, two of my friends with special needs. Logan and Dougie both face unique challenges with the precise timing required for percussion and with fitting in with the rest of the band. To ensure they are included and prepared, I dedicate extra time after rehearsals to review their parts and use subtle taps on their backs during concerts to help them stay on tempo. As I juggle my own responsibilities while assisting them both, I embrace their trust and listen as their rhythms align with the rest of the ensemble.

“It’s Time to Unleash the FURY!!!” After every performance, I huddle the team to recognize members who displayed showmanship and passion by asking them to lead our “Silent Sam” chant. When Logan and Dougie take the lead, their proud smiles mirror my own, reflecting growth not just as drummers but also in their confidence and sense of belonging in the band. I hope my efforts at inclusion can help to prevent feelings of isolation that drive school shootings like the one my classmates and I survived.

The boom of the bass drum. The crash of the cymbals. These sounds aren’t a cacophony of random percussive noises, but rather a symphony of connectivity and emotion that feels just like home. Through every beat and note I play, I endeavor to continue to inspire and promote empathy and acceptance; in myself, in my audience, and in my community.

Quiet. I always found comfort in quiet. While other children shrieked around the playground, I enjoyed solitary play with my dolls and having calm pretend tea parties with my parents.

November 6th, 2008. My little brother Max was born and the peaceful solitude of my only-child days was shattered. While I enjoyed quietly brushing my doll's hair for hours, Max would scream in frustration after only one or two puzzle attempts. Though I was assured crying toddlers were normal, I suspected that Max was different. Every tantrum seemed more intense, each day filled with more and more tears.

Being in public with Max was especially hard. At the grocery store, other shoppers turned their carts, while we shopped for milk and bread with a screaming child. Walking down the street, other families avoided eye contact so they didn’t have to encounter Max. Each venture outside filled me with both apprehension and shame.

I felt responsible for protecting him, shielding him from the judgmental glares of others, and helping him find the ability to better express himself. When we learned the correct terminology - a “mood disorder” - I spent hours each day filling my sticky toddler iPad with my rudimentary Google research. I learned that the main cause of Max’s tantrums was his inability to express his feelings. So, I taught Max how to manage his frustration by talking to me before he started crying. How to express his desires healthily by breathing and using his words. As the years passed I got better at helping him even as I amassed more and more knowledge through independent research, using a wide assortment of tips curated from Wikihow, NYU articles, and even parenting blogs on how to help children with mood disorders. Along the way, I learned how to adjust to having a sibling who had mental health issues, and having my quiet life turned into a circus.

As I learned to read Max’s cues, I started to notice the Maxes in my class - kids who sat alone at lunch, struggled with their schoolwork, or went simply unnoticed. I began sharing my lunch with Theo, who had autism, tutoring Chloe through Science, and teaching Michele how to dance. Every day, I made it my intention to share my friendship with everyone, leaving everyone feeling included, and if nothing else, they had at least one friend.

Though Max started to grow out of his tantrums, he faced other challenges. He was never invited to birthday parties or play dates, mentioned other friends at school, and often came home without a smile. It hurt me to see him so alone, without any close friends, because he couldn’t pick up social cues or solve 2+2 as quickly as his classmates. I saw the detrimental effects it had on him. I knew what it was like to be isolated or bullied, so watching it happen to him was hard.

Soon, I started an anti-bullying Instagram page, speaking about my and Max’s experiences with bullying. I talked about bullying and noninclusive environments and how they affect people’s mental health. I collaborated with many small businesses to advocate for the cause. As my account gained traction, Max also found his confidence and started to make friends with other kids just as special as him. After each school release, he ran home with a smile, eager to tell me about his adventures with Lorenzo and Nico.

By helping Max grow, I grew too. I learned the importance of having a good support system, the value of inclusivity, and every person’s capacity for empathy. Today, I look forward to each grocery store visit with Max. Instead of tantrums, we share conversations about what we are feeling. Judgmental sneers are replaced with smiles and waves. I’ll always treasure my only child days. But through Max, I found not just the joy of a sibling but the power of kindness.

My heart raced as the rhythmic clapping of my classmates pulsed through me—terrifying yet exhilarating. Chosen to perform in the front row alongside the admired sophomore Aybüke, the spotlight felt blinding, igniting a swirl of anxiety. What if I stumbled? Panic threatened to pull me under as I faced a sea of eager faces. But as our dance song echoed in the auditorium, a shift occurred. This was my high school debut, and the stakes felt astronomically high. Then I caught Aybüke’s confident smile, her words ringing in my ears: “It’s not about perfection—just believe in yourself.” With that, I let go of the pressure and danced. 
Little did I know, this first step into the spotlight would lead me to another stage as a leader rather than just a performer. 
Two years later, I found myself in the spotlight as the host of a debate tournament—an unexpected twist for someone who once feared the stage. It felt daunting, especially after years as my class's lead speaker, grappling with intense pressure. Hosting wasn’t just about logistics; it involved coordinating teams and ensuring everything ran smoothly. Initially, I felt overwhelmed trying to follow the rules from my first hosting experience, and chaos ensued. I soon realized the rigid structure stifled the event's energy, so I mustered the courage to suggest changes to my teacher—and he approved! 
With newfound freedom, I transformed the atmosphere. I added music, encouraged freshmen to dance, and created a fun environment to ease pre-debate stress. My mission was to turn debate from a source of fear into something enjoyable, and when students call me “abla,” meaning “older sister” in Turkish, it reinforces my belief in what I’m doing. 
Then came the big moment—a lead speaker didn’t show up. Cue panic! Rushing backstage, I found her trembling. I gave her my best “older sister” talk: “I know this feels terrifying, but trust me, you’ve got this.” Meanwhile, my inner thoughts were less graceful: Please just step in and speak. Please, please, please. Luckily, she did! And as she walked on stage, I realized hosting wasn’t just about running the show—it was about helping others find their confidence, just as I once needed. 
Fast forward to my junior year, and I found myself facing a new kind of challenge: organizing a Scrabble event—the first-ever led by a student at my school! We were excited, feeling like we were creating something special, but as the event drew closer, things took a turn. My teacher threatened to cancel it, and the pressure I had been putting on myself skyrocketed. 
Me to myself: “Wait, I’m trying to create something meaningful here! These younger students need this chance to shine.” But despite my efforts to stay calm, the stress started to weigh on me. Juggling my health, grades, and the looming possibility of the event being called off, I could feel it all taking a toll. 
In those moments, I remembered my first dance performance—how I had transformed fear into energy. I realized I needed to do the same here, stepping up as a leader, not just for myself but for the others who believed in me. Determined to make this event a reality, I embraced the chaos and powered through, even when my health began to suffer. 
Now, as I prepare to waltz onto the college stage, I see a canvas splashed with curiosity and creativity, ready for every voice to shine. My journey has taught me that leadership isn’t about being perfect or stealing the spotlight—it’s about building a platform where everyone can share their story. Inspired by my past, I hope to foster collaboration in college, creating a vibrant playground of ideas where dreams are nurtured and celebrated. And of course, I’m looking forward to dancing through it all with my peers, even if I occasionally step on some toes—metaphorically speaking (probably).

I grew up in a house, on a hill. Down that hill, I’d ride—my hair streaming and unbound—feeling reckless, uninhibited freedom that only comes from knowing your empty cul-de-sac by heart. I biked too fast to ever worry about encountering neighbors; I’d simply smile cheekily and ride on.

One afternoon, I’m barreling down with standard careless abandon when a flash of white hair—my elderly neighbor’s—momentarily blinds me. Since we last spoke five years ago, I almost forgot she lived next door.

The shock sharpens quickly into fear: I’m 15-feet-away from committing vehicular manslaughter…before even turning 16. A miraculous, last-minute swerve and clumsy apology later (what do you say after nearly killing your elderly, recluse neighbor?), I’m dethroned from my chariot and waiting for penance.

Instead, silence between us sits heavy and uncomfortable. Accustomed to breezing through life on shallow relationships, I’m oddly expecting something deeper from this interaction, though I’m not sure what. Perhaps this called for venturing beyond the surface of lives around me.

“Careful, your bike might get stolen leaving it there.” My neighbor’s sudden warning slices through the silence, her voice tinged with bitterness that feels foreign for our small, uneventful cul-de-sac. I nod silently, wait just long enough for her head to become a distant white pinprick, then surreptitiously abandon my bike to the roadside anyway. In typical teenage fashion, I don’t listen.

Two weeks after, I’m panting laboriously uphill and wiping futilely at sweat-stung eyes when I spot my neighbor at her mailbox. Stinging sight or not, the red stain of foreclosure notices is hard to ignore.

Spurred by some strain of curious guilt, I find myself pulled into conversation. She speaks of her husband, taken by Covid, and her son, who stopped calling. She speaks of nights spent in solitude; the looming threat of eviction; the unforgiving nature of time.

My heart aches with newfound understanding, bitterness that once seemed so alien sliding down my throat thick as tears. I nod silently. Except this time, I’m listening.

Days later, my fist hovers at her door. Mama sent me to leave a note about unruly crabgrass, but as I stand there, my hand trembles. Asking that—or anything—of her wouldn’t be fair. Instead…“Can I help?”

I only regret not helping more. When the crabgrass I painstakingly pulled grew gangly again, I almost didn't notice my neighbor moved away. Still, her absence lingered because her presence--raw and short-lived as it was--had differed. How often had I ridden past her house, observing overgrown weeds—thinking of the lonely, resilient woman living inside? I was hardly a perfect neighbor, but want more time to try. Perhaps I’d deliver coughdrops to her mailbox, as crabgrass released pollen through fall. Or I’d invite her on evening strolls. Above all, I’d slow down and listen.

Speeding through life on surface-level interactions kept me from seeing the complexity of those around me. Moreover, taking relationships for granted often misconstrued the value of genuine human connection. Life isn't defined by transactions and posturing small-talk, but by listening and understanding—reaching out and building bridges. Though establishing richer connections requires time, proactivity, and occasionally-almost-running-over-your-neighbor, I’ve discovered these investments make relationships truly fulfilling.

Beyond my neighborhood, this means holding extra meetings—impromptu 1AM "therapy" sessions—to support a WiSTEM Leadership member recovering from grief. It’s joining organizations like Project Green Schools where mutual interest initially bonds, yet further interactions foster profoundly more diversity. It’s inviting inspirations as discussions-to-be-had, not just LinkedIn-connections-to-be-made. It’s dedicating an environmental career to serving my contemporaries in anticipating the needs of generations I may never meet.

Finally, it’s initiating beautiful, messy, complex conversations—learning from anyone, anywhere. Math teachers make excellent philosophical discussion partners; 5th-graders dispense the sagest relationship advice. The neighbor I've met the least taught me the most poignant lessons about life.

No matter where the future takes me or how fast I’m thundering down a hill, I’ll always slow down to say hello.

Not many teenagers know how to cook funnel cakes and deep-fried Oreos, but I do. My father taught me.

Unexpectedly, my father was let go from his job, burdening my family financially.

For nine years, my father would leave his family for 52 nights to sell funnel cakes and deep-fried Oreos in Bristol, Tennessee. My father would often lose forty pounds while working at the light show, not because he was dieting but because he saved every dollar possible for his family rather than spending money on food for himself.

One year, I was able to help my father for the entire 52 nights. My school was virtual due to the early stages of COVID-19, so I took the opportunity to be with my father. I helped tie down all of our appliances in the food trailer and packed my suitcase full of clothes.

My father fistbumps me in tradition as we set our five-hour journey toward Bristol, Tennessee. "Son, it's just the boys!"

As we approached Bristol Motor Speedway, my body was filled with excitement. We unloaded the trailer, wired our electricity, and finished setting up our appliances. After a few hours of work, our next journey was moving into our apartment across the street. Once inside, I unpacked my clothes in my new room and came out to chicken wings on the counter. My Dad and I talked about how much fun this year would be, and then we went to bed.

The following morning, I woke up with no breakfast on the table. My mother usually cooks for everyone, so this was not a pleasant surprise. Instead, my father rushed us out the door to buy product for opening night. "Is this how it's always going to be?" I thought as my empty stomach rumbled.

As the sun went down, my nerves kicked in. It was the opening night of the light show, and I didn't know what to expect. My first customer approached the window, and I took their order. "Can I order deep-fried Oreos and a funnel cake?" It was my first time deep frying anything. Despite my anxiety, I plopped the Oreos in the batter and carefully placed them into the hot fryer. Positioning the Oreos together, I poured the funnel cake batter next to the Oreos, and after five minutes, I took them both out. "Perfect!" my Dad said after watching me hand the customer their food.

As the show went on, our days got longer. We worked 8-9 hours on weekdays, and on weekends, we worked 11-12 hours. If we were not selling food, we were buying ingredients, getting money from the bank, or counting yesterday's sales to compare them to last year's numbers.

As my body ached and my feeling of being homesick grew, all I wanted was to be home with my family and sleep in my bed.

On the 28th night of the light show, I was given the opportunity to go home and be done. Instantly, I was on board to leave, but the thought of leaving my father alone for 24 nights made me decline the offer.

As three weeks passed, my father and I had to disassemble our trailer and pack up for good. Fulfilled with accomplishment, I realized after seven weeks of grease and getting covered in funnel cake batter, my father and I were finally coming home together.

As we got in the truck, ready for our five-hour drive home, my father grabbed my shirt and hugged me. "I'm so proud of you, son," he said. "For 52 nights, you woke up in the morning, put in the hours, and never once complained. I love you."

Smiling, I glanced out the window as my throat tightened. Riding home, I realized that what I had done for the last seven weeks, my father had done for the previous nine years, and I am filled with a sense of unwavering appreciation.

Deep Blue Sea. Three words, one movie, and a fear that changed the way I looked at something as simple as a shower. Sitting in our cozy lounge, the five of us gathered around the screen as Deep Blue Sea aired on the television. My family and I, blissfully unaware, watched the movie with excitement. I didn’t feel scared at all while we watched the movie. It wasn’t until later, when I went to take a shower, that I froze, unable to turn on the showerhead, as the fear suddenly hit me.

In my young imagination, the showerhead became a doorway from the deep, through which these enormous sharks would emerge, their big bodies somehow fitting through the small nozzles to consume me whole. I couldn’t handle it; I had to take control. Over the next few weeks, I became obsessed with avoiding the showerhead, making a system out of buckets and tap water to wash myself. It was my way of holding the fear at bay, a method of ensuring that no whale could surprise me not when I had carefully limited the water’s source. This became a ritual, a daily exercise in making the unknown just a little more manageable.

That shark phobia subsided as I got older, but this innate desire to be in control of my environment and to prevent surprises persisted. It didn’t manifest in buckets of water anymore, but in other ways, like reviewing the syllabus repeatedly to ensure I’m not caught off guard by unexpected assignments, and asking for clarification on what’s expected in group projects. At school, I am always seen double-checking project deadlines and constantly refreshing the online grade portal to avoid any surprises.

Not everyone understands. I’ve been told by my friends and my siblings that my habits of over-planning and needing to know everything in advance are crazy and ruin the joy in surprises. And when I recount my childhood fear of sharks, the one that kept me from using the showerhead, it always leads to laughter, as if I’d told some elaborate joke.

At first, I wondered if this habit was rooted in that same childhood fear of sharks. Maybe it wasn’t the creatures themselves that scared me, but the unpredictability.

However, I realized that while my need to control situations helped me stay organized and prepared, it was starting to hold me back from enjoying experiences fully. I would get anxious when things didn’t go exactly as I’d planned.

I’ve always tended to over-plan, especially with group projects, believing that being in control would ensure success and reduce surprises. However, as school grew more demanding, this need to oversee every detail became overwhelming for me and those around me. For instance, while organizing a school event, I took charge of everything from coordinating guests to managing medals and certificates. The stress piled up, leading me to send a rare message in the group chat: “I need help.” That was my wake-up call. I decided to step back and try a new approach. I gathered the team, assigned specific tasks, and made a point to check in less often. Although it was challenging at first, I gradually learned to let go and trust that everyone would handle their responsibilities. My parents also noticed the change, commenting that I seemed less tense and more balanced in how I approached my responsibilities.

As I gear up for college, I have come to realize something freeing: life is full of inevitable twists and that’s alright. Throughout my academic life, I’ve often encountered the saying "the business environment is dynamic." As I prepare to major in this field, I've come to understand that I need to embrace this reality by letting go of my desire to control surprises and instead learn to adapt to whatever comes my way. Lastly, some mindful techniques won’t hurt either.

When asked to write an essay that reflects me as a person, I’ve had much difficulty in determining who that person really is. In my seventeen years of life there have been many different versions of me to walk this Earth. The question is just which me is the most me? Is Emily Cassidy the real me or is it [Name] Cassidy. Is it the lesser known nicknames Ry, Ryzeec, or Rhino? All of these names and nicknames make up who I am. They represent the multiple different versions of myself that have appeared at some point in my life and still appear daily.

Emily Cassidy is my given birth name, but my parents had every intention of my going by the name [Name]. My sister and I are the second generation of this tradition that started with my father and uncle who also go by their middle names. Nonetheless, there have been countless times I have been called Emily and accepted it. Emily Cassidy is the version of me that is met in formal situations or in passing. Emily represents the version of me that is very reserved and shy, mostly out of fear. It has been quite a while since I have let someone refer to me as Emily without correcting them and I think that that shows how I have matured into a more secure person.

[Name] is my real and true name. It is the name that comes to mind when most people think of me, and the name I identify myself with most. [Name] is me: a person who is sensitive, caring, bold and friendly. She knows how to stand up for herself and she loves to interact with everyone she can. She loves to do volunteer work because her strongest passion is to help those around her. In my own eyes I am [Name], but if you ask the people closest to me they would tell you about the various nicknames I go by.

The fact that I am able to say I have even one nickname shows me that the people around me truly know me and choose to have a deep connection with me. Ry is a name I get called by frequently. It is more of a casual and broad nickname that many people use, and I think of Ry as the tenderhearted person I am at my core. Ryzeec is the more fun version of me that loves to hang out with her friends, and shows her great sense of humor. She listens to unique music and expresses herself any way she can. Rhino is the little girl that is still inside of me. Whenever I am called this it makes me think of the summertime being by the pool with my Grandpa, a time I reminisce on frequently. I have loved the water as long as I can remember and so does “Rhino” who still lives in me. Each of these nicknames means so very much to me. They signify that I have formed deep connections with those around me and I am immensely proud of myself for that. As a person who deals with a lot of self doubt it is so heartwarming to know that people love me enough to get close to me. These relationships are invaluable to me because they have truly shaped me into the person I am today. I am proud to say that I have been able to form these deep connections.

While [Name] is the name I go by most frequently, Emily [Name] Cassidy along with her nicknames is the true me. Every person I've been now plays a part in the girl who is writing this essay today. Emily [Name] Cassidy is a person who is tender but also strong, loving and caring, and a girl who I have grown to be very fond of.

**The knock wasn’t my mother’s gentle tap.**

I squinted, trying to make out the silhouettes through the small window. 
“Oh, come on, [Name], just open it!” my brother shouted impatiently from the other side.

This wasn’t my first or last time hesitating in the face of fear. As a child, fear came from countless unsettling videos about skinwalkers—human, but not quite—haunting me for months. Their knocks reminded me of my powerlessness. To cope, I memorized the way my family knocked, taking comfort in familiarity.

For me, fear was never the dark itself, but what lies within.

The unknown in fiction always intrigued me. Facing something unfamiliar, I felt as helpless as a character in a Junji Ito horror manga—always expecting the worst, ignorant of escape. Yet, their bravery in navigating the dreadful unknown was a trait I wished for.

Fear costs opportunities, and after losing many, I dove headfirst into my biggest one—public speaking—knowing I had to face it directly.

“Bilal won’t make it in time!” Maryam, the book club leader, said nervously, pacing back and forth. 
We were at the Baghdad International Book Fair, set to give a presentation in just two hours. With no preparation and no time to spare, I stepped in. Panic gripped me as I sifted through notes about Albert Camus’ The Stranger, my palms slick with sweat. Public speaking had never been my strength, and here I was, about to face an international audience.

As the crowd's hum dimmed, I stepped onto the stage. After a few encouraging glances from my co-presenter, my thoughts crystallized into a cohesive presentation, quickly becoming a crowd favorite. It wasn’t perfect, but a start nonetheless.

That day, I realized fear could be rationalized—not just for myself, but for others. It was the start of a journey to guide others, as I guided myself.

As a facilitator at Speak with Rawan, an online English-teaching nonprofit, I saw that same fear in my students’ eyes. Many fumbled with their words, anxious that their English wasn’t enough. Week by week, we worked together. They improved—and so did I.

Ahmed, in particular, stood out. His rare participation to the rest. Reaching out to him privately, I discovered that his social anxiety had kept him from engaging. From then on, he began attending class early, and together we worked on pronunciation and vocabulary until conversation flowed naturally. Over time, Ahmed became one of the most active participants in class. The strategy we developed—preparing ahead, practicing in private—was something I later adopted for my own obstacles.

Last year, I organized our first school charity bazaar, leading students from all grades. The confidence I gained from public speaking helped me see how uniquely different, yet surprisingly similar, we all are when given time and attention.

At the event, I launched my jewelry business. With just $100 for materials, I left nothing to chance. My fingers were stiff and calloused, crusted with the dried remnants of glue that clung stubbornly to my skin, as if refusing to let go of the work I’d poured into every pre-order I made before the event and every pink flyer I hung. By the event day, even after discounting leftover stock, I walked away with an $800 profit—all thanks to my bestseller: the beaded strawberry necklace. The profit enabled me to reinvest in my business with an Epson printer and fill the gap in our donations for a local orphanage.

Over-preparation became my weapon, planning for failure my blueprint for success. 
As I transition to the next chapter of my life, I’m excited to help others reach their true potential, like Ahmed, or encourage them to surpass their fears, as my friends did for me. Life’s uncertainties are like the skinwalkers I once feared—at first, they are mysterious and daunting—but with understanding, they turn into chances to explore and grow.

The Courage to pursue my dreams against all odds. I have always wanted to be a nurse since before I could remember everyone in my family are in the medical field so I feel like that was a big part of my choice. The start of my career was freshman year of high school I wanted to apply to a nursing program, but I was not eligible due to the grade I was in I felt that was a setback but it was actually a booster for me. I took all the Health science classes my school could provide and any other classes that would help me in my future. I also volunteered at the nursing home where my aunt works helping out with activities and participated in the walk for Alzheimer’s. My tenth grade year it was time to apply for the nursing program I've been waiting for and on June 8th, 2023 I received my acceptance letter with the verse Matthew 19:26: “With God all things are possible” I was so excited. The first day of my nursing course I was so scared even though this is what I’ve been waiting for out of my whole class I was the youngest so I knew I had to give it my all I study hard and worked my best the whole semester then came time to test for state board. Through extensive research, I discovered that the College of LSA embodies the ideal environment for cultivating my knowledge, fostering my passions, and contributing meaningfully to the community I call home. I am eager for the opportunity to immerse myself in this dynamic community, where I can expand my knowledge and make a lasting impact on those around me.

Academically, I am specifically drawn to the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology, which offers an exceptional environment for students to explore the fascinating complexities found in living organisms. With the University hosting over six hundred operational laboratories, I eagerly anticipate actively applying my knowledge as I progress further through my education. I also particularly appreciate the inclusion of collaborative field research and independent study as a part of the curriculum. Participating in both of these activities throughout my education will assist me in excelling academically and lead me to develop my critical thinking skills further.

Another appealing aspect of the University is its dedication to fostering innovative research. As a prospective student, I am excited for the opportunity to engage in passionate research projects that involve my field of study. Innovative research, such as the MGI, proved to be not only fascinating but wildly compelling. As my undergraduate education concludes and I pursue graduate-level education, I aspire to contribute to similar research.

As a queer student who grew up in a rural village, I also anticipate engaging with my peers and participating in various campus organizations. In having previous experience volunteering for the Michigan Democratic Party, the UMICH Votes Coalition is an effort I would love to take part in. Opportunities like this would allow me to learn from others, contribute to meaningful discussions, and enrich my life with many lifelong connections. Community initiatives such as The Detroit Partnership offer me additional opportunities to support the surrounding community on a consistent basis. These organizations support my belief that everyone is vital in fostering communities based on mutual respect, collaboration, and foundational trust.

In summary, the College of LSA offers academic breadth that will fully support my academic ambitions and is home to a beautifully diverse community that I would be honored to be part of. I envision myself thriving in an environment that nurtures innovative thinkers and genuinely empowers students to become catalysts for change.

As a child, my youth consisted of traveling to Mexico with my dad to see my maternal grandmother, to visit her in her home in El Bajío, a region in the center of Mexico, characterized by dryness, and mountain ranges. As we would get off the plane, I would feel the dry air enter my lungs and smells of clay fill my nose. The ride to my house was long, the terrain was filled with cacti and cattlemen. I would pass old buses with ladies carrying bags and old men sitting with canes. In the distant mountains behind our home, we'd see small towns poking out of harsh terrain and fields of Pirul trees. During our trip, my dad would take me to a church in the middle of the Bajío, San Martin de Terreros. On the way to the sanctuary, there were many small towns, surrounded by nothing. I would stare into the distance and wonder how many people lived in those villages. 100? 200? 300?

Pueblos without names, groups of people who knew nothing else except their lives in the desert. How did people get food, what jobs did they work, I had so many questions. As time went on, I was older and learned more about my parents' home, how poverty affected them, and what being a third-world country meant.

My parents would share, they had never gone to a hospital as children. I wondered how many had died because they didn’t have access to medicine when they needed it. I knew my paternal grandmother, who I had never met, died of cancer. They didn’t know why she was so weak and frail, and when she found out. It was too late. Even if she knew, she wouldn’t have had money to afford those treatments. I ponder about how many other people suffered like my grandmother with an illness she never knew she had, due to poverty. The people, in small towns, without official names, lived far away from major cities.

In researching what people suffered in rural areas, food scarcity was a major issue. An important term in that field is food deserts. I wondered if there was a medical equivalent of a food desert, an area that didn’t have sufficient or quality healthcare. These small pueblos suffered through medical ‘food deserts’, there were no hospitals nearby and healthcare was not available to them.

As I went back to Mexico every year, the cycle repeated itself. I would wonder the same exact question. How many people died in those towns due to lack of healthcare, how many unmarked graves were in the desert that had a story that wouldn’t be shared with the world due to medical needs that were never met?

In those deep thoughts, as I listened to Banda music my dad played, or my mom, who had gotten her permanent residency a few years prior, chew on her coconut slivers. I wondered how I could do something about a systemic problem in Mexico. I wasn’t sure at the time, but it inspired me to work towards a change. I wanted to help those children in the villages who did not get to see a pediatrician regularly as I did back home. I wanted to help those mothers who suffered from medical problems, or had no guidance when it came to children. I wanted to help fathers who worked tirelessly through their pain. I wanted to help those elders, who had arthritis or slowly lost their teeth.

At that moment, I wanted to dedicate my life to helping others. I thought of the people in the villages in the Bajío Desert. They deserved someone in their lives willing to help them, and I’d try to dedicate mine to help those who I could. Maybe, one day, I could go as far to help the people in the pueblos.

When people bring up physics, most will think about gravity or momentum. However, I think of Gaussian surfaces—any closed surface used to measure how field lines are entering or leaving a certain region. And when I say “any surface,” I do mean “any surface.” Whether physically practical like a cylinder around a current-carrying wire or something more abstract like a sphere around an ice cream scoop, there’s a Gaussian surface to be found. While these surfaces may seem like an abstract concept limited to the physics lab, they have taught me lessons that span far beyond the classroom.

Just as there’s freedom in selecting a Gaussian surface, I find a lot of value in the freedom of being able to investigate whatever piques my curiosity. My countless hours delving down the notorious “Wikipedia rabbithole” has led to genuine academic growth — by uncovering an article about the Japanese Yamauchi clan, I was able to investigate the relationship between the Japanese feudal system and the nation’s industrial revolution, giving me a great topic to write a history paper about. Meanwhile, my long-standing love for FC Barcelona has led me to a 253-day Catalan streak (and counting) on Duolingo. Like Gaussian surfaces, the freedom to explore my curiosity is a core part of who I am, allowing me to embrace the unpredicted and trust my curiosity to guide me to gain new and valuable experiences.

However, the freedom inherent in choosing a Gaussian surface can be misleading at times. Applying a Gaussian surface requires using a surface integral with a vector dot product—which, in English, means things can get messy if the wrong Gaussian surfaces are chosen. This applies to life as well, where calculated choices are crucial. When I founded a student-ran string quartet with my friends, I initially was inspired by my love for freedom, advocating for a looser and more flexible organization structure. This caused a couple performance mishaps (jumbled programs, lost music, you name it…), so recognizing, my friends and I created strict rehearsal schedules and repertoire.

Moments like these teach me to value trade-offs between freedom and meticulous decision-making. As the president of my school’s Academic Team, I made sure to apply this philosophy, spending hours making careful decisions such as drafting balanced team rosters and picking diverse trivia topics to drill the team on each week so that they can excel in tournaments. Through my efforts, the team has elevated to consistent top 3 finishes. Thus, although freedom is essential to my life, I take pride in my simultaneous ability to employ order in all that I do.

Did you know that no matter how much two Gaussian surfaces differ in shape, the laws of physics guarantee that they will share unexpected key properties as long as they contain the same charge? Along a similar vein, I derive joy from finding the metaphorical charge that links different things together. For example, the “charge” that is love for music has connected me to new communities through violin performances at senior centers or art festivals. Whether it’s being able to dazzle them with the technicality of Mozart or hear them sing along to Taylor Swift instrumentals, the smiles and compliments from the audience are as gratifying as solving the hardest physics problem. That’s why, when an audience member yells “one more song!”, I’m always eager to concur and continue sharing the gift of music. It’s my belief that by devoting myself to my passions, I can bring together diverse groups of people and ideas.

Gaussian surfaces are known for their extraordinary versatility, being used to solve many types of problems in electromagnetism. However, the values they comport are just as universal. Looking ahead to my future, I hope to apply these lessons by trusting my creativity to guide me through [some specific class], fostering order by demonstrating confident leadership in [some specific club], and finding common threads between people [by volunteering for XYZ].

“Where does a cat go when it’s thirsty?”
Isla, one of my school’s first graders, asked me after I corrected misspelled words.
“Where?”
I squatted down to see her at eye-level.
“The cat-fe!”
She burst out laughing. I paused only a second before joining her, doing my best to force chuckling sounds out my teeth.

In the energetic first grade with 23 kids, Mrs. Hovancik often asks me to keep an eye on Isla, who was diagnosed with autism and ADHD. Throwing tantrums when her scissors went missing, interrupting teachers, and redoing work repeatedly in her chubby handwriting, Isla was a challenging student, but it was difficult to divorce my sense of stability and self-worth from her moods. One day, after she pushed my hand away shouting that she didn’t need help, the whole class witnessed me bolted from the room barely holding back tears of hurt. Cheap sympathy and fake laughter couldn’t go any further for my loving, patient teacher’s aide profile. I had to work harder.

I began looking past words, carefully observing Isla’s mood, reactions, and context of those jokes, while recording data like a researcher. As observations and reading inspired each other, I began reading books and articles like Autism: A New Introduction to Psychological Theory and Current Debate. From these materials, I learned about the inner experiences of autistic individuals and how their special perceptions impact how they interact with the world. I also decided on autism as my research focus in the Pioneer Research Program, which is an undergraduate-level academic research initiative for high school students. I learned about the nuances of autism from this curriculum, including the neurodiversity theory and useful techniques for enhancing communication. My knowledge connected with what I saw in Isla because her jokes, though playful, often represent her unique way of processing the world around her—sometimes using humor to ease confusion or express herself in ways that words alone cannot.

Although research and abstract theory was helpful, observation took me further than anything else. The more I observed Isla, the more I realized that laughter was her invitation into the world. When Isla couldn’t follow directions or it got too noisy in the classroom, she would repetitively shake her head and yell loudly due to overstimulation, which I mistook as defiance. After she calmed down, a joke would be told to me as compensation. Whenever others weren’t paying attention to her, like whenever I compliment another kid, she would tell me a joke and ask whether or not it was good. Also, she had trouble finding partners to work with due to her impatience. Wanting a partner, she would pull a classmate aside to convince them with her jokes.

Through my observation, Isla began to understand me too. When I asked, “Why do you only tell me jokes?” She was quick to answer. “You hear them.” And, with time, our relationship became one of trust, rather than one of duty or obligation.

As I enter college and Isla enters middle school and high school, we both have a lot to learn. But, because of her, my relationship to laughter, whether my own or others’, has changed for the better. Each time a classmate in college laughs while we are in the neurodiversity advocacy club or laughs at a punny joke related to special education major, I will think of Isla and the many ways that a person can relate to laughter. And while I hope to be forcing far fewer laughs in college, I will never forget the power of empathy and the immense joy that was behind so many moments with Isla, even if her joke was not funny whatsoever.

A massive structure loomed overhead, seemingly defying the laws of gravity. Constructed of glass and steel resembling a ship’s hull, it left me staring in awe, as questions flooded my mind: How is this design possible? How far does the overhang extend? What does it look like inside? I was attending my first game at the new U.S. Bank Stadium, home of the Minnesota Vikings.

Entering the stadium, we headed up the escalators where I could see the angled glass facade opening to the Minneapolis skyline framed by large engineered trusses. Between downs, my eyes studied the impressive design. The game ended with a Vikings win, but my fascination with stadiums had just begun. This motivated me to research other football, baseball, and soccer stadiums. I decided to challenge myself by modeling them on a smaller scale.

I saved up for months until I could buy a diode laser cutter. The day it arrived, I set it up in the garage, lined up a balsa wood sheet, put on my mask and protective glasses, and pressed ‘start.’ It took many tries, countless hours, and numerous late nights hearing, “[Name], you should get to bed soon,” not realizing it was already past midnight. Eventually, my first stadium was complete and was given to my sister, Evelyn, as a graduation gift. As her friends admired the gift, they eagerly asked for their own replicas. Realizing there was a broader interest, I knew this could become more than just a hobby. Thirty minutes later, Custom3DesignShop was carved into existence on Etsy.

Just days later, the 'cha-ching' of my first sale echoed my excitement. People valued my craftsmanship. However, as Minnesota's crisp fall wind blew in, finding a way to move my business indoors became necessary, especially if I wanted to capitalize on the holiday season. My current machine did not have ventilation making an upgrade necessary. This also would improve my quality and efficiency. To maximize profits, I developed an Excel spreadsheet to track expenses and set season-based prices. After two months, I accumulated enough surplus profit to invest in an enclosed CO2 laser cutter— the Glowforge Plus.

After honing my design and manufacturing skills, an opportunity presented itself allowing me to refine my interpersonal communication skills. A Culver’s franchise owner and marketing group inquired about replicating the first Culver’s restaurant. During our Zoom call, I had to ensure I understood their vision of modeling the building at an eye-level view layered with wood to create a three-dimensional piece—a technique I had never tackled before. Using active listening with clarifying follow-up questions, I was chosen for this commissioned project. Knowing this piece was a gift for a founding member of Culver’s, I had to deliver. After several AutoCAD drafts, and numerous email exchanges, their enthusiasm for the final product made all the effort worthwhile.

Upgrading the laser cutter was essential for advancing my business, just as a strong engineering program is crucial for my academic growth. Managing my business has taught me that refining designs, improving efficiency, and developing new skills are vital steps, revealing that success comes from hard work and continuous improvement. Likewise, my self-improvement through professional communication and customer satisfaction has prepared me for my collegiate journey and beyond.

Reflecting on my original fascination with the U.S. Bank Stadium, I am committed to bringing the same curiosity and creativity to campus. This mindset will drive me to contribute to university initiatives like robotics competitions, woodworking clubs, and supporting sports teams with the same enthusiasm I bring to engineering.

I anticipate rigorous academics, challenging projects, and diverse viewpoints. However, the problem-solving skills, advanced techniques, and business acumen I’ve gained are invaluable as I embrace these opportunities to fuel my passion for engineering. Looking ahead, I aspire to ignite the same awe and inspiration in others that U.S. Bank Stadium sparked within me.

It was eight in the morning, and my grandfather, dressed in his cotton dhoti, closed his eyes, hands folded, offering his daily prayers to the rising sun. I stood by the door, watching him with a mix of curiosity and admiration as he prepared his medical bag, ready to leave for a rural eye camp. As a retired ophthalmologist, he was no stranger to these camps. Little did I know that today, I would gain a new vision.

As we drove through the narrow paths surrounded by expansive fields of grains, my scenery transitioned from the grays of high-tower buildings and chaotic traffic to the vibrant green fields and pastel-brown houses with tiled roofs. As we approached the camp in the small open building, women covered their heads with sarees from the scorching sun, and men in dhotis dabbed their faces with handkerchiefs, patiently awaiting my grandfather’s arrival. As the rickshaw stopped, the crowd quieted, their hands folded in reverence, their eyes bright with hope.

Looking at the poster outside the building, more villagers entered, many of whom had never gotten their eyes checked due to financial constraints. Inside the makeshift clinic, I watched in awe as my grandfather moved from one patient to the next, his hands steady but gentle. His voice was calm, explaining to each person how they could protect themselves from cataracts and other threats. It was after the treatment that the room came alive—their relieved smiles lit the room, and their gratitude weighed heavy in my chest. That feeling stayed with me, a quiet but powerful reminder of the difference one individual could make.

As the sun dipped below the horizon and the clouds greyed, my morning excitement faded on the way to Indian Classical singing class. As I entered the room, my teacher handed me the tanpura, a drone instrument. Each note of the Bilahari raga unfolded, its patterns familiar but never quite sinking in. The rhythm of the tala beat in the background was a steady pulse I tried to follow, but it was out of reach. The swaras pulled me in one direction, then another, like threads I could never quite weave together. So, I just plucked the strings of the tambura, my thoughts drifting back to the eye camp—the smiles, the hope, the purpose. Music felt more like a routine than a passion, a discipline I hadn’t fully embraced its value.

Two years later, everything changed. I could no longer witness my grandfather’s rituals or connect with the tempo of nature. I found myself in a suburban American town, where the vast highways of the U.S. replaced the Hyderabad streets. Everything felt foreign—the sense of a fast-paced life and the sound of English spoken all around me.

During this transition period, I started to bridge the differences between the two worlds by reflecting on that transformative day two years ago. The precision and empathy my grandfather showed the patients mirrored the support and encouragement I received in America. The education system pushed me to chase my dreams and values, teaching me rigor alongside compassion. Likewise, sangeetham, which once felt forceful, became a source of comfort. Singing the ragas now connects me to my roots and the rich musical heritage of South India.

Today, as I reflect on my journey from that eye camp to my life in America, I realize how clarity can take many forms. Just as my grandfather restored vision for his patients, my experiences have given me a clearer vision of who I am and who I want to be. The blurred lines between cultures and aspirations have come into focus, revealing a path uniquely my own. As I look to the future, I hope to bring the same focus and compassion I saw in him through healthcare—helping others find clarity in their lives, just as I’ve found in mine. That is the vision I want to bring to my community.

A voice calls my name. I stand up and slowly walk up to the microphone placed before hundreds of eyes from all over the state gazing at me. I wait for the next question. “Which country has less than five million people: Namibia, Singapore, or Indonesia?” the voice echoes. I think about it, take a deep breath and answer. However, I’m met with reality as the sound of the buzzer sinks my heart. I am eliminated from the State Round of the Geography Bee. After the competition, dismayed by my futile efforts, I begin reflecting on my journey of becoming the “Geography Guy”.

My journey began from my uncle’s gift: an iPad. While looking for apps to play on it, I found one about geography. Out of childish inquisitiveness, I began playing and was immediately reeled in like a fish. My unstoppable thirst to learn led to countless hours playing this game. By the tender age of six, I could recall all the world’s countries. Since then, I’ve been intrigued by maps of all kinds. Many view maps as plain two-dimensional objects for navigation. I see keys to diverse landscapes, cultures, histories, and landmarks of global communities. These lines and shapes fascinated me because of their practical impact and historical significance. My curiosity-driven research channeled my interest further. When I learned about the Geography Bee, I worked hard for months, determined to give it my all. After extensive preparation, I found myself advancing to the State Round. By then, my middle school friends referred to me as the “Geography Guy”.

On the drive home from the competition, I continued reminiscing about all these positive and fun experiences, gradually turning my dismay into a revitalized motivation. I realized that my love for geography wasn’t just remembering trivia and the subject of noteworthy competitions. It was about comprehending the world and understanding climate patterns, cultural and political barriers and ongoing political and environmental issues. I applied my knowledge and fascination beyond the scope of competitions. I helped my peers understand the material during classes out of sheer interest, and I launched a YouTube channel to dispense my knowledge in entertaining and creative ways, earning subscribers along the way. Behind every video was an eager boy pouring hours into brainstorming, filming, drawing, and editing.

While exploring these topics, with my laptop on my thighs, I was captivated by how technology provides access to a wealth of information, recognizing that it can assist with problems worldwide. I realized I can make impacts with these interests and skills. For example, when I interned at the City of Austin, I built a mobile app that helps the public find clean water sources in Austin to combat dehydration, a pressing issue. I challenged myself to analyze an enormous amount of geographical data from sources like OpenStreetMap and ArcGis, present the water sources in a user-friendly manner, and program in Swift for the first time. I decided to dive into tutorials and ask my teammates for help, self-teaching and learning over time. My dedication and resolve enabled me to become self-reliant within two weeks. I also helped my teammates get acquainted with code management tools and website development. Together, we established rapport and I gained experience and developed soft skills, like communication and problem-solving, along the way.

As I provide myself with further experience and knowledge, I shall strive to develop solutions, such as combatting effects and patterns of climate change and constructing algorithms to improve and sustain agricultural processes. I can proudly say that as I am about to enter college, I am as determined, if not more, to leverage modern technology and my love and enthusiasm for geography to learn more about our world and make a positive impact. If enjoyment, hard work, and determination brought me this far, I’m confident they’ll drive me to achieve more in the future.

After all, I am the Geography Guy.

**Code Red: I am under attack!** In the battlefield of my basement, I narrowly miss being hit before diving to take cover behind the sofa until the rain of stuffed animals and pillows ceases. I wait for the right moment, then unleash havoc. I pick up all the ammo on the floor, and like John Wick, I hurl stuffed animals at my friends with perfect accuracy.

Pillow fights are a middle school girls’ sleepover staple. Another staple: Truth or Dare.

“Let’s play Truth or Dare!” my friend exclaims. We gather around in a circle, ready to spill the juiciest secrets in our tent made from the fuzziest blankets. And the game begins.

“[Name], truth or dare?” my friend asks me.

“Truth!” I excitedly call out.

My friend pouts and whispers, “You’re no fun, you always pick Truth.”

I stop, wanting to retaliate, but she’s right. I've never chosen to take the dare. Honestly, I was afraid of the unknown. It made me feel uncertain, and I hated not fully understanding what was to come. The unknown is limitless, meaning endless possibilities of what I might be forced to do. All I saw was potential humiliation and defeat. Tongue-tied, I brushed off my friend’s words and tried not to dwell on them.

As I grew older, sleepovers became rare, nestled in childhood memories. When I was dropped off at RYLA during my junior year of high school, it was the first time in a while I was staying somewhere overnight—a sort of sleepover. RYLA, the Rotary Youth Leadership Awards, was a four-day overnight program where selected teenagers from New Jersey came together to become impactful community members and also build connections and leadership skills.

In a place where no one knew me, I had the chance for a rebirth. Destiny was in my hands, and if I could turn into anyone, I chose to be a risk-taker. But change required forcing myself to try new things. I started with small steps, like learning to double dutch with my friends for the first time, until I evolved to singing “Happy Birthday” in front of my RYLA peers in Korean. My cracking voice and off-tune singing revealed my flaws. But, instead of ridicule, I embraced my shortcomings. Each small risk led to more challenges, and I slowly became self-assured in my abilities. My confidence radiated, and I found peers turning to me for help and acknowledgment by the district governor of Rotary District 7475.

Many believe you cannot be reborn, but I beg to differ. Once I learned to indulge in the unknown, I felt like I started a new life. By taking risks, I unlocked doors to numerous opportunities. I no longer perceived the unknown as a threat; instead, it became a ground for growth and potential. This redefined my perspective on life, and I no longer hold myself back in fear of repercussions. I know I will continue to utilize risk-taking in making future decisions. Occasionally, I want to take the easy route, like deciding whether to take a challenging AP class over a free period. But then I think back to RYLA, reminding myself that avoiding risks never pays off as much as challenging myself with the unknown.

On the last night of RYLA, all the girls huddled together in the dorm's living room. We wanted to spend the last night together before pursuing our future dreams. It was hard to imagine we were nearly high school graduates. To celebrate our youth before adulthood, we played a simple round of Truth or Dare, just like when we were kids.

“[Name], truth or dare?”

“Dare.”

“Stan, is that really you, bro? You look like the kid from Up!”

Without even seeing their screens, I knew what my classmates were laughing at: old photos and videos of me at piano competitions. “Nice flick of the wrist, [Name]!” they ridiculed.

I’ve played piano since I was five, but after being teased in sixth grade, I decided to switch hobbies. I let piano slide to the wayside and picked up a basketball instead.

From running daily all-out miles on my treadmill to shooting free-throws in 105-degree weather for hours straight, I devoted myself to becoming the best player in the school.

Still, throughout middle school, my parents continued to sign me up for piano competitions, so after class, I dragged myself to the keyboard, dreading the hours of drilling. By high school, I stopped competing altogether.

Instead, I put my efforts towards playing music I genuinely enjoyed. No longer worrying about perfecting an uninteresting piece, I explored new styles of music on YouTube, where I dreamily stumbled across Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse. I found myself reinvigorated by the glimmery texture of the passages, and thanks to the atypical melodies, practice felt more natural again.

I recalled the months I spent religiously following Plyomorph’s jumping workouts to be able to dunk at five foot six. I applied the same consistency to hit every note in Chopin Ballade 1’s notoriously difficult coda. Whereas before I used to study Devin Booker’s midrange pull-up, I now studied YouTube concert performances by Seong Jin Cho, drawing inspiration from his ability to unearth hidden melodies in his music.

At the same time, I picked up a third hobby: cooking. From learning how to dice an “onyo” with Chef Jean Pierre to making my first grilled cheese and tomato soup, I must pay homage to my two great teachers: Max the Meat Guy and Joshua Weissman. Though I sometimes spilled some diced onions while tossing them in the pan, I found moments of peace and solitude replaying Debussy passages and my alley-oops to my teammate as I seasoned my proteins and minced my garlic.

Two months ago, I pulled up [Name] Du’s picture for the Great Composers Competition, undoubtedly one of the images which garnered mocking laughs from my classmates. I was struck by both how childish I looked and how childish the reactions were.

I closed my laptop, walked to the piano, and pulled up Debussy. Then, after a two-hour practice session, I signed up for the Ross Mckee Piano Competition, the first competition I ever chose for myself.

Driving home from practice, my teammate, Parth, opened up to me: “No one else knows this [Name], but my dad doesn’t want me to play basketball anymore.” The goofiest, most dedicated person I knew struggled with having passion for the sport. Shooting fewer threes after practice and lifting less, I saw him going down the same road that I had with piano.

As cheesy as it might have been, I gave him the words that I needed most in 6th grade: “Focus on what your goal is, and don’t worry about anything else.”

Whereas in middle school and my early years of high school, piano symbolized my confinement to teenager norms and an Asian stereotype, today the instrument is an embodiment of my ability to start new endeavors with ambition and infuse interdisciplinary thinking between the arts, sports, and even cooking. The black and white keys are tangible proof that I can be authentic to myself while also maintaining autonomy.

In college and beyond, I’ll embrace my uninhibited curiosity, knowing that I will pursue every facet of myself without feeling ashamed. I won’t have to pick and choose because I can study classical music while immersing myself just as much in engineering, both stemming from my passion for creativity. And of course, I can always take my mind off exams and work by playing pickup ball at the gym, playing L’isle Joyeuse (for my roommates this time!), and maybe even cooking a comforting grilled cheese and tomato soup from time to time. Just for me.

At the age of ten, I felt like my whole life was set up to resist.

In the sweltering heat of a Babylon summer, a small desert town two hours from the capital, I was having my daily battle of survival–a battle not just against the elements, but against forces that sought to uproot the very fabric of our community. A big ISIS bomb went off shattering the glass of my room, and even though this was the town’s fifth car explosion that week, this time it targeted my school. That night, laying in bed, the weight of fear and loss pressed down on me like the sweltering heat itself.

“Yalla [Name] – today you fight, understood?” My father mumbled to me as we walked to school. As I stepped through the main gate, a metallic smell engulfed my nostrils; my airways constricted, a typical asthma symptom. I kept going.

Soon after class started, blasts echoed in the distance. Instinctively, I sprung into action: comforting my peers, and ensuring everyone was in a safe place while teachers frantically called their families to check in on them. “It’s alright rifak, they can’t hurt us here,” I said with teary eyes and a pounding heart, but my father’s words always echoed in my mind: resist.

I disagree with my father on the way I should resist. While my father contributed to the military efforts by donating aid and weapons, I embodied combat resistance by joining the volunteer community in my town. When everyone saw the horrors of destruction and death, I saw a gift of the communal bond of the advent of opportunities to help.

To resist was to volunteer; I began to volunteer with a local team. We did not have a name, only passion, and enthusiasm for a better Babylon to help children from conflict-torn areas get educational opportunities through workshops and sessions on leadership, conflict resolution, and climate change. A child approached me and whispered, “You know they asked us what we want to become when we grow up. I want to be just like you. I want to help,” I shed a tear. People realized that instead of fighting, they could volunteer.

To resist was to survive; I started making the daily dangerous journey to Baghdad while working two jobs to support my family. I went there to learn, sharing thoughts and project ideas as we sat near a cozy campfire playing the guitar and singing “Babar Fil”, a song we all used to listen to as children while organizing events and activities to train the people of the community on essential skills such as peace-building, conflict resolution, and organizing skills. I also worked as a freelance graphics designer, making around $50 a month, just enough to get by.

To resist was to promote peace-building efforts; organizing the IQ Peace Festival, I witnessed more than 1000 Iraqis, disregarding their race, religion, or sect, together celebrating our diversity instead of using it as a war tool. Together, we fundraised money to promote peace and used the funds towards a national orphanage. I transferred this same experience to my small city by organizing the “Lamhat Taghyeer” festival, meaning “A Sight of Change,” with promotions from the Iraqi Al-Amal Association, a well-known national organization, and the Norwegian Embassy. Coming back from UWC in December 2022, committed to my cause more than ever, I organized another peace festival.

To resist in college will be to utilize education as a tool to develop and empower communities to navigate crises effectively and support them. I will bring not only my deep commitment to the community but also a determination to engage in dialogues, lead initiatives, promote peace, and collaborate with peers to address global challenges.

I will continue to build a safer community, resistant to ideologies of destruction and terror, and resilient like me, a “lion of Mesopotamia” from a small town in Babylon.

How to Build a Lightsaber

“Gullible is written on the ceiling!” I looked up. I couldn’t help it. Fourth-grade-me took everything at face value, and, unfortunately, there were plenty of kids at school keen to capitalize on my willingness to believe. The most frequent offender was Liam, a redhead who could tell a story so well that my family later coined a term for his absurd tales and statistics: “Liam facts.”

One day at recess, Liam and I were discussing The Empire Strikes Back, and, as mega-fans of the Star Wars franchise, we were eager to get our hands on some real lightsabers. Liam had the solution. He asserted that if you took a sheet of tinfoil, folded it into a saber, and buried it, when lightning hit the burial site, a lightsaber would form. Foolproof strategy, right? As soon as we went in for lunch, I got my hands on a tinfoil sandwich wrapper, and when the day was over, I raced home to begin my project. I remained optimistic for weeks after the burial, but to my dismay, no lightsaber materialized. I realized then that I can’t trust everything I’m told.

The seed of skepticism that this realization planted in my mind has grown over the years. The world, once defined in black and white, the dark side or the light side, has taken on more nuance. In the pursuit of finding an outlet for my newfound skepticism, I devoured newspapers and developed a love of narrative nonfiction, but I couldn’t settle on an activity that extended beyond myself.

Then I discovered Speech & Debate, a community of open-minded individuals who were happy to tell you when you were wrong. Fourth-grade-me would have been appalled. No plastic lightsaber battles? No Episode V reenactments? Public speaking?!?

Getting started was difficult. On top of my personal reticence, there was no school record of success or coach for my event, Congressional Debate. So, I watched hours of online debate rounds on YouTube, learning from the best. I went to every tournament that my parents would drive me to. I practiced speeches in front of my sister. Slowly, a skillset developed. Instead of pre-writing speeches ahead of tournaments, I learned to outline arguments and fill out my points as the debate progressed. This adaptive style worked, and my performance improved.

Beyond personal success, I was also able to build a base of institutional knowledge at my school that hadn’t existed when I started. I created PowerPoints, lecture videos, and prep templates, which explained how novices coming up after me could become good debaters. And whether it be 11pm prep calls the night before a tournament, or working with middle schoolers to identify the right mix of argumentation and rhetorical flourish, I get an unmatched thrill from being able to give back to an activity which has given me so much.

I wouldn’t have thought that the most gullible kid in fourth grade could make it far in an extracurricular built on skepticism, but it demonstrates the power, to paraphrase Yoda, of not just trying, but doing—of putting yourself out there, joining that debate team, taking that leap of faith, even if it makes you uncomfortable. It is only one club at one school, but the more people who are able to articulately fight back against the “Liam facts” of the world, the better.

As I look toward college, I hope to find a school committed to truth-seeking and armed with the resources to make my quest for a more fact-based world a lifelong adventure.

Last spring, as I was uprooting dead plants in my backyard, I stumbled across a folded piece of tinfoil buried a few inches underground. When I look at that tinfoil, it reflects back a guy who still enjoys science fiction but believes the ‘force’ is in the facts.

I stood beside the stonecutter, gripping the rock I had spent $200 on, with my heart pounding. As I handed the man the stone I spent hours picking, I felt the tension in the air. Would the hard shell give way to reveal the jade I hoped for?

I was traveling in Guilin, China at the time. Wandering around, I found a group of people pondering over some stones in their hands. Guilin, with its rich landscapes and unique topography, is renowned for producing jade. Like the California gold rush, people are on their quest to get rich or go home. Hoping to find treasures, I grabbed the flashlight and joined the crowd. After hours of digging in the unrelenting mud, I finally held a rock in my hands, only to discover that the inside wasn't the coveted jade but a common gem. It wasn’t worth what I paid for. Disappointed, I left the rock in my suitcase and never looked at it again. However, for my 15th birthday, my mom made the stone into a stunning rabbit pendant and gave it to me as my present. Everything about the experience changed.

Value isn't just about material worth; it's also about meaning, purpose, and significance. In this case, even a simple stone becomes valuable as it represents a cherished memory. I will always treasure this pendant. It reminds me of an important lesson: anything can be valuable if you give value to it. I learned to determine what is valuable to me, and how to share my value with others.

I learned to overcome challenges as I value the opportunity to develop perseverance and to acquire new skills. I hated taking leadership roles, public speaking, all the responsibilities terrify me. However, now I help fundraising and planning events at my city hall. Being a leader gave me strength when I witnessed my contributions make positive impacts for the team, and it brings me happiness knowing that others depend on me.

I learned to adore my hobbies not because I’m especially good at them but because they represent who I am. I’ve been playing the piano for 8 years. Although I didn’t win any serious awards, it has value to me, and to others. When my dad gets off from work exhausted, I play the songs he loves to make him relax; at gatherings, I play a song or two to create a cheerful atmosphere. These moments, when I share my passion and create meaningful memories, they become valuable to me, and hopefully to others.

I even began to value mistakes. Failures used to intimidate me. It’s interesting how I’ve come to value mistakes in the same way I’ve learned to value objects. Just like how a rough gem needs to go through a process of polishing to reveal its beauty, I realized that my mistakes are part of my own polishing process. I’m taught mistakes can be fundamental milestones to success and can lead to unexpected discoveries and innovations. I used to joke about a friend's height, not realizing it hurt his feelings. I've since learned to be mindful of others' emotions and avoid commenting on personal attributes. Most importantly, I learned how to respect others. I may not be a jade, but like my pendant, through constant polishing brought about by life’s stumbling stones, I become more valuable to those around me and myself.

Often, new discoveries require only a change of perspective. Guided by my mother, she helped me see the true worth of not only an item, but how value lies not solely in the surface. I found the world can be full of surprises when I step back and view things from different angles. Every experience, even the bad ones, with an open-minded approach, can become part of a larger portfolio, shaping who we are and what we value. I no longer search for a perfect, exclusive “jade”; instead, I look forward to uncovering every unique gem that I can craft, refine, and share with others.

Consenting adults who fight in private places generally don’t break any laws—I checked.

As teenagers, we weren’t adults, so we couldn’t technically consent.

The hook is…we weren’t fighting, either.

We were grieving.

Welcome to Fight Club.

Every meeting starts the same way: we go around the room and everyone shares who they lost, and how. My dad died in the height of quarantine, which meant that I never actually shared my story in person before—until upper year when I learned about Fight Club. Discussing our losses didn’t feel uncomfortable, because we had the chance to be completely honest, not having to sugarcoat the reality of losing someone dear to us. We found comfort in our shared experiences (“Who’s coming for Parent’s Weekend?!” is a question we all dreaded each October).

We shared triggers we faced in our everyday lives—mine was the cardinals outside my dorm window, since my dad and I used to photograph birds together. Greg shared with me the importance of reframing how I perceived triggers—instead of being reminded of the loss of my father, it was a reminder of the love that he shared with me. Instead of feeling unsettled by nature, I began to immerse myself in its beauty, from clam digging to watching the sunrise on the Squamscott River.

Recognizing nature’s ability to heal, I decided to lead Fight Club on walks in the Exeter woods during our meetings. We practiced breathing and mindfulness meditation while navigating the Orange Trail, and I saw my peers grow calmer over time. While nature could not erase their indelible wounds, it acted as a soothing balm, drawing us closer together as a new family.

Gaby was against the idea of nature walks due to a fear of bugs and losing cell reception. I understood her fears (my sister is just like that!) and suggested that we do a short walk and meditation to see if she liked it, with pizza afterwards. Experiencing the serenity of nature during that first walk, Gaby eventually decided to continue joining our hikes, and eventually was inspired to lead the initiative senior year.

I was inspired to help others in whatever way I could after seeing the impacts I could have on other students. From my first meeting forward, Fight Club was never confined to Fight Club. As co-head, I maintained an ongoing dialogue with our faculty advisor about students who had been profoundly affected by loss. I heard about Josh, a new senior who had lost his father, and invited him to join our first meeting. I wanted to give back to a community that had given so much to me.
