At the end of our meeting, Josh nervously approached me to discuss his Meditation, a reflective 15-page essay that seniors read in front of their English class. He was hesitant to write about his father’s death but I encouraged him to be open about his struggles, just like he was in Fight Club. When he confided in me that he was terrified at the prospect of crying while reading his meditation, I suggested he read small excerpts out loud to me. Throughout the madness of senior fall, I’d meet with Josh four days a week in the library where he’d read his work aloud several times. Armed with supportive statements and a literal mountain of chocolate chip cookies, I showed him he could take every punch the world gave him.

Helping Josh find the strength to share his story not only deepened our friendship but also reminded me of where I had started in my grief journey. Fight Club isn’t just about fighting grief by yourself—it’s about boxing together.

The intercom blasts, “Welcome to the OC Maker Faire” while the first wave of the 3,000 attendees stream into the building. As they make their way to my table and study the various Kintsugi pieces on display, their expressions change from curiosity to understanding, as they start to see the purpose behind the art. From a practical standpoint, Kintsugi is a Japanese artform that repairs broken bowls and dishes with glue. To me, it is so much more than that: it is about finding beauty in brokenness and restoring something seemingly damaged beyond repair.

Having grown up in a family that upcycles and minimizes waste, I discovered Kintsugi after I had accidentally broken my mom’s ceramic plate. One thing I shared at my exhibit was that each broken piece mends differently. One fragment might take to the glue well and fit quickly back to its spot, but another piece may take several tries of re-gluing, and sandpapering to have it fit back. If I rush the process, everything comes apart again. In many ways, human health is affected by different fragments in one’s life, such as poverty, racial injustice or unequal access to healthcare. If one or many of these fragments do not come together in the right place, the health and well-being of the individual can fall apart.

A few years ago, I walked into the hospital with my parents to find my grandfather laying in the bed with a round, plastic bulb full of blood above his head. My grandfather had been assaulted by a mentally ill homeless man, resulting in a brain bleed. Miraculously, my grandfather was coherent as the blood was being drawn out of his skull. He shared that he decided not to press charges. “WHY?” I exclaimed, angrily. I didn’t understand why my grandfather would let the man get away with what he had done. My grandfather gently explained that the man was a transient who had been in and out of jail with no home. “Is jail really what he needs? Because if I lock him away, I choose to look at him as nothing but a criminal, deserving to be forgotten. I want to still view him as a human being, someone who is hurt, in need of help, grace and compassion.” While I was still upset, I was deeply moved and challenged. I wondered about this man’s life, his circumstances and if he had ever had the chance to heal and rebuild. The idea of creating beauty in spite of brokenness in life’s injustices and struggles resonated with me on a deeper level. I took a Sociology class where I discovered Paul Farmer’s book, “To Repair the World,” that reveals a 2002 study that “recommended letting 25 million people–all living with AIDS in Africa at the time–die because they thought it would be too expensive to save them.” It was 28 times more “cost-effective” to prevent new HIV infections than treat people with AIDS. I sat there thinking about how the death of 25 million people sent a message to an entire continent, to their families and future generations that their humanness was not worth repairing and that they have been discarded by the world in the name of “cost-effectiveness.” While, ironically, Accra, Ghana is burdened with the world’s addiction to overconsumption, drawing in millions of second hand clothing that pollutes its lands and waters. Why is cost-effectiveness not applied to overconsumption but applied to saving human lives? As I prepare for a career in medicine and health advocacy, I want to study social structures from the patient’s perspective to help them access care because I believe that healthcare is a human right. Even when the individual or situation seems damaged beyond repair, seeing their humanity is the way to see beauty in a broken world.

**Beijing 2023:**

Though I entered Beijing feeling like a foreigner in my own hometown, I left with an understanding that while places and people change, the bonds we share evolve.

—--

I navigated through hutongs (alleyways), searching for tangren (sugar figurines), remnants of my childhood in Beijing. Familiar sights and sounds had vanished. It was as if my memories were fading in real time, overshadowed by this new, modernized city.

Amidst this unfamiliarity, I spotted her—an inconspicuous street vendor with a small styrofoam stand displaying sugar figurines. When she noticed my interest, her face lit up. She quickly explained her freshly made maltose, but I was barely listening. I was too busy savoring this moment; a connection to a Beijing I feared was lost forever.

I pointed to my zodiac sign, a little golden pig, and watched in awe as she worked her magic. As I attempted to communicate in my rusty Beijing accent, a mix of shame and longing washed over me. I was a foreigner in my own hometown, stumbling over words that should have come naturally. But she didn't judge. Instead, she refused my attempts to pay extra, recognizing the effort in my fading local dialect.

—--

The aroma of braised abalone wafted through the air as I entered the estate of Master Wei, a former state banquet chef. I carefully bowed and seated myself as I gazed around the siheyuan, the courtyard house enclosed by intricately carved wooden eaves and red pillars that starkly contrasted the bustling Beijing beyond its walls. It felt like I had traveled back fifty years in time.

Master Wei’s hands trembled as he spoke about culinary trends, addressing my father directly. I caught every other word—cutlery, diversified development. For those I couldn’t, I turned to my phone. Old Chinese expressions and industry-specific terms swept into my brain. Master Wei smiled as he watched my desperate translations into Baidu. I barely understood half of what he said, but his smile said more than words could.

Before we left, Master Wei washed his hands with his teacup and shook mine. I was taken aback. In traditional Chinese culture, washing hands before a significant action signifies respect and purity. In that handshake, he recognized my effort to reconnect with my roots, even when the language and history felt distant.

—--

More than ordinary changes quietly revealed themselves as I sat at the family dinner table.

My great aunt’s hair, once a salt-and-pepper mix, was now completely white. When did she stop dyeing it? The realization hit me. These changes, barely noticeable day by day, had accumulated into a stark reminder of the time I'd been away. How much of my family's stories had I missed out on?

Yet, as I noticed these changes, I also felt excitement. Each new detail was an opportunity to reconnect, learn, and grow. Perhaps in exploring these changes, I could bridge the gap between the person I had become and the roots I had left behind. “Remember when I used to run around here during New Year celebrations?” I said as I watched her eyes twinkle. As we exchanged stories, she laughed, reminiscing about my childhood. Her laughter reminded me that while time passed, our connection never truly faded, but instead waited to be rekindled. It wasn’t too late to reconnect.

—--

I walked away from the street vendor, clutching my little sugar pig. I left Master Wei’s courtyard house, speechless after our handshake. I sat with my great-aunt, silently noting the changes that marked the passage of time. In each of these moments, I wanted to speak, but the words caught in my throat.

I boarded my flight with new connections that only emerged through leaving and returning, awakening a deeper desire for reconnection that I never knew I had. And, like the sugar figurine in my hand, I will carry these moments with me: sweet, lasting, and full of meaning.

As the daughter of an Active-duty military service member, I am aware of the dangers faced by those who serve, however, I was unprepared for when those dangers would personally impact me. As an 8-year-old, the memory of looking into my parent’s faces while at the departure gate in Spain, and seeing an expression I have never seen before, is etched into my memory. On March 22, 2016, the Brussels Airport was attacked by terrorists, leading to the deaths of 32 people. The consequences of that attack have shaped my journey of personal growth and resilience.

As an “Army brat”, I’ve had the honor of traveling with my family to each Duty station. In 2014, my family was reassigned to the Netherlands. The transition from American to European culture was challenging, but I found a close friend in Noe, whose family was also in the military. Noe and I bonded over our love for reading and jumping rope during recess. Our families became inseparable and planned a vacation to Spain in the Spring of 2016. At the last minute, Noe’s family canceled their flight to Spain and rerouted to the United States to visit family while my family went to Spain.

Early on March 22nd, as my family boarded our flight back to Brussels, Noe’s family was leaving for America from there. Minutes before our flight was scheduled to take off, we were abruptly forced off the plane. There had been a terrorist attack that would soon be heard around the world. The chaos that unfolded, combined with our inability to contact Noe’s family, marked the beginning of my journey through grief and anxiety.

Although my family was safe, returning home amidst the turmoil was challenging. We later found out that Noe’s mother had been killed in the attack, and her family had suffered severe burns. The shock of learning about their suffering and the gravity of the situation at such a young age was overwhelming. The realization that this could have been my family, motivates me to cherish each day and appreciate the gift of life.

Unbeknownst to me at the time, the airport attack would become a catalyst for how I live my life. This experience has shown me the importance of resilience—staying focused on the present and not being overwhelmed by past traumas or future uncertainties. I have dedicated myself to volunteering, running, and embracing every opportunity for personal and academic growth. I commit myself to pursuing each goal with determination, out of respect for those who no longer can.

By volunteering with the United Service Organizations (USO) at the airport, through various campaigns like the USO Canine Comfort Crew, I have discovered the value of giving back. I take great pride in helping those who selflessly sacrifice for our country, and I have come to appreciate that everyone’s story should have a voice.

Within my community, I inspire others to embrace running as a powerful tool for managing stress, a practice I turned to during some of life’s greatest challenges. As a High School Ambassador for the local running shoe store, I motivate people of all ages to find strength and joy through movement. Whether I'm leading others or running solo, this activity remains a source of happiness and integral part of my life.

Academically, I have proactively prepared for my future by attending pre-college summer programs. These experiences have strengthened my commitment to my goals. I am determined to seize every opportunity available to me as I learned early on, tomorrow is not promised.

As I prepare for college, I am confident that the resilience and drive I have developed will support my future success. The Brussels terror attack, while a painful memory, has taught me the importance of perseverance and reinforced my commitment to making the most of every opportunity. I choose to let this memory fuel my ambitions rather than deter me.

My hair levitated majestically behind me as I fearlessly galloped my horse up the mountain. I was Zendaya in the Lancome-Idole Fragrance ad, or so I imagined. Alas, it was an eighth-grade daydream. Still, this ignited my horseback riding fervor and a deeper understanding of marginalized voices.

Lessons started as a fantasy, but reality soon set in. My idealistic vision quickly shattered with distrustful horse kicks and falls. But dreams become reality through hard work. With patience emanating through every brushing and cleaning of the horses' hooves, I earned their trust, including that of Fiona, a massive white horse, who, in time, nudged me for an affectionate nibble or two. The moment she ultimately rested her head on me, I was ecstatic. I promised myself to never take this feeling for granted.

Months passed, and I felt at home with Fiona and her troop. Inspired by their acceptance, I desired to help others find similar belongingness. With this thought, I embraced the role of Handita in "Amma's Ashes," a film about a queer teen, Gump, navigating a conservative family. I mirrored Handita (Gump's cousin) when my friend Nathaniel faced slurs in the mall. His sheepish smile masked his deep longing for acceptance. I warmly hugged him, affirming that I'd always be there for him. Nathaniel stood a little taller with a confident smile.

Fracturing my collarbone on the first filming day, I was ambivalent about whether to fight through the excruciating pain. But hearing our stylist Luka's story of being denied service in a bar for being non-binary, I decided to continue for the film's timely release. This film was more than my pain or performance; it was about giving voice to those silenced by prejudice, especially in the South Asian community, who needed to hear the message to break away from identity prejudices like shunning people out for their gender or sexual identity and labeling non-heterosexual sexuality as a psychological disorder.

"Amma's Ashes" premiered at Sacramento's historic Crest Theatre in October 2022, winning several global accolades. I was glad to have contributed to creating a more inclusive community through the film's widespread impact.

Gaya, our director, warmly hugged me for persevering through her dream project despite my critical fracture, silently acknowledging my resilience. The moment reminded me of Fiona, where subtle gestures speak volumes. When Fiona fidgets, I adjust her harness; when she raises her hind leg, I know to step back. After riding for five years, she's comfortable relinquishing her reins to me.

Comprehending Fiona has allowed me to hear people through their silence, especially my neurodiverse music students at WeEmbrace, whom I've been mentoring for four years. On my first day, Manav threw Legos at me. Seeing him with a fire truck, I played a firefighter song that instantly lit up his face, and we started bonding from that moment. Another student, Anurag, who consistently refused to participate in class, sang like a bird after I motivated him with the promise of using a vacuum cleaner after class, knowing his love for them. When Sakshi squints, she's focusing. When Raha covers her mouth, she wants to speak but is shy; I encourage her to speak up. I'm incredibly proud of my students, especially as they went from barely singing to performing at WeEmbrace events. My silent communication with Fiona has opened my eyes to a profound curiosity about how unspoken language shapes human relationships.

Walking. Trotting. Cantering. Galloping. My journey of navigating through stages of horseback riding has evolved from fantasy into more than a skill; it taught me to form unconditional bonds. Creating spaces of wholehearted acceptance and resilience, I strive to be a 'Fiona' for others. As I explore new horizons, I'm eager to take my horsemanship to probe the intricacies of human relationships with patience. I aim to continue mentoring others and embrace new challenges while galloping from my small realm to larger arenas.

On the first New Year’s I didn’t celebrate, Mrs. Erwin, my fifth-grade science teacher, welcomed me into her home with a bear hug. My parents rushed to Boston, where my brother Charles was transferred for a challenging brain tumor surgery. He was 12.

At the Erwins’, I spent the days devouring home-cooked alfredo and watching X-Men movies. But at night, we prayed for my brother.

Charles returned two weeks later, a determined smile on his pale face. Yet, for the next two years, my emotions were tethered to the status of his treatment. Between online classes at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, I’d help my mom make Charles’ favorite sushi rolls while he could still enjoy them. I hoped Charles would recover and continue his obsession with ancient Greek military strategy and telling his stories about our old scoutmaster who “fought in the Civil War.” But on November 6, 2020, my hope was lost. Science had come up short for my brother, and I felt helpless.

At the lowest point in my life, I grew quiet in the science classes I once loved. It wasn’t until AP Chemistry in sophomore year when that changed. Applying logic to complex chemical reactions that had hundreds of practical uses, my helplessness gave way to determination. Weekends spent tinkering with my homemade galvanic cell and scouring LibreTexts articles on organic chemistry led to creating meme-infused flashcards for my class. Likewise, watching kids’ expressions shift from confusion to astonishment as I taught them about chirality at the “Chemistry Makes Scents” station at the McWane Science Center, I re-experienced a joy I’d missed out on during my middle school years.

Slowly, like a catalyst assisting to form new bonds and molecules, chemistry helped me heal.

Determined to find real-world applications of my chemistry knowledge, I emailed a dozen university professors who conducted fascinating research. Luckily, Dr. Zhou, a monk-like professor who always answered my questions with her own, admitted me to her lab. With the ultimate goal of regenerating heart muscle after a heart attack, Dr. Zhou gave me a straightforward task: investigate the role of paraspeckles, special organelles in the cell nucleus… where However, I was quickly humbled by this seemingly small task. If McWane’s programmed demonstrations were a middle school science fair volcano, real-life experiments in the lab were Mount Vesuvius.

Through numerous failed attempts to produce beating muscle cells, I discovered the limits of textbook knowledge. 11 PM Slack messages to Dr. Zhou became routine: “Should I use less puromycin?” “Could cold exposure prevent paraspeckle formation?” In the lab, I asked anyone and everyone for help–I even pestered the eternally-busy postdoctoral scholar Anteneh until he spent many weekends teaching me his 14-day direct cardiac reprogramming protocol.

After months of experimentation and countless late-night drives from the lab, I finally saw muscle cells under the confocal microscope in their breathtaking beauty–intricate networks of interlaced filaments glowing red, dotted with shimmering green paraspeckles.

Equipped with the knowledge of how to design experiments that probe into the unknown, I felt empowered, even though my data didn’t support my initial hypothesis. Those results drove me to further push the boundaries of science and contribute to more discoveries. Similarly, the loss of my brother gave me an unshakable conviction: to conquer deadly diseases.

For nearly two years, I’ve spent over 1000 hours researching how to heal the injured heart. Sometimes, as I peer into the microscope to examine scar cells transforming into cardiac muscle, I’m reminded of my own journey. Scarred, but with the support of my mentors and the exhilaration of scientific discovery, I’ve healed enough to pump life back into my community. My calling is to combat life-threatening diseases– to assist those who are struggling in their journeys, just as Mrs. Erwin, Dr. Zhou, and many others have done for me.

Sesame Street by the Sea. That's where I grew up, in a small coastal town called Lewes with a diverse cast of characters. It is a living classroom with the backdrop of bike trails, waterways, beach days, and the smell of salt in the air. This town has taught me the value of a caring community.

For the most part living in Lewes was always stress-free. Summer days were filled with the usual events. Community 5ks, family beach days, catching waves, or gathering a group of neighbor friends to fish. Everyone lives their lives their own way with a sense of mutual respect. It was safe, comfortable, and predictable… until it wasn’t. On July 16th, 2024, I woke up to my mom in tears and received the news that two of my friends had been killed in a car accident. The tragedy happened on a road I regularly take to ponds, the beach, church, and work. It's an unavoidable road to the entrance of my neighborhood. I couldn’t process the information that was given to me. It didn't make any sense. How could something like this happen? I sat on my bed with my thoughts for about 10 minutes. Should I go over to the family's houses and support them? Do I wait and give them space to process? I ultimately decided to go to Elijah's house as I was much closer with his family. I was met at the front door by Eddie, Elijah’s brother, and a good friend of mine. Water was flooded in our eyes, and we couldn’t compose many words, but his “I love you, Bro” told me that I made the right decision by being here. If my nose wasn’t so runny I’m sure I would have smelled the fresh hot bagels that were brought over by the neighbors. The home was filled with familiar faces: Coach Frederick—the high school football coach, Dr. Kane—my doctor, and a handful of my closest friends. I sat in silence among everyone else, and in the silence I found comfort being with people who I care for. Sitting on that living room couch, I truly understand and appreciate what I have in my life; not just having friends to fish with or a beach to visit every week, but a community that deeply cares for one another and that teaches me how to care, too.

I try anything and everything that I can do to show my support, whether it is sharing my favorite memories, listening to their stories, or just being with the families in silence. My family and I cooked meals for Elijah and Ryan’s families. The families are not grieving alone as the incident affected everyone in the town. I fill trucks with grills, food, and coolers for a BBQ Fundraiser to honor my friends and benefit the first responders. A wooden cross now sits at the crash site, and Elijah and Ryan's names are etched into the grain. I sometimes forget that they are never really coming back. Passing the scene always tightens my throat and waters my eyes. Despite the painful tragedy that this cross reminds me of, I’ve focused on what this event has really taught me. Life is short. Nobody will remember how many soccer goals I scored, or how many A’s I earn. The connections I make and the impact I have on people while pursuing these achievements is much more valuable. Now that I know how fast and unpredictable life is, I plan to make the most of every moment I get with people I love.

Looking forward is difficult right now, but I know that the experiences that I have had with everyone in my small town will help me to better my next community in college and beyond, where I will celebrate, collaborate, compromise, and, when necessary, comfort.

"[Name] on me. [Name] on three. One! Two! Three! [Name]!" This chant, which my friend started as a joke, spread like wildfire through the marching band, plaguing me as the new rookie before every halftime performance.

As a “freshy” and lacking social interaction due to the pandemic, I was super embarrassed by this chant. As I watched the formerly distant upperclassmen become friends with us and then cry on their senior night, I realized that our section leaders genuinely cared about our section and us underclassmen.

Junior year, I also wanted to be an upperclassman who made our section feel cared about. At band camp, when I was in line during our instruction next to a freshman who didn’t understand the size of a backward march. Looking at their tiny steps backward, I explained that initially, people tend to take small backward march steps, so the next repetition, they should try to increase their step size. Rehearsing in Georgia’s humid heat, I had sweat pouring down my back within 10 minutes. Marching band is basically a cardio workout, so during our next break, I told our section to make sure to drink plenty of water, as well as explained how to breathe diaphragmatically (breathing using abdominal muscles), in order to put out as much sound as possible. On our next repetition, I heard section members around me take deep breaths and our sound was instantly more powerful.

Marching band has been the most integral community I’ve been a part of. From the touching moments of senior night to learning to love the “[Name]” chant, to teaching breathing techniques, marching has taught me the meaning of community, a lesson that will stay with me as I head to the University of Michigan and audition for the marching band.

As I walk into my freshman biology class, I'm hit with the pungent smell of formaldehyde from our dissection lab. I was super pumped to participate in this lab since our previous opportunity was canceled due to virtual school. Since both my parents have a PhD in biology, I was excited to delve deeper into a world I had heard about, but never truly experienced. As I carefully slit the outside of the earthworm, spreading open the skin using T-pins and labeling the anatomy of the innards of the worm, I felt like a proper scientist.

As I progressed through school, my interest in biology further developed. In AP Biology, despite my shaking hands, I loved the process of using pipettes to insert samples into a gel tray for a gel electrophoresis lab and analyzing data from various case studies, to the aquatic microorganisms we studied under our microscopes. Coming out of the pandemic and reading the weekly CDC news updates, I realized how important hands-on biological research and data analysis was to combat the spread of COVID-19.

That is why I’ll pursue a Bachelor in Biology at Georgia Tech’s School of Biological Sciences and later apply to the BSBIO/MSBINF program to further my passion for becoming a Bioinformatics scientist, analyzing biological data to help the public. Through student organizations such as Tri-Beta Biological Honors Society and Bioinformatics @ GT, I’ll be able to apply the knowledge that I learn in high-level classes (such as BIOS 3451 — Cell & Molecular Biology Lab as well as BIOS 4150 — Genomics & Applied Bioinformatics), to real-world situations. Through the countless research and internship opportunities Georgia Tech has, (such as the Jordan Lab) I know that in the future, I’ll be the best prepared as a skilled Biologist, ready to tackle the challenges of tomorrow.

It was February 10th the last day of J.V Basketball, and I had my AP seminar presentation the next day. As I walked into the library, my palms were sweating, my legs were shaking, and even with a week of practicing, I felt completely unprepared. The presentation went horribly. I could barely understand what I was saying, and it was in that moment of embarrassment that I realized something needed to change. 
After the presentation, I had to take a long look in the mirror that night. I’ve always felt hindered by a fear of speaking to others. Whether it was making a presentation in front of the class, or starting a one-on-one conversation with someone I didn’t know. I was always afraid to use my voice and speak to other people. 
As I continued watching videos on confidence, I noticed a common theme among the videos: going to the gym. Initially, I didn’t understand how working out would help, but I decided to start going. Over time, I became more serious about my routine, setting specific goals for both my diet and workouts. After a few months, I realized that accomplishing these small goals boosted my confidence. With each achievement, I felt more comfortable in social settings, finding it easier to make friends and interact with others without feeling nervous.
As the year went on, I realized that my growth extended beyond just my physical appearance. I learned the value of discipline and how setting goals could apply to all aspects of life. I began using this mindset in other areas. I started volunteering on weekends to help the community and also to meet new people. In school, I challenged myself with a more difficult schedule during my junior and senior years while maintaining a high average. I set a goal to get in the 1500s on my SAT because only ten to twenty people in my school have ever done that. These small goals helped me build genuine confidence, as I no longer had to fake it. I went from being a shy kid with little confidence to a more confident and well-rounded person. 
Towards the end of my junior year, I started to think about what I wanted to do after high school. After some time I considered a career in finance. The fast-paced and competitive environment in finance caught my interest. I was interested in the challenge of mastering analytical thinking and problem-solving, both are essential to have in the field. The same principles that helped me succeed in the gym, determination, patience, and consistency, will be vital in building a successful career in finance. Also, my newfound confidence will help me excel in interviews and create strong relations with co-workers. I’m eager to take on the challenge of pursuing a career in finance and use the experience to continue to help me grow. 
Looking back, that presentation wasn’t a failure but a turning point that would change my life. It pushed me to take control of the things I felt most insecure about and develop confidence I thought I would never have. Whether I’m in the gym, the classroom, or in my career, I will know how to get through a challenge. It will take determination and making little improvements each day to push past that challenge. As I move forward into college and prepare for a career in finance, I am committed to continuing this journey of personal growth and embracing new opportunities to succeed.

Just laid on my bed, tucked myself in the comforting warmth of my blanket ready to sleep, and suddenly I hear my door squeaking. I knew it was my little brother Rakan, he never quits challenging me. He jumped on my stomach while holding his car toys and I just ate a big shawarma.

“I’m sleeping! I have an Arabic shawarma… uhh an Arabic exam tomorrow!”

There he is laughing away and pointing at me repeating “Arabic shawarma!”. He wouldn’t stop laughing and I knew it. Whilst holding my stomach from pain I yelled “Get out!”

A week later, I got into a game that goes around a similar story of brotherhood between me and Rakan. It led me to believe I could be a better brother. She grew fond of it too and I said “It made me feel like I was a miserable brother to Rakan”. She held my hand and said “That’s how children are, maybe you think he’s different but when you were his age we didn’t just give some of our time, but our life. I know you love him but just look at him as the child you were.” I told her I would try my best, putting in mind how exhausting he is.

The next day, my best friend Ibrahim came to gift me a sleek silver watch for my birthday. As we sat down Ibrahim asked “Where is Rakan? It’s been a while since I played with him.” I responded “Are you sure you want to see him again? You remember when he kicked your stomach last time?” But Ibrahim was eager to see him so I called for Rakan. As soon as I opened the door, he came rocketing in and jumped on Ibrahim’s stomach. I was going to warn Rakan to stop, but I remembered what Mom said, so I let him enjoy his moment. After they hugged and played, Ibrahim and I sat down to talk about what we’ll do after graduation, but instead of leaving, Rakan kept jumping around Ibrahim. Watching Ibrahim grow uncomfortable, after telling him to calm down three times, I finally snapped “Rakan if you don’t stop I will not let you stay any longer!” He looked at me with his eyes welling up and his lips slowly quivering. I got up to hold him. “I’m sorry I’m sorry I didn’t mean to. Come here besides me.” I said. “I would rather have him make more noise than see him cry.”

At that moment, I understood that he’s a kid just like I was. When I saw someone I loved, I got excited just like Rakan so why would I stop him from being who he is? A few days later, my mother asked me to take Rakan to get groceries for lunch. Knowing how noisy he is, I was going to say no, but I didn’t want to refuse mom. I turned on the car and a sudden bang hit the window. I saw nothing when I looked out the window, then I looked down and found little sneaky Rakan. I laughed and said “Enough now. Let’s go.” Right before our turn home, I remembered that Rakan loved to act as he could move things by superpowers. I said “Stretch your arm and pull the car to the right to turn!” I turned the steering wheel with his hand movements and said “Mom! Did you see that? He’s Superman!” He looked at me with a grin of utter pride.

Tucking Rakan into bed that night, he whispered, “Can we play superpowers tomorrow?” I smiled and nodded, realizing how impactful it was changing my attitude towards him. It helped me to be more loving and patient. In those small and chaotic moments, Rakan taught me the importance of cherishing the simple joy of childhood. I’m forever grateful for my little hero.

The pendulum swings left. 
Looking at the mirror, I see a white mustache and my precious uniform. I think I am a super proud and well-dressed dictator. I finish the milk Mommy made for me and eat the breakfast. Then, I head to my headquarters. 
I am seven. I am the president of my class. I raise my voice a bit when they're not on their desks before our teacher arrives. In our student times, each of them are my friends, and I am theirs. I feel happy. 
The desolateness of a ruler without the people struck out quickly. My mother finding a new job in a different city caused my first exile. My best-president medal was packed and unpacked numerous times as we continually moved in and away. Until high school, I was the president again, sometimes the friend, and sometimes isolated; but eventually, each shift was followed by the other, in an erratic order.

The pendulum swings right. 
As an animal adapts, I tried to survive in the chaotic habitats: school and home. Although I liked being a chameleon with dynamic colors, I sometimes craved to be an ordinary, static creature, like a tree perhaps. Regardless, the predator was the same: irregularity. My armor against the hunter was constant, so I decided to embrace math and physics: the most trusted endeavors. 
I am fifteen. I did not enjoy the extra augmented mechanics summer course in freshman year. After three-all nighters studying physics, I decided it was not my thing–eventually failed. However, the search for the constant kept itself alive. Ironically, it was a math project session on Carmichael Numbers that rekindled my interest in humanities and social sciences, fields full of inconsistency. When our professor told us about the incompleteness theorem by Gödel, the only thing I thought was constant, math, gave in on me. My long-lasting journey of seeking certainty was devastatingly demolished. I decided to look for something completely different, even quite the opposite. 
I befriended the beast that haunted me through every move and school change: uncertainty. 
I delved into the Black Swan incident to explore the ineffectiveness of inductive methods to reach certainty. I researched Turkey’s changing position between NATO and Russia under the scope of realism and liberalism, political theories where proof and certainty is unreachable unlike math. Whether it be an MUN conference, or a simple meeting on the boarding, I loved how different voices arose to strive with a common issue, creating a harmony in the disorder. My passion became to finish a task with the elevated feeling of ignorance, knowing that each discovery revealed more unknowns to exist, little calves of the beast. 
The openness to change, which causes many others to be intimidated, is what drew me in; maybe because I had already found out certainty is unattainable in life.

I am seventeen. In this philosophy camp of a math village, I am now responsible for cleaning the dishes of the people with Emir, whom I just met a few days ago. Standing between Emir and an “abi”, a Turkish expression for “older brother” , I control and manage the single sink to distribute water evenly and effectively. 
With some sweat, dirt, and tears, we finally finished the most compelling task of the week. I went over to hang my apron. 
I recognized a rectangular object between the swings of the pendulum: a mirror. 
I see my apron. It is the same color as the uniform of a child dictator I once knew ten years ago. Shiny buttons are replaced with stuck-on food residues.“Everything constantly changes” I thought. The Earth moves in space, continents shift, seeds bloom to be wise oaks, parents get old, families move…I realize that it is just a dance: the synchronous rhythmic gestures of us. Together, in an ever-changing ballroom. I feel happy… dancing with people. 
And thus the pendulum turned into a metronome.

"ARE YOU A GIRL?” (NO, this is not the first time I am facing this question)

Being surrounded by girls from every corner of the classroom–East, West, North, and South–is a choice few boys in my country make. However, I did so. I opted for the humanities stream, which is considered to be appropriate only for girls, and deemed unsuitable for boys as they are ‘born’ to study STEM subjects, according to the Indian society.

I chose to be surrounded by girls. I play with them. I share my lunch boxes with them, and have hour-long conversations. I became the only boy at my school who willingly took humanities. I decided to become a ‘brave girl’ instead of a ‘suppressed boy.’

***

Every Friday nights and weekends (SPOILER ALERT! No parties are on the agenda), I become high on demand, almost like a VIP. Because Mondays are Test days, and my friends have many last-minute doubts that they want to get cleared from me. Instead of juggling between several different phone calls, I started organising group calls on WhatsApp. With a book in one hand and phone in the other, I become their pseudo-teacher and answer all their questions.

Even though my mother often asks, “If you spend your time helping your friends, then when will you do your own preparation?” Honestly, I don’t have an answer to her, except, ‘I cannot say NO to them when they need me the most.’

***

During our free periods, our classroom transforms into a gaming zone. Destroying the seating arrangements, we push four pale yellow tables together to form a large one and arrange ten to twelve chairs in a giant circle around the newly formed giant table. Kanika then pulls out her deck of black-backed UNO cards from her bag, and like a casino dealer, swiftly distributes them. As I had forgotten how to play, I sat between Prachita and Kanika–both UNO champions–because I wanted to learn the game at any cost. Both the girls guided me whenever I made an illegal move.

At first, I lost almost every round, but with each defeat, I picked up the tricks of the game. I patiently learned that UNO is not only about rules but tactics, and soon I was almost equivalent in their strength.

***

I have a very strange habit of INTROSPECTION every night. As I lie in bed and cocoon myself with a blanket, my eyes closed and face towards the ceiling, black bubbles of thoughts start erupting through my mind, and I question every step that I take that day. I analyse my actions whether they were right or wrong, and if wrong, how I could have corrected them or how I could have responded to a situation differently. It’s like a silent conversation with myself. And because of these beautiful introspective nights some of the embarrassing moments of my childhood are still kept alive in my memory and never allow me to repeat my mistakes.

At the end of the day, when I recall those blissful moments–whether it's feeling proud for standing up for my decision to take Humanities, cracking little bit of jokes in the middle of group discussions which sharpened my humour, or learning to play UNO in eleventh grade which reminded me that learning has no age barrier and you should never feel shy to learn new things from others–it gives me INNER PEACE. These little interactions are my world and bring me joy during stressful times.

At college, I want to form such timeless bonds that I, and most importantly, my future friends will remember throughout their lives. That's the kind of person I hope to be. During my four years as an undergraduate, I want to create more colourful memories and relationships that are invaluable and bring smiles to my friends’ faces even when they have left college, got a job, and have grown terribly old.

Among the squirming newborn cavapoos, one tan pup with a white cross on his back stood out. We were picking up the dog of my dreams, a reward for years of persistence and persuasion. “Teddy”—the name an homage to my favorite ice cream shop in my dad’s hometown in Ireland—was mine. I had dreamt of a dog to run around my grandmother’s backyard with and watch Ted Lasso on the couch with. The YouTube videos I had watched showed dogs that were cuddly and affectionate. But when Teddy became family, he seemed to want nothing to do with me. I was devastated.

In his first five months, Teddy ran away from my hugs and kisses, giving me the most evil side eyes. I felt there was no room for growth between us. However, I began to recognize Teddy’s quirks and adjusted my habits. Since he would back away whenever I reached towards his head, I kept my hands behind my back until he seemed comfortable. Realizing he hated eye contact, I gave him long butt rubs rather than stare into his eyes. Instead of picking him up, I danced with him to 2010 Justin Bieber and High School Musical. I finally felt momentum when, instead of dodging my hand like Muhammad Ali, Teddy began to lean into my affection. Finally, we were two creatures learning to connect. I never forced Teddy to accept my gestures of affection. I simply met him where he was emotionally and adapted to show my genuine love for him. The journey with Teddy taught me about adjusting to different experiences in life, about determination and about that willingness to fight for something better – even if you’re not sure how.

My friendship with Will began at Intramural Basketball in 4th grade. Our brother-like telepath was best showcased when we simultaneously texted each other the same thing after being accepted to the same high school: “LET'S GOOOO!”

However, we played different sports our freshman fall and winter, living separate lives and making new friends. That spring, we would make plans, but end up hanging out with our own new friends instead. Our friendship continued to wane, leaving me devastated, until one night I thought of my journey with Teddy. My mood instantly shifted. For the first time in over a year, I believed that I could restore what Will and I once had.

So, I drafted a letter, addressing our friendship, to give to Will at the retreat we were both leading. “YOLO!” I said, after nervously dropping it off in his room. I worried that showing vulnerability would diminish what Will already thought of me. I wrote that seeing our friendship slowly fade had been killing me inside, and after recounting some of my fondest moments with Will, I explained that I wanted to rebuild our special relationship. Questions swarmed my head, wondering if I had made the right decision, until I received a text: “Love you so much, bro.” Ever since reading that text at 12:45 AM in a cold retreat house, Will and I have grown closer than ever, acting as constants in each of our lives amidst the challenges that life brings.

With both Will and Teddy, I embraced discomfort in hope of deepening the relationships in my life. While there were many times that I could have given up, I persevered, in pursuit of what I value. I fought for friendship and won. My experiences with Teddy and Will reflect my ability to act on and adjust to different circumstances beyond my interpersonal relationships. Adaptability and determination were crucial skills to have when I needed to improve playing soccer with my non-dominant foot to make varsity as a sophomore or when I experimented with all kinds of food in order to overcome my food sensitivity diagnosis. Even though the lessons I’ve learned from Will and Teddy might not always work out, they will act as a source of strength and comfort when my relationships and other aspects of my life require patience and determination.

Apple.

For the past three years, my morning routine has revolved around both the little, red fruit and the mighty tech conglomerate.

Every morning at 6:30 a.m., I plop down at my dining table and start nomming on some peeled Gala apples. To me, Galas are far superior to Honeycrisps or Fujis (despite what the very objective applerankings.com says). How do I know? Well, last year, I taste-tested every apple available at my local Safeway. Even now, I can tell when my dad accidentally buys forbidden Fujis.

Anyways, back to my routine: as I devour each apple slice, I can feel the fructose coursing through my veins as I gradually grow more and more alert (I don’t need caffeine!). I reach for my iPhone; I tap open Apple News. My feed is a mosaic of different news outlets, from NYTimes to the Wall Street Journal for “serious” journalism on international politics and technology, to Game Rant for the latest updates on Nintendo games and League of Legends. I spent months curating this feed by pinning following a multitude of journals so that I can get a multitude of perspectives that a single news site or an echo chamber algorithm cannot provide.

In the spring of 2023, ChatGPT just started being popular - multiple new stories on Apple News speculated about how ChatGPT could disrupt healthcare, finance, and even education. As I scrolled through Apple News one morning, I remember reading one article by the NYTimes titled “Alarmed by A.I. Chatbots, Universities Start Revamping How They Teach”. I learned how ChatGPT was forcing teachers to change how they taught writing, lest all assignments from this day forth be deluged by an ocean of plagiarized, AI-generated essays.

I found this deeply problematic. This article and most similar viewpoints lacked nuance - they viewed ChatGPT purely as a tool to cheat. However, I took a more nuanced view that was rather novel at the time - generative AI is not the problem, nor are the students. Students only use AI because they can get away with it. (I would like to make it clear I don’t use generative AI personally or academically.) Teachers currently use grading methods that are insensitive to generative AI’s greatest flaw - its unoriginality. I liken ChatGPT’s writing to a Fuji apple: its writing looks good on the outside… but tastes rather bland on the inside. Thus rubrics need to change to reflect that - instead of looking for 5 paragraph essays and use of evidence to support claims (does it look like an apple?) rubrics should be focused on the originality and quality of the argumentation (does it taste like an apple?). This is the idea I expressed in my Scholastic award-winning piece “ChatGPT’s Potential in Higher Education.”

To me, apples represent how routine can inspire nuanced thinking. I believe these technicalities matter, because the slight discrepancies in which we individually view the world can lead to original thought and actions that spark the greatest questions and innovations. This value is something I try to carry with me in every activity I’m a part of. In my engineering class, it was the routine of helping my classmates with gas law problems that inspired me to notice air would be an effective and cheap insulator for my solar oven project. Similarly, it was the daily routine gameplay of various card games that made me differentiate the nuance between traditional card games that encourage playing on-curve and the gambling-esque nature of Marvel Snap, leading to the creation of my very off-curve Jubilee deck. As my daily routines change as I move into college and career, I hope to discover new nuances, just as apples did in high school.

The screen was blank; only a blinking white line urging for thrilling tales penetrated the nihility. I've encountered the sight countless times before; this time, it pleaded for a warrior's story. With my flurry of clacking keys, Subjugator materialized in an explosion of pixels, her holographic shield pulsating with energy as it carved through the digital void.

The sci-fi warrior is a recent character for online roleplaying, an activity I discovered during COVID-19 by doom-scrolling through YouTube recommendations. Boredom seemed impossible when Record Player spat pancakes at the 100-foot-tall dragon Captain Suzika. Within four years, I was raining down electron beams on vicious Kneall spaceships as Subjugator.

Unsurprisingly, thrilling intergalactic war became a respite for weathering 8-to-4 school grinds.

But Orion, the rust-colored Skywing, showed how roleplay held more value than fanciful acting. When joyful hours bonding with strangers on Discord, planning Orion's next adventure on steamship S.S.No with dragon and human comrades, contrasted with reality-me struggling to bother the McDonald's cashier for an extra spoon, I wondered if digital-me could develop these human connections in reality. Mirroring how Orion guided recruits, I guided classmates through debugging Arduino wires sending false positives to finite-state machines. As Orion battled saboteurs from Villain Clubhouse, I replicated his confidence in proving the connection between the post-WWII baby boom and the rise of feminism to history teacher Dr. Anderson.

Future lessons came from wandering Flareon Floof, whose trial of adaptation to settled life in urbanistic Astral City inspired my stylus to dip into digital art after Floof's portrait became my first artwork. When my hand felt heavy with the weight of a client's art commission, reminiscing about Floof's tribulations in gaining his adoptive parents' trust convinced my hand to draw the next stroke; it was either make good on your efforts or disappoint expectations.

Sure, roleplaying is acting, but being inspired by Orion's engine maintenance was real. After joining my high school's robotics team, Orion accompanied feverish 6:00 P.M. build sessions fueled by Popcorners as we obsessed over gear ratios and rubber bands' tensile strength for catapults, played around with RPM and wheel diameter for drivetrains, and tested double-acting pneumatic against its single-acting kind. During unexpected robot breakdowns mid-competition, I channeled Orion's quick thinking when patching holes in a sinking boiler room to use zip-ties to repair our robot. Pushing for team leader after unbearable micromanagement from previous leaders earned a snarling lecture from Floof about falling into the same pitfall. Once leader, I obliged by trusting sophomore Ricky to infuse PID control and C++ code into our robot. Relinquishing the driving role to freshman Jackson was unexpected, but his years of RC driving outperformed my competition nerves, teaching me the importance of dividing tasks.

Subjugator's battle-trained eye spotted opponents stealing our unscored triballs. Right before our last competition, to convince my team of a new counter-strategy, I channeled Subjugator's eloquence during the Human-Xeno War, where she roused fighting soldiers. The combined effort between me, my team, and my characters resulted in our first semi-final victory, including hoarse cheering and a crushing team hug.

By having me forge characters and roleplays, the blinking line trained me to solve problems step-by-step, like writing a story line-by-line; before long, enjoying roleplaying transformed into pursuing Mechanical Engineering. Roleplaying still survives in 10-tab Googling sessions about Boolean Algebra, matching my enthusiasm when researching Galaxy's 11 spaceship categories for Subjugator's backstory. However, I question if roleplay's lessons can survive the future's veil of mystery, which chills my blood like exoplanet Aqueous II's eternal winter. But like Subjugator exhaling puffs through clenched teeth as she wretches herself from wreckage, I mirror her resilience through inhaling Thoraeu's legacy of environmentalism and Ted Talks on Convolutional Neural Networks to bear the duties of modern adulthood. Wielding responsibility, human connections, and the blinking line of creation, I'll slice apart the university's challenges to engineer Subjugator into reality and subjugate a nihilistic future into a hopeful story for humanity.

I felt my parents’ love before I knew any words. Yet outside my home, words seemed to have more meaning.

I was six when I started to learn Kuchipudi, an Indian classical dance form with roots in Southern India. My love for dance was soon overshadowed by the comments I received. I got consumed by the "You're wasting my time" or "You have no hope," phrases I’ve heard too many times to count. My guru’s cutting words and humiliating ways were so foreign. I was taught the importance of a guru-sishya relationship, yet I could not connect with a woman who didn’t understand me. Every class, I collected her insults like puzzle pieces. It didn't get better as time went on.

When the six-year puzzle was complete, I told my mother I was done with dance. The sentence broke her, but my feelings of resentment pushed out the empathy in me.

The initial feeling of freedom slowly turned into regret for abandoning an art that was so intrinsic. Conscience was telling me to rejoin, but I ignored them. I let my head control my heart. My classmates were years more experienced, and it was probably just too late.

I opened the door to my mother sitting alone in her bedroom late at night. There she was, watching my first dance performance with tears silently falling down her face. At the moment, I didn’t know if those tears were due to the joy of seeing her little girl dance out her own childhood dream or lament that she would never be able to see it again. Looking back, it was a mixture of both. To this day, she doesn't know I saw her crying and I do not know if she ever will.

Left with me was a feeling of guilt for being the root of my mother’s hopelessness. Shame as I was too weak to handle beration. And confusion - wondering if I could truly be my mother’s child without Kuchipudi. To dance again, I would need to have a difficult conversation with my guru.

After 3 years of no contact, I decided to have a talk with her and explain my crossroads. I knew I wanted to come back to this art, but I also knew it couldn’t happen without a change. I poured out everything that had stuck with me for the past 9 years. The comments I perceived as insults, the empty feeling I got every time I left dance class; it was a monologue. And I was met with a response I did not expect. “Why didn’t you tell me earlier?”

Now, when I leave dance class, I am happy with myself and my abilities. I take in the constructive criticism I receive and use it for good. However, this contentment took 9 years.

When I see my third-grade student crying while attempting a division problem, I put away her worksheet and show her grouping with my fingers without her asking. I see her red wrinkled face and furrowed eyebrows come to terms with the quotient. I notice the high schooler across the table say he understands a problem, yet the blank stare and fidgety hands say otherwise. I walk through the problem to make sure it's intuitively understood because actions really do mean more than words. I lead the stretches with the little ones at my dance school and ask how they feel. I tell them to speak up when they feel discouraged so they don’t make the same mistake I did.

Three hours after school ended, I realized I was the only one still in my eighth-grade digital art class. I quickly exited the Google Meet tab I’d left forgotten behind the canvas. The rows of faces I’d been scrutinizing for so long hadn’t been the video cameras of my classmates, but rather faint sketches of my original characters, framed in panels. I had always wanted to make my own comic.

The summer after ninth grade, I was determined to accomplish this through a WEBTOON (webcomic) contest. I soon realized what bringing my artistic vision to life entailed: each panel that had cost seconds to read cost hand cramps and (to my horror) white hairs to make. Even after simplifying the line art and shading, I was scrambling to finish hours before the deadline, wondering what else I could compromise on.

I paused. Was this really how I wanted to present my story?

Instead of submitting my webcomic, I revisited each panel, meticulously rendering the scenes and mulling over the dialogue until I was satisfied. Four weeks later, I finally posted my webcomic online. My friends shared in my enthusiasm over the final result, admiring the drawings of characters I’d only told them about and bemoaning the ending cliffhanger. Strangely, I also wanted to know what came next: rather than a sense of accomplishment, reading my comic left me with an urge to return to my drawing tablet and create another.

Though I couldn’t commit to midnight drawing sessions during the school year, art seeped into the experimental setup I drew for my ink chromatography lab report and the visuals I used to illustrate my science fair project to peers and judges. As I adapted to explaining triboelectrification within a three-minute time frame, I found that diagrams offered my audience an intuitive understanding that neither text nor photographs could provide. In teaching others, I had found my next comic idea.

In junior year, I started Pandotoons Studio to make scientific comics for kids. Because my friend Brianna handled the coloring, I could focus on the aspect I loved most: transforming ideas into sketches. From a lesson on heat transfer inspired by anime cooking scenes to an introduction to Java classes and objects using a fantasy-themed story, I wanted to present concepts in an approachable manner.

As time went on, I continued producing comics with a growing team: as our beta reader, Brianna’s little brother provided “nine-year-old approval” before I sent the comics to my supervisor at the Fuller Center (non-profit childcare center), who helped us distribute the printed comics. As I watched the rows of kids stooped over a comic about the water cycle during summer break, this time I really was proud of my comic.

But some topics weren’t as easy to visualize. When Brianna suggested mentioning the lithosphere in our “Layers of the Earth” comic, I was conflicted. Would we portray the lithosphere as one layer, or separate the crust and mantle into two? Each diagram online had a different opinion. Spiraling down science articles gave us our answer: do both. The lithosphere and the crust/mantle belonged to two separate representations of the Earth’s layers, physical versus chemical. Seeing the two diagrams side-by-side, my own misconception I’d carried since sixth-grade Earth sciences was cleared. Funnily enough, I’d learned the same way I sought to teach.

For me, comics are the most genuine expression of empathy. As a reader, I’ve come to appreciate the painstaking effort behind each panel and the glimpse it offers into the creator’s world; as a creator, I’ve learned to work with the reader in mind, whether they’re a hurried science fair judge or a spirited third grader. As I enter college, I hope to continue exchanging visions with an ever-growing audience.

**Homeland**

It was 3 am I was walking down the stairs of Mimi’s house in Shobera, a buzzing neighborhood. Earlier that day we ate KFC in her dining room but on the floor, and went to get zalabia hot dogs from our favorite place, I remember the way it tasted sweet with syrup but the hot dog taste compensated for the sweetness. Uncle Manfhaty owned a bicycle shop in front of her apartment, where I learned to bike, with my dad, one hand on my back and the other on the bicycle guiding me down the narrow alley as there were cars parked on both sides of the street eventually I scratched one of them. At the end of the block was Pizza Hut, but it wasn’t like the one in America, it was better, everything was actually fresh, the store’s atmosphere felt more familiar and friendly, and their stuffed crust was phenomenal. But even further down the block was the Ful place where my family and I got ful and falafel sandwiches after a weekend at my grandma's house.

Her house smelled of food, she would be cooking for us all day all kinds of food my favorite of hers was rokak. She would greet us at the door with my uncle they both would pick us up and smoosh us. I remember her room the way it was laid out, her vanity which was filled with all kinds of creams, and her closets which were so full of cloth she had three closets that all reached the ceiling. I remember she told my sister and me that she’d saved us dresses from her childhood and couldn’t wait to have us wear them as teenagers. That night I was sitting in what used to be my mother's room, I refused to leave, I refused to leave her, I refused to this apartment, I refused to leave this neighborhood, I refused to leave this life.

My dad on the other side of the world facetimed me and promised me a pretty mug once I got there, he was smiling but I was crying. I hugged her tightly and she was crying too, we walked down the stairs from the 5 levels with every step I cried harder. It was quiet down on the street very unusual, I looked around quickly at the street decorations that extended from the balconies of each apartment, I looked at the steps of the building, the gate of the buildings, and the number next to it. I looked down the narrow road again the lights lit organishly the cars still crowding their sides. Soon I was in the car going off to the airport. This was my last goodbye, to this life, to my childhood. I had left behind this little girl who at the age of 5 would walk to the fiteer store nearby and La Poire to get desserts and after lib for a snack. I left a girl who saved money all year so that in the summer she would go down to the shack at the end of her road to get a snack and foal with her sister for breakfast after her parents left for work. Sometimes she would go to her grandma’s house to try to catch Dora at 7:30 am on MBC3 and stay until 8 pm when the Totally Spies came on. The little girl who once refused to leave her Mimi’s house after a weekend visit, crawled on the floor by the shoes cupboard and cried.

I slept the whole way to the Heathrow Airport or that’s what it felt like. I woke up frightened from the coldness of the airport. My mom had bought me a sandwich but I wasn’t hungry, not for this food. Why did they say it wouldn’t be forever when it is? Why was it that my childhood had to stop at 9 years old?

Reflecting on it now, however, makes me realize how much I was shaped by it. Coming to America made me self-reliant, I matured faster than the people around me. I didn’t take this life for granted. I wanted to make this move worth it, I strived for opportunities and knowledge that I perhaps wouldn’t have found in Egypt. This experience made me grow closer to my family, they were a constant in my life and the support that pushed me to look beyond my losses. My home will always be in Egypt but as long as I am with my family I know life will keep going forward.

Growing up I rarely had water—regular water, that is. It was always bubbles. I prefer fizzy to flat. Sparkling over still. The bubbles quench my thirst more effectively. Sparkles are the key difference to life’s taste and texture. Seltzer is scintillating. Revitalizing. Fizzing. Cooling. Tingling. So rather than being dull, I choose to sparkle. To me, sparkle means to bring a fresh perspective, embrace the unexpected, impact others, and be spontaneous.

“What’s your favorite holiday?” Mine changes every day. It’s my favorite conversation starter. Let me check my calendar: February 24. National Sparkle Day. March 30. Manatee Appreciation Day. July 27. National Seltzer Day. July 26. National Disability Independence Day, where equal opportunity is promoted for those with disabilities. Awareness is raised. Barriers are broken.

At Camp ANCHOR, July 26 is lived out every day. There, I have had the privilege of working with campers of all ages with a wide scope of disabilities. Spending two summers and many winter nights at ANCHOR was the epitome of experiencing the unexpected.

“Help me put my dress on,” Dawn told me. “You are going to be a bridesmaid and marry me and Nathan!”

“All the volunteer girls’ flip-flops!” Max proclaimed, looking 20 pounds heavier with all the shoes stuffed underneath his shirt.

“Apple Music,” the only words I heard Robby utter the entire summer. Stunned, I handed him my phone.

All these individuals need varied forms of attention and care. I’ve pushed wheelchairs for some campers, but gotten piggyback rides from others. I’ve drawn for campers unable to draw on their own, and I’ve had other campers draw for me, like Cy, whose cartoons are still displayed in my bedroom. I’ve created a secret handshake with Johnny, who’s four times my age. I’ve sat in a front-row seat at Mike's Middle Camp Presidential Campaign.

Once, at the Camp Dance Show, while performing with Terrance to “The Sound of Sunshine,'' I saw his caregiver in the audience cheering us on. Curious, I started to wonder beyond the scope of my campers, asking myself, what is it like for the caregivers of the disabled? It was genuine moments like these that made me devote my junior year research project to the well-being of these campers’ caregivers, looking into caregiver burden, anxiety, and coping strategies. My ultimate research goals—exposing detriments of negative coping in this cohort and highlighting the need for improvement in support systems.

In some cases, I sparkle by “strongly encouraging” spontaneity in others. For example, one evening while dining with my family on vacation in Florida, I saw posters of manatees plastered on the restaurant walls. Intrigued, I began wondering about these mysterious creatures while waiting for my grilled cheese. I surreptitiously stepped away from the table to make a call. As I sat back down, I proudly announced, “Everyone better get to bed early tonight. We’re swimming with manatees tomorrow.” I had booked the 6am session. Yikes.

Expected complaints and retaliations followed. Still, before the sun was up, my family and I were getting ready to swim alongside sea cows. With the tight wetsuit clinging to my body, I took the first step off the boat into the chilly water, bubbles tickling my numb feet. As the sun rose on Crystal Springs, large, warm, gray rocks emerged. A manatee was swimming right underneath me! I shrieked with amazement; then I heard other shrieks echo across the river. As quickly as it had started, though, it was over… POP. Like bubbles escaping from a seltzer bottle.

Like bubbles, sparkling things pop eventually. Unlike bubbles, the impact of sparkling things on others lingers. I strive to make others feel sparkly, which helps me sparkle more. To change people’s lives is to shine. So yes, when given the choice of water, I prefer sparkling.

Every time.

At the bottom of the sea, a dark figure blends into the shadowy water with jet black fins and a hero’s posture. Above even the birds in the sky, a mighty dragon lazily lets out a languid yawn. Every pokemon card tells a story, and it took a global pandemic for me to discover a rekindled interest in the intricate designs of my favorite cards. Nowadays, I mark the date of new card box releases, track the market activity of cards on my wishlist, and take my chances in opening packs of cards from my local target, wondering if I’ll pull that elusive Greninja EX.

But of course, pokemon cards are more than a trip down memory lane for some; they’re an investment. For at least a couple of weeks, cards will hover at a reasonable price, but as hype builds outside of the pokemon community, the vultures will come knocking. Scalpers take interest in the rarest and most popular cards and can double their market price overnight. Missing that initial release period means potentially missing out on those prices forever, and with my busy schedule, that simply wasn’t acceptable. I needed to be able to predict which cards would be a target of interest for third parties; in other words, I just needed to know which cards I had to move fast to buy so I could spend my limited monthly budget optimally. That summer, I began working on the project that would end up being my Pokémon Magnum Opus: An AI model that could predict the most valuable/popular cards of any given box release.

I began by scraping the attributes, titles, and rarity ratings of every card from various releases, feeding the data into a model to categorize between cards of interest and not of interest to third parties. The Naive Bayes model architecture was chosen due to its proven performance for text classification, such as identifying spam emails. Thus, I developed a method to quantify the price surge potential of a card title like “Rayquaza VMAX (Alternate Art Secret)” against something more common like “Oddish 4/147 Burning Shadows Regular”.

The first model iterations already showed promise, identifying patterns that I expected it to see, such as knowing that Alternate Art and Holo cards were far more enticing than their regular forms. After including data about the pokemon moves on the card, however, it also started to find patterns that I didn’t even see myself, such as how cards with moves that ‘sound’ good for the competitive pokemon scene also increase in value significantly. I had created a model that could even see the hidden gems I left unnoticed. As long as the card’s specifics were publicly available, I could predict the general price trend of the card with roughly a 75% accuracy. My wallet could finally breathe a sigh of relief.

Whether it be applying the ML skills I learned through medical research to pokémon cards, it’s the fusion of the different pieces and skills that comprise me that allows me to see some of the subtle luster in the everyday and the mundane. As I prepare to step onto a college campus next year, I’m committed to nurturing a sense of curiosity—both in myself and in those around me—by exploring the overlooked details that make our world endlessly fascinating.

In front of awaiting gazes, I began my program on a rickety piano at the veterans hospital. The notes rang out timidly, creating unusual harmonies with the out-of-tune strings. I was not equipped for this, trapping myself within fast passages and harshly hammered-out melodies. I felt defeated. Legendary pianists could always make the simplest melodies the most memorable, captivating the audience no matter the circumstance. So why couldn’t I? How could I return with something greater to convey?

Perhaps there was something deeper hidden in the notes on the page. I became a detective as I combed through Chopin's manuscripts, analyzing phrases filled with longing, nostalgia, and pride. I was a historian as I examined composers’ backgrounds, interpreting what the dynamic of “loud” means to a jolly teenage Mozart vs. a nearly deaf, middle-aged Beethoven. I hypothesized about the purpose of marking “appassionata” here and “tranquillo” there. The keys became my canvas for experimentation with tone, color, and style.

I carved out stories for pieces of music. Linking Chopin’s Scherzo No. 3 to Little Red Riding Hood, I imagined the trepidation of the opening figures mirroring the little girl's journey through the dark forest, with the wolf sneaking up to her as the bass notes creep up the chromatic scale. I twisted fairy tales in different ways, envisioning the final Agitato climax as a person on horseback chasing the wolf down, a valiant force to amend the tragic end. I embodied many characters as my fingers tossed around musical motifs, each voice forming different personalities through sound and articulation: the narcissistic king, the lonely child, the infatuated newlyweds, and countless others.

Twice a month, I returned to the veterans hospital, armed with new tactics and tools: my stories. I connected veterans’ experiences in combat to the spirited “Heroic” Polonaise and brought comfort with the all-too-nostalgic “Can’t Help Falling in Love.” I noticed the stillness of the room as the veterans and hospital staff were completely absorbed in my music, with arms tensing up as the rollercoaster inched up the hill or cheeks relaxing with a gentle lullaby. After each performance, my veterans always asked me, “When will you come back and take us on another journey?”

I couldn’t stop there. I played a solo recital in my home country of Taiwan during my junior year. After immigrating to America at age five, I watched my cousins learn to walk over blurry videos, and they knew me through my piano recordings. My recital turned these vague impressions into concrete memories. For many in the audience, classical music was foreign territory. With animated waltzes to imitate youthful laughter and fiery preludes to echo lively dinner conversations, I worked to illustrate digestible ideas from complex music. The audience felt as one, pulses rising and falling with every twist and turn. After rounds of applause and shouts of “encore,” I concluded with renditions of Taiwanese folk songs, which prompted everyone to sing along, saturating the hall with voices of all registers. Despite coming from disparate cities across the world, we were united.

Musical storytelling has infiltrated numerous parts of my life. My AP Biology teacher’s lectures became vivid as I imagined the organelles in a cell as different musicians playing in an orchestra. When I performed as a soloist with a symphony, I represented the nucleus, signaling with my gestures and expression for the lines to develop as they passed between instruments like a cell synthesizing a protein. While writing a mock inaugural address for English, I choose my words carefully, emulating a composer who uses rich and dissonant chords rhetorically.

Storytelling through music has become an invaluable tool for understanding, helping me connect disparate ideas, experiences, and people. Systems are interconnected like how notes make up a phrase: an ecosystem with interdependent creatures, cultural traditions that extend across borders, and how each person contributes to society. In college and beyond, I will continue to embrace the process of experimentation and discovery, building connections with my stories in hand.

Ctrl C + Ctrl V: an attempt to copy and paste the success of others onto my life’s goals. Esc: an attempt to escape from my problems after hitting a dead end. Finally, my favorite– Ctrl Z: undo. My life can be described with keyboard shortcuts.

Amidst quarantine year, I made a blog named Ctrl Z. As I grew comfortable, blogging became my outlet to share my life experiences, aspirations, and even frustrations. At first, Ctrl Z was just a trick harboring no significance. However, over the years, the name of my blog has become my story, the keybind I associate with undoing past mistakes.

Growing up as the only child of an immigrant household, I was constantly compared. When I got hurt trying my first serve, I quit tennis. After my hands froze over the keys during a recital, I quit piano. Hoping to surpass expectations through talent, I gave up my passions. I feared failure, unable to accept imperfection.

I came upon coding: a skill with endless use. I was inexorably drawn to it – after all, wouldn’t it be nice to be a coding genius? The very first time my code flashed an error message, I X’d out of the window. Frustrated and stumped, I left the computer and went to bed. But that night, as I tried to sleep, I couldn’t stop thinking about Lightbot, the robot that I had been programming. Why couldn't it reach the exit? I rose from my bed, tiptoeing to the computer. Though the error was painful to see, I scanned my code furtively. There! A misplaced semicolon. With a couple keystrokes, the robot moved. The next time Lightbot got stuck, I only felt mild confusion before returning to my code. I had gradually learnt that I was capable of solving these problems all along (nothing was more satisfying!), even finding enjoyment in debugging.

The most frustrating error I’ve encountered took three days to fix. During my junior year effort in the congressional app challenge, I took a step away from working with teammates (whom I had won with the previous year), trying my hand in a solo project. While I dreamt of an app with my first try, my expectations were quickly grounded. I watched in horror as the AI I was using spit out gibberish, from cryptic JSON files to old Latin texts. I pored over each line of code over and over again, searching through all corners of the internet. While it was a frustrating experience for me, I was excited to move forward, to learn from my oversights. Through days of mind-numbing debugging and multiple errors, one after the other, I finally saw my end result, an app of my own that I was truly proud of.

My change of mindset helps me empathize with peers who feel inadequate in certain aspects, fearing failure like I used to. It was during my time at governor’s school that I was given further perspective on overcoming fear. Through shared love of music, I made a dear friend, just a year younger than me.

“I don’t really get these proofs,” he lamented. “I was never really good at math… why did I choose this class?”

Reminded of how I had felt inadequate in the same way, I undertook the role of mentor. Helped him practicing proofs into late nights, I saw each countless concepts solidify in his mind, as he gained confidence. Before my friend presented his final project on the fourth dimension, he smiled.

“I’m glad I chose math," he said to me.

Once, I dreamt of a life without challenges. Now, I look forward to every single one. Once, I bristled at a small error preventing my robot from moving. Now, I love late nights debugging complex algorithms. Today, I look upon Ctrl Z as a tale of not failure, but growth.

My heart pounded as I scanned the crowded shoreline, my eyes darting between colorful tents and the throng of vacationers milling about. After emerging from the surf and amid the chaos, my sister had taken a wrong turn and wandered down the opposite side of the beach, almost disappearing before being found a mile down the shore.

Grace was diagnosed with autism at the age of two. From that moment on, her life was a whirlwind of constant doctors’ appointments, speech therapy sessions, and special education plans.
