During our early years together, we skirted around each other. She didn’t know how to start a conversation with me. I wasn’t sure how to approach her.

Passing years left behind new responsibilities. “Remember, don’t open the door for anyone” became a parting call from my parents as they left for work, trusting me to watch over her when we were home alone. Initially a chore, my tasks turned into sparks of connection and discovery. We transformed her verbal tics together into humorous gibberish words with ten different variations (like guhgyosi, which had no meaning but made us laugh), later naming and adding new Pokémon to the 800 in her guidebook during a Death Valley road trip. My camera roll still has a photo of her holding zoo binoculars the wrong way around; concrete evidence of a bond I hadn’t expected to find.

Over time, I added a new responsibility to my list. Self-assigned, not given. It started with answering her questions about Spanish homework, and soon not a week would go by without her bursting through my door with a bright orange “Avancemos!” workbook in her hands, filled with questions about conjugations and verb usage. Social cues soon became part of the routine, as I taught her how to navigate conversations, recognize tone, and recognize genuine friends. Little by little, whether that be her greeting to a peer being met with a “hi Grace!” and a smile, or a 98% on her Spanish test, I saw her begin to build her own bridges to the world around her.

I wasn’t the only teacher in our pair. Her ability to straighten a slouched, dejected posture into a giggling and bouncing bundle of energy amused and inspired me. I learned not to dwell on past mistakes or failures, and that optimism for the future can be its own form of resilience. Her passion for art served as a reminder of ingenuity born from creativity, both metaphorically and literally (her drawings are still constantly scattered all over the house).

Most of all, I learned to enjoy the mundane moments in life while concurrently pursuing excitement and adventure–to embrace but also escape monotony. The skills and patience I built teaching my sister paid dividends when muddling together with a four-year-old through 10 minutes of trial and error to master syllable pronunciation techniques. A search for thrilling competition led me to Science Olympiad, where I also discovered the peacefulness of repetitive building, destroying, and rebuilding needed to construct a balsa wood tower (capable of holding 14kg at 8 grams!). Hungry for an outlet that encouraged both creativity and discovery, I dove into research, exploring new topics and innovative fields, creating a (sometimes ironic) smile on my face even during grueling hours of debugging and testing.

My heart no longer pounds looking for a lost sister, but at the prospect of applying old lessons and learning new ones. She’s taught me that being unorthodox is just another way of being unique. It’s in the unexpected and unpolished moments that we find depth, and I want to bring that same openness to communities that are ready to embrace not just who we are, but who we might become.

Balancing on a step-stool while clenching a tape measure with her teeth, my mom meticulously marked the wall for my new Pokemon posters. As she whipped out the hammer and laser level, I wondered out loud why the corners had to be perfectly aligned. No one was going to see it anyway. Why did it matter if it was a couple degrees slightly off?

Straight-faced, she responded simply in Vietnamese, “Làm việc Làm đúng,” which means, “Do a job, do it right.”

I didn't understand the meaning of her words at first, thinking they were just about hanging posters or folding laundry, things that didn’t seem to matter. It was just another one of her sayings that I quickly forgot.

It wasn’t until much later, on the soccer field, where her words dug deep into my mind. At first, I treated soccer as a fun activity, putting in minimal effort and still receiving praise. My coaches raved about my potential, but just like my mom’s words, I brushed them off, jogging through sprints without touching the lines. But when I joined a new competitive team, the gap between myself and my teammates became clear. I went from playing entire ninety-minute matches to sitting on the bench, glancing at my coach wondering if I was even going to play.

In the car, as I sat in defeat, my mom quietly said, “Làm việc làm đúng.”

Weeks later, I opened my front door and was surprised with shouts of “Happy Birthday!” My family and friends welcomed me with overflowing plates of fried rice, Vietnamese egg rolls, and my favorite ginger tofu. As I wolfed down mountains of ginger tofu, I noticed my mom watching with a smile. Beyond food and drinks, my mom carefully planned everything including invitations and decorations, to make sure I felt cared for. It was there when I started to notice that “Làm việc Làm đúng” wasn’t just about doing tasks, it was her way of expressing love and how those small details made everyone feel valued and appreciated.

Embracing my mom’s teaching, I committed to do it right for soccer. During late nights and early mornings, my best friends became a ball, a wall, and a soccer field. I studied YouTube highlights of Neymar and professional wingers, trying to absorb their techniques. I searched for drills like Effective Moves to Beat Your Defender to advance my training regimen. Through my grueling cone sprints, I learned doing a job right also meant not cutting corners, giving your all into every repetition, and holding yourself to a high standard. Some mornings, the rain gave me a free shower, soaking my clothes and turning the ball into a moist brick. Those hours alone on the field, surrounded by a maze of cones, became my sanctuary.

Noticing my efforts, my coach gave me the opportunity to start a game. At halftime, I slumped on the bench with my face buried in my arms and tears slipping through my fingers. But the next day, I was back on the field.

In every training, I pushed myself to the limit, racing in every sprint and fighting for every loose ball. My teammates began to notice my dedication and gave me pointers on things I can improve. A defender named Julian and I would analyze our weaknesses, strategize to address them, and dive into hypothetical scenarios to enhance our game IQ. My efforts weren’t just about personal improvements anymore. I was raising the standard for the whole team, pushing us all forward.

I started doing it right in all aspects of my life. From designing exciting practices for my youth basketball team to staying up perfecting dance choreography for my K-pop group to even crafting Peppa Pig-themed math lessons to keep my summer camp students engaged, I go the extra mile to make sure those around me have a smile on their face. In the future, whether I'm developing mathematical models to optimize equitable resource distribution to underrepresented groups or building inclusive communities on campus, I will create spaces where everyone’s quirks, personalities, and voice are valued, nurturing a true sense of belonging.

Now, after soccer practice, I flatten the eggroll wrapper, tucking the filling inside and mirroring the precise motions my mom taught me as we prepare dinner. As the kitchen fills with the familiar aroma of ginger tofu and our shared laughter, I fold each corner with care, doing a job right just like my mom. Together, we seal the edges with egg wash and slowly smooth out each wrinkle.

How can the universe be so beautiful? It’s what my 8-year-old self thought when I saw the staggering size of Saturn’s rings, the darkness inside the black hole Gargantua, and the chalky surfaces of the icy planet Mann in the movie Interstellar. Although my young brain wasn’t able to understand the societal messages about the self-destructive nature of humans, or the physics of how general relativity affects time, it was keen enough to fall in love with the beauty of space, the somethings and nothings, and the possibilities of infinity.

Two months later on Christmas morning, I rushed downstairs to see if my wish list came to fruition, and there among the small boxes was one large one from “Santa,” wrapped and placed under the tree. That night, I carefully put the telescope together, making sure every screw was tightened just enough and each little knob was adjusted just right so that my view would be perfectly focused. When I was finally able to look through the small lens and see my first “high-definition” view of the moon, I instantly felt curious to learn more about the cosmos, and learn more I did.

Entering my adolescence, YouTube became my best friend. As I stayed up late at night watching videos about astronauts, NASA, and their mission to better the human race, I found myself wondering what I could do to help better the world. I found I was most attracted to the idea of human advancement, meaning how I can foster my abilities for improving the lives of others. The stepping stones toward this goal are each video I watch, each article I read, and each piece of information that I consume about space and astronomy.

However, I started to lose sight of this goal when I entered high school. AP tests, finals worth 50% of my grade, and 10-part projects took up all my time. Instead of wondering about the universe, I was constantly occupied with due dates, syllabi, and numbers. Missing the time I spent learning about my goal of human improvement, I decided to connect my academic life with my personal interests. Instead of writing school papers on “The History of The English Language” I chose subjects like “The Effects of Space Exploration on Earth’s Environment.” Connecting my “regular” school assignments to my particular passion made it possible to connect my structured assignments with my curiosity and personal goal of bettering the lives of others, and I found that, as a result, not only did I excel in school but I enjoyed it as well.

Looking into the lens of a telescope helped me define a clear goal for what I want to do in life, and I am proud that I have learned how to recognize the many opportunities around me to learn more in pursuit of my goals. Registering for all the CS classes in my school and self-learning an array of different programming languages to work on different projects has given me the ability to delve deeper, like doing and publishing research on AI, and giving my knowledge to younger kids, teaching them how to program for themselves. To me, teaching these young kids how to code isn’t just to give them technical skills, but to open the door for them to find their own personal passions, whether it has to do with computer science or not.

And as for myself, I will be back in IMAX watching Interstellar this winter when it re-releases, except now with my new goal set in my mind. While Cooper and his crew traversed wormholes and the 4th dimension to save our species, we might not get there in my lifetime. But I want the work I do in mine to improve life for future humans, whether it's working in a NASA lab helping improve the environment, or in Mission Control helping future exploration.

**Seeing Snow**

While the sun bestowed on Superman his powers of x-ray vision, I gained the superpower to see in the glow of lamps and the sun, spindly phytoplankton, shadows that cast the secrets of the universe. At the height of the pandemic, visual snow first appeared unexpectedly.

The literal translation of visual snow is seeing snow, which many assume from winter stock photos, or watching falling snow ornate one’s hair with crystals. But my snow is another kind, a grainy old television with sparks, like at the ends of fireworks, that scurry throughout the sky.

During the pandemic, question after question bombarded my mind as I sought an answer via Google search. The algorithm seemed to memorize my frantic behavior, plastering false ads about health and medicine to exploit my desire for answers.

One evening during my family’s tennis games, I shared these inexplicable changes with my mother: “Mama, at night, I close one eye and see a fossilized fly imprinted on my vision.” I swung the racket, missing the tennis ball. “Sometimes I see white light dots.” Are you bringing this up again? I put down my racket and headed to the end of the court to pick up the tennis ball. “I did some research. I think it’s visual snow, but I don’t know.” No, you know for sure. “Why do I never stop sharing?” Because you want sympathy; you want a doctor to answer all your questions that you already answered; you want to witness the beautiful sky again.

“Okay,” my mom replied. She stood on the tennis court with a detached expression. Not only did my mother and the doctors misinterpret my self-reported symptoms and fail to address visual snow, but I also misunderstood. When a doctor grazed a metal bar against my leg and asked me if its temperature had changed to test the reaction of my nerves, I misinterpreted his question for a stark difference to a subtle difference in temperature. In an endless battle to translate my experience to other people along different perceptual lines, I discovered storytelling, where words compensate for my vision.

After one week, I was to attend my first summer workshop for my creative nonfiction course. In the narrow library strip under a lattice of gray arches, I sat in company with my classmates’ essays. Within my hands were the tangible work of their stories, which spoke to me an entire history imperceptible face-to-face: the charismatic father who dragged her family to camping, my classmate’s isolation from her Vietnamese culture, a passion for roller skating, the reality of the international college counseling industry. There’s something distinctly intimate in close reading and annotating a classmate’s cherished memory, which they purposefully wrote at their desk, reflecting on what moment to share or what themes to convey. At that moment, reading was like walking blindly into their stories, where their words simulated ecosystems created from their memories.

On the day of the workshop, I felt a strange anxiousness building in my chest. My five classmates, who I only knew for one week, would read, in the six pages, four years of my life. I remained silent while the flipping papers fluttered around the oval table. Their voices ricocheted across the room. For once, my writing on visual snow spoke for me, combining personal narrative, research, and philosophy. Near the end of my critique, one of my classmates, Julia, commented how her ignorance of visual snow dissolved after reaching the end of my essay. Many experiences are left unspoken. People live along their unique lines. But at this moment, our lines intersected.

Vision snow did not reveal to me the universe, but writing did reveal to me underrepresented stories and personal journeys. With writing, I gained the power to command language and wield stories to express myself and, foremost, to connect with others.

As the lights dimmed and the music began, I reflected on the events that brought me here. My community’s inability to help those suffering the consequences of war fueled an anger born of helplessness. With angry chants and dehumanizing language defining the discourse, I recognized the need to change the conversation, to proudly showcase our culture and humanity. I imagined an event that would use a special language, a language capable of reaching past rational thought and speaking directly to people’s souls: the language of movement. With that, "Lemat Fenaneen: Artists United for Gaza Relief" was born.

The opening song was, “Jerusalem, The Flower of all Cities,” my grandfather’s favorite. It was a tour of the temples, churches, and mosques of that city, and every element of my choreography - the turn of my head, the slow softening of my fist - conveyed reverence for those suffering the indignities of war. Under the spotlight, I wrapped my arms around my body and swayed back and forth, honoring the Jewish worshippers at the Western Wall, calling attention to the universality of suffering. Inspired by their perseverance, I remembered the challenges I had overcome to stage “Lemat Fenaneen,” the resistance of my school to host any event acknowledging the conflict in Gaza, the reluctance of the dance community to perform during the war. I rallied allies, and together, we overcame. Twenty-five of Jordan’s top dancers, choreographers and musicians joined me that night, unified behind a message of compassion.

Back on stage, I feared an audience unversed in the language of movement would fail to internalize my message. Placing my hands together in a symbol of Christian prayer, I found strength in those who taught me to value compassion and humanity above all else. I reflected on my family, Venezuelan and Palestinian, united in so many ways, not least their Christian faith, its unwavering focus on love. The same hand position, also used in Buddhist prayer, took me to Kathmandu, to the home of the State Oracle of Tibet, the Khadro-La. There, I spent countless hours learning how the rhythmic chants of her Gelugpa School could help adherents on their path to transcendence, a path I dreamed of traversing, of sharing with others, through the language of movement.

I also took inspiration from those who first taught me this language. The sharp swing of my arms took me to my mother, a Flamenco dancer who performed with me in her womb, who moved my arms rhythmically before I took my first step. The twist of my hand transported me to Bangkok, the Khon teacher stretching my fingers painfully as I practiced the revered role of Hanuman. A pirouette sent me back to the Washington Ballet and Irina Wunder, her admonishments as spirited as her ballet combinations, who taught me that a graceful gesture could convey as much meaning as an explosive jump.

In my final movement, I placed my forehead on the floor, the humble act of Islamic prayer, and gazed up at the 500 faces of those who had come to support me. I saw Mr. Waheed, the Palestinian janitor cleaning the theater that night. He was wiping away tears. The audience had engaged fluently, naturally, with the language of movement.

"We have art in order not to die of the truth," Nietzsche said, and it was the truth of war that motivated me to speak the language of movement that night. We raised US$18,000 for the Jordanian Hashemite Charity Organization’s Gaza relief effort, and for the first time, I shared my artistic voice with the world. I learned that audiences, even those suffering through war, would embrace the essential wisdom of compassion. At university, I hope to meet others who will introduce me to new artistic languages and concepts. I also hope to continue what I started with “Lemat Fenaneen,” using the language of movement to communicate directly to peoples’ hearts.

Standing there, the unknown freshman, I felt my heart racing, a wild drum echoing in my chest. The entire school was watching, and beside me stood Aybüke, the sophomore everyone admired. The rhythmic clapping of my classmates pulsed through me like a heartbeat, both terrifying and exhilarating. It wasn’t my first time dancing, but this was different. The spotlight warmed my skin, yet my palms were slick with sweat. ‘What if I stumble? What if I become the talk of the school for all the wrong reasons?’ I could feel those fears swirling inside me, threatening to pull me under. But then I remembered Aybüke’s reassuring grin, her gentle reminder that it wasn’t about perfection. If I could just let go, dance with belief in myself, I’d shine. And shine I did.

Two years later, I found myself hosting a debate tournament—a role usually given to language majors. As a STEM student, it felt unexpected and daunting, especially since it was my first time organizing an event. Hosting nearly 30 debates over two years, the stage began to feel like home. Each time I stepped up, I grew more confident, realizing that hosting, like dance, required presence and belief in myself. The stage was no longer intimidating; it became a space where I could lead, connect, and make a real impact.

Five weeks into hosting the debate tournament, the energy in the room was electric, yet I felt a ripple of tension when the lead speaker of one of the teams hadn’t shown up. Panic surged through me as I rushed backstage. There she was, visibly shaken, her hands trembling. ‘I know how stressful this is,’ I said softly, my heart racing. ‘But I’m here with you. Just focus on me while you speak.’ In that moment, I drew on my own experiences of stepping onto a stage filled with anxiety. ‘It’s okay to feel nervous,’ ‘You’ve been chosen because you’re the best. Just stepping out there is already a courageous act.’ As I watched her take a breath and step onto the stage, I felt a rush of pride—not just for her, but for every freshman I had guided through their fears.

Founding the Scrabble Club wasn’t just about organizing a game; it was about proving that we could create something meaningful on our own. Despite teachers brushing me off, I refused to let go. Every meeting ended with unsigned documents, but I kept pushing, staying late to handle paperwork myself. When my teacher threatened to cancel the event, I hid my panic behind a calm smile, reassuring my younger peers, “We’ve got this.”

On the day of the tournament, seeing the room filled with students debating words felt like victory. Their excitement reminded me why I fought so hard. We had done this—despite every obstacle—and in their eyes, I saw the impact of believing in something bigger than ourselves.

Through all of this, I’ve learned that true leadership isn’t about control; it’s about being supportive, kind, and authentic. It’s about showing up for others, even when things get tough. In the process, I discovered my full potential and developed a deep gratitude for the world around me. In finding ways to help others, I truly found myself.

Now, as I look to the future, the stage no longer feels intimidating—it feels like a canvas waiting for my brush. The lessons I’ve learned—from trembling on stage to guiding others—have transformed how I approach challenges. As I step into college, I carry with me a belief that leadership is rooted in authenticity and support. I’m excited to create inclusive spaces where everyone can thrive, just as I once did.

“Come on, guys!! Jump HERE and drive!” I had rehearsed this repeatedly - in the mirror to myself, and shouting to my parents after dinner as practice.

During the last week of my sophomore fall season, Coach Barb pulled me aside to tell me, “I’m not letting you race this Saturday because you don’t show enough emotion.”

Her words stung me as I sat beside her, contemplating the year and a half I’d spent coxing. My heart sank down to my stomach.

Did I throw myself too far out of my comfort zone? I’m someone who would rather spend a day reading the “Tiny Love Stories” section of the New York Times than scream my head off at Six Flags with my friends. Did I have the potential to be a good coxswain given my naturally quiet disposition?

I reminded myself why I’d joined the crew in the first place: it was to escape the swim team (they were a little intimidating and practiced at 6 a.m.), but more importantly, it was to develop my initiative, and above all, courage.

I quickly got to work. For the remainder of the fall, I would ask my friends after each practice for suggestions. Sylvania would ask me to be harsh when talking to her and to tell her what place we were in, while Ophelia asked for an incentive/threat during a race. So the next week, I told them that they would have to row a 2k if they slacked.

As winter term began, I practiced talking in front of a mirror and yelling at my family, incorporating the suggestions from my rowers. I also made a mental list of every area I wanted to work on, such as using an expanded vocal range when talking, timing everything I say with each stroke, and using my choir experience to crescendo during heated moments. Youtube videos of coxswains slowly became my favorite procrastination strategy. I would also repeatedly listen to my friends’ favorite coxswain recordings, including one where the coxswain repeatedly yelled, “Let’s get to nationals!” and created a picture of getting on a plane to Sarasota.

When springtime came and Coach Barb and I met to discuss my coxswain recording during practice, she remarked, “I love how you got so excited during that last hundred. None of the other coxswains showed this much emotion while rowing.” I beamed, knowing that all the pain and toil these months had been worth it.

In addition to helping me (literally) find my voice, being a coxswain has helped me grow in my ability to bring individuals together. When I run rehearsal in choir as a conductor, I communicate my interpretation to the singers through my voice and hands. And as a prefect, I rally the underclassmen around Dunkin’ Donut trips.

As I start my senior season in the fall, I confidently articulate my expectations for the rowers as they row around the lake. I tell them the story of a stroke: “Reach out and catch, lock the blade in, and drive with your legs. Use your lats to keep your body forward. Then swing your body, then arms, and relax out of the finish.” I emphasize ratio and relaxing on the recovery every few strokes while urging them to swing and suspend, reminding them of their favorite “butt-off-the-seat drill.” While encroaching upon a boat ahead of us, I would yell, “Oh my gosh, I’m at the bow of Izzy’s boat! Now I’m at Emily! Now Sarah!” And one day after a power piece, Coach Barb once again remarked, “All eight of you just flowed together so well!” I know that the momentum that I helped build in the boat will carry me through college and beyond.

"Why is my name [Name] Veeramachaneni, not Jan Allen? I want to change it." I asked my parents this question almost daily, feeling the pain of everyone's constant mispronunciations. Rather than attempt to pronounce my name correctly, teachers often asked me, "Can I call you Miss JV?" In class, I couldn't ask or answer questions, hesitating to do anything because I felt self-conscious about my name--it was as if I didn't have an identity.

These encounters not only affected my self-esteem but also became a hindrance to social relations. Additionally, my "V" last name placed me last in every alphabetical list and activity. While selecting classes, I couldn't choose AP US History, my favorite subject, since it was already full. When choosing a field trip, I ended up with botanical gardens instead of my first preference, fleet week tour. Disappointed with everything, one day, I returned home determined to persuade my mom to change my name--I would only return to school with a new name. It was then that my mom shared the meaning behind my name. [Name] means "one who cares for the people" in Sanskrit.

Her words made me think back to a social media post I had done for a Women’s Day project, highlighting names of influential people like Nobel prize winners Aung San Suu Kyi and Malala Yousafzai. Although their names might be considered difficult to pronounce, people consciously try to enunciate them correctly because of their achievements. After the Board of Education recognized my post, my name slowly began gaining recognition. So, I decided that to be understood and respected by others, I needed to understand and appreciate my name first. I had to influence people to work on pronouncing my name correctly while living up to the meaning of my name.

This realization and my first win in a debate tournament provided the self-confidence I needed to continue. Debating topics such as Vote 16 and the benefits of social media ignited a passion for civic engagement and community responsibility that turned into an initiative to combat everyday biases that students encounter.

To create a friendly environment in our school, I started the Alliance Against Bias initiative to raise awareness about the implicit biases that we may have toward people with unique names, appearances, or traditions. My presentation of accomplished individuals with distinctive names, like the Dalai Lama, Mahatma Gandhi, and actress Arizona Muse, showed that all names are valuable and carry significant meaning. This presentation discussed how mispronouncing names can undermine an individual’s identity and sense of belonging. Following the presentation, I was overjoyed when my friends and teachers finally learned how to pronounce the name of a freshman perfectly: Jaahnavi Rajendran.

The impact of this project, coupled with an ongoing dialogue about respect and inclusion, made my peers and teachers understand how important it is to respect each person's identity. Now that I better understood myself, I began to take my advocacy further. Knowing that my friend Anna felt alienated because of severe acne, I asked my biology teacher to talk about hormones when she was teaching us about enzymes, underlining that such changes are a part of normal development. Finally, I devised an impartial rotation system that alternates annually between A to Z and Z to A, randomizing the order in which our last names were used in picking classes or activities so that each student gets a fair opportunity.

These days, my name gives me the resilience to face any challenges. I have learned self-acceptance and perseverance from being the girl whose name was always mispronounced and hardly recognized to becoming a leader whom everyone recognizes. My name reminds me to care for those around me, from close friends to complete strangers. And now, as I enter the next phase of my life, I carry the resolve to face new challenges and fulfill my name’s meaning--caring for people.

Until junior year, my classroom hosted a 23’’ wall stain—some dubbed it “Whiteboard” (although solving a quadratic equation solicited three scrubs). Initially silent as stains relocated onto my laptop, I spoke up when sinusoids strained my teacher’s muscles.

“Do you remember our motto?” my principal frowned, sipping her macchiato. I’d outwitted and defrauded my timer of 41 minutes to convert this 7:35-before-class coffee habit into five-week-long lobbying. “Non multa, sed multum,” she inhaled. “We prioritize depth, not breadth.” “Sure, but… why can’t depth develop into breadth?” Her eyebrows intersected. “You mean?”

I meant interactive boards—distance-learning greatest lesson. Their DahuaTech manuals, YouTube unboxings—I inspected them all, mastering Infrared Touch-Technology and Anti-Light Interference in Vietnamese before selecting one—LPH86-ST420. My principal snorted though. Its price tag bellowed “$2250,” no less than 25 chairs! Yet, after holding an ergonomics-crash-course sit-down—literally—to convince 23 shrugging mates to initial a #WHITEBOARDLOVERS petition, I won.

Winning that whiteboard revolutionized our educational space. Traditionally, we’d flip through 2064-page Greek-Italian dictionaries to translate 8-to-12-line extracts—my friends’ eyes avoided epsilon contact; bathroom-bound escapes outperformed inflation; heads bowed during cold-calling. But now… “It’s a δεινόν tool—idea-making—can’t we try it?” I cornered my teacher. Rolling her eyes, stammering her consent, she propelled me to power the whiteboard’s note-on mode, investigate Lysias’ defense, and inflame everyone’s analytical spirits: “Were you Lysias, how’d you defend Euphiletos?” my best educator voice thrilled.

Under my teacher’s incredulous eyes, hands sprang up like mushrooms. From the right-back corner, Flavio shouted to “show the tears,” while Sofia in the front whispered: “Exploit the victim’s immorality?” Framing the passage with these ideas, “Testing time! Instead of line-by-line translation let’s color evidence on the screen to falsify these hypotheses,” I proposed. Quickly, an explosion of magenta, marigold, and mint turned the whiteboard into a choral painting.

It was a messy masterpiece. It was a little modernist. But its moving commonality modified and rectified my educational role: while many teachers equate education and spoon-feeding, few embody its original meaning—educo, “bring out.” I want to be one of them. But bringing out what? A class? What constitutes one? “Class” means “fleet” in Latin. And fleets have destinations, right? What’s mine? What’s my role?

I’m captain, but of a curious type—curious about people’s ideas, including the 25 Normale-Summer-School peers I stockpiled in frescoed seminar rooms—savoring tiramisu—to create a forms-of-government tier list. Aboard Stanford-Encyclopedia-of-Philosophy caravels, I discovered tribalism, minarchism, SULTANISM! I programmed single-transferable-vote ballots—past-midnight odysseys—holding and handing smartpens, steering and stirring deliberation (epistocracy ranked C—too nerdy!). In setting out for such adventures, individual initiative sustains my captainship, democratic curiosity my journey.

Yet, I’m sometimes blown off course. My school newspaper’s an example—I strategically twice-bake cantucci to feed editorial-discussion-warm-up, Gossip-Girl-Serena-vs-Blair disputes because when I write on the whiteboard “Paper-Scraps Hygienic Crisis?”, and Sveva substitutes that with “Second-Floor-Bathroom Pads’ Emergency!”, I know she’s well-meaning (how couldn’t someone prioritizing cosmopolitan humility over Parisian effervescence?). Fellow sailors’ accountability (and my gratitude) tastes sweeter than those almond biscuits—infinitely more.

That’s why I want everyone to board our ship—our whiteboard! Schoolhouse attests to this addictive inclusion. Engraving Ayobami’s thoughts beside Hasini’s on Freeform whiteboards (and Super-Mario-x-Baby-Boss-Dance-Monkey memes), I veer why-you-say-B propellers towards my favorite Ugandan and Lebanese to anchor educational optimism—they matter, their opened microphones matter, referring to each other by name matters! Their ensuing OHH-I-get-it-now-thank-you boarding always curves my cheeks. Why?

Because in my life, education and class overlap—always and everywhere. In my life, assembling a class wherever education isn’t conducive and collaborative enough is personal—a commitment I’ll push forward in college. Alongside inspiring individuals, I’ll cover whiteboards with sketches of turtles outrunning Achilles, with brainstorms to publicize undergraduate magazines on Instagram, and doodled MUN-team selfies as screensavers.

However, to make that possible, minds need spotless creative space. So I’ve brushed stain removers—LPH86-ST420—onto my high school’s 27 classrooms’ walls. With these infinite white canvases, I’ll craft art from dirt, truth from blots, life from education—a liberal arts education.

I remember sitting in my room, my fingers tracing the edge of my desk as I listened to him speak. Every time Deepak returned from his trips around the world, he would come home and tell us all about it. This time, however, his upbeat voice carried a heaviness that made me sit up straighter. He told me about his visit to northern Tanzania where women and children had to walk nine hours —just to get water. I could hear his words, but the silence in between his sentences hit me the hardest. My chest tightened, and the comfortable surroundings of my own room began to feel like a cage—suffocating because I knew I couldn’t just sit there and do nothing. A part of me wanted to believe that these stories were too far away to be real, but deep down, this couldn’t be ignored. Before I knew it, I was on my way to Losimingori, Tanzania.

That December, I was walking with my new friend, Joseph Shuaka, a boy my age. Joseph is part of the oldest tribe in the world, the Maasai. We walked the 5-mile trek through the drought-stricken plains of northern Tanzania to visit his home. I picked up my pace, the dry earth crunching beneath my sneakers. Joseph led the way with effortless grace and speed, in his cut-up tire shoes. As we approached the crest, the land opened up before us, below, a dry riverbed wound through the arid hills like a scar. Joseph’s stories of waking up at 3am, daily, to fetch water played in my head, each detail sharpening my resolve. The weight of our conversation about his family hung heavy on my mind. It was time to turn those words into action.

That was five years ago. I returned and shared the Maasai crisis with anyone who would listen. Fundraising and deploying the first 100,000-liter rainwater harvesting was a first step. The following year, six high school friends joined me to deploy three more rainwater units and measure the impact on the community. The women now only walked two to three hours, leaving enough time to create jewelry and grow crops. It was exhilarating to see children running freely across the land, attending school, instead of walking for water.

Now that the community had access to water, many new questions emerged: How much water can one family take? Should this water be shared with animals? With the Maasai leader's help, I organized a series of community gatherings with elders, women, and teenagers. Because of our language barriers, our conversations consisted of drawing and tone of voice rather than words. Ideas flowed here; the adults drew a bucket with an upside-down umbrella to catch rainwater, the teenagers wanted to get a drone for medicine delivery. One of the elders, who was skeptical initially, started to plan “water councils” for equitable access.

For the tens of thousands of Maasai living inland, the community wanted to deploy smaller units in each family’s living area. With no maps and no infrastructure, it was unclear how far deep and where. Using open-source satellite imagery and machine learning, I detected the locations of 500 living units. 100 rainwater harvesting units have been deployed this year.

Looking back, my conversation with Deepak was the spark that ignited a transformation I hadn’t anticipated. I started this journey wanting to help, but as I’ve walked alongside the Maasai, I’ve realized that this work isn’t just about providing water—it’s about reshaping my understanding of responsibility. I’ve witnessed the power of technology combined with empathy and action. Just yesterday I smiled when Joseph messaged “I am starting nursing school”. There is still so much to be done—more units to deploy, new technologies to integrate, more lives to change.

My heart was palpitating, and I nervously glanced at the school gate, and then back at my textbook. As the clock struck five, the lights went out. Under the cover of darkness, I filed into the stuffy classroom to secretly repeat everything I had learned to more than twenty girls from my neighborhood aged 14 to 17. I worried that the Taliban, who banned education for all girls, might come to check on the school. My eyes remained chained to the gate. I stayed vigilant since the lighting was poor, and danger was always lurking in the shadows. For the last year and a half, I lived in fear, knowing I would be tortured and lose my education if we were discovered.

While I worried about the girls’ future, my parents were afraid for my safety. The first time I stood against my parents’ will, I advocated for the girls’ right to continue attending the crammed classroom. This courage definitely comes from those times that we sang songs, played truth or dare, engaged in hopscotch and watched movies on Thursdays that made this small community worth not less than a family. Despite the insistence, I pushed on, spending hours preparing and creating engaging lessons and activities in order to set a kinesthetic learning environment. I had taken a survey and had given them questionnaires through which I figured out their learning style. During my vacation and on holidays, I would help them to review their UWC scholarship applications. An invaluable opportunity to study IB abroad. Six of them were shortlisted for interviews as a result.

I was raised by my father to believe that education was the cornerstone of personal growth, and to know that my female peers had been denied this right and pushed into marriage encouraged me to continue working in risky ways. We could only contact each other via encrypted messages online, but half of the girls could not afford a connection. I spent one third of my own salary $60 from an internship to cover their internet fee for a few months. Because they couldn’t go to school and online education was not feasible for them. I talked to several principals in my region to see if they were inclined in donating. I was nearly giving up while I understood they were unable to help. My mind was scratching, pondering to see how I can find a way to work out this issue. Suddenly, an idea came to my mind, to start STEM online education through International Students STEM Organization. I spoke to my friend Abigail and we decided to hold a Zoom meeting, where I proposed the opinion. As the founders and Presidents, we opened a GoFundMe fundraising campaign. Together, we raised $1,362 to cover the girls’ internet fees monthly.

In the evening class, Maryam and Zinab stayed calm and did not participate in the activities. I asked myself am I not doing enough? But a few days later, I noticed Maryam shed her shyness and eagerly enter into discussions after our Friday stream of consciousness sessions to hearing Zinab become motivated through her own engagement. Compared to my lasting fear, I became strong enough to continue this educational quest and all my free time has now become dedicated to creating programs for the girls and even teaching in secret during the weekends. Although fear of punishment constantly consumed me, my heart is warmed seeing Maryam and Zinab rediscover their love of education.

I don’t let fear rule my future. I strive to someday ensure that education is not only a right for all Afghans, but for everyone regardless of age, gender or race. In college, I will continue to strengthen this belief. Reality and danger never prevent me from doing exactly what I believe is the right thing to do. After witnessing all twenty-seven girls hone the capacity to navigate the constant obstacles, I am proud of us.

**Lemon Juice + Baking Soda = ???**

Instead of the blast I braced for, I heard the explosion of my teacher’s voice: “ETHAN, WHAT DID I JUST TELL THE CLASS NOT TO DO!”

I loved the vivid revelation of the reaction’s resonance and rhythm; yet that night, my parents labeled me a “problem child.” Until then, I had always adhered to their expectations. When they told me to stop dismantling arcade machines and hunting for Pokémon cards in local flea shops, I buried my passions under their approval.

But if I hadn’t gone through with that experiment, I would have never experienced that vitality I thought had faded away. Standing there, still smelling like lemon juice, the lines between being a good son and being true to myself blurred. I questioned who I was really trying to be—and I wasn’t sure I liked the answer.

Determined to bridge the gap I now felt with my parents, I hosted family-nights filled with playful reenactments of Moana and the occasional offbeat sing-alongs to Frozen’s “Let It Go.”

But when our dinner table remained thick with unspoken tension, I turned toward deciphering human connection. Countless 1 A.M. readings about repressed emotions and psychotherapy became my refuge for lucid-dreams. As I devoured TED talks from psychologists like Eleanor Longden, I uncovered concepts like intrapsychic conflict. How could I make my parents understand me? Maybe I had to first understand them.

I discovered the brain is more than its physiological intricacies; it’s the traversing medium for the psychic heart. Mirroring the emotions of others, the brain intertwines our internal states with those around us. As I dived into studies on affective empathy, I learned from organizational psychologist Adam Grant that mutual understanding and generosity are key to repairing broken bonds. The next time my mom said, “I don’t want you spending the entire day at the flea market,” I didn’t complain or comply. Instead, I asked myself what lay beneath her words. Her concerns hinted at deeper fears of me drifting into my own world, fears of watching her son grow increasingly distant.

The following weekend, I invited my parents to the flea market. As we entered its chaotic atmosphere, I noticed my mom nervously lingering at the entrance.

“Why don’t we check out that booth?” I suggested, nodding towards a modest stall. She hesitated, but soon followed. I picked up a familiar vase, its floral pattern evoking a nostalgic memory. “Mom, remember the blue orchids I gave you last Mother’s Day?” She looked at the vase, flickers of recognition flashing in her eyes.

“They died quickly,” she replied, her voice softening. I held the vase out to her. “What if we tried again?” The question hung in the air until she eventually grabbed the vase. “We should,” she agreed, warmth breaking through her expression as we embraced the idea together.

Reinvigorated, we navigated the bustling market, finding common-ground amid the vintage trinkets. I eagerly led Mom and Dad to my favorite stall of Pokémon cards (this time they shared in my joy). Together, we laughed as my dad donned a distressed clown mask, his faded-red nose bobbing comically like Tigger from Winnie the Pooh.

As dusk soon came and we left the market, I found that it was through inviting my parents into my world that I had finally built a bridge between us. By interpreting their words with generosity, I shared my vulnerabilities, unearthing the complexities behind my “problem-child” label. It was embracing my true self and finding shared moments that reconciled our unspoken differences.

This lesson has enriched my work in Nigeria, where communities shattered by child loss face disease, inadequacies in healthcare, and contaminated water. Encouraging members to share their stories, I foster spaces for healing, transforming individual sorrow into communal strength. In these moments, I watch as families unite to confront their shared challenges, lighting a path toward a better future for all of us.

“Place the basket under the counter,” the cashier snapped at my mom, frustrated by her limited English. Shaking his head, he muttered, “Do I have to say it in Chinese?” Sensing the anti-Asian sentiment that was rampant during the pandemic four years ago, I wanted to confront him, but my mom quietly paid, and we left.

I was frustrated with my mom for holding me back. “In America, not speaking up is seen as a weakness,” I told her. But my mom disagreed, offering traditional wisdom: Wae Yu Nae Gang—have inner strength and a gentle exterior. Seeing how far apart we were culturally triggered years of internal struggle to reconcile my conflicting values.

Initially, I tried to “go all American.” Throughout eighth grade, I rejected anything Korean, even refusing to speak Korean in public. Eventually, I realized I couldn’t erase years of upbringing. Living without my culture felt empty, and it became too agonizing to hold out. I accepted that I am Korean, after all.

As I began high school, I fully embraced my identity and grew comfortable sharing it with friends. My friend Tony nearly cried when he tried Buldak Ramyun—a fiery instant noodle—but now he’s a fan. I also showed off my BTS dance routines and sang their Korean lyrics for my friends. In those moments, I felt like my true self. This was home.

Even as I reveled in this rediscovery, I couldn’t shake the memory of that day at the supermarket—a reminder that beyond the comfort of friends and school, the real world loomed. I wondered if leaning into my Korean identity wasn’t a way of avoiding harsh realities. These reflections made me realize my internal conflict wasn’t about choosing between two values but understanding their nature. What does it mean to be Asian American? If I don’t understand who I am, how can I expect others to?

Books like Minor Feelings by Cathy Park Hong and The Making of Asian America by Erika Lee deepened my understanding of Asian American history and culture. However, my curiosity extended beyond books—I wanted to see how my cultural identity manifested in the real world.

For me, the clues came through my social involvements. I began teaching Korean to sixth graders at my church, recognizing that language is key to understanding culture. Encouraged by my friends’ growing interest in my Asian American stories, I organized our school’s first-ever Asian American heritage exhibition, showcasing generations of family photos and artifacts as president of the AAPI Club. I served as a panel member on K-Your Personal Achievement Radio Talk Show, discussing whether enjoying K-pop or Korean food makes us any less American. Most recently, after my Chinese teacher, Ms. Yang, highlighted the lack of political support for teaching Asian American history in schools, I launched a passion project this past summer to petition the California Legislature for its inclusion in public education.

Although these experiences began with my curiosity about my cultural identity, they ultimately gave me the inner strength my mom spoke of. The confidence I gained from sharing knowledge, the beaming pride on my student’s face when she won a Korean writing competition, the connections I built with friends as we relived tense moments during the LA Riots, the celebratory high-fives after closing the Asian American exhibition, and the electrifying sense of validation I felt when my survey revealed overwhelming support for including Asian American history in curricula—those moments were far more powerful and fulfilling than any confrontation with that cashier could ever have been.

My internal struggle between competing values taught me it’s not which values I choose but how I practice each—not using them to avoid challenges but taking them head on, leveraging my inner strength. Moving forward, I’m committed to embracing all aspects of my identity and advocating for the Asian American community while building solidarity with the diverse communities I will encounter in college.

Before my mother could call me, I would rush down the stairs lured in by the fragrant aroma and a hungry belly. By the time I made it to the living room, my family would be waiting, and we would surround the big rondeau pot anticipating to feast on my mother's savory chicken biryani. We enjoyed the food and enjoyed ourselves; laughed over cartoons and talked more than any period of the day. To me, biryani filled more than my belly.

It had been weeks since I last ate my mother’s food. An argument came crashing like a tsunami and I had been displaced from my family. Taken away by the engulfing power of Child Protective Services, I was put into foster care. Fortunately, I was taken care of by a family friend.

I called him Uncle and his family was warm and accepting, and did not question my circumstances. This does not mean everything flowed smoothly, I missed my parents and had to make changes to my life; some minor, and some major. The biggest change was adopting their vegetarian lifestyle.

The dishes they made were familiar but I couldn’t see myself being familiar with only eating vegetarian food. They followed vegetarianism due to religious constraints, and I respected their commitment; however never being able to experience the juicy, tender chew of meat wasn’t something for me. I didn’t know if I could manage, but I had to try.

Instead of shying away from unfamiliar vegetables, I always made sure to eat all of them, not only, to appreciate their efforts but also to acquaint myself with various flavors I had no prior interest in. Slowly, childhood nemeses turned into delectable friendships; broccoli didn't seem so bad, and bitter gourd not so bitter.

I was reunited with my family. I felt whole again, as if I had returned to my original self, but also different. After living several months without meat, I expected there to be a warm reconciliation with becoming nonvegetarian again, but I held a newfound disgust.

After being a vegetarian for eight months, reading Michael Pollan’s The Omnivore’s Dilemma inspired me to change my long-held eating habits. Pollan went into depth on the cruelties committed against the well-being of farm animals. I was especially devastated when I understood and researched the harsh reality of chickens. They were confined in an eternal prison, cramped together, with no sunlight or fresh air until they were slaughtered, packaged, and eventually ended up in my mother’s biryani.

After settling back home, this dark secret gnawed at my mind. I realized I could not be blissfully ignorant and continue eating meat so I took a stand.

A week after returning, my mother made a special chicken biryani dinner to commemorate being together again. A momentous dinner meant for a special occasion. I tried discreetly scooping only the rice onto my plate without adding any chicken. However, I was caught.

It took some time to convince my parents to let me stop eating meat. They said I needed protein and that making separate veg food would take extra time. I relented and stood my ground stating there was protein in plants with the added benefit of essential micronutrients that couldn’t be found in animals. I showed them documentaries on the cruelties done to farm animals and the benefits of eating a vegetarian diet. Finally, I told my mother about simple dishes I learned from living in Uncle’s house. They saw my passion and protests during dinner and allowed me to be a vegetarian.

It may have meant learning how to cook, having to prepare my own food, and accompanying my mom on grocery trips, but if it meant I wouldn’t need to partake in harming beings who deserved no harm, even if it meant just one less person adding chicken on their grocery list, I felt I could make a difference.

The basement steps felt like the edge of a cliff.

I heard my name called from downstairs—my dad. He stood at the bottom, saying he wanted to talk to me about something he used to do: programming competitions. The second I heard those words, my mind went blank. I stood atop the stairs, clenching the railing as hard as I could even though I had walked down those steps hundreds of times. For the past four years, I had poured myself into the hardware side of robotics. The thought of switching to something new, something so distant from what I knew so well, terrified me. I wasn’t about to let go of the one thing I felt comfortable with.

I knew this was important to him, so I decided to give it a shot, with the intention of just trying it and then returning to what I knew best. He showed me the setup, gave me some resources, and left me to it. Alone, I sat there, staring at the computer, thinking back to gear, screws, and chains I felt familiar with. Every night, I’d tell him what practice problems I completed, as if checking off a box. But there were moments, often unexpected, when I’d solve a problem or figure out some trick and feel a tiny something. It was strange—I wanted to walk away from this, but I just quite couldn’t. I didn’t know if it was the urge to impress him or some unfamiliar pull drawing me in.

In a few days, there was going to be an online competition. Dad said he would participate in it too. But when I saw the close to ten thousand people already registered, my fingers trembled, struggling to control the mouse. I stared at the number, my heart racing, as the timer on the screen kept counting down. Yet, it didn’t make sense. If I truly wanted to leave this like I first intended to, why would I be afraid? In thought, the countdown reached zero and I scrambled to click the little “Enter Contest” button. When I finally clicked it, it was like crossing a barrier that I didn’t know I cared about. Seeing my name on the scoreboard, even if it was closer to the bottom than the top, gave me reassurance that I belonged. The fear of leaving behind what I knew was fading. I was still far from where I wanted to be on that scoreboard, but now, there was promise.

In the following months, I kept going. Letting go of the doubt, I genuinely enjoyed going down the list of problems, learning a new algorithm, technique, or trick with each one. It was just me now; I wasn’t doing it as a chore. Sometimes I would get stuck, staring at the screen like I did before. It made me frustrated, even question myself, but that initial grasping fear was gone. I looked at the screen now thinking about the problem at hand, not the intention of leaving.

Looking back now, years later, I realized pushing through that initial reluctance and fear gave me something I truly enjoy. What I first thought of as annoying, my dad asking me to give it a shot, gave me the little bit of strength to go past what I was comfortable with. That little nudge can make all the difference, and it’s what I aim to offer to students in my competitive programming club. Just like my dad did for me, I do contests alongside students to encourage them to move past any fear they may have. As I move on to broader scopes, I hope to continue bringing that gentle push, guiding those around me to move towards new frontiers. Yet no matter how far, I will always remember standing at the top of those basement steps, unsure of just how far they’d take me.

Growing up, my family was always busy elsewhere. My brother, ten years older than me, was always out somewhere else with his friends. My father, who had come to America only to find his agriculture degree suddenly useless, would dedicate countless hours studying programming to get himself a job. And on the days my mother couldn’t drive me to school, I would find myself waving goodbye endlessly even after her car had disappeared around the corner of our dead end.

In my free time, I would read and watch cartoons about other kids exploring forests and rivers with their neighbors’ kids and wandering from one place to the next. In my neighborhood, however, the great outdoors constituted one-way streets piled with cars and the occasional row of trees, and there was no one besides my brother below the age of thirty on my street. Even then, he eventually left for college when I was eight.

I was still young, but I had to learn to make do with myself. This often involved exploring things on my own. Why does my bicycle balance when I pedal, but not when I stay still? Why does the small Lego fire truck move faster than the bigger one when I push it?

When I got my first laptop at age ten, I was exposed to a whole new world, and I was no longer limited by my physical street. I could also finally get the answers to any new questions I had within a minute’s search, whether through YouTubers like Veritasium or Minute Physics or online forums like Stack Exchange. Through them, I discovered Fourier series, refraction, and relativity. These concepts involved math and intuition I didn’t quite understand yet, but I was captivated by physics from the start.

At the same time, I was also getting into programming. Both my father and brother would spend hours writing line upon line of code, and I wanted to learn too. After I read through a tutorial off W3Schools, my first program, which simply printed “Hello World” onto a black and white console, was certainly not the grandest thing ever, but it had made a lasting impression on me. I dived deeper and deeper into the world of programming, creating Connect4 games and chemical equation balancers. Similar to physics’s ability to describe our natural world, I was fascinated by computer science’s potential to create a digital landscape.

As I grew older and entered my first physics class in tenth grade, I started to fully appreciate the nuances of physics. Suddenly, I could model how an object falls or break down the torque behind something as simple as opening a door. Physics was much more than just formulas; it was a way to decode the world around me. I wasn’t content just understanding it—I wanted physics to be a part of my everyday life. As my coding skills grew alongside my newfound physics knowledge, I began coding collision simulators and robot lift programs that made use of both physics and programming to bring the concepts I’d learned to life.

Growing up, I had always longed for the same social experience that everybody else seemed to have. I longed for the nasty sibling fights, the exciting outdoor adventures, the ability to just walk next door and have somebody my age to talk to. But now, I realize that it was what was once a burden of an isolated life that ultimately sparked the drive in me to explore, take initiative, and ultimately break out of the confines of my dead end. Now, I break out of my chains, into the future—studying computer science and physics as I look to be the difference for another eight-year-old boy longing for more.

“Mom, could you drop me to the park to play basketball with my friends?”

“Can’t right now. You're 17 years old and should have gotten your license.”

In Florida, there are over 16 million licensed drivers, but I am still not one of them. That’s because I failed the Florida Driver's License Test. Let me explain.

When most of my friends started getting their permits at 15, they celebrated, repeatedly singing Olivia Rodrigo banger, “I got my driver's license last week,” flexing their latest achievement. By the time you read this, I’ll have turned 18—still without a license, still hearing my friends echo that song in my head. Whenever I mentioned my unlicensed status, my friends’ reactions were always the same: shock.

"You haven’t got your license yet? Get your life together!”

“If it were the AP Driver’s License Test, you would’ve passed it with a 5."

“All you gotta do is say the importance of wearing your seatbelt.”

“Guess it's true, common sense is not so common after all.”

And the bantering kept on coming. Usually, I brushed these comments off, but eventually, it got to me and I started to wonder—why did I fail?

On that regular Saturday morning, I had walked into the DMV nonchalantly, arriving an hour early, hoping to get in and out quickly, but the line was an eternity. Instead of using that time to learn the material, I dove into my other interests. I watched videos about the logistics of moving the world’s largest building, learned about the ethical implications of semiconductors, and even studied for next week's biology quiz. By the time I took the test, well… the rest is history.

So, did I fail because I didn’t study during those two crucial hours? Not entirely. There’s more to it. Normally, when I have an exam, I’m laser-focused. I prioritize it. But this time, I really didn’t care. Not once was I excited about getting my license, unlike my friends, who couldn't wait to hit the road. I never dreamt of driving to Key West or navigating the mayhem of Florida traffic. My mind was always elsewhere—buried in academics, ethical dilemmas, and random trivia topics.

I was so absorbed in my academic life and hobbies that I forgot about the practical importance of real life. Even if I consider myself to be an “academic warrior,” that doesn’t always translate into success in the real world.

I had more than enough time to prepare for the DMV test, but I kept putting it off. I treated the DMV test like a casual walk-in without bothering to study at all. That overconfidence became my downfall. I was living in a world where I believed intellect was my shield, thinking it would carry me through the DMV test, but instead, I was humbled. Intelligence alone doesn't solve every problem. As Aristotle wisely said, “The more you know, the more you realize you don’t know.”

Now, every time I finish school at 4:30, I race across the street just not to miss the public bus. It's a constant reminder of my failure and the lesson I learned: nothing in life is so simple that you can just wing it. Whether it’s academics, cooking, or passing a “simple” driver’s test, you must commit to it with your whole heart and effort.

Bill Gates once said, “Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose.” My overconfidence and single-minded focus on my interest made me overlook the basics. But life simply doesn’t work that way. That's the beauty of it, everything has to be earned not given.

Now, by the time you’re reading this, I’ve already booked my driver’s license test for December—just after my birthday. This time, I’ll be ready. Then, I’ll be able to go play basketball with my friends anytime I want.

It's 9 pm on a Tuesday– I am 15 and spread starfish on the cool floor. My cheeks are a rosy shade of pink, my limbs feel like jelly, and all of the stress, adrenaline, and exhaustion from the past 24 hours melt off of me as I mold with the cool hardwood.

My mom looms over me, blocking the soft ceiling light. Don’t say it, don't say it. Let me rest, Please. “P, up. Now. Your fundraiser is tomorrow. The musubi won’t make itself.”

***

Growing up, musubi had always been our dish. Although we were both no strangers to the kitchen– I, an avid baker; she, an excellent chef. No dish had ever brought us shoulder to shoulder, cooking together like musubi had.

We would start in the evening, soon after she returned late from work. Enraptured and overjoyed by the rice, nori, and musubi that littered our kitchen, I wouldn't even glance up to see the setting sun or notice the house slowly falling into a slumber. This experience I associated so strongly with comfort that I jumped at any opportunity to make musubi together.

But somewhere, as middle turned to high school and 123 grades turned to ABCs, making the dish became tedious, more like a chore. Along with varsity basketball, where one missed free throw earns us a 30 second sub liner and liquid legs; volunteering, where dozens of kids rush at me screaming the lyrics to “This Little Light of Mine” (last week’s song); and tutoring, where my fifth grader “Emery” runs circles around me as I try to explain the correct order of adjectives; The musubi became just another box to check off on my growing to-do list. I had completely forgotten its original flavor.

***

At the end of the night, around 1 am, my head begins to droop and my eyes burn with the salt of spam and sweat– but a job started must always be finished. 6 hours later I’m out the door– backpack around my shoulders, posters held under my pointer finger by sheer will, and a 2 by 4 box in my hands filled with 200 musubi.

Hundreds of people stop at our beat-up plastic table– some to browse and some to buy. Regardless, their eyes light up with excitement in the face of our 200 musubi pyramid. After handing me a crisp $5 bill, they unwrap the sticky saran to unveil the gorgeous stack of seaweed, rice, and spam underneath. With one bite a smile stretches across their face and they all share the same sweet grin of satisfaction as they indulge in the musubi filled with love and my own history.

The joy spread across their faces is so reminiscent of my own before the act of making musubi was buried in my overflowing plate. Looking back, just a glance to the side would have broken my “perfect” musubi illusion– my mom’s tired eyes, heavy sighs, and shifts from side to side as she attempted to relieve the soles of her feet were all too apparent to anyone outside of myself. Nevertheless, she stayed by my side, toiling away in the dark of night to create small squares of heaven that forever encapsulated our memories in its flavor.

***

For the first 15 years of my life musubi was “my” thing: I made it with my mom and I made it for others. But perhaps musubi was never about me at all, it always has been and always will be a dish defined by the people I share it with. A staple for my mom and I to bond over, a meal to be shared between teammates, a fundraiser foundation that connects us to something greater, and a reminder to follow through and appreciate those who have followed through for me.

I will continue to form these “musubis” in my life– striving to make connections stronger than the nori that wraps the musubi tight and even deeper than the giant vats of white rice that have filled my childhood.

I failed the first test I ever took; it was a test I didn't even know I was taking. Ten days after I was born, I was diagnosed with bilateral profound hearing loss. It meant I couldn’t hear anything, not even a jet airplane. At ten months old, I received cochlear implants, for which I am eternally grateful. The implants allow sound to travel through electronic signals to my auditory nerve, where my brain takes over. The journey between silence and sound has defined much of my life.

My ability to choose silence has been one unexpected gift of receiving cochlear implants. When I disconnect the headpieces, I experience quiet, bliss, and focus that few others can understand. Without my “ears,” I can run faster, study harder, and dive into my latest novel without distraction. I have learned to cherish these moments. When I reconnect, I immerse myself in the world through learning, music, and engaging with others, fully aware of the preciousness of sound.

The road to sound, however, was challenging. Even though I received cochlear implants at a very young age, I still had to spend over 800 hours in therapy learning to talk and listen. Each word mastered was a hard-fought lesson in perseverance. That might sound grim, but I remember the sessions as joyful, filled with detailed conversations about snowmen, dolls, and monkey bars. Catching up with my hearing peers built a work ethic that continues to drive me.

My journey didn't stop at learning to talk and listen. Participating in scientific research has been a way for me to blaze a trail for others while validating my skills, and as a bonus, researchers pay in Amazon gift cards. I have been referred to as a "poster child," a "curve buster," and an "outlier" in the best way. My first study, aptly named The Baby Lab, involved me toddling around a toy-filled room, an audio recorder strapped to my chest. Researchers celebrated every utterance, tracking my language development, executive function, and quality of input.

Since that first lab, I have participated in more than 15 studies nationwide, from Madison to Nashville and Omaha to Arizona. With each experience, I learned about research—how it worked, who it helped, and how I can impact the future. One of the most significant studies I joined took me 750 miles from home. Researchers tweaked the electrodes in my cochleas for three years to enhance my hearing. I was not just a participant. I was contributing to science, which transformed my life by improving my hearing capabilities and growing my passion for discovery. It introduced me to world-renowned professionals and made me a pioneer in testing hearing technology.

Hearing loss ultimately led me to join my public school’s Science Focus Program, be a leader on our state championship speech team, and win a scholarship for my talk on optimism. These activities help me practice and flex the skills I have been working on for a lifetime. It feels poetic and paradoxical that language has become one of my greatest strengths, and listening to music one of my favorite activities.

As a mentor to families choosing cochlear implants, I share my journey’s ups and downs. I want to give them hope and practical tools to help their children thrive. I encourage families to fill their homes with sound, engage in conversation, and maximize early brain and language development. For me, the support of my family, friends, and teachers has been vital. They helped me push beyond my limits and discover that vulnerability and strength go hand-in-hand.

My journey from silence to sound is a lesson of determination. It illustrates the transformative power of science, highlights my ability to rewrite the journey, and helps to define my future research aspirations. I look forward to turning more obstacles into opportunities and passing every test that comes my way.

When you love to do something, you want to do it every day until you’re sick of it. Like that one song on repeat in your Spotify playlist or a TV show you can’t stop watching. The song I have on repeat is painting.

Walking into my room you’ll find jars of turpentine on the dresser and oil paint staining the carpet. I’ll be at my desk, with a small mirror by my side that I use to study my own movements as I simultaneously sketch the protrusions of my knuckles and the hollow of my ears onto a page. Sketchbook after sketchbook, I captured the most overlooked details of my life on paper.

It’s undeniable; I have an addiction.

“What are you gonna do with all these books?” my dad asked one day while looming over the stack of pages next to me.

“I don’t know, publish them?” I answered jokingly.

Publishing my art has always been a distant fantasy. I came from a family of doctors, engineers, and statisticians. Growing up in a world of black and white and nonfiction debate, pursuing art felt like a rebellion against my heritage. Yet, I couldn’t stop making art. Part of me looked up to the fact that Fridah Kahlo didn’t start painting until she was 18 and that Monet only started in his 40’s.

I couldn’t help but think, what if it wasn’t just some childhood fantasy?

Fast forward to junior year, I found myself officially earning the title of ‘artist’. It was the day before my painting The Girl With the Bucket was ready to be shipped to Capitol Hill for the Congressional Art Exhibition. Staring into the red crimson painting in front of me, all I saw was a canvas and a blank artist statement next to me. When it came to definitions, I found myself back in that polarized world; explaining why I paint in one paragraph suddenly became harder than actually painting.

I continued drafting my statement all throughout the morning with fragmented sentences until my next class: Calculus. As soon as class starts, the board immediately becomes filled with mathematical symbols, equations, and diagrams arranged neatly in sections, a structure that brought a sense of order to the chaos of my earlier thoughts. Watching this process unfold, I realized that painting, in its way, was just like Calculus: both required deep planning, executing a solution, and presenting that solution to others. While in painting, each stroke is carefully considered to bring my vision to life, in Calculus, each line is built towards a final solution. Standing up at the board, I began to write the solution to the problem with my hand moving as if I was holding a paintbrush, formulating line after line until finally crafting a complete picture. With the final step completed, I took a step back like I did with a finished painting, feeling the sensation of achievement and successful creative expression. Art was unlike any other subject I loved so much in school. Yet, I began to notice even more parallels in my other classes: the assembly of detail in the anatomy texts for Biology, the physics behind every optical illusion of perceived depth, and the narrative analyzed scrupulously in English.

I realized that art was not so different from other professions I isolated so harshly. I may not come from a family of traditional artists, but behind the empathy my dad builds with his patients and the narratives my mother writes through data points, artistry is in my blood.

Years ago, I couldn’t explain the definition of an artist. Today, when I become an artist, I also become a mathematician, physician, and storyteller. Being an artist allows me to dream extravagantly, yet with the spirit to materialize it. With my brushes and paint by my side, I am ready to blend the world of art and science into something extraordinary.

I was mid-bite through my celery stick when Mrs. Kinsey asked our class why the vegetable was so tough to chew. Her question was one that I had never thought to ask—a fact oblivious since the day I discovered celery. Mrs. Kinsey’s questions kickstarted my new personal quest: rather than seeking just answers, I began seeking questions instead.

My trivia mindset strengthened when I was studying for Science Olympiad. I supplemented my learning through real-world connections and discovered new interests in my day-to-day life. While exploring topics that piqued my interest, I found myself revisiting Mrs. Kinsey’s first trivia question after eight years: Why is celery stringy? This time though, I was determined to have an answer longer than two alien words I could barely pronounce: “xylem” and “collenchyma.” In search of more explanations behind earth's natural phenomena, I taught myself botany, and soon, I began to self-learn other advanced concepts of biology and chemistry, chasing every opportunity that fed me the answers that school left unanswered.

Determined to chase this dream, I found myself 2000 miles away from home at the UC Davis Young Scholars Program. In my world of computational chemistry, before I found success in the technical aspect of coding, I prioritized understanding how my code translated to real-world scenarios. I found these answers through reading research papers, finally allowing me to uncover the current impact science was making in the world. But it took me hours to digest a full paper. In every sentence I read, I paused to decipher an endless amount of scientific jargon; in every citation I came across, I tunneled down a rabbit hole of related papers. I thought back to Mrs. Kinsey’s trivia game where I found pride in grasping concepts and being able to explain it easily to others. To relive this excitement, I incorporated similar ideas to improve my readings: I brought my code to life through the lens of journal concepts and its impact on people. The once scrambled anagram of letters in my code mirrored the wet lab methods listed in papers, and the once confusing set of dancing molecules mirrored the molecular interactions I read about in journals.

I spent the next summer at UT Austin, again happily surrounded by an endless access to top-of-the-class research. With my newfound skill, I met with professors and read their papers from various fields of science. I was determined to share all my new perspectives on how research was currently advancing our world. Knowing that papers are usually dense and intimidating, I wanted to spark the curiosity of students in a fun way, especially for the younger audience. I created a YouTube channel called “The Abstract”—which acts like an abstract of a paper—a peek into cool science for anyone to explore further.

While volunteering in Mrs. Kinsey’s old room, I wanted to pass forward the curiosity she sparked in her students. Through a 15-minute video, I condensed the college-level course of materials science into concepts 4th graders could easily grasp and find fascination in, explaining why the Apple Watch had a green light through fun animations. When I was faced by their wonder-filled eyes and specific questions, I knew I had effectively taught the students to question their daily observations with science.

No matter the changes Mrs. Kinsey’s room may undergo, the memories that strengthened my passion for learning will always remain. In the moments I find myself snacking on celery, I wish I could go back and thank her for the curiosity she passed on to me. Starting from within her room, I will pass on the lessons Mrs. Kinsey taught me so that science can become more than just an abstract concept.

“We are products of our past, but we don't have to be prisoners of it.” - Rick Warren

Throughout high school, I always thought pure talent would take me far. For a while, I gave little effort compared to my classmates because I could keep up academically.
