I soon discovered that talent alone is not enough to achieve ultimate success. I began to see my peers catch up, and some even surpassed me academically. I started reflecting on myself, concluding that establishing success would take my best effort.

I had always been a helping hand for my classmates because they knew how academically gifted I was, but over time, people less frequently came to me in need of assistance because they had decided that it was crucial to focus on self-improvement rather than relying on others to forge their path to success. Eventually, I realized that I would never learn from my mistakes if I continued to believe that being talented was enough to succeed.

I tried out for the debate team during my sophomore year in high school, and I qualified because barely any people were trying to participate anyway. A couple of months later, I went to my first tournament. I despised public speaking, but I was confident because I thought arguing so much with my friends and family for fun over the years would be a solid foundation for debate. I had no idea who my competition was, but I believed nobody was good enough to beat anyone from my school. The moment I heard my opponent’s speech, I felt like somebody punched me in the liver. I was supposed to give a rebuttal and ask questions regarding my opponent’s speech during cross-examination. However, I sat in my chair, paralyzed from realizing he had just destroyed me. I finally decided to forfeit and left the room in a hurry.

On my way back to join the rest of the team, I contemplated everything that had happened within the past fifteen minutes. My friends came over and asked how my round went, and all I could say was, “I just got obliterated.” As I sat down, waiting for everyone else to finish competing, I re-evaluated myself as a student and a person. I realized that I had lived sixteen years without ever experiencing defeat as harshly as I had done moments ago. I told myself that if I participated in a debate tournament without doing any preparation on the topic or solidifying my speech, I would never become a top contender in the district.

As a result of this experience, I changed my mindset from believing in pure talent to actually using it by applying it while I studied to prepare for something instead of just winging it. A fire ignited inside me, burning with determination to capitalize on this new mindset as I completed my high school education. The process of reaching new heights began, and along the way, new perspectives contributed to my academic success. People pave their own paths to success, so I strived to understand others’ points of view to forge my own path. After looking through multiple lenses, I was reassured that nothing could obstruct my road to success, enabling me to surpass my classmates academically again. The road began when I was ranked tenth in my class, and as I kept applying the new mindset in my studies, I progressed to rank three. This climb was challenging due to the difficulties I experienced as I adjusted to high school. Through this journey, my strengthened mental resilience allowed for this constant improvement.

To this day, I maintain the mindset that learning requires humility; otherwise, I would not be at the top of my class. Although I have experienced the consequences of defeat, I will inevitably face defeat many more times in life. It is too early for me to conclude that I have learned my lesson, but I know that next time errors and defeat come my way, I will be prepared to face the consequences and respond in a way that will help me grow not only as a college student but as a human being.

My hair levitated majestically behind me as I fearlessly galloped my horse up the mountain, peering at the world around me. I was Zendaya in the Lancome-Idole Fragrance ad. Alas, it was an eighth-grade daydream. Still, this ignited my horseback riding fervor and deeper understanding of marginalized voices.

Riding lessons started as a fantasy, but reality soon set in. My idealistic vision quickly shattered as I endured distrustful horse-kicks and numerous falls. But dreams become reality through hard work. Brushing and cleaning the horses' hooves diligently led to fewer kicks and an affectionate nibble or two. Fiona, a large white horse, ultimately rested her head on me, nudging for a pat. Stroking her, I was ecstatic about finally being accepted, promising to never take this feeling for granted.

A few months passed. I was loved by Fiona and her friends. Accepted in their world, I developed a passion for helping others find the belongingness I experienced. To make a difference, I embraced the role of Handita in "Amma's Ashes," a film about a queer teen, Gump, navigating a conservative family. My values deeply resonated with Handita's (Gump's teen cousin), supporting my friends like Nathaniel, who are teased for their identities. When someone yelled the "F-slur" at Nathaniel in the mall, his sheepish smile tried to mask his deep longing for acceptance. I warmly hugged him, affirming that I'd always be there for him.

Fracturing my collarbone on the first filming day, I was ambivalent about whether to fight through the excruciating pain. But, hearing our stylist Luka's story of being denied service in a bar for being non-binary, my decision was clear. I had to continue for the film's timely release, especially for the South-Asian community, who needed the message to help break away from identity prejudices.

"Amma's Ashes" premiered at Sacramento's historic Crest Theatre in October 2022, winning several global accolades. I was glad to have contributed to creating a more inclusive community through the film's widespread impact.

Our debut director, Gaya, warmly hugged me for persevering through her dream project despite my critical fracture, silently acknowledging my resilience. She reminded me of my bond with Fiona, where subtle gestures speak volumes. When Fiona fidgets, I adjust her harness. She raises her hind leg; I give her space. Riding for five years, she's comfortable relinquishing her reins to me. I can understand her unspoken language.

Comprehending Fiona has allowed me to hear people through their silence, especially my neurodiverse music students at WeEmbrace, whom I've been mentoring for four years. On my first day, Manav threw Legos at me. Seeing him with a fire truck, I played a firefighter song that lit up his face instantly, and we started bonding from that moment. Another student, Anurag, unfailingly refused to participate in class. Knowing his love for vacuum cleaners, I incentivized his time, promising to let him use one after class. This motivated him to sing enthusiastically. I'm beyond proud of all my students, especially as they went from barely singing to performing in front of audiences at WeEmbrace events. Some personal knowledge about others and genuine empathy can help build heartfelt relationships. When Sakshi blinks fast, she's amused. When Raha covers her mouth, she wants to speak but is shy; I encourage her to speak up. I understand my students, and they see me as a trusted friend.

Walking. Trotting. Cantering. Galloping. Navigating through stages of horseback riding over the years, I experienced unbridled joy. Initially starting as a fantasy, riding has evolved into more than a skill; it's about forming bonds with my horses. Creating spaces of wholehearted acceptance and resilience, I strive to be a 'Fiona' for others. As I explore new horizons, I'm eager to take my horsemanship to probe the intricacies of human relationships with patience. I aim to continue mentoring others and embrace new challenges while galloping from my small realm to larger arenas.

Digging through stacks of paper, curled and worn from months of mental-health research, I took a deep breath and smiled to myself. The moment had come. Removing my laptop from my backpack—nestled alongside my familiar copy of Thoreau’s Walden—I finished final preparations for my Zoom with renowned sports psychologist Dr. Jonathan Fader. I expressed my admiration for his charismatic TedX talk and the effective strategies developed to help all of us perform at our highest potential—the same tools he teaches his elite athletes. Then, I posed the question at the heart of it all: "My generation is the most anxious and depressed on record, will you join my mission to equip us with the tools we need to face adversity and thrive?" During our conversation, he stressed the importance of building mental resilience in schools and was compelled to join Chasing Excellence: Fueling Success through Mental Wellness, the speaker series I founded to address the mental health crisis and combat stigma. His support propelled the initiative beyond what I had imagined.

Two years earlier, I was tasked with finding value-driven solutions to societal problems for a theology class. As I researched global issues, I wondered how teens could generate responses to crises even adults struggle to solve. But learning about young activists like Malala Yousafzai, who defied the Taliban to champion education for girls, inspired me. After discovering Amnesty International’s fight against human rights abuses in Saudi Arabia, I enlisted classmates to sign the "Free Saudi Arabia’s Voices of Change" petition, demanding the release of free-speech activists like Salma al-Shehab, unjustly imprisoned for advocating women's rights. Emboldened by taking action to impact an important cause, I began turning my attention to an issue that had plagued my community: mental health. Our school community was devastated when we lost, my best friend’s sister, to suicide, and I became determined to find ways to prevent such tragedies from happening again.

Recognizing that mental health struggles are often invisible, I devised an early intervention plan to host community-wide assemblies to capture our hard-to-reach teenage audience. With the core student council, I surveyed the student body to identify our most pressing concerns—like how unrelatable most materials are and how uncomfortable students feel seeking help from a guidance counselor. As I canvased the student body, Ava shared she was too embarrassed to seek help about her troubles surrounding her parent’s divorce. Tailoring the program to students’ needs, I resolved to erase the misconception that seeking help is weak and expand access to mental health experts - that were engaging and impactful.

After sending countless advocacy emails—and negotiating expensive speaking fees—I was thrilled to have Dr. Fader launch the series. Following his powerful talk, I watched students, including Ava, approach him with personal questions. It was a watershed moment for the series, proof that students were connecting and opening up as I’d hoped, learning we aren’t alone in our experiences. I signed on more thought-leaders addressing critical topics from 'Navigating Social Media to 'Defeating Your Inner Critic to Dealing with Toxic People. Each of these experts strengthened our foundation for mental wellness, which is crucial for unlocking our full potential and creating a better world together.

Returning to Walden as the speaker series unfolded, I realized how Thoreau’s philosophy of living life in its simplest terms—and finding your true self in the process—related to my own journey. I, too, aimed to live deliberately, honoring my values, striving to support others, and leading by example. Paving the way for my mission to continue long after I graduate, I’ve also proudly created an ambassador council as well as a business model and blueprint for other schools. Looking to my future academic home, my hope is to continue this platform to drive positive change to address our generation's health crisis. Seeing Chasing Excellence grow well past my greatest expectations has taught me that community action provides purpose, nourishes my spirit, and helps others flourish.

Clack. I flipped the light switch for the living room—it’s the opposite direction of the switch in my old house in Guangzhou, China. Slowly, the flickering light steadied to reveal couches covered in plastic, a tiny fireplace with blackened logs, and a round table surrounded by four wooden chairs.

That night, my dad cooked for us—tomato pasta, a dish we’d had many times. But in this unfamiliar place, it became our only nugget of familiarity. “In celebration of America!” my dad exclaimed as we sat around the table, staring at the mound of golden pasta, contemplating our futures in Gum Shan—Gold Mountain, as the Cantonese called San Francisco.

Clack. My dad had locked himself inside the study again. For the last eight years, I watched as my dad gave everything to chase his American dream—waking at unholy hours to catch the stock market, running errands, and collapsing into bed by evening. It took a toll on his health, both mental and physical. His eyes, heavy with dark bags, gave away the strain.

I couldn’t help but see myself in him—isolated and overwhelmed. I had felt the same way when I first arrived, struggling with the language and feeling like I had to do everything alone. But over time, I learned that connection, no matter how awkward, was the key to moving forward.

It was the first day of xc practice, and I just had the most unfortunate start by showing up unceremoniously late and rocking a misshapen buzz cut with a lopsided V on the back of my head. Suffice it to say that this bold fashion statement wasn’t exactly intentional (my mom was testing a new “fade” technique she’d just learned), but heck did my teammates chew me out for it (“let’s run behind [Name] because V is for VICTORY!!!”). For the first time in my life in the US, I was part of a team, even if my role was “the funny kid with the haircut that resembles victory”.

Through that experience, I learned to value my community and the support it offered. My dad, however, hadn’t yet experienced this in the U.S. I had become who I am today because of the guidance of others, and now it was my turn to guide him. As I contemplated how to bond with my dad, I thought back to the tomato pasta we’d eaten our first night in the U.S., and voila–cooking was one of my dad’s favorite pastimes, and he’d have to spend plenty of time teaching me, a complete amateur. With this in mind, I knocked on his door to pitch the idea to him.

The door flung open with surprising ease. Inside, the desks were yellowing at the edges, cluttered with pills, papers, and half-empty water bottles. My dad sat slumped at the far end, peeking at me behind his ten-year-old laptop.

“What do you need, Ah Go?” he asked in Cantonese.

“Dad, can you teach me how to cook?”

He paused, looking up at me, a hint of intrigue in his tired eyes before he turned back to his screen.

Silence. Did I annoy him? Should I leave? Doubts darted around in my head, but I stayed.

Suddenly, my dad let out a long sigh and shut his laptop.

“On second thought,” he said, “let’s cook. I’m hungry anyway.”

As he stood, there was a lightness about him, like he’d shrugged off a heavy burden.

Clack. My dad set the knife down as we admired his perfectly sliced tomatoes beside my misshapen ones. Perhaps he wanted to reminisce, because we decided to cook tomato pasta. As I manned the boiling pasta and my dad stirred the tomatoes, my stomach rumbled—not just for the meal, but for the renewed sense of hope in our relationship. My dad and I shared a smile for the first time in a long, long time.

I’m the person who swaps out garam masala for a dash of hot sauce in my mom’s biryani. My anti-traditionalism keeps me distant from cultural relics; however, today is different.

In India, Diwali brought our neighborhood together. Upon moving to the U.S., we clung to Diwali as a familiar constant amidst unfamiliarity. Here, my anti-traditionalist stance makes an exception.

As I walk downstairs, the scent of incense embraces me. My mother hands me a diya and my rebellion softens; I’m simply partaking in a tradition that’s larger than myself. Diwali isn’t just about lighting lamps; it’s about light over darkness, good over evil. In the flickering flame, I see the resilience and courage of my ancestors. Despite my instinct to rebel, this diya calls me to embrace these values. I set aside what felt “right” for so long, realizing that transformation comes from embracing the unfamiliar.

I face the mirror, noticing my kurta missing my preferred neutral colors. My “Clothing” Pinterest board would scoff, but I feel gratitude. Two years ago, this kurta felt like a costume--a reminder of my “otherness.” Now, it feels like a piece of home. Wearing it isn’t about abandoning who I am but integrating a deeper part of myself.

Recognizing the value of tradition, I step outside with fireworks, nerves tingling. This Diwali, I’m lighting the first fuse. I used to watch from the sidelines, but now, I feel bold, stepping into the role meant for me.

A rush of doubt hits me, causing jitteriness, but I push it aside. Those watching aren’t spectators--they’re family. This moment is about more than fireworks; it’s about embracing tradition and connecting to those before me.

As the fireworks burst, people cheer, drowning out the pops and crackles. As I’m surrounded by my loved ones, I feel more connected to my tradition than ever before. Everything feels right, and my sense of belonging intensifies, only made possible by embracing the unfamiliar.

Months later, I’m at Rockefeller University, preparing to present research on fear behavior in mice--ironically, while still managing my own--to a room of seasoned researchers. The daunting task stirs familiar nerves, echoing the hesitation I felt at Diwali. It wasn’t just a fear of my research faltering; it was the deeper question of whether I belonged in this space, much like my hesitations around tradition. Diwali had reminded me how disconnected I felt from my culture, how I struggled to fully embrace my heritage. In that gray room, I felt the same tension.

But then I remembered how I once resisted Diwali itself--the uncomfortable clothes and the feeling of not quite fitting in. Yet, challenging that discomfort had revealed something profound: tradition is a source of strength.

Presenting wasn’t about proving myself--it was about contributing to a deeper understanding of fear by finding the most optimal model to overcome it, much like my journey through Diwali. I had found confidence in my tradition, and now I had that same confidence in my work. As I shared my insights, the room lit up, as if the diya within me was illuminating my words.

These lessons are universal, from the presentation room at Rockefeller to the peer counseling programs I hope to join on campus, I aspire to help others navigate their own complexities--feelings of belonging, identity, and self-acceptance. I’m eager to join initiatives that explore cultural influences on mental health and advocate for healthcare that honors diverse backgrounds. Just as I overcame doubt and embraced my culture through Diwali, I want to help others find the courage to honor their own traditions. This advocacy is about creating a space where mental healthcare acknowledges the weight of cultural heritage. I envision myself connecting research with campus organizations to raise awareness about mental health challenges, especially in excluded communities. I'm determined to ignite a sense of belonging that inspires others to step into the light of their own traditions.

My mom pulled my hair back and loosely folded it up. Although she acted indifferent, I knew she was bothered. “You’ll look like a boy.” I yanked the scissors from her hand and went–
chop, chop, chop.

I combed my fingers through my hair, but the strands stopped prematurely. Rather than black hair flowing down to my hips, only rough edges poking my neck remained. Yet, despite this new “boy-ish” hairstyle, I felt more feminine and more like myself than ever before.

My wardrobe mainly consists of t-shirts, some jeans, and athletic shorts. Those clothes aren’t particularly my style, but I was scared to try on different clothes to find it and those were my default since birth. While I have inherited many stylish blouses and pretty skirts from my mother, they only remain occasionally used. I didn’t know what style I liked, but I had figured out that I didn’t like hers.

After cutting my hair, I experimented with more diverse gender expressions, from wearing dresses, and clothing I hadn’t even looked at in years, to applying Pacinos Signature Line’s matte paste to my hair. Short hair forced me to attempt new hairstyles other than a simple ponytail, and even the easiest styles looked pleasing. Though my mom stared at my hair like the devil sat on it, I realized that my joy came from my courage to be myself, for myself, and not for others.

Propelled by this confidence boost, in my junior year, I decided to take another leap and host a singing show in front of a thousand-person audience at the Pioneer Theatre Guild, despite having no experience in acting or singing. While I felt ostracized after someone mentioned that my skin was tanner than the other cast members, I made no intention to dab myself with white setting powder. While the other female hosts searched for dresses, I searched for a suit. Stepping out into the hot lights for the first time, I swelled at the feeling of not just representing my true self, but also those in the audience who also wanted to take the stage. A full year later, I still feel proud when I get recognized for my iconic velvet suit.

Though each of these moments had their difficulties, each brings me an extra pep to my step. Even my once scornful mother is finally beginning to pick out suits for me rather than dresses. Her acceptance makes me feel satisfied and drives me to tighten our relationship by attempting to understand her fashion sense and what she feels comfortable in.

As I continue on to college, I will continue to challenge stereotypes and explore my identity, be that through becoming one of the pioneering Asian women in comedy or becoming a lead medical physician. I also want to continue to act as the advocate not only for suits, but for whatever others wish to try; I want to help lift up others' voices now that I’ve found mine. As I leave high school, I will continue to exist as my authentic self, whatever form that may take, and lift up those around me as I do so.

In 1816's ashen summer, an eighteen-year-old unwed mother would pen Frankenstein–one of the earliest conceptual precursors to human-machine integration. In the company of accomplished, male writers several years her senior– Lord Byron and Percy Shelley–Mary Shelley was spurred by a dare to conjure a ghost story. As a first-generation college applicant two hundred years hence, I can empathize with how she must have felt when others underestimated her because of her age and gender, and, like my parents, her lack of formal education. I too have felt the weight of others' patronizing expectations, their raised eyebrows a silent challenge: "Can you craft a tale worthy of our time?"

Undeterred by the established authors, she went on to tell a story that would haunt the corridors of literature, science, and philosophy for centuries to come. Ironically, Shelley's tale of terror, depicting horrors born from one man's hubris, in her cautionary opus of ambition unchained, inspires me to pursue my passion and embrace my ambitions.

Science fiction captivates me as the perfect blend of escapism and scientific exploration. It offers a sandbox for the mind, where imaginative freedom can partner with intellectual rigor, allowing me to explore fantastic concepts and push the boundaries of scientific possibility. This fascination led me to my own Frankenstein-like project during my freshman year while working on a competition with my school’s science team. For the bioengineering competition hosted by UC Berkeley, we endeavored to address issues involving congenital pulmonary stenosis, the reduction of blood flow caused by the narrowing of the pulmonary valve within the heart. Current treatments–mechanical valves prone to clotting, bioprosthetic valves lacking durability–are more stopgap than solution. Neither can grow with the patient so replacement surgeries are necessary–a Promethean punishment for the crime of being born with a faulty heart. Having few parameters or limitations imposed on us, we aimed to develop a creative approach to tackle quandaries that have stumped scientists for years.

Our solution was a mechanical heart valve encoated with a layer engineered from the patient’s own tissues seeded with a growth factor to provide regenerative capabilities. After I researched scientific literature spanning all disciplines involved with the project, including cardiology, tissue engineering, and developmental biology, we identified cutting-edge techniques in each field to create our device. Like a mad scientist, late nights blurred into early mornings as I created, rejected, and then reimagined iteration after iteration of possible computer-aided designs, often exploring ideas as speculative as those Mary Shelley conceptualized for Dr. Frankenstein’s science. Each iteration was a lightning strike, occasionally illuminating new possibilities, and other times scorching previous assumptions to ash. Our device, like a benign tumor, would grow throughout the recipient’s lifetime, providing a crucial element for pediatric patients while having innocuous effects on adults. The thrill of potential discovery and the challenge of being told my ideas were based on unsound science fueled my determination as I ventured into uncharted territory.

This breakthrough came not as a moment of sudden clarity but as a gradual convergence of ideas. My project, like Frankenstein’s monster, became a fusion of the artificial and the natural—a marriage of human tissue and engineered scaffolds that blurred the lines between man and machine. Just as Frankenstein, which revolutionized literature and introduced a monster that would become a worldwide cultural icon, was created out of Shelley’s irreverence to convention, I discovered that scientific breakthroughs often emerge from minds willing to challenge the status quo. As a first-generation college applicant and aspiring scientist, I carry with me the spirit of Mary Shelley – a reminder that innovation knows no pedigree. Exploring the intersections of imagination and science, I plan to venture beyond conventional limitations, and through my own version of alchemy, I intend to breathe life into groundbreaking advancements that will transform the seemingly impossible into reality.

“Where does a cat go when it’s thirsty?”

Isla, one of my school’s first graders in the class I help in, asked me after I corrected misspelled words.

“Where?”

Immediately knowing it was another joke, I still squatted down to see her at eye-level.

“The cat-fe!”

She burst out laughing. I paused only a second before joining her enthusiastically, doing my best to force chuckling sounds out my teeth so she would think her not-so-great joke was comic gold.

In the energetic first grade with 23 kids, Mrs. Hovancik often asks me to keep an eye on Isla, who was diagnosed with autism and ADHD. I sympathized with the poor child, feeling the responsibility to dote on her. Though she was always in trouble—throwing tantrums when her scissors went missing, interrupting teachers, and redoing work repeatedly in her chubby handwriting—I contained myself to always be gentle with her. Yet honestly, no matter how deeply I love her, Isla was getting on my nerves. Nobody knew that my patience was thinning, until one day she pushed my hand away shouting that she didn’t need help, and the whole class witnessed me bolted from the room barely holding back tears of hurt. Cheap sympathy and fake laughter couldn’t go any further for my loving, patient teacher’s aide profile.

“I love Isla, and I know she has autism and ADHD, but her bad temper and bad jokes...” I said while unwillingly yet helplessly exposing my true thoughts to Mrs. Hovancik. She paused, her pen still resting on the homework she was correcting, and looked at me thoughtfully. “Why do you think she told you those bad jokes?”

“I think she’s just being naughty, but I’m not sure...”

She smiled, her voice soft but serious. “Think about it. Observe her.”

Maybe by answering questions understanding would happen—for both of us. So I began looking past words, carefully observing Isla’s mood, reactions, and context of those jokes, while recording data like a researcher. As observations and reading inspired each other, I began reading books and articles, even choosing autism as my research focus in the Pioneer Research Program. Then, I summarized patterns and observed in those directions.

I began to understand the things Isla couldn’t communicate. Her jokes weren’t just silliness or misbehavior, they were something deeper. Sharing humor was her way of feeling connected to others, feeling in control, and understanding confusing situations. When she couldn’t follow directions or it got too noisy in the classroom, she would repetitively shake her head and yell loudly due to overstimulation, which I mistook as defiance. After she calmed down, a joke would be told to me as compensation. Also, she would use her jokes as a means to gain attention. Whenever I compliment another kid, she would tell me a joke and ask whether she was good.

And she began to understand me too. When I asked, “Why do you only tell me jokes?” She was quick to answer. “You hear them.” Feeling incredibly warm in my heart, I understood past words: it wasn’t her acknowledging that I have two functioning ears; she saw my clumsy attempts at knocking on her door, and laughter was the invitation into her world. I no longer reacted with cheap sympathy and fake amusement, but genuinely laughed with compassion at her bad jokes because I could understand what she felt and needed. Our communication elevated to a spiritual level as we echoed.

As Victor Hugo wrote, “Laughter is the sun that drives winter from the human face,” joy is universal even though jokes are not. Though she is still a little stinker, and she sometimes doesn't stay inside the patterns, I will never run out of patience again. For now our relationship is built on mutual, deepened understanding. After all, I’m not a savior, just a “bad joke” for those who put their hearts in my hand.

This is my Ball Street Journal.

As the doctor examined me quietly, his expression grew serious. Looking at my skinny Indian physique, he said, "Your testicle hasn't descended, and you're sixteen?" My stomach tightened.

"No, should it have?" I replied, anxiety creeping into my voice.

In the heart of my Sikh-Hindu family, modesty is the law of the land. This curtain of discretion inadvertently obscured a serious medical issue. Words like 'infertility,' 'cancer,' and 'surgery' flooded my mind, wrapping me in a quiet dread. Above all, one question echoed relentlessly: Do I really control my own destiny?

The day of the surgery was a blur of sterile white walls and the sharp scent of antiseptic. A surgical team corrected nature's developmental error: my left testicle, entangled in my lower abdomen, was cautiously dropped to its rightful place. As I recovered, my anxieties shifted, sparking a more profound realization about the nature of control—and my role in it.

This experience was a stark reminder of life’s unpredictability, but it also taught me something vital: while fate throws challenges our way, we are not powerless. I had to take charge of my health when no one else could. The responsibility for my body was mine alone—and with it, I realized, so too was the responsibility for shaping my future.

After my surgery, I realized that health, like wealth, requires careful management and foresight. The same diligence I applied to my recovery taught me that our futures—whether in health or finances—are not left to fate alone. I began to view financial well-being as another form of self-care, a way to ensure a secure future not just for myself, but for others. This realization spurred me to take charge of my financial education and inspired me to help others do the same.

At school, I threw myself into the Student Investment Fund, where we managed a $25,000 portfolio, navigating financial markets and honing our analytical skills. It was an exhilarating and eye-opening experience. But I also became keenly aware of a troubling gap. In my predominantly Latino community, many students didn't have access to this kind of knowledge. Just as my family’s modesty kept me in the dark about my health, their socioeconomic circumstances kept them in the dark about their financial futures.

This realization ignited a sense of urgency in me. I began to wonder: If I had the tools to shape my destiny, why shouldn’t others? Why should someone’s zip code determine their financial literacy?

Determined to bridge this gap, I launched financial literacy workshops at our local community center. In the midst of explaining credit scores, something unexpected happened. An adult chaperone in the back, who had been quietly watching, suddenly leaned forward and started speaking rapidly in Spanish. Though my Spanish was limited, I understood the repeated word: importante. She was telling the kids that this part was crucial, explaining how credit scores impact everything from loans to housing in their community.

The room's atmosphere changed in an instant. Students who had been passively listening suddenly reached for their notebooks, pens ready to catch every detail. Their eyes, which had been wandering, now locked onto me. It was in that moment that I truly understood the impact of what I was doing.

After class, I watched one student excitedly show her notes to her waiting mom. The girl's eyes sparkled like stars as she flipped through her notebook, pointing out key concepts with her pencil. Her mother leaned in, nodding intently, her weathered hands gently touching the pages as if they held precious gems. The pride on both their faces was unmistakable, lighting up the dimming community center hallway. Right then, I saw how this knowledge could spread beyond just the classroom, like ripples in a pond, potentially changing not just individual lives but entire families.

Looking back, my surgery was a pivotal moment that deepened my understanding of responsibility and self-determination. It showed me that true growth comes from not just overcoming personal challenges but using those experiences to empower others. Control isn't just about reacting to life's unpredictability—it's about proactively shaping your future and helping others shape theirs.

Twelve years ago, a wide-eyed child sat in his grandmother's living room surrounded by familiar toys, waiting impatiently for his father's arrival from a long trip. The television mumbled in the background as he played, picturing the stories his father would tell and his excitement of being back together. His thoughts, however, were elsewhere, focused on his father walking through the door.

The world he knew was about to change and he had no idea. His mother walked into the room, followed by his grandmother. There they had delivered the news that forever changed his life. At first, he laughed thinking it was a joke, but eventually reality set in: his father was gone and would not be coming back. The hope he was holding onto so tightly broke. Something far far more complex replaced the innocence of a safe world—hope in all its fragile, powerful forms.

Eight years ago he discovered that hope did not always translate into quick satisfaction. He looked at a Nerf gun he had been dreaming about in a Toys "R" Us store. His mother gently said as they got closer to the aisle that they couldn't afford it. They walked out of that store empty-handed. Still, he insisted that eventually things would get better. Hope turned into a quiet force guiding him across the ups and downs of life.

Six years ago, during the global pandemic, he put his hope to the test. Bored and isolated from friends, he decided to gather the one-hundred dollars he had been saving and make his first investment in the stock market. He dove head first into the chaos of AMC and GameStop, riding the unpredictable waves of the market. Soon enough he had made his first profits. This event wasn’t just about the money for him—it was proof that he could create opportunities instead of waiting for things to happen. And when those earnings were needed to help his mother pay the bills, he didn’t mind. More than anything, it was the belief that he could navigate any storm that mattered most.

Two years ago, a scrawny fourteen-year-old faced another upheaval: relocating from New York to South Carolina. This was the ninth time he'd packed his life into boxes. But this time seemed different. The thick Southern accents, the slower pace, and the unfamiliar atmosphere overwhelmed him. But with each new beginning, he adapted. He relied on hope, not as a naive belief that everything would fall into place, but as motivation to change his circumstances. Moving wasn’t just about finding a new home—it was about finding resilience within himself.

Hope, I've discovered, is both a blessing and a curse. It propels us through the darkest times, providing a glimmer of hope when all seems lost, but it also exposes us to sorrow when reality falls short. That day in my grandmother's living room was the first time I fully understood this contradiction. I realized that hope is more than just a passive emotion; it is an intentional choice to believe in something better, even when the world gives every reason to doubt.

Though the path ahead is uncertain, reflecting on this duality has shaped my journey. Growth does not come from avoiding adversity, but from facing it. Every move, loss, and challenge has motivated me to adapt, persevere, and thrive. Hope has been my constant companion, not only in times of success, but also in the quiet determination that pushes me. It is not a guarantee of an easy life, but rather a belief in my ability to overcome any challenges that may emerge.

The air in the ring felt heavy, laden with nervous energy. Knight, restless beneath me, shifted as though he could sense my unease. My heart raced, my knuckles white as I clutched the reins. I had already fallen twice in as many weeks, and as the gate clanged shut, I could feel it coming—the inevitability of another failure. A dog nearby barked. Spooked, Knight bolted, galloping at full speed. I didn’t stand a chance—in a blur of motion, I found myself on the ground. The world spun as I tried to get up. The lesson continued, my body going through the motions, my mind stuck on the shame of another fall.

Afterward, my instructor approached. Her words were measured, a polite suggestion that perhaps riding wasn’t for me, that I should pursue “something easier.” A heavy silence hung between us during the car ride home. My father’s voice, when he finally spoke, was gentle, but his words were more painful than the fall itself. “We can always try something else, [Name]. This is clearly too much for you.”

His words stung, not just because he was my dad, but because everyone around me had decided my limitations without my permission. At nine, I didn’t have the words to articulate my frustration, but I refused to let their doubts define me. I insisted on finishing the season. But inside, a battle raged. Getting back on a horse after a fall isn’t just about physical recovery—it’s a quieter, more internal struggle. Doubts gnawed at me. I grappled with them every night, fear hovering, like mist over water—soft, but clinging and dense. What if it happened again? What if I really wasn’t cut out for this? Every ride became an exercise in quelling my doubts.

It took years, but as my abilities improved, the "what ifs" subsided, replaced by the sheer exhilaration I felt riding. I started to focus entirely on the present moment: the wind in my face, my connection with the horse. Riding became my sanctuary. Everything else—fear, uncertainty, parental expectations, stress—faded away.

With each new jump and course, I learned to face the unknown. Some days the terrain was tricky, the wind pulled differently, or my horses were moody. But I started to listen—to anticipate without trying to control, to adjust my approach as needed. Riding became less about mastering the course and more about embracing whatever it brought.

The lessons from the barn seeped into my life. As high school approached, I faced a difficult decision. Most of my friends were heading to a magnet school in another town. I had the option to join them, to bask in the comfort of old friendships, but it would mean giving up riding. Or, I could strike out on my own.

I chose the latter. Riding taught me that uncertainty is inevitable; I could shy away from it or embrace it. Starting high school without friends was daunting; social circles were set, and I found myself on the outside, looking in. But I reminded myself of those early days riding, when fear felt all-consuming.

I decided to join marching band. I wasn’t the most coordinated; playing saxophone while marching chair-step felt impossible. Being voted "Most Improvement Needed" by our section was mortifying, but I knew I would get better. We won regionals, nationals, even performed at Giants Stadium and Disney—I had a blast. Though I left band as a junior to focus elsewhere, I had already made enough friendships to anchor me, by now fully immersed into the school community.

Looking back, I remember that terrified nine-year-old, struggling with failure and doubt. She never could’ve imagined leading a club, winning blue ribbons, much less guiding young riders when they stumble. Now, as I face new challenges, a familiar voice stirs within, urging me to get back on that horse, reminding me that every fall is just an opportunity to rise again.

Sitting on the grass bank I am surrounded by fifteen anxious year nine students who are about to start high school together in a couple of weeks, they have never met before and as a prefect and mentor, I must help them connect over the next 3 days. “You don’t have to do it if you don’t want to”, I had reminded Jack. Yet now he was high up shaking the entire way across the high rope course, slower than everyone before him. He spends only a minute up in the air, but as his feet touch the ground, he beams. Despite only knowing the others for a couple of days and his anxiety at the sight of heights, he sits next to me clapping and cheering for those who are up on the high ropes. He encourages his newfound friends to give it a try as well and keeps them company as they wait.

Reminded by Jack’s kindness, I continued to encourage the students as they worked through a military-styled training course. Knowing that regardless of how hard they are pushed it would keep them going. On the camp’s last day, fifteen strangers had turned into fifteen friends.

***

“It’s as simple as Greet, Serve and Close” my manager Simon says. It’s my first day and I’m learning the trade secrets in retail - the warm greeting and reassuring smile that keep customers engaged. At the counter, Simon takes an immediate interest in every customer he meets, greeting them genuinely, and sharing fun stories or even a joke. Later a customer walks in angrily with a fraying jersey demanding a refund. It’s 3 years old, and despite the 30-day policy, Simon puts it through with a smile. Regular customers also come in, Simon has remembered their names and checks in with them about the shirt or blender they bought a couple of weeks ago.

Simon was always going above and beyond and was able to build a sense of community with every conversation. Clocking out after my day with Simon reminds me “regardless of what we sell, we must always serve”. I left that evening eager and prepared for the new customers I would meet tomorrow.

***

It’s another beautiful summer Christmas. Blooming red Pōhutukawa or New Zealand Christmas trees line the golden sandy beach across the road. In our kitchen, my grandmother glides like a ballerina past haphazard pots, bowls, and stovetops. I can smell the glazed ham in the oven. The smoke rises from the barbeque whilst I dream about her classic macadamia ice cream in the fridge. As is tradition I offer my helping hands. She passes on her tips and tricks like instead of wasting the fat from the ham using it to make crackling and basting regularly to get it juicy. Everyone helps, preparing food, getting drinks, or setting up the outdoor table. Our traditional annual Christmas gets all generations involved. Later the feast blankets the table and she looks up proudly, knowing it will impress.

Every year her hospitality brings our family together for a banquet. For just a few hours the phones are put down, the news is turned off, and we feast, laugh, and tell stories. Love takes on many different forms, for my grandmother, it was the pride in her Christmas meal, her way of reminding us she cares.

***

My learning was never constrained by the 4 walls of the classroom. From the high ropes course to a department store checkout counter to my family’s Christmas table, I was privileged to grow under the kindness of others. Through kindness, I’ve learned to always be encouraging, how to build connections and build a community with strangers, and the importance of tradition to bring friends and family together. And as I continue through college collaborating in science and technology, I'll always share that kindness and desire to give back to the communities that have supported me.

“Stan, is that really you, bro? You look like the kid from Up!”

Without even seeing their screens, I knew what my classmates were laughing at: old photos of me at piano competitions.

I’ve played piano since I was five, but after being teased in sixth grade, I decided to switch hobbies. I let piano slide to the wayside and picked up a basketball instead.

From pounding heavy balls in my garage to non-stop hours of free throw shooting, I devoted myself to becoming the best player in the school.

Still, throughout middle school, I dragged myself to the keyboard as I prepared for competitions that my parents put me in for. By high school, I stopped competing altogether.

Instead, I put my efforts towards playing music I genuinely enjoyed for myself. I explored new styles of music on Youtube, eventually coming across Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse. Unexpectedly, I found myself falling in love with the glimmery texture of the passages, and bringing myself to practice felt more natural again.

I recalled the months I spent religiously following Plyomorph’s jumping workouts, dunking tennis balls to be able to dunk at five foot six. I applied the same consistency to be able to hit every note in Chopin Ballade 1’s notoriously difficult coda. Whereas before I used to study Devin Booker’s midrange pullup, I now studied YouTube concert performances by Seong Jin Cho, where I’d draw inspiration from his ability to bring out hidden melodies in his music.

At the same time, I picked up a third hobby: cooking. From learning how to dice an “onyo” with Chef Jean Pierre to making my first grilled cheese and tomato soup, I must pay homage to my two great teachers: Max the Meat Guy and Joshua Weissman. Though I sometimes spilled some diced onions while tossing them in the pan, I found moments of peace and solitude replaying Debussy passages and my alley-oops to my teammate as I seasoned my proteins and minced my garlic.

Two months ago, I pulled up [Name] Du’s picture for the Great Composers Competition, the image which garnered mocking laughs from my elementary classmates. I was struck by both how childish I looked, and how childish the reactions of my friends were.

I closed my laptop, walked to the piano, and pulled up Debussy. Then, after a two-hour practice session, I signed up for the Ross Mckee Piano Competition, the first competition that I signed myself up for.

***

Driving home from practice, my teammate, Parth, opened up to me. “No one else knows this [Name], but my dad doesn’t want me to play basketball anymore.” The goofiest, most dedicated person I knew struggled with having passion for the sport. Shooting less threes after practice and lifting less, I saw him going down the same road that I had with piano.

As cheesy and cliche it might have been, I gave him the words that I needed most in 6th grade: “Focus on what your goal is, and don’t worry about anything else.”

Whereas in middle school and my early years of high school, piano symbolized my confinement to teenager norms and an Asian stereotype, today the instrument is an embodiment of my ability to start new endeavors with ambition and infuse interdisciplinary thinking between the arts, sports and even cooking. The black and white keys are my tangible proof that I can be authentic to myself while also maintaining autonomy—it represents how I’m able to be proud of working on different aspects of myself, even if it is unconventional.

In college and beyond, I’ll embrace my uninhibited curiosity, knowing that I will pursue every facet of myself without feeling ashamed. And of course, I can always take my mind off exams and work by playing pickup ball at the gym, playing L’isle Joyeuse (for my roommates this time!), and maybe even cooking a comforting grilled cheese and tomato soup.

**Essay:**

Numbers taste like orange juice. 7×7=49 feels like a Thursday. I can sense gravity with every step. My lucky charm? A picture of a young Bill Gates captioned, "Be delusional." For years, I viewed the world through a lens that defied conventional logic, feeling out of place. But once I embraced this unique perspective, I realised that unpredictability excites me. How I navigate it shapes who I am.

As an 11-year-old, awake at 4 a.m., I often wondered, "Is eating sugar really a sin?" Huddled under the kitchen table with sticky hands, sweetness, like joy, felt forbidden—something to be earned, not freely given. I carried this notion for far too long, believing happiness had a price.

That belief unravelled one day at the hospital where my mother worked. A frantic man rushed through the doors, desperate over his wife’s critical condition. My mother, calm and composed, coordinated the paramedics, reassured him, then disappeared into the operating room. I sat beside him in the waiting room, the air thick with his panic. Emulating my mother’s compassion, I offered a Snickers. He reluctantly took it, and with his sigh of relief, the truth became clear—joy isn’t granted, it’s inherent to us all.

This shift in perspective echoed my earlier efforts to rationalise fear. Like joy, fear became something I aimed to understand and navigate.

As a child, I recall watching a petrifying video about skinwalkers—creatures that mimic humans with unnerving accuracy. I became fixated. To soothe my anxiety, I memorised the knocks of my family members. If it wasn’t my mother’s soft tap or my brother’s unmistakable slam, the door stayed closed. Fear was never about darkness—it was about the uncertainty lurking within it. To me, fear was a puzzle to be solved.

As I grew older, fear took new forms. I’d nervously sift through piles of notes before meetings, stumble over my words on stage, or send my co-presenter a silent plea for help. My early attempts at public speaking weren't perfect, but I persevered. As a facilitator at "Speak with Rawan," I saw that same fear in my students’ eyes—fumbling with their words, anxious that their English wasn’t sufficient. Week by week, we worked together; they improved—and so did I. One student, Ahmed, embodied resilience, pushing through his struggles and inspiring me to continue confronting my own fears.

Motivated by this experience, I organised my school’s first charity bazaar, raising significant funds for a local orphanage. Later, I became a cultural ambassador and led a research program involving over 200 participants, building on my experience mentoring six students in a smaller initiative.

Yet fear is just one piece of the puzzle. My solutions often mirror the quirkiness of my fears. For example, I once created nine separate Google accounts to throw off potential hackers—a playful strategy that evolved into my go-to approach for online safety.

Last year, I launched a small jewellery business with just $100 for materials. I left nothing to chance. Meticulously pricing each piece, I ensured that even the worst-case scenario would break even. Weeks before the event, I began advertising at school, designing custom pieces for students who pre-ordered and helped spread the word. By the day of the event, I made more items than necessary. Even after discounting the leftover stock, I walked away with an $800 profit. Over-preparation became my secret weapon, and planning for failure turned into my blueprint for success.

Whenever life hurls an unexpected challenge my way, I approach it the same way I did with the skinwalkers: I identify my fear, dissect it, and devise a strategy to manage it. Whether it’s memorising familiar knocks or launching a business, I don’t merely react to the unknown—I anticipate it. Life’s uncertainties aren’t obstacles to fear but opportunities to embrace. The secret isn’t to evade the unknown; it’s to confront it with ingenuity, humour, and a healthy dose of over-preparation.

If Kintsugi has taught me anything, it would be that there is beauty in brokenness. Taking something injured and infusing life into it is at the heart of this Japanese artform. Sure, Kintsugi (kin means golden and tsugi means joinery) involves mending broken pieces of ceramic together to salvage a bowl or dish and turn it into art, but it is so much more than that. It is stewardship, taking care of something valuable, something entrusted to you. Kintsugi is the process of making something new out of what would have been discarded.

I grew up in a culture of mending and upcycling. For instance, our neighborhood has an annual garage sale where I’m able to connect with neighbors and exchange stories about the items for sale. These interactions are not just transactional, they are often enlightening. One time, a neighbor came by asking how old our t-shirts were and when I asked her why that mattered, she explained that t-shirts nowadays shed microplastics into our environment so she prefers really old t-shirts that are 100% cotton. This idea of minimizing microplastics in our world led me to my recycling initiative called Recycle Your Contacts! because whenever I looked down at my bathroom trash, it was always full of contact lenses and their packaging. I recruited four of my friends and we scheduled pick-ups with our neighbors to take their used contacts and packaging to official Bausch and Lomb recycling centers, saving 5,000 used contacts from polluting our environment.

So when I accidentally broke my mom’s ceramic dish, it was natural for me to try to mend it instead of throwing it away. During my Google search I came across a picture of a repaired ceramic bowl with golden lines running through it, labeled “Kintsugi.” I read a few articles on it and contacted a local Kintsugi teacher, Fumika, to learn this esoteric art. Since then, I have repaired 10 ceramic pieces and exhibited them at the OC Maker Faire to inspire the 3,000 attendees to rethink what they consider damaged and useless. Can they see the hidden value? Can they see the beauty?

This idea of mending and reusing is also something I wear. I refuse to throw away my shorts just because they are torn. My friends often ask me, “Why pay $10 to fix your shorts when you can get new ones for $40?” I explain to them that the $10 goes a lot further than they think: it keeps my shorts out of landfills and allows me to support a small business in my community. Restoration has value.

I have even found a way to salvage while playing baseball for my high school. During practice, a lot of our foul balls end up over the fence into the adjacent post office backlot, seemingly lost in the postal abyss. I was able to meet with Doug, the post office facilities manager, and he agreed to collect the baseballs if I would take them off his hands. We continue to work together and have been able to return hundreds of baseballs to my team. Was this the reason we won CIF in 2024? Probably not, but I like to think it played a small part.

I have carried this theme of stewardship over to my podcast on creating awareness for antibiotic resistance. By 2050, antibiotic resistance could kill more people than cancer, and a major driver of resistance is the misuse of antibiotics and a broken antibiotic pipeline. When I interviewed Dr. Su Chiang, Senior Alliance Manager at CARB-X Boston University, we talked a lot about the importance of stewardship as new antibiotics are developed. How do we ensure new antibiotics can continue to fight resistant bacteria globally? Stewardship and sustainable access. I am eager to continue finding ways to mend the brokenness in our world as I pursue medicine and health advocacy.

It was 10 pm and my eyes were fixed intently on the endless columns and rows displayed through the mosaic of spreadsheets on my Macbook. Budgets and timetables! A revolution cannot be started without funding, and funding cannot be acquired without a budget. I was deeply engulfed in my new business plan for LaunchX, building what I believed would revolutionize food management at home. That was my idea of a Saturday well spent. My team and I built an app that scans receipts and barcodes of food to minimize waste, provides recipes based on what is available in the fridge, and keeps track of inventory. My vision for this app was to make it simple for people to save time, money, and the planet, all from the comfort of their kitchen.

Busy with my project, I ignored the incessant buzzing of my phone until my best friend, Sara, decided to stop texting and start calling. For days, she had been urging me to join her and her sisters on a summer camping trip. “The adventure will make you an outdoor girl, Saanvi!” she promised. She was relentless. Eventually, I gave in.

I had gone on many hikes before, but backcountry camping was a different beast altogether. I loved the idea of REI more than the actual use of its wares. Regardless of my doubts, I decided to take a chance and join the intrepid group traipsing through primitive roads and imperceptible, lightly blazed trails—fending off black bears and rock scrambles. Plied with promises of heavenly cinnamon rolls – “Backcountry food is the best,” Sara swore, I thought, maybe I really was an outdoor girl, or maybe I just could not bear the feeling of disappointing her.

Everyone I talked to about camping at High Point State Park gave the experience excellent reviews. I imagined unearthing some deeply buried self-truth, uncovering unknown survival skills, and coming away a more fulfilled person.

This was not the case.

There were no cinnamon rolls. I realized this while crouching under a tarp on the shores of Sawmill Lake in a torrential downpour, drinking watery beans and rice out of my blue plastic camp bowl. There was, however, an abundance of flies with whom I shared the bathroom, and rain so heavy that if you attempted to leave the bathroom, you might require a boat.

Although waking up at 4 a.m. to watch the sunrise at the High Point monument proved infinitely worth it, with brushstrokes of amethyst and vermilion scattering across azure skies, I’ve come to terms with the fact that I prefer my spreadsheets, brainstorms, and business plans. I am not an outdoor girl; I am a “concrete girl.”

James Joyce said, “A man’s errors are his portals of discovery.” The lesson my friend wanted me to take from camping was not the one I left with; I discovered, instead, that I must trust myself. I went into the trip almost certain that I was not a hardcore backpacker, yet with some inherent mistrust of my instincts. Those instincts proved correct. As my best friend and I squinted at our summer reading by the inadequate LED glare of our headlamps, I learned to practice self-advocacy and determine where the lines fall.

So, camping in High Point State Park proved almost paradoxically valuable. By not listening to my inner voice in the first place, I became aware of the importance of doing so. This adventure hasn't stopped me from trying new things, but now it is easier to align my interests with my activities and prioritize my well-being over seeking other’s approval. Even if I did scrawl my frustrations in my journal on numerous occasions, and write about how much I missed my gray yarn blanket, I do not regret the experience. I tapped into a deep well of resilience I had previously written off. Who needs cinnamon rolls when you have that?

I crouched down facing my grandma and mimicked her hand movements carefully, burying my second corn seed two inches deep into the soil. As she stood up and walked a few feet down her row, I followed.

“Tarvata (Next)?” I asked.

“Malli (Repeat).”

I repeated these steps around twenty more times before I grew tired and asked how much longer we would continue in this scorching 104°F heat—at this point, sweat was dripping down my face and my pants were entirely covered in soil. Even the cows in the nearby shed seemed to moo in sympathy for me.

My grandma chuckled and replied, “Ippude modalettam (We just started).”

It was the summer before my sophomore year, and I quickly realized that farming was anything but simple. However, despite this difficulty and unpredictable climatic conditions, my grandparents were optimistic and proudly called themselves “andariki thindi pettevallam (the feeders of the world).” I, on the other hand, felt more like a feeder of the mosquitoes, returning home daily with my arms covered by countless bites.

Yet, as I watched my grandparents work tirelessly and take pride in their identity as farmers, I questioned why I felt the need to hide from mine. Before I arrived in the US at the age of seven, my parents shaved my head for religious reasons. Unfortunately, starting my first day of school with a bald head wasn't the only challenge I faced: struggling with poor English, I was placed in an English as a second language program for the next three years. Not wanting to stand out more than I already did, I rarely spoke out during class, afraid of bringing attention to my accent and poor grammar. In an attempt to “fit in,” I hid my true self, never sharing details about me such as my passion for dance or the different holidays we celebrated at home.

But, why did I have to hide? Why did I need to be quiet?

These questions constantly echoed in my mind after hearing my grandparents proudly talk about their work on the farm. After all, why couldn’t I also be proud of myself and how far I came?

I wanted to change.

With a different mindset, I entered my first year at IMSA (Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy). I gradually started raising my hand in class and talking to new students during lunch—these small changes opened up more opportunities. Encouraged by a senior, I signed up to choreograph the sophomore dance for our annual Diwali show. While teaching my culture to my peers, I learned more about theirs. Bih-sana, one of the other dancers, introduced me to traditional African dances, and I was amazed by how different—yet equally exciting—they were compared to Indian classical dances.

This experience helped me build some of my closest friendships at IMSA and gave me the confidence to use my voice in new ways. I became more involved with the NorthSouth Foundation, a non-profit where I coached middle schoolers. Noticing the large communication gap between the 4,000+ youth members and administrators, I created the junior board with another volunteer. Our goal was to start more youth-driven initiatives and create a space where high schoolers could expand on each others’ ideas and present them to admins.

Whether it was encouraging a freshman volunteer to voice his idea about incorporating games into coaching or calming a dancer’s nerves backstage, I helped those around me struggling with self-confidence, knowing exactly how it felt to be in their shoes. These past few years, the strength and optimism that I built through my grandparents helped me learn not only how to advocate for myself but also others. In college, I hope to continue to grow by learning from those around me as well as share what I know, whether it's the lessons I learned on the farm or small Telugu words like “manam (we).”

“17 chimes, for 17 victims…” I strike the chimes in my 17-note solo of “Forever and Always, A Reflection,” alongside the reporter narrating the NBC 5th anniversary feature dedicated to the lives lost on February 14th, 2018 at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School.

I call Parkland, Florida home. On that day, I was forced to hide inside a bathroom along with my classmates. We huddled together, uncertain and scared by actions driven by hatred, stemming from feelings of exclusion and isolation. For years now, music has played a role in how I processed that day and how I reconnected with my community.

“Wouldn’t that make your headache even worse [Name]?” my science teacher asks, as my head pounds. This was the third day that week I asked a teacher for a pass to spend their class period in the band room. In the aftermath of the shooting, I’ve struggled with painful migraines that worsened into prolonged episodes that forced me to quarantine in dark rooms to avoid excess stimulation.

In my search for relief, I tried various medications hoping to find a solution that would help me fully engage in daily activities.

But it’s not Advil or Tylenol that works, music is my medicine. A headache strikes on the bus to school in the morning? I throw on my headphones, losing myself in the rhythm of our halftime show track. A stressful school day filled with important tests and after-school math practices? I escape to the band room to improvise a beat with friends. Through these musical outlets, the weight of each demanding day is lifted.

Slowly, the soothing sounds of the band room seeped into other areas of my life. Prior to the Boston University’s RISE research symposium, I harnessed the effect of rhythmically tapping on my chest to calm my nerves before presenting in front of a crowd gathered around my poster. During the district playoff game against the Nova Titans, I led a pulsing chant and stomp to energize my volleyball teammates before we clinched our victory. These small musical rituals have calmed me, centered me, and guided me towards greater confidence and stronger leadership.

When selected to be the section leader as an incoming sophomore, I was initially nervous about being the youngest leader in the band, especially because of Logan and Dougie, two of my friends and section members with special needs. Logan and Dougie both face unique challenges, not only with the precise timing required for percussion, but also with fitting in with the rest of the band. To ensure they are included and prepared, I dedicate extra time after rehearsals to review their parts and use subtle taps on their backs during concerts to help them stay on tempo.

“It’s Time to Unleash the FURY!!!” After every performance, I huddle the team to recognize one or two members who displayed showmanship and passion by asking them to lead our “Silent Sam” chant. My favorite memory is of Logan and Dougie taking the lead, their proud smiles reflecting their growth not just as drummers, but in their confidence and sense of belonging within the band. I hope my efforts at inclusion can help to prevent feelings of isolation that drive school shootings like the one my classmates and I survived.

The boom of the bass drum. The crash of the cymbals. These sounds aren’t a cacophony of random percussive noises, but rather a symphony of connectivity and emotion that feels like home. My journey as a musician began in the aftermath of a tragedy, which brought chaos to my mind, but I learned to calm it through music, a skill that I later shared with my peers. Through every beat and note I play, I endeavor to continue to inspire and promote empathy and acceptance; in myself, in my audience, and in my community.

“CAN YOU PLEASE stop chopping the trees down?”

Along the landscape of Minecraft, I was the lumberjack. I looked around fervently with an ever-changing purpose, struggling to attach myself to anything. I wove my way through various professions - one day, I was a farmer, improving the foliage and creating a flourishing province. The small DVD became an outlet for my expression, yet its limitless bounds were drawn from my limited childhood.

I was overwhelmed when Dr. Raghunathan diagnosed me with eczema. In a few months, the wounds I would get from falling on concrete plagued my youthful skin. My parents–unfamiliar with my condition–hurried to dermatologists to “fix” me with woven gauze and sharp needles.

With each intensifying itch, I sought refuge behind bedroom doors. Armed with a cardboard box in hand reading “Xbox 360”, my dad approached me. On YouTube, I frequented stampylonghead’s builds and gained inspiration to make a boat. I needed spruce wood, various colors of wool, and a lot of water. The culmination of my work was a rectangular prism with an odd-looking triangle on top, which my dad misinterpreted for a hat. I couldn’t blame him. Although I wasn’t the best builder, I captured beauty in designs others overlooked, developing consistency, resilience, and passion for engineering. Surprisingly, with medication and time, my eczema slowly faded. I would finally fit in.

However, this notion collapsed in 11th grade when I had a flare-up. I stared into the mirror and noticed the wounds that crept up on me. It grew worse for a moment when in study hall, my friend Raghava bluntly asked, “What happened to your face?”

The room fell silent. I wanted to crawl under the floor as my lacrimal glands activated. Should I tell him that a cat scratched my face? “It’s just a skin condition” I stammered. At that moment, I felt ambivalent; the profound mixture of fear and self-acceptance diffused in the air, leaving fleeting traces. Mr. Bulusu’s chemistry lessons prevailed: “Paper chromatography helps separate mixtures.”

I felt that I was on my own part of that paper. Was I different?

“I have eczema too,” he confessed. Raghava handed me a bottle of Aquaphor, urging me to use it. His empathy, however, extended beyond a dab of Aquaphor. It reminded me that the feeling of one thousand needles in my arm hurt, but each wound became a fragment that I could sew back together by leveraging the needles. Through robotics, I could fulfill myself by helping others realize their potential.

Rummaging through old bolts and creating models with computer-aided design (CAD) turned into my evenings in high school. I met Ansh, who taught at the Sri Venkateswara temple and bursted into the room one day avidly recounting his lessons. Unlike Ansh, however, many students struggled to find themselves. Thus, I led a woodworking project where we assembled field elements to test our robot. The procedure was essential: I ensured team safety, referenced the CAD, and grabbed the tools. Each piece slowly came together; however, it became increasingly difficult to move. I sat there and considered the physics where placing a dolly under the hunk of wood with a larger radius can produce a greater torque. Once we finished, sweat and smiles arose in the room, and a missing fragment of myself finally felt complete. I formed connections with people from all walks of life: the new kid, 4-eyes, or the jock.

Why be another healthcare project? I became accustomed to eczema’s presence in my life. It wasn’t only my biggest obstacle, but also my thread with its robust ways of being spun to nurture my growth. From Minecraft to Robotics, my virtual escapade paved a path to defeat my condition. Robotics is invaluable because while it would’ve been easier to isolate, the meaningful ties I wove one wound at a time built my courage and capability to help others mark their own spot on that piece of paper.

It was 3 AM and I found myself standing in front of a dimly lit Waffle House in an unknown county. Upon entering, I was welcomed by the scent of slightly overcooked bacon and seats sticky with syrup. The waitresses looked up from their phones, vexed that their silent night was being interrupted by an unexpected busload of 17-year-old boys. For the first time in my life, I was away from my family, entering a Waffle House with a group of strangers I had met only hours ago. I was embarking on a dream experience that only 400 rising seniors in Florida get to experience each year. American Legion Boys State is one of the biggest student mock government and leadership programs across the nation. I was burning with excitement. Having been homeschooled my whole life, I was excited to make new friends and improve my leadership and public speaking skills.

When the bus arrived in Tallahassee, we hit the ground running. From sunrise to hours past sunset, we set up our mock government and held elections and party meetings. Even though I had never been more exhausted in my life—getting less than six hours of sleep each night—I put my all into the rigorous program. I ran for every position I could, staying up past midnight to write the next day’s speeches. At first, I lost every election. Every time they announced the winner, my heart sank. So I studied what the election winners were doing, critiqued my speeches, and asked myself what I could do to make my campaigns better. I realized that the people winning the elections were showing past experience in the roles they were running for, so when it came time for the House of Representatives election, I highlighted my legislative experience working as a Page on the Florida Senate floor and shared my detailed plan for how I would work with my fellow delegates to pass legislation. The work paid off, and I won my first election. But I won more than just an election, I also made lasting friendships, learned to persevere through failure, to be adaptable when my original plans didn’t work, and to keep my promises by staying true to my platform.

I maximized the weeks leading up to this experience by researching my legislative bill about the expansion of Florida SR-29 and US-27, which I would later present and successfully pass in the mock House of Representatives. In my preparations, I spoke with my County Manager and met with the Vice-Chairman of the Florida Transportation Commission as part of my extensive research, both of whom I knew from Youth Leadership Collier, a local program I had previously participated in. The bill was inspired by the infrastructure issues my hometown is experiencing due to explosive population growth. There has been a huge influx of people moving to Naples, but the roads were not designed to handle so much traffic. On the East Coast of Florida, there are numerous highways to help move traffic along, but in Southwest Florida, we only have one: I-75. Noticing these massive traffic issues has inspired me to pursue a degree in Civil Engineering, with the desire to improve Florida’s transportation infrastructure through proper design and infrastructure improvement. In the meantime, I’ve been doing what I can to bring light to this current issue Floridians are experiencing through my conversations with County and State leaders as well as with my friends at Boys State. On campus, I will inspire my fellow engineering students to work with me to find new solutions to improve our state infrastructure as well. I enjoy bringing people together to work towards finding common ground to achieve results that benefit us all, like traffic relief, as I did at Boys State.

“Wake up and smell the coffee!” This mantra passed down from my father and literally by my first-generation Colombian mother through her dark roast Juan Valdez, defines the rhythm of my life. As an early riser, it’s a call to seize each day beside those improving the world through love and leadership.

As a second-generation Latina living in the multicultural landscape of Miami, I travel regularly to Colombia with family and one of my earliest coffee memories is sitting on my grandmother’s colonial-style balcony overlooking the small town where real work is reflected by the blisters and scars on the people. I remember that morning having a “wake up call”, realizing not everyone is given the same opportunities. I felt a pang of humility followed by a wave of determination realizing I wanted to dedicate my life to make change beyond my own.

Immersed in a Spanish-speaking household rich in love and fervor, my dentist-parents from humble beginnings instilled an old-school work ethic that felt like a second skin--upholding human values that extended beyond professional drive. My father (who loves a strong cappuccino) introduced me to Operation Smile, a humanitarian non-profit dedicated to treating kids born with facial deformities. At age ten, I discovered photo albums documenting medical missions to remote areas of Middle Eastern and Asian countries. The devastating images showed hallways lined with kids ashamed of having gaping holes between their mouth and nose, and some left on the orphanage doorstep as “throw away babies”. They had no one, nor able to eat, speak, or appear in public ordinarily. I was shattered by the hopeless faces, but knew I needed to translate emotion into action, doing more than just watching.

As an incoming freshman, my principal took a chance on me, giving administrative overrides to be approved as the Founder and President of the Operation Smile Club. I was determined to do my part despite fears about failure, embarrassment, and worst of all--peer rejection. After a first year of success, I recruited even more members to join the OS Team traveling in Vietnam, becoming a combined U.S-Vietnamese student youth group. By this point, I practically lived off Vietnamese salted coffee (ca phe muoi) while giving presentations at Vietnamese schools and orphanages. The long days were worth it as our team’s efforts supported over 150 surgeries. This showed me ordinary people can make extraordinary contributions. I realized what I’ve done these weeks is what these doctors have done for 20 years, and I'm filled with a sense of unrelenting gratitude.

I think of the father who walked 10 miles carrying his eight-year-old on his back wishing for the surgery, teaching me lessons on true hope and human perseverance, as well as values of unwavering compassion and respect for human dignity first instilled by my favorite dentists. When overwhelmed not being able to help everyone we wished, I stayed grounded to my favorite JFK quote, “every accomplishment starts with the decision to try;” I'll never stop trying to bring a smile to the face of anyone who is hopeless. The following year, our team re-organized and returned to Vietnam, gaining university partners while being televised on national news.

In my daily Miami life, I don’t take for granted the privilege of simply being able to walk into a coffee shop. Traveling the world as a student volunteer on medical missions and repeated visits to Mom's homeland, reaffirmed in me the importance of humility, gratitude, and grit. When volunteering locally at the Cleveland Clinic Hospital, I never just order a coffee for myself, but surprise the staff with a pick-me-up. A small gesture can perk someone’s day. Small efforts grow and can create a movement.
