As I sit here sipping a chocolate light roast, I do so with a heart full of hope and a soul filled with the knowledge that no matter the circumstances, I’m ready to brew change.

Dear Philly,

It feels so far away, but I still remember the terrible fear when I first met you - those dangerous questions, me trying to flee, you pursuing determinedly. You upset me back then - but today… oh, Philosophy, thank you so much for that!

Oh well, I must stay true to your character - reflection, not rhetoric. Back then, my “truth-worship” was, in fact, preaching my inherited ideas - but self-criticism, you said, and took that parrot and made him human. I was terrified of your consequences, but flailed helplessly in your tide - and then I submitted, telling you, in a small voice: hold me tight, my god, and I'll serve you.

My fear was not unjustified. I would go on to sacrifice my sanity and my family for you; I served a lower god until I sacrificed him too; everything, everything, for you! How many nights have I tossed in my bed silently, so terribly lonely? It was all your fault. All it would have taken is for me to be religious again, to think less and follow more - everything would have been normal.

I refused to. I guess I had grown used to your companionship.

Today, I see what I couldn’t - you teach best during adversity. And who am I to criticize you, my teacher? The depth of thought you instilled took me to glittering corporate parks and the most prestigious summer camps in the country. The empathy you brought out makes me walk in desolate slums, trying to help. I’ve organized food drives and tried raising societal attitudes on maids. Beyond providing smiles and kind words, I’ve largely failed - but I’m confident that together, we will bring about meaningful change over the years.

Yes, together - today, I say what I couldn’t: I will not, cannot, stop loving you.

How much you’ve changed me! You showed me that society cannot benefit if I talk to you alone, so I started sharing you wherever I went - annoying some, befriending others, but always a thought provoker. I no longer back down when people debate me - heck, I start the debates; you shaped me into something bolder. I faced religious indoctrination, sneerers, and isolation, and I lived; the scars you gave me made me stronger.

I think about younger Safwans and I smile - remember that hardline Muslim who wanted to be martyred in jihad? Or the sworn atheist who would eliminate organized religion? You claim to lead to "the truth", but you only make me more wary of the word by the day. Today, I hold only one principle: free expression without fear. Every time I think I understand something, you always prove me wrong, though: so perhaps I’ll even flip on this. They tell me I’m a hypocrite, but Philly, there is no shame in flipping - only in hiding.

You and I have changed too. From the boy who would ponder questions in his head, to the young teen writing down thoughts alone on the beach, to us today. Weekly exploration issues, sociopolitical discussion everywhere, the PPP Project - we spend so much time together, brazenly celebrating our relationship. Fundamentally, however, we’re still the same: we may be dancing in a more expensive ballroom, but our thrilling and beautiful dance, that critical obsession with why, has never changed.

I'm leaving for college soon, and my life will undergo yet another transition. Transitions scare me no more, though - they only open up more doors to you. I reflect on the past. Truth-worship has given way to truth-love, darkness extinguished by the hope of light, the pursuit of a life of image uprooted by a life of pursuit of meaning. I live for you, I long for you. As we near a decade of our relationship: hold me tight, my girl, and I'll hold you.

Yours, forever,
[Name]

When I was in fourth grade, I earned the most traumatizing five dollars of my life.

I won the money from a game at my weekend public speaking class, and the game had only one main rule: you had to talk about the prompt for a full minute. The catch was, you couldn’t stop, stumble, or use filler words: uh, uhm, like, I mean, you know—anything that signified a pause in thought was forbidden. Break a rule, and you were out. Succeed, and a crisp five dollar bill was yours to keep. It seemed simple, but I couldn’t even breathe at the thought of playing.

The problem was, I had recently diagnosed myself with the fear of public speaking. The first speech I had attempted one solemn afternoon came with a side of salty droplets that streamed down my face as I stumbled back to my seat, embarrassed that I couldn’t get an actual word out of my mouth before uttering a fateful “uhm.”

Seven years later, I find myself striding back to my seat with a smile. Ten-minute presentations are my muse, and I’m ecstatic before any speaking activity. In the way that I used to participate in speaking games during my weekend classes, I’ve also formulated my own rulebook to navigate my route in speechcraft. There’s a small slip of paper taped on my desk, a reminder of the steps I’ve developed to confront every difficult oration. The rulebook is as follows:

Rule #1: Plan. Plan early, if possible. One of the most stressful speeches I gave in recent memory was the AP Spanish Language exam’s cultural comparison speech. Knowing that Hispanic culture was a realm that I was barely familiar with, I began cultivating a laundry list of information about my chosen country, Panama, months ahead of the exam. I drilled the facts into my head, reciting speeches countlessly to ensure it stuck. When I nervously entered the speaking section the day of the exam, I felt like I had struck gold. Shining in black letters was a prompt that I knew exactly how to respond to.

Rule #2: Focus. An element of speech I had a hard time embracing was the idea of delivering, instead of talking. It wasn’t until I participated in original oratory competitions that I recognized the way I recited words could matter even more than the words themselves. I couldn’t just blurt out phrases and expect people to empathize and understand. Instead, I had to focus on the pace of each sentence, the pitch of each word, and the volume of each syllable. Focus, because the details matter. At competitions, I would talk to walls to practice, honing in on the minutiae details of my voice, knowing each tweak could evoke a variety of reactions.

Finally, rule #3: Finish. I learned this lesson as a yearbook editor-in-chief, where speeches at the beginning of each class became a formality. At the end of each monologue, there’s always been one phrase that we have to chant before anyone starts working, “Break on three!” Then, we count up to three and begin work, our voices unified as we scramble to our respective tasks. A speech’s final impression should be as great as its first. Make an impact that will set people into motion.

These days, I no longer fear using my voice. My three rules reassure me each step of the way, providing consistency in the most nerve-wracking situations. As I move forward from these fears that so vividly defined my childhood weekends, I continue to communicate to others in a multitude of facets to help others become empowered to share their own values and experiences. And while I no longer receive five dollars for every minute that I speak without fluency breaks, I’m always happy to put in my three cents to shape a more transparent, communicative future.

Humans aren’t the only ones who use the WWW.

Like the URL prefix, nature has its own WWW– a complex network of roots, fungi, and bacteria termed the “Wood Wide Web”. The idea that a constellation of organisms worked together to create a hidden yet vital communication network fascinated me. I dug through YouTube videos decoding the mycorrhizal network and unearthed research suggesting even more sophisticated functions of trees. Uncovering the WWW uprooted my assumptions about the natural world and human connections. Maybe we aren’t as disconnected from each other as I once thought.

Stepping into Chesterbrook, my local assisted living home, my ideas of connection were further challenged. I imagined the age gap would make my volunteer days feel more like caretaking than genuine connection, struggling to find common ground.

My first assignment whisked me into the unfamiliar biome of the exercise room, where several rows of chairs sprouted from the ground. For the next month, I would be performing a “sittercise” routine with the residents, but with no prior experience, I slinked away to the back row, hoping to camouflage. My attempt didn’t last long - soon, a group of residents surrounded me, playfully giving me a “C” grade on my routine. Slow, mischievous smiles spread through the group, and I joked back, embracing the playful atmosphere.

Propelled by their encouragement, I improved rapidly, eliminating simple errors as I perfected my routine. By the event’s end, I was in the middle of the room, chit-chatting with a gaggle of jubilant seniors. Neither they nor I wanted the session to end.

Determined to unearth this connection, I scoured the internet to understand the activity that connected us. I learned the physical benefits of sittercise - improved flexibility, stronger joints - and unearthed new moves by watching other instructors on YouTube, jotting down toe taps and other techniques to share with my sittercise squad.

One day, halfway through our routine, our sittercise DVD suddenly glitched. After 15 minutes of troubleshooting, the number of disappointed faces spread. I knew I had to improvise. Drawing on my newly acquired knowledge, I led a live routine, incorporating new moves and music. Knowing some residents had hip pain, I adapted the routine, introducing an upper-body “breaststroke pull” exercise inspired by my swimming routine. I unearthed late 20th-century music, incorporating songs like “It’s Raining Men” and “Rhythm of the Rain.” We sang as we exercised, wrist circles and arm raises becoming our dance moves. By the end, my squad unanimously graded my routine an “A+”, declaring it the best routine they’d ever done.

Seeing how sittercise fostered connections, I sought ways to expand this web, linking students at my school with the residents. Now, on weekends, the sounds of Debussy and Schumann fill the room, sparking eruptions of claps and bravos. Knowing the residents’ love for music and engaging with the younger generation, I started bringing the Musicians Association club to perform. Debbie, a longtime attendee of our performances, excitedly calls down the other residents when we arrive. As I perform their favorite tunes on my clarinet, I see the residents swaying joyfully to the rhythm. My classmates perform next, gaining confidence from the residents’ unyielding support. Through a shared love of music, our roots, once hidden, have intertwined, creating a flourishing social network.

By initiating these connections, I became a part of this interwoven ecosystem - like the trees in the WWW, I forged an unlikely connection with a community that strengthened me as I strengthened it. Just as resources flow from older trees to younger ones in the WWW, the residents taught me that true strength lies in our ability to connect, support, and uplift one another. From a veteran tree to a sapling, from the Chesterbrook residents to myself, I learned how to connect across differences. Beneath the surface, endless possible connections are waiting to be unearthed.

The air in the ring felt heavy, laden with nervous energy. Knight, restless beneath me, shifted as though he could sense my unease. My heart was racing, my knuckles white from clutching the reins. I had already fallen twice in as many weeks, and as the gate clanged shut, I could feel it coming—the inevitability of another failure. Knight suddenly bolted, galloping at full speed. I didn’t stand a chance against two thousand pounds of angst. In a blur of motion, I was thrown to the ground. The world spun as I tried to get back on my feet. The lesson continued, but I was no longer a part of it. My body moved through the motions, but my mind was stuck on the shame of another fall.

Afterward, the instructor approached us. Her words were measured, a polite suggestion that perhaps horseback riding wasn’t for me, that I should pursue “something easier.” A heavy silence hung between us during the car ride home. My father’s voice, when he finally spoke, was gentle, but his words were more painful than the fall itself. “We can always try something else, [Name]. This is clearly too much for you.”

His words stung, not just because he was my dad, but because everyone around me, without my consent, had decided my limitations. At nine, I didn’t have the words to articulate my frustration, but I refused to let their doubts define me. I insisted on finishing the season, driven by a stubborn determination I hadn’t known existed within me.

But inside, a battle raged. Getting back on a horse isn’t just about physical recovery—it’s a quieter, more internal struggle. Doubts gnawed at me long after that last fall. I grappled with them at night, letting fear creep in like an unwelcome guest. What if it happened again? What if I really wasn’t cut out for this? Every ride became an exercise in quelling my doubts.

Slowly, things shifted. As my abilities improved, the questions started to subside—"what ifs" eventually overwhelmed by the sheer joy and exhilarating freedom I felt riding. I started to focus entirely on the present moment: the wind in my face, my connection with the horse. Riding became my sanctuary. Everything else—fear, uncertainty, expectations, stress—faded away.

With each new jump and course, I learned to face the unknown. Some days the terrain was tricky, the wind pulled differently, or my horses were moody. But I started to listen—to anticipate without trying to control, to adjust my approach as needed. Riding became less about mastering the course and more about embracing whatever it brought.

The lessons from the barn seeped into my life. As high school approached, I faced a difficult decision. After two years of social isolation due to COVID, most of my friends were planning to attend a magnet school in another town. I had the option to join them and bask in the comfort of old friendships, but it would mean giving up riding due to the distances involved. Or, I could strike out on my own—leaving behind the only social safety net I had known.

I chose the latter. Riding had taught me that uncertainty is inevitable, and I could either shy away from it or embrace it. Starting at a new high school was daunting; the social dynamics had already been set, and the thought of making new friends was intimidating. But I reminded myself of those early riding days, when fear felt all-consuming. I let uncertainty shape me - this was just another opportunity to grow.

Riding continues to guide me, shaping who I am today. My parents often cheer from the sidelines, no longer questioning what I can or can’t do. Like me, they’ve come to understand that the most important part of any journey isn’t controlling the course, but trusting yourself to navigate it, with confidence and an open heart.

My mom pulled my hair back and loosely folded it up. Although she acted indifferent, I knew she was bothered. I nodded my head and remained insistent that she should cut it. 
“You’ll look like a boy.” She hated the idea of her daughter looking like a son. I yanked the scissors from her hand and
Chop. Chop. Chop.
As my reflection gazed back at me, I combed my fingers through my hair, but the strands had stopped prematurely. Rather than black hair flowing down to my hips, only rough edges poking my neck remained. 
And yet, despite my “boy-ish” hairstyle, I felt more feminine and more like myself—a girl.
I experimented with more diverse gender expressions, from wearing dresses, a clothing I hadn’t even looked at in years and admittedly still do not prefer, to applying Pacinos Signature Line’s matte paste onto my hair. Though my mom stared at my hair like a devil sits on it, I realized that my joy came from my courage to change myself towards my likings, not others. 
After experiencing this confidence boost, in my junior year, I decided to take a leap and host a singing show in front of thousands with the Pioneer Theatre Guild despite having no experience in acting or singing. While I felt ostracized after someone mentioned that my skin was tanner than the other cast members, I made no intention to dab myself with white setting powder. While the other female hosts searched for dresses, I searched for a suit. Stepping out into the hot lights for the first time, I swelled at the feeling of not just representing my true self, but also many others I know were in the audience who also wanted to take the stage. Even after a year, I still feel proud when I get recognized for my iconic velvet suit. 
I took this confidence and eventually translated it to Band, where the girl to guy ratio is 1:3. In Band, there was always a man in charge: band director, drum major, principal chair, colorguard captain, etc. Even when I was Head Librarian with a team of female librarians, the eyes of my peers wander the room as I talk to them, ignoring my efforts. Although I felt frustrated with this disrespect, I still assisted my peers and demonstrated that women can take charge too. After a few long weeks, the band directors expressed gratitude to the librarian team at the end of a drill in front of the band. At last, I heard the claps of appreciation.
Though each of these moments have had their difficulties, each brings me one step closer to my true self. This has had a positive affect on my life at home, as well. A year after the haircut, my mom is finally beginning to pick out suits for me rather than dresses. Her acceptance of me makes me feel satisfied and drives me to tighten our relationship.
Similarly, my manager at work often complains about how other employees leave random boxes behind, resulting in her cleaning it every week. Everytime, I encouraged her to stand up for herself and let the boxes stay. Despite her habits, she resisted the urge. Now, they’ve slowly been disappearing without her acting on it. She smiles and calls me her megaphone—amplification of her voice when she needs it.
As I continue on to college, I will continue to challenge stereotypes and explore my identity, be that through becoming one of the first Asian women to take the stage or leading bands as a female. I also want to influence others to express their resistance to conforming. I know in college I’ll find others like me, but I’m not afraid to be the first either. As I leave high school, I will continue to exist as my authentic self, whatever form that may take, and regardless of others misconceptions.

The body smashed into the ground.

I couldn’t avert my gaze. Without being seen, I witnessed John Wick kill his target with ease. The sticky floors, burps of reclining chairs, slurping of Coca-Cola, and buttery scent of overpriced popcorn couldn’t distract me for a second.

BANG!

Another kill.

Movies aren’t just my favorite pastime. They’re an underworld business, and there’s a strict code that must be followed. Unhealthy snacks must be had, missions can only be completed after dusk, and phones must be powered off, not just silenced.

From the child-like fever dream of “My Neighbor Totoro” to the cocaine-induced financial crisis of “The Wolf of Wall Street”, I've eliminated a variety of targets. However, not every mission has been successful, with failure shooting me in the leg in the cyberpunk biker-gang world of “Akira.”

Mild New York Winter of Junior Year 
7PM

The chilled air, packs of Little Bites beside me, and darkness of my phone screen all alluded to another success… I pressed play. Not even 10 minutes traversing post nuclear Tokyo, I became aware that this wasn’t a quick eliminate-the-target mission. The real mark wasn’t just the movie itself, but the depth of its detail, and my focus was on one object in particular: the Kaneda Bike.

Like every other mission, I started with recon on the film, which led me to a reddit thread about the feasibility of the bright red motorcycle. There, I learned more details about the bike, such as how it's able to lower, and extend itself using cool active suspension. My introductory research of the target told me 1 thing: It was going to be much more difficult than just looking at the art book of the film, watching Katsuhiro Otomo interviews, and creating a model of the bike in CAD. Realizing the disadvantage I was at, I briefed Mr. Regini, my school’s engineering teacher, on the project, and soon after, he was my guy-in-the-chair, guiding me towards my target.

We learned about attempts to recreate the bike in real life, the most successful of which being by Matus1976. His work uncovered a structure towards digital recreation that I could follow. But recon is only the preparatory step, not the full mission. After regular meetings, and weeks of refining the caster angle and long wheelbase, I had a basic Solidworks model of the 1988 anime bike’s functions. Still, there was one opponent blocking me from my target. The egress. The reclining seat would be incredibly difficult to get out of without a mechanic allowing the entire front end to raise up, but no successful attempts at recreating the bike had this mechanic. A workaround I discovered were mechanically sliding armrests that offer support when standing that eject out of the frame, however the distribution of force would’ve been weak when attempting to stand, making the bike unstable and prone to falling.

Lots of meetings with Mr. Regini, and weeks of 1AM sessions spent watching to make this simple mechanic work, trying to take down my target’s second-in-command, and the resources I had for this mission ran low. I was incredibly close, with the target in my sights, but they were able to escape. Despite narrowly evading death and not achieving my ultimate objective, I was able to use the skills I learned to help fix the wiring on Mr. Cador’s motorcycle, and mod the local middle schoolers’ electric bikes to go even faster, assisting them on their own missions.

This business is not one where perfection is expected. In order to survive, it’s essential to adapt and improvise on the fly. And in the event mistakes are still made, as long as you’re still alive, learn from them and continue on. The next four years of my targets will be the most guarded yet, but I am sure I can thrive, eliminate them all, and not get excommunicated in the process.

Leaning into the mirror, I brush strokes of thick, green paint across my face, contorting my youthful features to resemble a terrifying hag. I widen my eyes in the reflection, marveling at my transformation into the Wicked Witch.

The spotlight beams on my tacky skin as I clench my broom, a scowl masking my nerves. Dorothy splashes me with water. I scream, thrash as I’m lowered into the pit, “Noooo!! I’m melting, I’m melting!!”

Initially, I was not thrilled about playing an ugly villain. However, my interpretation evoked an alternate perspective: she was mourning the death of her sister (thanks Dorothy). More importantly, performing as the Wicked Witch taught me how powerful female roles are often misunderstood as villainous.

Unjust, villainous caricatures of women go beyond fairy tales. In 2016, I watched Hillary Clinton on TV, perplexed and angry as she faced both overt and subtle sexism for the same assertive traits that are praised in men. At home, I saw my mother, a single mom, experience the same systemic sexism, as she struggled to balance a full-time job with raising two kids, due to insufficient childcare.

Rather than remain a spectator, I sought to take the advocacy of female roles in the performing arts and apply it to areas where women are still underrepresented. This led me to create Leadership for Women, a club where I invited speakers like Congresswoman Grace Meng and LAPD Deputy Chief Ruby Flores to share their powerful journeys: oftentimes they were the only women in a room full of men, yet they confidently made executive decisions. With these influential figures, I facilitated guidance and education between female mentors and young girls about various career paths, as well as how to pursue/reach leadership positions in male-dominated fields.

Listening to speakers involved in the public sector helped me recognize the importance of governance and its potential to be an outlet for my passion, drawing me to Youth and Government (YNG). I discovered that YNG could expose me to decision-making processes and highlight how salient issues, including gender inequality, could be addressed through policy. Though it was a mock legislature, YNG connected me to real lawmakers in Sacramento.

I remember anxiously clenching my papers at Bill Hearing Night, where proposals could potentially cross Governor Newsom’s desk. “State your name and delegation”. “[Name] Wang from the SPPY-WY delegation”. Standing firmly at the podium, I glanced towards the table of all male panelists and faced an auditorium full of 87 people. I was terrified of my audience but I drew from my mother’s resilience. I spoke with conviction, explaining how my bill provided tax breaks to corporations who implemented on-site child care facilities.

My bill did not pass. I truly felt like the Wicked Witch–misunderstood. As I looked back at the panel that did not resonate with or understand the issue, I reflected on their decision and realized diversity is crucial in leadership and policy-making.

At National conferences, this frustration fueled me as I scrambled from building to building in business attire, handing out badges and encouraging girls to pre-register to vote. Despite the discomfort of my outfit and getting in teenagers faces, I was determined to maximize outreach and spread the message of the impact of not only the youth voice, but the female voice. These girls can alter the stigma around women in politics and stand behind gender equality.

Playing the Wicked Witch pushed me beyond my comfort zone, teaching me to embrace roles that challenge traditional perceptions. This performance emboldened me to defy stereotypes both on stage and in real life. In college, I want to expand my advocacy beyond theater to drive societal impact in business and politics. Though the Wicked Witch may have melted, her fearlessness endures in me as I embark on my journey to become a powerful women leader.

A rebellion

“[Name], would you like to join AMC competition?”, “[Name], would you like to join Rockery club?”, “[Name], do you want to prepare for your SAT exam?”, “[Name], would you practice your piano?”. “No”, “No”, “No”, “No”. You are right, I may not be a good Asian son of a tiger mom. Sorry, mom, I may not like what you visioned me to be, a good “[Name] Federer” type of kid.

A quiet Saturday morning, sun shed glimpses of warmth on my piano, a regular time I need to practice, only birds chirping, I need to practice it again and again, a piece I am already so familiar with. But isn’t that bird singing its own song? I practice for what? To get a piano level certificate? And what next? I can’t imagine where I will be since we have Lang Lang, but I like the bird’s freedom. “Mom, I want to stop the piano class. I’ve already got a good base in music theory. Can I compose my own song?” I get my parents’ support, I can freely write something, I hum for myself, relaxed and encouraging.

One year after, I showcased my first award-winning piece in Vienna Ehrbar Hall Golden Key Music Festival, the notes flowing out of my fingers, but my mind and heart pulled back to the summer three years ago when my parents took me back to China, where we needed to take the train to another city. The station was crowded, all travelers rushing to get on the train, only a man was sitting on a chair with a cigar in his hand, he is not afraid of missing his train? Instead, he enjoyed being there alone with the smoky air and lost. After one cigar, he stood up, walked back to the waiting room, I could tell he was ready for the next train. Isn’t he refreshed! I am impressed by his composure, the calm rhythm, arising in my mind a piece of calm, no rushes, no hustles. I would like to praise this strong moment, my confidence in getting lost, and bounce back. The opportunity is there, and I am ready to get on. I ended the piece with a very pleasant tick tick sound of a train, that is my steady steps toward uncertainties.

As I get into 10th grade, school work starts to build up. My school has an SAT boot camp, mom asked me to prepare for the exam. But I don’t have a feeling to get too much into it because that is, after all, a test of IQ when it is originally designed to verify the aptitude for learning when it is first introduced to the US army. If we overdo the testing, the test result is defeating the purpose. I decided to use my own approach to prepare for it. Bought the SAT prep book, took 5 mock exams, and found out where I get mistakes, then summarized the lessons, making sure I don’t make the same mistakes, and I know my level, just move on take the test, that’s true to myself.

I don’t want to join the AMC competition because all you do is just practice, the solutions are there, it’s not creative to reinvent the wheels. I aspire for something new, not tried by other people, not repeating the same again and again to perfect it. After all, new challenges are always there, new solutions have to be out to resolve them. I want to tell mom, I will be ok without following your designed path. I don’t have to join the rockery club to demonstrate I want to do science research. The AI world needs someone creative, not repetitive. I will be ok dear mom.

“Laoba, stay safe!” echoed young [Name]’s voice, chasing after her dad barefooted amidst the dark night. Just minutes before, she was in bed, ready to sleep, until the car engine roared outside the window. Vroom, off it went as she witnessed the lights trail off in the distance bidding farewell.

Her dad was always on business trips. On the few occasions that he visits home, he never fails to bring her a piece of dark chocolate.

“Any other chocolate would ruin your teeth,” he sternly noted.

While other kids savored the sweetness of milk or white chocolate, she remained loyal to the bittersweet bar. These chocolates were very dear to her, a comforting remnant of her dad’s presence.

As she grew older, the more she realized that her dad was everywhere, but home. His occasional stays between the never-ending business trips shortened with each visit.
Ring ding~ “LAOBA!” She exclaimed as she yanked the door open at his unexpected appearance.

“Hi [Name],” he responded with a weak squeeze and proceeded to his room. 
Where was her chocolate? He always came home with chocolate in hand; maybe he was too tired today, he had never once forgotten.

The next day, as she groggily made it to the kitchen for breakfast, her dad had already left for his trip with no chocolate in sight. Ever since then, he had never brought her chocolate from his trips again.

As years passed by, my family moved to Hong Kong for better educational and occupational opportunities. Being the only mainland Chinese student in an international school, I was constantly grappling with language barriers and cultural differences. I found solace in the simple act of treating myself to chocolate even though I no longer receive them from dad. As he grew forgetful of our traditions, so did my independence to protect my vulnerability from being expectant of others. Chocolate became a tangible reminder that I am capable of providing myself with the comfort and happiness I longed for. The security I found in self-reliance transformed into a shield against potential disappointment as I became reluctant to fully trust and connect with my community. At that moment, I believed that only I will always be there for myself.

Due to a relationship mishap in high school, I moved alone to America for a fresh start. I couldn’t fathom sharing a room with a roommate I barely knew. I feel that my right to privacy was evoked, having to live so closely with another. I had always remained bottled up until I couldn’t disguise my emotions at the saddening news of my dog passing away. She reached out, offering comfort when I needed it most. Overwhelmed with grief, I found solace in my roommate's unexpected compassion. For the first time, the following day, we shared a meal together. In that simple act of kindness, our bond budded beautifully. Through these small, heartfelt interactions, my roommate’s persistent kindness blossomed over my walls. The bond transformed my dissociation into our deep sense of sisterhood. I learned the profound impact of genuine connections and how even the smallest gestures can create lasting, meaningful relationships. It reshaped my understanding of friendship and community, demonstrating the power of empathy and the beauty of finding family.

Soon after, came my junior year graduation. My dad arrived with a bouquet of flowers and a bar of chocolate in his hands. I looked into his eyes and smiled with the strength I built through this journey. Chocolate will always be chocolate, and I will always be human, but what truly sets us apart is how one enriches and packages themselves. Just as each chocolate has its unique wrapping, it’s my individuality and growth that sets me apart.

“Thanks laoba” I whispered as the wind carried my voice away.

Cherish the way you evolve, just as each piece of chocolate finds its special place in the world.

Every May, the bushes across my boarding house crowd with blossomed peonies, their bright pink petals a joyful proclamation of the end of the harsh winter and the arrival of the warm summer. I find myself drawn to the flower I was named after, the “king of flowers” in Chinese culture, renowned for its exquisite beauty and unique intricacy.

My name was always a source of discomfort for me. I resented the fact that it was often mispronounced by teachers, and its uncommonness only served to make me stand out even more. But it was when I found myself at a new boarding school in Sevenoaks, a staggering 9,532km from home, that I truly despised it.

Like a bee in a field devoid of flowers, I felt lost and out of place. Even casual conversations about popular TV shows left me feeling isolated. While my peers excitedly discussed Ant and Dec, I could only nod in confusion, convinced they were talking about a wildlife documentary. Instead of being a peony, I just wanted to blend in with the roses.

On Easter of year 10, my dad and I visited the Keukenhof flower festival in Amsterdam, where an abundance of flowers bloomed vibrantly amongst the grass. I noticed that despite all the flowers’ intrinsic differences, they all flourished brilliantly, one next to the other. Learning about the anti-inflammatory powers of the [Name], and the “1000-year-old [Name] Tree” in China, which has been credited for its resilience and versatility, I began to appreciate the flowers’ unwavering confidence. It is only with the [Name]’s inherent characteristics that the richness and glamour of the garden can be cultivated.

Below the dreary April sky, raindrops of adrenaline suffocated the London Olympic Pool as my teammates argued, disagreeing with the order of the relay. My struggle to fit into my new life taught me that it is not intrinsic similarities that tie people together to success but the acceptance of differences, just like how it was through the [Name]’s healing powers that the garden in Amsterdam could flourish with vitality. Transforming into the [Name] flower, I mediated the diverging opinions of my teammates, concluding in a compromise and healing the wounds of conflict. 5 minutes later, our team were crowned the first Winners of the Bath and Otter Cup in our school’s history. Hand in hand, united as a team. Once again, the [Name] flower had utilized its healing powers.

Peonies require a period of harsh winter dormancy before they bloom. Under the thick blanket of British precipitation, the suggestion of returning home, the yearning for comfort and familiarity, dwindled at me like a bee prowling at a flower. However, just as the bee knew if it persisted, honey could be collected, discipline and resilience were an ingrained aspect of my Cantonese upbringing, and I knew I would rise high and mighty through engendering a vivacious spirit against discomfort and hardship. I started to face the unknown: unknown knowledge, culture, sayings and experiences with a mountain of curiosity as opposed to fear. Soon enough, May arrived, the peonies began to bloom, and I came to appreciate my unique obstacles of understanding as an intellectual and curious mystery, a droplet of water in my everblooming flower.

Understanding different perspectives and people and learning from them has cultivated a diverse and exhilarating learning environment for growth, where there is an endless supply of things to learn, understand, teach and tell. Like petals, my differences shower me with knowledge of varying perspectives and experiences, which are loosely folded and stacked together, forming an intricate blooming flower.

In July, my dad visited me at school, and I pointed out a peony I saw, he insisted it was a rose. In fact, it is a Paeonia lactiflora hybrid: a [Name] Rose Mix, a symbol of my journey of embracing my unique identity and the diversity of experiences that have shaped me.

I stared at the many iterations of my name on the piece of paper in front of me in deep thought. I was writing my letter to Santa, asking for Pokemon cards, and had to sign it. By my Dad’s logic, it felt perfectly reasonable to turn this into a “teaching moment”, lecturing me on the legal implications of a signature. “Your signature binds you…legally…impersonating you…jail time…” I tuned out after the first sentence, turning my attention to my signature. Eventually, I gave up, entrusting my future self to this momentous task, settling for an uninspired printing of my name.

Signatures were the tokens of adult life—businessmen signing checks, politicians signing bills, and athletes signing autographs. I crafted many signatures, yearning for a relic of my unique presence, an exercise in independence, a unique culture of the self.

I was a perfectionist when it came to my signature. A signature had to represent “you”, not least from a legal standpoint. My signature was more than just a reiteration of my handle in society; it was a map of the self.

It starts with a graceful sweep of the pen, looping up and down, to create an “f” in equilibrium, sleek in shape but strong in disposition. The pen then levels off, delineating the rest of my name with the loops and curls of “…rank.” Then, with a sudden speed, the “tail” of the “k” rises up as another character begins to take shape. Two crescents with the sharpest of angles trace out the Chinese character for my last name, “王” in cursive, ending in a sleek horizontal line, fading into nothing. In one smooth, fluid pen motion, twirling and dancing on the paper, the trail of ink paints out me.

Each loop and curl adds pizazz to the aesthetic but is also a reminder of the distinctiveness of my personal journey. Insofar as making my signature legible, the exaggerated curves do not curry any favors, but they still flow through my name just as my passions and interests flow through my person, carrying conviction as an indivisible part of my existence. My signature is a statement on my individuality.

The blending of my English name and Chinese last name also blends the cultures that shape me. The elegant integration of Latin letters and Chinese characters brings about the essence of my identity, with the ending line tracing out a blank space, inviting further additions. My signature is a celebration of the cultures that represent me, but also of my willingness to interact with others.

The unique attention paid to each character delineates my keen attention to detail. Every stroke of the pen is made with intention and purpose, as the whole cannot be complete without the precision of every part, and so is my identity without every minute detail. My signature is a memo to the self to value all.

Moreover, this peculiar dedication to the perfection of my signature bears testimony to my devotion to the self. The process of gradual but perpetual improvement with every signing paralleled my outlook on this world. With every new attempt, the pen completes another brilliant dance of selfhood, adding new details to the autobiographical play that is the signature. Precision and concreteness mark the signatures after lengthy bouts of time spent understanding the laws of physics. Chaotic and visceral is the penmanship of signatures after hours spent writing unfamiliar words in Arabic script. Tentative but emphatic define the signatures in my diaries after sudden spells of introspective self-reflection.

Behold my evolving map of the self: since its first iteration, change has been abundant. Despite its multiple evolutions from experience, the signature still represents me. The legal implications of signatures will restrict me from changing it. But more importantly, I will maintain my identity, although changes to the style will always be welcomed.

Maybe I loved signing my name because of a deep desire for self-expression. Each stroke represented my curiosity, my zealousness, and my unwavering enthusiasm. Behold the evolving script of my identity: tough change through growth can only enrich it; it will stay true to its origins.

1, 4, 9, 16, 25—perfect squares.

Coin flipping, dice rolling, card drawing - binomial distribution

Circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola—conic sections

Math is comforting in its consistency. As long as you take the right steps, you’ll arrive at the correct answer. But what defies predictability? A mysterious illness with random, erratic symptoms.

Since my “diagnosis,” my life has become anything but logical. Each day brought new, unpredictable challenges—rashes one day, severe headaches the next, and extreme stomach pain on another. Different doctors offered conflicting opinions, leaving me without a clear path to surgery or specific treatment. For someone who thrives on order and logic, this lack of structure was terrifying.

The year I spent away from school felt like a grueling battle against an invisible enemy—no logic, no structure, no nothing. Each failed treatment, each dead-end diagnosis, left me feeling more powerless. My mind, used to neat equations, was forced to confront chaos; and my body, once predictable, had turned into a puzzle I couldn’t solve.

What was ironic about my eventual recovery is that, though we ended up finding a medicine that worked for me, it still didn’t explain my illness or the cause of my symptoms. It was a partial answer, found through endless trial and error, offering no real clarity. So when I finally felt well enough to return to school, the first thing on my list was to regain the structure I had lost– timetables, deadlines, routines. But one part of school remained unpredictable: people.

One of the challenges after returning to school from a year of being hospitalized is that your classmates are no longer the ones you knew well. The isolation is one thing, but the age gap is another– most of them were a year or year and a half younger than I was, and I found myself being addressed as “hyung,” a term of respect for older boys in Korea. Polite? Sure, but it’s definitely a point that makes you feel out of place.

Determined to keep everything under control, I came up with a common denominator: Icebreakers. Not like the “2 truths and a lie” type of ones—like the literal, coolmint flavored icebreakers. An effective, light-hearted intro route to making new friends.

But as I quickly learned, people don’t follow a formula, the same way my illness and my eventual recovery didn’t have a streamline of equations that made sense. Some conversations never went beyond offering a mint. Some didn’t even want the mint. No matter how much I planned, I couldn’t "solve" social dynamics like an equation. People were unpredictable, each with their own complex patterns.

The funny thing is, I don’t know exactly what worked in the end. One day, I found myself laughing with my classmates, the conversations flowing naturally, without any reliance on the Icebreakers in my pocket. On other days, the mints I brought as an icebreaker came after the conversations started, not before– totally against my initial hypothesis, and that was okay. And soon enough, I no longer religiously carried a pack of Icebreakers in my pocket to school.

In those moments, I realized that the real solution to all my quests, the illness and making friends alike, came from the very fact that I didn’t know. What I viewed as a partial, incomplete solution to my illness, in retrospect, was a miraculous moment of trial and error finally finding its course. The Icebreakers, which I thought would bring order and structure, never even ended up being used in the way I intended. My illness was unpredictable, and so were the people around me. Both situations defied the structure I wanted to impose on them.

At last, I was able to understand the true value behind my quest for patterns. Each journey was able to show me that the real journey I was searching for was not the final answer but more of the process of getting to it. Unpredictability can’t always be solved by forcing it into a structure. It’s handled through improvisation, trial and error, and—most importantly—the power of letting go.

As a daughter of an Active-duty military service member, I am aware of the dangers faced by those who serve, however I was unprepared for when those dangers would personally impact me. On March 22, 2016, the Brussels Airport was attacked by terrorists with explosives, leading to the deaths of 32 people. This day is etched into my memory, and the consequences of that attack have shaped my journey of personal growth and resilience. At just 8 years old, I faced the impact of such a tragedy and began to explore my inner strength with the guidance of my parents. This experience has shown me the importance of resilience—staying focused on the present and not being overwhelmed by past traumas or future uncertainties.

In 2014, the Army reassigned my family to the Netherlands from Virginia. The transition from American culture to Europe was challenging, but I found a close friend in Noe, whose family was also in the military. Our families formed an immediate connection and planned a joint vacation to Spain in the Spring of 2016. But that trip was not meant to be. At the last minute, Noe’s family canceled to visit family in the States. My family proceeded with our trip to Spain. On the morning of March 22, as my family and I boarded our flight back to Brussels, Noe’s family was leaving for America from Brussels airport. Minutes before our flight was scheduled to take off, we were abruptly forced off the plane due to a terror attack.

The chaos that unfolded, combined with my family's inability to contact Noe’s family, marked the beginning of my journey through grief and anxiety. Although my family was safe, navigating back home amidst the turmoil was challenging.

We later found out that Noe’s mother had been killed in the attack, and her family had suffered severe burns. The shock of learning about their suffering and the gravity of the situation at such a young age was overwhelming. The realization, this could have been my family, drives me toward the importance of cherishing every day.

Unbeknownst to me at the time, the airport attack would become a catalyst for how I live my life. I have dedicated myself to volunteering, running and embracing every opportunity for personal and academic growth. I am committed to pursuing my goals with determination. By volunteering with the United Service Organizations (USO) at the airport, I have discovered the value of giving back to military families. I take great pride in helping those who selflessly sacrifice for our country, and I have come to appreciate that everyone has a story deserving of being heard.

Running has become an essential part of my life, serving as an outlet for managing anxiety and life’s challenges. I also encourage others in my community to use running as a means of stress relief. I am a High School Ambassador for a running shoe store where I play a vital role in empowering people of all ages to embrace running, walking and movement to improve their physical and mental health. This role allows me to be a leader in my community.

Academically, I have taken proactive steps to prepare for my future by attending pre-college summer programs. These experiences have strengthened my commitment to my goals. I am determined to seize every opportunity available to me as I learned early on, tomorrow is not promised.

As I prepare for college, I am confident that the resilience and drive I have developed will support my future success. The Brussels Airport terror attack, while a painful memory, has taught me the importance of perseverance and has reinforced my commitment to making the most of every opportunity. My journey of personal growth, supported by my parents and enriched by my extracurricular activities, continues to empower me. I choose to let this memory fuel my ambitions rather than deter me.

“Do your best, but you don’t have to be the best,” Papa always told me.

A cliché saying I secretly rolled my eyes to, turned a prophecy in disguise.

Above all else, how does one best cancer?

Before morphine took over, I’d make him avocado juices and stovetop banana oatmeals, adding unsolicited peanut butter or condensed milk: desperate calories I thought would counter his depleting weight.

On the days he seemed lethargic, I’d send him YouTube videos of low-impact exercises. “You don’t have energy because you never move, Pa! It’s an ongoing cycle,” I’d insist. But he’d just agree, smile, then return to lying on his side.

When he was eventually bedridden, all I could do was prevent pressure sores—the relentless ticking of the clock louder than his breaths, more alive with movement. I stared at the mocking hand with bitter determination.

How could time live on, without guilt?

How do tiny metastasised cells best my father?

I’d even failed him.

***

In tandem was another attempt of mine, 9 years in progress.

At 6 years old, I noticed my 19-year-old brother often punched his forehead or screamed and slammed objects unannounced when he became overwhelmed.

So I tried, for many years, to take him away from overstimulation, maintain a quiet environment. But his episodes would surge unpredictably, like storms appearing on a clear day. Unlike clouds and wind, I struggled to identify the sources of his distress, often unable to sense them myself.

Years passed and I grew older, him being a constant. Merely telling him to stop only provided temporary relief and soon became ineffective. He was… gnawing himself from the inside, lacking purpose.

When this came over me freshman year, I started teaching him something after dinners and on the weekends. Having a more concrete goal to trudge towards was helpful for both him and myself.

He’d always liked making stories and drawing with a notebook and ballpoint pen, a hobby he transferred to Canva.

We’d watch the Avengers film together. When the English vocabulary and grammar I taught him were growing sufficient, he finally understood the subtitles.

But still, every step forward seemed like two steps back, and we were running on an unending marathon track that only ends when we do. A success or failure depends on the day.

***

Sometimes, hope is found and then lost, over and over, or never there at all.

Not even a few months after Papa’s passing, my 7-month journey began: leading our biggest school event since the pandemic.

Certainly, not what I thought. Supportive teachers and constructive criticism quickly devolved into dismissiveness and outright hostility. Constantly skipping meetings, ignoring text messages, or for one, being unmistakably condescending and hateful. “I’ve never and will never pray for you” or “You’re all bound for failure”. Taking students’ ideas and rebranding them as their own.

No. We could not be hopeless. At least the end goal was clear.

With a few others, I decided to handle every aspect of the event ourselves. I developed the theme and concept, crafted countless proposals and spreadsheets, oversaw various divisions, managed our website, and conducted nearly daily meetings with teachers during breaks or after school. I coordinated with sponsors, guest stars, and vendors, led fundraising events, and tackled many other tasks.

Despite people’s praises, were the sacrifices worth it?

I found my answer in the smiling, singing crowd: including the committee, who were once discouraged zombies.

***

Unlike the last fragment of my story I just told, most others don’t give the privilege of goodbye or closure. They pass without farewell, time refusing to wait. Although this will inevitably happen, I wish differently for others. Whether it’s finding inspiration in their favourite superhero movie, or having actual medical tools and advancements to battle life’s goliath, everyone deserves to feel that they were able to do their best. And I will be the one to empower them.

The day I arrived at San Francisco International Airport five years ago, I knew I had stepped into a different world. Raised in Korea, I was deeply influenced by “Yugyo Sasang,” Korea’s adaptation of Confucian principles, which I call “Yugyoism.” This philosophy emphasizes respecting authority, valuing modesty, and prioritizing group harmony. For me, blending in and suppressing my voice for the benefit of the group felt natural; acting otherwise seemed self-centered and out of place.

My initial days in America were a series of culture-shock moments that forced me to rethink how I interacted with people. In class, I discovered that my reluctance to volunteer answers, stemming from my desire to avoid standing out, was often misinterpreted by teachers as disinterest or a lack of confidence. Group projects were another challenge; failure to speak up when necessary often resulted in me taking on most of the work while others, who contributed little, received the credit.

But the most impactful experience involved my mom at a supermarket. When I was fourteen, a cashier treated her rudely because, although she was college-educated in Korea, she was not accustomed to American English and she didn’t immediately understand his simple instructions. “PLACE THE BASKET UNDER THE COUNTER!” the cashier yelled impatiently. Frustrated and unsure how to respond, I quickly whispered the translation to my mom. She blushed in embarrassment, paid without a word, and hurried out. That night, I couldn’t sleep, replaying the incident and considering a complaint to the manager. My frustration grew, not just at the cashier but at myself for not speaking up. This experience made me question my cultural values, realizing that while Yugyoism offers valuable guidance, it shouldn’t prevent me from standing up for myself and others. This realization sparked a determination in me to break from Yugyoism and start voicing my opinions more assertively.

Consequently, I began participating more in class discussions, ran for student government, and joined the Model United Nations, all of which helped me find my voice. As my confidence grew, I started advocating not just for myself, but for others as well. When a quiet classmate was repeatedly excluded from school projects, I took it upon myself to persuade my group to include her. When our class felt a teacher’s exam policy was too rigid, I initiated a conversation with the teacher on behalf of the class to request a reconsideration.

My growing involvement in advocating for myself and others naturally led me to seek out more formal opportunities to develop these skills. This drive took shape in the form of an internship at the LA District Attorney’s Office. Initially, I imagined myself observing courtrooms and the prosecutors’ oratory skills, but I quickly learned advocacy extends far beyond the courtroom. Effective advocacy demands not only making one’s voice heard, but also conducting thorough behind-the-scenes work to ensure it is heard correctly. Another valuable observation I made was how, in maximizing efficiency in the office, the DA’s office valued hierarchical order, seniority, and teamwork – principles that resonate with Yugyoism instilled in me by my parents.

As I delved deeper into these reflections, I began to see that the values with which I was raised could coexist with, and even enhance my new American mindset. This realization led me to reflect on how Yugyoism and American values aren’t necessarily at odds. Respecting elders, valuing hard work, and prioritizing the greater good are universal virtues, not just Korean ones. The difference lies in how they’re practiced. With this understanding, I reembraced Yugyoism, now integrating it with my American perspectives. This evolved perspective, which I call “Yugyoism version 2.0,” allows me to honor traditions while assertively voicing my views.

I still remember the public humiliation vividly: my mom’s face was reddened with embarrassment as the cashier glared at her, frustrated that she didn’t immediately understand his instructions due to her limited English. Thinking this was uncalled for, and perhaps even tinged with an anti-Asian sentiment, I stepped in to confront him. But my mom stopped me, quietly paid the cashier and we left the store.

I felt frustrated not just at the cashier but at my mom for holding me back. I told her, “In America, not speaking up is seen as a sign of weakness,” and urged her to leave behind Korean values that didn’t fit. My mom disagreed, saying it was her fault for not knowing English well enough, and promised to study it harder. Then she shared another nugget of Korean wisdom: “Wae Yu Nae Gang.” It’s no use appearing strong on the outside. What matters is inner strength.

“There she goes again, with her Korean values,” I thought. There was a growing cultural gap between my mom and me since moving to America five years ago, but this time it felt personal. I replayed the supermarket incident in my head, reflecting on what it meant. Then, something about what my mom said clicked: What good would confronting the cashier have done? Did I even understand where this Asian hate comes from or how to really address it?

Reflecting on this, I realized that reconciling the supermarket incident may not be as simple as choosing one set of values over another. As my inner conflict between dual value systems continued, they gradually began to merge, with my mom’s Korean values taking an important place in the integrated version. While it is important to stand up against injustice, it requires inner strength not to act rashly.

I wasn’t sure where to find this inner strength, but realizing the key was to educate myself, I first delved into books like The Origin of Others by Toni Morrison and The Making of Asian America by Erika Lee. These books taught me that Asian hate is another sign of human frailty: we fear, and so we hate, what we don’t understand. Much like how I instinctively took the cashier’s actions personally and wanted to lash out at him, those who harbor anti-Asian sentiments do so because they have limited understanding of Asian Americans.

Although it was never my intention to educate others about the Asian American experience, it kind of happened naturally as my knowledge spilled over. It began with casual conversations with my non-Asian best friends introducing them to Asian American cultures and history. After experiencing the exhilaration of discussing real-world Korean American issues on The Sisa Journal’s K-Your Personal Achievement Radio, as president of AAPI Club, I organized our school’s first ever exclusive library exhibition on Asian American heritage. I also began teaching Korean to sixth graders at my church, and this past summer, I launched my passion project to petition the California Legislature to include Asian American history in public education.

These efforts all came together to teach me that my mom was right. Educating myself about the Asian American experience gave me the strength I had been searching for. The confidence I gained from sharing what I knew, the emotional feedback I received from friends, and the sense of vindication I felt when my survey showed that the public overwhelmingly supported integrating Asian American history into school curricula, were all so much more powerful than simply lashing out at that cashier would have been.

Now, when I see my mom practicing her English every day on YouTube—building her own inner strength—I smile, knowing I’ve found mine, too. In the end, I realized that my mom’s Korean values and my American ideals aren’t in conflict after all; they complement each other perfectly, just as we have always done as mother and son.

“Mes élèves, le changement fait de nous ce que nous sommes (Change makes us who we are).”

My French teacher once asked our class, “If you could define your life in one word, what would it be?”

When it was my turn, I responded with “changement (change).” To me, change, specifically in the area of friendships, has provided the most poignant, influential, and meaningful experiences of my life.

Lucas was my first friend: the first person who liked me just because I was me. We never expected anything from each other except ourselves. Eddie was unimaginably kind. I met him on my first day in grade 4, and through our time together, I learned what true compassion looked like. Nelson was loud, assertive, and everything else that I wasn’t. Though different in many ways, he taught me how to get out of my comfort zone and stand up for what I believe in.

My life has been filled with transitions — new schools, new experiences, and a sea of new friends. With each farewell, however, I became more guarded because I didn’t know if my new relationships would endure. Drifting apart from a close friend carried the sadness of watching a fond attachment fade into a memory.

Ironically, it was a simple conversation with Nelson that gently unraveled my old frame of mind. As we strolled around my school’s quad, he unexpectedly expressed how grateful he was to be my friend. Caught off guard, I could only ask him “why?”

“You’ve given me kindness and understanding I didn’t even know I needed. I will never forget that.”

Although Nelson likely didn’t understand the significance of his words, at that moment, I finally started to recognize the impact I could have on others. I’d always been focused on what my friends could give me, but for the first time, I realized I had something meaningful to offer them. I realized that the strongest friendships were always two-way streets, and mine was actually open.

My change in perspective also helped me recognize the influence my old friends had on my life. By realizing the ways I could help others, I became more cognizant of the ways they helped me. Their lessons combined with my own morals have guided my actions and shaped the person I’ve become.

When I set up chairs for a 7am rehearsal at six, it was because just like Lucas, I wanted to help out simply because I cared. As I saw the glimmer in Tom’s eyes as we finished his English assignment, it reinforced to me that kindness is its own reward — something Eddie taught me all those years ago. Finally, when I struggled to launch my non-profit tutoring organization because I was afraid of outside opinions, Nelson gave me the confidence I needed to create the community I’ve built today.

At long last, I understand the importance of creating relationships: Even though goodbyes are inevitable, the memories we create, the lessons we take away, and the influence we have are forever. I used to think I was losing a piece of myself every time I moved away, but now I know I was really gaining a new one to add to my ever-growing puzzle.

Equipped with this understanding, I am finally ready to embrace the change around me because, for the first time, I know that I am moving forward, not backward. As I move into college, I’m excited to join a new community where I can use the pieces I’ve collected throughout my life to enrich the lives around me. I’m confident that I will be able to foster a supportive environment with my peers since I know it’s the people that create our experiences, who have the greatest impact on our lives.

“Charge!” The clash of weapons and cries of horses ring throughout the plains of the battlefield as the main character of the manga Kingdom, Ri Shin, looks on. Kingdom dives into the journey of Shin, a war orphan during China’s warring states period who aims to become the “greatest general under the heavens.” As Shin rose the ranks, growing from a lowly peasant foot soldier to a mighty general, he created numerous bonds with his comrades, even the king himself.

Just like many others, I isolated myself during the COVID pandemic, losing contact with many of my classmates and friends when we lost our ability to talk to each other between classes and in the halls. Without connections with my friends and interest in my activities, I began to read manga. After we returned to school, while reading another manga during free time in class, my classmate came up to me. “You should try Kingdom, it’s peak!” My interest piqued and I quickly became immersed in the massive battles and struggles of Shin. Inspired by how Shin built bonds throughout his unit as well as with other generals, I was motivated to emerge from my shy, isolated shell in order to reconnect with my peers. I began recommending the manga to my peers, slowly reconnecting myself as we discussed various story arcs and characters. We would spend all lunch discussing how powerful it was when Shin and the king of Qin fought off all the other kingdoms and nearly had tears in our eyes when Shin finally inherited his late mentor’s legacy, wielding their glaive on the battlefield. As we talked more about Kingdom, we also began giving recommendations on other manga, as well as awaiting the newest leaks of our other favorite mangas.

Just like Shin forging connections on his journey to become a general, through Kingdom, I was able to reforge lost connections that I previously had, but more importantly, grow out of a shyer, introverted version of myself that had set roots during the pandemic. Kingdom has helped me grow as a person during a pivotal part of my life and I’ll carry the lessons I’ve learned into college and beyond.

I’ve never believed in Santa. If he was real, I should’ve received a delivery from him by now. Mom claimed that gifts were merely courtesies wrapped in shiny paper; instead, I was raised by acts of service: magical conjurings of peeled longans on my desk when I arose from naps and unspoken reservations that entitled me to the last drumstick at dinner. As a child looking to expand my toy empire, I wanted to disagree, but with frequent reminders on how money comes from hard labor, I reluctantly withheld my rebuttal.

Labor looked like the torn hangnails on Mom’s hands from folding hundreds of pounds of laundry every day. Labor felt like the cracked skin on Dad’s fingertips due to overexposure to detergents and fabric softeners. The image of their worn hands grasped my heart with guilt whenever I dared to feel disappointed by the absence of presents under my imaginary Christmas tree.

***

When Dad's birthday approached in late July, I had no idea what to get him. Hand-written cards got buried in the basement, while homemade cakes got devoured by my sister and me (Mom said he couldn’t have any because of his high cholesterol). For Dad, practicality determined the value of a gift. Yet, when I asked him what he wanted, all he said was “You need to take care of yourself before taking care of others.”

In half spite and half determination to prove I could do both, I spent my last summer tutoring middle schoolers. I ceaselessly answered questions like, “Is 1 a prime number?” (no), “Were you nervous like us when you took your SHSAT?” (yes), and “Can you make penne alla vodka?” (kind of). As I left camp with cash weighing down my jeans pocket, my heart lightened, relieved that for a while, I could skip the trimonthly dread of asking my parents for allowance. After budgeting for the school year, I scoured “Best Father Day Gifts!” articles until I landed on a product that resurfaced memories of gingerly applying a herbal-smelling pain relief balm on Dad’s back: a Viktor Jurgen massage pillow. It’s practical, perhaps dull, but just his taste.

With a bunch of bananas (potassium for the cramps), I delivered the pillow while reminiscing about the hours of work and contemplation that brought it to Dad’s hands. The gift was simultaneously an act of service and a declaration that often, albeit silently, echoed across this house: “I love you.”

While he gleamed with a smile that showed off his chipped front tooth, my vicarious happiness showed me the symbiotic beauty of gift-giving. The $24.99 transaction in my Chase account never failed to flood my heart with pride every time I logged in to see the deduction again.

Although the bananas have long been digested, the pillow now has a permanent spot on our living room couch. Dad’s unexpected attachment to the pillow proved that it wasn’t that my parents didn’t like gifts, they just never had the chance to receive them, having grown up poor and immigrated to America in their youth. But now I can buy my own presents, so I can buy the presents my parents won’t get for themselves too.

In my family, we show affection through acts of service, but now, I’m also our designated gift-giver. By exploring love beyond the forms I was conditioned to, I’ve transformed the gifts I once shunned as a child into symbols of love for my family. As I continuously add new expressions of love into my repertoire, it becomes clear that affection isn’t bound by any single cast; whether through sharing BBQ Pringles with my fellow foodies or mindfully responding to all fifty Instagram reels that my friends send, I’ll continue pioneering the multifaceted nature of love. The next birthday coming up is my own, but I already know what books I should surprise my bibliophile sister with in November.

In 7th grade, my science teacher, Mr. Mahoney said, “Who knows? One day you might actually cure cancer!”

As cheesy as it sounds, I imagined myself holding a bottle with that magic potion.

Except the cure wasn’t for me. It was for my grandpa, who was diagnosed with Stage III pancreatic cancer. During my grandpa’s chemotherapy, I watched as he went from a cane to a wheelchair to lying in bed. My last memories of him were him screaming for help after falling off his mattress at 5 am.

Though my grandfather’s plight was what first drew me to cancer biology, I quickly found the study of genetic regulation, from DNA methylation to alternative splicing, to be both personally fulfilling and intellectually engaging.

This past summer, I had the privilege of studying transcriptomics and RNA sequencing at the Lin Lab. I especially loved two papers I read about how the chemotherapy drug 5-AZA-CdR activated endogenous retroviruses to initiate an immune response, one of which was co-authored by Dr. Baylin. Furthermore, I learned wet lab techniques like qPCR and Western blot, as well as TEQUILA-seq (the Lin Lab’s cutting-edge RNA sequencing technique!). But the best part was confirming the results from my favorite papers with my own qPCRs, which further fueled my excitement for exploring genomics in cancer!

Still, I was left with many questions: How are reads mapped to a reference genome? What is the full potential for RNA sequencing?

At Hopkins, I hope to once again take advantage of its wealth of research opportunities to learn more about cancer and epigenetics, by joining Dr. Baylin’s lab. I would also take the first-year seminar, Phage Hunters, with Dr. Fisher, where I would enhance my knowledge of sequencing and genome analysis with bacteriophages. On weekends, I would be doing community service with groups from the Center for Social Concern, such as Food as Medicine and Baltimore First. Furthermore, I would love to explore how religion, morality, and music intersect research with bioethics and music classes, and I would supplement those interests through groups such as Stepping Stone Ministry and Musicare. I want to contribute to Baltimore, by serving the hungry, sharing my love for music, and spending time with the seniors, and helping the children.

Lastly, I was inspired by the community at Hopkins. After talking to Sophia Phelan and Wilson Liou, I learned about how they were both constantly encouraged by their passionate peers and teachers. Here at Peddie, I’ve grown so much because of how my friends and teachers have inspired and cheered me on. I hope that I can embrace the same kind of community here at Hopkins, where I can learn from so many amazing people.

It is tempting to attribute an outcome to a singular cause. Reality is rarely so straightforward.

As a child, an introverted child, and a child raised among family members who seldom opened up to one another, I was not prepared to do the nuanced introspective work that would have led me to a sufficiently complex response to my challenges.

"Beachball" was my childhood nickname. Weighing a whopping 190 pounds at 13, it’s no surprise my two brothers and I could easily devour meals meant for eight adults. Our mom, always worried that we might go hungry, never missed a chance to pile our plates high–fueling our insatiable appetites. Eventually she stopped posting family photos on Facebook when “chubby” was no longer cute. I would often joke that I could donate half of my daily caloric intake to kids in the Congo battling hunger and still stay healthy.

While my weight gain was a growing problem, it became one of many. I isolated myself during school recesses, dodging chatter with peers and finding solace in empty corners. Not to mention, my family’s cultural norms meant I was not getting emotional support from home. My thoughts festered without others to guide me through the haze surrounding my struggles.

I blamed my weight for everything. Losing this weight would change me. It would fix me.

I threw myself into a single-minded, obsessive regime–counting calories, spending hours at the gym, forcing myself to lace up the same white-striped tennies when the clock hit 10 PM. Surprisingly, an unexpected factor solidified my routine: the Langley Marching Band.

Summer band camp required me to adopt a strict regimen that fit perfectly into my envisionment: it consisted of four hours of grueling early-morning outdoor rehearsals followed by four hours of intense indoor practice. By the end of Week One, I was exhausted, panting from the cadence of drills, my body surrendering to fatigue–but things were proceeding exactly how I had foreseen. I got into the best shape of my life, halving my body fat percentage from 25% to 12% and hitting a 315-pound bench press at 15.

But as I hit the goals I never thought I’d reach, many of my challenges–most of them, in fact–remained. At school, the distance I thought would narrow between my peers and I stayed. I was still the quiet one, isolated from joy and camaraderie. At home, I still struggled to find topics for conversation with my reserved family members.

What was I missing?

A candid conversation with a close friend sparked a realization: my journey had always been for myself.

The lack of grand congratulations or differing treatment from family members after losing the weight underscored that my transformation needed to be more than just altering others’ perceptions, I needed to begin embracing a sense of personal fulfillment that had eluded me for years.

My weight was just one symptom of a broader problem: a reflection of the introverted persona I had developed over the years. Confidence and passion had left me during my asynchronous school years, leaving a void I filled with copious greasy DoorDashing. Food was a refuge, a way to cope when emotions felt elusive. I realized my reliance on food to fill a chasm left by a lack of emotional support was just a symptom of my introversion, which in turn was a defense mechanism against my deep-set fear of failing social interactions. The whispered comments and exclusion were not caused by my weight, but merely worsened by it. Misidentifying relationships between factors can obscure the true nature of my challenges, especially if I think I can only change certain factors–like my weight–and not others that may be harder to approach–like asking myself the questions I need to ask.

Now that I’ve completed my weight-loss arc (for now), I continue to strive to adopt a more well-rounded mentality, one that–like a beachball–can always bounce forward.

A man stands knee-deep in a vat of crimson dye, working in the tanneries of Morocco, his hands stained from hours of labor. The air is filled with the scent of leather, clay, and sweat as he perfects his craft amidst utilizing a variety of colors: deep indigo, burnished gold, and vibrant scarlet. In the deserts of Dubai, a fire dancer performs under the night sky, spinning with passion as flames flicker and leave arcs of light. His precise, controlled movements electrify the air, with the heat of the flames overtaking the stage.

These are both moments from my recent family travels. As the family's unappointed travel planner, I carry out the responsibility of watching YouTube videos, to diving down the rabbit hole of Reddit, to make sure each trip is excellent. However, it didn't always go to plan, like the time we were stuck in Hyderabad airport for multiple days.

Ever since I was a kid, I often wondered how life was around the world. As I went through my daily routine, I wondered, What are other kids doing around the world at this very time? What do kids around the world do for fun? These questions propelled my curiosity to learn more about other cultures.

As I traveled, my curiosity expanded to the spiritual and religious practices of different cultures. Raised in a Muslim household, I became fascinated by how diverse rituals, beliefs, and traditions, such as those in Hindu temples and European cathedrals, influence other areas like healthcare.

When I visited India in ninth grade, I witnessed healthcare firsthand. At my grandfather’s clinic, patients traveled from distant villages, many lacking access to basic medications. I wondered: How do healthcare systems serve rural populations with limited resources? How do traditional practices blend with modern medicine? This curiosity led me to a program at Georgetown, where I worked with doctors from Nigeria.

That summer I spent my time learning about different diseases plaguing villages in Bauchi, Nigeria. From Acute Respiratory Illness, to Malaria there was a lot of sickness, but a lack of education and awareness. Doctors explained the lack of healthcare infrastructure and how folk beliefs lead to myths being spread. Through the program I met a young boy named Mohammad, he was malnourished, with large, weary eyes that spoke of both innocence and suffering. What made this encounter unique was the medium through which we connected—a virtual environment created through an Oculus Rift headset.
