I greeted him softly, “How are you feeling, Mohammad? What’s bothering you?”

He whispered, “I feel hot, and my head and stomach hurt.”

After asking for his temperature, I saw he had a high fever. When I asked how long it had lasted, he winced and said, “A few days.”

Through the training I received from my collaborating Doctors and the symptoms he described—high fever, chills, headache, and nausea—I began to suspect malaria, a common but serious illness in the region. I asked him a few more questions, trying to gather as much information as possible.

I learnt that malaria is relatively easy to prevent with mosquito nets, and bug spray. However, this education was not spread. I worked with peers to create an educational conference in the village, with fun activities to teach kids about malaria prevention.

Public health is my passion. It disturbs me that children die every day from preventable diseases simply because they are born in places with fewer resources. While the U.S. is developing groundbreaking treatments for cancer, diseases like polio still ravage parts of the world. Just as the tanner in Morocco and the fire dancer in Dubai are shaped by their environments, so too are healthcare systems shaped by culture, history, and access. I want to be part of the solution and plan to continue to engage in public health in every way I can: in the field, in college, and through global health organizations.

“[Name], can you make 40 Hexagon cookies with the company logo by tomorrow?” Here came another last-minute request. I wasn’t sure how I could finish them all by myself, on time. My passion for baking took an unexpected turn in 2020 when I enrolled in a business class. The final assignment was a revenue competition, for which I created my own online store, 8aCookie.org. In 24 hours, I had requests for over 480 bespoke holiday cookies.

I kept pushing myself to do more, thinking I was fine. The consistent long nights and early mornings exhausted me, grinding out cookie after cookie, all while juggling school, mid-terms, volunteering, and a 10-hour-weekly dance schedule. My heart was racing, and I began dreading the thought of piping another cookie. In the end, I won the competition, but I lost the joy I used to have for baking.

So, I put down my spatula, stopped taking requests, and finally let myself breathe. Relief washed over me, but it was accompanied by a growing sense of emptiness. Reflecting on my childhood, I remembered watching baking shows where contestants made exquisitely decorated confections. At ten years old, I taught myself to bake, scoured websites for recipes, and browsed books in search of dessert ideas. I remember standing in my kitchen, barely able to see over the countertops, cooking up a storm, mixing icing, experimenting with different designs and unique flavors, without realizing hours had gone by. What began as a hobby turned into something more when I debuted my cookie stall at Metro Detroit Youth Fair in June 2019. Selling themed sugar cookies, I tasted the sweetness of my first baking profit.

Stepping back from baking reminded me that it hadn’t always been a stressful chore. It used to provide me with a relaxing, creative outlet. When I baked, my mind quieted down and I found my bliss. The world felt so calm, as if it had fallen into a deep sleep. All the noises and distractions around me disappeared. In these moments, I am in my element and channeling my creativity.

As the seasons moved on, I picked up my tools again, but this time for myself. Motivated to explore new desserts, I experimented with everything from tiramisu to crème brûlée to strawberry shortcake. Sitting and staring at a crumb coated cake, I began visualizing new designs, and let my creativity flow through the piping bag. The joy I once felt slowly returned. I put on my favorite show, and started icing cake after cake, admiring my desserts as they came to life. While it felt good to hear people rave that my cakes were "better than those at Tous les Jours", it was the tranquil feeling of the baking process that mattered the most to me.

Armed with a new perspective on balance, I began accepting orders again. Now I focus on making larger, custom orders for special occasions, instead of rotely frosting the same design all day. In addition, I was careful to not overcommit myself. Once again, I found peace in the process. My skills flourished, my passion for baking was reignited, and I felt rejuvenated.

There will always be moments in life when I feel I am racing against the clock or overwhelmed with choices. Combining my passions for baking and business was exciting, however it is important to strike a balance between bringing happiness to the customers and to myself. Though it was hard to find my flow again, I’m glad I didn't give in to pressure and quit. Now that I have learned to not bury myself in work, I find joy in each order that comes my way, and anxiously wait for my next project. Mastering the art of balance is essential in life, school, as in baking. Like sugar and salt, they could complement each other in desserts with the right mix.

“Stan, is that really you, bro? You look like the boy from Up!” Without even seeing their screens, I knew what my classmates were laughing at: old photos and videos of me at piano competitions. My cheeks flushed.

I’ve played piano since I was five, but after being teased in sixth grade, my peers discovering that I wasn’t just the energetic basketball player they knew me as, I shattered my concert pianist dreams, wanting to be the commonly accepted athlete.

As I practiced less and stopped competing in competitions, my parents became confused as to why I lost my passion. “It’s just not fun anymore,” I said, looking at the picture of me dressed in my white suit smiling sheepishly.

Yet, I knew quitting wasn’t an option, not after playing this long. But if I was going to do it, I wanted to truly dedicate myself to it.

In the following months, I found myself drifting back to my keyboard more.

Exploring new styles of music, I delved into Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse. Unexpectedly, I found myself falling in love with the glimmery texture of the passages. I applied the same diligence I devoted to hitting 10 straight free throws after each practice to drilling the middle arpeggio section. Whereas before I used to study Devin Booker’s midrange pullup, I now also studied YouTube concert performances by Seong Jin Cho where I’d draw inspiration from his ability to bring out hidden melodies in his music.

At the same time, I picked up cooking, even though I’m known as a klutz. From learning how to dice an “onyo” with Chef Jean Pierre to making my first grilled cheese and tomato soup, I sought out YouTube and Google to kick off my cooking journey. Though I sometimes spilled some diced onions while tossing them in the pan, I found moments of peace as I seasoned my proteins and minced my garlic, my mind no longer a mess of schoolwork, piano, and basketball.

As my recipes went from simple chicken thighs to complex stews and gourmet pastas, I noticed that in the same way I perfected my touch in my fingers to create certain textures in piano, I had to practice the timing in moving my pan to flip my vegetables. I also developed a rhythm when making the once simple grilled cheese and tomato soup, first sauteing my onions, roasting my tomatoes while the onions cooked, and heating up my grilled cheese the moment I put the tomatoes and onions together.

Being able to utilize all my talents to complement each other, I felt deeply connected to all three as a result.

I pulled up [Name] Du’s picture for the Great Composers Competition, the image holding the memories of all the laughs garnered by my classmates, causing me to never want to compete at competitions and put my face on the internet again. Years later, I realized I missed that feeling of walking onto stage in the competition heat and playing, looking at the audience in my peripheral vision as I lifted my head up. I signed up for the Ross Mckee Piano Competition, where they’ll record me and put my videos online.

Whereas in middle school and my early years of high school, piano symbolized my confinement to teenager norms and an Asian stereotype, today the instrument is an embodiment of my ability to start with ambition and continue with the same vigor in any context, whether that’s laying the ball in the rim or laying my steak in the pan. The black and white keys are my tangible proof that I can be authentic to myself while also maintaining autonomy—it represents how I’m able to be proud of working on different aspects of myself, even if it is unconventional.

Sitting in a sweat-filled room, my hands form a visor to shield my eyes from all stimuli. The words, digits, names, images, cards, or people laying my hands eagerly wait to be absorbed. My brain frantically battles to forget the pressure of the awaiting audience while retaining the information in front of me. Yet, after swift negotiations, my mind accepts a compromise to remember both.

Despite being a competitive memorizer, I have an average memory. I can’t tell you what I ate for breakfast two mornings ago. My mom always scolds my blank face when my relative I had last met eight years ago asks if I remember his name. I can't barcode-scan a string of digits or a chemistry textbook page into my memory in a split-second.

Instead, all information I receive passes through my sanctuary for memorizing information—my memory palace. Mentally, my home is parted into ten rooms, each room with five items. The data I receive is streamlined into a visualization I can assign to each location. During recall, my mind saunters through my palace to decode each item in each room.

For each event, I use methods to encode information into items to set in my palace. For example, each playing card simplifies into a person, action, or object, to form compact stories. In groups of three, numbers become consonants to build the skeleton of a word or phrase to be visualized as an image—213 becomes [T]a[ll] [M]an.

However, these techniques left my progress at a plateau as I failed to perform alongside my competitors. I needed to alter my methods. I initially experimented with including audio in my palace, but it left me with a headache-inducing cacophony impossible to decode. Instead, I endeavored to enhance the images in my palace. Interestingly, the more detailed and bizarre the image, the better I could visualize and retain it. 213 transformed from a six-foot man to a living colossus, his elongated head jutting through the ceiling and piercing my palace roof.

With my experience adapting techniques, I wanted to decipher how my skills could be utilized in the context of memory loss. After researching studies on cognitive training, I found that the same principles that I employ in competitions have been developed into memory programs; my knowledge could be applied to prevent memory decline and dementia.

Over six months, I worked individually with professors involved in memory research. Together, we extracted information from various memory training studies and the knowledge I have attained as a memory athlete. Meeting weekly, we tailored a training session to suit seniors at assisted living homes. There, I presented a variety of exercises from memorizing unrelated words to visualizing short stories to remember information.

Without the regulations of an academic study, my volunteering was liberated from monotony; I could adjust the activities to accommodate for their abilities just as I had with my techniques. Originally, body parts were marked as locations for the participant’s “memory palace” to create uniformity for large groups. When some participant found that the proximity of the items blurred her memory, I suggested shifting to utilizing her apartment as a memory palace.

Often, when memorizing many sets of data in a short timeframe, the images previously visualized may overlap with current images. As some struggled with this interference, I recommended a method I use before memorizing new information: imagining a tsunami cascading through their memory palace, submerging and washing away each item.

Through this experience, I found joy in crafting solutions to take advantage of individual strengths. In the future, I am interested in researching the mental processes behind how we overcome weaknesses. How can we utilize our brain’s idiosyncrasies to achieve success? While I may never instantly absorb the names of my long-lost aunts and uncles, I can always use systems to memorize them. Until I learn their names, however, my mom will still scold me at our next family reunion.

In the soft glow of a spring evening, a sudden hiss startles my lemon-coated 13-year-old self. I flinch, bracing for the Citron lemon to explode again, but it’s instead my teacher’s voice: “ETHAN, WHAT DID I JUST TELL THE CLASS NOT TO DO!”

The unpredictable eruptions and splashes weren’t just chaos to me; they vividly revealed how varied amounts of lemon juice could alter the reaction’s resonance and rhythm. In that moment of rebellion, I felt like my child-self: experimenting with bizarre gum flavors, ecstatic to share my umami pickle-flavored concoctions with my family.

Yet later that night, my parents called me a “problem-child,” their disappointment creating a palpable rift between us. It was a conflicting feeling. I had always adhered to their expectations, believing it was the easier path. When they told me to stop hunting for Pokemon cards in local flea shops or to stop dismantling abandoned arcade machines, I complied without question. I buried my passions under the weight of their approval.

But standing there, still smelling like lemon juice, something shifted. If I hadn’t gone through with that experiment, if I’d played it safe like always, I would have never experienced that vitality I thought had faded away. The roles between being a good son and being true to myself blurred in that moment. I questioned who I was really trying to be—and I wasn’t sure I liked the answer.

Determined to mediate the "problem-child" within me, I looked to close the separation I now felt with my parents. Initially, I tried hosting family-nights filled with improvised playings of Moana and the occasional offbeat sing-alongs of Frozen’s “Let It Go.” Surely, I thought, this would mend the fracture that had grown between us.

But when our dinner table remained thick with unspoken tension, I dived into the study of human connection. Countless 1 A.M. readings about repressed emotions and psychotherapy became part of my evening routine. How could I change who my parents were, I wondered. Perhaps, I had to first understand myself. As I watched TED talks from psychologists like Eleanor Longden, I discovered concepts like intrapsychic conflict and affective empathy.

I also learned the brain as more than its physiological intricacies, serving as the traversing medium for the psychic heart. Beyond its unnatural harmony, the brain assigns cognitive experiences to emotions, transmitting them back to the heart and shaping the way we connect with others. Many can face external conflict but only a few dare to look inward and also face their own. I wanted to be one of them.

As I focused my research, I delved deeper into studies on affective empathy, learning from organizational psychologist, Adam Grant, that mutual understanding and generosity is the key to repairing broken bonds. I learned to see myself through my parents’ eyes and observe their reactions not as obstacles, but instead “emotional data” that I could utilize.

I began with light-hearted humour (like my goofy imitation of our dog’s dinner-time antics) and impromptu science experiments at our table (such as homemade lava lamps). Then, once the air felt lighter, I hosted events with my local neighborhood as we watched coordinated playings of Moana and sang even more offbeat versions of “Let It Go.” As I watched the kids—Alex stumbling over a speaker, David creating oceans from seashells, and Grace eating popcorn with her family—I saw my parents smiling, reflecting the same joy they once had whenever I would share my pickle-flavored creations with them.

**OOMPH.** I hit the floor, gasping for breath.

Dad, my archenemy, waltzed over, lip-syncing the final verse. I had lost.

“NOOOOO” I wailed.

Dad whooped victoriously. My brother and Mom, sitting on the couch, tried not to burst out laughing as Dad struck his over-the-top victory pose once again—arms wide, head thrown back as he grinned from ear to ear.

In my family, it was tradition that we gathered once a month to sing. Sometimes until as late as 3 AM, we screamed, laughed, and danced our hearts out, hosting events from Disney acapellas to sing-off jams. As a quiet child, I initially hesitated to join. But I found my voice over time, discovering joy in my family’s smiles.

Since my 13th birthday, though, I noticed subtle changes: the sprinkling of white hairs near Dad’s temples, the dark rings under Mom’s eyes. Their long days of labor were taking a toll while I remained sheltered in our tradition’s warmth.

Every time I voiced my concerns, my parents brushed them aside. “Don’t worry, just focus on your studies,” Dad laughed. “Silly, we haven’t felt better.” Mom smiled. But I wasn’t reassured. I wanted to help, yet I was convinced they didn’t think I was strong enough to help them. Their early-morning meetings and late-night shifts sapped them of energy and joy, all so they could provide for me and my brother—and all I could do was watch. Even during our cherished singing nights, their once-genuine smiles began to appear artificial—as if they were holding on to those moments for our sake rather than their own.

One day, I stopped attending the singing nights. As my family whooped and chanted inside the living room, I huddled in the corner of my bed. One month passed. Then two. Then four. Over time, I grew distant from my parents, rejecting their questions and concerns, hoping they would realize my protests.

I wanted them to realize they didn’t need to work so hard for me; I could do it myself. I received high marks in school. I made money as a waiter, and since I stopped attending the singing nights, I took on even more.

But, as time passed…I grew tired. Sleep eluded me as I hunched over textbooks at 2 AM, eyes bleary from hours of cramming and meal-prepping for my brother. My phone remained still, notifications of once-frequent messages dwindling as close friends became strangers. But I was strong. I need to prove it.

One day, my younger brother sought me out in my cluttered room, his face steely and determined. “Let’s go karaoke.”

I set down my pencil. “I have an exam tomorrow.”

“Let’s go karaoke,” he repeated.

“I can’t, I…”

“Let’s. Go. Karaoke.”

I hesitated. As I looked up into his eyes for the first time in months, I saw fear and anxiety. I saw tears glistening as his steely composure began to crack. I saw the same whirlwind of emotions I experienced when facing my parents. As I glanced through my doorway, I saw their eyes on me, shining with worry. In that moment, I realized that in my efforts to prove myself, I had taken their psychological places.

So I went to karaoke. I threw myself into it with everything I had, and although it was a chaotic, off-key mess, it was genuine. As I looked around, I saw my parents, faces lit with wide smiles not artificial but real, bursting with relief and happiness. As they sang with us that night, I realized. Their sacrifices were because their joy was within us. Through each lyric; each laugh; their wrinkles and white hairs seemed to fade just a little more.

In the following months, reconnecting with my family taught me various lessons. Yet, the most profound ones came from the times I stumbled - burnt dinners, forgotten assignments, vulnerable moments. Those were the times my family stepped in. I learned to see unity—beauty—in our countless small sacrifices: Mom's knowing glances as she poured me tea at midnight, Dad's silent pride as he helped me study. It was through the harmony of our voices, each note imperfect, yet together, that I learned to truly sing. To sing knowing that other voices supported mine underneath.

I never understood the whole concept of two Christmases. When people find out your parents are divorced, it seems that everyone's first thought is to say, “Hey, at least something good came out of it.” I know I never got to have two Christmases, Since the age of 4, I’ve spent every holiday with my mom, my sister, and the same 6-foot, slightly lopsided artificial tree.

Having to navigate through life without a father is something I wouldn’t wish on anyone. Every single crossroads in life where you need just a little bit of guidance is made that much worse when you have to navigate it without a father figure. There's no one there to check up on you to keep you out of trouble as a kid when mom’s sleeping, or when she’s working multiple jobs to ensure we’re living in the same place next month. There’s not always someone there to ensure your grades aren’t slipping and give you a little extra help if you need it.

It seems that being poor can make every problem just a little bit worse too. Being poor with a single parent means that the family dog has to be given up because there just isn’t enough time or money to take care of it. Being poor means that the family can’t leave the abusive boyfriend without fear of missing meals.

Despite these difficult circumstances, I consider myself extremely lucky. Thousands, if not millions, of children are growing up with the same story (more or less) as my own. However, there is a reason why the next breakfast that I eat will not still be bought with food stamps. There is a reason that, after all of this hardship, I am able to write this essay in the sanctity of my own home, on my very own computer, sitting next to my two oversized, sleeping cats. The reason why my story diverges from theirs is solely because of my mother.

Whenever I find myself doubting my abilities, or unsure about committing to something, I think back to my mother. It takes a special kind of person to continue to pursue education while raising two children on their own, all while making sure those two children have something to eat that night. It takes a special kind of person to work 10 hours and still find time to bring their kids to their Russian classes. It takes a special kind of person to simply keep getting up in the morning and give an ounce of effort in those circumstances.

My mother has paved the way for me to be my own special kind of person. When I was handed the tattered, faded green soccer captain armband my junior year, I thought I was in way over my head. What if the rest of the team doesn’t respect me? Or what if I’m just not capable of leading people? I recall staring at the ground, and I remembered how my mother would ensure we always had enough money to get me new cleats every year. I knew then, that I was capable of leading them, as she has always believed I can. When the ominous sign-up sheet was posted on the band room door for drum major auditions, I didn’t even give a moment of thought to it. Why would I even be considered? However, I looked back to everything my mother has done for me, and everything she’s been able to accomplish, and I put my name down.

I may not know where my path will take me next in life. Maybe I’ll be replacing that old, ragged tree for my next Christmas. However, I know that whatever I do, I will know that I can do it, as my mother has always shown and believed in me.

I watched as my sister’s hands trembled while she hung up the phone. Her voice faded as my heartbeat drowned everything out, like turning a corner in a haunted house. By now, these calls were predictable—quick, whispered preludes to approaching police sirens. We hid in the closet, trapped in fear, feeling like Hester Prynne and Pearl—excluded and anxious. Though paralyzed, curiosity propelled me. Little did I know, the scene that unfolded would change me forever.

The floorboards creaked as I reached for the door, which resisted slightly—as if it knew. As I opened it, three engines roared up the street—the police, bringing a fleeting sense of relief. The fight would stop. But then I saw it—my father’s hands around my mother’s neck, her face turning pale. Like Scout outside the jail, I froze, eyes wide, witnessing the dark side of humanity. The last sight I have of my father is the blue and red lights flickering off his face. That night, I vowed to choose creation over destruction, strength over violence.

Three years later, Brian entered my life—a new father figure filling the void. He built a childhood for me that sparkles in memory, like sun on crisp autumn mornings. I remember leaves scattering off my football helmet as Brian, whistle in hand, led the team through drills. His influence was profound, especially the day he adopted his nephew, Connor.

Connor’s parents struggled with addiction, leaving Brian with a difficult choice: protect his financial stability or risk his nephew’s future. He chose Connor. “We must,” he asserted, eyes reflecting the streetlight. This taught me that following your heart over common sense is often the morally just path, even at personal expense.

For the next two years, I watched Brian and my mother tirelessly care for Connor as my room transformed into half Mickey Mouse, half Dallas Cowboy. One day, despite financial struggles, they surprised me with tickets to a Cowboys game against the Giants. My heart pounded with joy—a moment that erased dark memories. Their determination to provide for me, even when it seemed impossible, showed me that perseverance can achieve anything.

These experiences instilled in me two profound lessons: to follow my heart over common sense when morality demands it, and that determination can overcome any obstacle. These lessons guided me when my conviction was tested during freshman year.

I launched a cryptocurrency project, investing all my savings. I managed correspondence and scrutinized market forecasts tirelessly. Two weeks before launch, the market crashed; 40% of liquidity vanished overnight. Faced with a tough choice—proceed for quick profit or refund the investments—I thought of Brian’s example. I chose to follow my heart, prioritizing integrity over potential gain. I refunded every dime, which meant my $50,000 investment evaporated.

Determined to rebuild, I worked as a lifeguard eight hours a day that summer. By autumn, I’d saved $3,000. Applying the lesson that determination can achieve anything, I used that seed money to launch an electronics business. Embracing resilience, I incorporated the lessons from my failed project. By the end of sophomore year, my business crossed six figures in revenue.

Reflecting on these moments, I realize what drives me. Though my father is gone, I have something to prove—not to him, but to myself and Brian. The Scarlet Letter from my past still pushes me. My therapist once asked, “Why are you doing all this? It’s almost like you’re trying to prove something to someone.” I stayed quiet, but I realized that letter still burns within me, pushing me to make a lasting impact and reshape the name my father and I share: [Name] Delossantos.

My heart was palpitating, and I nervously glanced at the school gate, then back at my textbook. As the clock struck five, the high school lights went out. Under the cover of darkness, I filed into the stuffy gray classroom to secretly repeat to more than twenty girls from my neighborhood aged 14 to 17 everything I had learned regarding skills for the twenty-first century – how to thrive in today’s environment. I stayed vigilant since the lighting was poor, and as is customary in Afghanistan, danger is always lurking in the shadows. My eyes remained chained to the gate. I worried the Taliban, who banned education for Afghan girls, might come to check out the school—an infrequent, but one which had still happened before. Knowing that arrest and severe punishment could occur, for the past year and a half, I felt afraid probably because of the torture and losing my own education.

I was raised by my father to believe that education was the cornerstone of personal growth, and to know that my female peers had been denied this right and pushed into marriage induced me to continue working in risky ways. Pushed me to have always contacted the girls through WhatsApp for our discussions and sharing new updates, rather than having any phone calls which could lead me to trouble. Half of them, with a low financial condition, could not afford the internet. I had to spend one-third of my own salary ($60) covering their internet fee for a few months. Because they couldn’t go to schools, and online education was not feasible for low-income families, I raised $1362 funds through GoFundMe, asked my friend Abigail for help—a senior student at UWC East Asia—to cover the girls’ internet fees monthly.

While I was concerned about the girls’ status quo, my parents worried about me. While I worried about their future, my parents were afraid of my safety. The first time I stood against my parents’ will, I advocated for the girls’ right to continue attending the crammed class. Every day, I used to hear my mother say, “Schools are banned for the whole Afghan girls; why do you endanger yourself for just a few girls?” Despite the insistence, I tried more every day, spending hours preparing lessons to make interaction games and activities in order to set a kinesthetic learning style environment—how they learned better. On vacations and holidays, I was helping review their United World College scholarship applications, where students come from around the world to study IB, which later six of them had been shortlisted for the interview. The principal of the school and I were so excited, as his bravery in permitting the girls to congregate in the school took his 16-year-old daughter into the second stage of UWC, too.

Although fear of punishment consumed me, I pioneered English workshops, Academic Success Courses, and virtual information sessions hosted with international friends. From seeing Maryam shed her shy skin and now eagerly enter discussions after our Friday stream of consciousness sessions to hearing Zinab remarking confidently to get charged with energy, my heart is warmed seeing my neighborhood friends rediscover their love of education. Compared to my initial fear, I became strong enough to continue this educational quest, and all my fun has now become scheming programs for the girls and sneaking even on the weekend to teach more.

After seeing three of these dynamic girls teaching basic English to children and all the twenty-seven girls now possess the capability to navigate the constant obstacles, I am proud of myself. I don’t let reality and danger prevent me from doing exactly what I believe is the right or good thing to do, and in college, I will strengthen this belief. Beyond college, I will someday ensure that education is not only a right for all Afghans but for everyone.

Growing up in a war-torn village, I learned early on that strict control and rigidity were essential for survival. I maintained order by following a fixed schedule and double-checking everything, believing that if I controlled every detail, I could shape any outcome. It worked—until it didn’t.

In freshman year, I launched SaveAzezo, an initiative to prevent frequent floods caused by the deforestation of our village's forest, Genet Terara. I wanted to protect where I cherished my childhood — from planting mangoes to listening to my grandmother’s stories of the legendary Queen of Sheba. Initially, I met with the problem of finding volunteers and securing funding as many saw the flood as divine punishment. My belief in controlling every detail led me to spend six weeks organizing meetings, distributing flyers, and presenting my idea at church. Yet, nothing changed. Frustration and anger filled me as I spent restless nights wondering how my thorough planning and dedication could lead to so little impact. Giving up crossed my mind, but it felt like betraying my grandmother and our cherished weekend memories.

One smoggy evening, I asked Mola, an elderly man, why they refused to join. He chuckled, shaking his head. “Prevent God’s punishment?” he said. Even though it was not my first time hearing this, something in his tone—perhaps the simplicity of his certainty—hit me differently. It became clear that while control had been essential for survival in the war, here it was only creating distance. Despite this realization, I struggled to let go of my plan as my instinct told me to hold on. However, the constant failure made me understand that my approach was too rigid, rooted in my perspective alone.

As the community had limited access to education, they did not believe that reforestation would stop the flood. While I could not change their deeply held belief overnight, I could bridge the gap between my vision and their belief by learning to speak in terms they could relate to. I began by speaking informally with community members. Through these conversations, I understood that many families were struggling financially. I saw an opportunity to present the project not just as flood prevention, but as a means of improving the community’s economic well-being by planting fruit trees. Communicating this idea on Sunday in church helped me gain their support.

My next step was presenting my project to the mayor to gain official approval. I crafted a detailed proposal highlighting reforestation's environmental and economic benefits, such as flood mitigation, improved soil quality, and sustainable income from fruit trees. By including the success story of Yacob’s Tree Planting Initiative in Addis Ababa, I secured the mayor's permission for the project.

The small adjustment in my approach created a tangible impact. After 26 days, my team of 43 people planted 1,000 seedlings including avocado, mango, and papaya. As weeks passed, we began to see small changes—the shade under the young papaya tree and the gratitude of the villagers who now picked fruits from the forest. Besides the direct impact, this initiative fostered a sense of community. Many people started engaging in caring for young trees. Now, elders sit around the forest every evening; children play on the ground; and schools use the place for field learning.

Trees sway with the winds to keep their strength, not by resisting every gust, but by knowing when to stand firm and when to bend with it. In much the same way, I learned to hold things tight as long as they are within my reach and to let go of things I cannot control. As I move forward into college and beyond, I know that unpredictability will continue to challenge me. Perhaps the beauty of life lies in the moments when we are forced to ask ourselves: how do we decide when to bend and when to stand firm?

Winnie-the-Pooh would've shuddered seeing honey, a colony’s lifeblood, bleeding from one of nature’s miracles—the once buzzing beehive. My beekeeping suit offered no protection from the massacre: thousands of contorted, lifeless bees victims of a vicious pest larvae army. A haunting odor—the combination of wet socks and decomposing oranges—clung to my nostrils. The root of this destruction was the small hive beetle.

Over the past 6 years, I’ve collaborated with Dr. Charles Stuhl at the USDA, independently prototyping treatments/devices and running experiments with commercial beekeepers. More specifically, I've been researching the global issue of eliminating invasive small hive beetles in an eco-friendly, low-cost manner. To me, research is a superpower, my tool to improve ecology and benefit farmers, the cornerstones of our food supply. Wielding my superpower to address real-world problems, I create “research-for-impact.”

My first research venture was born on a fishing trip when I was 12-years-old with a friend and his grandfather, a generational beekeeper who narrated how pest infestations had destroyed his apiaries. His heartbreaking story inspired me to immerse myself in the world of bees. Devouring every bee-related book I found, I learned that one-in-three bites of food comes from bees and 50% of US hives are dying annually. Seeking to deepen my knowledge, I attended Dr. Jamie Ellis' honeybee anatomy lecture at the University of Florida's Bee College Conference. Later working in his lab, I researched commercial pollen substitutes to support hive growth. My findings, published 1st author in a peer-reviewed journal, fueled my passion to aid beekeepers; I was hooked.

But it was the destructive small hive beetle that truly captured my attention. At the time, beekeepers had two treatment options: expensive/toxic pesticides or ineffective organics. Were those our only options? As someone who was used to upcycling plastic bottles as plant vases, surely I could find a do-it-yourself option around my house. My first mission? Determining the most attractive natural bait–oils, yeasts, fruit purees, beer, etc.–placed in plastic in-hive traps. The beetles, like humans, were lured by an irresistible organic bait: beer. Beer proved highly effective, outperforming the leading organic option by 33-times.

Next year, I pushed further, synthesizing a cheaper, more effective blend based on beer’s chemical composition. Testing it against the only EPA-approved pesticide, my blend was equally effective and 4754-times cheaper. But I didn’t stop there. The following year, I harnessed the power of machine learning and IoT technology, I created BeetleGuardAI–the world’s first 3D-printed solar-powered traps with fully-automated beetle-capture counts and predictive-modeling for beetle management. BeetleGuardAI saves the industry $8 billion+ annually, safeguarding beekeeper’s livelihoods. The downside of my work? Getting hospitalized for three-dozen stings. The upside? Enough honey for Pooh, Piglet and Tigger.

Undoubtedly, the greatest gift of research-for-impact is sharing my ideas. Witnessing my love of beekeeping impacted by climate change leads me to represent youth at UN conferences, calling-for-action for sustainable agriculture. Fostering environmental wonder and responsibility in younger generations, I read my children’s book The Bee Story in libraries and lead STEM-workshops in schools. Speaking at 30+ beekeeping organizations from 18 states and 4 countries, I receive heartfelt mail from overjoyed farmers on the difference my research has made in their hives. The gratitude in beekeepers’ eyes, sight of thriving colonies, and knowledge that I'm making a difference–these are the moments that energize me.

But nothing compares to lifting a hive's lid, the sweet aroma of honey and harmonious buzzing symphony relaxing me. Most people would recoil seeing hundreds of dead beetles drowned in my beer traps. But in my eyes, the annihilation of these colony-killers represents a victory, not just for beekeepers and farmers, but to “research-for-impact.” Through my experiences, I’ve learned to emphasize relentless curiosity and unwavering determination. Witnessing our ecosystem’s fragility instills me with profound environmental responsibility and commitment to harnessing sustainable innovation to protect what matters most. Driven by my love of learning and desire to positively impact society, I’m dedicated to further amplifying my impact. After all, a world without honey is a world without Pooh-Bear, and that’s just un-bearable.

As the relentless Tanzanian sun beat down on my neck, I walked alongside my new friend, Joseph, on the rugged path toward his home. Joseph was about my age and part of the oldest tribe in the world, the Maasai. On our walk, I began to grasp the gravity of the water crisis in his community. 30,000 Maasai walked nearly nine hours every day searching for water. He explained that climate change and deforestation destroyed the soil of his land, exacerbating the droughts that killed cattle and floods that destroyed homes. After two hours, I stopped to rest. As I reached into my backpack for my water bottle, a wave of guilt washed over me. This bottle was something that Joseph’s family spent every hour searching for, and here I was with such easy access to it.

For the first time, I felt guilty about drinking water.

That was five years ago. I fundraised enough money to deploy a single 100,000-liter rainwater harvesting unit in Losimingori, Tanzania. Still, after deploying it, I realized that this single unit would never solve the water access problem for thousands of Maasai. The following year, I fundraised and returned to Tanzania to deploy three more units and lead six high school students to measure the impact on the community. Through my interviews, I saw how the unit changed the lives of 4,500 Maasai who lived nearby. The women who previously walked nine hours daily for water now only walked two to three hours to the unit. There was a cascading effect on the rest of the community. Children could use water for bathing and fell ill far less frequently, leading to better school attendance. Women had time to create jewelry, grow crops, and generate additional income.

While the situation had improved in a small area, I heard concerns from the community: How much water can one family take? Should water be shared with animals? How do we help the thousands? With the Maasai leader's help, I organized a series of community gatherings with elders, women, and teenagers. Because of our language barriers, our conversations consisted of drawing and tone of voice rather than words. Ideas flowed here; the adults drew a bucket with an upside-down umbrella to catch rainwater on the go. The teenagers wanted to discuss drone delivery logistics. One of the elders, who was skeptical initially, started to plan “water councils” for equitable access.

One specific idea I pursued with the Maasai community was subsidizing multiple 5000-liter rainwater harvesting units and deploying them in the family's living unit [Boma]. I optimized the placement of these units using remote sensing and machine learning. Through the actual deployment, I learned that engaging the community through both the development and deployment of a project ensures future maintenance. The community takes ownership and treats the project as their own and a permanent solution rather than a temporary fix. So far, we have deployed ten units, and 150 more families have signed up. We are on the way to deploying the following 100 units this year.

I love the Maasai. I love Joseph. And I lead these projects only because I love everything about this job. Love is why I wake up at 3 AM on vacation in New York to talk to engineers in Israel, Maasai in Tanzania, and fund managers in California. Love is why I did a 96-hour trip to speak at a global conference while preparing for my math test.

Joseph’s family welcomed me with open arms in his home. As the sun dipped below the horizon and stars emerged unimpeded by city lights, I felt a deep connection and purpose. My trek with Joseph was more than a journey—it was a path toward solving the global water crisis through collaboration, compassion, and perseverance.

Flashes of red filled the studio as long silk fans snapped open and shut in perfect unison. Walking into the room felt like stepping into a world of ancient elegance, where every movement carried millennia of Chinese tradition—a world that seems foreign to me now. For three years, I had battled with excruciating cramps due to an obstructed unicornuate uterus, which made dancing nearly impossible. Standing there, I questioned whether I could still find my place here or reclaim the dancer I used to be.

Walking away might’ve been easier, but it would’ve meant abandoning a part of me. Chinese dance was never just an activity; it was a way to connect to my culture and be intimately bound up with my sense of self. But with my diagnosis, I knew I had to adapt. I started researching stretches my body could endure and discovered the importance of a balanced diet to reduce inflammation. And so, my evenings turned into a mix of homework and oversplits, my muscles howling as I memorized polar functions for the next day’s test. I seized every opportunity to stretch, viewing the playground equipment as a chance to prop my leg up. I even learned to modify dishes like mapo tofu, cooking with less oil to prevent flare-ups of pain. Randomly falling asleep in the frog pose or experimenting in the kitchen became the new normal. Gradually, my flexibility and muscle memory returned.

This progress ignited a flame in me, renewing my sense of purpose. And yet, something still felt missing. My girls, who I saw more than my own family at times, were still gone and so was my laughter. I missed how they’d linger after rehearsals, go over the dance in silly variations, and share matcha pocky between breaks. I waited for weeks until it became clear that I now had to take on the roles left behind by the older girls; I was the only one left to spot front walkovers when the teacher was busy and offer words of encouragement. After noticing the parallels between my younger self's struggle with the fan shen—a vertical cartwheel with windmill-like arms—and the younger dancers' challenges with the choreography, I gathered the courage to suggest meeting on Saturdays to help. They agreed, and from then on, Saturdays became our Saturdays. I would demonstrate how to isolate different body parts, moving slowly and clearly to show the subtleties. “Watch how my fingers lead the movement,” I said, as the younger dancers mimicked my actions, their eyes tracking their own fingertips. I would observe their attempts, notice where they faltered, and step in. Gently arching their backs, I directed them, “Try to find your balance here,” as I guided their front walkovers.

Through taking on these new responsibilities, I recalled the warmth of the older girls' hands carefully arranging my hair and perfecting my makeup before recitals. Their care made me feel loved and like I belonged, even as one of the youngest on the team. Wanting to pass this tradition down, I learned how to draw a perfect winged eyeliner in under a minute, apply fake lashes in one go, and style a bun that stayed flawless through every performance. It felt like a way to give back to the community, ensuring the little ones felt as special and cared for as I once had.

Little by little, I saw their confidence build up; little by little, my void was filled. Through this journey, I discovered that moving forward wasn’t about waiting for the past to return but about actively shaping the present and embracing new roles. Helping the younger dancers ignited a sense of responsibility that I’m eager to bring to college, whether by organizing Chinese community programs that blend culture with creativity or by continuing to mentor and inspire others in different aspects of life.

It all began when I was eight years old, watching a football game. Dallas vs Washington, tied, 2 minutes left. On the edge of my seat, I watched DeSean Jackson fumble a punt return that Cowboys punter Chris Jones recovered. That fumble led to a Cowboys touchdown, key to their victory as they overcame a following Washington touchdown to win on a field goal as time expired. Without that fumble, the Cowboys likely wouldn’t have won as Washington could have scored as time expired, winning the game. Alas, as Chris Jones secured that football on the ground, the Cowboys secured a place in my heart. That Cowboys win initiated a lifelong fandom and a love for football that have both skyrocketed since. In fact, my passion for talking about the Cowboys landed me an interview for the position that I have proudly represented since tenth grade: my school football team’s head manager.

Upon joining, I knew my football knowledge would increase, but I didn’t expect my social life to blossom too! Previously, I didn’t have to socialize to get through school and therefore chose not to. Unfortunately, that isolation was causing me unhappiness. I wanted more friends to share life’s joys with. Luckily, being head manager thrust me into new social waters. I’ve attended every practice, from those at 3 PM to the ones at 6 AM, while staying until 10 PM to film every game. Every second is spent with the same people, and I grew comfortable getting to know them. They’re my second family. I talk with players about school, football, and more while eating weekly lunches with the coaches. I’m even comfortable enough to tutor players, helping two with separate English assignments between school and practice while encouraging them to talk to teachers about their grades.

The relationships I built at football broke me out of my shell early into my first season. In my Human Geography class, I shocked myself by raising my once shaky hand in a confident burst of determination, answering a question about population. I saw myself change into a strong participant as I nailed the answer.

As a veteran manager, I was entrusted with more responsibility. When other managers had questions about water distribution or equipment, they came to me. I responded in kind, taking charge to keep things running smoothly.

In junior year, I began a quest to get our school band to play the anthem before football games. We had been using a recording which failed to showcase the skills of our musicians. I contacted the band and athletic directors, lobbying for weeks to get it done. I can’t begin to describe the joy I felt when our pep band finally played the glorious notes.

This summer, while volunteering with the University of Maryland’s equipment managers, I saw my supervisors being tasked with great responsibility as they led us through swarms of laundry and mountains of boxes. Any failure would cause the program to collapse, but they commanded our unit with such precision that nothing could go wrong. Teaching 12 college kids the ropes while managing business on their computers and on the field must have been hard, but they never showed it. Surprisingly, they tackled these tasks in a similar way to how I have at the high school level, which gives me confidence that I’m ready for the next step.

I also gained valuable experience and smiled more than I can ever remember. Every task brought me joy, affirming my intentions to pursue a similar job while in college. I know I belong in sports management. I know I can handle the responsibilities. I know I will love the work. Most importantly, I know how I got here. I always thought football was just an interest holding a clipboard on the bench, but now I can see that it has been my starting quarterback the whole time.

“You’re addicted!” 
All too often I’m hit with this accusation. People coming across, scanning, hurling with furtive glares, almost like ritual. And I don’t deny. My addiction permeates across piling notebooks, bedsheets, left-hand and most profoundly me. Unfortunately, It is my life now. You might wonder: “Is it sniffing lines, rolls, or ethanols” 
Actually, none of the above. My addiction just needs pens (sometimes, markers). Fishing for blanks within my radius to fill them with disorders, alphabets and patterns until ink invades every inch, I scribble.

It began when the twelve-year-old me couldn’t scribble over the expanding blank drowning his life- order. Order, like many other Indo-Bengali-Hindu families, is escaping chaos. While dadu-grandfather found order from 1975’s artilleries, my baba-dad from economical pandemic, each becoming north stars of a community hovering back-and-forth the country’s historical margins. Inspired, I dutifully shadowed their footsteps, pursuing every accolade, only to set sights on the next. My mantra: the topper joined MUN, I must join MUN (MUN= the variable). Bleary-eyed, my to-do lists would lengthen. Yawns fought ambition as I pictured my parents' proud faces. One more achievement and I'd shine the light.

It was seventh-grade, when that light started flickering. From stuttering to inadvertently breaking things, I only down-spiraled: unfocused-at-lectures, tests-riddled-with-big-red-dumplings, interrupting-every-conversations, checked. By the time eight-grade came, I was infested with glares from everyone, dissecting my missteps, murmuring mockery. Embarrassed, I tried everything: from whipping my limbs to adopting silence- If I don’t talk, I can’t stutter. But, ADHD doesn’t listen to DIY efforts; missteps multiplied. My portfolio flattered honors, presidentship, and isolated contempt when I left BMS citing ‘medical leave of absence’.

My order was gone. I hoped Baba would guide me to restore it. But, with days passing desolate, shrouded in tears and silence, I knew even he couldn't. Instead, I found myself subconsciously scribbling on bedsheets. Another symptom emerged, and likewise, it was uncontrollable, but also unharming. Words, numbers, patterns let me speak freely, without judgment. Silence couldn’t bring such euphoric bloodrush. As days passed, Silence still felt suitable, since ADHD meant pity from others. But I was determined to find order. Hence I scribbled, and it worked. The year-long turmoil ended with weightloss, resocialization, and a realization. Order is an illusion: life is an unpredictable brushstroke, rarely conforming to neat lines and stubborn efforts to perfection only drains its vitality. To truly define the 'I' in 'I am,' I must appreciate life beyond fixated rulebooks, finding beauty in every scribble of chaos and disorder, wallowing their underlying hope. I began and never stopped.

Analyzing deconstructed calculators to perfecting biryani spice-ratios, my random scribbles undoubtedly screamed ‘me’. Vandalizing during interminable Zoom calls, my pen taking flight as I brainstormed words over murmuring melodies and A#'s, although I'm not anything like Taylor Swift. Deadbolted group discussions would lead to group-scribbling, to see which art style would feature next on Qalaqriti. As days became weeks, patterns emerged in these scribbles: Python, LLM-tokenization, tensorization. What began as a frantic attempt to fill the void transformed into an invaluable companion, keeping me awake without any espressos to fill my 2 A.M. journal, fine-tuning C++ roadblocks or hypothesizing potential biases in commercial LLM-NLP chatbots. Overcommitted. Yes. Tired. No. With markers swirling in my ink-blotted hands, releasing inquiries and piling ideas from my flooding brain, I found my constellation of light shining in these scribbles.

I wish I could end here, exulting my newfound superpower, undefeated. But life is an unpredictable brushstroke. Sometimes, I prefer silence and scribbles both. It sounds contradicting, however my addiction isn’t about triumphing over ancestral expectations or subduing ADHD, but embracing my disorders I fritted most. Though baba and my paths diverge, our determination to our identity remains constant. In the end, it is also that undeterred curiosity to understand and explore the universàle that defines me.

All too often I get asked- “Why you do it?” And I simply say: to be [Name], I scribble.

The clatter of baseballs and the rhythmic whoosh of the pitching machine filled the air as my younger brother and I stepped into the batting cage. Fueled by excitement and overconfidence, I set the machine to its highest speed. The first pitch shot toward me like a speeding bullet. Swing after swing, my bravado dissolved into frustration—my high expectations blinded me to setting unrealistic goals.

During my sophomore year, I set out to break my bench press record, initially planning a 5-pound increase. But after seeing my classmates' records, I ambitiously attempted 125 pounds, far greater than anything I had attempted before. The weight felt excruciatingly heavy, and after failing the rep, I felt disappointment wash over me. I had chased an unreasonable goal, but this experience forced me to learn from my mistake. The value of this failure in teaching me a lesson was profound.

My increased ambition is due to my main goal: surpassing my father in any aspect, whether that is interpreted as net worth or enjoying more freedom in life. My father's elevated standards and ability to build the roadmap to what he wants have always set the bar high for me, and it's that same bar I feel required to raise. I don't view this as a rivalry; I view it as the age-old idea of a son wanting to accomplish more. My father has always encouraged me to look past the limits and find a balance between ambition and fulfillment. My pursuit of surpassing him excludes competition—it's about internal growth, learning from his achievements, and applying the lessons to forge my path. It's a reminder that while I may seek to exceed his accomplishments, balancing ambition and thoughtful planning is the real challenge, and this balance is crucial for a holistic approach to personal growth.

Growing up, my father instilled in me the importance of setting high standards and striving to exceed them. I distinctly remember him telling me that having ambition but no direction is like driving with no roadmap. There's a chance you might get to your destination, but the odds are minimal. My father taught me to build a roadmap for my goals in life and to make sure that roadmap combined my surging ambition with considerations of what I am capable of. This mindset has helped me understand that success isn't about reaching the highest level the fastest. Success is about making planned progress. Looking back, my approach to growth has changed drastically: aim high but always keep sight of the steps needed to get there.

Overreaching in pursuing excellence has taught me a valuable lesson: ambition without awareness can lead to failure, frustration, or harm. I risk falling short and damaging my confidence when I push myself beyond reasonable limits. I now know that unchecked ambition can cloud judgment, making it harder to see when I'm setting myself up for disappointment. There's more at stake than a missed goal; it's my ability to grow steadily and sustainably. Recognizing this has become crucial to my development. I've learned to embrace a more patient approach. When I recalibrate my goals, these moments of humility, where I acknowledge my limitations and adjust my ambitions, have been instrumental in my personal growth, emphasizing the importance of self-awareness in my journey toward success.

Looking back, I realize that success comes from setting manageable goals and pushing beyond them. It became clear that there's a difference between striving for excellence and overextending. Understanding this distinction has been central to my personal growth and guides my approach to future development and mentoring others. Now, with the lessons I have gained, I can go into the batting cage and hit the fastest speeds. Because of these progressions I made, I can now lift more weight than my friends from my sophomore year.

“Wake up and smell the coffee!” This mantra passed down from my father and literally by my first-generation Colombian mother through her dark roast Juan Valdez, defines the rhythm of my life. As an early riser, it’s a call to seize each day beside those dedicated to improving the world through love and leadership. 
I’m a second-generation Latina living in the multicultural landscape of Miami, but travel regularly to Colombia with family. One of my earliest memories attached to coffee is sitting on my grandmother’s colonial style balcony overlooking the small and simple town without many developed resources. I remember that morning on the balcony realizing not everyone is given the same life opportunities. This was my “wake up” call, and now, I'm committed to dedicating my life to creating a ripple of change that expands far beyond my own. 
Immersed in a Spanish-speaking household rich in love and fervor, my dentist-parents from humble beginnings instilled in me an old-school work ethic that felt like a second skin--upholding human values that extended beyond professional drive. My father (who loves a strong cappuccino) introduced me to Operation Smile, a humanitarian non-profit dedicated to treating kids born with facial deformities. When age ten, I discovered a photo album documenting medical missions to remote areas of Middle Eastern and Asian countries. The images were devastating, especially photos of hallways lined with kids who looked ashamed having gaping holes between their mouth and nose, and some dreadfully left on the orphanage doorstep as “throw away babies”. They had no one to care for them, nor were they able to eat, speak, or appear in public normally. I felt upset by the hopeless looks on their faces, but knew I wanted to translate emotion into action and help write the next chapter. 
As an incoming freshman, my principal took a chance on me, giving administrative overrides to be approved as the Founder and President of the Operation Smile Club. I was determined to make a difference, despite fears about failure, embarrassment, and worst of all--peer rejection. After a first year of success, later during my sophomore year, I recruited even more members to join the OS Team traveling to Vietnam as a combined U.S-Vietnamese student youth group. By this point of life, I practically lived off of Vietnamese salted coffee (ca phe muoi) while giving presentations at Vietnamese schools and orphanages. The long days were worth it as our team efforts supported over 150 surgeries. This outreach experience showed me ordinary people can make extraordinary contributions. I think of the father who walked 10 miles carrying his eight-year-old on his back wishing for the surgery, and I'm grateful to these impoverished people who taught me lessons on true hope and human perseverance, as well as the values of unwavering compassion and respect for human dignity first instilled in me at home. I love staying grounded to my favorite JFK quote, “every accomplishment starts with the decision to try;” I'll never stop trying to bring a smile to the face of anyone who is hopeless. The following year, our team re-organized and returned to Vietnam, gaining university partners and being televised on national news. 
In my daily Miami life, I don’t take for granted the privilege of simply being able to walk into a coffee shop. Traveling the world as a student volunteer on medical missions, as well as repeated visits to mom’s homeland, reaffirmed in me the importance of humility and gratitude. When volunteering locally at the Cleveland Clinic Hospital, I never just order a coffee for myself, but surprise the staff with a pick-me-up. A small gesture can change someone’s day. Small efforts grow and can create a movement. As I sit here sipping a chocolate light roast, I do so with a heart full of hope and a soul filled with the knowledge that no matter the circumstances, I’m ready to enact change.

I was enduring this conversation, slumping in bed while breathing heavily. It was my first time gasping through an asthmatic attack. Since birth, I have struggled with pneumonia, but by age 10, it seemed to vanish. At 15, this problem surged back as a consequence of Delhi's (my residing city) escalating pollution. Long walks, going to the gym, and most heartbreakingly, playing my beloved volleyball, all come to an end. These changes eroded my self-confidence, as excelling in volleyball and maintaining a fit physique were the only things, I treasured fervently. In those moments, my mental state was none less than the sinking ship in the middle of the ocean. Each wave—whether crippling asthma, weight gain, or estrangement from my friends—pushed me deeper into the abyss.

Growing up, I saw my mom worshiping God daily. One day, curious with the whole idea, I asked her, "Why do you go through all this formality?" She replied, "It keeps me relieved that at least someone is there in my bad times." Intrigued by her answer, I started searching for spirituality. I began worshiping with her and visiting temples, establishing an inverse relationship between my stress and confidence—stress diminished, and confidence grew.

I wanted to learn more about the beauty and mystery of spirituality that heavily shaped my life; that’s why I began watching the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, ancient Indian epics, and started reading Hindu scriptures like the Bhagawd Gita. These revelations greatly shaped my perspective on life’s trials. Specifically, Lord Krishna’s (Hindu God) struggles in the Mahabharata stirred something within me: If even a god faced endless challenges, how could I, a mere mortal, shrink from my own?” This reflection inspired me to face my biggest problem: asthma.

I began my journey by practicing basic breathing exercises from YouTube. Initially, I struggled- holding breath was troublesome. I wouldn't say that I was consistent, but with time, I saw progress with my lung capacity, still walking and running was challenging. I began daily park visits, starting with 100 meters of walking and steadily extending the distance. While I adapted to walking, running was much harder; when I started running, I felt the shortness of breath, fast heartbeats, and sometimes even fainting. Therefore, to make my body immune from these hurdles, I increased my meditation and exercise routine and made the toughest decision: sacrificing fast foods.

Despite my endeavors, I was inconsistent. One day, I noticed a child playing volleyball alone, propped up by a tree. I approached him and asked why. He confided that his skill inadequacies led to his exclusion from the school team. I was aware of my health conditions, but I knew this child needed help. I started teaching him volleyball after finishing my running sessions, and that is what made me conquer my inconsistency for two continuous years. After two years, I could proudly say: I was the richest man—not in wealth but in resilience and fortitude. From striving to walk to running 10-kilometer marathons and receiving appreciation from the state itself, I had conquered my asthma.

For others, this could be a story of strength, spirituality, determination, and patience—and many ways, it indeed was. But for me, this was beyond all these values. It gave me a lesson in creativity and innovation. I found every obstacle as an invitation to innovate. Whether inventing special breathing exercises or devising ways to teach volleyball with limited physical ability, my adversities made me think out of the box. I realized that creativity was not confined to art or science: rather finding unconventional solutions to problems life throws at you.

Equipped with these experiences, I look forward to receiving more invitations for innovation in research, sports, and service to humanity at college.

A slight breeze flowed through the hot, humid kitchen as “Liza” by the Sonny Stitt Quartet played softly. Milk was boiling in a pan, steeping the black tea leaves. After 10 minutes, I transferred it to my Batman mug, added sugar, and took a sip: it was bland. Again.

My repeated efforts to create the perfect cup of tea always fell flat. Every afternoon, I grappled with it, using only the three primary ingredients - tea leaves, milk, and sugar. Each attempt showed nothing more than a slight change as I remained loyal to the basic ingredients. This faithfulness mirrored my approach to life.

I started taking Bharatanatyam lessons when I was three years old, and I adored them. Like with my tea, I repeatedly practiced my steps, striving for perfection with each one. However, dancing the same steps over and over eventually led to boredom, and I became disillusioned with my tedious schedule of going to school, coming home, and practicing. Still, I was reluctant to deviate from the path, uncomfortable with new experiences.

Then, one afternoon, as I was rifling through the cupboards for sugar, I found some other items - turmeric, honey, and a small bottle, labeled “tea masala”. Having run out of sugar, I had to use the honey instead, adding tea masala to balance out the increased sweetness. The newly spiced tea brought forth an epiphany. Because of my adherence to dance, I had missed opportunities by refusing to try new hobbies or classes, believing they would take time away from my practice.

Slowly, I started taking up new opportunities, trying the violin lessons that my parents had been suggesting for years. As I struggled with complex pieces, such as Claire de Lune, I started embracing mistakes as part of the learning process and overcame them to polish my playing. Just as the masala and honey provided new layers of complexity to the tea, these violin lessons taught me patience and perseverance which I started applying to every aspect of my life. The lessons also led to appreciation for the music which I danced to. By listening carefully to the lyrics and shifts in notes, I learned to match my expressions to them, improving my storytelling through dance.

As my tea improved, I decided to share it with my family. As we all sat around the dining table one afternoon, I felt joy at seeing their enjoyment. Drinking the tea with my family gave me a feeling of unexpected contentment. That slight emotion sparked a great interest in community service. I wanted to spread joy in my greater community, so I started volunteering at a hospital. When I trained for the emergency department, one comment from my supervisor stuck with me and changed my perspective on life: “I don’t have to train you; I get to train you.” It made me view new challenges as opportunities to learn rather than obligations. Watching the doctors interact with the patients and help them enthusiastically through their struggles inspired me to be even more empathetic to others. Because of this newfound love for my community, I became inspired to try more group performances. Being one of the senior students, I was used to dancing solo, believing that performing complex dances was more impressive. However, I realized that adapting to my groupmates’ moves and helping them with steps was much more notable.

My days and personality became much richer as my tea transformed into a symphony of flavors. Each ingredient provided a new layer of complexity: the honey brought forth resilience and regard, and the masala a love for the community. As I continue exploring and refining my passions, I hope to add depth and richness to my journey with each experience, savoring the process of growth and discovery along the way.

Quiet. I always found comfort in quiet. While other children shrieked around the playground, I enjoyed quietly playing with my dolls and having calm pretend tea parties with my parents. As an only child, I looked forward to our special time alone, just the three of us, soaking up every drop of undivided attention.

November 6th, 2008. That was the day my little brother Max was born and my peaceful solitude was shattered. While I enjoyed quietly brushing my doll's hair for hours, Max would scream in frustration after puzzle attempts. I suspected that Max was different from other kids; even his tantrums were more intense and more frequent.

I felt responsible for protecting him, shielding him from the judgmental glares of others. When we learned the correct terminology - a “mood disorder” - I spent hours each day filling my sticky toddler iPad with my rudimentary Google research. I learned that the main cause of Max’s tantrums was his inability to express his feelings.

I taught Max how to manage his frustration by talking to me before he started crying, and how to express his desires healthily by breathing and using his words. As the years passed, I got better at helping him cope with what he was feeling rather than him screaming, using tips everywhere from wikihow to NYU articles on children with mood disorders. Along the way, I learned how to adjust to having a sibling who had mental health issues, and having my quiet life turned into a circus.

Being in public with Max was especially hard. Other shoppers turned their carts, while we shopped for milk and bread with a screaming child. Walking down the street with other families avoiding interaction so they didn’t have to encounter Max. Their avoidance of eye contact and attempting to avoid interaction reeked of judgment and filled me with shame. I felt so judged and isolated, so I could only imagine how Max felt. I started to notice the Maxes in my class - kids who sat alone at lunch, struggled with their schoolwork, or went simply unnoticed. I began sharing my lunch with Theo, who had autism, tutoring Chloe through Science, and teaching Michele how to dance. I made it my intention every day to share my love and friendship with everyone, leaving everyone feeling included, and if nothing else, they had at least one friend.

As Max started to grow out of his tantrums, he faced other challenges. I noticed him spending lunch by himself and coming home without a smile. It hurt me to see him so alone, without any close friends, because he couldn’t pick up social cues or solve 2+2 as quickly as them. I saw the detrimental effects it had on him and how all of his progress started to backtrack. I knew what it was like to be bullied, so watching it happen to him was hard. But I am a resilient person. I always know how to turn negative things into positive ones. Soon, I started an anti-bullying Instagram page, speaking about both my and Max’s experiences with bullying. I collaborated with many small businesses to advocate for the cause. This gave me a platform to speak on my experiences with bullying because my whole life, I watched people pick on my brother for his differences. As my account gained traction, Max found his confidence and started to make friends with other kids just as special as him. He started coming home with a smile on his face and eager to tell me about his adventures with Lorenzo and Nico.

By helping Max grow, I also grew too. While gaining knowledge and helping Max stop screaming in public and complete a puzzle without crying, I learned the importance of having a good support system and inclusivity. Today, I look forward to each grocery store visit with Max. Instead of tantrums, we share conversations about what we are feeling. And judgmental sneers are replaced with smiles and waves. I’ll always treasure my only child days, but I found that having Max as my brother was way better. I learned so much at such a young age, and plan to impact society by promoting inclusivity and spreading kindness.

I’m the person who swaps out the typical garam masala for a dash of hot sauce in my mom’s biryani. My anti-traditionalism keeps me distant from cultural relics; however, today is different.

**

In India, Diwali was a family event that brought our neighborhood together. Upon moving to the U.S., we clung to Diwali as a familiar constant amidst unfamiliarity. Here, my anti-traditionalist stance makes an exception.

**

As I walk to the living room, the scent of incense embraces me. My mother hands me a diya, and I place it alongside others, feeling its glow within me. My rebellion softens; I’m simply partaking in a tradition that’s larger than myself. Diwali isn’t just about lighting lamps; it’s about light over darkness, good over evil. In the flickering flame, I see the resilience, optimism, and courage of my ancestors. Despite my instinct to rebel, this diya calls me to embrace these values and my place in a legacy greater than myself. It's a moment of setting aside what felt “right” for so long, realizing transformation often comes from embracing the unfamiliar.

**

I face the mirror, noticing my kurta missing my preferred neutral colors. My “Clothing” Pinterest board would scoff, but I feel gratitude. Two years ago, this kurta felt like a costume--a reminder of my “otherness.” Compared to muted jeans and hoodies, the vibrant colors and intricate designs felt like I had shed one identity to embrace another. Now, far from the local store in India where my Aya bought it, I feel I’m carrying a piece of home with me--a tangible link to my roots. Each year I wear it, my internal conflict eases--I’m not abandoning who I am but integrating a deeper part of myself.

**

Recognizing the value of this tradition, I step outside with a box of fireworks, nerves tingling. This Diwali, I’m lighting the first fuse. I used to watch from the sidelines, but now, I feel bold, stepping into the role meant for me.

My shaky hands steady as I realize that those watching are not just spectators--they’re family, sharing this moment connecting my past to my present. I can’t help but feel a rush of doubt. What if I mess up? What if this moment doesn’t live up to their expectations? These thoughts cloud my mind, but I remember the journey it took here; through facing my fears and challenging my comfort zone that I learned the true meaning of perseverance.

As I light the fireworks, people cheer around me, their cheers drowning out the pops and crackles. I blend into the environment, feeling more connected to my tradition than ever before as I’m surrounded by my loved ones. It feels as if everything has come together perfectly, and the feeling of belonging intensifies amidst the sparkles of celebration--only possible by embracing the unfamiliar.

**

Eight months later, I find myself in a gray room at Rockefeller University, preparing to present research findings to a room full of seasoned researchers. The daunting task stirs familiar nerves--I fear my voice will crack, that my insights might falter. My instinct is to stay quiet, but just as I have stepped outside my comfort zone each Diwali, I push myself to confront my nerves. I present our work and with each word, the dull room reflects a diya--lighting with my colorful passion.

Just like I learned to navigate strong conflicting emotions through Diwali, I aspire to help others navigate their own complexities--feelings of belonging, identity, and self acceptance--through my studies in the field of psychology. I’m eager to join initiatives that explore cultural influences on mental health, advocating for dynamic healthcare that honors diverse backgrounds. Whether it’s through research on how cultural identity shapes behavior or involvement in student organizations that promote well being for a variety of communities, I’m determined to ignite a sense of belonging that inspires others to step into the light of their own traditions.

Restlessness was my constant companion. My little legs were perpetually in motion. Running, kicking, jumping, and climbing, they were always taking me exploring. Although my adventurous tendencies were great for exercise, they fell short in other areas.

At school, I would frequently blurt out answers without raising my hand, and my first time as the line leader was also my last. I would fidget with anything I could get my hands on: pencils, scraps of paper, leftover cookie crumbs. The only item that managed to escape my constant fiddling was a good book. Whenever the teacher said it was reading time, all of my classmates would groan in despair. For me, however, reading time was the best part of the day. Each page was a buffet freshly prepared. Long sentences were like a medium well filet mignon, a tad bit chewy, but bursting with an umami flavor to reward you for your effort. The shorter sentences were bites of an envy apple, crisp and fruity. Dialogue was my favorite. It was what brought the story to life. It made the words on the page speak to me, and I could hear the unique and vibrant voices that brought each character's personality and emotions to life.
