In contrast to my eating habits, I was a picky reader. I seldom went beyond my favorite genre—fantasy. Why would I read a non-fiction book and stay on Earth when a good fantasy book could transport me to worlds beyond the Milky Way Galaxy? Frequently, I would find myself lost in complex plotlines where magical spells, whimsical beasts, and heroic quests intertwined to hold my imagination hostage.

As my voice became deeper and my frontal lobe developed, my body stopped restlessly moving—yet my mind didn’t. Journeying beyond the comfortable realm of fantasy, in place of goblins and dragons came atoms and kinematics. I began to devour the solar system and periodic table, exploring the paths of subatomic particles and asteroids. Soon I was tasting math and physics, where formulas and theories became a playground for me to chase the invisible oscillations of electromagnetic waves, the hurricane of thoughts racing through my head imitating their patterns. My curiosity was not just limited to science. I began to sample more mature kinds of literature—philosophical, historical, and mythological literature became my favorites. As Hercules nimbly dodged and voraciously slashed at the heads of the Hydra, I could feel the weight of his courage, compelling me to face my own battles with the same bravery. Studying how Dmitri Shostakovich anguishedly crafted his symphonies amidst the starvation in besieged Leningrad, I couldn’t help contrasting my peaceful surroundings with his relentless suffering. As I listened to a live performance of his 7th symphony, every single note caused my skin to prickle, a vivid reminder of the dire circumstances in which he composed this symphony. Whenever chaos and stress arise, I find myself going back to the lessons and teachings of Marcus Aurelius. Closing my eyes, I pause to breathe deeply, my troubles washing over me like a wave, as he might have done before war.

Just like my legs once did, it is my mind that takes me exploring. The whirlwind my legs used to create became thoughts spinning in my head, propelling me forward onto academic and intellectual pursuits. Like a chef, I am continuously trying new recipes, tasting fragrant aromas, and sharing the fruits of my labor with others.

“Mom, watch out! You’re gonna derail the Azusa!”

My mom narrowly missed the white engine barreling down the sloped track from the dining table to the floor. Besides expanding my mind, every new piece of track I added to my “landscape” opened more stations and destinations my family had to step over. Leading out of the living room station hub, the tracks diverged in the dining room, passed through the bedrooms and across the genkan (where we removed our shoes) before returning back to the hub.

Passengers on the miniature plastic trains would wave goodbye as the trains disappeared over the horizon into the kitchen. After each train departed, I wondered where my passengers wanted to go. I always needed more tracks and trains. But the more I added, the more I had to redirect or leave cars on sidings. It would be years before I’d be coding algorithms for interval scheduling maximization and optimizing the number of trains that could arrive within a given time frame. Until that future arrived, I had to step over interlocking tracks, lift derailed boxcars, and watch trains crash.

“Can you move the tracks near the kitchen somewhere else?” my mom pleaded.

“No! They have to be there, or else the passengers from my bedroom are not going to make it on time!” I replied, holding two boxcars.

I didn’t realize it at the time. The insurmountable (or so they seemed) problems and frustrations that came from trying to remember which trains were leaving from which rooms and which ones were arriving from other rooms and wondering if I could ever solve the problem of trains crashing out of sight in other rooms were what drove me to seek solutions in programming.

Today, my parents no longer have to worry about kicking over engines or tripping over tracks. Instead graphs and simulations manifest my passion for modeling. The waving passengers exist only as numbers, but their presence is more important than ever. With every simulation I run, I imagine thousands of businessmen and students standing shoulder-to-shoulder in unbearably crowded trains. I run these simulations every morning, as I get ready for school. I’ve set up scripts to give me the numbers of people I’m going to be sharing a train with, along with reminders of any homework I have to finish.

As I left my home one fateful winter day, I got an alert on my phone saying my first train was delayed. I got to the platform, and there were already twice the number of people my simulations had predicted. I found a seat and pulled out my laptop. There was no use fretting over a train that wouldn’t be here for another half-hour. I spent some time adjusting my simulations. Rubbing my hands together to keep warm, I pressed play and estimated that 300,000 commuters across Tokyo were currently reexamining their life choices.

I was prepared the next time my train was delayed—instead of waiting on the platform, I timed my commute to when the trains started running again. What started out as a way to make my day easier evolved to larger and more complicated analysis projects. What if we shuttled trains using the opposite track during rush hour? The more data I cataloged, the more threads I drew between the different projects I undertook. My mind was the biggest network I had created, and I found myself spending more and more of my free time at school engrossed in the complex systems of Tokyo.

Tracks no longer wind through my home, even though my wonderful parents would have let me keep them until I was an adult. Those tracks led me to recognize the lack of earthquake shelter infrastructure in parts of Japan and develop a shelter placement algorithm.

Progressing beyond those tracks allowed me to create a network larger than I could have ever imagined.

Have you ever donated any of your clothes to a Goodwill store? If so, there’s a chance they could be hanging up in my closet right now. About four years ago, I was introduced to the world of the Goodwill Bargain Bins, and I haven’t been the same since. These bargain bins are Goodwill’s liquidation point, where items that don’t sell at regular stores end up. This is also the final stop for these clothes before they head to the landfill.

Picture this: a giant warehouse filled with large, blue bins on wheels. Within these bins lies every object you could imagine, from your best dreams—a current Urban Outfitters Nirvana sweatshirt—to your worst nightmares (no comment). What makes this place even better is that you pay by the pound, and the more you buy, the cheaper the pricing gets. It sounds like heaven, I know, but there’s more. These bins are lined up in rows, and every thirty minutes, the current bins are wheeled out and replaced by new ones brimming with treasures.

There’s a catch, though. As the new bins roll out, it’s like the starting bell of an epic battle. Shoppers, armed with their reusable bags and an eye-on-the-prize mentality, circle the bins like hawks. The moment the staff gives the go-ahead, it’s a mad dash! You dive in, elbow-deep in a sea of clothes, toys, and mysterious gadgets, hoping to unearth that one hidden gem. Imagine digging blindly through utensils, pots, and pans when you hit the jackpot: a 1980s vintage rock band tee in mint condition (pro tip: the best tees are always wrapped around the glassware)!

My whole life, I had never embraced a style. I typically wore whatever clothes my mom or grandma bought, and I was content with that for a while. But right before high school, I decided I wanted a closet refresh. I was about to enter a new era and wanted my clothes to reflect a new, grown-up me. It was a battle to convince my mom to take me to the store because it was over an hour away, and she was a little suspicious since she had never heard of anything like it before. My eyes widened as I tried to take in the overwhelming number of items everywhere. As I dug through the clothes, I started finding pieces for the new me.

As the visits continued, my style began to expand and become more expressive. I picked out clothes that I normally wouldn’t have purchased at a store. I made it into a game to see what new outfits I could create with these items. Imagine grabbing an NFL t-shirt, a 1970s patchwork comforter, a plain gray Champion crewneck, and XXL jeans, and designing an eclectic, one-of-a-kind winter jacket. I never knew the sewing lessons my mom signed me up for when I was little would come in handy. My friends always say they love my style, and a few have even bought some of the clothes I’ve created.

In a world where fast fashion dominates, my journey with Goodwill Bargain Bins has taught me the true value of sustainability and creativity. Each visit is not just a shopping trip but an adventure, a treasure hunt that allows me to express my unique style while making a positive impact on the environment. By giving these discarded items a second life, I challenge the notion that worth is determined by price tags or brand names. Instead, I find beauty in the worn and the used, and in doing so, I contribute to a more sustainable future. So, the next time you donate your clothes, remember—they might just end up in the hands of someone like me, ready to be transformed into something new and cherished.

The tantalizing aroma of ginger chicken or the crunch of fresh vegetables from the market connects those who have a shared love of food. A meal shared together can build conversation, reminding us of our grandma’s cooking from when we were young. However, despite the fact that food connects people, I found that it tended to make me feel disconnected from those I cared about.

The disappointed look on my grandma’s face after my automatic response of “I’m sorry Bà, but I can’t have that” would eat me up from the inside out. The glass cup of Chè Ba Màu (a Vietnamese dessert), meticulously crafted by my grandma, would sit forgotten on the table, its grass jelly floating solemnly in the ivory coconut milk - a forbidden dessert filled with sweet temptation.

I held resentment towards myself and my body. In my family, food is the ultimate form of love, yet I found myself unable to embrace it. Instead, I felt deeply embarrassed, as though I were painfully out of place in a body that didn’t listen to me.

Frustrated by my allergies, I decided to immerse myself in learning life sciences to take control of my inability to consume dairy. As I began to understand the molecular workings of life, I found excitement in all aspects of biology beyond my allergies. Hours spent reading through research papers regarding the immune system opened the floodgates of my interest in plant biology, cancer research, HIV/AIDS, and more. I discovered that the scientific name of asparagus was actually Asparagus officinalis (a monocot species) and I learned how to use western blotting to identify proteins.

As I indulged myself in learning the inner workings of life (to the point where I would become bloated from reading so many different scientific research articles), my curiosity grew to become more than myself, something which I wanted to share with the rest of the world. Maybe in the ways that I couldn’t connect with others through food, I could connect with them through scientific discovery instead.

For the past few months, I worked as an intern for the Seattle Children’s Research Institute (SCRI), where I broadened my understanding of pediatric cancer research, specifically in neuro-oncology. In ways that I couldn’t before, I shared delectable meals with the researchers I met, gorging myself in the knowledge and skills I learned both in and outside the lab. John, my mentor, shared an abundant feast of knowledge, teaching me the ins and outs of microchimerism. In turn, I taste tested each dish, refining my palette by fervently asking questions such as how are GFP’s (Green Fluorescent Proteins) used for protein localization? Or, what is the best way to collect samples from lab specimens?

Although I haven’t found a cure for my allergies, I’ve discovered how to overcome my barriers with food, fostering connections with researchers and patients who are eager to exchange knowledge and learn alongside me.

I continue to bridge the divide caused by my allergies, connecting with my family members as I discover new ways to adapt various recipes in the name of science. Through trial and error, once dairy chocolate chip brownies have now been tweaked to become vegan brownies. I am the mad scientist in my family’s kitchen, sharing my crazy experiments with my family in hopes of creating a dairy-free concoction that tastes just like its dairy-filled counterpart.

While my journey in science started as a way to understand my allergies, my interest in my body developed into my drive to help others through research and discovery. Biology excites me as it helps us understand these differences and overcome challenges like mine. I aim to continue my pursuit of autoimmune disorder and pediatric cancer research to help kids enjoy their grandma’s cooking without worry.

A shared love of food unites people despite cultural or lifestyle differences. A meal shared together can build conversation. However, the joy of a shared discovery and knowledge can nourish the soul just as deeply as my mom’s comforting, homemade Bún bò Huế.

My mom pulled my hair back and loosely folded it up. Although she acted indifferent, I knew she was bothered. I nodded my head and remained insistent that she should cut it. She furrowed her eyebrows and tried to convince me once again.

“You’ll look like a boy.” She hated the idea of her daughter looking like a son, and my disregard for her desire made her snap.

Chop. Chop. Chop.

As my reflection gazed back at me, I tried to comb my fingers through my hair, but the strands had stopped prematurely. Rather than black hair flowing down to my hips, only rough edges poking my neck remained. Despite my “boy-ish” hairstyle, somehow I felt more feminine and more like myself—a girl.

I am an error in the grand system of society. Perhaps not a mistake, but an outlier. I’ve desperately wanted to blend in with the gender norms my entire life. Somehow, I still stand out. According to the standards of sexual preference, I am too masculine to be attracted to men. I relate to the comedian, John Mulaney, who said about himself, “I think heaven built ¾ of a gay person, and then they forgot to flip the final switch.” I bear all the typical stereotypes of a lesbian, and yet, I miss the core of it all: attraction to females.

After growing out my hair, I realize that people will continue to judge no matter what I do, but I don’t care. Although I had no experience in acting, I hosted a singing talent show in front of thousands with the Pioneer Theatre Guild. While my skin was tanner than the other cast members, I made no intention to cover my color. While the other female hosts searched for dresses, I looked for a suit. I represented not only myself, but many others I know were in the audience who also wanted to take the stage. Even after a year, I still get recognized from my iconic suit. Similarly, in band I always had to look up to the Head Librarian in another band because he had so many more inches than me. However, I made sure he didn’t look down on me. I took up many leadership positions as the Head Librarian of my band, rank leader for colorguard, and section leader for flutes. I dedicated many hours to the band, printing out music and volunteering at music festivals, illustrating that all musicians are the same outside of the band. In such a male-dominated band, I demonstrated women can take charge too.

Stereotypes are restricting chains binding one to the fundamental equations of identity. A woman does not need to be feminine. A man does not need to be masculine. The liberal public has somewhat accepted this ideology. I propose to further this philosophy. A masculine woman does not have to be a lesbian. A feminine man does not have to be gay. There should be no association between following gender norms and sexuality. My “boy-ish” hairstyle won’t help my case in defending my heterosexuality nor assist my paltry attempt to fit in. However, it is one step closer to finding my true self. Even if I was born as an outlier, I’ll find a place where I equal the equations of identity. A year after the haircut, my mom is finally beginning to pick out suits for me rather than a dress.

In college, I will continue to challenge stereotypes and explore my identity, be that through becoming one of the first Asian women to take the stage or through leading the bands with a height disadvantage. I know in college I’ll find others like me, but I’m not afraid to be the first either. As I leave high school, I will continue to exist as my authentic self, whatever form that may take, and regardless of the misconceptions from others.

**Jolting up from my mattress, I peered into the hallway to investigate the ear-splitting sound. My gaze swept past shattered plates and bowls to my father, who lay on his right, clutching a torn tablecloth that couldn’t prevent his fall. I rushed towards him and shook his torso with desperation. After an eternal minute, his eyes opened.**

The next few moments were a blur: as my mother helped him sit up, I brought him water. After taking a clumsy sip, my father instructed me to leave so he could speak privately with my mother. I left—but secretly listened.

“...stress...suddenly fainted…”
“...H-1B visa…11 days to get a job…deported to India…” 
“...no time…talk later.”

At age 13, I’d heard of the H-1B visa—but I never thought that a ticket into America would have an expiration date. I had to find a better visa for my family. I scavenged through immigration articles, struggling with terms like “Form I-129” and “212(D)(3) Waiver.” After hours of translating legalese, I concluded that my father needed permanent residency, not an H-1B.

“With a green card, you can find jobs more easily, and you can't get deported for being unemployed," I explained to him later that evening. I knew he'd realize I'd eavesdropped—but his relief was my priority.

Yet his eyes weren’t relieved—just defeated.

“Adhi, I filed for a green card six years ago.”

For the next three days, I pored over policy papers, trying to understand the long wait. I learned that the Immigration Act of 1990 restricted each nationality to 7% of employment-based green cards granted annually. Indian immigrants, constituting 68% of employment-based applicants, faced a 195-year wait for permanent residency. Until then, we were shackled to a life of temporary H-1B contracts, perpetually teetering on the tightrope of deportation.

Why did society ignore this inequity?

In the week approaching deportation, tension escalated with every day that passed; finally, my father revealed our fate.

“Adhi…”
He smiled. 
“I got hired. We can stay.”

With watery eyes, we embraced, grateful we’d escaped deportation. Yet, I couldn’t escape indignation. When the tribulation of over a million Indian immigrants remained invisible to society, I had to bring our plight to light. I wouldn’t be hushed by historical silence.

I was going to shatter it by raising my voice.

***

Gripping the lectern, I scanned the dimly lit auditorium. Five hundred unknown faces stared back.

I froze.

What if my speech angers them?

I then spotted my father in the audience. Suddenly, I was speaking—with passion.

“Society condemns illegal racism but ignores legal racism,” I denounced, thinking of 400,000 Indian immigrants expected to die before being naturalized.

“Each voice added to the chorus amplifies the call for immigrant justice,” I declared, rallying the audience to join the fight for reform.

I wasn’t speaking for applause or acclamation, but to ensure no child would have to witness a parent collapse from stress caused by systemic injustice.

After my five-minute speech, dozens of strangers surged toward the stage.

Uh-oh. I braced for hostility.

“Go into politics, young man,” encouraged an African-American gentleman, sharing the discrimination he faced because of his skin color.

“Run for Congress,” suggested a Czech lady, revealing her own father’s struggles immigrating to Canada.

As the once quiet audience now shared stories fervently, I realized that silence wasn’t the absence of dialogue—but its suffocation. All it took was for one person to initiate the dialogue to create waves of discourse that rippled across the shores of change. Just like my father’s fall ignited a fire in me, my words could ignite a fire in others.

As I stepped off stage, my father approached me with eyes that were no longer defeated—but proud. With watery eyes, we embraced—not for escaping deportation—but for putting our pain into purpose.

Wheeling sixteen wooden planks, a 50-ft roll of chicken wire, eight bags of dirt, and a huge shovel up to the register, I invested every bit of chore wages and birthday money into the Lowe’s clearance section. My objective? To grow a Burmese Sour tomato. That chicken wire still borders the four garden beds I assembled in my backyard, with the help of my dad’s nail gun.

It all started five years ago when I was reading a picture book to my little sister Ritika, and we spotted an ugly-looking tomato. “A Burmese Sour tomato,” I read, examining the lumpy fruit and wondering what it would taste like. My sister and I borrowed five farming textbooks from the library, watched YouTube videos about soil chemistry, and scoured Reddit threads from r/GardeningUK to r/PerennialVegetables. I bought a pack of 15 seeds from possibly sketchy Etsy sellers and planted them in trays. After two weeks, 60% of the seeds sprouted, and by late August, we’d counted 41 ripe tomatoes in the garden.

One sunny afternoon, my neighbor Ms. Thien spotted the funny-looking tomatoes on her morning jog. She mentioned she’d been trying to make her grandmother’s special curry but couldn’t find a grocery store that carried the key ingredient: Burmese Sour tomatoes. She’d offered me 8 dollars for 4.

That afternoon, I set up a Facebook marketplace account. As word spread, Mr. Wu from down the street wanted Chinese yams; my friend’s uncle Mr. Patel wanted Goji berries; and even my Spanish teacher Mrs. Carrasco put in a request for Peruvian Loche squash. Of course, growing these vegetables wasn't as simple as deciphering the handwritten notes, sprawled in passionate handwriting from the Etsy sellers. Each new request led me to explore obscure gardening forums, dive into random blogs, and DM experts (aka people who posted about their successful yields) to hound them with questions.

The more unusual the vegetable, the longer the conversations lingered. I’d spend many happy hours sharing gardening tips through Facebook Messenger chats, or explaining why I couldn't sell crosnes for 10 dollars a pound if I’d wanted to make a profit. With my first few sales, I bought a plastic greenhouse and grow lights from AliExpress so I could plant sprouts earlier in the year.

As the demand for the produce grew, I began tracking my expenses and returns, quickly realizing that running a garden wasn’t just about digging in the dirt; it was about crunching numbers and crafting marketing plans if I wanted to break even. When the plants seemed to compete with each other for sunlight and space, I’d hit the dreaded wall of diminishing returns. It was clear that simply growing more wasn’t the answer. So, I got creative, diversifying the crops, branding them as rare and exotic, and watching as my profit margins bounced back.

The diversity of these vegetables demanded highly individualized care, so I dove back into YouTube as I integrated my first Arduino system into the greenhouse, complete with sensors to monitor soil moisture, humidity, and temperature. The Arduino ecosystem allowed me to automate drip irrigation, grow lights, and thermostat cycles. The following summer, I built a compost tumbler with a 55-gallon plastic drum my neighbor was throwing out along with an air compressor I found on eBay and drove two hours to pick up.

Five summers later, I’m still the steward of the garden. I’ve tried to bequeath the garden to my sister, but she refuses on account of the creepy crawlies. Nevertheless, as I plant the sprouts for this season, I look forward to the new things that will grow from the soil. My mom hates how ugly it gets in the winter –- the pile of wood and wire covered in snow, but she’s promised to keep it there when I leave, Burmese sour tomatoes and all. In that way, I will always be close to my roots.

Jump.

It’s funny how a single word can capture everything I’ve done, everything I’ve feared, and everything I’ve become.

“Why do you even bother with dance?” My friend’s voice cut through the noise, sharp and certain, as I sat, lacing up my shoes. It stung—maybe because part of me wasn’t so sure either. Dance was that thing you did for fun, right? Not something you "bothered" with. Their words hit me harder than I cared to admit, making me question if my time on the dance floor was really worth it.

I stood there, as the freshman nobody knew, side by side with a senior that everyone admired. My hands were trembling, but my feet? My feet were ready to fly. That first leap onstage—let’s just say I didn’t crash and burn, though my heart felt like it was doing cartwheels. In the following months, I found myself in front of crowds at other schools and festivals. With every performance, I danced not just for others, but for the parts of myself I was still trying to find. I wasn’t proving something to the audience anymore; I was proving something to me.

But it wasn’t always this easy.

Jump.

It happened again when my English teacher, of all people, handed me an opportunity that seemed ridiculous: hosting a debate tournament. Now, I was a STEM student—numbers and equations were my rhythm, not words in front of an audience. But somehow, there I was, standing on the edge of another metaphorical cliff, staring at almost 300 people. I thought, “This isn’t me. I can’t do this.”

Spoiler alert: I did.

In the crowd, I spotted a freshman—her hands shaking like mine had been not long ago. She looked terrified, like someone had asked her to jump from a plane without a parachute. I recognized that fear. I lived that fear. So I took her aside, shared my own story—the nerves, the shaking, the uncertainty—and told her how I had learned to jump anyway. I watched her face change, just a little, the fear still there but softened, like clouds clearing away to let the sun through. Leadership isn’t about being the loudest or the most in charge. It’s about standing at the edge of a high diving board, feeling the rush of fear as you prepare to leap into the unknown, and then taking that jump with the confidence that your own leap will inspire others to take their own courageous dives.

Jump.

That freshman? She nailed her speech, just like I knew she would. Watching her take the stage was like watching a younger version of myself, except this time, I wasn’t the one trembling.

For a long time, I thought jumping meant conquering fear. Turns out, it’s more about embracing it—knowing that fear will be there, whispering doubts in your ear, and deciding to leap anyway. With every jump I’ve made, I’ve grown. From timid freshman dancer to confident leader, from stage-fright to stage-steady, I’ve learned that my power doesn’t come from being fearless. It comes from jumping into the unknown and finding out what I’m capable of along the way.

Jump.

My friend’s words still echo sometimes, like a faint breeze on a quiet night: “Why bother?” But now, they make me smile. Because the truth is, I don’t just "bother" with dance, or with leading, or with stepping up when others need me.

I jump.

“6’6 FORWARD, NUMBER 12, ALI AHMADDD!”

As the only Pakistani-Arab athlete on the Lovejoy High-School basketball team, I’m no stranger to curious glances and hushed whispers when the announcement of my name as team captain echoes through our gym. I can sense every gaze and the subtle shift in the crowd's energy. I won’t lie– it stings being seen as different– but the sting of watching my brother bullied for his differences cuts far deeper. That’s why, when I’m not practicing free throws, I'm pushing the ball forward for neurodiversity awareness.

My older brother, Ahsan, is autistic, and in seventh grade, he was taunted and tripped by a classmate, an incident which broke his wrist. In the weeks following his emergency surgery, Ahsan’s pain-filled cries tormented the halls of our home while I kept mine muffled in my pillows.

I wanted to know why. Why does Ahsan’s brain make him hyper-fixate and rewatch the same Cars movie scene, 100 times? Why do some differences lead to social exclusion while others are more readily accepted? Why did socializing come so naturally to me, allowing me to enjoy hooping with peers who might otherwise tease someone like my brother?

Seeking answers, I turned to neuroscience. Conducting independent research with a UC Davis PhD candidate, I bushwhacked into the cerebral jungle. Over the course of 10 arduous months, I scoured hundreds of databases analyzing brain scans of autism patients. Using machine learning, I found that technology can help diagnose kids before they show symptoms, allowing for early intervention and eventually preventing future struggles caused by autism.

I wondered: if early diagnosis had been an option, how different could Ahsan’s life have been? Could his struggle to recognize social cues or repetitive hand movement – both of which made him a ripe target for bullying – been mitigated?

But I knew that research alone wouldn’t change the everyday indignities faced by my neurodivergent peers. Before I was captain, teammates would groan when a neurodiverse kid tried out for the team, impersonating flailing arms. I recall seeing one such student sitting alone in the locker room post-tryout, tears streaming down his face. To this day, I deeply regret not standing up for him as a freshman. And yet, it was this same regret that drove me to create A Beautiful Mind, an anti-bullying after-school club. My vision was simple: to create fun activities that bridge gaps between neurominority and neurotypical kids.

During our weekly club hangouts, I formed a special bond with Thad. His enthusiastic recitations of dinosaur facts remind me of Ahsan’s passionate monologues about model trains. Thad never directly divulges his emotions — I can only sense how he may desire having friends or being invited to a birthday party. So, on Thad’s birthday, our club organized a dinosaur-themed party, transforming Mr. Seidel’s art room into a lush jungle. Throughout lively rounds of Jurassic Park trivia, Thad eagerly shared fun facts about velociraptors (Did you know that they were only the size of a turkey? Jurassic Park lied!) to a roomful of laughter.

Ahsan, Thad, and countless other neurodiverse individuals have taught me that the busiest room can be the loneliest room. Although serving as the first Pakistani-Arab captain to lead our team to the district championship is immensely fulfilling, my true purpose lies beyond shooting hoops. For every Ahsan and every Thad, there needs to be a steadfast ally– a captain, a brother– who has their back. For every researcher dedicating toiling hours to understand autism, there must be someone who empathizes, laughs with, and shares the struggles of those who they research for. And for every kid that is singled-out for being different, there must be a cheerleader who champions and uplifts precisely what makes them unique.

At university, I’ll continue to break stereotypes. I’ll join others working towards the same ideals. Together, we’ll try to make the busiest room a little less lonely.

Do you love your ears? Well, I love mine. Not because they’re bigger or better looking but because they listen intently. Growing up, my mom would clean the entire house, from the basement to the bedrooms, a few times every month. She’d start cleaning by entering her bedroom and opening Pandora to play whatever Carlos Vives or Shakira had recently released. The music was so loud I could hear it at every square inch of the house. The sound of stomping feet dancing along to the music would shake the walls. For a while, I was used to the routine. I’d tune the noise out of my head and continue to build my Legos. One day, I stopped just hearing. I decided to listen. Listen to how the singer evoked the song's mood by the inflections in their voice. Listen to how the drummer controls their volume to influence the intensity. Listen to how the bassist lays down the tempo and sound with the baseline. Once I began to listen, I was obsessed. I couldn’t ever go back to just hearing.

Now, after eight years of playing saxophone, I listen like it's the last time I might hear anything. I’ll listen to music to sing along, learn a part I have to play in a jazz band, or even transcribe a lick from a solo I love. Every day, I pull my headphones out of my pocket and flip the latch open. I slip one bud into my ear, cue whatever song I’m most intrigued by, and begin scatting along to the solo. I do it daily, even when I get strange looks in the hallway, because the more I listen, the more I learn. Some assume that just because you listen more than others, you don’t understand things as quickly, but it couldn’t be further from my truth. I listen with intent because it’s what teaches me best. Whether playing a tune with a band I’ve never played with or listening to my PLTW professor talk about calculating trusses, I’m listening to learn.

Listening to various jazz solos by artists like Charlie Parker and Sonny Rollins helped me develop my jazz vocabulary. I’ve applied listening not only to the arts but also to academics and athletics. Listening to my swim coach explain why I needed to narrow my breaststroke kick helped me achieve my goal time at the DuKane conference, and listening to my PLTW teacher provide feedback on my tank design allowed me to understand why I needed to redesign. I used feedback to resolve issues, such as programming a system in the VEX V5 software that utilized distance sensors to rotate the tank if it detected a wall within a 5-inch proximity. Whether it’s grasping the complexities of AP Physics or understanding ideas from a materials engineer assisting in shaping military technologies, my ears are a gateway to learning from those with expertise. They allow me to delve deeper into a world of unknowns but have the confidence that regardless of difficulty, I’ll be able to thrive.

Listening has shaped how I approach every aspect of my life, from music to academics. It’s about more than just absorbing information at the surface level; it’s about understanding the nuances that occur that others might miss. Whether perfecting my breaststroke, analyzing a jazz solo, or redesigning a failed model, listening allows me to extract critical details and conquer any obstacle. Like in music, engineering is about understanding patterns, details, and ideas, and I’m eager to immerse myself in the experience. Listening with intent has taught me that true understanding comes from having a purpose behind my intentions. My ears aren’t any different from anyone else, but they help me discover what others often overlook. And that’s why I love them.

The first thing I remember asking my mom to buy off Amazon was a Rubik's cube. The next thing was a Sudoku book. Then a chess board. Brain teasers. Solitaire. Nonograms. See the pattern?

It’s clear to me that those orders, the toys and puzzles that required thinking, that required problem solving, weren’t just a meantime for me to play with. They allowed me to channel an inclination to problem solving and thinking into something tangible, something I could hold in my hands.

Inevitably, when I got my first laptop and my mom introduced me to the first line of code: (“Hello [Name]!”);, computer science bridged my love of puzzles to a career path. It was a natural choice, and I fell in love with the world where I could create, innovate, and manipulate my own ideas into reality.

Computer science became a natural extension of my mindset- an extension of the way I approach the world. Finding patterns in nonograms or trying to beat my brother in chess, the thrill of thinking and figuring things out stuck to me. Programming brought these traits into a new focus- giving me the tools not just to find problems to solve but to create the problems themselves and find the solutions.

What started as a basic love for brain teasers grew into a connection with the processes behind applications. Computer science is a manifestation of the curiosity and desire to solve as a child, but now with the complexity of math and abstract thought, and personal results to show for it. The character traits I’ve always had are no longer put to use on toys for my enjoyment, but now are my professional foundation. Computer science has never just been a career choice- but a natural evolution of who I’ve always been.

“SOUTH RIM TRAILHEAD,” a sign reads. I sigh, unprepared for the 12-mile hike ahead. Maroon peaks battle with the blue sky, sand dances across the ground, and Meerkats peek out from the hills. But the heat makes me itch, and by the time we summit, I’m completely exhausted- only to realize I forgot my lunch in the car.

While it’s a privilege to RV trip across 700 miles of Texas, walking through Big Bend and hiking through the Chihuahuan Desert with family and friends- I wasn’t thrilled, especially after sitting on a cactus. To me, hiking was like a chore; a constant battle with exhaustion. The only reason I went on hikes was because my father didn’t give us another option.

After a hike up Guadalupe Mountain, our group gathered for dinner in an RV. The room hummed as conversations floated through the air- I argued with my sister about opening a window, and my friends were yelling over an UNO game. Despite my dread for the upcoming hike the next day, I chose to savor the moment, and enjoy our present connection. In the midst of it all, the TV was playing a slideshow my dad created with pictures from our past trips.

As images roll by of us posing at the top of Mount Rainier, of us flashing the peace symbol dripping in sweat at the Grand Canyon, of our weary smiles at the top of Logan Pass; I realize those early mornings and long hikes were my dad’s way of gifting us memories, his way of teaching us to appreciate the world. While, yes, hiking might be exhausting, I’ve gotten to see so many national parks with my family; and create so many experiences.

But just because I realized hiking was a way to make memories didn’t mean I immediately loved it.
“Wake up,” My mom whispers. “We’re doing the Window Trail.”
I rub my eyes with the tips of my fingers, shaking my head. Dang it.

I didn’t enjoy hiking until our trip to Alaska. The Last Frontier brought something out in me; I was truly interested in the land, the potential of untapped wilderness to explore, and for the first time, I took the lead on the hikes- just like my dad. I pointed out fish in rivers, I learned the past of the Fjords, and I dragged my family up the Kenai Mountains. On that trip, I understood. I understood why he took us to hundreds of trails- not just to show us nature, but rather, to show us ourselves.

Now, it helps me to see parallels between challenges of hiking and daily life. Just as a hiker conquers obstacles and finds joy in journeys, I approach every challenge with a sense of goals and an appreciation for the growth they provide. When I’m programming and faced with a bug, I see each line of Java I have to go through as a step along a rocky path, each error resolved an incline I’ve completed. When I’m struggling with weights at the gym or losing a tennis match, I remind myself that every rep and point is a small victory- a step closer to my goal. As I take on the trails of life, I’ll never forget the paths I walked with my dad.

A tough hike, to me, is now a source of strength, a reminder of the importance of perseverance. Each step on a trail, once heavy with fatigue, is now a gift. I know the spirit my dad forged within me during those hikes will continue living inside me until the day I die. And when my trail becomes hard, I remember the lessons of our hikes. Even the most difficult parts can reveal the most amazing views, and every step forwards is a chance to discover something new.

Fate clatters to a standstill and I realize I'm holding my breath, the tension at the table thick enough to cut. My sister breaks the silence:

“5 and 3, so 8.”

My uncle erupts with excitement at the roll—I can’t help but smile, his joy is infectious! My aunt groans as her civilization’s supply drought continues. I offer her a few of my bricks and she embraces me in a loving hug.

***

Growing up in Singapore, family moments like these were frequent. I’d spend weekends marveling at giant pandas with my aunt and laughing at my uncle’s howler monkey imitation—he was more car alarm and circus clown than animal! But after moving to New Jersey in 2016, visiting my extended family required a grueling nineteen hours squeezed into 32x18-inch seats through jolts of turbulence. Separated from the familiar faces of my previous home, I sought comfort through a virtual solution.

I scoured the internet until I struck gold with Colonist.io, an online Settlers of Catan platform. With its endless strategies, element of chance, and ever-evolving nature, the game was an instant hit, making everyone feel included regardless of age.

My aunt’s tortoise-paced play earned her the title “The Sultan of Slow-Mo” and prompted us to set a fifteen-minute timer for her turns! Meanwhile, my uncle hoarded resources like a dragon guarding riches, often leading to hilarious disasters when he lost half his precious stash! Laughing with my family, even through a screen, made the oceans between us a little smaller.

As our games continued into high school, I grew more grateful for the support my relatives provided me. Despite my busy schedule (balancing school, sports, and extracurriculars was like stealing the longest road from my dad: almost impossible!), my relatives always found a time that worked, often staying up late for our Catan calls. Their unconditional presence inspired me, so I made it my mission to be there for others.

At Mega V Day Camp, Marcus frequently sat alone with his Nintendo Switch while other campers played dodgeball. I noticed he’d often steal longing glances at our camp activities before retreating to his device. I knew that feeling of loneliness all too well, so I joined him, at first just watching, then slowly inquiring about his game. He eventually gave in, passionately describing Link’s perilous quest to defeat the tyrant Ganondorf and restore balance to his kingdom. I saw an opportunity! The gym became a battlefield with every throw and dodge an attack against Ganondorf’s evil forces. It wasn’t long until the Switch sat unattended.

While serving food in Newark, I met David, a man who lost his job as a mechanic and fell into a life beneath the city bridges. When I handed him two sandwiches, his expression revealed… disgust? He pointed to the label—cucumber and cheese (one of my favorites)—and looked at me with skepticism, but after trying it, his eyes widened in surprise, and a smile spread across his face as he devoured the rest of his meal. He explained he hadn’t eaten like that in a while and was looking forward to my next delivery. The sincerity in his voice was raw, and I left knowing a small sandwich could bring me contentment in a way no amount of wealth ever could.

***

In both life and Catan, every road starts with a single brick. And I’ve found that the best roads connect us in ways that distance can’t diminish. Whether it’s sharing resources online with my aunt, roping Marcus into the Mega V joy, or brightening David’s day, I strive to be a builder of roads.

Life, like Catan, is better enjoyed with others. I’m here to build bridges of kindness, trade smiles, and rack up those victory points by spreading joy, so let the dice roll!

Matryoshka - a Russian nesting doll. I have had the same set since birth, but unlike the typical set with uniform designs in various sizes, my dolls were unique. Each had a different profession emblazoned on its front in delicate paint strokes. From teachers to mathematicians, scientists to painters, every profession was represented. The smallest doll was a writer, holding books close to her chest.

These dolls mirrored my own shifting ambitions as my interests changed. As I grew into a logic-driven mathematician, writing became my outlet to create worlds with infinite possibilities and endless answers.

Inevitably, some of the matryoshka dolls got lost, just as some of my dreams faded. When I submitted an article to my school newspaper but found that mine was the only one not published, I decided that writing wasn’t for me. My matryoshka dolls became more rigid in their identities and the smallest writer was left behind.

In my sophomore year, the school newspaper stopped publishing. The decline in participation made me wonder if I wasn’t the only one who had lost touch with the art of writing. I didn’t want to keep my writer nested inside my outer matryoshka dolls — the mathematician, teacher, and economist.

I searched for solutions that would have inspired me to pick up my pen again; something online, so that it would be easily accessible for everyone to read at all times, and something with a broad theme, so I could write about anything I was interested in. Looking up, I realized that there was one thing that could allow for discussion about a spectrum of viewpoints, and it was already all around me: color.

That was the birth of my own school magazine, which allowed myself and others to write creatively outside the confines of the classroom. It became a space for me to express my thoughts and explore creativity without the pressure of grades or expectations. Without the boundaries of subject-specific essay structure, ideas flowed out of me like never before. With every new theme, I rediscovered the joy of writing—something that had once felt burdensome when measured against others' standards. Exploring architecture, history, religion, and poetry added vibrancy to the linear structure of my academic curriculum and taught me to learn for learning’s sake.

The broad nature of the themes also encouraged other participants to explore topics that they usually wouldn’t. A submission that stood out to me came from my physics tutee, who had shied away from writing due to a lack of experience. Through encouragement and hours spent brainstorming and editing, I helped her produce a detailed article on sustainable technology, which she proudly printed out and gifted to her parents.

As the magazine was online, I couldn’t help but keep up with the statistics it generated; the shares, page visits, and submissions that came in every day. But this time, they were not a measure of success, but proof that my ideas had had an impact on those around me.

Through ‘The Colour Chronicles’, I learned that my passion for writing wasn't about getting approval from others. It was about sharing my voice and inspiring others to do the same. The writer matryoshka doll, once discarded and forgotten, now stands proudly among the others on my dresser. It serves as a reminder that curiosity and education are not something to be judged by external factors but by the fulfillment it brings within.

My matryoshka dolls continue to grow alongside me, strengthening each other with each new addition. The mathematician will perform groundbreaking research and the artist will embrace new technologies to capture the world around her. The teacher will use any opportunity to enrich others and the author will continue to use her voice to foster community. With each passion within me supporting the others, they create a whole that is richer than any single pursuit.

**Essay:**

My younger self writhed in his grave as I watched my sister drizzle glossy melted chocolate over snowy vanilla ice cream, desperately searching for its flavor in the ice cube on my tongue. Was this worth it?

Let’s revisit my younger self entering sophomore year. The scale read 98.75 kg; these four flickering white characters were the puppeteers controlling my strings of confidence, leadership, socialization, and health.

Alone during the Covid-19 lockdown, I realized self-disgust, not external judgment, was the puppeteers’ lifeblood. A dormant figure was unshackled from the puppeteers’ grasp: discipline. I began dragging myself to 3 km daily, walking 100 meters for every 200 I “ran” envisioning a six-pack soon.

Two months. 45 runs. Scale: 99.50 kg.

Where had I gone wrong? Upon advice from my fitness junkie cousin Shaurya and Greg Doucette’s YouTube videos, I began meticulous caloric tracking and implemented strict meal timings to compliment daily runs. “Nudge” by Thaler and Sunstein introduced “snudges” (self-nudges); fruits at the kitchen’s entrance and junk deep inside created a “walk of shame”. Each step forward was a step away from my goal. Come senior year, the scale read 67.85 and I had never felt healthier. Take that, puppeteer #4!

Two lessons emerged from the dead puppeteers’ ashes. Motivation is merely the ignition - discipline is the fuel for the engine of success. Secondly, consistency is essential to divide ambitious dreams into smaller goals.

Returning to school, I unearthed a passion for MUNs previously suppressed by puppeteer #1, setting an ambitious dream of spearheading my school conference. I constructed smaller goals: enrolling in available MUNs, winning awards and moderating debate, mirroring my division of 3 km into jog, walk, repeat. Each goal was a step transforming the timid Ethiopian delegate hiding behind his placard in freshman year into the USG of Finance handling the entire conference in senior year. Allocating the $17,000 budget reminded me of caloric tracking; working with three conference days and funds instead of three meals and calories. Managing this while fending off a sea of pink sticky notes with IB deadlines scrawled over them, every minute became crucial.

I voluntarily led Project Ancora, an organization of 50 volunteers fundraising for an animal charity (Causes for Animals). Checkmate, puppeteers 2 and 3! However, I caught myself hyper-focusing on merely one of two requirements just as I had on exercise, neglecting diet. Here, focusing on personal hard work I neglected delegation causing a plateau at $1,000. I once again broke down our goal into door-to-door fundraising, merchandise sales, event profits and optimized donor ROAS (return on ad spend), delegating these to volunteers. Combining personal consistency and delegation, we raised $7,500 winning the YFC Merit Award.

The best reward, however, walked through my creaky door in a yellow tank top and denim shorts months later. After making me promise I wouldn’t laugh, my sister said with rare seriousness, “I want to lose weight like you. How did you simply drink water watching us eat your favorite Din Tai Fung dumplings? Why didn’t you give up after failing miserably for months?” I smiled. In classic sibling style, she managed to weave in “failing miserably” in a compliment.

I explained how empowering gradual change through discipline was, helping her visualize this through a video game character slowly leveling up. Only here, the currency was sweat and willpower, not Fortnite V-Bucks or Clash Royale gems. I learnt a lot in the coming months while teaching; she introduced me to scrumptious lower calorie desserts as well as LoseIt!, an effective calorie tracking app. I felt our bond strengthen with her painful side-glance watching our parents enjoy melted chocolate and vanilla ice cream. She was sucking an ice cube.

My sister showed me my biggest change wasn’t physical. I had learned how to learn. How to continually improve myself. This change had transformed seeds of discipline into a blossoming tree with branches of time management, leadership and delegation. It transcended weight loss and four puppeteers, preparing me for any future challenges.

The cold metal of the chair bit into my skin as I sat, hands trembling, in the Taliban detention cell. Two meals a day—if I could keep them down—were the only breaks from the unceasing barrage of questions. “How dare you defy the supreme leader's law?” they roared. I couldn’t stop thinking—how does a simple desire to learn become a threat to an entire regime?

After the Taliban takeover, my once-uninterrupted 1,368-hour streak on my Pomodoro app, spent mastering Khan Academy math videos, was replaced by the daily grind of tracing my earnings. I became the breadwinner of my family.

Schooling also became a distant dream. It was like sixth grade when a rocket bullet hit my primary school; Baba would never again risk my life for school until I spilled onto the floor, fainting on the third day of my hunger strike, protesting for my right to learn. Now, I gave up bearing the despair, watching the lives of millions of kids taken, beyond fainting.

I soon revived a once-abandoned academy to covertly homeschool girls in STEM subjects. We concealed textbooks veiled in religious covers, offering them a glimpse of the education they were being denied.

Inevitably, our underground movement was caught when I confirmed my identity to the Taliban patrol. As I endured the grueling interrogation, my heart shattered upon realizing that 29 classes, sheltering 300 students, were dismissed. Sitting there, I couldn’t resist questioning, "Why are you so afraid of educated girls?"

"You want some weaklings to rise above us?" they told me.

With each blow of the Kalashnikov butt to my body, I realized that oppression can fuel resilience. The more I endured, the clearer it became that we have only one true weapon to fight for our rights: education by any means necessary.

Upon reuniting with my family—teary-eyed—I set out to make Khan Academy STEM lessons accessible in a language millions of Afghans could understand. During the day, I hosted live Zoom sessions with peers, tutoring confined students in STEM subjects. At night, I stationed myself on the stair landing, careful not to awaken my family with the murmurs of my voice echoing through the walls. Wrestling with technical terms that lacked direct translation, I replayed videos countless times to craft analogies and even coined new terms to simplify complex concepts.

I envisioned lighting up every TV screen with Dars. Initially, I approached many requesting their help in creating an encrypted site to store and share educational resources. After receiving multiple rejections, I decided to self-teach and do it independently. I learned web development through trial and error. When the site crashed due to a security vulnerability, I studied encryption protocols to ensure my homemade defiant content was protected. After drafting many versions, my publicly available website was finally born. Later, I was choked up hearing my voice on Meraj TV as the videos were broadcast to thousands of viewers.

With the funds raised by my online students—one even sold her family’s only goat—I put my savings towards buying enough DVDs. I collaborated with local drivers and village elders to deliver them to places where the term "education" had become a whisper.

As I update the green dots on the villages’ map, I read Zahra’s letter; a 14-year-old girl from western Kandahar, wrote, “With the educational kits, I no longer have to disguise myself as a Bacha Posh to attend boys' classes. As someone from an illiterate family, our TV-education screen brings us together at night, as mates."

I’ll continue finding new ways to circumvent gender-apartheid laws—a fight for equity that would not have been possible if I hadn’t survived the interrogations. As I move on to college, I want to make sure no other student mind-drifts during a calculus lesson, fearing the next sound of a boom might be from their class. With 2.5 million confined girls, my journey is far from over—I’ve just begun.

My French teacher once asked me, “If you could define your life in one word, what would it be?”

I responded with “changement (change).”

Throughout the course of my life, change, specifically in the area of friendships, has provided perhaps the most poignant and influential experiences of my life.

Lucas was unconditional. I first met him when I was two weeks old. Together, we went from gibberish to words, crawling to walking, and babies to brothers. Growing up, he was the first person who taught me what it meant to have a best friend: someone who liked you more than anyone else just because you were you. But then I moved. From the bustling city to the placid suburbs, our daily playdates slowly became sporadic reunions.

Edward was perfect. During our first recess, I remember sitting with him under a maple tree and mustering up all my courage to ask, “Hey, do you like Pokemon?” Our similar interests quickly helped us become friends, while our similar personalities helped us become inseparable. Yet, there was always one thing about Eddie that separated him from anyone else I’ve ever met: his heart. He consistently went out of his way to help people and never berated my mistakes. During our years together, he showed me true kindness, and it meant the world to me. But then I moved. Again. From public to private, my once blissful school days suddenly became long, isolated hours trapped behind a mask.

Nelson was different. He was loud, he was energetic, he was assertive. He was everything that I wasn’t. Although I initially thought we wouldn’t end up becoming good friends, he proved me wrong. Through the time we spent together, I learned that despite his boisterous personality, there were also layers and depth to his character that I had initially missed. In fact, what I grew to admire most was his selfless personality and how it inspired his actions. Whether it be standing up for freshmen against bullies or for me against rude strangers in the mall, he’s always ready to speak up for others.

I’ve never struggled to make new friends. My challenge was always leaving them behind. Every time I moved, it felt like I was starting a part of my life over from scratch. As I grew older, I started to question the point of creating new relationships if I was just going to keep losing them. Over time, I became afraid of getting too close to people because I wanted to spare myself another inevitable loss.

One day in my English class last year, my teacher put up a particularly memorable quote on the board: “People will forget what you said, but they will never forget how you made them feel.” As Angelou’s words entered my mind, so too did a sea of emotions as I remembered all the time I spent with my friends, past and present. Pensively staring at the wall beside me, I started to reflect on everything I had gained from my previous relationships. I learned to appreciate the value of my past experiences and became reinvigorated to make the most out of my new ones.

At age 16, I’ve moved houses four times, schools five times, and friends more times than I can even remember. However, unlike the places I’ve been, the people I’ve met have all taught me valuable lessons that continue to impact the person I am today. Learning unconditional friendship from Lucas has helped me become someone who is always ready to help others; learning kindness from Eddie helped me become a strong leader in my school’s band and Wellness Council; and when I spoke about the importance of mental health at a large conference, I never would have had the confidence if it wasn’t for Nelson. I used to think I was losing a piece of myself every time I moved away, but now I know I was really gaining a new one to take its place.

Equipped with this understanding, I am finally ready to embrace the change around me because, for the first time, I know that I am moving forward, not backward. In college, I am excited to create new relationships and continue to grow alongside my peers. I hope I can add something to their lives the same way my friends have done for mine.

$4.7 million—that’s the amount of funding my local school district is losing this year. Back in June, I overheard Ms. Roth, the Science Teacher at Shawnee High School talking to my neighbor about budget cuts and her dire need for test tube holders and aprons. I politely interrupted, and asked if she thought a wish list for school supplies would benefit teachers. Her face lit up, “Absolutely! We need basic supplies, but it would be wonderful if teachers could request items specific to their subjects." We discussed the idea further, and I promised to work on it. My friends Reid and Danny, who were with me, started brainstorming ideas on the way home and were excited to get started. Being from a small log-cabin community, many of our teachers are also neighbors and coaches making this initiative deeply personal.

Over the following weeks, we formed a team and kicked off The Supply Project, a drive to support 13 local schools and over 700 teachers. We organized six events and established three drop box locations. On a sunny Sunday, volunteers set up our donation table outside the local ShopRite. Initially, several people showed interest and donated, but many quickly moved on. One man approached but after Maggie explained our cause, he muttered, "I already pay my taxes!" before walking away. While surprising, his reaction helped us understand the challenges and reluctance we were up against. Weeks earlier, teachers had begun using our online wish list to request items like whiteboards, math fidget spinners, carpets, and book bins—tools necessary for enhancing education, not personal luxuries. Knowing that we needed to refine our message, and sensing my team's discouragement, I ordered pizza and called a meeting at my house. Danny was heated, and started the discussion, “We need to highlight that public funding is inadequate.” I knew he was right and chimed in, “Eight teachers requested flexible seating to better support their ADHD students, which has no funding. Ultimately, these supplies are for the students also.” We spent two hours talking about the social challenges and decided our approach needed to be more personal, mentioning teachers' names, their subjects, and the schools they worked at. This strategy (and taco pizza) revitalized our mission, and we were determined to change public perception.

The next day, when confronted with "Do you know how much teachers earn- and they get summers off?" we were prepared with real-life examples. For instance, Jason Jenkins, the high school woodworking teacher, took on various side jobs, including making a vinyl record holder for my family. Mrs. O’Brien, our 6th-grade math teacher, was preparing and delivering meals. We also emphasized that teachers often spend summers planning their curriculum. Armed with printed examples of needed supplies and their significance in enhancing learning, we engaged effectively with people. Asking, "Did you grow up or go to school here?" sparked conversations, breaking down barriers and encouraging many to donate. For days we engaged, debated and sympathized with passersby. We knew these events wouldn’t solve the widespread issue of underfunded schools, but we were committed to supporting the teachers we cared about. After six fundraisers and nearly $10K in supplies and donations, Mrs. Roth was the first to receive a “Supply Box.” It contained not only her test tubes but highlighters, colored sharpies, scissors, sticky notes and paper to last the entire year.

Motivated by this experience, I plan to start a new initiative focused on tackling food insecurity this year. From my involvement with TSP, I understand better the complexities of community social impact projects and the importance of finding common ground for solutions. When I embark on my college journey, I plan to persist in championing this approach. The prospect of interacting with faculty, peers, and other members of the campus community excites me, as I am convinced that respectful dialogues foster the best ideas and the most profound growth.

My mom pulled my hair back and loosely folded it up. Although she acted indifferent, I knew she was bothered. I nodded my head and remained insistent. She furrowed her eyebrows and tried to convince me once again.

“You’ll look like a boy.” She hated the idea of her daughter looking like a son, which I unfortunately have been doing almost my entire life. My disregard made her snap.

“Do whatever you want, the hair grows on your head anyways.” She threw down my hair and sat down nearby. I hesitated. Even though I was almost an adult, I felt like a child deciding whether or not she should spend her hard-earned money on a Harry Potter Lego set. I wanted to feel mature and independent, but what if I was merely throwing a tantrum in a 16-year-old body?

Chop. Chop. Chop.

As my reflection gazed back at me, I tried to comb my fingers through my hair, but the strands had stopped prematurely. I peered at my side profile. It looked so… different. Rather than black hair flowing down to my hips, only rough edges poking my neck remained. It confused me. Despite my “boy-ish” hairstyle, somehow I felt more feminine and more like myself—a girl.

Even with long hair, my friends called me gay and were just waiting for me to “come out of the closet.” I felt lost. How do I come out of somewhere I’m not in?

After I had cut my hair to express myself more, the allegations of being gay only strengthened. Even my mother had fallen for it. She finally asked the question that I suspected she had for a while.

“Do you intend to act as the male role in a relationship?” aka: You’re gay, right? It pained me that even my own mother categorized me by the standard formulas.

Why does everyone define my sexuality from my personality, not my romantic interests? Society wishes for me to find and express my true self, and yet tries to mold me into someone I’m not. What should I value more, fitting in or finding me?

I am an error in the grand system of society. Perhaps not a mistake, but an outlier. I’ve desperately wanted to blend in with the gender norms my entire life. Somehow, I still stand out. According to the standards of sexual preference, I am too masculine to be attracted to men. I relate to the comedian, John Mulaney, who said about himself, “I think heaven built ¾ of a gay person, and then they forgot to flip the final switch.” I bear all the typical stereotypes of a lesbian, and yet, I miss the core of it all: attraction to females.

After growing out my hair, I realize that people will continue to judge and assume no matter what I do. Stereotypes are restricting chains binding one to the fundamental equations of identity. A woman does not need to be feminine. A man does not need to be masculine. The liberal public has somewhat accepted this ideology. I propose to further this philosophy. A masculine woman does not have to be a lesbian. A feminine man does not have to be gay. There should be no association between following gender norms and sexuality. My “boy-ish” hairstyle won’t help my case in defending my heterosexuality nor assist my paltry attempt to fit in. However, it is one step closer to finding my true self. Even if I was born as an outlier, I’ll find a place where I equal the equations of identity.

In the future, I will continue to challenge stereotypes and explore my identity. With these experiences, I now have the courage to find my own path. In an environment that values individualism, I shouldn’t assimilate into existing equations and instead, rewrite them to define who I am.

"Wake up dude, it's time for anchor watch." I'm suddenly shaken awake by one of my crewmates at 2 AM, passing off his job of making sure that the anchor wasn’t dragging and other vessels weren’t approaching. Accepting my fate, I groggily climb the ladder to the boat's upper deck into the darkness of the ocean night.

The summer of my freshman year, I got the opportunity to attend Seabase High Adventure, a unique Boy Scout experience of living on a sailboat while exploring coastal environments. Although my crew was all in the same troop, I was worried about how well we could mesh together in such a tight new space with people already complaining on the car ride there.

The sun's orange glow paints across the afternoon sky as we slowly motor behind Rodriguez Key, our anchorage for the night. After finishing up grilling up and devouring burgers for dinner, our Captain, Chuck brought out an old conch horn from his cabin and asked if any of us wanted to try playing it. Flattening my chin, I took a deep breath and buzzed my lips against the small opening at the end of a conch. The conch produces a resonant tone, echoing through the afternoon sky. Astounded by the huge sound of the conch, I called over my other scouts, encouraging them to give the conch a try, and one by one, our crew began taking turns, playing the conch into the setting sun. During this setting sun, I discovered how through my leadership, I could join together with my peers to form stronger connections.

The next morning after our conch playing, It was my turn to act as the grubmaster for the day. Alongside my scoutmaster, I dipped slices of bread into a mixture of milk, eggs, and cinnamon, before placing the slice onto the grill. While we sat around our cabin table eating breakfast, chatting, and looking forward to the day's activities, I was reminded of the bonding our crew had while we played the conch the previous evening, and realized our crew had become stronger, no longer worrying about personality differences.

As we progressed through the trip, from snorkeling the vibrant “Donut” reef, filled with schools of blue tand and banded butterfly fish, to swimming over shallow seagrass flats onto Indian Key State Park and exploring its ruins, our community grew stronger and stronger with each passing day. I took on long anchor watch shifts from 12 to 4 am for my crewmates and cooked for them, learning how to properly make dishes such as fried rice and cinnamon french toast. Though at first I was nervous about the trip, I’ll always remember the bonding we had as a crew and the moments we shared.

Three years later, I was now the Senior Patrol Leader, tasked with coordinating events and leading the troop. Our troop was on our annual backpacking trip, tackling a 10-mile loop and with almost 2000 feet of elevation gain for 6 miles straight, some of the newer scouts on the trip began to fall behind. Knowing I was the SPL, I knew I had to help. When we paused for a water break I joined the newer scouts in line and checked up on them, making sure they were drinking enough water and feeling alright, and after we finally reached our campsite, cooked meals for them as a grubmaster. As I’ve become an older leader, I can’t help but remember our crew on our sailboat, inspiring me to forge greater bonds within my troop.

Through scouting, I’ve developed crucial skills that have helped me grow as a person. My experience through outings like Seabase has taught me empathy and leadership, which I strived to achieve as SPL. Furthermore, I’ve built a community and memories I’ll never be able to replace, and I hope to do the same in college.

As my student slid his queen to deliver checkmate, winning the state championship, a surge of pride filled my chest. I recalled standing on a similar stage nearly a decade ago, crowned the national kindergarten chess champion, a victory I once thought would be near my pinnacle in chess. Yet, in this moment, I realized that seeing my student triumph eclipsed all my personal accolades.

I was 4 years old when my dad enrolled me in my temple's morning chess class. What started as a weekly hobby quickly grew into a daily obsession. The effort I poured into chess quickly intensified, culminating in my first major victory at the 2012 Kindergarten National Championship, marking the start of a seven-year journey of winning numerous state and national titles. During these years, my days were consumed by chess—an hour-long class before school, followed by two or more hours of practice after. The thousands of hours I dedicated to the game forged a lasting work ethic, one that would become the cornerstone of my success far beyond the chessboard for the rest of my life. Yet, despite the immense success and productivity, my interest in chess had dimmed; I was no longer playing for the love of the game but for reasons that felt increasingly hollow, such as fueling my addiction to the fleeting thrill of victory.

It wasn’t until COVID forced the world to pause that I finally had the chance to reflect on my fading connection with chess and reassess my relationship with the game. I learned that if I wanted to derive happiness in a healthy way from chess, I needed a different approach. This is when I was first given the opportunity to teach it, originally through Zoom at the very same temple where I had first learned chess. At first, I did not understand my place in teaching because there was no winning and losing in the traditional sense, and this led me astray since that was the one purpose I had thought chess had truly served for me. Over time though I had grown to like it, but it wasn't until we returned to in-person classes that I started to realize that my true success and passion in chess was through the success of my students rather than my own.

In the face-to-face classes, the excitement of my students quickly became infectious, and I began to see the kids I taught as younger versions of myself, which motivated and immersed me in the world of teaching. Their curiosity and determination reminded me of the fulfillment I had once found in chess, and with each lesson, I found myself rediscovering that same passion. I realized that I could find joy in something I excel at in a way that I had never considered before. The proudest moment of my teaching career came when a student I had mentored for two years won the state championship for her grade. As I watched her hold her trophy, beaming with pride, I realized that this moment meant more to me than any of my own victories. It wasn’t about the trophy—it was about the journey she had taken, a path I was grateful to have helped on.

My temple provided me with a full-circle opportunity to give back to the same community that taught me a game that provided me with so much. The journey of giving back has deepened my connection to chess and to the community that nurtured my earliest ambitions, reshaping my understanding of what it truly means to succeed.

While many see Young Sheldon as just a sitcom, for me, the Coopers have been more like my extended virtual family. Over the last eight years, I grew up with them alongside my own loving family. Over time, I’ve come to see pieces of myself reflected in each of them.

George Cooper Sr. — stubborn, hardworking, a man's man. Initially, I saw him as a strong, distant father figure, but over time, I discovered his quiet compassion. In one episode, George stands up for Sheldon when he's bullied, teaching him that kindness and empathy are more effective than aggression. This moment resonated with me when my cousin was bullied. Witnessing his pain was difficult, and I realized how easy it is to feel powerless in such situations. Inspired by George, I encouraged my cousin to address the bullies with calm and compassion, sharing how their words hurt him. This approach slowly changed the dynamic. The bullies' attitudes softened, and over time, some even became friends. It showed me that kindness and understanding can often reach people in ways that anger or retaliation can't. This experience made me reflect on how empathy not only defuses conflict but also helps build bridges between people.

Missy Cooper — spirited, creative sibling: Missy’s boldness and fairness mirror my drive to challenge norms and use creativity to make a difference. In another episode, Missy challenges her school’s strict dress code, which she feels unfairly targets girls. Instead of quietly complying, she boldly and creatively confronts the rule, showing her sense of justice. I relate to that same drive. Like Missy, I’m motivated to address unfair issues, which led me to create Faktual.ai. This platform combats misinformation and social inequality. During the 2024 Indian National Elections, it gained local attention for fact-checking and promoting unbiased information. The platform uses AI to detect misleading content and highlight credible sources, helping people make informed decisions. Through this project, I’ve learned perseverance, adaptability, and the importance of balancing technical challenges with ethical responsibility. These experiences have shown me the value of using technology to drive positive change and address important societal issues.

Sheldon Cooper — Genius, socially awkward, and endlessly curious. While I may not be quite the genius he is, I share his passion for diving deep into complex ideas, particularly in computer science. Like young Sheldon experimenting with science, I started exploring technology from the age of 8, building small projects with Arduino, sensors, and Raspberry Pi. As I grew, my curiosity shifted toward AI, moving me from simple programming and robotics to researching AI and its ethical implications. Over the last two years, I fine-tuned my own AI text classification model based on my research and completed a successful internship at Clix Capital, where I led a team of four high school students to develop an AI-powered customer service bot. The project impressed the company, and I even received a job offer from the CEO, which I politely declined to focus on college. Much like my early curiosity with technology, my journey has been shaped by a relentless pursuit of knowledge. Through persistence and learning from challenges, I’ve pushed the boundaries of what’s possible, finding joy in solving complex problems. The experiences I’ve had, from building small projects to developing AI-powered solutions, have shown me the value of exploration, growth, and the power of continuous learning.

The qualities I’ve admired in the Coopers—George’s quiet compassion, Missy’s bold creativity, and Sheldon’s relentless curiosity—mirror traits I’ve cultivated over the years. At college, I will bring this same blend of empathy, innovation, and passion for learning. I’m eager to contribute through technology projects, collaborative problem-solving, and creative thinking, always striving to make a positive impact, and to continue learning from and with those around me.

Thirty-four. Most people would say it’s too late to start over. But not my mother. She was just getting started. After decades of deferred dreams, she enrolled in law school, ready to rewrite her entire path.

My own life, however, took an unexpected turn. It transformed into a non-stop “what’s next?” show, thanks to my little brother and sister! Spilled milk, hair-pulling, endless “Why?” questions, and “I’m hungry!” cries became my daily routine. To help Mom, I tried my hand at cooking. My first attempt at spaghetti? A clumpy mess!
