Cleaning, cooking, and chasing after my siblings for hours on end wasn’t how I pictured spending my days as an eleven-year-old. It wasn’t the life I imagined, but it was the life I had. My mother needed me, and I knew that.

Four years later, there she was, all dressed up in her graduation gown. My mother looked incredible, and for the first time, I saw a smile that reached all the way to her eyes. “I couldn’t have done it without you,” she said, embracing me in a rare hug. “I love you, my girl.”

Tears streamed down my face—tears of joy—and in that moment, I knew everything I’d been through was worth it.

Khaled Hosseini once said, "A society has no chance of success if its women are uneducated." With the Taliban’s takeover of my country in August 2021, I couldn’t shake the weight of that truth from my mind. I spent months locked away in my room, feeling as if the walls were closing in on me. The creak of the old wooden door became a constant reminder of my confinement. The same injustice that had robbed my mother of the right to education for years was now stealing mine, and millions of other girls'.

I couldn’t bear the thought of all those girls missing out on even a basic education, so I began to wonder how I could be part of a movement to fight for it. With the Taliban everywhere, watching and listening, the risk was immense. If they discovered a school for girls, they would shut it down and take everyone away.

But oppression? Even a needle can fight back. 
That’s how the idea of Golden Needle shaped in my mind. It was more than just a sewing school.
I created an affinity group of peer activists who shared a love for education and were willing to share their knowledge. We teach math, physics, chemistry, and English, all while pretending to be sewing teachers to stay safe. Our sewing supplies are always on hand, ready to be used as cover if someone comes to inspect. A sudden knock on the door can send us scrambling to hide our books under stacks of fabric. Who would have thought that a simple conversion from inches to centimeters could lead to algebra discussions? One moment we’re fine-tuning seam allowances, and the next, we’re solving for x!

The silence at Golden Needle is a reminder of our secret and the risk we take every day. Yet this silence isn’t merely a void; it’s filled with excitement, the sound of pages turning, and the hunger for knowledge that no one can silence. It’s a feeling that whispers, “We are here. We are learning. And we will not be stopped.”

Today, over two hundred girls attend Golden Needle. The girls at my secret school—with their curious faces, eager eyes, and strong will to learn—inspire me to keep going. Together, we’re sewing a future, one tiny, hopeful stitch at a time.

Until every girl can step into a classroom without fear, my work is far from done. But as I step into the next chapter of my life—college and beyond—I’ll continue to fight for the right to education and carry the voices of the girls at Golden Needle with me.

Every May, the bushes across my boarding house crowd with blossomed peonies, bright pink with gaiety, signaling the decline of the tumultuous winter and wake of the impending summer. I admire the flower I was named after, the “king of flowers” in Chinese culture, famous for its unique intricacy.

Despite the flowers meticulous beauty, I had always hated my name. I hated the fact that no teachers could pronounce my name correctly and how because it wasn’t a “generic name,” made me stand out from everyone. However, I never hated it more than when I arrived at my new boarding school 9,532km from home.

Here, once again, my name proved to be the back of sandpaper. This time, though, it was much more than just my name: it was my hair, my accent, my culture, my mannerisms and opinions which singled me out. It was barely even the fact that I looked different from all my classmates in school and teammates at my swim club, but the way they talked to coaches with nonchalant honesty and gossiped about their favourite Love Island Couple, which I did not watch, called Eggplant, aubergine and perhaps even the fact that they did not wash their hair after they swam that baffled me. Most importantly, though, was that I did not feel as if I belonged: while everyone had a family and a home to return to, grew up eating fish and chips, and watched the same Ant and Dec, I felt as if I did not share the similarities which like an invisible thread, tied all my teammates together. When I did return to my unhomely home, the boarding house, the sky a blanket of darkness and the walk back a shivering gust of nervous wind, it was difficult to converse with my roommates about how I couldn’t just “miss a training” or “stop in the middle of the pool because I was tired.” Like a maze with no exit, everywhere I went, I felt a sense of isolation and horrifying unfamiliarity. Instead of being a peony, I just wanted to be amongst the roses.

In Easter of year 10, my dad and I visited the Keukenhof flower festival in Amsterdam, where many tulips, peonies, roses, and daffodils bloomed vibrantly amongst the grass. I noticed that despite all the flowers’ intrinsic differences, they all flourished brilliantly, one next to the other, all belonging to the luscious garden. Just like the flowers, I realized that belonging is not defined by intrinsic similarities but fostered through the acceptance of differences: differences in language, culture, upbringing, ideas and hobbies.

Side by side, folding dumplings together in the kitchen in our boarding house, I shared aspects of my cantonese culture to my new friends, while we cheered on the England football team playing on the television. While my unique cross-cultural experiences never gave me the traditional sense of “belonging” or “home”, what it did give me was a home away from home, a sense of belonging in being different and an opportunity to understand and immerse myself in so many friendships: being able to compete at English Nationals in Sheffield, debating at the heart of University College London, helping out young children every Thursday at a local primary school, eating pineapple bun at a Cha Chaan Teng and watching the rugby sevens in Hong Kong. Like petals, my differences shower me with knowledge of perspectives and experiences, which are loosely folded and stacked together, forming an intricate blooming flower. Understanding different perspectives and people and learning from varying experiences and stories from others has cultivated a diverse and exhilarating learning environment for growth in me where there is an exciting supply of things to learn, understand, teach and tell.

In July, my dad visits me at school, and I point out a peony I see hiding amongst the bushes; he insists it is a rose. In fact, it is a Paeonia lactiflora hybrid: a [Name] Rose Mix.

Walking down the trail, I felt a tug pulling me back a couple of steps. As I looked over to Ray, I wasn’t surprised to find him motionless, sniffing the same blade of grass that he has been sniffing for years with the same enthusiasm. However, with only 4 minutes left in my morning walk, I hurriedly tugged at the leash, begging my four-legged friend to move along.

I tied my hair and began my tasks as usual. Driven by the fear of falling behind, I kept my schedule as busy as I could with 7 AP classes and a ton of extracurriculars. While working, the sudden non-stop dinging started filling my ears. Frustrated, I wondered, Who's texting me on do-not-disturb mode? My phone lit up displaying the 10 messages from Keerthanaa, my best friend, the last one reading “can’t wait to see you at 7 PM tonight.” A surge of panic replaced my steady heartbeat as I forgot and had to balance this commitment in my already busy day. I knew that I couldn’t miss her Arangetram, an Indian classical dance debut that she had been working towards for 10 years. Wasting no more time, I worked frantically, while her Arangetram loomed over me like a dark cloud.

At 7:08, I was seated in the auditorium, and at 7:10, her performance began. With each beat of the music, her dance drew the audience in, yet I found myself detached, as the pressure of what awaited was a constant beat running through my head. The loud applause brought me back to reality as I saw Keerthana bow out and come running to me.

‘You were mesmerizing,’ I said with a wide smile, hoping to mask my lingering anxiety, only for her to lean in, her eyes searching for more than just a polite compliment, as she asked, ‘Which sequence was the best?’

There was an awkward silence for about 10 seconds as I tried to jog my memory. A pang of guilt hit me for not being fully present during her performance, while I noticed the change in her facial expression—a clear sign of disappointment in me.

The whole night I was disturbed, as I had never witnessed this sense of disappointment from anyone. I had always equated working hard and being busy to success, which I believed invoked a sense of pride not just in myself, but also for those around me. But this moment of realization forced me to confront a deeper truth—that I had been so focused on future achievements that I was missing out on the present.

I began to notice how the satisfaction I chased from adding more rigorous courses and extracurriculars remained elusive and exhausting. I slowly incorporated changes to stop cramming every day with activities but rather tried to focus and enjoy the ones I chose. I backed down from participating in multiple activities, such as Girls Who Code, Robotics Club, and online courses which all shared a similar focus on technology to concentrate on fewer, more meaningful commitments like the Student Council, where I went from being just another member to becoming a District Officer for 312 schools, finding my passion in giving back to my community.

This shift wasn’t easy, but as there were more white spaces in my calendar, it showcased the flexibility, spontaneity, and potential for a deeper connection to the world around me. Instead of leaving my dinner table early, I started to stick around and enjoy the family time and laughter we shared. I gave myself the permission to go out with my friends, learning that success doesn’t always need to be measured by how busy I am, but by how much I allow myself to truly live.

Even my morning walks with Ray have turned into moments of peace, rather than just another task. When I think about his routine of stopping at the same blade of grass over the years, I wonder—was it his way of telling me to slow down and embrace the present?

“6’6 FORWARD, NUMBER 12, ALI AHMADDD!”

Rising from the bench, I high-five 12 teammates. Broadcasting my name as a starter for the Lovejoy High School basketball team is something my school may not be used to hearing. As the sole person of color on my team, it’s unusual for a Muslim kid with Pakistani-Arab heritage to be selected Team Captain by the head coach.

It may come as a surprise, but when I’m not sinking free throws, I’m fighting against bullying and pushing for neurodiversity awareness. My older brother, Ahsan, is autistic, and I’ve seen his struggles and trauma. In seventh-grade English class, Ahsan was taunted and tripped by a classmate. He fell and broke his wrist, as the principal called my frantic mom. In the weeks following his emergency surgery, Ahsan’s pain-filled cries tormented the halls of our home while I kept mine muffled in my pillows.

I wanted to know why. Why does Ahsan’s brain make him behave differently — hyper-fixating and rewatching the same Cars movie scene 100 times? Why do some differences lead to social exclusion while others' idiosyncrasies are more readily accepted? How could I enjoy hooping for hours with the same guys who’d tease someone like my brother?

Seeking answers, I turned to neuroscience. Doing independent research with a UC Davis PhD candidate, I bushwhacked into the cerebral jungle. We scoured hundreds of databases analyzing brain scans of autism patients, trying to decipher common threads. Using machine learning, I unearthed a strong connection between atypical brain activity and autism. This discovery suggests that technology can help diagnose kids before they show symptoms, allowing for early intervention and eventually preventing future struggles caused by autism. I wondered if early diagnosis had been an option, how different Ahsan’s life could have been. Could his struggle to recognize social cues or repetitive hand movement, which made him a ripe target for bullying, have been mitigated? As I delved into my research, I became fascinated by the neuroscience-technology nexus and its potential to improve lives.

But I knew that research alone wouldn’t change the everyday indignities. Before I was captain, teammates would groan when a neurodiverse kid tried out for the team, impersonating flailing arms. I recall seeing one such student sitting alone in the locker room post-tryout, tears streaming down his face. I regretted not standing up for him as a freshman, a regret that weighed on me constantly. Later, I established A Beautiful Mind, an anti-bullying after-school club. My vision was simple: to create fun activities that bridge gaps between neurominority and neurotypical kids.

During our weekly club hangouts, I formed a special bond with Thad. His enthusiastic recitations of dinosaur facts remind me of Ahsan’s passionate monologues about model trains. Thad never directly divulges his emotions — I am only clued in enough to know that his desires are like anyone else’s: friends, especially those who remember your birthday. So, on Thad’s birthday, our club organized a dinosaur-themed party, transforming Mr. Seidel’s art room into a lush jungle. Throughout lively rounds of Jurassic Park trivia, Thad eagerly shared fun facts about velociraptors (“Did you know that they were only the size of a turkey? Jurassic Park lied.”) to a roomful of laughter.

I know now that there is no “right” way for the brain to work. Ahsan, Thad, and countless other neurodiverse individuals have taught me that the busiest room can be the loneliest room. And although being the first Pakistani-Arab captain to lead the basketball team to the district championship is fulfilling, my true purpose goes beyond basketball. For every Ahsan and every Thad out there, there needs to be a basketball captain who has their back. At university, I’ll join others working towards the same ideals. I’ll continue to break stereotypes. Together, we will try to make the busiest room a little less lonely.

Jason swears as he tumbles headfirst out of the portal, his helmet the only thing keeping him from eating concrete. Then he pushes himself up, taking stock of his surroundings, and swears again.

He recognizes the skyline around him, but as if everything has been picked up and shifted four inches to the right. Some of the buildings he doesn’t recognize; others that he remembers are missing. There’s no Wayne Enterprises branch in sight. Unease starts to gather in the pit of his stomach. Whatever that portal had done, this was no simple displacement.

My fingers pause on the keyboard. What comes next? I try to picture myself in Jason's shoes, stranded in a foreign world with no idea how to get home or where to even start. Personally, I’ve never been tossed through a portal and ended up in a universe that didn’t belong to me, but I’ve had experiences that have felt pretty close to it. My interdimensional portal has been the gates of my high school during the first day of freshman year, the five-hour car ride to my residential summer program, even the door of my Jewish friend’s house as she invited me to dine with them on Shabbat.

For me, writing serves as a medium through which I can examine familiar feelings through unfamiliar eyes. When I sit in front of my laptop or curl around my awkward phone-screen keyboard in bed, what I’m really doing is exploring the dozens of complex characters at my fingertips. Jason’s uncertainty facing the unknown, Kaeya Alberich’s complicated relationship with his brother, Henry Strauss’s desperate desire for acceptance—even if they live in worlds with unexplained magic or impossible feats of science, their emotions, the motives that drive them, are universal. As I explore their stories and continue their journeys, I glimpse my reflection in each character, learning more about myself and the person I want to become.

Writing is more than just an introspective tool, though; my storytelling follows me into the real world. When my piano teacher challenges me to replay my Beethoven again — this time “with more emotion!” — I try to envision myself as the depressed nineteenth century composer as I place my fingers back on the keys. While trying to explain cell organelles to a roomful of disinterested elementary schoolers, the idea strikes me to frame it as a story about a team of construction workers; soon, some of the students are even asking questions. As I help a reluctant patient make his daily exercise round of the surgical ICU, I ask him to think of it as an adventure, dramatically narrating the obstacles — the nurses and the help desk — along the way, and he’s smiling when we return to his room.

Unlike the fictional characters that I write about, I don’t have an authorial hand guiding me along a predetermined path. All I can do is remember the aspects of each character that I admire the most, and do my best to continue my own journey. As Jason uses his new start to unleash his inner nerd, devoting himself to his studies like he’d never had the chance to before, I double down on my efforts to finish my chem project before midnight. While Kaeya takes the first tentative steps towards reconciliation with his brother, I vow to stop bickering with my sister and let her use the Spotify… sometimes. Before I nervously strike up a conversation with my psych class seat neighbor, I remind myself that it hadn’t been until Henry finally stepped outside his familiar, but isolating, apartment that he had finally met friends who truly saw who he was. As every character I’ve journeyed alongside gradually finds their way to a happy ending, I grasp onto the threads of myself that I’ve found through each of their stories, and prepare to weave a new narrative: my own.

Tears blurred my eyes as I stepped off the hulking cruise ship. The weight of saying goodbye to my uncle, who had ALS, pressed down on me, knowing the Grim Reaper was looming. Amid the chaos of customs, I noticed my uncle's wheelchair shoot forward like a spaceship. Suddenly, the front wheels lifted off the ground, and we all gasped.

My aunt hollered, “Tom, did you just pop a wheelie?!”

Everyone erupted with laughter. I glanced over and saw his tired blue eyes twinkle as he smirked. At that moment, I realized how I wanted to live my life. "Pop a wheelie" became my rallying cry, a reminder to find joy even in the darkest times.

Before my Uncle Tommy's illness, I hadn’t experienced real tragedy or heartache. His strength in the face of ALS taught me that the world keeps moving, even when yours feels like it's stopped. That morning, his wheelie and our laughter overshadowed our pain. I vowed to hold that moment close to my heart.

Shortly after his passing, I stood at a crossroads. Theater had always been an important part of my life, but the stories I told were filled with Disney-themed happy endings. During my sophomore year, I had the opportunity to audition for *Bare: A Pop Opera*, a production that tackled difficult topics like mental health, body image, sexuality, and suicide. It was outside my comfort zone, but I auditioned with vulnerability, determined to take on these heavy topics. Every time I doubted myself during rehearsals, I heard Uncle Tommy’s voice urging me to “pop a wheelie.” I would breathe deeply, close my eyes, and remember how he faced his illness with grace and courage. This memory continues to fill me with the motivation to embrace challenges with positivity, even when things feel difficult.

When faced with adversity, I draw strength from my uncle’s wheelie. From the beginning of his illness until the very end, he never stopped living life to the fullest. His perseverance, hope, and resilience are values I strive to carry into my own life. During a high school tennis match, discouraged and down 2-4, I envisioned his wheelchair lifting to the sky, driven by Uncle Tommy with a sparkle in his eye. My nerves faded. 3-4, pop a wheelie. 4-4, pop a wheelie. 5-4, pop a wheelie. 6-4, winner.

That moment on the cruise ship shifted my perspective and inspired my desire to help others with terminal illnesses find moments of joy. It sparked my interest in palliative care, a field that blends medicine, psychology, and ethics to address not only physical symptoms but also emotional and spiritual needs. I’m captivated by this holistic approach, which goes beyond curing illness to provide comfort, dignity, and emotional support. My uncle’s brief moment of joy amidst his illness showed me the profound impact small acts of happiness can have, and I am committed to bringing that same peace to others. If I can help just one person in hospice find their "pop a wheelie" moment, I will have made a difference.

My uncle's death was tragic, but I will always be grateful to him for the perspective he gave me. I now strive each day to find joy and perseverance in the face of life’s challenges. Sometimes, all you need to do is "pop a wheelie."

I declare myself to be a strong anti-traditionalist.

I’m the kind of person who swaps out the typical garam masala for a dash of hot sauce in my mom’s biryani recipe. My anti-traditionalism typically drives me away from outdated cultural relics; however today is different.

In India, Diwali was an important family event; almost everyone in our neighborhood would join our celebration. Upon moving to the U.S., we clung to Diwali as a familiar constant amidst a new world of unfamiliarity. Here, my anti-traditionalist viewpoint makes an exception.

As I walk to the living room, the scent of incense wraps me in a warm hug. My mother hands me a diya, and as I carefully place it next to the other illuminated diyas on the windowsill, the glow of the flames reflects in my heart, making the room--and me--complete. At this moment, I feel the weight of my rebellion melting away. I’m simply her daughter, participating in a tradition that connects me with something larger than myself. Diwali isn’t just about lighting lamps; it’s about celebrating the triumph of light over darkness, good over evil. In that flickering flame, I envision the values that guided my ancestors: resilience, optimism, and courage to shine in the darkest times. This diya calls me to embrace these values and reminds me that I’m part of a broader legacy of stories.

I stand in front of the mirror, taking note of my kurta missing my preferred neutral colors; I sense my “Clothing” Pinterest board scoffing at my fashion choice. Despite this, I feel a sense of gratitude. Two years ago, this simple piece of clothing felt like a costume--a reminder of my “otherness” I wore in discomfort. Compared to the muted jeans and hoodies, the vibrant colors and intricate designs felt like I had to shed one identity to embrace another. When I wear this kurta in the U.S., far from the local store in India from where my Aya bought it, I feel I’m carrying a piece of home with me--a tangible link to my roots. My internal conflict I've been wrestling with eases everytime I wear this stretched out kurta. Each year, I’ve come to understand that wearing this kurta is not about abandoning who I am but integrating a deeper part of myself.

As the night deepens, I step outside with a box of fireworks, feeling a tinge of nervousness reflected in my jitteriness. This Diwali, it’s my turn to ignite the first fuse. In previous years, I watched from the sidelines but now, I feel bold; I’m stepping into the role I yearned for.

My shaky hands steady out when I realize that those watching are not just spectators but family, sharing this moment which connects my past to my present. As I light the fireworks, people cheer around me, their voices deafening the loud pops and crackles. I blend into the environment, feeling more connected to my tradition than ever before as I’m surrounded by my loved ones. It feels as if everything has come together perfectly, and the feeling of belonging intensifies amidst the sparkles of celebration. Today is the exception. As I’m surrounded by the shimmering lights and my family, I realize that embracing the unfamiliar unlocks an unimagined depth of belonging.

As I reflect on this gradual yet powerful change, I set my sights on bringing the same courage to future communities, particularly in the field of psychology. I am passionate about joining initiatives that explore cultural influences on mental health where I can advocate for a more dynamic viewpoint of healthcare that honors diverse backgrounds. Whether it’s through research on how cultural identity shapes behavior or involvement in student organizations that promote well being for a variety of communities, I’m eager to apply my own experiences to help others navigate their own internal conflicts. I hope to ignite belonging that inspires others to step into the light of their own traditions.

Playing FIFA 21 with my brother became a turning point in recovering my family's dynamics. Every time I grabbed the controller, the excitement on my face was something I will never forget. Maybe it was one of the few moments where I felt relief and carefree. However, looking back, things were different 3 months ago.

It was summer 2021 where I picked up my brother, who is 10 years older than me, from Suvarnabhumi Airport. His return marked the end of his studies at Lancaster University, where I was excited to reconnect as we aren’t close as he's always abroad. But through our brotherhood, unbeknownst to me was the darkness that has been haunting him: depression and social anxiety.

Soon after his return, I noticed something was off. He would often lock himself in his room, being unresponsive to our family outside. This suspicion was then escalated during our trip to Japan, where as our family strolled down the street of Tokyo, he vanished into the crowd. Whilst my parents tried finding him, I was stunned: barraged with conflicting thoughts - fear, confusion, helplessness. After countless hours of missed phone calls, he simply returned to our hotel. Shrouded in complete silence. The lingering tension disrupted our family dynamics completely.

After our trip, my brother severed all ties with our family, throwing accusations of being unsupportive of his depression. However, perhaps driven by a subconscious urge, he still allowed me to talk and visit him. Whilst I felt helpless during his disappearance in Japan, this was now the opportunity for me to aid my now distressed parents.

This has ignited a period where I visited my brother, hoping to mend our family. This is through weaving in subtle hints within our conversations that my family always welcomed him home, but he never budged. But each interaction, each game of FIFA 21 (where I always lost miserably), became a piece in the puzzle I was trying to solve. These moments felt like I forged a new bond and memories, and not just trying to amend something that was lost.

Determined to help, I committed long hours into researching depression online. Yea I was creeped out at times, but you know what? My parents are placing hopes on me and I can’t let them down. Eventually, the research has fostered my knowledge of mental health and inspired me to support my brother with a deeper sense of understanding.

"What if I fail? What if this doesn't work out?" I questioned myself.

However, whilst these storms of thoughts clouded my head, I never once thought of giving up. I kept persisting to break down the barrier between my brother and family, no matter how long it takes. Although it had little effect on my brother, this strengthened my determination to mediate and bring our family back together.

But then, it finally happened. My brother texted me at 2pm with a message that I will never forget: “I love you”. As simple as that. From that moment onwards, it was clear that his return was imminent.

I was speechless. Overwhelmed with joy, I immediately ran to my parents to tell them what had happened. Hearing their happiness is special. It proved to me that the dedication I poured in wasn’t for nothing.

As my brother returned home, the family dynamics that I yearned for was beginning to take shape. This moment was instrumental in allowing my parents to reconcile with my brother, steadily recovering his depression.

The highs and lows in my life have undoubtedly transformed me to become someone that can mediate and ignite meaningful change within my community. With my newly discovered self, I hope to apply my ability as a conduit both inside and outside the campus setting, helping to create and restore meaningful relationships. That’s what it means to be part of a family, and that’s what it means to be me.

When people bring up physics, most will think about gravity or momentum. However, I think of Gaussian surfaces—any closed surface used to measure how field lines are entering or leaving a certain region. And when I say any surface, I do mean any surface. Whether it’s physically practical like a cylinder around a current-carrying wire, or out of one’s imagination like a sphere around an ice cream scoop, there’s a Gaussian surface to be found. While these surfaces may seem like an abstract concept limited to the physics lab, it has taught me lessons that span far beyond the classroom and into my daily life.

I often treat my day-to-day activities like one big physics problem—just as there is freedom in selecting a Gaussian surface, I find a lot of value in just going with the flow. I remind myself of this after every school day, where in order to unwind, I put on my “potpourri” Spotify playlist, composed of over 2000 of my favorite songs that I’ve accumulated over these past few years. I often spend hours on end delving down the infamous “Wikipedia rabbithole”, leading me through articles about topics ranging from lists of past Grammy winners to the Japanese Yamauchi clan. Meanwhile, my long-standing love for FC Barcelona has led me to a 239-day Catalan streak (and counting) on Duolingo. As a proud proponent of the whimsical, I embrace the unpredicted, trusting my curiosity to guide me to new and valuable experiences.

Did you know that no matter what the shape of a Gaussian surface is, the laws of physics guarantee if two of them contain the same electric charge, they will share other unexpected key properties? Similarly, I find joy in finding threads between vastly different concepts; the metaphorical charge that links different surfaces together. As a pious player of NYT games, the critical thinking skills that have come with solving puzzles are instrumental in my experiences with competition math, where paths to solutions are often winding and complicated. Meanwhile, the pattern recognition abilities I’ve honed through years of observing different flowers and ferns in nature have made it infinitely easier to sight-read sheet music, allowing me to quickly learn pieces by Beethoven and Tchaikovsky. As a student invested in all areas of study, I’ve become infatuated with the idea of conducting research to expose beautiful connections between seemingly different subjects.

However, the freedom inherent in choosing a Gaussian surface can be misleading at times. Applying a Gaussian surface requires using a surface integral with a vector dot product—which, in English, means things can get messy if the wrong Gaussian surfaces are chosen. This applies to life as well, where meticulous decisions and calculated choices are crucial. As the president of my school’s Academic Team, I have to make careful decisions daily by drafting balanced team rosters to achieve results at tournaments, as well as picking diverse trivia topics to drill the team on each week. When performing with my student-run string quartet, we have to cherry-pick pieces to play based on the event; it may seem weird playing Mozart and Elvis in the same program, but we’ve done it. Even in the wake of my “potpourri” Spotify playlist, I have a collection of smaller playlists for every little thing that I do, from late-night cram sessions to working out to mid-afternoon naps. Although freedom and creativity are essential to my life, I take pride in my simultaneous ability to employ order in all that I do.

Gaussian surfaces are known for their extraordinary versatility, being used to solve almost all types of problems relating to electromagnetism. However, the values they compart are just as universal. Just as they’ve taught me that order and creativity can co-exist, I’ve come to realize that it’s crucial to always look beyond what may seem to separate different ideas. As I look to my future, I hope this same belief will elevate me to new heights in my campus and career endeavors.

My passion for baking took an unexpected turn in 2020 when I enrolled in a business class. The final assignment was a revenue competition, for which I created my own online store, 8aCookie.org. In 24 hours, I had requests for over 480 bespoke holiday cookies.

“[Name], can you make 40 Hexagon cookies with the company logo by tomorrow?” Here came another last minute request. My mind was racing, and I wasn’t sure how I could finish them all by myself. I kept pushing myself to do more, thinking I was fine. Once I turned my passion into a business, something in me changed. I began dreading the thought of piping another cookie. Instead, I was exhausted with the consistent long nights and early mornings, grinding out cookie after cookie, all while juggling school, mid-terms, volunteering and a 10-hour-weekly dance schedule. The enjoyment I once had for making desserts, was gone.

So, I put down my spatula, stopped taking requests, and finally let myself breathe. I felt relieved, but at the same time, there was also a feeling of emptiness that grew. I looked back on my childhood, watching baking shows where contestants made exquisitely decorated confections. This inspired me, at the age of ten, to teach myself to bake. Scouring websites for recipes, and looking through books to find dessert ideas. I remembered standing in my kitchen cooking up a storm, mixing icing, experimenting with different designs and unique flavors, without realizing hours would go by.

As the seasons moved on, I picked up my tools again, but this time for myself. I was motivated to try some other desserts, from Tiramisu to crème brûlée to strawberry shortcake. I found myself sitting and staring at my crumb coated cake, visualizing new designs. Then, I let my creativity flow through piping.

The feeling of joy started to return. I put on my favorite show, and began icing cake after cake, admiring as my desserts came to life. While it felt good when I heard people rave that my cakes were "better than those at Tous les Jours", it was the process itself that mattered most to me. I began accepting orders again. This time, however, I was careful to not overcommit myself. Once again, I found peace in the process. My skills flourished, and my passion for baking was reignited.

Now when I bake, my mind shuts off and my smile comes back. The world feels so quiet, as if it has fallen into a deep sleep when I’m immersed in baking. All the noises and distractions around me disappear. In these moments, it is me in my element and my own creativity.

There will always be moments in life when I feel I am racing against the clock. One of the most important lessons I’ve acquired is the value of finding my flow and prioritizing. Combining my passions for baking and business was exciting, however it is important to strike a balance. Like sugar and salt, they could complement each other in desserts with the right mix.

As I wrap up my last year of high school, and move on to the next stage of my life, I know that I need to maintain the right equilibrium, and take the time to smell the roses.

Slingshotting Angry Birds into the structures of egg-hungry pigs was my introduction to video games. Seeing the debris fly and the birds’ abilities excited 5-year-old me. But, it wasn’t until early sophomore year when I stumbled upon Brackey’s YouTube channel that I discovered the behind-the-scenes world of Indie game development. Enthralled by the intersection of coding, math, art, storytelling, and psychology that went into each game, I was determined to make one of my own.

After school, I ran home and focused on my studies in hopes that I could allocate at least 3 hours to learn game design. I enjoyed the coding and visual effects the most, uploading some of my discoveries to YouTube, in hopes of helping other aspiring developers as I struggled in the early stages of learning due to a lack of resources.

Further, I made a community Discord server dedicated to sharing information among aspiring developers. Through this community, I met other developers seeking to make a game, and overzealously, we joined forces. In the beginning, it seemingly went well; Zavier was producing detailed yet optimized 3d-models, Maine and Ao were designing beautiful environments, and I was coding the backend systems.

But after a year, a series of circumstances occurred that resulted in us disbanding: Zavier had GCSE exams, Maine got a full-time job, and Ao had someone close pass away and took a step back from development. Devastated at first, I thought I should’ve done something, but I knew that these circumstances and others’ commitment was outside my control. The only thing I could control was how I chose to move forward.

Thinking I could just pick up where we left off, I examined the assets we created and found that they were all over the place. We were so caught up in our own work that we neglected communication and planning, making things that weren’t related at all, part of a greater lack of management. I would have to restart largely from scratch.

I began by carefully planning out the components of the game I needed to make on a Trello board. Reading through the list of tasks, “build character controller, implement first-person viewmodel, secure caster module—” I realized there was too much work to do alone, but I also remembered that with teamwork came the issue of commitment.

Referring to my dad’s old management books and a bit of Reddit, I discovered a potential solution: contractors. Since they only worked on small components of projects at a time, there was little commitment required.

Unfortunately, I needed money to pay for contractors. I wasn’t of age yet to get most jobs, and washing the dishes could only go so far. But the answers were right in front of me—literally. I already had a YouTube channel that qualified for monetization, and there were old Legos collecting dust in my room that had accrued value. By selling some of those Legos, I gained a small startup fund, and through monetizing my channel, I made steady income to fund my game.

After obtaining funding, I did the coding and visuals and found suitable contractors to work on the models and environments by setting up online interviews and portfolio reviews. Unlike before, I made sure everyone was on the same page by referring back to the Trello board and following up every couple days. Piece by piece we built the game, and in summer of 2024, we finally released it.

Though I wanted to be like the Angry Birds and smash through my obstacles, through this journey, I’ve come to see myself in the pigs. They’re resourceful inventors, building elaborate cities and clever contraptions, using only primitive materials available to them, which I found akin to how I utilized what I had at hand to build my game. But above all, despite getting knocked down by birds and challenges alike, we always rebuilt, always improved, and never lost sight of our respective goals.

The smell of pancakes and the faint sound of Saturday morning cartoons filled the air as I sat at the kitchen table, savoring a perfect warm summer day. But rather than the familiar sounds of comic book heroes blaring from the TV, it was the colorful world of Equestria that filled our living room. It wasn’t always easy for me to follow the adventures on screen. Despite being born in Chicago, my first language was Tamil.

While most children started speaking full sentences in English by the age of two, I don't think I even started saying words until I was three. Consequently, growing up in English-language learning classes and speech therapy sessions became a regular part of my routine, helping find my voice. But it was My Little Pony that taught me how to use it.

Every morning growing up, my brother and I would eagerly jump out of bed to run downstairs to our dining room TV. Cozying up on my sofa with a bowl of corn flakes and of course, My Little Pony.

Twilight Sparkle, the main character, embodied the element of magic. Watching her and her friends, I saw how they turned everyday problems into magical adventures. Twilight’s inventive spells and problem-solving inspired and echoed my own experiments at home.

Store-bought toys never captivated me as much as creating my own obstacle courses with upside-down chairs, slanted books, and stuffed animals. The kitchen became my lab for brewing potions, and my bedroom transformed into a workshop for makeshift machines. One afternoon, as I watched the Flim Flam brothers struggle with their apple cider machine, I found myself doodling on a scrap of paper. Sitting cross-legged on the living room floor, I sketched out a few ideas for how their machine might work better. It was just something I did without thinking—letting my mind wander, much like I’d seen Twilight do in her own way.

Another episode had Twilight Sparkle using a spell to create a makeshift bridge out of nearby materials. Inspired by her ingenuity, I decided to build a Rube Goldberg machine to turn on my bedroom light switch. It began with a book knocking over a marble down a toy track, triggering dominos that led to a toy car hitting a lever. The lever released a string tied to my chair, pulling a weight to flip the light switch. Watching the chain reaction unfold was mesmerizing and seeing it come to life made me realize how much every little piece mattered.

As I got older, those Saturday mornings with My Little Pony influenced more than just my TV choices. The atypical fascination I had for Twilight and her adventures drove me to approach problems with a new perspective. What started as a whimsical interest evolved into a life of constantly disassembling every moving machine I encountered, simply to see how it worked.

This mindset followed me into school. Joining the Robotics team and building complex machines let me turn my ideas into real, working projects. The curiosity that once kept me glued to the TV as a child now fueled my passion for engineering.

My Little Pony to me was never really about the battles in Equestria or the magic of friendship—it was about the small, everyday victories that taught me to keep going. The magic of those Saturday mornings wasn’t about grand adventures but about the small, everyday discoveries that shaped who I am. From fixing toy fans to tackling robotics challenges, it’s the same sense of wonder and creativity that drives me today. As I move forward, it’s this mindset—rooted in those early moments with my brother—that I carry with me into every new challenge.

“Everyone has weakness but it is only a weakness until they find someone who can help make it their strength.” Alone one can only do so much but when unified with people you trust you become greater than ever before. I have known this feeling most of my life but I really began to feel it this year as I joined the Unified Bowling team for my high school. I got the blessing to work with many kids who were born with mental disabilities that are seen as a weakness. Throughout my work with them I learned to the greatest extent of who they truly are and together what we could become.

Before my junior year of high school I would be involved a little bit and knew many of the kids who participated but I decided I should join for the first time. At first I was filled with nerves walking in on the first day of practice. I had spent little time periods with some of the kids but not like this. Which caused many thoughts and questions to circulate around my head. I have been in situations like this before so I took a deep breath and shut all the negative thoughts away. My nerves and slight embarrassment faded as a player on the team Noah immediately got a smile as I walked into the special education classroom. This feeling of giving a huge smile to someone just by walking into the room selfishly made me feel very good about myself. This small moment was the key to give me the confidence to be myself every time I was with them.

Soon enough I knew everyone on the team. I didn't just know them but built good relationships with many other people that will last forever. My love of working with these kids grew exponentially as I really got to know them and got to continue working with them as we hosted the Special Olympics at our school. I was thrown off the roof about the opportunity of being able to work with a friend one-on-one. I was given the blessing of spending the day with Timmy and learning more about him than I ever would if I had continued to watch from the sidelines. This experience showed me more that they are just as strong as any other person.

Even though some people may view the kids I work with as being worse or weaker than others, when I was with them they were able to make me into a better version of myself everyday. The never ending joy, love, determination, the list goes on and on was able to make me a better person than I thought I could be.

Smiling triumphantly, I set aside my well-worn copy of Thoreau's Walden and tidied the acceptance letter for my proposal on top of the mountain of research and e-mails I'd accumulated—reminders of my lengthy quest to resolve the teen mental health crisis. Eager to bring my mission to life, I logged into my Zoom meeting with Dr. Fader, the renowned sports psychologist. After expressing admiration for his method of using sport performance psychology - to help everyone win at the game of life, I dove into my most pressing question: “How can we equip my generation with the tools necessary to succeed?” During our hour-long conversation, Dr. Fader stressed the importance of cultivating strong mental health habits early, commending me for being the first student to approach him with an initiative for improving teen well-being. Ultimately, he agreed to join Chasing Excellence: Fueling Success through Mental Wellness, the speaker series I’d founded to empower students and combat mental health stigma. His support would launch the series further than I’d ever imagined.

Chasing Excellence began as a seed planted during a theology class assignment. Tasked with finding value-driven solutions for societal problems like censorship, I wondered how teens could be expected to generate responses to significant crises even adults can’t solve. However, after researching Amnesty International’s work in Saudi Arabia and enlisting classmates to sign the “Free Saudi Arabia’s Voices of Change” petition—demanding the release of free-speech activists like Salma al-Shehab—I learned that, when acting together, my generation can make a difference. Drawing inspiration from Malala Yousafzai, who identified the importance of education in empowering Pakistani girls to stand up against the Taliban, I grew determined to improve my own all-girls school, where I’d recently realized the need for mental-health support. When an injury sidelined me from lacrosse, I was struck by the impact of missing daily practice with my team—losing the camaraderie and structure was harder than I’d expected.

Following an instinct to host our expert speakers in community-wide assemblies, I ushered mental health out of the shadows and created a space for support and self-care, while offering a break from our demanding schedules. With the core student council, I surveyed the student body to clarify our values and identify concerns—like the isolation Ava shared in our conversation about her troubles at home. Tailoring the program to students’ needs, I set our series’ missions: (1) erasing the misconception that seeking help is weak, (2) expanding access to professional advice and resources without fear or embarrassment, and (3) sourcing engaging speakers to captivate the attention of hard-to-reach teens. After sending countless advocacy emails—and negotiating down expensive speaking fees—I was thrilled to have Dr. Fader launch the series. Following his powerful talk, I watched students - 7th to 12th graders alike - approach him to express excitement over his techniques. It was a watershed moment for the series, proof that students were bonding and opening up as I’d hoped, learning we aren’t alone in our experiences. I signed more pioneers in mental well-being—including Bailey Parnell, Brett Ledbetter, and Vanessa Van Edwards—who each strengthened our foundation for mental wellness, crucial to unlocking our full potential and creating a better world together.

Returning to Walden as the speaker series unfolded, I realized how Thoreau’s philosophy of living life in its simplest terms—and finding your true self in the process—related to my own journey. I, too, aimed to live deliberately, honoring my values, striving to support others, and leading by example. Paving the way for my mission to continue long after I graduate, I’ve also proudly created an ambassador council as well as a business model and blueprint for other schools. Looking to my future academic home, my hope is to continue this platform to drive positive change to address our generation's health crisis. Seeing Chasing Excellence grow well past my greatest expectations has taught me that community action provides purpose, nourishes my spirit, and helps others flourish.

“This nest isn’t big enough for the both of us!” 
The bluejay stared down his rival, ready to make him pay for stealing the last of his seeds. With one talon in front of the other, the bluejay was determined to get his revenge…

At least, that’s what I think would've happened if I could actually hear the birds chirping.

Back in reality, I fiddled with my guitar strings as my teacher reminded me that this duet was an argument between two birds. All I heard were different tones of vibrating nylon. Why couldn’t I feel the intensity? That's how most lessons ended. I stuffed my gripes into my Roadrunner case, ignoring them another week. I couldn’t mimic bird chirps or bell chimes, and I definitely couldn’t mimic a garden rose (maybe I’m not alone on that one). Yet at the time, I had no issue with this. After all, my music was still accurate. However, my purely analytical approach produced a monotone landscape of just treble and bass.

Even though my creative gene laid dormant, its origins were clear. In Chennai, I sat by Ammama’s side while she created Tanjore paintings. At first, it was mere observation. My gaze flipped from her brush’s steadfast voyage across the canvas to depict Ganesha to the glistening layers of gold leaf pressed upon the painting. I didn’t understand why she needed both gold leaf and paint; yet, when I looked at the whole piece, my eyes glistened beyond metallic luster. For the first time, I saw what art could be, and I needed answers. The intricate canvas overwhelmed me, so I looked to my Ammama for guidance, to which she happily obliged. As she highlighted the depth created by combining three-dimensional gold and flat brushstrokes, I began to understand the importance of contrast. With my original approach to art, one medium would have sufficed. After all, I’d still depict Ganesha. However, when the two mediums built upon their differences in accompaniment, Ganesha seemed to come alive.

Back home, the canvas shifted to my wooden fretboard. Now, Royal Conservatory sheet music resided on my stand, but my old approach wasn’t working. Forced monotony split my potential voice into unrecognizable fragments. My most complicated piece, Miami, shared no connection to the city, its laughter and life was compressed into the musical equivalent of TV static. I tried all sorts of remedies, from exaggerated movements to visualization with my eyes closed, but these approaches were unsurprisingly unsuccessful. Frustrated, I returned to familiarity for comfort. The ridges and valleys of gold formed by my Ammama’s loving fingertips yearned for my attention, and the soft outlines left in her brush’s wake fed tranquility to my soul. What made this piece undeniably my Ammama’s? The answer was simple, she didn’t force things together. So, I slotted Miami back on the stand, and as my eyes darted from the high G note down to the low E note, I saw an opportunity. My index finger softly plucked my cheerful trebles, and my thumbnail struck down on my thunderous basses. Finally, the story began to unfold. My chords morphed into a family’s harmonious laughter, standing out in the city’s bustling nightlife. My soundhole became a megaphone for a complete, multi-dimensional story, leading me to triumph with First Class Honors.

Nowadays, contrast still pushes me forward on my artistic journey. The scent of my Ammama’s mallipoo-braided hair may be half a world away, but her lessons still resonate. I proudly stand on the shoulders of a giant, creating beauty through accompaniment.

Obviously, my guitar still can’t literally chirp, but actively inviting difference fuels my creativity. Yet, even though my guitar’s laminate wood base is the basis of my expression, it’s not its limit. So, I’ll continue to embrace contrast throughout my life, using my own versions of gold leaf and brushstrokes not to break, but to build.

As the doctor examined me quietly, his expression grew serious. Looking at my skinny Indian physique, he said, "It hasn't dropped, and you're sixteen?"

"No, should it have?" I replied, my stomach tightening.

In the heart of my Sikh-Hindu family, modesty is the law of the land. Underneath the vibrant bustle of my multi-generational home lie deeply-seated values of privacy and discretion. Photos of baby bums at bath time are ok, but family nudity ends there. This curtain of modesty inadvertently obscured a serious medical failure.

“It will drop, just give it time,” the doctors said when I was very young. This casual assurance was accepted without question, initially unchecked then subsequently forgotten. Now, the clock had run out: what was meant to 'drop' never did.

Words like 'infertility,' 'cancer,' and 'surgery' ran rampant in my mind wrapping me in a quiet dread heavy and thick as fog. Above all, one question lived rent-free in my mind: Do I really control my own destiny?

The day of the surgery was a blur of sterile white walls and the sharp scent of antiseptic. Lying prone on the cold operating table, I grasped my mom’s reassuring hand as I felt the cool rush of anesthetic enter my veins.

A surgical team attempted to correct nature’s developmental error. My left testicle, entangled in my lower abdomen, was cautiously and optimistically dropped to its place.

It might be nuts, but, as I recovered over the next month, the miasma of anxieties transformed into a more complex awareness of the human condition and a desire to take action.

While doctors and my parents were invaluable advisors, I alone bore the ultimate responsibility for my well-being and future. Money I once spent on video games began paying for a gym membership and supplements needed to strengthen my body. Among the clanking weights and the steady rhythm of treadmills, my daily hour-long sessions in the gym began to forge a deep strength of character and self discipline.

Mastering my physical and mental health sparked an awakening to the realization that I could control my own destiny. This empowerment through self-discipline and awareness naturally expanded into another critical area of self-governance: financial literacy.

At school, I was deeply involved with the Student Investment Fund, where we managed a $25,000 portfolio, diving into complex financial strategies and market analyses. This experience was enlightening, but also sobering—I was acutely aware that the students in my town were deprived of this critical knowledge, simply because of their zip code.

Witnessing this void firsthand sparked a burning desire within me to bridge this gap. Despite being a young Indian American in a predominantly Latino community, I realized that my role extended beyond my own ethnic boundaries—I could be a beacon of hope and guidance for other kids who shared a similar shade of brown skin.

The first workshop session unfolded in a small, sunlit room at the local community center, where the eager murmur of anticipation filled the air like static. As I stepped through the door, the sight that greeted me was both heartwarming and overwhelming—more faces than we had chairs, with latecomers dragging in extras from nearby rooms. Young students, some barely into their teens, packed the room, their eyes wide and attentive, reflecting a thirst for knowledge that surpassed all my expectations. As I began discussing the basics of investing, hands shot up like sprouts in spring, questions pouring out with the urgency of a breached dam. Each inquiry, each curious, earnest face showed the vital importance of this knowledge to their futures.

The financial literacy workshops I initiated were not just about teaching budgeting or how to check a credit score; they were about imparting a sense of control and capability. By equipping these young students with financial tools, I aimed to help them see that they, too, could shape their destinies through informed choices and disciplined action.

Cute.

A word that makes most teen boys cringe—but undeniably, the stuffed Highland cow and Andean llama who adorn my pillows are adorably cute. Who could resist Hamish’s rustic bovine hairstyle, or Cusco’s banana-shaped ears?

But you know what’s not cute?

Total nuclear annihilation.

I’ve committed a significant amount of my past—and future—to disarmament policy and activism… though strangely, my interest in the cause stemmed from the same sentimentalism that led me to adopt Hamish and Cusco: my love of the natural world. During freshman year, I dived headfirst into environmental work, which unexpectedly sparked my interest in disarmament.

Through the Climate Action Leadership group, I met Dr. Helfand, a physician-environmentalist who co-founded the International Physicians to Prevent Nuclear War, which received the 1985 Nobel Peace Prize. After a fascinating conversation about the intersection between environment, public health, and disarmament, I asked to continue our discussion over a walk around Exeter. As we walked on Swasey Parkway observing a family of ducks, I couldn’t help but imagine the aftereffects that Dr. Helfand shared with me—the monstrosity of a two-mile wide fireball emerging with the mushroom cloud of debris shortly thereafter.

Although people may realize that nuclear conflict would cause environmental damage, many would be shocked to hear that it would plunge us into an Ice Age. From uninhabitable lands to contamination of air and waterways, all ecosystems would be disrupted severely.

While discovering nuclear disarmament was simply a byproduct of my environmental activism at first, it also fueled my desire to take action. For instance, after learning that carcinogenic chemicals were contaminating NH water sources, I led a group of students to the NH Statehouse to present a testimonial. Despite facing a well-funded lobbyist from D.C., we were able to share the experiences of local members of the community who had been impacted—eventually swaying the hearing in our favor. Environmental justice, I realized, is inseparably intertwined with any progress in environmental policy.

This realization informed every subsequent action in my fight for disarmament—which improved my ability to recruit. For example, when I met Sarah, an Andover student at the Eight Schools Environmental Conference, she fiercely contended nuclear weapons are integral to national security. However, after showing her the degree of biodiversity loss and the disproportionate impact on impoverished communities, she joined our interscholastic task force. Today, she’s among our strongest advocates—even presenting at the Massachusetts Statehouse.

Through all my efforts, Dr. Helfand continually provided mentorship. During one meeting, he said something I’ll never forget:

“Throughout history, people have never had the same opportunity as you—to save the world.”

While college applications are on had been on my mind, like many other high school seniors, I differ from many of them in one key aspect: my goal is to save the world. —but this awakened a new goal: saving the world. That’s why, instead of freshman orientation, I’m participating in diplomacy as a representative of the same organization Dr. Helfand founded two scores four years ago. My French is improving—though I still sound “sort of like a baby” while debating the codification of Article IV of the Non-Proliferation Treaty. While still balanced on the precipice of a dangerous stalemate, I’m honored to share the boulder, growing heavier every day with considerations just as intersectional as the nations we’re trying to save.

Yet beyond my grueling hours at the UN, I’m savoring the small, everyday aspects of Swiss life: commuting to Geneva, indulging in kafi-crème beside Jet d'Eau Fountain. At the conclusion of the Fall 2024 Summit, I shall immerse myself in an internship far more prestigious than Goldman (at least according to Cusco): Altiplanic Animal Attendant on a Peruvian llama farm. Because despite the urgency of disarmament, it is important to take time to enjoy the planet I’m striving to save. Counterintuitively, the peace I feel while surrounded by Cordillera summits and cuteness of the camelid variety, stokes my internal fire.

Because nuclear annihilation is not cute.

I always wondered how she never got tired of that sound.

Sunday mornings began with the clamor of mung beans crashing against a battered metal pan. With each flick of Amma’s wrist, the beans leaped into waves we sailed together my hands diving in to sift the stones she left behind. Impatient, I would give up after a few minutes, leaving her to finish what I saw as a waste of time.

My races against the clock weren’t limited to Sunday mornings. Whether it’d been taking a contested three-pointer the moment I caught the basketball or scarfing down Amma’s special vegetable pulao in under a minute to tune into Naruto, I thought moving quickly would help me outrun the possibility of falling shortof, letting me achieve an “efficient” lifestyle. Instead, my approach narrowed my vision – a path such as one that could have led to a game-changing shot or the enjoyment of a home-cooked meal was always left unexplored.

It was yet another Sunday morning, and I found myself helping by Amma, asking to help her sift beans until none remained. This was a chance to explore a path I had always wandered away from, and I longed to see what awaited me at the end. But, as my fingers began to work, a familiar restlessness tugged at me – we could sift beans until sunset and still barely have enough for a single bowl of kaalu palya. What was Amma seeing that I wasn’t?

Drowning in the sea, I leaned in towards her, searching for an answer. With a calm gaze and upturned lips, she helped me understand the motivation for her patient sifting – an unforgettable meal for our family. Rather than dreading the task, Amma saw it as an opportunity, one where she could savor every small action on the long road to creating something meaningful.

Each following Sunday became a slab of stone, with my newfound knowledge as my chisel. What if I adjusted the pressure of my fingertips as I dug through the beans, feeling for the smallest imperfections, or changed the angle at which I flicked the pan to separate more stones? Each decision took time, but they brought me closer to sculpting a meal filled with love, imbuing my once-dull movements with intention.

I started to synchronize my movements with Amma’s steady rhythm, finding solace in what let her push through so easily. In the process, I began to discover what was left unnoticed. The sound of the mung beans blended with the faint scent of turmeric floating in the air and I could feel the warm sunlight dissipating as I let time get the best of me. Eventually, the urgency that held onto me loosened its grip, guiding me to steadier waters.

Nowadays, I’m not afraid to “waste” my time and take risks, using patience as a pole to calmly trek on scenic paths from start to finish, just as I did in my adventures with Amma. When I became interested in applying deep learning to Parkinson’s Disease, I unhesitantly dove in headfirst. For weeks, I sifted through every code bug just as if they were beans, learning about countless model architectures along the way. Or when I spent hours scavenging my pantry for the most protein-packed ingredients to perfect my specialty shake, the possibility of making something undrinkable didn’t scare me. I had learned to power through, experimenting with hidden gems like PBFit and chia seeds, embracing every attempt that brought me closer to success. The once-tiring sound of mung beans clattering against Amma’s pan reminds me to calmly yet curiously navigate my sea, knowing that the time I invest in exploring new possibilities will not only yield the right results but will allow me to savor the details I once ignored. I will always carry the lessons I learned from those Sunday mornings, finding purpose even in the smallest, seemingly mundane moments.

The song was, “Jerusalem, The Flower of all Cities," my grandfather’s favorite. It was a tour of the temples, churches, and mosques of the holy city, and every element of my choreography - the joining of my hands, the slow softening of my fist - echoed its call for coexistence. Given their pain, I feared that those I most hoped to speak to - the children on the front row, my friends who sat helplessly as their relatives suffered, Abu Ziad, the Palestinian janitor cleaning theater that night - would reject my message. Worse, I feared they would fail to engage with the language I have spent my whole life learning: the language of movement.

Doubting its universality, I reflected on those who first taught me this language. The sharp swings of my arms took me to my mother, a Flamenco dancer who performed with me in her womb, who moved my arms rhythmically before I took my first step. The twist of my hand transported me to Bangkok, the Khon teacher stretching my fingers painfully as I practiced the revered role of Hanuman. A pirouette sent me back to the Washington Ballet and Irina Wunder, her admonishments as spirited as her ballet combinations, who taught me that a graceful gesture could convey as much meaning as an explosive jump. A solemn expression took me to Amman, to Rania Kamhawi, who reminded me to speak to peoples' hearts, not just their minds. I strove to be a worthy translator for my teachers, watching as audiences around the world were moved by their message.

Questioning whether a message of coexistence could be accepted in the face of war, I remembered those who taught me to search for humanity in everyone. Placing my hands together in a symbol of Christian prayer, I reflected on my family, Venezuelan and Palestinian, united in so many ways, not least their faith. The same hand position, also used in Buddhist prayer, took me to Kathmandu, to the home of the State Oracle of Tibet, the Khadro-La. There, I spent countless hours learning how the rhythmic chants of her Gelugpa School could help adherents on their path to enlightenment. Many artists recognize this path, a path in search of transcendence, a path the language of movement has helped me discover.

"We have art in order not to die of the truth," Nietzsche said, and it was the truth of war, the casual calls for violence, that motivated me to speak the language of movement that night. But this time, I was not translating. It was my voice. In my final movement, I placed my forehead on the floor, the humble act of Islamic prayer, and gazed up at the 500 faces of those who had come to support me. The first person I saw was Abu Ziad. He was wiping away his tears. Many others joined him.

The audience had engaged fluently, naturally, with the language of movement. We moved beyond reductive binaries, beyond good and bad, Palestinian and Israeli, terrorist and oppressor, the language of movement delivering grace, humanity, and reverence for the sacred directly to our souls. I learned that the most essential truths, the truths of kindness, forgiveness and compassion, are often the most easily understood, and that I have the ability to share them through the language of movement. I also learned to trust - to trust the audience, to trust their willingness to embrace a humane message, to trust the universality of art - and thus to overcome my insecurities. Over 25 of Jordan’s top choreographers and dancers came together with a shared vision that night, adding real-world impact to what was, for me and many others, a transcendent experience. It was a moment I hope to replicate for the rest of my life.

Today, I’m wearing googly-eyed burgers and monochrome aliens.

I’m talking about my socks, of which, I allegedly possess the world’s largest, most funky and mismatched collection. Although a seemingly small detail of my overall outfit, they’re impossible to miss. The practice of wearing my outlandish, distinctive socks has accidentally become a physical metaphor for my experience living with cerebral palsy (CP).

Last year, when I scheduled a meeting with a school administrator to bring up an issue with elevator accessibility, I stumbled into the room and fell awkwardly. As I picked myself up, the administrator noticed my “Central Perk” socks. “Do you like Friends?” she asked, and before long we were discussing “The One with Rachel's Sister." My socks helped inspire a successful “elevator pitch.” Admittedly, my socks are weird, unpredictable, and blatant, but these same descriptors can be applied to having CP, and both remain things that make me a distinct individual.

Often, I am reminded not to take others’ reactions too seriously and, instead, remain easygoing. Like in my interaction with the police officer; while his questioning was rather presumptuous, I spun the moment into a net positive. I started mismatching my socks amidst the suffocating chaos of my sophomore-year exam period. With little time to sort my laundry, I picked two green socks off the pile and rushed to my math assessment. Later, tapping my foot inside the testing room, I looked down and tarnished the unyielding silence with a liberating chuckle. I had avocados on my left foot and geometric jellyfish on my right.

My socks’ uncanny oddity perfectly matches the misfit that I am; yes, they’re normal socks, but something is a little off. Although most physicians classify me as “high-functioning” – able to get from A to B on NYC public transport – I simultaneously struggle with everyday tasks like opening a can of tomato soup (I own a pair of Campbell’s socks). Despite knowing I’ve earned my place in most rooms, I often wonder if I truly belong. When I first entered high school, my peers all seemed to have an incredible talent in music, sports or academics that set them apart. What I believed made me different was inherently a disadvantage. For this reason, I initially questioned my team’s decision to elect me as next year’s Varsity track captain. How could their slowest runner lead a serious team? I may finish last in every race, but I’m always first at practice. My holey vibrant socks tell the story of my training to be a para-national track champion. That’s the catalyst I inject. During an away meet last year, I cheered so vigorously that a teammate joked they may be able to hear me back at school.

My feet, the most flawed part of my body, are laden with calluses and deformed with hefty bunions, collapsed arches, and heels that have never hit the ground. Growing up, I wore unattractive, knee-high white socks pulled back down over my orthotics. For a teenager, this turned heads for the wrong reasons. Now opting out of regular orthotics usage, I’ve spent the past few years rebelliously relishing my opportunity to turn heads for the right ones. People used to ask about my orthotics, but now they ask about my socks.

Ironically, I highlight the part of my body that I should despise the most, but it would be difficult to hate my feet when they have come to shape me. Perhaps, wearing funky, mismatched socks was never an accident and, instead, an avenue to showcase who I am. I intend to wear them for a very long time.

On the first New Year’s I didn’t celebrate, my fifth-grade science teacher, Mrs. Erwin, greeted me with a bear hug as I entered her home. My parents rushed to Boston, where my brother Charles transferred for a challenging brain tumor surgery, his fate uncertain at age 12.

At the Erwins’, devouring home-cooked alfredo, watching X-Men movies, and playing Halo, I almost forgot about our family’s troubles. But every night, we prayed together for my brother.

Charles returned home with a determined smile on his pale face. I kept praying for the next two years, my emotions coasting up and down as he was treated at Cincinnati Children’s, then Johns Hopkins, then Alabama Children’s. Between online classes at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, I would help my mom make Charles’ favorite sushi rolls while he could still enjoy them.

Knowing little about cancer, I expected my brother to recover. He’d continue obsessing over ancient Greek military strategy and telling me stories about our old scoutmaster who “fought in the Civil War.” But that didn’t happen. Charles’s smile faded on November 6, 2020. Science had come up short for my brother, and I had nothing to offer, even if I was the “science kid” in Mrs. Erwin’s class.

During the lowest point in my life, I was quiet in my ninth-grade science classes. It wasn’t until AP Chemistry in sophomore year that the spark reignited. Being able to apply logic to complex chemical reactions, my helplessness gave way to determination. Weekends spent tinkering with my homemade galvanic cell and scouring LibreTexts articles on organic chemistry led to creating meme-infused flashcards for my class. Likewise, watching kids’ expressions shift from confusion to astonishment as I taught them chirality at the “Chemistry Makes Scents” station at the McWane Science Center, I began to feel a renewed connection with science. Chemistry reinvigorated my curiosity, but seeing its impact on people helped me heal. Still, I wanted to take it further– to see how science could improve the lives of people like my brother.

Inspired to engage in scientific research, I reached out to a molecular cardiology lab run by Dr. Zhou, a monk-like professor who always answered my questions with her own. I was quickly humbled by our research on cardiac muscle regeneration. If McWane’s programmed labs were a volcanic eruption at a middle school science fair, real-life experiments in the lab were Mount Vesuvius.

After numerous failed experiments trying to produce beating muscle cells, I discovered the limits of textbook knowledge. 11 PM Slack messages to Dr. Zhou became routine. In the lab, I pestered the eternally-busy postdoctoral scholar Anteneh until he spent a weekend teaching me his reprogramming protocol. There was no eureka moment, but after months of experimentation and countless late-night drives from the lab, I finally saw muscle cells under the confocal microscope in their breathtaking beauty. Soon enough, experiments became drafts that became published scientific knowledge with the potential to help cardiologists address the aftermath of heart attacks.

Equipped with the knowledge of how to design experiments that probe into the unknown, amazingly, I feel empowered instead of helpless in the face of setbacks. Having witnessed scientists tirelessly pushing the frontiers of medicine, I am optimistic that the fates of kids like my brother will change soon.

For nearly two years, I’ve spent over 1000 hours researching how to heal the injured heart. Sometimes, as I peer into the microscope to examine scar cells transforming into cardiac muscle, I see a reflection of my own journey. Scarred, but thanks to the intrinsic beauty of science and the support from my mentors, I’ve healed enough to pump life back into my community. My calling is to join the front lines in combating disease: to assist those who are struggling in their journeys, as the Erwins and many others once did for me.

After many exhilarating experiences throughout my high school years, I have realised that learning can occur in the most unexpected places and from the most unexpected people. These are lessons I will continue to carry with me.

***

Sitting on the grass bank I am surrounded by 15 anxious year 9 students who have never met before but are about to start high school together in a couple of weeks. Jack sits next to me hiding towards the back of the group looking up at the high ropes course, I can see the raw shock in his eyes as Ethan floats effortlessly in the air. Jack’s face begs “Don’t pick me”. Later the instructor asks if anyone else wants to try, Jack looks around sheepishly, he’s the only one who hasn’t gone up yet. To my surprise, Jack stands up and walks across. “You don’t have to do it if you don’t want to”, I remind Jack. He responds defiantly, yet fails to mask his quivering voice. His legs tremble as he slowly ascends and he only spends a minute up in the air but as soon as his feet touch the ground his smile glows.

Despite only knowing the others for a couple of days, he sits next to me clapping and cheering for those up on the high ropes. In a situation where many would keep to themselves, Jack’s encouraging spirit makes everyone feel welcomed allowing him to connect with his newfound friends.

***

“It’s as simple as Greet, Serve and Close” my manager Simon says riding next to me in the elevator down to the department store floor. It’s my first day and I’m learning the trade secrets in retail, the warm greetings and reassuring smile that keeps customers engaged. At the till he takes an immediate interest in every customer he meets, greeting them genuinely and even going as far as complementing one customer’s avant-garde bag. Later a customer walks in angrily with a fraying jersey demanding a refund. It’s 3 years old, but despite the 30-day policy Simon puts it through, the customer leaves elated. “That customer has got to be delusional”, but deep down it’s clear Simon will do anything to please a customer.

Simon’s first impression on me was extraordinary, the sign of a master at work. I was reminded that it was a desire to be kind and helpful that made Simon so great in retail, something I was eager to apply.

***

It’s another beautiful summer Christmas. Blooming red Pōhutukawa or “New Zealand Christmas trees” line the golden sandy beach across the road.
