Yet in the back of the kitchen, my grandmother glides like a ballerina past haphazard pots, bowls, and stovetops. I can smell the glazed ham in the oven and see the smoke rising from the barbeque whilst I dream about her classic macadamia ice cream in the fridge. Despite running her kitchen like a military general, she will take my helping hands. She passes on her tips and tricks, I never realised there was a better way to beat eggs. Later the feast blankets the table and she looks up proudly, knowing it will impress.

Every year her hospitality brings our family together for a banquet. For just a few hours the phones are put down, the News turned off, and we feast, laugh, and tell stories. Love takes on many different forms, for my grandmother, it was the pride in her Christmas meal, her way of reminding us she cares.

***

My learning has hardly been constrained by the 4 walls of the classroom. From Jack’s unfaltering encouragement to my grandmother's endless annual Christmas feast to working in retail, I have learnt that above all we must be kind. Whether it’s a close family member, a stranger, or perhaps a newfound friend, people remember you above all for how you made them feel. I hope to use my college degree to continue uplifting those around me.

13,153. That’s the number of miles I biked over a consecutive 772-day span. The average commuter drives 12,000 miles per year. I biked more than that in just two years. You’d think that a streak of that caliber would’ve been planned, but mine was actually an accident. One spring day, I biked 16 miles, and I had a good time, so the next day I did 12, and then 18, until I was biking at least 15 miles every day. Biking gave me a new freedom. I felt like I could go anywhere. But with each day I biked, the more bound I became to the streak.

I recorded my rides on an app which kept my statistics and provided me with a map of my rides. I’ve loved maps since I was little. I would spend hours staring at them, at specific countries and regions. The atlas was my best friend. My knowledge of global geography moved to a knowledge of local geography, as I’d match the map on the app to where I had ridden.

I biked in rain, in hail, even in snow. I remember the distinct feeling of my bike's studded tires rolling over fresh powdery snow, where you feel like you have no control, and yet somehow, everything works. I remember biking with my father on a warm sunny day where some dark clouds came out of nowhere and instead of drenching us with rain, pelted us with icey clumps of hail. I remember enjoying riding in torrential downpours, as once you’re wet, you’re wet, and as long as it’s not too cold, it’s fine.

My schedule became busier, which resulted in me resorting to boring, ‘easy’ rides to complete my mileage quickly, causing me to view biking as a chore. My least favorite kind of ride was when it was drizzly and all I wanted to do was stay indoors. It was on one of these rides where my crankiness got to me, and I knew I would have to end my streak. Of course I could’ve ended the streak whenever it seemed convenient, but the reality was, I wouldn’t let myself betray the streak. I had to end it when it seemed right.

I decided that my streak would end when I’d return to Tbilisi Georgia, where my mother grew up, that summer. I had often found myself imagining being back there, walking around with my grandmother to go get tonis puri, Georgian bread baked in clay ovens, or playing on rusty Soviet swings, or taking the deep, rattly, escalator down to the subway. I felt that my love for Georgia was a worthy thing to end my streak for. I’d try to remember the smell of Fig trees and the sounds of cicadas, which defined the summertime night. My mother loved visiting her friends and family, but hated the complex where she grew up, as it reminded her of times when she lived without electricity and regularly running water. But for me it’s different. It was where my family lived. The crumbling structures really didn’t register as depressing, but rather, as my beloved summer home.

It was confirmed that we’d be leaving for Georgia on August 3rd, meaning it would also be the last day of my streak. During the final month, I remember starting to second guess my ending of the streak. I felt like a part of me was going to disappear.

The day of my final ride, I came home with an hour left before we were to head to the airport. For maybe 20 minutes, I sat in my garage thinking about what I had just completed. The streak taught me what it meant to do something not because you have to, but because you promised to. And now at the end, I learned how to let go.

Ever since, I’ve recorded a walk everyday.

$4.7 million—that’s the amount of funding my local school district is losing this year. In June, I overheard a conversation between the Science Teacher at Shawnee High School and my neighbor about budget cuts and her need for supplies like test tube holders and aprons. Having founded a non-profit called Change Has Started the previous year, my team was on the lookout for a new project. Realizing this could be it, I politely interrupted Ms. Roth, introduced myself, and apologized for eavesdropping. I asked her if she thought teachers would appreciate a wish list form for needed supplies. She was thrilled with the idea and offered her help. With five successful fundraisers under our belt, my team was energized and ready to take on this challenge. We were, however, unprepared for the challenges we’d encounter when launching The Supply Project (TSP).

Just 30 minutes into our first event, it became clear that not everyone was on board. 'I already pay taxes' was the first of many complaints. I was taken aback, as supporting teachers seemed obvious to me, and I was unprepared to respond. A few weeks earlier, teachers had started filling out our online wish lists and requesting items like whiteboards, math fidget spinners, flexible seating, and book bins - all resources aimed at enhancing the learning environment. These weren’t for personal gain; they were tools for better teaching. With five more events ahead, I realized we needed a strong message. My team was also feeling disheartened, so I called a meeting at my house to address the feedback. We needed to demonstrate that public funding wasn’t enough and that teachers lacked additional resources necessary for student success. Our impromptu two-hour meeting ended with everyone ready to tackle the challenge. The next day, when asked, "Do you know how much teachers earn?" we were prepared. Reid quickly countered the argument, that teachers' salaries are over $100,000, by asking, "Who says that's enough? Why is it okay for others to earn more, but not teachers?" The response was the familiar gripe: "They get summers off."

And there it was, a sentiment founded on resentment that teachers had summer vacations while others worked. But we were armed and ready with real-life examples. Our woodworking teacher, Jason Jenkins, took on side gigs, including making a vinyl record holder for my own family. Mrs. O’Brien, our 6th-grade math teacher, was preparing and delivering meals. We also explained how the curriculum takes place during the summer. Despite the many challenges that weekend, we engaged the public and shared our message. We had examples of the needed supplies and their significance. We aimed to make personal connections, using the names of teachers, their subjects, and their schools. Asking, “Did you grow up or go to school here?” helped break down barriers, and many eventually donated. These events wouldn’t solve the widespread issue of underfunded schools, but we were committed to supporting the teachers we cared about. After six fundraisers and nearly $10K in supplies and donations, Mrs. Roth was the first to receive a “Supply Box.” It contained not only her test tubes but also enough supplies to last the entire year.

This year, I will start a new initiative focused on tackling food insecurity. From my experiences with TSP, I understand better the complexities of addressing a topic like this and the importance of finding common ground for solutions. When I embark on my college journey, I plan to persist in championing this approach. The prospect of interacting with professors excites me, as I am convinced that respectful dialogues foster the best ideas and the most profound growth. My aspiration is that all 40 members of my non-profit service group can adopt these principles, allowing me to proudly declare, Change Has Started.

Quiet. I always found comfort in quiet. Stereotypically, children my age were having play dates, running around playgrounds, screaming at the top of their lungs. On the other hand, I enjoyed having calm tea parties and gently playing with dolls for hours with my parents, soaking up every last drop of attention they gave me. As an only child, I looked forward to having alone time with my parents. I felt safe knowing I had their love and affection to myself. Being an only child I never had to fight for my parents' attention, it was a luxury. Little did I know, this would soon change.

November 6th, 2008. That was the day my little brother Max was born. Max and I were very different, I was day and he was night. While I enjoyed brushing my doll's hair, Max would get frustrated and start screaming after less than 5 minutes of attempting to put together puzzle pieces. I knew from a young age that Max was different from other kids, considering his constant wailing. Therefore, I felt responsible for protecting him. Many would describe me as Max’s second mom because everywhere Max went, I followed, especially from the moment I learned that he had a mood disorder. From the moment the doctor diagnosed Max, I pulled out my sticky 2012 toddler ipad and opened google. I spent hours each day researching everything from what a mood disorder is to how to cope with it, attempting to help my brother. I taught Max ways to prevent himself from having meltdowns and along the way learned how to adjust to having a sibling who had mental health issues.

Impact. Being in public with Max screaming at the top of his lungs was especially hard. Shopping for milk and bread with a screaming child by my moms side while other shoppers turned their carts, swiftly walking away, attempting to avoid interaction with Max and my family. I felt so judged and isolated so I could only imagine how Max felt. As the years passed I got better at helping him cope with what he was feeling rather than screaming, using tips everywhere from wikihow to NYU articles on children with mood disorders. After putting myself in Max’s shoes I realized how he must feel when he is having shopping carts avoiding him. From that moment on I started to sit with kids who sat alone at lunch, clapped for everyone even those who typically would go unnoticed, and tutored those who struggled with school work. I made it my intention everyday to share my love and friendship with everyone, leaving everyone feeling included and if nothing else they had at least one friend.

Setbacks. As Max started to grow out of his tantrums and use the coping mechanisms I provided, he began to be bullied at school. It hurt me to see him be isolated by his peers because he couldn’t pick up social cues or solve 2+2 as quickly as them. I saw the detrimental effects it had on him and how all of his progress started to back track. I knew what it was like to be bullied so watching it happen to him was hard. But I am a resilient person. I always know how to turn negative things into positive ones. So, I started an anti-bullying Instagram page, where I gained a large following and collaborated with many small businesses to advocate for the cause. This gave me a platform to speak on my experiences with bullying because my whole life, I watched people pick on my brother for his differences. By starting an anti-bullying movement on social media, I hoped to make other kids like Max feel seen so they know they are not alone. As my account gained traction my brother started to make friends with other kids and fit in. He started coming home with a smile on his face and telling me about his day.

Resilience. Although it took hours of reading and research, I not only helped Max grow, but I also grew myself. While gaining knowledge and helping Max stop screaming in public and complete a puzzle without crying, I learned the importance of having a good support system and inclusivity. Today, I go to the grocery store with Max and instead of shopping carts being pushed away from him, people walk by him and greet him with a smile. Although I previously enjoyed being an only child and having time to watch Dora the explorer with my parents, I found that having Max as my brother was way better. I learned so much at such a young age, and plan to impact society by promoting inclusivity and spreading kindness.

The biggest mistake someone can make is avoiding pig-blood cake. Enveloped in a warm summer breeze, drowning in sweetened soy sauce and peanut powder, this delicacy can be found in any of Taiwan's renowned night markets. Second only to boba as the tastiest street food, they were a mystery I avoided as a child, fearful of its speckled surface.

Finally, one day, I gave into Baba’s purposeful appreciative noises for the delicacy. Upon biting into my first pig-blood cake, I was met with a subtle nuttiness and rich, umami flavor; I was hooked. I began to observe that new experiences can be very rewarding.

Slowly, I eased into overcoming my smaller fears of riding the California Screamin’ roller coaster and petting my grandma’s mean German Shepherd. Despite this, my fear of socializing was present when our middle school volleyball team hosted tryouts. I had contemplated the new sport as a replacement for elementary handball, and these recent triumphs pushed me to do so. I recall nervously sweating when we were told to find someone to pass back and forth with; yet, seven years later, Angelynn is still my warm-up buddy. I began to communicate for the ball landing between seams, and my clarity strengthened other relationships outside of the court. Furthermore, I learned that under pressure at match-point, I cannot play with hesitation: I must continue to swing the ball deep.

Unfortunately, swinging deep sometimes has consequences. Being the adrenaline junkie that I am, my sharpened courage led me to attempt freestyle skiing, and my knee gave out as I slid off the rail. Surgery was necessary and my quadriceps tendon graft required a longer recovery process than usual. That weekend, there were enough tears to synthesize my own ski resort. However, I did begin my physical therapy journey which evolved into working out and daily runs. Eight months post-surgery, I ran my first 10-kilometer race. At eleven months I could play again! As Mama’s Facebook post put it, “When we asked her if she’d go skiing again, she said ‘Of course! Do you think Eileen Gu only fell once? She worries me!’” The four surgery cuts remind me that although my tears are valid, it is essential to keep moving forward.

In doing so, I recognized that my favorite aspect of these unfamiliar situations, equally as invaluable as the lessons learned, was sharing them with new friends. When I had the random thought to pen-pal, I met a Canadian living on the border of Ontario and Quebec. Our exchanges inspired me to take French, which grew into a love for studying languages. This chain of events brought me to the first day of my Ryman Arts scholarship, where Regina introduced herself as an artist from Kazakhstan. I just had to talk to her, as I was learning Russian, and we have shared art critiques ever since. In like manner, when I chose challenging courses to maximize my time off from volleyball, I established Sunday study groups with my classmates. We laughed together, shared (stole) each other’s food, and helped one another with tricky homework questions. My friendships showed me how everyone brings a unique stall to our community’s night market.

I aspire to be a policymaker because the marginalizing within our society demands urgent reform. Why do politicians categorize people together and deem them as ‘other’ when we are all human? I now realize that my childhood hesitation of socializing was rooted in a fear of not being accepted. Thus, my college education will equip me with the resources to become a leader who promotes a culture of exploration and empathy. Standing in the Taiwanese night markets, the unconventional appearance of a pig-blood cake is now a reminder of the richness that lies beneath seizing new opportunities. Despite how quick I am to pounce on the unfamiliar, Mama still taught me to finish what I started -- even the stinky tofu that I did not like as much.

"Do you hear that?" I asked my mom, but the answer was already surging through our door, sweeping away everything in its path.

Our village’s forest, Genet Terara, gives us everything from food to a place of calm. In the middle of the forest was our garden, where I cherished most of my childhood from planting mangoes to listening to my grandmother’s stories of the legendary Queen of Sheba. However, urbanization and deforestation turned the green forest into a barren field, resulting in frequent flooding. Soon after, I lost my grandmother. I wanted to preserve what my grandmother and ancestors had cherished, but how? How could I succeed in a community that didn’t believe in me?

Growing up in a community that saw left-handedness as a curse, I lived in fear of failure and being labeled as different. The skepticism I faced whenever I tried new things made me hesitant to act. However, watching the empty field that once was my first school weighed more heavily on me than fear of failure.

Determined to honor my grandmother’s legacy, I launched SaveAzezo, a student-led initiative to create environmental awareness in Azezo. Initially, I gathered a small number of students who shared my concerns. We held weekly meetings at our school library to brainstorm ways to combat the flooding. The idea to plant 1,000 trees emerged as we researched various environmental solutions.

To implement it, we started by attracting volunteers. Securing funds, however, was difficult. No one was willing to contribute as they perceived the flood as divine punishment. When we explained the reasons, they said, “You’re too young to understand.” We tirelessly crafted informative flyers and distributed them door to door. Nothing changed. I remember spending countless nights wondering if maybe I was cursed and my efforts were futile. It was disheartening, but it showed me that good intentions weren’t enough. I had to bridge the gap between my vision and their reality and learn to speak in terms they could relate to.

Realizing we needed a new approach, I researched the economic benefits of reforestation and discovered that planting fruit trees could provide additional income for the community. Communicating this idea helped us gain their support.

My next step was presenting my project to the mayor. I crafted a detailed proposal highlighting reforestation's environmental and economic benefits, such as flood mitigation, improved soil quality, and sustainable income from fruit trees. By including data and success stories, I secured the mayor's permission for the project. This showed me how aligning a vision with the needs of others could transform a simple idea into a shared goal.

After 26 days of setbacks, we planted 1,000 trees. As weeks passed, I began to see small changes—the shade under the young conifer tree and the gratitude of the villagers who now picked fruits from the field. Besides the direct impact, this initiative fostered a sense of community. Many people started engaging in caring for young trees. Now, elders sit around the forest every evening; children play on the ground; and schools use the place for field learning.

This experience shaped my life. Whether tackling complex calculus problems on the whiteboard or speaking up in debates, I learned that confidence is cultivated not in success, but in the willingness to keep trying even in the face of fear. I had to be a strategist, a negotiator, a listener, and a motivator. This taught me the importance of multiplicity in leadership, which helped me balance schoolwork with many extracurricular activities. In planting those trees, I had planted something deeper within myself: a belief that I could grow beyond the limits others placed on me.

Now, instead of a flood’s surge, I hear the rustling of leaves. One day, while standing among young trees, a person approached me and said, “Now, if we flood, at least we'll have fruit to eat while we swim!”

A summer of learning about both life and death

This summer was an experience of a lifetime that led me to grow in more ways than one! I am on the shy side which can make it challenging at times to step outside of my comfort zone. That would all change for me in just a few short months. I heard about a new summer opportunity, and without knowing what to expect, I bravely signed up for an internship at Sarasota Memorial Hospital. I had some previous medical term knowledge from helping to care for my aunt after her heart transplant and hearing a family friend talk about the challenges that come with a child born at 27 weeks weighing only 1lb. 15oz.

Out of over 300 total internship applicants, I was one of four selected to work in the amazing Mother Baby Unit! I was excited yet unsure about what this opportunity was going to bring. The internship started out simple with me sitting behind the check-in desk, but it ended with me in the operating room standing right next to surgeons!

I had no idea when I started this internship that I would go from the shy quiet girl who was terrified to enter a delivery room, to a brave and curious girl asking for more surgery observation time. I gained a new sense of confidence that I never knew that I had! Each day I would go to work, not knowing what the day would bring and wondering what opportunities would be waiting for me. I experienced high intense situations, and I overcame the fear and uncertainty that came along with childbirth.

“Never trust your fears, they don’t know your strengths” - Athena Singh.

At first, I was terrified and only observed from the back corner of the delivery rooms. By the end of the 8 weeks, the nurses would wonder where I was if I was not eagerly waiting at the elevator. It was a persistent beeping overhead that alerted me to a possible life-or-death situation where a mother or baby was in distress. Nurses and doctors would run pass me down the hall racing for the elevator! With my heart pounding, I would run to catch up! Equipped with medical booties, masks, and a cap, I quickly scrubbed in to be part of the delivery watch team.

Each delivery was unique and different. I saw a delivery that made my stomach twist and turn. The mother was in labor for hours then rushed in for an emergency C-section. Her baby was stuck! The doctors and nurses applied intense pressure to the mom's stomach, it made me uneasy. I also experienced a devastating situation where one twin sadly did not survive. This gave me a new understanding about how precious life can be, as my heart ached for the grieving parents. Those experiences led me to ask to visit the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit. I was welcomed in to learn about how to care for the premature babies in the NICU. I helped to feed, change, burp, and admit the tiniest of babies. This was an opportunity that many 17-year-old teens could only dream of having!

By the end of the summer, I had witnessed an astonishing 13 Caesarean sections and 4 regular births! I started to feel more comfortable with the intensity of various situations and before I knew it, I was overcoming fear while taking part in new lives coming into the world! I have a new understanding and appreciation for both doctors and nurses and the love that they have for their patients. I gained a new understanding of myself as well. You want to know about who I am? I like to help others. I now know that during intense situations I can engage and thrive! I learned that I am braver and stronger than I ever thought that I could be!

My mind soared through intergalactic space, spiraling in and out of galaxies, watching giant stars shrink until they looked like splatters of paint on a dark canvas. My body sat on a bench at the front of the stage and my fingers twirled across the 88 keys of the piano, spelling out Hans Zimmer’s Cornfield Chase. They were far from perfect, but they were infused with a passion. I didn’t care if people judged me for the mistakes I made, I was too immersed in the piece to notice.

I had only recently returned to piano more than a year ago, inspired after watching a piano rendition of Unravel. I decided to sweep the dust off my upright Yamaha and try my hand at the long-neglected instrument. For two weeks, I argued with my technique, my fingers stumbling across the keys arrhythmically. A familiar sense of frustration overtook me and I was reminded of the reason I quit. It was so disappointing that I knew exactly how to play, the map of the song engraved into my mind after countless readings of the music, and yet my fingers couldn’t find their spots. I had little joy when I sat down in front of the piano, only determination to play the song precisely, and then annoyance when I inevitably messed up. I once again abandoned the piano.

Then one day some weeks later, I happened to come across another video of Unravel, this time a live performance. The pianist who performed it played with immense emotion; his body swayed from side to side, his eyes closed yet his fingers so precise as they danced up and down. The piece itself also seemed to come alive, almost as if there was a holograph above the piano, with each note adding more and more detail. It was incredibly vivid, beautiful, and different from the way I played. I so desperately wanted to master the piece that I forgot why I wanted to do so in the first place – to immerse myself in its splendor.

And so I approached the piano with a different mindset. I let go of the anxiety arising from the incessant desire to hit the right key. I let go of the old fear of playing the piece wrong in front of my teacher. I realized that the joy of playing the piano didn’t come from playing it correctly, rather, it came from playing it passionately and sharing my emotions with the audience. For the piano will play itself and the notes will connect together when you imagine yourself deep into the piece, focused less on hitting each individual note in the right spot and more on making the piece come alive. Passion and emotions breathe life into music. They ignited the spirit and drove me to perform Interstellar at the talent show at the Yale Summer Program in Astrophysics, something the young boy who was nervous to go to every recital would’ve never imagined doing voluntarily.

As a chess master and aspiring mathematician, chess and math have shaped my rational mind, while playing piano revived the emotional part of my life and reminded me of the importance of passion. When I play chess, I’m captivated by the strategic battle on the 64 squares, more than my desire to win tournaments. When I do math, I appreciate its elegance and creativity, beyond performing well at competitions. And when I play the piano, I relish the emotional conversations with the composers and audience, more than the urge to hit every note accurately.

As Beethoven put it, “to play a wrong note is insignificant, but to play without passion is inexcusable.” I hope to bring the same to college, pursuing the things I love not only for the achievements I may accomplish but also for the fervor they instill within me and the languages they bestow on me to connect with more people.

Eyes closed, palms pushing against each other, back straight, thighs almost parallel to the ground. My muscles felt like a breath of wind away from collapse. Why am I even in Ma Bu?

Breathe. There are three things in practicing Fu Jow Pai. One, to learn how to learn. So that’s why a form can’t be understood by rushing through it. Two, to learn how to practice. A better question to ask is, what is the stance trying to teach me?

I was still looking for the third answer as Sifu signaled the time for empty-handed sparring.

***

The headworn microphone has long been taken off, but I still wondered if the ghost of it would pick up my heartbeat. My speech finished, my story delivered, I sat down as the Urban Arts fundraising event moved onto the next segment.

To my left was my mom. Her usually active phone camera sat quietly tucked away, and I met her watery astonished eyes. My speech was almost entirely in English. But the one thing she understood meant the most; 学无止境 in Cantonese means limitless learning. I would later deliver to her a translated version of my story on the trip home.

To my right was Arthur H. Kohn. He studied at Columbia, graduating in 1986! I asked about how his interpretation of Contemporary Civilizations has evolved with his life experiences. We still keep in contact, and I left that conversation excited for classes I haven’t taken yet.

In a moment of quiet, I looked down to see the navy-blue Ma Mian Qun I wore. It didn’t resemble the face of a horse that its English translation suggests. Still, as a style of clothing from ancient China that suited horse riding, I’m reminded of Ma Bu, or Horse Stance. I was quite literally wearing a piece of Kung Fu.

I think it goes deeper though. I think the third point I was searching for all along is right here. Kung Fu is learning how to apply what I learn. Just like how Arthur took his double major in philosophy and economics into philanthropy. Or like how I want to bring philosophy and East Asian studies into the Cantonese community.

***

Columbia is the only place I can take Cantonese classes and Culture, Mental Health, and Healing in East Asia at the same time. There’s a unique opportunity in taking World Literature Revisited II to learn about how translation differentiates Comparative Literature and World Literature through the lens of Cantonese. I want to continue triweekly Kung Fu practice and re-experience The Fantastic World of Knights–Errant in Chinese Literature curriculum as I sit lower in Ma Bu.

Like Professor Mercer at the Center for New Narratives in Philosophy, I’m the first in my family to go to college. I’m excited to work with her in Just Stories because Embodied Learning can also be applied to the Cantonese community, teaching them to be “agents of change” in a country that sees their language shrinking. I’m inspired by philosophical thought and discussion closing cultural and economic distances.

In Kung Fu, there is quiet soundness in the way we speak to ourselves. In Kung Fu, language is not stoic but rather saturated with intention. We have built Kung Fu into our hands. Our bodies are those of warriors and minds are those of scholars. It is a huge responsibility. It is tough. But this is how we practice martial arts. In life.

It was freshman year English class when I started wondering how to pull off my ears.

The blaring noise of my glucose monitor was interrupting the discussion of *The Count of Monte Cristo* and I was desperate. It had already beeped twice announcing my low glucose level, yet I hadn’t drunk my juice.

As I felt heads turn and eyes fixated on me, I realized my teacher was asking who enjoyed the book. I raised my hand immediately - the revenge, drama, spite…what was there not to love? I was enthralled with Dantés and the letter that sealed his identity and future at the Château d’lf.

Noticing no one else had raised their hand, I began lowering it. But my teacher stopped me, asking why it had resonated with me. I didn't respond; I wasn’t sure what resonated meant. I left the class half-embarrassed, half-curious and half-pale.

In hopes of finding an answer, I started looking at books from another lens.

It was then when literature became a mediation, as I found the beauty in the reflexive nature of characters. Woolf’s passages serve as testaments to this phenomenon, as Mrs. Dalloway’s introspective thought pattern reflected my own.

But I was still stumped on Dantés.

One year into this habit, I received a call from Valeria’s parents. Worried for their 5-year old daughter recently diagnosed with diabetes, they asked to meet. Pressure surged through my veins - surely they expected an example for Valeria.

Going into the hospital, I felt myself stuttering even at hello but as the conversation flowed, so did my words. I told her I enjoyed the talks from curious classmates when they asked why I had a “chip” on my arm.

To my surprise, switching the narrative helped: by telling her it was going to be okay, I felt at ease; by acting confident with my condition, I realized how good it felt.

Her little arms leaned into a hug after we had finished talking, and I let out a sob.

Realizing I wanted to become a role model for kids like Valeria, I picked up a book I had avoided since my diagnosis: *My Beloved World* by Sonia Sotomayor.

The prologue started and I traveled back in time: I was in my kitchen, hands trembling, parents screaming, just to get my first insulin shot. Sotomayor’s diabetic experiences mirrored mine; I felt seen.

It then hit me. I understood why *The Count of Monte Cristo* resonated with me: unconsciously, I had found comfort in Dantés' struggle to defy the label of traitor others had given him. Dantés’ ambition to escape it mirrored my need to conform.

While I found consolation in Dantés, I found strength in Sonia. Similar to how she was scared to be vulnerable as it's not customary for a justice, I tried to blend in with my classmates.

Today, I not only find myself in books but in people. Especially those patients I’ve visited: Coco, José and more, have motivated me to turn my vulnerability into action by raising awareness for diabetes and founding T1DOSE.

I’ve realized there is no need to fix my inner Dantés, but to accept his racing thoughts and let it coexist with my courageous Sonia. At the end of the day, the Dantés in me still gets uneasy because of the beeps, but the Sonia in me breathes, and lets the 3 beeps be.

“Is that really you, [Name]? Look at those chubby cheeks!” My classmate jeered, the rest of my peers not even bothering to contain their cackles. Without even seeing their screens, I knew what they were laughing at: photos of me in ironed suits at competitions and hoards of piano videos.

I’ve played piano since I was five, even placing in international competitions. With my parents’ encouragement, I dedicated myself wholeheartedly to piano. That is, until the 6th grade, when my tablemates and I decided to Google each other’s names. My cheeks flushing, I vowed to become an NBA player, shattering my concert pianist dreams.

However, I found myself on the bench halfway through the junior season, silently comparing the sport I once loved to a dull nine-to-five. Wallowing on that bench, I realized something: when I start new activities, I commit myself to them completely, but that exciting, fresh feeling doesn’t last forever. Especially not when other challenges, like classmates’ judgment or parental pressure, arise.

My basketball struggles during the season made me rethink piano. I'm going to maximize my potential in something I’m gifted at. In the following months, I brought myself to the keyboard daily. Still, I found myself blanking out, playing with no real purpose nor structure. I needed a cause, a reason to do something every day, and I came up with two: my mother, who drove hours taking me to school then piano then basketball; and my father, who paid for each and every lesson happily.

I constructed a practice plan, warming up with scales and arpeggios, followed by one-hand rhythmic practices in difficult passages of my pieces. Unexpectedly, I found myself immersed in the unique style of impressionist music while playing Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse, a style I hadn’t yet played.

I built up to practicing for two hours everyday again, making sure to give myself the freedom to play catchy pop songs from the radio. Finding ways to de-stress, like taking break days, allowed me to balance piano even as my schedule became tighter with AP tests and off-season open gyms. This stability allowed me to joke around with my teammates at the gym and still feel energized enough to practice the coda in Chopin’s Ballade No. 1 afterwards.

Throughout that time, new classmates found out about my playing—this time through the local news station covering my pianist and basketball player dual-identity. Showing their other friends, I wasn’t ashamed as they stumbled upon “[Name] Du (11) Variations in f minor HOB17:6 by Haydn.” In fact, I embraced the idea of being good at something unexpected. For example, I picked up cooking, even though I’m known as a klutz. From learning how to dice an “onyo” with Chef Jean Pierre to making my first grilled cheese and tomato soup, I sought out Youtube and Google to kick off my cooking journey. Though I sometimes spilled some diced onions while tossing them in the pan, I found moments of peace as I seasoned my proteins and minced my garlic, my mind no longer a mess of schoolwork, piano, and basketball. As I continued reading Marcella Hazan’s take on the best bolognese sauce, I integrated cooking into my lifestyle, embracing all aspects of myself by prioritizing my wellbeing and happiness.

Although an unlikely combination, playing piano serves as a reminder to remain consistent, and going to basketball practice helps me take breaks when I’m exhausted from hours of drilling phrases. My uninhibited curiosity will propel me in developing new dimensions of my identity, and I embrace this, knowing that in college, I will pursue every facet of myself without feeling ashamed. And of course, I can always take my mind off projects and exams by playing pickup ball at the gym, playing L’isle Joyeuse (for my roommates this time!), and maybe even cooking a comforting grilled cheese and tomato soup.

She dove in front of me to try and save the ball. After going to overtime with one of our biggest rival schools in the last set of my sister’s senior night volleyball game, we lost by two points, 17-15, and my sister’s mistake on game point had lost us the entire game. She completely lost it and ran off the court, crying because she had just lost her senior night.

In the car that night, on the way back home, the usual conversations were replaced with silence. In that silence, I began replaying the last moments of that game in my head. I looked over at her and it suddenly hit me that the ball she dove for had actually been in front of me. She’d sacrificed herself to save me from having to carry the mistake myself. A mix of guilt and comfort washed over me, knowing she’d sacrificed her own moment for me. I realized that she tended to prioritize me before herself a lot. From giving rides to my friends and I after school to helping me at school whenever I needed her, she’s been putting my needs above hers. “You know that ball was actually in front of me right,” I said as we turned into our driveway. “I know,” she responded.

From that time on, I no longer saw our car rides as time-consuming and mundane, recognizing the confined spaces of that car as an opportunity for us to understand each other and build our relationship. Learning new things from each other everyday like handling different situations at school and home and continuing to gain perspective, I’ve learned that the foundation of all things in life is the relationships connected to those experiences. With her behind the wheel and me in the passenger seat, even though our time spent together were just car rides, it was the little things every day that mattered.

After my sister left for college, I knew things were going to change, one of them being I would have to drive my brother around. In my mind, I saw this change as having to start over, especially because we were not close at all. We barely had anything in common at this point in our lives and didn’t have as much to talk about, but I reminded myself he was going into his first year of highschool and was probably excited to not have to drive around with my mom, which was exactly how I felt 2 years prior. I realized this was an opportunity to create the same comforting environment that my sister established for me. “Here you can take the AUX,” I offer as we pull out of the driveway. As we drive with his music playing in the background, we don’t feel the need to converse. The silence in the car feels natural and comfortable, finding reassurance in knowing that we don’t need words, but just the simple presence of each other, to connect and bond. Just like how I managed to shift the silence with my sister, I learned how to create a comfortable silence with my brother.

Now, when my sister comes home from college, I’ve learned to appreciate our car rides together. Whether we’re driving 5 minutes to Downtown Chandler for a quick breakfast or driving an hour to a flea market, I hold those moments close to my heart. From seeing the sacrifices my sister has made for me to learning to be comfortable with new spaces with my brother, all those unstructured moments of time, dedicated to just being with each other have built the closest relationships in my life. Whether or not I have a car, I hope to take this mindfulness on relationships to college and continue stepping out of my own experiences and seeing the value in bigger pictures.

“Can I really do this?”

For three years, I had dealt with excruciating cramps, which made dancing nearly impossible. It wasn’t until my mom’s persistence that led to the grand unveiling: an obstructed unicornuate uterus. Walking back into the dance studio after the surgery wasn’t easy. The once familiar place had changed; Sydney, Kaelyn, and Stephanie had graduated, and new faces filled the room. My body had also changed; my once flexible limbs now resisted every command. Watching the others, their fans snapping open with precision and their graceful “orchid palms” capturing the essence of China’s 56 ethnic styles, filled me with self-doubt. I questioned whether I could still find my place here, whether I could reclaim the dancer I used to be or if that part of me was lost forever.

Walking away might’ve been easier, but it would’ve meant abandoning a part of me. Chinese dance was never just an activity; it was a way to connect to my culture and just be myself. And so, my evenings turned into a mix of math concepts and oversplits, with homework often propped open next to the mat and my muscles howling as I memorized polar functions for the next day’s test. Randomly doing a front walkover, leaping in the air, or falling asleep in the frog pose became the new normal. I seized every opportunity to stretch, viewing the playground equipment as a chance to prop my leg up and the street curbs to perfect my lines and balance. One move I focused on perfecting was the “fan shen,” where I would pivot on one foot, sweeping my other leg and arms around in a circular motion. Gradually, the burn and foreign feeling subsided. The muscle memory I had relied on returned.

This progress ignited a flame in me, renewing a sense of purpose. Yet, something felt missing. My girls, who I saw more than my own family at times, weren’t back and neither was my laughter. I waited, and waited, for weeks until it became clear to me that I now had to take on the roles left behind by the older girls. It started with spotting backbends on the mat when the teacher was busy or throwing in reminders to straighten the knees and keep the chest up. However, as I observed them struggling with the choreography, I realized they needed more than just occasional tips–they needed the extra guidance I had received when I was their age. During a stretching session, I gathered the courage to suggest meeting on Saturdays to refine our routine. They agreed, and from then on, Saturdays became our Saturdays. I broke down each movement, explaining how to isolate different body parts and showing how the eyes should follow the fingertips to bring more emotion to a routine. I demonstrated how to find balance during long sequences of fan shen’s, passing down all the secrets my older girls had shared with me.

Growing up, I was always spoiled by the older girls who took time each recital to do my makeup and hair. Their pampering not only made me feel loved as one of the youngest kiddos there but also gave me a sense of belonging. Wanting to pass this tradition down, I learned how to draw a perfect winged eyeliner in under a minute, apply fake lashes in one go, and style a bun that stayed flawless through every performance. It felt like a way to give back to the community, ensuring the little ones felt as special and cared for as I once had.

Little by little, I saw their confidence build up; little by little, my void was filled. Through this journey, I discovered that moving forward wasn’t about waiting for the past to return but about actively shaping the present and embracing new roles. Struggles are inevitable, so it’s up to me to navigate across them and find my place.

My biggest secret: my favorite book is a gay romance. Growing up in Brevard County, Florida, where hundreds of both classic and modern books have been banned from school libraries, and being a member of a conservative church, most people in my life consider same-sex relationships taboo. However, there I sat reading on an airplane, during junior year spring break, utterly captivated by the love story of two male Trojan War heroes: Achilles and Patroclus.

My love of ancient Greece started with childhood library visits. I still have the pink notebook holding my own pencil copies of the vibrant Goddess Girls cover art depicting the powerful female goddesses. My elementary-age obsession was reignited years later by Madeline Miller’s The Song of Achilles.

After my initial read, I felt Miller’s words calling me back to her work. I created a summer-long project: dissecting the book. I designed my own annotation system. I assigned seven colored tabs to seven different categories: beautiful quotes, ties to the Iliad, interesting Greek myth references, song lyric connections, important plot developments, foreshadowing, and character descriptions.

Each summer day I read, tabbed, highlighted, circled, and wrote for hours. I filled the margins with lighthearted remarks, analytical comparisons to additional sources, and grief-stricken exclamations. My annotated copy became an embodiment of my enthusiasm and devotion, and by the end of summer, my now-worn book had become my most prized possession.

My plunge into the ancient world was enriched by numerous female classicists including Madeline Miller, Jennifer Saint, and Emily Wilson. Miller’s Circe flipped The Odyssey’s narrative into a female-driven story. In Ariadne, Jennifer Saint holds Theseus accountable for abandoning Ariadne to die, as opposed to the traditional version where he “forgets” her and is exempted from consequences. Wilson used a novel translating technique to emphasize the lyrical nature of Homeric poetry. My laundry sessions and drives were infused with her captivating 20-hour translation of the Iliad.

That summer, I read to my little brother each evening, filling nights with vibrant stories from my own childhood copy of D’aulaires’ Book of Greek Myth. Playing the catchy tunes of Epic: The Musical on family road trips, my parents joined in with their children’s caterwauling. Despite our shared enjoyment, I was too scared to disclose the catalyst that reignited my passion for Greek mythology: a love story between two men.

However, when reading the last chapter of D’aulaires’ book recounting the Trojan War, the urge to share the heroes’ love story grew unavoidable. So, I calmed my nerves and shared with my brother the details of the story that I so deeply adored.

A month later, right before piano lessons, I declared my love for the book to my sister Eliza. Despite her shock, she was intrigued and later read the book. The story likewise enthralled her and prompted deep discussions regarding LGBTQ+ rights. Next, my father. To my immense relief, he welcomed my words with understanding. He even shared his own experiences of supporting his best friend from high school, Craig, who is gay.

My motivation to share these stories is largely influenced by the determination of female classicists. After watching six hours of interviews with Miller, I learned that she feared being criticized for her Trojan War retelling; however, after ten years of writing in secret, she shared it with the world. Her courage to share these perspectives of the often overshadowed has encouraged me to speak up in my own way— art.

I share my voice on classical studies through my Senior year AP Art Sustained Investigation. Although struggling to find the courage, I push away fears of judgment from classmates and my family, and create artworks exploring the complexity of romantic relationships in ancient mythology.

I look forward to studying Classics in college. I hope to share my unique viewpoint by following in the footsteps of the classicists that I admire and learning from future mentors.

After running into heavy traffic, my attention shifted from the I-880 highway to my four oddly quiet passengers. Looking around, I found my mom next to me staring intently at her phone, as well as my friends’ collective six eyes glued to their phones in the backseat

“So we gonna keep ignoring the no-phone policy?”

Groaning, they shoved their phones into their pockets. “Grandpa T strikes again,” jested Siddharth.

“Grandpa T wants us to talk about something,” I replied, laughing off the joke.

“About what?”

“Anything.” There was a pause. “What y’all think about the trolley problem?”

Akarsh enthusiastically jumped in, explaining with conviction that pulling the lever to save four people by sacrificing one was the most sensible answer. I felt immensely gratified. Riding with Great-Grandpa G and his original no-phone rule for sixteen years had shown me that being in a space where people are both eager to speak in support of their opinions and humble enough to stay open-minded is absolutely riveting. Without fail, each of these car conversations with my dad always brought with it some new insight or change of opinion, resulting in deeper personal connections with him and any other family or friends in the car. It was this exact magic that I hoped to emulate after getting my own license, and despite the occasional “Grandpa T” joke, I was always pleased to see it coming alive in front of me.

Continuing the conversation, I argued that pulling the lever was a poor choice because it entailed taking direct responsibility for killing the one life that would be sacrificed. I was extremely fixated on this opinion until my mom called it selfish, only for Jeffrey to call it humble, only for Siddharth and Akarsh to exclaim that saving a net total of three lives mattered much more than humility. The discussion went back and forth for an hour. By the time we reached San Francisco, there was no right answer that we could agree on. Forget a consensus—none of us were even sure of our own opinions after the conversation. I walked out of the car full of uncertainty, and I was more uncomfortable in that moment than at any other time in my recent memory.

Dilemmas and paradoxes had always irked me because they never proved to be truly unanswerable. The egg unquestionably came before the chicken, and yes, Pinocchio’s nose would grow if he said “my nose grows now.” This obsession with finding answers even when there seemed to be none bled into all aspects of my life. It was one of the reasons why I loved discussions—regardless of whether I was right or wrong, there was always an answer at the end of the conversation that allowed me to develop a stronger opinion about the topic. Chatting about the trolley problem was the first time I was forced to accept that there was no correct answer at all, and it was difficult because it was different. However, complexity continued to rear its ugly head in ensuing discussions on topics such as abortion and religion, and I continued to grapple with weighing conflicting opinions against each other. Struggling to reconcile the nuances of different subjects in this way was important because it showed me that issues are rarely black and white, and—much like coffee’s bitterness does—it gradually grew on me. I learned that avoiding the habit of forcing differing opinions into simplistic right-or-wrong classifications allowed me to strike a balance between staying true to my own values while appreciating the merits of others’ beliefs. As I transition into a college community of people from all over the globe, I look forward to connecting with a range of different viewpoints by approaching conversations with the recognition that all perspectives hold elements of both good and bad. Would I pull the lever? No. But would I criticize someone else for pulling it? Absolutely not.

As the hot Mediterranean sand burns my feet, I rush to the crystalline water for yet another discovery: an admirable shining conch added to my life-long collection of seashells. The new little fellow is welcomed among a dozen similar findings, all cramped up in the macramé bag I eagerly hold in my sunburnt hands. While admiring Saïdia’s gentle waves embracing the shore, I reminisce about the ferocious and untamed tides of Rabat where my seashell obsession had first begun.

Moving five times across Moroccan cities in less than a decade was never a tear-soaked drama. With each new landscape, I discovered a unique aspect of my country’s traditions, history, and dialects. As I learned Algerian words from the east, Spanish from the north, and French from the west, it seemed as though communicating with others was an innate talent. Nevertheless, socializing while solving bugs at coding school or building national networks through local Model UNs was easier than blending in with those communities. ‘Where are you from?’ was more dreadful to me than “What’s the limit of f(x)?”. Just like a sea conch, I could constantly welcome hermit crabs from different seas, but was I just an empty shell after all?

Digging my toes through the wet sand, I carefully put to my ear the rose whelk I picked up from my array of souvenirs. Almost instantly, a raging thunder intensifies and the cries of sailors echo as their incinerating ship battles through the waves of the Atlantic. The adventurous voyages of Jules Verne or Hercule Poirot always ignited an electrifying thrill in me. Indulging in a sci-fi or crime novel was not only blissfully sniffing its fresh pages, but also creating new topics of conversation. Wormholes? Multiverse? Serial killers? I’m in for a 3-hour TED Talk. My pleasure was at its peak whenever I saw my younger sister sitting at the edge of her seat; waiting for me to uncover the kidnapper’s identity in L’affaire Tournesol, or radically refusing to sleep until she finished reading my old Tintin adventure books.

I put down my whelk and scoop a handful of minuscule sand grains. Quartz. Feldspar. Crushed pieces of shells and corals. Minerals and organic materials from different origins; mixed up, united even, to create a harmonious golden shore. This time, I teleport to the Al Haouz earthquake period. Although I’d only felt a five-second shake that night, my friends in Marrakech lived through chaos. Immediately, the same ‘sandy’ scenery of solidarity connected Moroccans worldwide to overcome the social damages of the 7.2-magnitude seism, and witnessing this heartwarming dedication also pushed me to take action. Joining the movement led to a dozen ten-kilo bags full of clothes, food donations, and survival essentials being gathered through my awareness campaigns on the Rising Impact pages, before being transferred to the Al Haouz region.

‘One man’s trash is another’s treasure’ took all its meaning. My sister’s inheritance of my childhood books and my people’s sacrifice for the common good made me realize the subjectivity of values and the human need to give in order to receive.

Passion and persuasion helped me rent my books during school breaks, filling me with joy as I pulled more people toward sci-fi and astronomy. Coding and collaboration allowed me to build miniature rockets and AI-based recycling prototypes for the AMAZE Space Camp or the DigiGirlz Entrepreneurship Competition, which I was then honored to teach to my Rising Impact peers. Just like shells live multiple lives on the beach – from shelters to sand and memory holders – Sharing our possessions and abilities is the key to influential cycles and human fulfillment. My interest in engineering, communication, and entrepreneurship was the treasure I received and still forge through these experiences, and giving my best to every community I join is a value deeply ingrained in my Moroccan blood.

Turns out, I have learned to be proud of being a shell.

I am Adirondack 46er #14653. Becoming a 46er is no easy task. It took me eight years of climbing through dense forest, roaring brooks, and boot-sucking mud to summit all 46 mountains over 4,000 feet in the state of New York. I hiked over 300 miles and ascended 70,000 feet. Spending time immersed in the wilderness showed me the restorative value of nature and the importance of unplugging from the fast pace of everyday life. When you hike in this terrain, you are focused on planting one foot in front of the other, trying not to trip over tree roots or slide down wet rocks. You are absorbed in the sharp smell of pine or looking at that strange, upside-down orange mushroom. You stand in awe, admiring wooded valleys giving way to the slopes of mighty crags that touch the clouds. One is not concerned about schedules, or any of the day-to-day tasks that yearn to be finished. Nature gives you a unique opportunity to set your mind at peace, be entranced in the moment, and realize how many of your worries are dwarfed by a mountain.

I recall my most memorable hike, up Wright Peak. My family was greeted by a volunteer who introduced herself and gently reminded us to be wary of the endangered alpine plants pocketing the mountain’s summit—some of which we may have accidentally stepped on. “They grow by the inch, and die by the ‘foot’,” she said. This person’s dedication—waking up before dawn, ascending one of the toughest 46ers, and then educating other hikers—left a lasting impression on me. Inspired by her commitment to preserve the very nature I use as a respite, I felt motivated to protect this opportunity for future generations, so that they may also experience nature’s remedy. So I decided to deepen my involvement in environmental activities within my high school and community. If something as simple as where I step can make a difference, just imagine what ecological improvements could come about by engaging others on broader environmental issues.

During my four years as a member of the Environmental Club, I have recruited students, teachers, parents, and the administration to participate in various projects like our recertification as a “Sustainable NJ School,” and an anti-idling initiative. My goal for these challenges was not only to spur the creation of gardens or alert my community to the pollution idling causes, but also to expose my district to how small efforts can result in significant changes. I was able to demonstrate how simply educating student and parent drivers, and promoting an anti-idling pledge, resulted in a 50% reduction of idling on school grounds. Or how through encouraging actions such as increased bike usage and serving locally-grown foods in our cafeteria, we were able to have a large enough impact to be recognized by the state Board of Education and NJ First Lady. While the results of my high school activities may be small compared to the scope of the global environmental issues we face, it has been heartening to observe my community’s increased participation and focus on tangible solutions.

My 46er and Environmental Club experiences have taught me that I should never be complacent with where I'm standing today, and that I am always capable of taking one more step. Whether one is hiking Couchsachraga Peak (whose Algonquin name literally means “dismal wilderness”), or amidst a school-wide effort to get certified as “NJ Sustainable,” we are always able to progress. For me, my latest step was becoming a volunteer trailhead steward for the NY Department of Environmental Conservation and the 46er organization. I now advise hikers on everything from proper footwear to “Leave No Trace” principles. My culmination of experiences have proven that it is the consistent efforts that ultimately yield incredible results and change. This ideology will serve me well wherever the next trail takes me.

In one hand, I hold a 400°C burning blade. In the other, a gray wire connected to a coil, ready to unwind at my fingertips. In front of me, I see colorful specks revealing themselves to be an assortment of tiny black, white, and red components when I look through my microscope. With my pair of trusty black and gold tweezers, I am set to assemble my jigsaw. Soldering fuses metal in extreme heat, creating miniature bridges between electrical components. When I solder, the delicate balance of power and responsibility rests at my fingertips - with one accidental slip, I could end up severely burning myself. Yet, I feel at ease wielding this instrument.

I was not always so comfortable operating with the burning blade. I was someone who preferred the sidelines, scared that a mistake could be disastrous. Despite being in jazz choir, I declined performing any solos fearing potential embarrassment. I saw firsthand the lack of girls in my school’s technology classes, but held back from taking action, fearing I wouldn't be taken seriously. And as I walked into the Sensor Systems lab, I certainly feared the smoke-emitting pencil-shaped blade capable of liquifying solid metal.

But as I continued touring the lab, I saw a lab member at the workbench working on an acoustic levitator - suspending matter in air against gravity using high intensity sound waves. Next to her, another person was creating a wireless charging pad for their earbuds with the same resistors and capacitors. I grew intrigued by how these few electrical components could be combined in producing practical applications. Where I once saw an intimidating tool of destruction, I began to see an instrument of creation. The soldering station was soon becoming my enchanted reckoning, compelling me to challenge my fear. I studied the process: heat the metal pad, melt the solder, fuse it, and replace the coil with the component to secure it. When my mentor gave me a practice soldering board to try out, I took a deep breath to calm my shaky hands.

With my right hand operating the iron and my left holding the coil, I proceeded with laser concentration. Like clockwork, after one second of contact between the iron and the coil, it began to melt. Immediately, I placed a resistor on the joint. It solidified. I stood with the iron raised as I looked at my practice solder board. Did I just do that?

Upon learning the basics of soldering, I started experimenting with old, discarded circuit boards. My first circuit was a simple LED smiley face made out of diodes and resistors. Yet, attaching the components to the breadboard led to numerous tweaking sessions to satiate my growing curiosity. What would happen if I swapped a resistor's position? How might rerouting a diode change the current flow? Could connecting two capacitors double the energy storage? One of my latest endeavors was building a renewable energy source made through little circuits compounded together. My prototype yields 30 watts of power, enough to light a large LED, yet I found the power of illumination in me far greater.

Overcoming my initial fear of the blazing soldering iron instilled in me a newfound sense of confidence pushing me to venture out of the sidelines - a compounding effect extending beyond the workbench. I grew from a timid girl afraid of public speaking to performing a Chet Baker jazz solo at my school’s fall assembly and presenting fundraising projects to an international panel of judges. I started a SWENext club at my school to build a community of women interested in technology and help others overcome similar reservations. Fear is at the root of many barriers we face but all it takes is one small push. I thank the soldering station for giving me the courage to make things happen. I will continue to embrace new opportunities and actively contribute to my community in college and beyond.

With half a sandwich in hand, I mindlessly rush through a labyrinth of passengers to catch up with my debate team, who have already sat down. But after passing security, I finally gaze up in awe at the bustling environment: Sky Harbor Terminal 4. Twice a month, my team and I scour this place for inspiration and, of course, a place to sit.

**Friday Before the Season Opener:**

AZCentral is my favorite store in Terminal 4, and as I walked by, a black forest ham sandwich caught my eye – and my stomach. But as I reach for it, my partner Arnav yells, “14 dollars?!” Unable to gauge how my beloved $10.00 sandwich could inflate so drastically, I searched “price hikes” on Google and found that Jerome Powell increased interest rates due to pandemic inflation. Calculating the impact of these rates, we determined that prices had to rise by at least 40% to maintain profit margins.

Throughout the flight, I discussed how Sky Harbor’s Hudson Group may be susceptible to rate changes due to their reliance on high retail loans. Learning that this dependence led to a whopping 15% price hike, I excitedly turned to Arnav, who, overwhelmed, asked me to “kindly stop.” But I was insatiable. As we returned, I immediately headed to start the Economics Club and host weekly discussions. Were price hikes due to greedy businesses or were there other effects at play?

Researching operation costs, I found a NYT article revealing how some businesses had rising costs in raw materials. Devastated, I wasn’t sure how to help – I certainly couldn’t prop them up myself! However, I knew how devastating it would be for these workers to lose their jobs if businesses shut down. I decided that a community approach would work best, and if I could increase sales at these local stores, I could help them stay afloat a little while longer. After reading countless marketing articles, I designed an Instagram post, offering discounts on clothing for strangers to participate in. When Bruce texted me about how “my post inspired him to buy a Devin Booker jersey before ACDEC nationals,” I felt so proud knowing that if I hadn’t discovered the problem, I might never have brought even just one extra customer to these stores.

**Wednesday Before the Harvard Tournament:**

Gulping down our coffee, Arnav and I were frantically finishing our case when the plane started boarding. But the novices, who were huddled together playing Brawl Stars on their phones, hadn’t. After losing every round, a novice named Luka asked me how to improve. Remembering my first tournament, when not even my captain helped, I felt terrible.

As I considered how Arnav and I were mindlessly preparing, I realized I could have been a better mentor for the novices. So, at our next club meeting, I tried to explain the importance of preparation. The blank stares signaled I was getting nowhere. Seeing the Exploding Kittens game on the table, I wondered if an analogy would work. I shot my shot: beneficial evidence for winning was like an action card, while ineffective evidence was like the exploding kitten card. The basic idea – you only win with enough action cards.

Gamifying prep meant cramped airport seats became Hamilton’s ideal prep time! As the next tournament neared, the novices were ready (even if only as we began to board), a sharp contrast from the pre-Harvard anxiety.

I’m proud my analogy worked, but what truly satiates me is knowing that these strategies continue to guide them long after I’ve left the club. My initial curiosity about their challenges led me to sacrifice my time to help them, empowering them in tournaments.

**Midnight at Sky Harbor:**

As I step into Terminal 4, the nostalgic scent of ham draws me back to AZCentral. I find my team in the corner, debating the Model Minority Myth from an Asian kritik. This flight is one of my last ones with my team, but my journey isn’t over yet. In fact, my new destination will be making my college campus a better place — whether it’s supporting my college debate team, or taking notes on 13th-Century English literature to share with the Office of Disability Accommodations, I’m eager to overcome setbacks, satisfy my curiosity, and help others.

The story of The Three Little Pigs always puzzled me. How could their houses be blown away so easily? 5-year-old [Name] knew if she could decide, her home would be the sturdiest ever. After all, go big or go home, right? Except just like the pigs whose houses had blown away, I couldn’t always go home.

The Straw House

When I was 9, I left my home for medical treatment. Medication was too expensive in the US so my parents could only afford me getting treated in China. Fortunately, my uncle could house me there until I was ready to return. My uncle’s cramped apartment reminded me of the first pig’s straw house. Temporary and uncertain, never feeling like my real home. Each night, he’d help inject my medication into my arm. Each night, he’d have a cigarette dangling from his mouth. Each night, I’d discreetly hold my breath as smoke seeped into the air. Even with the sting of the needle, I did not release my breath. I did not want lung cancer from secondhand smoking on top of everything. My uncle knew how bad smoking was for his lungs yet continued with his ways, and it wasn’t just him. The strangers in the city, the distant relatives, my grandpa, and my dad secretly did too. The lack of autonomy and unwillingness to change knowing the harm stung more than any needle ever could. For two years, the stubborn atmosphere of tobacco dominated the makeshift straw house. It was as if the rudimentary build indicated its existence would come to an end. Like it was supposed to be blown away. A necessary experience to restart for the better. So when the straw house blew away and carried the heavy smoke with it, it was more refreshing than concerning.

The Stick House

5 years later, I left home again. This time, the stick house was more sophisticated and better planned. I packed away 15 years of my life to live out the philosophy of going big or going home at TAMS. To go big was to know the unknown, to question the status quo, to gain autonomy in my own pursuits. So I tried exactly that. Cases advocating for marginalized minorities at debate tournaments exposed me to societal issues I was too ignorant to know. Discussions about critical race theory in medicine with my English professor expanded my understanding to develop solutions that considered both the social and technical aspects of the problems I cared about most. Countless hours spent on rooftops from sunset to midnight for robotics meetings, coding, and brainstorming. Chipotle runs with my Ballot Executive Board family where we share our club visions. 2AM conversations about determinism versus free will with my roommate as we share a bowl of ramen. But most importantly, my research in lung cancer along with some guilt-tripping eventually got my dad to quit his smoking habits of 6 years. Each experience turned into a collection of sticks with different shapes and sizes that ultimately created the stick house. An indispensable learning curve that molded my consciousness toward my actions, perception of the universe, and what I care about.

The Brick House

To be entirely honest, I’m still working on the brick house but I know that home doesn't need to be confined to the four walls of my parents’ house, my uncle’s apartment, or my dorm at TAMS. It is the home of my thoughts, values, and experiences that have molded me into who I am today. Somewhere I can return to upon soaking in new interactions, exposures, and concepts to develop my own solutions, understandings, and original thoughts. Something continuously open to expansion, renovation, and collection for as long as I’m alive. With each huff and puff of life, a chimney or a door might occasionally be blown off but nonetheless, my brick home remains. Even if it requires some repairing.

Like most artists, I’m starving. Chicken pot pie, leftover fried rice, a crushed croissant – none of these options appeal to my taste. By the time I look at the clock, it’s well past midnight. My routine “late night snack” has once again become a courageous expedition to the kitchen, opening an array of cabinets as quietly as possible to not make a commotion.

In our house, no meal is instant. Finding anything edible becomes a labyrinth of recipes and creativity. Tomato noodle soup? Time to slice up tomatoes and venture outside into the garden for fresh scallions. Pesto tortellini? I’d rather wait till morning.

Instead of setting the house on fire, I typically embark on a less hazardous operation: painting. With my brushes, turpentine, and oil paint surgically laid out by my side, I am eager for yet another artistic procedure. Unlike the immaculate placement of my materials, a 36 by 30 canvas suspended before me comprises of one thousand chaotic — yet elaborate — brush strokes. It was the first time using oil paint on such a large canvas; it’s vast workspace intimate yet daunting. Little by little I cover the canvas with light, steadfast brushes of color. My brush hovering just slightly above as I consider the best placements for each stroke. At 1 AM, my stomach grumbles. A healthy reminder that time is still passing. Ten minutes for a detailed eye – another ten for the right. Each one gazing lazily downwards at the objects in their foreground. But yet, my eyes wide open and energized for the next ten minutes working on their lips, the next ten on their nose, and the next ten on the flush of their cheeks. Finally, at 2 AM, I pull myself away from the canvas.

Initially, I started painting as a way to satiate my hunger. When I found myself wide awake at night haunted by the dreadful confinements of boredom, a sketchbook became my meal that I devoured page after page. From the most mundane and overlooked details of everyday life, I strived to capture these elements in my work. The natural drift of my brother's arm as it fell over the couch ledge; the pattern of the neighbors sweaters blending seamlessly with my mothers; my own movements that I study in the mirror – the protrusion of my elbow and the hollow of my ears.

Even when I find myself in absence of inspiration and innovation sitting in front of a canvas, I found art in academics. The same admirable qualities of painting appeared in my Calculus problem sets: planning, executing, and presenting a solution to others. The assembly of detail and vitality in the anatomy texts in Biology. And finally, the conclusive narrative analyzed scrupulously in English.

Oftentimes when people ask, what are your favorite hobbies? Painting is always my first response. But during a visit to my room, you’ll most likely catch me doing anything but paint. You'll find me preparing a mixture of varnishes; two parts matte, one part gloss to cast the perfect reflectivity and transparent shine unachievable by just one compound. You’ll catch me tying a string to the ceiling and letting it cast a perfectly linear shadow onto my canvas – acting as a template for the sunlight peeking through the clouds which I gloss over with titanium white.

When I become an artist, I also become a chemist, mathematician, and engineer. Being an artist allows me to dream extravagantly, yet with the spirit to materialize it. As I continue to learn how to see the world from different perspectives, I’ll keep experimenting with new ideas. One day, perhaps, I’ll learn how to cook something as delicately as I carry my brush strokes. For now, though, creating art will never fail to satiate my hunger.

It was “five o’clock” in the afternoon. As the school lights went out, I entered the gray stuffy classroom to secretly teach more than twenty girls I aimed to help under the cover of darkness. I stayed vigilant since the lighting was poor, and as is customary in Afghanistan, danger is always lurking in the shadows. I kept looking up at the gate of the school aware of the imminent risks. I began lesson to the girls aged 14 to 18 in attendance. While they shared their experiences, my eyes remained chained to the gate. I worried the Taliban who banned education for Afghan girls might come to check out the school, an infrequent practice, but one nonetheless possible. I was afraid what would I do if they came? This has been the situation for the past year and a half.

I was raised to believe that education was the cornerstone of personal growth, to know that my female peers had been denied this right and demanded into forced marriage pushed me to continue working in risky ways. Helping them obtain their education by any means possible, online or offline. Since online education was not affordable for the girls coming from low-income family, I managed to raise funds, talked to my friend Abigail for help after setting up a zoom meeting, to cover their internet fees monthly through GoFundMe and some like-minded people, while assuring them that they would have my support throughout the entire process.

Although fear consumed me, I exerted all efforts to improve their future by pioneering numerous workshops, academic courses, virtual information sessions hosted with international friends, and helping with scholarship applications not only for academic purpose, but for their capacity building all-around. And my work is already paying off. From seeing Maryam shed her shy skin and now eagerly enter discussions after our Friday stream of consciousness sessions to hearing Zinab remarking confidently to get charged with energy. I see friends rejoicing on the weekend to have fun. But all my fun is scheming programs for the girls and sneaking even on Fridays to teach more.

While I was concerned about the girls’ status quo, my parents worried about me. While I worried about the girls’ future, my parents were afraid of my safety. For the first time, I stood against my parents’ will and advocated for the girls’ right to continue going to the crammed class. A few weeks ago, as my father and I were walking home late after a particularly Thursday night-feast invited by one of those girl’s families to celebrate their daughter’s graduation for completing an English course with me, my father slowed down his pace. He turned to me, coughed and said, “At first, I didn’t think you could do it. But you proved it every day, woke up every morning, and worked in the hours. And never, did you say you were ever tired.”

He embraced me in a very rare hug. “I am so proud of you, son,” my father said. “And I want you to know that I love you.” Then he kept walking. I followed my father like a meter in distance. I was obsessed with a sense of unbounded gratitude and felt proud.
