I am particularly determined to continue striving for my goals after seeing three of these dynamic girls teaching basic English to children and all the twenty-seven girls now possess the capability to navigate the constant obstacles. My main goal now is to provide education for all Afghans, no matter their gender or age, allowing our community to thrive. To many, these may all be impossible dreams, delusions even. To me, they are the air that fills my lungs, the water that quenches my thirst and the resolve to achieve whatever I set my mind to.

My life can be described with keyboard shortcuts. Ctrl C + Ctrl V, an attempt to copy and paste my life’s goals into reality–to echo the success of others–like copying and pasting lines of code. Esc, an attempt to escape from my problems after hitting a dead end, like closing out of my coding environment for the night. Yet none of these keyboard shortcuts seem to describe my life as well as Ctrl Z, undo.

I grew up as a constantly compared child. In an effort to surpass expectations, I tried countless activities but often fell short. I gave up activity after activity, hoping for something to come naturally, hoping to no longer be seen as inferior. I was afraid of failure, and unwilling to accept my imperfections.

Despite my struggles with confidence at a young age, I had no shortage of ambition. I desired to prove to myself that I was worthy of my dreams, to realize my full potential. While my younger self hoped for instantaneous change, my growth from fear’s grasp was gradual.

Amidst quarantine year, I made a blog named Ctrl Z. While I intended for the blog to be a way for me to display my coding skills, blogging became a comfort of mine. Over the next two years, I would share not only code but my life experiences, aspirations, and even frustrations. I discovered the charm of Ctrl Z with my first lines of code. At the time, the simple shortcut was just a neat trick harboring no significance. However, over the years, the very name of my blog has become a testament to my resilience, a core principle of my learning methodology. I often wonder how many times I have used Ctrl Z throughout my blog’s lifetime, an uncountable number.

Upon accelerating past the goals I set back then, I realize the one thing vital to each–be it small–success was the failure I originally feared. Each mistake and each correction following presented new learning experiences. Daunting challenges that once seemed insurmountable, filled with endless room for failure, were eventually overcome, mistake after mistake. While success tasted sweet, the process became its own reward. I have only recently realized how vital failure has been to my learning process, appearing time and time again in all aspects of my life.

In my problem-solving journey, I have failed test case after test case, deployed faulty apps, and experienced no small amount of confusion in data analysis. Although I initially was terrified of acknowledging my imperfection, each new experience provided a way for me to learn from my mistakes. I found that my fears began to gradually subside with each passing day. Failure morphed from an imposing wall into my greatest teacher–I no longer viewed it as a dead end.

My change of mindset and reflection on my past self has yielded a unique perspective. I often empathize with peers who say that they are not made for certain subjects, feeling discouraged and quitting. I hope to one day be able to provide hope for those who feel the way I used to, an encouragement to take the first step. Today, I have overcome my struggles with self-doubt. I have learned to apply my learning philosophy to all aspects of my life. With each use of Ctrl Z, I gain a little more respect for my own growth, becoming a little better than yesterday. I gain confidence as the once meaningless shortcut becomes part of my identity. Day after day, year after year, I have grown from a once fearful child into someone unafraid to step into the future, no matter what failures or successes wait.

I’m an everyday rapper. Unfortunately, my “rap,” or speedtalk, doesn’t have much musicality. Instead of an album of carefully curated 3-minute-long songs, I have a OneDrive folder of PowerPoint presentations that should be slowed down by 20%. In fact, when my teacher raised her hand to give me the 2-minute warning for my AP Psychology final presentation, I sped up my talk time so much that my classmates began laughing at how fast I was going (we finished 1 minute faster than rehearsed). While I’m not as fast as Eminem, I can still skyrocket through presentations, lighting up the room as I energetically talk. As a true crime fanatic who just completed a 2.5-month long group research project on how CNNs could be used to determine a boltcutter size, I was excited about the opportunity to present our findings to Congresswoman Kim Schrier before we were struck with a problem – although we had timed our presentation for 10 minutes, Congresswoman Schrier was on a tight schedule and could only stay for 5. I was in a pickle – most things in my script seemed too necessary to cut. But with verses like, “wehadtoaugmentimagestoartificiallygeneratemoredata-,” we rhythmically blasted through the presentation while not omitting crucial information.“That was awesome,” Congresswoman Schrier said with a smile as we ended right at 5 minutes. “So much work explained so quick.” My teammates and I flashed each other a grin. Not only does speedtalking allow me to get through information faster, but it excites and captures people’s attention. With my rapid-fire lyrics, my speedtalk energizes the room, leaving my audience both engaged in the content and amused by my tempo. I engage in freestyle battles with my peers as well, bouncing creative ideas off each other. Sitting on a call with my design team while brainstorming ideas for the Mustang Math Tournament (MMT) merchandise, Sarah asked, “How does this snake design look?” “I like how it wraps around the pencil, but try making it more angular. It’d match the theme more,” I quickly commented, moving the conversation along as we worked towards our first product for the tournament: an MMT 2024 competitor t-shirt. My ability to speak my mind without hesitation allows me to openly contribute creative ideas without fear. I’d rather quickly blurt out wacky gems, such as suggesting making our tournament design theme centered around the Google Snake Game (we actually did) without contemplating if it’s good or bad, possible or impossible – because there’s always a possibility that it’ll inspire someone else. My energy and ability to throw out rapid, rough contributions encourages unique ideas, leading to new iterations that otherwise might not have been thought of. But imagine the power behind your two favorite rappers collaborating on a hit. Sitting in my Key Club advisor’s room, I was energetically going on about how the advertising for our donated goods yard sale could be improved when I noticed Anoushka – a freshman who was very involved in our service projects but was often too shy to speak up. As I wrapped up my thoughts, I added, “Anoushka, what do you think we could do better for next year?” Although surprised, she quickly took the floor, sharing her thoughts about starting donation collections earlier in the year – an idea we hope to implement this year. I’ve grown to value listening just as much as sharing. Giving everyone the stage to speak is more important than always sharing my own thoughts, as hearing from varying perspectives lets me learn from how others think. Plus, the integration of diverse opinions from my peers creates a melting pot of brilliant ideas – a combination of the best of us all. My ability to speedtalk has encouraged me to approach knowledge in a similar way; allowing myself to quickly but confidently piece together creative ideas that captivates others and encourages collaboration. I’ll drop bars about the crisis of the depleting ozone layer, explaining to my peers how we’d be at a larger risk for skin cancer. I’ll propose ideas to my friends about potential apps we could develop, such as creating a resource to find local small businesses to support. But now, I’ll also be listening. I’ll listen to my peers rapidly explain sorting algorithms, making unique allusions to aid their explanation. I’ll listen to my roommate’s advice on my latest portrait drawing, tweaking the colors based on her suggestion. After all, the beauty of music doesn’t solely lie in its creation, but also its appreciation.

I remember hearing the oboe for the first time. I was seated in the high school auditorium for my brother’s concert, admiring the warm blend of sounds. The band dropped to a pianissimo, and the rich sound of the oboe emerged into a solo. I felt the sound penetrate my heart with its endless depth and soul. I had been playing clarinet for a year, but when it came time for me to move to middle school, I jumped at the chance to learn the oboe.

From the first note, I knew the oboe embodied everything I loved about music: distinct, complex, and full of personality. Each day, my practice corner drew me in as I learned how to tame the buzz of my reed. After a year of daily scales and technical exercises, I auditioned and got into my school’s Wind Ensemble. In one piece we played, there was an especially exposed oboe solo. I was so excited when I found out, but as we practiced, I realized it also made me nervous. The very uniqueness and personality of the oboe that first drew me in were also the same qualities that made me feel the most vulnerable when I played it. Sensing my unease, the band director asked if I wanted a flutist to accompany me. I could play it flawlessly with the flutist beside me, but that fell short of my expectations. I knew that by giving up my solo, I was also cheating myself. A few days before the concert, I asked the band director if I could play it alone, and he agreed. Despite originally doubting myself, I played it perfectly that night. I felt that with enough confidence, I could do anything.

A year later, when the world went into lockdown, the camaraderie of playing together was impossible. Instead, we recorded ourselves playing alone. The disorientating change of filling a much smaller room with sound combined with the dreaded weekly recordings that exposed my every mistake slowly made my sound smaller and meeker. Still, whenever someone asked me about my interests, playing the oboe was the first thing that came out of my mouth. It wasn’t just something I was good at—it made me ME.

When we returned to in-person learning the following fall, my band director pointed out that I pinched my reed shut with my embouchure and angled the bell toward the ground, contributing to my smaller sound. Kayla and Andrew, older oboists who played beside me, helped me realize that the oboe’s unique sound wasn’t something I needed to hide. If I’m not contributing to the band’s sound, why be part of it? Kayla’s tone was gorgeous, and in her solos, her oboe soared above the ensemble, passionate and powerful. She and Andrew shared assurance in their skills, and I found that playing alongside them helped me find my own voice. I was learning that it’s okay to be heard.

One night, my school had a band concert that all my old music instructors attended. I spotted my brother cheering me on from the audience. I had just been accepted into All-Region ensemble as first chair oboe, and the thought of my recent success meant I was even more excited than usual for the concert. Throughout the performance, I felt like I was one with the band rather than fixating on my volume as an individual. On the downbeat of my solo, I shocked myself with the clarity and boldness of my sound. I had finally gained control over my instrument. Throughout that movement, I felt free to focus on my phrasing and musicality without worrying about how my sound was perceived by others. As I remember how Kayla and Andrew had inspired me throughout high school, I hope to have a similar impact on others.

I see the oboe as reflective of my growth as a person throughout these years. As I’ve found my courage as a musician, I’ve also found it in other aspects of my life. I’ve figured out how to lead a group, be a valuable part of it, and contribute effectively no matter my role. Looking back, I realize I was foolish for doubting myself. The volume of my voice is just as important as the volume of my music. I am more than the accompaniment—I dream of a melody of my own.

It looked like the aftermath of a Looney Tunes episode. The garden, once filled with fragrant strawberries and delicate blueberries, now lay in disarray—burrows, overturned soil, and scattered petals. Annoyed, I stood guard and hours later caught the culprit red-handed (or rather, tomato-handed): a chubby, knockoff Punxsutawney Phil, whom I named [Name] Scott, after the irrepressible boss from The Office. For days, this groundhog and I engaged in a battle of wits. I tried everything—from acting as a human scarecrow, to blasting bear sounds, and even putting out Halloween decorations in July. But these solutions only garnered me weird looks from my neighbors. Exhausted, instead of trying to outwit [Name], I began observing. Patterns emerged: his timing, his preferences, and even the specific paths he took through the garden. Interestingly, he avoided the garlic plants, likely due to their pungent smell, which gave me an idea: What if I moved the garlic plants next to the tomatoes, his favorite snack? To my delight, the strategy worked. [Name] soon stopped raiding my garden, deterred by the garlic’s odor. This experience wasn’t just about battling with a groundhog; it reinforced my belief in the power of observation, data gathering, and rational thinking. Whether it was creating my own paper fighter jet after watching the movie Top Gun or experimenting with switches for a custom keyboard, my passion for innovation and science was always sated by calculated experimentation and logical problem solving. Eventually, that passion segued into a fascination with medical science—what better way to seek out the answers of life than by tackling actual life-and-death issues?

Wanting more hands-on experience, however, the summer of my sophomore year, I started shadowing a doctor. One day, as I was making appointment reminder calls, I was thrown off guard when a patient answered the phone, cutting off my typical introduction, with a desperate “Do I have cancer?” My palms grew damp as the weight of her words sank in, and I frantically looked for the doctor, but she was speaking with a patient. "I... I don’t know," I finally stammered. The words felt inadequate, almost hollow, as if they could never hold the gravity of what she was asking. There was a brief silence on the other end. “I’m sorry,” she said, her voice trembling. “I shouldn’t have asked you that.” "No, it's okay," I said. "I’m here to listen if you need to talk." As we continued talking, I learned that she was a single mother of two toddlers, juggling two minimum-wage jobs just to make ends meet. Her fears weren’t solely about her own health; they were deeply tied to her worry about who would care for her children if something happened to her. As I hung up the phone, I felt a rush of emotions. I was so used to thinking of medicine mainly as a puzzle—a neat picture made of diagnosis, treatment, and recovery. But as I imagined this patient’s two toddlers playing in their living room, unaware of the possibility of losing their mother, the puzzle pieces scattered, revealing gaps I hadn’t considered. While I intellectually understood before this internship that there was a human element to medicine and that solutions are rarely straightforward, the experience brought those complexities into sharp focus.

Through small moments like these, I witnessed firsthand patients’ various fears, values, and idiosyncrasies. And because of that, I gained a deeper appreciation for the fact that pursuing a life in science and medicine is about more than logic. It’s about understanding the human experience, embracing the uncertainties of life, and providing comfort even when answers aren’t clear-cut. And while research could provide answers, it was the human connections that gave those answers meaning. After all, people aren’t as simple as a set of data or even as a pesky groundhog: they are complex, dynamic, and beautifully unpredictable.

“So, what’s the latest tea?” my dad prodded me as I got into the car. He had been learning my generation’s lingo to embarrass me, and this had become our ritual as we drove home from school. Whether sharing school gossip or a crash course on the latest Dua Lipa single, car rides with Dad were always fun. I was the Mini-Me to his Dr. Evil—we shared a strong bond spanning our love of astronomy to our reliance on logic and rational thinking to solve problems. Little did I know that these simple moments would soon become priceless memories. A few days later, my dad was diagnosed with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer.

As an aspiring scientist, my first instinct when he was diagnosed was to make sense of this inexplicable disease. As I opened his first few lab reports, I began plotting his significant vitals on an Excel sheet. Bilirubin: 2 mg/dL. Iron: 40 mcg/dL. Although the trend lines were not ideal, I willed them to move in the right direction. For the first time, I was going against logic as I desperately wanted to believe that numbers could lie.

Five weeks went by. I kept updating the Excel sheet with new readings, wishfully thinking that the vitals would eventually stabilize. Bilirubin: 8 mg/dL. Iron: 45 mcg/dL. The trendlines kept fluctuating, and so did my confidence in my dad’s prognosis. On a warm summer evening, with my parents at the hospital, I decided to make some boba from a Costco kit. As the small tapioca pearls clinked against the cup, I remembered my dad’s excitement when he first bought me the boba kit. I poured some milk and added ice. Reality began to sink in. Maybe this would be the last treat he bought for me.

Eight weeks. Bilirubin: 18 mg/dL. Iron: 60 mcg/dL. The erratic trend lines mirrored my growing sense of helplessness, making it harder to maintain any rational thought. Two weeks later, my father succumbed to his illness.

Rationality had always been my strongest suit. But, perhaps, my grief could be a source of strength too. What began as a desperate question of ‘Why him?’ soon motivated me to learn more about the enemy: pancreatic cancer. This evolved into a passionate endeavor to research the disease’s mechanisms. During one of my late-night research scours, I stumbled upon a cancer-causing process where one cell type transforms into another to fight inflammation in the pancreas, a process known as acinar to ductal metaplasia (ADM). I became intrigued by this mechanism. Datasets on pancreatic cancer were not easy to find. To make adequate use of the few publicly available records on ADM, I taught myself Python and R programming. For better data visualization, I developed statistical models similar to those I used to monitor my dad’s vitals. I started off making these plots using my own calculations and functions. However, there was a critical flaw with my technique that reported exaggerated changes in genes with low activity. When my AP Biology and AP Statistics knowledge fell short, I sought guidance from experts in the field of bioinformatics to refine my models. Taking their input, I changed my approach to implementing DESeq2, a more reliable computational biology tool. This helped me find a strong correlation between two genes (C2 and FOLR1) and ADM, which conformed to observations in existing studies. Using these findings, I wrote a research paper titled ‘RNA sequencing of human acinar to ductal metaplasia’.

I hope this paper makes my dad proud, or as he might have said, ‘hyped.’ Sharpened by the resolve to combat this disease, my short research journey has nurtured my ambition to pursue a career in biomedical engineering. I aim to apply rational thinking and my personal experiences to develop innovative diagnostic and therapeutic tools to help families like mine. My father’s battle with cancer may have ended, but my fight is just beginning.

I had an innate curiosity about the inner workings of a computer, and what better way to find out than putting one together? I started my journey overwhelmed by the abundance of foreign terms: cas latency, overclocking, megahertz, etc, but my excitement soon grew the more I learned. I enlisted my dad’s help when it was time to begin building. We persevered through this foreign land, careful when configuring the BIOs and unperturbed by our motherboard’s strange layout. Although the finished product can be found online for some cash, these memories cannot be fabricated.

I wait for the 30 minute timer to go off, salivating at the thought of eating the sweet kozhukattai. I spent the last 30 minutes molding pieces of dough into circles, then handing them over to my mom or Rajima to place the coconut jaggery paste in the center and fold over the edges. In the meantime, we clean up. I put the dishes away as my mom washes them. The timer goes off and we wait for the piping hot kozhukattai to cool down. Then, we feast, offering them to everyone in the house to enjoy with us. Rajima, my dad’s mother, was the first to introduce me to this delicacy. Her profound selflessness and humility manifest through her cooking. As I relish the sweet dumplings, I find myself reflecting on the origins of this dish and me, and they both lead back to her.

I wait with my hand raised for Mrs. Coaston to notice me, and this time I’m aware how I don’t hesitate when I say the answer: “line 7 is missing a semicolon” I observe how when I join a conversation, I don’t overthink what I’ll say or how I’ll say it. Although I stutter here and there, my voice now booms with confidence that it didn’t always have. Therefore, when I weave through the tables of boisterous elementary school kids and spot Suhana sitting in solitude, I attempt to coax her out of her shell. When 6 year old Theo nervously steps into Kumon by himself for the first time, I welcome and encourage him to take a seat. I talk to these kids, urging them to express their feelings and validating their thoughts. I look at them and am reminded of young Kaovya. I give to them what she would have loved: a helping hand in her quest to leave her comfort zone.

When I look back on these moments now, it’s not the end result that comes to mind. I think of the times before. Memories of my dad and I sitting on our living room floor past midnight, computer parts scattered across the rug are now more valuable to me than the computer we built, the one I'm typing on right now. The stories told by Rajima and my mom as we kneaded the dough between our hands are more sweetly remembered than the taste of the sugary kozhukattai. The friendships made from helping others step out of their comfort zones are more cherished in my heart than the fact that my palms no longer sweat when I anticipate having to speak.

I used to abhor the three-hour lines for a rollercoaster or the eight-hour car rides to our next vacation, but I’m now grateful for them as they are where the best memories usually lie. I’ve learned perseverance, humility, and selflessness. I’ve come to appreciate how the beauty of the destination is found in the journey, and I’m excited for all the adventures yet to come, in college and beyond.

**The Observation**

Amid the squeak of fans in the bleak Physics lab, with each page turn of my End-of-Term exam paper, I found more than just equations. It was here, amidst faded diagrams and formulas, that I began to view my life through the lens of the scientific method. Admiring the work of scientists like Newton, I proposed a thought experiment—Just as a scientist observing situations to understand the unknown, I started questioning my preconceived notions, identifying patterns in my life, and uncovering the profound changes that shaped those paths.

**The Hypotheses**

As I grew older, I reflected on how my Jamaican heritage influenced my approach to life’s challenges—an aspect I once considered mundane. How did Jamaica’s messages of resilience and empowerment impact my perspective? Could applying a scientific approach help me overcome obstacles? When did this cultural spark lead to a significant shift in my life? These questions marked the beginning of my self-discovery journey.

**The Experiment**

Under the mango tree in my backyard, while listening to Jimmy Cliff’s "The Harder They Come," I experienced a pivotal moment. High school had felt like a series of uninspiring activities and essay assignments, with my family pushing me to join clubs I found unengaging. Eager for change, I decided to follow my true passion. Inspired by the lyrics, “Well, I don’t care what they say; I don’t care what they do,” I spent my holidays not on a PlayStation 4 like many of my peers at the time, but immersed in YouTube programming tutorials and eagerly exploring the microcontroller toolkits I had specifically requested for Christmas. This newfound enthusiasm caught my family’s attention, leading them to encourage me to apply for a highly competitive '4-Week Free Algorithm Summer Program for High School Students.' Being accepted into this inaugural program was a transformative experience, allowing me to pursue my interests and find new community and friends, many of whom I still keep in touch with today.

**The Analysis**

After completing the program, my desire for growth accelerated and took the shape of an exponential curve. I navigated through various opportunities, facing trial and error, rejection from programs like Jamcoders, and periods of stagnation. Despite these challenges, I remained resilient. I took on diverse roles that aligned with my aspirations, from volunteer tutoring at my high school in Information Technology to securing internships locally and abroad. My journey also led me to launch a global educational nonprofit, teaching over 100 high school students from six countries. This endeavor demanded significant resourcefulness and determination, especially in overcoming hurdles related to funding, payment systems, and skill recruitment. Inspired by the challenges I faced in establishing this nonprofit, I now advocate for better access to online payment systems for Jamaicans. Just as Jamaicans use dried coconut to create "Coconut Drops," I crafted my experiences as an outlet for my passion and a unique expression of my personality—my own version of "coconut drops."

**The Conclusion**

Throughout my journey, I embraced the wisdom of Jamaican playwright Miss Lou: "Wi likkle but wi tallawa," meaning that Jamaicans have the remarkable ability to overcome challenges despite our small size. This saying, combined with the rigor of the scientific method, guided me in discovering new patterns through experimentation and perseverance. The rich cultural vibrations and music continue to inspire me, reminding me of the importance of resilience, cultural heritage, and a methodical approach to overcoming life’s obstacles. These lessons will continue to guide me as I navigate my future.

Later, my mother told me, “No sound came out as you screamed.” I was in India, eating delicious dosas and playing Pokémon on my DS. My arm went numb, with serrated teeth imprinted—blood flowing out. We rushed back to the States, where I spent the next few weeks in and out of the ER. I remember the first immunoglobulin shot: it was as big as my arm, thicker than peanut butter, and took a minute and a half to go in. Combined with my 104-degree fever and pounding headache, the pain was unbearable. Even after recovering physically, I was still shaken. Unable to control life’s unexpected obstacles, I cut out everything risky. My risk calculus mindset persisted, until it contaminated an activity I loved.

The aroma of the masala in the pot was interrupted by a harsh charcoal-like smell—then the pain exploded. Cooking made the outside world become an afterthought. But the burn flashed my eyes every time my mind thought about cooking. Interestingly, I saw my mom cook with a glow, despite her own scares. Eventually, my longing for cooking overwhelmed the fear, and I asked her how to cook safely. The kitchen counters became spotless, oven mitts ready by the stove, and I prayed for safety before making meals. My love and confidence in cooking returned as I began cooking again, and I gradually resumed activities I’d exiled, like tennis. In addition to reintegrating previous joyful pastimes into my life like cooking or riding my bike, I welcomed newer activities such as riding roller coasters or rock climbing. My perception of these opportunities focused on excitement instead of fear. When it came time to eventually interact with a dog—my cousin’s dachshund Maxwell—memories of regaining happiness after returning to hobbies like cooking and tennis quelled my initial anxiety. And sure enough, as I extended my hand, Maxwell showered me with affection: simple petting turned into hugging. As the years went by, my love of dogs returned with interest, deepening my affection for animals. Along with having two dogs of my own, my high school years have been spent at a no-kill animal sanctuary, rehabilitating horses, goats, and even pigs, walking, brushing, and feeding them.

Healing from the rabid dog bite emphasized that even severe anxieties and pain can be unraveled and reoriented into finding joy and purpose. Along with my personal growth, my experience expanded into providing support for others. As my sister spoke, my knees buckled, tears beginning to fall. Hearing that Isha attempted suicide put a 200-ton weight on my heart—I could only muster a hug. I felt powerless. Isha’s emotions weren’t in my control. My family and I began learning how to support her through Dialectical Behavioral Therapy classes. Sitting through the classes brought unexpected hope, every success story made my heart flutter. During interactions with Isha, my focus was on “radical acceptance,” active listening, and validating her feelings. As I learned to support her in a new role as her brother, Isha began receiving help from counselors and mental health programs. To complement her therapy, I took Isha on adventures like Topgolf and Six Flags and bonded over making puris and potato curry. I saw her smile almost return. Over three years, her suicidal ideation consistently dropped until it disappeared entirely. During a family photo, for the first time in years, Isha genuinely smiled, radiating happiness.

The dog bite reinforced that my capabilities exceed dealing with life’s challenges as I can grow and excel because of them. With Isha, I learned how to implement my experience as a basis of support, using the activities I applied to overcome my risk-averse mindset to provide exposure and happiness into her life. While I’m not old enough to join the Crisis Text Line yet, I’ll continue to use my skills to build connections with my peers and community, emotionally supporting and growing with them now, and in the future.

Leaning into the mirror, I brush my face with heavy strokes of thick, green paint, contorting my youthful features to resemble a terrifying hag. I stare in the reflection and widen my eyes as I see transformation into the Wicked Witch.

The spotlight beams on my face, I immerse myself in the character and scene. My scowl masks my nerves, as I clench my broom and glare at my sworn enemy. Dorothy splashes me with water. I scream and thrash as I’m lowered into the pit, "Noooo!! I’m melting, I’m melting!!!".

Initially, I was not thrilled about playing an ugly villain. The Wicked Witch of the West is perceived as pure evil, deserving no kindness. However, my interpretation evoked an alternate perspective: she was mourning the loss of her sister (who Dorothy killed) and reclaiming the stolen Ruby slippers. But more importantly, performing as the Wicked Witch taught me how to be a powerful female voice in a role that is considered a villain.

But unjust, villainous perceptions of women go beyond fairy tales. In 2016, I witnessed Hillary Clinton, the first woman to secure a majority party’s nomination for president, face overt and subtle sexism. She was criticized for her aggressive, assertive behaviors, traits seen as strengths in men. This demonstrated to me the systematic barriers that hinder women from achieving leadership positions at the highest levels. I witnessed that same challenge at home as my mom, a single mother, struggled to balance her work life with taking care of two kids due to insufficient childcare.

I had many female role models within the Performing Arts but few in politics or business. Rather than remaining a spectator, I sought to take the advocacy of female roles in the performing arts and apply it to sectors where it is not as developed, leading me to create Leadership for Women. In this club, I brought speakers, such as Congresswoman Grace Meng and Deputy Chief Flores, to share their powerful journeys: oftentimes they were only women in a room full of men but still had the courage to make executive decisions. It has since become a vital part of my class’ cultural activities. Their powerful stories educated and inspired us to pursue leadership positions in male-dominated fields. Still, I wanted to expand my impact and understanding of this challenge outside of high school.

Listening to speakers involved in the public sector helped me recognize the importance of governance and its potential to be an outlet for my passion. I discovered that Youth and Government provided a political platform, giving me exposure to decision-making processes and how salient issues, including gender inequality, can be addressed through legislation.

Within my delegation, my mother’s struggle inspired me to propose a bill that provides tax breaks and state subsidies to corporations who implement on-site child care facilities. My efforts targeted the time and money dedicated to familial responsibility and advancing for working mothers. Despite disliking public speeches, I spoke with conviction. At conferences, I helped the California Secretary promote the importance of voting. My motivation, as I scrambled from building to building in pumps and business attire, was remembering my sole purpose and intention: to maximize outreach and spread the message of the power of not only the youth voice, but the female voice. By making social media posts and handing out badges, I encouraged girls to get civically engaged and pre-register to vote. These girls represent the next generation and their input can change the stigma around women in politics.

Performing as the Wicked Witch broke me out of my shell and gave me the confidence to shatter stereotypes. I seek to amplify my voice beyond just theater and continue advocating for diverse individuals who may be misunderstood. While the Wicked Witch melted, her spirit of unwavering fearlessness will guide my journey to help the next generation of girls in business and politics.

“We have to catch up,” I whispered, urgency sharp in my voice. “Andy won’t wait.” 
“Then let’s go,” he replied, eyes alight with the spark of adventure. “We need RC.” 
My heart raced with anticipation. “We’ll catch Andy. We’ll be his favorites again.” 
And so we did—time after time, each journey a new twist on the classic Pixar tale. However, suddenly, all our storylines ended—not because we ran out of plot twists, but because this plot twist was devastatingly real. 
It happened without warning. As my father gently caressed my grandmother’s hand with his calloused fingers, I watched her eyelids softly rest. In just two months, overgrown grass replaced the laughter that once filled our backyard. I became familiar with my father’s midnight travels and his waking to yet another pack of cigarettes. This was the opposite of a Pixar story; this was real life. 
I missed the man who could be Buzz Lightyear to my Woody and Jackson Storm to my McQueen, all in the same day, just to transform back into my father by sundown. I saw my uncle heal, at least in appearance, so why couldn’t my father? Countless visits to the behavioral psychology section of my school library became part of my daily routine. I learned about the brain and heart, the tangible affecting the intangible. I studied therapeutic interventions from reframing to hypnotherapy and the neuroscience behind psychiatric illness. Through my research, I discovered that many resist healing because they refuse to acknowledge what’s broken. So, I decided, I must show irrefutable proof to my father of his broken side. I gathered clips and audio recordings that captured the person he had become. It wasn't easy—guilt weighed on me as I pieced together scenes of him smoking outside, lost in thought, yelling, and making my mother cry over pain I still felt myself. But when I finally showed him, tears welled in his eyes. The truth had to shatter him so that the healing could begin. I knew my father wouldn’t talk about his feelings, so I made Woody do it for him. This time, our stories were not the classic Pixar stories with their assured happy endings; they were struggles waged in the void left by Andy, knowing we could never reach him again. We began with positive affirmations (“Andy may be gone, but his love and memories are a part of me, giving me strength every day”). Then, we’d move to sessions. 
“Andy will always look over you from afar, but he wouldn’t want you to lose your partner.” I said in my best Buzz Lightyear voice. 
“I don’t want to lose your mother,” he would slip up, “but it feels like my pull string is missing; I can’t say what I need to anymore. What if I can’t be that leader for you and your mother without Andy beside me?” I noticed his Woody voice was absent. 
I mirrored his body language, nodded in affirmation, and listened actively as our story flowed between the realms of reality and Pixar. This continued for several months. At last, one night, my father and I had a session where the flow between Pixar and reality was interrupted. This time it was a dialogue between a son and his father. A son and his father who were ready to move to infinity and beyond, knowing Andy was smiling over them. Through helping my father rediscover his happiness, I found my own. My father and I will never catch up to Andy, but we’ve learned to live in the light of his love. And now, be that through mental health workshops in front of entire schools or simple interviews to hear how someone recovered from their mental health challenges, I realize that I want nothing else but to help others find their own RC, to encourage them to seek help amidst the plot twists of their stories until they too can move to infinity and beyond.

A massive structure loomed overhead, seemingly defying the laws of gravity. Constructed of glass and steel and resembling a ship’s hull, it left me staring in awe, as questions flooded my mind: How is this design possible? How far does the overhang extend? What does it look like inside? I was attending my first game at the new U.S. Bank Stadium, home of the Minnesota Vikings. After entering the stadium, my dad stopped to take in the view, but I had my mind set on seeing the structure from the inside. We headed up the escalators where I could see the angled glass facade opening into the Minneapolis skyline framed by large engineered trusses. We reached our seats just in time for the Skol chant, evoking a unifying energy that boomed through the stadium of seventy-three thousand people. Between downs, my eyes studied the impressive design.

After the Vikings won, my fascination with U.S. Bank Stadium grew, motivating me to research baseball, soccer, and other football stadiums. I decided to challenge myself by replicating them on a smaller scale. As it turns out, figuring out how to model a football stadium that took years to build is even more confusing than the whole ‘football’ versus ‘soccer’ debate. I saved up for months until I could buy a diode laser cutter. The day it arrived, I set it up in the garage, lined up a balsa wood sheet, put on my mask and protective glasses, and pressed ’start’. It took many tries, countless hours, and numerous late nights hearing, “[Name], you should get to bed soon" not realizing it was already past midnight. My first prototype wasn’t perfect, but I was confident this idea could grow into a business. Thirty minutes later, I had my first Etsy business account—Custom3DesignShop. Hearing the first "cha-ching”' notification a few days later affirmed others valued my hard work.

However, I realized continuing my work outside in the frigid Minnesota winter wouldn’t be feasible if I wanted to capitalize on the holiday season. I determined an enclosed machine would be essential, allowing me to move my work inside while improving the quality and efficiency. I developed an Excel spreadsheet to track expenses and set season-based prices to maximize profits. Additionally, I expanded my listings with a variety of sizes and border options to appeal to a broader market. After two months, I accumulated enough surplus profit to invest in an enclosed CO2 laser cutter— the Glowforge Plus. Refining my interpersonal communication skills has been vital in communicating with customers.

A Culver’s franchise owner and marketing group approached me to recreate the first-ever Culver’s building from an eye-level view—a challenge I had never tackled before. During our Zoom call, they were initially surprised by my age but were quickly convinced of my capabilities. Knowing this piece was a gift for a founding member of Culver’s, I had to deliver. After several drafts and numerous email exchanges, their enthusiasm for the final product made all the effort worthwhile.

Striving for excellence is recognized in my customer reviews. One customer who ordered a soccer—or should I say football—stadium said; “Working with [Name] was an absolute dream…my husband is a HUGE ManUnited fan, and I wanted to give him a stadium replica that we could hang in our new home!” Stadiums are more than just structures; they are capsules of the shared history and community sports create. My work serves as a reminder of these cherished memories. I’m eager to immerse myself in the college sports spirit while aiming to innovate for the future. I look forward to using my passion for engineering to tackle new challenges, whether designing stadiums, advancing robotics, or working on rockets. My enthusiasm for sports and innovation will drive me to contribute to a vibrant campus community, where I can help create lasting memories and craft solutions that make a meaningful impact.

Matryoshka - a Russian nesting doll. I have had the same set since birth, but unlike the typical set with uniform designs in various sizes, my dolls were unique. Each one had a different profession emblazoned on its front in delicate paint strokes. The largest, the mother of the group, bore math equations and a ruler. The next, chemicals and a Bunsen burner. As the dolls grew smaller, their ambitions evolved: from teachers to doctors, scientists to painters, every profession was represented. The smallest doll was a writer, holding an array of books close to her chest.

These dolls mirrored my own shifting ambitions as my interests changed and I couldn’t bear to sit idly. Some days I was the painter, splashing watercolours across the table as I tried to depict my family as stick figure drawings. Other days, I was an engineer, folding yesterday’s artwork into a paper airplane that could soar across the living room.

Inevitably, some of the matryoshka dolls got lost, just as some of my dreams faded. When I submitted an article to my school newspaper but found that mine was the only one not published, I decided that writing wasn’t for me. My matryoshka dolls became more rigid in their identities and the smallest—a writer— was left behind.

In my sophomore year, the school newspaper stopped publishing. The decline in participation made me wonder if I wasn’t the only one who had lost touch with the art of writing. When I found my writer doll behind my bookshelf, a forgotten symbol of a passion I had once loved, I realised that to truly grow, I had to push myself to explore every path before me.

That was the birth of my own school magazine, which allowed myself and others to write creatively outside the confines of the classroom. It became a space for me to express my thoughts and explore creativity without the pressure of grades or expectations. With every new theme, I rediscovered the joy of writing—something that had once felt burdensome when measured against others' standards.

Through ‘The Colour Chronicles’, I learned that my passion for writing wasn't about getting approval from others. It was about sharing my voice, and inspiring others to do the same. The writer matryoshka doll, once discarded and forgotten, now stands proudly among the others on my dresser. It serves as a reminder that curiosity and education is not something to be judged by external factors but by the fulfillment it brings within.

As I reflect on my journey, I see how my matryoshka dolls have grown alongside me. The mathematician now relishes late-night study sessions with friends, working through complex problems and experiencing the thrill of success. The artist no longer limits creativity to paper but captures the world's beauty through the lens of a camera. The teacher aspires to inspire, understanding that true success lies in sparking curiosity and fostering growth in others. And the author? The author has embraced writing as a means of connection and growth, discovering the power of communication to foster community.

With their diverse professions, the matryoshkas represent the many facets of who I am and who I aspire to be. They remind me that I don’t have to choose one path over another but can embrace all my interests, allowing them to coexist and complement each other. Just as the matryoshka dolls fit neatly together, each passion within me supports the others, creating a whole that is richer than any single pursuit.

In the end, my matryoshka dolls are more than just toys; they are symbols of my journey—of curiosity, leadership, and intellectual growth. They stand on my dresser as a testament to the many paths I will explore and the endless possibilities that still lie ahead, each one waiting to be discovered, just like the dolls within the nesting set.

On the day I was leaving Magadan, relief was hovering in my mind. Sandwiched in the plane seat, I kept promising to myself, “I’ll never miss this godforsaken place.” The image in the plane window was a testament to my pledge: the Soviet-style terminal epitomized all the tombstone-gray architecture you can find in Magadan, while the further snow-capped mountains symbolized winters that run wild here from October to May.

Hardly had I fastened my seatbelt when my attention was diverted by the video screen in front of me. It showed a map of Russia with Moscow and Magadan at its extreme ends and an inscription above—5,904 kilometers. After living for sixteen years in a place separated from the world by endless forests, being far away felt like nothing new. Still, a sense of isolation persisted, coloring even the brightest moments.

Although I tried to banish my loneliness by exploring the town’s taiga surroundings, it refused to let up so easily. Ironically, swarms of mosquitoes sent me back to my book-filled room. There, I found escape in Merriam-Webster crosswords and Oxford grammar guides, each page a step away from isolation and deeper into the world of English. Under the pressure of remoteness, I converted English into a gateway to connect with the outer world.

The narrowly yanked-out perspicacity and malediction, the finally mastered subjunctive—all made their way into writings I created in preparation for the All-Russian School Olympiad and speaking sessions I organized with fellow English enthusiasts from all across Russia. What had appeared to be arcane vocabulary and grammar transformed into tools for expressing myself across physical boundaries.

But the story didn’t end there. As I learned more about ties between the United States and Magadan, including its sister-city status with Anchorage, I set out to study their foundations. Soon, English was supplemented with American history, and I found solace at my school library, perusing the dusty *American Pageant* about Ronald Reagan’s jaunty charms and Teddy Roosevelt’s Cuban arms.

Through my reading bouts, I explored the deep connections between the U.S.A. and Russia, overshadowed by mainstream political agenda—how Russian immigrants like Nabokov and Stravinsky shaped American culture and how American corporations like Ford and General Electric were involved in the Soviet industrialization in the 1930s. While aiming to further elevate my interests, I was also witnessing how global ties were tumbling under the perils of populism, racism, and propaganda.

This motivated me to create Intertalk, a space where everyone could get an unbiased sense of world affairs through intellectual discourse in English. Initially a schoolwide club, I eventually expanded it to a virtual format to make it accessible to anyone living in remote areas across Russia, just as I did. Intertalk is not merely a place where my passions for American studies and international affairs converge in discussions on the Spanish-American War cartoons and Wilsonianism—it’s where I apply those interests to promote objectivity and global awareness.

In 1944 U.S. Vice President Henry Wallace visited Magadan, then a Gulag prison camp, and, deceived by local authorities into believing that those who worked there were “volunteers,” praised it as a “combination of Tennessee Valley Authority and Hudson’s Bay Company.” Afterward, he obviously had to take his words back.

Seventy years later, Magadan may still project a grim image for some, but for me, there is infinitely more behind that bleakness: under those decrepit façades lies my cradle of intellectualism, one that I unequivocally cherish. My thoughts were interrupted by the plane finally accelerating. Through the window, I could still see the same brutalist terminal and frosty mountains, but this time they weren’t off-putting—they overflowed with meaning. They inspired me to foster connection through discussion and commonality of interests. They symbolized my drive to bridge the gaps that define today’s global fragmentation in the same way I had bridged thousands of kilometers between Magadan and the world.

There I was, holding my hand hovering over the table, heart pounding, leg bouncing, my mind racing through each possibility looking for an escape. With low time, the only move I found was to sacrifice my knight to stop his attack. 
I was in 10th grade, playing Kevin at the North Penn Chess Club. He was one of the top players and the only other highschooler in the room.
It’s over, I thought. I knew that anyone with Kevin’s rating would be able to capitalize on the material and time advantages I just gave him with ease. As soon as he took my knight with his pawn, I found myself saying, “I resign,” and shaking hands. After the game, Kevin moved my queen to h5 and pointed out a counterplay that he had been worried I might play. I shook my head, realizing I had been so fixated on taking back the useless pawn that I overlooked other opportunities to counterattack. I couldn’t help thinking if I had more time I might have found it and had a chance.
I asked him if we could continue the game for fun. He agreed, and we played on for the next hour as if I hadn’t prematurely resigned. For the next hour, I played with more ease without having to worry about the consequences. I exerted constant pressure and waited patiently, allowing him to make mistakes while defending. It wasn’t long before he blundered a piece, and I swiftly finished out the game. 
I felt a surprising sense of satisfaction, even though I had officially lost.
Instead of walking away from a loss frustrated, I found myself drawn to the idea of asking my opponent to review the game with me–an opportunity to uncover their strategies I might have not seen. I wanted to dissect their ideas so I could implement them in my future games or predict moves more easily. I also researched top players like Anand and Kramnik who are known for being calm during tense positions and time pressure. The main thing I learned was to be present in the moment and to love the game so that you don’t stress about the result. I felt the best way to do that was to play as much as I could, making North Penn Chess Club a weekly event.
Talking to my opponents after the games allowed me to become closer friends with all the regulars there. Kevin later became a key player on my team when I invited him and two other kids from my high school to form a club team for the K-12 state tournament. There was Greg, the funniest old man, who always wore shirts with sayings like “I play chess therefore I exist.” He’s the kind of player who can play like a grandmaster the whole game, then miss a mate in two, and laugh about it afterward. I also met a 7th grader named Alan, who’d often stay after tournaments to review games with me or play practice matches. I loved these sessions because Alan would teach me fun gambits that he would find on youtube.
The experiences I’ve had from chess give me the confidence to try difficult things in school and other activities. Even when I put effort into a well-thought-out plan and it fails, chess taught me it's not the end; it’s an opportunity to keep counterattacking. I learned more from the chess community than from the games.. Kevin taught me to be comfortable speaking to someone better than you which helped me talk to teachers and other students more. Greg and Alan taught me how to be present and be interested in what you are doing. 
Chess has taught me that every challenge is just another move in the grand game of life and each one has many lessons and approaches.
“I resign” has been taken out of my dictionary.

Costco trolleys are more than just practical tools; they hold cherished memories for me. On August 20, 2022, after finishing a geometry test, my parents treated me to my favorite Costco strawberry ice cream and pizza. While helping them load our groceries, I noticed an abandoned cart drifting toward an old green car. I quickly handed my cart to my mother and rushed to stop it, but it rear-ended the car just seconds before I could intervene. Flustered, I quickly tried to put the cart away before noticing an angry man approaching and yelling, “Why did you hit my car? Do you not know how expensive it is?” I stammered, “I was only trying to get the cart from hitting your car, sir.” As he continued shouting, I felt my resolve softening. I was trying to do something good yet here was this 40-year-old man yelling at me. Just then, from the corner of my eye, I saw my father hurrying over despite our strained relationship, arguing on my behalf. I said, “I ran to get the trolley so it wouldn't hit your car; if you don't believe me, please check the CCTV camera.” After a few minutes, a woman from another car confirmed my attempt to stop the cart, and the man backed down. I left in tears, headed to my library interview. Later on, before my interview, my father pulled me aside and said, “Don’t let others’ actions or reactions influence you. Keep your head up and go crush that interview,” and although my father doesn't show physical affection, I knew in those moments, his words of encouragement were a bigger hug than I would ever wish for.

Nervous from earlier events, I faced four competitors. After waiting forever, I was called. The interview went well, and when asked why I wanted to be a leader, I said, “To become a guiding force for others and to stand strong with them in adversity and to support those who believe in me. There will be times when change is rejected; as a leader, I want to support my peers to bring that change.” Later that day, I received an email: I had been selected as the leader! My goal was to raise mental health awareness. Despite challenges, including inconsistent timing and insufficient members, I proposed and got approval for a mental health fair for all ages. We featured relaxing activity booths, hired a mental health counselor, and included therapy dogs and meditation experts. The fair’s success, reflected in the joyful attendees, reinforced my resilience and showed me the positive impact of my efforts.

That day, my father's words taught me that true leadership and resilience go not only hand in hand but also are about more than just words—they are about standing steadfast for those who believe in you. Leadership means defending and supporting others even when it's difficult, while resilience is about unwavering self-belief in yourself and others when faced with setbacks. Through our combined efforts of hosting a mental health fair, I learned to be patient yet resilient. Leadership doesn't always mean being the only one at the top, it also means sharing and helping others around you as well. Although, the challenges made me doubt myself, just like I had in the Costco parking lot; this time, however, I had the support of my community and teammates. With their support and belief in me, I could lead the fair successfully. This year on August 20th, when I pass my driver's test (if I can do parallel parking correctly) the first place I would like to visit is my local Costco with my dad to get a vanilla sundae in one hand and a Costco trolley in another.

The savory smell of my mother's fresh-made dosa wakes me from my eleven-hour slumber. On my journey to the kitchen, I observe an empty carton previously filled with alphonso mangoes. It haunts me. In a cold and dark corner, leaning over next to the wilting plants, my father sits on the shoe bench, putting on his colorless sneakers. I don’t bother to make conversation since I figure I would get the classic “hmmm”, the sheer frequency of the sound dehumanizing my own father. Amongst the chaos of making sure the dosa is crisp and the chai doesn’t boil over, my mother sentences me to a trip to the market with my father. My futile rebuttal goes unnoticed, so I accept my fate.

During the car ride, my fierce wave of interrogative attacks is swiftly shut down by his defense of “hmmms.” I give up on making conversation; it is as awkward as always. When we arrive, I retreat to a corner, scrolling through the abyss of Instagram reels. When I look up, I am amused by a sight never seen. It is as if he is passionate about the task at hand, which is examining mangoes. He presses each one gently, studies the scent, determining whether it is worthy of his basket.

At once, my mind is invaded with insatiable curiosity. How exactly does he know what the right amount of give on a mango is? What scent is he looking for? Do these tests actually work? Why is he putting so much effort into such a mundane task? The curiosity eats me up; I have to know more.

This curiosity pushes me to sit through those painfully awkward drives and ask questions, even though his answers are often dry. I become a sort of apprentice, learning the fundamental formulas of the webbing test, press test, and smell test.

“I’ve always wanted to have a garden of my own.”
“Why not?”
“It’s too much work,” “The soil may not respond well.”

This interaction during a routine mango picking session represents a fundamental difference in mentality between me and my dad. Although I grew up comfortably, fostering a riskier and dream-like mindset, my father’s tough life experiences made him highly risk-averse, explaining the barrage of excuses.

I had to save him from himself and get him that garden. I spent early mornings before school researching, scouring the internet for easy plants to raise. I spent my time after school exhaustingly taking soil measurements, my hypothesis backed up by vague memories of Mr. Blair’s AP Environmental Science class. I spent my post-dinner wind-down time toiling among the bugs to measure the depth, nutrient supply, and ratio of silt and sand to pure soil. I spent hasty passing periods desperately scribbling down my notes at the library, exhausting the plethora of basic gardening books. I spent my time with Mr. Goldenburg, drinking from his holy grail of debate knowledge, curating a Suits-worthy opening statement. Inevitably, my stubbornness emerged victorious, and after the performance of a lifetime, there we were, marveling over the beauty of our empty lawn, plotting our dream garden.

In the proceeding months, we found ourselves planting seeds, nurturing the soil, and relocating plants to ensure the success of the garden. As I enter the garden at the rooster's call, I stumble on my father’s sneakers, its now vibrant color ensues a sense of warmth in me. In my mind, I thought it was the vibrance of the garden infused within him. I consider it, shake my head, and run out to the vast lush to join my father, where we harvest our fruit, a faint, united smirk on our faces.

While I write this, eating the fruit of our efforts, every love-infused fiber, the sweetness fueled by pride, keeps me going, carrying my father’s spirit of embracing the mundane and pushing for perfectionism no matter where I go.

Hotpot, the most popular Chinese cuisine, consists of cooking raw ingredients such as thinly sliced meat and vegetables in a spicy boiling broth. As a hotpot fanatic who grew up in a family addicted to those spiced dishes, my life has been defined by the simple sauces, ingredients, and broths prepared around the hotpot table.

My favorite sauce is soy soup and peanut butter mix. It mirrored my relationship with my sister, a rivalry of flavors of spicy and cold, sweet and bitter, Eastern and Western, all combining to create a stark but wondrous taste.

My contention with Sis over what is more important, art or science, has aged over a decade. She would luggage me on tours to see Picassos, Monets, the Met, and the Forbidden City to prove her point, while I dragged her on visits to see innovation centers, AI therapists, and auto-delivery drones. We mutually hated each other’s locations like the opposite textures of fluid soup and sticky butter – fifteen-year-old me would question the purpose of visiting palaces that were built by dead people and were no longer relevant, while she would snap back that robot psychiatrists were dystopian. Nevertheless, the rivalry opened us both to a different but flavorful side of the world. After going on dozens of art visits, I do (sometimes) notice sparks of beauty in the intricate zigzag patterns on the walls of Chinese temples and Monet’s magnificent brushes of sunlight, and I’m sure that one day I’ll make Sis feel the same about science too.

My favorite ingredient is fresh tofu. Boiling the dish taught me an appreciation for patience – with thorough culinary preparation, the initially bland block could transform into a flavorful, silky delight.

Zihan is an 8-year-old I met through my club Teens who is half phonologically deaf and about to turn full, but after obliterating me forty times in a row in LEGO tank warfare, his normally quiet self would turn into the most talkative, excited person in the room. Sometimes, the roleplays did get repetitive after ten or twenty rounds, but just like in preparing fresh tofu, it takes time and care to make something special. Every time Zihan crushes over me with his army of five enlarged battle tanks against my only mini truck that was also missing a wheel, dancing around the room after his triumph and enthusiastically making hand gestures all over the air to remind me that he just beat me again, it always makes me feel that the afternoon spent crawling on the ground with him was so worth it.

My favorite broth is the four-grid flavored. Everyone can find their preference in the four-grid – there is tomato soup for youngsters, mushroom flavored for elders, mildly spiced for veggies, and ultra-spiced for the courageous.

This inclusive spirit is something I’ve carried into another passion of mine: creating a supportive online space for teenagers to connect and share their experiences called To-Listen. From connecting with Anna, a second-year middle schooler feeling anxious that she can’t find a friend whom she can bond with on a heart-to-heart level; to Julia, feeling pressured to act like the “good child” as the older sibling of a low-income rural family and afraid to express her negative emotions in front of her parents and friends; to Jake, who just wanted to be wished happy birthday by a fellow peer – every time I helped a previously unspoken voice open up and feel included, my heart is always filled with warmth and pride. The process of uncovering an unspoken story is never easy. It can take days, weeks, even months of subtle encouragements “you’re not alone”s, and sometimes even a cat emoji.

I may be far from the perfect sibling for my sister, playmate for Zihan, and companion for Anna, Joe, and Jake – but I am committed to growing alongside them, embracing our differences and learning from each experience we share.

As every fresh tofu block transforms into a steamy delicious delight with the help of my favorite sauce and broth, I am reminded that true strength comes not from starting out as the perfect ingredient, but from recognizing that with openness, patience, and love, any initially bland tofu block has the potential to become a flavorful and unique delicacy.

In the early days of my non-profit, I experienced a wave of enthusiasm and support that was nothing short of exhilarating. The initial fundraisers were met with open hearts and generous contributions, sparking a sense of community and shared purpose. Little did we know that these early triumphs would soon be tested when we launched The Supply Project (TSP), an initiative aimed at fundraising for teachers.

TPS was supposed to be a continuation of our triumphs, but it quickly became evident that not everyone shared our enthusiasm. As a 17-year-old, I found myself unprepared for the harsh reality of public opposition. The initiative to support teachers, which seemed undeniably good, drew unexpected criticism during our first fundraiser. "I already pay taxes" became a refrain we started to get used to. Each comment chipped away at my initial optimism, forcing me to confront the complexities of social advocacy. Yet, each dismissive remark also fueled our resolve. We had to refine our messaging, emphasize the tangible impact on classrooms, and demonstrate that public funding alone was insufficient.

This unexpected challenge steeled us; it wasn't just about fundraising anymore—it became a fight to validate the necessity of supporting educators directly. By the second day of our campaign, when one gentleman inquired, "Do you know how much teachers make?" we were ready to engage in the dialogue. The ensuing conversation has replayed in my thoughts countless times. His argument, claiming teachers earn over a hundred thousand dollars annually, was swiftly countered by Reid Cooper, a member of my team. "Who says that's sufficient? It's acceptable for others to earn more, but not teachers—why?" The man's retort, which we had heard before, was, "They get summers off." And there it was, a sentiment rooted in resentment or envy that teachers were enjoying their summers while everyone else worked; but we knew this wasn't true. Our woodworking instructor Jason Jenkins took on side jobs, recently crafting a vinyl record holder for us, and Mrs. O'Brien, our 6th-grade math teacher, was preparing and delivering meals. In our little town teachers were everywhere working side jobs.

We encountered numerous challenges from the opposition that weekend, and we honed our skills in engaging with the critics. Sometimes they laughed at our persistence and donated a few dollars; sometimes, they didn't. While we're unsure if we changed any opinions, we know we earned their respect. That initial backlash was deflating, but it taught me resilience and strengthened my commitment to making a difference in less supported or understood areas.

The experience also added a new layer of education to our foundation. As we brainstorm our next project, I find myself researching the social aspects of each idea, preparing for informed debates with real data. As a team, we now regularly talk about opposing viewpoints to better understand different perspectives. It’s become a fun debate where we try to outdo one another, but ultimately helps us to understand our initiative and goals in a broader light. This journey has taught me that true change begins with listening and bridging gaps between differing viewpoints.

My experiences have shaped me into someone who seeks not only to connect but also to foster meaningful dialogue. As I transition into college life, I aim to champion this approach, believing that real change is rooted in the exchange of diverse ideas and respectful dialogue. This approach ensures that my foundation, aptly named "Change Has Started," achieves its mission of bringing about positive transformation. In my small corner of the world, with my small group of 40 students we are making this happen. And we will live by the words of someone way wiser than us, “Be the change you want to see in the world.” - Gandhi.

**Discuss an accomplishment, event or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others. (650 words max)**

98.75 kilograms. Entering sophomore year, these flickering white characters barely visible beneath my protruding stomach were the puppeteers controlling my strings of confidence, socialization, school participation and sports. As COVID-19 forced Singapore into a lockdown, the four puppeteers were ecstatic expecting a fifth to soon follow. They were wrong.

A dormant figure unbeknownst to the puppeteers sprung into action. Discipline. I used the extra time during lockdown effectively, walking 100 meters for every 200 that I “ran” dragging myself to 3 km daily. Two months later, I whipped out the scale: 99.50. Where had I gone wrong?

Advice from my fitness junkie cousin Shaurya and hours of Greg Doucette’s YouTube videos directed me towards meticulous caloric tracking. “Nudge” by Thaler and Sunstein introduced me to “snudges” (self-nudges); they proved a useful ally for discipline in the war against the puppeteers. Fruits at the kitchen’s entrance and junk hidden deep inside alongside eliminating snacks, reducing carbohydrates and strict meal timings formed five pillars of my dietary journey. It hurt. Sucking an ice cube while my younger sister drizzled melted chocolate over snowy vanilla, my younger self writhed in his grave screaming “WHY?”. I channeled this pain into energy running daily. Gradually, pain metamorphosed into pride. I chuckled saying “Size 32 shorts please!” at the cashier, vividly remembering tears rolling down my cheeks as I missed the bus attempting to bridge the chasm between button and hole of my size 34 shorts months prior.

Approaching senior year, the scale read 67.85. No puppeteers. Numbers I controlled. Three key lessons stood atop the puppeteers’ graves as school reopened. Daily runs taught me motivation is overrated; discipline is essential. I learnt that consistency constructed the seemingly small steps converting dreams to goals. Lastly, expect mistakes. Learn from them. I unearthed a passion for MUNs previously suppressed by puppeteer #1, setting an ambitious goal of spearheading my school conference. I constructed smaller, achievable targets just as I divided a daunting 3 km into segments of jog, walk, repeat. I enrolled in available MUNs, won awards and moderated debate at conferences. Each goal achieved was a tiny step transforming the timid Ethiopian delegate hiding behind his placard in freshman year into the USG of Finance handling the entire conference in senior year. Allocating the $17,000 budget for 300 people reminded me of caloric tracking, and I enjoyed drafting the $3000 grant application whilst fending off the sea of pink sticky notes with IB deadlines scrawled over them engulfing my splintered desk. Simultaneously, I led Project Ancora, fundraising for an animal charity, CAS. Plateauing at $1,000, I realized personal discipline going door-to-door was insufficient and I learned delegation to my 46 volunteers. Deconstructing fundraising into merchandise sales, event profits and optimizing ROAS (return on ad spend) to attract donors, we raised $7,500, winning the national YFC Merit Award.

My discipline’s greatest test was yet to strike. Incessant elbow clicking I naively attributed to “too much writing” was actually Early Onset Elbow Osteoarthritis caused by a prior imperfect surgery, explained the doctor, as I stared at the (fittingly) crackled glass table. He said there was no cure, it would get worse and I should avoid the gym. These hammer blows catapulted me into a self-pity spiral for months. I decided the debilitating smell of medicinal cream and a hundred different braces that didn’t alleviate pain (but seriously undermined my fashion sense) couldn’t define me forever. I found a sports orthopedist who recommended solutions instead of proclaiming “No Cure!”. He recommended returning to the gym (much to my delight), identifying pain points and challenging mental strength, a challenge I embraced. Writing worsened the pain, so I decided to learn writing with my left hand. Transforming illegible scrawling into English posed the toughest test yet to my discipline and consistency. I rewrote the same paragraph daily, gradually reducing it from 7 lines to 4. I modified my gym routine and found exercises that alleviated pain. I felt akin to a child understanding how his body worked, learning through trial and error. Accepting and acclimatizing to slight constant pain was essential, but the condition began conceding against my relentlessness. I do not know what the future holds; I do know I will find a way to adapt and persevere through anything thrown at me. I hope to continue leveraging the adaptability, leadership and discipline that my journey has imparted while learning new skills.

Theorem: I suck. I suck at talking to people. 
Proof: Sitting at my desk, I watch as other kids laugh and throw around buzzwords I don’t understand. Thrown into a bustling middle school in Seoul, my funky English-Busan dialect sparked barely-muffled snickers, making it impossible to socialize. My dad’s sudden exit from my life in second grade had already shaken my confidence in people, and now I retreated even further. Here, math became my refuge, offering comfort and order amid social chaos. Stewart's theorem didn’t require me to decode hidden meanings in a sideways glance or guess the right moment to laugh. Seeking solitude also drew me to tennis: just me and a ball I could control.

Theorem: Tennis is a game of numbers. 
Proof: By using geometry to maximize my opponent's running distance and probability to target weak shots, tennis felt natural through my mathematical lens. 
“Aditya, [Name], third doubles.” As a freshman, I squeezed onto varsity, eager to explore the new world of doubles. 
But the random variable named Aditya flipped my game upside down. We both swung at the ball—or didn’t swing at all. He’d rush forward unexpectedly, leaving the court wide open. We kept losing. Something was wrong.

Theorem (revised): Doubles tennis isn’t just a game of numbers, but one of synergy. 
Proof (by contradiction): A(Aditya) + B(Me) don’t achieve our maximum when we are individually optimized. 
I thought we could fix our issues mathematically: maximize A and B, and A+B should be maximized as well. But we both tried our hardest to reach every ball, leading to collisions and frustration. 
As we continued playing, I realized instead that success required adjusting our styles to complement each other. Aditya started leaving volleys for me, and I let him take overheads where he excelled. 
But the breakthrough came when I understood Aditya as a person. He was talkative and thrived on encouragement during tense moments, so I began offering support after missed shots. In turn, he matched my calm focus during critical points. We started to win and gradually grew as a team.

Teamwork taught me what numbers and logic couldn’t. More importantly, I realized connections, like mine with Aditya, aren’t predetermined—they're created. Slowly, I stopped fearing daily interactions and instead saw them as opportunities to connect. I began to believe in people. I began to believe in myself.

Theorem: Human relationships are really, really, powerful. 
Proof: I started in familiar territory: math team. The next school year, I stepped up and ran for president, now more confident in voicing my ideas. I created teaching sessions, curriculum and all, and built a strong, tight-knit community. 
My brain had always wanted to speak, and finally, my voice was ready to follow, making connections for those who couldn’t. I yelled in rainy weather for veterans who couldn’t leave their homes. I petitioned to create a chess club for elementary schoolers without a voice in the PTA. Through this newfound power, I saw firsthand the impact I could make on my community.

But the most profound connection I developed was right at home. 
(Part B): My mom and I were making bibimbap together for dinner. Softly, I asked: “Mom, what was it like when you first came here?” At first, she hesitated. But gingerly, she opened up: talking about the loneliness of being in a new country, working jobs to make ends meet after my dad left, and the guilt she felt for not being able to give my sister and me everything she wanted. Listening to her, I began to see my mom as a person with her own dreams, fears, and struggles. I realized that fulfilling my household responsibilities wasn’t enough; I needed to be a shoulder for her to lean on. 
That night, I hugged her tight, grateful for the relationship we were building—one rooted in understanding, empathy, and the courage to share our vulnerable selves.

Theorem: The world isn’t a place that can be defined by a hard set of rules, as I once thought it was. 
Proof: The most beautiful rules aren’t the ones you can simply calculate. It's the ones you create yourself. It’s illogical, but I’m slowly, slowly understanding the logicality of it.

“Helicopter ride?” I asked, making a whirring noise and a spinning motion.

Emanuelly stretched out her arms in response, which I took to mean a ‘yes.’ Grasping securely onto her wrists, I spun her in circles so fast that her legs lifted up off the ground. As the familiar playground blurred out of focus, all I could see was her gleeful expression. Soon, each of the kids wanted a turn and they organized a rotation that lasted until I was too dizzy to walk.

My attempt to spice-up the regular playtime routine of the kids at the Haven House seemed to be a hit.

On our class walk the next day, we crossed a bridge over Highway 101 and watched the waves of cars below. Whispering to teacher LaDaysia, I told her my top-secret plan and she agreed to help. After a few moments, we used our arms to make a tugging motion, pantomiming honking a horn. Immediately, dozens of cars and trucks started honking in response. At the first honk, Darelilla jumped back in surprise, but I reassured her it was just a friendly gesture.
