Quickly, the kids’ initial confusion was replaced with giggles, twirls, and cheers, as they made this dull concrete bridge their stage for a spectacular moment.

Grinning, I took in the bizarre spectacle; the kids jumping up and down with excitement, the people in the cars beaming back, and the teachers struck with contagious joy. More than anything I was moved by the capacity of a mere arm motion to turn an ordinary walk or a boring commute into a meaningful moment.

Unfortunately, not every moment at the Haven House had such a joyful tone.

That day Casey had one of his frequent ear-splitting tantrums, which derailed the classroom. I felt an overwhelming sense of helplessness and tension; while the teachers did their best, they weren’t equipped to handle the behavioral challenges that came with his non-verbal autism. Without access to speech or occupational therapy, his educational progress was stalled.

That morning, Darriella came to school with dark bags under her eyes. Teacher Teri explained that when her untreated eczema flared up, she was so uncomfortable she could hardly sleep. This clearly carried over to the classroom, manifesting as uncharacteristic disinterest and distraction.

Seeing their struggles reminded me of the stark educational challenges these kids face, which eclipsed playtime boredom.

The topic of educational inequality in the Bay Area wasn’t new to me. I had spent the better part of the year researching disparities, pouring over journal papers, and interviewing numerous local stakeholders. While that research provided critical insights, interning at the Haven House brought those insights to life, making me even more determined to tackle the problem, at least in some small way.

After researching age-appropriate topics, creating a lesson plan, and presenting to the internship coordinator, she agreed to let me lead a lesson where the kids used snap-on components to create circuits. As they chased after the discs that their circuits made go flying and eloquently explained the concept of electricity, I knew the lesson was a success.

Looking to the broader community, I worked to bring Rise-Up STEM workshops to more libraries across San Mateo County and translated materials to Mandarin and Spanish, expanding access to a wider group of students. I ensured the robotics summer camp I was planning would be completely free and started building relationships with established organizations tackling educational inequality to reach more low-income students for next summer.

Big problems like educational inequality compel us to tackle them in whatever small ways we can, even when no practical solutions are in sight. Yet, amid these daunting challenges, there is always the opportunity to create moments of joy and connection. As I continue to take on big problems like these, I will treasure the significance of small moments of joy, knowing they alone can make a great difference.

Cushioned by the well-loved seats of bus 61C, I watch as the dad across from me attempts to corral his squirmy son into a pair of neon yellow crocs. I’m heading to the university lab while a couple bickers over a shopping list, a computer science student dives into a problem set, and the Pittsburgh skyline blurs past the windows. My 7:30 morning commute last summer was hectic but, immersed in its whirlwind of noise, I took complete peace in my own world.

When I visited my Dad’s side of the family last year however, I traded that comforting pace for slow World Cup reruns on our faded red couch. Every night by the TV was a kind of limbo, pocketed with Taco Bell Chalupa ads in which I tried to speak with my grandfather. “¿Eh?”, Papa Ramón would squint, as I fumbled through a mix of sign language and broken “Spanish”, turning tomato-red in my attempts to learn about his life as a mathematician. But, when I (grudgingly) solved triple integrals in my chewed-up notebook, his eyes lit up.

“¿Matemáticas?” Mathematics? He asked, gesturing to my integrands. With slow, deliberate page-turning, I retraced my equations line-by-line as he nodded and smiled. Even as I struggled to find the Spanglish word for “derivative”, and though it looked more hieroglyphic than mathematic, my roadmap of numbers brought us together. Engineering wasn’t only a tool to solve my technical problems—it let me build a bridge of language and understanding, even if it took a little extra time.

Yet I still found my 7:30 bus ride peace in what I thought engineering had to look like. Just before junior year winter break, I wrestled our team’s robotic grabber for four consecutive nights at the Tech Room Three. Now dubbed the “spatula” by my “teammates”, its 270° swing gifted me gray hairs and a graveyard of servo motors as I rushed through one haphazard iteration after the next, refusing to move slowly.

When I chose to diagram version four on our team’s whiteboard however, every hardware member gave their input on where we could improve. Three hours later, with too many Lay’s bags littering our bench, V5 was complete. Was it better? Absolutely, a similar version won us a ticket to the world championships.

Better yet, the same “real” engineering involved a collective blueprint of pausing, listening, and understanding, the same tools I used to connect with Papa Ramón.

Don’t get me wrong, I love the technical aspects of engineering—wrestling robotic arms at the tech room and 3D-bioprinting collagen blood vessels are my idea of a good time—but it was on bus 61C last summer that I learned its more personal application.

I waved to that kid, now sporting his neon Crocs, and started a game of rock-paper-scissors. The Pittsburgh skyline blurred past the window as usual but, as with both with my grandfather Papa Ramon and robotics, I slowed down with intention. As I lost round after round (he wasn’t the most honest opponent) and smiles grew on both our faces, I learned that “engineering” is as much as about relationships as it is about results.

Slowing down, whether on the bus or in the lab, didn’t mean I lost momentum. It let me build bridges—of bioprinted collagen and laughter—that made my life richer: between teammate and teammate, rock-paper-scissors opponents, grandson and grandfather. As we the boy and I laughed while zipping through Point State Park, I felt more relaxed than I have in years.

I know I’ll have to move quickly in college, racing from class to class while sprinting through my projects. But as I’ve grown up, I’ve learned discovered it’s not only okay to enjoy the slow moments, what I didn’t used to believe was “engineering”—sometimes it’s more important. Each time Papa Ramón calls my Dad on the weekends, he asks how I’m doing with su ciencia, my science. My words spill out faster than I can translate them, teaching me that science, like life, is richer when shared.

“Wow, you wrote that much? You know it doesn’t matter, right?” That is what I frequently hear from classmates whenever I get an opinion feedback form with all the lines filled out. No matter if it’s a teacher impressions review or something as mundane as how we liked the color of a wall. I would always write with honesty, no matter how positively or negatively I felt about it. Occasionally I got in trouble for this as I got disgusted looks from classmates or was even asked by teachers to paraphrase and to put more “neutral” sentiments on such reviews. I never understood why these expectations were the standard as everyone asked each other for opinions. The more I pondered, the more I questioned why people continued to sugarcoat their true opinions and feelings even when asked for an “unfiltered” opinion. I knew it wasn’t because of societal expectations, as most forms were anonymous, so one could be however they wanted with no direct consequence. Despite that, I still couldn’t quite form an idea of why. Then, on a random Friday afternoon, the answer emerged from the most unexpected of people: my father.

We were flipping through Netflix trailers, I asked him, “Papi, does your job ask for your opinions?” Unexpectedly, he went on a rant. The business is a startup, and even though they state that they value opinions, they do the opposite. Such as their development of a new artificial intelligence system, but due to time constraints, employees constantly fix the systems, losing customer data and support. Many attempted to state that the system development needed more time but kept applying temporary fixes, leading to another failure. A vicious cycle. The problem is that people feel unheard and unimportant in what they do. And that to me didn’t seem like the way I wanted to live my future life as an adult. Despite that, I decided to implement ways to allow people to feel heard and important in my ways. I was already a tutor at my school, but I wasn’t involved until I started actively thinking, “How can I make this more effective?” My first challenge was with a freshman who had learning disabilities with reading and struggled with algebra. We, however, found a way to break down each math concept to its fundamentals, not skip any steps, and say every step was done to solve the equation. It took longer to finish a question, but it effectively taught someone how to solve problems themselves. Then I continued to help others. It didn’t matter if I would only have them for a few days or a couple of months; I would continue to apply this mindset to allow opinions to be heard. It motivates me to want to become an industrial engineer where not only STEM is the focus but also direct feedback to make existing systems better or even build something from scratch. I want to be someone everyone knows will consider their thoughts and enact positive, lasting change. To convince others to not be afraid to express their true thoughts and opinions, just as little [Name] wanted.

“I want to be a biscuit,” I almost say. But I (sensibly) answer the inevitable question posed by adults when they discover I’m a senior. On a typical Saturday, our walls were draped in silvery shadows from the low-hanging clouds, raindrops a (steady) soundtrack to clattering in the kitchen. I aimed to perfect my biscuit recipe once and for all. What’s the secret? Butter or shortening? Milk or buttermilk? The optimal ratio of ingredients? In my home, one teacher speaks volumes and the other is silent. Mama, the first in her family to attend college, grew up as a first-generation immigrant in New Orleans. She once told me, “making Southern biscuits helped bridge the gap between my heritage and American culture.” There’s a (spirited) debate in my family about which biscuit profile–fluffy or flakey–reigns supreme. I’m squarely in the flakey camp. I gently placed the pan in the oven and began cleaning the flour-dusted countertop. My thoughts drifted to Mama and the stark differences between our childhoods. Maybe because she had limited opportunities, Mama instilled in me the importance of using mine to “be a leader and leave the world better than I found it.” I wasn’t sure what she meant until I started examining the world around me.

From my car seat, I observed White men insult Black men while Grammy hurriedly pumped gas, ignoring my questions about “that” word. I encountered (resilient) men pushing carts sagging with heavy blankets. I watched elderly faces flush red with embarrassment as their credit cards were declined at the drugstore. Subtle biases surfaced in my own life, too. Receiving backhanded compliments about my “Wasian” identity reminded me that privilege doesn’t erase prejudice. Like the time I was told, “your eyes are so pretty even though you’re Asian.” I sang Hannah Montana’s “The Best of Both Worlds” to diffuse the tension. While stuck in a claustrophobic car, my Driver’s Ed teacher questioned my mixed-race identity; I felt like a curiosity. I’ve spent most of my life living on the hyphens of White-Asian-American. But Mama always told me to “put things in perspective.”

My growing understanding of social injustices fueled my (tenacious) drive to lead meaningful change. But I equated leadership with being the line leader, issuing commands to (boisterous) Kindergarteners from the front. Over the years, I’ve grappled with the notion of the perfect leader, feeling squeezed into a prescriptive mold that I don’t fit.

My wandering thoughts were interrupted by a rhythmic chime, the timer insisting it was time to pull the biscuits from the oven. Some biscuits looked like tipped top-hats, others resembled (overzealous) sunbathers, the Maillard reaction too enthusiastic. Regardless, they revealed delicious layers. This time, a pattern caught my eye: biscuits baked close together pulled each other up, rising taller than those that stood alone.

Each batch of biscuits was a lesson wrapped in (craggy) crust. Biscuits changed my view of both leadership and myself; they taught me that I don’t have to be perfect to be delightful. I no longer view leadership as dictating plans and commanding others to follow. Over time, I’ve learned that just as biscuits rise higher when leaning on each other, we too reach greater heights when we support those around us. One way to uplift others is using humor to bridge connections and encourage collaboration. At the Gates Foundation, I put this into practice, and the team I led voted me “most likely to make everyone burst out laughing.” This (supportive) space allowed us to rise together, like biscuits, to reach our goals.

So, how do I answer that inevitable question? A dreamer, a baker, a daring change-maker? My two teachers inspired me to pursue human rights law. The layers in my biscuits also reflect the (parenthetical) layers in me, shaping how I want to lead in the future.

In my personal life, college, and career, I hope to always be a biscuit.

**Student Essay:**

A slight breeze flowed through the hot, humid kitchen as “Liza” by the Sonny Stitt Quartet played softly. I had milk boiling in my favorite pan, steeping tea leaves. Once the tea was done, I transferred it to my Batman mug, added sugar, and took a sip: it was bland. My effort to recreate my mother’s familiar tea fell flat, and I became determined to figure out the cause. Every afternoon, I grappled with the tea, using only the three necessary ingredients - tea leaves, milk, and sugar - and methodically changing the amounts of each ingredient. The jazz in the background, rich with improvisation, starkly contrasted my rigid approach - often frustrating me and leading me to turn the music off. The strictness mirrored my approach to life itself. I became dedicated to dance when I was three years old, and the many years of dancing meant my life became a tedious loop of practicing and studying. I would attend school every day, come home, do my homework, and practice dance: a set formula. Again and again, I was merely going through the motions.

Although bored with tedium, I strove for perfection. Just as I did not want the tea’s taste to be potentially spoiled with new ingredients, I did not want my time wasted on a possibly fruitless endeavor. I was reluctant to deviate from the path, uncomfortable with spontaneity and new experiences.

Then, one afternoon, I walked into the kitchen to make tea, noticing my mother had decided to make it instead. When I glanced at the counter, I saw a small bottle labeled “tea masala” and a few shavings of ginger. The reason for my tea’s blandness became clear: my horizons were too narrow. As I added these new ingredients to the tea while listening to “The Lamp is Low,” I reflected on my endeavors in life. I had missed opportunities by refusing to try new hobbies or classes, believing they would not be my cup of tea. Slowly, I dipped my toe into something new, taking up the violin lessons my parents had suggested for years. Realizing this, when my parents suggested starting violin lessons, I tried them. As I struggled with complex pieces, such as Claire de Lune, I started embracing mistakes as part of the learning process and overcame them to polish my playing. Just as the masala and ginger provided new layers of complexity to the tea, these violin lessons gave me patience and perseverance which I could apply to every aspect of my life. I learned to be steady when faced with new challenges and to push through them with determination.

As my tea improved, I decided to share it with my family. As we all sat around the dining table one afternoon, drinking tea and listening to “The Girl from Ipanema,” I felt joy at seeing their enjoyment- sharing my tea with my family gave me a feeling of unexpected contentedness. That slight emotion sparked a great interest in community service. I wanted to spread joy in my greater community, so I started volunteering at a hospital. When I trained for the emergency department, one comment from my supervisor stuck with me and changed my perspective on life: “I don’t have to train you; I get to train you.” It was transformative. It made me view new challenges as opportunities to learn rather than obligations. Watching the doctors interact with the patients and help them enthusiastically through their struggles inspired me to be even more empathetic to others.

My days and personality became much richer as my tea transformed from a single note to a symphony of flavors. Each ingredient and process provided a new layer of complexity: the masala and ginger brought forth resilience, and sharing the tea gave me a love for my community. As I continue exploring and refining my passions, I hope to add depth and richness to my journey with each experience, savoring the process of growth and discovery along the way.

“6'6 FORWARD, NUMBER 12, ALI AHMADDD!” As I rose from the bench and high-fived my 12 teammates, the announcement of my name as a starter for the Lovejoy High School basketball team echoed through our gym. It may come as a surprise from the basketball captain but when I’m not sinking free throws, I’m standing up to bullies and pushing for neurodiversity awareness.

My older brother, Ahsan, has autism. Back when my brother was in 7th-grade, he was taunted and tripped by a classmate during English class. He fell and broke his wrist, as the principal called my frantic mom. Requiring emergency surgery, Ahsan’s pain and social anxiety rocked me. While Ahsan’s pain-filled cries tormented the halls of our home, I kept mine muffled in my pillows. I felt a mix of rage and helplessness. That moment sparked a fire in me – a determination to create a world where neurodiversity is celebrated, not stigmatized.

I wanted to know why. Why does Ahsan’s brain make him behave differently — hyper-fixating and rewatching the same Cars movie scene 100 times? Why do some differences lead to social exclusion, while others' idiosyncrasies are more readily accepted? There were nights I lay awake, overwhelmed by the enormity of the challenge. How could I, a young student, really make a difference? But then I'd remember Ahsan’s pain, and I knew I had to take a stand.

Seeking answers to these questions, I turned to neuroscience. Doing independent research with a UC Davis PhD candidate, I bushwhacked into the cerebral jungle. We scoured hundreds of databases analyzing brain scans of autism patients, trying to decipher a common thread. Using machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence, I unearthed a strong connection between atypical fMRI brain activity and autism. This discovery suggests that such methods can help diagnose kids at risk for autism before they show any clear signs, allowing for early intervention and eventually preventing future struggles caused by autism. I couldn’t help but wonder if early diagnosis had been an option for Ahsan, how different his life could have been. Could his inability to recognize social cues or repetitive hand movement, which made him a ripe target for bullying, have been mitigated? The more I delved into my research, the more I became fascinated by the nexus between neuroscience and technology, and their potential to improve lives.

But I knew that science research alone couldn’t fix our broken system. Back at school, I worked with my principal to establish A Beautiful Mind, an anti-bullying after-school club. My vision was simple: to create fun activities such as “Buddy Bingo” and “Harmony Quest” which bridge gaps between neurominority and neurotypical kids.

During our weekly club hangouts in Mr. Seidel’s art room, I formed a special bond with Thad. His enthusiastic recitations of dinosaur facts remind me of Ahsan’s passionate monologues about model trains. Thad never directly divulges his emotions — I am only clued in enough to know that his desires are just like anyone else’s: the desire for friends, especially those that remember your birthday. So, on Thad’s birthday, my friends and I organized a dinosaur-themed party, transforming the art room into a lush jungle. As we played a lively round of Jurassic Park trivia, Thad eagerly shared fun facts about velociraptors (did you know that they were only the size of a turkey? Jurassic Park lied), a truth that had us all chuckling.

Ahsan, Thad, and countless other neurodiverse individuals have taught me that there is no “right” way for the brain to work. Ahsan gave me the purpose in life I never knew was coming. And though leading my basketball team to the district championship is fulfilling, my true purpose goes beyond basketball. I hope to transform my community into a locus of acceptance, where all perspectives, whether typical or eccentric, are honored and valued as equal. So, when I see an overlooked peer at university, I won’t stay quiet. I’ll try to make the busiest room a little less lonely. The journey has just begun, but I’m ready for the challenging road ahead.

I rubbed my sweaty hands on my pencil skirt, trying to ease the tightness in my chest. One by one, the tournament director read off the names of the competitors who had advanced to speech finals. Come on, I silently begged, [Name] Li. [Name] Li. When the director walked off the stage without calling my name, the tightness in my chest grew as if somebody had reached in and started squeezing my insides.

When I first read stories of anti-Asian hate crimes during the COVID-19 pandemic, I felt the victims’ pain and frustration even without having ever been assaulted myself. I began investigating the history of discrimination against Chinese Americans and the past of mass lynchings and xenophobic legislation horrified me so much that I knew I had to share this history with others.

As I was speaking in a conservative Christian community, I got used to hearing startled “ohs” when I told people the subject of my speech. Even though some people told me to lighten it up, I didn’t want to water down my message when it meant so much to me. I shared childhood stories that I never told people. My shocked friend exclaiming, “You’re Chinese? I thought you were normal!”. My karate partner making me pronounce my “R”s and then saying in confusion, “But people like you can’t do that.” When I put so much of myself into this speech but only got a sixth-place ranking on the ballots, I couldn’t help wondering—did anyone even hear me?

Still, I was determined to keep going. At the Regional Championship, things would finally change. People would finally understand me and I would walk across the stage amid a thunder of applause to receive a 1st-place trophy. But there I sat slumped in my chair while everybody cheered and high-fived. Tears began streaming through my carefully applied eyeliner. Then, my friend reached out and wrapped me in a tight hug.

“It’s okay to cry,” she murmured in my ear. More and more of my friends surrounded me. They embraced me even as my tears left wet marks on their blazers. They comforted me even when they had their own speeches to practice. I tried to shove down my tears but the more love I felt, the more violent my sobs grew.

When we drove home from the tournament, I remembered a mom coming up to me and telling me that her friend had been moved to tears by my speech. I remembered another ballot telling me I would never know how much my speech meant to her. Maybe it only touched a few people, but those moments still mattered.

I would end this season with only a few small medals but those judges, listening to me, felt the passion I felt. My friends, showing love to me, felt the heartbreak I felt. Through their feeling, they helped me feel heard. I often resented the people uncomfortable with my message because I couldn’t comprehend why they would be. To free myself from this bitterness, I learned to imagine experiences that would have led them to their beliefs and realize that perhaps if I underwent the same experiences, I would be right by their side.

Those who supported me taught me to help others feel loved and heard. Those who questioned me taught me to interact with other viewpoints and show them grace. After this season, I would never compete in this speech again but if I could learn to understand others’ emotions and perspectives, its impact didn’t have to end.

This past season, quite a few friends cried on my shoulders in the bathroom stalls. Quite a few friends ranted to me about their struggles and passions when they felt frustrated that nobody was listening. I never could have grown into that person without each disappointment shaping my ability to empathize with others.

“Stop romanticizing dreams,” he roared, his voice cracking with fury. The clamor of shattering glass and my sister’s heart-wrenching cries was tearing the night away. This was the first time I had witnessed my father's unstrained anger. Right. For the first time because of me, because I didn’t get into the university… as he had envisioned for me.

On the summer night of the 11th grade, lying in bed, I couldn't stop my hot tears from falling. My throat went hoarse. My cheeks felt numb. I couldn't remember how many times I had fought with my parents over my university decision this week. Looking at the cupboard and seeing my 7.5 IELTS certification, I didn't feel any joy like what my friends normally did. That was the third certification that the British Council sent me within three months and it still had yet to meet my parents' expectations of a so-called: "English-major student" and "future English teacher". Scoring 8.0 on IELTS, winning a grand-prize in an English Regional competitions, gaining 9.0 GPA, these were not goals. These were requirements. The requirements that secured my slot in Ho Chi Minh University of Education.

As I stepped foot into my senior year, I had always been told that I must be an English teacher. The appealing salary and stable life that the job offered in my country became the main goal for many, but never mine. Despite fights over my own agency and intellectual freedom, I was still dragged down by my father’s examples of people failing to earn decent money, or articles reporting the number of employees that Amazon had sued because a certain piece of technology was replacing a certain position.

Unmotivated, weary, and reckless, I trudged through my last year of high school. Every requirement they set, I achieved. Every class they signed me up, I passed with flying colors. Still, none of them satisfied me. Watching friends discussing their future paths and the schools that they could freely select at the very last days at school, I could only sit in the corner and gaze at them with deep envy and complete helplessness.

When I thought nothing could hamper me from living the life that my parents had thoroughly designed, the sudden flashback on the four-year journey of the first Vietnamese K-pop idol - Hanbin as he stood in front of thousands of fans and delivered the ending speech: "... We only live once," once again, rekindled my courage and reaffirmed my commitment to pursuing my true passions. Arriving home from the concert, I immediately erased the school that I had worked so hard for 3 years from the university national website and resumed the unfinished business plan that I had meticulously jotted down since grade 10.

The following nights of searching for baking tricks and learning the business operation complexities myself was daunting. But, the power of dreams pulled me through. Day after day, my small online business - Nguyen Hoang bakery - gradually witnessed from a familiar face to familiar faces. The beaming smiles and rushing words as I handed my customer her orders one day: "Hey, we love your cakes. They're amazing," finally made me feel me.

Now, typing out these words as I wrap up this essay, I felt nothing other than free. Headlines about the increased salary that English majors would gain after graduation that my dad sends me every day, or comments telling me thoughtless no longer stop me from trying. Risking a stable future that the English teacher offers in exchange for a blurred vision of 10 years ahead seems unsmart, but I know, living a one-tracked life and one day ending it up with what-ifs is even more absurd and wasteful. So, as long as I "live", I will continue to dream, remake my stories, and fill it with lessons and growth.

Here’s the story of my 80-year-old roommate and I:

Grief first visited when I was six years old. My grandfather, my Daadu, was gone. I wailed for days, desperate to have him back. My family tried to console me with words, and hugs and candies but nothing and nobody seemed to quell my screaming sorrow. A soft sniffle that silenced me in the end. It came from my grandparents'—now my grandmother’s, Daadi’s,—room. I peeked through the door and saw her putting away his clothes into boxes, clutching one of his shirts to her face as she stifled her sobs. When she noticed me, she quickly wiped her tears and offered an affectionate smile. It was the first time I saw an adult, one of my adults, cry. I realized then that my grandmother must have been hurting even more than I was. While I cried openly, surrounded by adults to console me, who was consoling her? She had lost her life's companion, her best friend, her roommate. I rushed to my room, threw open my wardrobe and grabbed as many clothes as I could in the span of my tiny arms. "Can I be your roommate, Daadi?" I asked, plopping the small heap of my clothes on her bed. It was meant to be a temporary arrangement to alleviate her grief. It’s been a decade since and we’re still roommates.

After moving the rest of my clothes into Daadu’s space in the closet, I snuck in some color into the minimalist gray room. I started with replacing the wilting funeral flowers with my story books. Noticing Daadi smile at these new additions, I left my toys around in the room for her like little landmines of love when I was away at school. Back from school, I accustomed myself to the constant faint babble of the news channel on the television, the aroma of fresh cups of tea every other hour, and the sunlight seeping through the tall windows. Our nighttime routines coalesced onto a shared bathroom countertop. The monotone bathroom was splashed with colorful hair clips, hairbrushes, and toothbrushes. In a month, the room went from theirs to hers to ours. Learning that my grandmother was grieving made me notice my parents’ grief too. A furrow had settled between their eyebrows. Despite her own grief, I saw how Daadi comforted them and I saw the strength of her compassion and resilience. I learned how, even in the depths of sorrow, we can find strength in caring for one another. It was in attempts to make my parents smile during those bleak weeks that I found my goofy sense of humor. So many of my personality traits are inherited from Daadi. The million-dollar confidence-boosting smile she flashes everyone she meets is a gift I frequently use. Everyone remarked on my newfound extroversion after moving in with Daadi. She is the genesis of my passion for theater. Noticing my newly developed goofy antics, she joined in and began delivering the day's newspaper headlines, adopting the persona of an irate news anchor. Mimicking her, got me both behind a newspaper, to keep myself informed, and in front of an audience, to keep them entertained.

As the months passed, grief slowly unclenched its grip on our hearts, and Daadi and I became inseparable. She taught me how to make parathas and I taught her how to make a sundae. The teamwork forged during the covert mission to dissipate sadness after Daadu’s passing took on a new purpose when we decided to channel our synergy as cooks to start a community kitchen in Daadu’s honor. Every Saturday we cooked and served meals to people living in poverty. A decade later, this tradition lives on and we now feed nearly 300 people each week. As I make space in my heart for new roommates, I hope they teach me new shades of resilience, compassion and joy just like my first, 80-year-old roommate.

‘ I bet you with a ticket to the US Open that you can’t beat me in this tiebreak. ’ My father declared, standing before me with his posture casually crossed, his familiar grin a tempting wager. "Sure, bring it on!" I didn't hesitate for a second to shout out, despite lying on the sunbaked court gasping for breath.

I’ve always known I can't beat him. The disparity in our physical strength and his lifetime of tennis experience makes it almost impossible. This wasn’t the first time he’d dangled a tempting wager in front of me. ‘I bet you with a new iPhone…’, ‘I bet you with a PS5…’, ‘I bet you with a trip to Europe…’, whenever I am exhausted or not having my mood of playing game with him, he always offered me with the most desirable items that I cannot say no to.

In our family, physical activity is a way of life, and tennis has become a cherished weekly tradition - play a hearty game with my parents and little brother after busy school schedules, and feel the dopamine rushing in while watching matches with my dad. More importantly, My admiration for Djokovic, which began when I was six, has fueled my desire to persist not only on the tennis court under the blazing 40-degree sun but also in other aspects of my life, like pushing through a challenging biology experiment that kept me up all night or mastering a new sport like sailing. "How did you manage to keep practicing for so long? You weren’t like this." my mom would often “troll” me, and my answer was always the same: "Because of the bets my dad made."

Then came the day of my first formal regional match, where I faced an African-American girl who was clearly a formidable opponent. The first moment I saw her serve, I knew I was not going to win this game. I gazed at my father to look for some comfort, asking, ‘why don’t you make a bet with me this time to give me some motivation? I am doomed to lose anyway.’ ‘The real trick of betting is that it gives you the power and motivation to push through a tough battle. Just remember what I said about how to adjust your mindset.’ said my dad.

The moment I stepped onto the court, I looked at that girl. Her eyes full of confidence, but I was also determined. ‘Be focused, excited, and relaxed.’ The familiar words echoed in my ears holding my body and spirit up and prepared me for the battle. I wiped the sweat from my hands onto my pants, as if shedding the stress, and gave my body a shake to clear my mind. With a sense of ritual, I would often reflect on my past conversations with my dad, almost like a mantra. He’d always ask me, “What’s out there to lose, other than this game?” What matters is the ball I am holding, every hit I try, and every time I pushed myself to run as fast as I can and stretch my arms to reach as far as I can. ‘Play point by point’ It was as if I could see my dad on the sidelines, telling me, "Play point by point." I kept fighting, holding onto every point.

Progressed into high school, weekly family game turned into monthly. But every time before test week, I would step onto the court as I felt myself constrained in the narrow focus and tennis was the only time my nose came out of the pile of schoolwork. I would put my head into a basket of balls to smell them before the games to feel the familiar item surrounding me. During the game, I forced myself to forget about the upcomings but focus on the going-ons. Those questions I got wrong under pressure felt like the shots that didn’t clear the net. But just like I wouldn’t stop practicing because of one missed shot, I won’t give up because of a few mistakes.

After the game, I’d lie on the court, watching the clouds drift by, greedily inhaling the aroma from the barbecue grill nearby. Free as a bird, my breath would gradually even out, a reminder that I’m exactly where I need to be.

Crossing the Pacific gave life to the pebbles. The unassuming flat disks that I had grown up with now took up ornate forms of soldiers and horses and royalty. I grew up playing weiqi, named “Go” in English, a traditional Chinese strategy game played on a 19 by 19 grid, with each player placing black or white stones to secure territory by surrounding space with a wall of stones. The complexity of the strategy, despite the simplicity of the game, fascinated me. Low-hanging trees would shelter the park from the summer rays of Shanghai as I pondered my moves. Locals often gathered around, some taking turns playing against me, curious to see an outsider play their game. However, I struggled to find weiqi players in Dallas. My mother was too busy raising me alone, and besides I had far surpassed her skill. In school, few had even heard of Go, and when combined with my innate reclusiveness, my search was futile.

My search came to an unexpected end. In the library, I found two opponents seated across from each other like countless times before. Yet, the pieces they played with were in the shape of elegant figures, a far cry from the mundane pebbles I was familiar with. As I watched the battle between the two generals commanding their armies, I became entranced by the game of chess. I’d learned the rules before, but I failed to see its similarity to Go.

The display I witnessed demonstrated simple mechanics woven into delicate, beautiful strategies. This was my calling, the medium by which I could again practice the art of strategy. I studied the intricacies, finding connections with Go everywhere I looked. Openings were not far off josekis, and while territory does not directly win, extra space leads to advantageous positions.

My transition from Go to chess was more to me than simply finding a new game to play; rather, it was a new outlet for creative expression. Every game is different, each with new problems to solve, generating new ideas, new lines to calculate.

The freedom to challenge norms and test novel ideas in unique positions defines the game, and victory falls to whoever outwits their opponent with creative planning. It also served as my bridge between the two cultures I struggled to reconcile. On one end was my conventional mother, raising me to follow the societal expectations of her traditions. On the other, I had to observe others and learn the expectations of American society, without the guidance of someone already familiar with that culture. This largely contributed to my feelings of isolation, as I struggled to connect with others, with whom I lacked commonalities.

I tended to stick with students of similar upbringing. With chess, however, I finally found a way to expand my social horizons. After chemistry class one day, someone I had met while playing chess asked me if I could tutor him. Off we went to the library where I answered his questions, explaining concepts he didn’t quite understand in a new light. As I finished up, someone else I didn’t know asked my friend if he had time for a game of Magic: The Gathering.

I stuck around to watch the game, and the strategy of the game piqued my interest. They taught me how to play, introducing me to many friends who shared this hobby. Another acquaintance from chess introduced my rowing team, enabling me to communicate more effectively with my teammates.

Fellow athletes started asking me for help with academics, which I readily supplied.

As my friends taught me the expectations of American society, I shared my culture with them as well: weiqi. The black-and-white pieces showed the division between yin and yang. The nine star points were the constellations of the sky, and the square board was the map of the world. As I dusted off the panel, it appeared larger than in my memory, as if the world had expanded—at least, my world had.

Dead grass stuck to my shoes, the smell of poop, and the blazing sun - a painful scene but a fate I had chosen for myself: the barn. Inspired by Zendaya's Lancôme Idôle ad in middle school, I became obsessed with horseback riding, convincing my parents to let me take riding lessons.

Riding started as a fantasy that I yearned to bring to life. Lessons began with brushing, scooping poop, and cleaning hooves while enduring kicks from distrustful horses with only ten minutes on horseback after all the grunt work. My fantasy disappeared. Frequently bruised from horse-kicks, I found myself ambivalent. Was all the hard labor and bruises worth learning this new skill? I chose to continue.

After two months, my favorite horse, Fiona, finally licked and nibbled me affectionately. I was ecstatic and felt accepted in the "horse-world." Our bond started growing. Fiona fidgets if harnessed incorrectly. When she raises her hind leg, I give her space. When she swishes her tail while riding, she is focusing. I understand Fiona; I often talk to her. I also understand people, even when silent. When Nathaniel, my choir best friend, smiled sheepishly as someone in the mall addressed him with the "F-slur," I hugged him.

I thought of Nathaniel while reading the "Amma's Ashes" script. The story's LGBTQ+ acceptance in the South-Asian community deeply resonated with me, having witnessed my friend's struggle and the stigma that exists. I accepted the role of a teenager. On the first shoot day, I fractured my collarbone. The ambivalent war resurfaced. Why me? Why today? With a looming film festival deadline, I couldn't sink Gaya's directorial debut. But. You're. In. Massive. Pain. My thoughts conflicted. If my pain wouldn't quit, neither would I. I chose to continue. I endured three weeks with my arm in a sling, ingesting painkillers, and removing the sling when the camera rolled - my choice again! "Amma's Ashes" premiered at Sacramento's Crest Theatre in October 2022 and featured my singing. My family's silent, warm hugs reassured me of their unwavering support whenever I needed them.

After years of horseback riding, I developed a strong sense of responsibility for all the horses, especially since they couldn't verbally express themselves. Once, I noticed Fiona's poop had an abnormal color, different from the usual brown. Alarmed, I called my trainer, Nicole, to check if a vet visit was necessary. "This looks bad," she replied. The visit confirmed a stomach bug with prescribed antibiotics. Cleaning up the poop doesn't bother me anymore; instead, it assures me of the horses' well-being. They are family.

I first met my neurodiverse students at WeEmbrace as their music mentor as a 13-year-old. When Manav threw a Lego piece at me, I wondered if the kids would ever accept me. I felt lost. Should I quit? I chose to continue. Seeing him holding one, I played the firefighter song to connect with Manav. He smiled. We bonded. As Anurag, my student on the mid-autism spectrum, performed on stage for the first time last year, a huge milestone, his mom and I celebrated together, tearfully. Like my horses, the kids have accepted me as their own, teaching me a deep sense of empathy while promoting inclusivity in my community.

For years, I've dedicated myself to horseback riding, my favorite weekend activity, which has helped me navigate other activities, instilling values earned from riding. Started with a Zendaya-esque vision, gradually and unknowingly Zendaya went out of the picture at some juncture of my journey, giving way to prioritizing commitment, resilience, patience, and perseverance over the illusion of glamor. From being the first horseback rider in my South-Asian family to breaking stereotypical academic expectations and entering the cinematic and musical spotlight, I aim to pioneer inclusive spaces while achieving my goals. As I move to bigger stages, rather than being "kicked," or "breaking my collarbone," I look forward to "breaking a leg."

**Essay:**

From the palm of my hand, the little golden face of Mao Zedong grinned up at me. I looked from the infamous dictator to my Grandfather. “Happy thirteenth birthday,” he beamed. I had only known him through my father’s stories of his illustrious photojournalism career during China’s Cultural Revolution. Now, a man who seemed like just a shadow of those stories moved in with us. Irritable and stubborn, he was deeply skeptical of the modern world around him, always fearing that something terrible was around the corner. I had hoped gifting me the Mao pin—the man behind atrocities he once captured—was part of some twisted joke.

Once my Grandfather returned to China, monthly FaceTimes became mandatory under my parents’ obligation. As his Alzheimer’s worsened, anything beyond his bad attitude seemed unsalvageable. It wasn’t until we touched on the Chinese Cultural Revolution in World History class that I thought to ask about his photographs. Then, like I had unlocked a time capsule, he shared not only his own experiences but also the stories of those he had captured through his lens, recounting the horrors, despair, and joys with the same vividness as the images themselves.

Despite not understanding all of his Chinese, I felt the emotions behind his words, detailing conflicts that I had yet to understand but desperately wanted to grasp. Seeing how my genuine curiosity was enough to brighten his mood, I realized what I was once quick to judge as stubbornness was really a testament to his resilience. At times, his justifications for the regime's atrocities as mere “bad decisions” challenged my empathy for him. Still, I admired his unwavering compassion for those he encountered. I refrained from debating him, choosing to listen and observe despite my misgivings; I aimed to offer understanding.

I turned to my own research as I tried to grapple with the complexities of my Grandfather’s past. When I began to share the conclusions, my peers struggled to understand how I could empathize with my grandfather; others were perplexed by the contradictions in his views. I had expected other people to “get it” like I finally had, but I soon realized that cultivating empathy in others was an even greater challenge than in myself. As I engaged with their perspectives, I saw reflections of my own past judgments, I came to understand that empathy and understanding required persistent selflessness to guide others towards it.

The hard truth was that there are no easy answers or clear-cut judgments; rather, empathy doesn't require agreement, and understanding doesn't necessitate endorsement. My grandfather’s photographs told the stories of individuals amidst historical upheaval, reminding me that no contribution is too small when it carries the weight of human experience. I found reasons to talk to peers that I had never interacted with before, while volunteering at local conventions to pay closer attention to the people I interacted with, fueled by a desire to unlock the intricacies of each individual.

My grandfather was never a conventional hero. Understanding the complexity of his character, I see firsthand how resilience can take different forms. My grandfather ensured that the truth would endure no matter his own beliefs. I strive to add my voice to the larger narrative, not to overpower, but to uplift those who are often unheard. I carry forward my grandfather’s dedication to truth, embracing a more vocal role that honors the same resilience he demonstrated. I speak out, but with the understanding that true change is rooted in empathy. My voice is not a contradiction of his silence, but a continuation of his legacy.

I keep his pins among pastel notes, friendship bracelets, and miniature trinkets in my pink cardboard memory box. Each time I add a new memento, Mao Zedong’s golden face greets me with a grin, reminding me that true understanding is an ongoing journey, not a final destination.

I could easily sense my grandparents' overt favoritism towards my aunt because she earned more money than my father. Tet holiday, a time usually filled with fireworks and laughter, turned into a haunting memory for me. Hidden behind the old wooden door, I witnessed a heated argument between my father and grandparents. He expressed his feelings of being unfairly treated and disrespected as both an older brother and a son, repeatedly asking my grandparents, “Why?” even though he knew money was to blame. His sobbing voice has replayed in my mind over and over since then. Whenever that scene came to mind, I couldn't help but ask myself: Are we poor? Am I spending too much money? What can I do? Why can’t my grandparents see my father for who he is? These questions haunted me, pushing me to take action.

Determined to ease my family’s finances, I devised a plan to sell something. After organizing a survey about hobbies and looking for the current trends among high schoolers on TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, I found a rising demand for festival pins and lanyards. Therefore, I volunteered as a ticket checker at numerous festivals. Thus, I acquired discounted or free pins and lanyards, which I sold to collectors and students from different schools at nearly double the prices. In the first month, I made 3 million Vietnam Dong. This income, though modest, significantly helped with our expenses.

While my business efforts lightened our financial load, I knew mending emotional wounds required more than just money. I wanted to improve the relationship between my father and my grandparents by drawing cheerful images of him into their minds. Accordingly, while I was playing cards with my grandparents and having waves of laughter, I deliberately told them how much I admired them through the stories of my dad. Then I continued to exemplify the stories, such as how they taught him martial arts, how my grandma encouraged him to study instead of dropping out, and how my grandpa worked so hard to cover my father’s university tuition. I reminded many positive memories of my dad they may have forgotten. In the end, I saw smiles on their faces.

Concerning my father’s feelings, to encourage him to reflect on his feelings and help heal his long-standing family pain, I selected several thought-provoking questions from a book I had read called Self-Discovery Journal by Tiffany Adams, as well as some sensitive jokes to engage him in my “therapy” conversation. At first, I invited him to play his favorite sport-snooker. During the game, I talked about my life at school, shared my thoughts, and asked him some genuine questions about life. When our first game was about to end, I purposely asked him to describe his ideal family. He seemed preoccupied and slowed down his cue. I noticed that and immediately began by telling my dream family. Recalling some of our memories—like the time when I stumbled into the cactus when he taught me to ride a bike or when he lost me in the middle of the park—I told him how much admiration I had for him and that I wished to be a father like that and have a family like ours. Although he remained silent throughout, when he hit the final black ball into the pocket, I knew my “soothing” conversation was effective.

Through this journey, I realized that bridging divides, whether financial or emotional, requires discretion to ask the right inquiries, patience to elicit different insights, and the gratification of connecting people. The act of showing up, sharing perspectives, and providing “soothing” conversations makes me feel truly valued. That’s the kind of person I hope to be and these are the qualities I hope to bring to a college community.

Right before my seventh-grade spring break, my middle school closed because of COVID-19. My friends and I high fived each other, reveling in our good fortune for the extended holiday and extra time to play video games and ride our bikes around the neighborhood. Of course, it didn’t quite work out this way. After my school closed, I transferred into Jeffco Virtual Academy, an online asynchronous school. I set my alarm to start my school day every morning at 8:30, tackling first the subjects I found the needed the most brain power. First biology, then math. Without the rigid structure of traditional school, it was up to me to get my work done – setting small goals each day in each class and meeting up with my teachers when I needed help. Because I was responsible for my schedule, I also had the flexibility to try new things. In the afternoons I completed a Udemy course in Unreal Engine and taught myself Blender, C++ and Python which I used to build my game development portfolio. I rebuilt my PC and built one for my brother. After a while though, it was hard not to feel a little isolated. As the pandemic eased and the boundaries of our socially distanced “bubbles” began to blur, I was eager for something new.

I enrolled in Colorado Early College which offered a fully concurrent enrollment program with Red Rocks Community College. Coming into a community college as a tenth grader, I knew the instructors and classwork would be demanding. But I didn’t think twice about leaving my social bubble behind. My first semester in tenth grade I was sitting in my Introduction to Chemistry class, held three times a week at 8 am. I was working on a titration lab. But my lab partner was late. Two weeks into the semester and he was almost always late. I was frustrated having to pick up the slack. I thought to myself, if I was able to get to class on time, why couldn’t he? Minutes ticked by and valuable lab time dissipated. He didn’t show up for class at all that day.

Fast forward a week. I’m back in my chemistry class and thinking about how I could get the lab done again by myself. He finally shows up, 20 minutes late. Before I had a chance to say anything, he turned to me with a defeated look on his face. “I’m sorry I’m always late. And I’m sorry about last week. I work the night shift at a pharmacy, and I don’t get off until 7am. I’m really tired. I think I’m going to have to drop the class.” I was stunned and suddenly felt very small. Before class I had a full night’s sleep and a solid breakfast. It didn’t even occur to me that people in my class might be working a night shift outside of school. All I could think to say in that moment was “Its ok. I’m sorry. That really sucks.”

Humbled by my lab partner’s dedication, troubled by his circumstances, I began to see my advantages, my own “bubble,” in a clearer light. Over the following week, I reached out to my lab partner, offering to study with him outside of class, share my notes, even see if we could bring in a third person to strengthen our team. In the end, he dropped the class despite my efforts to help. While I can never really know all of the circumstances that led to that decision, I still struggle to understand how this could happen, if the outcome might be different were he in my shoes. My junior year brought me to General Chemistry I, and a new lab partner. During the ice breaker session led by my instructor, I made sure to ask about his life outside of class and to let him know I’d be there to help any way I could. While I can never really know all of the circumstances that led to that decision, I still struggle to understand how this could happen, if the outcome might be different were he in my shoes.

Nestled in my blankets, my six-year-old self listens to the soft crackling of the radio. My mother turns the dial to 99.1 FM—CBC News Radio. She whispers the announcers' words, her voice stumbling and repeating as she teaches herself English. As I grow older, I sit with her during those nights, and together we repeat each word until they become ours. I often felt helpless when my mother struggled with words that came easily to me. Sensing my worry, she would laugh and reassure me. “Tomorrow night, we will try again!” Years later, I stop my brother from throwing out the old radio during spring cleaning. It was no longer used, replaced by my crisp English and my mother’s new job as a teacher. Yet a part of me still lies in that radio.

I wonder how many other people still listen to 99.1 FM at night, reciting until the stars come out? How many other people, like my mother, didn't have English education in a foreign land? So, when I saw the flier for volunteer English teachers at the FCJ Refugee Center, I knew I had to sign up. I wanted others to learn English in a classroom with a teacher, not alone with a radio, as my mother had. Every Wednesday, in a dimly lit classroom, I labor over punctuation, watching my students learn about grammar. I share stories about Canada—explaining the cultural significance of Tim Hortons, and the best public parks downtown. One of my students, Shokria, tells me about her journey from Afghanistan, her excitement for building snowmen, and surprisingly, her love for raising chickens—a passion we both share. I help her prepare for a job interview, teaching her the phrases and questions she might face, like I once did with my mother. And this time, with experience in teaching, I didn’t feel so helpless. When she joins the next class beaming, the entire class celebrates the good news of her successful interview. Over two years, I watch my students grow and find their best lives in Canada. They will never need to rely on a radio to learn words.

As I watched my students, like Shokria, grow confident in their new language, I remembered my own journey with words. There was a time when I feared words, when they felt like hurdles too high to jump over. My sentences would clumsily clamber over each other, forming jagged peaks across my page. My ‘r’s and ‘l’s blended together — replicating my mother’s English. To me, words only existed in the morning news, weather reports, and commercials. But as I grew, so did my relationship with words. Fighting through speech therapy in elementary, I found solace in debate. By speaking about problems I cared about, I slowly mended my broken radio English. Over time, debating world problems became more than just an intellectual exercise—it became personal. Arguing that a country’s belief in the sanctity of borders should not overshadow the humanity of refugees brought me back to those dimly lit classrooms, where I taught dozens of refugees navigating their new lives. Debates about assimilation reminded me of my struggle between Canadian and Chinese identities, and finding middle ground through a radio that combined both to learn English. Clashes over the viability of ethical agricultural regulations felt deeper because the backyard chickens I raised would have been sent to an industrial farm. In every speech, I discovered something new about myself and the world.

Those speeches led me to teach debate. Whether it’s students at my business or classmates eager to learn at debate club, I want to share my words and the discovery of my voice with others. Teaching debate, whether to students or classmates, became my way of sharing my voice. The radio now rests quietly on my desk, its job done, but its legacy continues as I help others find their words. I’m reminded that I’m still that child, learning beside my mother, holding onto the lessons we shared.

I often got blisters from practicing so much, where BandAids became a constant necessity. I had them ready at any moment, so much so that I was the designated person on the team to give BandAids to my teammates who needed them. The number of BandAids I have gone through is innumerable, but to me, they represent my hard work and the dedication I put into bettering my skills and pushing myself to my limits.

I was 10 when I went to my first practice with a boy’s team. I remember the silent, hour-long drive to La Cañada. I was so angry at my dad for making me go and the butterflies in my stomach made me feel sick (on top of the fact that I was hyper-prone to car sickness). My dad tried to cheer me up numerous times but no matter how tempting it was to break my facade of anger and tell my dad about my day at school (our little “tradition” on my drives to practice), I wanted him to know how unforgivable this was. When we arrived at the field, I walked alongside my dad. I made sure not to walk behind him no matter how much I wanted to shrivel up and hide in my dad’s back pockets. I knew right off the bat that I had to seem confident and not shy away from a conflict because knowing myself, I knew if I walked on the field with a cowardly attitude, I would most likely play like a coward. As soon as I touched the grass, heads turned and whispers started. The feeling of being watched and judged was no stranger to me because of my many years of piano recitals and tests, however, this feeling was entirely different. It was probably the top 10 worst feelings of my life. In the next two hours, I experienced a new form of soccer. The way the boys played was a totally different game than the girls. It was faster, more technical, and clever in all the ways possible. I could barely keep up. I felt helpless and ashamed that to them I was a representation of what a typical girl played like. I drove home with a wet shirt–part sweat, part tears–and an inkling that that wouldn’t be my last time playing with the team.

I practiced tirelessly outside of regular practices, working twice as hard to demonstrate my commitment and skill. I spent hours honing my skills and focusing on every aspect of the game. I knew that I needed to be twice as good to earn half the respect, and I was determined to do just that. Every practice, whether it be with a team or by myself, I would tape up the soles of my feet in order to mask the pain of the new blisters that formed from the day before.

However, the actual technical part of boy’s soccer was not the only tough part about playing on a boy’s team. Communication was key. I had to be louder and more assertive to show that I belonged. Before the start of practice, the players formed into circles to pass the ball around. I made it a point to join in, showing that I was part of the team and that I was present. This experience taught me the importance of perseverance and the power of pushing through discomfort.

When I switched to a new team, I found it easier to become part of the team because of what I learned from my previous experiences. However, the effort to be included didn’t stop. I still had to continue to work hard and push myself beyond my comfort zone. Through these experiences, I learned that challenges are necessary for growth. They pushed me to improve, to ignore the pain, and to keep going even when it got tough. The BandAids on my blisters were more than physical aids, they were a symbol of resilience and determination, a reminder that pushing through pain and adversity is essential for growth and success.

As I shift my gaze, the world falls away. I am one with the wall, captivated by the intricacy of the cracks and edges in the rock that span hundreds of feet above and below. I steady myself, filling my lungs with chilling air. It’s cold up here. From the moment I placed my hands on the wall hours earlier, I felt a sense of calm… a sense of purpose. The rough texture of sandstone against my fingertips, the subtle shifts in my footing, and the rhythmic sound of my breathing electrify my senses. I reach for the next hold, each move choreography as I dance my way up the cliff face. I am a climber. While outdoor climbing is my Zen, competitive climbing drives me, demanding both physical power and exceptional mental toughness. Each competition route unique, requiring intense determination and strategic precision to conquer. When competing on the lead wall, I tune everything out as I focus on the countless simultaneous factors I must consider: The time counting down… Conserving my energy… Remembering my beta… Where to rest… When to clip… Which move to make next… Dynamic? Static? Should I be climbing faster? The wall is unforgiving; an incorrect shift in weight, a foot placed 1mm off course, or a slight break in concentration is all it takes and suddenly I’m off, dangling in mid-air. So, each decision is a fight to stay on the wall. “One more move. Just one more move.” It’s the difference between advancing to the next round and my season being over. I rely on this mentality as life has become more challenging, this past year, testing me like no other: a brutal academic course load, intense training, national/international competition, the sudden and unexpected death of my coach, my team of seven years disbanding. I draw upon the strength of this mindset to fight through and emerge improved. I have become strong. Climbers excel when knowledge and strategy are shared, realizing true potential when working together. During the route viewing period before competition, I take the lead in gathering my competitors around me to share ‘beta’ (specific strategy to complete each climb). Counterintuitive? Perhaps. But competing for me is only satisfying when everyone can perform at their best making success that much more satisfying. This perspective has been a catalyst for my personal growth, deepening my understanding of the value of collaborative effort, insightful guidance and genuine selflessness. Through these experiences, I’ve had the opportunity to collaborate with climbers from around the world, gain invaluable insight from professionals in the sport, and thus rally myself and my team to success. I have become a leader. Climbing culture is nuanced from country to country. When I compete internationally, I let go of the security of familiar procedures and comforting traditions. Will I be able to communicate effectively? Hopefully. Will I have time to warm up? Maybe. Will I know what time I’m climbing the morning of competition? Probably not. And that’s OK. I have learned to embrace ambiguity and uncertainty, thriving in unfamiliar situations. As a Mexican American competing for both Mexico and the United States, I have learned that differences are not barriers but opportunities for learning and growth. Traveling with my Mexican team has taught me adaptability and patience, being interviewed by local media in Spanish has taught me confidence and poise, and failing in front of a large, international crowd has taught me composure and perseverance. “Me he vuelto resiliente.” (I have become resilient.) Striving for achievement in climbing has taught me invaluable life lessons, profoundly shaping my identity with strength, leadership, resilience, and more. As I look forward, I’m excited to continue this personal journey as I continue climbing and embark on a brand-new challenge - college. I feel prepared and eager to engage and make a meaningful impact—not only within my university and community but ultimately on a global scale as well. I am ready.

The stench of potatoes engulfs acres around me as I wade through a green sea towards Mr. Urbach. Our hands embrace, his calluses tearing into my delicate sophomore palms. Although we speak English, we possess distinct native languages: his, of generational farming and pestilence, and mine, of technology and creativity. As he explains his troubles—"scan crops... identify blight... tedious walks"—my internal dictionary fires away, and our lingual circles of expertise begin to overlap in a Venn diagram to ease Oregonian crop loss: scan – Computer vision!
i·den·ti·fy – Machine learning!
te·di·ous – Robotic automation?

Eventually, I present my paper-mâché of fragmented ideas: a machine learning-powered robot. Intrigued but skeptical, Mr. Urbach questions its accuracy, interpretability, and feasibility. I scrawl his reservations, determined to address them. After months of tinkering with a several-hundred-line Python script, Mr. Urbach's initial concern resurfaced—my algorithm was disappointingly 63% accurate).

Back at my drawing board, faint lines of past ideas now criss-crossed into pestering ghosts. Despite my determination to design a better model architecture, the whiteboard remained, well, white. Seeking refuge, my mind drifted to art, a blue Expo taking shape in black ink—the cap, body, and finally, text. But as I fumbled with the disturbingly uneven X, it clicked. In art, I've long known most subjects can’t be captured in a single stroke. Shouldn't the same hold true here?

I scribbled a new approach—breaking crops into leaves and then classifying each individually. Once translated to code, my art-inspired architecture achieved a 99.8% accuracy. The language of art saved our project and enlaced another lingual circle to our Venn. Mr. Urbach’s next concern lurked until PhytoBot was built, losses mitigated, and hyperparameters fine-tuned. The lingering problem materialized: How do I share PhytoBot’s findings? I recalled decomposing languages as I helped my grandmother, Dadi, prepare for U.S. citizenship. I realized I had to translate PhytoBot’s findings from a language I knew so well to one Mr. Urbach and farmers worldwide understood.

To develop translation software, I revisited what re-sparked my coding interest: Python’s Turtle library. Although designed for educational drawings, and in my case, a fifth grader’s charmingly, unnecessarily coded “Happy Birthday Mom!”, it now generated interpretable maps, translating blight positives to red indicators. Instead of overwhelming Mr. Urbach with data, I visually showcased them on the farm he knew—with my teaching lingual circle, our problem-solving Venn and PhytoBot were complete. Fortunately, these very lingual circles have enabled me to creatively tackle problems countless times. That's why the “A” in STEAM is much more than an often overlooked letter to me; it’s the lens through which I see the world and its problems, the color that paints an incomplete label to be one that truly encompasses who I am. That’s why I’ve found such joy in developing from an intern to an intern mentor in my lab, guiding a team from no programming experience to a machine learning manuscript at CSYA, and introducing kids to coding at Code Ninjas. I’ve come to cherish sharing my languages as an extension of my love for the languages themselves. And although the language of technology enables me to translate ideas to reality, from my first science fair project—an auditory racing game for the visually impaired—to an app to simplify colored pencil matching, I realize now it's the multilingualism of my approach that empowers me to tackle the issues most important to me and my communities.

break·down – Object detection
in·ter·pre·ta·tion – Visualization

These words, among others, were added to my mental dictionary throughout this project. My ever-growing dictionary has continued to fire away as I’ve taken skin cancer, spatial transcriptomics inference, and drug design head-on. As I flip to the next chapter, I’m eager to continue filling blank pages in my dictionary. But even more so, I can’t wait to overlap with others, fluent in their own lingual circles of thought, to bring innovative, multilingual solutions to the global challenges ahead.

Optics is the behavior of light, and it’s also the source of my grievances. At eight, I recall deciphering small greens and red circles plastered across the test book, hiding nines and twos beneath them. After just six questions, I was diagnosed with colorblindness. I was gripped with feelings of inadequacy, but was this really a “vision disorder”?

*** 
“Here you can see the blue emission line of hydroge- You know that’s purple. Right?” interjected Katie. Warm blood surged to my palms and face. I can recover from this. Eager, young students filled with palpable enthusiasm awaited my explanation to my light demonstration.

Katie was unlike any other student I had. I distinctively remember how she grappled to understand the basic interactions between forces. Often times the difficult equations clouded her understandings to the real physical interactions. From the very first class, she fearlessly questioned how I dissected each 2D-kinematics problem, and, most admirably, asked what “sine” and “cosine” was. Through this eight week journey, Katie showed me bravery.

Every Sunday, I learned to be the best teacher I could be; endless enthusiasm and a side of detailed pre-prepared handwritten lesson plans.

***
4:45 a.m. Why? 4:51 a.m. Why? Comforting darkness and the soothing warmth lull me back to complete my doze. The blaring alarm never felt more disgusting. Flashes of the unsightly red time from yesterday’s meet sears into my early thoughts. I rewatch yesterday’s swim on my phone.

“Cold”, “Icy”, “Uncomfortable”. As I jump into the pool, these adjectives ring clear in my sluggish mind. Though difficult, I remain attentive to fixing the errors from the meet. My rippled journey is only beginning. With each lap, I replay the Youtube lessons and stroke modifications I attentively outlined the previous night. Today, I work to correct yesterday’s slow turn and implement a faster execution of the pull. However tiring an additional dolphin kick is, I push myself to do two extra.
Swimming is my teacher.

*** 
Mozart’s Twelve Variations gave birth to Twinkle Twinkle Little Star. Mozart also strengthened my love for music. My sophomore and junior years were my most personally challenging years. Losing a friend to suicide and mounting pressures of getting recruited skyrocketed.
But, in these dark moments, connecting with music provided ineffable solace. From the connection of the rosin bow that struck the soothing rich G-string to the melodic pedal that effortlessly linked dissonance, my colorless life was filled with rich gradients.

***
Colorblindness is my superpower. My superpower that motivates me to identify and connect with qualities beyond the surface. Also a gift that allows me to help others understand what they too cannot yet grasp. With compassion and a love to learn, I aspire to be the best teacher for others.

How is quantum superposition even possible? How do scientists know dark matter exists? Despite my trepidation in identifying colors in emission spectrums and heat maps, learning physics is the place where I can satiate this curiosity to explore beyond fundamentals. Junior summer, I carried out my own astrophysics research that explored exoplanet detection and habitability. Pouring over past research papers and meticulously learning coding packages, I was thoroughly entranced by how I could apply basic concepts like the Law of Gravitation to modern fields.

From black to brown hair, I bravely approach any challenge that comes my way. My fiery hues within my world have shaped me to become one unafraid to fail and give my absolute best in my endeavors. While it took much time to accept my colorblindness, I am beholden to the coloring it adds to my life. There is one beacon of light that connects me, physics, my colorblindness, and the world of my imagination, in which colors will always be in their fullest form. Through this, I have been presented with fiery inquisition and endless exploration.

On a chilly September morning, I laid on damp planks, straining to dip an oxygen probe into pond water as my Environmental Science friends gripped my ankles. The pier was just tall enough that nobody’s arms reached the water without such a maneuver. I needed to sample as deep as I could for the most accurate reading. Next, we hopped over puddles and trampled wet leaves to get to our second site. As my team filled a massive plastic tube to measure turbidity, I worried: a sample from shallow waters could negatively impact our data. I ventured off onto rocks, squatting and inching further down. I collected the perfect sample, but felt water collecting in my shoes. My friends were horrified by my leaking sneakers. We worked so hard to excel on this lab and in our class, but I wondered if our efforts were enough.

Our teacher, Mrs. Girardi accompanied us on our next expedition to the pond. We were to evaluate the ecosystem well-being by measuring the biodiversity of macroinvertebrates. We carried a pile of green rubber out of Mrs. Girardi’s trunk. We took off our shoes and shimmied our feet through the rubber pant leg into the boots of the galoshes. The sand-covered belts took an effort to tighten. When I entered the pond, the water pressure caused the galoshes to tighten around my legs. I could feel the resistance of cold water as I waded forward. While I used the net on a pole to scrape the bottom of the pond, I was grateful to Mrs. Girardi for showing me that I can go deeper into the water with the right equipment.

Mrs. Girardi’s thoughtfulness extended beyond her classroom. She spoke to me about every season’s sport, job, and class I was invested in. Amazingly, she did this for every one of her students. She made sure to avoid assigning major labs and homework during playoffs. She balanced work with fun, the right attitude becoming our “right equipment”.

My high school soccer team was always competitive, and occasionally tensions boiled over and feelings were hurt. As a freshman on varsity, I believed that competitiveness was everything: this mindset helped me make the team. By junior year, Mrs. Girardi’s influence encouraged me to find a new role on the team. Driving to games, I lead my teammates through visualization of their best plays and lightened the mood with humor. At the end of the season, I was elected a captain and received the “fun captain” regalia: the Freaky Hat, my most prized piece of equipment. The Freaky Hat is a deflated yellow and white soccer ball, collapsed into a hollow hemisphere, adorned with a screw-on plastic chinstrap. Many pentagons and hexagons are decorated with inspirational notes left by captains of the past two decades. The hat reminds me to balance my drive with positivity.

Mrs. Girardi’s lessons apply to my choices outside of school. My parents grew up in Soviet bloc housing and find suburban lawns mystifying. As soon as my feet could reach the pedals of the ride-on mower, I took over lawn care. I avoid pesticides and herbicides that harm native species. I skip mowing in May for the pollinators and whenever there’s a new litter of cottontail rabbits. My lawn is certainly not a monoculture. I mow to meet the expectations of my community with minimal harm to the environment.

This August I entered Mrs. Girardi’s classroom as a teaching assistant, eager to help this year’s class learn and explore. When my soccer season ends, I’ll write my own note on the Freaky Hat and crown the next “fun captain”. As my time in high school comes to a close, I look forward to wading my galoshes into new, deeper lakes of college life.

“All you want to do is play basketball!” My dad shouts. After storming away, I find myself in the shower, legs wrapped in my arms, thankful that the water drowns out my sobs. I’ve played piano since I was five, even placing in international competitions. With my parents’ encouragement, I dedicated myself wholeheartedly to piano. That is, until the 6th grade.My tablemates and I were Googling each others’ names, and a quick search of mine yielded “[Name] Du age 9 Sonata Op.10 No.1 by Beethoven” and pictures of me in tuxedos suited for competitions. Everyone erupted into laughter, bewildered as to why the athletic boy they thought they knew played piano.
