My cheeks flushing, I vowed to become an NBA player, never to play piano again.However, I found myself on the bench halfway through the junior season. The moment I compared basketball to a nine-to-five job, I realized that when I start new activities, I commit myself to them completely. But that fresh feeling of newly-found love doesn’t last forever, especially when challenges, like classmates’ judgment, get in the way. I had to find a way to preserve my interests without burning out. My basketball struggles during the season made me rethink piano. In the following months, I brought myself to the keyboard slowly—one hour at a time. Still, I found myself blanking out, playing with no real purpose nor structure. Why couldn’t I focus? Maybe I needed a cause, a reason to do something every day. I thought about my mother driving me an hour from school to piano then back for basketball practice and my father paying for my piano lessons. Seeing their sacrifices, I made them my cause. I constructed a practice plan, warming up with scales and arpeggios, followed by one-hand rhythmic practices in difficult passages of my pieces. Unexpectedly, I found myself immersed in the unique style of impressionist music while playing Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse, a style I hadn’t yet played. I built up to practicing for two hours everyday again, making sure to give myself the freedom to play catchy pop songs from the radio and even take a few days off. Finding ways to de-stress allowed me to balance piano even as my schedule became tighter with AP tests and off-season open gyms. The balance allowed me to joke around with my teammates at the gym and still feel energized to practice the coda in Chopin’s Ballade No. 1 afterwards. Throughout that time, new classmates found out about my playing—this time through the news station covering my pianist and basketball player balance. Showing their other friends, I wasn’t ashamed as they stumbled upon “[Name] Du(11) Variations in f minor HOB17:6 by Haydn.” In fact, I embraced the idea of being good at something unexpected. For example, I picked up cooking, even though I’m known as a klutz. From learning how to dice an “onyo” with Chef Jean Pierre to making my first grilled cheese and tomato soup, I sought out Youtube and Google to kick off my cooking journey. I was able to find calmness and alone time in the time I was seasoning my proteins and mincing my garlic, helping me take my mind off of schoolwork, piano, and basketball. As I continued reading Marcella Hazan’s take on the best bolognese sauce and watching Max the Meat Guy and Guga’s guide on steaks, I integrated cooking into my lifestyle, embracing all aspects of my identity by prioritizing my wellbeing and happiness. Standing in the shower a few months later, I thought back to the furrowed brows and loud cackles my online photos garnered from classmates. My peers were right to laugh, because it was surprising—I am a basketball player, but I am also a pianist. Although an unlikely combination, playing piano serves as a reminder to remain consistent and not be afraid of failure when messing up a move in front of the team, and going to basketball practice helps me take breaks when I’m exhausted from hours of drilling phrases. My uninhibited curiosity will propel me in developing new dimensions of my identity, and I embrace this, knowing that in college, I will pursue every facet of myself without feeling ashamed. And of course, I can always take my mind off projects and exams by playing pickup ball at the gym, playing L’isle Joyeuse (for my roommates this time), and maybe even a nice, comforting grilled cheese and tomato soup.

"5, 4, 3, 2, 1!" The siren sounded, and all the bakers stopped. Some were frustrated with their unfinished cakes, others embarrassed by their creations, and a few thrilled with their avant-garde designs. This countdown is a familiar scene from the baking competition show “Zumbo’s Just Desserts”, where bakers face time-pressured challenges in a set decorated like “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory”.

Since childhood, I’ve been captivated by baking shows like Zumbo’s. Enchanted by the beautiful confections, at the age of ten, I taught myself to bake. It didn’t matter how busy I was with dance classes, competitions, school, or volunteering. With baking, I could simply focus on the cookies I was making. My forte was intricately decorated sugar cookies. As I piped on every detail, I felt my cookies come to life. It was as if the world had gone to sleep, and it was just me working. In these moments, it was me in my element, with my own thoughts and creativity.

What began as a hobby turned into something more when I debuted my cookie stall at the Metro Detroit Youth Fair in 2019. Selling themed sugar cookies, I tasted the sweetness of my first baking profit. This experience led to more opportunities, including creating dog cookies with CombatV.com and making baking videos for the First Aid onSite Foundation. I also donated cookies to organizations such as Alternatives for Girls, finding fulfillment in bringing joy to others through my creations.

However, my passion for baking took an unexpected turn in 2020 when I enrolled in a business class. The final assignment was a revenue competition, leading to the creation of my online store 8aCookie.org. In 24 hours, I had requests for over 480 bespoke holiday cookies. I was overwhelmed with what was being asked of me, but with their cheerful expression on their faces, I couldn't say no. Nevertheless, this started to take a toll on me.

In two weeks, I single-handedly designed and decorated each cookie. I kept pushing myself to do more, thinking I was fine. However, by the end, I was burnt out. I began dreading the thought of piping another cookie. Baking was no longer fun. When I thought I was done with one order, there was a new request; I was exhausted. The consistent long nights and early mornings, grinding out cookie after cookie, all while juggling school, mid-terms, and a 10-hour-weekly dance schedule, grew to be too much. It was no longer a way for me to escape from the stresses in my life. I needed a break.

So, I put down my spatula, stopped taking requests, and finally let myself breathe. I felt relieved, but at the same time, there was also a feeling of emptiness that grew. As the seasons moved on, I picked up my tools again, but this time for myself. I thought I should try some other desserts like cakes and crème brûlée. I let my creativity flow through piping, and once again, found peace in the process. From fondant cakes to chocolate mousse, my skills flourished, and my passion for baking was reignited. While it felt good when I heard people rave that my cakes were "better than those at Tous les Jours", it was the process itself that mattered most to me. The world feels so quiet when I’m immersed in baking and decorating, all the noises and distractions around me just disappear.

There will always be moments in life when I feel I am racing against the clock. But one of the most important lessons I’ve learned is the value of finding my flow and balancing my priorities. As the Australian pâtissier Adriano Zumbo said, “There are no mistakes in life... only experiences.” As I enter college, I’m eager to embrace new adventures, pursue my passions, and find my zone in my academic journey.

Every night, my dad’s voice rings out from his office, “TIME FOR BED!” As I rush to finish my projects, he reluctantly waits until midnight before he kicks me out of my room since he understands the frustration of waiting a whole day to work on a passion project.

It all began during quarantine when my dad and I found ourselves desperate to escape our boredom. One afternoon, we decided to rummage through several dusty, forgotten boxes in the garage. Among them, we stumbled upon a half-empty storage box filled with beads and tools he had once used to craft jewelry before I was born.

With nothing else to do, we revived his long-forgotten hobby as he taught me the basics. As we created more, our designs diverged: his pieces became bold, statement jewelry, while I found myself exploring bead wiring and bead weaving. As I strung through bead after bead, my curiosity grew and I wanted to explore other non-physical crafts as well. During 10th grade, I joined my robotics team as a business manager, but I would oftentimes hang out with the programmers of the team. Eventually, they helped me become interested in computer science, which happens to be one of my dad’s passions, so I asked him to be my mentor as I began self-studying Java. While doing practice problems, I would sit at my desk brainstorming a problem or typing away a solution, but sometimes a bug would trump me for hours. Frustrated, I went to my dad for help, asking him to explain my mistake. After correcting my bug, he would sit with me longer, helping me solve other problems or explaining new fundamental Java concepts to me. He believed that passion should be reflected in knowledge, so he made sure that I knew the language fully to reflect my capabilities.

Eventually, these helpful sessions expanded from debugging code together into designing projects. During Aerial Robotics, I created a program that was able to recognize hand-drawn numbers with the handy assistance from a premade machine learning platform. When I finished Multivariable Calculus, I wanted to recreate this number-recognizing AI purely from math, and, determined to help me, my dad relearned the necessary math himself. When I dove into cybersecurity, I learned that my dad already had a solid grasp of it from the programming perspective, but his knowledge didn’t extend beyond that. So, when I learned how to analyze networks at school, I ran back home to teach him how to as well. That night evening, we watched countless Youtube videos poring over how to use various programs that analyzed networks.

However, the most interesting craft we’ve made, though, is our scrapbook. When I became the Virginia Junior Classical League (VJCL) Historian, I excitedly told my dad about the year-long project ahead: a scrapbook. The scrapbook depicts a year’s worth of events that Virginia had held in regards to Classics. I was always seen carrying my camera around, snapping photos of students studying around a table and quizzing each other before a Latin contest. When I first told my dad about the project, his eyes lit up with excitement and he immediately offered to help.

Since I knew I had my dad by my side, I took creative liberty to go above and beyond, especially in designing the cover of the scrapbook. We spent hours together researching for the right materials and brainstorming ideas. We started with a plate of wood and spray painting it black as a base. Then, I air-brushed the wood to mimic a purple galaxy splashed with gold stars, both of which are symbolic colors of royalty in Rome. With my dad, we carefully drilled holes in the shape of a constellation Auriga, which is known for its ingenuity. Then, we threaded star-shaped beads through the holes, illuminating them with fairy lights to create a beautiful, glowing galaxy.

For the past few months, I have been working tirelessly on the scrapbook, often staying up until midnight to perfect each spread. As I grew up, he ensured that his endless curiosity and passion would be instilled in my life since these were his core values. With my father’s Muse-like guidance, he was able to push the boundaries of my creativity to produce extraordinary creations. As I embark on new projects with him before heading off to college, I’m proud to call him my Muse.

It was 3 AM and I found myself standing in front of a dimly lit Waffle House in an unknown county. Upon entering, I was welcomed by the scent of slightly overcooked bacon and seats sticky with syrup. Dishes clanking, the waitresses looked vexed that their silent night was interrupted by an unexpected busload of 17-year-old boys descending upon them like ravenous wolves. For the first time in my life, I was away from my family. I just got off a bus crowded with a bunch of strangers I had only met hours ago. Was this a nightmare?! No, I was embarking on a dream experience that only 400 rising seniors in Florida get to experience every year. American Legion Boys State is one of the biggest student mock government and leadership programs across the nation. I was fervid. Having been homeschooled my whole life, I was excited to make new friends and improve my leadership and public speaking skills.

When the bus arrived in Tallahassee, we hit the ground running. From sunrise to hours past sunset, we set up our mock government, holding elections and party meetings. It was so rigorous that I got less than 6 hours of sleep every night. Even though I had never been more exhausted in my life, I kept putting my all into the program. I ran for every position I could, staying up past midnight writing the next day’s speeches. At first, I lost every election. “And the winner is Richard!” My heart sank. Not me (again). So I studied what the election winners were doing, critiqued my speeches, and asked myself what I could do to make my campaigns better. Richard had clearly shown experience for the role, so this time I gave specifics like my legislative experience working as a Page on the Florida Senate floor, and shared my detailed plan for how I would work with my fellow delegates to pass legislation. It worked! Although I didn’t win every election, the lasting friendships I made from introducing myself to new people every day, and the lessons such as resilience during failure, persuasiveness in sharing my platform ideas with others, adaptability when my original plans didn’t work, and accountability to stay true to my platform when I got elected were the valuable lessons I learned during my campaigns were worth more than any title.

I had maximized the weeks leading up to this experience by researching my legislative bill about the expansion of Florida SR-29 and US-27 which I would later present and successfully pass in the mock House of Representatives. In my preparations, I spoke with my County Manager and met with the Vice-Chairman of the Florida Transportation Commission as part of my extensive research, both of whom I knew from Youth Leadership Collier, a program I had previously participated in. My inspiration for this bill came from growth and infrastructure issues my hometown is experiencing due to explosive population growth. So many people are moving to Naples, but the roads were not designed to handle the traffic. On the East Coast of Florida, there are numerous highways to help move traffic along, but in Southwest Florida, we have one highway: I-75. Noticing these massive traffic issues has inspired me to pursue a degree in Civil Engineering, with the desire to improve Florida’s transportation infrastructure through proper design and infrastructure improvement. In the meantime, I’ve been doing what I can to bring light to this current issue Floridians are experiencing through my conversations with County and State leaders as well as with my friends at Boys State. On campus, I will inspire my fellow engineering students to work with me to find new solutions to improve our state infrastructure as well. I enjoy bringing people together to work towards finding common ground to achieve results that benefit us all, like traffic relief as I did at Boys State.

“Vehicle versus Pedestrian” I heard the ambulance paramedic say. Then the robotic voice on the overhead repeated, “Trauma, Room 16, 15 minutes out.” The announcement sent the Emergency Department doctors and nurses into action, transforming Room 16 into a war room where they would soon fight death. Told to watch at Room 16’s window, I was frozen with apprehension as the Emergency Medical Technicians wheeled in the pedestrian and the medical team prepped him for life-saving surgery. His shirt was ripped, blood everywhere, and his face was unrecognizable. My sole focus was on the shaky rise and fall of his chest, and I prayed hard for it not to stop. Before I interned at Portsmouth Hospital, I thought when bad things happened to me, it was the end of the world. My junior year, I was the last of two players cut from the varsity soccer team. I spent all summer training, not taking even one day off. I was absolutely devastated. How could life be so unfair? But, as I watched this courageous team work to save this patient’s life, I thought, “He was once someone’s baby.” This was not Grey’s Anatomy. I started to realize how small my world and my problems really were.

In awe, I often witnessed the nurses do the job of 10 nurses. I started to understand why they had little left in them to teach me. So I learned by watching. Each new trauma only meant a more complex juggling act for the Emergency Department nurses who attempted to balance traumas and their numerous stressed patients. Overwhelmed nurses mean longer wait times, which create angry patients. If a room upstairs wasn't prepped efficiently, triage would grind to a halt. All the while, I would tend to a litany of patient complaints, many of them superficial, and patients not giving a thought to their nurses’ workload. I tried to see both sides of the issue and was determined to create a solution that addressed both plights. My final internship presentation advocated for a volunteer patient companion program to provide “sitters” for patients that needed constant monitoring. This would free up the nurses for duties requiring higher-level skills. It would also shorten patient wait times and improve the systemic flow of the department.

After my internship, I requested special permission to continue volunteering, this time in the Intensive Care Unit and Seabrook ER. The nurses tell me they are relieved they don’t have to stop their rounds to answer family phone calls and escort ICU visitors to critical patient rooms and the Emergency Medical Technicians could go back to duty instead of registering or sitting with patients. Music to my ears! I knew many of my peers also wanted exposure to impactful work and more meaningful volunteer experiences. So I’m now working with a school advisor and the hospital volunteer coordinator to create a program at my high school that marries these jobs with high school students who want to be part of a medical team.

The worst part of this work for me is I often don’t know what happens to a patient. As I left my shift that pivotal night wondering if the pedestrian was stabilized, I overheard the head nurse say they would need to get out a body bag. My heart sank. The time I spent in the hospital opens my eyes to life in perspective. Whenever I don't want to do training runs for soccer, I remember the amputee patients or car accident victims who can't run. The hospital teaches me to respect the difference between pain that is permanent versus temporary. I now appreciate the privilege of living, knowing there are patients in the ICU literally living off of machines. I’ve seen families lose loved ones in the ICU, but my parents are still alive. Each day is no longer just another day, but the gift of another day.

“This app is easily the best product here!”, an EdTech professional told me after my nerve-wracking presentation. I had just presented my project LessonGPT, an app to generate lesson plans with LLMs, at the DigiCode-Ed Challenge. Despite receiving positive reception from most participants, I lost. Was it because my presentation was bad? Did the judges not like me? I didn’t really know. Just three months earlier, I had survived a near-death car accident, which left me determined to use every moment meaningfully. Losing this hackathon reignited my fear of dying without accomplishing anything worthwhile. As a highly functioning internet addict, I responded to these feelings by drowning myself in YouTube videos. While scrolling, I was recommended a video about Existentialism by Crash Course. Intrigued, I clicked on it and proceeded to binge the entire Crash Course: Philosophy series, much to the chagrin of my mom (who wanted me to study for an upcoming physics test). Growing up in a fiercely competitive Indian culture had conditioned me to prioritize winning over others' well-being. The course made me realize that, instead of focusing on winning, I should help others (using my programming skills).

This perspective shift came from combining two ideas in the YouTube series: utilitarianism, a framework that values actions that make the most people happy as the most “correct” actions, and existentialism, which suggests that we should live autonomously according to our own values because we will eventually die and be forgotten. This led me to show my app to my vice principal, Mr. Atkins, the next day. I realized that lesson planning formed a bulk of my school’s administrative work, and, keeping in mind that teachers are infamously overworked, I wanted to reduce my teachers’ workload. At lunch, I entered his office and stuttered out a few words about the app’s ability to create complete lesson plans from basic information about the lesson like its topic and learning objectives (which teachers can fill in less than 30 seconds). He began to smile when I showed him the demo and immediately called our school's chief innovation officer Mr. Dhanak to see if we could implement the app in school. We quickly planned to launch the app on the forthcoming Teachers' Day, as a gift to all the teachers. That summer, I worked on the app by iteratively organizing feedback sessions with my school's senior leadership team and writing code to incorporate their suggestions. When I made this app, generative AI technology wasn’t well-documented, so I often experimented through trial-and-error to understand how the technology worked. I found this process really fun (it reminded me of doing research). Months later, I stumbled into the auditorium as the Teachers’ Day Assembly started, worried that I’d fumble my app presentation again. At the end of the assembly, my principal invited me onstage to demo the app. I walked through the app and, when my presentation was done, resounding applause filled the audience as the teachers gave me a standing ovation.

After a full year of use, the app has significantly helped teachers, amassing over 100 users, and generating over 1300 lesson plans. Later, on November 13, I woke up to find my app featured in an article on Gulf News, my region’s largest newspaper. I felt validated and proud, which conflicted with my newfound appreciation for utilitarian existentialism. Didn’t I recently decide I wanted to be motivated by a desire to help others, not a desire for recognition? I still struggle with the constant internal battle between being extrinsically motivated by recognition and intrinsically motivated by a desire to help others. But I’m gradually learning to prioritize the latter, seeing technology as a tool to help others — not a selfish way to gain fame. At college, I’ll use the education, network, opportunities and organizations that I receive to create more altruistic technology and scale it up to as many users as possible.

The robot burned down in Colorado’s Marshall Fire. There was less than a month until the competition. During the next team meeting, the usual excitement was gone. We had a lot of things to do in this crucial final push, and now, we didn’t even have a robot. The thought of giving up was making its way around the room through whispers as we quietly stood.

As the team captain, I decided to take action; not trying wasn’t an option. Before I was about to speak, a teammate, visibly nervous, mumbled, "There is no way we are going to make it." I was also unsure, but if I was nervous, how would the team feel? Needing to set an example, I desperately calmed my nerves and managed to reply with a positive expression, "We are going to make it. We are going to make it because we will start now." I could sense why everyone was so nervous: they just didn't know where to start. Understanding that staying active would be crucial to reinstating team morale, I began to come up with small tasks for each team member: 3D-print the frame brackets, order the linear slides, drill out the side panels, cut the polycarbonate for the bumper, and so on. With a way to help, phrases like, "I’ll get to work on that!" were filling the room. Having a starting plan raised spirits, but I knew that having a physical robot, even if incomplete, would make all the difference in keeping the team motivated and hopeful.

So, right after the meeting ended, I got to work. The grueling effort was unending. Every day I would come home from school and start setting chains, tightening screws, aligning bevel gears, connecting aluminum frames, and more. One night, I woke up confused. The only sound was the ambient buzz of the 3D printer. I couldn’t see anything, but I felt a pile of hardware, then a motor. To my shock, I had fallen asleep building the robot. At least, when the team saw the progress, albeit incomplete, morale soared.

My plan was working, but by the eve of the competition, not everything was done. The team met after school, scrambling to work on presentations, practice runs, and other administrative tasks. With nine p.m. approaching and the six a.m. wake-up, I ended the session. I needed the team to be at their best the next day, so rest would be essential. I stayed up by myself amending the autonomous programs. As the hardware lead, I have assisted with software, but now it was just me and the code. Free to explore the vast hierarchy of files, I tinkered with computer vision, input integration, and pathfinding. Designing algorithms and learning new tricks allowed me to solve intriguing problems on a medium unlike anything else; in a way, it was like leading the computer. When I finalized the programs, it was two in the morning. Exhausted, I trudged to bed. My focus was on tomorrow, but I made a quick note to explore this area further.

From this experience, I have learned that, for me, leading can be summarized by two words: doing and understanding. Since the incident, I have applied these principles. When a contest goes poorly for a member of my competitive programming club, I reassure them that setbacks are normal. I understood the feeling and showed my past challenges. Then, I start practicing myself, encouraging them to do the same. I also mentor an FLL team. Though I cannot do any work for them, I can still utilize the same concepts; by saying things like, "Wow! That idea is really interesting, let's look into it," I try to convey enthusiasm and motivate the students. I hope to use my learned skills in leadership to inspire those around me on campus to grow and contribute, whether in clubs, organizations, or potential businesses.

At the checkout in a bookstore, the salesman asked Isabela, “Would you like to sign up for our newsletter?”

“Sure!”

While filling up her details, the salesman added, “We have a fun tradition here—we sign our clients by their nickname. What should we call you?”

A simple question. Yet, the girl stared at the blank piece of paper for a full 20 seconds, unable to pick what nickname to use...

Bebela? 
The nickname given by her family—“Bebela’s show is about to start!” the 3-year-old Isabela would shout, her voice echoing through the living room, calling people over. With a shampoo bottle as her microphone, she’d perform with all the confidence in the world, strumming imaginary guitar strings.

At the music competition, Bebela stepped on stage, her heart pounding. She began singing, her voice steady until—“…oops!” she faltered, missing a note. That didn’t make her run away from the stage. Instead, she laughed it off and continued her performance. 
At home, practicing with a shampoo bottle, her voice grew stronger, her techniques more polished. However, errors were part of the performance and a path to improvement.

Isa? 
At church, they called her Isa. Every Sunday, she could be found sitting in the same pew flipping through the well-worn pages of her Bible. These moments quietly shaped her, instilling a drive to serve those around her by taking action. Inspired by Bebela’s fearlessness, she founded her church’s youth band, took on numerous volunteer projects, and embarked on trips.

On one of those trips, she met Emily, a girl living in a riverside community deep in the Amazon. Toys and school supplies couldn’t hold her attention, though she was still quiet in a corner.

“Would you like to draw?”

“No, thank you,” The girl murmured, walking away from the group and sitting near the river.

“Is everything okay?”

“I feel very lonely here, there are dangerous people around in the woods and I am not allowed to play outside anymore.”

That wasn’t what Isa expected. What Emily truly needed wasn’t anything material or grand gestures, but simply a willing ear ready to listen. The words of the once quiet girl shifted Isa’s focus from doing what she thought was helpful to simply being what others truly needed.

Egídio?

The name used by Isabela’s peers—her surname. Egídio was the one who’d argue for that extra 0.1 on a grade and the 9th grader already juggling an internship. She strived for excellence as for her being flawless meant she was on the "right path."

“The committee is going well; I might even win something!” Henrique said confidently.

Egídio, however, wasn't self-assured at all, she wasn’t even having fun at the MUN. Pressure, need for an award and fear of failure weighed heavily on her. Encouraged by Isa’s quiet nudge within her, Egídio confessed her fears.

“The only one expecting you to bring home an award here is you, ” Henrique pointed out. “ Rethink! What do you really want to take away from this?”

Answering “get an award” seemed so vain now. Would achieving what she wanted to be worth it without challenging herself, stepping out of her comfort zone, or learning something new?

The next day, Egídio tried to let go of the need to be flawless.

“Let’s hear everyone out, every input is valuable”

She wasn’t just trying to prove herself; she was trying to grow, to learn from others

“You seem different today,” Henrique remarked.

Egídio knew why. Now, she’s bringing home the “imperfect” experience, full of teachings and breakthroughs of her limits.

Isabela snapped out of her thoughts, realizing she had kept the salesman waiting.

"You know what? Surprise me."

As he jotted something down, Isabela smiled. She didn’t need to check what name was written. Bebela, Isa, Egídio—they weren’t separate identities to choose from. Each one was a piece of her, woven together to make her as a whole.

“THE OCEAN! WHERE’S THE OCEAN?” I imagined the pufferfish thinking as it frantically sped around the tidepool. Crouching on slippery rocks at the pool’s edge, I felt completely enraptured, watching the biggest, coolest animal I’d ever seen in a body of water this small.

Most of my memories of the beach are like this one. Whether standing in pristine white sand or on gray pebbles, under serene skies or within howling winds, engulfed by smells of salty sea spray or decaying seaweed, I’ve always been captivated by the miniature ecosystems in tidepools.

At first, the water seems utterly still: tidepool organisms have evolved to hide from prying eyes. Only through patience would the shy critters open up to me: a hermit crab stretching its legs, a barnacle testing the water with feeding appendages, a brittle star awkwardly waving its arm. I learned that patience brought rewards. Exploring baking, I accrued experience with its chemistry then moved on to experimenting with my own recipes. My first efforts at a protein pancake had the texture of cardboard, somehow both burnt and raw, but it revealed a new “creature” to coax out. I patiently tweaked ingredient proportions and selections, adjusted temperature and cook time, and ate hundreds of decreasingly sandy pancakes to arrive at my current fluffy cinnamon disc: success after two years squatting at the edge of this tidepool!

When sitting patiently reveals nothing noteworthy, I’ll risk slipping and getting wet to flip over rocks. I sure thought I’d get wet sand in my Crocs when I founded my local tutoring organization. It took months to get past a Google Doc of hopes and dreams, because I feared wasting hundreds of hours without discernible community benefit. However, I’d tutored elementary schoolers Emilio and Vishnu, whose underprivileged backgrounds and pandemic setbacks caused them significant struggles with English and math, and watched Emilio become proficient at decimal-laced long division and Vishnu soar to reading at middle school level. So, I cast my worries aside, and “got my feet wet,” putting up flyers all over town and displaying a sign as I walked around our local town fair on a hot summer day. By advocating for my plan and overturning the first rock, I saw a squad of colorful little crabs scuttle out into view, ready to reinforce their academic fundamentals.

Not all tidepools reveal critters, no matter how many rocks you flip. Sometimes you must try another pool, as resiliently as the creatures within them must persist through the buffeting tide. I competed in my regional viola competition last year, determined to reach State. My parents had invested a mind-boggling amount of time and money ferrying me to and from lessons for years. My conductor had pushed me to new limits during tiring after-school rehearsals. I zealously practiced daily for hours, feeling hopeful when individual notes started translating into the movement of my body, when miniscule adjustments in bow position and arm weight turned sheet music into storybooks, reflecting my soul on the composer’s. I really felt like I’d turned over every rock in the pool.

Yet, I didn’t qualify for State. Initially devastated, I collapsed on the floor, bemoaning the time and effort wasted, until I realized I'd emerged from the crashing waves with a new level of passion, ambition, and appreciation for music. I waded forth armed with the knowledge that, award or not, I had become a more expressive human, ready to prove myself at next year’s competition.

Whenever I visit a beach now, I still scan the tidepools, gleefully recalling memories of discovery. I’ve come to recognize that I’m like the pufferfish, itching to move beyond my high school tidepool to the ocean. Entering the great expanse, I’ll build on what I’ve learned in the tidepool, practicing patience, facing failure head-on, and leaving no stone unturned. I look forward to moving from just wet feet to full immersion.

My mom was crying; she looked defeated. "You are becoming just like him… you are turning into your grandfather!" That stung… I stormed out, one part of me seeing the truth in her words and the other side rejecting it.

In my early teens, as a computer nerd, I found refuge in Internet forums. There, I was treated as an adult, but I unknowingly spiraled down questionable subforums with toxic ideologies. I found myself a mentor, Andrew Tate, a hyper-macho influencer. With his million-dollar mansions and Bugattis, it seemed like he had all the answers.

When high school started, I severed ties with middle school friends, labeling them not manly enough. Rather, I focused on intense workouts. By sophomore year, my classmates couldn't recognize me; I was buff and assertive. Inspired by my newfound mentor, I had transformed from a nerd to a gym rat, armed with protein shakes and a vocabulary that consisted mainly of 'bro.' I was convinced I'd found my path. I thought I could apply a testosterone-filled mindset and technology to solve any problem. However, my warped worldview led me to start resenting girls, thinking they have it easy. I began dismissing my female friends' opinions, damaging those relationships and isolating myself further.

Meanwhile, I also grew isolated from my family. As first-generation Turkish immigrants, my family lacked the support of extended relatives; we only had each other. But, I refused my mom’s attempts to connect and skipped all family tea times and outings. My self-imposed isolation didn't just harm me; it weakened the tight-knit family we'd always relied on. I projected a self-reliant manly image, but inside I felt lonely and insecure.

My mom's tears shattered this facade.

Her words were a wake-up call. I knew she was right, and it was scary. My grandfather was the embodiment of toxic masculinity. He mistreated his wife and his daughters and abandoned them to move to Germany, becoming an absentee father. Although my grandfather tried to make amends in his fifties, the damage was done.

I was terrified of heading down a similar path of desolation. This moment of truth revealed how much I had been radicalized. With a renewed perspective, I investigated Tate’s ideology and found it masked in lies. His promises of an "alpha" lifestyle were just deceitful ways of selling his online courses by manipulating young men and making money out of thin air.

I asked myself, ‘How can social media have such a powerful influence?' While researching this, I discovered that the International Conference on Web and Social Media would be held in Buffalo, NY. Volunteering there opened the door to a collaboration with the organizing professor to investigate online radicalization processes. It was time to trade in my 'alpha male' card for a ‘social impact researcher’ lab coat. I wanted to redeem myself and make a difference. I learned about how toxic masculinity often serves as a gateway to more extreme incel ideologies. I collected gigabytes of data from Reddit and built machine-learning models to identify pathways funneling young males into harmful ideologies.

This work evolved into a paper I submitted to the top machine-learning conference, NeurIPS. This research experience also sparked my interest in humanities and sociology. By integrating my interests in sociology with technology, I founded a nonprofit, Code Social Good, to create positive change and combat online radicalization processes. I hope to prevent others from experiencing the same isolation and pain.

All the experiences in this journey redefined manhood for me. I mistakenly equated it with projecting toughness and dominance, seeking respect through a macho facade. Now, I understand true manhood as internal growth and earned respect. Instead of judging, I’ve learned to love and appreciate myself and others for who they are. So these days, when my mom invites me for a Turkish tea session, I don't think twice about dropping my work and joining my family.

Quick! Pick one: rock, paper, or scissors (RPS)? It doesn’t matter which one because I will likely beat you 9 times out of 10. What does this say about me?

Apparently, a lot.

The discovery of my “talent” occurred sophomore year. My English teacher said she’d get rid of a homework assignment that was due at the end of the week. It was a 5-page paper none of us had even started. All we had to do as a class was nominate someone to beat her at RPS. I was the one who not only beat her but proceeded to beat my entire class. It was so bizarre that when I went to soccer practice that night, I beat my entire team, including my coach. I felt so “lucky” until my curiosity pushed me into researching what I thought was a game of chance.

In actuality, RPS involves observation, mindfulness, manipulation, emotional intelligence, strategy, and skill. This is according to an article I found in Psychology Today. It got me thinking about who I am as a person. I broke it up into 3 categories: academics, sports, and relationships. In academics, I challenge myself with accelerated classes. The hardest one was AP Calculus, but I ended up getting an A in the class because of how I approached studying. It’s one thing to learn problems but test taking is a hurdle for me. I needed to strategize time management to make sure I’d complete all the problems. I really thought out my approach before each test. I was generally successful using smart study methods I learned and not pushing myself too hard. Using my watch and prior to the test, I timed out my math problems, allowing no more than a few minutes per problem to make sure I wouldn’t run out of time. This meant I needed to have a really good understanding of implementing what I’d just learned. I had to challenge myself to not be afraid to ask questions if I didn’t understand something. Before this strategy, I would just hope to, “figure it out.”

In sports, I’ve been told I am “coachable.” I pick up on instruction quickly and can apply it too. I am a soccer defender. A player on another club team is about 5 inches taller than me and very fast. She plays for Columbia University this year. One on one, I learned that if she took off, I’d have a hard time catching her, so instead, I was physical as soon as she got the ball and kept her close to the line. I studied her moves enough to successfully defend her and keep her away from the net. I also learned that she is lazy and doesn’t want to run the entire game.

I try to tire her out by pacing her up and down the sideline. By the second half, she is wiped out. I was proud of myself for coming up with a solution quickly that greatly benefited me and my team.

In a social aspect, I have noticed that although I am good at making new friends and being a leader, I struggle with communication about topics that aren't surface level. I find it hard to open up to others about serious events going on in my life, which has made me grow distant from my closest family and friends.

When I realized this, I wanted to make a change. Every day, I try to challenge myself by strengthening all of my relationships by being honest with how I feel, and prioritizing when I need some ‘me’ time, so I can improve my mental health.

All of these parts of myself are vital to who I am at my core. They are consistent works-in-progress, but I know that if I keep pushing myself to overcome these obstacles, I can be the best version of myself. If for nothing else, I’ve learned that nothing is a game of chance but rather a platform for opportunity.

“Boom, boom, boom”. It’s dark and the pounding won’t stop. I’m afraid to open my eyes as I realize it’s the intruder, kicking in the door under my bedroom window. It’s the middle of the night. Where are my mom and sister? My dad is away on business. “Boom, boom, boom” the thud of the suspect’s shoe is faster, more frantic, making my head pound. "[Name]!” “[Name], are you okay? Can you hear me?” I startle with the realization that someone is calling my name. Cautiously, I open my eyes to see people looking down at me, over me. I realize I’m not in my bed, frozen in fear, while a stranger tries to kick down my door. I’m on the soccer field. Relief washes over me as I realize he can’t harm me, but then panic tingles in my chest as the realization becomes more clear: I’ve hurt myself. I remember. I went for a header, my opponent yanked my jersey, pulling me to the ground. My head hit the turf first. I have a concussion.

There isn’t anything astounding about my injury. It’s what happened afterwards. The concussion put me out of school for 2 weeks, confined to my room, no social media. That’s 14 days of no homework as a junior with AP and honors courses during the Fall semester. Even with concussion protocol in place, my teachers showed little grace. My counselor even tried to intervene to help alleviate my workload, but for the first time since Freshman year, my grades were in trouble. I admit there was a moment when I asked my dad, “what’s this all for, anyway?” Feeling isolated and unsure, it forced me to get to know myself better. Through that loneliness, somehow self preservation got the better of me and my faith provided the courage for me to keep going. Not only did my grades climb that Spring semester, but I was cleared to play on my high school varsity soccer team.

Ironically, the silence my injury brought, helped me discover my voice. I started every game and became a leader on our team. I made the 4 Freshmen players my personal responsibility, integrating them in with the upper classmen. My coach’s appreciation came with a promise to make me captain my senior year. Our season was nothing short of spectacular. We made it to the North Coast Section Championship game. We hadn’t won in 10 years. Down by one with only minutes to go, as a defender, I scored the game tying goal from the 20 yard line. That sent us into overtime. We won in double overtime! I will never forget the exhilaration I felt on that field. When I got in the car with my parents, I put my head between my knees and said, “what just happened?”. The moment overwhelmed me. Everything I had questioned before, had answers. I understood. My hard work, and self doubt paid off. I finally knew who I was. I’m the one who won’t give up. I’m the one who will continue to challenge myself, and understands the importance of conquering together.

I am a, “trapped junior”. The label comes from my sport. The inference comes from within. In US club soccer, players are divided up by birth year, not grade. My birthdate is September 15th, 2006. Most kids in my grade were born in 2007. I’m older in my grade yet always the youngest and a grade behind on my soccer team. I’m referred to as a, ”trapped JUNIOR “ because that’s the year you really feel it. It’s my senior year now but my entire team is gone. They graduated last year, leaving me behind to either quit or find a new 2007 team. I’d be lying if I don’t admit my personal struggles with the negative connotation associated with the word, “trapped”. I gave it a heartbeat. The fortuitous nature the barriers my birthdate presented had a profound effect on how I felt about myself. I never knew where I fit. Looking back, it also helped me discover who I really am.

Stuck on the second team until high school, I made a bold move to switch clubs to move to the top team. This would give me access to playing in front of college soccer coaches. The next year, a former teammate followed. She is now playing D1 soccer in college. She says I gave her the courage to try because I showed her it was possible. Still the youngest on the team, I worked hard and was voted Captain my junior year.

My experiences pushed me to help others see beyond their circumstances. I applied and interviewed for a leadership program for the non-profit, Girls Soccer Worldwide. I mentored underprivileged girls ages 6-14 years old. Soccer became a building block for their confidence; a first step towards finding their voice. I encouraged shy girls, like 10-year-old Angelica, to participate and realize that she has the power to choose a better life and escape being trapped in her current situation, forever.

As a senior, I can now recognize how being labeled as, “trapped”, actually motivated me to strive for better. I evolved as a leader who encourages others to create opportunities and not accept a one-dimensional reality.

My mother sat quietly on the couch staring straight ahead, dazed and confused. She resembled a drugged out addict from a movie I once watched. In fact, her eyes, once bright with life and love, were now dull and vacant. Gone were the moments I sadly took for granted, like dancing to her favorite Taylor Swift songs or casually asking about my day. Instead, she sat there in silence, completely disconnected from the world around her. I would look over with sadness as the Mom I knew and loved was unfairly stripped away, replaced by this emotionless zombie-like figure. This was the scene at our house after every soul draining chemotherapy session. There is no way to sugarcoat the emotions. It absolutely sucked. Cancer gets all the attention but for me, watching the effects of chemo on my brittle Mom was infinitely worse than the diagnosis itself. It was painful, confusing, and frightening all at the same time, but in many ways, it was also the spark that transformed me internally and fueled the depths of my compassion and empathy. I wish a million times over that it happened under different circumstances but the genuine concern I developed for others as a result of this tormenting journey ultimately shaped my growth as a budding entrepreneur, a nurturing leader, and staunch community advocate.

Since starting a sports card trading business in 5th grade, I have had this relentless spirit to build something great. But for me, the love of business seemed to center around money alone. It didn’t come from the lens of helping society first. That is until I saw the heartache of cancer and chemo, which led to much needed personal introspection. From then on, I shifted my focus to finding actionable ways to improve people’s lives above all else. So I brainstormed for months, intent on improving food quality to prevent chronic disease, and came up with a patent pending product that makes it easy to grow high quality food through an app driven backyard garden. My hope is to reduce cancer cases and save families from traumatic ordeals. While the business idea has won awards and attracted interest from investors, what truly excites me is the message spreading to vulnerable people, with local newspapers covering my story and social media influencers sharing our vision with their followers.

Constantly wondering why disease set its sight on my Mom and fully absorbing what each impacted person must be feeling, also helped me become a more understanding leader. I used to think I was exceptional at inspiring others. I get along easily with people from all walks of life, leading the brightest minds inside the classroom while managing competitive and sometimes aggressive personalities in athletics. But I realized I often led from the front, focusing on efficiency and completion rather than collective empowerment. Once I embraced leading with compassion, I figuratively started leading from the back, making sure I took time to understand each person’s story, what drives them, and what limitations or circumstances might be hampering them. I used this approach at the Wharton Global Youth Academy to help a team member overcome stage fright and we ultimately won best overall presentation. Looking back, it was most meaningful to see him build confidence in something that will carry long into the future.

Through this journey, I found my authentic self. I went from checking all the right boxes because they were the expected path to pursuing endeavors that truly mattered to me and, more importantly, things that would benefit the broader community. In recent years, that meant bonding with foster children, teaching the underserved about Bitcoin and financial technology, mentoring first-generation students, and coaching a girls flag football team. While I am as determined as ever to be extraordinarily successful, I no longer strive for self recognition but rather to create meaningful change in those I have the privilege to interact with. Like my mother, many are going through their own private battles and I want to make sure their voice is heard and life uplifted.

Just a year ago, I had never won an arm-wrestling match with anyone, save my 86-year-old grandmother—and I honestly think she let me win. That discovery came after my unceremonious defeat in a round-robin Math Club tournament. Determined to remedy my abysmal record, I chose to do the unthinkable: weightlifting.

I burst into the training room at 7 am the following morning. Surrounded by six-foot-tall athletes lifting barbells larger than my head, it was an intimidating introduction, to say the least. They only worsened my anxiety as I scrambled to the weight rack, trying not to reveal my total lack of arm strength. Even then, I forged on.

For the first few weeks, every workout left me sprawled on my bed, unable to move a single limb. I felt entirely out of my comfort zone. Climbing the single flight of stairs to my dorm room was an excruciating ordeal. Coming back to the gym each day was a tiresome test against my resolve, more than a mere physical battle. But still, even when quitting felt like the obvious choice, the burn of my muscles showed me that, with each set, I was rebuilding my strength in ways seen and unseen.

Slowly, but surely, I adjusted. Recognizing that the same workouts those other athletes used were not always conducive to my own growth, I altered them to myself. Rather than flailing with the heaviest weights, I worked with the ones that matched my strength, using my newfound motor control to master the correct form. When I failed to do regular push-ups at first, I learned to do inclined ones instead, slowly lowering the slope as I grew stronger.

The gym transformed into my sanctuary. Machines that once struck me with terror now laid comfortably in my grip, leaving behind familiar calluses in my palms. The first time I finished a full set of deadlifts at my bodyweight, I felt like I was floating. It was ironic that lifting such heavy weights could make me feel lighter than a feather. Every day in that sweltering hot room served as a reminder of my continued resolve.

I first realized just how far I had come on a Costco run during winter break. Getting those enormous 50-pound bags of rice into our cart had always been a two-person job—Costco was not designed for the weak. This time, however, I lifted the bag into the cart myself, before my mom had a chance, feeling inexplicably proud. I recognized then that my newfound strength had the potential to benefit those around me, too.

As I told my mom about my weightlifting journey, I thought of her severe osteoporosis. After researching treatments for low bone density, I knew weightlifting could make a difference. I walked her through the beginner exercises: unweighted squats, resistance band stretches, and light bicep curls. It was slow going, but as the numbers on our weights grew, so did the smiles on our faces.

Realizing the positive influence weightlifting could have, not only on my mom, but on other girls, I shared it with my friends at school, convincing even those who avoided the gym like the plague to join me for workouts. Together, we formed a community in that once-foreign training room as we cheered each other on.

Weightlifting is not only about building muscles (though, for the record, I have now won arm-wrestling matches against more than just my grandma). It’s about the courage to break boundaries and my resilience to continue on, even when the weights feel too heavy to bear. The bonds that I have formed in the gym with my mom, my friends, and even myself, have shown me that we are strongest when we lift together.

My journey is far from over, in the gym and beyond, but the strength I have gained from weightlifting will guide me along in every obstacle I face. I know now that nothing is too out-there if I reach for it, and whether I am winning arm wrestling contests or breaking through new obstacles, there is nothing I can not lift.

I declare myself to be a strong anti-traditionalist. 
I’m the kind of person who swaps out the typical garam masala for a dash of hot sauce in my mom’s biryani recipe. I take pride in being titled “Most Likely to Rebel” by my friend group, especially after I attended a family wedding in my Converse sneakers instead of fancy sandals. Typically, my anti-traditionalist stance drove me to avoid participating in cultural traditions because I viewed them as outdated relics. However, today is different.

In India, Diwali for our family was always an important event; almost everyone in our neighborhood--strangers and the like--would join our celebration. Upon moving to the United States, we yearned to keep this ritual consistent and replicate the same environment we had in India. I wished for Diwali to remain familiar while entering a realm of unfamiliarity; for this, my anti-traditionalist viewpoint makes an exception.

As I walk to the living room, the scent of incense fills the air, wrapping me in a warm hug. My mom hands me a diya, and as I carefully place it next to the other illuminated diyas on the windowsill, the glow of the flames reflects in my heart, making the room--and me--complete. At this moment, I felt the weight of my typical rebellion melting away. I’m simply her daughter, participating in a tradition that connects me with something larger than myself; part of a legacy that spans generations.

I stand in front of the mirror, taking note of my kurta missing my preferred neutral colors; I can sense my “Clothing” Pinterest board scoffing at my fashion choice. On any other day of the year I would have the urge to throw a hoodie over the kurta and wear baggy jeans, but Diwali is different. As I glance at my reflection, I feel grateful for this kurta; even though it’s been worn and stretched out over the years, it feels right. My internal conflict I’ve been wrestling with--between holding onto my usual identity and embracing tradition--eases everytime I wear this stretched out kurta. As we celebrate Diwali each year, I’ve come to understand that wearing this kurta is not about abandoning who I am, but about integrating a deeper part of myself.

I hear feet shifting near our house’s entrance. As I open the door, I’m greeted with a splash of colors from our familiar guests’ sarees and kurtas; their faces shine with the glow of the diyas around our house. I remember each and every one of them; they’ve been coming to celebrate Diwali with us since we moved here. Upon seeing them, I couldn't help but smile, ignoring the soreness in my face; I was unaware that I could smile widely.

As the night deepens, I step outside with a box of fireworks, feeling a tinge of nervousness reflected in my jitteriness. This Diwali, it’s my turn to ignite the first fuse. In previous years, I watched from the sidelines but now, I feel bold; I’m stepping into the role I yearned for.

My shaky hands steady out when I realize that those watching are not just spectators but family, sharing this moment which connects my past to my present. As I light the fireworks, people cheer around me, their voices deafening the loud pops and crackles. I blend into the environment, feeling more connected to my tradition than ever before as I’m surrounded by my loved ones. It feels as if everything has come together perfectly, and the feeling of belonging intensifies amidst the sparkles of celebration. Today is the exception. As I’m surrounded by the shimmering lights and my family, I realize that embracing the unfamiliar unlocks an unimagined depth of belonging.

As I reflect on this gradual yet powerful change, I set my sights on bringing the same courage to future communities. I hope to ignite belonging that inspires others to step into the light of their own traditions.

13 has always resonated with me—not for its mathematical properties or its association with social and religious stigma, but for something much more personal. My mom being one of 13 siblings is what helped me when my parents separated. I felt distressed. Not only did 7-year-old me not process the idea of my father abusing my mother, but immediately moving from Richmond, VA to my grandparent’s house in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia served as both a cultural shock and a social challenge as I had no memories there. When we moved to Tabuk, our family dynamic shifted dramatically from being an isolated unit in Richmond to joining a large extended family with 24 first cousins. Initially, I struggled to fit in, feeling outcasted due to the cultural differences and my limited Arabic. However, my Aunt Munira, the eldest, helped me adjust by reassuring me about my mother’s well-being and that we had the support of our extended family. She helped my mother find a great Arabic tutor for me and encouraged me to overcome my shyness with my cousins. From then on, when I needed someone to confide in after the divorce I sought Auntie Munira, who comforted me and helped me recognize my new role in my young sister’s life. I embraced this role, becoming her after-school math tutor and the confidant for her young dramas — the same as Munira was to me.

At 15, after settling into my new life and embracing Saudi culture, a significant event occurred: my youngest aunt, Arwa, had her first child, Mohammed. I was thrilled to be like an uncle to him. When I visited a few months later, I took care of him while my aunt ran errands; he pushed my creative boundaries in unexpected ways. He was a loud baby. He cried the whole time his mother was out. I tried everything—humming songs, changing his diaper—but nothing worked. Finally, I realized he might be hungry (he was). As he calmed on my lap, I sat in the silence wondering if a similar persistent alert could help care for houseplants—something harder to ignore than a phone alarm. Inspired, I created a 'crying plant' device using a XIAO ESP32S3 and a water sensor, which plays Mohammed’s cries when the soil is low on moisture, honoring him for giving me the idea.

While children stretched my imagination, our weekly family gatherings sometimes grounded it; as I grew older, I joined the older table, where professionals shared the harsh realities of their work. Yet this year, in contrast, Aunt Areej's fintech startup Sa'ah ignited a spark in me. I found purpose in her vision to create Saudi’s first mutual fund marketplace, seeing an opportunity to apply my programming skills to make a big impact. After researching the challenges of regulatory compliance and system integration in global markets, I returned to discuss my findings. After bouncing ideas off of each other for enough time, she kindly offered me a role as an office intern, which later evolved into a front-end developer. There, working through legislation and navigating the Capital Market Authority license was more challenging than I anticipated. Despite front-end work not being my preference, I’m proud of the impact I’ve made. My contributions, though small, represent the culmination of everything I’ve learned—from coding to compliance.

The foundation of the intern, brother, and person I am today was built long before this internship, shaped by my thirteen aunts and uncles. Collectively, they were my anchors, helping me process my emotions and passions. Individually, whatever high my passions gave me, they bumped it up one octave: Abdulrahman got me into football, Ahmed taught me to drive, Abdulaziz sparked my love for math, Turki taught me to cook, Ali shared travel tricks, Ibraheem inspired my love for poetry, Taghreed helped me secure my first research internship, and Nora’s garden made me love houseplants. As I move forward, I carry their lessons with me, eager to continue making an impact wherever I go, knowing that my next role as an active student will be built on the solid foundation they’ve helped me create.

“Does my language shape my thoughts? Can I ever really share a thought with no ambiguity?” This text on a meme I saw while scrolling Instagram instead of doing my chemistry homework sophomore year altered how I perceived every interaction I’d ever had. At that moment, I thought back to all of the times I was trying to communicate a brilliant idea or some funny joke I thought of, only to spit out a completely different and considerably less clever statement. Even attempting to draft this very college essay, the same process occurred. I would think of a great idea, write it down, and halfway through drafting it, I would become bored of this unfamiliar mess I created. Every day following that, I wondered how to remedy this disconnection between the creator and the communicator and if I’d ever be able to express the mere essence of an original idea. 
I tried several different strategies to test my theory. I attempted to use weightier words and longer sentences in the “spray and pray” method, assuming that, if I spoke enough, my initial point would eventually come out. People usually fell asleep after failing to hear anything for over thirty minutes. I took my second shot by using my body language more, which effectively showed the intended emotions yet failed to share my actual thoughts. I could identify this by listening to their response, which always led to me repeating my question with new phrasing and them becoming frustrated thinking they had already accurately answered it. The back and forth drove me crazy, and I feared I would forever harbor this fundamental gray area in identifying exactly what occurred between my ears. Failures ranging from intentionally abusing metaphors to amplifying my spoken volume left me hopeless for a cure. 
That was until I signed up for a month-long language program in the Brittany region of France. I figured I would be fine considering my experience in French, but it would prove to be one of the most challenging experiences of my life. Not only was I alone in a foreign country, but I had to communicate in a foreign language accurately and effectively just to find a toilet. I was naturally terrified since I had not yet seen the solution to my dilemma and was now shifting cultures in only three flights. My time there began with me using one or two-word phrases to express basic needs. This rapidly evolved to encompass telling stories of my time there and conveying opinions on French art. I had realized the key to my struggle: I was overthinking everything. 
The solution came from the discovery that statements translated between English and French are typically quite different in content, but identical in substance, which required a level of poetic creativity I had never needed before. I finally understood that I was so obsessed with getting my exact thoughts across I failed to realize the power of thought comes from its application. Words alone aren’t enough to convey all of the ideas in my head, and this revelation invigorated a new sense of curiosity in me. 
I now seek knowledge in all forms, whether written, spoken, or shown. My interest in math became an interest in the language of numbers and discovering the message behind each expression. In choir, I find the notes to be a method of transmitting emotion aided by the words they carry in crafting a clear message that makes audiences feel just what the composers intended. Communicators long before me faced the same problem as I, and chose to readily abandon the conventional method of presentation to opt for more unique styles of disclosure. Language will always influence how I think, and there will forever be a layer of confusion in my words. However, I will no longer let perplexity stop me from experiencing the beauty of creative expression.

"[Name], pack everything now. We are never coming back." My mom's voice shattered the stillness of a humid summer afternoon. In an instant, the stable life we had always known in the bustling heart of Shanghai was ripped apart by one person's unforgivable betrayal. The urgency was palpable. Our hearts pounded with disbelief. My sister and I packed suitcases to the brim. As the city lights of Shanghai blurred behind us, we boarded a flight into the unknown.

I was brought to a boarding school in Switzerland. Numbed from the sudden change, I found solace through scribbling in my journal, filling pages with hypotheses about my life. I questioned my mother’s decision and imagined how our lives could have been different. Our new “home” became whichever hotel rooms could fit those six suitcases.

Amidst this instability, I witnessed a profound change in my mother—once strong and unshakable, she became vulnerable, grappling with the weight of betrayal. We were now adrift, struggling to maintain financial security while searching for a permanent home in a foreign land. My mother carried the burden of holding our world together, which seemed ready to crumble at any moment.

It was in her struggles that I found the strength to shift my focus. To figure out ways I could better support her, I initiated daily mother-daughter appointments. Whether the activity consisted of a hotel courtyard stroll, school summaries, or translating immigration documents, every moment spent together gave me a precious glimpse into her life.

One of the most challenging responsibilities I took on was managing my mother’s divorce case. With my mother emotionally drained, I found myself navigating the complexities of legal jargon, deadlines, and evidence gathering. I spent hours researching legal terms and even liaising with our lawyer. When our lawyer suggested a seemingly unfair settlement, I stepped in, advocating for a better outcome. I recall the weight of that moment, knowing our family's future was at stake. In the end, my efforts secured a settlement that protected my mother’s financial stability.

But that wasn’t enough. Throughout the ordeal, my mother struggled to hold herself together, teetering on the edge of a nervous breakdown. I wanted to cheer her up. I wanted to help her rediscover who she was. We joined a gym, pushing each other through every workout and celebrating even the smallest victories. I also helped her work on an application, and now she’s preparing to dive back into the academic world, pursuing another master’s degree in the States. With time, I began to understand her decision to uproot our family. With each goal we achieved, I saw her confidence grow. Together, we began rebuilding the life we lost.

Through the experience of uprooting, my feelings of loss have transformed into a drive to help others who face the same uncertainty I once did. During my internship at the shelters, I encountered women and children thrown into the unknown, grappling with fears and insecurities that felt all too familiar. As we connected, I was driven to help the families feel a sense of belonging, even in the most uncertain of environments. Through my communal spaces of work, I help organize activities that bring people together. Whether I'm serving meals or helping the children with their homework, I listen to their stories as if they were my own. These small gestures create moments of normalcy and connection, helping them regain a sense of stability.

My journal reflects my change. The pages that once held complaints are now filled with ideas on how to help these families find their footing. In doing this work, I’ve found that I belong here, among these people, more than I ever did in the bright lights of Shanghai. As I move forward, I am driven to build a future where I can continue helping others find their footing—just as I have found mine.

After hearing the sound of the tires stopping on the warm spring pavement, I leaped out of the car and raced around the vehicle to meet my mother, my face brimming with excitement. I was an exuberant 12-year-old boy delighted at the chance to get his first guitar, his first real guitar, that is, anyway. Not the tiny child’s guitar I had been playing since Christmas before last, no, not that at all, a real full-sized ax. And so, the sun shining and my heart racing, we went inside.

At the front of the local Ted Brown Music, we met a man who took us to the back room. The room, usually kept closed, was perfectly humidified and had bright, shining chordophones that stretched the walls. These guitars covered every square inch of space in the room except for a small looping walking path, so they were accessible. I must have done that loop around the room several times, but eventually, I landed on one I liked, so the man took it off the wall and handed it to me, and I played the one song I knew that didn’t require a pick.

The guitar I picked that day was a Yamaha FS-TA; it was a brown wooden color with the edges singed deep charcoal. It was a fantastic instrument that has allowed me to grow my guitar playing tenfold. Despite it being a great instrument, there wasn’t a lot of thought that went into that choice. Less research and more; I think that one looks cool. I hadn’t asked many important questions when choosing my first guitar. My second time around, my approach to selecting a six-string would be different.

It began in October 2023 when I was playing guitar in my church and noticed my guitar sounded a little tinny through the speakers. My guitar never sounded as good plugged in as when I practiced at home. And with my birthday around the corner, it was the perfect time to look for a new guitar. This time, though, I wasn’t going to stroll into the store and pick out one I liked but instead do thorough research.

I looked at a myriad of guitar brands and settled on two that I liked, Martin and Taylor guitars. They represented craftsmanship in their field and had many guitars I admired—Martin with their OM models and the D18, a dreadnought guitar that was just plain cool. However, the D18 did not have electronics and was a little out of my price range, so I kept looking. That’s when I landed on Taylor Guitars.

I was hungry to learn everything I could about the brand. I found that their guitars were equipped with quality electronic systems, ensuring that my guitar would sound great when plugged in. I also appreciated the brand’s efforts to be environmentally conscious and sustainable in an industry that relies on old-growth trees.

I looked through their 100 series collection to find one that suited me. The one I liked the most was the 114ce, which has a solid Sitka spruce top and a walnut body that gives the guitar a beautiful, bright sound. It was a perfect fit for me, and I found it in a warm, sunburst color at my local music store.

This research journey I underwent was important to me because I value thoughtful decision-making. It would have taken less effort to pick out one of the many guitars at the store with a few good reviews. Still, my new process of browsing through articles, researching a brand’s history, and learning about guitar making to find a guitar that met my needs demonstrates my willingness and desire to become a more knowledgeable person. That is the person I strive to be, and that is what I hope to contribute to a college campus.

Chewed paper is my favorite thing in the world. To clarify - I don't chew paper (even if I did, no medieval torture device could get that information out of me). What I mean is papier-mâché: chewed paper. Before I could even write on paper, Kaka, my grandfather, taught me to mix it with water and turn it into art. He engrossed me with an anecdote about NASA using papier-mâché to build mockups of spacecraft, and when we made those spaceships, he even let me use his prized hot-glue gun to trace the NASA decal on it; I felt like Thor being handed Mjölnir. FAST. Face, Arms, Speech, Time. It's how you know that someone's having a stroke. An acronym now stapled to my skin, reminding me of how we lost Kaka.

After we lost Kaka, I read countless research papers like 'Epidemiology of hypertension' and scoured websites like Medscape, trying to grasp how this 'silent killer' could take him away, leaving us to mold the unanswered pages. The frigidness of the kitchen floor and my cheeks overrun with tears, each wave of grief was like flipping through the same pages of a book over again. I couldn't seem to mold this grief into art, though, like I could paper. Papier-mâché didn't seem as comforting now without Kaka’s hands guiding me. So I focused on playing kho-kho, a traditional tag sport that Kaka used to play with his eight siblings. But on the verge of winning a game, as I leaped to tag a defender, I lost more than the match. Diagnosed with a chronic fracture at fourteen, I lost the ability to ever play kho-kho again. My broken leg felt like gloopy paper, too watered down to save, too damaged to be art anymore. My room, filled with papier-mâché wall decors, felt wistful.

I remember Kaka telling me I was like a honeybee when I worked - so focused that not even a trumpet playing could disturb me. Kaka helped me discover not only my strengths but also my passions, so I hobbled back to him. This time, I knew I wanted to tie my fondness for papier-mâché with my love for service - both inspired by Kaka. So I gathered plenty of used paper by organizing a drive around my neighborhood. As much as my leg hurt, my hands were eager to get back to my inherited passion. With twists of my wrists, I used wads of old paper to shape caricatures, including some of myself. Although my crutches hindered my stride, they fueled my drive to be better. So I decided to sell the caricatures at an art expo and allocate the funds to Unnayan, an organization for older individuals with special needs that Kaka used to donate to. I had felt powerless in my efforts to help Kaka. But my new friends at Unnayan - Arham, Mahanta uncle, Kritika - were people whose lives I could help shape the way Kaka had shaped mine. I saw glances of Kaka in them, but more importantly, I saw parts of me that I cherished. As soon as my plaster was removed, I started volunteering at Unnayan actively. The residents found papier-mâché too messy at first; I had to experiment with different pastes and bases so they could enjoy it as much as I did. Once they did, I took it one step forward and hosted my first fundraiser in Lumding, a town near me. It featured papier bowls, vases, and figurines, all made by Unnayan residents and by me. Since then, I've spent my weekends organizing more fundraisers and events, steering initiatives to ensure that the residents receive the support they need.

Now, whenever life presents me with gloopy, mulchy problems, I say "Thank you!" and wonder how best to turn them into art. Every discarded object, and each individual, has something that can be redeemed and reshaped. As for my new endeavor, college, I plan to either join a crafts club or start my own, so I can continue growing my passion for repurposing discarded items. I am excited to build a dorm community around reuse and upscaling, inviting my dormmates to donate their waste so we can build papier-maché together, just as I did with Kaka and the residents of Unnayan, and sell it to raise funds for charities. The mushy, chewed-up paper inside all of us is just waiting for someone to believe in it, for someone to mold it into magnificent cartonería.

The screen was blank. Only a blinking white line interrupted the grayness. I've witnessed the sight countless times, but the line ceaselessly urged for thrilling tales to fill the nihility. This time, it pleaded for a warrior's story. My fingers flew across the keyboard in response; as I slammed "Enter," Subjugator shattered the void with the thrust of her holographic shield.

The sci-fi fighter is a recent addition to online roleplaying, an activity I stumbled upon while doom-scrolling through YouTube recommendations during the COVID-19 pandemic. Gone were dull days as Record Player spat pancakes at the 100-foot-tall dragon Captain Suzika. Within four years, I was raining down electron beams as Subjugator against alien spaceships of the vicious Kneall. Unsurprisingly, intergalactic war was a welcome reward for weathering the 8-to-4 school grind.

But Orion, my rust-colored dragon, showed how roleplay was much more than fanciful acting. Inspired by joyful hours bonding with strangers on Discord over planning Orion's next adventure on steamship S.S.No with dragon and human comrades, I realized I (who struggled to bother the McDonald's cashier for an extra spoon) could develop these human connections in reality. Mirroring how Orion guided recruits, I guided struggling classmates through debugging fickle Arduino chips and wiring. As Orion gained confidence to battle saboteurs from Villain Clubhouse, I replicated his strength in proving the connection between the post-WWII baby boom and the rise of feminism to my history teacher, Dr. Anderson.
