Bringing Orion's wisdom to hobbies, I cracked jokes in front of an audience before my nerve-wracking piano rendition of Zenzenzense.

The lessons didn't stop with Orion: my fiery Flareon Floof, who dipped his paw into the complexities of Astral's city life after a nomadic childhood, inspired my stylus to dip into digital art after Floof became my first artwork. When my hand felt heavy with the weight of a client's art commission, reminiscing of Floof's tribulations of gaining his adoptive parents' trust convinced my hand to draw the next stroke; it was either make good on your efforts or disappoint expectations and a proud $40 wasn't a disappointment!

Sure, roleplaying is acting, but Orion's engine maintenance on S.S.No sparking an interest in my high school's robotics club was real. Orion also accompanied feverish 6:00 P.M. build sessions fueled by Popcorners as we obsessed over gear ratios and rubber bands' tensile strength for a catapult, mixed and matched RPM and wheel diameter for a 6-wheel drivetrain, and mastered double-acting pneumatic pistons with solenoids and reservoirs, all for a winning robot. Becoming team leader earned a snarling lecture from Floof against micromanaging every job like previous leaders; I consented by trusting sophomore Ricky, who excelled at coding C++, and freshman Jackson, whose RC experience outweighed mine. And when examining previous losses to strategize victory, Subjugator's battle-trained eye spotted how opponents stole our unattended triballs for their goal. After winning our first semi-final victory, followed by a crushing team group hug and hoarse cheering, a latent passion finally awakened. That blinking line in roleplay, which created my characters and their lessons, transcended into my hands to gift a desire to pursue Mechanical Engineering to improve my robot-building skills and witness those teammates' weary smiles.

As I stare down the uncertain future, its veil obscuring my next steps chills my blood like exoplanet Aqueous II's eternal winter. But roleplay taught me to transform nihility into a story; the worrying future is simply another blank screen for an epic roleplay. Like Subjugator exhaling clouds of condensation through clenched teeth as she wretches herself from her ship's wreckage, I mirror her resilience through inhaling Thoraeu's legacy of environmentalism and Ted Talks on Convolutional Neural Networks in readying myself to bear the duties of modern adulthood. Wielding lessons of responsibility and human connections in one hand and the blinking line of creation in the other, I'll slice apart the challenges of university and manifest my digital dreams into tangible realities to pen my future.

All I could feel was the relentless pounding in my head. I heard the constant beeping from my IV pump. The extreme pain overwhelmed my 15-year-old body. It was an attack on the brain. At first, I thought it was simply one of my mild headaches from school stress or not drinking enough fluids. But what I had contracted was something far more serious: meningitis.

I sat through earth science class trying to keep my focus on the lesson. I heard my teacher say that she often gets migraines triggered by weather or air pressure changes, especially in the spring. Once the clock on the wall read 2:40, I practically jumped out of my seat and took the two buses home. My mom gave me two Advil pills after hearing about my excruciating headaches. Two hours later, Mom came to check up on me with a concerned face as though she already knew I was still feeling pain and immediately took me to the hospital. On the way to Northwell Cohen’s Children’s Medical Center, I felt my heart pounding, thinking about all of the possible outcomes of my sickness. The diligent doctors took my temperature which turned out to be over 100° F. They took a sample of spinal fluids from my lower back during a lumbar puncture to help diagnose the illness. At that moment, all I could do was wait with my mother by my side to get the test results back. Nighttime arrived and the doctors told me I had to stay in the hospital overnight.

On my hospital bed, I pondered the question of what the meaning of life is. I deeply appreciated the care I had been given by the doctors, nurses, and my mother during one of the most challenging times of my life. They weren’t only treating my sickness but also offering hope and comfort for those five dreadful nights. On the third day, I had an MRI and a CT scan performed on me to help the doctors diagnose my illness. That night, the neurologist came into my hospital room and told me that I had contracted viral meningitis. I felt relieved to know what I had been battling against and grateful that it wasn’t something more severe as they told me I would feel better within the next few weeks.

Months after my recovery, I realized how fragile life is, and that I should be grateful for every moment of it. I discovered that I want to spend my life helping others in service. I started to become more involved in my school community by volunteering at park cleanups and soup kitchens. As my love for helping others deepened, I joined summer service programs to learn more about the importance of service. In my junior year, I volunteered at Ozanam Hall Nursing Home, helping elderly residents get from one place to another, whether it be to their rooms, physical therapy, the garden, or an event. I volunteered at Saint Mary’s Hospital where I led in pediatric care, working in the recreational area; I enjoyed brightening the days of the children with special healthcare needs. At the hospital, I worked with a child named Nehemiah whose favorite activity was watching fun YouTube videos. I loved hearing all of Nehemiah’s eager comments about the Marvel toy opening YouTube videos that I helped him put onto his iPad. As I read the book “Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs” to the children, I remember seeing their excited faces, bringing me a sense of purpose. Then, I thought of the doctors at Northwell Cohen’s Children’s Medical Center and their selflessness in putting their time in to serve others. Their dedication inspired me to pursue my dream of studying medicine to be able to help others and make a significant impact in people’s lives.

In the quiet moments when the world seems to pause, there is a scent that brings me back to a variety of nostalgic moments—my dad’s cologne. It was there as the rain came down in a melodic pattern that made me smile and rise, as my eyes adjusted to the scarlet morning light and saw my mother’s prized colorfully distinct garden. It followed me among the harmonious bustling of the streets, in the insults in myriad languages exchanged at traffic lights, and in the food stands outside my grandmother’s house. It remained amidst the thousands of miles in an economy-class seat with no legroom or even on the gloomiest New England evenings. Why was it with me?

Tennis was where this scent became the unexpected MVP, anchoring my passion for the sport and connecting me to cherished memories. I spent countless evenings at Amerige Park, where the rhythmic sound of tennis balls meeting racquets mingled with the distinct, comforting fragrance of the cologne under the familiar town lights. Years later, I remember my first varsity match vividly—the tension of the competition, the cool evening air, and a large audience watching from a distance. As I stood at the baseline, waiting for the serve, the familiar scent of my dad’s cologne seemed to envelop me, transforming the pressure of the game into a home-like environment. That night, amidst the cheers and the intense focus of the match, the fragrance was more than just a memory; it was a reminder of my father’s support and the countless hours of practice that had led me here. Each point I won was underscored by that comforting aroma, turning the court into a space where past and present came together, helping me regather myself even amidst the chaos of the game.

The scent followed me to Switzerland, blending with the crisp, refreshing air. Riding the angelic gondola up the mountain, I found myself in a tapestry of experiences - the chilly wind hitting my face, the laughter and jokes of my family, and the random bursts of “That's a great photo spot!”, all connected through that comforting tang from home. Although my face was numb and my brother's cries echoed through my frozen ears, at that moment, the smell of my dad’s cologne was there, an invisible thread connecting me to the love and security of home. It was in between these exciting moments that I started to truly understand the deeper significance of the fragrance.

However, it wasn’t only in these beautiful moments that I felt such a connection present. I was sitting on the red couch in our loft, when my chest spiked with a burning pain, so sudden and strong that I felt fear like I had never before. Faces filled with worry, my parents quickly measured my blood pressure and found it was dangerously high, resulting in a rush to the local ER. Yet as I lay in the hospital bed covered with surprisingly comfy blankets, I felt comforted by not only my family’s presence but by the faint scent of the cologne lingering in the otherwise classic hospital air. It was an extreme low, yet I experienced the same sensations I had at Amerige Park and in the Swiss mountains. Later that month, all the pieces came together at my physical, where I learned that I had Celiac Disease and severe vitamin D deficiency. In between cardiac workups and a few strands of greying hair, the same scent was a reminder of my family's unwavering presence through every twist and turn.

Looking back, I realize that the cologne is more than just a nice fragrance. It represents the essence of my life’s journey—connecting my beautiful childhood memories with the challenges of everyday life and the aspirations for my future. Whether I’m relishing the simplicity of a tennis match, soaking in the beauty of a distant mountain, or finding solace in a hospital room, it embodies the little things that bring joy and glee in a world that often pushes us to feel otherwise. This scent carries with it the lessons learned from my past, the strength I hope to continue to gain, and the hope I hold for the future. As I move forward, I strive to carry all this with me, a symbol of my journey and the resilience that defines me. It’s a reminder of the connections I cherish and the small, meaningful moments that shape my life.

After steering through security, I crash into an island overflowing with seats and windows: Sky Harbor Terminal 4. I'm here twice a month with my debate team— we're pirates, searching not for treasure, but scouring the airport for inspiration and a place to sit.

Friday Before the Season Opener…AZCentral is my favorite store in terminal 4, and as I walked by, a black forest ham sandwich caught my eye—and stomach. But as I reached for it, my partner Arnav shocked me with the astonishing price. Unable to gauge how my beloved $10.00 sandwich jumped to an egregious $15.00, I Google searched “price hikes of sandwiches at airports.” As we waited for our flight, Arnav and I found that the Fed had increased interest rates. Calculating the downstream revenue for owners, we realized in order to keep business afloat, AZCentral needed to increase prices by 50%.

I talked non-stop throughout the flight about AZCentral and continued into discussions about the Hudson Group and Bunky Boutique. Shortly thereafter, Arnav had enough, asking me to “kindly stop” discussing sandwich pricing, but I was insatiable. So as we arrived back home, I immediately went to Mr. Novak’s room and filed paperwork to start the entrepreneurism club and host weekly discussions. Were these price hikes actually the fault of the airport businesses or was there some other economic effect at play?

Once, a NYT article revealed how some airport businesses actually had it rough. Devastated to find out, I wasn’t sure how I could help—I certainly couldn’t afford to prop them up myself!

However, I knew I would miss the aromatic smell of cheese, so after reading countless marketing articles, I decided to design an Instagram post, giving hefty discounts to viewers.

Ecstatic to have helped out airport sandwich shops and have introduced my teammates to questions about aggregate supply, now I sail back to AZCentral in search for more treasure: a new discussion. I bring the team with me to excitedly discuss a bank’s inflation targeting policies—a footlong Subway in hand, of course.

Wednesday Morning Before the Harvard Tournament… Gulping down our Starbucks lattes, Arnav and I were frantically working on our case. When the plane started boarding, we finished. But the novices hadn’t. They were huddled together playing Brawl Stars on their phones.

I was initially frustrated, feeling it was a waste of money on plane tickets if they weren’t going to put in the effort. However, when one of the novices, Luka, asked how to efficiently prepare, I realized I was the problem. I was so busy working on my own case that I hadn’t shown them how to adjust to the fast-paced airport life.

So, at our club meeting after the tournament, I explained how to prepare through the lens of Exploding Kittens. Beneficial evidence for winning a round was like an action card, while each ineffective evidence was like the exploding kitten card. The basic idea—you only win Exploding Kittens with enough action cards. Gamifying prep meant cramped airport seats became Hamilton’s ideal prep time!

As the next tournament nears, the novices are ready (even if only as we begin to board the place), a sharp contrast from the pre-Harvard feeling of anxiety. They've turned the once daunting task of preparation into a fun and strategic game inspired by Exploding Kittens.

I’m proud that my analogy worked on them, but also that the strategies I taught continue to help them thrive in the hectic airport environment and in the tournament rooms even after I leave the club.

After an 11pm Flight Back to Phoenix… As I step foot in the bustling terminal, the scent of reminiscent sandwiches hits me, prompting me to return to AZCentral. I found my team already in the corner, arguing over another round of losses.

I don't have many more plane rides with my debate team left, and I'll cherish every one. I learn something new each time—just last month I learned about government issued automatic stabilizers for the economy! I'm proud to have convinced others of the fun we can have diving down rabbit holes and researching about our debate topics.

“Create a moment!” my coach shouts by the fencing strip. Her guidance has never led me astray, but I can’t control reality: my opponent, the years of experience they have over me, and the mere seconds left. How can I create a moment?

…On the Strip:

When I first started fencing, my favorite part was the weapon: elegant and the only way to score. I was so protective of it that every time the referee called “allez!” (go!), I would only step back, never forward. My weapon had enough of my protectiveness and broke after I lost one too many bouts to this compulsion. I had never yet dared to lay a screwdriver on my weapon, instead watching others fix them with cautious interest. Only after taking apart my sacrificed blade did I understand the exact mechanics behind a touch—where the electrical signal came from—and realize that I was limiting my fencing just to save an arrangement of springs, buttons, and wires that needed me to take action and score.

…To Do Both:

My eyes water at the bright, overlapping blocks on my Google Calendar. I’ve qualified for the upcoming fencing Summer Nationals, but they conflict with summer classes at school. As if sensing my distress, my cat clambers into my arms. I reminisce about the day I took him home, when online classes had just ended—and I know how to solve my dilemma.

I immediately open a new tab to search for online credits, dual-enrollment, and whatever else is available. Scrolling, scrolling, score! Classes matching the ones I’ll be missing. I finalize my registrations with a satisfying click.

The week of the competition rolls around. I watch recordings on bumpy flights, scribble notes with hotel-branded pens, and finish homework just in time to rush off to compete. I relish every moment that allows me to continue my academics without sacrificing my passion for fencing.

…When All Fails:

Summer has just started, and I’m panicking at 8:30 am on a Monday at a public library. I’m there to host a summer camp for middle schoolers; my two teammates just texted me: one has COVID, and the other has a family emergency.

I shoot back: “No worries! We prepped the materials already, so I can teach your slides, too.”

With my years of experience teaching online and in-person, I’m used to improvising for the unexpected. I take a deep breath and push the button for the projector. The screen stays blank. Right as I’m frantically looking for a secondary switch, controller, or anything to magically save the situation, students start showing up. Thirty-odd pairs of expectant eyes are on me, and my confidence in leadership shatters. I shakily ask everyone to do introductions. After a minute or so of talking, I see students start taking out devices, and I don’t tell them to put them away. I can’t talk for two hours without my materials, anyway. My eyes drift over their screens before I realize how I can keep the camp engaging.

I put up a Zoom ID on the whiteboard and ask each student to join with their devices. We spend the class roleplaying customer interactions, designing games, and analyzing online sources. Students discuss fervently—never a moment of silence—and I was saved from my crisis. This was much better than anything I could have planned.

Over years, there is some part of me that is still scared of breaking a weapon, limited to traditional paths, or holding on to a need for control as a leader. With each broken blade, calendar shuffle, and lecture-turned-interaction—my perception of restrictions breaks—I create a moment. I start to fence with purpose (even beating a 2024 USA Olympian in a bout!), take more opportunities to learn outside traditional classes, and lead with the goal of empowering others, stepping back from the spotlight. In challenging moments, I hear my coach’s voice, saying: “Create a moment!”

One summer evening before eighth grade, I glimpsed a tiny shadow darting through the fading light in our backyard. That’s when I met my unexpected role model—Hummingbird Mama. That first evening, Hummingbird Mama struggled to stay awake, her head faintly bobbing with fatigue in her coin-sized nest. Yet by the next morning, she had adorned the nest with delicate lichen leaflets, preparing a home for her soon-to-be newborns. Her resilience reminded me of my father, who, without a college education or connections in America, has been the sole breadwinner for our family. For eight years, I woke up at 6:00 a.m. to him quietly starting his day in the stock market, often finding him later hunched over at the dining table, defeated.

In a perfect world, Hummingbird Mama would have a partner to share the burden, just as I wished to lighten the load for my father. When I offered to help in seventh grade, he sighed, “You don’t have to do it, Ah Mui,” he said in Cantonese. “I’m no banker, you’re a girl, and this is a hard industry. Bills and taxes, you can help with. But this—my prime time is over…” He spoke of getting a retail job after my brother and I graduate high school and returning to China when he saves enough to care for our ill grandparents. I couldn’t accept his surrender. After much convincing, my dad handed me two 800-page books on stock technical analysis in Cantonese. I devoured them, journaling hundreds of pages of experimental notes on my and I’s swing-trade transactions. The market became our common battleground. My dad was right—it is hard. During a fintech research cluster, I was the only student without coding experience. Yet through pattern recognition, I learned to translate the logic diagrams scribbled in my investment journal into regression and decision tree models. Applying more statistical analysis in the due diligence reports for my dad, we saw his annual return improve from barely breaking even to over 60% for the past two years.

Sophomore year, my mom trusted me to invest a portion of her lifetime savings, hoping it could be a retirement pension. I spent three months carefully growing it by 30%, only to lose it all within a week in a mistimed Nasdaq short. Despite recovering the trade, the tension in my parents’ voices and the worry in their eyes stayed with me. I understood then that investing wasn’t about chasing profit; it was a lifeline for families like ours, navigating the fragile American Dream.

Two days before Hummingbird Mama went into labor, a fledgling who couldn’t feed itself landed in our garden, crying for food. Despite rushing to complete her nest, Hummingbird Mama fed this newcomer too—every fifteen minutes for four days straight. She taught me that resilience isn’t just perseverance; it’s about extending yourself for others, even when it’s difficult.

Inspired by her, I crafted my journal notes into a financial literacy curriculum. Collaborating with educators at Envisioneers, an extended learning provider for under-resourced schools in the Bay Area, I brought the curriculum to life as a 10-week after-school program. Over three semesters, our program reached 90 students across eleven campuses. I’ll never forget Yonardi’s high-five after his first stock report or Sylvia’s smile after her business pitch. They reminded me of my younger self, thirsty for knowledge.

One day, Sylvia confided that her family was considering returning to Guatemala due to financial hardships. I realized our work is about more than numbers—it’s about empowering communities to hold on to their dreams through students like Sylvia, like myself.

My tennis coach often teases, “Little Mighty [Name].” Whenever I hear this, I think of Hummingbird Mama, watching proudly from the camellia bush as her fledglings flutter between the poppy branches. She taught me that true might isn’t just about soaring, but building and building others up. Every day, I strive to be just a little bit more like her.

“Privilege to do business with you, sir,” I proofread my father’s email in 5th grade. Watching my parents run their cutlery export business, I learned early on the dynamics of international trade. "Walmart would purchase 50,000 fork and spoon combos at once," my father would say. "The unit price was so low, and we could barely cover the cost. But the volume… it was an order manufacturers and intermediary agents like us could only dream of."

This sparked my fascination with the global marketplace, where unequal power dynamics create disproportionate value. At a young age, I noticed how trade relationships, though voluntary, often left smaller players at a disadvantage. This early insight planted a seed that grew into a deeper investigation of global supply chains and ethical business practices.

In the summer of 2019, I stumbled upon the stock of Lithium Americas, a lithium mining company, as I explored the intersection of sustainability and profitability in the electric vehicle sector. My initial investment was purely speculative, but as I delved deeper into the company’s operations, I encountered lessons far more valuable than the eventual 300% surge. Researching the company’s development plans for their Nevada mining site, I found a petition by local residents opposing the project. It was the first time I encountered the term “greenwashing,” and I began questioning the environmental claims behind “sustainable” industries.

My curiosity led me further into the upstream supply of lithium, much of which is concentrated in the Lithium Triangle in Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina. Five years of studying Spanish allowed me to read court documents and interviews with indigenous communities, learning how lithium mining was exacerbating droughts by depleting local water supply, creating a situation where water has to be transported by truck into town weekly. I was struck by the disconnect between these communities’ struggles and the data-driven narratives in the business media like The Economist.

This marked the beginning of my deep dive into the complexities of global supply chains, where environmental ethics, corporate responsibility, and international trade intersect. I expanded my research by reading about Chinese legislation on Baidu and following manufacturing experts on Weibo to understand the entire battery value chain. I realized that consumer-facing companies have the power to trickle down change if they are willing to sacrifice short-term profits for long-term sustainability.

I found myself discussing this during office hours with Professor Malkiat Sandhu, with whom I took macroeconomics at my local community college. He encouraged me to challenge mainstream media beliefs and provided opportunities to attend seminars at Stanford's King Center for Global Development and the Hoover Institute. There, he pushed me to ask my probing questions and engage with scholars and policymakers, particularly on the disparities between multinational policies and business ethics within the value chains of battery and semiconductors. Through these experiences, I began to see how potential solutions for global dilemmas could be modeled from a multidisciplinary perspective that blends economics, public policy, and global politics.

The Huntsman Program is the ideal environment for me to continue this work at the intersection of business and international studies. The dual-degree structure will allow me to combine rigorous economic analysis while exploring the cultural, political, and ethical contexts in which global business decisions are made.

I am particularly drawn to the Andrea Mitchell Center for the Study of Democracy and Penn’s sustainability initiatives, where I hope to explore how multinational corporations can be held accountable for their environmental and social impacts while remaining competitive.

Whether it'd working as a consultant at a firm like McKinsey, Bain, or Boston Consulting Group, engaging in ESG investment ventures, or advocating for policy change from within an international organization, I am committed to contributing to global initiatives that push for transparency and equity for underrepresented communities in supply chains. The Huntsman Program’s unique integration of business and international studies is precisely what I need to prepare for this challenge.

**98.75.** The “big four” that controlled me as I entered sophomore year. These flickering white characters on the black and grey machine against the pale orange marble floor were the puppeteers that controlled four key strings of my life: confidence, social skills, school participation and sports. You probably know these puppeteers by their deceivingly innocent name: weight. A generally quiet student, I scored well on written tests but feared oral components where the puppeteer controlling my confidence overpowered knowledge. Everyone loved the jokes I cracked about my weight; this coping mechanism orchestrated by puppeteer two controlling my social life defined my personality. I distinctly remember my sports teacher, Mrs. Nilima, taking our weight in primary school and turning towards me in shock, exclaiming “You’re heavier than me!”. I laughed it off as always, masking pain with humour, almost instantly forgetting all embarrassment as the school snack bell’s chime reverberated around the dark auditorium, my cue for a daily caramel “Mickey Mouse Ice Cream”.

Covid 19 led to a nationwide lockdown just as I entered sophomore year in 2020 at almost 100 kg. The four puppeteers were ecstatic, expecting a fifth in mere days with restrictions on physical activity and unfettered access to my favourite LG fridge steps away from my room. They were wrong. The fifth and final spot in my mind was occupied by a dormant figure unbeknownst to the puppeteers - discipline. Alarmed by the fifth puppeteer looming large, he sprung into action as I decided I would use the extra time in the lockdown effectively. I began running daily, walking 100 metres for every 200 that I “ran”, dragging myself to 2.4km. Afraid to see the fifth puppeteer rear its ugly head, I repeated this for 2 months before checking the scale with naive anticipation replacing usual fear. **99.50.** I was distraught and on the verge of quitting, but I couldn’t allow the (almost) five puppeteers to banish my discipline back into dormancy. What had I done wrong and what could I do better? I called up my cousin Shaurya, who had recently lost weight, and his first four words revealed my mistake - “What did you eat?”. I realised I was merely focusing on one of two essential aspects for weight loss and adopted a more systematic approach.

CICO - Calories in Calories out - became my mantra as I realised I needed to burn more calories than I consumed accounting for lower metabolism. Instead of my favourite foods, I devoured information from YouTube channels, primarily Greg Doucette, on effective calorie tracking. Reading “Nudge” by Thaler and Sunstein at the time provided unexpected help; I discovered the game-changing idea of a “snudge” or self-nudge. Changing my snack drawer to contain less junk and more fruits along with a habit of studying for hours on end before my designated running time helped running seem like a break, an exit mechanism, and I enjoyed it more. This became an effective ally for the disciplinary figure’s battle against voices screaming for food constantly (no doubt a last ditch effort by the puppeteers to regain control), allowing me to eliminate snacks, reduce carbohydrates and eat dinner at 5 pm. The number on the scale begrudgingly began decreasing.

The Big Four’s stronghold over my mind weakened, discipline growing in stature having fended off the incoming puppeteer. Meeting another overweight friend after the lockdown at Domino’s, I chugged glasses of water watching him eat as I explained my lifestyle changes. We soon found ourselves competing to lose weight; he took a more exercise heavy approach than my dietary focused one, allowing constant mutual learning. At a family gathering months later, a smile broke across my face when my aunt offered everyone else melted brownie with vanilla ice cream barring me: “I know he won’t eat”.

Returning to school after the lockdown, far more self assured, I unearthed a talent for debating at MUNs that the puppeteers had suppressed, transforming the delegate of Ethiopia hiding behind his placard in freshman year to USG of Finance running the conference in my junior year. I was elated to share my journey with other students as deputy head boy, including students looking to lose weight and a proud badminton doubles partner who had believed in me for years. Three years after the lockdown, approaching senior year, I looked down at the flickering white characters. **67.85.** Four numbers that I controlled.

It doesn’t take much to make my day. Some good food, a supportive remark, a compliment. A friend of mine used to tell me that I had a nice smile, yet she probably didn’t realize what those words meant to me. After years of feeling insecure about my crooked teeth and enduring two years of braces, her compliment made me want to smile more. It was as if she had given me permission to embrace a part of myself I had always been hesitant to show. That’s when I began to realize the impact words and actions could have on others. I started paying closer attention to the good in people, and offering as many compliments as I could.

The concept of being able to have such an impact on others began to take root during my sophomore year, when my dad asked me if I wanted to help launch the newest service in our family business: digital loyalty card programs for restaurants. During the hot summer days, you could find my dad and I at our dining table, scavenging papers of prototypes and product presentations. In the evening, you could find us in the car, driving for hours on end to go to as many local restaurants as we could before night fell. I started by eagerly waiting in the car while my dad handled the meetings, then to accompanying him while he did the talking, and finally, taking a role in the pitches myself.

During our sixth checkup meeting with the owner of the small Thai place near our house, we discussed the usual—number of installed cards, improvements, ideas for new social media content, and more. As we talked, the owner began to tell us about his niece, a girl my age who lived far away. “She is ambitious, just like you,” the owner remarked. “I haven’t seen her in years, but watching you help me through this process makes me feel like she’s right here with me.” As we sat there in a brief moment of silence, the ceiling fan whittling softly overhead, I watched a thin layer of water form in his eyes. I learned that my actions not only have a direct impact–a goal of increasing business—but also an indirect impact in people’s lives, in more ways than I know.

This understanding influences various aspects of my life. Among my friends, I became a source of support, like when a friend FaceTimed me in tears after a recent breakup, saying she needed to talk to someone who could make her laugh and feel better. At home, when my mom told me that our conversations help her destress, I realized the comfort I could provide. At school, when I was selected to be a “Red Jacket” student ambassador by my teachers and administrators, I saw that people around me felt my impact. In my community, seeing the joy of the women at a domestic violence shelter when they received my handmade care packages showed me the difference small acts of kindness could make. Even across the world, when I found myself helping kids in my grandpa's village with their English homework, sharing laughs as they tried to mimic my American accent, I saw the impact firsthand when I was greeted the next day with a box of homemade sweets and a thank you note scribed in neat English.

Each of these moments reinforced what I had come to believe: that my actions, big or small, have an effect on others. Whether it’s through a compliment, a business interaction, or a simple conversation, I’ve learned that the impact I make is real, even if I don’t always see it right away. As I move forward, I carry with me the understanding that every interaction is an opportunity to leave a positive mark on someone’s life. And that’s a lesson I’ll never forget.

I am all too familiar with the sound of vigorous applause after a recital, with my face flushed and my mind relieved as I bow. But this performance was different. It was my first solo recital in my home country of Taiwan, a grand undertaking to showcase my piano studies over the last nine years. I began my program with works by Frederick Chopin, one crafted to intertwine the rustic nature of Polish dances with melancholic nocturnes. I could not believe nearly 300 people came just to hear me. Who am I, and why am I even worth their time?

Early on in high school, through frustrated tears and countless drills with the metronome, I confined myself to the ceaseless work toward perfection for the next piano lesson, the next performance, and the next competition. Quickly, my hands became virtuosic and my fingertips callused. However, despite my technical proficiency, a nagging doubt remained in my mind.

I had always been told I wasn’t “musical.” But I was playing music! How was I not musical? With the subjectivity that is art, what determines if music is “musical”?

Perplexed by this elusive goal, I redirected my focus from practicing for precision to instead exploring various musical facets. I was a detective as I combed through Chopin’s manuscripts decorated with penciled-in edits and melodies filled with longing, nostalgia, and pride. I was a historian as I examined composers’ backgrounds, interpreting what the marking of “loud” means to a jovial teenage Mozart versus a nearly deaf, middle-aged Beethoven. Through contemporary ensemble and musicianship classes at SF Conservatory Pre-College, I learned to dissect pieces by thinking like a composer, weaving together harmonic structure and form.

I amalgamated my studies with my technical experience, discovering how to make meaning from the collection of notes on the page. I spent sleepless nights conjuring music and experimenting to find my personal style, using the push and pull of timing and attack of the keys to craft a unique experience. I headed down unpaved paths guided by my ears, leaving behind doubts of “am I good enough?” to explore the boundless freedoms of music.

This translated into performances that resonated with diverse audiences. I played on the rickety, out-of-tune piano at my local veterans' hospital, connecting veterans' experiences in combat to the spirited “Heroic” Polonaise and bringing comfort with the all-too-nostalgic “Can’t Help Falling in Love.” Though these performances didn’t garner grand applause, it was perhaps more rewarding to see feet tapping to the beat or eyes fluttering closed in a state of serenity.

I played for my family, mentors, and friends during my solo recital in Taiwan. After immigrating to America at age five, I felt perpetually isolated from my extended family back home. As I saw my cousins learn to walk over blurry videos, they knew me through my piano recordings. My recital turned these vague impressions into concrete memories. It became a celebration of life as I shared the euphoria of the harmonies resolving after tension rose, of turning simple melodies into unforgettable moments. After rounds of applause and shouts of “encore,” I concluded with renditions of Taiwanese folk songs which prompted everyone to sing along, saturating the hall with voices of all registers. Although people came from across the country to hear my recital, we were united.

I reimagined the kind of musician I want to be and embraced the subjectivity that makes music powerful: the way music resonates through people’s bodies in countless forms, the way it spurs the tear ducts or invigorates the spirit of different people in different ways. Whether for an audience of several hundred in a concert, my twelve loyal supporters in the hospital, or myself alone in front of my piano, I make music that is undoubtedly “musical.”

When I was young, my imagination soared wild with dreams of being a fearless field meteorologist. I pictured myself chasing EF5 tornadoes, feeling the swirling winds and captivated by their unpredictable nature. Tornadoes rarely occurred where I lived, so I settled for giving weather reports to my stuffed animals. During our teatime, I’d put on my best high-pitched voice and ask: 
“[Name], What’s the weather like tomorrow?”
“Sunny!” I’d always answer.

Although I was “Sunny [Name]” to my stuffed animals, school had always been a different case. I hadn’t spent more than two years at a singular school, and close friends were few and far between. As I boldly strutted up the stairs into New School Number Four, I was ready to change this… until I got a face full of rainwater, shaken off from someone’s umbrella. I wiped it off and soldiered on, but it just felt like the first rumble of thunder in the new life I wanted to build. I felt a dazed cloudiness, passing by students with their school sweatshirts, belonging. But all these years of making friends just to never check in or declining invitations to catch up—of course I felt lonely!

There was no single moment where I figured things out, but after reading self-help books and binging numerous podcasts, I finally saw how passively I'd lived, waiting for opportunities and people to voluntarily walk into my permanently crossed arms. I forced myself to embody sunny [Name] and struck a conversation with the girl next to me in chemistry class. That same weekend, I peer into a classroom of chattering students cutting out dragon lantern fixtures for Lunar New Year. Heart pounding, I open my mouth and address no one in particular. 
“Hi, is this class K-1? I’m [Name], your new teacher’s assistant.”

As taking initiative and speaking up became easier and easier, I set what seemed like a small goal for myself: to make someone smile, every single day. Maybe it was to offer a pencil to Alex in English class or to compliment Kasey’s space buns in class K-1, whom I grew to adore. I grew to anticipate the rush of dopamine after seeing the smile, the happiness on someone’s face after I’d said something nice. Soon, I wasn’t just attempting to emulate the sunnier, bolder version of myself: I was embodying her.

As organizing fun games with my Chinese class grew into planning events for the community as a whole, I grew more comfortable in the driver’s seat—on the road to chase my own tornadoes. Being a child with a wild imagination, I was captivated by anything and everything. Why was the sky blue? Why did tornadoes only form in one region of the USA? The unpredictable patterns in the sky mirrored the complexities of the brain, both filled with mysteries waiting to be unraveled.

My curiosity evolved, and I found a new “tornado” to chase—lab research. Driven by my newfound confidence, I hungrily drove towards it. I eagerly immersed myself, not by dutifully following procedures, but experimenting to refine them. Being a positive force in the lab not only created a ripple effect of support, but also bridged the gap between surface level and creating deeper relationships. All it took was that first step, initiating that first conversation.

As I’ve grown older, my idea of a “sunny” [Name] has changed. I’ve found that my love for the weather isn’t just grounded in things like the uncertainty of chasing tornadoes; it’s the idea that life itself is unpredictable. Change is the only constant in our lives—so by seizing the moment, I’ve truly learned how to live mine. As I continue taking charge, I hope to channel that same passion-filled tornado that drives me forward—but in others. In the midst of the whirling storm, I feel peaceful, knowing that each moving cloud has its definite path, as do I.

Getting out of bed is hard. Dozens of complete 1000-piece jigsaw puzzles stretch my bedroom floor, necessitating groggy Hopscotch jumps to avoid dismantling my masterpieces. Since my kindergarten teacher introduced a 500-piece San Francisco puzzle, I’ve spent twelve years of weekends twisting and turning pieces, pleading for an interlock. Initially frustrated, I’d use scissors, leaving new tabs and blanks that artificially matched. Strategy can only do so much: starting with corners and edges impedes messy matching and delayed disaster. Why? A jigsaw fundamentally requires trial-and-error. This taught me to build success off “random” accidents, and equally important, to continual trialing in the absence of success.

One month after I started powerlifting coaching, an initiative I hoped would replicate my success as an athlete, my first client, Noah, hit a plateau on his bench press. Having experienced a similar situation, I suggested increasing the frequency of sessions he benched, as I had done. He didn’t progress over the following month. Noah’s bench was a puzzle set with an extra amount of pieces. Locating faults in his training would first weed out irrelevant pieces. Was it his sleep or recovery? No, Noah got his eight hours and never missed a meal. Let’s track all possible metrics for future data: intensity, volume, frequency, and rate of perceived exertion. My scientific curiosity also propelled me to dig through kinesiology staples, such as The Body in Motion and Anchored, to identify possible programming faults. These were like the corner and edge pieces. Taking notes from powerlifting forums, like StrongFirst, and other coaches, such as Rondel Hunte, allowed me to cross-examine case studies. Within this rabbit hole, I located the culprit. Noah’s long arms, produced more systematic fatigue - he had to exert more force to lift the barbell a longer distance. He needed a personalized program with greater intensity and lower frequency. Within eight weeks of implementing an accessorized five sets by five repetitions program, his bench max skyrocketed by thirty pounds.

Trial-and-error preaches perseverance, but also rationality. In my first East Palo Alto Tutors Interact Club session with Daniel, a 6th grader, he seemed disinterested despite my plethora of jokes and brooded about something other than learning algebra. Despite decreasing lecture time and increasing break frequencies, my efforts yielded not even piecemeal improvement. I yearned for the simplicity of short-CUTTING to force connections. Just like checking the picture on the outside of a jigsaw’s box, I sought help. After speaking with Daniel’s dad, I was shocked to learn that his uncle had passed away a few days before our first session. To make lessons more engaging and less stressful, I used Math Playground’s database of Sudoku-esque puzzles infused with algebraic concepts. I had Daniel visualize and eliminate possible numbers for each square. Even if he was correct, I proposed alternate solutions, which he shut down with a “I told you so” explanation. At the end of the session, I offered my condolences and asked about his favorite activity with his uncle. For the first time since we started tutoring, he looked up at the camera and said it was playing soccer with him at sunset. Our conversation proceeded from soccer to In-N-Out to his life aspirations, as we giggled and eagerly planned the next meeting. By trialing through possible explanations for Daniel’s gloom, I was able to piece together a puzzle that provided both profit for his learning and our relationship. Equally important, was not acting rash and cutting corners, an approach that lacks empathy and identifies minimal areas for growth.

My trial-and-error solving mindset isn’t perfect - it may be time-consuming and can’t be a solo project. But its beauty of being augmentable and incomplete allows every one of life’s challenges to piggyback on another piece, identifying growth, like how my perseverance introduced rationality and empathy. Looking at the sea of organized puzzles rooted through my floor, maybe accidentally stepping on them wouldn’t be disastrous. The journey of tinkering piece by piece grounds me to make the world a tab less puzzling.

Children's book authors excel at crafting lovable characters. But slouching on a miniature desk, second-grade me cursed Peggy Parish for creating Amelia Bedelia, the all-too-literal fool. Maid to the Rodgers family, Bedelia waltzed with unwarranted certainty through each page, never failing to spectacularly misinterpret tasks: "Draw the drapes" resulted in her painting of curtains. A fellow Amelia, Bedelia naturally became my nickname. Yet her trail of missteps was the path I feared most.

Since elementary school, I searched for certainty. My nickname warned me that mistakes could become my identity. My hunt for the definitive accelerated my love for math, a haven of reliable, repeatable answers. I have pursued numerous math-oriented activities, including volunteering at a free after-school program for local immigrant and low-income children. As a member of Fieldston's Community Service Advisory Board, I spend Thursdays with these second graders, aiding with math homework and sensory time. The afternoons are filled with giggles and front-toothless smiles.

One afternoon, I sat coloring between two girls, Jenna and Shayna. Jenna, scribbling with her pink marker, suddenly announced that Shayna was in the wrong classroom. Shayna's eyes widened with fear. Unsure if it was true, I tried redirecting the conversation back to drawing, as my pre-volunteer training advised. Jenna ignored my diversion. "You don't get it. She's not with her class right now because no one likes her." Shayna weakly retaliated, "That's not true." As I broke into the interaction, Jenna's voice sharpened as she insisted. "I'm not lying. Ask anyone, even Teacher Rosie!" Then I stumbled.

In past conflicts, my pre-volunteer training guided me step-by-step, like a formula. I knew what to do when kids pried for personal information, got distracted, or whined—but this moment spanned unmapped ground. Jenna was serious about threats, and I knew contradicting her could escalate things. Shayna was quickly transitioning from composed to… less so. Teetering on an imaginary pool of tears, I stared at Jenna and asked about her school day. Jenna returned to her drawing, rolling her eyes, but my heart felt strained with apologies for Shayna. On my train ride home, I relived the situation with regret, calling family and friends and asking what would have been the "right" move.

I wanted to solve every situation like the Problems Of the Week in math—dissecting, analyzing, and confidently taking my next steps. I feared moments like Jenna’s outburst, ones I was inadequately prepared for. As insults and tears continuously surprised me, I reevaluated my overly methodical framework. I spoke with older volunteers and researched teacher tips for behavior management. Similar to my training, I learned many procedures. But the lead teacher gave me new advice: “Trust yourself, you’re not expected to do everything perfectly. I’m still learning to guide them myself” she said with a smile.

After much advice, I began balancing logic with my gut reaction, accepting my faults, while continuing to uplift the Shaynas. Weeks later, go-lucky Ashton whispered that his grandfather died. I hugged him, and instead of standard condolences, I started asking him about his favorite memories. After Ashton mentioned playing dominoes with his grandfather, I promised to bring some and play with him the next week. Dominoes dominated our conversation for the rest of that afternoon. I still hesitated too long to come up with an initial response, but Ashton’s eventual smile and following “Thank You” letter affirmed my new instincts.

I now admit my mistake: Amelia Bedelia and I have always shared more than a name. For years, I ran away from her habit of mistakes, only to retrace her path of literalness. It manifested differently, but ultimately, we both needed to embrace ambiguity. Although I still wince out of habit when someone calls me her name, I no longer fear the comparison. Instead, my childhood nemesis reminds me to appreciate all questions without immediate answers.

"This can't be real, can it?" I thought to myself. A sudden jolt rattled my body, accompanied by the sickening sound of crumpling metal. My heart pounded loudly in my chest. Panic overtook me as I realized what had happened — I had failed to notice the oncoming traffic before continuing forward, due to the construction work happening. My father and I sat at the intersection by Chinatown, staring at the dented, dust covered car sitting in front of us.

Although no one was hurt, every time I looked at the empty spot in our garage, where our 2017 Toyota Camry used to be, I felt a solemn sense of responsibility. When insurance called, I shrank back, expecting to get yelled at. To my surprise, my dad tossed me the phone, having me handle the situation.

Though daunting, I took it upon myself to resolve this issue. Every action was mind-numbing, from remembering every second of the accident to describing the damage down to the shattered headlight and front bumper dangling off the car, wincing as I remembered the jarring force of the crash. I felt overwhelmed, yet I continued to push through, making more calls with insurance agents.

Seeing my parents' trust in my ability to resolve this situation showed me just how much I wanted to become someone others could fully rely on.

As a dental assistant, I embraced this newfound mentality. In the past, I was occasionally negligent: missing details in patient files, or not noticing when Dr. Jiang needed a different dental instrument handed to him. However, I now walked into the treatment room with a new air of confidence, determined to meet every patient's needs. A blonde, middle-aged woman had come into our clinic, needing to get her crown replaced. During the two-hour long process, I quickly prepared and handed dental instruments to Dr. Jiang. I tirelessly monitored the patient, removing any excess saliva she had, being careful to avoid the sensitive tooth that needed the dental crown. Outside the treatment room, I triple-checked patient insurance and expenses for accuracy, knowing both the dental office and patients were relying on me.

Yet, despite my best efforts, such reliability can only stretch so far.

During our group mousetrap car project for physics, we were required to have the car roll a randomized distance. I was committed to crafting the perfect car, recording the number of rotations, down to the millimeter, needed to reach every possible distance we could be assigned. I spent hours adjusting the length of the lever arm and string, creating makeshift tires with blue and green balloons for extra friction.

However, with the upcoming rotation test also in physics, I found myself struggling to make time for both assignments. Eventually, I chose to devote my time to the mouse trap car project, knowing that my partner Abhinav was relying on my meticulousness to succeed. Though I struggled on the rotation test, it felt vindicating knowing our team was able to succeed because of the extra details I had spent time on. I learned to choose my battles wisely, and to absolve myself from the unrealistic expectation of extreme detail in every situation.

While the aftermath of the car accident has gradually receded, the accountability and reliability I gained have not. From biochemistry to environmental chemistry, I know I can only dedicate myself to a few subjects and wish to find those where my reliability and attention to detail can have the largest influence. Being dependable and focused will be essential, no matter the field I pursue, and I resolve to channel these qualities into establishing meaningful connections. I hope to continue being meticulous and deeply accountable for all aspects of my research, no longer just for my own benefit, but for the benefit of those around me, leaving a far more positive and lasting impact than the one left by my car.

The bedroom which I once considered a safe haven had transformed. My 6th-grade imagination ran wild, with shadowy figures lurking in every corner and poltergeists creeping closer with each creak of the house. Heart pounding and teeth chattering, I wondered why I hadn't urged my friend to leave my house earlier. I had always been apprehensive about anything spooky, but this childhood instance differed. While I usually managed to avoid our horror movie nights, my friend had made it her mission to expose me to the genre by telling me stories laden with ghosts, killers, and other cliched characters. The most terrifying part of the experience, though, was what happened when I didn’t sleep well.

Bleary-eyed and irritable, I exhaustedly stumbled through the next few days. The lack of sleep took its toll, making it a Herculean endeavor to focus on my math problems. Even the park, my usual post-school sanctuary, no longer held any interest. How, I wondered, could a few days without sleep cause such a shift in my well-being?

Late nights became routine in high school as I balanced academics, extracurriculars, and socialization. Knowing this was a common phenomenon among my peers, I joined the Hamilton Lab at Rutgers University to investigate further. In the lab, I helped develop the codebook for a study exploring the links between social media, sleep, and suicidality. I also learned that systemic factors play a significant role in sleep quality, with many facing challenges beyond their control, such as inadequate time for sleep due to multiple jobs or an absence of a safe sleeping place. My laptop was filled with annotated studies and highlighted articles each contributing to my understanding of this issue.

Just knowing this information wasn’t enough. It couldn’t possibly be left exclusively to me—- I needed to ensure it resonated with others. I shared my insight with community members at Rutgers Day, and I spoke to a girl who excitedly told me that she would implement the sleep strategies we discussed. As participants jotted down their thoughts and favorite activities on our booth's whiteboard, I realized how powerful these conversations could be. Something shifted for me that day—it wasn’t just about research anymore. It was clear that this was the beginning of a deeper commitment to advocacy, one that would continue to grow.

Through these experiences, I noticed a lack of youth involvement in the mental health initiatives centered around them. To combat this, I helped organize RISE Day, where 16 teenage advocates from different backgrounds across New Jersey came together to explore psychology research and mental health resources, and develop impactful community initiatives. The long hours spent collaboratively drafting the grant, constructing our presentation, and co-writing an abstract on the importance of youth advocacy were all worth it. Our animated lunchtime discussions about the gaps in school mental health support only strengthened my connection to the mission we were all so invested in.

Today, I’m proud to say that I am not just an advocate for the importance of sleep. Advocacy plays a central role in my life, whether I’m demonstrating deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prevention techniques to my community, recruiting volunteers to donate blood at the Piscataway Street Fair, presenting recommendations for systemic healthcare issues to my congressman, or deciding what genre of movie our family watches on the weekend (not a scary one).

I aspire to be a physician in the future—not solely treating a patient’s medical condition, but being the strongest supporter in their health journey. I will advocate for them despite the biological, socioeconomic, or policy barriers they may face and contribute to community initiatives that will further our collective health. A future without advocacy is frightening to me, and I intend to pursue it in college and beyond. My patients can rest easy knowing their doctor has their back!

It all began when I was eight years old, watching a football game, when Desean Jackson fumbled a punt return and gave the Dallas Cowboys a win. That moment initiated my love for football and my Cowboys fandom. Since then, football has been a major fixture in my life. Even though my elementary school days were spent loafing around at recess and quietly listening to my teachers talk about multiplication, when Cowboys games were on I was on my feet cheering for them and excitedly running around my basement when they scored. I soon became a superfan as my love for football flourished. I searched for data and studied concepts like mesh, a short passing concept. Eventually, my passion for football started expressing itself whenever possible. Even when I went into the administrative office to discuss an unrelated situation regarding school buses, I ended up talking football with the Vice Principal. After he recommended me to the head football coach, I became my school team’s lead manager. As I got acclimated, I changed from an aimless and socially isolated teenager into a social butterfly with clear life goals. Football created a safe haven for me to escape the anxious moments of school. I felt comfortable talking to the players and coaches and bonded with them over lunches and greetings in the halls. Finally experiencing social comfort, I began chatting with my tablemates in classes. This paid off, establishing three strong friendships soon after my first football season.

I also started talking more with my teachers, cultivating relationships with them just as I bonded with the coaches. The social environment of the football team helped alleviate my fears of social embarrassment as I was accepted for who I was. I gained confidence and my class participation increased, culminating when I answered difficult questions in my Calculus BC course despite knowing that I may have been incorrect. Along with working to build relationships, I gave the job my all. I attended every practice possible, whether they started at 6 AM or 3 PM, and stayed until 10 PM so I could film each game. I gleefully stepped into any necessary role, helping with equipment, water, the medkit, filming, and even tutoring. My first year, I was asked to tutor a player who was struggling with schoolwork. I spent hours between school and practice helping him complete English assignments, one being related to Of Mice and Men. I volunteered my tutoring free of charge to help anyone who needed help maintaining the required 2.0 GPA to play.

I acquired a leadership role after my first year when I became the longest tenured team manager. When other managers had questions about water distribution or needed any equipment help, they came to me. Additionally, I connected our school’s pep band and athletic director so our students could play the pregame national anthem instead of using a recording that we didn’t even make, finally succeeding towards the 2023 season’s conclusion. Managing the team made me think about pursuing a football-related career, but volunteering with the University of Maryland’s equipment management team made it a top choice. Despite being the only high schooler dealing with the complex scripts and copious equipment supply, I felt comfortable. I quickly learned tasks and became trusted to operate chains at practice, do laundry, and even drive gator trucks around during field cleanup. As I accrued more hours there, I saw the importance of effective work behind the scenes. Whether it was giving players skull caps, decaling helmets, or cleaning sweat-drenched clothes, it became obvious that any equipment room issue would become the program’s issue. The equipment room doesn’t get public recognition, but the team would be unrecognizable without their hard work. As football has influenced me increasingly throughout the years, I’ve learned many important lessons about both life and myself while obtaining a passion to pursue a career in it.

My dad is notoriously difficult to buy gifts for. It’s nearly impossible to predict what he’ll like, since he rarely buys himself anything. For years, my birthday gifts to him consisted of coffee mugs and sweaters: simple, functional things with no personality whatsoever. I was determined that his fiftieth birthday present would be different. But I was stumped. What could I give him that wouldn’t be another piece of meaningless clutter? After weeks of thinking hard, I stumbled on the answer the day before his birthday.

I’ve been singing Hindustani classical music for the last decade, and though my dad never took formal music lessons, our love for music brings us closer. As we listen together, I point out soft classical melodies underlying the Hindi songs he loves, like Raag Kalyan woven through Moh Moh Ke Dhaage and Jab Deep Jale Aana. When I start humming a song, he never fails to start whistling the next few lines from wherever he is in the house, a back-and-forth that becomes our special duet. Our busy schedules mean that we don’t spend much time together. But on the few Saturday evenings we find time to sit side-by-side on the sofa, immersed in the melancholy or lighthearted strains of whatever new Hindi song has caught our fancy, that gap dissolves.

I noticed him listening to the 1965 song Piya Tose Naina Laage Re on repeat. It’s a childhood favorite of his, with a darting rhythm and lighthearted tone. My planned gift was a recording of myself singing it, complete with keyboard music in the background (played by my sister). And I only had a day to do it.

While my dad was out of the house, I sat down to try to recreate the dancing melody of the original, doing my best to mimic its leaps and sways while adding in some riffs and runs of my own. My sister and I figured out little keyboard improvisations to sprinkle throughout the song too, places where it briefly spun the melody into something new. Finally, we began to record. Between all the mistakes and unsatisfactory attempts, it took four hours and over thirty recordings for us to find one we liked.

The next morning, my dad’s face lit up when he heard the recording. This gift was no coffee mug. He’s kept it on his phone ever since, and I’ll catch him listening to it now and then, head tipped back and eyes closed. The song pops up often in our whistling-humming duets, and it’s a reminder of the way music brings us together.

This experience showed me the meaning of gifting. At the beginning of the pandemic, masks were scarce, with boxes disappearing as soon as they arrived. My mom and I bought fabrics from our local Joanne’s and set to work sewing, only meaning to make a few masks for ourselves. It was then that a Nextdoor post caught my eye; a nurse who worked at a nearby hospital had sent out a plea for masks, saying that she and her fellow healthcare workers desperately needed some.

I took it as a call to action and picked out the prettiest designs I could find: shimmering stars and planets against a dark background, lively purple flowers, and bold aqua swirls. Who said masks had to look drab? Over the next few days, we set to work sewing a heap of colorful masks.

Gift-giving, I realized, comes from a deep place in your heart. It is the desire to present something surprising and beautiful, not merely functional. It is the determination to spend hours creating for the reward of a momentary smile. It is the recording of a nostalgic song that conjures childhood memories, a vibrant mask that lights up grim hospital corridors. As the giver, you are left with the awe-inspiring feeling of having created a brief spark of joy with your gift.

Rockets flew overhead, and with each explosion, our house shook and the window curtains flew. Living in Gaza, I never knew if the next rocket would hit too close to home. This constant fear made me realize how fragile life is and pushed me to value my education as a way to make a difference.

My parents grew up in Gaza, Palestine, and moved to the U.S. in 2000 to escape war and provide a better life for me and my siblings, making me a first-generation American. In 2012, we moved to Gaza for the first time since they left and I attended kindergarten and first grade. This experience gave me a taste of life in the place where my family came from and allowed me to connect with my relatives and experience the culture that shaped my parents. During my time there, I saw firsthand the struggles many families faced due to high unemployment and economic instability. It was common to see children in the streets begging for food or money. Daily life was very difficult for everyone due to the lack of quality basic living conditions. Electricity and air conditioning were available for only a few hours at unpredictable times, which was awfully challenging during the hot summers.

In 2014, our attempt to settle was disrupted when a huge war broke out. I vividly remember the chaos—crowds of people running and screaming, missiles in the sky, and the intense fear with each sound of explosion. Sitting in the corner of our house with my brothers and cousin, all of us crying as the walls shook around us, made me appreciate the safety and educational opportunities I have in the U.S.—privileges most children in Gaza don’t have. Despite leaving under such stressful circumstances, these experiences have motivated me to take full advantage of opportunities that many privileged people take for granted.

Returning to the U.S. after experiencing life in Gaza greatly influenced my perspective on education and career goals. Witnessing the lack of access to quality healthcare and education in Gaza pushed me to pursue a career in healthcare—a field that many in Gaza dream of entering but cannot due to limited opportunities. My relatives in Gaza often express how they wish for the educational resources and opportunities I have in the U.S., which has made me even more encouraged to make the most of my education.

Determined to take full advantage of the opportunities available to me, I have been working at a clothing store after school and during summers. This job has taught me responsibility and the value of hard work. It has allowed me to pay for my car, clothing, and phone expenses, taking some of the weight off my parents’ shoulders. Additionally, I send money through my parents to help my family in Gaza, knowing that even a small contribution can make a huge difference in their lives. This experience has strengthened my commitment to a career in healthcare, where I can use my education to help others and make a positive impact.

The challenges I witnessed in Gaza, combined with the opportunities I have in the U.S., have inspired me to pursue higher education and a career in healthcare. I am motivated by the hope that one day, I can save lives and create environments where patients feel welcome and safe. I aspire to become a healthcare professional who can clearly explain complicated medical concepts to patients, allowing them to make informed decisions about their health. In college, I am eager to learn more about medicine and health issues, and to gain the knowledge and skills necessary to make a meaningful contribution to communities in need. My journey has taught me the importance of education and service, and I am excited to bring this passion to my future studies and career.

I stared at the random colors of our parquet: golden oak pieces neighbored with dark walnut ones and occasional red mahogany imposters (not a stylistic decision, but my dad’s way of economizing, naively assuming furniture would cover the mismatch). We’d been sitting in our living room in complete silence for hours. My dad’s simultaneous desire and fear to share something was palpable, but he refused any help, ensuring us he was fine. He hadn’t eaten or slept in days. The anxiety-managing techniques, meditations, or breathing exercises I showed him didn’t work anymore, and all I could do was hold his unusually cold hand.

Then he sprang up, checked the wall clock, and, with his hazel eyes a bit glossy, said, "Stop. I have 30 minutes left." He pivoted towards me and, exhaling a deep, shaky breath, began explaining: “There's no choice. It's like choosing between God or mankind's extinction. Count 12345 until you pass out. I have four minutes…” He gave me his saddest, most hope-filled eyes, causing my stomach to hollow. But no matter how much I tried, I couldn't decipher this code. He was either communicating with aliens, becoming psychic, or I was losing my mind.

Then he rushed to the kitchen, and somehow I instantly knew he was looking for alcohol and chased after him. He was about to drink when I hovered over his back, snatching a bottle out of his hand. It seemed like he was stuck in a loop, a nightmare he couldn’t escape. My eyes darted to his and I bit my lip to keep it from trembling, because I couldn't see my dad in them.

Anxiety swarmed around my lungs, and my eyes burned with tears. I dropped my head back, trying to control my breathing and stay quiet, while praying to all the gods so that the ambulance would arrive faster. After 20 minutes a ginger woman and a tall man in uniform finally came in. Their calm composure enraged me, because I couldn’t sit still. I needed them to understand, help Dad, not interrogate about suicidal thoughts and religious affiliations.

The woman instructed me to leave, so I went to my bedroom, where, of course, I googled the symptoms and thought dad had dementia. I comforted my younger brother, although I feared dad would never be the same, never be our dad again.

I felt guilty about accusing him of not paying attention to me, unless giving unsolicited advice, expecting me to parent my brother, and fixating on my flaws over strengths, making me feel like I wasn't good enough to be loved. I'd been selfish, thinking it was only me who got hurt, when I made mistakes and hurt him and others too. Not with malice intent, but because that was the only way I knew. I did it out of love, and my dad did too.

He might’ve not been there for me in ways I wanted, but he was there in ways he could. He taught me to spackle walls (an amazing skill for a confectioner) and drive a clutch, delivered my cake orders, and saved me from Baba Yaga, a local crazy old woman I was TERRIFIED of.

It wasn’t instant, but slowly the anger dissipated, and I forgave dad and myself.

I changed my communication strategy, showing love in new, healthier ways.

After three weeks in a psychiatric hospital, dad got diagnosed with Acute Polymorphic Psychotic Disorder.

The first time we talked on the phone, I was relieved to hear he was himself again. Dad thanked me for my advice, which prompted me to see my strength in being sensitive.

No, I don’t want to become a psychologist (although considered), but I do want to use my traits and knowledge to help someone. Whether it be through teaching languages, baking cakes, or sharing tips on how to stop worrying about saving money on your parquet.

Apple. For the past three years, my morning routine has revolved around both the little, red fruit and the mighty tech conglomerate. After waking up at around 6:30 a.m., I plop down at my dining table and start nomming on some peeled Gala apples. To me, Galas are far superior over Honeycrisps or Fujis (despite what the very objective applerankings.com says). How do I know? Well, last year, I taste-tested every apple available at my local Safeway. Even now, I can tell when my dad accidentally buys forbidden Fujis! Anyways, back to my routine. As I devour each apple slice, I can feel the fructose coursing through my veins as I gradually grow more and more alert (I don’t need caffeine!) By 6:40 a.m, I'm pretty awake. Instinctively, I reach for my iPhone 11, then tap open Apple News. My feed is a mosaic of different news outlets, ranging from NYTimes to the Wall Street Journal, from more hobbyist Game Rant to more technical Popular Mechanics.

Something I’m proud of is how I try to ward against building an echo chamber. Most people don’t know this, but Apple News operates just like a social media site. In the beginning, my feed was littered with Buzzfeed articles and celebrity news. Now, my news sources inform me of new political analysis, technological developments, and my guilty pleasure, game news!

In the Spring of 2023, ChatGPT just became popular, and not many people were familiar with its capabilities. As I scrolled through Apple News one morning, I saw multiple stories speculating about how ChatGPT could “disrupt” healthcare, finance, and most importantly, education. I remember reading one article in particular, titled “Alarmed by A.I. Chatbots, Universities Start Revamping How They Teach” by the NYTimes discussing how ChatGPT was forcing teachers to change how they taught writing, lest all assignments from this day forth be deluged by an ocean of plagiarized, AI-generated essays. I found this deeply problematic.

As someone who spends his free time reading Large Language Modeling research papers and has even contributed to one, I was quite familiar with how ChatGPT was trained. Because of this, I thought many articles were vastly overestimating GPT 3.5’s competency, believing that it would be able to write essays that were indistinguishable from normal students. However, I liken ChatGPT to a Fuji apple: its essays look good on the outside… but taste rather bland on the inside. To share this idea, I wrote an argumentative essay titled “ChatGPT’s Potential in Higher Education,” arguing that if teachers are worried their students will use AI-plagiarized essays, they probably need to change how they grade. Instead of rubrics looking for 5 paragraph essays and use of evidence to support claims (does it look like an apple?) rubrics should be focused on originality and quality of the argumentation (does it taste like an apple?).

While this article did not make the cover of Apple News, it taught me the importance of science communication. Although the technology may be here, the importance, capabilities, or implications of emerging technologies like generative AI are not made clear to most people. Thus, it’s up to people who are familiar with its power to inform the public. That’s why I hope to couple my existing research experience with my love for argumentation to communicate groundbreaking discoveries to the public. My apple routine every morning grounds me, but it also serves as a daily gateway to the world, ready to explore new ideas. My routine grounds me, but it also propels me to new perspectives, and consequently new ways of thinking and argumentation. My routine grounds me, but it prepares me for a new, novel day. To me, originality is the true mark of a remarkable person. Therefore, I plan to refine this routine in new environments and with new information to enhance my ability to think uniquely.

I am ready. My mom has taught me everything I need to know, including how to double-thread my needle, and how to keep close gaps between stitches. As I ask Alexa to play an energetic Bruno Mars playlist, I sit cross-legged on the living room carpet with my mom’s sewing box and the black Isshin-ryu karate gi that I wear weekly for classes.

It is spring break of my junior year, and I recently earned my first-degree brown belt and a brand new set of patches to adorn my gi with. Eager to start sewing, I begin stitching two patches that mean the most to me. I place the fist-shaped Mizugami patch on the right of my gi top, and the circular star-throwing patch on the bottom of the gi pants.

Mizugami is the Japanese goddess of water, known for her strength and protective nature. My sensei, who is much like Mizugami, has mentored me since I first started karate in 2017. One core memory with sensei occurred after my first star-throwing tournament a year after starting karate; I froze while competing with my older opponents, and missed all the targets.

Sensing my discouragement, my sensei encouraged me to keep going. She reminded me that becoming a strong student cannot happen overnight. Sensei recommended that instead of doing star-throwing, I focus on sparring as it would be both physically and mentally rewarding. I took her advice, and understood that the only way to improve my karate skills would be to challenge myself and practice. I began attending classes multiple times a week and chose to fight more experienced students. Gradually, I began to see my efforts pay off, as my sparring abilities improved and I became a more dynamic fighter.

As I improved, I became an assistant teacher who motivates younger students to challenge themselves. I remember a class a few months ago where high-ranking students, with brown belts and above, sparred with low-ranks. During the class, I was sparring with a seven-year-old girl, but she kept running away whenever I moved towards her. After our sparring session, she explained that sparring older ranks made her feel nervous and outmatched. This was when I realized she was making the same mistake that I made during my first tournament. To help alter her mindset, I encouraged her to view higher ranks as mentors instead of opponents, and to understand that she will improve the more she practices.
