Although it wasn’t an immediate transformation, watching my student become increasingly confident in the sparring ring was extremely rewarding.

From this experience, I’ve found that the most meaningful mentorship has been a combination of lessons I’ve learned from overcoming challenges like my tournament, and advice from my sensei. A few hours and dozens of Bruno Mars songs later, I finally complete my patchwork. As I admire my newly adorned and colorful gi, I am reminded of the importance of paying forward the contributions others made to help me. I am proud of overcoming the challenges I faced in the past. They are valuable assets I use to teach my students, and help them avoid the same mistakes I made. By doing this practice, I am able to pay forward the invaluable guidance my sensei, mom, and sparring opponents gave to me. I hope down the line, my students will continue the chain of paying forward their own experiences to future students.

What do tangerines and basketballs have in common? 
1. They are round. 
2. They are orange. 
3. They show me how little I know.

“Para mi hermana,” Emiliano explained as he slid the last of the tangerines into a well-worn backpack. I felt the red shame of guilt creep into my chest. I had budgeted only two tangerines for each kid who registered. Clearly, not enough. Despite my meticulous planning, I had failed. Maybe Emiliano – who silently watched me with large, cocoa-colored eyes, sharp with intelligence, thirsty to understand his new world– didn’t need basketballs.

Basketball exhilarates me and makes my body sing; it challenges me, sometimes heartbreakingly. In my sophomore year, when playing college ball still consumed me, hours-long rides home from AAU tournaments often left me sobbing into my seatbelt, twisting away from my dad to shield him from my suffering. An only-six-foot-tall point guard has to be exceptional, it was agony to learn I wasn’t that. The pain was visceral; it almost cracked me in two. Yet after that sorrowful season, I reassessed and rebooted. I devoted more time to academics and Hoops & Books, a non-profit I had started for kids, which was growing quickly, both in popularity and in my heart. Their guileless joy on the court and the excitement radiating from their sweaty faces swelling my soul like no three-pointer ever had.

I had begun offering the free hybrid basketball/reading classes after I noticed too many kids emerging from the fog of Covid struggling with mental and physical health; many schools in my area only offer PE once a week. Basketball keeps me disciplined, motivated, focused. Physical activity regulates emotions and leads to better academic outcomes. I am passionate about sharing this with kids who don’t have access. When initially crafting the program, I carefully selected drill sequences and books about athletes from the “Who Is?” series I had loved as a kid. Only as an last-minute afterthought did I bring snacks to munch while we read cross-legged on the gym floor.

That day, Emiliano, his family fresh from Ecuador, fixated on the tangerines. In his soft Spanish, he asked if he could have extras to take home. I told him he could have as many as he wanted. His mother, proudly watching him from the sidelines, surprised me when she, too, slid several of the orange orbs into her purse. After reading time, Emiliano made another beeline for the snack table, collecting the last of the tangerines, and triggering my shame.

Tangerines and Basketballs. Bread and roses. We need to feed both body and spirit, but isn’t one more essential than the other? I was giving out roses when perhaps what was needed was bread. I couldn’t know Emiliano’s exact situation, but I do know, from years of volunteering at a food bank, that far too many families can’t access affordable, healthy food.

I also wondered if the citrus fruit reminded Emiliano of his sunlit home. I thought of my grandmother, who left Cuba at about his age, also a refugee, arriving with a single suitcase. The first food she fed me as a child was another round, orange, tropical fruit– the mango. I was instantly enraptured by its singularly sweet, liquidy meat. I'm convinced Abuela’s enduring enthusiasm for a fruit she still buys in bulk is because its explosive sweetness brings her more than corporal sustenance. Likewise, for me, mangoes – along with lechon that falls flaky off the bone, and salty black bean stew– will always be synonymous with Abuela’s embrace. Sometimes, the bread is also the rose.

The crucial discovery: the afterthought, the almost-overlooked element of a project, can end up being central. The tangerines can become as important as the basketballs. I remain open to signs of this, staying flexible and able to pivot when new information presents itself. Only then can I be most useful. I now understand when helping others, they should drive the bus, not you. They will tell you what is needed if you are listening. I now run Hoops & Books within NYC Public Schools where there’s a large migrant community. Many of the books I bring are now in Spanish. I'm still figuring out how to make the biggest impact where there’s the most need, but I am listening, carefully. I believe college will make me more effective in my quest by deepening my understanding of the forces that shape our societies. Ultimately, I hope it will lead me to a career in government, as an educator, or as an attorney advocating for those who can’t as effectively advocate for themselves.

Now, I always bring extra tangerines.

Red snappers, king crabs, and tiger shrimp glistened under a Saturday sunrise at the Newport Beach fish market. Growing up, I spent countless weekends there, peering over the ice stacks, developing an eye for the freshest, sweetest catch. But often, my gaze wandered longingly to the ice cream shop. As I tugged at my father, he would remind me of a Chinese idiom, “One cannot have both the fish and the bear’s paw.” With our trunk full of seafood, there would be no room for ice cream.

My sweet tooth wasn’t deterred. Before each subsequent trip, I tucked a watermelon Jolly Rancher under my tongue. Relishing my candy, I felt giddy and invincible, equipped with a deft fishtail and powerful paw. I could have seafood and sweets, if only I snuck them in.

The summer after my freshman year, my mornings started with seafood. I turned the crabs on my plate to research specimens, waking at daybreak to study marine shore crabs in the Alberto Lab at UC San Diego. During early hours of low tide, I scrambled across miles of beaches, piers, and harbors, catching growing crabs, testing how temperatures shift their habitat ranges. Then, burying science at sunset when the tide receded, I embarked on another adventure—a poetry workshop, riding the waves of verse. Those evenings after a day of lab work, I co-hosted “Around the World of Poetry in 80 Days” through Polyphony Lit, an international magazine publishing teen writing edited by teens. I joined editors from 80 hometowns to teach virtual lessons on writing inspired by my cultural geography. After finalizing lesson plans each night, I set my alarm again to dawn, awaiting low tide. Science and poetry were celestially distinct, separated by the solar rising and setting.

One day, exhausted by a crab that escaped out of its tank, I stayed overtime to complete an experiment and scrambled to start my writing lesson. On Zoom, my poetry peers, surprised by my hectic apologies and the aquariums visible in my background, poured out floods of questions. Where was I? What had I been doing? I feared I would be viewed as an imposter upon revealing my scientific research, but I found myself excited by their biology questions. I did not always have answers. I’m not sure, I replied to a kid asking me if crabs had personalities, but I will find out.

I was buoyed by sharing, not hiding, biology with poets. For them, I began gathering videos of crabs, sea anemone, starfish—intertidal creatures turned poetic muses. I taught science-inspired poetry, with crabs as proud representatives of my tongue, my home.

Poetry challenged me to put down the caliper and take time for patient observation. I began to notice how these crabs acclimate to stress, adapting to rising temperatures and water levels. Some lashed out aggressively; others passively cowered. I investigated how their personalities influence survivability to climate change, then adopted their versatility in writing. In poetry workshops from Sewanee to Iowa City, I arrived ready to crack open my hard exoskeleton, offering vulnerability and tenderness for my peers, seeking solutions to our own chronic wear and tear. I returned to science, reminded by an imaginary crab’s pinch of the lives intertwined with my research.

I thrive in the intertidal zone between sciences and the humanities. At my STEM school, I added the “A” for “Arts” by starting a STEAM for All chapter, an interdisciplinary volunteer organization that has taught kids about epidemiology and electrochemistry, creative writing and ceramics. I co-founded a poetry club delivering lessons to patients at children’s hospitals, using writing therapy to supplement traditional healthcare.

I enjoy the iridescent joy of poetic creation and stepping paw by paw across terrains of biology, chemistry, physics. I am driven by logic and numbers, compassion and stories. I can have my fill of seafood and keep enough space for sweet dessert.

Despite not having created anything like Picasso's Guernica or da Vinci’s Mona Lisa, I stand just as proud as the greatest artists in the world. Three years ago, I sat hunched on the floor of my bedroom, meticulously refining and retouching the details of a portrait of my grandmother. That same piece, along with a stash of unfinished paintings, leaned against my wall for years. Despite having nothing left to add, I remained too unsatisfied to apply their final coats of emulsion, leaving them undone. Constantly finishing each painting session with a palette stacked with layers of dry paint with no visible progress on my work, I began dreading art entirely. I was convinced that if an artwork could not be perfect, I’d never find fulfillment in it.

This fear of inadequacy extended beyond my art. It held me back from pursuing projects as I worried I might fall short of excellence, forcing me to find excitement in new canvases and interests. Perfection became my prison.

Frustrated, I explored ways to continue my art without being trapped in the routine of making a sketch and painting over it only to abandon it forever. With several youth artists, I organized art workshops for a group of orphans, stepping into a new milieu where my art could find fresh meaning.

At first, I struggled to break the silence in our workshops. Though we all spoke Tagalog, the children were reserved, distant, and hard to reach. But seeing this divide, I knew that I was in for it. It became my goal to blend the striking contrast between our volunteers and the children. The art itself eventually served as a bridge between young people of different realities with little in common except a shared interest in painting.

I showed the children how to achieve the three-dimensionality of impasto with a painting knife; meanwhile, kids began to open up, sharing their childhood experiences on the streets of Manila. For our first collaborative piece, fifteen children and I gathered around a large wooden panel. As we worked together, we experimented with acrylic paint. I guided them through the process of layering and blending, even if it meant more paint ended up on their clothes than on the panel itself. By the end of the day, we transformed the blank canvas into a vibrant, unifying mosaic, each brushstroke bringing a child’s unique contribution to life. Watching the children's hands awkwardly control their brushes, I felt a new kind of satisfaction—not from achieving perfection, but from creating something with a real purpose.

Our techniques weren’t flawless, but this experience put smiles on their faces and allowed all of us to appreciate art for what it truly is; beyond its beauty, it is a way to connect, share, and inspire. I knew it was no masterpiece, but the creation was imbued with our handprints and shared creativity.

I used to think that perfection was what I was seeking in art and in everything I did. But as I encountered and built relationships with kids with experiences so harsh, I came to realize how imperfect and flawed our world really is. My frustration in art became embarrassingly trivial compared to the brutal realities many children my age face. Now, I hope to help others find value in their unique voices and abilities, and through this, address the disparities that hold so many back.

When I look at my stash of unfinished paintings, I no longer see them as disappointments but as reminders to keep moving forward. While within me will always be the little boy who strives to be exemplary in all he does, I have broken free from the prison. By working on every piece and project with purpose, I will find pride and fulfillment in everything I do—even if it isn’t always so ‘perfect’.

“LOGAN PASS TRAILHEAD,” a sign reads. I sigh, totally unprepared for the 12-mile hike ahead. The sun blazes, turning the landscape into an oven. I wipe sweat off my forehead, adjust my backpack, and set off. Granite peaks battle with the blue sky, wildflowers dance across the valleys, and mountain goats graze. But the heat and endless trail make it hard to enjoy. By the time we reach the peak, I’m drenched in sweat—only to realize I forgot my lunch in the car.

I was raised with balance. My parents push me to excel in academics, sports, and behavior. But they also encourage me to have fun. They’ve always let me take my own path in life. But our hiking trips were contrasting—I wasn’t allowed to go my own way. There, I had to follow my dad through miles of trail; day in, day out. It was a privilege, yet also a source of frustration.

In winter of 2020, since airlines were down, our family and friends decided to do an RV trip across 700 miles of Texas. We walked across barren West Texas deserts and climbed mountains in the Guadalupe range. We marched through Big Bend and hiked through the Chihuahuan Desert with family and friends. I wasn’t thrilled, especially after sitting on a cactus.

On New Year’s Eve after hiking up Guadalupe Mountain, our group decided to have dinner in one of the RVs. The room hums as conversations float through the air and food sizzles on the stove. I argue with my sister about opening a window, and my friends are yelling at each other about an UNO game. In the midst of it all, my dad calls out, “Everyone, look at the TV!” To my surprise, he prepared a slideshow night with pictures from our past trips. We recount old memories and laugh, flipping through the highlights of our vacations. Memories of our struggles and triumphs, from Yellowstone’s geysers to Yosemite’s granite peaks, all mix together.

As images roll by, a shift begins within me. For the first time, I see not just hiking, but the experiences we created beating nature’s challenges. A pose at the top of a mountain. A weary smile, flashing the peace symbol drenched in sweat. The experiences he created shaped me. Realization hit like a wave and washed away resistance from the past. Those early mornings and long hikes were my dad’s way of giving us memories, and his way of teaching us to appreciate the world.

These days, it helps me to see parallels between challenges of hiking and daily life. Just as a hiker conquers obstacles and finds joy in journeys, I know I have to approach every challenge with a sense of goals and appreciate the challenges for the growth they provide. When I’m programming and faced with a bug, I see each line of Java I have to go through as a step along a rocky path, each error resolved an incline I’ve completed. When I’m struggling with weights at the gym or losing a tennis match, I remind myself that every rep and point is a small victory— a step closer to my goal.

As I take on the trails of life, I’ll never forget the paths I walked with my dad. A tough hike, to me, is now a source of strength and a reminder of the importance of perseverance. Each step on a trail, once heavy with fatigue, is now a gift. Over the years, my dad has shown me that it’s in these everyday moments like casting a line fishing, a family dinner, talks on the patio with my friends—that I find true meaning. And when my trail becomes hard, I remember the lessons of the hikes. Even the most difficult parts can reveal the most amazing views, and every step forward is a chance to discover something new.

Unlike the heroes in my favorite comics, I don't possess the ability to run through walls or heal from any wound. Reality is different—I rely on insulin and a needle to survive. The memory of feeling the hospital's cold vinyl floor on my warm feet on my eighth birthday will never fade. Learning about the chaos of type one diabetes was almost more scary than waking up in the hospital. At eight, the permanent nature of diabetes was overwhelming. Nearly a decade later, living with type one diabetes as a teenager is turbulent. Constant change fueled my fear, keeping me from going out with friends or attending school events—even those I helped plan. It is a vicious cycle I only broke in my junior year. But I cannot blame my hermit-like lifestyle as a freshman and sophomore purely on fear. Fear isn't just the absence of bravery; it's the barrier we must overcome to find courage. During my sophomore year, I struggled to find that courage, often letting my fear dictate my choices. However, it was in small, seemingly insignificant decisions—like choosing to enroll in an elective class outside my comfort zone—that I began to challenge my fear and take the first steps toward bravery.

It came later, however. Even though I was excited to learn about entrepreneurship, my first thought when walking into class was about the close proximity to the nurse's office (an absurd idea, looking back). You would expect a teenager to think about who looks friendly and easy to approach in the class—that was not me. However, my focus quickly shifted from diabetes as I experienced Mr. Davidson's unique approach and engaging subjects. I quickly realized I would learn more in entrepreneurship than in any AP class. As my interest in all things business and economics grew, I started to come out of my shell. After a while, going to Mr. Davidson's class during lunch became a habit, until he asked me a non-academic question one day. "What are you going to do?" I only understood what he meant once he turned on the projector and displayed an image Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs glared at me. The room was struck by silence until the 5th-period bell rang out, breaking my reflection. As I left, he said, "Don't come back until you have an answer," knowing I was ready to do more.

I knew I could be doing more as well, so I was looking to take on some risk. I decided to leverage my time and energy to apply to a full-time dual enrollment business associates program at Montgomery College. The application was more than I bargained for though. Due to software compilations, my entrance exam score didn't get linked to my ID, and I had to take all of the supplementary classes and pass them to get into the program. That half summer, I spent six hours alone on campus taking notes, asking questions, and developing relationships with the professors teaching the supplementary classes. Getting the best grade possible wasn't a want for me, it was a need. I felt the fire of competition.

By the beginning of my junior year’s second semester at Montgomery College, I connected with my cohort; for the first time, I scheduled and led study sessions, peer review sessions, and project meetings. I had the independence and confidence to start something myself. I left the shell I was once in behind. Building on this momentum, my friends and I founded a business club to explore markets and mentor the next group of high school students. This venture deepened my understanding of business, allowed me to embrace leadership, and allowed me to share my experiences with others despite the chaos of diabetes. Through the club, I've gained opportunities and experiences beyond what I once imagined, and I'm eager to share my insight and push forward in my future endeavors.

Lies.

June 14, 2023

Most of the people at the Digital School X coders(hq) hackathon — ranging from seasoned professionals in EdTech to students younger than me who had just started coding — told me my app LessonGPT was the most useful product there. They lied. I still lost. Was it because of how I presented the app? Did the judges just not like me? I didn't really know.

Just three months earlier, I had survived a near-death car accident which left me determined to use every moment meaningfully, knowing I could die at any time. But losing this hackathon reignited the same fear of dying having not accomplished anything worthwhile. As the highly functioning internet addict I am, I responded to these feelings by drowning myself in YouTube. While scrolling, I was recommended a YouTube video on Existentialism by Crash Course. Intrigued, I clicked on it and then proceeded to binge the entire Crash Course: Philosophy series, much to the chagrin of my mom who was complaining I wasn't studying for a physics test I had the next day.

The course made me realize that, instead of focusing on winning awards, I should help others. This perspective shift came from combining two ideas: utilitarianism, a framework for judging the morality of actions by which the actions that make the most people happy are the most “correct” actions, and existentialism, which suggests that because we will die and be forgotten eventually, we should live autonomously according to our own values, not society’s expectations.

This led me, the following day, to show the app to my vice principal, Mr. Atkins.

June 15, 2023

At lunch, I entered his office and stuttered out a few words about how the app works. Then, I saw his eyes light up. “This is amazing! It’ll really help reduce teacher workload. By when can you have it adapted to our school’s lesson plan format?”

“Uhh…maybe within this week, if I lose enough sleep.”

“Relax. Take your time. Let me call Mr. Dhanak” (Mr. Dhanak is my school’s chief innovation officer). We instantly planned to launch the app on the forthcoming teachers' day as a gift to all teachers.

Between June and September, I continuously organized meetings with my school's senior leadership team to get feedback on my app, wrote code to incorporate their suggestions and then organized further meetings. I finally felt like I was actually using each moment correctly, motivated by a desire to help others.

5th September 2023: Teacher’s Day Assembly

I stumbled into the auditorium as the assembly started, worried that I’d fumble my app presentation again. As the assembly was ending, my principal Ms. Khambatta invited me onto the stage to show the app. I walked through the app and, when my presentation was done, there was a resounding amount of applause in the audience as the teachers gave me a standing ovation. I guess I didn’t fumble the presentation. The app has now significantly helped teachers, amassing over 100 users, and over 1300 lesson plans have been generated using it.

13th November 2023

I woke up to my app featured in an article on Gulf News (my region’s largest newspaper). I felt a little validated and proud. This confronted me with my newfound appreciation for utilitarian existentialism. Didn’t I just decide I wanted to be motivated by a desire to help others, not a desire for recognition? I still struggle with this dilemma everyday. I face a constant internal battle between being extrinsically motivated by recognition and intrinsically motivated by a desire to help others.

But I’m gradually learning to prioritize the latter, trying to see technology I create as a tool to serve others — not as a selfish way to gain fame or achievement. I’ve learnt that true fulfillment comes from making a difference, and college will provide me with the tools to do so.

After steering through security, I crash into an island overflowing with seats and windows: Sky Harbor Terminal 4. I’m a pirate, but rather than searching for treasure, I’m here twice a month with my debate team, scouring the airport not just for a place to sit, but also for curiosity and inspiration.

The first time, Friday Before The Season Opener…

As I visited Sky Harbor, it was a tempting sandwich in my favorite store, AZCentral, that caught my eye – and stomach. But as I reached for it, my partner Arnav claimed it was too expensive. Unable to figure out how my beloved $9.50 Subway sandwich had jumped to an egregious $15.00, I searched the price hikes of sandwiches at airports. As we waited for our flight, Arnav and I researched the ins and outs of interest rates on Subway sandwiches. It was curiosity that led me to learn about how my home airport worked as a business.

As our airport discussions broadened outside of AZCentral and into discussions about the Hudson Group and Bunky Boutique, my curiosity drove me to start an entrepreneurism club and host weekly discussions. How do monopoly’s pricing strategies actually compare to startups? Were these price hikes actually the fault of the airport businesses or is there something bigger at play?

Slowly, insights about how some small businesses actually had it rough came to light. I found out how some airport sandwich shops were close to filing for bankruptcy. I felt devastated, however, my curiosity led to me pitching an interactive game to help market for these businesses.

All in all, these questions have ignited the flame of curiosity in me, and my teammates! Now, when I head back to AZCentral, I find myself and others excitedly discussing monetary policy– a footlong Subway in hand, of course.

The second time, Wednesday Morning Before The Harvard Tournament…

Gulping down our Starbucks lattes, Arnav and I were working on our case. When the plane started boarding, we finished. But the novices hadn’t. They were huddled together playing Brawl Stars on their phones.

While I was initially frustrated, I slowly recognized that it was my fault. It was one of the most prestigious tournaments of the year, and I hadn’t shown them how to adjust to the fast-paced airport life.

Initially, their lack of focus frustrated me, especially given the high stakes of the tournament. But then, I realized that it wasn't just about their inexperience; it also reflected my failure to guide them effectively in this fast-paced airport life.

So, at our next club meeting, I explained how to prepare successfully through the lens of Exploding Kittens. Beneficial evidence for winning a round was like an action card, while each ineffective evidence was like the exploding kitten card. Soon, cramped airport seats became Hamilton’s ideal prep time!

As the next tournament nears, the novices are ready, a sharp contrast from that feeling of incompletion. They've turned the once daunting task of preparation into a creative and fun yet strategic game inspired by Exploding Kittens.

I felt safe knowing that the airport strategies I taught had helped them thrive in the hectic airport environment, channeling their hunger to not only become more curious but also creatively bloom.

The last time, 11pm on a Flight Back To Phoenix…

As I step foot in the bustling terminal, the scent of ______ sandwiches hits me, prompting me to return to the food aisle of AZCentral, hoping to uncover familiar flavors and recall past discussions. My team sits at the corner, arguing over another round of losses, not in Brawl Stars, but in Exploding Kittens.

As the plane takes off and this high school era comes to an end, a wave of pride washes over me. It’s as if every memorable moment at the airport replays in front of my eyes; those curious conversations with Arnav and the creative card games to prepare cases, I proudly reflect.

For years to come, I’ll cherish the remaining months flying home to Sky Harbor. At the same time, I’m excited to find new communities in college where I can inspire others to keep hungering for!

Quiet. I always found comfort in quiet. While other kids my age were having play dates running around playgrounds, I enjoyed sitting alone in silence. As a kid, I looked forward to staying up late when no one was awake, and my house was submerged in silence. I felt tranquil knowing I had the whole world to myself, even if it was only in the middle of the night. My world shifted when I got my first pair of headphones on my 9th birthday. They kept the world silent, tuning out the chaos around me. I took them everywhere, so without them, I fell apart.

November 6th, 2008. That was the day my little brother Max was born. Many would describe me as Max’s second mom because everywhere Max went, I followed. I knew from a young age that Max was different from other kids. “Normal” kids don’t have 10-20 screaming tantrums every day, but Max always did. When he was diagnosed with a mood disorder, I wasn’t surprised. I always felt burdened by Max’s constant screaming tantrums, but that never stopped me from being a good sister. I was there to fix any inconvenience that bothered Max to prevent him from screaming. I tried to mold Max into a normal kid because I found it insufferable being in public with him screaming at the top of his lungs. I felt helpless, watching people pass by Max during his tantrums, quietly judging my family. Although Max seemed like a mess, he wasn’t. However, many people would never even attempt to try and get to know him because of his disorder.

These moments impacted who I am today. They made me realize that other people's opinions did not always matter, because they did not know our family based on one small interaction. This realization made me strong and resilient. It wasn’t unusual for Max to get bullied. I taught Max to ignore kids who picked on him because he’s so special and they will never be lucky enough to get to know him.

Dance. Dancing became my “sweet” escape from public outings with my brother. His constant blood-curdling screams drove me into dance, which became my second home. Dancing gave me a chance to express myself. At dance, it wasn’t about how Max felt, it was about me. I looked forward to hearing the music play, dancing, and releasing all the emotions I bottled up throughout the day while tending to Max’s. Coming home from dance after a long day, I knew what was waiting for me at home. As I walked through the door every day, I could hear the music calling to me, ignoring Max’s screams. My headphones were my lifeline; they tuned out the chaos around me and helped me discover my love for dance. After spending each day caring for Max, I always had something to look forward to.

Resilience. Although Max’s mood disorder may have seemed like a setback for me, I always recognized it to be where I found my love and passion for music and dancing. People around me would describe me as a resilient type of person. I always know how to turn negative things into positive ones. I started an anti-bullying Instagram page, where I gained a large following and collaborated with many small businesses to advocate for the cause. This gave me a platform to speak on my experiences with bullying because my whole life, I watched people pick on my brother for his differences. By starting an anti-bullying movement on social media, I hoped to make other kids like Max feel seen, so they know they are not alone. I am so grateful to have Max as my little brother because he has led me to do amazing things in the past seventeen years of my life, so I can only imagine what is to come in the future.

Hotel room, 11 PM, January 9th, 2023. The noise from a video call with a friend disturbed my brother’s sleep. Suddenly, I heard shouting, heavy footsteps, and the thump of the cellphone thrown onto the ground. My heart pounded, and tears filled my eyes, while I reached for the blurred black spot on the white floor. To my brother’s relief, the cracks on the screen were the only visible damage. Intangibly, however, they marked the rupture of a friendship.

My brother Eduardo, about seven years older than me, has played different parts in my life’s chapters.

During elementary school, he was my role model. Yellow, orange juice, and cat: respectively, our favorite color, drink, and the pet we asked our parents for (though we ended up getting a dog). As a five-year-old, I thought these elements were the essence of Eduardo’s identity and decided to make them my own. Plus, his academic skills: my brother’s high grades set the standard I aimed for. I would spend hours on homework, perfecting my drawings and reviewing sums and subtractions. Quickly, the first fruits from my dedication appeared: the so-desired teacher’s happy face stickers.

From middle school to early high school, he was my friend. Even though my favorite color changed to purple, and passion fruit juice became my beverage of choice, I still shared many traits with my brother, like our enthusiasm for math and logic. The challenge problems in my geometry tests from 7th grade introduced me to the thrill of solving math exercises. The frustration of not finding an immediate solution often transformed into the satisfaction of discovering the right answer when changing my approach - sometimes, highlighting congruent sides revealed an isosceles triangle. While showing me the values of persistence and adaptability, problem-solving also allowed me to spend time with my brother: we bonded over TED-Ed riddles and puzzle videogames, and he taught me math topics ahead of my class. My connection with Eduardo seemed key in my pursuit for my identity.

For ten months in high school, he was a distant presence. After the cellphone incident, we stayed apart, each waiting for the other to make the first move to reconnect. Away from Eduardo’s influence, I discovered new passions on my own. I felt more confident about my future after understanding how to combine my interests in problem-solving and life sciences with my desire to address environmental challenges. A YouTube video discussing the research on transgenic plants with enhanced carbon sequestration sparked my curiosity for biotechnology. This led me to explore the field through an online course in bioinformatics and a group project on biodiesel for the school science fair. By producing fuel from the oil found in food parts usually thrown away, like avocado peel and papaya seeds, I learned the importance of precision and attentiveness: a small change in the mass of NaOH could originate soap instead of fuel (which ended up happening more than once). As I put my ideas into practice and explored new areas of knowledge, I found satisfaction in forging a path distinct from Eduardo’s.

Today, he is my family. Too proud to accept responsibility for our conflict, I refused to admit that I missed my brother. That is, until my mom told me Eduardo was diagnosed with mild autism. I knew these two words didn’t say more than a lifetime spent together did. However, they helped me understand the challenges my brother faces daily, and, as a result, the importance of family: more than quality time, it provides support – which we couldn’t give each other for months. Regretting my absence, I wrote him a letter, acknowledging our past mistakes while asking him for a fresh start.

Relationships aren’t easy. As academic pursuits, they require commitment, perseverance, flexibility, and carefulness. But, with time, the cracks in my relationship with Eduardo were repaired, just like the ones in my cellphone.

As Naresh buried his face in his hands, I felt a pang of guilt—paralyzed by my own grief and clueless on how to support my best friend. Muthu Mama, his dad and like a second father to me, had passed away just hours earlier from a cardiac arrest. After many sleepless nights, I realized I couldn’t stay passive in my regret forever. Muthu Mama had always been there for me; I needed to be there for Naresh.

Muthu Mama encouraged me to research the physics of speed skating—centripetal forces, dynamic friction—so I could better teach techniques such as the Hawk to novice skaters. Why not apply that same research-oriented approach to grief? I delved into psychology journals at the local library, seeking to understand how I could help Naresh overcome grief.

These journals often mentioned Kubler-Ross's five stages of grief, a framework I initially applied to understand my own pain. As I dug deeper, I discovered that support is sometimes just about actively listening and creating a safe space for someone to express their feelings without judgment.

A month later, I lay in bed, unable to sleep, thinking about the annual barbecue dinner Muthu Mama always hosted on this day. Then, the phone rang—it was Naresh. I knew he would ask me to visit, but every part of me wanted to stay hidden under the covers, still grief-stricken. However, I realized his pain was probably worse than mine.

I biked over immediately, and we sat on his porch in silence. Eventually, he began to speak, his words unraveling the shock of how his dad was "just... gone." I listened and put my hand on his shoulder, my own tears held back, knowing he needed me to be strong. We stayed there until dawn broke, and as he finally drifted off to sleep, I knew my distress could wait. He needed me more.

In the following months, I visited daily to lend an active ear. However, Naresh struggled with returning to speed skating. Lacing up his skates was a reminder that his father wouldn’t be there at practices anymore. Muthu Mama’s encouragement to never give up resonated with me, so I began researching again to help Naresh until I came across the idea that losing a loved one can challenge our core beliefs. I realized Naresh needed something more than just emotional support to heal—he needed a new sense of purpose that could coexist with his grief.

To help him, I initiated “Skate For Hearts,” a fundraiser to honor Muthu Mama’s memory where we would skate 1200 miles to raise $12,000 for the American Heart Association. When I mentioned it to Naresh, he hesitated. But when I explained that every mile we skated was a step toward preventing others from losing loved ones, a glimmer of determination returned to his eyes. He agreed to skate!

Over the 1200 miles we skated together in August 2024, Naresh’s smile slowly reappeared, and his once contagious laugh returned. Each mile brought back a piece of my best friend that I thought I had lost. I hope our fundraiser has helped others reclaim those precious moments with their loved ones, just as it did for us.

Guiding Naresh through grief, I’ve not only navigated my own distress but also learned that true strength comes from the support we offer each other. I want to continue supporting others facing similar challenges by building medical devices and software that can detect health conditions early, allowing people to enjoy cherished moments with loved ones. As I step into this next phase of life, I’m committed to fostering connections and support within my community, whether with roommates, classmates, or professors.

Optics is the behavior of light, and it’s also the source of my grievances. I realized I was colorblind when I was eight years old. At the doctor’s office, I couldn’t piece together the “supposed” numbers that hid under similar shades of colors. Small greens and red circles plastered across the colorblind test book, hiding nines and twos beneath them. Failing miserably, I was diagnosed with colorblindness within six questions. In the most scientific sense, I am colorblind because I lack a set of cone cells that detect colors of light. I have come to evolve beyond that definition though. Colorblindness is my unique perspective within the world and forces me to connect likes with likes and identify qualities beyond the surface. Despite my trepidation in identifying colors in emission spectrums and heat maps, learning physics is actually where I can satiate this curiosity to explore even further. How is quantum superposition even possible? Physics is the reservoir from which I can observe the world beyond societal delineations. When I first started exploring physics in high school, I struggled. It was hard for me to move beyond the memorized formulas into real learning. Exploring the real learning in my Junior year is where I began to fully conceive the beauty behind physics. Whether it was visually seeing how light could be refracted entering water or seamlessly using integration-by-parts to grasp the flux of a donut hole, each new concept illuminated my colorless imagination. Even though my interests culminated in providing a lens to understand why I was colorblind, I wasn’t finished. I sought to carry my curiosity beyond, to analyze the most efficient freestyle pull in swimming and direct my own astrophysics research on exoplanets. My experience in navigating colorblindness kindles my passion for helping others; whether it is assisting swimmers after a passing teammate or simplifying dark matter and dark energy to third graders, I aim to help others and teach what they too cannot yet fully grasp. By teaching Jacob, I can see how he thinks of his breaststroke pull as a reversed heart, giving me insight to how I can also improve the angle in which I pull. Through compassion and a multitude of perspectives, I have a superpower that illuminates others’ world. Nonetheless, the fiery hues within my world have shaped me to become one defiant to fail and give my absolute best in my endeavors. Blue stands clear on my palette, a comfort I can always rely on. Blue is the color of the water I swim in, the first activity I truly loved. Blue is also the shivering, icy 5 am wake-ups I groggily attend, motivated to put slow performances to sleep. Vibrant blue showed me the art of chasing after what I love. Indigo, violet, and other purples are colors I cannot recognize. Purple is yearning, a brother trying to separate and fold laundry for two sisters. Purple’s mysterious dark hue surrounds the late, second shifts that my dad works, meticulously piecing together pipes, unclogging toilets, and fixing drywalls. Purple’s essence is behind each moment of success. Orange and yellow are bright. They are highlights scattered across my piano and cello music scores. They are areas that need improvement. However, amidst the emphasis on repeat signs and mezzo fortes, I can craft a soothing masterpiece that places me in serenity. The connection of the rosin bow that strikes the soothing rich G-string and the melodic pedal that effortlessly links dissonance are brilliant orange sunsets. Music compliments the color challenges and stress in my life. There is one beacon of light that connects me, physics, my colorblindness, and the world of my imagination, in which colors will always be in their fullest form. Through this, I have been presented with a gift of fiery inquisition and endless exploration.

As I browse the 99 Ranch Market aisles in search of ingredients for a new batch of dumplings, I ask myself: chicken or pork this week? In other words: which part of myself do I choose to embrace tonight?

***

“When you were little, I thought you were so skinny that no matter how much I fed you, you would never gain weight. Clearly, I was wrong,” my mom sighs, running her palm across my torso, convincing my fourth-grade self that thinning my body was the only way to achieve validation and love from my mother. From this night on, our household began to strictly consume low-fat foods, a world-record amount of tofu, and, most strikingly to me, only white meats. Pan-fried dumplings, a weekly staple in my diet, became a rare indulgence to be earned through academic success. Our dinner table transformed from a bonding haven where my mom and I prepared our favorite dishes together into a place of shame and insecurity.

***

Grudgingly stir frying chicken, garlic, and an array of Chinese seasoning sauces, I sighed, wishing I could be out with friends rather than alone in my kitchen. After earning my driver's license in junior year, my mom started working again, freed from driving me to and from school, violin lessons, and debate meetings. Her job required a 2-hour commute daily, leaving me to take on the responsibility of cooking our meals. Yet, despite gaining the freedom of administering my own diet, I dreaded trading my after-school power naps for cooking and meal-planning. Each new recipe I had to invent through the rations of my household’s limited ingredients granted another headache. But I couldn’t bear the thought of leaving these responsibilities to my exhausted mother after her tedious work schedule.

***

“STOP– don’t eat that! You’ll get salmonella.” I yelled, snatching the spoon of raw filling from one of my provisional student’s hands. “This is how we do it.” I empty the spoon onto a small plate and microwave the filling, just as my mother had once taught me. As the founding board chef of my school's new Food & Culture Club, I was giving my own masterclass on preparing dumplings, demonstrating how to properly taste the filling. Portioning out the now-cooked pork mixture to each board member, I felt increasingly satisfied, watching each of my temporary food critics give the filling a nod of approval. Guiding my classmates on rolling, filling, and folding hundreds of dumplings, just as my mother had once done for me, brought me a sense of both comfort and achievement, helping me realize just how valuable the time I spent cooking with my loved ones truly is. For the first time since the fateful shift in my family’s diet, I began to cook for my own enjoyment.

***

“Folding looks beautiful. Just like how I taught you as a little girl,” my mom approved. Despite the pride I gained in my cooking from my peers, my feelings towards the dumplings were ultimately dictated by my biggest critic, the mentor who taught me to make dumplings in the first place. Having expected a beration of criticism, I was stunned into silence, watching as my mom finished the entire portion of dumplings I brought home. I stare at her empty plate in gratification, knowing that finishing the dish was her own way of demonstrating gratitude. A wave of relief came over me as I realized that she enjoyed my food, despite its sodium content or protein type.

***

Facing the debate between pork loin or chicken breast tonight, the decision seems clear. Although I’m no stranger to opting for the “healthier” option, allowing myself to eat meals I truly enjoy now determines my diet. With each roll, fill, and fold, I honor my mom’s teachings, passing on her knowledge to others and sharing her love through each dumpling. So, for tonight’s batch, I’ll definitely be going with pork.

I can make toilet paper rolls become bunnies. I first stumbled upon the Amur Leopard in my brother’s National Geographic magazine. I spent that night huddled under my blanket, reading about the species and their endangered status. By morning, I had a plan to wrest the species from the jaws of extinction. My afternoons became filled with unusual duct tape crafts, and menageries of sock puppets which I took from door to door, determined to raise money and awareness. As I clicked the “Donate” button, I felt like I was helping an effort larger than myself. It was the first time I brought purpose to a cause I was passionate about.

In my eighth-grade history class, we discussed educational inequity and its impact on social mobility. As the daughter of first-generation immigrants who came to the US to pursue higher education, I experienced first-hand how transgenerational emphasis on education translated into more opportunities. I came to understand that the performance gap in education started early in life and was largely determined by socioeconomic status. It came down to opportunity and not ability. Like when I first read about the Amur Leopard, I felt that familiar tug – Could I do something about this injustice? I needed to.

As I researched more, I sought to create a tactile educational program for students seeking STEM resources. I wanted to create a fun learning space in which students could be exposed to similar enrichment resources that piqued my curiosity and interest. What began as late nights with friends, sending emails, and wrestling with WordPress, soon turned into mornings spent explaining fossils and adaptations to eager students. When 7-year-old Eva excitedly showed me her Play-Doh superhero during our genetics session at her local library, I was reminded of those afternoons spent sticky with duct tape residue, building something meaningful.

At seventeen, I am still eager to create and solve. Learning about a non-profit that provides devices to teach digital literacy to students in Kenya, I was keen on contributing. After recruiting my peers, we partnered with Loglogo, an at-risk all-girls school in rural Kenya to conduct weekly classes. I was struck by the strength these girls had. Seeking reprieve from child marriages and abusive families, they chose to continue to invest in their education. During a lesson, Mercy describes how she can use the video feature to look back at her football (soccer) games and practice her technique, and Ruth eagerly describes the Instagram page she wants to create to share her soup recipes. They are eager to learn and grow. Their positivity radiates from my screen and inspires me to take action in what I believe in. As I continue to forge these global connections, I find my perspectives broaden as distances shrink.

Although market research (my dad) might suggest that people would rather wear their socks than play with them, I treasure each of my endeavors. They are vehicles for me to make sense of the world. Wherever my interests take me, I strive to advocate for the issues I see in the same way: dynamically, with energy and exigency. As the world around me motivates me to create, build, and solve, I hope to carry myself with the same determination and faith as my seven-year-old self.

I have learned that the ability to take action is a privilege– one that I refuse to waste. I hope to continue to learn and gather experiences, expanding the possibilities of what I can do. As I move forward, I know each new endeavor will find its place alongside the toilet paper roll bunnies and sock puppets in my personal hall of fame.

The robot burned down in the Marshall Fire. There was less than a month until the competition.

During the next team meeting, the usual excitement was gone. We had a lot of things to do in this crucial final push, and now, we didn’t even have a robot. Giving up, something that had never come up in past discussions, seemed to take center stage that day. A part of me also wanted to give up, and if there had been only a week left before the competition, I probably would have. Although it would be tight, I knew we had a chance. As the team captain, I decided to take action as soon as possible. I realized that having no robot meant that progress in other areas would be slowed: we really had two weeks to rebuild. There was a real chance that we wouldn’t make it, but I tried to appear calm when speaking to not add more fuel to the fire.

I could sense the reason everyone was so nervous: they just didn't know where to start.

If we were going to make it, team morale would be a crucial aspect, and no one is happy if they want to help but feel like they are doing nothing. For this reason, I decided to give everyone some small tasks: order this part, drill these holes, 3D print that part, and so on. Everyone left with something to do, some way to help.

These small tasks would help, but they wouldn’t rebuild the robot in two weeks. If the team came back to the next meeting and there still wasn’t a physical robot they could see, it definitely wouldn’t help morale.

So, I got to work on building it. It was relentless: tightening countless screws, drilling, connecting frames, aligning gears, setting chains, everything to rebuild the robot. One time, I fell asleep while building the robot. I woke up next to a heap of nuts in the middle of the night, completely confused as to where I was. Even the 3D printer was working overtime, buzzing through the night.

My strategy seemed to work.

During the next meeting, the team came back with their small tasks done.

When they also saw the robot, which at that time was a drivetrain with the skeleton of the frame, you could feel that the overall feeling in the room was better than before. Again, I spoke in a calm voice to pack in reassurance; was I that calm inside? No, not really. But now the team had hope that we could make it, and this inspired them to help out more.

I continued to work every day after school. At every meeting, the robot was a little more finished, and the team was a little more excited. When they saw the robot getting closer to completion, it motivated them just a little more. That was what I was going for.

It was the last evening, and not everything was done.

We met right after school, working on presentations, practice runs, and Q&A. It was approaching nine, and we needed to wake up at around six for the competition. I knew that everyone would need to perform well tomorrow, so I decided to call the session over and let everyone rest. I stayed up until two, finishing the autonomous programs.

The burned robot tested me as a leader and as a person. I could've not stepped up from the get-go, but for me, leading means doing. When you do, you show an example that motivates others. To me, leading also means understanding. To get the most help from my team, I needed to understand what they were feeling. These two principles are key to me, and they guide the way I lead; they are what I want to bring to the people, clubs, and potential businesses on campus.

Droplets of blood trickled down his forehead and snakelike patterns of stitches glistened in the white hospital light. I had never seen Chetta like this before.

When I first learnt that my older brother was hit by a car, I didn’t know how to react.

The word “Chetta,” Malayalam for brother, had followed me for years. The pressure I put on myself to compete with Chetta’s musicality filled me with blind ambition. Despite endless hours of strain, I was determined to surpass his achievement with every new melody I blew into my flute or saxophone. But each of my performances at the Balaji temple only deepened an insatiable void in my heart.

After the accident, Chetta started to change. Sustaining a major concussion, he struggled to keep up with his freshman year in college while fighting severe depression and anxiety. I couldn’t see him as the idol who propelled me to empty heights anymore. All I could see was my brother, struggling, and I had to support him.

As weeks passed, I made the conscious decision to become a friend rather than a rival. Seeing him struggle with coursework, I flipped our conversations into practice problems and our regular FaceTime calls into review sessions. Watching MATH110 lectures together distracted us from his ailments as he slowly regained his smile — a smile I had once taken for granted.

At the same time, I found myself enthralled in these new topics, asking a tornado of follow-up questions. By exploring the links between game theory, cryptography, and antitrust policy, I wondered: How can technological innovation transform foundational economic systems? Though difficult at times, these investigations felt right; they motivated me to appreciate the discussions as they were—with no covetous spirit spoiling them. Life had given me a platform to explore my thoughts, while shedding light on a fun, empathetic relationship.

Without a perfect Chetta to chase, a new north star guided me: Curiosity. I started to combine my newfound wonder with my talent in South Asian music. Instead of straining for endless hours to perfect a melody, misguidedly trying to compete with Chetta, I discovered new thoughts steering me towards musical politics, caste discrimination in Tamil Nadu, and intra-brahmin secularization in the arts. Through this, I broke an unwritten rule in my hypercompetitive community by indulging myself in anthropology research that stirred my mind instead of restricting myself to a stigmatized workaholic life.

Becoming my brother’s support system placed me in a service role for the first time, leaving a lasting impression on my heart. I found that being an ally was rewarding and was inspired to channel my energy towards serving others instead of my own ambition. By kickstarting a non-profit centered around relationships with the elderly and malnourished, I found that the people who I helped taught me unique and invaluable truths. As I delivered Mr. Palmissano’s Trader Joe’s Syrup or Grandma Joyce’s lychees, I experienced genuine gratitude. To my amazement, my self-doubt began to fade as I uncovered newfound purpose.

As the competitive craters in my heart filled, new depths exposed themselves in my life-long bond with family. Through this experience, I realized all the struggles, both physical and mental, my mom and dad have faced — struggles my blinded mind previously ignored. Over the next three years, this realization was tested when both my grandfather and little cousin developed cancer. Rather than burying my feelings by solely feeding my academic and musical ambition, I rose up, becoming a pillar of comfort for my family in their time of need.

Chetta has always shown me that being ambitious can lead to a certain level of success. However, tunnel vision created by competition and self-aggrandizement leads to hollowed-out achievement.

Paired with empathy and understanding, a drive directed by an inquisitive mind will allow me to explore the world freely. Chetta no longer defines my aspiration. I am free to be me.

It was 96 degrees outside, but when I stepped through the gates, my body felt cold. A pale white sign painted with black lettering above a barren wall read “Arbeit Macht Frei,'' meaning “Work Sets You Free.” This was a common Nazi maxim. As we walked through the barracks, the tour guide explained the conditions the Jews were forced to endure. Starvation, forced labor, overcrowding. Terezin was not a death camp, still, over 33,000 people died there, not to mention 90,000 sent to extermination camps. Those weren’t numbers. Those were people. Each person with a life, a family, and a stolen future.

My grandmother Raya, a widow and immigrant from Ukraine, was lucky. She could’ve had her future erased like the other 6 million Jews who died during the Holocaust. Her mother and sisters died in the massacre of Babi Yar, but she survived, and despite the horrors she witnessed, she was the most positive person I’ve ever met. As I was growing up, her visits from San Jose to our home in Southern California were full of excitement and storytelling. She was a great listener and incredibly responsive to my need to communicate. Even though I was young, our discussions were always satisfying and insightful. When I explained my deepest frustrations, including a knee injury that forced me to quit soccer, or struggles to make friends, I distinctly recall how she ended these conversations: "Vsyo budet khorosho Shany!" (Everything will be alright).

Over the past six years, though, my Grandma Raya has been battling depression. Around my twelfth birthday, I became aware that something was off. On the phone, grandma seemed subdued. I desperately wanted to help her. After researching her diagnosis, I learned that loneliness and depression are linked. So, I began Skyping with her two times a week. Grandma looked forward to our calls because she opened up to me about her joys and sorrows. She also told me about her past - how she grew up, her family, and the atrocities she witnessed during WWII. I listened in awe. I could see what she saw: the soldiers in uniform, the broken glass scattered on the ground, the snow lined with boot tracks. Those vivid images motivated me to visit Terezin in the summer of 2023 in order to help me understand my grandmother, and these tragic events.

Five years ago, when I discussed how much I enjoyed Skyping with my grandmother, my Sunday school teacher suggested I join a group called Mitzvah Centers in Southern California. I did, and in 2019 became a pod leader, arranging visits to various senior residential facilities. Every other week a group of 5-8 kids, including myself, got together and visited the seniors.

We sat and listened to the residents who had different stories to tell. One person had a son who was injured and unable to visit, another had no living relatives, and another discussed how busy her children were. What I remember the most, though, are their smiles when we walked in. During COVID, these activities were temporarily put on hold, but the Mitzvah Centers eventually supported Zooming with the seniors. Although I have moved to Texas, I continue to exchange stories with these people because I have realized that it not only benefits them, it helps me, too.

My grandma has helped me appreciate the power of storytelling and that our stories bring us together. Through communication, we learn from one another and gain perspective. Through my interactions with my grandma, and the people I have met through the Mitzvah Centers, I have become a more compassionate, resilient, and positive person. Listening and being kind are Mitzvahs (good deeds), and the more Mitzvahs there are in the world, the less room there is for the hatred that led to places like Terezin.

The sound of my heart pounding reverberated through the room, accompanied by the constant chattering of my teeth. I questioned why I hadn't urged my friend to leave my house earlier. My gaze was fixated on my bedroom door, desperately searching for any hint of a supernatural stranger. Although I had always been known for my apprehension about anything spooky, this childhood instance was different. While I usually managed to avoid our horror movie nights, my friend had made it her mission to expose me to the genre by telling me “scary” stories laden with ghosts, killers, and other cliched characters. The most terrifying parts of the experience, though, were what happened when I didn’t sleep well.

Bleary-eyed and irritable, I exhaustedly stumbled through the next few days. The lack of sleep took its toll, making it a Herculean endeavor to focus on my math problems and leaving me constantly anxious. However, this experience sparked my curiosity about the profound impact of sleep on mental health. How could a few days lacking it cause such a shift in my well-being?

In high school, late nights became routine as I balanced academics, extracurriculars, and social activities. Knowing that this was a common phenomenon among my peers, I joined the Hamilton Lab at Rutgers University to investigate further. In the lab, I reviewed research on the links between poor sleep and suicide risk, and helped develop a sleep intervention for teens. I learned that systemic factors also play a significant role in sleep quality, with many facing challenges beyond their control, such as inadequate time for sleep due to multiple jobs or an absence of a safe sleeping place. My laptop was filled with annotated studies and highlighted articles, each contributing to my understanding of this issue.

Now what? Just knowing this information wasn’t enough. It couldn’t possibly be left exclusively to me—I wanted to ensure that it resonated with others as well.

I shared my insight with community members at Rutgers Day, listening to their stories about sleep and mental health and offering strategies for more impactful rest. As they jotted down their thoughts and favorite activities on our booth's whiteboard, I realized how powerful these conversations could be. That day, something shifted for me—it wasn’t just about research anymore. It was clear that this was the beginning of a deeper commitment to advocacy, one that would continue to grow.

Beyond the community, I found opportunities to share my knowledge with other young advocates. One notable instance was my involvement in organizing RISE Day in collaboration with the lab, where teenagers came together to explore research processes and psychology careers and develop impactful community initiatives. From drafting the grant, to refining our presentation and co-writing an abstract on the importance of youth advocacy, every step was a chance to grow and connect with others who shared my passion. During lunch, our animated discussions about the gaps in mental health support in schools only strengthened my sense of purpose and my connection to the mission we were all so invested in.

Today, I’m proud to say that I am not just an advocate for the importance of sleep. Advocacy plays a central role in my life, whether I’m demonstrating deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prevention techniques to my community, recruiting volunteers to donate blood at the Piscataway Street Fair, presenting recommendations for systemic healthcare issues to my congressman, or deciding what genre of movie our family watches on the weekend (not a scary one).

I aspire to be a physician in the future—not solely treating a patient’s medical condition, but being their utmost supporter in their journey, advocating for them despite biological, socioeconomic, or policy barriers, and contributing to community initiatives that will further our collective health. A future without advocacy—not just in health either—is a frightening concept, and I intend to pursue it wholeheartedly in college and beyond.

“Did you forget your name?” he asked with an awkward laugh.

After the monotonous chorus of introductions had echoed, it was finally my turn to speak. My mouth hinged open, lockjawed and gaping, but the words died in my throat. Silence pressed on me like a wet blanket, smothering me in its embrace. It was interrupted by the muffled laughter trailing the teacher’s question. Then followed the insensitive yet impressively spot-on imitations by my classmates. Seconds later, I heard it again, the same monotonous chorus. He’d skipped me.

I stutter, but not q-q-quite like Porky Pig. Mine isn’t repetitive, but more a silent force blocking the path from my brain to mouth, preventing thoughts from birthing words.
Simple acts—calls, orders—became daunting obstacles. Sentences were battlegrounds, words minefields of potential humiliation. I clung to the belief I wasn’t broken, merely wired differently. Yet, each botched word saw me surrendering ground in the tug-of-war with societal perception. To protect my fragile reality, I’d resigned myself to silence.

My chest tightened hearing that harrowing question. It was a spectre that haunted each first day, each icebreaker, each introduction—each time I had to say my name. It mocked the effort I was wasting stifling my voice. My stutter was a Chinese finger trap—hating and resisting only fueled the vicious cycle. This “imperfection” was woven into my identity, as defining as my fingerprints; it was exhausting trying to hide it. I sought to break the silence. A tally counter, my companion, clicked with each stutter while I walked to class. My hand, a reluctant actor, raised; my mouth, a stubborn gate, swung open. Words, those elusive sprites, danced just out of reach. Click—another tally for the counter. I acknowledge each stutter, training my subconscious to accept each falter as a whim in my speech. Although each choked word sent my heart racing, I refused to let the blip keep me in its vise-like grip.

Weekends found me in unfamiliar corners of my city. I approached each encounter like a soldier charging toward a battlefield with nothing but a sign reading, “I stutter; come say hello.” My heart pounded in anticipation.
Some paused, their brows furrowing in confusion. Others approached, their eyes betraying curiosity. We spoke; My sentences were a mosaic of fractures. I smiled. Click. I owned each word and danced with my stutters, each misstep a part of the choreography. In those suspended moments, when time dilated as my words hung mid-air, “Wow,” I’d quip at the end of a hard-won sentence, “I thought that’d take an eternity.” Laughter mingled with my staccato speech, and a revelation dawned: I was broken, but that made me whole.
Disfluency, rather than defining me, refined me. In the quiet spaces between syllables, where words hesitate, I discovered the value of Socratic seminars. I learned to understand people’s differences and the weight behind each fragmented sentence. Witnessing how supposed curses become blessings, I now use each conversation as a chance to forge resilience. However, stuttering isn't just my tale. It's a narrative stifled by ignorance and the pressure of perfection. If society knew to stop treating their 'imperfections' as faults to overcome, 75 million people wouldn't feel trapped as I did. StutterStrong is my initiative to make that happen, celebrating every stumble, hesitation, and imperfect cadence. I’ve given 13 presentations on stuttering, keynoting at African Stammering Connections. I’ve met other stutterers, inspiring them to embrace their unique quirk as I did mine. One of whom, Aaira, I helped start her own campaign. I stutter. And th-th-that's all, folks! That's all there is to it. I stutter. And much like Porky Pig, confidently. I make calls. I place orders. My true mission, though, lies in reaching out to that ashamed boy struggling to force a smile on hearing that question. I want to talk to him, show him that there’s nothing wrong with being flawed, there’s nothing wrong with forgetting his name.

After steering through security, I entered an island overflowing with seats and windows: Sky Harbor Terminal 4. I’m a pirate, but rather than searching for treasure, I’m here twice a month with my debate team, scouring the airport for items that satisfy my hunger to improve: as the plane takes off, it's as if my dreams are taking off too.

Once, a tempting sandwich caught my eye – and stomach. As I reached for it, my partner Arnav claimed it was too expensive, launching a debate about the airport’s unjust sandwich monopoly. Eventually, we settled with interest rates, and their impact on my beloved $9.50 Subway sandwich, now $15.00. But I was dissatisfied. Why? Upon returning home, I started to research the price hikes of sandwiches at airports, but couldn’t find anything. As my research broadened to monopolies and startups, I had an eagerness to study businesses. Eventually, my curiosity drove me to start an entrepreneurism club and host weekly discussions – a more productive way to find answers. Slowly, insights about how some small businesses actually had it rough came to light. As we discussed everything from monopolies on airport food to Jerome Powell’s policy on interest rates, I’d ask. Are these price hikes actually the fault of the airport businesses or is there something bigger at play? [All in all, these questions have ignited the flame of curiosity in me. Maybe it's because of the Subway sandwich or because of the discussions with Arnav. Whatever it is, at the airport, I feel a stronger connection to my curiosity.

Gulping down our Starbucks lattes, Arnav and I were working on our case, writing and finding evidence to perfect it. When the plane started boarding, we finished. But the novices hadn’t. Huddled together playing video games, they were clueless as to what they needed to do. I thought I had failed them, but since it was one of the first tournaments of the year, I decided to teach them how to adjust to this life through fun activities. At the club meeting afterwards, I explained how to prepare successfully through the lens of Exploding Kittens. Each beneficial evidence was like an action card while each ineffective evidence was like the exploding kitten card. At the airport, I hosted typing competitions through Monkey Type and imitated a dog through charades to teach the novices how to creatively prepare their cases and speech on the go, despite the limited working conditions. Teaching unconventional strategies like Exploding Kittens, typing competitions, and charades will not only fulfill my hunger to have fun, but will help others find creative ways to practice despite the airport environment.

The paintings at the airport were like colors of a palette splashing me, and yet no one glanced. How could this mural be so overlooked? I desperately wanted to help these artists receive recognition, so I recruited volunteers to operate a competition. I was scared. Was I qualified to run this competition? But after confiding with my team at the library, I felt empowered since their support infused me with a clearer vision to tackle the project. By inviting professional artists to judge, we attracted hundreds of aspiring artists to submit their works, ranging from Japanese watercolor paintings to contemporary art on the Seven Wonders. As the competition came to a close, my team and I proudly showcased all of these works to the judges on Zoom, receiving a flood of comments: “Wow! These artists are so underrated!” Many of these judges even offered internships and scholarship money. Although I wasn’t able to highlight those airport pieces. If I learned something it’s that you can’t save everyone, but you can try. By helping others persevere, I’m satiating the hunger to help others receive recognition.

Hunger is the feeling of Sky Harbor Terminal 4. Each time going back to the airport, nostalgia runs rampant. The scent of sandwiches reminds me of my curiosity, the ubiquitous Starbucks reminds me of creativity, and the new paintings inspire me with themes for next year’s competition. In college and beyond, I will continue to uphold these traits through questioning lectures about economic theory, persevering even when my brain tells me to stop, and helping others with group projects that I’m not a part of.

Noise reverberates around Bus 11 as it rumbles down Madison Street, but I can’t hear it. Instead, a search for the perfect song meets its resolution. My headphones buzz with a song not meticulously executed but entrenched in the human sound of gospel and blues - Duke Ellington’s “The Shepherd” is the perfect vessel for my band’s unique, raw sound.

Convincing the band of The Shepherd’s merit necessitates immediate action. When I finally arrive home, I skid over to the piano. As I listen to The Shepherd on repeat, I recreate its liking in a three-part formula: first, converting pitches into numbers and symbols; second, identifying the current key; and lastly, combining the two to create a visual – the matching notes on the piano light up as my hands dance over the shifting chords and scales. In the following weeks, I seek to develop my understanding of the song – its improvisational solos demanding an intimate knowledge of the harmony. School lunches spent practicing start to intrigue passerby bandmates. Soon many of my closest musicians are on board.

Still hungry for understanding, I keep searching further. I meticulously dissect The Shepherd, leaving no recording untouched. Throughout all takes, one key soloistic idea remains the same - a simple yet definitive perfect cadence. This use of a timeless resolution between musical phrases creates a flow that fragments ideas through time but connects them through harmony.

With the core elements in place, I expand my influences. Blending Oscar Peterson's bluesy licks, Jacob Collier's ornate composing, and McCoy Tyner's pentatonic qualities, I carefully craft a sound uniquely mine. Invigorated by my developments, I seek out my band director. He listens attentively as I demonstrate the product of my dedication. When I finish, he calmly delivers his thoughts. “It sounds… busy and contrived.” A disheartening blow. That night as I play, I feel stagnant. My ideas - repetitions of the past, growing repulsive as they age. Days pass searching for inspiration to break the hold of habit.

In a hopeful attempt, I seek guidance from my fellow soloists. One group chat and premature arrival later, I anxiously sit on my friend’s couch, my foot tapping sporadically to an imaginary groove. When everyone arrives, conversation begins immediately. As we discuss, we search to support and revise my old methodology. Reflection leads us far into the past as we toss around the influences of Duke Ellington and The Shepherd. The impact of religion seems especially strong in this piece: hopeful gospel rebutting the sorrow of blues, like a preacher delivering uplifting speeches to the dispirited congregation. This call and response of praise and amen seems to be mirrored between soloists and the band. Maybe “The Shepherd” is the preacher, leading his congregation of sheep to safety. Electrified by this new revelation, we all grab our instruments and attempt to incorporate this metaphor into our playing. An abstract process takes shape we each assume a distinct role: Timothy, the trumpet, acting as our words of wisdom; Gianni, the trombone, asking for guidance; and me, the piano, interjecting “Amen” and “Hallelujah!” with my conversational chords. This alteration to our approach challenges the constraints instilled by the rigidity of music theory. Over weeks of before-school meetings, we use the metaphor of The Shepherd to create a thematic and communicative performance that remains authentic to its history. This technique even carries over to my solo with my left and right hands assuming the roles of congregation and preacher respectively.

The solution to captivating music entails more than just checking off a list of criteria. I’ve found it requires a willingness to experiment, reverence towards historical origins, and most importantly, respect for the critique of others. This experience has enforced the importance of community in my approach to problem solving, allowing novel influences to build on my foundational knowledge. Whether it’s music, programming, or day to day issues, collaboration shapes my innovation.

390mg of caffeine. Panera’s Charged Lemonade, with as much caffeine as five cups of coffee, was a requirement for every 4:30 am store opening. Whether I was on all fours cleaning drainage clogs that flooded the back of the restaurant with over an inch of murky “water”, sopping up the aftermath of a spilled soup catastrophe, or detoxifying tables a pigeon chose to make its overnight nest, the drink was a necessary evil.

My coworker Yaya said she could only make it through an eventful day at Panera because of our caffeine-infused concoctions. Although our signature “energy drink” powered us through the day, it was available to anyone, including children. Kids playing tag during the lunch rush wasn’t ideal, but it kept work exciting. However, Yaya and I had the most fun experimenting with our vast array of food toppings. Unfortunately, we’re still waiting for the Panera marketing team to get on board with our Buffalo Mac & Cheese Chicken Sandwich, obviously topped with peppadew peppers and frizzled onions (the best toppings at Panera). After only a month on the job, Yaya and I had formed a close relationship. She became my role model at work for her unrelenting confidence—despite standing at a whopping 5’3’’, she projected her voice so powerfully that even grown men feared her. Yaya helped me get comfortable with interaction and confrontation rather than shying away.
