I quickly became much more confident interacting with customers, so much so that I even got promoted to shift leader. As school started, I reduced my hours to only work the weekends, assuming Yaya did the same. I soon realized working wasn't a choice: she worked thirty hours weekly to cover food, clothing, and medicine. Working was a way of life that left little room for homework or the dream of attending college. Her hard work had a different urgency–one I had never experienced. Over time, I couldn’t help but notice the challenges my classmates were quietly enduring. Like Yaya, many were juggling school and work, but lacked the resources to fully pursue their academic goals. Their access to computers was limited to the school day, leaving limited time for exploration beyond the basic requirements. This growing awareness left me caught in a struggle of logic and emotion. Leveraging my newfound communication skills, I reached out to individuals and companies for donations of old computers, and despite initial rejections, my tenacity paid off. Two years later, Ms. Parker, my school’s social worker, tells me with a beaming smile how eighteen students have personal computers for the first time. Additionally, in the guidance computer lab, counselors work with other low-income students on the college application process. Ms. Stewart, the Robinson High School social worker, explains how a student living in a motel next year can still graduate through online school. After working with program coordinators to form lesson plans for resume-building and interview skills, every visit to Loretta Ingraham Community Center leaves me with a profound sense of pride and satisfaction at how eager students are to learn when given fair access to resources. These students, despite their struggles, share a determination to fight for their future. Between their multitude of responsibilities, from being workers, caregivers, and breadwinners, it’s easy to let school drop as a priority, yet as a society, we must create a system that incentivizes them to pursue further education.

The hard work and resilience I saw in Yaya and so many other students inspired me to leverage my newfound skills to create opportunities for others and while I’ve been able to help a meaningful number of local students, the journey towards educational equity is far from over. As I continue to navigate my academic and personal growth, I’m committed to expanding these efforts, guided by the lessons from the caffeine-charged mornings at Panera: that hard work, whether fueled by caffeine or compassion, can transform lives.

May 16th, 2024. An unforgettable gray afternoon that seemed like any other, quickly turned into a day that would redefine me. I drove home after robotics, exhausted and ready for a power nap. I shrugged off my backpack and collapsed onto my bed around 5:30 PM, ready to wake to my alarm at 7pm. Little did I know, nature had a different wake-up call planned. Thirty minutes later, a crack so vicious that it seemed to mark the beginning of the end roared in my eardrums. Bricks, once a part of a sturdy roof, hailed from the ceiling above, immediately followed by the trunk of a 300-foot tree. Confused and groggy, I felt my right thigh throbbing from the debris (later diagnosed as internal bleeding by the EMT) but adrenaline drowned out all other thoughts. Instinctively, I ran out of my room, stumbling on the soggy carpet, clad in nothing but my pants. The power had gone out, making the hallway dim, but my mind was crystal clear: check on my family.

My mother and father had hopelessly watched the tree fall from the second-story window while my cousin just arrived home from work, walking into a scene straight out of a disaster movie. It was only after ensuring everyone’s safety that the reality of the situation dawned on me—this wasn’t a dream: this was chaos. I noticed the sound of water—a lot of water. A clear wall poured in through a gaping hole in the living room, courtesy of the tree branches now decorating our interior. Buckets hastily grabbed from my outdoor garage became tools to desperately save what we still had. My family and I worked together, sweeping water out of our front door and moving precious items upstairs, drenched in a mixture of rainwater and sweat. After the weather calmed down and our brooms broke, the harsh truth settled in: our house was uninhabitable. As we packed up dry clothes, we said our last goodbyes and drove away, setting out for shelter.

A hotel room with bland decor and a constant hum of air conditioning, a stark contrast to the warmth our house emitted, became our temporary home for the next three weeks. Despite the chaos around me, life continued. Finals were right around the corner and adaptation became a necessity. The squeaky and shiny wicker basket chairs in the hotel lobby restaurant replaced my dad's old office chair, and was where I found myself balancing schoolwork with endless paperwork, insurance claims, and repair plans. It was definitely not the crash course in adulthood that I had imagined, but was undoubtedly effective.

As the weeks passed by and I returned to a normal schedule, I was struck by the funny way life teaches lessons. The very bricks that caused damage to my thigh had also saved my life, preventing the tree from crushing me in my sleep. Being so close to death has a way of sharpening perspective, revealing what truly matters. Suddenly, even the mundane moments I once took for granted have now become golden. Waking up in my own bed feels like a luxury. Dinner with my family has become a celebration. I now face the trials and tribulations life gives us in a positive light with a renewed sense of purpose.

But the aftermath wasn’t just about survival but rather about transformation. The storm, with all its chaos, had revealed a resilience that hadn’t been tested before. It didn’t just tear through my ceiling; it tore through my old ways of thinking. There is no need to announce the newfound strength—it's evident in the paperwork filled out, the final exams taken, and all the other steps taken. The storm has left a mark, but in the process has shaped a determined spirit. When the unexpected strikes (literally), there are two choices: crumble or rise. My choice was made in the split second of chaos, in the everlasting days of cleanup, and in the quiet moments of reflection. The number of trials ahead is unknown, but one thing remains certain—I’m more than ready for it, paperwork and all.

My father opened the lid, eyes widened with fright, and dropped the wax laden lid to the ground. Squadron 1 took off in perfect formation, attacking the cracks in my dad's supposedly bee-proof jeans. I was terrified and scampered indoors. My introduction to the bees began with me running away. One hot Mumbai summer day, as the school bell rang, my mom called to inform me that traffic was terrible. I decided to ditch the school bus and take a combination of Metro and Autorickshaw that would stretch over 6 miles that took an hour for me to reach home, all because the local authorities were repairing a 2x3 meter patch of road.

That long ride home gave me some time to think about the fascinating disconnect between natural systems and human-engineered systems. Bees, like ants, have highly evolved social systems and methods of communication. Living in the overpopulated metropolis of Mumbai, I see the absence of the hypnotizing productivity with which a swarm works. Why can’t humans be perfectly cooperative like the ants?

I dug into the problem through the lens of swarm intelligence, a theory on the behavior of self-organized systems. A bee hive hanging from a branch can spread over a large area in response to an external force, increasing the strain on each individual bee, but reducing the overall pressure on the hive. The selflessness and flexibility of the bees were missing in the jam, where drivers jostled and fought for their turn to escape the bottleneck.

Making qualitative sense of the situation didn’t satisfy me. Like any child of mathematics, I needed some numbers to play with. Looking for a framework that would guide me, I trudged through massive volumes on Transportation Science by leading operations research journals like INFORMS and the International Journal of Transportation Science and Technology. I read Dr. Victor Knoop’s article on interactions between drivers at intersections and a study on Markov modeling of vehicular flow by the General Motors Laboratories. I realized that making sense of the chaotic Indian traffic won’t come out of a few research papers about “organized” road systems. I would need to combine that research with my own understanding of swarm intelligence.

My research on swarm intelligence inspired my TED ED Student talk on how ants and bees can serve as a template for the attitudes of our drivers. I connected the chaos on the streets to my research on swarm intelligence, hoping to inspire my audience. Furthermore, I extended the principles of swarm intelligence to theorize about Indian traffic. Online mathematical modeling techniques helped me simulate traffic conditions like acceleration, lane changes, and traffic lights, and questions like “How much does a sudden lane change by one driver affect the flow of traffic?” By a lot!

The connection I made between my backyard bees and traffic made me realize that impactful ideas can come out of our unique experiences. For over four years, I have helped the members of the TED ED Student Club realize that their stories matter in a global context. I helped a 15-year-old marry their obsession with comics and love for psychology, establishing a link between cliffhangers used in panels and the closure obtained by using our imagination.

I look forward to learning more from my friends living in hives. With groundbreaking research being done into swarm intelligence techniques like ant colony optimization, I want to find solutions for problems beyond traffic that are inspired by natural systems in the medical field, where waiting times for patients can be optimized or with law enforcement where response times can be reduced. I see myself in a university that promotes innovation and unique thinking, where I can engage in constant collaboration with multidisciplinary professors and peers about my interests. Until then, I’ll keep observing my backyard bees, looking for inspiration to solve new problems.

“All you want to do is play basketball!” My dad shouts. After storming away, I find myself in the shower, legs wrapped in my arms, thankful that the water drowns out my sobs.

I’ve played piano since I was five. Placing in international competitions at a young age, my parents encouraged me to dedicate myself to piano, and I embraced it. That is, until the 6th grade, when my classmates found out. My tablemates and I were Googling each others’ names. Everyone started laughing when a quick search of my name yielded a handful of my piano videos on YouTube and pictures of me in jacketless tuxedos suited for competitions. They were bewildered as to why the athletic boy they thought they knew played classical piano. My cheeks flushing, I vowed to become an NBA player I never wanted to play piano again.

But as I continued basketball throughout junior year, I found myself on the bench halfway through the season, and soon basketball felt like a nine-to-five job. I realised when I start new activities, I commit myself to them completely at first. But that fresh feeling of newly found love doesn’t last forever, especially when challenges, like classmates’ judgment, get in the way. I had to find a way to sustain an activity, preserving my interest without burning out.

My basketball struggles during the season made me rethink piano. In the following months, I brought myself to the keyboard slowly—one hour at a time. Yet I found myself blanking out playing with no real purpose and structure to my practice sessions. First, I needed a cause, a reason to do something every day and a goal to work towards. I thought about my mother driving me an hour from school to piano then back for basketball practice and my father paying for my piano lessons. Seeing their sacrifices, I made them my cause. I constructed a practice plan, warming up with scales and arpeggios, followed by one-hand rhythmic practices in difficult passages of my pieces. Unexpectedly, I found myself immersed in the unique style of impressionist music while playing Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse, a style I hadn’t yet played. I built up to practicing for two hours everyday again, making sure to give myself the freedom to play catchy pop songs from the radio and even take a few days off. Finding ways to de-stress allowed me to balance piano even as my schedule became tighter with AP tests and off-season open gyms. The balance allowed me to joke around with my teammates at the gym and still feel energized to practice half of a piece afterwards.

Standing in the shower a few months later, I thought back to the furrowed brows and loud cackles my online photos garnered from classmates. My peers were right to laugh, because it was surprising—I am a basketball player, but I am also a pianist. Although an unlikely combination, playing piano helps me conduct my basketball skill set in developing new footworks and moves, with piano helping me stay in tune by making me be patient but also reminding me to stay consistent.

While the joy of a newfound hobby might fade, by sticking with piano, I discovered a new type of joy: being able to work closely with peers that inspired me with their passion. People at school would never see the laughter from trying out unorthodox voicings with my string players during our practice sessions, but I don’t need to be what they expect me to be.

Like me, millions of other pianists struggle to have structure in practice sessions. Knowing my fascination in classical music, machine learning, and problem-solving, I want to make it my mission to create an app to help people improve their skills each session. My fascination will propel me to develop new dimensions of my identity. I embrace this, knowing I can have multiple, and these passions will only be strengthened when I join clubs to inspire and to be inspired.

I have a hatred for loud noises, but today my noise-sensitive eardrums make an exception. 
I declare myself to be an anti-traditionalist, but today my beliefs make an exception. 
I have never worn a dress on any of the other 364 days of the year, but today my style makes an exception.

As I walk to the living room, the scent of incense fills the air, wrapping me in a warm hug. My mom hands me a diya, just like she has every Diwali, and I carefully place it next to the other illuminated diyas on the windowsill. At this moment, I’m no longer a typical angsty teenager. I’m simply her daughter, participating in a tradition that connects me with something larger than myself. Today is the exception. 
“Pari, mej lagao,” (Pari, set the table) my mom hollers. To her, I will always be known as “Pari.” Today is the day when this name carries deeper significance to me. As I set the table with the handmade ladoos and chaklis, I slip into the role of the daughter she knows--someone who upholds rituals passed down through generations. For a day, I’m not [Name], the anti-traditionalist. I’m Pari, the daughter who embraces Diwali. Today is the exception. 
I stand in front of the mirror, adjusting the pink silk kurta that feels foreign on my skin. My kurta is missing my preferred neutral colors, and I can sense my “Clothing” Pinterest board scoffing my fashion choice today. On any other day of the year, I would have the urge to throw a gray hoodie over the kurta and wear my wrinkled baggy jeans, but today feels different. As I glance at my reflection, I realize that this kurta, though alien to my everyday fashion style, captures the very essence of Diwali with its vibrant color and glistening buttons. At this moment, the kurta no longer feels distant on my skin. The fabric envelopes me, reminding me that sometimes stepping out of my comfort zone brings me closer to who I am meant to be. Today is the exception. 
I hear feet shifting near our house’s entrance. As I open the door, I’m greeted with a wonderful splash of colors from our guests’ sarees and kurtas. I watch as each person enters our house and removes their shoes, placing them in the rack I decorated with bright garnishing. Their faces shine with the soft glow of the multiple diyas around our house. I can’t help but smile, ignoring the soreness due to seldomly smiling for the other 364 days of the year. Today is the exception. 
As I move through the crowd handing out the gulab jamun and pani puri I helped my mom make, I feel a sense of accomplishment. The syrup-soaked gulab jamun and the tangy pani puri--each bite a piece of our collective effort--are met with wide smiles and compliments. When I share the story of how we ruined the gulab jamun twice before our success, the guests laugh. I laugh with them, feeling pride in my own failures. Today is the exception. 
As the night deepens, I step outside with a box of fireworks, feeling a mix of excitement and nervousness. I ignite the first fuse, and as the sparklers transform into colorful patterns, I'm captivated by their beauty in the night sky. The once-dreaded pops and crackles now sound melodious as my friends and family cheer around me, their happiness amplifying the fireworks’ bright display. I blend into the environment, feeling more connected to my tradition than ever before. It feels as if everything has come together perfectly, and I realize amidst the sparkles of celebration that I truly belong. Today is the exception. As I’m surrounded by the shimmering lights and my loved ones, I realize that embracing the unfamiliar unlocks a depth of belonging I had never imagined. 
The exceptions make me who I am.

It had been more than one year since women were banned from attending school after grade six, getting university degree, or attending informal courses in Afghanistan. It was five o’clock and class for the boys in my town, Dashte-Barchi, had just ended. As the lights went out, I entered the grey stuffy classroom to commence lessons for the more than twenty girls I aimed to help under the cover of darkness. That day, not unlike any other, I stayed vigilant since the lighting was poor, and as is customary in Afghanistan, danger was always lurking in the shadows. I kept looking up at the gate of the school as if I might control whatever might happen.

I began by distributing the twenty first century skills sheet to girls aged fourteen to eighteen in attendance. I asked everyone to reflect on a time when one of these skills had helped them. While they shared their experiences, my eyes remained chained to the gate. I worried the Taliban might come to check the schools, an infrequent practice, but one no less real. What would I say if they came? This has been the situation for the past year and a half. Many of the girls’ families were demanding that they get married. On many occasions, shaken by this news and the emotional build up I experienced, particularly hearing from Zinab, about arranged marriage demanded by her family, I was frozen, pacing the room, lost on how to respond. This pushed me to continue working with the girls to help them obtain their education by any means possible, online or offline. I managed to find a way to cover their internet fees monthly and assured them that they would have my support throughout the entire process.

Although fear envelops me, I exert all my effort to help improve their future. Compared to a year ago, the girls’ English proficiency and computer skills have improved beyond what I taught them. We have supported each other in our quest for knowledge which has inspired me to continue this educational mission. Despite the challenges and setbacks due to the heavy restrictions, we learned mutually through numerous workshops, academic courses, cultural events, and virtual information sessions hosted by international friends, and working on the scholarship applications for Afghan girls. The day I was informed that six of the girls I taught had been shortlisted for the United World College Scholarship, I was exceedingly excited and could not believe our success.

We are all one human family, worthy of the same access and equity. The memories I hold from this time in my life, will live in my work and pursuits forever. The strength I have earned comes from those that sang songs, played truth or dare, engaged in hopscotch and watched movies on Thursdays with me. Many of these girls had never utilized platforms for online education. Even after mock sessions, they made errors. After a Zoom workshop in the crammed room with Dr. Lee-Ann Laffey from the U.S., the girls’ behavior shifted with adaptation, effective communication and connected worldwide through virtual education.

Almost a year and half has passed since my first lesson. I feel honored to have helped these girls with their schooling, overcoming depression, isolation and the immense frustration that touched them in this situation. All twenty-seven girls now possess the capability to work through any obstacle. They long to plunge themselves into remote educational opportunities to further their interests. I am particularly determined to continue striving for my goals after seeing three of these dynamic girls teaching basic English to small children. These girls have taught me how to stand up against difficulties and how to overcome the challenges despite the fear and risks involved. My main goal now is to be able to provide education for all Afghans, no matter the gender or age, allowing our community to thrive regardless the situation.

My name is Ni-shi. Ni from my dad Nitin. Shi from my mom Shilpa. Admittedly, being named after a portmanteau wasn’t their best idea, but they liked it. If you ask me, they couldn’t come up with any other names. In a world where one crafts one's path of individuality and progress, I felt like kintsugi, the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with gold. However, it wasn’t just two pieces - I have unique fragments of everyone I have ever met.

I am fragments of Juli, a close friend from Uruguay, who taught me laughter can bridge any gap, whether linguistic or cultural. Even as we debated the intricacies of separating chemical compounds from lunar dust for profit at the International Space Settlement Design Competition, I was never too busy to encourage her to pitch her ideas or smile at a sleeping friend switching his pose every time we walked in the room. In those moments, as we combined broken Spanish with Google Translate, I learned that collaboration, infused with humor, can turn any challenge into a shared victory.

I am fragments of Thomas, a little boy with arm mobility issues I developed a toy to help, who taught me that every drop of love that you pour into the world gets poured back into you in the form of pure joy. As my team Arc Reactor labored to turn his gaze into a trigger switch for a Mickey Mouse Toy, the ongoing joy and gratitude from his mother and the Lakeview School never let us forget the positive impact we were having. As I coordinated visits, developed code, conducted interviews with his family and teacher, evaluated mechanisms, and collaborated with my team, our combined efforts created a meaningful bauble.

I am fragments of Ada Lovelace, the mother of programming, who taught me to always keep developing novel ideas and encouraging others to come along with me. As I encourage girls to come to Computer Science Club meetings and learn the basics of boolean algebra or tutor freshmen in conic sections, I feel her spirit in me. As I seek out professors to mentor my robotics team in implementing odometry techniques without standard libraries, I know I am carrying on her legacy. Her pioneering work as the Enchantress of Numbers drives my commitment to prototype innovative solutions for today’s pressing challenges.

I am fragments of Thomas Edison, who despite never meeting, taught me the value of spreading knowledge with the world and embracing the cultural divides that never really divide us. As I guide patrons through a small but quaint museum and tower memorial, fueling their infinite curiosity and teaching them of his unconventional path, I meet people from all over the world - from China to Poland to my hometown of Edison, New Jersey.

I am fragments of Bear, my Goldendoodle who reminds me to stop and smell the roses and to remain flexible. Even as he runs around the yard or pulls me endlessly, keeping an open mind and an even more calm disposition is critical to avoid pulling my hair out in stress. His determination to get a bite of my dinner reminds me to always pursue my dreams and never give up, just tackle things from a different angle.

My name - [Name] - may be a combination of my parents’ names, but my identity is a mosaic of everyone I have ever met or pet. I am a work in progress, a kintsugi of experiences just like the world - made of people from various walks of life and connected by the common thread of passion, empathy, and creativity. Each fragment, like the gold in kintsugi, contributes to a greater, more beautiful whole.

Examining the soil between trees, I discovered that us humans aren’t the only ones who use the WWW. Referred to by scientists as the “Wood Wide Web,” the mycorrhizal network allows the exchange of nutrients and even warning signals between trees to strengthen each other. I used to believe that trees were individual organisms that competed for survival. Yet, discovering their hidden network fundamentally uprooted my assumptions about the natural world and of human connections.

When I began volunteering at Chesterbrook Residences, I was nervous that our fifty-year age gap would mean my days would be spent taking care of the residents and struggling to understand conversations. However, my first assignment – morning sittercise – made me realize these residents would also strengthen me. Three giggling ladies, Julia, Esme, and Evelyn, playfully graded me as I stumbled through a routine they had mastered. My earlier apprehension melted away as I did knee hugs and shoulder rolls alongside them, belly laughing as if we had known each other for years. In just an hour, these ladies made me feel like family.

Next, I headed to the bingo room, which had a reputation for being famously competitive. Not wanting to disturb the games, I instinctively hovered along the wall. But it wasn’t long before a group motioned me to the center of the room, and in moments I had an extra bingo card and a generous chunk of chips. By staying open to new experiences and connecting with these residents, I let go of my previous doubts and became a tree in the Chesterbrook Web. Whether it was creating an original routine for my sittercise squad or inviting more residents to bingo, I was now connected to a whole network of people who revitalized me.

Seeing how a small action could trigger new and meaningful connections, I sought ways to connect the retirement home with students at my school. Now, on weekends, the sounds of Debussy and Schumann fill the room, encouraging eruptions of enthusiastic claps and bravos. Knowing the residents’ love for music and engaging with the youth, I started bringing the Musicians Association club to perform at Chesterbrook. Before each recital, Debbie, a longtime attendee of our performances, excitedly calls down the other residents. As I perform familiar favorites, such as Autumn Leaves and Love Theme from Cinema Paradiso, I see the residents swaying to the rhythm as they become immersed in the sounds of my clarinet and piano. When I finish and bow, a wave of claps and bravos erupt from the audience. Initially nervous to perform, my club members slowly gain confidence and expression from my and the residents’ unyielding support. Through a shared love of music, the Chesterbrook residents and student musicians have inextricably linked their roots.

Volunteering at Chesterbrook taught me that below the surface, there are millions of possible connections waiting to be made. I foster dialogues about cultural diversity through hosting international food-making events, eagerly sharing the significance of Mid-Autumn Festival as I guide participants in making their own mooncakes. With a hawk perched on my left glove, I welcome D.C. youth to connect with their environment, offering encouragement as they nervously attempt to pet the hawk. Just as resources tend to flow from older trees to younger ones in the Wood Wide Web, the residents taught me the true meaning of connection and modeled how to bring others of different backgrounds together. I know now that true strength lies in our ability to connect, support, and uplift one another. In each new community I join, I will grow my network and extend my roots to others in the flourishing social ecosystem I am making.

In the span of a month, I didn’t make the math Olympiad team; got rejected after three Valorant tryouts; and my newly achieved six-pack left me looking good—yet knocked out in the ring :) Was I destined to fail? No, I got Knapsacked. Formally, the knapsack problem is about optimally choosing items with weights and values while staying under a limit to maximize value. I imagined myself jumping out of a window with all my ambitions, only to fall splat on the ground, weighed down by the very dreams I tried to carry. (Ouch.) Carrying my knapsack, the challenge was choosing which jewels—math, Valorant, boxing—would weigh me down the most. Mathematically, this problem is NP Complete (unsolvable) if you can only take a jewel fully. But in real life, as in math, it’s solvable when you can take parts of a jewel; for example, Valorant can become just a pastime. So how do you choose? Similar to when coding the solution, you calculate each jewel’s value-to-weight ratio. Every grueling boxing session pushed me to my limits, building my confidence and pride. Math, though, went deeper—it wasn’t just a challenge. It reshaped how I see the world. Every problem left me not only fulfilled, excited, and in awe of the creativity one can muster when all other avenues are blocked, but also with a new lens to view life through. My most valuable jewel, though? Family. Leaving Mama and Dana in the care of my younger brother Sulaiman, I chose to take on this jewel fully before I leave. As we teared up cutting those heart-wrenching onions and hissed at the oh-so-sour limes while perfecting my world-famous Michelin-star molokhia recipe, I wanted to ensure he was ready to handle the beautiful chaos that is our family. Every day, we’d cook lunch if not dinner as well. Not one month later, he had the basics down—adding cheese to Dana’s favorite scrambled eggs and turning on our old rusty stove without getting electrocuted. More importantly, I told him that while other families might have it easier, having to take care of them shaped in ways he couldn’t imagine. Learning to deal with a 10 year olds tantrums isn’t that different from learning to listen to friends in need, you have to deal both with care and patience–Rocky is Rocky, because his road was just that: rocky. My new approach: collect as many shiny jewels as I can before they become too heavy. Learning to kickflip and working towards a national speedcubing record both hit that sweet spot of my competitiveness. Yet, both humbled me as I drastically overestimated my talent. But that’s the beauty of it—both introduced me to communities of skaters and cubers, where I didn’t need to go super in-depth to feel connected. I found the best value-to-weight ratio, but I also realized the importance of fully capturing certain jewels. The past three months, I’ve been diving deep into one of those jewels: learning JavaScript, Next.js, and more libraries than I can count building both mobile and web apps. This combines the constant learning of math, the painstaking discipline of boxing, and the feeling I get when this time, my efforts help others solve problems I once had–even if as simple as making time lapses (check out lapsey on the app store.) Thinking of the challenges I choose as jewels that get heavier over time helped me realize what I truly value–learning, but also connecting. I’ll enter college mindful of my heavy knapsack—one that will continue to shine, but hopefully, never land me fallen splat on the ground.

Whiteboards weren’t something I used to get excited about. Until my junior year, my classroom‘s wall hosted a 23’’ wall stain, which some dared to call a whiteboard. It was so small that you had to clean it thrice to solve a quadratic equation. I never complained though. Bigger issues—a world pandemic—were underway. But when everything normalized, I spoke up.

“Do you remember our school’s motto?” my principal frowned (adding brown sugar to her smokey macchiato). 
“I do, but—” (I woke earlier for a month to turn her 7:35am-before-classes coffee habit into lobbying occasions).
“Non multa, sed multum”, she proclaimed, “we prioritize depth, not breadth.” 
“Sure, but… why can’t depth develop in breadth?”
She fell silent. “What do you propose?”

If COVID-19 taught me anything, it was Zoom boards’ power. That was my proposal. So I scrutinized all interactive-whiteboard YouTube unboxings and manuals, educating myself about Infrared Touch-Technology and Anti-Light Interference in Chinese and Vietnamese.

After an espresso-powered, nocturnal, cost-benefit analysis, I found it — LPH86-ST420. Although my principal preferred new chairs, I persuaded my classmates to sign a petition for a whiteboard-instead-of-chairs exception. She conceded.

The whiteboard revolutionized our physical and educational space. Traditionally, we’d flip through 2064-page Greek-Italian dictionaries to translate 8-to-12-line extracts—agonizing for my friends. Eyes inspected all but deltas and epsilons; bathroom-bound escapes increased faster than inflation; heads bowed during cold-calling.

Then the whiteboard came. “It’s a δεινός tool. Can’t we try it?”, I cornered my teacher. Rolling her eyes, she stammered her consent.

I’d just activated the whiteboard’s note-on mode when my teacher, smiling shrewdly, told me to analyze Lysias’ speech defending a lover’s murderer. I guarded against asking, for example, παύσηται’s tense. Wasn’t it too narrow? While translating is contingent upon grades, developed-through-translating skills could serve us well beyond high school.

I instead inflamed everyone’s analytical spirits: “If you were Lysias, how’d you defend Euphiletos?” Wise, indeed. Hands sprang up like mushrooms. Under my teacher’s incredulous, sparkling eyes, a debating fever spread.

From the right-back corner, Flavio shouted that Euphiletos had to “show the tears”, while Sofia in the front row whispered: “Exploit the lover’s immorality?” “Awesome! Time to test these ideas!” Rather than line-by-line translation, I proposed to use colors to hoop on the new whiteboard’s screen evidence to falsify different hypotheses. Quickly, an explosion of magenta, marigold, and mint turned the whiteboard into a choral painting.

However, this experience didn’t remain constrained to my classroom. This summer, I organized ultimate-Mario-Kart-Wii sessions for my little cousin and his friends to wonder how blowings move cars. When he, grimacing at his releasing-smoke-rings Honeycoupe, asked why karts exploded, “Up to you to discover”, I replied.

Today, he can detail automotive engineering better than I can, and some of his friends dream of becoming engineers.

Similarly, the Super-Mario-cute-dance memes I intersperse throughout my Schoolhouse sessions ease tensions among diverse learners, clearing the ground for discussions I simply light:
“Ayobami, why B?” Then I step back, sipping my subtly sweet, velvety matcha tea until the last option standing wins.

Today, I can see how social connections unearth personal motivation, so striving to make learning as collaborative and conducive as possible is something personal—a commitment I’ll push forward in college. With the diverse, bright people I’ll meet, I’ll cover whiteboards with utility functions to investigate home biases in trade, with ways to publicize undergraduate magazines on social media and make simulations inclusive for Intercollegiate ModelUN delegates.

Everyone must be free to own and share their mind. So I endeavor to espouse and embody that lifelong, not-confined-within-classroom-walls, aspiring-for-timeless-learning mission called liberal arts education. However, I recognize to make them blossom, minds need fertile soil. So far, I’ve been the plower, fighting to secure plows—LPH86-ST420—for all 29 classrooms in my high school and using them to uplift others and myself.

Now I get excited about whiteboards and in college, my excitement will only intensify.

Sitting in the airplane’s cockpit, I marveled at the rigid feeling of the master switch or the delicate touch of the throttle lever. As though I were in the simulator, I started running down the “Engine Start” checklist: Mixture (RICH), Throttle (OPEN ¼ INCH), Beacon (ON), Master Switch (ON), Ignition Switch (START). The long nights in the simulator paid off as I flew through the checklist effortlessly, breathing life into the aircraft.

Stopped in my tracks, I was diagnosed with Crohn’s Disease; my life changed instantaneously as food became a precious commodity. Crohn’s also drained my energy very quickly. Naturally, my life of soaring through the skies was put on hold. Google quickly became my best friend, and finding Crohn's-friendly recipes became my new hobby. While Googling, I found the Crohn’s and Colitis Foundation, which provided me with recipes for some of my favorite foods, like pancakes. Instead of using hard-to-digest ingredients such as milk and flour (gluten), the recipe called for white rice flour and no milk at all. Trying new foods became a sort of research project. A cucumber, for instance, had rough skin and hard-to-digest seeds, but the softer inner layer was perfect for me. I applied that logic to tomatoes, removing the rubbery red skin and tiny seeds. Whenever I ate something new, I used my own makeshift checklist: Skin-PEELED, seeds-REMOVED, NewFactor-NOTE.

Feeling healthy, I applied for my FAA Medical Certificate, a requirement to continue flight training (solo). However, because of Crohn’s, it was deferred. Without it, I couldn’t become a pilot. All those hours in the simulator–were they worth it? I reached out to Aviation Medical Examiners, specialists at Mike Monroney Aeronautical Center, and pilots, and kept hearing, “It’s just gonna take time, but you’ll get it.”

Although those words haunted me, I wondered if I could apply my condition to my flight training. What if I could simulate a flight while fasting for a few hours? Iron deficient and still working on clinical remission, my body quickly became less sharp. In the simulator, I ran through the same checklists that I would in a real aircraft. I noticed that my use of checklists remained similar to that of real life, but my attention to detail lacked while flying. Simple tasks, such as leveling off and maintaining a heading, were less accurate, and critical phases of flight, such as landing and takeoff, felt more overwhelming. Although I expected those effects, I needed to feel them to make improvements upon them.

Eating enough [Crohn's-healthy] food (rice, eggs, pancakes) rejuvenated my headspace. Instantly, I saw improved directional control, and I picked up on small cues to pitch up (pull up) a bit or add more power to maintain a stabilized approach to land on the runway. It was interesting how slight changes in physical health could affect performance so much. Pushing the experiment further, I simulated an emergency– a complete engine failure–while hungry and fatigued. Thus the memory items on the checklist that should’ve come to my mind instantly were slower to come up. That, too, was expected, but again, feeling it in the simulator was eye-opening.

Building on those experiences, I seriously considered health before each flight, constantly verbalizing the six checks on the IMSAFE checklist: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating. To share what I’d learned and connect with the aviation community, I joined my local Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA). There, I found several pilots and discussed the impact of Crohn’s on the body, helping them understand how physical health directly influences flight performance and mental capabilities.

As I write this, I’m finally in clinical remission, and I’ve just received my FAA Medical Certificate after nine long months–Special Issuance, of course, because who doesn’t like a challenge? With the certificate in one hand and the checklist in the other, I’m ready to finish my training safely and obtain my Private Pilot’s Certificate.

Fate clatters to a standstill and I realize I'm holding my breath, the tension in the air thick enough to cut. My sister breaks the silence:

“5 and 3, so 8.”

My uncle cheers with excitement— I can’t help but smile, his joy is infectious! My aunt groans as her civilization’s supply drought continues. I offer her some of my bricks and she leans over to give me a loving hug.

While growing up in Singapore, moments with family were endless. I remember spending Saturdays marveling at giant pandas with my aunt and laughing as my uncle performed a howler monkey imitation more car alarm and circus clown than animal!

After moving to New Jersey in 2016, visiting my extended family now required a grueling nineteen hours squeezed into 32x18-inch seats through jolts of turbulence. Separated from the familiar faces of my previous home, I searched for a virtual solution.

I soon found an article, “12 Ways To Beat Loneliness,” praising the benefits of playing games and maintaining online contact with relatives. Bingo! I scoured the internet until I struck gold with Colonist.io, an online Settlers of Catan platform. With its endless strategies, element of chance, and ever-evolving nature, the game was an instant hit, making everyone feel included regardless of age.

My aunt’s tortoise-paced play earned her the title “The Sultan of Slow-Mo” and prompted us to set a fifteen-minute timer for her turns! The laughter following the inevitable “Diiinnngggg!” never failed to brighten my day. Meanwhile, my uncle had a knack for hoarding resources like a dragon guarding riches, often leading to hilarious disasters as he lost half his precious stash to the roll of a seven! Joking with my uncle, even if only on a video call, filled me with the sense of warmth I remembered so fondly from our Saturday trips.

Moments like these etched themselves into the family lore, making the oceans between us a little smaller.

The Catan sessions were the highlight of my week, but as high school ramped up, balancing school, sports, and the twelve-hour time difference led to every week becoming once a month. The sense of separation started to bubble up again, but hours of online Catan had taught me the importance of creating and maintaining relationships with supportive role models. Inspired, I sought out people who could fill the gaps left by my older relatives.

My first experience with Devin, my swim instructor, was marked by water up my nose and erratic splashing; his efforts to corral my abysmal butterfly technique were in vain! But as my form (slowly) took shape, so did our bond. We discovered our shared passion for Alphonso mangoes, compelling me to reserve a special spot in my fridge full of golden fruits to share.

Overtime, Devin became more than just a coach; he became a friend and confidant, someone who joined my dad and me on lighthearted runs and workouts. He even participated in the occasional Catan game, replicating a sense of home I hadn’t felt since my days in Singapore.

As I reflect on my previous constructions, I study the Catan playing field—littered with roads stretching across plains and curving around mountains, each hex tile bringing me nearer to the people I hold close. This powerful world, residing in a six-inch device in my pocket, will always be ready to blossom anywhere with a stable internet connection.

In college, I’m eager to connect with my peers, embracing their unique playing styles with an open mind and enthusiasm for cooperation. And my journey in higher education, like a Catan board, will be full of challenges and opportunities for innovation, whether I'm modeling the orbits of asteroids or delving into the atomic intricacies of semiconductors. With the same collaborative spirit and adaptability from my family game nights, I’ll be ready to navigate the scholarly settlements of my college journey. Let the dice roll!

Two enormous footprints mark the ground before me. Surveying their length, I step forward, planting my feet among them, curiosity and unease swirling within. I was born to a family of three living in a two bedroom triplex. From the beginning, the fragile footprints beside my tiny feet began to lay the foundation of my character. Unlike most babies, I wasn’t selfish; I even compromised. Shocking, right? If my brother wanted the pullback NASA Discovery toy, I would give it up for nothing in return. In front of Tātayya’s (grandfather’s) home, I fed Nutella chocolate sandwiches to the monkeys of India, fueling their curiosity at the expense of my lunch.

Even when I’d incorrectly pronounce the letter H as “hech,” I still persevered through an unfamiliar culture becoming a leader too: coordinating neighborhood games, teaching math, and creating a 4th grade economy with “P-Dollars.”

Amidst my journey to maturity I found solace in what became my passion – bringing joy to others. Even in moments of frustration, like losing Mr. M’s month-long math odyssey on the final day, the triumphant smiles and contented eyes of others spread a warm happiness within me. I thought this would define who I was. Except, I sensed a deep-rooted hole within myself. What is my “why”? It was apparent the footprints in front of me blurred, mirroring the erosion of my identity.

This seemingly simple question became difficult to answer. As I grew older, I felt lost leading to self doubts of my authenticity. I laid staring at the cracked corner of my white ceiling for hours, no longer finding the courage to venture outside on my RipStik or fundraise with my Skittles donation jar in hand. Searching for clues, I turned to Project 351, who previously engaged me in year-long service opportunities. Knowing their extensive programming offered insight, I attended their annual reunion.

Stepping into Foxborough’s Gillette Stadium, I immediately noticed many bridge builders facing a single jumbotron. There, six letters seemed to dance, assembling an ancient zulu word in large, colorful font, meaning ‘I am because you are.’

By emphasizing the need to be open and available to everyone, Ubuntu illuminated the concept of interconnectedness. For the first time, I acknowledged the bond that transcended words and gestures, forming a delicate web of empathy between myself and others. Consciously observing the intricate patterns of relationships woven by life, I learned that pure elation serves as an indicator of my efforts, not a motivator. Rather, it is truly an innate responsibility to foster and nurture the strength of other people’s beings that drives me forward.

Mind and heart united, my service expanded from simply emotional satisfaction to understanding and prioritizing material needs, widening the footprints beneath me. I gained awareness and purpose. Recognizing Am'ma’s (Mom’s) nostalgic-rich “Michelin Star'' chicken biryani she cooked for my birthdays was a privilege, I learned that my community urgently needed both the comfort and necessity of food. Inspired, I coordinated an annual food drive at Chelmsford High School. Reminiscing of the black Adidas hoodie I wore throughout freshman year, I noted the anxiety and inhibition my clothing insecurity caused that others shouldn’t endure. In response, I led teams to fundraise clothes for Cradles to Crayons. Witnessing hundreds donate, roll collection carts of food, and carry gallon bags of clothes confirmed my presumption that our humanity is tied. Now, I know the footprints I constantly envision are made by the ideas, efforts, and wisdom I gain from those I meet and impact. They became mine to shape and solidify, conjuring giants from universal bonds whose shoulders my intellect and aspirations rest on.

I may be 6'0'', but, once I take my stance, I am uplifted past the horizons by the collective efforts of my community within each footprint. Through college and adulthood the imprint I stand on will grow, and soon enough I’ll reach the moon thanks to Ubuntu.

Butterfly ankle braces. That’s the first thing I saw on the girl who was being pushed into the classroom on a wheelchair. The room hushed, then erupted in whispers. “What’s wrong with her?” The words stung, even as our teacher introduced her as Starla, explaining her Spastic Cerebral Palsy– a term that meant little to my six-year-old self, yet everything to Starla’s daily life. During recess, I went up to Starla and told her how pretty the butterflies on her ankle braces were. Seeing her smile when listening to me obsess over butterflies, I knew we were going to be good friends.

Starla’s elementary school years weren’t easy. While we ran carefree on the playground, she fought for each step. As we tackled multiplication and division, she wrestled with forming full sentences. Many things we take for granted required extra effort from her, but she kept moving forward at her own pace. I helped her practice phonics and cleared obstacles so her wheelchair could move freely. As time passed, we grew close and discovered shared interests, like having little brothers and love for mac-n-cheese. Years later, Starla’s condition had improved dramatically. She went from relying on a wheelchair to walking with my support during our class trip.

After transferring to a new school, I lost contact with Starla since neither of us had phones. My new private school introduced me to smart, wealthy, and privileged friends, but none were like Starla. Feeling a void, I sought out opportunities to help children like her, and began volunteering at Friendship Circle, a program dedicated to connecting special needs children, and I formed special bonds with many. One camper, Timmy, shared with me, “At school, kids make fun of me, and I never want to smile, but at Friendship Circle, I want to smile every day.” This is when my heart feels fullest– being with these pure, innocent children, sharing all the love I have and giving selflessly, knowing that every moment with them is a gift.

On a typical day at Friendship Circle, I spotted a girl who looked familiar. As I glanced over, I immediately recognized Starla’s butterfly braces! Before I could react, she approached me the moment she saw me. It was incredible to reconnect after four years, yet it felt like no time had passed. I was overjoyed to hear the significant improvements in Starla's life. We’ve stayed connected ever since and I’m thrilled to see her thriving in high school now.

Starla and Friendship Circle friends inspired me to share the joy of community service with others. I joined the Global Outreach Club at school, progressed from a member to officer to co-president, I led my classmates and friends to Focus: HOPE to help low-income seniors, held fundraisers for anti-human-trafficking organizations, supported local animal shelters, and introduced them to the Friendship Circle to connect with special needs children. Our club grew from fewer than ten members to over 150. At my school, many students from upper socioeconomic backgrounds, who had never previously engaged with those facing basic needs, had their first community service experience through our club. I am so proud that my effort has led and influenced more peers to embrace and contribute to our community.

Like Starla’s butterflies, we each possess unique patterns that enhance the beauty of life. Despite her physical constraints, Starla moved through her life with unwavering determination, just like the vibrant butterflies dancing around her ankles that symbolized her inner strength and spirit, guiding her toward joy, independence and freedom.

Starla’s journey and my community service experiences have revealed the immense power of embracing our unique strengths and empowering others. Driven by Starla’s resilience and the Friendship Circle’s impact, I am dedicated to transforming lives and forging a vibrant, inclusive world that celebrates our diverse differences.

Backstage, beads of sweat dripped down my face as I counted the steps before my entrance. Immersed in Tchaikovsky’s music, I stepped onto the stage. Tchaikovsky composed The Nutcracker during the lowest point in his life – grieving the death of his sister. Despite his sorrow, the audience hears only the enchanting music. Similarly, as a ballerina, I conceal my struggles behind a radiant smile, presenting elegance while the audience remains unaware of the effort and pain behind each performance.

Growing up, I was taught to value inner beauty over outer. Yet, each time I looked in the mirror, I struggled to believe. In my immigrant household, my parents often urged me to toughen up, reminding me that many people face greater hardships. I tried to apply this perspective when faced with my own challenges. However, this lesson was put to the ultimate test when even stepping outside my house became a challenge for me.

I first noticed strands of hair on my pillow and clumps in the drain. Initially dismissing it, I was alarmed when I saw my hairline receding in the mirror. Diagnosed with alopecia, a condition that left me grappling with my self-image, I found myself spending significant time getting ready to go outside. The routine of putting on a wig, drawing on eyebrows, and perfecting my makeup became a necessity and a reminder of what I lacked.

Before my diagnosis, I danced with confidence. But as alopecia began affecting my appearance, my self-consciousness grew. Each class was shadowed by the fear that my condition would become evident, affecting my dancing. Ballet itself was a demanding ritual—rigorous training, constant practice, and maintaining perfect technique often felt overwhelming. Yet, just as I found solace in ballet despite its demands, I found perseverance in my routine for alopecia. Routines can be burdensome, but they can transform into sources of resilience.

Determined not to let alopecia control my life, I sought solutions tirelessly, from dermatologists to unconventional treatments, but to no avail. High school was not designed with balding teenagers in mind. Tchaikovsky's sister passed away shortly before he began composing the score. Although he wanted to refuse commission, he felt compelled to continue. He channeled his grief into his music, creating compositions that resonated with his longing. Similarly, I grieved the time I used to dance without worry. I learned to channel that pain into furthering my artistry, transforming my struggles into a source of creative expression. By shifting my focus from my appearance to the joy and passion of dancing, I found a renewed sense of purpose.

I could feel the anxiety bubbling up, but as I looked at the faces of my fellow dancers on stage, I saw genuine support and encouragement. They reminded me that we were all in this together, each with our own struggles and triumphs. It was in that collective moment, I allowed myself to be fully immersed in the moment.

My climactic performance of The Nutcracker ended with a flourish. As the Lead Spanish dancer, I stood before the crowd. Blinded by the spotlights, bravos sprinkled across the audience as I took my bow. Much of what happens in life is beyond our control, but how we respond is within our power. Rather than hiding in self-pity, my acceptance of my canvas allowed me to see vulnerability as a source of strength rather than a weakness.

Behind the seemingly plain canvas, I now see a confident young girl whose character defines her. Appearance is not what fills our canvas with beautiful colors and strokes; it is our personality and our actions. Seeking new experiences and making connections broadens our understanding of others, transforming grayscale images into dynamic portraits. Living with alopecia has taught me invaluable lessons about resilience, self-acceptance, and the power of vulnerability. Through life’s challenges, I will carry on the grace and resilience instilled in me by ballet.

When I handed over the check to SVDP, the current president took a moment to pull me aside, expressing his thanks for my efforts. He shared his observation that younger generations seemed increasingly resistant to service, yet here I was, making a difference. Initially, I had founded this organization to engage my peers, but now I found myself driven by a new mission. I wanted to elevate our cause, not just by encouraging participation, but by inspiring my friends to recognize the power of service. Our first project had thrived, but I was acutely aware that there was so much more potential to unlock and achieve together.

During our March madness bracket fundraiser, I had encouraged each of our 30+ members to convince 5 people to buy a bracket for the 50/50 pool. At the end of the event we had doubled the money raised from the first fundraiser. The tears from the mom's face when she saw that local high school kids had helped her son grow a step closer to affording a service dog was enough for me to realize how special my team was to our community.

Over the next few smaller events that we hosted I noticed relationships being built both inside and outside of my organization. While we were connecting with our community through service I had noticed that my organization was becoming a community in itself. Most of the members are my friends and they divide into 3 schools in the surrounding area.

Through the events I noticed friendships being made and saw my hometown friends start to build relationships with my school friends. As these friendships strengthened, so did their love for service. They now saw service as a time to spend together and help others.

Before starting CHS I had been that kid who always wanted the world to be a better place but never thought I could do anything about it. After seeing the impact I have created within my community and my members, I realized that I am the person who can create change not only in the things I can do for my community but also drive personal growth in my friends and members.

While I will eventually have to leave Change Has Started to another person when I go to college, I don't plan on merely joining one. My goal in college is to find the leading service organization on campus and work my way to the head of it.

I believe this is completely possible because my experience with Change Has Started and would love to take it to a larger scale.

As I sat in my mother's walk-in closet, clutching my trembling little sister and whispering reassurances I barely believed myself, I felt a surge of gratitude for my mother's preparedness—her weapons and the steady hands that held them. The window that once seemed the perfect place to watch sunsets had now become a source of my intrusive thoughts. What if someone outside sees us? What if they do not want to leave any witnesses? My mother gave us two specific instructions: call your father and brother to confirm they are not the ones in the home and keep your sister calm. I stayed on the phone with my father as he raced home. The next three minutes seemed to run in slow motion, each second ticking by in rhythm with my heartbeat. My mind raced with worst-case scenarios from crime shows as my mother searched the house. Her diligence and preparedness became apparent as she finally discovered the "culprit"—a YouTube video playing loudly on my TV, mimicking human presence. Relief washed over us, followed by laughter, as the "mystery burglar" turned out to be a YouTuber. I sat there with my father on the phone, now with tears of joy. My mother hugged us, and I asked her to get weapons for every corner of the home. What once seemed dangerous and evil now felt like the only thing that could have saved us had there been an intruder. I had to rethink my belief system about gun control, which moments before had a clear-cut response.

Growing up in a tranquil suburb, I was shielded from the harsh realities of violence and crime. My perception of guns was shaped by the media's portrayal of gun-related tragedies, leading me to believe that guns were inherently dangerous and unnecessary. I associated gun ownership with reckless individuals who posed a threat to public safety. All my knowledge of weapons came from crime TV, Law & Order, and documentaries, which I still struggle to pronounce fluently.

This experience sparked my interest on Second Amendment rights. I began to research more on the issue, discovering the complexity of the debate. I delved into the historical context of the Second Amendment, the nuances of regulations, and varying perspectives on gun ownership. My research revealed that control measures can have unintended consequences, such as disproportionately affecting marginalized communities or infringing upon individual liberties. I discovered that unreasonable regulations have far-reaching effects, as seen in countries like Venezuela and Cuba. In contrast, Nordic countries with strong middle classes and robust education systems achieve lower crime rates, demonstrating that a well-informed and empowered citizenry can coexist with responsible gun ownership. This highlighted the need for nuanced approaches to gun control.

My journey made me realize that despite my youth, I can contribute to the problem if I am not tolerant. It made me gain a deeper appreciation for the complexities of the issue and work towards finding common ground. My initial aversion to gun ownership stemmed from fear and misconception. I had assumed that guns were inherently dangerous without considering the context and responsibilities surrounding their ownership. I came to understand the importance of responsible gun ownership, paired with sensible regulations and education. A mindset that had undergone a significant transformation, but I gained understanding of the responsibility—one that requires education, empathy, and courage.

The path to peace lies not in disarmament, but respect—respect for others' rights, respect for human life, and respect for the complexities of our world. This experience taught me the importance of questioning and challenging my beliefs to reach a more informed and empathetic understanding of complex issues. As Benito Juarez wisely said, "Among individuals, as well as nations, the respect of the rights of others is peace."

Chewed paper is my favorite thing in the world. I don't chew paper (even if I did, no medieval torture device could get that information out of me). What I mean is papier-mâché: chewed paper. Before I could even write on paper, Kaka, my grandfather, taught me to mix it with water and turn it into art. While my friends got chocolates from their grandfathers, mine handed me scrap paper from the bin. Not that I complained! Kaka enthralled me with an anecdote about NASA using papier-mâché to build mock spacecrafts. I was so intrigued that I badgered him to spend three mornings straight sculpting with me, only resting to enjoy some til pithas, sesame cakes. He even let me use his prized hot-glue gun to trace the NASA decal on the spaceship, and I felt like Thor being handed Mjölnir.

FAST. Face, Arms, Speech, Time. It's how you know that someone's having a stroke. An acronym stapled to my mind now, a harsh reminder of how we lost Kaka. I read countless research papers, and scoured websites on hypertension trying to understand his demise. I remember Ma sobbing on the kitchen floor, each wave of grief like turning over the same pages of a book over and over again. I couldn't seem to mold this grief into art, though, like I could paper. Papier-mâché felt too close to my woe, so I focused on playing kho-kho, a traditional tag sport that Kaka used to play with his eight siblings. But on the verge of winning a game, as I leaped to tag a defender, I lost more than the match. Diagnosed with a chronic fracture at fourteen, I lost the ability to ever play kho-kho again. My broken leg felt like gloopy paper, too watered down to save, too damaged to be art anymore.

With nothing to do but smell the musty plaster on my leg, I started learning 3D modeling, digital art, and even played the ukulele. All of it amused me yet lacked what I craved most, a thread to Kaka. My room filled with papier-mâché walldecors felt wistful. I remember Kaka telling me I was like a honeybee when I worked - so focused that not even a trumpet playing could disturb me. Kaka introduced me to my best parts, so I led myself back to him. I gathered plenty of used paper by organizing a drive around my neighborhood. With twists of my wrists, I used wads of old paper to shape caricatures, including some of myself. The way that Kaka had taught me to turn gooey mush into art, I fashioned myself into an impressionist painting: smudged, imperfect, but authentically, originally me.

The caricatures I made were sold, and the funds were allocated to Unnayan, an organization for older individuals with special needs. I had felt powerless with Kaka. But my new friends at Unnayan—Arham, Mahanta uncle, Kritika—were people whose lives I could help shape the way Kaka had shaped mine. As soon as my plaster was removed, I started volunteering at Unnayan actively. My first fundraiser was in Lumding, a town near me, and featured papier bowls, vases, and figurines, all made by Unnayan residents and me. Since then, I've spent my weekends organizing more fundraisers and events, steering initiatives to ensure that the residents receive the support they need. Now, whenever life presents me with gloopy, mulchy problems, I say "Thank you!" and wonder how best to turn them into art. Every discarded object, and each individual, has something that can be redeemed and reshaped.

As for my new endeavor, college—I plan to either join a crafts club or start my own so I can continue growing my passion for repurposing discarded items. I am excited to build a dorm community around reuse and upscaling, inviting my dormmates to donate their waste so we can build cartoneria together, just as I did with Kaka and the residents of Unnayan. The mushy, chewed-up paper inside all of us is just waiting for someone to believe in it, for someone to mold it into magnificent cartonería.

I always wondered how she never got tired of that sound.

Sunday mornings always began with the clamor of mung beans crashing against a battered metal pan. With each flick of her wrist, the beans would leap into the air, forming into waves before settling back on the shore. I would silently sail along this sea of seeds with my amma, gently diving my hands in to fish out the stones she left behind.

Time didn’t exist to my amma while she was lost in her work. With her trusty pan, she would spend hours sifting beans without complaints. On the other hand, I would give up after a few minutes to chase the next adventure, wandering off long before she was finished. I lacked the patience she had built up through years of practice, worried I would “waste” too much time focusing on one thing.

Whether it be in taking a contested three-pointer one second after I catch the basketball, scarfing down my amma’s special vegetable pulao in under a minute to tune in to Naruto, or biking to school at full speed two minutes before the bell rings, my childhood has always been one big race against the clock. I thought moving quickly would help me outrun the possibility of falling short, letting me achieve an “efficient” lifestyle. While this approach to life made perfect sense to my childhood self, it narrowed my vision, forcing me to look at the world on the surface level.

It was yet another Sunday morning, and I found myself by my amma. To my surprise, she asked me to sit with her until there were no beans left to sift. I hesitated at first. We could sift beans until sunset and still end with barely enough to make a single bowl of kaalu palya. But, I decided to trust her, forgetting my doubts and fully committing myself. The mung beans began to crash into the pan once again, but this time, it felt different. My amma guided me to match the steady rhythm of her movements and the usual rush began to disappear. As I picked out the stones from the edge of the pan, she helped me realize one goal: helping prepare an unforgettable meal for my family. Each stone got me one step closer, and I savored every little victory. Regardless of the hours I spent with my amma, my actions finally had a purpose. What once seemed like an endless task turned into a routine experience that slowly guided me to steadier waters, putting me on the path to outgrow my impatience.

Nowadays, I am not afraid to “waste” my time and take risks, approaching every part of my life with the patience I learned from sifting seeds. I now enjoy digging down into rabbit holes and exploring topics beyond the surface with no fear of how time-worthy they may be. When I spent weeks working on a way to combine attention mechanisms and 3D object detection, I didn’t feel the need to switch gears because the code would take too long to debug. Or when I spent hours finding the most protein-packed ingredients to perfect my specialty shake, I pushed through even with the possibility of making something undrinkable.

My experience with my amma also taught me to appreciate the little details. I stare off into the distance fifteen minutes after waking up, thinking about the rest of my day. I fold my paper into three sections and carefully trace the creases with a ruler before solving a math problem. I even split up my Oreos and slowly enjoy each piece. The once-tiring sound of mung beans clattering against my amma’s pan serves as a reminder to navigate my sea with patience and a clear mind. I will always carry the lessons I learned from those Sunday mornings, staying curious and finding purpose even in the smallest, seemingly mundane moments.

Returning to China after seven years abroad, seated around the same family dining table as every Spring Festival, I had become a stranger in my own family. My family had not seen or heard from me in years. My only presence was their rare glimpse of me in their WeChat feeds. ErYi LaoLao stood from the table. Her voice, rich with a Beijing accent, rang out, “Tell us about yourself.”

I felt exposed. My gut feeling told me I wouldn’t be truly seen here. Seven years earlier, I had failed to hide my face when zealously reciting poetry. I had vowed I would never be so embarrassed again.

“I mean, it’s been pretty busy…”, I fumbled with my response.

Laughter rung around the table as I spoke of my travels and academic pursuits. I strategically omitted the parts I feared they would criticize. I cleverly packaged myself as a high-achieving scholar, but it didn’t feel like me. It reminded me of my childhood performance when I stopped mid-recite–except this time, I knew to fear their judgment. As I recited my life, feeling a raw vulnerability, I realized how much of myself I had hidden away–even from myself.

—--

The aroma of state banquet cuisine wafted through the air as I entered the estate of Master Wei, one of the “Four Little Chefs of Beijing.” I carefully bowed and seated myself as I gazed around the Si He Yuan, a traditional Chinese courtyard house.

Master Wei’s hands trembled as he spoke passionately about culinary trends, and offered my father advice. I caught every other word—Cutlery, “diversified development”—mixed with words I couldn’t type into Baidu fast enough to translate. His voice, though shaky, carried the weight of decades of experience. The mix of old Chinese expressions and industry-specific terms swept into my brain, but I could barely understand. I felt out of place under the old eaves of his yard, unsure how to fit into this world.

Before we left, he asked for water. Instead of drinking it, he washed his hands—frail yet strong—and shook mine. I was taken aback. In traditional Chinese culture, washing hands before a significant action signifies respect and purity. The handshake, laden with respect and connection, bridged his generation of experience and wisdom with mine on a personal level. I realized legacies aren’t just in words and expertise but in the quiet, meaningful exchanges connecting generations.

—--

The dining room buzzed with the low hum of important conversation on tables and nightmare at a glance—chaos of children under the table, giggling and chasing each other.

“Good luck,” my dad said, nodding toward the unruly kids.

Determined to keep them quiet, I first tried offering food. But the kids, mid-bite, continued their antics, knocking over glasses and climbing under the table. Nearby diners shot me disapproving looks while the adults at our table maintained their polite facade. As I felt the weight of responsibility overwhelming me, an idea sparked.

“Psst…Want to play a game?” I whispered.

Their eyes lit up with curiosity. “Let's see who can stay the quietest for the longest; the one who makes the least noise wins!”

The promise of a game instantly captured their attention. The chaotic scene soon turned into a quiet, focused contest. As the adults continued their discussion, I couldn’t help but marvel at how a simple game could bring order to the chaos.

True growth, I've discovered, often emerges from the most unexpected places. In each uncomfortable scenario where I didn’t know how I would be perceived or if I could manage the situation, I found myself growing to embrace these moments of uncertainty and vulnerability. In college, I am excited to continue embracing these challenges, entering new spaces and scenarios where I can explore, adapt, and grow even further. Now, I am not just reciting my life. I am starting to live it.

The boom of the bass drum. 
The crash of the cymbals. 
The sharp strikes on xylophones and the precise rhythms of the snare drums overwhelm my ears. 
Yet, this chaos, this cacophony of random percussive noises, sounds just like home.

“Wouldn’t that make your head even worse [Name]?” my science teacher asks as we ascend the stairs together, my head pounding as I await her decision. This was the fourth day this week I had asked a teacher for a pass to spend their class period in the band room. It’s not Advil or Tylenol that works for me. As someone who deals with severe headaches, I have learned that medicines or prescriptions are not always the best answer. Instead, music is my medicine.

As I look over my percussion family, flashing quick smiles to my closest friends playing alongside me, I feel the comfort of our tight-knit community washing away the exhaustion from a demanding week of school. Understanding how music helps me overcome my personal challenges and tackle each school day with renewed energy inspires me to engage with others more empathetically and channel even more passion into my playing. This insight has deepened my commitment across all my communities—whether in band, volleyball, math competitions, or with my family—as I recognize the role my contribution to our collective effort plays in uplifting each member. Recognizing public speaking as an area I sometimes lack in, I have utilized music as a tool to strengthen my performances. Before important presentations – whether it be presenting at a research poster symposium or giving a pep talk to my volleyball team – I harness the calming effect of rhythmic tapping on my chest or legs to help mitigate my nervousness in front of larger crowds. This ritual has significantly contributed to developing my confidence as a public speaker and a leader.

“17 chimes, for 17 victims…”

I strike my mallets to accompany the NBC reporter as he narrates the feature on “Forever and Always, A Reflection,” dedicated to the lives lost during the Marjory Stoneman Douglas tragedy on February 14th, 2018. I live in Parkland, 1 mile from the high school. On that day, I was forced to hide inside a bathroom along with the rest of my elementary school math team for hours, uncertain and scared.

When the NBC feature for the composition aired, my parents and I received messages from many old friends, all reaching out after seeing me on TV. This experience made me realize that my fellow musicians and I had been part of something much larger—a debut performance that resonated deeply with our community. In my band, which has a no-cut policy to welcome musicians of all skill levels, I serve as a section leader with a strong commitment to inclusivity. Witnessing such events at such a personal level has greatly shaped my approach to leadership, in which I am particularly dedicated to ensuring that every member of our band feels valued and included. This especially comes into play in regards to two members of my section that have special needs. I make it a priority to ensure they are fully integrated into our section and treated with the same respect as everybody else. By fostering an inclusive environment, I strive to counteract the outcasting that can lead to tragic outcomes, reinforcing the positive, unifying capabilities of music within our community.

My growth as a musician, starting as an elementary schooler that wanted nothing to do with joining a band class, to a middle schooler who discovered a talent, and finally a musician that can appreciate how great of a gift music can be as a catalyst for community-wide healing, has shed light upon the capabilities of the music I create to inspire and promote positive change in my next audience: the world?

My eyes locked on the number; my face was lit with the blue glow of my computer screen; my sweaty hand clenched the mouse. I refreshed the “Views” page, anxiously hoping today was the day I’d become famous. June 16th, 2023: My journey began. The Timeless Tales of History YouTube channel was born. I sprang into my chair, beyond ecstatic, uploading seven videos in just the first two days. As I launched this project off the ground, I elevated my work from humble screen-recorded PowerPoints to meticulously polished films crafted with advanced video-editing software. All this was done as I chased my biggest dream: millions of views.

One early Tuesday morning, my phone vibrated for what seemed like hours. I glanced over. A gleam of excitement filled my eyes. Was Genghis Khan the WORST Ruler in History: the first video to cross 1,000 views! This initial success stoked the flame inside me, strengthening my motivation. I slumped over my laptop, my fingers dragging me through dozens of articles as I read through the life of Mao Zedong, the death of Rasputin, the actions of Vlad the Impaler. Like a machine, I cranked out new scripts and constructed fresh animations. Nothing would stop me… or so I thought.

Throughout these months, the siren call pulling me back to continue researching and editing was simply the numbers. As a result, my initial passion gradually waned. Each video was a labor of love into which I poured my whole heart, yet their lack of recognition made me question the value of this endeavor. I found myself, in the face of a small adversity, committing the gravest of crimes: giving up.
