April 20th, 2024. My father’s eyes meet mine. His deep voice cuts through the silence of the room. He inquires about the status of my channel. With a sense of disappointment, I casually mention my sporadic upload schedule. I look up. A weary smile filled his face. He tells me “[Name], the worst thing you can do in life is give up hope. Please… do not ever give up hope.” His words danced through my head that evening. Why did I begin to make videos in the first place? Was my journey all in the pursuit of likes, comments, and subscribers, or was it to make elegant content that gave insight into history’s most important pieces? My mind defined success as popularity, but my heart defined success as personal satisfaction. By shifting my focus from short-term achievement to long-term gratitude, my passion was reignited.

That night, the Timeless Tales of History was reborn.

8:00 AM. The bright sunshine pierced through my window. I bounced out of bed, determined to make today’s video my magnum opus to date. The quest for the perfect subject began, with hours of fervent research and excited script writing. I edited into the wee hours of the next morning, adding novel effects and synchronizing the captions. I pressed “UPLOAD” with a combination of nervousness, relief, and most importantly, satisfaction. The views came thundering in. 1,578 4,912 10,595 Not only did the video shatter my expectations, it felt deeply rewarding to compose a piece that resonated with my audience.

My journey through content creation has not been limited to crafting videos: it has been a long, winding path of self-reflection and exploration. I’ve grown to understand that achieving success in any field demands a degree of perseverance, a resilience when met with setbacks. Having navigated the challenges I’ve encountered, my goal is to continue facing life, head on, armed with this powerful weapon of perseverance.

A light chord fades in and lands on a satisfying note, breaking the silence. I enter high school, a blank slate, recent memory consisting only of Zoom and videogames. I do what everyone else does. I say what everyone else says. I fit in perfectly. I can read the room and be who I need to be. I make sure my situations are at worst awkward, and never embarrassing.

As more chords follow, a simple melody takes shape. Apart from my best friend from elementary and middle school, I make a lot of acquaintances, but nothing too intimate. I notice people that I want to get to know, but not enough to put myself out there.

A soft vocal joins the melody and ushers me along. I study hard and take any opportunities that come to me. I have motivation to do something special, but see no clear path to get started. I maintain the status quo, excelling at what I know I need to do, without pushing too far beyond that.

An orchestral hum of an airy pad fills the background. At home, I feel trapped under constant berating from my father, to the point that neighbors call child services multiple times. With my unhealthy living situation draining all my energy, I get nothing done.

A light beating of drums inserts itself into the mix. Sophomore year arrives. I finally make a new close friend. He introduces me to bass-driven EDM genres and artists. I dismiss most of it as weird at first, but eventually find myself deep into the community, listening to artists with fewer than 100 monthly listeners.

The ever-louder pounding rattles on, with chord stabs mixed in. Unknown emotions come out from deep inside as I listen to the music. My body moves autonomously, unafraid and daring. I don’t just hear the music, I feel it. It resonates all the way down to my core. Each beat pulses through me like a second heartbeat, the rhythm alive and insistent. I break free and resolve to no longer take a backseat in my own life.

The kick rapidly picks up pace. Tension builds like a stretched rubber-band, about to snap. I realize that I need to take action instead of just fitting into the mold. I muster the courage to take control of my own environment: I convince my parents to let me move in with my mom. I continue to nerd out over underground EDM, even though almost everyone I know finds the music weird. I don’t care anymore.

Thick supersaw stacks erupt, soaring like untamed spirits, weaving tales of joy and sorrow in the language of sound. The snare cuts through with surgical precision, a beacon in the swirling sea of bass. Strategically placed drum fills and growls perfectly break up the drop. The sound frees and soothes me. I reach out of my comfort zone again and again, knowing I have the music to turn to. Though uncomfortable at times, I expand my friend group, developing deep, meaningful relationships. Social events plaster my calendar and I feel creative and inspired at home. I create my own opportunities instead of waiting for them to come to me: my own game, my own research, my own startup. I am carving out my own path and trailblazing.

A euphoric release follows. The elements melt away and only an angelic voice and a few quiet synths relay the heart of the melody. I will leave high school, a colorful canvas backed by a vibrant soundtrack of life, recent memory consisting of leadership, service, personal autonomy, and much more. I constantly outdo my past self, becoming a better version everyday. I speak up for those without voices. I stand out perfectly, just where I want to be.

The first time I stepped into Bal Sabha (kids’ assembly) as a child, I would’ve never imagined that the mandir (Hindu temple) would become my second home. I remember clutching my father’s hand, overwhelmed by the towering fifth-graders and the hum of prayers that filled the air. It wasn't until, four years later, when I met my spiritual Guru Mahant Swami Maharaj that I understood the true gift I had been given.

In 2017, my brother and I found ourselves in a line that seemed to stretch endlessly, winding through the corridors of the BAPS mandir in Atlanta, Georgia. The anticipation in the air was tangible. We were minutes away from meeting our Guru. Finally, we stepped forward together. There he was, seated with a warm, welcoming smile. The exchange was brief, just a few words. But it was the kind of moment where time seemed to stand still and the world outside ceased to exist. Soon, the moment passed, and it was our time to leave.

“Wait,” my Guru’s voice called out. We stopped in our tracks, turning back towards him. He reached out to us, his hand holding two large chocolate bars. The gesture was simple but heartfelt, a symbol of his care that words can’t describe.

As I grew older, my role within the mandir community began to evolve. My Guru’s teachings (the very lessons I had been taught as a young child in bal sabha), guided me as I took on responsibilities like organizing youth assemblies and coordinating various events. Each task was an opportunity to practice the values that I had learned. The mandir became more than just a physical space; it was a manifestation of the principles my Guru had imparted on me.

Over the years, this realization has grown into a deep sense of gratitude, one that has shaped my life in ways I never expected. One moment stands out. I was leading a team activity when a young teen, shy and unsure, hesitated to join a group.

The buzz of chatter filled the room, but Dhyan stood on the sidelines, hands buried deep in his pockets, eyes cast down.

“Dhyan…”, I hollered from across the room. “Where’s your team?”

The words echoed, but he didn’t move, didn’t look up. I made my way across the room, weaving through clusters of excited kids already lost in their plans.

When I reached him, I bent slightly to meet his eye level. “Do you have a team?” I asked, though I already knew the answer.

He hesitated, his voice barely above a whisper, “Not yet.”

I glanced around, noticing the tight circles of three that had already formed—each group enthusiastic, their chatter filled with laughter.

“Come on,” I said, gently nudging him forward. “We’ll find you a spot.”

As we walked, I could sense his unease, the way his steps dragged a bit behind mine. It wasn’t just about finding a group; it was about helping him find his place, his voice.

Finally, we found a group! I introduced him and they welcomed him with warm smiles, but I could still see the flicker of doubt in his eyes.

As the weeks passed, I observed a remarkable transformation. Slowly, Dhyan began to blossom. His confidence grew as he began to find his place within the group. Two years later, he isn’t simply a participant anymore—he is a leader, guiding others with the same warmth and encouragement that had once been extended to him.

Reflecting on these experiences, I realize how much I’ve grown because of the guidance I received from my Guru through the community he built. The gratitude I feel isn’t just for the teachings themselves, but for the impact they have on my life. They have shaped my actions and defined my sense of purpose. Through the gift of mandir, he gave me a compass to navigate life with integrity and compassion.

January 1, 1836. United States of America.

As I immerse myself in the society of pre-Civil War America [in Victoria 3, a nation-industrializing video game], I queue up buildings in anticipation of the inevitable war. Setting the game to speed five, I start a six-year deficit spending spree as I fight off the Seminole and Sioux, walk the tightrope between John Calhoun’s slavers and Henry Clay’s abolitionists, and conduct trade negotiations with Britain and France. After more prudent investments, political maneuvering, and some technological research, I soon lead the Union to victory by 1863. Ready to establish a footprint on the international stage, I zoom out to view the world map. I almost miss it entirely at first. While the German states had united (a rarity for the German AI), France had surprised me by forming the Paris Commune - something I’d never heard of. While I continued gameplay, I couldn’t help but wonder what the Paris Commune was. I struggled to concentrate as that little thought lived rent-free in my head. Eventually, I’d had enough. I closed the game, googled “Paris Commune,” and clicked on the Wikipedia article.

“The Paris Commune was … the Third Republic in September 1870 … ” Wait. The Third Republic? With my curiosity piqued, I continued reading. Even when it satisfied my initial curiosity (angry working-class Parisians and a war-induced famine led to a socialist revolt) it raised more questions. Since when was Paris the traditional home of French radical movements? And if the third version of the republic existed in 1870, when was the first republic established? How?

Cue a three-hour, long-winded Wikipedia rabbit hole, where questions led to articles, and articles led to questions. The article on the Third Republic led me down four clicks to an article on the French Revolution. Remembering it being brought up in APUSH as a brief aside from a discussion on the American Revolution, I believed it was just a minor footnote in history; however, when I read that its ideas were the cornerstone of liberal democracy, more questions emerged. Where did these democratic ideals come from? What factors led to the monarchy collapsing in the first place? How important was this revolution anyway? Even the Wikipedia article, for its excruciating detail, hadn’t left me completely satisfied, leaving my questions simmering on my mind’s back burner.

I found my answers on vacation. When browsing the shelves of Seattle’s indie Lionheart Bookstore, a book caught my eye: A New World Begins: The History of the French Revolution. Although I didn’t immediately remember that three-hour session six months ago, I still bought the book thanks to my curiosity. Opening its pages for the first time at my desk, I was immediately thrown back into the world of revolutionaries and counter-revolutionaries. I would quickly learn that the French Revolution wasn’t some “footnote in history” - it had a greater impact than anything the American Revolution could have had.

Even as I finally understood the Revolution’s political movements and social influences, I soon realized what others already had about me: I have an insatiable thirst to not only learn, but to understand. Whether it’s examining opposing perspectives of the nuclear energy debate to deciphering the nuances of Indian culture to learning the recipe for a delectable Gujarati khichdi (still experimenting there, I promise!). I’m simply not satisfied by what; I need to know why. How. Most importantly, though, I yearn for that deeper understanding of whatever I put my mind to. As I enter the next chapter of my life, I will continue to ask questions, dig deeper, and thoroughly research intriguing topics as I pursue my future aspirations.

On August 19, the day I was leaving Magadan, among the thoughts hovering in my mind was one of relief. Sandwiched in the plane seat, I kept promising to myself, “I will never miss this godforsaken place.” The image of Magadan was a testament to my pledge: indeed, what other impression can you have about a misty port town, where winters run wild from October to May and where almost all buildings are tombstone-gray copies of each other? Suddenly, the pilot’s fumbling English boomed from the loudspeakers, urging passengers to fasten their seatbelts. The most obvious instruction sparked my musings about whether I could discern the pilot’s message through those half-muted s’s and rambling r’s. But before I could come up with anything, the answer presented itself on the video screen in front of me. It showed a map of Russia with Moscow and Magadan at its extreme ends and an inscription above—5,904 kilometers.

After living for sixteen years in the place separated from the rest of the world by endless forests, being far away felt like nothing new. Still, I never managed to find a moment when I wouldn’t be gutted by isolation. And however strenuously I tried to banish it—by trying to enjoy the town’s taiga surroundings or going fishing with my parents—it wasn’t willing to let up simply like that. In fact, it was me who always ended up banished by thousands of mosquitoes, and the nauseating plaice smell back to my book-stuffed room, where I would find my escape in Merriam-Webster crosswords and Oxford grammar guides.

Under the pressure of remoteness, I converted English from a run-of-the-mill subject into a gateway to bring myself closer to the outer world: the narrowly yanked-out “perspicacity” and “malediction” were steps towards comprehending the wordiest articles in The New Yorker; the finally mastered subjunctive was a leap to connecting with fellow English enthusiasts across physical boundaries. But it didn’t end there. As I learned more about ties between the United States and Magadan, including its sister-city status with Anchorage, I set out to explore those connections. Soon, English was supplemented with American history, and I found solace at my school library, perusing the dusty American Pageant about Ronald Reagan’s jaunty charms and Teddy Roosevelt’s Cuban arms, Andrew Jackson’s zealous populism and Woodrow Wilson’s hopeless pacifism. Later on, it was the eventual severance of those ties—the long-gone student-exchange partnership between my school and Alaskan schools—that spurred me to research the ebbs and flows of connection internationally: how World War I crashed the Concert of Europe into austere interbellum, how the unipolar moment transitioned to the increasingly fragmented world we find ourselves in today.

In 1944 U.S. Vice President Henry Wallace visited Magadan, then a Gulag prison camp, and, having been deceived by local authorities into believing that those who worked there were “volunteers,” praised it as a “combination of Tennessee Valley Authority and Hudson’s Bay Company.” Afterwards, he obviously had to take his words back. Seventy years onward Magadan may still project a grim image for some, but for me there is infinitely more behind that bleakness. It was its remoteness that inspired me to create spaces of connection through culture and commonality of interests at my school and beyond. And although it was awfully easy to fall into the trap of criticizing Magadan for its inhospitable weather, decrepit infrastructure, and dismal past—something I’m certainly guilty of—it was within its dreariness that I discovered my cradle of intellectualism, something I am eternally grateful for. My train of thought was yet again interrupted by the plane finally accelerating. As the pine trees were waving goodbye to me through the plane window, realization was overtaking relief. Following the orders from the pilot, I tried to set my seat back in the upright position but didn’t manage to—it was broken, as was my imprudent promise.

“No results found”. I felt like Schrodinger’s cat, stuck between the excitement I had to explain my video on superposition to my cousins in Patna, and the dismay I felt when I realized I was trapped by a language barrier I never knew existed. As I stared at the blank screen, trying to search for an effective way to explain what the double slit experiment was in a regional dialect of Hindi known as Bhojpuri, I realized what I had been missing all these years.

I was mystified by the world of subatomic particles from a young age. Trying to wrap my head around the separate rules of classical and quantum mechanics, I watched videos from famous lecturers such as Michio Kaku, reading about different unification theories such as string theory and quantum loop gravity. I even made videos on YouTube myself about different topics within quantum mechanics, eager to share the knowledge I had attained. However, it always felt like I was missing a crucial component that would later form my identity.

During the summer after my freshman year I went to Patna, a small city in northern India. This seemingly normal family trip would be the trip that defined my future path. My cousins happened to see my video and I was eager to further explain to them why a particle could also be considered a wave. As I launched into my explanation, their confused expressions stopped me short. The problem wasn't just the language barrier—they spoke Bhojpuri, a Hindi dialect—but a lack of accessible resources in their language. This was further exacerbated as I scoured the internet for resources in Bhojpuri but could only find a paid Bhojpuri translator instead of articles specifically for their language. I started questioning how they even pursued their own interests with this barrier blocking access to the vast amount of online resources. They said they had to deal with this every time, using their choppy understanding of English rather than their mother tongue to attempt to learn a new concept. I felt so helpless, how would knowing entanglement or knowing quantum tunneling help me in this situation? That’s when I realized I had no direction, no end goal, no purpose I was working towards.

After this epiphany, I realized I was missing impact. I wanted to build something that would help people like my cousins and revolutionize education by allowing people to use technology in the sphere of their own culture.

This is where I started my research into artificial intelligence. I saw in AI the potential to democratize knowledge on a scale previously unimaginable, since it could be used to build a tangible platform that others could use. I had always been a coder since middle school but AI was a quickly developing field where I truly believed I could make an impact due to the parallels I saw with quantum mechanics. I dove into machine learning and natural language processing, seeing parallels with the quantum concepts I loved. The way AI models consider multiple possibilities simultaneously before picking one solution mirrors quantum superposition, just as how a particle is thought to be in multiple places before converging on the most probable location.

I used the skills I obtained in machine learning and fullstack development to help with projects and research papers that aligned with my goals, moving my knowledge from out of my head onto projects that would help bring education to various people and cultures.

This journey from quantum-obsessed kid to aspiring AI researcher has shown me the unexpected ways scientific passion can evolve. Like a quantum particle tunneling through seemingly impenetrable barriers, my love for science has found a new expression—one that I believe can punch through the walls separating millions of minds from the wonders of scientific discovery, all starting from an unexpected discovery on a “normal” trip.

The biggest loss to cable TV was my cousin and I not appearing on Shark Tank. At seven years old, I knew that viewers wanted to see two scrawny girls, just shy of three feet, pitching “Design It Up,” a business aiming to upcycle everyday items into works of art.

My venture was born from stumbling upon a National Geographic article on the Amur Leopard. Enchanted, I spent the next nights huddled under my blankets, voraciously reading articles and watching videos about the species and their endangered status. Could I do something to help? I was confident I could, one toilet paper roll bunny at a time. Soon after, I roped my cousin in, and Design It Up was created.

My afternoons became filled with increasingly unusual duct tape crafts, gossamers of dried hot glue, and sock puppets. Going door to door, we sold our creations and handed out flyers, hoping to raise money and awareness.

For as long as I can remember, I’ve cared about things almost too stubbornly; As I clicked the “Donate” button, I felt like I was helping an effort larger than myself. It was the first time I brought purpose to a cause I was passionate about. I realized that I didn’t have to wait till I was older–I am capable of creating an impact now.

In my eighth-grade history class during a lesson on the Boston Busing Crisis, we discussed educational equity and its impact on social mobility. Like when I first read about the Amur Leopard, I felt that familiar tug – could I do something? Where should I start? These initially hopeful questions turned into soured expressions of reality: Is this too large and complex for a fourteen-year-old? Unlike when I was younger, I knew more about how expansive and deep-seated these macro-economic issues were, and felt I couldn’t create an impact. With this exaggerated form of rationality, I was trapped in a state of inertia, worried that I was in deeper water than I could swim in.

After unearthing an old Design It Up flyer, I was reminded of the joy of experimentation and puzzling to find a solution. Seven-year-old me was not worried if her plans would come to fruition or what people would think, but delighted in her ability to act. When I was young, I was not scared of failure. Years later, I reminded myself not to be as well.

As I researched more, ideas collided, fractured, and merged into a tactile educational program for students seeking STEM resources. What began as late nights with friends, sending emails and wrestling with WordPress, soon turned into mornings spent explaining fossils and adaptations to eager students. Now, when 7-year-old Eva excitedly shows me her Play-Doh superhero during our genetics session at her local library, I am reminded of those afternoons spent sticky with duct tape residue, building something meaningful.

At seventeen, whether I’m teaching digital literacy classes to students in Kenya or working to create a supportive environment for women in debate, I strive to advocate for the issues I see in the same way: dynamically, with energy and exigency. Although market research (my dad) might suggest that people would rather wear their socks than play with them, I find joy in the evolution of an idea– watching it take shape and gather momentum.

As the world around me motivates me to create, build, and solve, I hope to carry myself with the same determination and faith as my seven-year-old self. The ability to take action is a privilege– one that I refuse to waste. I relish the process and no longer fear an imperfect final product. As I look forward to my next project, I’m reminded of the playful experimentation that started it all, knowing that each new endeavor will find its place alongside the toilet paper roll bunnies and sock puppets in my personal hall of fame.

“She has no problems.”

This was the fifth time the doctors had dismissed the unexplainable pain after my period that lasted for twenty days every cycle for the past three years. Despite countless visits, doctors firmly assured me that nothing was wrong. Yet, the relentless and excruciating cramp frequently left me bedridden for days on end, and dancing, which I had done since I was three, became nearly impossible. It wasn’t until my mom’s gut intuition and persistence that led to the grand unveiling: an obstructed unicornuate uterus.

Returning to dance after the surgery wasn’t easy. The studio had changed; the older girls had graduated, and new faces filled the room. My body had also changed; my once flexible limbs and graceful fluidity now resisted every command. Watching the others, their fans snapping open with precision and their movements embodying the artistry of Chinese dance, left me painfully aware of my own inadequacy, filling me with self-doubt.

But I was determined to regain everything I had lost. My evenings turned into a mix of math concepts and oversplits, with homework often propped open next to the mat and my muscles howling as I memorized polar functions for tomorrow's test. Randomly doing a front walkover, leaping in the air, or falling asleep in the frog pose became the new normal. I seized every opportunity to stretch, viewing the playground equipment as a chance to prop my leg up and viewing the street curbs as practice for perfecting my lines and balance in “fan shens,” a move resembling a windmill. Gradually, the burn and foreign feeling subsided. The muscle memory I had relied on returned.

But my girls weren’t back and neither was my laughter.

“You wanna get McDonald’s ice cream with us after?” This simple invitation sparked the beginning of new friendships. As I joined the group on their weekly excursions to McDonald’s, the smell of forbidden hot fries and the taste of velvety ice cream became symbols of camaraderie. The carpools to the studio and back were filled with Snapchat filter tests, entertaining impersonations, and endless gossip. Barbecue nights of chatty conversations transformed our connections from dance mates to trusted friends. Everyone’s unwavering support and unconditional help, whether that be restitching costumes or words of affirmation, made this team feel like an extended family.

Amidst these months, however, a foreign figure stared at me in the mirror. The medication I had taken during my recovery caused significant weight gain. Each glance at my squishy stomach, thick thighs, and four incision scars felt like a betrayal from the person I used to be.

But scraps of bright red and white fabric were my fairy godmother. The costumes, intricately designed, bibbidi bobbidi booed me into someone I could feel proud of. No longer hiding behind a facade, the happiness and elegance radiated in my appearance and spirit once more.

Although insecurities still shine through occasionally, the mirror’s judgments have become reflections of my strength and resilience rather than critical remarks. Turns out, the magic in dance was exactly what I needed to find myself again—not just in the movements or routines, but in the passion, journey, and love I received. I discovered within myself that I was able to reclaim the joy of the happy little girl I once was, now reshaped by the challenges and strength I experienced along the way.

“Next up, let’s welcome number 2383…”

The bright lights hugged me, and adrenaline surged through my veins. This is where I belong. From a young girl with stage fright in a silly unicorn costume to a confident performer in a beautiful flowy dress, I’m back to own the stage.

I loved my grandma’s car. I loved the way it hugged the road with its low suspension, and its bright blueberry-colored exterior. I loved the way her ancient sunglasses sat on the dashboard, and the flickering of the faulty speedometer. I loved the rattling of her keychain filled with accessories from her favorite charities. But most of all, I loved her collection of classical piano CDs that crammed into the armrest.

“You used to be able to play this?” I asked her as Liszt’s Liebestraum No. 3, echoed its mesmerizing beauty and virtuosity around the car. “Yes, and I bet you will someday too,” she responded wholeheartedly. My grandma and I drove around her condo often, and when we did, classical piano was always playing. The music served as a bonding point for us, and something I enjoyed learning how to play for her when I got home.

As I got older, I grew a new appreciation for these classical pieces. Fascinated by the meaning of each composition, my grandma and I frequently conversed over them—especially when it was Rachmaninoff's. While practicing his powerful, uncanny chords, I felt transformed into the snowy Red Square in Russia, sensing his essence in the room and his own interpretation playing out in my hands. Music has this wonderful ability to encapsulate people and memories: something I had to learn the hard way.

Sadly, my grandma passed away from cancer last summer. I felt like I lost my best friend, but I still had the one thing that connected us so well - music.

That summer, I made a promise to myself that I was going to learn Liebestraum. Being the most played CD, it was our favorite piece, and my most vivid memory from our rides; however, learning it was no easy task, and it would become the first advanced piece in my repertoire.

I clocked in hours on the piano bench. Fingers stiff and sore, I continued to run through giant leaps and melodious chords. Some sections, like the middle in C major, seemed unconquerable, but the tiny portrait of my grandma placed atop the piano motivated me to push through. After meticulous effort, I started playing in tempo. The music painted a beautiful scene of love—with soothing cello-like melodies, dreamy cadenzas with speedy tempos, and nostalgic passages—making Liebestraum a piece that reveals the encapsulated memories we shared together and reflects the values she taught me.

Carrying two heavy bags filled with clothing, I stepped into my grandma’s car for an excursion to drop off donations at church. “Why do we always have to do this?” I remember constantly pondering on the way. At the time, I was blind to the significance of my grandma’s actions, but over the years, I have come to appreciate her altruism. Inspired by her legacy for others, I want to give back and benefit our community through charity—and even music.

One of the best things about music is its ability to share a story, and I got the chance to share what Liebestraum means to me by performing at my school’s charity concert. The lights dimmed, and with the spotlight flashing on the grand piano, I hurried to the bench. With over six months of work, and 1000 eyes darting on my hands, I felt uneasy, but I was eager to play my heart out. As I gently lifted my hands, finishing the performance, the cheers from the crowd grew. Although not physically present, I knew my grandma was proud, and as they brought out the large check for the local charity, I felt content knowing that my playing had a positive impact.

I love my car. A gift from my grandma, “Blueberry” is a reminder to live graciously and generously. When the CDs play, I picture all of the happy memories we had, and I feel determined to keep our bond alive through music.

12 seconds left on the clock. It was the game, and we were going to lose because of a silly mistake I made. 4…3…2… I scored the game-winning layup. My heart and left leg skipped in unison as I sprinted back to defense. Three whistles marked the end of the game and the beginning of a celebration as we confirmed our advancement to the championship. Barely 12 seconds elapsed before our jubilation was abruptly interrupted. My teammate, Fenet, suddenly collapsed to the floor. My coaches and teammates rushed to her. I couldn't do anything to help, so I just watched from a distance. To our relief, she regained consciousness a few minutes later. She hadn't eaten food all day and had fainted. My heart regained its normal rhythm. My inability to understand what had happened and respond accordingly brought back an unwelcome memory.

Baba, my father, passed away of a heart attack one unassuming morning three years ago. I remember how sick he had been in the days leading up to it. “Nothing major, nothing Baba can’t handle.” I had thought. One Saturday morning, my parents decided to head to the hospital for a check-up. 10 AM: Baba got in the shower. I was worried. “Should he be in there alone?” Suddenly, we heard a loud thudding sound. We rushed to the bathroom door only to find it locked. My brother beat the door down and on the tiled bathroom floor lay Baba, gasping, struggling to breathe. It was the middle of the rainy season, yet the sun hung brilliantly in the sky, its intense radiance casting a glaring light that seemed almost cruel, a stark contrast to the nightmare that was now our reality. Seconds...minutes elapsed before we finally made it to the hospital, but Baba had already left us.

For months afterwards, every minor incident heightened my heartbeat. I constantly checked others’ breathing as they lay asleep. I felt uncomfortable with someone locking the door while alone. Finally, daunted by the prospect of again being unable to act, I enrolled in a first aid summer course. Simple yet invaluable, we learned the Heimlich maneuver: a technique used to save someone who is choking. We explored a multitude of scenarios - bleeding, body injuries, bone fractures, dislocation, burns, bleeding, poisoning. And with a mannequin as our patient, we learned how to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation. CPR. “Gasping is not proper breathing. Gasping requires CPR," our first aid trainer Dr. Elias stressed. If only I had known. The 'if' tormented me, but I had to look forward.

Chest compressions are supposed to be deep, so deep that there is a possibility of breaking ribs. Pushing into the dummy’s chest, with ‘Stayin Alive’ by Bee Gees playing in the background, I remember being nervous at the thought of putting that much pressure on a real human being, but I also remember thinking that if it were a person lying in front of me, I wouldn’t hesitate for a second. ‘The golden hour’ is a term used to describe the very first hour following a traumatic incident. Without the knowledge to act promptly, that gold turns into stone and the opportunity to save a life fades. Such incidents can be unpredictable, and any hour could suddenly become a golden hour. Having the knowledge to act when that time comes is empowering.

Today, I walk with more confidence and less fear of the next second bringing with it the unknown. As I traverse the streets of Addis, I consciously lift my head, always on the lookout for anyone needing my assistance, in need of first aid. Dreading it, but never avoiding it. Seconds could make the difference between life and death. I vowed to myself to never again let those precious moments pass by as a spectator. I live to abide by that promise.

**Burnt and Knapsacked**

My right eye throbbed as I lean my 165 lbs on the red corner of the ring, spitting what little water I had under my mouthguard into a bucket.

This was my last hoorah.

Sixty seconds later, I was knocked out.

Setting aside how lazy my jabs were the last round and the sheer force of the gut punches I took, something deeper was at play: The Knapsack Problem. Imagine a robber, limited to carrying 50 pounds; he must choose the most valuable jewels to steal while staying under the limit. I’d never tasted failure this bitter before. Math camp was challenging but I always passed; Valorant’s rank hell was mean, but I eventually climbed to the top 0.1% of players; and while everyday in training felt like a marathon, I lost 50lbs preparing for this moment.

Despite this, I found myself staring at my gray ceiling with a busted lip, watching my friends go to Japan’s IMO while I’d exponentially get crushed after every failed Valorant tryout.

Was I meant for failure? No. I got Knapsacked. Like an algorithm taking on too many inputs to compute, I overloaded myself. I imagine jumping out of a window with all my ambitions, only to fall splat on the ground, weighed down by the very dreams I tried to carry. (Ouch.) So, how do I choose?

Or maybe, why did I even consider going pro in Valorant and boxing?

I realized that whether it’s diving into a new math problem or entering a new Valorant game, the feeling is the same. In math, I try theorem after theorem, construction after construction, while in-game, I fake rotations, play slow, or sometimes use a teammate as bait until that feeling of success starts to hit. In both, the better you get, the harder that feeling becomes to reach—so you go into olympiads or attempt to go all Muhammad Ali.

Unlike math, in real life, optimization and prioritization aren’t the same. Optimization is about efficiency; prioritization is about what matters most. Cooking Dana’s favorite Kabsa every Friday isn’t efficient, but it’s a priority. I choose the jewels that matter, even if it means not optimizing every moment.

With my heavy knapsack on my back, I began a new approach: collecting as many small but valuable jewels as I could. I’d learn anything that interested me but as soon as learning more became too heavy, I’d reconsider the value of the jewel.

My first small jewel? Learn to kickflip. It took a month of rolled ankles and two broken skateboards, but once I added it to my knapsack, I moved on. My second: learn to code a full-stack app—one that conveniently solved my problem of giving up when trying to make time lapses. And the latest jewel I’m working on adding: getting a national speedcubing record.

Even so, other jewels are worth the heavy weight. I focused on helping out my family by training my younger brother, Sulaiman, to take over. I spent the time I previously used for reviewing my Valorant games teaching him how to add the perfect amount of cheese to Dana’s favorite eggs or showing him how to open our old rusty stove without getting electrocuted (but that’s a story for another time).

Thinking of the challenges I choose as jewels that get heavier over time helped me realize what I truly value. I think long and hard before going the extra mile to capture the full jewel, and I understand now why, ever since I was a kid, I’ve obsessed over new hobbies. That feeling of discovery is something I’ll never let go of, whether it’s tackling hard math problems or learning a new skill. I’ll come to college learning who and what deserves the most space in my shiny knapsack that’ll only get shinier—but hopefully, never too heavy.

As I stood on the gravelly road of Sonsonate, El Salvador, the sound of roosters crowing broke the pre-dawn calm—a sharp contrast to the hum of Los Angeles traffic I was used to. A visa loophole forced me to leave the only home I had ever known, and I found myself thousands of miles away, struggling to make sense of a land both familiar and alien. The hands that once wrote essays and biked around the city now bore the rough calluses of harvesting fruit and caring for cattle—a bitter irony that in this place, I could work, while the country I called home had barred me from doing so. Far from the urban jungle of California, El Salvador greeted me with vibrant, lush landscapes. The scratchy soursop fruit that pricked my fingertips as I toiled connected me unexpectedly to the ground of my ancestors. This routine became my new normal for over three years, immersing me in a culture I had long felt distant from. Yet, I found myself stuck in an existential limbo, caught between immigration laws and legal loopholes, feeling neither fully Salvadoran nor entirely American. Being sent back to the country of my birth after living my whole life in the U.S. left me feeling like I didn’t truly belong anywhere. The distance from my family was the hardest part—a constant, gnawing loneliness that no amount of work or lush scenery could ease. I decided to channel my pain and turn the fields of Sonsonate into my classroom, where I learned perseverance and patience in ways no textbook could teach. One day, I stooped over for hours gathering fruit while the merciless sun hammered down on my back. My hands were blistered, my muscles ached, and there was no end in sight. Back in Los Angeles, challenges often came with quick fixes—a tutor for a tough class, a doctor’s note to skip gym—but here, there were no shortcuts. The only way forward was to push through the discomfort and find a rhythm in the work. With time, I came to see that my everyday work was about reclaiming control over my life rather than only survival. Sitting on a hillside seeing the sunset over the mountains in my second year away from home, I came to see I had not only survived but also clearly accomplished something. Every fruit I picked, every cow I looked after, was evidence of my resiliency—a silent protest against the forced relocation I had gone through, a means of expression, "I am still here; I am still standing." This insight changed my perspective: I was actively involved in my own story rather than only a victim of events. Having saved enough money for tuition, I re-enrolled at Santa Monica College under a student visa and felt as though I was recovering a piece of me. Coming back to the United States was about seizing control of my destiny, not only about returning to familiar surroundings. School became my refuge, a place where I could reestablish the life I was forced to leave behind and reconnect with my family. My time in El Salvador fundamentally changed my perspective and sparked a desire for advocacy—especially for immigrant groups dealing with legal and identity issues. While at Santa Monica College, I developed a visa guidance program for overseas students negotiating the challenging legal terrain of seeking an education in the United States. At nearby middle schools, I also assist and tutor undocumented students, providing direction and encouragement while they tackle similar obstacles. The desire to be a catalyst for change inspires me to keep studying and significantly influence the lives of those going through the same challenges I once did. What I discovered in the classrooms of Santa Monica College and the fields of Sonsonate inspires me to write the next chapter. With each step forward, I aim to transform obstacles into opportunities so that others don’t have to endure the burden of displacement I once did.

Stepping into Kindergarten career day, my mind was filled with endless fantasies. I dreamed of becoming a chef, combining spices in precise proportions to produce the perfect taste. But that was soon replaced with the prospect of being a mayor, where I could fix all the “dog poop landmines” in my local park with a single pen stroke. As I continued to visualize these endless scenarios, it was impossible to choose between these incredible options until a man in a white lab coat took the presenter’s seat.

The man in the white lab coat worked for the local hospital, but not as a nurse, doctor, or surgeon. He was a research scientist, identifying biomarkers for diseases like diabetes. As a clean room filled with pristine and complex lab equipment materialized on the smartboard, I instantly knew that lab research was for me; I yearned to wear the white lab coat, the visual representation of his unrelenting pursuit to improve society.

However, that elusive “lab dream” was soon tucked away along with the rest of my imaginations.

Every Friday afternoon in 7th grade, the first thing I would do after school was to turn on the Discovery Channel to watch BattleBots. I was obsessed and soon wanted to be involved in (less violent) robotics myself. Though I couldn’t find an existing robotics team that took middle schoolers, I did find two enthusiastic friends, and we co-founded our own robotics team.

There was nothing special about our rookie team; we were just three middle schoolers with nothing but a kit of basic parts. After conducting much “exploration” with our glorified Legos (which was greatly accelerated by having six hands instead of two), we gathered our limited knowledge (mostly from some YouTube videos) to assemble something we could safely call a “robot”: it had four functional wheels and a claw to pick up giant 2x1 Lego bricks from the foam competition field. Additionally, it could quack like a duck from an onboard speaker.

Upon entering into our first competition, we were met with an unpleasant surprise – our robot could only quack and didn’t even move well. As I cautiously manipulated the joystick, time seemingly stopped as I twisted and turned my whole body in an attempt to turn our robot using an Xbox controller. Unable to hear anything or even look at the match timer, driving the robot was a surreal experience. Aside from leaving the venue at the end of the day with pieces of bent aluminum held together by zip ties, I also left with empowerment to build something better, stronger, and more complex for our next competition.

I desperately needed this empowerment if I were to rebuild a robot from scratch in four weeks. Despite my 3D printer constantly jamming and accidentally burning out half of our motors after grossly overestimating the power of a 12V battery (which turns out is very little for its massive size), I yearned to build that better, stronger, and more complex robot every night—even during winter break in a ski resort hotel room in Lake Tahoe.

In no time, the four weeks had passed. We also spent another week drive-testing my new creation to fix any remaining drive-base problems and simplify driving it. While my creation didn't win a huge trophy, we placed in the top third and won the "Judges' Award" – recognizing our enthusiasm, can-do mindset, team spirit, and robot performance.

In 9th grade, my robotics journey continued. My team merged with a local, better-resourced team, and our combined forces won our regional championship twice. At the 2024 World Championship, my team competed with the best teams worldwide and reached a new high: division finals. These achievements wouldn’t have been possible if I hadn’t initiated and nurtured my rookie team.

Fast-forward to this year: I am analyzing satellite data to develop computerized techniques (using the skills and knowledge I acquired in robotics) to predict geomagnetic storms that disrupt our electrical grid and communications network. It feels like a dream come true, reminiscent of my aspirations during Kindergarten Career Day—just without the white lab coat. I pursued my dream with resilience and hard work, overcoming obstacles to eventually achieve my goals. It is a testament to the power of a stubborn mind, fierce imagination, and unyielding determination. It embodies the very essence of my journey, from dreaming of a white lab coat to standing amidst a robust robotics team.

The old lady took her last breath as the bright blue of her eyes dulled. Her screen went dark for the last time. As I unplugged her from the wall, I bid her one last goodbye. My chromebox had served me well, but she was now old and slow. She took forever to wake up and was prone to unpredictable narcoleptic sleeps. I decided it was time for an upgrade. Computer parts were a puzzle that some had managed to solve. Maybe it was my innate curiosity on the topic, or the fact that I was just bored, but I decided to take on this challenge. I decided to build my own PC. I would come to know what words such as cas latency and overclocking meant, yet at that time I was beyond overwhelmed. The world of PC building seemed like it had its own language, but I was nonetheless eager to explore it.

As I familiarized myself with the computer parts, I grew to love computer engineering. However, my quest wasn’t without its obstacles, one being a GPU shortage. Because of COVID, this integral part of the computer was scarce, and the ones you could find were sold at exorbitant prices. Would I have to wait until GPU's returned? My solution: iGPU's, an integration of the CPU and GPU. Not only were they in stock, they were also cheaper. I meticulously researched the options, continuing on my adventure.

A month later, I had finally crafted the perfect list of the six essential components I needed to begin building. After impatiently waiting weeks for each part to come, I finally had all the boxes stacked together in the living room. Hours went by as we built. I enlisted my father’s help for the trickier steps, such as placing the CPU down without touching the pins at the bottom and then applying thermal paste on top. I was scared of ruining this tiny, expensive piece of equipment, but I had managed it even with shaky hands. A PC is very picky. Each part comes with a plethora of variations, some incompatible with others. My research had confirmed that there were no incongruities in my build, but you can never know. Hours of time and hundreds of dollars were banking on this moment. The question now was: does it work? I held my breath as I turned it on. I waited patiently for any signs of life... crickets. I ensured all the wires were connected correctly and scoured the Internet in search of a solution. However, all doors led to the same consensus: I had failed. It was past midnight and I could feel my hope slipping away.

Suddenly, I hear my dad’s voice yell, “[Name]! Come here!” One of the RAM sticks hadn't been fully pushed in. With anticipation, I clicked the on button and watched as the surrounding fluorescent circle glowed. It worked!

I continue to chase this feeling of accomplishment. After delivering 2000 tennis balls to a local dog shelter or having my video game code run with zero errors, I feel proud. Taking up projects had become a constant in my life, and gratification became the fuel for my ambition. I’ve learned that failure is a part of life as well, accepting the rejections that come from cold-calling sponsors for my blood cancer fundraiser and dusting myself off after losing a heated tiebreaker in a tennis match.

As I look at my two computers, the retired chromebox sitting to the left of my monitor, and the flourishing PC I built sitting to the right, I embrace the beauty of the journey. I cherish the memories of initiative, resilience, and curiosity that have molded me into the person that I am today. Even now, when asked where I got my PC, I swallow down my excitement before saying, “Oh that? Yeah, I built it!”

Have you ever felt like the hours take way longer than they should and the subway conveniently breaks down and the rush-hour conspires against you? The bus slows to a maddening crawl and the weight of work and responsibilities grows ever higher and the sky outside is a sick joke of sleet and rain? So you tell yourself “it’s Thursday, one more day, one more late night, then everything will be ok.” But you don’t believe yourself, day after week after month after year of saying the same thing. So your eyes fill. You’re losing it. But you don’t know what to do. I couldn’t tell you when I began to understand that something was wrong. All I know is that it was very bad that evening. And when that happens to you, you become tremendously willing to examine some other alternatives for how to live.

So I’d delete social media and cancel streaming services thinking distraction was the issue. Or then for three weeks I’d try time-blocking techniques and run a mile every morning. I thought if I worked a little bit harder, was a bit more disciplined or that next thing worked I’d finally get on top of everything, then everything would be ok. But what it really was, was a 17-year-old kid who exhausted a couple other ways to live, really took them to their conclusion, and was able to do almost everything he needed to do, but never everything. My dad could tell I was drowning. So one morning in June he told me to pack a backpack and that Wednesday we were on a red-eye. He would bring me to one of his favorite places. We would hike through Big Sur and speed through Highway One and dream that golden dream.

I remember we were hiking when we stopped and sat on a rock that looked down towards the sea. The slope to the sea was dotted with shrubs and trees, and the swell of clear water was as blue as the sky. The sea shimmered in the sunlight and the warm air smelled of salt and water, stirred by the breeze, stretched infinitely beyond. We sat there for almost three hours. It was the same feeling with which I woke on the morning we were in the Sahara. I was eight and he made me get up and I was groggy and cranky until outside the tent I saw a hundred miles of orange sand in every direction, of absolutely gorgeous unspoiled nothingness while the sun slowly rose out of the dunes.

For the first time in a while, I was able to breathe, free from scheming and calculating and worrying. It reminded me of what life is like—instead of being a relief from it—and I remembered the world is indeed a big and beautiful place. For a few weeks after it was to feel your eyelids pulled open. I was alert and attentive and optimistic and every day was a joy to wake up to and I was becoming a better person. But the insidious thing is I gradually, unconsciously, slipped back into my default setting: the rat race, the slave to my head, the constant sense of needing more of, of having lost, some infinite thing. I couldn’t help myself.

Maybe it’s because the world of money and power is mired in a pool of fear and frustration. Maybe it’s me. So it’s extraordinarily hard to stay conscious and happy day in and day out. Maintain awareness of what is so real and essential, so hidden in plain sight, that I have to keep reminding myself time and again to say that “thank you” and think positively and live in the present. It involves attention and discipline and it’s the job of a lifetime but it’s surely worth more than anything else. It’s the pursuit of happiness.

On Dec 23, 2015, a mini glass carriage fell on my head.

I was diagnosed with a condition that would affect me for the rest of my life: “being the most awesome person ever.” While this condition was diagnosed by a little girl holding an ice pack on her head, it was written and sealed in a pink journal of mine, therefore making it official.

Since that day, I’ve been a diligent collector of all my life’s moments: Jan 2015, my first entry! June 2017, I saved a hurt bird. September 2020, I was awarded in school for having good character. April 2021 I hit $1000 in sales. March 2022 I embarrassed myself at the student vs staff volleyball game. May 2024, my family and I watched the stars. These snippets comprise a pink journal with pages that have housed the past decade.

Collecting has always been second nature to me. Go into my room, turn right, and open the small closet. In the corner, you will see a mini box of every birthday card I’ve ever received. Pick up the brown bag next to it- stacks of hotel keycards, Ashley paint sheets, quarters from every state, and all my school projects since kindergarten. One more small right, a cubby for my pink notebook, craft supplies, and pens of every color you could imagine. Everything I collected had some sort of value to me- even the Welch’s gummy wrappers I collected as a kid simply because I was drawn to their sweet, artificial fruit scent.

Of all my collections, I've found writing to be the most fulfilling. Each page in my notebook allows me to relive exact moments from my past as if they were happening all over again. In some pages, I can feel the fear I had before an interview or the joy I felt being named MVP of a hard-fought tournament. In other pages, there's the ache of tears that left my eyes dry from my grandfather's passing, while others have the sheer anxiety of being a teenager. Some pages have the peace of morning walks with my headphones, while others have the chaos of family reunions in India.

This habit of note-taking extended beyond memories—I began writing down every idea that crossed my mind. When I started my small business, I kept scrap papers on my bedside to jot down thoughts as I lay awake. I have a binder of everything I’ve ever pondered—projects, research, workout routines, side hustle concepts, and more. Sometimes, when inspiration struck and my binder was out of reach, I’d scribble on my pants and take a picture for later. I’ve always felt that there was more to my obsessive note-taking than just collecting memories. Perhaps I was afraid of forgetting, scared that if I didn’t write these memories down, they’d slip away and be lost in time forever.

Or perhaps, this is my way of trying to live life to the fullest, a response to a childhood scare when my parents were mistold at my birth that I was deaf. Every sound, every conversation, every whisper became precious to me. Perhaps my journal is my way of capturing life’s symphony, ensuring that even if silence came, I’d have a record of every note.

But maybe, just maybe, it’s the continuation of a wild imagination—a promise that the notebook is a sanctuary for the girl with an ice pack on her head. A promise that there’s always an answer through hardships and something to celebrate. A promise to cherish the gift of life, and will someday be a legacy of laughter, love, and a life well-lived.

New Yorkers call it Richmond Hill; we call it “Little Guyana.” I grew up around the tangy aroma of curry on the street, around bustling Guyanese bake shops, rhythmic calypso music, and thick Caribbean accents. Every guest who walked into our house, every customer who entered my parents’ office, was known as an “aunt” or “uncle.” It didn’t matter if we were related by blood because we shared a culture that, in a way, went far deeper. Growing up in Little Guyana felt normal, a perfect combination of my American surroundings and Guyanese heritage.

Then, in middle school, I moved from Little Guyana to Long Island, and my sense of identity completely changed. I switched from my predominantly Black school to a largely white school, where I was one of only two Black girls on campus. No “aunts” or “uncles” were in this community, no curry or Caribbean accents. It was only a few months until I started receiving hateful comments on social media about my race. I responded by desperately trying to fit in, to the point where I worked with a speech therapist to scrub out every hint of my accent. It was a feat of cultural shapeshifting, but no matter what I tried, my heritage still made me an outsider. Even worse, I also became an outsider in Little Guyana. “[Name], you act so American now,” my family would say when I visited. “What happened to being Guyanese?” I felt like I was being torn in half, one foot in my Guyanese heritage, another in my American community, somehow a stranger to both.

Entering high school, I knew there was only one solution to this tension: I needed to visit Guyana. I had traveled to Guyana when I was young, but my memories were filtered through a child's eyes, long before my identity began to fray. I finally visited when I was in 9th grade, and as I stepped off the plane into the warm, humid air, I immediately felt a sense of belonging. Over the next few weeks, I walked through Bourda market in the scorching sun, spoke Creole with shop vendors, and smiled as adults called me “pickney.” It felt like home, a home I had always known, even though I grew up 2,600 miles away. When I returned to Long Island, I was determined not to hide my Guyanese heritage, but to embrace it.

When I returned from Guyana, I not only wanted to better express my identity, but help other people find strength in theirs. I became a leader in my school’s Black Student Union, where I hosted events about different national identities and mentored Black students at my local middle school. I started attending events with Jack and Jill of America, which aims to improve quality of life for Black children. I was selected as a leader in my school's first ever Peer Mentoring program, where I help students of different races and find the right community for them. My identity once made me feel like a pariah in my community, an outsider looking in. Now, only three years later, it has become the centerpiece of my most meaningful activities. All of this stems from that first trip back to Guyana, when my identity became a source of strength rather than a reason for doubt.

This entire journey – from Little Guyana to Guyana itself - has made me more confident in my identity and inspired me to support my community. In a way, it feels like coming full circle. I still visit Little Guyana today, where I smell the same tangy curry, hear the same Caribbean accents, and see Guyanese children playing in the parks. It’s a reminder that I belong, not just in Little Guyana, not just in Long Island, but in all the places I’ve ever called home.

Children's book authors excel at creating lovable characters. But slouching on a miniature desk, second-grade me cursed Peggy Parish, the creator of [Name] Bedelia, an all-too-literal fool who shared my first name. Maid to the Rodgers family, Bedelia waltzed with unwarranted certainty between each page, never failing to spectacularly misinterpret her tasks: "Draw the drapes" resulted in her oil painting of curtains. Indisputably hilarious, “[Name] Bedelia” quickly became my go-to nickname. Yet her trail of missteps was the path I feared most. Determined to shed any likeness to her, I found a haven in the reliability of math.

Every Thursday, I volunteer for a free after-school program for immigrant children. One afternoon I sat filling in inked lines with two second-grade girls - Jenna and Stella. Jenna was loud and cliquey, always laughing, while Stella preferred quietly building sandcastles. Jenna, scribbling with her pink marker, suddenly announced that Stella was in the wrong classroom. Stella's eyes widened with fear. I tried to shift the conversation as trained, back to drawing. Jenna ignored my diversion. "You don't get it. She's not with her class right now because no one likes her." Stella weakly retaliated, "That's not true." As I broke into the interaction, Jenna's voice sharpened as she insisted. "I'm not lying. Ask anyone, even Teacher Rosie!" Then I stumbled.

Whenever issues previously arose, my pre-volunteer training guided me, like the familiar PEMDAS, step-by-step. I knew what to do when kids pried for personal information, got distracted, or whined—but this moment spanned unmapped ground. Jenna was serious about threats, and I knew contradicting her could escalate things. Stella was quickly transitioning from composed to tearful. Staring down Jenna, I asked about school that day. Jenna returned to her drawing, rolling her eyes, but my heart felt strained with apologies for Stella. On my train ride home, I relived the situation with regret, asking family and friends what would've been the "right" move.

I wanted to solve every situation like a POW - dissect, analyze, and confidently take my next step; A to B, B to C. I feared moments like Jenna's sudden outburst, ones I felt inadequately prepared for. As insults, tears, and snot continued to surprise me, I began reevaluating my overly methodical framework. I started to balance logic with my gut reaction, accepting my faults, while continuing to defend the Stellas. The result was __________ When I reflect on my actions, I avoid ruminating on the "correct" move I didn't make. I've begun internalizing that, for any choice, one answer, or any answer, might not exist.

Like [Name] Bedelia in her misadventures, I was naively coddled in the literal. I trusted every next step existed and would carry me to *the* solution. Now I can admit my mistake: [Name] Bedelia and I were always similar. While it manifested differently, we both needed to embrace approaching the world less concretely. I still wince out of habit when someone calls me her name, but I no longer fear the comparison. Instead, my childhood nemesis reminds me to appreciate all questions without immediate answers.

“6'6 FORWARD, NUMBER 12, ALI AHMADDD!”

As I rose from the bench and high-fived my 13 teammates, the announcement of my name as a starter for the Lovejoy High School basketball team echoed through our gym. In Lucas, a predominantly white suburb of Dallas, it might be surprising to hear this name associated with basketball. People often assume that a basketball captain looks a certain way—perhaps not like a Muslim kid with Pakistani-Arab heritage, brown skin, and curly black hair.

But I refuse to be confined by stereotypes. While sinking free throws has its moments of satisfaction, when I’m not practicing basketball I’m advocating against bullying and pushing for neurodiversity awareness. My older brother is autistic, and I’ve seen firsthand his struggles. Back in middle school, my 7th-grade brother was taunted and tripped by a classmate. He fell and broke his wrist, as the principal called my frantic mom. Requiring emergency surgery, my brother’s pain and social anxiety rocked me.

Both joy and torment drive my neurodiversity advocacy. Often, an irritated groan greets any neurodiverse kid trying out for the team. As a freshman, I recall seeing one such student sitting alone in the locker room post-tryout, tears streaming down his face. A machine's cogs turn as they always have, as they were told. The instructions are clear: preserve the status quo, maintain the unwritten rules. As expected, a freshman's tears in the locker room were not part of our protocol. Regrettably, I followed my instructions. I preserved the status quo. I maintained the unwritten rules. These experiences left me questioning the norms that perpetuate such exclusion. Why does my brother endure daily bullying since he’s neurodiverse? Why does his brain make him behave differently — hyper-fixating and rewatching the same Cars movie scene 100 times? Don’t we all have our own quirks? Why is it that my brother’s differences lead to social exclusion, while others' idiosyncrasies are more readily accepted?

Seeking answers to these questions, I’ve turned to neuroscience. Partnering with a UC Davis PhD candidate, I dove into the cerebral jungle, wrestling with neural pathways between 200 nodes in the brain scans of autism patients. Using machine learning, we unearthed a stark connection between atypical fMRI brain activity and autism. This discovery suggested that such methods could be applied to children even before they show clear signs of autism. I took this truth and published my research paper, which aims to facilitate early intervention strategies that can significantly reduce symptoms and improve long-term outcomes for those affected by autism. Closer to home, I’ve worked with my principal to establish A Beautiful Mind, an anti-bullying after-school club to support peers who fall on the autism spectrum. The school's initial resistance was a veritable fortress to our neurodiverse classmates. I hammered out a compelling proposal and provided evidence of the need for such a program, and after months of persistence the school approved it.

Hanging out in the club, I’ve befriended one classmate specifically, Thad, who’s obsessed with dinosaurs. Thad forces me to reflect upon my brother, guilting and motivating me to channel my voice against social exclusion. Thad never directly divulges his emotions — I can only sense how he may desire to have a group of friends or be invited to a birthday party. So, on Thad’s birthday, we organized a dinosaur-themed party, hanging brightly colored streamers from the ceiling to create a canopy of greens and oranges that mimicked a lush, dinosaur-filled jungle. When Thad walked in, his eyes widened with amazement. As we played a lively round of Jurassic Park trivia, Thad eagerly shared fun facts about velociraptors (did you know that they were only the size of a turkey? Jurassic Park lied.), a truth that had us all chuckling. My duty doesn’t end here. I didn’t expect to always be treated as the neurodiversity advocate. But somehow, I wanted people to remember that I was always that kid with that brother. He taught me that the busiest room can be the loneliest room. Sometimes we look at people like my brother, like Thad. But rarely do we see them. And yet, I see them, hear them, and (I hope) I understand them. So, the next time I see an overlooked peer at university, I won’t stay quiet. I’ll break protocol, I’ll reverse direction. I’ll try to make the busiest room a little less lonely.

On the first New Year’s I didn’t celebrate, my fifth-grade science teacher greeted me with a bear hug as I entered her home. My parents lugged my two suitcases up to Mrs. Erwin’s doorstep, said their goodbyes, and left for Boston, where my brother Charles was rushed for brain surgery. After learning about Charles’s deteriorating condition, the Erwins didn’t hesitate to take me in. At the Erwins’, devouring home-cooked alfredo, watching X-Men movies, and playing Halo with their son Joseph almost made me forget about our family’s troubles. Getting to school early to help Mrs. Erwin set up felt like, a distraction. But every night before bed, we would pray together for my brother.

Charles returned home with an ever-determined smile on his pale face. I kept praying, hoping modern medicine would bring back the funny, cheerful brother I used to follow around and fight with. As I began middle school, Mr. Erwin became my new principal. We’d fist-bump in the halls and reminisce about the two weeks I spent living with them, but beneath our casual conversations, a thinly-veiled worry lingered between us.

For the next two years, I was caught in a cycle of helplessness as my brother’s cancer progressed. Whether making egg fried rice between online classes or adjusting Charles in bed, I did whatever small things I could, knowing they would make little difference. Despite treatments at Cincinnati Children’s, Johns Hopkins, and Alabama Children’s, Charles’s smile faded away on November 6, 2020. For my brother, science had come up short.

Before Charles's illness, I was the kid who always had the answers in science class, the one who believed that every problem could be untangled with enough knowledge. The year he passed, I found myself sitting through science classes, each course just another credit. It wasn’t until AP Chemistry in sophomore year that a spark reignited within me. The logical structure of chemical reactions offered a sense of clarity and control that I desperately needed. Weekends spent tinkering with galvanic cells and scouring Wikipedia articles led to creating meme-infused flashcards for my class. As I helped my friends understand complex theories, I felt useful again. Running the “Chemistry Makes Scents” demo at McWane Science Center, I watched kids’ expressions shift from confusion to astonishment as I taught them about chirality. Science isn’t just about equations or experiments—it’s about the impact I make on others.

Wanting to engage with science in a way that affects real people, I sent out dozens of cold emails to labs. However, I was quickly tempered by the reality of research. If McWane’s programmed labs were a volcanic eruption at a middle school science fair, real-life experiments in my molecular cardiology lab were Mount Vesuvius. Instead of a grad student, Dr. Zhou, a monk-like professor who always answered my questions with her own, introduced me to the best practices of the lab. After numerous failed experiments and stacks of marked-up manuscripts, I realized that textbook knowledge wasn’t enough. Late-night Slack messages to Dr. Zhou after yet another failed experiment became routine. I pestered the eternally-busy postdoctoral scholar Anteneh until he taught me how to effectively induce a fibroblast into a cardiomyocyte. Gradually, the muscle structures in my reprogrammed fibroblasts revealed their breathtaking beauty under the confocal microscope, and soon enough, experiments became drafts that became published scientific knowledge.

It was evident that science faced an insurmountable challenge in eliminating my brother’s cancerous cells without harming his brain tissue. But now, designing experiments to answer unsolved questions, I feel empowered instead of helpless in the face of setbacks. I have moved from the passenger seat to the driver’s seat, optimistic that the fates of kids like my brother will change in the near future—despite my rudimentary driving skills. The loss of my brother has given me an unshakable conviction to continue pushing the boundaries of science and conquer deadly diseases.

For nearly two years, I’ve spent over 1000 hours researching how to heal the injured heart. Every other day, as I peer into the microscope to examine scar cells transforming into cardiac muscle, I see a reflection of my own journey—scarred, but healing, and ready to pump life back into my community, or by supporting the journeys of others whose problems are not yet untangled, as the Erwins once did for me.

The pants thief struck again.

Frantically foraging around my house, I finally uncovered the culprit: my small closet, sheltering lost pants in its abyss. Reorganizing this newly indicted criminal, I observed my pants repeatedly sliding off the hanger and vanishing from my usual line of sight—a critical flaw in my closet’s functionality. My routine "hang-it-over" method had failed me.

My pants, bunched up and hanging low in my closet, often slid to one side of the hanger due to an imbalance in weight, making them hard to find. I asked my mom to buy clip hangers (since I saw them used in stores), but with an abundance of regular hangers available, she refused.

Searching "How to hang pants,” I scoured YouTube for a solution, but my attempts were met with failure. The popular Savile Row fold didn’t work for me, presenting the same issues as my routine method. With the "wrap-over-hanger" method, the pants lay above the hanger like a scarf, but the flimsy plastic hangers couldn’t support the weight of my heavy cargo pants. Within a week, a few hanger tops snapped off. My closet became a crime scene with the pants thief outsmarting my every move. After hours of experimentation, I realized I needed a better, more personalized approach.

Delving into the world of hangers, I discovered more varieties than I ever imagined from velvet to metal and triangle to rectangle. Similarly to how I used pros and cons lists to choose the best gym to attend, I made a tier list ranking the best types of hangers.

Through experimenting, I deconstructed plastic hangers, bending and taping pieces to create various shapes. By repurposing leftover metal wire from my armature sculpture, I crafted a right-trapezoid-shaped hanger and reinforced it by weaving a second wire around the first. With a spiral-textured design, this hanger successfully prevented pants from sliding off. Merging the 'wrap-over-hanger' method with my trapezoid creation to elevate the pants into my line of sight, I achieved a personalized, efficient solution, arresting the pants thief once and for all. Despite the struggle, designing taught me patience. To find the perfect solution, I needed to embrace a cycle of trial and error, learning from each attempt. This approach has not only become integral to my creative process but also to navigating new hobbies and experiences. Just as I had woven wire to create the perfect hanger, I soon found myself weaving a different type of creation—this time with colorful threads.

Bracelet-making, like my hanger project, demanded its own cycle of trial and error. The process mirrored my earlier challenge: hours of experimentation and failed attempts. Similar to how I had deconstructed hangers, I now unraveled and retied knots from six or more different-colored strings. For every successful bracelet, three ended up in the trash. Yet, each failure paved the way for better results, until my hands and the thread harmonized.

By gifting these bracelets to my friends and hosting informal bracelet-making workshops, I tied bonds through these colorful strings. Before, I underestimated the value of handmade gifts (Amazon gift cards were my thoughtless go-to present), but witnessing my friends' appreciation for my custom-tailored patterns made every hour of struggle worth it. Eager to connect with more people, I started sharing my creations with the online bracelet-making community and even developed my own designs and templates, including whimsical ones like a “Perry the Platypus” pattern. Seeing others post photos of their creations using my templates brought me immense joy. My closet no longer burdened my morning routine as I had vanquished the pants thief but fueled my desire to connect through design. Whether it’s designing my school’s yearbook cover, a website for repurposing used tennis balls, or a deck of playing cards by replacing the standard Bicycle designs with Chinese lanterns and dragons, I build connections with others and bridge my diverse interests through design. By bringing my imagination to life, I can share my creations and extend my passion to others—a pursuit I plan to continue in college.

If I was asked to describe my life these past few years, I can best describe it as a fruit basket. Full of good and bad fruits, sweet and sour fruits, and some fruits you have to cut inside to see the true colors of them. The fruits in my basket can be best known as everything that changed in my high school years.

For my first 2 years of high school I had many of the fruits I enjoyed the most. The fruit that when you take the first bite of juice drips down your chin and you know that you are going to enjoy it. My fruit basket stayed like that for all of freshman and sophomore year and they were the best fruits that I have ever tasted.

While I entered my junior year of high school, those sweet and juicy fruits that I always enjoyed started to change and become sour. While many of the fruits came sour I also stumbled upon many fruits that I wouldn't know if they would be sweet and sour and their colors were hidden inside. I came to the realization that my fruit bowl didn't include anymore of my favorite fruits and it had forever changed.

My friendships in junior year of high school can best be described as sour and hidden. Many of my friends became people I didn't even recognize anymore. It took my 2 years of being friends with them to finally notice their true colors, much like a watermelon or cantaloupe that the colors inside are hidden until you cut them open to reveal those colors.

When my fruit bowl began filling up with these sour and hidden fruits, I began to not wanna eat them anymore. I didn't want to touch another piece of fruit again no matter if it was sweet or sour. I knew exactly how they tasted and how I would never enjoy them. My fruit bowl was forever changed from that point moving forward...

I began to get very tired of these fruits and wanted a change. I was tired of not having the fruits I knew that I once loved at one point. But I came to the realization that the fruits that I once loved had forever changed and went from sweet to sour.
