Instead of sticking to the same fruit I knew and loved, it was time for me to adventure with new fruits and go back to old fruits that I loved as a child and once forgot about in my teenage years.

While my fruit bowl began to look different, it changed for the better and taught me life lessons. Sometimes in life the fruits you once loved will taste much different than they once did. I learned that no matter what you do, you are going to acquire many sour fruits and will have to try many different types of fruits you never thought you would, no matter the stories of good or bad you once heard of them. You have to give every single fruit a chance.

My fruit bowl is changing every day and I now know to not get caught up with all of those sour fruits again as they impacted my life in a way that I never saw coming and changed my overall impression of many fruits in my basket.

The window was open, and a slight breeze flowed through the hot kitchen. I had milk boiling in my favourite pan, steeping tea leaves. I added the tea masala and ginger as the milk turned darker brown. When the leaves had steeped enough, I transferred the tea to my Batman mug and mixed in some sugar and turmeric honey. When I finally sipped the tea, I was elated: the tea was exceptional, a testament to my months of toiling.

I only used three ingredients - tea leaves, milk, and sugar - during my first few attempts. I was convinced that mastering these basics would be enough, much like how I viewed my own endeavors. Fourteen years of dancing had left me unwilling to try anything new; although I loved to dance, the routine of practicing made my schedule mundane. As I spent many afternoons drinking tolerable tea because I did not want to risk ruining its mediocre taste with new ingredients, I spent many days with the same mediocre routine of dancing and studying.

One afternoon, I was rifling through the cupboards to find the tea leaves jar when I came across a small bottle labeled “tea masala.” It was a blend of spices—cardamom, cinnamon, and nutmeg. I was initially hesitant about whether or not to sprinkle it in, but listening to “Liza” by the Sonny Stitt Quartet led me to experiment with the spices as the quartet experimented with their notes.

When I sampled the tea, I was struck by an acute realization: I had to broaden my horizons. My unwillingness to take on new opportunities had made my days uninspiring, much like the tea. I had missed out on different opportunities by refusing to try new hobbies or classes out of the belief that they would definitely not be my cup of tea.

So, inspired by my success with the masala, I also decided to add spice to my schedule: I picked up violin lessons. Learning to play complex pieces on violin made me much more patient than before. I struggled with playing “Clair de Lune” but the journey through it gave me a new understanding of how to allow myself to make mistakes and work through them.

I knew the ginger would complement the spices well, so I decided to mix in some. As I added it to my tea, I added my own ginger to my days by volunteering at a hospital. Initially, I was hesitant because I wasn’t willing to write off my lazy Sunday mornings as a commitment. When I trained for the emergency department, however, one comment from my supervisor shifted my perspective: “I don’t have to train you; I get to train you.” It made me view new challenges as opportunities rather than obligations. Volunteering in the ER allowed me to view the patients’ resilience and patience despite their struggles, inspiring me to adopt a more stoic mindset in the face of problems.

Still not completely satisfied, I added turmeric honey. The honey waltzed beautifully with the other ingredients, symbolizing my research project. The photos I had to take for that project showed me different issues that members in my community struggled with, driving me to investigate one of them so that I could help my peers. The project taught me empathy by putting me in others’ shoes and making me determined to find a solution for their problems through contemporary research.

As my tea transformed from a single note to a symphony of flavors, my days became much richer, and my personality improved drastically. Each ingredient provided a new layer of complexity: the masala gave open-mindedness, the ginger brought forth appreciation, and the honey infused empathy. Now, when I drink my tea while listening to “The Lamp is Low,” I reminisce how each ingredient came together perfectly to create the finest cup of tea and a much better version of myself.

The pre-dawn calm was broken by the sound of roosters crowing, a sharp contrast to the dissonant hum of Los Angeles traffic to which I had been accustomed. As I stood on the gravelly road of Sonsonate, El Salvador, I felt the weight of my circumstances settle heavily on my shoulders. The outline of the Izalco volcano menaced in the distance, symbolizing the beauty and ambivalence I felt about my life up until that point. At the age of twenty-one, I had been forced to self-deport from the United States due to a legal loophole surrounding the visa I had been on since the age of two, leaving behind the only life I had ever known, made to go to a land both unknown yet familiar to me.

For the first time in my life, I found myself alone in a completely foreign country, fighting to survive. Finding a steady job proved to be a challenge, but eventually, I found a job harvesting fruit and caring for cattle in the mountains of Sonsonate. The irony hit me like a truck: in the country where I had lived all my life, my visa prevented me from working, yet in a land that felt foreign to me, I was allowed to work simply because I was born there.

Far from the urban jungles of California, El Salvador welcomed me with its vibrant and lush scenery. I rose with the sun, whose golden radiance warmed the crop fields every morning. The earthy aroma of dirt permeated the air along with the promise of harvest. The scratchy soursop fruit that prickled my fingertips while I toiled as a ranch hand connected me unexpectedly to the ground of my ancestors. For over three years, this daily habit became my pattern, engulfing me in a culture from which I had long sought to separate myself.

However, my forced departure was anything but perfect. Despite being my mother tongue, Spanish felt alien to me and brought up memories of the identity dilemma that had long plagued me. I felt caught in an existential limbo defined by immigration laws and legal loopholes, neither entirely Salvadoran nor totally American. I was expelled from the nation I had lived in my whole life and returned to my birthplace, making me feel as if I truly didn’t belong anywhere.

Yet, the fields of Sonsonate became my classroom, teaching me resilience and patience, virtues that textbooks in Los Angeles had never imparted. Every fruit I collected served as a silent protest against the forced relocation I had experienced and a monument to my adaptation.

I was eighteen years old, just out of high school, and I had no idea what the future had in store before this forced departure. My education was unexpectedly cut short, leaving me disoriented and disengaged from my goals. I felt like I was reclaiming a part of myself when I re-enrolled at Santa Monica College after moving back to the United States, this time on a student visa. The institution became my haven, bringing me back to my family and giving me a second opportunity to follow my aspirations with a fresh perspective.

Spending time in El Salvador changed my perspective. It sparked an interest in advocacy, especially for immigrant groups navigating the tricky waters of legality and identity. At Santa Monica College, I turned my experiences into advocacy aimed at influencing public policy and helping others in similar circumstances. The desire to be the catalyst to make this change drives me as I try to keep on learning and have a significant influence.

What I have discovered in the Santa Monica College classrooms and on the Salvadoran fields inspires me to write the next chapter. With each step forward, my goal is to transform obstacles into opportunities so that no one else has to endure the burden of displacement that I once did.

As the doors to Target open, I head up the escalator and round the corner. My eyes are greeted with many words:

Dogs. Birthday. Get Well.

My fingers glide between the many cards in front of me. Some are blank; others are full. Some even sing. One catches my eye – its design is simplistic, and its inside is bare. Its face speaks three words: Happy Father’s Day.

***

I have done this before, and today seems no different. I grab my pens and once-clear colored pencil box and begin by echoing the card’s words, careful not to tarnish the card’s frail composition. Dear Dad, Happy Father’s Day.

Then, as my words dig faster and deeper into the card, I reminisce about the year past: our Korea trip that introduced me to the world beyond our small island; his rice cake soup that always wrapped my tummy in a warm embrace; the late k-drama nights with popcorn and furikake. Thank you, Dad.

Finally, I signed. Love, Your Son, Jeremy.

Basketball. Airplane. Easy to draw Korean soup. After “drawing” everything that could represent my words (i.e. placing my phone under and tracing the screenshots line for line), a blank space in the corner still stared back. But after stuffing it with a simple face made of a pair of glasses and a mustache, I was finally finished.

I closed my eyes peacefully as Mom drove me to Dad’s house.

***

The next morning, I sneak downstairs and scream, “Happy Father’s Day!”

“Thanks, Jem!” he says. “You’re finally up!”

I run to my backpack and reveal my masterpiece. “Ja jan!” Opening the card, his eyes travel up and down, my heart following the same trajectory. Finally, he speaks. “Jeremy, what’s this?” he says, pointing to a corner of the card.

“Oh, that?” I say. “I didn’t know what to draw, so I searched up Father’s Day images and that popped up.”

He closes his eyes along with the card. “Jeremy, what does Father’s Day mean to you?”

***

Nine hours later, Mom picks me up after dinner. I still don’t understand. I had perfected my craft for nearly a decade. And yet, maybe that was exactly why. What had once been a token of gratitude became an apathetic chore. I had forgotten the meaning behind my actions, and all that was left was a dull husk of what once was. It was as plain to see as a face made of a pair of glasses and a mustache. I crumple into a ball. I squeeze harder. A dampness envelops my eyes. I realize it’s not what I did: it’s what I did not do. I wince. But not because of regret. Although guilt pervades my heart, the desire to never feel this pain ever again courses throughout me and I am filled with a sense of reinvigorated purpose: To do everything I can wholeheartedly. I learned back then that halfheartedness is plain to see. But now I know that wholehearted, burning passion outshines it. For when I look back on the life I have drawn, I don’t see an emotionless face: I see faces screaming “Bravo!” and applauding me in standing ovation after performing Sarasate’s Zigeunerweisen; I see the roaring faces of teammates cheering me on to the finish of a cross country championship 5k; I see the face of a friend cracking a smile for the first time that day.

That is the kind of future I intend to draw.

“All you want to do is play basketball!” My dad shouts.

Storming away, I sit in my shower, legs wrapped in my arms, thankful that the water blocks out my bawling.

I’ve played piano since I was five. Placing in international competitions at a young age, my parents encouraged me to dedicate myself to piano, and I embraced it. That is, until the 6th grade, when my classmates found out.

My tablemates and I were Googling each others’ names. Everyone started laughing when a quick search of my name yielded a handful of my piano videos on YouTube and pictures of me in jacketless tuxedos suited for competitions. They were bewildered as to why the athletic boy they thought they knew played classical piano. My cheeks flushed. I never wanted to play piano again. I wanted to be an NBA player.

When I started playing piano, I woke the whole house up from playing before the sun rose. Now I stayed half an hour after practice to get shots up. I realized when I start new activities, I commit myself to them completely for short periods of time. But that fresh feeling of newly found love doesn’t last forever, especially when challenges, like classmates’ judgment, get in the way. I had to find a way to sustain an activity, preserving my interest without burning out.

Perhaps that activity was piano. In the following months, I brought myself to the keyboard slowly—one hour at a time. Yet I found myself blanking out playing with no real purpose.

I needed a cause, a reason to do something every day and a goal to work towards. I thought about my mother driving me an hour from school to piano then back for basketball practice and my father paying for my piano lessons. Seeing their sacrifice, I made them my cause. Practicing piano, I was able to remain consistent since I had a clear goal in mind. Unexpectedly, I found myself immersed in the unique style of impressionist music while playing Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse. I built up to practicing for two hours everyday again, making sure to give myself the freedom to play catchy pop music songs from the radio and even take a few days off; finding ways to de-stress allowed me to balance piano even as my schedule became tighter with AP tests and open gyms. The balance allowed me to joke around with my teammates at the gym and still feel energized to practice half of a piece afterwards.

Standing in the shower a few months later, I thought back to the surprised reactions my online photos garnered from classmates. My peers were right to laugh, because it was surprising – I am a basketball player, but I am also a pianist. Although an unlikely combination, playing piano and basketball help me orchestrate my basketball skill set, with piano helping me stay in tune by being patient and giving myself time to develop.

Excelling at something means embracing it. While the joy of a newfound hobby fades, when I stuck with something, I discovered a new type of joy developed: being able to work closely with peers that inspired me with their passion. People at school would never see the laughter from trying out unorthodox voicings with my string players during our practice sessions, but I don’t need to be what they expect me to be.

Like me, millions of other pianists struggle to have structure in practice sessions. Knowing my fascination in classical music, machine learning, and problem-solving, I want to make it my mission to create something to help people improve their skills each session. My fascination will propel me to develop new dimensions of my identity, pulling me in even further directions. I celebrate this, knowing I can have multiple at once and knowing taking breaks is part of the process. When I need a break, I’ll go back to playing L’Isle Joyeuse (maybe for my roommates this time) or going to the court to play pickup basketball.

It was 5:00 PM and class for the boys in my town had just ended. As the lights went out, we entered our classroom to start our day under the cover of darkness. The electricity had been suspended and the gray old fan, hung silently on the wall, not to be turned on. What a hot day! Like always, the class with its malodorous atmosphere was unbearable, but we were used to it. That day, we started class with half seated in broken chairs to continue our lesson. I began by distributing the 21st century skills sheet to all twenty girls in attendance. I asked everyone to ponder of a time when one of these skills helped them. They thought for a few minutes and then suddenly, Maryam raised her hand and said “collaboration…my friend, Hamida, was absent and I did her assignments last week and vice versa,” All laughed heartily!! I glanced at Maryam and shook my left eyebrow, it was indeed a good response, I said. While everyone was busy sharing their experiences, my eyes stared at the gate as if I was waiting for someone. In fact, I was afraid of the Taliban who might come to check on the schools, what would I say if they came? Exactly, a few weeks ago, they had banned all the informal courses beside of the school and university education for girls older than 13. For the first time, we were in the small class measuring four by three meters and I worked with each of the twenty girls individually. I felt incredibly emotional, I was on the verge of tears after understanding some of the girls’ families were demanding that they get married. Shaken and moved by this news, I tried to inspire them get an education by any means possible, whether online or offline while I promised to cover their internet fees and assured them of having all my help. So far, we come to the class and I help them not only learn English but strive to assist them to learn self-worth and boost skills. Albeit I am afraid, we have done great things so far and attained extraordinary achievements inspiring me to continue this educational quest. Despite the challenges and setbacks due to lots of restrictions, we have spent a long period of time together learning from each other through many workshops, academic courses, public speaking, debate competitions, cultural events, virtual information by international friends, and working on the scholarship applications for Afghan girls. The day I was informed that six of those twenty girls, which later grew to 27, had been shortlisted in UWC Scholarships, I was super excited and could not believe our success. We are nothing more than a family, I might have these memories alive forever: that sang songs, played hopscotch and watched movie, on Thursdays games. Sometimes we struggled with troubles; for instance, none of these girls had utilized platforms for an online education, particularly, even after plenty of mock sessions, they made errors, but after a workshop with Dr. Lee-Ann Laffey from United State through Zoom App they became super motivated and invigorated to connect to the world of virtual education. Today, I am more than honored to could help these girls from depressions, isolations and frustrations, particularly, seeing three of these dynamic girls teaching basic English for small kids is a humongous success for me. All of the 27 girls no longer ask me a ton of questions, because they possess the capability to work them out on their own. I feel thrilled that they are long to sign up for online summer schools, workshops and short courses all on their own compared to the past when they did not even know how to use Gmail. To be honest, these girls taught me how to stand up against difficulties and how to overcome the challenges confronting in my life.

I was an adventurous mountaineer, determined to reach my final destination: the bathroom counter. I was on the hunt for a strange treasure, to say the least. Rather than the traditional trove of ancient artifacts and precious jewels, I was searching for something far more valuable: the instruction labels glued along the sides of every tube and bottle on the cluttered countertop.

I sought out my treasure with great determination, pudgy legs flailing beneath me as I scrambled onto the counter with the grace of a bullheaded six-year-old, but to me, they felt like the most powerful objects in the world. Every time I read one of those elusive labels, I was in awe at the critical information they divulged: who knew putting on sunscreen could be so very complex? I was intent on knowing the instructions for everything, filled with the confidence that I could tackle anything so long as I had a trusty set of instructions by my side.

But, in time, I came to recognize that there weren’t cut-and-dry instructions for everything in life. That realization hit me in the most unexpected of places: mathematics. I had returned to school one morning with a neatly written solution to the Algebra I homework, thrilled at my success after wrestling with it for almost the entire evening. I felt certain that I had solved the problem exactly as intended, only for my teacher to furrow his brows the moment he started reading my solution.

I had never seen him look so confused before, and already, I was sinking into my seat from the humiliation. But then he grinned, tilting his head in amusement as he declared: “I don’t know how, but you’ve thought of a completely different solution—fascinating!” He then excitedly displayed my solution to a room full of onlooking students, gesturing wildly as he spoke. For the first time, I had unwittingly broken free from the instructions I so loved to follow.

Mathematics gave me the confidence to venture into life without the need for instructions at every corner. For if there could be more than one right answer in a field bound by such strict axioms—and after a grueling but fascinating term of set theory, I would certainly know—there was no reason for me to enforce any other arbitrary boundaries on my life.

Of course, instructions are still useful at times. I could not have discovered so many obscure mathematical theorems without the aid of my handy textbooks or learned to run my school's mathematics contest without the guidance of those who came before me. But even with those instructions, I no longer feel bound to them. Whether by making my own discoveries through original research in statistical redistricting simulations or simply adjusting our Math Club training program to better fit the needs of our team, I feel confident in the knowledge that I can simultaneously learn from and contribute to the instructions of those who came before me, too.

And even when there exist no instructions for the journey I am embarking on, I have made uncountable changes to the way I confront life’s uncertainties. From starting weightlifting with zero knowledge of the sport whatsoever to writing journalism articles about subjects I had been too uncertain to confront before and, later, founding my own publication to spread that initiative amongst more students, I have learned to thrive in that feeling of not quite knowing.

Over the years, I have recognized that I can only truly grow by throwing myself into situations where I do not know the answers. By letting go of the constant need for instructions, I no longer fear the unknown, but embrace the chance for me to write instructions of my own.

**Essay:**

My strongest passion has always been football. I’ve loved the game since I was seven, when football immersed itself in my life. I’m a Cowboys fan, and I’ve maintained that fandom for a decade despite their bitter rivalry with the main NFL team in my area. Despite not expressing much independence in elementary school, I truly came into my own when playing or watching football. It makes me my own person, emphasizing my differences and separating me from my cookie cutter surroundings. My Cowboys fandom has remained by my side through countless days and nights as I cheer for them regardless of situation. This dedication carries over to academics, as I persevere through setbacks with relentless studying instead of dropping the class. Football expresses my loyal nature, sticking with the Cowboys despite playoff failures. I never ditch those whom I’m loyal to and I work through tough times instead of giving up. Further displaying my passion, I never ignore chances to talk football. Even when I had to go into the administrative office to discuss an unrelated situation where my ability to safely ride the bus home was at risk, I talked football with the Vice Principal. One thing led to another and he recommended me to the head coach at my high school. This led to me becoming the team’s lead manager, subsequently provoking a major shift in my identity. Before, I was quiet and introverted in school. I had few friends and no idea where I wanted to go in life. Even after a year of high school, I felt out of place. However, upon joining the football team, I knew I belonged. Football created a safe haven for me to escape the anxious moments of school. I felt comfortable talking to the players and coaches and bonded with them over lunches and greetings in the halls. I even began flourishing in other social situations, participating in classes more frequently than ever. I wouldn’t have unearthed this side of myself without football. I found passionate dedication within myself as I attended every practice and game possible, whether they started at 6 AM or 3 PM, and stayed until 10 PM for each game so that I could film for the team. I gleefully stepped into any necessary role, including helping with equipment, water, the medkit, filming, and even tutoring. That was when I realized that I desired a career in football and to work with a football program at college. I’ve also recently volunteered with the University of Maryland’s equipment management team, doing laundry, sorting equipment into shelves, and operating chains at practices. My time there was fulfilling, reinforcing my desire to pursue football. Even though I was in a college equipment room, I felt like I belonged and was happy. My interest in football gave me a concrete idea of what I want in a career, even inspiring my secondary career interest, statistics. I searched for numbers and data so I could understand football to a greater degree, giving me a lasting intrigue regarding statistics. I just took a summer program on statistics run by the University of Pennsylvania which affirmed my interest in the subject. I’m interested in learning more about statistics at the college level as well. Loving football inspired me to devote my time to it; I’m excited to continue expanding my interest in the game. Football also introduced me to the importance of work behind the scenes to success, first in my role as a high school manager and then as a volunteer at the college level. Without clean laundry, well-conditioned equipment, and effectively spotting the football, practices would be a sweaty, jumbled nightmare. Similarly with academics, without studying and devotion one can’t get the most out of classes. Football has become much more than an interest to me, changing my personality for the better and giving me a blueprint for success.

Gusteau would be proud. Children often daydream about having superpowers: superhuman strength, teleportation, or telepathy. I don’t covet those types of comic book attributes. Instead, I have a true superpower that’s not limited to the pages of comics. In the great tradition of Bobby Flay and Anthony Bourdain, I can cook! I take pride in the fact that I don’t have to rely on my mother for my next meal. From a young age, I’ve loved to combine ingredients into delicious recipes. And I’m not talking about cup ramen or the kimchi fried rice that many of my friends sometimes make for themselves after school (That said, I can put together a mean interpretation using old-school kimchi, spam, nori, tuna, and a fried egg). Instead, on any given Saturday afternoon, you can find me recreating some of the appetizing recipes that I saw in my favorite movies, like the confit byaldi iteration of “the Peasant dish” that Remi prepares in “Ratatouille,” or the four-cheese grilled cheese sandwich that Jon Favreau’s character in “Chef” makes for his son. Cooking has introduced me to a variety of cultures from around the world without me ever having to set foot on foreign soil. My culinary exploits have taken me to Mexico, with beef burritos accompanied by homemade guacamole and salsa, to Japan, with pork tonkatsu and curry with croquettes, and to India, where I dabbled in palak paneer with basmati rice. I get to bring these cultures home and share them with my family over hearty meals, prompting conversations about the ingredients and other traditions. There’s something truly magical about making and sharing delicious food that can transcend language and cultural barriers. The first major test of my superpower was making crème brûlée, a French dessert that I first perfected in the 7th grade. Through rigorous trial and error of making multiple batches where the egg custard didn’t set just right or the caramel top didn’t crack when hit with a metal spoon in just the right way, I finally made a recipe that I was proud of. Family members and friends who tried the dessert were equally wowed. As I honed my superpower into my teenage years, I knew I was not without my kryptonite. As a freshman, I could barely complete factoring algebra questions while my peers seemed to be able to breeze through whatever formula was on the quiz on any given day. I was constantly overweight in middle school, with over 40% body fat, and no matter how much time I spent in the gym, I couldn’t seem to lose the blubber. I failed to make the school basketball team my first three years of high school, despite the hundreds of hours that I spent getting shots up in the gym; perhaps it was my height, my below-average vertical, or my lack of cardio that kept me out of my coach’s eyes. In a society like Korea, which places utmost value on visible achievements like academics, appearance, and sports, I almost always felt inadequate. Thankfully, cooking was my safe haven from this torment. Cooking gave me a sense of assurance—my dishes would be appreciated for their creativity and taste. I wouldn’t be judged by an arbitrary performance metric, like how I did on a surprise quiz in my chemistry class. Cooking was such a confidence booster because I could create something purely from my own personal trials and judgment. That freedom inspired a mentality that continues to catalyze my personal growth in so many different areas, such as debate, journalism, and academics. In the movie “Ratatouille,” perhaps Chef Gusteau was thinking of me when he said that “anyone can cook.” Regardless, this ability transformed a feeble little boy into a superhero in the eyes of his family and friends. But more importantly, it helped me realize that creativity and confidence will always be the primary ingredients for my success.

The sound of fate clattering against the hardwood floor penetrates the air. A few seconds later, fate rolls to a stop. Silence. I hold my breath.

“5 and 3, so 8.”

My dad cheers with excitement — I can’t help but smile. My mom groans as her civilization’s supply drought continues. I offer her some of my bricks and she leans over to give me a loving hug.

***

Growing up in Singapore, I remember spending Saturdays with my uncle at the zoo, marveling at giant pandas and laughing at his howler monkey imitation. Meals with my aunt felt special too — she would occasionally leave the bank early to join in with my palak paneer obsession.

When I moved to New Jersey in 2016, my ability to spend time with relatives was impeded by nineteen hours of cramped seats and the occasional jolt of turbulence. Separated from the familiar faces of my previous home, I turned to the internet for a solution.

I dove into media about combating isolation and soon found an article, “12 Ways To Beat Loneliness,” praising the benefits of playing games and maintaining online contact with family. Motivated, I spent hours after school searching for the perfect virtual activity until I found Colonist.io, an online Settlers of Catan platform. The game was an instant hit, with its endless strategies, element of chance, and ever-evolving nature making everyone feel included, regardless of age.

My aunt’s lethargic playstyle earned her the title “World’s Slowest Player” and prompted us to set a fifteen-minute timer for her turns! “Diiinnngggg!” The laughter following the timer’s ring while she was still deciding her move always lifted my spirits. Meanwhile, my uncle’s tendency to hoard resources often led to uproarious clashes with the supply-stealing robber. Joking with my uncle, even if only on a video call, filled me with the sense of warmth I remembered so fondly from our Saturday trips.

It was moments like these that etched themselves into the family lore, making the oceans between us seem a little smaller.

The Catan sessions were the highlight of my week, but as I transitioned into high school, balancing both school and sports with the twelve-hour time difference led to every week becoming once a month. The sense of separation started to resurface, but hours of online Catan had taught me the importance of creating and maintaining relationships with supportive role models, inspiring me to seek out people who could fill the gaps left by my older relatives.

My first experience with Devin, my swim instructor, was marked by water up my nose and erratic splashing; his efforts to corral my abysmal butterfly technique were in vain. But as my form improved with every lesson, I discovered our shared passion for mangoes, compelling me to save a few from every box to share.

Over time, Devin became a close family friend, frequently joining my dad and me on lighthearted runs and workouts. He even played Catan with us sometimes, replicating a sense of home I hadn’t felt since my days in Singapore.

***

As I reflect on my previous constructions, I study the playing field — littered with roads stretching across plains and curving around mountains, each hex tile bringing me nearer to the people I hold close. This world, residing in a six-inch device in my pocket, will always be ready to blossom anywhere with a stable internet connection.

In college, I’m eager to connect with diverse individuals, embracing their unique playing styles with an open mind and enthusiasm for collaboration. And my journey in higher education, like a Catan board, will be full of challenges and opportunities for innovation, whether I'm modeling the orbit of asteroids or delving into the atomic intricacies of semiconductors. With the same collaborative spirit and adaptability from my family game nights, I’ll be ready to navigate the landscape of my college journey, regardless of how the dice roll.

I rapidly scrolled through the answers on the Quora webpage and found an answer that helped. “Finally, I’ll be able to read this over and go to bed,” I thought. I had been studying for hours now and felt my eyes begin fluttering shut as I struggled to maintain consciousness. I started reading a long explanation about why there is a negative sign in the “work done by conservative force” formula, jotting things down in my notebook as I glanced back up at the screen.

Right below it, however, something caught my eye. It was an answer to a related question discussing how the universe would end. Out of a sense of morbid curiosity, I clicked ‘read more.’ My heart sank as I read the entire description about how all life in the universe would slowly, painfully end.

Obviously, this put me in a rut. I had lived my entire life under the assumption that what I do has value because it might be remembered by those that come after me, and this would lead to some sense of ‘immortality’. This had informed some of the projects I had pursued earlier in grade 9 and 10 like Nocrastination, my gamification research paper, etc. which were meant to be memorable for journal acceptances or placing highly in competitions. But after reading this answer I realised that assumption was false. Eventually, I would be forgotten because those that remember me would die. Although we may remember greats from a few centuries ago like Galileo, Archimedes, etc, we’ve still forgotten about many ancient civilisations and, thus, they are dead to us both physically and in memory. I realised that my work would suffer the same fate too, and this caused me to question why I was doing anything. For the first time, I had to genuinely confront my mortality. I solved this problem as I solve many problems in life: by learning.

At the time, I was using the “Crash Course: Physics” series on YouTube to study. I felt like concepts from philosophy — a discipline focused on answering the kind of fundamental questions I had started asking myself about my existence and purpose — could help mitigate my existential dread, so I turned to the sister series “Crash Course: Philosophy” and binged the entire course in one day. A few ideas deeply resonated with me.

Existentialism made me realise that we have absolute freedom to do what we want to with our lives and live authentically to our values because, in the long term, no one would care anyway. This led me to give up any of the engagements I had that I was doing just for the sake of college applications and did not genuinely believe in — including volunteering and debate — and instead focus on what I really loved, which was programming.

With utilitarianism, the idea that the moral correctness of an action can be measured through how much happiness it produces for how many people, I realised what I should actually strive to do: help people. This was not just born out of a selfish desire to be immortal, but instead by a redefinition of my moral compass. As a result, I would later focus on getting the app I created in junior year, LessonGPT, to teachers who would actually find it useful in reducing their workload and overwhelm rather than just having impressive competition placements.

Combining the idea of utilitarianism and non-human animals, I turned into a vegetarian and stopped eating meat.

And the concept of ‘eudaimonia’ — a “life spent well” where one is constantly pushing themselves and trying to improve — led me to challenge myself by joining the IB diploma programme and partaking in an extremely challenging course on quantum computation by CCIR in junior year. Oddly enough, a simple physics formula led me to rethink how I look at the world.

Captain Ahab had Moby Dick, Don Quixote had his windmills, and even Harry Potter had Voldemort. For me, I have the distinct privilege of having one Mr. Rudolf Clausius as my foil. It is not my life’s work to defeat Mr. Clausius mind you but it is my Sisyphean struggle against his discovery; the 2nd law of thermodynamics and its proclamation about entropy and systems progressing to disorder that is my life’s calling. Battling against an immutable planetary law, creating order, and deriving a solution in a universe of unlimited possibilities drives me. Ever since I can remember, I have enjoyed transforming an entropic mess of thousands of pieces of cut cardboard into a beautiful picture. The larger the jigsaw puzzle the greater the sense of triumph after persevering for hours to finally find the dreaded “missing piece.”

As I grew older, puzzles helped me to make sense of the mysteries of the world around me. One of my passions, coding, is like linking pieces of a jigsaw puzzle together. Cooking is a challenge in finding the right combination of raw ingredients to optimize flavor. Working with people on a Physics project or leading a Cyberpatriots team are all brain teasers in finding the optimal way for working cohesively for our common success.

Playing doubles on the high school varsity tennis team provided one of the most complex conundrums to solve. Most see a physically demanding sport where hand-eye coordination and physical conditioning are paramount. The game that I play prizes fast thinking, creative problem solving and most importantly, a multidisciplinary thought process. While my body is moving fast on the court, my mind speeds even faster. Questions race through my mind like a whirling fan on my home-built computer during a match. What are my opponent's best shots? Which of my shots do they struggle with? How do I take away my opponents’ biggest weapon? How can I set up my teammate for success? As each point goes by, my mind formulates a plan and through trial, I am searching for the “missing piece” to ultimately gain the advantage.

Knowing the rules of tennis will allow you to play the game. Knowing and ultimately applying Physics and Geometry will allow you to be successful. Understanding the moment arc of a tennis swing and the geometry of a tennis court to optimize coverage of the open space are keys to victory in the tennis puzzle. Also vital in tennis and life’s other puzzles are simplicity and curiosity. Oftentimes, simplicity wins. The most consistent stroke in tennis is the one that is most easily repeated and often the one that has the least wasted movement. The simplest game plan is the easiest to actually execute on the court. Following my innate curiosity has led me to seek knowledge whether it is in a book, video lesson, or speaking with coaches or other players, for a deeper understanding. The more knowledge that I have, the more options I have to find an optimal path to victory.

Entropy is all around us. I know that I will lose to Mr. Clausius and his 2nd Law much more often than I win. Finding a solution to create order drives me. My life’s calling, and one that I plan to further develop the necessary skills for in college, is to solve a puzzle of a lifetime; discovering the next big scientific breakthrough to help humanity. Whether it is climate change, pollution, clean water, or how to properly harness AI, these massive puzzles will require a multidisciplinary, creative puzzle-solving approach to tackle. In college, I will bring my sense of framing the world into puzzles, share my entropic perspectives, learn from others, and just as importantly, bring the joy and optimism that comes from seeing a world of puzzles. After all, puzzles, no matter the difficulty or the challenge, were created for fun.

Whiteboards weren’t something I used to get excited about. And that’s because I’ve never had a reason to do so. Until my junior year, hanging on my classroom’s wall was a 23’’ wall stain some dared to call a whiteboard. It was so small that you had to clean it up thrice to solve a quadratic equation. I never complained about it though. Bigger issues took all the attention, namely a world pandemic. But then, when everything went back to normal, I spoke up.

“Do you remember our school’s motto?” my principal asked me (adding brown sugar to her smokey macchiato). “I do, but—” (I woke up earlier for a month to turn her 7:35am-before-classes coffee habit into lobbying occasions). “Non multa, sed multum,” she proudly proclaimed, “here we prioritize depth, not breadth.” “Sure, but… why can’t depth develop in breadth?” She fell silent. “What do you propose?”

If COVID-19 taught me anything, it was the beauty of Zoom interactive boards—white and endless like snow. My classroom needed one. So I scrutinized all interactive-whiteboard-related YouTube unboxings and manuals, educating myself about Infrared Touch-Technology and Anti-Light Interference in Chinese and Vietnamese. After an espresso-powered, nocturnal, cost-benefit analysis, I found it—LPH86-ST420. Although my principal preferred new chairs for students, I persuaded my classmates to sign a petition for a whiteboard-instead-of-chairs exception. She conceded.

Versioni represent my curriculum’s cornerstone. However, flipping my 2064-page Greek-Italian dictionary to find any of 24 Greek letters’ 453,783 possible combinations to translate 8-to-12-line extracts felt mechanical and meaningless—until my junior-year teacher spent an entire lesson challenging me to wonder how one word—δεινός—could simultaneously mean “horrible” and “marvelous.” The translation became instrumental in interrogating, interlinking, and internalizing writings. Not so for my colleagues. Although the goal was novel, the practice of one-line-per-student translation wasn’t. During classes, eyes ceaselessly wandered, inspecting anything other than deltas and epsilons; bathroom-bound escapes increased faster than inflation; heads bowed during cold-calling. My friends’ agony turned tangible.

Then the whiteboard came. “It’s a δεινός tool—positively, of course. Can’t we try it?” I cornered my teacher. Rolling her eyes, she stammered her consent. I projected the versione and activated the whiteboard’s built-in note-on mode. Hopeful, I was returning to my desk when my teacher, smiling shrewdly, told me to turn around and analyze the extract—a Lysias’ speech defending a man who murdered his wife’s lover. I beware of asking, for example, how to translate παύσηται. It was too narrow. While translating is contingent upon passing exams, other skills developed through translating could serve us well beyond high school. Therefore, I inflamed everyone’s analytical spirits: “If you were Lysias, how’d you defend Euphiletos?” And I had my answer but didn’t regurgitate it straightaway, because why should’ve been the answer? It wasn’t more valuable than any of my classmates’.

Wise, indeed. Hands sprang up like mushrooms. Under my teacher’s incredulous, sparkling eyes, a debating fever spread. Flavio from the right-back corner shouted that Euphiletos had to cry to move the judges, while Irene in the front row whispered: “Exploit his wife’s immorality?” “Great! Now, how to test these ideas?” Without the board, we’d have employed line-by-line translations. But now, I proposed to use various colors to hoop on the screen evidence to falsify different hypotheses. Quickly, an explosion of magenta, marigold, and mint turned the whiteboard into a choral painting.

I believe in the liberal arts mission, that students must be free (liberalis) to own and share timeless learning, developing mind habits transcending the present. However, I recognize that to make them blossom, talents need fertile soil. That’s been my duty so far. Today that I’ve secured an LPH86-ST420 for all 29 classrooms in my high school, I get excited about whiteboards—and will continue to do so in college and beyond.

Snakefruits brown and scaly. Rambutans red as rubies. In my mother’s garden, at the tender age of five, I learned how small we indeed are against the grand tapestry of nature. At school, I was struck by the alluring beauty of endangered species like the Sumatran tiger, the Bali Myna, and the Tapanuli Orangutan. Yet, a harsher truth emerged from my mother’s teachings and the lessons at school: humans possess an immense capacity for destruction far surpassing nature’s ability to defend itself.

My advocacy journey began in the summer of 2023 when I interned at Fairatmos, Indonesia’s first climate tech company. I had always had a passion for technology, tinkering past midnight with scripts in my Roblox Studio as a child and studying Python as soon as I got to middle school. But I didn’t know that I could combine my love for tech with my passion for climate advocacy until I interned at Fairatmos.

The summer of 2024 marked an exhilarating turn in my journey as I returned to work on Fairatmos' conservation project in Cilacap. When I mentioned going there and staying in a remote village for my internship, even my mother resisted, citing how vastly different things would be from the comforts of our home in Jakarta. However, I insisted that I must go there to gain firsthand experience in conservation efforts, and protect the fragile ecosystem that the local residents dearly preserve. Eventually my mother relented.

The Cilacap mangrove swamp, spanning 5,000 acres, is a vibrant ecosystem teeming with biodiversity essential for carbon absorption. And yet, the work itself was gruelling, as my hands grew rough and my nails cracked from the physical labor. The oppressive sun often left me dizzy with heat exhaustion, while the constant ache in my body reminded me how far I was from home. Nights brought little relief as I cried silently in my cramped quarters when fatigue and loneliness consumed me.

However, as I interacted more with the local community, I began to see the resilience of the villagers, who faced these challenges daily with unwavering determination. Their stories of survival and hope in the face of adversity inspired me to push through my own discomforts. I realized that the work we were doing was not just an academic exercise – it was vital for the livelihoods of the local residents and the survival of Cilacap forest.

At the village, I had the privilege of exchanging captivating stories and innovative business ideas with the locals. From Harris and his fellow fishermen, who optimized spaces around mangrove roots for aqua farming, to Kuntoro, who cooked delicious toffee candies from mangrove fruits, I was struck by the resourcefulness of these community members. The community’s resourcefulness and vibrance were present in students as well. I guided Rachmat on the programming skills needed to become an ethical hacker, while Zakri worked with me on an Excel sheet to forecast the financial return of establishing an eco-tourism business in Cilacap. These children, full of life and dreams, fueled my determination to safeguard our planet for their future.

In my university life, I envision collaborating with students, alumni, faculty and sustainable local businesses to build an app dedicated to the preservation of the Cilacap mangrove forest. This app stems from my deep seated belief that technology, when harnessed creatively, can be a powerful force for change. By offering eco-tourism, virtual tours and adopt-a-tree program, giving users the ability to donate to crowdfunding campaigns, and allowing local residents of Cilacap to sell sustainable foods and eco-friendly merchandises, the app will generate sufficient revenue to fund conservation efforts.

My climate advocacy journey has shown me that a dedication to environmental advocacy, grounded in humility, intellectual curiosity, and common sense, can drive meaningful change. By continuing to nurture my passion for nature on campus, I hope to inspire others to join me in protecting our planet for generations to come.

Her frail hand rested on mine, fingers trembling slightly. My great-grandma recounted her distressing experiences of being blind in a low-income area without a sufficient support system and how she needed people to assist her with basic tasks: navigating the apartment complex, reading, and using auto rickshaws (the local transportation system). Her eyes welled up with tears as she recalled being isolated–reduced to a liability by people who were supposed to treat her like a human being. I didn’t know how to comfort her; I was completely clueless. What could I possibly say in my broken Telugu that would alleviate her struggles? Guiltily, I retreated to what was familiar to me–googling. As I scoured the internet for ways blind individuals could live independent and fulfilling lives, I came across The American Federation for the Blind which introduced me to assistive technology.

I researched various forms of assistive devices, such as hand-held video magnifiers and screen readers in hopes that at least some of my great-grandma’s troubles would fade away. After making several pros and cons lists, I concluded that purchasing an electronic device called the BrailleNote Touch would manage some of my great-grandma’s most strenuous tasks–navigation and reading–while also helping her connect with others through accessible messaging apps.

But my thoughts became an intangible mess when I looked at the price. It was over five thousand dollars. My muddled thoughts began assembling themselves into questions. How can blind people with financial constraints access these devices? Did they have to go through the same distress my great-grandma did? I didn’t want anyone to experience the same hardships that reduced my great-grandma's hope to shattered remnants. I knew I had to do something about the disparities in access to assistive technology.

While researching, I decided to play Bolt Thrower’s Those Once Loyal (my favorite death metal album at the time). I recalled how at first the music loomed over me like an indecipherable wall of sound (just like how the problem I was trying to address felt), but as I dissected each instrument, I understood how they collectively contributed to the big picture. After brainstorming, I tried applying this approach to analyze each disharmonious cause of the problem: the financial constraints were the guitar, the geographical barriers were the drums and the social stigma was the bass.

I delved deeper into the underlying causes by browsing through the resources listed on the websites of countless nonprofits. Just like a death metal song where the instruments required further investigation due to their complexity, the root causes also had many complex layers that needed dissecting. I found out that the financial constraints mainly arose because many blind individuals were unemployed and unable to afford the prohibitive costs of assistive technology, despite their role in making it easier for blind individuals to join the workforce. The geographical barriers were primarily due to the limited reach of distribution networks and manufacturers in countries with developing economies. The stigma caused by people associating assistive technology with increased dependence leads to less funding for training on assistive technology use.

Since the causes were so interconnected, I resolved to launch an initiative to tackle the issue comprehensively. I would focus on supplying expensive devices (such as refreshable braille displays) to low-income blind individuals and people in developing countries where these devices aren’t commonly available. To tackle the stigma and societal barriers, I wanted to implement accessibility workshops to raise awareness about the benefits of using assistive technology. Of course, I recognized that as a high schooler, I needed to work with many organizations that assisted blind individuals globally to make a widespread and long-term impact. Drawing inspiration from the intricacies of “inaccessible” music provided me with renewed insight on expanding the accessibility of assistive technology; it showed me how to turn disharmonious problems into harmonious solutions–transforming dissonance into innovation.

Chewed paper is my favorite thing in the world. I don't chew paper (even if I did, no medieval torture device could get that information out of me). What I mean is papier-mache: chewed paper. Before I could even write on paper, Kaka, my grandfather, taught me to mix it with water and turn it into art. In retrospect, this was rather an odd thing to teach a child. While my friends got chocolates from their grandfathers, mine handed me scrap paper from the bin. Not that I complained! One anecdote about NASA using papier-mâché to build mock spacecrafts had eight-year-old me building mock spacecrafts! But the hands that had so deftly shaped my dreams grew wrinkled and finally fell still. FAST. Face, Arms, Speech, Time. It's how you know that someone's having a stroke. An acronym I have stapled to my mind now, a harsh reminder of how we lost Kaka. I remember my mother sobbing on the kitchen floor, each wave of grief like turning over the same pages of a book over and over again. I couldn’t seem to mold this grief into art though like I could paper. Kaka's stroke could be blamed on hypertension, and my mother had it too. I recall reading research papers on HBP, learning how to perform CPR, and cooking heart-healthy meals ... I needed to be ready if, the next time, it was Ma instead. I wanted to grasp onto everything, but it was all too FAST. My nervous limbs— no longer busy with the patient art of papier-mâché— sought other forms of release. I started playing kho-kho, a traditional tag sport, but this was temporary too. On the verge of winning a game, as I leaped to tag a defender, I lost more than the match. Diagnosed with a chronic fracture at fourteen, I lost the ability ever to play kho-kho again. My broken leg felt like gloopy paper, too watered down to save, too damaged to be art anymore. With nothing to do but smell my musty plaster, I found my way back to someone I missed dearly. Now it wasn't all moving too FAST. I gathered plenty of used paper by organizing a drive around my neighborhood. With twists of my wrists, I used wads of old paper to shape caricatures and myself. The way that Kaka had taught me to turn gooey mush into art, I fashioned myself into an impressionist painting: smudged, imperfect, but authentically, originally me. The caricatures I made were sold, and the funds were allocated to Unnayan, an organization for older individuals with special needs. I felt powerless with Kaka. But my new friends at Unnayan - Arham, Mahanta uncle, Kritika - were people whose lives I could help shape the way Kaka had shaped mine. As soon as my plaster was removed, I started volunteering at HUM actively. I began brainstorming possible ways I, a single 16-year-old, could make an impact. I decided to raise funds that could help manage their vulnerabilities. My first fundraiser was in Lumding and featured papier bowls, vases, and figurines, all made with scraps found in the garbage. Since then, I've spent my weekends organizing more fundraisers and events, steering initiatives to ensure that the residents received the support they needed. Now, whenever life presents me with gloopy, mulchy problems, I say "Thank you!" and wonder how best to turn them into art. My creative skills are my inheritance, and I intend to nurture them through and beyond college. Every discarded object, each individual, has something that can be redeemed and reshaped. The mushy, chewed-up paper inside all of us is just waiting for someone to believe in it, for someone to mold it into magnificent cartonería. When I start college, I plan to either join a crafts club or start my own so I can continue growing my passion for repurposing discarded items. I am excited to build a dorm community around reuse and upscaling, inviting my dormmates to donate their waste so we can build cartonería together as one.

The last time I had banana pancakes made by my mother was on a Sunday morning in third grade. I loved savoring the sweet stickiness of the mashed bananas mingling with the dry, fluffy pancakes. During that summer, after a day of playing with friends at the park, we would hear the 6 p.m. chime echo through the city. That was our cue to head home.

One evening, when I arrived, I noticed my mother acting unusually. On the kitchen counter sat an empty can of cheap beer. Her hands trembled as she prepared dinner, and she accidentally dropped her plate. The sound of it shattering was becoming all too familiar—this was the third plate she had broken that week. My mother, moving slowly and with a vacant, almost ghostly look in her eyes, resembled Cinderella sweeping up the broken pieces. My father loomed over her, shouting angrily. Tears welled up in my mother’s eyes as she muttered, “I just want to get out of the house.” My father’s response was harsh: “Stop spending money on alcohol and just earn more.” After a heated argument, my mother, dazed, grabbed her bag and left, saying, “From now on, you will handle all the household chores yourself.” My sisters and I cried and tried to stop her, but she shook us off and ran away. The next day I came home to find her back in the kitchen, preparing dinner as usual. This pattern of excessive drinking, arguments, and leaving only to return the next day became a regular occurrence. My parents couldn’t divorce, since my mother, working part-time for minimum wage, could not afford living, so the cycle persisted.

In a family of five, with no personal space of my own, I grew weary of coming home to my mother’s inebriated state. To escape, I spent more time at the library or park, coming home late. In junior high, after learning about child labor and environmental issues related to my favorite clothing brands, I started a student organization with friends. We stayed up late discussing solutions and planning activities. These pursuits occupied my mind and pushed thoughts of my mother to the background. However, when I returned from a year of studying abroad in Canada during my sophomore year of high school, I noticed my mother’s drinking habits had worsened, and their arguments had intensified. It was even sadder to think of the warm, familial gatherings I had experienced with my host family and friends in Canada. Determined to understand my mother better, I decided to have a conversation with her alone. It was then that my mother told me for the first time (drunkenly, of course) about her life. She revealed that her father had died of alcohol-related causes when she was four, and her mother, suffering from schizophrenia, had been unable to work. Consequently, she had worked part-time throughout her school years and had no choice to go to college. It was only at eighteen that I began to understand my mother’s struggles. I deeply regretted the way I had looked down on and ignored her, failing to appreciate her challenges and limitations. I had always blamed her for our problems, but I realized that the real issue was the environment surrounding her and the way we interacted. Since then, I spend time with her, talking, going out, and even giving her handmade aprons—though she rarely uses them. While she still enjoys drinking, our conflicts have lessened. This coming Sunday, I’ll be making banana pancakes with my mother.

“6’6 FORWARD, NUMBER 12, ALI AHMADDD!” Rising from the bench, I high-five 13 teammates. Broadcasting my name as a starter for the Lovejoy High School basketball team is something residents of Lucas, a Dallas suburb, may not be used to hearing. As the sole person of color on my team, it’s unusual for a Muslim kid with Pakistani-Arab heritage, brown skin, and curly black hair to be selected Team Captain by the head coach.

It may come as a surprise for the basketball captain, but when I’m not practicing my free throws, I’m telling off bullies and pushing for neurodiversity awareness. My older brother is autistic, and I’ve seen firsthand his struggles. Back in middle school, my 7th-grade brother was taunted and tripped by a classmate. He fell and broke his wrist, as the principal called my frantic mom. Requiring emergency surgery, my brother’s pain and social anxiety rocked me.

I wanted to know why. Why does my brother endure daily bullying since he’s neurodiverse? Why does his brain make him behave differently — hyper fixating and rewatching the same Cars movie scene 100 times? Why isn’t he treated the same?

Seeking answers to these questions, I’ve turned to neuroscience. Doing independent research with a UC Davis PhD candidate, I investigated autism diagnoses. I’ve spent hours upon hours analyzing brain scans of autism patients, trying to decipher a common thread. I’ve even interviewed dozens of families dealing with autism, along with experts, for my Neuroverse podcast.

Closer to home, I’ve worked with my principal to establish A Beautiful Mind, an anti-bullying after-school club to support peers who fall on the autism spectrum. Hanging out in the club, I’ve befriended one classmate specifically, Thad, who’s obsessed with dinosaurs.

As we bake Christmas-themed sugar cookies, Thad rattles off fun facts about velociraptors. (Did you know that they were only the size of a turkey? Jurassic Park lied.) Cutting green-and-red frosted Grinch-shaped treats into dinosaur shapes, we chuckle as I botch up the cookie. Thad never directly divulges his emotions — I can only sense how he may desire having a group of friends or being invited to a birthday party. Thad forces me to reflect upon my brother, guilting and motivating me to channel my voice against social exclusion.

Both joy and torments alike drive my neurodiversity advocacy. I could’ve chosen to stay silent like many of my basketball teammates — some of whom also have neurodiverse siblings. Often, teammates will groan when a neurodiverse kid dares to try out for the team, impersonating flailing arms and a missed open layup. As a freshman, I recall seeing one such student sitting alone in the locker room post-tryout, tears streaming down his face. I regret not standing up for him then amid peer pressure.

Now, it’s a funny sight: a brown-skinned liberal Muslim basketball captain overseeing a squad of nearly-all white, conservative Christian teammates. I’ve stayed quiet long enough.

Growing up, as the only Muslim family in a Southern Baptist neighborhood, I felt uneasy leaving school early on Fridays to attend jummah salah, mosque prayer. “Jokes” about Islam are often thrown around in the cafeteria or gym locker room. When I was younger, I tried my best to laugh along in a feeble attempt to fit in. Now? I care less about their comfort level and more about my own. Yes, I pray in Arabic. Yes, I speak Urdu at home. Yes, I have an autistic brother. They’re all reasons why I stand up to the bullies — if they weren’t taunting the autistic kid, they’d be making crass Islamophobic remarks.

My duty doesn’t end here. There’s more work to be done. Anytime a peer on the autistic spectrum is bullied, I feel as if I’m the one personally taunted and jeered.

Today, when I hear “6’6 FORWARD, NUMBER 12, ALI AHMAD!” called on game nights, I stand tall with pride, honing a voice to stand in neuroscientific and racial solidarity.

Eighth grade has just ended, and it’s the first weekend of summer vacation. For the first time in a while, bright rays rest upon my enchanted face, waking me from a half-day slumber. The house is quiet. Mom is out teaching piano. Wandering the apartment, I find the bathroom and brush my teeth. As I rinse my mouth and splash my face with cold water, I remember. I put on my running clothes. I tie my shoes tight. Tomorrow is that day.

As the doors to Target open, I head up the escalator and round the corner. My eyes are greeted with many words. Dogs. Birthday. Get Well. My fingers glide between the many cards in front of me. Some are blank, others are full. Some even sing. One catches my eye – its design is simplistic, and its inside is bare. Its face speaks three words: Happy Father’s Day.

I have done this before, and today seems no different. I grab my pens and once-clear colored pencil box, and after vigorous squiggles taint an ancient math quiz, two strokes appear in the card. Dear Dad. I begin slow and soft, echoing the card’s words. Happy Father’s Day. Then, as the pace quickens and my words dig deeper into the card, I reminisce about the year past. Thank you Dad. Finally, I sign. Love, Your Son, [Name]. On the other side of the card, I lay the pen to rest. Basketball. Airplane. Easy to draw Korean soup. After “drawing” everything that could represent the words in the card (a.k.a placing my phone under and tracing the screenshots line for line), a blank space in the corner still stared back at me. And so, with a stroke of genius, I googled Easy to Draw Father’s Day Images. While scrolling through possible drawings, I spot one seeming relatively doable: A simple face made up of a pair of glasses and a mustache. Finished with my masterpiece, I close my eyes peacefully to nap as Mom drives me to Dad’s house.

The sound of birds and skateboards wakes me up. I sneak down the stairs to see my dad on the couch watching soccer. I jump and scream, “Happy Father’s Day!” He puts down his sadly unspilled coffee. “Thanks Jem!” he says. “You’re finally up!” As I reach the bottom of the stairs, I run to my backpack and reveal my surprise. “Ja jan!” Dad, this is for you!” Opening the card, his eyes travel up and down, my heart following the same trajectory. Finally, he speaks. “[Name], what’s this?” he says, pointing to a corner of the card. “Oh that?” I say. “I didn’t know what to draw, so I searched up Father’s Day images and that popped up. I think it's a guy with glasses and a mustache.” He closes his eyes along with the card. “[Name], what does Father’s Day mean to you?”

Nine hours later, Mom picks me up after dinner. I still don’t understand. What went wrong? I had perfected my craft for nearly a decade. And yet, maybe that was exactly why. I had written these cards time after time in an increasingly monotonous manner, and it showed. It was as plain as a face made up of a pair of glasses and a mustache. What had once been a token of gratitude became an apathetic chore. I had forgotten the meaning behind my action, and all that was left was a dull husk of what once was. I crumple into a scrunched ball. I squeeze harder. A dampness envelops my eyes. I realize it’s not what I did: it’s what I did not do. I wince. But not because of regret. For although guilt pervades my heart, the desire to never feel this pain ever again courses throughout me, and I am filled with a sense of reinvigorated purpose: To do everything I can wholeheartedly.

The sun cast long shadows as I walked Sophie down our familiar suburban street. It was during one of these routine dog-walks that I first noticed him—the stranger who would set me on a path I never saw coming.

"Namaste," he said, pressing his palms together at chest level and offering a slight bow. The gesture caught me off guard, and I awkwardly nodded and waved in response. The melodic flow of Hindi filled the air, and I found myself frozen, unsure how to respond. Noticing my hesitation, he seamlessly switched to English. "I'm Mr. Ahuja. I'm new here, just moved to be closer to my grandchildren."

"In India, we greet each other like this," he explained. "Namaste means 'I bow to the divine in you.' Would you like to try?”

Taken by surprise and not wanting to be rude, I awkwardly mimicked his gesture.

“Namaste?”

Mr. Ahuja's face lit up with approval. I felt a mix of embarrassment and an odd sense of accomplishment. From that day forward, a spark of curiosity drew me to Mr. Ahuja, and our interactions became a daily ritual. To my delight, he began sharing stories about India—not the dry historical accounts from school or my parents' occasional anecdotes, but tales full of color and intrigue.

One evening, as we discussed the local Indian community, Mr. Ahuja mentioned the nearby temple. "The temple is always looking for volunteers," he said, his tone more insistent than casual, clearly hoping I’d take his advice. "It's not just about helping out—it can deepen your understanding of the topics we’ve been exploring."

Although I was somewhat reluctant to spend time at the temple, the conversation replayed in my head.

And so, a few weeks later, after some reflection, I volunteered at the temple, to help set up for Diwali. The vibrant colors, the scent of incense, and the warmth of the community sparked a connection to something I had always tried to run from before.

Growing up, I often laughed along with jokes and stereotypes about Indians in media and among friends. The exaggerated accents, the head-wobbles, the "thank you, come again" quips—they were everywhere. However, Mr. Ahuja's influence made me reflect on my Indian heritage and see my culture anew. The intricate rangoli designs I once dismissed as old-fashioned, now appeared as stunning works of art. The Bollywood movies I used to roll my eyes at, revealed layers of social commentary I’d never noticed before. I found myself standing taller, more confident in my identity, and increasingly drawn to the idea of visiting India, which seemed absurd just a few months ago.

The impact of Mr. Ahuja's mentorship became evident as I immersed myself in temple activities by organizing the Navratri-Garba event, where students and parents wore colorful traditional Indian attire, and danced to Indian music. I connected with my neighbors; attending the annual Lunar New Year and Eid celebrations, trying different cuisines and sharing cultural elements such as folk tales and music. At the annual Katy Holi celebration, I bridged cultures by inviting my non-Indian friends to join the cricket tournament. Although initially hesitant amid the unfamiliar game, with some friendly encouragement and quick lessons, they found themselves batting and running alongside the Indian uncles in their crisp white kurtas. The air buzzed with a mix of Hindi, English, and our excited shouts as boundaries were hit and wickets fell.

This journey has even inspired me to plan a trip to India after graduation, ready to explore my roots—not from any obligation, but as an opportunity to reconnect.

Mr. Ahuja’s influence and these experiences have deepened my confidence in my cultural identity and enhanced my cultural competence. Nowadays, when I walk past that bench, I see more than just an elderly gentleman. I see a contagious catalyst for change, a reminder that both growth and connection often begin with a simple "Namaste" and an open heart.

I gazed downwards at Sally, my face red hot with a confusing mix of enduring rage and embarrassment. Don’t make me do this to you, I thought. I gripped the shovel in my hand tighter as I recounted the series of events this morning that led to this moment: I had packed Sally up in a plastic bag and brought her to school. As part of our grade 8 Life Science coursework, we had to grow and document the life cycles of our own sunflower plants. Sally was my sunflower seedling, whom I had taken great care of over the past few days—watering the soil regularly and making sure it received 8 hours of direct sunlight per day. As I placed Sally beside my peers’ seedlings, the class burst out in laughter. Sally was short—about 4 centimetres tall, its seed leaves still intact, its stem thin and frail, its true leaves tiny and timid with a subtle yet jarring hue of purple. My peers’ seedlings were mostly twice Sally’s height, their stems thick and healthy, their leaves bright green, luscious, and sprawling. "[Name], your plant looks like it’s dying!" one of my classmates commented obnoxiously.

Sally bore a stinging resemblance to myself. As an immigrant, I stood out in school as the guy who was slow at English lessons and spoke with a funny accent. I was passionate about discussing current affairs, but my social ineptitude barred me from joining the debate team. My attempt at leadership ended up with me crying in the shower because I was "too quiet" during the Prefectorial Board selections. I was often the last pick in sports—my frame was small and I was too clumsy to stop hitting my own face with the ball. Sally reminded me of everything I hated about myself. As I peered intensely at Sally, her leaves, bowed down and flimsy, seemed to call out to me in pity. Then, a tiny, diamond-shaped growth caught my eye. I was pretty sure it was an apical bud—at least that’s what we learned in Life Sciences. That meant Sally was about to grow new leaves. I loosened my grip on the shovel. Maybe, I should give Sally another chance, I thought.

My leap of faith led to weeks of biological research and exploration. I quickly realized that ensuring moisture and sunlight was not enough—many other factors were in play for optimal plant growth. Sally’s purplish leaves resulted from phosphorous deficiency caused by low pH. To balance soil pH, I added well-rotted manure from the neighbourhood garden to Sally’s pot. Reading scientific studies on the aerobic respiration of roots made me realize my soil was too cloggy and compact. As a workaround, I employed my earthworm friends from the neighbourhood park to create tunnels in the soil to improve aeration. As a result of my persistent troubleshooting, Sally’s growth picked up. Her leaves had shed their hues of purple and grew abundantly, and her stem stood tall and proud. Months later, a tiny, spherical growth caught my eye. A smile lit up my face. It was a flower bud. Sally was blooming.

My success journey with Sally sowed the seeds of my can-do attitude in life. After countless hours of Kumon practices and reading aloud, I topped the class in English. Volunteering for class presentations and debates helped overcome my fear of social interactions. In high school, I joined the school MUN team and put myself in front of my peers to campaign for the Student Council. Seeing Sally realize her potential, though, brought me more joy than anything I could have done for myself. I never became the best at sports, but my undying love for basketball led me to pioneer the first batch of school team to play for the ‘A’ Division National School Games, creating an opportunity for my like-minded peers to compete. My favourite pastimes became gifting the joy of music to underprivileged children in my community and sharing my healing journey from a slipped disc with athletes suffering sports injuries. Every time I feel like giving up, on myself or others alike, I remind myself of that bright yellow sunflower, grinning at me with an exuberance of triumph and gratitude.

Pacing the floor of my tiny room at Crumlin Children’s Hospital in Dublin, Ireland, I taught myself to French braid hair. My arms, covered in red blistering sores and aching from the IV of antivirals, worked relentlessly as I sectioned off three strands. After a few hours of walking in circles and with very tired arms, I managed my first French braids. I was elated. Despite the skin infection causing giant, pus-filled sores that covered my entire body, at least my hair looked pretty. It was the happiest I had been in days. More importantly, I felt determined to reclaim a sliver of normalcy amidst the chaos of my circumstances.

For a long time, I grappled with the self-pitying question: “Why me?” Having a chronic skin condition at thirteen—producing dry, itchy, red patches and periodic infections—felt tragic. I obsessed over every flare up and was convinced I looked grotesque. A move from the cool, rainy days of Dublin to the harsh, humid climate of Texas worsened my skin condition and tested my fragile self-confidence. Despite consulting numerous doctors, none could offer effective solutions, leaving me feeling discouraged.

In the unassuming setting of my freshman biology class, my curiosity ignited. Captivated by the giant heart diagram that adorned our classroom floor, I imagined being a surgeon, like Meredith Grey from Grey’s Anatomy while dissecting a giant rat. Biology sparked a deep interest in the human body, especially my own health condition. Science provided perspective: for every problem, there is an answer, and with determination, there is a solution. I started to view myself not as a victim but capable of taking control of my own story. In my newfound assertiveness I Googled the best places to live for tree allergies. Within six months, we relocated to Colorado seeking better management of my condition.

There, I met Dr. Sartori, a pivotal figure, who entered the room singing an Italian song that included my name. As he attentively listened to my medical history, I felt truly seen and understood for the first time by a doctor. A biologic injection, Dupixent, was a game-changer. Dr. Sartori’s impact went beyond alleviating my symptoms; he made me reflect on what it means to be both a compassionate and effective physician.

With a new home and clearer skin, I felt like I had a blank slate. My confidence grew as I challenged myself by joining the field hockey team, enrolling in multiple AP classes, and contributing to my community by volunteering. Monday nights, volunteering at a home for single mothers and children escaping domestic violence, I met fourteen-month-old Hannah. Although identified as developmentally delayed, her resilience both humbled and inspired me. She craved constant attention and was severely underweight, unable to crawl or stand on her own.

Drawing on insights from my AP Psychology class, I recognized the developmental milestones she had yet to achieve. Each week, I brought her brain-boosting food and worked diligently to help her crawl, and eventually stand. I vividly recall the moment she smiled for the first time as I rolled a ball to her.
