Playing a small role in positively impacting her life deepened my understanding of human development and psychology, but also reinforced my belief in the transformative power of human connection.

While braiding my teammates’ hair on long bus rides to games, I’m reminded of teaching myself to braid my own hair while in the Children’s hospital in Dublin. That seemingly small accomplishment empowered me to realize that even in the face of struggle, I am stronger than I think. I continue to learn that if I am determined, curious, and selfless, I will make an impact on my own life and the lives of others.

I arrived in Colorado as an insecure girl, and I now confidently lead my teams as captain, impact lives at FLS, and pursue my dream of becoming an empathetic and compassionate pediatric doctor.

"I'll have to find out what happens to Raskolnikov later," I think to myself as I let Crime and Punishment, my favorite book, slip from my fingers. Hastily, I put on my swimsuit and run downstairs.

Noticing my rushed steps, my mom yells: "Come back here right now! You're going to catch a cold!" But she knows it's too late. Glimpsing at the window, I realize the arrival is imminent: I sense a heavy gust of wind on my chest and hear the flickering leaves of the huge tipuana trees outside.

When I pass through the building's gates, a downpour of heavy rain covers the whole street and I am thrilled by the earthy scent that rises from the ground: petrichor. As people hurry to their homes not to get drenched, they look strangely at me while I get on my old Caloi bike and start to pedal. Now, I am committed to going to the Ibirapuera park, whose tropical plants and Streptomyces bacteria provide my favorite petrichor blend.

"I need to make haste," I think. "If I get there before the rain ends, I can really catch that geosmin —"

Bang!

Disconcerted, I try to get up from the asphalt. The cyclist, who crossed the red light, says: "Sorry, bro. I had to rush for a delivery and this rain just sucks. Are you OK?" But, before I answer, he hops back onto his bike. As he leaves, I realize not everyone is enthusiastic about the arrival of petrichor like I am.

Weeks later at church, I could still feel the pain from the crash, but it was nothing compared to what I was about to see.

"Hundreds have lost their homes," my friend declared as he showed pictures of frightened people in places devastated by landslides. These images taught me that one of my country's worst climate catastrophes was happening a few hundred miles away due to rainstorms. Immersed in my own privilege, I had overlooked how some of my most pleasant moments were synchronized to the destruction of many people's lives in my community.

This news disturbed me ever since. Knowing how petrichor — or, indeed, any other phenomena — worked was only a selfish mental exercise if I couldn't associate it with a larger purpose.

"This isn't the right number," I heard numerous times as I tried to reach my state's civil defense. "You should call someone else.''

The crash and the photos I saw at the church were the greatest wake-up call ever: I gathered sensors and wires to develop a prototype aiming to predict landslides, seeking support from civil deference. No one seemed to answer, but that didn't appease me: I decided to try a different approach, reaching out to victims themselves.

"Hi, [Name]! I am [Name], a young scientist with a project to predict landslides. My friend at church told me you were personally affected by the catastrophe this year. Would you be willing to let me test my simulator at your place?"

When I finally saw her house, which had almost been taken down with the cliff during a landslide, I was relieved for the first time in my life that it wasn't raining. The months that followed weren't easy: I spent several late nights doing calculations and had to dig the earth in the middle of the rainforest behind [Name]'s favela until I finished my plan: by installing an underground humidity sensor, the risk of landslides could be detected before disasters happened.

Nowadays, I find the same excitement predicting landslides as when I search for petrichor. However, my new quest has new motivation— I have a bigger purpose. From people living in favelas to delivery guys, I want more people to experience rain like I do — not with fear, but with joy. Both of these pursuits symbolize my hope for something better, my growing determination to support people to cherish rain as an auspicious arrival.

As I rocked back and forth in my chair, I held an ordinary 3x3 Rubix Cube in my hands attempting to bring all six sides into unity. The cube felt like a kaleidoscope of possibilities, each twist revealing a new pattern of colors. I sat in my room, the sunlight streaming through the window, casting playful shadows on the walls as I focused on the challenge before me. The familiar click-click of the Rubix Cube echoed in my quiet room, each movement a step closer to solving the puzzle. It amazed me how there were 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 combinations to this ordinary cube, but only 1 combination where all sides possessed a singular color, forming a solved cube. With every twist and turn, I began to view each unsolved side as a reflection of my own activities and experiences throughout high school. Over time, these seemingly disparate sides started to align, eventually revealing my true character and giving me a better understanding of who I am.

My Saturdays were typically a hectic schedule as I woke up early to put on my red Mathnasium shirt, brown khakis, and white adidas shoes. It was 10:00am and I arrived at work where I would grade countless papers and provide tutoring for my students. Typically, my students would ask me, “Hey [Name], how do I solve this factoring problem?”. Immediately, I would show them the step-by-step procedure and have them try it on their own. After answering a few questions by themselves, they would finally understand how to encounter a challenging topic, and I would see a glowing smile across their face. This brought me a sense of satisfaction knowing that I helped my students learn something new. After a busy day at work, I would come home and find time to work on learning something new. I usually worked on my website where I learn and publish about the electronics platform, Arduino. I saw this as an adventure, as I was brainstorming new ideas for projects. Learning programming languages, such as C and Python, and circuit breakdowns of Arduino was just one thing. Publishing these projects to get feedback was where I found my enjoyment. With their insightful feedback and support, I was able to further pursue additional projects and create more tutorials.

As I journeyed through high school, I participated in many activities. At first, I wasn't able to see how all my activities revealed my true character. These activities represented the scrambled sides of the Rubix Cube as if they were unique from each other. But it wasn't until junior year when these sides began to align and form a completed cube, revealing my personality. I realized I wanted to create a positive impact on a larger community, and this gave me a better understanding of myself. I enjoy my time at Mathnasium as I tutor students because witnessing their growth made it clear that I had a desire to see the impact I could make in any field I was a part of. I continue to endeavor on multiple Arduino projects because it reaches over 130 countries with 5000+ monthly visitors. My website motivates me to continue my work because I enjoy creating an impact on a larger audience. Following my passion and seeing a tangible result brought me satisfaction to a level that motivated me further.

As I bravely take a new step into my college career, I seek to create an impact on my new community. In the same way, I brought unity to the Rubik's Cube, I hope to bring this personality and contribute meaningfully to the University of Florida, living out the motto “civium in moribus rei publicae salus”. The welfare of the state truly does depend on the morals of the citizen, and I believe the citizen that I am today will help contribute positively to the community at the University of Florida.

How can one person deliver 2 billion presents in one night? Growing up, I chose to treat this as a paradox because ever since I can remember, Santa has been there for me. I still vividly remember the Christmas he brought me something I didn’t even think was possible: a lustrous silver bell from The Polar Express (my favorite movie) that could only be heard by “true believers.” Although initially skeptical, when I first heard that beautiful, resonant chime and saw my parents had no reaction, all my doubts disappeared.

Unfortunately, as you may expect, my childhood innocence didn’t last forever. Eventually, in 6th grade, I discovered the harsh truth. When my mom finally broke the news to me, I simultaneously experienced an overwhelming sense of disbelief and loss. I had always found comfort in the thought that Santa was watching out for me, and in an instant, that safe space was gone.

For a long time, I struggled to reconcile the joy I experienced through the ideal of Santa and the disillusionment I experienced over inevitably finding the truth. However, one day, in a conversation with my best friend, somehow, the topic came up, and he told me that he had actually found out about Santa at just five years old.

Ever since he’s always believed Santa “was pointless” and “never someone important.” It was in that simple moment that I finally resolved my inner conflict and understood something that has helped shape me to this day.

I realized that Santa was never just a kind old man who flew around the world at three times the speed of sound. To me, Santa represented ideals that I wanted to live up to; he was selfless, generous, and unconditionally kind. Ultimately, I realized that even though Santa was never real, the things he stood for and the ways he’s shaped my life were, and these benefits far outweighed the initial sense of loss I felt.

From a young age, I knew that if I could help others in some small way, that was something I wanted to do, just like Santa did. This is what led me to start an online tutoring service that connects like-minded high school students, who also want to give back, to younger ones who need support. Although it was hard at first, I kept going because I was genuinely passionate about helping others receive the opportunities they might otherwise not have access to. This project also led to me developing an interest in learning about the ethics of educational access as it relates to finance.

As a result, I then searched for research opportunities related to the topic and soon found myself learning about the economic impacts of AI on society; I was very grateful because this was also something I wanted to pursue further in college.

Finally, although I may not have understood at the time, I now realize that my parents maintained the Santa facade for so long because they wanted to give me a childhood filled with fond Christmas memories; especially because it was something they rarely had as immigrant children. I’ve become so grateful to them for what they did because I’ve realized how significant those past experiences were. They’ve helped shape the person I’ve become today and I couldn’t be more appreciative of their influence.

In the future, I am inspired to use what I’ve learned to contribute to the things I believe in. I always want to see the bigger picture and never fail to recognize the importance of ideals. In the end, I still believe in Santa because he lives in what he represents. I believe in all the amazing things he’s done for my life, and I’m proud to say I still hear the chime of my silver bell; it’s safe to say he will definitely be coming to visit my kids in the future.

Getting out of bed is hard. Dozens of complete 1000-piece jigsaw puzzles stretch my bedroom floor, requiring groggy Hopscotch jumps to avoid dismantling my masterpieces. Since my first-grade teacher revealed a 500-piece San Francisco puzzle, I’ve been fascinated by the piece-by-piece creation of my favorite landmarks and alluring utopian cityscapes. I often spent recesses twisting and turning pieces, pleading for an interlock. Frequently frustrated, I’d use scissors on a piece, leaving new tabs and blanks that created an artificial, forced match. Strategy is partially important: starting with corners and edges impedes messy matching and delayed disaster. But a jigsaw's fundamental truth is that it requires trial-and-error, something I'd have to accept. Jigsaw tactics are akin to the mentality of “luck is no accident”, which teaches me to take advantage and build success off “random” accidents.

One month after I started experimenting with powerlifting coaching, an initiative I hoped would replicate my success as an athlete, my first client, Noah, hit a plateau on his bench press. Having experienced a similar situation, I excitedly suggested increasing the frequency of sessions he benched, just as I had done to overcome the same stagnation. However, he didn’t progress at all over the following month. Embarrassed, I convinced myself that his external factors were the source of error. But no, his sleep and recovery were spot-on. Noah’s bench was a disorganized puzzle set with an extra amount of pieces. Locating faults in his training was comparable to weeding out irrelevant pieces. We started tracking all possible metrics: intensity, volume, frequency, and rate of perceived exertion. My scientific curiosity also propelled me to dig through kinesiology staples, such as "The Body in Motion" and "Anchored," to identify possible programming faults. These were like the corner and edge pieces. Within this rabbit hole, I located the culprit. Because of Noah’s long arms, benching produced more systematic fatigue than someone with more leverage – to achieve a full range of motion, he had to exert more force to lift the barbell a longer distance. He needed a personalized program with greater intensity and lower frequency. Within eight weeks of implementing an accessorized 5 sets by 5 repetitions program, his bench max skyrocketed by thirty pounds. The puzzle was solved.

Trial-and-error doesn’t always work. While tutoring a middle schooler, Daniel, my first three sessions were difficult, as he exhibited minimal excitement following my plethora of established jokes and seemed to brood about something other than learning algebra. Despite decreasing lecture time and increasing break frequencies, my efforts always yielded no piece-by-piece improvement. I began to wish I could go back to being a kid - where I cut pieces to force synthetic connections. Instead, I turned to what I once considered blasphemy - asking for help. After speaking with Daniel’s dad, I was shocked to learn that the kid’s uncle had passed away a few days before our first session, and understandably, he was preoccupied.

In our fourth session, making little headway, I taught through something other than a whiteboard. Using Math Playground’s database of jigsaw puzzles infused with algebraic concepts as a base, we also enhanced reasoning and logic skills with simple Sudoku. As Daniel worked through each grid, I asked him to visualize and eliminate possible numbers for each square. Even if he was correct, I playfully proposed alternate solutions, each of which he masterfully shut down with a sassy, “I told you so” explanation. At the end of the session, I offered my condolences and asked about his favorite activity with his uncle. For the first time since we started tutoring, he looked up at the camera and said it was playing soccer with him at sunset. Our conversation proceeded to traverse from soccer to In-N-Out to his life aspirations, as we giggled and eagerly planned the next meeting.

My trial-and-error-solving mindset isn’t perfect - it may be timely and sometimes requires additional assistance (like looking at the box). In college, I look forward to trialing through problem sets testing elasticity and market analysis with my handbook of formulas and theories. But, I equally look forward to enlisting the help of my peers and professors, where I’ll find my own explanation through various proposed solutions. Looking at the sea of organized puzzles near my bed, maybe accidentally stepping on and dismantling them wouldn’t be disastrous. The journey of tinkering piece by piece and inevitable errors provides wisdom, making the world a tab less puzzling.

It was in English class when I started wondering how I could pull off my ears. The blaring noise of my glucose monitor was interrupting the discussion of The Count of Monte Cristo and I was desperate. It had already beeped twice announcing my low glucose level, yet I hadn’t drunk my juice. Wondering if my classmates would be mad if it beeped a 3rd time, I placed my thumb on the “off” button just in case. As I zoomed out of my strategy, I realized my teacher was asking who enjoyed the book. I raised my hand - the revenge, drama, spite…what was there not to love? I was enthralled with the character of Dantes and his aliases after being falsely accused of treason. But when I noticed no one else did, I began lowering it. However, my teacher stopped me, asking why it had resonated with me. I didn't respond; I wasn’t sure what resonated meant - I left the class half-embarrassed, half-curious and half-pale (the juice was still in the box). The question stuck with me: How did the book appeal to me on a personal level? In hopes of finding an answer, I started looking at books from another lens, getting into the habit of asking that same question at the end. I think everyone does this, but mine was a bit more systematized: in the last page of the book, I made sure to write down a reflection. But I was still stumped on Dantes.

Two years into this habit, I received a call from Valeria’s parents. Worried for their recently diagnosed 5-year old daughter, they asked to meet. I was nervous - would I be lying by saying it’s “going to be okay” or radiating a confidence that I had not yet found within myself? Nevertheless, I accepted and did both. But it felt different: by telling her it was going to be okay, I felt an ease that I too was going to be okay; by acting confident with my condition, I tricked myself too, realizing how good it felt to be optimistic. Her little arms leaned into a hug after we had finished talking, and I let out a sob. Even though she might’ve felt I helped her, she healed me in far more ways. That conversation helped me begin to embrace my condition. I knew I wanted to be a role model for young kids just like her.

Inspired by Valeria, I picked up a book I had avoided since my diagnosis: My Beloved World, by Sonia Sotomayor. The prologue started and I traveled back in time: I was in my kitchen, hands trembling, parents screaming, just to get my first insulin shot. Sotomayor’s experiences mirrored; I felt seen. It then hit me.

I understood why the Count of Monte Cristo resonated with me: unconsciously, I had found comfort in Dante’s struggle to defy the label others had given him. His eagerness for revenge mirrored my yearning for conformity. While I found consolation in Dantes, I found strength in Sonia. Similar to how she was scared to be vulnerable as it's not customary for a justice, I tried to blend in with my classmates.

Today, I not only find myself in books but in people. Especially those patients I’ve visited: Coco, Alondra, José, Alejandro and more, have motivated me to turn my vulnerability into action by raising awareness for diabetes through hospital visits, talks and founding T1DOSE. Yes, there are hazards to openness, but they seem minor to the possibility that someone might see themselves in me. I realized there is no need to fix my inner Dantés, but to accept his racing thoughts and let it coexist with my courageous Sonia. At the end of the day, the Dantes in me still gets uneasy because of the beeps, but the Sonia in me breathes, and lets the 3 beeps be.

When I was eight years old, I fell in love.

Celestial, unassailable, and ineffable—the stage stood there in all its grandeur. Delicate snowflakes pirouetted and leaped with ethereal grace, their costumes shimmering under the stage lights like frosty diamonds. From that moment on, I knew exactly what I wanted to be.

Years of relentless practice and perseverance followed that moment of enchantment. Each step and each leap brought me closer to my dream of dancing on stage, particularly when I was chosen to perform as Lead Spanish in "The Nutcracker." However, the path to that stage was fraught with challenges beyond my control, even beyond the choreography itself.

Backstage, I stood with beads of sweat dripping down my face, counting the steps before my entrance. I immersed myself in Tchaikovsky’s music as I stepped onto the stage. Tchaikovsky composed The Nutcracker during the lowest point in his life, grieving the death of his sister. Despite his sorrow, the audience hears only the enchanting and glamorous music. Similarly, as a ballerina on stage, I concealed my struggles behind a radiant smile, presenting elegance and grace while the audience remained unaware of the effort and pain behind each performance.

Growing up, I was always told not to judge a book by its cover and that inner beauty matters more than outer beauty. Yet, each time I looked in the mirror, I found it hard to tell myself that and believe those words. Being in an immigrant household, my parents often reminded me to toughen up, pointing out that many people faced hardships far greater than mine. Taking this into account, I tried to apply this perspective when faced with my own challenges. However, this lesson was put to the ultimate test when even stepping outside my house became a challenge for me. When I looked in the mirror, I didn't see a typical teenager; I saw a blank canvas. I felt disfigured.

Diagnosed with alopecia, a condition that left me grappling with my self-image, I could never quite recall the last time I didn't spend a significant amount of time getting ready to go outside. The routine of putting on a wig, drawing on my eyebrows, and perfecting my makeup became a necessity rather than a choice. This ritual felt like a burdensome reminder of what I lacked.

I sought solutions tirelessly, from dermatologists to unconventional treatments, but to no avail. High school was not invented with balding teenagers in mind. Despite this, the stage beckoned. Tchaikovsky's notes were filled with richness, my tutu glistened—all of it beautiful. How could I give up something so profound? Tchaikovsky's sister passed away shortly before he started composing the score and although he wanted to refuse the commissions, he couldn't bring himself to do so. I couldn't either.

Pose. The dance ended. Blinded by the spotlights, bravos sprinkled across the audience as I took my bow. Much of what happens in life is beyond my control, but how I respond to these events is within my power. Rather than hiding in self-pity, my acceptance towards my canvas allowed me to see vulnerability not as a weakness, but as a strength. Life takes everyone by surprise, but the challenges are what teach us the lessons and make us stronger.

Behind the seemingly plain canvas, now I see a confident young girl whose intelligence, kindness, and character truly define her. Appearance is not what fills our canvas with beautiful colors and strokes; it is our personality and our actions that do so. Seeking the unknown and making new connections fills our perspective on other people's canvases, transforming them from grayscale images into vibrant, dynamic portraits. Living with alopecia has taught me invaluable lessons about resilience, self-acceptance, and the power of vulnerability. Through life’s challenges, I will carry on the grace and resilience instilled in me by ballet.

His head slammed into the concrete with a sickening thud. I stared at him, frozen in shock, as the afternoon sun cast a golden hue over his unconscious body there on the ground.

On a mid-October afternoon, the scent of Jasmine filled our backyard on Desert Cove as the sun glinted off our grassy backyard. During a heated soccer game, I shoved my brother too hard, and his head slammed into the concrete border of our yard.

The lessons of compassion and forgiveness typified my youth. Every night at supper, my grandmother Sabah would recite Surah Ash-Shura from the Quran, followed by Rumi's poem, “ The Seven Advices”, her voice calm and kind. At my Jesuit school, I vividly recall the teachings of Father L. as he told the story of Jesus asking Heavenly Father to forgive the men who crucified Him, challenging us to forgive as the Lord intends. Though these teachings were always present, they felt distant and abstract until that day.

As I knelt beside my brother, seeing his unconscious body and feeling the weight of my actions, all our petty arguments over the Spider-Man movies seemed trivial. The days of hospital visits and anxious waiting blurred together. I repeatedly returned to the third-floor ICU at Shea Hospital, watching the beeping monitors and mentally replaying the moment I shoved him. The fear that his injury might be permanent and my fault haunted me.

On the third day, I brought our favorite SpongeBob figurine, hoping it would comfort him if he woke up. Sitting by his bed and reminiscing about our shared laughter, I realized how much I missed our simple joys like watching CartoonNetwork together. When he finally opened his eyes, relief washed over me. Holding his hand, I whispered, “I’m sorry; I just wanted you to think I was cool—good at soccer.” The tears in my eyes were not just for the accident but for our distant relationship which I deeply regretted.

Initially overwhelmed by guilt, I avoided him, fearing his resentment. I began by offering help him with his geometry homework and inviting him to join my friends for basketball. He initially refused, telling me he was worried about rough-housing. I was sad, at first, that he would bring up the injury I caused him, but I reassured him that I would be more careful, and that I wanted to never hurt him again like that. Our games became a routine and I consistently initiated small conversations. In the weeks that followed, we began to share clothes and meals, something we had never done before. We binged all nine Spider-Man movies, debating intensely over the ”Into The Spider-Verse" and “No-Way Home” one. In the end, we both agreed that “Into The Spider Verse” was the best because of its enjoyable adventure with heart, humor, and plenty of superhero action.

Now, as we go to the gym every weekend, I see how my brother and I have grown from siblings to true companions. Our relationship is defined by our willingness to forgive and support each other. It took a traumatic event, but I see my brother differently now, and it inspires me to extend olive branches wherever I can.

As I prepare for college, I know my roommate and I will encounter disagreements, whether over noise levels during late-night study sessions or differing lifestyles. But no matter how intense our squabbles get, I'll always remember the curative power of forgiveness. Reflecting on that autumn day when I chose to shove my brother, I understand how forgiveness shapes meaningful connections. The day I chose to extend my hand and reconnect with my brother was the day I truly understood the power of forgiveness. This lesson has become the cornerstone of how I approach conflicts and relationships in my life.

My mom and I have killed over one hundred people.

In the video game Fortnite. (That was almost really bad, wasn’t it?) Our journey to becoming mother-son assassins began when my mom told me that growing up, she had always wanted to become a sniper. The problem, she explained, was that she could never stomach the idea of killing real people. I realized I had just the solution. Handing my mom a controller and booting up the Xbox, I introduced my mom to Fortnite for the first time. Have you ever seen those videos of baby giraffes trying to walk? That’s what it felt like watching my mom’s first round of Fortnite. I was subjected to a Promethean cycle of dying, resurrecting, and dying again as I taught her the purpose of every. single. button. (love you, mom!) Initially, I’d grab her controller when she was about to lose a fight (or walk off a cliff). But gradually, I stopped. Unsurprisingly, she died a lot more, but I began to realize that every mistake I didn’t fix was a chance for my mom to learn, even if it did mean we’d lose.

The love for failure I cultivated on the couch next to my mom shows up when I push for a new bench press max or have to re-re-re-read through a difficult nuance of Kant’s moral imperative. As I see myself improving with failure, I’m filled not only with a sense of resolve but also unconditional gratitude. If everything that happens is either a success or something preparing me for success, why shouldn’t I be rejoicing at every moment? In Fortnite (and in life), having what Nietchze described as a “why to bear any how” allows me to continuously develop, without fearing what I can’t control.

Despite this newfound patience, I didn’t trust my mom’s still-developing Fortnite skills. I thought that her more conservative strategy wasn’t as good as charging in guns-blazing. However, after she started to survive without my help, I realized (as all teenagers do) that I might not have all the answers. Only when I humbled myself and admitted my approach wasn’t perfect were the talents of others able to shine. This lesson has demonstrated itself in my debate career. Junior year, I did the majority of work for our group of six people, which was sometimes helpful, but often devastating when my teammates used material unfamiliar to them. My senior year, our coach resigned and I was faced with the same decision: keep trying to carry the debate team alone, or change something. I knew from losing at Fortnite that a leader who wasn’t scared to depend on others was worth five times more than someone who tried to do it themselves. This year, through calling more leadership meetings and elevating others’ strengths, I’ve tried to develop a culture of interdependence instead of one where we charge forward alone.

Dozens of rounds after our first drop into the Fortnite map, me and my mom finally secured our first Victory Royale! My mom’s excited shouts of joy made me light up. I was filled with a growing sense of satisfaction, not only at her progression but also at mine. What began as a mission to help my mom achieve her childhood dream fulfilled me even more than her. Although you may think that winning Fortnite means I pretty much have the meaning of existence figured out, I know there’s still an infinite number of things to learn. I can’t wait to find new obstacles to push me beyond my limits and make me rely on others. Whatever’s set to challenge me next, from something as small as a Fortnite round to something as existential as an epistemological debate, I know those hours sitting on the couch next to my mom has prepared me for it.

I can’t wait to teach my dad.

The problem in front of me was clear: Given a few months and a Person object p (where p is the high school graduate), return a 650 word essay that perfectly encapsulates the entire 18 years of existence of the high school graduate. The faint glow of the computer illuminates steep piles of notes scattered across my desk. I lean back in my chair and glance over at the clock in the corner. It’s midnight. How am I ever going to finish this? I’ve now spent the last few weeks feeling desperately lost about my personal statement — coming up with a dozen drafts and yet not feeling satisfied with any of them. I can feel my eyelids start to flutter. I fight the feeling, but I know I’ll lose consciousness soon.

Then something clicks. I jolt awake and frantically begin tapping away at the keys. Writing your personal statement is exactly like solving a programming problem. I take a minute to consider this, balancing it against my suspicion that delirium is getting the best of me... No, this is a great idea. I begin to lay out the steps and match them to my current predicament.

Step 1: State the goal to achieve in an unambiguous, specific and direct manner
In programming, this step allows us to identify the tasks ahead without any ambiguity. The same applies for personal statements — after all, the prospect of writing a 650 word essay that “encapsulates all 18 years of my experience” is, to say the least, daunting. After some research, I realize that the goal I was really targeting was: Given a few months and a Person object p, return a unique (i.e. different from most other essays), personal (i.e. revealing an important insight about your personality) and focused (i.e. focusing on one event, person or activity) essay that accurately represents who you are as a person.

Step 2: Try solving the problem yourself. Take the given example inputs, work through the problem and convert them to the corresponding outputs.
The next step programmers take is to figure out how the algorithm works. You do this by trying to solve the problem on your own (like a math problem). This process allows programmers to identify specific patterns and procedures they can use in their solutions. While the personal statement is obviously not a math problem, I realize that I can still try to find patterns and procedures — just in a very different manner. I could use the pattern finding skills I developed by pouring through papers while doing research projects. I begin opening endless tabs of YouTube videos made by students who got accepted to their dream universities and analyze them to understand what techniques made their personal statements so effective.

Step 3: Outline the algorithm to use
After that, programmers outline the algorithm’s steps. Based on the information I previously learned, I begin to create an outline for the algorithm involved here using a mind map. Mind maps are a technique I’ve used extensively because they allow me to focus on logical understanding and reveal unintuitive insights.

Step 4: Write the code
This is where programmers actually write the code they’ll use to solve the problem. This code is written according to the outline of the algorithm created previously. In the context of college essays, I realize this just means writing my essay according to the steps of the algorithm I had previously created.

Step 5: Test the code
The last and most hated part of the programming process is testing the code. In the context of college essays, it’s not so bad. I realize this step involves showing my essay to my friends, family, teachers and counselors. They'll likely give me feedback that I can then use to refine my essay. Speaking of which, I’ve gotta go “test” this essay with my parents now. Hopefully they aren’t too confused by this insanity…

The screen was blank, with only a blinking white line interrupting the grayness. I had grown accustomed to the sight, but the line's urgency for combating the void never ceased. This time, it was pleading for a warrior. My fingers flew across the keyboard in response; as I slammed "Enter," Subjugator shattered that void with the thrust of her holographic shield.

The sci-fi fighter is a recent addition to online roleplaying, an activity I stumbled upon while doom-scrolling through YouTube recommendations during the COVID-19 pandemic. Its opportunity to let my imagination run wild by acting out fictional characters fascinated me. Within four years, I was raining down electron beams as "Subjugator" against alien spaceships of the vicious Kneall splashing excitement into an 8-to-4 school day surrounded by sleep-deprived students toiling for A's.

But my first character, a rust-colored dragon named Orion, revealed roleplay was more than fanciful acting. As he conquered the seas with dragon and human comrades on steamship S.S.No, unforgettable memories of feverish planning and joyful bonding with strangers on Discord servers inspired 13-year-old me (who struggled to bother the McDonald's cashier for an extra spoon) to develop those human connections in reality. Mirroring how Orion guided recruits, I guided struggling classmates through debugging fickle Arduino wires and chips and sketching diagrams of revolving parabolas around the y-axis, each explanation as detailed as the sunset scene casting the intertwined shadows of Orion and Permafrost against the ocean. As Orion gained the confidence to battle against saboteurs from the Villain Clubhouse, I replicated his strength in challenging Dr. Anderson's perception of the post-WWII baby boom's effect and cracking jokes with the audience before my nerve-wracking piano rendition of Zenzenzense.

The lessons didn't stop with Orion: my fiery Flareon Floof, who dipped his paw into the complexities of Astral's city life after a nomadic childhood, inspired me to dip my stylus into digital art. When my hand felt heavy with the weight of a client's art commission, reminiscing of Floof's tribulations of gaining his adoptive parents' trust convinced my hand to draw the next stroke; it was either make good on your efforts or disappoint expectations, and a proud $40 indeed wasn't a disappointment (fusing a spaceship with a girl was a challenge for my first commission)!

Sure, roleplaying is acting. But without the seas of Pyrrhia kick-starting Orion's adventure, I might've chosen a different life path; acting out Orion's maintenance of the S.S.No's engine sparked an interest in joining my high school's robotics club. As I sketched drivetrain designs and assembled catapults, Orion and I brainstormed how to improve our robot builds. Gaining the team leader position earned a snarling lecture from Floof, warning not to micromanage every role like previous leaders; I placed my trust in towering Ricky, who excelled at coding C++, and freshman Jackson, whose RC experience outweighed mine. When examining previous losses to strategize a victory, Subjugator's battle-trained eye spotted how the opponent stole unattended triballs for points. After winning our first semi-final victory, followed by a crushing team group hug and hoarse cheers, my passion for engineering robotics became clear. That blinking line, which created my characters and their lessons, had transcended into my hands.

Those who have created their mark on history, the cumulative efforts of science since the dawn of man, and the pens of authors more influential than any weapon all involve humans who've used their blinking lines to complete their story. And like Subjugator crashlanding into a thicketed forest of an unknown planet, I feel my story will continue on to discover my impact on the world. As her white-haired silhouette pries herself from a muddy crater, I wield the lessons of human connections and responsibility in one hand and the blinking line of creation in another, slicing through the void of tomorrow for my next roleplay: conquering the trials of university to engineer my intangible imagination into reality.

It’s bad when tech support knows your voice. It’s worse when they start providing restaurant recommendations.

My first birthday invitation referred to me as allari pilla (mischievous girl in Telugu), proudly mentioning that I could run around and break my dad's computer. I’ve broken three more since (along with many other devices).

Each situation got dubbed a nickname: Citrustrophe, Cookiecrash, and Ice-aster.

Citrustrophe: Immersed in updating my art business's website—hundreds of tabs open and Gracie Abrams blaring—an idea sparked, causing me to leap from my seat, accidentally dousing my laptop in lemonade. Despite hours of troubleshooting with online support, diligently following each instruction, it succumbed to its sugary demise.

Cookiecrash: While baking cookies to share with friends, I was viewing a complex recipe on my laptop. Amidst the frenzy of measuring ingredients and mixing batter, I spilled flour across the keyboard. My frantic attempts with compressed air and YouTube tutorials yielded no results.

Ice-aster: I was savoring the leftover ice from my energy drink—a normal habit of mine—my damp fingers touched my laptop one too many times while organizing my next art exhibition.

Disheartened after the third mishap, I recognized I wanted to seize control of the situation. I began following an online course with videos regarding refurbishing computers. This decision stemmed not only from my need to repair what I damaged but also my fascination with how things work. After spending time taking reference pictures for a painting I spent my entire weekend contemplating how a camera works. How do various focal lengths alter perspective in photography? How does it know what to focus on? Another time I disassembled an old alarm clock. "What makes the hands move precisely at that speed? Why does it produce that ticking sound?" Each answer sparked new questions, fueling my quest for knowledge.

Initially, the complexity made me feel my time could be better spent elsewhere, and I considered quitting. Troubleshooting guides and repair tutorials felt like labyrinths with countless late nights spent grappling with hardware issues and deciphering technical jargon. Tackling a relentless cycle of computer issues seemed less daunting in comparison. However, with tools and screws scattered like breadcrumbs around me, I persevered. The more I learnt the more my frustrations transformed into a genuine appreciation for the craft and eventually a hobby.
The quiet hum of the fan and the screen's glow slowly coming to life filled me with satisfaction. Each part I replaced, upgrade I installed, and connection I re-soldered symbolized a fresh start. I realized these repairs were more than technical fixes; they represented the beauty of impermanence and the potential for renewal.
After learning in World Geography about the detrimental impacts of the digital divide, I decided to put my skills to better use. I collected discarded devices from my community to refurbish and donate to those in need locally and abroad, like in India. I installed educational software and internet browsers, ensuring the computers were equipped for learning and connectivity. One recipient, a bright student named Aanya’s smile lit up the photo as she unboxed her refurbished laptop, eyes sparkling with dreams of online courses. Witnessing recipients' gratitude highlighted the power of transformation.
These experiences taught me that impermanence often leads to abandoning things easily. However, with creativity and flexibility, we can cause beautiful transformations. This mindset applies not only to objects but also to opportunities. Endings can pave the way for new beginnings when approached with the right perspective.
Sixteen years later, my passion for exploring the unknown continues to thrive. I’ve learned that just as a broken computer can be revived, so can discarded opportunities reflecting the potential for renewal in both technology and society. I aim to channel my skills and curiosity into making a meaningful impact, repairing and innovating wherever I go. I aspire to inspire others to see potential in what is often discarded, fostering new beginnings from apparent endings.

Snakefruits brown and scaly. Rambutans red as rubies. In my mother’s garden, at the tender age of five, I learned how small we truly are against the grand tapestry of nature. At school, I was struck by the alluring beauty of endangered species like the Sumatran tiger, the Bali Myna, and the Tapanuli Orangutan. Yet, a harsher truth emerged from my mother’s teachings and the lessons at school: humans possess an immense capacity for destruction far surpassing nature’s ability to defend itself.

My advocacy journey began in the summer of 2023 when I interned at Fairatmos, Indonesia’s first climate tech company. I had always had a passion for technology, tinkering past midnight with scripts in my Roblox Studio as a child and studying Python as soon as I got to middle school. But I didn’t know that I could combine my love for tech with my passion for climate advocacy until I interned at Fairatmos. What captivated me about Fairatmos was its groundbreaking business model, which seamlessly integrates nature-based solutions—like carbon sequestration through forests and mangrove swamps—with cutting-edge technologies, including satellites and drones, to measure the net additionality of carbon offsets precisely.

The summer of 2024 marked an exhilarating turn in my journey as I returned to work on Fairatmos' conservation project in Cilacap. When I mentioned going there and staying in a remote village for my internship, even my mother resisted, citing how vastly different things would be from the comforts of our home in Jakarta. However, I insisted that I must go there to gain firsthand experience in conservation efforts, and contribute meaningfully to protecting the fragile ecosystem that the local residents dearly preserve. Eventually my mother relented.

The Cilacap mangrove swamp, spanning 5,000 acres, is a vibrant ecosystem teeming with biodiversity essential for carbon absorption. Yet, industrialization, illegal logging, and pollution are slowly destroying this vital ecosystem. The disappearance of these mangroves would leave Cilacap vulnerable to increased coastal erosion and flooding, jeopardizing the livelihoods of local communities, who depend on the mangroves for fishing and aqua farming. Protecting and restoring the Cilacap mangrove swamp was, therefore, urgent.

Initially, adjusting to the internship demands amidst the village’s poor living conditions was challenging. However, my self-pity disappeared as I grew to appreciate the mission’s significance. At the village, I had the privilege of exchanging captivating stories and innovative business ideas with the locals. From Harris and his fellow fishermen, who optimized spaces around mangrove roots for aqua farming, to Kuntoro, who cooked delicious toffee candies from mangrove fruits, I was struck by the resourcefulness of these community members.

The community’s resourcefulness and vibrance was present in the students at the local school as well. Rachmat, for example, asked about the programming skills needed to become an ethical hacker. At the same time, Zakri worked with me on an Excel sheet to forecast the financial return of establishing an eco-tourism business in Cilacap. These children, full of life and dreams, fueled my determination to safeguard our planet for their future.

In my university life, I envision collaborating with students, alumni and sustainable local businesses to build an app for the Cilacap forest. This app will generate revenue for conservation through in-person eco-tourism packages, virtual tours and paid webinars. It would facilitate donations through a secure portal and allow crowdfunding campaigns for specific projects. It will also include an e-commerce platform for sustainable foods, eco-friendly merchandise, and an adopt-a-tree program. Finally, through the app, I will increase user engagements through interactive learning modules, community forums, volunteer programs, educational partnerships, research collaborations, and corporate sponsorships, to raise awareness about Cilacap mangrove ecosystems.

My climate advocacy journey has shown me that a dedication to environmental advocacy, grounded in humility, intellectual curiosity, and common sense, can drive meaningful change. By continuing to nurture my passion for nature on campus, I hope to inspire others to join me in protecting our planet for generations to come.

**Essay:**

The sound of fate clattering against the hardwood floor penetrates the air. A few seconds later, fate rolls to a stop. Silence. I hold my breath.

“5 and 3, so 8.”

My dad cheers with excitement — I can’t help but smile; his joy is infectious! My mom groans as her civilization’s supply drought continues. The sound triggers a memory from my childhood game nights. I offer her a few of my bricks and she leans over to give me a loving hug.

***

For the first nine years of my life, I thrived in Singapore. I remember spending Saturdays with my uncle at the zoo, marveling at giant pandas and laughing at his howler monkey imitation. Meals with my aunt felt special too — she would often take time off work to join in with my palak paneer obsession.

When I moved to New Jersey in 2016, however, the happiness I shared with relatives was barred behind nineteen hours of cramped seats and the occasional jolt of turbulence. Separated from the comforting routines and familiar faces of my previous home, I turned to the internet for a solution.

I dove into headfirst into articles about combating loneliness and soon stumbled upon a blog praising the benefits of family game nights. Motivated, I spent hours after soccer practice searching for the perfect virtual game until I found Colonist.io, an online Settlers of Catan platform. After a few video calls with my family to learn the game rules, it didn’t take long for a weekly round of Catan to become routine.

My aunt’s lethargic playstyle earned her the title “World’s Slowest Player.” She was so slow we started setting a fifteen-minute timer for her turns! The ensuing laughter when the timer rang never failed to lift my spirits. Meanwhile, my uncle’s tendency to hoard resources often led to hilarious clashes with the supply-stealing robber. Laughing with my uncle, even if only on a video call, filled me with the sense of warmth I remembered so fondly from our Saturday trips.

It was moments like these that etched themselves into the family lore, making the oceans between us seem a little smaller.

The Catan sessions were the highlight of my week, but as I transitioned into high school, once a week turned into once a month. Trying to balance school and sports with the twelve-hour timezone difference was exhausting.

The sense of separation from years earlier started to resurface, but this time, I was armed with a new understanding of human connection; My hours of trading wood for brick in Catan weren’t for nothing:

My first experience with Devin, marked by chlorine and erratic splashing, was quite a spectacle — his efforts to corral my abysmal butterfly technique were in vain. But as my form improved with his coaching, I discovered our shared passion for mangoes, prompting me to save a few from every box to share.

Over time, Devin became a close family friend, frequently joining my dad and me on lighthearted runs and workouts. He even played Catan with us from time to time, replicating a sense of home I hadn’t felt since my days in Singapore.

***

As I reflect on my previous constructions, I study the playing field — littered with roads stretching across plains and curving around mountains, each hex tile bringing me closer to my family. This world, residing in a six-inch device in my pocket, will always be ready to blossom anywhere with a stable internet connection.

In college, I’m eager to connect with diverse individuals and role models, embracing their unique playing styles with open-mindedness. And my journey in engineering, like a Catan board, will be full of challenges and opportunities for innovation. But I know that with the same collaborative spirit and adaptability from my family game nights, I’ll be ready to navigate the landscape of my college journey, regardless of how the dice roll.

“Where is your manager, I need to speak to them.”

Yikes, not the best opener I thought to myself.

As the lady behind the counter told me in broken English that I couldn’t speak to the manager, I took a mental note to never ask that again. I went back to the car, smiled, and added my first tally mark to my list. 1 down, 64 more to go.

During the hot summer days, you could find my dad and I at our dining table, scavenging papers of prototypes and product presentations. In the evening, you could find us in the car, driving for hours on end, racing the sun to go to as many local restaurants as we could before night fell. This was the start of our journey to expand our family business, 20X Media: an all-in-one platform for customer management, growth tips, you name it. Our plan was to offer restaurants a loyalty program based around the idea of digital stamp cards/rewards programs that incentivize customers to come back. I started by eagerly waiting in the car for my dad's meeting recaps, then accompanying him while he did the talking, and finally, taking the lead on pitches myself.

The more restaurants we visited, the more disappointing the results became. Each rejection felt like a door slamming shut, quieting the hopeful ideas in my head. Maybe I just wasn’t cut out to be a female entrepreneur. I was certain of that after 17 rejections. Yet, my dad congratulated me. In fact, he challenged me to get 65 rejections before I graduated.

On the 23rd try, we finally hit a breakthrough. The small Thai store near our house, one of my favorite places to eat, became the setting for our first success. As my dad and I sat down with the restaurant owner, the familiar aroma of lemongrass and basil filled the air, creating a comforting atmosphere that contrasted with my nervous excitement.

The ceiling fan whirred softly overhead as my dad finished his part of the presentation, discussing statistics and business reports. I could see the owner's eyes light up with interest. Then, it was my turn. Taking a deep breath, I launched into explaining the process of how our loyalty program works and why it's important for small businesses like theirs.

The owner nodded, his fingers tapping thoughtfully on the wooden table. "This could really bring in more regular customers," he mused aloud. To our delight, the owner agreed it was a good idea and even offered us some food to take home. As we sat in the car, basking in the glow of our first success, I couldn't help but laugh a little to myself about what had happened. It was laughter not only from the joy of successfully onboarding a restaurant, but a reflection of the person I'd grown into. Starting in high school, I couldn’t even order food for myself. I was so nervous to talk to the baristas that I always had my brother do it for me. I skipped many school events like homecoming, the school volleyball tournaments, football games, and more, because I wasn’t comfortable putting myself out there. I was a terrible public speaker, and I even froze in front of my judge at the state competition my first year in DECA.

A week has passed, and I visit the same Thai restaurant, now marketing the flyers I had developed, plastered all over the windows and tables inside. The bell rings as I walk in and the owner gladly directs me to my seat with a grin, recognizing me from afar. From the corner of my eyes, I see a curious family wiggle over to the corner to sign the QR code on my flyer to register for our program, before our eyes meet.

Not a single object on my desk has been moved in years, even dead pens. Chipped cookie tins and mason jars filled with brush pens and special-edition calligraphy tips sits in the corner, eager to embrace additions. Scattered notebooks and sticky-notes of 2 A.M. font practices create Jenga-pile barricades, a simple tap away from collapsing. Yet, nothing (emphasis on nothing) gets moved. Instead, this maze of lettering and calligraphy tools only builds. What seems like clutter to most, in reality, is a bourg that tells an untold story of emancipation.

My journey with lettering began quite early. Waiting for hours outside cardiologists’ offices contemplating why my dad periodically hid from me and why my mom refused to answer, I remember ripping out chunks of newspaper headings and imitating sans-serif fonts with hospital gel pens. As a reserved little girl who grew accustomed to silencing herself—but still managed to formulate strange notions and interrogations every millisecond—I simply copied characters to fill temporary voids my own repression enlarged. My mantra: do not ruin the harmony of congruent letters. Silence and congruence only became synonyms.

Gripping the same inflexible pens that haunted me of deafening silences in hospitals, at home, and everywhere I went, I used countless notebooks to perfect each character: same size, same strokes, same ink intensity. My desk became a canopy of immaculately lettered alphabets for years, echoing an obsession with orderly compliance and muting an ardent wildness. Nothing would change.

That was until, in freshman year, I unintentionally bought a Tombow Fudenosuke brush pen, not knowing it was for calligraphy.

It was nothing but odd: every stroke was painstakingly different from the previous, and it would not conform to structure.

I couldn’t throw it out though….

Months of battling with it led me to begin accepting the unconventional cursive it produced. Strangely, when I used it, something enchanted me—an inexplicable part of me liked that it was obdurate, even against my own will. I was free from rigidity when I held it, and every use crafted a novel lettering style Canva or the newspaper had yet to discover.

If I had only ever forced myself to copy those symmetric letters, what was wrong with embracing calligraphy’s subdued anarchy?

That distinctive style unexpectedly gave me comfort, one that coerced me to speak and ask, loudly. And before I was conscious of it, it became mine, all while those gel pens dried out.

While my Tombow passed away sophomore year, it left with an everlasting influence. I was used to breaking old precedents without the fears that used to restrain me: I remodeled the organizational structure of the Youth Passion Project; I changed the protocol in my project on lupus to adopt a new technique never studied before; I considered new protein interactions in my neuropsychiatric lupus project I was scared to; I played games with my students during tutoring sessions; I asked my parents and teachers questions; and I made jokes during my AcaDec competition speeches. I learned to value the brilliance hidden within every unspoken thought I suppressed, all because of a pen’s ability to do what I never could.

Even today, my Tombow has an abode in that constantly evolving village, and those bittersweet gel pens will never be exiled either. It’s been years since they passed, but they rest on a make-do grave next to assemblages of old letterings that piles of my own fonts have overtaken.

My desk houses more brush pens now, though, all ready to venture through eccentric avenues. In the process of lettering, inexplicably, I freed myself of the shackles that reticence and submission once gripped me with, with pens becoming the liberators of odd fonts and my outlandish ideas. As I continue collecting these instruments of discovery in college, my new desk will certainly mirror newer stories but never substitute those jars of dead pens at home.

Chewed paper is my utmost favorite thing in the world.

I don’t chew paper (even if I did, no medieval torture device could extort that information out of me). What I mean is papier-mâché: chewed paper.

Before I could even write on paper, kaka, my grandfather taught me to mix it with water and turn it into art. In retrospect, this was a rather odd thing to teach a child. There were days I thought I was Truman from the Truman show and this man is an actor paid to prank me. While my friends got chocolates from their grandparents, mine brought me more and more paper. Not that I complained. One anecdote about NASA using papier-mâché to create mock-ups of spacecraft had me intrigued. Then he actually made me a spaceship with paper and eight year old me knew then this man wasn't an actor but really my kaka.

But, with time, the hands that had so deftly shaped my dreams grew wrinkled and finally fell still. FAST. Face, Arms, Speech, Time. An acronym I have stapled to my mind now. It’s how you know that someone’s having a stroke. But, at ten, I didn’t know, didn’t understand the reason for his sudden disappearance. I only remember my mother sobbing on the kitchen floor, each wave of grief like turning over the same pages of a book over and over again.

Through the haze of it all, I recall learning how to perform CPR, reading research papers on high blood pressure as my mother had it too so I needed to be able to help if the next time it was Ma instead, learning how to cook meals for the household…anything that could help lessen the burden and stuff the gaping hole in my chest. (Nothing was) FAST (enough).

My nervous limbs—no longer tethered to the patient art of papier-mâché—sought other forms of release. I started playing kho-kho and sports stadiums became my refuge. But, this was temporary too. On the verge of winning a game, as I leaped to tag a defender, I lost more than the match. Diagnosed with a chronic fracture at fourteen, I lost the ability to play kho-kho again.

My broken leg felt like gloopy paper, too watered down to save, too damaged to be art anymore.

But, time heals—or, in this case, dries. In time, my tears and my plaster dried. And the smell of my musty plaster drying led me back to someone whose fingers I’d held as I’d taken my very first steps.

I bought myself plenty of paper. With twists of my wrists, I used wads of old paper and new metal crutches to shape myself into someone Kaka would be proud of. The way that he’d taught me to turn gooey mush into art, I fashioned myself into an impressionist painting: smudged, imperfect, but authentically, originally me.

I wasn’t able to help Kaka or Ma in their times of need. But, I could carry forward my kaka’s legacy and the values that Ma had instilled in me. So, I dragged myself to a place where I could see glimpses of him. As soon as my legs recovered, I started volunteering at the Unnayan, an organization for older individuals with special needs.

Since then, I’ve spent my weekends organizing fundraisers and events, steering initiatives to ensure that the inmates received the support they needed. I was alive and breathing and grateful. And Arham, Mahanta uncle, and Kritika were people whose lives I could help shape better the way I had shaped mine.

Now, whenever life presents me with gloopy, mulchy problems, I say “Thank you!” and wonder how best to turn them into art. My creative skills are my inheritance and I intend to nurture them through and beyond college. Every discarded object, each individual has something that can be redeemed and reshaped. The mushy, chewed-up paper inside all of us is just waiting for someone to believe in them, for someone to mold them into magnificent cartonería.

Abraham Lincoln said, “yes,” so I have to oblige, I thought. I was in 5th grade and had just asked my Abraham Lincoln bobblehead if I should play basketball. Every slight nudge sent the peculiar figure into a hypnotic cadence, acknowledging every thought with unquestionable agreement. He was Honest Abe, he’d never lie to me, I’d say. But, his absence of diverse answers and communication led me to explore the special stories of people around me.

***

“Bye-lo, bye-lo!” It was these daily farewells from our 70-year-old bus driver, Mr. Gary, that kept me motivated during arduous times. During bus rides, he’d let me slip in 15 minutes of computer work on an AP Seminar project on pharmaceutical prices while displaying his love for Elvis’ songs. I’d talk to him about anything: his enjoyment of talking to high schoolers, his eccentric experiences as a policeman, and his hope about his upcoming heart surgery. Through each start of the engine, Mr. Gary with his unwavering positivity has taught me the value of optimism. He has inspired me to cultivate joy for others by organizing flourishing Friday debates in school for any student to engage on exciting topics, playing Elvis songs in the background.

***

Stranger danger. Albeit a common phrase, it was how I felt trembling towards a doorbell, attempting to present a caricatured version of my confidence for a donut fundraiser. I stumbled on words and scattered my eyes, avoiding eye contact. But, each doorbell I rang gradually eased me into conversing with people. However, a vital factor made it easy: everyone’s happy if you offer donuts, chocolate, and all things sweet. Politics wasn’t as sweet. I quickly understood that when my first calls to voters featured silence, “not interested”s, and one particularly furious voter criticizing my “rendition of conspiracies”. But each rare conversation was too eye-opening to avoid, hearing voters’ livelihoods and what they care for. It was with these voters that I organized postcard campaigns and canvassing, utilizing novel political messaging. Whether it's selling cookies or selling the merits of single-payer healthcare for Georgia politicians, I rejoice indulging in the dangers of talking to strangers.

***

I swung the door open. My heated face became cognizant of the swirling coolness of the Boston air. I had exited an exhilarating debate round regarding right-to-work laws, harboring a longing desire to know how the judge evaluated the correlation between unionization and outsourcing. While debate tournaments were instilled with competitiveness, it was these moments in between rounds I was fond of. I spoke with debaters from JR Masterman delineating their struggle as a small school to financially access coaching and others discussing inequalities stemming from debate. These anecdotes encouraged me to harness my talent and initiate free coaching, targeting students from low-income Title 1 Schools and rural regions. The “OHHHHs” of the first few students served as an alluring incentive to go further and let others swing their doors of debate open.

***

“You may not have noticed, but I’m actually blind.” I met Germaine Barrett, a strong advocate for debate, when I traveled to Jamaica, and never had he mentioned his blindness till then. Through his unyielding spirit and candid observations, he offered me a glimpse of his world, shaped not by sight, but by the sounds of yearning Jamaican students debating in aging buildings. My days involved helping him navigate new terrain and co-facilitate classes filled with energetic discussions such as comparing social contract theory to anarchy for hundreds of students. Germaine’s pragmatic approach to his hurdles reshaped my perception of resiliency from one of just being blinded by grand gestures to prioritizing consistent acts of perseverance.

***

As I hop on the bus to college, I am enthusiastic about building upon these fountains of narrative I’ve been inspired by. I won’t be a bobblehead in agreement as I intersect my interests in debate and political advocacy to spark real change.

"This can't be real, can it?" I thought to myself. A sudden jolt rattled my body accompanied by the sickening sound of crumpling metal. My heart pounded loudly in my chest. Panic welled up inside me as I realized what had happened - I failed to notice the oncoming traffic before continuing forward due to the broken light. My father and I sat there at the intersection by Chinatown, staring at the dust-covered car sitting in front of us.

The car accident in my junior year of high school made me recognize the value of everyday moments of focus. Though no one was hurt, I felt a solemn sense of responsibility for the damage my actions had caused. I took it upon myself to deal with the insurance company. Every action required much concentration; I needed to remember every second of the accident, provide accurate personal information, and thoroughly understand the insurance process so that the insurance company would fully cover the expenses. Throughout this entire situation, my parents were never mad or disappointed; they simply wanted me to work through this conflict and gain experience from it. Their steadfast support for my growth instilled a sense of accountability and a need to become more reliable, pushing me to become more meticulous with my actions and to fully commit to the tasks at hand, becoming someone others could fully rely on.

At work, I embraced this mindset. Being an assistant at my dental office required diligence and care. In the past, I sometimes became distracted at work, missing details in patient files, or not noticing when Dr. Jiang needed a different dental instrument, but now I felt a renewed sense of determination, committed to being fully present and attentive. A blonde, middle-aged woman had come into our clinic, needing to get her crown replaced. During the two-hour process, I quickly prepared and handed dental instruments to Dr. Jiang. I constantly hovered over the patient, removing any excess saliva she had, being careful to avoid the sensitive tooth which needed the dental crown. Outside the treatment room, I triple-checked patient insurance and expenses for accuracy. Knowing both the dental office and patients were relying on me, I couldn’t afford to miss any details and cause unnecessary costs. Many patients, and even Dr. Jiang, noticed and began to thank me for my thoroughness.

As I adapted, I encountered a few hurdles. During our group mousetrap car project for physics, we were required to have the car roll a randomized distance. I was committed to crafting the perfect car, and recording the number of rotations, down to the millimeter, needed to reach every possible distance we could be assigned. However, I found myself frustrated, struggling to find time due to the upcoming rotation test also in physics. Eventually, I chose to devote my time to the mousetrap car project, knowing that others were relying on my meticulousness to succeed. Though I was unable to focus on the rotation test, it felt good knowing our team was able to succeed because of the extra details I had spent time on. I learned to choose my battles wisely, and to absolve myself from the unrealistic expectation of meticulousness in every situation.

While the aftermath of the car accident has gradually receded, the accountability and attentiveness I gained have not. Reflecting on this experience, I realize that though the car accident was a harsh reminder of the consequences of inattention, it has made me more dependable and helped develop a renewed sense of focus which I now apply to the work I do. As I continue into college, I hope to continue being meticulous and deeply accountable for all aspects of my work, not just for my own benefit, but for those around me as well. I want to contribute a reliable and focused mindset and inspire others to do the same.

**What We Owe Ourselves**

Have you ever felt the feeling of someone stepping on your chest and making it near impossible for you to breathe? This past year it felt like the school year had just started and I looked down and I looked back up and it was week fifteen and I was drowning. I wanted to hit the ground running so I took on way too much and while no one thing was overwhelming a combination of things caught up to me. At the end of each day I was tired and stressed and all I wanted to do was have a good supper and crash but there was still a pile of work I had yet to do. But the instant I began to consider if this was making me unhappy, I thought “everyone else seems to be doing fine, maybe I’m just lazy.”

I think most folks know the feeling all too well.

But what do we owe ourselves?

Sure, everything I did felt like I had a good reason for doing it; everything was something I wanted to do and cared deeply about. But the work gradually felt like it became a checklist to complete instead of something that actually helped me learn and grow as a person. And no matter how hard I worked I was able to do almost everything I needed to do, but never everything. So I thought if I worked a little bit longer, was a little more efficient or a bit more disciplined I could finally get on top of everything, and then life would be good.

But that’s not real. That pretend land where everything is flowing neatly and efficiently and happily, that doesn’t exist.

Self-deception remains the easiest deception. Everyone, myself included, has all these goals and ambitions, hopes and dreams. Some part of me tolerates nothing but self-perfection, thinks that “if I could just achieve X and Y and Z, everything would be ok.” The insidious part of all this is I genuinely don’t know if this is a culture problem or a me problem. But what if I spend my entire life waiting for the day that I can appreciate the things in front of me, only to realize that I could have done that decades ago?

The answer isn’t to sacrifice your sanity and achieve that goal because that never ends. There’s no guarantee you’ll be happy in ten years, you can only be happy right now. The goal of life shouldn’t be to reach a place where we can finally feel happy, but to live a life where we’re happy doing what we’re doing every day, filled with joy at the fact that slowly but surely, we are better than we once were.

Things that have made my life really beautiful haven’t been achieving some peak level of efficiency or fulfilling some ambition, after all. It’s the small things that I remember.

This summer my dad and I hiked through a small strip of the California coastline. I remember we stopped and sat on a rock that looked down towards the sea. On the shoreline of the sea there were pebbles and boulders, and the swell of clear water was as blue as the sky. The sea sparkled in the sun as it looked across to the shrubs and the trees that dotted the plain to the mountains. The shrubs and the trunks of the trees below were dusty and water, stirred by the breeze, stretched infinitely beyond.

We sat there for almost three hours. I didn’t think about to-do lists, work, what will I have for dinner; I just stared at the waves and I was happy.

We owe ourselves happiness. To live in the present. To be filled with joy at the fact that we’re alive. To take ourselves less seriously, make more mistakes and, decades later, look back without regret.

Most of us are instructed to have certain priorities when we are young to get us through life. For me, I was taught good grades matches your intelligence; intelligence means you don’t make stupid choices or mistakes; and the wrong choice can ruin your life. 
I believe all and none of them. 
Going through 12 years of schooling, I have seen my dad who once excelled in school, now imprisoned for skipping out on debt and abusing, buying, and dealing drugs. As young kids, we didn’t see the bruises in his arms, dry skin, headaches, or mood swings. What we did hear was the midnight screaming from beneath our blankets. But my mom heard, felt, and saw it all.

And it’s why, during that time of living under an abusing father, she went undercover. Doing all the preparation beforehand, she knew we would only have one day to pack up everything and move safely. Never having a steady, climbing job before, she found her first software job and plucked my 11-year-old self and two younger siblings to a rundown rental. From this, we went on a new adventure of autonomy while my dad chose to further fall into the reliance of alcohol, smoking, and heroin. After being in jail a few times, 7 years later he is finally in prison allowing my family to feel a little safer.

However, moving so suddenly, packing up everything we could within a workday changed my whole outlook. Not only did my once outgoing personality become timid, suppressing my past, but I also welcomed others to open up to me more. I set myself as the therapist, negotiator and role model of the family. My siblings looked up to me in how I managed my longtime friendships and schoolwork. Whilst my mom revealed things about my dad with drugs that not many elementary school kids could not say they shared.
Admittedly, leaving my dad affected me more than I would like to admit. Namely how focused I became on what could lie in the future. My family’s safety, money issues, and being a minority race in my school were only a few things I became anxious about. Always trying to think ahead and plan out multiple solutions worked my brain overtime. But my mom came to my rescue when I needed her most. She proved to me that a doubtful choice can change your life for the better; shown when leaving my dad. This demonstrated to me life is about taking calculated chances, giving me the courage to find my footing in a love for writing and learning about the business world. 
While it took until senior year, I observed how as we grow, we are told many things most people must follow. But we are not told how this advice is set as an overall scale. As you mature, it is your job to find that balance in school, work, family, morals, and hobbies to what best fits your personal scale of growth. 
For my scale, performing well in school means hardworking and ambitious. Making mistakes allows you to acquire knowledge for fast thinking and problem solving. And now I explain to those younger that whether it be what college they choose or ice cream flavor, it will not ruin their life. It is what you do after choosing that will alter your life for the worse, or for the best. It's why I know I won’t regret going to (college), as long as I continue to keep that balance of working hard, keeping my family close, and continuing to make mindful errors.

Music intertwines seamlessly with everything I learn and do. Whether doing homework or reading, music makes the learning process more enjoyable and enhances my understanding of the material. Music adds to everything by providing a sense of familiarity and clarity which I’ve found helps with my studies and supports my overall well-being in no small measure (pun earnestly intended).

One day in the car, Journey's "Don't Stop Believing" came on, and I was immediately captivated. I spent hours trying to play it on the half-sized guitar my dad gave me when I was four, but I couldn't get it right. After one lesson, my teacher said I was too young. Determined, I taught myself. My fingers stumbled, and I often felt frustrated, but I kept going. Six months later, I played a set of songs at the local library, including "Don't Stop Believing." My old teacher was in the audience, and his surprised smile was unforgettable. He invited me back for lessons, and I've been with him ever since. Soon, I took up piano, saxophone, and singing.

At thirteen, I discovered the song "To You" by blxty and mental, which opened my eyes to new music genres. I think it was then that my deep interest began to evolve into a passion for music. I fell in love with unique melodies that could evoke both joy and sorrow. I began longing to create something as beautiful. I started by recreating songs and then producing my own music. I reached out to popular artists with thousands of followers who inspired me, and to my surprise, they responded positively. Connecting with them brought me immense joy, and soon, our conversations led to collaborations where I was invited to produce and sing with them.

Encouraged by those collaborations, I thought it might be a good idea to share my music with the people around me. I volunteered to play at a senior memory care center specializing in dementia, hoping my music might bring comfort and joy to the residents.

It didn’t.

It was a humbling experience seeing how much my music didn't resonate with the audience. But I didn’t dwell too long - the answer actually came rather quickly once I realized the problem: I went home and spent some time learning older songs. Songs they knew. Songs from their youth.
