Thankfully, my next visit went quite differently than the first. One unforgettable moment came when an elderly woman with dementia recognized "Que Sera Sera" and sang along with tears in her eyes. Since then, I've continued volunteering, discovering through my own experience how music can potentially touch lives and uplift people. This strengthened my belief that music can evoke deep emotions in others just as it does for me.

But that’s not it. Music finds its way into everything I do and think about. Especially at school.

I often find connections between music and academics, drawing parallels that may not always seem logical to others. In a research lab analyzing genes, I linked DNA sequences to musical patterns. I would associate each sequence to a rhythm, and I'd hum these tunes in the lab. This made my work exciting as each DNA sequence created a new melody. Later, I was surprised to learn that researchers have created music from gene sequences, a technique known as "Protein Music”. Then I thought I wasn’t crazy after all. Music truly is everywhere I look.

Whether studying the sciences or humanities, I envision integrating music into my studies and interactions, connecting with people of all ages and backgrounds. Music has evolved beyond a passion, it has become an integral part of my inner stability.

So don’t be surprised if I’m using a music composition notebook to write down notes during a physics class.

Having an older brother sucks. It sucks when he always overshadows you. It sucks when he always beats you in soccer matches. And it really sucks when your parents, teachers, and friends all compare you to him.

Obviously, my brother is that brother. When we were at Kennywood, I had to ride the same rides he did even though I was three years younger. When we were playing our favorite video game, I had to finish faster than him in every race even though he had played for longer. And when I entered high school, I had to join the same clubs he did and do the same sports he did, just so I could be as good as him. That was the goal of my life: to be better than my brother at anything.

This began to change during my sophomore year of high school. One day, in the middle of math class, my teacher overheard me telling one of my friends that I was better than my brother at calculus. She then asked me a question no one had before: Why do you want to be your brother instead of being your own person? At the time, I just answered that it was funny. Inside myself, I knew this was a lie but even I could not find a true answer. Why did I want to be like my brother? Was all I was a copy of him?

For the rest of class, I could not stop thinking about these questions. I wanted to know who I was, not who I was trying to be. That night, I went home and convinced my parents to let me volunteer at the local veterinary hospital. I always had an interest in the healthcare field but I was fearful that if I pursued something different than my brother had, I would not be as good as him. Even so, I needed to understand who I was, and the only way I could do this was by overcoming the fear of failing to be him.

Over the next two weeks, I worked with nurses and other volunteers to treat a variety of illnesses. Although I learned that I would not want to be a veterinarian, I enjoyed helping others, even if it was through their animals. With this new experience, I decided to explore my interests, which I had never done before. I began to train harder for the upcoming track season and ran my fastest mile. Additionally, I participated in a driving race for our school’s robotics team and won, meaning I would drive our robot at the next state competition.

Although I was interested in these things, I could not stop thinking about my experience at the veterinary hospital. I loved identifying the illnesses of animals and making them, and their owners, comfortable and happy. Due to this, I applied for a volunteering position at a children’s hospital. I was quickly notified that I had been accepted as a volunteer and would start working later that month.

I found my true love for the medical field working as a volunteer. While I had always enjoyed playing sports and participating in clubs, I never felt as satisfied as I did now. Working with doctors and nurses to comfort and distract children was rewarding for me and I felt that I was making a difference in the world, one kid at a time. As my junior year approached, I continued this by running for president of my school’s national honor society. After learning that the association fundraised money for the Make-A-Wish foundation, I felt that I had to be a part of it so that I could ensure that as much money as possible was raised.

So who really am I? If my math teacher asked me that question again, I still would not be able to give her a definite answer. But I now know what I want to be: a person who makes a difference in the world.

Getting out of bed is hard. This is not because of my habitual all-nighters or crippling caffeine addiction. Rather, dozens of complete 1000-piece jigsaw puzzles stretch my bedroom floor, making for groggy Hopscotch jumps to avoid dismantling my masterpieces.

Since my first-grade teacher pulled out a 500-piece San Francisco puzzle, I have been fascinated by the inevitable, piece-by-piece creation of my favorite landmarks and alluring utopian societies. I often spent recesses and lunches twisting and turning pieces, pleading for an interlock. Frequently frustrated, scissors were utilized on a piece, leaving new tabs and blanks that created an artificial, forced match.

I soon learned that first locating important pieces, like the corners and edges, was crucial to eventual success. Blindly pairing middle pieces could work, but it often created unnecessary matching and delayed disaster. Still, a jigsaw’s foundation is its trial-and-error procedure, something I would have to accept.

This reality would craft my approach to problem-solving even outside the classroom. One month after I started experimenting with powerlifting coaching, my first client, Noah, hit a plateau on his bench press. Having experienced a similar situation, I excitedly sent him my program, expecting similar improvements. However, his progress remained stagnant over the following month. Embarrassed, I convinced myself that his external factors were the source of error. But no, his sleep and recovery were spot-on.

I then decided to think of Noah’s bench as a disorganized puzzle set with an extra amount of pieces. Locating faults in his training was conducive to weeding out irrelevant pieces. We started tracking all possible metrics: intensity, volume, frequency, and rate of perceived exertion. My scientific curiosity also propelled me to dig through kinesiology staples, such as Physiology of Sport and Exercise and Becoming a Supple Leopard, to identify possible programming faults. Within this rabbit hole, I located the culprit. Because of Noah’s long arms, benching produced more systematic fatigue than someone with more leverage. He needed a personalized program with greater intensity and lower frequency. Within eight weeks of implementing this, his bench max skyrocketed by thirty pounds. The puzzle was solved.

Thinking back, the perspective of accepting faulty matches propelled my initiation. Each problem was simply a data point, beneficial for understanding what worked and what didn’t. Visualizing this issue as a puzzle produced results for my client while I learned that unique body leverages would require personalized solutions.

Also, I realized that puzzles themselves could be a solution to problems while tutoring a middle schooler named Daniel. My first three sessions with Daniel were difficult, as he exhibited minimal excitement following my plethora of established jokes and seemed to brood about something other than learning algebra. I was shocked to learn that his uncle had passed away a few days before our first session, and understandably, the loss of this close connection preoccupied his mind.

In our fourth session, I decided to teach through something other than a whiteboard. Using Math Playground’s database of jigsaw puzzles infused with algebraic concepts as a base, I encouraged Daniel to explore the Internet’s vast number of jigsaws. He proceeded to share his screen and avidly worked through a puzzle. As he worked, I offered my condolences and asked about his favorite activity with his uncle. He instantly lit up and said it was playing soccer with him at sunset. Our conversation proceeded to traverse from soccer to In-N-Out to his life aspirations. The end of the session came too soon, as our microphones burst with giggles and we eagerly planned our next meeting time. Within a month of introducing puzzles, Daniel’s grade jumped by two letters.

Through these experiences, I discovered that jigsaw puzzles’ problem-solving capabilities can simultaneously create connections between people in diverse niches and communities. Still, my trial-and-error-solving mindset isn’t perfect. But that’s its beauty: continuously adding pieces - something I anticipate doing in college.

Looking at the sea of organized puzzles near my bed, I now realize that accidentally stepping on and dismantling them wouldn’t be disastrous. The journey of tinkering piece by piece and inevitable errors provides wisdom, making the world a tab less puzzling.

Laying there on the floor, he was unconscious. It was a warm autumn afternoon, and the sun cast a golden hue over our backyard. During a heated soccer game, I shoved my brother too hard, and his head slammed into the concrete border of our yard.

The lessons of compassion and forgiveness typified my youth. Whether it be my grandmother’s nightly recitation lines from the Quran and the Persian poet Rumi during our evening prayers emphasizing kindness and love or the teaching of Father L. at my Jesuit school challenged us to forgive as the Lord intend. These teachings were always there, but they seemed distant and abstract in that moment of panic and regret.

As I knelt beside my brother, seeing his unconscious body and feeling the weight of my actions, all our petty arguments over the Spider-Man movies seemed trivial. The following days blurred into hospital visits and anxious waiting. Each day, I returned to that sterile room, haunted by the fear that his injury might be permanent, and that it was my fault. On the fourth day, I brought our favorite SpongeBob figurine, hoping it would comfort him if he woke up. Sitting by his bed and reminiscing about our shared laughter, I realized how much I missed our simple joys like watching CartoonNetwork together, and the laughs we shared. When he finally opened his eyes, relief washed over me. Holding his hand, I whispered, “I’m sorry; I just wanted you to think I was cool—good at soccer.” The tears in my eyes were not just for the accident but for our distant relationship that I deeply regretted.

Initially overwhelmed by guilt, I avoided him, fearing his resentment. But my guilt made me seek redemption. I started by helping him with geometry homework and inviting him to join my friends for basketball. Though initially hesitant, he agreed after I reassured him that our sibling bond was more important than any game. Our games became a routine, and I consistently initiated small conversations, even when awkward. In the weeks that followed, our relationship improved. We began to share clothes and meals. We even watched all the Spider-Man movies together, and like true brothers, we agreed on the best one. This change profoundly impacted me. I learned to appreciate his perspectives and understood that vulnerability and honesty are a crucial part of forgiveness.

This newfound understanding of forgiveness wasn’t just for my family. During an overnight volunteer camp, I met Brad, a fellow camper struggling with anger issues. One evening, borrowing my treasured Celtics headphones, Brad accidentally broke them. Anger surged within me, but recalling my forgiveness to my brother, I held back from shouting abruptly. I took a deep breath and said, “It’s okay, accidents happen.” We worked together to fix the headphones by duct taping them, and later on he invited me to join his friends at the campfire. By the end of camp, we had become close friends, taking long walks together and going on mountain biking every afternoon after lunch. This act of forgiveness allowed Brad and I to see each other in a new way which otherwise would not have been possible.

Now that we go to the gym every weekend, I see how my brother and I have grown from siblings to true companions. Our relationship is defined by our willingness to forgive and support each other. This lesson permeates all my interactions. In Mr. Hutton's A-PUSH class, I initiated a "Cultural Exchange Chat" where students shared their heritage through food and stories. When Leo, whose family recently moved from Guatemala, shared his experiences of border crossing, I gained a perspective that enriched my understanding of patience.

As I prepare for college, I'm sure my roommate and I will encounter disagreements, whether over noise levels during late-night study sessions or differing lifestyles. But the lessons of forgiveness I’ve learned will help us navigate these conflicts – I expect to solve by listening and forgiving allowing me to quickly forgive and be more solution-oriented.

Reflecting on that autumn afternoon, I understand how forgiveness shapes meaningful connections. The day I chose to extend my hand and reconnect with my brother was the day I truly understood the power of forgiveness. This lesson has become the cornerstone of how I approach conflicts and relationships in my life.

**My need to understand their Why**

As a keen political aficionado with a deep understanding of governmental intricacies… wait, let me start over: I am a politics nerd. I listen to Supreme Court arguments as I fall asleep. It’s not about memorizing the cases but understanding the underlying motivation and perspectives behind the questions and tone. The “Why”.

My passion for understanding the “Why” was key to my decision to apply for and serve as a United States Senate Page. I will always remember the feeling of lying on the Rotunda floor at 3 a.m., being met by complete silence and solitude, while gazing up at the Apotheosis of Washington, brightly lit by one of the many lunettes. But what was the most meaningful part of being a page was the opportunity to connect with people and delve deeply into their unique perspectives.

Living with 29 other pages and stripped of our phones, many of us wandered around like zombies the first few weeks, figuring out how to best interact with peers from vastly different backgrounds and beliefs. One day I had an idea; I’ve always enjoyed cooking as a way to foster connections and get to know people, and I decided that soup was the answer. Soup, on one hand, is a comfort food that helps people let their guard down. On the other hand, soup is such a versatile food that anyone can add ingredients of their choice. I got things started and as soon as the smell of onions sautéing filtered down the hall, a group began to gather. With the smell of soup levitating throughout the residence, pages perked up and slowly a group was formed. In our soup, Spencer (UT-R) added jicama to give the soup a subtle sweetness and crunch; Yosef (TX-R) grated ginger to add a slight kick; and Jessie (MD-D) and I together chose parsnip, finishing the golden elixir with a slight earthiness.

As the soup simmered, guards dropped and we hung out in the kitchen stirring the soup occasionally as an excuse to be there. I started asking some questions. That later evolved into a two-hour conversation where we talked about our hometown cultures and upbringings. Spencer and I came from wildly different environments. While religion has had little impact on my political views, Spencer conversely talked about how religion has a major impact on his values and views. Spencer believed firmly that abortion was wrong, stemming from his Mormon faith. As his opinion – and faith – was staunchly different from those I was surrounded by in my hometown, I asked him many questions, wanting to understand more. Appreciative of my interest, this eventually led to an invitation from Spencer: “Just come to my church.”

So I did.

I didn’t really know what to expect going to the LDS church. But what I found was an incredibly welcoming community that was eager to answer any questions. Going to Spencer’s church sparked something in me and I began to think. I realized that going to different places of worship would be a great way to really dive deep into the communities and belief systems that often shape others’ perspectives. So for the duration of my time in Washington, I challenged myself to go to everyone’s place of worship: Aleyah’s Methodist church, nestled behind the Nats’ stadium; Chace’s Baptist church, in southwest Capitol Hill; All Saints Day Mass, near the Capitol; and Sloane and Piper’s synagogue – which eventually led me to go to the White House menorah lighting ceremony.

By attending religious services with friends, I gained a deeper understanding about their backgrounds, communities, and values that influenced their perspectives. Behind every opinion and belief is a person with a unique story. In the end, it’s through the conversations and the willingness to learn from others that we truly understand the world around us. As someone aspiring to shape public policy, I believe that seeking diverse perspectives and understanding their why is essential to crafting policy with the greatest possible impact.

Whether it’s soup that’s made from a mix of different ingredients, or honest conversations, the only way to truly understand someone’s opinion is to engage with it – and ultimately make the world a better place. Their “why.”

Forty years ago, at the onset of communist rule, in a small town in Eastern Slovakia, a young man stained his hands with charcoal and acrylic paint to save up money and attain his dreams of becoming a doctor. It’s hard to believe that the same young boy over the years molded himself into the strongest man I know today: my dad.

While my childhood weekends were spent experimenting with colorful scribbles as a way of creative expression, my dad’s childhood was spent producing flawless features of human faces, so they could be used to make income. For me, art was a creative outlet. For my father, art was how he survived. By sharing with me his story of resilience, my dad inspired me to use art not just as self-expression, but as social entrepreneurship.

Surrounded by paintings capturing daily realities of my father’s life, I began to be interested in the stories hidden underneath enigmatic human faces. Yearning to better understand people and the world around me led me to French-Slovak literature. Perusing French oeuvres written by Czechoslovakian authors in political exile like Milan Kundera, I recognized French language as a utensil I could use to paint my own views and draw the lines between distant cultures. The first time I used this artistic tool to inspire change was through my advocacy at the Model European Parliament Conference. As I joined the EU Commission and found myself on the center ground between divided delegates over the issue of climate justice, I realized the role of French as a double-edged sword. In my speeches, I strived to garner support by highlighting detrimental consequences of inaction, citing Camus’s philosophy of existentialism to show how perceiving climate-imposed disasters as inevitable leads to the destruction of our surroundings. Many students later told me this allusion helped them understand the danger of complacency, convincing them to collaborate. I was thrilled to see how this creative use of French helped us pass a bill that would impose protective measures in vulnerable communities.

Empowered on a mission to use French as a common thread and garner change to the lives of those in need, I joined French Doctors Without Borders. There, I was humbled to shake hands with brave volunteers who dedicate their lives to saving malnourished children in Yemen. Seeing photographs from their missions stirred a sense of urgency within me. I realized the impact I could make by combining my artistic passion with humanitarian efforts.

Merging the persuasive voice of a delegate with values ingrained in me by my dad, I negotiated contracts with international facilities to start visual art competitions at my school, collaborated with schools across Czech Republic, and held a fundraising art auction at Manes Gallery to empower medical communities in Yemen. From writing proposals to serving as student coordinator and auctioning artwork that raised $14.8k to provide families with daily necessities and healthcare, I witnessed how with each task I truly reaffirmed the collective power of art in my own community. Using my voice to advocate for others made me realize my own capabilities in influencing change – amplifying abstract beauty of art by turning it into something universal that brings joy to people’s faces despite the odds they face.

Slowly but surely, I breathed life into a canvas that was once blank.

As a child I couldn’t fully comprehend the power of art beyond the surface. Now, I realize that its beauty is often invisible to human senses. Through my dad, I learned the importance of humility and resilience in the creative process – letting the effects of art to be experienced rather than heard or seen. By combining social advocacy with scientific studies, I hope to contribute to the future where creativity and science work hand-in-hand to solve global challenges. I’m eager to bring my perspective and drive to Yale, enriching my academic journey and campus community.

“All you want to do is play basketball!” My dad shouts.

Storming away, I sit in my shower, legs wrapped in my arms, thankful that the water blocks out my bawling. They just don’t understand.

I’ve played piano since I was five. Placing in international competitions at a young age, my parents encouraged me to dedicate myself to piano, and I embraced it. That is, until the 6th grade, when my classmates found out.

My tablemates and I were Googling each others’ names. “S t a n l e y D u…” pops up a letter at a time, and then everyone started laughing. They see a handful of my piano videos on YouTube and pictures of me in tuxedos suited for competitions. They show the rest of the class, everyone laughing at the outfit, bewildered as to why the athletic boy they thought they knew played classical piano. My cheeks flushed. I had a realization: piano made me un-cool, and from that moment, I decided I wanted to be an NBA player.

When I started playing piano, I woke the whole house up from playing before the sun rose. In 3rd grade, I practiced wall ball in my garage from the moment I got home from school until dinner to be the best player at recess. Now I stayed half an hour after basketball practice to get shots up. I realized that when I fell in love with things, I put my entire consciousness into it. But that fresh feeling of newly found love doesn’t last forever.

That realization made me rethink basketball. I had put all my eggs into the basket—and in doing so, I lost my vision for piano. I wanted to give piano a second go. This sentiment was further heightened when thinking about my father staying up late at night to tutor me with math and my mother driving me all the way from school to piano, then to basketball practice: I was humbled by their actions, and made them my cause. I started by practicing more religiously again instead of lying to them about playing piano the two hours they were at Costco.

Unexpectedly, I found myself immersed in the unique style of impressionist music while playing Debussy’s L’isle Joyeuse, wishing my lessons were longer than an hour. I began to practice for two hours everyday again, even as my schedule became tighter with AP tests and basketball open gyms. It just took some time management.

Standing in the shower a few months later, I thought back to the surprised reactions my online photos garnered from classmates. My peers were right to laugh, because it was surprising – I am a basketball player, but I am also a pianist (even if I look goofy in a tuxedo!). Playing piano was the chance for me to immerse myself in a different dimension. I realized, months after falling back in love with the piano, that excelling at something meant embracing it. People at school would never see the genuine joy from nodding at my string players before killing a performance in front of hundreds of people, and that is fine – because I don’t need to be what they expect me to be.

Dropping others’ opinions of me, I started caring only about my own passion and happiness. I started cooking, even though I’m known as a klutz. Now I make butter-basted steaks, and I don’t feel ashamed that I am a chef.

As I find new interests in college, my drive to excel will propel me to delve deep into them. But more importantly, I’ll embrace all aspects of my identity, knowing I’m not limited to one identity. Sometimes I’ll take a step back and think back to my roots, whether that be playing L’Isle Joyeuse for my roommates or going to the YMCA to play pickup basketball.

Sitting in a beautifully manicured park, adjacent to an imposing glass building, on a crisp Monday morning, my eyes were drawn to an insect on a nearby branch. It struggled to climb, slipping and falling, its weight overpowering the friction of its tiny feet – it triggered memory of my dad’s story about ants carrying food despite repeated setbacks. I arrived early to avoid traffic on my first day of a work experience program. Entering the reception, I saw the company’s core values displayed prominently, similar to the IB learner profiles at our school’s reception. I had subconsciously absorbed these profiles for years. Once in class, we were asked to choose our top three learner profiles; I picked Thinker, Risk Taker, and Inquirer. I always thought if I aspired to be these or already was. Later, at a parent-teacher conference, my teacher praised me for keeping the class lively with thoughtful questions.

I found myself in a large room with four other high school students, we were asked to observe customer service staff at Clix Capital answering emails. We were instructed to observe quietly and not disturb anyone’s work. After two days, initial excitement had turned into boredom. We were to present our observations to the senior manager at the end of day 4. At the start of day 3 in the morning, I could see the confusion and boredom on the faces of my fellow high schoolers. At that point I realised this experience is not going to go well unless I do something useful.

At that moment reflecting on my past, I remembered how, even as a child playing with Lego bricks, I always tried to improve existing designs. I wanted to innovate and see how I could make my creations more complex and functional. As I grew older, my interest in technology deepened. I began experimenting with Arduino, a platform that let me bring my ideas to life through coding and electronics. I spent countless hours learning to program sensors, motors, and lights, always trying to push the limits of what I could create. Then, more recently, using python and large language model I created a chatbot that could answer anything from our economics textbook – my Economics teacher loved it.

I gathered my fellow students in the cafeteria, proposed a plan, and assigned tasks. We needed answers to five questions from the customer service staff. Three hours later, we found that over 65% of queries were simple and repetitive. I proposed building a prototype to read incoming emails, use an AI language model to understand queries, and query the database for automatic email replies. I told the team they don’t have to work on this if they don’t want to, but everyone got excited to present something meaningful to the senior manager and agreed to work together. I managed to convince the IT manager to give us test system to experiment.

By the end of day three, we had the evening and half of the next day to finalize our solution. I spent the night coding. The next day, I showed my team the working prototype. They had made the presentation slides and we practiced the presentation and demo together.

During our presentation to the senior manager, he was astonished by what we had achieved. He sent multiple wordy emails to the test address and received an accurate response in seconds. He admitted he hadn’t expected much, but our solution impressed him. At the end of the work experience week, the CEO of the company called me into his office and asked, “Would you like to come and work for us?” I was flattered and humbly mentioned that I was still in high school and would like to complete college before considering work.

How to Build a Lightsaber

“Gullible is written on the ceiling!” I looked up. I couldn’t help it. Fourth-grade-me took everything at face value, and, unfortunately, there were plenty of kids at school keen to capitalize on my willingness to believe. The most common offender was Liam, a redhead who knew how to tell a good story. He was so notorious at my house that we later coined a term for his absurd stories and statistics: “Liam facts.”

One day at recess, Liam and I were discussing a Star Wars movie we had recently watched: The Empire Strikes Back. Soon enough, we were eager to get our hands on some real lightsabers. Liam had the solution. He asserted that if you took a sheet of tinfoil, folded it into a saber, and buried it, when lightning hit the burial site, a lightsaber would form. Foolproof strategy, right? As soon as we went in for lunch, I got my hands on a tinfoil sandwich wrapper, and when the day was over, I raced home to get my experiment going.

Despite my optimism for weeks after the burial, to my dismay, no lightsaber materialized. While in retrospect my desired outcome was unachievable from the start, my younger self’s realization that not everything I’m told can be believed was profound.

The seed of skepticism that this realization planted in my mind has grown over the years. The world, once defined in black and white, the dark side or the light side, has taken on more nuance.

Nowadays, I do less looking up at ceilings and more digging into the veracity of what is being said. I was thrilled to find a community of similarly-enthused truth-seekers on my high school's Speech & Debate team. The younger version of me from fourth grade would have been appalled. No plastic lightsaber battles? No Episode V reenactments? Public speaking?!?

Yes, getting started was difficult. On top of my personal reticence, there was no coach for my event, or school record of national success. So, I watched hours of online debate rounds on YouTube, learning from the best. I went to every tournament that my parents would drive me to. I practiced speeches in front of my sister. Slowly, a skillset developed. Instead of pre-writing speeches ahead of tournaments, I learned to outline arguments and fill out my points as the debate progressed. This adaptive style worked, and my performance improved.

More than personal success, though, I was able to create a base of institutional knowledge at my school that hadn’t existed when I started. I created PowerPoints, lecture videos, and prep templates, which explained how novices coming up after me could become good debaters. And whether it be frantic 11pm prep calls on Discord the night before a tournament, or reviewing judge feedback with middle schoolers to help them find the right mix of argumentation and rhetorical flourish in a speech during a Tuesday practice, I get an unmatched thrill from being able to give back to an activity which has given me so much.

I wouldn’t have thought that the most gullible kid in fourth grade could make it far in an extracurricular built on skepticism, but it demonstrates the power, to paraphrase Yoda, of not just trying, but doing—of putting yourself out there, even if it makes you uncomfortable. It is only one club at one school, but the more people who are able to articulately fight back against the “Liam facts” of the world, the better.

Last spring, as I was uprooting dead plants in my backyard, I stumbled across a folded piece of tinfoil buried a few inches underground. I still keep it in my desk drawer as a memento. When I look at that tinfoil, it reflects back a guy who still enjoys science fiction but believes the ‘force’ is in the facts.

I was ashamed of my dad. In the high-achieving environment of Silicon Valley, where success is measured in stock options and job titles, my father was an anomaly—a stay-at-home dad. While other dads boasted about their roles in tech giants, and their giant paychecks, mine spent his days at home. At dinners with other families, the air would thicken with awkward silence when people asked my dad what he did for a living. I'd shrink in my seat, wishing I could disappear. In a world where his gender was defined by corporate ladders and corner offices, my father seemed to fall well short.

As I grew older, I began to see my dad's role through a different lens. I realized that being a stay-at-home parent wasn't just a full-time job—it was an around-the-clock commitment that demanded more dedication than any corporate position. His day started at dawn and often stretched late into the night, seven days a week. There were no vacations, no sick days, and certainly no promotions.

The more I observed my father's daily life, the more I understood the depth of his commitment. It dawned on me that my dad had given up a conventional career not out of laziness or inability, but out of love for me. His sacrifice allowed him to be uniquely active and present in my life, shaping me into the person I am today. Whether it was solving our elderly neighbors' computer problems or running errands for sick community members, I learned early on from my dad about the importance of service and compassion. Gradually, my shame began to transform into something else—a profound sense of gratitude. As that shame withered away, I also noticed how he carried himself with quiet pride. He never felt ashamed about his role or tried to inflate its importance. He was unapologetically himself.

This recognition of my father's authenticity came at a crucial time in my own life. While society encourages boys to seek validation on football fields and in gyms, I had discovered my passion for the gentle hobby of grafting designer fruit trees. My hands preferred to splice branches over throwing spirals or sinking 3 pointers. While my friends animatedly discussed Steph Curry's no-look pass or the 49ers' Hail Mary win over the Rams, I would be quietly thinking of z-grafting techniques, or adding apriums and pluots to my fruit salad tree.

In a culture that prizes toughness and athleticism, how could I explain my love for something so delicate? My interest, seemingly at odds with societal expectations of masculinity, became my own private shame. I hid them away, pretending to love sports and mocking anything remotely "feminine." But as I watched dad live authentically, despite societal judgements, I began to wonder: Why was I so afraid to be myself?

I realized that my passion for grafting wasn't just a hobby—it was an integral part of who I am. The fusion of diverse branches, strength from the grafted unions, and richness of the fruit taught me how growth can come from embracing differences and finding strength in unlikely connections. By ignoring this part of myself, I would be just as disingenuous as if my dad had pretended to be an executive.

I decided to reject toxic masculinity and embrace my authentic self. My interests and passions are uniquely mine, finding strength in pursuing them regardless of others' approval. Moving forward, I am determined to use my perspective to challenge societal norms and foster inclusivity for those with diverse interests and identities.

Through Dad, I've learned to prioritize compassion over conventional success, to see worth beyond job titles, and to appreciate beauty in simple, selfless acts. Just as my prized heirloom “Indian Free Peach” graft resiliently withstands fungal and viral onslaughts each year, dad gracefully weathers society’s barrage of thoughtless comments. More importantly, he has helped me find my voice and confidence in defending both his choices and, by extension, my identity—like my “Baby Crawford Peach” graft, that was overlooked at the UC Davis Labs until it revealed its authentic self: unassuming, yet bursting with potential. These days, when someone asks me what my dad does, I say he has the best job in the world—he’s MY stay-at-home dad. And I am proud of him!

The biggest mistake someone can make is avoiding a pig-blood cake. Enveloped in a warm summer breeze, this delicacy can be found in any of Taiwan's renowned night markets. Second only to boba as the tastiest street food, they were a mystery I avoided as a child, fearful of its speckled surface.

These bustling markets represented my childhood. Akin to my initial aversion to pig-blood cake, I reread the same Harry Potter books. I found it difficult to make friends after moving homes and refused to go on roller coasters. However, this was just the first stall in my life’s night market.

Upon biting into my first pig-blood cake, I was met with a subtle nuttiness and rich, umami flavor; I was hooked. When my parents announced a trip to France, the home of Fleur Delacour from Harry Potter, my intrigue was overshadowed by the thought of venturing into new territory and unpredictable routines. I was left pleasantly surprised by Parisians chatting at café storefronts and millennials of history casually sitting in opulent buildings. My initial discomfort melted away, and I ripped into the escargots (I surprised myself too), returning home wishing I had at least taken their super dense bread with me.

In the next stall of my night market, I tried out for the middle school volleyball team. I was contemplating it as a replacement for elementary handball, and my positive time in France pushed me to embrace one more new adventure. In the past seven years, I now dive for every ball, even when it seems unsalvageable, as it is essential to our success. My teammates and I trust each other, and I call for the ball landing between our seam. Most importantly, under pressure at match-point, I cannot play with hesitation: I must continue to swing deep. This newfound courage did result in a knee injury later down the line, but I at least returned with a consistent gym schedule and somehow, a love for what I previously considered a punishment: running; completing my first 10-kilometer race eight months post-surgery!

In the markets’ game stalls, my cousins and I were always tempted to play more after winning a stuffed animal. Volleyball caused me to love speaking to others, and I began a correspondence with Greg, a Canadian living on the border of Ontario and Quebec. We exchanged stories about life in our respective countries, and I was particularly astounded that their beaches are often lakeshores. He was the first of many pen-pals: Lina sent photos of Malaysia’s clear waters and Vicosse taught me the French version of “lol” (mort de rire). Culture led to the language stall, and of course I started with my friends’ native tongue. Fortunately, the Mandarin spoken with my family allowed a head start with tone and pronunciation. French placed emphasis on the clarity of speech and the introduction of grammatical gender. I carried this over to Russian, which ironically I chose because of Greg, as we agreed on a language challenge for our meet-up at Disneyland. Right now, I am learning Taiwanese with my mom, as I felt guilty for not knowing the aural tongue of my parents. Beginning as a fuel for my curiosity, I soon realized that the greatest reward was community in the most unanticipated of places. During my Ryman Arts scholarship, I became best friends with Regina, who grew up in Kazakhstan, due to our common language of Russian. She helped me improve beyond what Duolingo taught me. In junior year, Rue was a new student from Toronto. Due to the exchanges with Greg and keeping up with Canadian politics, we shared common ground and she became another best friend.

The unconventional appearance of a pig-blood cake is now a reminder of the richness that lies beneath new experiences. I will still reminisce on my favorite memories: I reread Harry Potter every year, and I begged my parents to go on a road trip in France for my sixteenth birthday. However, I also know that there are still many stalls to visit, and the prize of knowledge will only tempt me more.

According to the Urban Dictionary, "I’m fine" is the most told lie in the English language, two words conveniently used as a mask to shield emotions, an automatic response to “How are you?”, a social ritual as integrated as shaking hands, a monologue built under the expectation of a positive response that rarely reflects a genuine inquiry of our emotional states.

I’m in pain. There is a particular kind of suffering that comes with silence. It is the quiet, unspoken agony, unseen and unheard by the world. For a long time, this was my reality. I lived in an environment in which talking about any psychological challenges or mental health was seen as a sign of weakness. “Everyone feels sad sometimes, just think positively”, people would say, a mantra that implied strength was synonymous with enduring hardships in silence. I knew I needed help, but I was terrified of admitting it, even to myself, as the voices of social judgment echoed in my head.

I’m not okay. As a child, I would spend hours lost in my thoughts, crafting stories and imagining futures where anything was possible. I remember always being fascinated by the world around me, constantly questioning and exploring, and eager to learn and experience new things. As I grew up, this insatiable curiosity made me determine specific goals for my future, leading me to a sense of purpose and direction. However, the sadness that I crept in quietly gradually consumed me. The vibrant colors of my dreams had faded to gray, leaving me feeling lost and disconnected. The goals that had once defined my identity disappeared.

I need help. One evening, my father and I were sitting in the living room. He had always been a figure of respect and authority in my life, but not someone I turned to for emotional support. “Are you okay?” he suddenly asked. I was surprised by my response, for the first time in a long while I couldn't hold the strength to say "I'm fine." Instead, my eyes watered and I released all the emotions I had hidden for a long time. As I spoke, I watched his expression shift from concern to understanding, and in that moment, I felt an overwhelming sense of relief. My father's compassionate response to vulnerability became a turning point in my journey toward mental health support.

I’m not alone. As I started my therapy journey and navigated my mental health challenges, I became increasingly aware of the prevalence of similar struggles among my peers and in the world. I felt a growing sense of responsibility to do something about it and advocate for mental health awareness. I realized that my story was not just about personal struggle but about the systemic issues that prevent many people from seeking help; misinformation, stigma, and fear or judgment. It inspired me to become a mental health activist. I founded a youth-led NGO that uses social media for change, raising awareness about the importance of mental health. Its name is Kaizen Community; the Japanese name Kaizen alludes to the philosophy of continuous improvement, which is the goal: a constant improvement in mental health at a personal and global level.

Starting was not easy, it required preparation, time, motivation, and perseverance. Overcoming challenges, I began to understand the true essence of leadership is inspiring and empowering others. With two years of Kaizen, we have encouraged people to become a force of transformation creating a safe space for vulnerability, in which scars became stories and the motivation to persist.

I’m growing. Throughout this journey I discovered vulnerability is not a weakness; it is a fundamental aspect of being human. The path to true well-being involves moving beyond the simplicity of "I’m fine" and embracing the complexity of human emotions. I am committed to continuing this path, contributing to a world where we can speak openly about mental health.

The Technology Student Association (TSA) has state and national conferences every year, and I’ve gone to many of them. One of my favorite things to do at TSA conferences is pin trading. Each state delegation in TSA creates a pin for their state every year. TSA has been around for a while, so there are a lot of unique pins to try and collect. Older pins are usually considered rarer than newer ones.

Pin trading is an important part of TSA culture, and people like to show off their pins. At closing ceremonies where formal attire is required, it is common to put your pins on the lapels of your suit jacket to display.

At conferences, I get to collect and trade pins with people from all over the US, including New York, Delaware, Kentucky, Illinois, Georgia, North Carolina, and many others. My favorite pins I have are a blue killer whale pin from Washington and a red pin with a white spinning gear from Texas.

Some people are avid collectors with hundreds of pins. I once met a lady who carried around a large felt map of the US. She placed all her pins from various states on the map and many people came up to trade with her.

The pins themselves aren’t even the best part. Just from talking to people about their pins, I get better at communication and small talk. If I am at an event and I don’t know anyone, it’s hard to find someone new and strike up a conversation. However, from pin trading, I’ve learned that you can’t just expect to be great at conversation from the get-go.

A useful analogy is a ping pong ball, ricocheting around the room. It gets faster as it bounces off more places. In the same way, you have to first talk to one person, and slowly your energy will grow as you talk to more people. Pin trading is good practice because you already have something in common to talk about.

Every year, my pin collection gets more impressive with rarer pins as a testament to my growing bartering skills. I have applied the talking skills from pin trading on many other occasions where I don’t know anyone. Pin trading helps me build communication skills and form new friendships, and it is one of my favorite parts about TSA.

At 16, I flew from Vietnam to Finland alone for high school. Sitting on the suitcase to squeeze in as many packs of instant noodles as possible, I tried to calculate how long I could survive with that amount of food.

My fear quickly turned into excitement when I landed on the other side of the world. One foot out of the airport, I filled my lungs with fresh air and my brain with dopamine. On the first call home, I told my family all about my breaking discoveries: the tap water that I could drink, the system of public transport that could take me anywhere in the country, and the soothing green color all over the place.

Overnight, my life changed drastically, but life back home did not. My family was still living the conditions that I left behind: suffocating polluted air, constantly honking traffic, and substandard food safety. On the other side of the call, my parents still wore the same clothes they did when I started middle school. The inequality between our lives has profoundly shaped my perspective.

Actually, life did change. My dad, a teacher, now also manages a beer warehouse. My mom, a bank employee, now also runs an online shop. My brother, a 13-year-old boy, now has no one to tell about the drama at school or ask for emergency homework rescue. My seemingly glamorous life abroad came at an expensive cost that required my parents to start working on weekends and my brother to cut down on hanging out with his peers. All so that I could afford a life in the happiest country in the world.

But the inequality does not just lie within my family, it lies within the countries in which we live. In Finland, education is free. My classmates' parents work as cleaners and shipbuilders. We all study the curriculum that would cost us thousands of dollars anywhere else in the world. For university, my friends could go to any university in Europe without worrying that it would break the bank. In Vietnam, to afford to go to school is an uphill battle for many low-income families. To feed their families, some of my cousins dropped out to work in casinos. Why would I be in a position so high up if I could not lift the people below me?

Though I want to share everything I have with my family, it is not quite rational or even possible to ship fresh air or clean water by post. Writing for my blog When in Finland has enabled me to share a part of my life with them. My mom, who has never traveled abroad, can now tell her friends how Finns spend their summer. My brother, who was never taught about politics, now knows what a democracy is like. More than a bridge within my family, When in Finland has grown into an organization that has reached over 2000 Vietnamese students where I provide free consultation and webinars to help them pursue better education opportunities abroad.

As the eldest daughter living abroad, I will always carry the guilt of having a higher living standard than the rest of my family. But a great part of that guilt will be turned into gratitude for being privileged and motivation to give back the privileges that I received from the sacrifices of my family. To bridge the gap within my family is to bridge the gap between our two worlds. Therefore, I am committed to helping every student I can reach to have access to quality education and better opportunities.

At 18, I flew back to Vietnam from Finland for the summer holiday. It was a summer of spending time with my family and meeting with students and parents to help them prepare for their journey abroad.

An explosion is coming. You can feel it in the air.

I jump on my bicycle and scramble out of the garage, clutching my phone. Troy’s voice crackles over the Discord call:

“Line of cumulus clouds moving east towards you. I see it on NEXLAB satellite.”

It’s a typical video call with fellow members of the Greater Philly/NJ/NY pre-college chapter of the American Meteorological Society. Every time there is a severe weather outbreak, I get the members together for a group storm-tracking session.

I pedal like my life depends on it. A quadrillion joules of convective energy barely contained by a temperature inversion was about to be released, like opening the lid of a pot of boiling water. Legs, don’t fail me now.

I zoom up the hill, and my jaw drops when I spot the horizon. The line of small cumulus clouds had merged into a gigantic rotating column rapidly ascending to tens of thousands of feet tall — a supercell. Its top fanned out into an anvil cloud a hundred miles wide, extinguishing the daylight in all directions. Faint grumblings of thunder groan as a low, horizontal wedge develops along the storm’s base.

“Uh, [Name] – is that a tornado?” asks a concerned Santhosh.

I pop in front of my phone’s camera, smiling.

“Nothing to worry about bro. That’s just the wall cloud.”

I am an atmospheric science nut. I love it because it’s like trying to solve a never-ending puzzle, as – thanks to the variability of weather and climate patterns – no two situations are ever identical. Though that storm didn’t generate significant damage, other times haven’t been so lucky. When several supercells generated by the remnants of Hurricane Ida struck my county in quick succession, they dumped several months' worth of rain in an hour - and generated an EF2 tornado that ripped roofs from buildings across town. Researching afterward, I learned that as global temperatures climb and evaporation intensifies, moisture levels in the lower atmosphere will increase, boosting convective potential energy. The likely result? Stronger severe weather outbreaks. And atmospheric science is one of the most important ways we can learn to mitigate its effects.

Currently, the best tool we have for weather prediction is numerical weather modeling. But it isn’t ideal, tending to lose accuracy more than a month out. When it comes to drought, one month simply isn’t enough time to adjust planting dates, switch crops, or enact anticipatory humanitarian action. While statistical and machine learning are better at generating accurate predictions for longer timescales, they struggle with spatial accuracy – a crucial element for thoughtful planning and response. I knew there had to be a better way.

So, I rolled up my sleeves. I experimented with a new ML technology to represent related climate regions as a network of connected locations in a graph data structure, ultimately training it to learn patterns of drought spread. It improved the spatial accuracy of ML drought predictions by 40%! A great first step, but there is still more progress to make. Next up, I’m planning to add weights between the connections themselves, allowing for the degree of connectivity to be customized based on factors such as topography or soil type.

My dream is to develop even more precise forecasts. It would allow us to drastically improve water management and save billions of dollars from flood and drought damage – not to mention countless lives. Studying earth science will transform my passion for the planet’s dynamics into knowledge that becomes a tool for thoughtful action. I am eager to use this expertise to make life in our changing world safer and more sustainable.

As the lighted candle filled the Garden City Transcendental Meditation Center with the scent of apple pie, my instructor, Harry, assured me that the process would—and should-- be effortless. Relaxing, I sank into the marshmallow easy-chair, closed my eyes, and silently repeated my secret mantra.

I admit: I didn’t achieve enlightenment that first session. Yet, over the next several weeks, as I meditated for twenty minutes, twice daily, a sense of calm settled, then spread.

Originally, my family and I turned to transcendental meditation to help my older brother, Alex, with his ADD. There were days when concern over Alex’s condition would trigger screaming matches. Listening to the turmoil, I realized that our family could only be as happy as our least happy member.

Yet, with each repetition of my mantra, I not only relaxed, but continued to step outside of myself. With Alex, especially, I wondered how it would feel to walk in his shoes. Awkward jokes. Occasionally excessive attempts to please. To me, his well-meaning idiosyncrasies were endearing; but I could see how others might be less forgiving.

As I peered past Alex’s smile to the eyes that betrayed sadness, loneliness, I resolved to meditate with him.

We went minimalist. No candles. No music. Just the two of us, our mantras pulsing silently to the rhythm of our heartbeats. A disciple of process, I reminded Alex of my Tortoise Approach to meditation—steady, consistent, no slacking. As the days stretched into weeks stretched into months, I beamed as I observed Alex growing more focused, more comfortable in his own skin. And when he became the one to nudge me awake after I’d accidentally fallen asleep during our session, I offered him a peaceful, proud smile.

Alex’s improvement continued. And as I deliberately positioned our meditations in the living room, for maximum visibility, the other family members couldn’t help but notice. First, my other brother, CJ, joined our meditation party, then Mom, then Dad. As we meditated, our heartbeats harmonized. But sensing opportunity in a captive audience, relaxing in post-meditation bliss, I started a new family tradition, the “Meditation Afterparty.”

Bonding in a sea of blankets, we freely swapped stories. My favorite: in Aesop’s, “The Eagle and the Arrow,” was the eagle karmically responsible for its own downfall? And what does this karmic boomerang imply about human interconnectedness?

Contemplating how the butterfly effect of my actions might ripple through a unified sea of humanity, I wondered if society might benefit from introducing meditation and wellness education to the less fortunate. Perhaps, even to one?

That’s why last fall, I launched “The Wellness Corner,” a regular column in the school newspaper--to share tips on practical philosophy, meditation, and well-being. And fifteen articles in, there was...silence. Weeks went by. No “likes.” No feedback. Nothing.

Then, one cold December day, I received an email from my classmate, Bernie. He mentioned that he’d been inspired by my column to take up meditation. “Could I contribute a piece on the Flow State?” he asked. I knew he was quiet and also, that he’d been struggling. But he’d been courageous to reach out.

And as I pored over his email, I thought of my brother.

Heart aflutter, pondering the karmic significance of my initiatives, I imagined the fluttering wings of the butterfly, sending out wisps of air, gaining in strength—manifesting in ways both mysterious and incalculable.

I envisioned my future. Meditating with college roommates pre-exam. Deconstructing Stoic life hacks during impromptu dining hall debates.

Then I dreamed of a better world--where, through meditation and wellness education, the lighted candles of peace shine, one enlightened soul at a time.

“The Wellness Corner” still hasn’t gone viral. The earth didn’t shake. But as my heart drummed louder, my paradigm shifted.

Perhaps, the ultimate impact of my initiatives will be like the wings of a butterfly—measured not by numbers, but by heartbeats.

I’ve always been a sucker for new experiences, especially when it comes to food. So after I stumbled upon Falafel Taco, a new Mexican-Israeli restaurant in my hometown, I knew I had to try it. Enticed by their inexpensive yet plentiful portions and unique flavor combinations, I would often stop by after my workouts at the Y or study sessions with friends at the library. Every time I came in, two things remained constant: 1) the owner Jonathan was always manning the store, and 2) I was one of the only customers.

Jonathan and I quickly became well-acquainted. Despite our vast differences, we connected through our appreciation for the plate. Whether it was their Mexican Latkes (Jonathan’s wife’s favorite appetizer) or their Ma Bett’s Old Clothes Taco (an homage to his grandmother’s slow-cooked brisket), every dish Jonathan concocted brought us closer together.

Yet, the more I learned about him and his business, the more puzzled I became as to why it was struggling. Why would such an affordable, delicious, and novel restaurant go unnoticed?

I took Jonathan on as my marketing agency’s first client that summer. While I taught him about customer personas, market segmentation, and situational analyses, he taught me about the best way to sear chicken shawarma (press down to get those grill marks!); how to make zhoug, an aromatic Middle Eastern herb sauce (use extra green chilies!); and how to wrap a pita even when it’s overflowing (cut the openings deeper!). Most importantly, Jonathan taught me something that transcends the realm of food – a lesson on the power of human connection.

A few months into our partnership, Jonathan began discussing the hardships of running a business. From high fees charged by meal delivery services to the lack of support from local community organizations, he began to break down. I caught a glimpse of a tear in his eye as his voice trailed off asking, “Who knows why people don’t want to come?”

I wanted to find a solution in the best way I knew how: I hit the books.

That summer, I consumed all the marketing knowledge I could. Long nights spent gaming with friends turned into dates with Berger’s *Contagious: Why Things Catch On*, Tungate’s *Adland: A Global History of Advertising*, and Rothenberg’s *Where the Suckers Moon: The Life and Death of an Advertising Campaign*.

As I explored these renowned campaigns, I began to understand the sheer impact advertising has. A single TV spot can reach millions of individual viewers, hundreds of thousands of whom would consider purchasing. Here, I realized that marketing is not a one-way channel – it involves a personal engagement with every viewer. We needed to connect with potential customers on a deeper level and convey what makes Falafel Taco truly special. As a regular at the restaurant and good friend of Jonathan’s, I knew exactly what that was: his food’s potential to bring people together.

Armed with a new selling proposition, we launched a campaign, but this time we focused on the connective power of food, with headlines like: “Fresh food for quality family time” and “Enjoy your dates with a side of Falafel Taco.” Slowly, customers started coming in.

My experiences with Jonathan have shown me that the best solutions are human-centric. At the heart of every decision, touchpoint, or advertisement lies a person, and only with empathy and understanding can we fully connect with them. While many people might not initially see the appeal of a Mex-Raeli dish, they definitely can see the value in experiencing something new with a loved one.

I recently made a visit back through those glass doors, now peppered with menus and flyers drawn by my own hand. Jonathan and I greeted each other with a smile and a nod, but this time we wouldn’t be able to talk immediately. This time, we had company.
