In college, I will stand on my family’s shoulders, knowing that the essence of who I am and principles I cherish, like my suitcase, will always be with me.

Growing up in the multicultural landscape of Miami, I’ve looked forward to sharing the blend of values, heritage, and leadership of my bilingual upbringing, with the desire to make a more colorful impact in the world. Speaking fluent Spanish opened twice as many doors connecting me with our global community and gaining exposure to people I may have never been aware of. This changed me as a person.

Cultural vibrancy met solid work ethic in my household, raised by a first-generation Colombian mother and Italian American father, both dentists, who stressed building a life dedicated on love, leadership, and improving others’ lives. I learned about taking risks by founding the Operation Smile Club chapter at my school, a global non-profit organization supporting free surgery for kids born with cleft lip and palate. Participating in their International Leadership Conferences as a team leader unlocked a hidden character trait. Our chapter, hungry for big impact, supported the work involved with us traveling on 2 international medical missions, partnering with UPenn and NSU Florida to treat orphans living in poverty within Vietnam. This taught me the lessons of team building, dreaming big, vision, taking risks, networking, and team trust.

These are bedrock experience values I’m hopeful to share with Babson’s community and draw from others in writing the story. Babson has a legacy reputation where young leaders thrive in becoming the best version of themselves. Integrating with the Babson family is something I wish to be part of as what I am about.

Years ago, I stumbled upon the bullet chess genius Penguin GM: Andrew Tang, an American International Master moving pieces seemingly at an incomprehensible speed.

I was fascinated by the intensity of each player's movements, the way each piece’s value for taking space was maximized. How did he play so accurately without running out of time?

Inspired, I sought to discover the truths of how one dissects and dominates chess without even the room to think, methodically training myself till the point where tactics and strategies become instinctual — pure intuition. As such, I played whenever I found free time and even cut down my sleep time to raise my elo.

Ultimately, though, it wasn’t Tang’s speed or ingenuity that enraptured me; it was the balance between chaotic haste and controlled deliberation that arose from the application of his intuition.

To me, intuition is something that blossoms through time while being unleashed through turbulence, like a seesaw between patience and wit – the art of discovery. When my mathematical hero, Archimedes, exclaimed ‘Eureka!’ through the streets of Greece, was the enlightenment a product of prolonged experimentation and calculation or was it an instant instance of intuition? I’d argue the former. This moment didn’t come about from an amateur stumbling upon a stroke of genius, rather the culmination of decades of effort.

Similarly, when the electricity shut down during my solo sophomore year over our largest annual jazz band performance, I had to improvise until the sound came back on. Now unchained to the song’s key signature, I began my unbridled interlude flowing from the modal scales and arpeggios of John Coltrane and the chromatic approach tones of Brecker licks. Only through intuition and instinct, built from the slow grind of practicing the saxophone and learning music theory, was I able to piece together a rapid salvaging of that catastrophe.

That very composure to exercise my intuition was honed through playing bullet chess, incited by my love for the fast and furious play of Penguin GM. Yet, seemingly juxtaposing myself, I’d describe myself now as a rather methodical and lax person, more like a tortoise than a penguin: more protective than courting disaster and more precise than hasty. But, as they say, ‘slow and steady wins the race.’ So, is there really a difference between the two?

We humans love to view life as a competition, one where outspeeding others means success. And to outspeed others means to be smarter than them. But intellect alone can’t amount to anything. One can know yet never use. I believe the vision to apply knowledge is what is crucial – and that comes from intuition. As Einstein said, “The only real valuable thing is intuition.”

Take resource optimization and problem solving as an example. Over my sophomore year, I worked in a photon beam microscope laboratory at NUS, analyzing how I could prevent a vacuum seal from trapping air bubbles. At first I failed by brute-forcing the gluing process, smacking them together and hoping for the best and with the few testing kits I had available, I had to find alternate ways to cut costs. Firstly, I had a hunch that heating the seal could help, so I constructed an insulated heating system that the seal could be placed in to settle, allowing the adhesive to dry faster, evidently resulting in pushing air bubbles out.

Additionally, during the testing process, I guessed the best condition for several variables with little empirical data such as the texture of the wall seal, adhesive type, and adhesive application method to succeed in creating an effective seal with as little testing as possible. Through these strategies, I finally created a vacuum seal able to withstand even the harshest of leak tests – the helium leak test, even strong enough to gain CERN’s strongest approval.

Life’s problems are countless. And intuition is my greatest weapon against them.

Who knew a labyrinth of iron and steel could become my personal mentor? Like many other boys my age, I found myself in the gym so that I could look better, be stronger, and get the girls. However, what I found was a fresh frontier brimming with marvels and profound lessons that I would soon discover.

My journey began with a few friends, all of us inexperienced but eager to explore. Our initial goals were probably to have massive arms like Arnold or get chiseled six-pack abs like CBum, but I quickly learned that this was way easier said than done. I once subscribed to a common thought: “I don’t want to get too big in the gym,” how naïve was I to think this? Some may believe that the gym is a magical place where the mere glance of a dumbbell will result in the spontaneous growth of muscle, but building muscle was indeed a formidable endeavor.

I didn’t want to embarrass myself my first time in the gym, so like any other challenge, I tackled this problem by doing some research. I looked into countless programs, watched tons of YouTube tutorials, and asked several gymgoers. Yet, I only found myself overwhelmed with such an overload of information, some of which was contradictory and confusing. So, with what I had, I knew all I needed to do was to get started. I gathered up the courage, stepped through the rusted-up and dented metal doors, and entered this new world.

By crossing those doors, I learned that the gym demands countless hours of grinding away at machines and dumbbells, pumping iron, especially on days when you don’t feel like it. The human body is a stubborn piece of machinery. It wants to maintain the status quo, also known as homeostasis. Muscular hypertrophy (growth) is the elusive result of putting immense stress on the muscles to the point where they suffer micro-tears. In response to the damage incurred, the body repairs and bolsters the muscles so they won’t get hurt the next time you work them. This biological process embodies the essence of “no pain, no gain.” Just like how muscles must endure stress and micro-damage to grow stronger, personal and professional growth often requires facing challenges and overcoming discomfort. Through these struggles and the pain they bring, we build resilience, develop newfound skills, and ultimately become more capable and robust individuals ourselves.

This notion extends beyond the gym. Challenges come in all different forms. Whether it is tackling a difficult subject in school, dealing with personal setbacks, or navigating complex social situations, challenges can always lead you to discover something new in yourself. I slowly began to recognize that these hurdles presented an opportunity rather than an obstacle; it was just a matter of perspective. I learned to embrace discomfort now that I understand that pain is a catalyst for development and evolution.

Through my journey in the gym, I have discovered the value of perseverance and the importance of pushing through. Ironically, the hard part while lifting isn’t actually the workout; it is the many instances where you are confronted with quitting. When the pain and the fatigue get to your head, you stop thinking about everything else. It’s split seconds like these where I will truly see if I will succeed or fail. Each ounce of sweat, each point of exhaustion, and each aching muscle reminded me of the dedication and resilience that I was building toward. This mindset of embracing pain for growth shifted my approach to life’s challenges, reinforcing that true strength and success are forged in the fires of adversity.

It is a June evening, with the sun dipping below the horizon of my city, a small desert town called Babylon. It is also a typical +120°F weather outside and one of the “power-off” days, where electricity gets cut for 4 days a week. The whole house started to shake, and in the midst of the chaos, a hush fell over the neighborhood. It is the horror of death that captured our thoughts and forbade any human to step foot and ask about what had happened.

It is another car bomb explosion, this time targeted towards my school’s main entrance. I am just a ten-year-old kid, and this evening, I could not hold up tears from dropping, maybe because I felt too numb and powerless to help this time.

Everyone expected school to be closed the next day, but to fulfill the curiosity of my ten-year-old mind, I went; I never thought for a minute that I would give up to terrorism, “Yalla [Name], today you fight, understood?” My father mumbled to me as we walked to school very warily in the morning. To our surprise, it is open. As I stepped through the main gate a metallic smell engulfed my nostrils; My airways constricted, leaving me tense. But I would not let my asthma bring me down, as my father told me: I fight.

As a band of explosions passed, my teachers panicked and rushed to call their families and check on them. Blasts echoed in the distance; As a student representative, I am responsible for maintaining my class' safety both physically and emotionally. “It’s alright friends, they can’t hurt us here” Tears are up my eyes as I repeatedly say this while everyone is crying. In times of crisis, it is necessary to have an effective mental fortitude to not give up on the purpose of the attack - to instill fear and prevent us from pursuing education, thereby numbing the potential of the next generation.

At the age of 12, I felt like my whole life was set up to resist; I think about it as a challenge. While my father contributed to the military efforts by donating aid and weapons, I sought a different way to combat terrorism; when everyone saw the horrors of destruction and death, I saw a gift of the communal bond of the advent of opportunities to help. I focused on making my community a better place rather than surrendering to the prevailing violence. I grew with this mindset when I decided to join the volunteering community, where I developed the skills I needed to make an impact and fight this idea of extremism. All of us, hand by hand, said no to extremism and started building mindsets before anything else.

At the age of 15, while my parents worked tirelessly to support our family, I had to shoulder my volunteer commitments and finances independently. Now I am moving to Baghdad, a two-hour ride every weekend to seek better learning opportunities, while working at two jobs virtually to support my family. The journeys were not necessarily safe, with many reported missing cars and random shootings on the highway, I knew if I needed to fight extremism, I would resist.

Now I am 19, the lessons of communal responsibility I learned have profoundly influenced my ambitions for the future. I used education to develop and empower communities to navigate crises effectively and support resilience. I trust that through quality knowledge and education, I will continue to build a safer community; a community more resistant to ideologies of destruction and terror, one that is resilient just like me, a lion of Mesopotamia.

From surviving the perils of war to leading impactful initiatives, I have followed a goal. I believe that through education and dedicated service, I can continue to drive positive change in communities, not just in Iraq, but wherever life takes me.

It was a warm autumn afternoon, and the sun cast a golden hue over our backyard. In a fit of frustration during a heated soccer game on my brother’s 13th birthday, I pushed him too hard and his head hit the concrete border of our grassy yard.

Raised by Persian grandparents whose Muslim faith was shaped by deep persecution, and educated by Jesuit teachers who demanded we behave as the Bible intends, I had always been surrounded by teachings of compassion. Yet, these lessons felt distant and abstract in that moment of panic and regret.

As I knelt beside my brother, seeing his unconscious limp body and feeling the weight of my actions, all our petty arguments over which Spider-Man movie was the best seemed trivial. The following days were a blur of hospital visits and anxious waiting in his shock-white room. Each day I returned to that sterility, I thought what if he was permanently hurt? And it was all my fault? On the fourth day, I brought our favorite small SpongeBob figurine, the one we always used to fight over, hoping it would comfort him if he woke up. As I sat by his bed, discussing our favorite episodes, I realized how much I missed our arguments and laughter. When he finally opened his eyes, an overwhelming wave of relief washed over me. Holding his hand, I whispered, “I’m sorry; I just wanted you to think I was cool – good at soccer, and all.” Tears welled up as I understood that our poor relationship was partly my fault for not being more considerate.

At a certain point, I ran out of cheeks to turn. Was I doing this right? Forgiving as the Lord does- was it about turning the other cheek or loving our enemy? I grappled with these questions after my brother’s accident. Initially overwhelmed by guilt, I tried to avoid him, fearing his resentment. But on a whim, I invited him to play basketball. He hesitated, but after some persuasion, he eventually decided to join me, and we started to reconnect. Our games became a routine. This act of forgiving for forgiveness’ sake, without pretense, without hate, without spite, or at least that’s what I learned from my grandmother’s interpretations of the Quran, helped me see that we could overcome our past conflicts.

This newfound understanding of forgiveness and kindness extended beyond my family. During an overnight school camp, I met Brad, a fellow camper with a rugged exterior. One evening, he accidentally broke my Celtics headphones. Anger surged within me, but I remembered basketball games with my brother. My first reaction was to lash out, but then I remembered that forgiveness can mend relationships. Taking a deep breath, I said, “It’s okay, accidents happen,” and offered to help him fix them. Together, we repaired the headphones, and then he invited me to join his group for a campfire. By the end of that camp, we were best friends, and we did almost everything together. Brad’s surprised reaction continues to live in my head, and I am grateful to have found another friend, just because I saw him as a friend, and was willing to forgive and move past a mistake.

Today, my brother and I are not just siblings but true brothers. Our relationship is defined by our willingness to forgive and support each other. This lesson is one I carry with me in all my interactions. When I arrive at my dorm, I will be open-hearted and welcoming, by organizing study sessions and movie nights with my dormmates. In the classroom, I will listen and engage with empathy, by encouraging open discussions during seminars. Reflecting on that autumn afternoon, I realize how forgiveness and kindness can shape our reality and help us see the best in others. This understanding will guide me throughout my life: in friendship, by resolving conflicts amicably; at work, with collaborating effectively with colleagues; and in community service, by showing empathy to those in need.

"This can't be real, can it?" I thought to myself. A sudden jolt rattled my body accompanied by the sickening sound of crumpling metal. My heart pounded loudly in my chest. Adrenaline shot through my body. I felt a sense of panic well up inside of me as I realized the truth - due to the broken light, I had failed to notice the oncoming traffic before continuing forward. My father and I sat there at the intersection by Chinatown, staring at the dented, dust covered car in front of us that I had just hit.

The car accident in my junior year of high school left a lasting impact on the way I viewed the world. Though no one was hurt, I felt a sense of solemn responsibility, guilt, and shame for the damage my actions had caused. I took it upon myself to deal with insurance, answering their calls with detailed descriptions of the crash and talking through claims with the insurance agents. Every action required much concentration; I needed to remember every second of the accident, provide accurate personal information, and thoroughly understand the insurance process so no unnecessary money was lost. Throughout this entire situation, my parents were never mad or disappointed; they simply hoped I had learned a lesson. Their encouragement for me to solve this issue alone ignited a sense of independence and responsibility within me, pushing me to become more meticulous with my actions and to fully commit to the tasks at hand, no matter how trivial.

The accident taught me that even the smallest mistakes could quickly turn into larger problems in the future. This new idea encouraged me to look deeper at the smaller details I previously overlooked. Working as an assistant at my dental office required precision and care - traits which I had come to value deeply. I completed each task with renewed purpose and diligence. Patient insurance needed to be triple-checked for consistency. Dental instruments needed to be spotless. During dental procedures, I made sure to remove every single drop of excess saliva in the patient's mouth. Consequently, many patients, and even Dr. Jiang, began to thank me for my thoroughness. With this new mindset, every task done was a step toward a transformation in my approach to life.

I implemented these transformations in my academic life as well. During my mousetrap car project for physics, we were required to have the car roll a randomized distance. In the past, I might have been content with rough estimates on how much to wind back our car, yet now I found myself recording the number of rotations, down to the millimeter needed to reach every possible distance we could be assigned. My precision earned us extra credit, resulting in a 105 on our project. My study habits, though already rigorous, started to shift. Rather than simply studying what I needed to, I looked further at how the information fit into the larger context of the world. I used to find torque and rotation a bore to learn, but as I researched its effects on car acceleration and towing force, I was captivated.

While the aftermath of the car accident has gradually receded, the sense of accountability and habit of attentiveness I gained has not. Reflecting on this experience, I realize that though the car accident was a harsh reminder of the consequences of inattention, it has allowed me to develop responsibility which I now apply to the work I do. The chemistry research I hope to do in college will demand high levels of precision and accuracy. I resolve to be more attentive than ever as I engage in experiments and collaborate with others. Whether it's measuring reagents or performing titrations, I am excited to carry my newfound approaches into college and continue to reach new heights in my personal growth.

My grandmother slides me last week’s The Daily Herald across our dining table. She takes my hand, tenderly guiding me through folding my first origami tray to fill with our snacktime sunflower seeds.

During quiet summer mornings like these, I’ve learned how to meticulously repurpose old sheets of newspaper into beautiful keepsakes, from molding the Chicago Tribune into flower vases to montaging vintage book covers. Joining her at the table, I followed her motions crease by crease, marveling at our shared creations.

“Polanyeyouyong,” she would tell me. Even scraps have their value. Despite her stinging memories of stitching together paper-thin clothes in the wintry cold, my grandma now laughs as she guides my hand through each embroidery pattern on her quilt. With every stitch she helped me sew, I saw that reusing items was, to her, an expression of familial love.

*****

During the academic year, I routinely wake up at 5am. Why? Because there's a classroom of students at the Dawamu School anticipating their afternoon lesson.

Born and raised on the outskirts of Nairobi, Kenya, Grand didn’t have someone to feed his curiosity surrounding computers. Hungry for knowledge, our virtual Code2Connect lessons soon expanded into chaotic “device-maximizing” open discussions. Together, we squeeze every bit of value out of his dilapidated laptop, from refining power settings to revamping hardware components. Fixing Grand’s defective webcam by installing a new driver, I finally can see the face behind the voice that had been so familiar to me over the months, and in that moment, all the miles between us seem to disappear.

Following my grandmother's expert origami folding techniques, I crease and flatten scrap cardboard from routine school lunch shipments, assembling drop-off boxes to collect dozens more used laptops and electrical devices to send to schools around the world. And each time I guide volunteers in nursing old game consoles back to life for our local libraries—”Wii-Serve Wednesdays,” we’d call them—I am inspired to know that each scrappy device donated by my peers invites a treasure of intellectual discovery, an invitation like my grandmother’s first origami lesson.

*****

“What a hoot!” Blenda hollers, after we spend the morning together with all the grandmas scrunching, banding, and squirting t-shirts senseless.

Blenda, hailing from Englewood, Chicago, is a two-time breast cancer survivor and caring grandmother, with her only daughter hospitalized from the disease. As she taught me the perfect baking soda-to-vinegar ratio needed to create my own fabric softener, I thought I’d teach her a clothing hack of my own.

So, prior to setting up for the Pink Divas and Gents Breast Cancer 5K, I invite Blenda and other grandmas to join me with some old white t-shirts and pink dye. While their days accompanying a belted cardigan were long gone, they’d found new life as pink pride headbands and wristbands.

Sporting their newly upcycled pink shirts, the grandmas groove and clap to the beat of “Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.” As Blenda waves me over, welcoming me to their dance circle, I break into a tentative two-step. But as the tempo picks up, I spontaneously bust into The Carlton! (or tried to, at least). Soon, the circle expands, and we happily throw extra pink gear to the participants that trickle in. As I tie my own t-shirt-bandana around my head while laughing uncontrollably, I realize that the value in repurposing isn’t simply in creating new clothes, but treasuring them together as a family.

*****

Grand now spends his weekends running a free computer repair clinic for his neighbors. Blenda now runs her own “Dye-namic Creations” class at her local YMCA. I still fold these paper trays in my dining room each morning, only now I do it with my seven-year-old brother. They all honor my late grandmother’s dedication to others. I, too, with an eye for value and a heart for others, will continue to transform trash into treasure, just as she did for me.

As the aromatic candle filled the Garden City Transcendental Meditation Center with the comforting scent of apple pie, my instructor, Harry, assured me that the process would—and should-- be effortless. Relaxing, sinking deeper into the marshmallow easy-chair, I closed my eyes and silently repeated my secret mantra.

I admit: I didn’t achieve enlightenment that first session. Yet, over the next several weeks, as I meditated for twenty minutes, twice daily, a sense of calm settled, lingered, then spread.

Originally, my family and I turned to meditation in an effort to help my older brother, Alex, with his attention deficit disorder. There were days when concern over Alex’s condition would trigger screaming matches. Listening to the turmoil, I realized that our family could only be as happy as our least happy member.

Still, meditation was my sanctuary. With each repetition of my mantra, I not only relaxed, but continued to step outside of myself, becoming more empathetic, more inclusive, more mindful of others. With Alex, especially, I began to wonder how it would feel to walk in his shoes. The awkward jokes. The occasionally excessive attempts to please. To me, his well-meaning idiosyncrasies were endearing; but I could see how others might be less forgiving.

As I peered past Alex’s smile to the eyes that betrayed sadness-- loneliness-- I resolved to meditate with him.

We went minimalist. No candles. No music. Just the two of us, our mantras pulsing silently to the rhythm of our heartbeats. As a disciple of process, I reminded Alex of my Tortoise approach to meditation—steady, consistent, no slacking. As the days turned into weeks turned into months, Alex became more focused, more comfortable in his own skin. Insomnia became less problematic. And when he became the one to nudge me awake when I accidentally fell asleep during our session, I happily acknowledged his progression.

As Alex’s improvement continued—and as I deliberately positioned our meditations, for maximum exposure, in the living room—the other family members couldn’t help but take notice. First, my other brother, CJ, “wanted in” on our meditation party, then my parents. As we meditated, our heartbeats harmonized. But sensing opportunity in a captive audience, relaxing in the afterglow of blissful meditation, guards down, filters off, I started the “Meditation Afterparty.” In what became a family tradition, we bonded in a sea of blankets, freely swapping life lessons and oddball personal anecdotes.

Witnessing the butterfly effect of Alex’s meditation-inspired improvement on the happiness of my entire family, I wondered if society too might benefit from introducing meditation and wellness education to the less fortunate. Perhaps, even to one?

That’s why last fall, I launched “The Wellness Corner,” my regular column in the school newspaper—to share tips on practical philosophy, meditation, and well-being. Unfortunately, without sufficient analytics, I was flying blind. Weeks went by. No “likes.” No feedback. Nothing.

And then, one cold December day, I received an email from my classmate, Bernie. We hadn’t spoken since elementary school, but he mentioned that he’d been inspired by my column to take up meditation and asked if he could contribute a piece on the Flow State. I knew he was quiet and also, that he’d been struggling. But he’d been courageous to reach out.

And as I pored over his email, I thought of my brother.

Heart aflutter, pondering the karmic significance of my initiatives, I imagined the fluttering wings of the butterfly, sending out wisps of air, gaining in strength, its power extending outward—manifesting in ways both mysterious and incalculable. I then imagined my future. Meditating with college roommates before exams. Deconstructing Stoicism and well-being principles with classmates.

“The Wellness Corner” still hasn’t gone viral. The earth didn’t shake. But as the pulsing in my ears drummed louder, my paradigm shifted.

Perhaps, its ultimate impact will be like the wings of a butterfly—measured not by numbers, but by heartbeats.

Snakefruits brown and scaly. Rambutans red as rubies. It was here, in my mother’s garden, at the tender age of five, where I learned how small we truly are against the grand tapestry of nature. At school, I marveled at the alluring beauty of endangered species like the Sumatran tiger, the Bali Myna, and the Tapanuli Orangutan. Yet, within my mother’s teachings and the lessons at school, a harsher truth emerged: humans’ capacity for destruction far surpasses nature’s ability to defend itself. The more I learned about the destruction of habitats and the accelerating pace of climate change, the more I knew I could not stand idly by. With the threat of human destruction, nurturing these living beings was not just a task but a necessity. That’s what ignited my path toward climate advocacy.

My advocacy journey truly began in the summer of 2023 when I interned at Fairatmos, Indonesia’s first climate tech company. I had always had a passion for technology, tinkering with my video games as a child and studying coding as soon as I got to middle school. But I didn’t know that I could combine my love for tech with my passion for climate advocacy until I saw the internship opportunity at Fairatmos. What captivated me about Fairatmos was its groundbreaking business model, which seamlessly integrates nature-based solutions—like carbon sequestration through forests and mangrove swamps—with cutting-edge technologies, including satellites and drones, to precisely measure the net additionality of carbon offsets.

The summer of 2024 marked an exhilarating turn in my journey as I returned to work on Fairatmos' conservation project in Cilacap. When I mentioned going there and staying in a remote village for my internship, even my mother resisted, citing how vastly different things would be from the comforts of our home in Jakarta. However, I insisted that I must go there to gain firsthand experience in conservation efforts and contribute meaningfully to protecting the fragile ecosystem that the local residents so dearly preserve. Eventually, my mother relented.

The Cilacap mangrove swamp, spanning 5,000 acres, is a vibrant ecosystem teeming with biodiversity essential for carbon absorption. Yet, this vital ecosystem is slowly being destroyed by industrialization, illegal logging, and pollution. The disappearance of these mangroves would leave Cilacap vulnerable to increased coastal erosion and flooding, jeopardizing the livelihoods of local communities, who depend on the mangroves for fishing and aqua farming. Protecting and restoring the Cilacap mangrove swamp was therefore urgent.

Initially, adjusting to the demands of the internship amidst the poor living conditions in the village was challenging. However, as I began to appreciate the mission’s importance, my self-pity disappeared. At the village, I had the privilege of exchanging captivating stories and innovative business ideas with the locals. From Harris and his fellow fishermen, who ingeniously optimized spaces around mangrove roots for aqua farming, to Kuntoro, who spearheaded local conservation efforts by commercializing snacks made from mangrove trees, the resourcefulness of these community members inspired me to support conservation initiatives that harmonize ecological preservation with economic livelihood.

At the local school, children brimming with hopes eagerly shared their ideas with me. Rachmat, for example, asked about the programming skills needed to become an ethical hacker, while Zakri worked with me on an Excel sheet to forecast the financial return of establishing an eco-tourism business in Cilacap. These children, full of life and dreams, fueled my determination to safeguard our planet for their future.

In my university life, I envision promoting eco-tourism and preserving mangrove trees in Indonesia, collaborating with students, alumni, and sustainable local businesses. I also plan to champion nature-based solutions as a powerful tool to combat climate change by establishing a nature preservation society on campus. This journey has shown me that a dedication to environmental advocacy, grounded in humility, intellectual curiosity, and common sense, can drive meaningful change. By continuing to nurture my passion for nature on campus, I hope to inspire others to join me in protecting our planet for generations to come.

“5 and 3, so 8.”

My dad cheers with excitement—I can't help but smile; his joy is infectious! My mom groans as her civilization’s supply drought continues—the sound triggers a memory buried within my childhood game nights. I offer her a few of my bricks and am met with a loving hug in return.

For the first nine years of my life I lived in Singapore. I remember spending Saturdays with my uncle at the zoo, joking about whether monkeys or pandas would make a better roommate (my uncle sided with monkeys, but pandas are the clear winner: they are living teddy bears!). Meals with my aunt were special too—she would often take time off work to join in with my palak paneer obsession. I’m convinced she was competing with my mom!

When I moved to New Jersey in 2016, however, everything changed; the joy with my relatives was now hidden behind nineteen hours of cramped seats and occasional jolt of turbulence. Separated from the comforting routines and familiar faces of my previous home, I turned to an unlikely antidote: Catan.

It was my idea; every weekend my relatives and I would gather for a virtual game session on Colonist.io.

My aunt’s lethargic playstyle earned her the title “World’s Slowest Player.” She was so slow we started setting a fifteen-minute timer for her turns! The ensuing laughter that filled the room always brought a touch of nostalgia, but the happiness that followed never failed to lift my spirits.

Meanwhile, my uncle’s tendency to hoard resources often led to hilarious clashes with the supply-stealing robber. Laughing with my uncle, even if only on a video call, filled me with the sense of warmth previously reserved for our Saturday trips to the zoo.

Moments like these etched themselves into my family lore, making the oceans between us seem a little smaller.

The Catan sessions became the highlight of my week, but as I transitioned into middle and then high school, once a week turned into once a month. Trying to balance school and sports with the twelve-hour time zone difference was exhausting.

As the sense of separation crept back into my life, I felt I was slipping into the same loneliness I had experienced years earlier. However, hours of trading wood for brick weren't for nothing. Armed with a new understanding of human connection, I found solution in my swim instructor, Mr. Devin.

My first experience with Mr. Devin, marked by chlorine and erratic splashing, was a bit of a spectacle: his efforts to corral my abysmal butterfly technique were in vain. But as I started to open up to him, what began as student and teacher morphed into uncle and nephew. Our weekly swim lessons became lighthearted runs and workouts, and then further evolved into manning the front desk together at SwimQuest.

We laughed about my initial swimming form, him comparing me to a walrus attempting ballet, and marveled at my push-up progression. We even shared my love for mangoes; I would keep a few from every box to share with him. Through our shared jokes, workouts, and mango moments, I felt so at home in a way I hadn’t since 2016.

***

As I reflect on my previous constructions, I study the playing field—littered with roads stretching across plains and curving around mountains, each hex tile bringing me closer to my family.

This world, residing in a six inch device in my pocket, will always be with me, ready to blossom anywhere with a stable internet connection.

I look at my playing pieces, knowing I still have more roads to pave, in college, and beyond.

My game is just beginning, and I can’t wait to meet everyone who will join me.

If you asked me what my favorite activity was during my spare time, I would have said creating vision boards for my future. One summer, when I was ten, I remember walking into Hobby Lobby, a crafts store near my home, with my mom to pick out colorful stickers of astronauts, and rocketships - symbols that represented the wonders of space exploration to me. After begging my mom to buy these stickers, I hurried home to add them to a white cardstock board. With that, my vision board was complete. I proudly pinned it up on my wall, marveling at this board that seemed to encapsulate all the wonders I aim to accomplish.

Ever since then, creating vision boards has become a cherished hobby. By laying out my aspirations on a vision board, I became the engineer of what seemed to me my ideal reality: I organized a blueprint for my dreams through vision boards, hoping to achieve them one day.

As I continued to create vision boards for every aspect of my life, I began to notice a troubling pattern. While I cherished the process, I found myself looking down on my current reality. I would look down on my status with friends, my mediocre accomplishments, and the fact that I wasn't living the dream life I had envisioned. These feelings of disappointment were the opposite of what my vision boards were supposed to evoke – fulfillment and overall gratification.

I remember how I was stressed about the success of my Aerospace Club even though I was looking back at my vision board that held all my desired outcomes. One night, I opened up to my mom about my conflict with my vision boards since she loved my hobby of creating them. Instead of giving her usual advice on why stress at such a young age is concerning, my mom came to me and read a line from the Bhagavad Gita in Sanskrit. I am no expert in Sanskrit so these words went through one ear and out the other. Fortunately, my mother noticed the confused expression on my face and carefully stated the meaning behind this phrase: "One should not focus on results; rather, enjoy the journey of their actions." Somehow my mom is always in tune with what I need to hear. I realized that most of the time when I started a project I cared about, I fantasized about the desired outcomes and stressed about the results.

Lying in bed late that night, I reflected on my past thought process. Instead of feeling overwhelmed about the possible success of my Aerospace Club, I should focus on the feelings of joy when creating an enriching experience for club members. I should feel the excitement, at the current moment, of picking out supplies so students can engage in interactive activities related to aerospace engineering. This positive shift in perspective filled me with newfound enthusiasm - the same feelings I experience if I had a successful club. So, instead of thinking, "When I get my result, I will be content," I decided to think, "As I work towards my goals, I feel energized." I went to bed with the satisfaction of this realization.

It would be a miracle if my brain could automatically rewire itself to think this way. The stress from "what ifs" and feelings of discontent still clouded my mind. However, on those specific, miraculous moments when I committed to my new mindset, I felt much freedom by embracing the positive emotions I wanted to channel.

I continue to create vision boards, but I have a different approach. Instead of fantasizing, I place the vision board aside and start living my current life where I cherish the journey of achieving my goals. I utilize my vision boards as an anchor, helping me feel who I want to be and achieve in the present moment, rather than an escape to reality.

I am a competitive memorizer with an average memory.

I don’t remember my 3rd grade vacation to Hawaii. I forget the directions to school, despite taking the bus there every day. My mom still scolds my blank face when my relative I had last met eight years ago asks if I remember his name. However, if you place 80 digits in front of me and give me two minutes, I can recite them in perfect order.

As I scan each digit, I transfer it into my palace—my memory palace.

Front door, mat, closet, console table, staircase.

Couch, fireplace, dining table, chandelier, utensil holder.

This seemingly arbitrary list of furniture is my sanctuary for storing memorized information. In my head, my home is parted into ten rooms—each room with five items. As I memorize random words, digits, names, images, cards, and people, the data is streamlined into a visualization I can assign to each location. During recall, my mind saunters through my house, patiently focusing its blurry lens to reveal the image at each piece of furniture then decoding it to obtain the original information.

Armed with this technique in the 8th grade, I signed up for a memory competition. For each event, I crafted methods to encode information into items to set in my palace. For example, I developed a system to translate each digit into a consonant through random connections.

1 looks like an L
Two becomes T

In groups of three, the consonants then form the skeleton of a word or phrase to be visualized as an image—213 became [T[a[ll] [M]an. Each playing card simplifies into a person, action, or object, with sets of three forming a compact story—Barack Obama sitting patiently on my bed, fishing for Mount Rushmore?

After a lack of success, I continued to adjust my memory techniques. Dissecting how my memory worked, I learned that I thrived on visual rather than aural or tactile stimuli; I found that the more detailed and bizarre the image in my palace was, the better I could visualize and retain it. 213 transformed from a six-foot man to a living colossus, his elongated head jutting through the ceiling and piercing my palace roof as I wave from my foyer.

The following year, I further enhanced my methods. I united the individual elements of each room into one scene; each image came to life to interact with the others. Now, a motorcycle barrels across my parquet flooring, erupting my oven into flames while a firefighting monkey appearing from the fridge commandeers an extinguisher to swiftly subdue the fire.

With my experience adapting techniques to leverage my memory, I wanted to decipher how my skills could be utilized in the context of memory loss. After researching studies on cognitive decline, I found that the same rudimentary principles that I employ in competitions have been developed into memory training programs; my knowledge could be applied to prevent cognitive decline and dementia.

Working with professors involved in memory research, we amalgamated information from various memory studies and the knowledge I have attained through competing. After tailoring a training program, I volunteered to teach these concepts at senior assisted living homes through a variety of exercises from memorizing unrelated words to visualizing short stories to remember information.

In the future, I am interested in understanding the brain, particularly in the context of overcoming weaknesses. How are some able to prevent cognitive decline during aging? How can we utilize our brain’s idiosyncrasies to prevail over challenges? How are some able to attain success without innate ability? Despite the variable nature of the methods in which the seniors completed the activities, the immense growth of those who believed in self-improvement remained constant. It seems the line between acceptable and exceptional is one’s self-imposed prophecy to be mediocre; for me, being average will never be my excuse to give up but my motivation to succeed.

Locked away in a self-imposed cage, I watched my peers enjoy and revel in their carefree moments of youth, clutching the key to freedom yet choosing isolation. It was another Friday night, but instead of being out with my friends, I was at my computer once again: studying, painting, creating, fearful that the moment I stopped, I’d fall further behind in my goal of achieving a blissful future.

At times, I would sit at my desk with a blank stare and a gut feeling that I wasn’t doing enough. This feeling would drown me, making escape seem impossible. Eventually, becoming overwhelmed by an intense sense of dread, not fully understanding where it came from. Later, I realized I couldn’t maintain this state of mind. It’s like trying to drive to the ends of the earth on one tank of gas. I just couldn’t do it; I needed to reevaluate myself and learn to relax.

“You should ask Jovani if he wants to come?”

“I mean, I could, but you already know he’s going to say no.”

One day, I said, “I’ll go.” And the darkness I’d been feeling, the insurmountable weight of pressure I put on myself to succeed at everything I do, lifted, and I didn’t feel bad.

The year I started hanging out with my friends and taking breaks was the most productive year of my life. I achieved the most awards that year, took part in multiple galleries, and did so without feeling depressed. I finally found my balance.

My love for learning is both a blessing and a curse. To me, knowledge is the most important thing in the world, and I yearn for it. Currently, I am learning different languages to better connect with the world. I have a decent grasp of Spanish, Portuguese, and my parents' language, Cape Verdean Creole. I learned to cook, making breakfast, lunch, and dinner for my family. I learned to cut my own hair. I have a job, I work almost every other day right after school. I have my art that I need to work on, studying for school, and studying things that interest me, such as investing and language learning. At one point, I was running a clothing brand and selling my paintings through a website, both of which I researched and developed myself through YouTube. Those two things tipped the scale, and I have taken a break from focusing on them, as my priority right now is getting into a great college. I again had to find what was tipping the scale and rebalance.

My move from middle school to high school is when my mind shifted to prioritizing my future and being willing to make the necessary sacrifices. This determination led me to leave my old friends and familiar environment in pursuit of better education, going to Cumberland High School, a school where I didn't know anyone, and an environment I wasn’t used to. Living about half an hour away from the school and everyone who went there, it was hard to adjust. Sometimes I would be the only African American in my classes. I felt like I stood out, especially coming from Pawtucket, which is known for being “ghetto” and having really bad high schools. I didn’t let that determine who I was. This attitude resulted in me scoring straight A’s in classes I genuinely enjoyed, even though I found it challenging to excel in subjects that didn’t captivate my interest.

Although I often find myself alone, studying and bettering myself, I have learned to create a balance. I understand that I can’t work like a machine and that taking time for my mental health can and will lead me to achieve greater things.

“I want you to go to JV practice today.”

It was 7:50 am on a Monday, the first thing I saw when I checked my phone after waking up. It was from my varsity basketball coach. I knew what it meant. I had been moved down to JV. When I go down to eat breakfast, I tell my mom the news, trying to stay calm.

But deep down, I’m angry. I’m angry that my mom and my dad forced me to go to piano class over basketball practice, and as a result, they had removed me from the position I fought to earn: a freshman on varsity basketball.

I’ve played piano since I was five. It felt natural; every teacher I searched for wanted me to study with them, I consistently placed in high caliber competitions in elementary and middle school, and I dreamt of playing Chopin’s Concerto Number 1 in Carnegie Hall once I grew up.

The first turning point was in 6th grade, when my tablemates and I were searching each others’ names. When my name gets searched, they laugh. They see handfuls of my piano videos online and pictures of myself in tuxedos suited for competitions. They turn around and show the rest of the class, everyone laughing at the outfit and bewildered why the energetic, goofy, athletic boy they knew played classical piano. My cheeks flushed. I had a realization: piano made me un-cool.

My resentment towards piano began to grow. From the outbursts in laughter when my basketball teammates and classmates found out to the stress from making the hour-long rush from piano to basketball practice to missing games and practices, I felt that piano was holding me back from reaching my potential in basketball.

Moving down to JV strengthened this resolve. I avoided practicing piano, waiting until late in the day to play, causing me to sleep late. My grades dropped, causing more arguments with my parents.

That summer, my dad made me stay up late to help me understand math. We grappled over worksheets my tutor gave me, going through the solutions one step at a time, making sure I understood every single one of them. When sophomore year started, I found myself performing at the top of my class for every test. I realized finally that my parents were trying to help me, even if it was at the expense of my anger towards them, and it was the same thing with piano. They saw the potential I had, and wanted me to shine.

I was so caught up in trying to be accomplished in basketball, I forgot why I played piano—because I had enjoyed it. I had enjoyed it, before I felt like people looked down on me for it, and that my coach disapproved of me playing piano. I found myself genuinely enjoying the music I was playing again, wishing my lessons were longer than an hour. I began to practice more again, even as my schedule became tighter. It just took some time management.

I realized that it didn’t matter what others expected me to be, and trying to follow other peoples’ paths was only going to stray myself further from mine. I am a basketball player, and I am also a pianist. I started to embrace myself for who I was, knowing that only then could I truly excel at what I loved to do. I also started new hobbies, such as cooking, even though I know people don’t think the clumsy me would be a chef.

I know that my classmates will still be surprised when they find out I am a pianist, and I know that my musician peers will still be surprised when they find out that I am a basketball player. But that won’t stop me from being the things that they don’t think I am.

4:45 a.m. Why? 4:51 a.m. Why? Comforting darkness and the soothing warmth lull me back to complete my doze. The blaring alarm never felt more disgusting. Flashes of the unsightly red time from yesterday’s meet sear into my early thoughts. My lats and thighs scream in agony from mere extensions. I have to wake up.

“If you want to be the best, you have to do things that other people aren't willing to do.” - Michael Phelps.

Humid, scorching heat stretches across the noisy streets of Shanghai. Amid the passersby, a frail grandmother pedals passionately to send her young grandson to swim training. The cost of such an experience? More than half a year’s supply of rice and modest vegetables. Packed dinner in hand, the son’s pregnant Mom rushes back from a nine-hour shift to take her blissful son to swim practice. I am the essence of sacrifice and unconditional love.

At the age of ten, I was a state champion, later winning nationals. Exhilarating: Confident. Loved. Three seasons later, I failed to qualify for a state championship. Coaching feedback shifted to pity, and for the first time, I experienced an overwhelming wave of loneliness. What was I without my medals? Later after the swim meet, for the first time in swimming, I subtly cried, freeing the disappointment and settling the expectations. Quit? Not a chance.

Why did I swim slow yesterday!? Walking to the pool was a battle itself. Chilling Chicagoan gusts breezed through my patchy winter coat and seeped into my inner warmth. Remnants of thawed snow freeze into slick, thin ice. I remain unfazed. Not because the cold didn’t get to me. Not because I wasn’t tired. Not because I enjoy the temperamental gusts that reinforce yesterday’s failure. I continue walking because I love swimming.

“Cold”, “Icy”, “Uncomfortable”. As I jump into the pool, these adjectives ring clear in my sluggish mind. Though difficult, I remain attentive to fixing the errors from the meet. No breath off the wall, three underwater kicks, no breath into the finish. Amid the chaos in the grueling main set, I am at peace; I am in control. I can fix my inconsistent flutter kick. With mounting expectations of recruitment and pressure to seek club positions, being in the pool no longer made me feel worthy.

But, it is in these draining practices that I feel invigorated with purpose. Tasked with a personal challenge to improve and, most importantly, an earnest responsibility to push my teammates through practices, I am driven to be their best teammate. These experiences root my love for swimming. When I can no longer lift another stroke, I subconsciously urge myself that I have to be there for my friends; No skipping. A simple “You can do this” to Claire pushes her to overcome her inexplicable aerobic fatigue. When Claire battles through and completes the set, my unceasing pain effortlessly subsides into admiration. Making it through these tough practices together and a team Einstein’s breakfast truly exceeds all my first-place finishes. From what is often considered an “individual” sport, swimming has shown me the impact of how simply caring and being there for others can make lifelong ripples.

From black hair to brown hair, I have witnessed how the power of support can deepen passion. Whether I’m extending my Introduction to Physics class or volunteering at swim clinics, I deeply value helping others overcome challenges through their hardest times; my hardest obstacles are the ones that I cross independently. Every morning as I gaze upon the medals that hang woefully by my drawer, the cheering and support of friends and family are evoked. Every morning. While I may not be the fastest swimmer or have the most impressive extracurriculars, I remain committed to improving myself and supporting others to the best of my ability.

A blinking white line is all that fills an empty void. It is a sight seen thousands of times before, reflected off glasses dimly lit in the fading light of 6 P.M; it is a sight that demands my fingers to hover above the keyboard of a silver HP Chromebook. The line suddenly shoots off to the right as my fingers descend upon the keys, clicking echoes around the bedroom. As words spill out from behind the line’s path, they warp and twist into shapes and colors. Sentence by sentence, a sea of trees sprawls from under a cliff, and the sun’s dying rays paint the sky and stain the ground below in reddish hues. Then, the clacking ceases. The line blinks again, but now in a freshly born world ready for its protagonists.

Online roleplaying: an activity similar to writing a book, involving acting out characters with other online users. By accident, I stumbled upon it while doom-scrolling through my YouTube recommendations during the COVID-19 pandemic. But immediately, I was fascinated by its opportunity to let my imagination run wild. From when I was thirteen, roleplaying became a way to express creativity when school demanded cognition. As my fingers churned out the actions of my characters, the fantastical worlds I partook in inspired a sense of adventure: dragons sailing on an Australia-sized pirate ship, Pokemon fighting against interdimensional threats, and the multiverse banding together to protect a sanctuary. Every story splashed excitement into an ordinary school life.

As my characters fought for their right to everyday life, I absorbed all the lessons and experiences they weathered through to apply in my own life. My rust-colored dragon Orion, who conquered the seas with his dragon comrades, revealed that people were not as judging as I thought. As my first character, he taught me the strength of human connections and the benefits of a good team. His lesson encouraged me to interact with more people in real life, from finding the courage to trouble the waiter for an extra spoon to challenging the thinking of classmates and teachers and assembling one of the best teams I have ever been in for robotics club. My firey Flareon Floof, who found his role in society after spending his life in the wild, showed me the weight of responsibility. He taught me that I had to finish that job, whether it was finishing my response in a roleplay or fulfilling a promise to a family member. His life pressed me to lead every group assignment to completion, consistently deliver a final product for my artwork, and avoid disappointing expectations from family and classmates.

Even if roleplaying is acting, it showed how the blinking line that created their worlds impacted my reality. With that realization, I started viewing the world around me full of blinking lines, waiting for someone to write and witness its story. With each calculus problem, line of sheet music, and part of the VEX competition robot, I feel that blinking line urging me to finish it. I study the blinking lines of the people who have completed their story: those who have created their mark on history, the cumulative efforts of science since the dawn of man, and the pens of authors whose words were more impactful than any weapon.

Roleplaying kick-started the vibrant and colorful imagination that swirls through my head. It showed me how to turn intangible thoughts into products for people to experience, whether they read my roleplays, used my tool to align books neatly, or drove the robot I designed to second place. Just like how a thrilling roleplay is formed line by line, I find the same joy in building a solution piece by piece. Roleplay showed that the power of creation lies with everyone, and I intend to use it to design and create solutions with the creativity it cultivated within me.

A coquí and a markhor walk into a room. The tiny Puerto Rican frog and the imposing Pakistani horned goat eyeball each other. "We are so different," declares the markhor. The coquí counters, "I believe we're quite similar." Delving into my bicultural identity, I've drawn unexpected inspiration from the coquí and the markhor, the national animals of my parents' respective homelands. Although they are vastly different creatures representing seemingly incongruent nationalities and cultures, both symbolize qualities that I have fused into my unique self.

Similar to the coquí, I am small, yet remarkably resilient. The coquí species has survived countless hurricanes that have ravaged Puerto Rico. I suffer from growth hormone deficiency and scoliosis and have endured hurtful bullying in the past because of my size. No matter what age I was, I was always the smallest one on the pitch. Despite my physical challenges, I have always chosen to fight to overcome my disadvantages and live positively. I always thought to myself, "It's not the size of the dog in the fight, it’s the size of the fight in the dog." In the same way that the coquí’s diminutiveness and unmistakable call make it unique, it is my size, might, and spirit that makes my individuality shine through.

Like the markhor, I embody determination and resourcefulness. The markhor adeptly navigates Pakistan’s demanding mountainous terrains and demonstrates adaptability in its foraging behaviors to endure extreme climates. I demonstrated my ingenuity and creativity during the challenging times of the pandemic by launching my own shoe design business. Today, I continue my entrepreneurial journey by managing Cartel Kicks, a sneaker and consignment reselling page on Instagram. It’s a highly competitive industry that has exploded in popularity in recent years. I am committed to leveraging my experiences and continuing to innovate to ensure that my business continues to thrive.

While different in appearance, the coquí and the markhor represent countries that cherish one value above all: family. From my mother’s Puerto Rican side, I learned about the strong bonds of family through our shared love of traditional food. Even though I grew up in Dallas, Abuelita made me cherish my Puerto Rican heritage when we sat around her kitchen table on the mountainside, waiting for her delicious funche, flan, and arroz con habichuelas y tostones. From my father’s Pakistani side, I have learned about the responsibility of taking care of my extended family. He has assumed the financial burden of supporting many relatives who have left Pakistan in search of a better life. I will be proud to follow in his footsteps in honor of my Pakistani roots. My parents have been able to raise a strong, close-knit family in a different country because they have found shared values to teach to their children. Quoting the poet Vin Diesel, “The most important thing in life will always be family.”

I distinctly remember coming across a quote that has stayed with me ever since: “Jack of all trades, master of none.” I have often questioned whether I truly fit in with my family. Whenever we visited Puerto Rico or Pakistan, I tried to communicate with my relatives using the limited language skills I had. However, I always ended up feeling disappointed in myself. I felt ashamed that I couldn’t fully immerse myself in either culture due to my American upbringing. As I’ve matured, I’ve come to realize that my diverse identity draws strength and inspiration from the rich cultures that enhance my life. Although I'm not a clone of either of my parents, I am still a product of their respective backgrounds. Yes, I am half-coquí, half-markhor, and a first-generation American bald eagle. But ultimately, I am 100% original. I am [Name].

Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, Acceptance? Stages of Grief 
A story of a young American woman challenging social norms and expectations? Vampires 
What do these sequences mean? They represent patterns - predictable, logical sequences that bring order to seemingly unrelated terms.

Ever since I was diagnosed with a mysterious illness with an unknown cause that forced me to take a gap year, my life has revolved around the quest for patterns. The unpredictability of my condition—its chaotic, unpatterned nature—left me yearning for structure and understanding in other areas of my life. This drive to find patterns and order became my way of coping with the uncertainty and chaos.

Jump Ropes: 1400. The ideal number of jump ropes I skip every day. It took countless trials and errors to arrive at this perfect number. Too few jumps left me feeling unsatisfied, while too many drained my enthusiasm. Settling on 1400 provided a balance between challenge and enjoyment. This routine, while seemingly simple, was the result of careful observation and adjustment. The music - maintaining a combination of new, exciting music every day to freshen up the day; the path - exploring new routes along the Han River, blending with the serene ambiance of nature, and finding the perfect spot where the view of the water was most inspiring. Each skip, a meticulous cobweb of various factors intertwined, was my own way, my own one and a half year old path accompanied with a 6 inch worth of growth.

Eclipse Mints: Step 1. Bring a pack of eclipse mints to school. Step 2. Sit next to someone who you want to be close with in class. Step 3. Give him a mint whenever he/she is trying to doze off. Step 4. Smile. This simple strategy has by far been the most effective, light hearted intro route to making new friends according to my experience, especially if you’re someone like me whos bad at striking up conversations naturally. Initially I approached this method as a mere tactic to overcome my shyness. Over time, however, this mint was more than just a friendly gesture. A mint, a shared laugh, a nod of gratitude—these subtle, non-verbal moments spoke volumes and often led to more profound conversations. Through these patternized acts I learned to read and respond to these cues, becoming more attuned to the needs and feelings of others. This approach didn't just help me make friends; it taught me to value and nurture the social bonds.

Clothes: Baggy jeans, denim jackets, leather bracelets, airforces. Fashion has always been my silent language, a way to express who I am without uttering a single word. Observing my own preferences in clothing, I noted patterns in the colors, fabrics, and styles that made me feel most confident and comfortable. This process involved experimenting with different outfits and paying attention to which ones garnered positive feedback like “You’re so drippy”, or simply made me feel good about myself. Each outfit became a blend of personal expression and careful selection, mirroring my internal journey. Initially, my goal was to find clothes that helped me blend in, but over time, I started to embrace bolder choices that reflected my individuality. This approach didn't just enhance my wardrobe; it taught me to celebrate my authentic self, understanding that true style is about confidence and self-awareness. Recognizing these patterns in my preferences and adapting accordingly became a powerful strategy for overcoming the challenge of self-expression, similar to how I approach other aspects of life.

Prime numbers: 2,3,5,7,11… These seemingly simple yet enigmatic sequence of numbers only divisible by 1 and itself, has always fascinated me. My journey of research that dives deep through the Riemann Hypothesis serves a testament for my will to uncover a pattern that has eluded discovery for hundreds of years. The hypothesis suggests a hidden order within the apparent randomness of prime numbers, mirroring how I seek patterns to navigate the complexities of life.

In both mathematics and everyday challenges, identifying underlying structures enables me to find solutions. This analytical mindset helps me break down complex issues into manageable parts, find order in chaos, and devise effective strategies. Whether solving a mathematical theorem or addressing personal obstacles, my passion for uncovering hidden patterns equips me with the tools to tackle real-world challenges with confidence and precision.

True Brothers

It was a warm autumn afternoon, and the sun cast a golden hue over our backyard. What should have been a joyous celebration of my brother’s 13th birthday turned into a moment that changed my life forever. In a fit of frustration during a heated soccer game, I pushed him too hard, and his head hit the concrete border of our grassy yard.

My journey toward understanding forgiveness began that day. Raised by Persian grandparents whose Muslim faith was shaped by deep persecution, and educated by Jesuit teachers who demanded we behave as the Bible intends, I had always been surrounded by teachings of compassion and resilience. Yet, in that moment of panic and regret, these lessons felt distant and abstract.

As I knelt beside my brother, seeing his unconscious form and feeling the weight of my actions, all our petty arguments over which Spider-Man movie was the best seemed trivial. The following days were a blur of hospital visits and anxious waiting. Each day I returned to the sterile room, my guilt and fear deepened. On the fourth day, I brought a small SpongeBob figurine, hoping it would bring him comfort if he woke up. As I sat by his bed, talking about our favorite episodes, I realized how much I missed our arguments and laughter. When he finally opened his eyes, a wave of relief and overwhelming emotion washed over me. Holding his hand, I whispered, “I’m sorry, I just wanted you to think I was cool.” Tears welled up as I understood that our poor relationship was partly my fault for not being more considerate.

My teachers in school used to say we must “Forgive as the Lord does,” a phrase I had dismissed as a meaningless cliché. In the aftermath of my brother’s accident, I struggled with this concept. Why should I forgive myself when the guilt was so overwhelming? Initially, I tried to avoid him, fearing his resentment. But on a whim, I invited him to play basketball. He hesitated but eventually joined me. Our games became a routine, and through this shared activity, we began to rebuild our bond. This act of mutual forgiveness helped me realize that our sins, though personal, could be overcome through understanding and compassion.

This newfound understanding of forgiveness and kindness extended beyond my family. During an overnight school camp, I met Brad, a fellow camper with a tough exterior. One evening, he accidentally broke my Celtics headphones. Anger surged within me, but I remembered my journey with my brother. Taking a deep breath, I said, “It’s okay, accidents happen,” and offered to help him fix them. Brad’s surprised reaction and the mutual respect that followed taught me that empathy and kindness could bridge divides and create meaningful connections.

Today, my brother and I are not just siblings but true brothers. Our relationship is defined by our willingness to forgive and support each other. This lesson is one I carry with me in all my interactions. When I arrive at my dorm, I will be open-hearted and welcoming. In the classroom, I will listen and engage with empathy. The knowledge that forgiveness and kindness can shape our reality and help us see the best in others will guide me throughout my life: in friendship, by resolving conflicts amicably; at work, by collaborating effectively with colleagues; and in community service, by showing empathy to those in need.

I thought I did everything right, but the delicate, whispery bodies of my lifeless ornamental shrimp, laying belly-up on the moss soil proved otherwise. Despite extensive research, careful acclimation in pH-adjusted water, and strategically placed moss balls, only a few of the original fifteen shrimp remained. Galaxy Pintos, Blue Bolts, and Orange-Eye Blue Tigers, these were no ordinary shrimp. I went over the variables in my mind. Did I acclimate too quickly? Overshoot on the hardness of the water? Was I too optimistic about my ability to raise these fragile creatures? Stunned and saddened, I was now confronted with my failure, listless shrimp lying motionless on the aqua soil.

Like other projects I've undertaken, I had to do a lot of convincing and strategic ignoring of objections for this endeavor. My mom's concerned gaze while I hauled five gallons of reverse osmosis water into the playroom is one I've seen before. But, I have always been stubbornly optimistic, rarely dissuaded by others' doubts. When faced with a less-than-desirable outcome, I see a puzzle to be solved or a person to be understood. When down a set in a tennis match, I remind myself that I’m just warming up and get to work analyzing my opponent’s game. For exams that prove to be trickier than expected, I consider whether I should do more practice questions, or study different material. And when gearing up to talk to skeptical state representatives and overworked school officials to advocate for radon testing in Pennsylvania schools, I consider what their priorities might be and reflect on how I might better address what is meaningful to them.

It is this stubborn optimism that prompted 8th grade me to call Bob Lewis at the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection after our home was selected for a year-long radon monitoring study. I have approached the need for radon testing in our schools from different angles, including research that demonstrated students are potentially exposed to 2x background radiation, tutorials for HVAC students about radon testing/mitigation, and presentations to our local/state legislators. Sometimes, I am congratulated on my work; other times, I am listened to politely and told it is unlikely this bill would pass. From stuttering conversations as a skinny eighth grader, to a TEDx stage, I’ve learned that analogies are my friend when explaining that our community is at an elevated risk for radon exposure. Explaining that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency action level for radon, 4 pCi/L is equivalent to smoking 8 cigarettes/day, paints a picture that is hard to ignore.

As the only high school student presenter at TEDx Northampton Community College, I did not want to waste this opportunity and practiced my presentation until I could give it in my sleep. However, the initial jolt of stepping onto the stage, lights blinding, I became frozen momentarily. But, I am at my core, a fighter, a believer in myself. A deep breath, a reminder to myself of why this is important, I faced an audience I could not see. I shared why our area had high levels of radon, a carcinogenic gas, and what we could do about it. When teachers, friends and neighbors share that they tested and mitigated their homes because of my talk, I am gratified, knowing that their homes are safer.

For my delicate shrimp, I set about making changes, adding minerals to help them properly molt their exoskeletons, enhancing their diet with flour-like, microorganism-containing food, and adding blue vitamin sticks to strengthen their exoskeleton. Bit by bit, I see the remaining shrimp become used to their new home. The dark blue color that indicated stress was fading, and they slowly turned light blue, a sign of good health. My efforts were rewarded a few weeks later. Little blue and white lines in the tank. Undeniable proof that my shrimp had adjusted to the tank and were healthy. Shrimp babies.

My grandmother slides me last week’s edition of The Daily Herald across our dining table. She takes my hand, tenderly guiding me through folding my first origami tray. The precious jewels that lay inside? Our snacktime sunflower seeds!

During quiet summer mornings like these, I’ve learned how to meticulously repurpose old sheets of newspaper into beautiful keepsakes, from molding Chicago Tribune newspapers into flower vases to montaging vintage book covers for our bookshelf. Joining her at the tableside, creasing each fold ever so precisely, every creation of ours seemed like a masterpiece.

“Polanyeyouyong,” she would tell me. Even scraps have their value. Having lived through China’s Cultural Revolution, my grandmother had no choice but to ration necessities like paper and cloth. Despite her stinging memories of stitching together paper-thin clothes in the wintry cold, my grandma now laughs as she guides my hand through each patterned embroidery on her blanket.

***

“Is there any way I can lengthen my laptop’s battery life?” Grand asked, unmuting his mic.

Born and raised on the outskirts of Nairobi, Kenya, Grand didn’t have someone to feed his curiosity surrounding computers. Hungry for knowledge, our structured virtual Code2Connect lessons soon expanded into chaotic after-school “device-maximizing” open discussions. Together, we squeeze every bit of value out of his dilapidated laptop, from refining power settings to revamping hardware components. Fixing Grand’s defective webcam by installing a new driver, I finally was able to see the face behind the voice that had been so familiar to me over the months, and in that moment, all the miles between us seemed to disappear.

Following my grandmother's expert origami folding techniques, I crease and flatten scrap cardboard from routine school lunch shipments, assembling drop-off boxes to collect dozens more used laptops and electrical devices to send to schools around the world. As I tenderly disinfect chipped 10-inch Macs or cracked tablets with isopropyl alcohol and a microfiber cloth, I take comfort in knowing that each scrappy device donated by my peers preserves a treasure of intellectual discovery. And each time I go to the local library to race children at Mario Kart using the previously damaged consoles they donated—“Wii-Serve Wednesdays,” we’d call them—I’m reminded of my grandmother’s words: it takes just a scrap to ignite a lifetime of passion.

***

“Would you be a peach and throw me a shirt?” Blenda hollers at me.

Blenda, hailing from Englewood, Chicago, is a two-time breast cancer survivor and caring grandmother, with two daughters hospitalized from the disease. As she taught me the perfect baking soda-to-vinegar ratio needed to create my own fabric softener, I thought I’d teach her a clothing hack of my own.

So, prior to setting up for the Pink Divas and Gents Breast Cancer 5K, I invited Blenda and other grandmas to join me with some old white t-shirts and pink dye. Together, we spent the morning scrunching, banding, and squirting them senseless. While their days accompanying a belted cardigan were long gone, they’d found new life as pink pride headbands and wristbands. (“What a hoot!” Blenda would say).

A horn blares. Before I rush to set up a registration tent, I look behind me to see Blenda and the grandmas together by the starting line. Sporting their newly upcycled pink shirts, they groove and clap to the beat of “Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.” As Blenda waves me over, welcoming me to their dance circle, I hesitatingly put forward a tentative two-step. But as the tempo picked up, I spontaneously busted into The Carlton! (or tried to, at least). Soon, the circle expands, and we happily throw extra pink gear to the participants that trickled in. As I finally tied my own t-shirt-bandana around my head, I realized that it wasn’t the concrete act of repurposing scraps that brought the most joy; it was the mountains of communities it created.

***

Looking back on these moments, I wonder: Maybe that's why I strive for compassion and creativity in everything I do. Grand now spends his weekends running a free computer repair clinic for his neighbors. Blenda now runs her own “Dye-namic Creations” class at her local YMCA. I still fold these paper trays in my dining room each morning, only now, I do it with my seven-year-old brother. I will never forget my late grandmother’s dedication to others. I, too, with an eye for value and a heart for service, will continue to make mountains out of scraps, just as she did for me.

Is it possible to fight a war in a day? According to my history teacher, yes. Actually, he was tasked with teaching World War I to eighth graders in less than a week. However, this would never be enough for me. I went home and searched on YouTube: WWI. I grabbed every article, watched every video, and listened to every lecture I could. In class, I constantly raised my hand, offering details about the Schlieffen Plan and the Battles of the Somme and Verdun. Ever since, I’ve been studying history just for fun.

Fast forward to high school. At my friend Kyle’s house, my friends and I noticed a small hole surrounded by even smaller mounds of dirt. Kyle told us it was a war trench he tried digging back in eighth grade. We all knew this would be our new project.

We didn’t get far before we had to leave, as the sun was setting. Later, I got a text from Kyle saying we should plan it out before continuing, so I decided to research WWI trenches.
