The next day I returned with notes, and our trench started to take shape in the following weeks, even though we were using only shovels, a bucket, rakes, a root cutter, and a pickaxe.

Once the trench looked somewhat complete, we had another idea: wear German or French attire and stage a battle along the hillside. Orchestrating this task, I researched uniforms of soldiers during Verdun. Using some money I’d saved up from working, I bought pieces of a German uniform and showed them to my friends. Everyone approved; however, construction still needed to be done, and winter was approaching, making it impossible to dig into the frozen ground. While we still work on it in small groups, we haven’t been able to fully complete it. Even though it’s a loss for me, I’ve gained a new appreciation for research and for sharing what I learned.

My love for learning doesn’t stop at history. Early in my music education, I wondered whether to continue the clarinet, but that changed once I joined the high school concert band. At the first concert, I arrived early to warm up, and as I entered the auditorium with my friends, we saw the dark stage with thirty silhouettes barely illuminated by the stage lights. When the lights turned on, we saw the glimmer of brass instruments, the rims of the drums, and the musicians' sunglasses reflecting the lights back at us. Our jazz band kicked off the night, and they played together perfectly, inspiring me to try out. I worked and saved money for a saxophone and started taking lessons. Eventually I got a better horn. I wanted to learn everything–how to play it right, how to improvise, how to create cool rhythms. After being accepted into jazz band, I asked for a keyboard, as if two instruments weren’t enough.

I still wanted to learn more. Taking private lessons, I learned soprano saxophone, along with alto sax and clarinet. I was playing three instruments in two bands. Still, I looked to add a different instrument, the guitar. Having gotten an acoustic that year, I saved up and bought an electric so I could learn all of my favorite songs. And even though my fundamentals still need improvement, I have learned so much more than I thought I could, surrounded by great people who are as passionate as I am.

When something interests me, even if it’s challenging, I go for it. My jazz teacher says I should start showing off when I have a solo, but that’s not me. It’s not what I value in music, or in history, or in any of my other passions. I’m just eager to learn as much as I can, in any way that I can, and share my knowledge with others.

Should I pick this glittery bear? No…too shiny. How about this Hello Kitty one? Ah…too childish. What about this clear green dinosaur? No, the more I stared at it, the weirder its eyes looked. In the center of cuteness, Seoul, Korea, I was on a mission to find the perfect sticker, but I wasn’t having any luck.

My love for stickers flourished when I received my first sticker book in third grade, quickly filling each page with diverse little beings. To many, the book was a chaotic mess, but in my innocent eyes, it was a work of art. As I grew older, I developed a professional eye for sticker collecting, and my criteria for new additions grew stricter, causing my once abundant sticker family to dwindle. I pinned my hopes on my trip to Korea—the mecca of stickers—to revive my collection. Despite thorough exploration, I failed to find a sticker that met my standards. I couldn’t even articulate what I was truly looking for—I just knew I hadn’t found it yet.

After returning from my failed expedition, a thought sparked in the midst of my frustration—could I create my own stickers? I carefully placed my Hello Kitty stuffed animal on my table, grasped my Apple Pencil, and opened a crisp white Note on my iPad, ready to glide away. There was just one problem—I was a terrible drawer.

My first doodles were laughable—eyes too close, head too big, and even Hello Kitty’s pink bow became a blob. But amidst my laughter, I found a freakish joy in letting my hands dance. I continued spewing the visions in my head onto my screen, from drawings of spam musubis to multitudes of bears (the easiest to draw).

Although some doodles were barely comprehensible to the uncultured eye, where palm trees resembled spiky hammers and a bowl of kimchi jjigae looked like a red vase, I identified what my sticker family lacked—a sense of home.

Eager to see if others shared my perspective, I began posting on Instagram, hoping for validation and feedback on my creations. My initial posts received astronomical engagement (from friends). Their supportive comments motivated me to keep posting. I relished the nervous excitement I felt when hitting "post" and seeing a once blank page filled with my weekly creations. From watching numerous YouTube tutorials to DMing local artists and sticker shops for guidance, I received unexpected results.

My five-second “animation reel” (only mouth movements, which still stretched my capabilities) ended up receiving 984K views, and this engagement quickly transferred over to my other posts. I couldn’t believe it. My simple drawings resonated with thousands of people online.

Seeing this support, I was empowered to start my own sticker business, Tofuboo Studio. Each sticker, created during countless hours spent slouching over my iPad and Silhouette machine, excited me in the creative process. My enjoyment led me to pursue various avenues within my business, deepening my connection and understanding of my tight-knit, multicultural community.

From engaging in pop-up events, where I bonded with my local audience, to collaborating with local organizations in creating stickers or a cultural-themed coloring book, I found immense satisfaction in immersing myself in my community and crafting items that truly represented home—not only for myself, but for others as well.

Being able to share something that wasn't a perfect work of art but was still "me" was freeing, allowing my creativity and thoughts to flow without the restriction of perfectionism. Each doodle, whether a bucket of Korean fried chicken or a bear sleeping, told a story—my story—in a pretty cute way. I don't think I’ll ever find the perfect sticker, and honestly, I’m no longer seeking to. The joy I’ve discovered comes not from finding but from making. And, I’ve learned that trying something new isn’t about being perfect or even good at the start—it’s about embracing the messy, imperfect process, and not holding myself back.

Snakefruits brown and scaly. Rambutans red as rubies. Welcome to the most enchanting place in the world: my mother’s garden. It was here, at the tender age of four, when I understood how small we truly are against the grand tapestry of nature. Plants cleanse our air, nourish us with their bounty, and transform our surroundings into breathtaking landscapes. Yet, within my mother’s gentle teachings, a harsher truth emerged: humans possess an immense capacity for destruction, far greater than the plants’ ability to protect themselves. Nurturing these living beings was not just a task but a necessity. This early lesson instilled in me a profound interest in horticulture and, eventually, an enduring fascination with the natural world.

At school, I marveled at the alluring beauty of endangered species like the Sumatran tiger, the Snow Leopard, and the Bali Myna. Yet, alongside this wonder, I felt a growing rage. The more I learned about the grave consequences of relying on fossil fuels—the destruction of habitats, the hastening of climate change—the more I realized I could not stand idly by. Watching the plants and animals I cherished being destroyed by human avarice and neglect was unbearable.

Future generations will face extinction if we continue to ignore the escalating threats of global warming, fail to drastically reduce our carbon emissions, and neglect the urgent need for comprehensive environmental policies and sustainable living practices. My burning ambition to protect what I loved transformed me into a climate advocate.

My advocacy journey truly began in the summer of 2023 when I interned at Fairatmos, Indonesia’s first climate tech company. I know that we cannot fight climate change with just sticks and stones. We need to leverage the latest technological advancements, from renewable energy innovations and carbon capture systems to AI-driven climate modeling and smart agriculture, to even have a fighting chance to survive this relentless rise in earth’s temperature. What captivates me about Fairatmos is its groundbreaking business model that seamlessly integrates nature-based solutions—like carbon sequestration through forests and mangrove swamps—with cutting-edge technologies, including satellites and drones, to precisely measure the net additionality of carbon offsets.

The summer of 2024 marked an exhilarating turn in my journey as I returned to work on Fairatmos' conservation project in Cilacap. The Cilacap mangrove swamp, spanning 5,000 acres, is a vibrant realm teeming with biodiversity and vital for carbon absorption. While staying in the village, I had the privilege of delving into captivating stories and exchanging innovative business ideas with the locals. From Harris and his fellow fishermen, who ingeniously optimized spaces around mangrove roots for aqua farming, to Kuntoro, who spearheaded local conservation efforts by commercializing snacks made from mangrove trees, the resourcefulness of these community members was truly inspiring. At the local school, children brimming with hopes and aspirations eagerly shared their ideas with me. Rachmat, for example, wondered what programming skills are needed to become an ethical hacker, while Zakri worked with me on an Excel sheet to forecast the potential return of building an eco-tourism business in Cilacap. These children, full of life, hope, and dreams, fueled my determination to safeguard our planet for their future.

After my sojourn in Cilacap, my commitment to climate advocacy crystallized with newfound clarity. In my university life, I envision promoting eco-tourism and preserving mangrove trees in Indonesia, collaborating with students, alumni and sustainable local business partners. I also plan to champion nature-based solutions as a powerful tool to combat climate change by establishing a nature preservation society on campus. This journey has shown me that a dedication to environmental advocacy, grounded in humility, intellectual curiosity, and common sense, can drive meaningful change. By continuing to nurture my passion for nature on campus, I hope to inspire others to join me in protecting our planet for generations to come.

For years I’ve had the ability to breathe life into an amalgamation of ivory keys, metal strings, and wooden hammers. This realization hit me as I sat down on the piano stool, the hushed chatter of the audience subsiding as my fingers eased on the smooth, polished keyboard. Years before, I would be left frozen in elementary school talent shows as the idea of a full auditorium engulfed my thoughts. As time passed, the audiences became merely a backdrop to a stage, my trepidation now replaced by a euphoric passion that extends far beyond the stage. My fingers flowed through the keys, and it felt as if I was floating alongside the notes, communicating with the audience through a language of melody.

I have always had a great appreciation for music; many of my fondest memories are of listening to the lively and pulsating rhythms of Latin music with my family and dancing (or at least trying) to songs by Willy Chirino and Celia Cruz. These vibrant tunes have been ingrained as part of my Hispanic identity and laid the foundations for my love of music. I would like to say that I have also enjoyed playing the piano since the beginning of my lessons, but that is not the case. When I started at age five, it seemed too challenging, and I thought it was as riveting as my household chores. However, once I began learning pieces by great composers, such as Mozart’s Turkish March or Beethoven’s Sonata Pathetique, I found myself intrigued by the possibilities of this instrument, and music became part of my daily life. I have often found myself reading, doing schoolwork, or even typing this essay while listening to music that ranges from Chopin’s ballades to Queen’s rock.

I yearned not only to understand this language of melodies but to fluently converse in it; I wanted to learn to play the notes that flowed into chords and built into beautiful harmonies. Every fumbled note was motivation to keep improving, and each conquered piece was a reward that urged me to move forward. Not only had I improved my musical skill, but I found that this personal relationship with music had transcended beyond the piano, shaping my determination to face challenges in other aspects of my life. Whether solving a difficult differential equation, analyzing the works of Shakespeare, or studying the neural pathways that control human functions, I found myself doing it with the same dedication and enjoyment as I would with a challenging etude.

Music has helped me form a deeper connection with people, which I feel while playing a lively duet with my little brother as my mom relives her ballet years and the rest of the family cheers and laughs along to the music, or performing "My Way" at a nursing home and glancing at someone in the audience reminiscing with a sparkle in their eye. I’m definitely no Liszt, but I for sure enjoy sharing music with others and watching it light up their hearts. The piano has also had a unique effect on my soul; whether as a way to freely express myself or to unwind after a long day, I often sought refuge immersing myself in the comforting voice of this instrument.

The piece reached its climax, as both hands’ melodies intertwined together emulating the sound of a symphony. A blend of relief and joy surged through my heart and onto the keys as the music began to reach its resolution, the harmonies of just a few seconds ago dwindling into a lone voice. The final chord was still resonating throughout the theater; just as I had instilled life into the piano, music has inspired me to look to the future, offering me a unique perspective in which I can appreciate the beauty of humanity’s expressions. Perhaps this peculiar four-legged wooden box is more alive than I thought.

As an aromatic candle filled the Garden City Transcendental Meditation center with the soothing scent of apple pie, my instructor, Harry, assured me that the process would be—and should—be effortless. Relaxing, I sank deeper into the marshmallow easy-chair, closed my eyes, and silently repeated my mantra.

I admit: I didn’t achieve anything close to enlightenment during that first session. Yet, over the next several weeks, as I meditated for twenty minutes, twice daily, a sense of calm settled, lingered, then spread. As I began to step outside of myself, I became more aware of the pulsing heartbeat of my own thoughts, more aware of the world around me.

I first noticed the early signs of mindfulness during Soo Bahk Do martial arts practice. Leading the other students through the Passai snake form, I sensed a heightened awareness of their breathing, their movements, as we harmonized in a cohesive flow. We never flowed like that before. And as even my most impatient pupils appreciated the joys of our togetherness, this harmony extended, over time, throughout the Dojang.

Home, however, was a work-in-progress. In fact, my home situation is what originally motivated my family to try meditation—in a collective effort to help my brother, Alex, with his attention deficit disorder. There were days when concern over Alex’s condition would trigger screaming matches. As I listened to the turmoil, I realized that our family could only be as happy as our least happy member.

Still, meditation was a safe harbor. And with each heartbeat, each repetition of my mantra, I not only relaxed, but also continued to step further outside of myself, becoming more empathetic, more inclusive. With Alex, especially, I began to wonder how it would feel to walk in his shoes. Interspersed between the awkward jokes and the occasionally excessive attempts to please were the laughs that went on for a bit too long. To me, his well-meaning idiosyncrasies were endearing; but I could see how others might be less forgiving.

As I peered past Alex’s smile to the eyes that betrayed a sadness—a loneliness—I resolved to meditate with him.

We went minimalist. No candles. No music. Just the two of us, our mantras pulsing silently to the rhythm of our heartbeats. As a disciple of process, I reminded Alex of my Tortoise approach to meditation—steady, consistent, no slacking. As days turned into weeks turned into months, Alex became more focused, more comfortable in his own skin. Insomnia became less problematic. And when Alex became the one to nudge me awake when I accidentally fell asleep during our session, I happily acknowledged his progression.

As Alex’s improvement continued—and as I deliberately positioned our meditations, for maximum exposure, in the living room, smack dab in the middle of our house—the other family members couldn’t help but take notice. First, my other brother, CJ, “wanted in” on our meditation party, then my parents. Our family dynamic began to change. And as our heartbeats harmonized, there was more tolerance, more lightness.

Witnessing the butterfly effect of Alex’s meditation-inspired improvement on the happiness of my entire family, I began to consider if society too could only be as happy as its least happy members. What if meditation and wellness education could be brought to the less fortunate? Perhaps, even to one?

That’s why last fall, I launched “The Wellness Corner,” my regular column in the school newspaper—to share tips on practical philosophy, meditation, and well-being. Unfortunately, as there were no analytics to help gauge its effectiveness, I was flying blind. Weeks went by. No “likes.” No feedback. Nothing.

And then, one cold December day, I received an email from my classmate, Bernie. We hadn’t spoken since elementary school, but in that message, he mentioned that he’d been inspired by my column to take up meditation and asked if he could contribute a piece he wrote on the Flow State. I knew he was quiet and also, that he’d been struggling. But he’d been courageous to reach out.

And as I pored over his email, I thought of my brother.

As I considered the karmic significance of my initiatives, my heart began to flutter. I imagined the fluttering wings of the butterfly, sending out wisps of air, gaining in strength, its power blooming outward, like the petals of a flower—manifesting in ways both mysterious and incalculable. “The Wellness Corner” still hasn’t gone viral. The earth didn’t shake. But as the pulsing in my ears drummed louder, my paradigm shifted.

Perhaps, its ultimate impact will be like the wings of a butterfly—measured not by numbers, but by heartbeats.

Henna, mehendi, maradhani, all are names for the beautiful Indian art form that shaped me. The artistic application of henna has been a fascination for me since I was five. It started out with an obsession of getting my henna professionally done on my hands. I would beg my parents for any opportunity to get my henna done. I would sit for hours while an artist applied henna to my hands relishing the cold feeling of the paste on my skin and the smell of ground leaves. A smell that never fails to bring a smile to my face. While henna certainly has very deep cultural roots to my ethnicity, henna has always been synonymous to happiness. Looking at my hands like a work of art and enjoying the beauty of simplistic design stained onto my skin. As I grew up, henna never lost the joy it brought me. My parents started buying me henna cones instead of taking me to get it professionally done. They saw how happy henna made me and encouraged me to try it out for myself. I started experimenting with my own creativeness, and I learned how hard it was to create art. I made so many horrific designs that I almost never wanted to touch henna again but the happiness it gave me and my persistence persevered instead of my want to give up. Henna taught me patience and resilience. I wanted to make sure a design that lasted for days on my skin was perfect. Every time I messed up, I would run my hands under hot water and try again, overlapping the stain of the previous design with a new improved version. Henna taught me how nothing comes naturally, and all skills must be honed with practice. Over time I learned to understand henna’s temperament and would practice with any free time I had. I also started applying henna for others at local cultural or school events. I shared my love for the art and allowed others to carry that joy with me. In the present, henna has transformed into a coping mechanism. Whenever I am stressed, overwhelmed, or bored, I reach for the henna cone. The familiarity of the art form soothes me and reminds me of how far I have come and how much a simple hobby can shape me. Henna is something I hold close to my heart and love to share with others. I will always appreciate this art form which has become an integral part of my being.

Locked away in a self-imposed cage, I watched my peers enjoy and revel in their carefree moments of youth, clutching the key to freedom yet choosing isolation. At the time believing that trading my childhood to focus on preparing for the future, was the mandatory price paid for a secure enviable future. But the journey of overworking myself eventually taught me that a life without balance is a life half-lived.

I have never been a follower, often avoiding anything I deem could jeopardize my future. While many of my friends and classmates were quick to purchase cars or engage in typical yet questionable teenage pastimes, I remained focused in my commitment to my goals. My interests and priorities were clear, and I was and still am willing to forgo immediate gratification to achieve long-term success. This determination led me to leave old friends in pursuit of better education, going to a school where I didn't know anyone, only going because I knew it provided the best education within my area. This attitude resulted in me scoring straight A’s in classes I genuinely enjoyed, even though I found it challenging to excel in subjects that didn’t captivate my interest. My high school experience was influenced by my passion for business and architecture. Being enrolled in a business pathway, I dedicated myself to excelling in these courses, maintaining an A average was a testament to my dedication. Formerly struggling, I slowly became better at math once realizing its importance in architecture, so much so that I am taking honors precalculus in my senior year. Also taking AP Studio Art to enhance my artistic abilities and CAD to improve my knowledge on the subject, taking these specific classes due to their correlation with architecture.

This summer, I have been studying pre-calculus in preparation for the upcoming school year, knowing that architecture is not just an interest but a goal set in stone. Architecture has always been a passion of mine, stemming from when I was in elementary school. My love for art and design combined with aspirations to design houses and see them come to life nurtured this passion. However, my journey has not been without its struggles; my inability to perform well in subjects I found uninteresting was evident during my freshman and sophomore years in honors English. Despite disliking the subject, I took honors classes regardless in order to challenge myself. Although Excelling in creativity and analysis on the rubrics, I found some of the technical aspects of writing difficult. Conversely, I thrived in honors English with an emphasis on communication, this being driven by my genuine interest in becoming a better communicator. Initially, speeches left me anxious and breathless, my interest helped me overcome these challenges and excel in the class. When it comes to architecture, it's this interest that drives me to perform better and study harder. I graduated with well above average grades, recognizing the importance of maintaining good grades for college. While my grades may not be outstanding; I genuinely put my all into achieving the goals I set for myself.

As I entered high school, I took a significant step in prioritizing my future over short-term gratification. I often find myself alone, studying and bettering myself, despite having many friends and enjoying social interactions. High school has transformed me into someone who goes days or even weeks without indulging in distractions. My journey has taught me the importance of balance—between ambition and living in the moment. Attending this college is an essential part of my path to becoming the architect I have aspired to be since childhood. I am committed to living the best life I can, understanding the work required to do so, and seizing every opportunity to grow and succeed. I hope to bring this same dedication and passion to your college, continuing my journey towards becoming the architect I’ve always dreamed of being.

“Build Ninjago Lego Samurai”. “Basketball”. “Do math homework (maybe)”. The words were scribbled across a faulty, dusted chalkboard through the careful maneuvers of a dissipating green chalk piece. The colors nearly faded, the words barely visible. It was my first ever to-do list at the age of seven. It kept my jumbled thoughts productive, my ambitions delineated, and my mom proud for actually trying to organize my mess-making instincts.

Upon selling my chalkboard on the Facebook marketplace, I delved into a physical calendar. Each distinct day featured my miniature handwriting delicately detailing descriptions of some personal innovation. On Christmas day, it was a Monopoly game family tradition I started. It spotlighted my dad’s transformation into his cocky alter-ego and my mother’s bloodthirsty competitiveness. At 2:00 AM every January 12th and April 15th, the calendar whispered “origami!”. I was no origami virtuoso, but I performed complicated manipulations (like the Yama-ori technique) to create birthday gifts like skydiving (my mom’s favorite activity) or sunglasses (my dad’s favorite style enhancer).

Being more technologically equipped led me to pursue different to-do lists. I became a Google Calendar enthusiast, MacBook Calendar connoisseur (although really confusing), and Phone Reminder merchant. One reminder, which was always displayed from 9:00 PM to 1:00 AM, was a special trademark: “Debate Research Time!!!”. It involved indulging in political scientist Ted Carpenter’s analysis of Russia’s disinformation warfare in the Baltic states. It entailed scavenging Google’s 12th and 13th pages for the perfectly curated research study on single-payer healthcare. It demanded the struggle to bypass the New York Times’ paywall.

Sometimes, the reminder said, “Practice Debate :O”, which meant many things. At times, it included ironing out my articulation, practicing speeches with a pen in my mouth, or saying “watermelon” in between each word of a speech. Other times, it triggered what my mom called “obnoxiously long showers” of me singing rebuttal speeches for my Aveeno shampoo bottle. Or it was debating skilled debaters like Gene and Anuj, soaking in their insights and conglomerating their debate styles to evolve my unique flair. Even still, these efforts did not gleam in rapid success; consecutive losses in debate rounds at the Glenbrooks and Lexington Tournaments culminated in an initial 0-8 record. That only served as a reminder to stick around for late-night 4-hour debate calls and finish that 7th re-do of a previous speech on West African urbanization I delivered in a round that I lost.

This birthed a fierce desire to spread the infectious joy of debating to others. While my initial Zoom classes unveiled just two participants, hearing students’ “OHHs” was an impenetrable incentive to rally Jamaican students and champion debate within Georgia’s school curriculums. And along the way, debate helped me fulfill another reminder: “Talk to people”. Debate reshaped me from being petrified of asking the McDonald’s cashier for extra ketchup packets to being comfortable delivering speeches to diverse audiences.

After a while, I switched back to an old-fashioned reminder approach: 8.5 x 11 paper. It exhibited a warzone of clashing pen ink of stark color differences and a unique linguistic style I could only decode. It got the job done, like crossing out my daily rendition of listening to archived NPR Politics Podcast episodes. When I ran out of paper, I turned to gum wrappers, writing jargon that signaled me to nervously wait for the 9:00 PM scheduled presidential debate.

Gradually, these to-do lists became less about productivity and more about mapping my growth. Whether it was “tournament this weekend!” or “iron clothes”, each gum wrapper, each calendar notification, and each cross-out symbolized a canvas of self-exploration. It charted my adventure from a young boy enamored with Lego Batman to a national debater eager to immerse the next student into debate’s beauty. And I look forward to plunging into a new adventure in college, one (or maybe 2-3) to-do lists at a time.

My bulky leather harness was not-so-discreetly hidden under my costume and made me sort of waddle in an ungainly manner. It was not a flattering look but that was the least of my concerns. It was time to hook my harness up to the cable wire and pulley system and “fly” above stage. I felt that familiar rush of excitement as the cable wire abruptly hoisted me 20 feet up. From this elevated vantage point, I could see that all 2,500 seats in Taft Theatre were filled.

As the namesake character in Casper, the Friendly Musical, my face was airbrushed an unsettling bluish white, complete with exaggerated blue freckles, an attempt to make me look more approachable and less cadaverous. My voice was cooperating as I began to sing my favorite solo, “Halfway Home.” Then I noticed the cable wire was spinning, which meant I was spinning too. This was not ideal because I soon found myself with my back to the audience. How, I wondered, could this be happening? I lost focus and my voice weakened. Beneath the stage makeup, my face blushed with embarrassment and my ears burned with heat.

Then I shifted my focus to all of the people who purchased a ticket for the show. Determined to give them a good experience, I came up with a solution. I slowed down the spinning by extending my legs and arms. Then I subtly swayed counter to the angular momentum. Facing the audience again, I finished the song with a crescendo of passion and tears of joy. Of the 17 times that I performed Casper, this show contained the only blunder. But I remember it as the time I gracefully recovered from an awkward situation by embracing the unexpected.

Ben, my older brother, is on the autism spectrum and does not like surprises. For many years, he didn’t understand why I even wanted to be involved in musical theater because he couldn’t relate to my enthusiastic nature. Ben doesn’t sugar coat his words and regularly tells me his opinion, whether I’ve asked for it or not. But one day, as he was watching me struggle to prepare for an important audition, his attitude softened, and he agreed to help. While Ben, my unlikely acting coach, flatly read aloud the lines of the other characters, I recited my lines from memory. I was having difficulties and desperately wanted to take a break. But Ben is a force of nature when it comes to stamina and attention to detail; so instead, we practiced late into the night. The next morning, I nailed that audition because I knew every line inside and out.

Since then, I’ve had many occasions to implement Ben’s relentless approach to preparation. This past June, I used “Ben’s method” when repeatedly rehearsing my PowerPoint presentation before sharing my research on “forever chemicals” with the Indian Hill Mayor and Village Council. Thoroughly prepared, I felt competent and at ease. I could therefore focus on conveying a sense of urgency and teamwork. This resulted in their unanimous approval to build a municipal filtration system capable of removing “forever chemicals” from our communities’ tap water.

Wanting to better understand what went technically wrong the night of my pulley system and cable wire snafu, I went to the I hardware store and purchased a pulley system of my own. After attaching its fulcrum to a sturdy branch in a large Oak tree, I used it to seamlessly transport all of the materials that Ben and I needed to build a treehouse for our younger brother. This project turned out to be incredibly challenging, but Ben and I enjoyed coming up with solutions to the difficulties we encountered. I still don’t know how the cable wire became twisted that pivotal night in Casper. But I do know that life is a journey filled with wonderful and ridiculous possibilities and I will come prepared.

Living with younger siblings is like being on a roller coaster of annoying behaviors and non-existent personal boundaries. Having successfully lived through this with two little sisters, I am here to offer my advice and six skills you will need for survival.

When it comes to handling younger siblings, it's important to realize that the arguments and tattle-tailing can be managed. My middle sister Sadie is quick-witted and great with a comeback. This is why I learned skill number one, the art of patience. Instead of escalating an argument, I take a deep breath and think before I act or speak. Patience has won me many battles!

Sometimes your siblings will make unreasonable requests (or demands) like wanting to use your brand-new skateboard or hang with your friends, which means you must master skill number two, negotiation. Instead of getting into a regrettable conflict, try to seek out a negotiation. This works well with my sister Keira. I found that always telling her no meant that she would inevitably sneak behind my back and try to get away with it anyway. I do however suggest you approach your negotiations carefully; headlocks and yelling will ensue otherwise.

With all siblings, get ready to ditch the concept of personal space. My bedroom is a shopping mall and ATM for my little sisters. While your parents may preach "sharing is caring," the loss of your brand-new sweatshirt will drive you mad. This is why it is essential to master the skill of organization. Now, I can’t say my room is in perfect order, but I have clear spaces for my favorite items and of course money.

Never anticipate having any sense of privacy in your personal relationships. Younger siblings want to know everything, and even if you don’t tell them, they will find out. Keep an eye out for the shadow of little feet outside your door, my sisters are like tiny investigators who love to hear everything my friends and I are saying. This is where you learn one of the most important skills, inclusion. No one likes to be left out, especially my sisters. I’ve learned to share stories and pictures of my friends and include them (a bit) when I have friends over. Even the littlest inclusion can go a long way to promote happiness.

There will be moments when you perceive your younger sibling as being from a different planet. They might share experiences that are difficult for you to fully understand, such as unequal treatment or bullying. As my sisters have gotten older, I realized that being a girl is a lot more complicated and stressful than being a boy. Their problems seem foreign from my own and I’ve struggled to process it sometimes. It is during these instances I mastered skill five; the art of listening. This can be a tough one for someone with a lot of opinions and suggestions, but sometimes it's OK not to respond, they just need someone to listen.

And that brings us to the last skill, and this one might take some time, acceptance. After all the patience you’ve shown, all the negotiations you’ve had, successful efforts at inclusion, and hours of listening you should have a pretty good understanding of who your siblings are. Last summer, I was leaving to go surfing and woke my sister Sadie up at 6 am to go with. On that day our relationship changed from siblings to friends. I have accepted, and even appreciate, all her quirks and comebacks. She has a picture in her room of the two of us walking to the beach that day with our boards. It’s a great reminder of all the skills my siblings have taught me, there are lifelong skills that have made me a better man and carry with me the rest of my life.

I was five when I discovered I could rearrange the sky. And no, I don’t mean literally moving it by hand—my creativity didn't stretch that far. Rather, I’m talking about the hot summer nights that I spent sitting in Pappa’s comforting lap. As we pieced together our own constellations using the canvas of stars above, I pretended I was an adventurer navigating uncharted territory, painting the night with stories as I traversed across the limitless expanse of space.

But one day, I came home from school frustrated, slamming a copy of a constellation map I had received onto Pappa’s desk. To my horror, I’d learned that the bright white lights in the sky had already been connected thousands of years ago—Draco, Orion, and Cassiopeia had existed centuries before I even made Spongebob and Garfield. I wasn’t a pioneer, I was a fraud…

“Why?” I breathlessly looked to my dad. “Why’d we waste our time?”

“We didn’t,” he said with a gentle smile.

I stare at the twinkling lights above for the first time in a long while. A high school senior now, I understand their origin: the Big Bang. Yet, my hands continued to gravitate upwards, entranced by the same old fascination I felt years ago. As I began to connect the dots my way, I finally realize what my dad meant: The constellation map never changed anything, I was going to end up with patterns in the sky either way. But getting to share those ginger moments with Pappa? Experiencing the elation in paving my own path through the stars?

Definitely not a waste of time.

I see myself in the cosmos as I work—dynamic and vibrant yet simply a vessel yearning to fill its gaps. But rather than a mosaic of black, white, and purple, the colors collected by the curious explorer inside me complete who I am. Days and hours rewind as I remember…

***

Staggering to my seat, I feel like an inflatable dancer outside those car dealerships. Taking a deep breath, I glance at my opponent: tall, confident, prepared. They say debate is a place to voice your opinions; I say it’s an opportunity to face your fears. Public speaking was never my thing, and stepping into that battleground felt like diving into deep water for the first time. However, I defended my argument, delivered my rebuttal, and before I knew it, walked away victorious… battle scars turned into radiant gold badges of determination.

Sweat perspires on my forehead as I look down at the blueprint… concrete, lumber, roofing. What had I gotten myself into? I had never handled a power tool before, let alone built an entire dog shelter. Nevertheless, it only took one step across the starting line to begin, sparking a journey of learning how to embrace challenges and lead a team. While realizing that it was never about completing my Eagle Project, but treasuring the friends I made along the way, I felt something by my feet: a dog, its fur warm brown, wagging its tail happily as if thanking me.

My fingers danced across the keyboard—Java, HTML, Swift: all languages, yet none that can be spoken. Still, I strive to communicate with my community through each. With each project I coded, I gave these programming languages a voice to bring about change. Whether it was a website to make Model UN more accessible to impoverished students abroad or an app addressing the mental health crisis within my school, no predefined boundaries held me back—I was chained only by the deep blue of my dreams.

***

Gold, brown, blue… each color I encounter enriches the palette of my identity, weaving complete a constellation that holds together who I am and what I cherish. As I continue seeking life’s adventures, I gather new shades along the way, setting the stage to ultimately shed light upon the world in my own Big Bang.

Rambutan trees. Tulips red as rubies. Welcome to the most enchanting place in the world: my mother’s garden. It was here, at the tender age of four, that I first discovered the wonders of nature. Plants could purify our air, provide us with food, and beautify our surroundings. Yet, within my mother’s gentle teachings, a harsher truth emerged: humans possess an immense capacity for destruction, far greater than the plants’ ability to protect themselves. Nurturing these living beings was not just a task but a necessity. This early lesson instilled in me a profound concern for plants, sparking my interest in horticulture and, eventually, an enduring fascination with the natural world.

At school, I marveled at the alluring beauty of endangered species like the Sumatran tiger, the Snow Leopard, and the Bali Myna. Yet, alongside this wonder, I felt a growing rage. The more I learned about the grave consequences of relying on fossil fuels—the destruction of habitats, the hastening of climate change—the more I realized I could not stand idly by. Watching the plants and animals I cherished being destroyed by human avarice and neglect was unbearable.

It was then that I realized enough was enough. If no one was raising awareness and taking action against climate change, our generation would not survive. Greta Thunberg’s words, “The climate crisis has already been solved. We already have the facts and solutions. All we have to do is wake up and change,” resonated deeply within me. My burning ambition to protect what I loved transformed me into a climate advocate.

My advocacy journey truly began in the summer of 2023 when I interned at Fairatmos, Indonesia’s pioneering climate tech company. I joined this company to explore the intersections between technology and climate advocacy. I took the initiative to learn and work on various tasks, each assignment broadening my skills and understanding. By the end of my internship, I had assisted the Fairatmos CEO in identifying strategic alliances with other global climate tech companies, including co-developing an application with a Canadian firm for monitoring and enhancing carbon sequestration in Indonesian mangroves. This experience enriched my advocacy journey, pushing me to explore innovative technological solutions to environmental challenges.

The summer of 2024 marked an exhilarating turn in my journey as I returned to work on Fairatmos' conservation project in Cilacap. The Cilacap mangrove swamp, spanning 5,000 acres, is a vibrant realm teeming with biodiversity and vital for carbon absorption. Staying in the village, I was privileged to hear fascinating stories and exchange ideas with the locals. From Harris and his fellow fishermen, who optimized spaces around mangrove roots for aqua farming, to Kuntoro, who was preserving local conservation efforts through the commercialization of snacks made from mangrove trees, these narratives highlighted the inseparability of human lives and nature. At the local school, children brimming with dreams and aspirations shared their ideas with me. Rachmat, for example, wondered what programming skills are needed to become an ethical hacker, while Zakri worked with me on an Excel sheet to forecast the potential return of building an eco-tourism business in Cilacap. These children, full of life, hope, and dreams, provided me with additional motivation to protect the planet we live on.

After my sojourn in Cilacap, my resolve for climate advocacy crystallized with even greater clarity. In my university life, I envision promoting eco-tourism and the preservation of mangrove trees in Indonesia with the help of sustainable local business partners. I also plan to champion green building initiatives and promote sustainable construction practices on campus, given the significant amount of carbon emissions in traditional building construction. My experiences with Fairatmos and in Cilacap have shown me that a commitment to environmental advocacy, combined with humility, intellectual curiosity, and plain old common sense, can drive meaningful change. By continuing to nurture my passion for nature, I hope to inspire others to join me in protecting our planet for generations to come.

As a first year in high school, I made the worst mistake of my life: pushing my brother so hard he hit the concrete.

It wasn’t easy dealing with a split household. On one hand, I believed in my Farsi grandparents, whose Muslim faith encouraged us to share moments of spiritual reflection, bow in unison, and tie together. On the other hand, my parents, who grew up in the confines of a suppressive regime in Iran, were hesitant to teach my brother and I about faith from their fear of persecution. They did, however, believe that faith is an integral part of being a complete person.

For me, this became a reality when I enrolled in a Jesuit high school, with the ethos “men for others,” with mandatory service hours. Even though I approached these hours with a sense of obligation rather than enthusiasm, I soon found some joy in the work; I felt some improvements within myself over time. After each session we gathered holding hands, talking about our personal lives and issues, reflecting on them.

As I returned back to the sterile hospital room, seeing my brother lying there unconscious after hitting the concrete, I truly thought. I realized how my jealousy and anger had driven a wedge between us. I thought about all the times we had fought over which SpongeBob episode was the best and how, deep down, I had always wanted to be closer to him. Even though these were silly topics, it was because I didn't know how to express how much I wanted to be closer to him. Fighting was the only way I knew how to communicate.

Over the next few months, I practiced what I had learned about forgiveness, kindness, and respect from my parents and the Jesuit teachings. I invited him to join me at the gym, play the piano with me, and share in activities I enjoyed. He initially refused, but through months of perseverance, I began to see his actions differently. His resistance wasn’t selfish; it was his way of trying to protect me! He didn’t want to see my teary eyes watching The Blind Side just as he had done when he tried to stop me from going on a ski trip, fearing that I would dislocate my shoulder again.

In one of the overnight volunteer camps, I had to seriously grasp the concept of “forgiveness” for the first time. It seems so obvious in retrospect, but I realize how much I have been ignoring this value in my own life after hearing the story of my campmate, Jacob, for having a darker skin color. So, at my camp, when Brad accidentally broke my Celtics headphones, I took a deep breath! Instead of getting mad, I chose to offer compassion and empathy, realizing that no one is perfect.

I carried this principle of brotherhood into my volunteer work at the shelter, where I was the first to serve Thanksgiving dinner and stayed 4-6 hours longer than anyone else to clean up afterward despite my fingers being cramped up from preparing so much food; I took the initiative to talk to John, Jill, and Mary to connect with them instead of just serving food. I had learned to be the bigger brother.

Today, my brother and I are not just siblings but true brothers. Our relationship is built on mutual respect and understanding, something I never thought possible. The journey was long and filled with challenges, but it taught me the value of family, faith, and forgiveness. Reflecting on our childhood conflicts and moments of reconciliation, I realize how these experiences have shaped my understanding of empathy and the importance of building strong family bonds. It all began with the desire to change, to forgive, and the support of my Jesuit school. These experiences have prepared me to face challenges in college and beyond with empathy and resilience, aiming to build meaningful connections and contribute positively to the community.

What if I were to tell you that I am a communication strategist extraordinaire at the ripe old age of 17?

“Plié, tendu, piqué, jeté, keep those legs strong dancers.” Music to my ears. For over 11 years, I was a classically trained ballerina; it transformed me into a graceful, magnetic swan. It was my entire world—until it wasn’t. The dreaded news came one day: my muscles couldn't keep pace with my bone growth, lacking the strength to support my joints. Tearfully, I danced my final ballet and hung up my pointe shoes. Transitioning to my school's dance team, old injuries resurfaced, leading to more tears and more retired shoes. During that time, a conversation with a friend ignited my interest in strength training. I vividly remember the day I joined him at the gym using a guest pass—it felt like confetti falling from the skies! The weight room quickly became my new dance studio. Since then, I’ve been hitting the gym hard for over two years, working out 5 to 7 days a week. Even though I am no longer sashaying across the dance floor, the rhythmic flow of lifting weights continues to feed the dancer in me. Still a dancer, now with muscles. I call this Brand Rebuilding!

Music concerts? Check. Festivals? Check. Sound waves blasting through my ears (and my mind)? Check. I proudly proclaim myself a musicaholic. My passion for music began with ballet, where I found classical pieces, especially Tchaikovsky's, absolutely captivating. Music is a universal language. It expands and unites people. Hip hop and rap express young desires, disapprovals, and rebellion like no other. Country music soothes my broken heart and stirs dreams of love. Pop music fuels my energy to dance with friends. Road trips with my mom must include head-banging to Queen's Bohemian Rhapsody. And at family parties, you'll find me swaying my hips to the beat of ethnic Armenian and Greek music, striking ancient poses alongside three to four generations of my extended family. I call this Brand Diversity. Hopa!

Something a little less enchanting than all the dancing and music in my life was my bumpy first two years of high school. My old academic software ([Name] 1.0) was glitchy, took uncalculated risks, had instances of boredom and lack of focusing, bouts of B-titis and C-titis, and adventures in la la land. Diagnosis and strategic learning techniques led to a software overhaul, complete with my patent-pending ADHD superpower boost that enables me to hyper-focus and develop mastery over things I am passionate about. Ladies and gentlemen, substantial progress has been achieved. Welcome to [Name] 2.0. I call this Public Relations!

My brand is, as we speak, under review by investors who are carefully evaluating whether they want to invest. As you complete this review, my hope is that you say “YES! I want what she’s selling. Rumor has it she is an excellent risk.” I call this Brand Recognition!

I realize I am not a traditional young leader. I am not the president of any formal clubs, nor do I have shelves filled with certificates or trophies. I do, however, have a laser beam focus on my goals, a knack for creative problem-solving, psychological curiosity, a killer Spotify playlist, and a regenerative spirit to overcome setbacks.

You see, a leader is not just someone who holds a top position or tells people what to do. A leader is also someone who wants to connect and understand what moves and inspires people. Expressing myself in artistic ways, immersing myself in creative worlds, and being innately curious of not only my own but in others' experiences is what makes me feel alive. After all, what the world needs more of is people who have come alive (thanks Howard Thurman), some muscle and hard work (thanks gym), and a little je ne sais quoi (thanks French class).

My grandmother slides me last week’s edition of The Daily Herald across our dining table. Gently humming to the melody of Edvard Grieg’s Morning Mood, my grandmother takes my hand as she guides me through folding my first origami tray to hold our snacktime sunflower seeds. Throughout my childhood, I’ve been taught how old sheets of newspaper can be meticulously repurposed to beautify our house—from creating flower vases holding lilacs with The Chicago Tribune wrapped around to assembling book covers to give our bookshelf that vintage feel. Joining her at the tableside, creasing each fold ever so precisely, every creation of ours seemed like a masterpiece.

“Polanyeyouyong,” she would tell me. Even scraps have their value. Having lived through China’s Cultural Revolution, my grandmother had no choice but to ration her necessities and not let a single thing go to waste. Despite her painful memories of stitching together old clothes to barely stay warm during the winter, my grandma now laughs with me as she guides me through stitching my own patterns on her blanket. With every stitch sewn into the cloth, I too learned to embrace compassionate reuse.

***

“How can I optimize my computer’s UEFI settings?” Grand said. Born and raised on the outskirts of Nairobi, Kenya, Grand didn’t have someone to feed his curiosity surrounding computers. With him seeking computer knowledge beyond our virtual group lessons, our formal Code2Connect sessions soon devolved from structured lectures into informal “device-maximizing” open discussions. Creating 1-on-1 lessons with Grand, together we squeezed every bit of value out of his dilapidated model laptop, from configuring the motherboard’s SATA ports to undervolting the CPU. For me, the fulfillment wasn’t just from teaching students Python, but from reviving the run-down laptops from junk to fully functional.

My evenings aren’t spent folding origami boxes, but cardboard. Using scrap cardboard from routine school lunch shipments, I create drop-off boxes to collect used devices. Tenderly disinfecting chipped 10-inch Macs or cracked tablets with isopropyl alcohol and a microfiber cloth, I take comfort in knowing that each device from my peers and library I receive is another brought back to life. And each time I go to the local library to race children at Mario Kart using the previously damaged consoles they donated—“Wii-Serve Wednesdays,” we’d call them—I’m reminded of my grandmother’s words: with my own two hands, I have the ability to uplift communities.

***

“Would you be a peach and throw me a shirt?” Blenda calls to me. Blenda, hailing from Englewood, Chicago, is a two-time breast cancer survivor and caring grandmother, with two daughters hospitalized from the disease. As she taught me the perfect baking soda-to-vinegar ratio needed to create my own fabric softener, I thought I’d teach her a clothing hack of my own. So, prior to setting up for the Pink Divas and Gents Breast Cancer 5K, I invited Blenda and other grandmas to join me with old white t-shirts and pink dye. Together, we spent the morning scrunching and binding our shirts with rubber bands and squirting them with pink dye. Using the ripped shirts that could no longer be worn, I turned them into headbands and wristbands to further our pink pride (“What a hoot!” Blenda would say).

As I finish setting up the final tent before the others arrive, I look behind me to see Blenda and the grandmas together by the starting line, singing and dancing in their newly upcycled pink shirts, grooving and clapping to the beat of “Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.” As Blenda waved me over, welcoming me to their dance circle, I also busted into The Carlton (or tried to, at least). As we happily threw extra pink gear to the participants that trickled in, I realized that it wasn’t the concrete act of repurposing that brought the most joy; it was celebrating it with the people around you.

***

Looking back on it now, maybe that's why I strive for compassion and creativity in everything I do. Now sitting alone in my dining room, being the only one to fold these paper boxes every morning, I will never forget my late grandmother’s dedication to others. I, too, with an eye for value and love for others, will continue to celebrate generous repurposing, just as she did for me.

I have forty-six individual alarms on my phone. It may seem unnecessary, but it’s a fine-tuned science. You see, I have long dealt with a tendency to forget. It could stem from a genetic disposition inherited from my mom or a case of living in the moment too much, but I digress.

I was long able to avoid (or rather, not notice) this proneness, gliding by as my parents directed me from birthday party to baseball tournament. It was a pleasant bliss.

When high school hit, my forgetfulness hit harder. Student council, JV baseball, honors classes, all clashing to seize my attention. With three siblings across different stages of education, I had to balance this workload with minimal intervention from my parents. And according to my standards, I failed miserably. Student council meeting period two? Missed it. Baseball practice after a class officers meeting? Late. I tried using my Apple calendar app, but its reminders would get swept into a sea of notifications. It simply couldn’t win over my attention.

As I contemplated whether some commitments should give way, a friend suggested I use alarms. Yikes, now that would be embarrassing. Few options were left and sophomore year arrived, so I gave it a shot.

I first tackled the alarm sound. By this time, many of the iPhone ringtones gave me micro-PTSD from waking me up for school. This had to be disruptive yet innocuous, unique yet appropriate, irritating yet repeatable. After many underwhelming sound tests, I found it: the duck alarm. Its quacking chimed through my thick pants pockets in any environment, instilling a sense of urgency and subsequent silliness.

I began setting alarms at the exact time of each event, be it an afterschool meeting or a landscaping job. These alarms were last minute insults to my forgetfulness; when the quacks sounded, I was already late. I began setting them exactly thirty minutes before each event. Then, I could remember momentarily. I’d be busy with something else, though, and the darned duty escaped my mind when the time came to go. Other times, my alarms didn’t activate. This necessitated the classic two-alarm strategy, in which a second alarm quacked fifteen minutes after the first. My memory increased incrementally, but not enough for me.

As the notoriously busy junior year came, I sat in my gaming chair and whipped out my whiteboard. What was I missing? The duck sounds caught my attention sufficiently. Two alarms accounted for a possible failure of one and the risk of forgetting again. Yes, forgetting again. The last confounding variables must’ve occurred after my alarms and before the event. Each situation was different, though. Some classes worked until the bell rang, and some baseball games started before the school day ended. So there wasn’t a set number; I’d have to calibrate each alarm to each situation.

This led me to alarm 4.0. The night before, I think of where I’ll be when the alarms sound. If it’s a class, I locate exactly when I’ll have free time or be packing up my materials (though it can’t be the time of the bell because the madness will drown out even the loudest quacks). I set two alarms about two minutes apart. The second alarm comes a minute before the latest departure to be on time. I recycle alarms to save time, and I use them to remember everything from club meetings to study sessions.

Although my memory hasn’t been fixed, setting alarms has instilled in me a notable time awareness. Alarm 4.0 and its previous iterations have allowed me to eliminate heaps of wasteful screen time. By cutting these out of my day, I have become more involved in my previous commitments and have comfortably tacked a few more onto my plate. In college, I will continue to pursue and expand these passions, even if it takes all forty-six alarms to do so.

The moment seemed to last an eternity. A sudden jolt rattled my body accompanied by the sickening sound of metal crumpling against metal. My heart pounded loudly in my chest as adrenaline shot through my body. I felt a sense of panic well up inside of me as I realized the truth - this was my fault. My father and I sat there at the intersection, in shock at the events which flew by in a matter of seconds. "This can't be real, can it?" I thought to myself.

The car accident in my junior year of high school was an experience which left a lasting impact on the way I viewed the world. I grappled with guilt and shame at my failure to pay attention. Though no one was hurt, I felt a sense of solemn responsibility for the damage my actions had caused. In the coming days, I found myself contending with questions and calls with insurance, accompanied by berating from concerned friends and family. I was grateful for the concern, yet in my mind I knew I had to change. Outside of insurance and money, there was no punishment. My parents weren't mad, or even disappointed; they simply hoped I had learned a lesson. Witnessing the encouragement my parents continued to give me, along with their determination to allow me to solve this issue by myself ignited a sense of independence and responsibility within me, inspiring me to become more meticulous with my actions and to focus fully on the tasks at hand, no matter how trivial.

After the accident, with the memories replaying in my head, I decided to refine my work ethic. I knew now the consequences of even the smallest mistakes, which could quickly turn into larger problems in the future. This new mindset significantly changed my approach to various activities, causing me to look deeper at the smaller details I may have previously overlooked. Working as an assistant at my dental office required precision and care - traits which I had come to value deeply. Each task was approached with a new sense of purpose and diligence. Patient insurance needed to be tripled checked for consistency. Dental instruments needed to be spotless. When assisting with dental procedures, not a single drop of excess saliva was left in the patient's mouth. With this new mindset, every task done was a step toward a transformation in my approach to life.

My passion for care and diligence has also transformed my academic life. This was particularly evident with the survey project in my statistics class. In the past I might have been content with rough data estimates, but I now found myself meticulously noting down the exact responses and each person in my population. During lectures, no point was too meaningless to note down, and no caption was too small to be ignored. My study habits, though already rigorous, started to shift. Rather than simply studying what I needed to, I looked further, understanding how the information fit into the larger context of the world. These actions have enhanced the appreciation of my studies, changing my perspective on learning and setting a new standard for persistence in all areas of my life.

While the aftermath of the car accident has gradually receded, the sense of accountability and habit of attentiveness I gained has not. As I reflect on this experience, I realize that though this has been a harsh reminder of reality, it has allowed me to develop traits which I can now apply to the work I do. As a child, I've always believed in the miracles and happy endings which were present in cartoons and T.V shows. But now, I've come to realize that these happy conclusions can only be achieved through responsibility and personal growth. The success we obtain in life is best characterized by the experience we gain through conquering challenges.

**Essay:**

AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. It was the first time I was passing through Emergency Room doors wearing scrubs and a badge. Looking back on those first days working in the hospital, I realize that I viewed people very differently than I do now.

In the summer following my freshman year in high school, I interned at UC Irvine Medical Center shadowing the Head of Emergency Medicine. It was around 11:00 pm, about halfway through one of my very first eight-hour shifts. The paramedics raced into the ER with a motorcyclist who had been hit by a drunk driver. The drunk driver, a woman, was in a trauma bay down the hall along with her eight-year-old daughter…and three police officers. I can still see the motorcyclist writhing in pain, the daughter wanting to play with me, and the handcuffs connecting her mom to a gurney.

This was the first time I witnessed the devastating impact of drunk driving. Three lives forever changed—in an instant. I can still see the ants that crawled over the motorcyclist’s severed leg as he died in front of me and the look of regret and despair on the mom’s face. I’ll never forget the intense sadness I felt for the young, innocent girl as I thought about my little sister and what she would do without my mom. My heart ached for her as the girl asked me, “Do you want to play rock, paper, scissors?”

On another shift, I watched a thirty-year-old man who had overdosed on heroin struggle while being intubated. As the nursing staff pinned him down, his huge green eyes locked onto mine, begging me to help him. Tears swelled in his eyes...and mine. I remember trying to reconcile my feelings with my prior beliefs. Drugs are wrong and people that use them get what they deserve—or so I once thought.

As I think back on those events, and others, my head spins with internal conflict about the relationship between crime and punishment as well as right and wrong. I am a math and science guy. Always have been. I am also a pragmatic guy. They go hand in hand, I suppose. Life as a doctor, always appealed to me because I thought medicine was black and white. My time in the hospital was the start of me realizing that medicine isn’t black and white at all.

I started observing patients in a different way. It wasn’t just about diagnosis and prognosis or ailment and treatment. People that were hospitalized because of their own mistakes, even their own stupidity, no longer “deserved what they got.” Those first shifts in the hospital were the beginning of a multi-year journey of developing compassion and empathy for people I didn’t know. I saw many patients in my two-plus years across three hospitals that were there because of poor choices they, or the people around them, made. The more patients I saw, the more I developed a deeper sense of empathy for others’ struggles and suffering.

I found myself being more attentive when listening to the stories that patients would tell about “how” or “why” something happened, where previously I would focus only on the facts that were relevant for making a diagnosis. I listened with intention and embraced the gray that lies between the black and white. I looked for opportunities to connect personally with people. I evolved from a pragmatic problem-solver to an empathetic and compassionate care provider—not just in the hospitals, but in life too.

I now look for opportunities to impact lives through understanding, whether it be in a hospital, during my volunteer work at the local Boys & Girls Club, or just interacting with people on a day-to-day basis. Technically, I won’t be “AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL” for a long time, but when I am I will help those in need not only with my pragmatic mind but also with compassion in my heart.

I thought I did everything right, but the delicate, whispery bodies laying belly-up on the moss soil proved otherwise. The stress of the new environment was too much. I had acclimated them slowly into the new tank, knowing that this was the most critical time. But my efforts were not enough. Only a few of the original fifteen remained. This was my first attempt at raising ornamental shrimp, unusually bright creatures that resembled tigers and panthers. The Galaxy Pintos with jet-black exoskeletons dotted by white star patterns, Blue Bolts that glittered aquamarine and crystal navy and Orange Eye Blue Tigers, tiny but splendid, with deep blue bodies, tiger stripes and bright orange eyes. Despite my extensive research, careful acclimation in pH-adjusted water and strategically placed moss balls, I was confronted with my failure, listlessly floating shrimp lying motionless on the aqua soil.

Stunned and saddened, I went over the variables in my mind. Did I acclimate too quickly? Overshoot on the hardness of the water? Was I too optimistic about my ability to raise these fragile creatures? Like other projects I’ve undertaken, I had to do a lot of convincing, and strategic ignoring of objections for this endeavor. My mom in particular had limited patience for this project. Although she usually supported my endeavors, she encouraged me to give this one up. I have always been stubborn, sprinkled with optimism, rarely dissuaded by others’ doubts. This stubbornness and optimism show up at different times and places. It shows up at tennis tournaments, after Dad and I have sized up the higher-seeded players. It kicks in right before big exams, when there is nothing left to do except a few pushups, and high knees to get the blood flowing to my brain. And I feel a rush of optimism every time I talk to local representatives, school board members, and state representatives to advocate for healthier indoor environments for my community and school. This stubbornness and optimism remain even after I've dropped a set, didn't get the test score I had hoped for and have been told no when I've shared suggestions on how to make our schools healthier.

When faced with a less-than-desirable outcome, I see a puzzle to be solved or a person to be understood. When I find myself down a set, I take a breath and remind myself I’m just warming up and get to work analyzing my opponent’s game. Should I start hitting to the kid's backhand? Bring him up to the net? For exams that prove to be trickier than expected, I consider whether I should do more practice questions, or study different material. When gearing up to talk to state representatives and school officials to advocate for radon testing in schools, I reflect on what their priorities might be and consider how I might better address what is meaningful to them. From stuttering conversations as a skinny eighth grader, to a TEDx stage, I’ve learned that analogies are my friend when explaining that our community is at an elevated risk for radon exposure. Explaining that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency action level for radon, 4 pCi/L is equivalent to smoking 8 cigarettes/day, paints a picture that is hard to ignore.

For my delicate shrimp, I set about making changes. I added minerals to the water to help them properly molt their exoskeletons. I mixed their diet with a flour-like food containing microorganisms. I added blue vitamin sticks that were thought to strengthen their exoskeleton. Bit by bit, I started to see that the remaining shrimp became used to their new home. The dark blue color that indicated stress was fading, and they slowly turned light blue. My efforts were rewarded a few weeks later. Little blue and white lines in the tank. Undeniable proof that my shrimp had adjusted to the new tank and were healthy. Shrimp babies.

When I was four, my mother introduced me to our enchanting garden, a place where rambutan trees and red tulips flourished. With gentle patience, she taught me the art of gardening. As my horticultural skills grew, so did my ambition. While trying to revive a dying peach tree sapling, I loosened the soil to aerate its roots and removed its dying foliage. To my astonishment and delight, new buds soon appeared, and the sapling transformed into a thriving tree. This episode taught me that plants, much like humans, can endure incredible stress but can flourish anew with tender care.

As time passed, my curiosity about the natural world deepened. At school, I learned about endangered species like the Sumatran tiger, the Snow Leopard, and the Bali Myna. I also learned the grave consequences of relying on fossil fuels, which hasten climate change. The realization that human actions can drastically curtail the longevity of our planet was a shocking revelation. I could not stand idly by, watching the flora I had grown to cherish destroyed by human avarice and neglect. This epiphany compelled me to pursue climate advocacy.

My initial foray began in the summer of 2023, when I interned at Fairatmos, Indonesia’s pioneering climate tech company. Meeting Ria, the CEO, was both awe-inspiring and intimidating, given her impressive background in a top consulting firm. However, as we conversed, I discovered that we shared many passions, including a love for technology and a deep concern for our planet’s well-being. After learning key concepts in the climate tech industry, I was assigned a variety of tasks, from marketing Fairatmos’ carbon certification tools through digital platforms to conducting in-depth research on Laotian provinces to assess their carbon offset potentials. Each assignment broadened my skills and understanding, much like a young wizard mastering new spells. By the end of my internship, I had assisted Ria in identifying strategic alliances with other global climate tech companies.

To further elevate awareness, I established my own LinkedIn page. Through this platform, I connected with over 600 like-minded individuals and became a climate journalist, regularly writing, sharing, and publishing articles, photos, and videos on topics ranging from carbon capture technologies to sustainable development goals.

The summer of 2024 marked an exhilarating turn in my journey as I returned to work on Fairatmos' conservation project in Cilacap. The Cilacap mangrove swamp, spanning 5,000 acres, is a vibrant realm teeming with biodiversity and vital for carbon absorption. I vividly recall the seven-hour train journey, followed by an exhilarating boat trip through the swamps. Upon arrival, the beaming smiles of the local people warmed my heart.

Staying in the village, our team of twelve organized basic health check-ups and offered health education to the villagers. We also played eco-games with local school children and taught them English. During my stay, I was privileged to hear many fascinating stories, from Harris and his fellow fishermen, who optimized spaces around mangrove roots for aqua farming to Kuntoro, who shared ideas to boost local conservations through commercialization of snacks made from mangrove trees. At the local school, Principal Tarsun and teacher Oktavelani recounted their childhood stories and their motivations to teach. Several schoolchildren, brimming with dreams and aspirations, confided in me, from Rachmat, who aspired to be an ethical hacker, to Bimo, who spoke excitedly about becoming a drone pilot, to Zakri, who envisioned building a local eco-tourism business. These personal narratives reminded me again that the preservation of nature and human lives are inextricably linked.

After my sojourn in Cilacap, my resolve for climate advocacy crystallized with even greater clarity. In my university life, I envision hosting talk shows that raise awareness about climate change. I also plan to champion green building initiatives and promote sustainable construction practices on campus. Finally, I look forward to collaborating with faculty members on projects aimed at tackling the most pressing challenges in achieving net zero emissions.

81 cards scattered all over the lounge. We lay on the floor, minds still racing from the adrenaline of the round. It was another one of our nightly SET sessions: three of us sitting in a circle with the twelve cards in the middle as we searched for a SET. SET is a classic game in the math community. Each card has four attributes, and a SET consists of three cards in which each attribute is either completely the same or different across the three cards. One of the first mathematical properties of SET that I figured out was that for any two cards, there will always be a third card that completes the SET.

When I attended the MathPath summer program, I was assigned to a class taught by Dr. V, a famous mathematician. One night I was struggling with one of his homework problems about the relationship between Fibonacci Numbers and the Golden Ratio. I went up to Dr. V to ask for help, and he gave me a hint. A few minutes later, I came back with the problem solved, so he gave me an extension about the problem to think about. This problem kept me awake all night. I scribbled ideas on a post-it but always crumpled it up as I got to a dead end. However, it finally clicked during lunch, and I immediately ran to find Dr. V and excitedly showed him my proof.

A year later, I attended MathILy-Er and took a class about the math behind the game SET. On the first day of class, we had a Do Now: What questions do you have about the math behind SET? This had me stumped for the entire five minutes we were given. Once the time was up, I lifted my head and saw a question written on the board: How many possible SETs are there in a deck of 81 cards? As we solved the question, so many more popped into my head: What if we expanded the deck so that each card had 5 attributes instead of 4? What if we played a variation of SET that involved four cards in a SET? What if the four attributes in a SET represented a four-dimensional plane? I enjoyed each problem we faced, writing our ideas on the whiteboard and mapping out the solution with my deck of SET cards. Even after the class ended, new questions kept popping into my head as we played our nightly SET games.

These experiences are just two of my SET cards in math. My experiences at MathPath and MathILy-Er made me realize what I love about math. Dr. V, once a young student like me sitting in a math lecture, now taught me to embrace the challenge in math. My friends from camp who I spent time with in the classroom and lounge, fueled with curiosity and excitement. Now, I need to show the younger generations the beauty of math. I’ve been tutoring math since middle school, interacting with tons of different people. One of my students, a fifth-grader named Emma, often struggled with the problems in my math competition classes. She would always attend my office hours outside of class time, and we would go through each question on the homework. During one lesson, I discussed the strategy of recursion in combinatorics problems. She was immediately captivated by the concept and in the following office hours session, we spent the entire time talking about recursion and all its applications in mathematics. I was inspired by how she embraced her curiosity for her subject despite all the obstacles and was grateful that I could help her find something that she loved.

Many people solely do math for the competition. Although I love spending my time grinding through competition problems, I’ve also learned that there is so much more to the subject. Whether it’s the obscure theorems about the Golden Ratio or the fascinating applications in card games, I have learned to pursue my curiosity and love for a challenge through math.

My unique talent reared its head during middle school. Some schoolmates' talents were merit-based, while others were athletic. Mine, however, was less typical.
