I had the unique ability to break my bones with minimal effort. It seemed like I could find a way to do it in the most creative manner possible—almost comedic. If it were possible to stumble, trip, or fall, rest assured, I would discover resulting from a fracture of some new part of me. Fractures occurred from something as simple as breaking a finger while casually walking up the stairs and catching my hand wrong against the railing to more elaborate events, such as barely falling off my bike and ending up with a fractured collarbone. However, my most humiliating moment involved falling off a seesaw from only two feet high, which resulted in an arm fracture so awful that my arm resembled Zeus' lightning bolt. At home, whenever we encountered someone new, my mother's introduction to me would always be "the twin that breaks easy."

Every one of my injuries brought forth a tale and, eventually, an interest in understanding our body mechanics, which included how nutrition aids recovery and sustains overall wellness. During a routine yearly physical before high school, the Doctor ordered bloodwork. The results returned, and the mystery was solved; I was Vitamin D deficient. This deficiency negatively aided my bone health but opened my eyes to how nutrition can significantly impact our bodies. For instance, I learned that Vitamin D is crucial for calcium absorption, which is essential for bone health. I then connected that what we eat affects our overall health positively or negatively. Therefore, proper nutrition, including a balanced diet rich in calcium and Vitamin D, would improve my performance in sports and aid my body in recovery from injuries.

My desire to pursue a career as a sports nutritionist was ignited by a mix of experiences and a deep passion for sports and fitness. I had to sit out and watch my soccer team play from the sidelines whenever I got injured. Being born with a deficiency made it frustrating not being able to take part in activities I enjoyed because of limitations. My dad instilled a love for staying active by encouraging my twin and me to run around the house when we had energy. Watching soccer while sidelined with injuries only fueled my passion for the sport, motivating me to investigate how nutrition could help prevent injuries. I never wanted to feel like I was holding back my team or myself because of limitations.

I have begun to dive into scholarly research integrating nutrition and human physiology to achieve this aim. I am learning how the various food components affect our body systems, ranging from structural aspects like bone health to functional aspects like muscle recovery. I am blessed to have access to practical clinical exposure by observing how dietitians are closely involved in patient care and recovery during rehabilitation. Becoming a sports dietitian is now my career goal, as they work with athletes to develop nutrition plans that optimize performance and promote overall health. This career aligns with my desire to overcome my deficiency alongside my love of fitness and sports. I wish to influence the lives of athletes and make their bodies as physically healthy as possible. I aim to promote nutrition as a core factor for healthy living and resilience, inspiring others to take charge of their wellness and seek greater heights in their sports pursuits. My objective is to pass down this wisdom and enlighten athletes on nutrition's role in injury prevention and recovery so that they can apply it for success along their athletic journeys. My apologies to middle school Alex, but instead of being known as "the twin that breaks easy," I aim to be recognized as the expert who helps athletes stay strong and healthy.

Panic gripped my chest as our plane pierced through Shanghai's smoggy veil. The city's iconic skyline—my home for eight years—shrank to a glittering toy set. Would my Mandarin dissolve like the disappearing landscape? Would I forget everything? The streets where I learned to ride my bike, the park where we flew kites in the fall, my best friend Lam Lam's laugh? No, I vowed. I won't forget.

In Singapore and later in America, I clung to my Mandarin like a treasured toy. Every night, I practiced writing characters until my hand hurt. '想' (xiǎng) evolved from simply meaning 'think' to embodying the ache I felt during monthly calls with Lam Lam. '家' (jiā) expanded beyond 'home,' becoming a sprawling web of family ties stretched taut across oceans.

My efforts paid off. At school, I led Mandarin tours for prospective families and tutored eager 5th graders like Emma and Sophia during lunch breaks. I showed them how every character tells a story, like '和平' (hépíng - peace), which combines '禾' (hé - grain) and '口' (kǒu - mouth), suggesting that when people have food, there is peace. Beyond the classroom, I sought out essay competitions, pitting myself against heritage speakers, climbing from Bronze to Silver, and eventually winning the prestigious Gold award at the Annual Chinese National Essay Competition with my essay "这是我的命运" - This Is My Fate among 8,000 entries from around the world! This accomplishment lifted the weight of the promise I had made, as an 8-year old to myself, staring outside the airplane window from my shoulders.

My obsession with preserving Mandarin had made me deaf to the lyrical Portuguese flowing through my home. One evening, my grandmother's and mother's conversation pierced my linguistic bubble. Struck by its melodic rhythm, so different from Mandarin's tonal precision, shame washed over me for neglecting this language. Despite being my grandma's main caregiver during the academic year, our shared time had become a clumsy dance of gestures and broken Portuguese—enough to ask "Do you need anything?" but falling short of the companionship she deserved. In my eagerness to cling to one identity, I had unintentionally distanced myself from another.

Determined to bridge this gap, I immersed myself in learning Portuguese. Convincing Middlebury Language School to accept me as their youngest student at the age of 16, I lived and breathed Portuguese for seven weeks, stumbling through conversations and conjugations, finding beauty in words like "saudade" (a state of nostalgic longing).

Returning from Middlebury, I felt an immediate shift in my relationship with Avo. Our once-silent walks through the neighborhood blossomed into animated conversations. As I helped her with daily tasks, I wasn't just caring for her physical needs anymore. I was finally a companion with each shared conversation. This connection brought me closer to my long-neglected Latina heritage. My fluency in Portuguese became a bridge to a part of myself I had almost lost.

My hard-earned language skills in both Mandarin and Portuguese, sparked broader interests. I delved into East Asian politics with books like "China's Grand Strategy" and explored Latin American history through "Veins of Latin America". The economic ties between these regions now felt both personal and vital.

As I prepare for university, I'm eager to study in departments of East Asian and Latin American Studies, exploring topics like China's digital economy alongside Brazil's burgeoning tech startups. I'm fascinated by the global cultural impact of South Korea's K-pop, particularly groups like BTS, and how it compares to the international reach of Latin American reggaeton artists.

Whether crafting policies leveraging China's e-commerce to boost Latin American businesses or developing cultural exchanges between South Korean and Colombian artists, I aim to catalyze cross-cultural dialogue. Just as learning Mandarin and Portuguese bridged divides in my life, I aspire to create spaces where diverse worldviews coexist. By fostering understanding that transcends borders and ideologies, I hope to contribute to a more interconnected, empathetic global community—one conversation at a time.

"Never double text a girl. Embrace boredom. Don’t try to do a backflip with no experience, and most importantly, take care of Mama and Dana."

Deciding to go to university outside of Saudi was one of the hardest decisions I ever made, but I know they’ll be in good hands. The past year has been training my heir: the all-mighty Suliaman. Left with a big-bros-genius-game-theoretical-guide to life—and occasional notes on dealing with Dana’s tantrums. We started with cooking basics; boiling pasta until it's al dente, adding the perfect amount of cheese to their favorite scrambled eggs, and most importantly: how to turn on our old rusty stove without getting electrocuted.

Then it was time for the good stuff. Mouthwatering homemade muttabaq and Robert Axelrod’s tournament. The tournament was built on a simple game, the prisoner’s dilemma. Two players can either cooperate or betray. Betraying leads to better results regardless of what the other chooses, yet mutual cooperation leads to a much better outcome than mutual betrayal.

As we prepared the minced meat with our cut onions, cumin, coriander, and black lime, I introduced it. Suliaman reciprocated with a smug, “Obviously betrayal is the logical action.” And then the game-changing word was introduced: repeated.

When we add numerous rounds and repeat this game, good faith comes into play. If I betray you now, I risk you betraying me next round and falling into a loop of mutual loss. I let him ponder the question of which strategies would work best before explaining Robert Axelrod’s paper and the original 14 strategies in the tournament over dinner.

The next day, we moved on to making molokhia. As we chopped the molokhia leaves and prepared the chicken broth, I explained how Tit for Tat was the best strategy, one which cooperates or betrays simply by copying what the other player did the round before.

Four years later, in 1984, Axelrod repeated the tournament, this time with 63 submitted strategies. He introduced noise to simulate misunderstandings (such as the famed nuclear attack false alarm, for which we owe Stanislav Petrov our thanks), and evolution where strategies would evolve over generations. Once again, the findings were clear. Successful strategies were all nice, forgiving, and clear, but never pushovers.

Cooking dinner became our daily class. Sometimes it was a failed game theoretical analogy that didn’t quite reach, other times it was straight-to-the-point advice. His favorites were definitely my many embarrassing stories from lessons I wish someone had taught me.

Finally, after months of cooking, it was time for him to graduate. His final project: a 6-course meal featuring dishes like lamb kabsa, stuffed grape leaves, and kunafa for Dana’s Birthday, with me simply following his instructions to the T. Six grueling hours later, Dana and her friends enjoyed what I claim to be a Michelin-star-esque meal (not that I have ever tried one).

Although Axelrod’s claims about the clarity of successful strategies have been met with skepticism, the lessons I hope have stuck with Suliaman—being kind, forgiving, yet firm—remain important. Teaching Susu was as beneficial to me as it was to him; it gave me the opportunity to reflect on and learn from my mistakes by explaining them to someone else. Trying to impart my fascination for game theory to him, looking for those real life examples, deepened my own understanding of the subject.

“The Loudest Kid in the Class of ‘21” – I was not. It was a joke. This was the sarcastic superlative I received when I graduated middle school. When asked to speak in class, my stomach curled, and my voice trembled. And when I finally finished speaking, my teachers would say, “We couldn’t hear you.” And I’d spend the next three hours recomposing myself. But I feel that four years later, I’ve lived up to the sarcastic title in my own way.

The process of becoming “The Loudest Kid” began my freshman year when I decided to join the speech and debate team in hopes of getting over my intense glossophobia: fear of public speaking. Predictably, at every competition, I landed myself at dead last. Repeatedly.

Despite this, my coaches maintained their faith in me. After hours spent performing to my bedroom walls, I slowly clawed my way up to national stages. I could now scream, cry, and yell in front of hundreds of people. My voice no longer shook.

Learning to use my voice was not just about gaining the courage to speak. It was about learning to persuasively and engagingly convey my ideas. Sometimes, it was by splicing together poetry I found on Instagram. It’s trying to choreograph a ten-second dance number to Madonna’s “Vogue” for the beginning of a speech. Speech creates a platform to share my creative voice.

My newfound voice enables me to do what I was previously too timid to do: amplify unheard voices. It’s important to me that I craft speeches that humanize the struggles of underrepresented people. For the past two years, I’ve told stories that amplify the voices of LGBTQ+ youth.

During my junior year, I told the story of Jacob, a transgender child who finds love for their identity by finding their voice and community. Living their story through every speech competition touched me because I went on a similar journey. I struggled to find love for my identity as a Black girl – especially when I first arrived at my predominantly White school in Johannesburg, South Africa. My friends said something to me that would stick with me for years. “Be careful in the colored neighborhoods – they like to steal.” As though they weren’t speaking to a “colored” person. Despite the sinking feeling, I just smiled and kept quiet. Unfortunately, incidents like these became common.

This incident weighed on me for years: I felt guilty for not speaking up in moments like those. I was fortunate to learn to use my voice, and extending that power of speech to my communities became so important to me. It was time to take it further and share that joy with others.

I set out to create diversity-focused workshops for students to speak up about issues that affect their communities. We brainstormed ways to create change, such as how to persuasively present underrepresented experiences to audiences who may not relate. They showed me not only the joy of speaking but also the knowledge that can be gained from diverse conversations. They represented to me how people can view the same issues vastly differently. I learned from them that solutions to seemingly irreparable issues can be found by collaborating with people of different backgrounds.

At the end of these workshops, participants expressed the solidarity found in being heard, and I was thrilled. It was gratifying to know that I could share the joy of finally being excited to use our voices.

Still, I noticed that some participants hesitated to speak in such a formal environment. This resonated with me because I used to feel the same trepidation. So, I organized lower-stakes opportunities to express our ideas, from diversity-focused movie nights to cultural fashion shows. The sights and sounds of joy – the laughter, the belting “LOVE” by Keyshia Cole, and the loud “That happened to me too!”’s – alone were worth finding my voice. My experience in going unheard for years has made it so important to me that I continue to platform marginalized voices in whatever way possible.

Since learning to use my voice, I’ve tried my best to use it to amplify and bring together other voices in an effort to prevent other people from going unheard. Speaking and listening gave me power, and it’s important to me that I extend that power to as many people as I can.

I can now confidently say that I am a “Loud Kid,” even if it’s not in volume.

I’ve always believed that kindergarten is the one place where it’s socially acceptable to have paint on your face, mismatched socks, and the occasional "uh-oh" moment. Kindergarten was a wonderland of colourful finger paints, where classroom was filled with songs that made boring ABCs sound like rebellious anthems of childhood. But this magical world also had its not-so-glamorous moments – accidents. We're talking about those "uh oh" situations where someone, well, you know. Now normal kids wouldn’t care to imagine the most abnormal things. But me? My young mind, fertile with imagination, found both wonder and confusion in everyday mishaps. Be it being scared from sharks to some poopy scares. It all started when my class fellow , Ahmed had a bit of an accident during a fun coloring activity. As per usual, our custodian Ms Shaista, a superhero in disguise, came to Ahmed’s rescue, and whisked him away . Now Seeing Ms. Shaista, our school janitor, rush in with a clear bag containing Ahmed's cleaned pants made me feel both relieved and curious when I was five years old. 
Now it wasn’t a normal bag. It was a transparent shopping bag and inside it was a crumpled up ball of something. It turned out to be ahmed’s pants. The dirty ones. Now for some reason my 5-year old brain imagined something else. Ms shaista had washed the pooped pants of course so they were wet and looked darker. You wouldn’t imagine what I thought it was. I THOUGHT THE BAG WAS HOLDING AHMED’S ACTUAL POOP so the school doesn’t have to keep it. (it was my 5 year old brain, come on)
I was horrified to see that. I thought to myself, why cant the school just flush it away? Why do they have to return it? How will Ahmed go down the street with the embarrassing bag until he catches the bus back home? Confused and frustrated by the bizarre incident, I began to question the entire school system, wondering why it operated in such an illogical and mysterious manner. 
The whole "poop-in-a-bag" situation seems absurdly humorous in retrospect. Although my worry was untrue, it did plant the doubting seed that has grown alongside me in Pakistan over the educational system.
Talk of certain Pakistani private schools prioritizing business above education is common these days. They give mediocre quality for outrageous fees. Parents are treated like second-class citizens as they are nickelled and dimed for everything from " fees" to "uniform upgrades," with no regard for the real education. It's a system that seems more focused on upholding a particular image than on fostering the development of young brains. Maybe my five-year-old self wasn't entirely wrong about the school system being, well, a bit sick. Back then, I questioned why they'd "return" poop. Later, I questioned why they prioritize profit over genuine education. 
As the president of the business society in 2022, my classmates and I developed a detailed proposal aimed at addressing these issues and fostering a more equitable educational environment. It was more of a far fetched approach but we had to take a chance. After seeing multiple deserving students leave LGS(my school), we wanted to make the school fees affordable for these students. The school undoubtedly denied our request of offering scholarships. Despite the setback, in 2023, I formed a tutoring club called “on the block”. Initially it was for the students who had left LGS, but in January 2024, I made it available for the students of my block. I will not lie, I do charge “some” price for my services but it is too less to what the school was charging. I have been joined by my friends who teach different subjects. 
Reflecting on those early days now, the memory of kindergarten stirs up a nostalgic blend of innocence and wonder, reminding me how those simple moments shaped my perceptions.

"Vamos, querida. It's time." My Brazilian mother gently pried me from my Chinese Ayi's embrace.

I gazed up at my Ayi's face one last time, the familiar creases around her eyes now cradling an unfamiliar sadness. "Remember me," she breathed, her words barely audible, like the last notes of a fading lullaby.

Even at eight, I understood what was at stake. This farewell was tearing me from the woman who, though sharing neither my surname nor ancestry, had nurtured me since birth. Mandarin was the lifeline tethering me to my beloved Chinese Ayi, to Shanghai's bustling streets where I first tasted freedom on two wheels, to the park where our joy danced with autumn kites. Each syllable cradled precious memories - the warmth of jasmine-scented embraces, the comfort of whispered bedtime stories. If I let my Mandarin slip away, our bond would surely fade into the background like Pudong Terminal disappearing below my airplane window as our plane reached cruising altitude. In that moment, I made a silent vow: "Wǒ huì huí lái. Wǒ bǎozhèng." (I will return, I promise.)

In Singapore and later in America, Mandarin became my secret rebellion against what seemed inevitable—forgetting. Night after night, characters danced before my tired eyes, transforming from mere symbols into vessels of memory and emotion. 'Xiang' (想) evolved from a simple 'think' into the ache I felt during our weekly calls. 'Jia' (家) was no longer just 'home' but a complex web of family ties stretching across continents.

At school, I insisted on taking Chinese as a first language. Beyond the classroom, I sought out essay competitions, pitting myself against heritage speakers, climbing from Bronze to Silver, and eventually the prestigious Gold award in the Annual Chinese National Essay Competition, an ambition born not out of competition but love. Weekends found me lost in the pages of Lu Xun and Eileen Chang, their words painting vivid pictures of a China I feared losing. Lu Xun's "My Old Home" resonated deeply, its exploration of nostalgia and disillusionment mirroring my own struggles between memory and reality. Eileen Chang's poignant declaration, "I want you to know there's someone in this world who's yours always," echoed in my mind as I grappled with my multiple identities. Tang Dynasty poems unfolded like intricate origami and sparked a curiosity about neighboring cultures. Soon, I found myself poring over Japanese haiku, noticing the subtle interplay of shared influences and unique expressions igniting twin passions: a love for East Asian studies and an insatiable hunger for languages.

It was this newfound interest that led me back to my Brazilian roots, to the language of my mother that I had long neglected. Portuguese, with its lilting cadences and warm vowels, became a counterpoint to the tonal precision of Mandarin. Yet it was my Brazilian grandmother—Avó—who caused an urgency in me. As dementia began eroding her mind and her English, I realized once again that language was a lifeline to the people I love.

At sixteen, I bargained my way into the Middlebury Language School's Portuguese program as its youngest enrollee yet. For seven intense weeks, I lived and breathed Portuguese, often waking up with unfamiliar words echoing in my mind. I discovered the profound beauty of "saudade," a word that encapsulated my own complex emotions – a bittersweet ache for a place I'd never known. My hard-earned fluency in Portuguese transformed my relationship with Avó, offering her an anchor when the tide of forgetting seemed to sweep her away. I gently whispered, "Calma, Avó. Não faz mal," soothing her with the familiar cadence of her mother tongue and watching relief soften her worried features.

Mandarin, Portuguese, Urdu, Japanese—each language I've embraced echoes my immigrant parents' wisdom. That moving forward doesn't mean leaving behind the people or parts of yourself you hold dear.

Years later, my promise fulfilled with a whispered "Wǒ huí lái le" as I embrace Ayi at the Pudong Terminal.

As a ninth-grade avid reader, I was shocked when few students revealed enjoyment upon reading *The Count of Monte Cristo*. I was enthralled with the character of Edmond Dantes, a callous man consumed by revenge, as well as by the jealous, spiteful characters who framed him for a crime he never committed. The evolution of characters, reasons behind their actions, and the circumstances they faced became a world of analysis. Many presented frustrations hindered by a reality that prevented them from finding resolution. Reading has allowed me to gain perspective as others' ink has helped me overcome my own adversity.

My own ink describes reliability, insight, savvy, and persistence. It portrays kindness, meaningful connections, and fierce academic drive. In sixth grade, my storyline transformed; a blotch of ink tinted my book forever. Darkness appeared in pages that had always been light and bright. As the author, I desperately attempted to clear the unwelcomed splotch- I erased, erased, erased- yet permanent ink did its job…remaining forever marked. A diabetes type 1 diagnosis was here to stay, tinting new chapters to come. I searched for meaning, but had no luck finding resolution. Unfortunately, Dantes’ frustration over his uncertain future described my own reality.

At first, swimming in the unwanted ink overtook my identity. Fixated on finding clearer water drowned me further. Ironically, once I returned to school after an extended hospital stay, I felt important. Mentors worried and classmates wanted information that I wasn’t ready to share. As a pre-adolescent who rarely seeked attention, I resented my uniqueness and stubbornly ignored my health issues. I wanted my story to be like everyone else’s. I often silenced the alarm set on my phone, avoiding any reminder of another blood sugar check. I refuted reality, smearing the nasty blotch instead of finding ways to outgrow it.

Perception mattered to me, so I convinced people that I was doing well. To them, the ink was clearing; I was no longer the diabetic girl. But in reality, it continued to consume me. I didn’t want to mature quicker, or differently, than my peers. WHY ME echoed constantly.

It was three years into my diagnosis that I finally began looking deep within. Curiously, it was another book jump started my transformation: *My Beloved World* by Sonia Sotomayor. From the first page I felt seen, not only did she struggle in the same ways I did at the beginning of her diagnosis: days coupled with stressed out parents, anxiety and fear, but she was also Puerto Rican. Her words shaped my perspective as I learned that “difficulty can tap unsuspected strengths.” I found myself smiling as I realized that this stain in my book was only a challenge, not a setback.

With a resilient, persevering, steadfast attitude, I began exploring an alternate version to what I had expected would become of me. Once I accepted that my circumstances were indeed frustrating, I forgave myself for what I had left unattended. The more I take care of myself, the less I question how others perceive me. Emotional strength energizes healthy growth!

Upon reflection, I now understand why I was one of the few students who enjoyed *The Count of Monte Cristo*: unconsciously, I found comfort in Dante’s struggle to defy the label others had given him. His eagerness for revenge mirrored my yearning for conformity. While I found consolation in Dantés, I found strength in Sonia.

Multiple colors now fill my pages, and that giant blotch has become a spec within my ever evolving variegated chronicle.

I was certainly prepared for my online weekend of debate competition, but I was off from the beginning, neither making persuasive arguments nor possessing the right headspace. After eight hours of grueling debating, I had two wins (one of which was because my opponent did not show up), followed by three straight losses. Undoubtedly, I was upset with my woeful performance, disappointed at the result.

Seemingly done for the day, I began to change out of my dress clothes when I suddenly got a call from my coach: The tournament needed a competitor with a losing record to be their fourth semifinalist, which, by merit, happened to be me. Back online shortly thereafter for the elimination bout, I was greeted by three judges and my opponent, the top seed, who had just beaten me in the previous round. Thinking about the imminent bout, I decided to myself to simply concentrate on performing well regardless of win or loss.

As the showdown was set to commence, I reiterated to myself this was more than just a competition but an opportunity to be challenged. Simultaneously, I felt a wave of willpower and clarity, uplifting me to a tremendous state of energy. The 50-minute debate drove on like a battle of heavyweights. I crafted each word in my speech to present my case, articulately rebutted my opponent’s arguments, and turned them onto my side of the debate. The back-and-forth contention between us were heated in a fierce dynamic yet exhilarating. As the round ended, I breathed a sigh of relief whilst the judges deliberated on this intense odyssey I had just gone through. Soon thereafter, the two-to-one decision came back as a total shock: I had beaten the best competitor in the tournament.

Nevertheless, I came back down to earth quickly as the finals still awaited me the day after. My opponent this time was the second seed who had also handily defeated me in the preliminary stage. Although nervous right as the round was set to begin, I got reassured by the thought that, after my upset of the top seed, it was deserving for me to be a finalist. The clock ticked on, but unlike my semifinal, my confidence grew by the minute. When it came time to cross-examination my opponent, my questioning was on point leading to winning some key concessions. Conversely, when I was under cross-examination, I applied both my wit and my thorough research on the topic to fend away any prodding attacks. When the round was ended, a strong sense of victory fell upon me. All three judges agreed, confirming my intuition.

In retrospect, I had won a trophy, yet the win was surpassed by something far greater: a model through which to both elevate myself and to encourage others towards any given goals. Before, a bad test score, loss in debate, or even an embarrassing social interaction could easily put me down. Instead, I now take any situation and utilized it as an opportunity for self-improvement, refusing to yield even when chances of promise are bleak.

This debate experience had brought me more than just a vision, but an effort that has nurtured me a new perspective: a mentality which took me to the heights of confidence, leadership, and vigor. Moreover, it facilitated a new drive at my heart to contribute my learned skills to others at any given opportunity.

I despise attention. The moment eyes turn toward me, my face flushes red like a tomato and my palms sweat like Niagara Falls. During recess, when my friends bickered to be Anna and Elsa in our reenactments of Frozen, I was content being Olaf, a side character in the background.

Ironically, despite my efforts to avoid attention, I often stood out. In class photos, I was the student a head taller than everyone else, poking out from the crowd. As the youngest in both my immediate and extended family, I was like a newborn baby in her bassinet swarmed by doting relatives at family gatherings.

My distinctness reached its peak at age eleven when I was diagnosed with a severe case of amblyopia, or lazy eye, a visual development disorder in which an eye fails to achieve normal visual acuity. The treatment required me to wear an eye patch over my left eye to stimulate proper function in my weaker right eye. My classmates quickly noticed and dubbed me the “pirate girl.” In hallways and cafeterias, curious and sometimes cruel stares penetrated my right eye.

Wearing the eye patch plunged half my world into darkness. Initially, I was frustrated, having to navigate the world with my “lazy” eye that could only afford to show me a blur. But with only one eye to see, I became more attuned to my surroundings due to my heightened awareness. I began to uncover the intricacies of human dynamics, noticing how people treated me differently because of my appearance. I also noticed subtle details children my age often overlooked, such as the contrasts between light and dark, various textures, and the seen and unseen. My observations translated into drawings, fueling my bond with art. I discovered a safe space to express my perspective of the world, all while avoiding attention, as an artist has the choice of remaining anonymous behind the canvas.

Years later, I came to cover not one eye, but both. I began participating in a sport called Showdown, a version of air hockey for the visually impaired, where all players, regardless of their natural sight, had to wear blindfolds to level the playing field. Though not visually impaired myself, I felt a deep connection to this community, having experienced judgment for my own visual difference in the past.

As I gripped the wooden bat and poised to strike the ball whose location I could only discern by sound, memories of my childhood began to resurface. I was once a quiet and restrained child, creating art in the solitude of my room. But amidst the visually impaired, I felt a sense of urgency—a need to speak up about their situation and advocate for the disabled community in an ableist society.

I returned to art, but this time I stood confidently in front of the canvas, advocating for marginalized communities. I reached out to elementary classrooms where I could present my children’s book featuring a visually impaired protagonist. After the read-aloud, the students crowded around me for signatures while teachers tried to usher them back into their classrooms. I found myself the center of attention, feeling like the next Beyoncé.

But this time, attention was not my foe but my ally. My face did not turn tomato-red; my palms did not sweat like Niagara Falls; and I no longer wanted to be just Olaf. I stood proudly in the spotlight, determined to shape a society where “pirate girls” are not set back by the ocean’s currents.

**True Brothers**

Growing up, my brother and I were always fighting, not like your typical siblings who might just wrestle or use a Nerf gun on each other, but we genuinely wanted to hurt each other. When I was seven years old, he nearly shredded my pinky off, sending me to urgent care. We were not fond of each other, to say the least.

As the older brother, I was always jealous of him getting all the attention everywhere we went, and hated the fact him idolizing me. But the one thing that always connected us was this made-up store called Pix-n-Bux. It had a secret password and involved trading goods between our rooms.

My brother and I loved playing sports, even though we weren't the most athletic. When COVID hit, we stopped playing sports, let technology take over our lives, and were never at a lower point. Our family felt isolated and all my brother and I would do was play video games and study.

After nearly a year of isolation, the first time we left the house was a revelation. Stepping outside, I saw the world in a way we never had before. Everything seemed different, brighter, and more alive. It was as if I had been given a second chance to appreciate the world and our place in it, but the distance between my brother and I remained.

My parents who grew up in the suppressive regime in Iran, had a difficult relationship with religion. The fear of prosecution made them hesitant to teach my brother and I faith; however, they believed that having faith is an integral part of complete human so a new chapter of my life started when I enrolled at a Jesuit high school, with ethos “men for others.” The school showed me a part of me that I didn’t know I had. I transformed into the best version of myself when I opened up to Mr. H., leading me to play basketball, wrestle, tennis, run track, join four clubs, and volunteer for three non-profits. This was good, but I wanted to be closer to my brother. Since we grew up the way we did, I didn’t think it was possible to have the brotherly relationship other siblings have. I thought nothing could save me until I went on a school retreat to Manresa, a well-loved as a place to decompress from the fast pace of campus life, and to pray, reflect and become closer to God and nature. other high schoolers dealt with drugs or vaping or sought freedom at the bottom of a bottle, we talked about our personal life and issues. When all said and done, all I wanted was to have a relationship with my brother.

It was through this retreat and my journey to faith that I began to understand the importance of forgiveness and reconciliation. I reached out to my brother, and for the first time, we had an honest conversation about our childhood, our feelings, and our dreams. We both realized how much we had missed out on by being at odds with each other. Slowly, we started to rebuild our relationship. We found common grounds in our shared memories and experiences, and we began to create new, positive ones together.

The lessons of love and kindness I learned at my Jesuit school and home and the spiritual awakening I experienced allowed me to approach my brother with a newfound sense of empathy and understanding. I saw him not as my rival, but as my brother, someone who had his own struggles and pains. This realization brought us closer than ever before.

Today, my brother and I are not just siblings, but true brothers. Our relationship is built on mutual respect and understanding, something I never thought was ever going to happen. The journey was long and filled with challenges, but it taught me the value of family, faith, and forgiveness. Reflecting on our childhood conflicts and the moments of reconciliation, I realize how these experiences have shaped my understanding of empathy and the importance of building strong family bonds. It all began with the desire to change, the support of my Jesuit school, and the guidance of my newfound faith.

After almost two weeks at the Haven House, I noticed the kids were getting bored of their regular playtime routine. I wanted to bring some new excitement to their day. “Helicopter ride?” I asked Emanulley, making a spinning motion. She stretched out her arms in response, which I took as a yes. I grasped securely onto Emanuelly’s wrists, and spun her in circles, so fast that her legs lifted up off the ground. As the familiar playground blurred out of focus, all I could see was her smile. Soon, all of the kids wanted a turn, and self-organized a rotation until I was too dizzy to walk.

On our walk later that day, we crossed a small field of grass, sparsely scattered with dandelions. I saw an opportunity. Darting around, I plucked one for each of the kids.

“Here, make a wish Sky” I said, slightly out of breath, as I offered her a dandelion.

"Have a wish ready Bella?” I prompted, handing her the fluffy weed.

“Yep!” she said, with a knowing smile.

When I offered Darriela one, instead of blowing away the fluffy seeds, she kept the flower in her hand. Noticing this, I looked around for another flower to give her. “Thank you teacher [Name]!” she examined, with a bashful gap-toothed grin. By the end of the walk I made sure she had a mini-bouquet of every flower I could find.

The next day, we walked a new path across a bridge over the highway, and watched the waves of cars rush below. Whispering to teacher LaDaysia, I told her my plan and she agreed to help. After a few moments, we used our arms to make a tugging motion, pantomiming honking a horn. Immediately, dozens of cars and trucks started honking in response. After the first honk, Darelilla was startled and leaped back, but I assured her that the noise was a friendly gesture, nothing to be afraid of. Quickly, the kids’ initial confusion was replaced with giggles, twirls, and cheers, as they made this dull concrete bridge their stage for a spectacular moment.

Grinning, I took in the bizarre spectacle; the kids jumping up and down with excitement, the people in the cars beaming back at them, and the teachers struck with contagious joy. More than anything I was moved by the capacity of a mere arm motion to turn an ordinary walk or a boring commute into one to remember.

On my last day with the kids, I squeezed into a tiny, child-sized chair and watched them rehearse their graduation songs (which are still stuck in my head today). Sitting there, I thought about the events we commonly celebrate, like birthdays, graduations, marriages, and baby showers. When I was younger, I thought these milestones were the only events worth celebrating. But as “Teacher [Name],” I learned the significance of creating and cherishing small moments of joy and connection. While those big moments are undoubtedly important, it’s the little ones every day that infuse life with meaning.

So why wait for an excuse to celebrate?

Fifty years ago, at the onset of communist rule, in a small town in Eastern Slovakia, each day a young man smelt his hands with charcoal and anillin paint to save up money and attain his dreams of becoming a doctor. It’s hard to believe that the same young boy over the years molded into the strongest man I know today: my dad.

While my childhood weekends were spent experimenting with colorful scribbles as a way of creative expression, my dad produced refined features of human faces and surrounding landscapes, of which only the flawless ones could be used to make income. So, while I considered art as the creative outlet, for my father, it was the medium of survival. Every time my eyes land on our paintings hanging side-by-side in my room, I’m mesmerized by the stark differences in our childhood, and how in sharing with me his story of resilience and unwavering determination, my dad inspired me to use art not just as self-expression, but as the medium of social entrepreneurship.

However, the yearning to explore the potential of art as the medium for change led me to transcend beyond the flatness of canvas.

The first time I was able to use creative expression to bring change was when I discovered my voice for unveiling beauty in the French language. As I joined the EU Commission at the Model European Parliament Conference and stood on center ground between advocates and politicians, I realized the role of the language as a double-edged sword. Through poetic melodies of French “discours politique” (political speech) I grappled to the bone in negotiations to pass the “bill” that would allocate resources to the minorities impacted by climate-imposed catastrophes. It was there I acknowledged how literary crafts of the French language enabled me to use it as a medium of connection between delegates of various nationalities. In that moment, French for me became much more than the arts or method of self-expression, it became a new path I could use to collaborate with others and together pursue civil engagement.

Empowered on a mission to use French as a common thread and garner change to the lives of those in need, I collided forces with French Doctors Without Borders. There, I was humbled to shake hands with brave men and women who dedicated their lives to saving malnourished children in Yemen. Seeing the photographs from their missions, showing my peers clothed in nothing but mere skin, I felt an urge to act.

Combining the persuasive voice of a delegate with values ingrained in me by my dad, I negotiated contracts with international facilities to start art competitions at my school, collaborated with schools across Czech Republic, and held a fundraising art auction at Manes Gallery to empower medical communities in Africa. A jarring sensation jolted through my body as I witnessed the powerful impact of my actions: art connoisseurs and enthusiasts of all nationalities coming together to pursue change. In the same way my dad ignited a spark of passion for art in my childhood self, it was in these moments that I truly reaffirmed the collective power of art in my own community.

Slowly but surely, I breathed life into a canvas that was once blank. I remember the stepping stones of my childhood recollections, seated by the table as my dad poured a cup of tea before picking up a palette, depicting the refined features of enigmatic human faces. Today, I realize that while art was created to be admired, its value is maximized when it bring beauty to the lives of others. Inspired by my dad, who was able to forge his passion for helping save human lives by bringing beauty to the world with his paintings, I too aspire to enhance the physical world around me through chemical engineering while using creative expression of French language as the medium for social change.

September 1st, 2017

The sound of fate clattering against the hardwood floor penetrates the still air. A few seconds later, and fate drifts to a stop. Silence. I hold my breath.

“5 and 3, so 8.”

My dad cheers with excitement - his settlements in the wheat field have paid off handsomely. My aunt groans as her civilization’s supply drought continues. I collect my resources, debating my next move.

***

For the first nine years of my life, I thrived in Singapore’s perpetual summer. Marked by Saturdays at the Singapore Zoo with my uncle, six hour movie marathons while traveling to India, and palak paneer beside my aunt at the British Club, I couldn’t have asked for more.

Come the move to New Jersey in 2016, and everything would change. No longer could I marvel at Giant Pandas and bask in the scent of fresh spices with my relatives. And those six-hour flights? Well, they became fifteen hours of neck pain and sleeplessness. Cut off from the comforting routines and familiar faces of my previous home, I turned to an unlikely antidote: Catan.

It was my idea; every weekend, despite significant time zone differences, my relatives and I would gather for a virtual game of Catan. These sessions, lasting just one or two hours, swiftly became the highlight of my week. Our gatherings were more than mere games, they were a way for us to reconnect as a family despite the miles between.

My mom’s relaxed and methodical playstyle earned her the title “World’s Slowest Player”, prompting playful jokes about setting a ten-minute timer for her turns. Meanwhile, my uncle’s penchant for resource hoarding often sparked clashes with the notorious supply-stealing robber, drawing laughter from everyone playing. These moments etched themselves into my family lore, making the oceans between us seem a little smaller.

Through the shared moments with my family during our games, I began to see a deeper significance in the roads we built—both in the game and in life. Each road in Catan linked settlements and resources, mirroring how our relationships and experiences connect the different parts of our lives.

My first road led to Mr. Vanasse, whose summer camp was a beacon of joy during my early years in America. His imaginative games and quirky humor never failed to light up my days and eased my transition from Singapore to New Jersey. Leading campers to victory in dodgeball and being a friend whenever needed were my way of ensuring that others could experience the same warmth and laughter that helped me feel at home.

My second road extended to Mr. Devin, my swim instructor from middle school who became a cherished mentor and friend. Our relationship evolved from lessons in the pool to lighthearted runs to feeding the fish every Sunday at SwimQuest. These shared activities echoed weekly excursions with my uncle in Singapore, further strengthening the road between us.

My third road progressed into the New York Math Circle classrooms. Initially, I was hesitant to attend the program; I was scared of taking the train to New York alone. However, with coaching from my parents and hours of studying the red line, my uncertainty gave way to joy and curiosity as I engaged in discussions about probability, proofs, and how many pigeons could fit on a subway car.

***

I look at my playing pieces, knowing I still have more roads to pave, in college, and beyond.

The game is just beginning, and it’s your move next.

Coming out as a transgender boy in middle school added another layer to my already complex life. I felt awkward, embarrassed, confused, and hurt, and I could never pull answers from my family members as to why my father and I had this distant and hard relationship. Why did I have to watch as other kids experienced a confident male role model in their lives while I had a father that I barely knew?

As I watched my father’s life expand, my brother and I took a back seat in his story. He gained a new wife, a fancy job, and twin boys, and he didn’t seem to need his older sons. We stopped seeing each other, from once a week to once a month to about twice a year, and my father's face became unrecognizable as he aged. He missed award ceremonies, art shows, parent conferences, and me growing up. I saw glimpses of his new life—starting a company, helping others with addictions, my stepbrother's first steps—until he slowly started fading away, and I saw none of it—no word from him for months at a time.

I was discovering my identity as a brother, a son, and a man, and I needed a support system to fill in the missing spots that my father left in me as I grew up. I leaned on the system I had: my friends, who tried their best to understand my situation. But more importantly, I realized I had to be there for myself and support my friends in return. Whether it be losing a parent like I had or missing the support they needed to succeed, I realized that by helping others, I was learning more about myself, gaining confidence, and healing. When my middle school decided to acknowledge Pride Month by presenting only a program on HIV and AIDs, it upset me and my LGBTQI+ friends. I petitioned the administration to allow me to create a slide show on the spectrum of gender and sexual identities and got to present it to the entire school. It allowed my friends and I to feel seen and heard, and I learned that sometimes I had to step out of my comfort zone and seek opportunities to foster change for myself and those around me.

Taking one step at a time, I went from offering a listening ear to friends in need to leadership positions within my 1400+ student urban high school. As vice president of the student council, I advocated for changes in school policies to promote gender equity and empower other transgender classmates, including doubling the number of gender-inclusive bathrooms and providing higher-quality period products. Over time, my efforts expanded beyond the school building. I launched a neighborhood pride t-shirt business that got local press attention (Time Out New York ran a feature), and I donated 100% of the profits to Covenant House, an organization that helps teens in crisis. I participated in a public gallery show, creating art to spread awareness of the situation of migrants in New York, and wrote YouTube scripts on adolescent mental and physical health for the Youth Medical Association. I recognized the power of collaborative effort and the impact it could have on those around me.

Whether it be through participating in leadership positions in my school or advocating for causes I feel strongly about, I want to create platforms where vulnerable and disadvantaged people can tell their stories. In the coming years, I intend to collaborate with campus organizations, utilize university facilities for diversity projects, and advocate for structural changes that would render society more tolerant and equitable. I will continue striving to uplift and speak up for those who feel marginalized or alone. The belief that real progress is possible only when we unite, support each other, and aim for an equitable globe motivates me to help others feel not alone and not hurt as I once did.

Soccer is so much more than a game. It is a feeling of teamwork, friendship, and pure joy. I loved this game throughout my childhood, and every time my bright orange cleats would touch the field, all of that day's negativity remained on the sidelines. Nothing brings down that feeling of pure bliss when my center-back defensive skills keep the opposing team from scoring. Unfortunately, like most tales from 2020, all good things came to a grinding halt due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

In Fall 2021, my soccer club finally reopened. Eagerly returning to my passion, I signed up instantly, now entering the high school age bracket. Sadly, my childhood joy faded. The team lost every game, players were hostile, and team comradery was non-existent. Being a freshman playing alongside high schoolers after such a long break made me doubt myself in a way I had never felt before. My confidence in the game became that of a new player. I decided to quit soccer. The passion flame for soccer was officially blown out.

When the next season approached, I told my family I was done playing. The shock was evident as they asked me insistently if I had changed my mind. Even my twin brother tried talking me out of quitting, as we had played together our whole life, but he was unsuccessful. Watching my brother's games from the sidelines during that season, I felt a tinge of regret. As each game went by, I watched my brother improve immensely while having fun. Witnessing his progress completely reignited my love for the game. I realized the only thing standing in my way was myself. In the final moments of his last game, with the opposing striker charging down the field, he made a crucial block that secured the win. The eureka hit, and I decided I wanted to be on the field and not sit on the sidelines anymore.

The summer was a period of intense training alongside mental and physical conditioning. I knew I had to push myself to achieve success and confidence. The temptation to quit arrived every morning at 8 am when the screeching sound of an alarm clock called for me, but I pushed on. I trained like a sponge, absorbing every lesson I could, soaking it like water. If doubt crept in, I remembered how the sidelines felt, which pushed me harder. As the days passed, my confidence grew, and I eagerly anticipated the upcoming season. It was a testament to my discipline and dedication that I could transform my desire to return to the sport into a reality.

When the season arrived, I felt like a small child full of joy on Christmas morning. Stepping over that line and onto the field again felt like home. Outrunning my teammates, chasing after wingers, and being a brick wall to all unlucky strikers made me the one player who never got subbed off the field by the coach every game. That season, we were the undefeated champions, and I was named the VIP of the season.

I have learned that my journey was about not just soccer but personal growth. With dedication and hard work, I can achieve anything I want. Soccer was not just a game. It transformed me from a boy who so quickly had his confidence shattered into a person full of determination and a desire to push through negativity and succeed.

The Aroma of Hope

Every Friday morning, the aroma of saffron would drift through the house, stirring me from my sleep. I would find my grandparents in the kitchen, my grandmother meticulously chopping herbs while my grandfather played the tar and sang. This was how our cherished Persian dish, ghormeh sabzi, was prepared at the heart of our home.

This dish, a symphony of herbs, beans, and tender meat, was the centerpiece of our family gatherings. My grandparents had always lived with us, and the fragrant scents of their cooking seemed as permanent as their presence. However, even the beloved ghormeh sabzi could not fend off the grip of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, which cast a shadow over my babajoon’s vibrant life.

The disease gradually drained his energy, yet he clung to his kitchen rituals as long as they could. The preparation of ghormeh sabzi became less frequent, and eventually, the ready-made versions we bought from the store could not fill the void left by the absence of our family tradition. I would sit with them, trying to recapture their wisdom, but often finding only fatigue in their eyes.

Communication with my grandparents was another challenge. They spoke only Farsi, and while I understood the language, my fluency was limited. Yet, we found a profound connection through shared prayers. As Muslims, our faith provided a bridge when words failed us. The rhythmic recitation of prayers, the communal act of bowing in unison, and the shared moments of spiritual reflection were powerful bonds that transcended language barriers. It was what tied us together.

One evening, in a moment of shared resolve, my mother and I decided to attempt the dish ourselves. We gathered fresh herbs, beans, and the most aromatic spices we could find. As the familiar scents began to fill the air, my grandparents were drawn into the kitchen, their faces lighting up with recognition.

Despite their frailty, they joined us. My grandfather’s once-strong hands shakily guided mine as I ground the spices, and my grandmother’s soft voice directed the chopping of herbs. Their movements were slow and unsteady, yet the determination in their eyes was unwavering. For the first time in months, the kitchen echoed with the clatter of pots and pans and the harmonious blend of aromas.

That night, we dined on ghormeh sabzi that was far from perfect; the seasoning was uneven, and the herbs were chopped irregularly. Yet, it was the most delicious meal I had ever tasted. As my grandmother offered me a spoonful, she said in Farsi, “Here, azizam. Eat it.”

Now, as I look back on that evening, I realize that moment was fleeting but precious. My grandparents’ health continued to decline, yet the memory of that shared meal remains vivid. Holding their hands, gazing into their eyes, I can still sense the warmth and love of those Friday mornings.

Witnessing my babajoon’s battle with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia ignited a passion in me to delve into medical research. I was determined to understand the intricacies of such diseases and contribute to finding better treatments. This drive led me to a biomedical engineering lab, where I spent countless hours researching and experimenting. The complexities of cellular behaviors and the promise of new technologies fascinated me, and I found myself immersed in the world of medical science.

Moreover, my journey did not stop in the lab. I began shadowing doctors and volunteering at local hospitals, eager to see the practical application of medical knowledge and to understand the patient experience firsthand. I witnessed the compassion and dedication of healthcare professionals, and the profound impact they had on patients' lives. These experiences solidified my desire to become a doctor.

The hospital corridors, filled with stories of struggle and hope, became familiar to me. I saw patients and their families facing uncertainties with courage, much like my own family had. Volunteering allowed me to support them, even in small ways, and strengthened my resolve to pursue a career in medicine.

The process of making ghormeh sabzi was more than culinary; it was an art form passed down through generations. Each herb chopped and spice ground was a stroke in the painting of our family’s legacy. Writing about these moments allows me to preserve what time and illness threaten to erase.

My grandparents always said, "love and kindness cures all sufferings.” Their legacy lives in the scents of saffron that linger in our home. Mine will be the words that capture and convey our shared history and the medical research that strives to extend and improve the lives of others. The motivation sparked by their struggle continues to guide me on my path to becoming a doctor, dedicated to making a difference in the world of medicine.

I initially believed the hardest part would be executing high Degree of Difficulty spins, flips, and somersaults into the frigid pool from heights that had only existed in my dreams. The exhilaration of emerging from the pool, refreshed and accomplished after a flawless dive, was just a small piece of a much larger sense of self-worth. Even before the first meet of the season, I had an audacious dream how fun it would be to aim high with a unrealistic goal of earning a Varsity letter as a Freshman. Challenges like managing anxiety and the pressure to outperform more experienced competitors were apparent to most. Yet, few knew that my greatest challenge wasn’t the ability to focus in a hushed natatorium with all eyes on myself while balancing on my toes hanging backwards off the edge of the board, it was feigning enjoyment each time I stepped onto the diving board, knowing my heart wasn't in it.

"But I can't quit. [Name] McCormick doesn't quit!” Right?

Summoning the courage to prioritize my own happiness was harder than sticking an inward xxx less than 8 inches from the tip of the board headfirst, but with the support from my family, I made the most gut-wrenching difficult decision of my life. Though walking away from diving was agonizing, it taught me invaluable lessons in resilience and inner strength. Embracing this challenge empowered me, showing me that I could uphold my self-worth and happiness.
